Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Rightly Self-awakened One.

Khuddakanikāye

In the Khuddaka Nikāya

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā

The Commentary on the Sutta Nipāta

(Paṭhamo bhāgo)

(First Part)

Ganthārambhakathā

Introduction to the Text

Uttamaṃ [M 1.0001][P 1.0001][V 1.0001] vandaneyyānaṃ, vanditvā ratanattayaṃ;

Yo khuddakanikāyamhi, khuddācārappahāyinā.

Having paid homage to the Triple Gem, supreme among those worthy of homage; of that which is in the Khuddaka Nikāya, taught by the one who has abandoned minor misconduct,

Desito lokanāthena, lokanissaraṇesinā;

Tassa suttanipātassa, karissāmatthavaṇṇanaṃ.

taught by the Lord of the world, who seeks release from the world—of that Sutta Nipāta, I shall compose a commentary on its meaning.

Ayaṃ [V 1.0002] suttanipāto ca, khuddakesveva ogadho;

Yasmā tasmā imassāpi, karissāmatthavaṇṇanaṃ.

And because this Sutta Nipāta is included only within the Khuddaka Nikāya, therefore, of this also, I shall compose a commentary on its meaning.

Gāthāsatasamākiṇṇo, geyyabyākaraṇaṅkito;

Kasmā suttanipātoti, saṅkhamesa gatoti ce.

Filled with hundreds of verses, marked by mixed prose and verse and by exposition; if it is asked why this has attained the appellation ‘Sutta Nipāta’—

Suvuttato savanato, atthānaṃ suṭṭhu tāṇato;

Sūcanā sūdanā ceva, yasmā suttaṃ pavuccati.

On account of its being well-spoken and heard, on account of its excellent protection of meanings, and because it indicates and yields them, it is therefore called a 'Sutta'.

Tathārūpāni suttāni, nipātetvā tato tato;

Samūhato ayaṃ tasmā, saṅkhamevamupāgato.

Having brought together such discourses from here and there into a collection, it has therefore attained this appellation.

Sabbāni cāpi suttāni, pamāṇantena tādino;

Vacanāni ayaṃ tesaṃ, nipāto ca yato tato.

And all the discourses are also the sayings of the Such-one, according to their measure; this is a collection of them from here and there.

Aññasaṅkhānimittānaṃ, visesānamabhāvato;

Saṅkhaṃ suttanipātoti, evameva samajjhagāti.

Due to the absence of distinct, other appellations or marks, it has thus indeed attained the appellation ‘Sutta Nipāta’.

1. Uragavaggo

1. The Chapter of the Serpent

1. Uragasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Uraga Sutta

Evaṃ [M 1.0002][V 1.0003] samadhigatasaṅkho ca yasmā esa vaggato uragavaggo, cūḷavaggo, mahāvaggo, aṭṭhakavaggo, pārāyanavaggoti pañca vaggā honti; tesu uragavaggo ādi. Suttato uragavagge dvādasa suttāni, cūḷavagge cuddasa, mahāvagge dvādasa, aṭṭhakavagge soḷasa, pārāyanavagge soḷasāti sattati suttāni. Tesaṃ uragasuttaṃ ādi. Pariyattipamāṇato aṭṭha [P 1.0002] bhāṇavārā. Evaṃ vaggasuttapariyattipamāṇavato panassa –

This collection having thus attained its classification, by way of sections, there are five sections: the Uraga Section, the Cūḷa Section, the Mahā Section, the Aṭṭhaka Section, and the Pārāyana Section. Among these, the Uraga Section is the first. By way of suttas, there are twelve suttas in the Uraga Section, fourteen in the Cūḷa Section, twelve in the Mahā Section, sixteen in the Aṭṭhaka Section, and sixteen in the Pārāyana Section—thus there are seventy suttas. Among these, the Uraga Sutta is the first. By way of textual extent, there are eight bhāṇavāras. Thus, with regard to its measure in terms of sections, suttas, and textual extent—

“Yo uppatitaṃ vineti kodhaṃ, visaṭaṃ sappavisaṃva osadhehi;

So bhikkhu jahāti orapāraṃ, urago jiṇṇamiva tacaṃ purāṇa”nti. –

“He who subdues arisen anger, as antidotes do spreading snake venom; that monk abandons the near and the far shore, just as a snake sheds its old, worn-out skin.”

Ayaṃ gāthā ādi. Tasmā assā ito pabhuti atthavaṇṇanaṃ kātuṃ idaṃ vuccati –

This verse is the first. Therefore, in order to compose a commentary on its meaning from this point forward, this is said:

“Yena yattha yadā yasmā, vuttā gāthā ayaṃ imaṃ;

Vidhiṃ pakāsayitvāssā, karissāmatthavaṇṇana”nti.

“By whom, where, when, and for what reason this verse was spoken—having clarified this procedure, I shall compose a commentary on its meaning.”

Kena panāyaṃ gāthā vuttā, kattha, kadā, kasmā ca vuttāti? Vuccate – yo so bhagavā catuvīsatibuddhasantike laddhabyākaraṇo yāva vessantarajātakaṃ, tāva pāramiyo pūretvā tusitabhavane uppajji, tatopi cavitvā sakyarājakule upapattiṃ gahetvā, anupubbena katamahābhinikkhamano bodhirukkhamūle sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambujjhitvā, dhammacakkaṃ pavattetvā deva-manussānaṃ hitāya dhammaṃ desesi, tena bhagavatā sayambhunā anācariyakena sammāsambuddhena vuttā. Sā ca pana āḷaviyaṃ. Yadā ca bhūtagāmasikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ, tadā tattha upagatānaṃ dhammadesanatthaṃ vuttāti. Ayamettha saṅkhepavissajjanā. Vitthārato pana dūrenidānaavidūrenidānasantikenidānavasena veditabbā. Tattha dūrenidānaṃ nāma dīpaṅkarato [M 1.0003] yāva paccuppannavatthukathā[V 1.0004], avidūrenidānaṃ nāma tusitabhavanato yāva paccuppannavatthukathā, santikenidānaṃ nāma bodhimaṇḍato yāva paccuppannavatthukathāti.

But by whom was this verse spoken, where, when, and for what reason was it spoken? It is said: It was spoken by that Blessed One—who, having received the prediction in the presence of twenty-four Buddhas, fulfilled the perfections up to the Vessantara Birth, was reborn in the Tusita heaven, passed away from there, took rebirth in the Sakyan royal family, gradually undertook the great renunciation, awakened to perfect enlightenment at the foot of the Bodhi tree, set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma, and taught the Dhamma for the welfare of gods and humans—by that Blessed One, the Independently Awakened One, the One Without a Teacher, the Perfectly Enlightened One. And it was spoken at Āḷavī. When the training rule regarding plant life was laid down, it was spoken there for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma to those who had gathered. This is the brief answer here. In detail, however, it should be understood by way of the distant origin, the not-so-distant origin, and the proximate origin. Herein, the distant origin is from the time of Dīpaṅkara up to the present narrative; the not-so-distant origin is from the Tusita heaven up to the present narrative; the proximate origin is from the seat of enlightenment up to the present narrative.

Tattha yasmā avidūrenidānaṃ santikenidānañca dūrenidāneyeva samodhānaṃ gacchanti, tasmā dūrenidānavasenevettha vitthārato vissajjanā veditabbā. Sā panesā jātakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttāti idha na vitthāritā. Tato tattha vitthāritanayeneva veditabbā. Ayaṃ pana viseso – tattha paṭhamagāthāya sāvatthiyaṃ vatthu uppannaṃ, idha āḷaviyaṃ. Yathāha –

Therein, because the not-so-distant origin and the proximate origin are included within the distant origin itself, the detailed answer here should be understood only by way of the distant origin. But since this has been stated in the Jātaka commentary, it is not elaborated upon here. Therefore, it should be understood according to the manner in which it is elaborated there. This, however, is the difference: there, the narrative for the first verse arose in Sāvatthī; here, it arose in Āḷavī. As it is said—

“Tena [P 1.0003] samayena buddho bhagavā āḷaviyaṃ viharati aggāḷave cetiye. Tena kho pana samayena āḷavakā bhikkhū navakammaṃ karontā rukkhaṃ chindantipi chedāpentipi. Aññataropi āḷavako bhikkhu rukkhaṃ chindati. Tasmiṃ rukkhe adhivatthā devatā taṃ bhikkhuṃ etadavoca – ‘mā, bhante, attano bhavanaṃ kattukāmo mayhaṃ bhavanaṃ chindī’ti. So bhikkhu anādiyanto chindiyeva. Tassā ca devatāya dārakassa bāhuṃ ākoṭesi. Atha kho tassā devatāya etadahosi – ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ imaṃ bhikkhuṃ idheva jīvitā voropeyya’nti. Atha kho tassā devatāya etadahosi – ‘na kho metaṃ patirūpaṃ, yāhaṃ imaṃ bhikkhuṃ idheva jīvitā voropeyyaṃ, yaṃnūnāhaṃ bhagavato etamatthaṃ āroceyya’nti. Atha kho sā devatā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesi. ‘Sādhu, sādhu devate, sādhu kho tvaṃ, devate, taṃ bhikkhuṃ jīvitā na voropesi. Sacajja tvaṃ, devate, taṃ bhikkhuṃ jīvitā voropeyyāsi, bahuñca tvaṃ, devate, apuññaṃ pasaveyyāsi. Gaccha tvaṃ, devate, amukasmiṃ okāse rukkho vivitto, tasmiṃ upagacchā’”ti (pāci. 89).

“At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Āḷavī, in the Aggāḷava Shrine. Now at that time, the monks of Āḷavī, while doing construction work, were cutting down trees and having them cut down. A certain monk of Āḷavī was also cutting down a tree. The deity dwelling in that tree said this to that monk: ‘Venerable sir, do not, desiring to make a dwelling for yourself, cut down my dwelling.’ That monk, paying no heed, cut it down nonetheless. And he struck the arm of that deity's child. Then this thought occurred to that deity: ‘What if I were to deprive this monk of his life right here?’ Then this thought occurred to that deity: ‘It would not be proper for me to deprive this monk of his life right here. What if I were to report this matter to the Blessed One?’ Then that deity approached the Blessed One and reported this matter to the Blessed One. ‘Good, good, deity. It is good, deity, that you did not deprive that monk of his life. If today, deity, you had deprived that monk of his life, you would have produced much demerit. Go, deity, in such-and-such a place there is a secluded tree; go to it.’” (Pāc. 89).

Evañca pana vatvā puna bhagavā tassā devatāya uppannakodhavinayanatthaṃ –

And having spoken thus, the Blessed One, for the purpose of subduing the anger that had arisen in that deity, then said:

“Yo ve uppatitaṃ kodhaṃ, rathaṃ bhantaṃva vāraye”ti. (dha. pa. 222) –

“He who indeed restrains arisen anger like a swerving chariot.” (Dhp. 222)

Imaṃ [M 1.0004] gāthaṃ abhāsi. Tato “kathañhi nāma samaṇā sakyaputtiyā rukkhaṃ chindissantipi, chedāpessantipi, ekindriyaṃ samaṇā sakyaputtiyā jīvaṃ viheṭhentī”ti evaṃ manussānaṃ ujjhāyitaṃ sutvā bhikkhūhi ārocito bhagavā – “bhūtagāmapātabyatāya pācittiya”nti (pāci. 90) imaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññāpetvā tattha upagatānaṃ dhammadesanatthaṃ –

He spoke this verse. Then, having heard the people complaining, “How indeed can the ascetics, the sons of the Sakyans, cut down a tree, or have one cut down? The ascetics, the sons of the Sakyans, harm one-facultied life!” and having been informed by the monks, the Blessed One laid down this training rule: “An offense of expiation for the destruction of plant life” (Pācittiya 90), for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma to those who had gathered there—

“Yo [V 1.0005] uppatitaṃ vineti kodhaṃ,

Visaṭaṃ sappavisaṃva osadhehī”ti. –

“Whoever removes arisen anger, as one dispels spreading snake’s venom with medicines…”

Imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi. Evamidaṃ ekaṃyeva [P 1.0004] vatthu tīsu ṭhānesu saṅgahaṃ gataṃ – vinaye, dhammapade, suttanipāteti. Ettāvatā ca yā sā mātikā ṭhapitā –

He spoke this verse. Thus this one single story is included in three places: in the Vinaya, the Dhammapada, and the Suttanipāta. And to this extent, that mātikā which was set down—

“Yena yattha yadā yasmā, vuttā gāthā ayaṃ imaṃ;

Vidhi pakāsayitvāssā, karissāmatthavaṇṇana”nti. –

“By whom, where, when, and owing to what circumstance, this verse was spoken; having explained its occasion, we will elaborate on its meaning.”

Sā saṅkhepato vitthārato ca pakāsitā hoti ṭhapetvā atthavaṇṇanaṃ.

That mātikā has been explained both in brief and in detail, setting aside the commentary on the meaning.

1. Ayaṃ panettha atthavaṇṇanā. Yoti yo yādiso khattiyakulā vā pabbajito, brāhmaṇakulā vā pabbajito, navo vā majjhimo vā thero vā. Uppatitanti uddhamuddhaṃ patitaṃ gataṃ, pavattanti attho, uppannanti vuttaṃ hoti. Uppannañca nāmetaṃ vattamānabhutvāpagatokāsakatabhūmiladdhavasena anekappabhedaṃ. Tattha sabbampi saṅkhataṃ uppādādisamaṅgi vattamānuppannaṃ nāma, yaṃ sandhāya “uppannā dhammā, anuppannā dhammā, uppādino dhammā”ti (dha. sa. tikamātikā 17) vuttaṃ. Ārammaṇarasamanubhavitvā niruddhaṃ anubhutvāpagatasaṅkhātaṃ kusalākusalaṃ, uppādādittayamanuppatvā niruddhaṃ bhutvāpagatasaṅkhātaṃ sesasaṅkhatañca bhutvāpagatuppannaṃ nāma. Tadetaṃ “evarūpaṃ pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ uppannaṃ hotī”ti (ma. ni. 1.234; pāci. 417) ca, “yathā ca uppannassa satisambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāpāripūrī hotī”ti ca evamādīsu suttantesu daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Yānissa tāni pubbe katāni kammānī”ti evamādinā (ma. ni. 3.248; netti. 120) nayena vuttaṃ kammaṃ atītampi samānaṃ aññassa vipākaṃ paṭibāhitvā attano vipākassokāsaṃ katvā ṭhitattā, tathā katokāsañca vipākaṃ anuppannampi evaṃ kate okāse avassamuppattito okāsakatuppannaṃ [M 1.0005] nāma. Tāsu tāsu bhūmīsu asamūhatamakusalaṃ bhūmiladdhuppannaṃ nāma.

1. Now, here is the explanation of the meaning. The word 'yo' refers to whoever—whether one gone forth from a khattiya clan or a brahmin clan; whether new, of middle standing, or an elder. 'Uppatitaṃ' means gone, having risen up higher and higher; the meaning is 'occurred,' which is to say, 'arisen' (uppanna). And this 'arisen' is of many kinds, by way of being presently-arisen, having-been-arisen, opportunity-made-arisen, and realm-obtained-arisen. Herein, all conditioned things endowed with arising and so on are called 'presently-arisen' (vattamānuppanna), referring to which it is said: 'Arisen phenomena, unarisen phenomena, phenomena that are to arise' (Dhammasaṅgaṇī, Tikamātikā 17). Wholesome and unwholesome states that have ceased after experiencing the taste of an object are reckoned as 'gone after having been experienced' (anubhutvāpagata); and the remaining conditioned things that have ceased after having attained the triad beginning with arising are reckoned as 'gone after having been' (bhutvāpagata). These are called 'having-been-arisen' (bhutvāpagatuppanna). This should be seen in such suttanta passages as: 'Such an evil view has arisen' (MN 1.234; Pāc. 417), and 'how the development and fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of mindfulness comes to be,' and so on. Kamma spoken of by the method beginning, 'Those actions previously done by him...' (MN 3.248; Netti. 120), though past, stands having made an opportunity for its own result by obstructing the result of another; and since the result for which the opportunity has been so made, though not yet arisen, will inevitably arise when the opportunity is thus made, it is called 'opportunity-made-arisen' (okāsakatuppanna). Unwholesome states not uprooted in the various planes of existence are called 'realm-obtained-arisen' (bhūmiladdhuppanna).

Ettha ca bhūmiyā bhūmiladdhassa ca nānattaṃ veditabbaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ – bhūmi nāma vipassanāya ārammaṇabhūtā tebhūmakā pañcakkhandhā. Bhūmiladdhaṃ nāma tesu uppattārahaṃ [P 1.0005] kilesajātaṃ. Tena hi sā bhūmiladdhā nāma hotīti. Tasmā “bhūmiladdha”nti vuccati. Tañca pana na ārammaṇavasena. Ārammaṇavasena hi sabbepi atītādibhede pariññātepi ca khīṇāsavānaṃ [V 1.0006] khandhe ārabbha kilesā uppajjanti mahākaccāyanauppalavaṇṇādīnaṃ khandhe ārabbha soreyyaseṭṭhiputtanandamāṇavakādīnaṃ viya. Yadi cetaṃ bhūmiladdhaṃ nāma siyā, tassa appaheyyato na koci bhavamūlaṃ jaheyya. Vatthuvasena pana bhūmiladdhaṃ nāma veditabbaṃ. Yattha yattha hi vipassanāya apariññātā khandhā uppajjanti, tattha tattha uppādato pabhuti tesu vaṭṭamūlaṃ kilesajātaṃ anuseti. Taṃ appahīnaṭṭhena bhūmiladdhuppannaṃ nāmāti veditabbaṃ. Tattha ca yassa khandhesu appahīnānusayitā kilesā, tassa te eva khandhā tesaṃ kilesānaṃ vatthu, na itare khandhā. Atītakkhandhesu cassa appahīnānusayitānaṃ kilesānaṃ atītakkhandhā eva vatthu, na itare. Eseva nayo anāgatādīsu. Tathā kāmāvacarakkhandhesu appahīnānusayitānaṃ kilesānaṃ kāmāvacarakkhandhā eva vatthu, na itare. Esa nayo rūpārūpāvacaresu.

Here, the distinction between the ground (bhūmi) and what is obtained from the ground (bhūmiladdha) should be understood. To explain: the ground (bhūmi) is the five aggregates belonging to the three realms, which are the object for insight. What is obtained from the ground (bhūmiladdha) is the host of defilements fit to arise in them. This, however, is not meant in terms of the object (ārammaṇa). For, in terms of the object, defilements arise concerning even the aggregates of those whose cankers are destroyed (arahants)—aggregates which are fully comprehended in their divisions of past, etc.—just as defilements arose for Soreyya the merchant’s son, the youth Nanda, and others, with the aggregates of Mahākaccāyana, Uppalavaṇṇā, and others as their object. If this were what is called bhūmiladdha, then because it would be unabandonable, no one could abandon the root of existence. Rather, bhūmiladdha should be understood in terms of the basis (vatthu). For in whatever person aggregates not fully comprehended by insight arise, in them the root of the cycle of rebirth, the host of defilements, lies latent from the moment of arising. This is to be known as 'realm-obtained-arisen' (bhūmiladdhuppanna) because it has not been abandoned. And for a person in whose aggregates there are defilements with unabandoned latent tendencies, those very aggregates are the basis for those defilements, not other aggregates. For that person, concerning the unabandoned latent tendencies in past aggregates, the past aggregates themselves are the basis, not others. This same method applies to the future and so on. Likewise, concerning the unabandoned latent tendencies in sense-sphere aggregates, the sense-sphere aggregates themselves are the basis, not others. This same method applies in the case of the form and formless sphere aggregates.

Sotāpannādīnaṃ pana yassa yassa ariyapuggalassa khandhesu taṃ taṃ vaṭṭamūlaṃ kilesajātaṃ tena tena maggena pahīnaṃ, tassa tassa te te khandhā pahīnānaṃ tesaṃ tesaṃ vaṭṭamūlakilesānaṃ avatthuto bhūmīti saṅkhaṃ na labhanti. Puthujjanassa pana sabbaso vaṭṭamūlānaṃ kilesānaṃ appahīnattā yaṃ kiñci kariyamānaṃ kammaṃ kusalaṃ vā akusalaṃ vā hoti, iccassa kilesappaccayā vaṭṭaṃ vaḍḍhati. Tassetaṃ vaṭṭamūlaṃ rūpakkhandhe eva, na vedanākkhandhādīsu…pe… viññāṇakkhandhe eva vā, na rūpakkhandhādīsūti na vattabbaṃ. Kasmā? Avisesena pañcasu khandhesu anusayitattā. Kathaṃ? Pathavīrasādimiva rukkhe. Yathā hi mahārukkhe pathavītalaṃ adhiṭṭhāya pathavīrasañca āporasañca [P 1.0006] nissāya tappaccayā mūlakhandhasākhapasākhapattapallavapalāsapupphaphalehi vaḍḍhitvā nabhaṃ pūretvā yāvakappāvasānaṃ bījaparamparāya rukkhapaveṇīsantāne ṭhite [M 1.0006] “taṃ pathavīrasādi mūle eva, na khandhādīsu, phale eva vā, na mūlādīsū”ti na vattabbaṃ. Kasmā? Avisesena sabbesveva mūlādīsu anugatattā, evaṃ. Yathā pana tasseva rukkhassa pupphaphalādīsu nibbinno koci puriso catūsu disāsu maṇḍūkakaṇṭakaṃ nāma rukkhe visaṃ payojeyya, atha so rukkho tena visasamphassena phuṭṭho pathavīrasaāporasapariyādinnena appasavanadhammataṃ āgamma puna santānaṃ nibbattetuṃ samattho na bhaveyya, evamevaṃ khandhappavattiyaṃ nibbinno kulaputto tassa purisassa catūsu disāsu rukkhe visappayojanaṃ viya attano santāne catumaggabhāvanaṃ ārabhati. Athassa so khandhasantāno tena catumaggavisasamphassena sabbaso vaṭṭamūlakilesānaṃ pariyādinnattā kiriyabhāvamattamupagatakāyakammādi sabbakammappabhedo āyatiṃ punabbhavābhinibbattadhammatamāgamma bhavantarasantānaṃ nibbattetuṃ samattho na hoti. Kevalaṃ pana carimaviññāṇanirodhena nirindhano viya jātavedo anupādāno parinibbāti. Evaṃ bhūmiyā bhūmiladdhassa ca nānattaṃ veditabbaṃ.

For the noble individuals from the stream-enterer onwards, in the aggregates of whichever noble person those defilements that are the root of the cycle are abandoned by that respective path, for that person those aggregates do not receive the designation 'ground' on account of being a non-object for those abandoned defilements that are the root of the cycle. For an ordinary person, however, since the defilements that are the root of the cycle are not abandoned at all, whatever action is performed—whether wholesome or unwholesome—the cycle increases on account of these defilements. It cannot be said that this root of the cycle exists only in the form aggregate and not in the feeling aggregate and so on, or only in the consciousness aggregate and not in the form aggregate and so forth. Why? Because it lies latent in all five aggregates without distinction. How so? Like the earth-essence in a tree. For just as a great tree, established on the earth's surface and depending on the earth-essence and water-essence, grows with its roots, trunk, branches, twigs, leaves, foliage, flowers, and fruits, filling the sky, and its lineage continues through a succession of seeds until the end of the aeon, it cannot be said: 'This earth-essence is only in the root, not in the trunk and so on; or only in the fruit, not in the root and so on.' Why? Because it pervades all parts—the root and so on—without distinction. In the same way, just as a person, weary of that same tree's flowers and fruits, might apply a poison called 'frog's thorn' to the tree in the four directions, and that tree, being touched by contact with that poison, would, due to the depletion of the earth-essence and water-essence, arrive at a state of no longer producing and thus be unable to generate a new continuum; in exactly the same way, a son of good family, weary of the continuation of the aggregates, undertakes the cultivation of the four paths in his own continuum, like that person applying poison to the tree in the four directions. Then, his continuum of aggregates, through contact with the poison of the four paths, is entirely depleted of the defilements that are the root of the cycle. All its varieties of karma, such as bodily action, having been reduced to a merely functional state, it is no longer capable of producing a continuum for a future existence, having arrived at the state of not generating a future rebirth. But simply, with the cessation of the final consciousness, like a fire without fuel, it attains final Nibbāna without clinging. Thus, the distinction between the ground and what is attained on the ground should be understood.

Apica [V 1.0007] aparampi samudācārārammaṇādhiggahitāvikkhambhitāsamūhatavasena catubbidhamuppannaṃ. Tattha vattamānuppannameva samudācāruppannaṃ. Cakkhādīnaṃ pana āpāthagate ārammaṇe pubbabhāge anuppajjamānampi kilesajātaṃ ārammaṇassa adhiggahitattā eva aparabhāge avassamuppattito ārammaṇādhiggahituppannanti vuccati. Kalyāṇigāme piṇḍāya carato [P 1.0007] mahātissattherassa visabhāgarūpadassanena uppannakilesajātañcettha nidassanaṃ. Tassa “uppannaṃ kāmavitakka”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.26; a. ni. 6.58) payogo daṭṭhabbo. Samathavipassanānaṃ aññataravasena avikkhambhitakilesajātaṃ cittasantatimanārūḷhaṃ uppattinivārakassa hetuno abhāvā avikkhambhituppannaṃ nāma. Taṃ “ayampi kho, bhikkhave, ānāpānassatisamādhi bhāvito bahulīkato santo ceva paṇīto ca asecanako ca sukho ca vihāro uppannuppanne pāpake akusale dhamme ṭhānaso antaradhāpetī”tiādīsu (pārā. 165) daṭṭhabbaṃ. Samathavipassanāvasena vikkhambhitampi kilesajātaṃ ariyamaggena asamūhatattā uppattidhammataṃ anatītanti katvā asamūhatuppannanti vuccati. Ākāsena gacchantassa aṭṭhasamāpattilābhino therassa kusumitarukkhe upavane pupphāni ocinantassa madhurassarena [M 1.0007] gāyato mātugāmassa gītassaraṃ sutavato uppannakilesajātañcettha nidassanaṃ. Tassa “ariyaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ bahulīkaronto uppannuppanne pāpake akusale dhamme antarāyeva antaradhāpetī”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 5.157) payogo daṭṭhabbo. Tividhampi cetaṃ ārammaṇādhiggahitāvikkhambhitāsamūhatuppannaṃ bhūmiladdheneva saṅgahaṃ gacchatīti veditabbaṃ.

Furthermore, there is another fourfold type of 'arisen' [defilement]: by way of active manifestation, the object being grasped, being unsuppressed, and being uneradicated. Herein, what arises in the present is 'arisen as an active manifestation.' Even if a defilement does not arise in the initial phase when an object enters the range of the eye, etc., it inevitably arises in the subsequent phase because the object has been grasped; thus, it is called 'arisen due to the object being grasped.' An example of this is the defilement that arose in the Elder Mahātissa when he saw an unsuitable form while walking for alms in Kalyāṇi Village. The application of this term should be seen in such phrases as, 'A sensual thought has arisen,' etc. A defilement that has not been suppressed by either serenity or insight, and has not been established in the mental continuum due to the absence of a cause to prevent its arising, is called 'arisen as unsuppressed.' This should be seen in passages such as, 'This concentration through mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated, is peaceful and sublime, an unadulterated blissful abiding, and it utterly disperses and quells evil unwholesome states as soon as they arise.' A defilement that has been suppressed by serenity or insight but not eradicated by the noble path is called 'arisen as uneradicated,' because it has not transcended the nature to arise. An example of this is the defilement that arose in an elder who had attained the eight attainments and was traveling through the sky when he heard the sweet-singing voice of a woman plucking flowers from a blossoming tree in a grove. The application of this term should be seen in such phrases as, 'By frequently developing the noble eightfold path, he dispels and eliminates evil unwholesome states as soon as they arise.' It should be understood that these three types—arisen due to the object being grasped, arisen as unsuppressed, and arisen as uneradicated—are included within the 'attained on the ground' type.

Evametasmiṃ yathāvuttappabhede uppanne bhūmiladdhārammaṇādhiggahitāvikkhambhitāsamūhatuppannavasenāyaṃ kodho uppannoti veditabbo. Kasmā? Evaṃvidhassa vinetabbato. Evaṃvidhameva hi uppannaṃ yena kenaci vinayena vinetuṃ sakkā hoti. Yaṃ panetaṃ vattamānabhutvāpagatokāsakatasamudācārasaṅkhātaṃ uppannaṃ, ettha aphalo ca asakyo ca vāyāmo. Aphalo hi bhutvāpagate vāyāmo vāyāmantarenāpi tassa niruddhattā. Tathā okāsakate. Asakyo ca vattamānasamudācāruppanne kilesavodānānaṃ ekajjhamanuppattitoti.

Thus, regarding this 'arisen' [anger] of the aforementioned types, it should be understood as 'arisen' in the sense of being attained on the ground, the object being grasped, being unsuppressed, or being uneradicated. Why? Because it is this kind that is to be disciplined. Indeed, only what has arisen in this manner can be disciplined by any means. As for that 'arisen' which is designated as a present active manifestation, as having passed and ceased, or as an opportunity created—in these cases, effort is fruitless and impossible. Effort is fruitless regarding what has passed and ceased, because it has already ceased even without effort. The same applies to an opportunity created. And effort is impossible regarding a present active manifestation, because defilements and their purification do not arise simultaneously.

Vinetīti [P 1.0008] ettha pana –

Now, in the phrase 'one disciplines'–

“Duvidho vinayo nāma, ekamekettha pañcadhā;

Tesu aṭṭhavidhenesa, vinetīti pavuccati”.

Discipline is of two kinds, and each of these is fivefold. It is said that this person disciplines by eight of these means.

Ayañhi [V 1.0008] saṃvaravinayo, pahānavinayoti duvidho vinayo. Ettha ca duvidhe vinaye ekameko vinayo pañcadhā bhijjati. Saṃvaravinayopi hi sīlasaṃvaro, satisaṃvaro, ñāṇasaṃvaro, khantisaṃvaro, vīriyasaṃvaroti pañcavidho. Pahānavinayopi tadaṅgappahānaṃ, vikkhambhanappahānaṃ, samucchedappahānaṃ, paṭippassaddhippahānaṃ, nissaraṇappahānanti pañcavidho.

This discipline is twofold: the discipline of restraint and the discipline of abandonment. Herein, each of these two disciplines is divided into five. The discipline of restraint is fivefold: restraint by morality, restraint by mindfulness, restraint by wisdom, restraint by patience, and restraint by energy. The discipline of abandonment is also fivefold: abandonment by substitution of opposites, abandonment by suppression, abandonment by eradication, abandonment by tranquillization, and abandonment by escape.

Tattha “iminā pātimokkhasaṃvarena upeto hoti samupeto”tiādīsu (vibha. 511) sīlasaṃvaro, “rakkhati cakkhundriyaṃ, cakkhundriye saṃvaraṃ āpajjatī”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.213; ma. ni. 1.295; saṃ. ni. 4.239; a. ni. 3.16) satisaṃvaro.

Therein, in passages such as, “He is endowed with this Pātimokkha restraint, possessed of it” (Vibh 511), is restraint by morality. In passages such as, “He guards the eye faculty, undertakes restraint in the eye faculty” (DN 1.213; MN 1.295; SN 4.239; AN 3.16), is restraint by mindfulness.

“Yāni sotāni lokasmiṃ, (ajitāti bhagavā)

Sati tesaṃ nivāraṇaṃ;

Sotānaṃ saṃvaraṃ brūmi,

Paññāyete pidhīyare”ti. (su. ni. 1041) –

“Whatever streams there are in the world,” (said the Blessed One to Ajita), “mindfulness is their obstruction; of the streams’ restraint I speak, by wisdom they are shut off.” (Snp 1041) –

Ādīsu [M 1.0008] ñāṇasaṃvaro, “khamo hoti sītassa uṇhassā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.24; a. ni. 4.114) khantisaṃvaro, “uppannaṃ kāmavitakkaṃ nādhivāseti, pajahati, vinodetī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.26; a. ni. 4.114) vīriyasaṃvaro veditabbo. Sabbopi cāyaṃ saṃvaro yathāsakaṃ saṃvaritabbānaṃ vinetabbānañca kāyavacīduccaritādīnaṃ saṃvaraṇato saṃvaro, vinayanato vinayoti vuccati. Evaṃ tāva saṃvaravinayo pañcadhā bhijjatīti veditabbo.

In passages such as this is restraint by wisdom. In passages such as, “He is patient with cold and heat” (MN 1.24; AN 4.114), is restraint by patience. In passages such as, “He does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensual desire, he abandons it, dispels it” (MN 1.26; AN 4.114), restraint by energy is to be understood. And all this restraint is called ‘restraint’ (saṃvara) from its restraining, and ‘discipline’ (vinaya) from its disciplining, of bodily and verbal misconduct and other things that are to be respectively restrained and disciplined. Thus, it should be understood that the discipline of restraint is divided into five.

Tathā yaṃ nāmarūpaparicchedādīsu vipassanaṅgesu yāva attano aparihānavasena pavatti, tāva tena tena ñāṇena tassa tassa anatthasantānassa pahānaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ – nāmarūpavavatthānena sakkāyadiṭṭhiyā, paccayapariggahena [P 1.0009] ahetuvisamahetudiṭṭhīnaṃ, tasseva aparabhāgena kaṅkhāvitaraṇena kathaṃkathībhāvassa, kalāpasammasanena “ahaṃ mamā”ti gāhassa, maggāmaggavavatthānena amagge maggasaññāya, udayadassanena ucchedadiṭṭhiyā, vayadassanena sassatadiṭṭhiyā, bhayadassanena sabhayesu abhayasaññāya, ādīnavadassanena assādasaññāya, nibbidānupassanena abhiratisaññāya, muccitukamyatāñāṇena amuccitukamyatāya, upekkhāñāṇena anupekkhāya, anulomena dhammaṭṭhitiyaṃ nibbāne ca paṭilomabhāvassa, gotrabhunā saṅkhāranimittaggāhassa pahānaṃ, etaṃ tadaṅgappahānaṃ nāma. Yaṃ pana upacārappanābhedassa samādhino yāva attano aparihānipavatti[V 1.0009], tāva tenābhihatānaṃ nīvaraṇānaṃ yathāsakaṃ vitakkādipaccanīkadhammānañca anuppattisaṅkhātaṃ pahānaṃ, etaṃ vikkhambhanappahānaṃ nāma. Yaṃ pana catunnaṃ ariyamaggānaṃ bhāvitattā taṃtaṃmaggavato attano santāne yathāsakaṃ “diṭṭhigatānaṃ pahānāyā”tiādinā (dha. sa. 277) nayena vuttassa samudayapakkhikassa kilesagahanassa puna accantaappavattibhāvena samucchedasaṅkhātaṃ pahānaṃ, idaṃ samucchedappahānaṃ nāma. Yaṃ pana phalakkhaṇe paṭippassaddhattaṃ kilesānaṃ pahānaṃ, idaṃ paṭippassaddhippahānaṃ nāma. Yaṃ pana sabbasaṅkhatanissaraṇattā pahīnasabbasaṅkhataṃ nibbānaṃ, etaṃ nissaraṇappahānaṃ nāma. Sabbampi cetaṃ pahānaṃ yasmā cāgaṭṭhena pahānaṃ, vinayanaṭṭhena vinayo, tasmā “pahānavinayo”ti vuccati, taṃtaṃpahānavato vā tassa tassa vinayassa sambhavatopetaṃ “pahānavinayo”ti [M 1.0009] vuccati. Evaṃ pahānavinayopi pañcadhā bhijjatīti veditabbo. Evamekekassa pañcadhā bhinnattā dasete vinayā honti.

Likewise, for as long as the factors of insight, beginning with the determination of mind-and-matter, proceed by way of non-decline, for so long there is the abandonment of this or that continuum of what is unbeneficial by means of this or that knowledge. That is to say: through the determination of mind-and-matter, the identity view is abandoned; through the comprehension of conditions, the views of causelessness and of wrong cause are abandoned; through its subsequent part, the overcoming of doubt, the state of uncertainty is abandoned; through the comprehension of groups, the grasp of ‘I’ and ‘mine’ is abandoned; through the determination of path and not-path, the perception of the not-path as the path is abandoned; through the seeing of arising, the annihilation view is abandoned; through the seeing of passing away, the eternalist view is abandoned; through the seeing of fear, the perception of safety in what is fearful is abandoned; through the seeing of danger, the perception of gratification is abandoned; through the contemplation of disenchantment, the perception of delight is abandoned; through the knowledge of the desire for deliverance, the desire not to be delivered is abandoned; through the knowledge of equanimity, non-equanimity is abandoned; through conformity, the state of opposition to the stability of phenomena and to Nibbāna is abandoned; through change-of-lineage, the grasp of the sign of formations is abandoned—this is called abandonment by substitution of opposites. Furthermore, that abandonment which is reckoned as the non-occurrence of the hindrances, which are struck down by concentration of the access and absorption distinction for as long as it proceeds without decline, and of the respective states, such as applied thought, that are inimical to them—this is called abandonment by suppression. Furthermore, that abandonment which is reckoned as eradication, owing to the cultivation of the four noble paths, whereby the thicket of defilements belonging to the side of arising, spoken of in the way beginning, “For the abandonment of views” (Dhs 277), can never again occur in the personal continuity of the one of the respective path—this is called abandonment by eradication. Furthermore, that abandonment of the defilements which is their being stilled at the moment of fruition—this is called abandonment by tranquillization. Furthermore, Nibbāna, wherein all formations are abandoned, being the escape from all that is formed—this is called abandonment by escape. And all this abandonment is called ‘abandonment-discipline’ because it is abandonment in the sense of relinquishment and discipline in the sense of removing. Or, because from this or that abandonment, this or that discipline arises, it is called ‘abandonment-discipline’. Thus, it should be understood that the discipline of abandonment is also divided into five. In this way, because each one is divided into five, these disciplines are ten.

Tesu paṭippassaddhivinayaṃ nissaraṇavinayañca ṭhapetvā [P 1.0010] avasesena aṭṭhavidhena vinayenesa tena tena pariyāyena vinetīti pavuccati. Kathaṃ? Sīlasaṃvarena kāyavacīduccaritāni vinentopi hi taṃsampayuttaṃ kodhaṃ vineti, satipaññāsaṃvarehi abhijjhādomanassādīni vinentopi domanassasampayuttaṃ kodhaṃ vineti, khantisaṃvarena sītādīni khamantopi taṃtaṃāghātavatthusambhavaṃ kodhaṃ vineti, vīriyasaṃvarena byāpādavitakkaṃ vinentopi taṃsampayuttaṃ kodhaṃ vineti. Yehi dhammehi tadaṅgavikkhambhanasamucchedappahānāni honti, tesaṃ dhammānaṃ attani nibbattanena te te dhamme pajahantopi tadaṅgappahātabbaṃ vikkhambhetabbaṃ samucchinditabbañca kodhaṃ vineti. Kāmañcettha pahānavinayena vinayo na sambhavati. Yehi pana dhammehi pahānaṃ hoti, tehi vinentopi pariyāyato “pahānavinayena vinetī”ti vuccati. Paṭippassaddhippahānakāle pana vinetabbābhāvato nissaraṇappahānassa ca anuppādetabbato na tehi kiñci vinetīti vuccati. Evaṃ tesu paṭippassaddhivinayaṃ nissaraṇavinayañca ṭhapetvā avasesena aṭṭhavidhena vinayenesa tena tena pariyāyena vinetīti pavuccatīti. Ye vā –

Among these, setting aside the discipline of tranquillization and the discipline of escape, it is said that by the remaining eightfold discipline, this one disciplines in this or that way. How so? For, while disciplining bodily and verbal misconduct by the restraint of morality, one also disciplines the anger associated with them. While disciplining covetousness, displeasure, and so on by the restraints of mindfulness and wisdom, one also disciplines the anger associated with displeasure. While enduring cold and so on by the restraint of patience, one also disciplines the anger that arises from this or that ground for resentment. While disciplining a thought of ill will by the restraint of energy, one also disciplines the anger associated with it. By bringing about in oneself those states by which there is abandonment by substitution of opposites, by suppression, and by eradication, while abandoning those respective states, one also disciplines the anger that is to be abandoned by substitution of opposites, to be suppressed, and to be eradicated. And here, it is true, discipline by means of the discipline of abandonment does not occur. But since one disciplines by means of those states by which abandonment occurs, it is said figuratively that ‘one disciplines by the discipline of abandonment’. At the time of abandonment by tranquillization, however, because there is nothing to be disciplined, and because the abandonment by escape is not to be produced, it is not said that one disciplines anything by means of them. Thus, among them, setting aside the discipline of tranquillization and the discipline of escape, it is said that by the remaining eightfold discipline, this one disciplines in this or that way. Or else—

“Pañcime, bhikkhave, āghātapaṭivinayā, yattha bhikkhuno uppanno āghāto sabbaso paṭivinetabbo. Katame pañca? Yasmiṃ, bhikkhave, puggale āghāto jāyetha, mettā tasmiṃ puggale bhāvetabbā…pe… karuṇā… upekkhā… asati-amanasikāro tasmiṃ puggale āpajjitabbo, evaṃ tasmiṃ puggale āghāto paṭivinetabbo. Kammassakatā eva vā tasmiṃ puggale adhiṭṭhātabbā kammassako ayamāyasmā…pe… dāyādo bhavissatī”ti (a. ni. 5.161) –

Monks, there are these five ways of subduing resentment, by which any resentment that has arisen in a monk should be fully subdued. What are the five? Monks, concerning the person towards whom resentment might arise, loving-kindness should be developed towards that person… compassion… equanimity… or non-attention and non-contemplation should be applied to that person; in this way resentment towards that person should be subdued. Or, concerning that person, the reflection on kamma as one’s own property should be established: 'This venerable one is the owner of his kamma… heir to his kamma.'" (A.N. 5.161)

Evaṃ [V 1.0010] pañca āghātapaṭivinayā vuttā. Ye ca –

Thus, five ways of subduing resentment have been spoken. And those which –

“Pañcime, āvuso, āghātapaṭivinayā, yattha bhikkhuno uppanno āghāto sabbaso paṭivinetabbo. Katame pañca? Idhāvuso[M 1.0010], ekacco puggalo aparisuddhakāyasamācāro hoti, parisuddhavacīsamācāro, evarūpepi, āvuso, puggale āghāto [P 1.0011] paṭivinetabbo”ti (a. ni. 5.162) –

"These five, friends, are ways of subduing resentment, by which any resentment that has arisen in a monk should be fully subdued. What five? Here, friends, a certain person has impure bodily conduct but pure verbal conduct. Even towards such a person, friends, resentment should be subdued."

Evamādināpi nayena pañca āghātapaṭivinayā vuttā. Tesu yena kenaci āghātapaṭivinayena vinentopesa vinetīti pavuccati. Apica yasmā –

Thus, in this and similar ways, five ways of subduing resentment have been spoken. Among these, one who subdues by any of these ways of subduing resentment is said to be 'one who subdues.' Moreover, since—

“Ubhatodaṇḍakena cepi, bhikkhave, kakacena corā ocarakā aṅgamaṅgāni okkanteyyuṃ, tatrāpi yo mano padoseyya, na me so tena sāsanakaro”ti (ma. ni. 1.232) –-

"Even if, monks, bandits were to savagely sever your limbs, joint by joint, with a two-handled saw, even then whoever of you should arouse a mind of hatred, he would not be one who carried out my teaching."

Evaṃ satthu ovādaṃ,

Thus, the Teacher's instruction,

“Tasseva tena pāpiyo, yo kuddhaṃ paṭikujjhati;

Kuddhaṃ appaṭikujjhanto, saṅgāmaṃ jeti dujjayaṃ.

Worse off is he who returns anger to one who is angry;

Not returning anger, one wins a battle hard to win.

“Ubhinnamatthaṃ carati, attano ca parassa ca;

Paraṃ saṅkupitaṃ ñatvā, yo sato upasammati”. (saṃ. ni. 1.188);

"He fares for the welfare of both, of himself and of the other,

Who, knowing the other to be angry, remains mindful and calms down."

“Sattime, bhikkhave, dhammā sapattakantā sapattakaraṇā kodhanaṃ āgacchanti itthiṃ vā purisaṃ vā. Katame satta? Idha, bhikkhave, sapatto sapattassa evaṃ icchati – ‘aho, vatāyaṃ dubbaṇṇo assā’ti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Na, bhikkhave, sapatto sapattassa vaṇṇavatāya nandati. Kodhanāyaṃ, bhikkhave, purisapuggalo kodhābhibhūto kodhapareto kiñcāpi so hoti sunhāto suvilitto kappitakesamassu odātavatthavasano, atha kho so dubbaṇṇova hoti kodhābhibhūto. Ayaṃ, bhikkhave, paṭhamo dhammo sapattakanto sapattakaraṇo kodhanaṃ āgacchati itthiṃ vā purisaṃ vā (a. ni. 7.64).

"Monks, there are these seven things liked by an enemy, that make one an enemy, which come to an angry woman or man. What seven? Here, monks, an enemy wishes of an enemy: ‘Oh, may this one be ugly!’ For what reason? Monks, an enemy does not rejoice in the beauty of an enemy. An angry person, monks, overcome and assailed by anger, even if he is well-bathed, well-anointed, with neatly trimmed hair and beard, dressed in white clothes, still he is ugly, being overcome by anger. This, monks, is the first thing liked by an enemy, that makes one an enemy, which comes to an angry woman or man."

“Puna [V 1.0011] caparaṃ, bhikkhave, sapatto sapattassa evaṃ icchati – ‘aho, vatāyaṃ dukkhaṃ sayeyyā’ti…pe… ‘na pacurattho assā’ti…pe… ‘na bhogavā assā’ti…pe… ‘na yasavā assā’ti…pe… ‘na mittavā assā’ti…pe… ‘kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ [M 1.0011] vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjeyyā’ti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Na, bhikkhave, sapatto sapattassa sugatigamanena nandati. Kodhanāyaṃ, bhikkhave, purisapuggalo kodhābhibhūto kodhapareto kāyena duccaritaṃ carati, vācāya… manasā duccaritaṃ carati. So kāyena duccaritaṃ caritvā…pe… vācāya…pe… manasā duccaritaṃ caritvā kāyassa [P 1.0012] bhedā paraṃ maraṇā…pe… nirayaṃ upapajjati kodhābhibhūto”ti (a. ni. 7.64).

"Furthermore, monks, an enemy wishes for an enemy thus: 'Oh, may this one lie down in suffering!'... 'May he not have much gain!'... 'May he not have wealth!'... 'May he not have renown!'... 'May he not have friends!'... 'At the breaking up of the body, after death, may he be reborn in deprivation, a bad destination, the lower world, hell!' Why is that? Monks, an enemy does not rejoice in the good destination of an enemy. An angry person, monks, overwhelmed by anger, assailed by anger, practices misconduct by body, speech, and mind. Having practiced misconduct by body, speech, and mind, at the breaking up of the body, after death, he is reborn in deprivation... in hell, overwhelmed by anger." (A.N. 7.64)

“Kuddho atthaṃ na jānāti, kuddho dhammaṃ na passati…pe…. (a. ni. 7.64; mahāni. 5);

An angry person does not discern what is beneficial, an angry person does not see the Dhamma... (AN 7.64; Mahāni. 5)

“Yena kodhena kuddhāse, sattā gacchanti duggatiṃ;

Taṃ kodhaṃ sammadaññāya, pajahanti vipassino. (itivu. 4);

Those beings who go to a bad destination because of the anger with which they are enraged—the wise, fully understanding that anger, abandon it.

“Kodhaṃ jahe vippajaheyya mānaṃ, saṃyojanaṃ sabbamatikkameyya. (dha. pa. 221);

Abandon anger, renounce pride, overcome all fetters.

“Anatthajanano kodho, kodho cittappakopano. (a. ni. 7.64; itivu. 88);

Anger gives rise to harm, anger disturbs the mind.

“Ekāparādhaṃ khama bhūripañña, na paṇḍitā kodhabalā bhavantī”ti. (jā. 1.15.19) –

"Forgive this one offense, O wise one, for the learned are not strong with anger."

Evamādinā nayena kodhe ādīnavañca paccavekkhatopi kodho vinayaṃ upeti. Tasmā evaṃ paccavekkhitvā kodhaṃ vinentopi esa vinetīti vuccati.

In this and similar ways, when one reflects on the drawbacks of anger, that anger is subdued. Therefore, one who, having reflected thus, subdues anger is also called 'one who subdues'.

Kodhanti “anatthaṃ me acarīti āghāto jāyatī”tiādinā (dī. ni. 3.340; a. ni. 9.29) nayena sutte vuttānaṃ navannaṃ, “atthaṃ me na carī”ti ādīnañca tappaṭipakkhato [V 1.0012] siddhānaṃ navannamevāti aṭṭhārasannaṃ, khāṇukaṇṭakādinā aṭṭhānena saddhiṃ ekūnavīsatiyā āghātavatthūnaṃ aññatarāghātavatthusambhavaṃ āghātaṃ. Visaṭanti vitthataṃ. Sappavisanti sappassa visaṃ. Ivāti opammavacanaṃ, i-kāra lopaṃ katvā va-icceva vuttaṃ. Osadhehīti agadehi. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā visatikicchako vejjo sappena daṭṭhaṃ sabbaṃ kāyaṃ pharitvā ṭhitaṃ visaṭaṃ sappavisaṃ mūlakhandhatacapattapupphādīnaṃ aññatarehi [M 1.0012] nānābhesajjehi payojetvā katehi vā osadhehi khippameva vineyya, evamevaṃ yo yathāvuttenatthena uppatitaṃ cittasantānaṃ byāpetvā ṭhitaṃ kodhaṃ yathāvuttesu vinayanūpāyesu yena kenaci upāyena vineti nādhivāseti pajahati vinodeti byantīkarotīti.

"Anger" (kodha) means the resentment (āghāta) that arises from any one of the nineteen grounds for resentment: the nine stated in the suttas in the manner beginning, "Resentment arises with the thought: 'He has done me harm'" (Dī. Ni. 3.340; A. Ni. 9.29); the nine established from their opposites, beginning, "He has not done me good," making eighteen; and, together with these, the inappropriate occasion, such as a tree-stump, a thorn, and so on. "Spread" (visaṭa) means extensive. "Snake venom" (sappavisa) means the venom of a snake. The word iva ("like") is a term of comparison; having elided the letter 'i', it is stated simply as va. "With remedies" (osadhehi) means with antidotes. This is the meaning: Just as a physician skilled in treating poison would quickly subdue the spreading snake venom that has pervaded the whole body of one bitten by a snake, using various medicines made from roots, stems, bark, leaves, flowers, or other such things, or from prepared formulas; even so, one who, by any of the aforementioned means of subduing, subdues—does not tolerate, abandons, dispels, and eliminates—the anger that has arisen in the way described and pervades the mind-stream.

So bhikkhu jahāti orapāranti so evaṃ kodhaṃ vinento bhikkhu yasmā kodho tatiyamaggena sabbaso [P 1.0013] pahīyati, tasmā orapārasaññitāni pañcorambhāgiyasaṃyojanāni jahātīti veditabbo. Avisesena hi pāranti tīrassa nāmaṃ, tasmā orāni ca tāni saṃsārasāgarassa pārabhūtāni cāti katvā “orapāra”nti vuccati. Atha vā “yo uppatitaṃ vineti kodhaṃ visaṭaṃ sappavisaṃva osadhehi”, so tatiyamaggena sabbaso kodhaṃ vinetvā anāgāmiphale ṭhito bhikkhu jahāti orapāraṃ. Tattha oranti sakattabhāvo, pāranti parattabhāvo. Oraṃ vā cha ajjhattikāni āyatanāni, pāraṃ cha bāhirāyatanāni. Tathā oraṃ manussaloko, pāraṃ devaloko. Oraṃ kāmadhātu, pāraṃ rūpārūpadhātu. Oraṃ kāmarūpabhavo, pāraṃ arūpabhavo. Oraṃ attabhāvo, pāraṃ attabhāvasukhūpakaraṇāni. Evametasmiṃ orapāre catutthamaggena chandarāgaṃ pajahanto “jahāti orapāra”nti vuccati. Ettha ca kiñcāpi anāgāmino kāmarāgassa pahīnattā idhattabhāvādīsu chandarāgo eva natthi; apica kho panassa tatiyamaggādīnaṃ viya vaṇṇappakāsanatthaṃ sabbametaṃ orapārabhedaṃ saṅgahetvā tattha chandarāgappahānena “jahāti orapāra”nti vuttaṃ.

That monk abandons this shore and the far shore. Thus, the monk, dispelling anger—since anger is entirely abandoned by the third path—it should be understood that he abandons the five lower fetters, which are termed 'this shore and the far shore'. For, generally, 'pāra' is a name for a shore. Therefore, because they are both the near shore and the far shore of the ocean of saṃsāra, they are called 'this shore and the far shore'. Alternatively, as in 'one who subdues arisen anger, like an antidote for spreading snake venom,' that monk, having completely dispelled anger by the third path and being established in the fruit of non-returning, abandons this shore and the far shore. Therein, 'this shore' is one's own being, and 'the far shore' is another's being. Or, 'this shore' is the six internal sense bases, and 'the far shore' is the six external sense bases. Likewise, 'this shore' is the human world, and 'the far shore' is the divine world. 'This shore' is the sense-sphere realm, and 'the far shore' is the form and formless realms. 'This shore' is existence in the sense-sphere and form realms, and 'the far shore' is formless existence. 'This shore' is individual existence, and 'the far shore' is the accessories for the well-being of individual existence. Thus, in this 'this shore and far shore', one who abandons sensual desire with the fourth path is said to 'abandon this shore and the far shore'. And here, although for a non-returner, due to the abandonment of sensual lust, there is no sensual desire at all for this state of being and so on, nevertheless, for the purpose of proclaiming the qualities of the third path and so on, having comprehended all these divisions of 'this shore and far shore', it is said that 'he abandons this shore and the far shore' through the abandonment of sensual desire therein.

Idāni tassatthassa vibhāvanatthāya upamaṃ āha “urago jiṇṇamiva tacaṃ purāṇa”nti. Tattha urena gacchatīti urago, sappassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. So duvidho – kāmarūpī ca akāmarūpī ca. Kāmarūpīpi duvidho – jalajo thalajo ca. Jalajo jale eva kāmarūpaṃ labhati, na thale, saṅkhapālajātake saṅkhapālanāgarājā viya. Thalajo thale eva, na jale. So jajjarabhāvena jiṇṇaṃ, cirakālatāya purāṇañcāti saṅkhaṃ gataṃ. Tacaṃ jahanto catubbidhena jahāti – sajātiyaṃ ṭhito, jigucchanto, nissāya, thāmenāti. Sajāti nāma sappajāti dīghattabhāvo. Uragā hi pañcasu ṭhānesu sajātiṃ nātivattanti – upapattiyaṃ, cutiyaṃ, vissaṭṭhaniddokkamane, samānajātiyā [M 1.0013][V 1.0013] methunapaṭisevane, jiṇṇatacāpanayane cāti. Sappo hi yadā tacaṃ jahāti, tadā sajātiyaṃyeva ṭhatvā jahāti. Sajātiyaṃ ṭhitopi ca jigucchanto [P 1.0014] jahāti. Jigucchanto nāma yadā upaḍḍhaṭṭhāne mutto hoti, upaḍḍhaṭṭhāne amutto olambati, tadā naṃ aṭṭīyanto jahāti. Evaṃ jigucchantopi ca daṇḍantaraṃ vā mūlantaraṃ vā pāsāṇantaraṃ vā nissāya jahāti. Nissāya jahantopi ca thāmaṃ janetvā, ussāhaṃ katvā, vīriyena vaṅkaṃ naṅguṭṭhaṃ katvā, passasantova phaṇaṃ karitvā jahāti. Evaṃ jahitvā yenakāmaṃ pakkamati. Evamevaṃ ayampi bhikkhu orapāraṃ jahitukāmo catubbidhena jahāti – sajātiyaṃ ṭhito, jigucchanto, nissāya, thāmenāti. Sajāti nāma bhikkhuno “ariyāya jātiyā jāto”ti (ma. ni. 2.351) vacanato sīlaṃ. Tenevāha “sīle patiṭṭhāya naro sappañño”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.23; peṭako. 22). Evametissaṃ sajātiyaṃ ṭhito bhikkhu taṃ sakattabhāvādibhedaṃ orapāraṃ jiṇṇapurāṇatacamiva dukkhaṃ janentaṃ tattha tattha ādīnavadassanena jigucchanto kalyāṇamitte nissāya adhimattavāyāmasaṅkhātaṃ thāmaṃ janetvā “divasaṃ caṅkamena nisajjāya āvaraṇīyehi dhammehi cittaṃ parisodhetī”ti (a. ni. 3.16; vibha. 519) vuttanayena rattindivaṃ chadhā vibhajitvā ghaṭento vāyamanto urago viya, vaṅkaṃ naṅguṭṭhaṃ pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā urago viya passasanto, ayampi asithilaparakkamatāya vāyamanto urago viya phaṇaṃ karitvā, ayampi ñāṇavipphāraṃ janetvā uragova tacaṃ orapāraṃ jahāti. Jahitvā ca urago viya ohitataco yenakāmaṃ ayampi ohitabhāro anupādisesanibbānadhātudisaṃ pakkamatīti. Tenāha bhagavā –

Now, to clarify that meaning, he stated the simile: 'Like a snake shedding its old, worn-out skin.' Herein, 'uraga' means one who moves by the chest—this is a synonym for a snake. It is of two kinds: form-assuming and non-form-assuming. The form-assuming one is also of two kinds: water-dwelling and land-dwelling. The water-dwelling one attains desired forms only in water, not on land, like the nāga-king Saṅkhapāla in the Saṅkhapāla Jātaka. The land-dwelling one attains them only on land, not in water. It is called 'worn-out' due to decrepitude, and has come to be called 'old' due to its long age. Shedding its skin, it sheds it in four ways: while remaining in its own species, with revulsion, by relying on something, and with strength. 'Own species' refers to the snake species, the state of being long. Indeed, serpents do not transgress their own species in five situations: at birth, at death, when in deep sleep, when mating with one of their own species, and when removing their old skin. For when a snake sheds its skin, it does so while remaining in its own species. And even while remaining in its own species, it sheds it with revulsion. 'With revulsion' means that when half of it is freed and the other, unfreed half dangles, it sheds it in disgust. And even while shedding it with revulsion, it does so by relying on the space between sticks, or between roots, or between rocks. And while shedding by relying on something, it generates strength, makes an effort, and with energy, having made its tail crooked, it sheds its skin while breathing out and making a hood. Having thus shed it, it departs wherever it wishes. In the very same way, this monk, wishing to abandon this shore and the far shore, does so in four ways: while remaining in his own species, with revulsion, by relying on something, and with strength. For a monk, 'his own species' is virtue, according to the saying, 'Born of a noble birth.' Therefore He said, 'A wise person, established in virtue…' Thus, this monk, established in his own species, with revulsion—by seeing the danger in this and that state—abandons that 'this shore and far shore' (differentiated as one's own being and so on), which produces suffering like an old, worn-out skin. Relying on spiritual friends, he generates strength, known as extreme exertion. In the manner described—'By day, with walking and sitting, he purifies his mind from obstructive states'—striving and exerting himself day and night like a snake; like a snake that has coiled its crooked tail into a seat and is breathing out, this monk too strives with unslackened energy; like a snake making a hood, this monk too generates an expansion of knowledge; and just as a snake sheds its skin, he abandons this shore and the far shore. And having abandoned them, like a snake that has cast off its skin, he too, having laid down his burden, departs in the direction of the Nibbāna-element with no residue remaining. Therefore the Blessed One said:

“Yo uppatitaṃ vineti kodhaṃ, visaṭaṃ sappavisaṃva osadhehi;

So bhikkhu jahāti orapāraṃ, urago jiṇṇamiva tacaṃ purāṇa”nti.

He who subdues arisen anger, as one would spreading snake venom with medicinal herbs; that monk abandons this shore and the far shore, as a snake its old, worn-out skin.

Evamesā [P 1.0015] bhagavatā arahattanikūṭena paṭhamagāthā desitāti.

Thus was this first verse taught by the Blessed One, with Arahantship as its pinnacle.

2. Idāni dutiyagāthāya atthavaṇṇanākkamo anuppatto. Tatrāpi –

2. Now the turn for the exposition of the meaning of the second verse has arrived. Therein also:

“Yena [M 1.0014] yattha yadā yasmā, vuttā gāthā ayaṃ imaṃ;

Vidhiṃ pakāsayitvāssā, karissāmatthavaṇṇana”nti. –

By whom, where, when, and for what reason this verse was spoken; having explained this method for it, I shall make an exposition of its meaning.

Ayameva mātikā. Tato parañca sabbagāthāsu. Ativitthārabhayena pana ito pabhuti mātikaṃ anikkhipitvā [V 1.0014] uppattidassananayeneva tassā tassā atthaṃ dassento atthavaṇṇanaṃ karissāmi. Seyyathidaṃ yo rāgamudacchidā asesanti ayaṃ dutiyagāthā.

This is the matrix. And so for all verses thereafter. However, for fear of excessive elaboration, from this point on, without setting down the matrix, I will provide the exposition of the meaning by showing the origin of each verse. As follows: 'He who has completely eradicated passion…'—this is the second verse.

Tassuppatti – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Tena kho pana samayena āyasmato sāriputtattherassa upaṭṭhāko aññataro suvaṇṇakāraputto therassa santike pabbajito. Thero tassa “daharānaṃ asubhaṃ sappāya”nti mantvā rāgavighātatthaṃ asubhakammaṭṭhānaṃ adāsi. Tassa tasmiṃ āsevanamattampi cittaṃ na labhati. So “anupakāraṃ mameta”nti therassa ārocesi. Thero “daharānametaṃ sappāya”nti mantvā punapi tadevācikkhi. Evaṃ cattāro māsā atītā, so kiñcimattampi visesaṃ na labhati. Tato naṃ thero bhagavato santikaṃ nesi. Bhagavā “avisayo, sāriputta, tuyhetassa sappāyaṃ jānituṃ, buddhaveneyyo eso”ti vatvā pabhassaravaṇṇaṃ padumaṃ iddhiyā nimminitvā tassa hatthe pādāsi – “handa, bhikkhu, imaṃ vihārapacchāyāyaṃ vālikātale nāḷena vijjhitvā ṭhapehi, abhimukhañcassa pallaṅkena nisīda ‘lohitaṃ lohita’nti āvajjento”ti. Ayaṃ kira pañca jātisatāni suvaṇṇakārova ahosi. Tenassa “lohitakanimittaṃ sappāya”nti ñatvā bhagavā lohitakakammaṭṭhānaṃ adāsi. So tathā katvā muhutteneva yathākkamaṃ [P 1.0016] tattha cattāripi jhānāni adhigantvā anulomapaṭilomādinā nayena jhānakīḷaṃ ārabhi. Atha bhagavā ‘taṃ padumaṃ milāyatū’ti adhiṭṭhāsi. So jhānā vuṭṭhito taṃ milātaṃ kāḷavaṇṇaṃ disvā “pabhassararūpaṃ jarāya parimaddita”nti aniccasaññaṃ paṭilabhi. Tato naṃ ajjhattampi upasaṃhari. Tato “yadaniccaṃ taṃ dukkhaṃ, yaṃ dukkhaṃ tadanattā”ti tayopi bhave āditte viya passi. Evaṃ passato cassāvidūre padumassaro atthi. Tattha dārakā orohitvā padumāni bhañjitvā bhañjitvā rāsiṃ karonti. Tassa tāni udake padumāni naḷavane aggijālā viya khāyiṃsu, pattāni patantāni papātaṃ pavisantāni viya khāyiṃsu, thale nikkhittapadumānaṃ aggāni milātāni aggiḍaḍḍhāni viya [M 1.0015] khāyiṃsu. Athassa tadanusārena sabbadhamme upanijjhāyato bhiyyosomattāya tayo bhavā ādittamiva agāraṃ appaṭisaraṇā hutvā upaṭṭhahiṃsu. Tato bhagavā gandhakuṭiyaṃ nisinnova tassa bhikkhuno upari sarīrābhaṃ muñci. Sā cassa mukhaṃyeva ajjhotthari. Tato so “kimeta”nti āvajjento bhagavantaṃ āgantvā samīpe ṭhitamiva disvā uṭṭhāyāsanā añjaliṃ paṇāmesi. Athassa bhagavā sappāyaṃ viditvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ obhāsagāthaṃ abhāsi “yo rāgamudacchidā asesa”nti.

Its origin: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī, in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Now at that time, a certain goldsmith’s son, who was an attendant of the Elder Sāriputta, had gone forth in the Elder’s presence. The Elder, thinking, “For the young, the meditation on foulness is suitable,” gave him a meditation subject on foulness for the destruction of lust. But his mind did not gain even a foothold in it. He reported to the Elder, “This is not beneficial for me.” The Elder, thinking, “This is suitable for the young,” instructed him in the same subject again. Thus four months passed, and he gained no distinction whatsoever. Then the Elder took him to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said, “It is not within your scope, Sāriputta, to know what is suitable for him. This one is to be tamed by a Buddha.” Then, by his supernormal power, the Blessed One created a lotus of radiant hue and placed it in the bhikkhu’s hand, saying, “Here, bhikkhu, take this and, in the sandy ground in the shade of the monastery, pierce it with its stalk and place it there. Then sit cross-legged facing it, reflecting, ‘Red, red.’” It is said that this bhikkhu had been a goldsmith for five hundred births. Knowing that the sign of red was suitable for him, the Blessed One gave him the meditation subject on red. He did as instructed and in a moment, in due order, attained the four jhānas there. Then he began to sport with the jhānas by the method of forward and reverse order. Then the Blessed One willed, “Let that lotus wither.” When he emerged from jhāna and saw that withered, dark-colored lotus, he gained the perception of impermanence, thinking, “This radiant form is crushed by decay.” Then he applied this perception inwardly as well. Then, reflecting, “What is impermanent is suffering; what is suffering is non-self,” he saw the three realms of existence as if ablaze. While he was observing thus, not far away there was a lotus pond. There, children descended, and having plucked lotuses again and again, they made a pile. To him, the lotuses in the water appeared like flames of fire in a reed thicket, the falling petals appeared as if entering a chasm, and the withered tips of the lotuses placed on the ground appeared as if burnt by fire. Then, as he contemplated all phenomena in accordance with that, the three realms of existence appeared to him even more intensely as a burning house, without refuge. Then the Blessed One, while seated in the Perfumed Chamber, released a radiance from his body over that bhikkhu. It enveloped his very face. Reflecting, “What is this?” he saw the Blessed One as if he had come and was standing nearby. Rising from his seat, he paid homage with joined palms. Then the Blessed One, knowing what was suitable for him, taught the Dhamma and uttered this illuminating verse: “One who has cut off lust entirely…”

Tattha rañjanavasena rāgo, pañcakāmaguṇarāgassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Udacchidāti ucchindati, bhañjati[V 1.0015], vināseti. Atītakālikānampi hi chandasi vattamānavacanaṃ akkharacintakā icchanti. Asesanti sānusayaṃ. Bhisapupphaṃva saroruhanti sare virūḷhaṃ padumapupphaṃ viya. Vigayhāti ogayha, pavisitvāti attho. Sesaṃ pubbasadisameva. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yathā nāma ete dārakā saraṃ oruyha bhisapupphaṃ saroruhaṃ chindanti, evamevaṃ yo bhikkhu imaṃ tedhātukalokasannivāsaṃ ogayha –

Herein, it is ‘lust’ (rāga) in the sense of finding delight; this is a designation for lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure. ‘Udacchidā’ means cuts off, breaks, destroys. Indeed, in verse, grammarians accept a present-tense verb for a past-tense meaning. ‘Asesaṃ’ means together with the underlying tendencies. ‘Bhisapupphaṃva saroruhaṃ’ means like a lotus flower grown in a lake. ‘Vigayha’ means having plunged into, having entered—this is the meaning. The rest is the same as before. What is meant? Just as these children, having gone down into a lake, cut a lotus flower with its stalk, a lake-born flower, in the same way, a bhikkhu who, having entered this world which is the abode of the three realms—

“Natthi rāgasamo aggi”; (Dha. pa. 202);

“There is no fire like lust.”

“Kāmarāgena [P 1.0017] dayhāmi, cittaṃ me paridayhati”; (Saṃ. ni. 1.212);

“I burn with sensual lust; my mind is consumed by burning.”

“Ye rāgarattānupatanti sotaṃ, sayaṃ kataṃ makkaṭakova jālaṃ”. (dha. pa. 347);

“Those who are infatuated with lust fall back into the stream, like a spider into the web it has made itself.”

“Ratto kho, āvuso, rāgena abhibhūto pariyādinnacitto pāṇampi hanatī”ti (a. ni. 3.56, 72) –

“Friend, one who is infatuated, overcome by lust, with mind consumed, even kills living beings.”

Evamādinayamanugantvā rāgādīnavapaccavekkhaṇena yathāvuttappakārehi sīlasaṃvarādīhi saṃvarehi saviññāṇakāviññāṇakesu vatthūsu asubhasaññāya ca thokaṃ thokaṃ rāgaṃ samucchindanto anāgāmimaggena avasesaṃ arahattamaggena ca tato anavasesampi ucchindati pubbe vuttappakāreneva so bhikkhu jahāti orapāraṃ urago jiṇṇamiva tacaṃ purāṇanti. Evamesā bhagavatā arahattanikūṭena gāthā desitā. Desanāpariyosāne ca so bhikkhu arahatte patiṭṭhitoti.

Following this method, by contemplating the dangers of lust, by the various restraints such as the restraint of virtue as described, and by the perception of foulness in objects both conscious and unconscious, while gradually cutting off lust, he cuts off the remaining portion with the path of non-returning, and with the path of arahantship he then cuts off the rest without remainder. In the very manner described before: “that bhikkhu abandons the near and far shores, like a snake its old, worn-out skin.” Thus, this verse was taught by the Blessed One with arahantship as its culmination. And at the conclusion of the teaching, that bhikkhu was established in arahantship.

3. Yo [M 1.0016] taṇhamudacchidāti kā uppatti? Bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati. Aññataro bhikkhu gaggarāya pokkharaṇiyā tīre viharanto taṇhāvasena akusalavitakkaṃ vitakketi. Bhagavā tassajjhāsayaṃ viditvā imaṃ obhāsagāthamabhāsi.

3. What is the origin of the verse beginning, “One who has cut off craving...”? The Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī. A certain bhikkhu, dwelling on the bank of the Gaggarā lotus pond, was thinking unwholesome thoughts due to craving. The Blessed One, knowing his disposition, uttered this illuminating verse.

Tattha tassatīti taṇhā. Visayehi tittiṃ na upetīti attho. Kāmabhavavibhavataṇhānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Saritanti gataṃ pavattaṃ, yāva bhavaggā ajjhottharitvā ṭhitanti vuttaṃ hoti. Sīghasaranti sīghagāminiṃ, sandiṭṭhikasamparāyikaṃ ādīnavaṃ agaṇetvā muhutteneva paracakkavāḷampi [V 1.0016] bhavaggampi sampāpuṇituṃ samatthanti vuttaṃ hoti. Evametaṃ saritaṃ sīghasaraṃ sabbappakārampi taṇhaṃ –

Herein, it is ‘craving’ (taṇhā) because it thirsts (tassati). The meaning is that it does not attain satisfaction with its objects. This is a designation for craving for sensual pleasures, for existence, and for non-existence. ‘Saritaṃ’ (a stream) means gone, proceeded; it is said to have stood pervading up to the peak of existence. ‘Sīghasaraṃ’ (swiftly flowing) means swiftly going; it is said to be capable of reaching even another world-system or the peak of existence in just a moment, without regard for present or future danger. Thus, this craving, which is a stream, swiftly flowing, and of every kind—

“Uparivisālā duppūrā, icchā visaṭagāminī;

Ye ca taṃ anugijjhanti, te honti cakkadhārino”ti.

“Exceedingly vast, hard to fill, is desire that spreads everywhere; and those who are greedy for it become bearers of the wheel.”

“Taṇhādutiyo puriso, dīghamaddhānasaṃsaraṃ;

Itthabhāvaññathābhāvaṃ, saṃsāraṃ nātivattatī”ti. (itivu. 15, 105; mahāni. 191; cūḷani. pārāyanānugītigāthāniddesa 107);

A person with craving as a companion wanders through the long course of saṃsāra; from one state of being to another, he does not transcend saṃsāra.

“Ūno [P 1.0018] loko atitto taṇhādāsoti kho, mahārājā”ti (ma. ni. 2.305) ca –

The world is deficient, insatiable, a slave to craving, O great king.

Evamādīnavapaccavekkhaṇena vuttappakārehi sīlasaṃvarādīhi ca yo thokaṃ thokaṃ visosayitvā arahattamaggena asesaṃ ucchijjati, so bhikkhu tasmiṃyeva khaṇe sabbappakārampi jahāti orapāranti. Desanāpariyosāne so bhikkhu arahatte patiṭṭhitoti.

Thus, by reflecting on the dangers in this way, and through the kinds of restraints such as the restraint of virtue that have been mentioned, whatever bhikkhu, having gradually dried it out and completely eradicated it without remainder by the path of arahantship, that bhikkhu at that very moment abandons every kind of craving, of this shore and the far shore. At the conclusion of the teaching, that bhikkhu was established in arahantship.

4. Yo mānamudabbadhīti kā uppatti? Bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati. Aññataro bhikkhu gaṅgāya tīre viharanto gimhakāle appodake sote kataṃ naḷasetuṃ pacchā āgatena mahoghena vuyhamānaṃ disvā “aniccā saṅkhārā”ti saṃviggo aṭṭhāsi. Tassajjhāsayaṃ viditvā bhagavā imaṃ obhāsagāthaṃ abhāsi.

4. Regarding “Who has uprooted conceit?”: what is its origin story? The Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī. A certain bhikkhu, dwelling on the bank of the Gaṅgā river, saw a reed bridge that had been constructed in the hot season when the stream had little water, being swept away by a great flood that came later. Struck with a sense of urgency at the thought, “Conditioned formations are impermanent,” he stood still. Knowing his disposition, the Blessed One uttered this illuminating verse.

Tattha [M 1.0017] mānoti jātiādivatthuko cetaso uṇṇāmo. So “seyyohamasmī”ti māno, “sadisohamasmī”ti māno, “hīnohamasmī”ti mānoti evaṃ tividho hoti. Puna “seyyassa seyyohamasmīti, seyyassa sadiso, seyyassa hīno, sadisassa seyyo, sadisassa sadiso, sadisassa hīno, hīnassa seyyo, hīnassa sadiso, hīnassa hīnohamasmī”ti mānoti evaṃ navavidho hoti. Taṃ sabbappakārampi mānaṃ –

Therein, conceit (māna) is an exaltation of the mind based on grounds such as birth. It is threefold: the conceit “I am superior,” the conceit “I am equal,” and the conceit “I am inferior.” Again, it is ninefold: the conceit “I am superior to one who is superior,” “I am equal to one who is superior,” “I am inferior to one who is superior”; “I am superior to one who is equal,” “I am equal to one who is equal,” “I am inferior to one who is equal”; “I am superior to one who is inferior,” “I am equal to one who is inferior,” and “I am inferior to one who is inferior.” That conceit, of every kind—

“Yena mānena mattāse, sattā gacchanti duggati”nti. (itivu. 6) –

“By which conceit they are intoxicated, beings go to a woeful destination.”

Ādinā [V 1.0017] nayena tattha ādīnavapaccavekkhaṇena vuttappakārehi sīlasaṃvarādīhi ca yo thokaṃ thokaṃ vadhento kilesānaṃ abaladubbalattā naḷasetusadisaṃ lokuttaradhammānaṃ atibalattā mahoghasadisena arahattamaggena asesaṃ udabbadhi, anavasesappahānavasena ucchindanto vadhetīti vuttaṃ hoti. So bhikkhu tasmiṃyeva khaṇe sabbappakārampi jahāti orapāranti. Desanāpariyosāne so bhikkhu arahatte patiṭṭhitoti.

By the method beginning thus, by reflecting on the danger therein, and by the aforementioned kinds of restraints such as the restraint of virtue, whatever bhikkhu, gradually destroying it, completely uproots it without remainder by means of the path of arahantship—which is like a great flood, due to the exceeding strength of the supramundane states—as the defilements are like a reed bridge, due to their weakness and feebleness. It is said that he destroys it by cutting it off through the method of abandoning without remainder. That bhikkhu, at that very moment, abandons every kind of conceit, of this shore and the far shore. At the conclusion of the teaching, that bhikkhu was established in arahantship.

5. Ti kā uppatti? Imissā gāthāya ito parānañca dvādasannaṃ ekāyeva uppatti. Ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati. Tena kho pana samayena aññataro [P 1.0019] brāhmaṇo attano dhītuyā vāreyye paccupaṭṭhite cintesi – “kenaci vasalena aparibhuttapubbehi pupphehi dārikaṃ alaṅkaritvā patikulaṃ pesessāmī”ti. So santarabāhiraṃ sāvatthiṃ vicinanto kiñci tiṇapupphampi aparibhuttapubbaṃ nāddasa. Atha sambahule dhuttakajātike brāhmaṇadārake sannipatite disvā “ete pucchissāmi, avassaṃ sambahulesu koci jānissatī”ti upasaṅkamitvā pucchi. Te taṃ brāhmaṇaṃ uppaṇḍentā āhaṃsu – “udumbarapupphaṃ nāma, brāhmaṇa, loke na kenaci paribhuttapubbaṃ. Tena dhītaraṃ alaṅkaritvā dehī”ti. So dutiyadivase kālasseva vuṭṭhāya bhattavissaggaṃ katvā aciravatiyā nadiyā tīre udumbaravanaṃ gantvā ekamekaṃ rukkhaṃ vicinanto pupphassa vaṇṭamattampi nāddasa. Atha vītivatte majjhanhike dutiyatīraṃ agamāsi. Tattha ca aññataro bhikkhu aññatarasmiṃ manuññe rukkhamūle divāvihāraṃ nisinno kammaṭṭhānaṃ [M 1.0018] manasi karoti. So tattha upasaṅkamitvā amanasikaritvā, sakiṃ nisīditvā, sakiṃ ukkuṭiko hutvā, sakiṃ ṭhatvā, taṃ rukkhaṃ sabbasākhāviṭapapattantaresu vicinanto kilamati. Tato naṃ so bhikkhu āha – “brāhmaṇa, kiṃ maggasī”ti? “Udumbarapupphaṃ, bho”ti. “Udumbarapupphaṃ nāma, brāhmaṇa, loke natthi, musā etaṃ vacanaṃ, mā kilamā”ti. Atha bhagavā tassa bhikkhuno ajjhāsayaṃ viditvā obhāsaṃ muñcitvā samuppannasamannāhārabahumānassa imā obhāsagāthāyo abhāsi “yo nājjhagamā bhavesu sāra”nti sabbā vattabbā.

5. What is its origin story? The origin story of this verse and of the twelve following it is one and the same. At one time, the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī. Now at that time, a certain brahmin, when his daughter’s betrothal was imminent, thought: “I shall adorn the girl with flowers not previously used by any common person and send her to her husband’s home.” Searching Sāvatthī, both inside and out, he did not see even a grass flower that had not been previously used. Then, seeing a large group of roguish young brahmins gathered together, he approached and asked them, thinking, “I will ask them; surely among so many, someone will know.” They, wishing to mock the brahmin, said: “Brahmin, there is what is called the udumbara flower, which has not been previously used by anyone in the world. Adorn your daughter with that and give her away.” The next day, rising early and having taken his meal, he went to an udumbara grove on the bank of the Aciravatī river. Searching tree by tree, he did not see so much as the stalk of a flower. Then, after midday had passed, he went to the second bank. And there, a certain bhikkhu, seated for his day-sojourn at the foot of a certain pleasant tree, was attending to his meditation subject. The brahmin approached that place and, without paying the monk any mind, at one time sitting, at another squatting, and at another standing, he grew weary searching that tree among all its branches, boughs, and leaves. Then that bhikkhu said to him: “Brahmin, what are you looking for?” “The udumbara flower, sir.” “Brahmin, there is no such thing in the world as an udumbara flower. That is a false statement. Do not weary yourself.” Then the Blessed One, knowing that bhikkhu’s disposition, sent forth a radiance and spoke these illuminating verses to him, in whom great reverence and application had arisen: “One who has not found any essence in states of existence…” All the verses should be recited.

Tattha paṭhamagāthāya tāva nājjhagamāti nādhigacchi, nādhigacchati vā. Bhavesūti kāmarūpārūpasaññīasaññīnevasaññīnāsaññīekavokāracatuvokārapañcavokārabhavesu. Sāranti niccabhāvaṃ attabhāvaṃ vā. Vicinanti paññāya gavesanto. Pupphamiva udumbaresūti yathā udumbararukkhesu [P 1.0020] pupphaṃ vicinanto esa brāhmaṇo nājjhagamā, evaṃ yo yogāvacaropi paññāya vicinanto sabbabhavesu kiñci sāraṃ nājjhagamā. So asārakaṭṭhena te dhamme aniccato anattato ca vipassanto anupubbena lokuttaradhamme adhigacchanto jahāti orapāraṃ urago jiṇṇamiva [V 1.0018] tacaṃ purāṇanti ayamattho yojanā ca. Avasesagāthāsu panassa yojanaṃ avatvā visesatthamattameva vakkhāma.

Therein, in the first verse, “nājjhagamā” means “he did not find,” or “he does not find.” “Bhavesu” (in states of existence) refers to the states of existence in the sensual realm, the form realm, and the formless realm; the states of existence of beings with perception, without perception, and with neither perception nor non-perception; and the states of existence with one, four, and five constituent aggregates. “Sāraṃ” (essence) means either a state of permanence or a state of self. “Vicinaṃ” (searching) means searching with wisdom. “Pupphamiva udumbaresu” (like a flower on an udumbara tree) means: just as this brahmin, searching for a flower on the udumbara trees, did not find one, so too, a practitioner of yoga, searching with wisdom, does not find any essence in all states of existence. He, seeing those phenomena through insight as impermanent and non-self, on account of their essencelessness, and gradually attaining the supramundane states, abandons this shore and the far shore, like a snake sheds its old, worn-out skin. This is the meaning and the construction. As for the remaining verses, without giving their construction, we will state only their special meaning.

6.

6.

“Yassantarato na santi kopā,

Itibhavābhavatañca vītivatto”ti. (udā. 20) –

“For whom there are no angers internally, and who has transcended this and that state of existence.”

Ettha tāva ayaṃ ‘antarasaddo’ –

Here, to begin with, this word ‘antara’—

“Nadītīresu saṇṭhāne, sabhāsu rathiyāsu ca;

Janā saṅgamma mantenti, mañca tañca kimantara”nti. (saṃ. ni. 1.228);

“On riverbanks, in resting places, in assembly halls, and on roadways, people gather and confer: ‘This and that—what is the difference between them?’”

“Appamattakena visesādhigamena antarā vosānamāpādi” (a. ni. 10.84);

“Anatthajanano kodho, kodho cittappakopano;

Bhayamantarato jātaṃ, taṃ jano nāvabujjhatī”ti. (a. ni. 7.64; itivu. 88) –

"A slight attainment of distinction leads to falling away in between."

"Anger is the generator of harm, anger provokes the mind; fear born from within, that people do not understand."

Evaṃ [M 1.0019] kāraṇavemajjhacittādīsu sambahulesu atthesu dissati. Idha pana citte. Tato yassantarato na santi kopāti tatiyamaggena samūhatattā yassa citte na santi kopāti attho. Yasmā pana bhavoti sampatti, vibhavoti vipatti. Tathā bhavoti vuddhi, vibhavoti hāni. Bhavoti sassato, vibhavoti ucchedo. Bhavoti puññaṃ, vibhavoti pāpaṃ. Vibhavo abhavoti ca atthato ekameva. Tasmā itibhavābhavatañca vītivattoti ettha yā esā sampattivipattivuḍḍhihānisassatucchedapuññapāpavasena iti anekappakārā bhavābhavatā vuccati. Catūhipi maggehi yathāsambhavaṃ tena tena nayena taṃ itibhavābhavatañca vītivattoti evamattho ñātabbo.

Thus, it is seen in many contexts such as causal factors, wavering minds, and so forth, in many meanings. Here, however, it pertains to the mind. The phrase 'in whom anger does not exist internally' means that since anger has been eradicated by the third path, the meaning is 'in whose mind anger does not exist.' Furthermore, bhava denotes attainment, and vibhava denotes loss. Similarly, bhava denotes growth, and vibhava denotes decay. Bhava denotes eternalism, and vibhava denotes annihilationism. Bhava denotes merit, and vibhava denotes demerit. In essence, vibhava and abhava are identical. Therefore, 'having transcended such bhava and abhava' refers here to the many kinds of becoming and non-becoming, namely, attainment and loss, growth and decay, eternalism and annihilationism, merit and demerit. This meaning is to be understood as the transcendence of these forms of becoming and non-becoming through the four paths, in the appropriate manner for each.

7. Yassa [P 1.0021] vitakkāti ettha pana yassa bhikkhuno tayo kāmabyāpādavihiṃsāvitakkā, tayo ñātijanapadāmaravitakkā, tayo parānuddayatāpaṭisaṃyuttalābhasakkārasilokaanavaññattipaṭisaṃyuttavitakkāti ete nava vitakkā samantabhaddake vuttanayena tattha tattha ādīnavaṃ paccavekkhitvā [V 1.0019] paṭipakkhavavatthānena tassa tassa pahānasamatthehi tīhi heṭṭhimamaggehi ca vidhūpitā bhusaṃ dhūpitā santāpitā daḍḍhāti attho. Evaṃ vidhūpetvā ca ajjhattaṃ suvikappitā asesā, niyakajjhattabhūte attano khandhasantāne ajjhattajjhattabhūte citte ca yathā na puna sambhavanti, evaṃ arahattamaggena asesā chinnā. Chinnañhi kappitanti vuccati. Yathāha “kappitakesamassū”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.122; 4.365). Evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

7. Referring to the phrase 'Whose thoughts...': here, concerning a monk, these nine kinds of discursive thoughts—namely, the three of sensual desire, ill will, and harmfulness; the three pertaining to relatives, country, and immortality; and the three associated with compassion for others, gain, honor, fame, and not being despised—have been thoroughly examined for their drawbacks in each case, counteracted by applying their antidotes, and dispelled by the three lower paths. They have been greatly scorched, burned, and consumed—this is the meaning. Having thus dispelled them, they are well eradicated internally, without remainder, so that they do not arise again in one's own continuum of aggregates, which has become internal, nor in the mind which has become internal. They are completely cut off by the path of arahantship. For what is cut is called 'kappita', as it is said: 'one whose hair and beard are cut'. This is how the meaning should be understood here.

8. Idāni yo nāccasārīti ettha yo nāccasārīti yo nātidhāvi. Na paccasārīti na ohīyi. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Accāraddhavīriyena hi uddhacce patanto accāsarati, atisithilena kosajje patanto paccāsarati. Tathā bhavataṇhāya attānaṃ kilamento accāsarati, kāmataṇhāya kāmasukhamanuyuñjanto paccāsarati. Sassatadiṭṭhiyā accāsarati, ucchedadiṭṭhiyā paccāsarati. Atītaṃ anusocanto accāsarati, anāgata paṭikaṅkhanto paccāsarati. Pubbantānudiṭṭhiyā accāsarati, aparantānudiṭṭhiyā paccāsarati. Tasmā yo ete ubho ante vajjetvā majjhimaṃ paṭipadaṃ paṭipajjanto nāccasārī na paccasārīti evaṃ vuttaṃ hoti. Sabbaṃ [M 1.0020] accagamā imaṃ papañcanti tāya ca pana arahattamaggavosānāya majjhimāya paṭipadāya sabbaṃ imaṃ vedanāsaññāvitakkappabhavaṃ taṇhāmānadiṭṭhisaṅkhātaṃ tividhaṃ papañcaṃ accagamā atikkanto, samatikkantoti attho.

8. Now, concerning ‘one who does not advance’ (nāccasārī), here ‘one who does not advance’ means one who does not rush ahead (nātidhāvi). ‘Nor runs back’ (na paccasārī) means one who does not fall back (na ohīyi). What is meant? For one who, with excessive energy, falls into agitation, advances; one who, with excessive slackness, falls into sloth, falls back. Similarly, one who exhausts oneself with craving for existence advances; one who indulges in sensual pleasures with craving for sensual pleasures falls back.
