One advances with the eternalist view and falls back with the annihilationist view. One advances by lamenting over the past and falls back by longing for the future. One advances with views about the past and falls back with views about the future. Therefore, it is said that one who avoids both these extremes and practices the middle way neither advances nor falls back. ‘He has overcome all this proliferation’—by that middle way, which culminates in the path of arahantship, he has overcome, transcended all this threefold proliferation, which is conditioned by feeling, perception, and thought, and is known as craving, conceit, and views. The meaning is that he has fully gone beyond.

9. Tadanantaragāthāya pana sabbaṃ vitathamidanti ñatvā loketi ayameva viseso. Tassattho – sabbanti anavasesaṃ, sakalamanūnanti [P 1.0022] vuttaṃ hoti. Evaṃ santepi pana vipassanupagaṃ lokiyakhandhāyatanadhātuppabhedaṃ saṅkhatameva idhādhippetaṃ. Vitathanti vigatatathabhāvaṃ. Niccanti vā sukhanti vā subhanti vā attāti vā yathā yathā kilesavasena bālajanehi gayhati, tathātathābhāvato vitathanti vuttaṃ hoti. Idanti tameva sabbaṃ paccakkhabhāvena dassento āha. Ñatvāti maggapaññāya jānitvā, tañca pana asammohato, na visayato. Loketi okāsaloke sabbaṃ khandhādibhedaṃ dhammajātaṃ “vitathamida”nti ñatvāti sambandho.

9. However, in the subsequent verse, the distinction lies in knowing, concerning the world, that 'all this is unreal'. Its meaning is: 'all' means without exception, complete and entire. Even so, here it refers only to the conditioned—the worldly aggregates, sense bases, and elements conducive to insight. 'Unreal' means devoid of true reality. Whatever foolish people grasp due to defilements—as permanent, or pleasant, or beautiful, or self—is said to be 'unreal' because it is devoid of such a nature. 'This' is spoken to show that very all in its direct manifestation. 'Having known' means knowing with the wisdom of the path, and that too without delusion, not merely as an object. 'The world' refers to the entire class of phenomena, such as the aggregates, and so forth, in the world of space, understood as knowing that 'this is unreal'—this is the connection.

10-13. Idāni ito parāsu catūsu gāthāsu vītalobho vītarāgo vītadoso vītamohoti ete visesā. Ettha lubbhanavasena lobho. Sabbasaṅgāhikametaṃ paṭhamassa akusalamūlassa adhivacanaṃ, visamalobhassa vā. Yo so “appekadā mātumattīsupi lobhadhammā uppajjanti, bhaginimattīsupi lobhadhammā uppajjanti, dhītumattīsupi lobhadhammā uppajjantī”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.127) evaṃ vutto. Rajjanavasena rāgo, pañcakāmaguṇarāgassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Dussanavasena [V 1.0020] doso, pubbe vuttakodhassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Muyhanavasena moho, catūsu ariyasaccesu aññāṇassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tattha yasmā ayaṃ bhikkhu lobhaṃ jigucchanto vipassanaṃ ārabhi “kudāssu nāmāhaṃ lobhaṃ vinetvā vigatalobho vihareyya”nti, tasmā tassa lobhappahānūpāyaṃ sabbasaṅkhārānaṃ vitathabhāvadassanaṃ lobhappahānānisaṃsañca orapārappahānaṃ dassento imaṃ gāthamāha. Esa nayo ito parāsupi. Keci panāhu – “yathāvutteneva nayena ete dhamme jigucchitvā vipassanamāraddhassa tassa [P 1.0023] tassa bhikkhuno ekamekāva ettha gāthā vuttā”ti. Yaṃ ruccati, taṃ gahetabbaṃ. Esa nayo ito parāsu catūsu gāthāsu.

Now, in the following four verses, these are the distinctions: being free from greed, free from lust, free from hatred, and free from delusion. Here, greed is in the sense of coveting. This is a designation for the first unwholesome root, which encompasses all forms of clinging, or for inordinate greed. As it is said: 'Sometimes, thoughts of greed arise even toward those like a mother, toward those like a sister, or toward those like a daughter' (Saṃ. Ni. 4.127). Lust is in the sense of attachment; this is a designation for attachment to the five strands of sensual pleasure. Hatred is in the sense of aversion; this is a designation for the anger mentioned earlier. Delusion is in the sense of bewilderment; this is a designation for ignorance regarding the Four Noble Truths. Here, because this monk, disgusted by greed, began insight meditation thinking, 'When indeed will I dwell free from greed, having abandoned greed?'—therefore, to show him the means to abandon greed, the showing of the unreal nature of all formations, and the benefit of abandoning greed, namely the relinquishment of both near and far, he spoke this verse. The same method applies to the following verses as well. Some, however, say: 'According to the method stated, for each monk who, disgusted by these qualities, undertook insight meditation, a single verse here was spoken for him.' Whatever is preferred may be accepted. This is the method for the following four verses.

14. Ayaṃ [M 1.0021] panettha atthavaṇṇanā – appahīnaṭṭhena santāne sayantīti anusayā kāmarāgapaṭighamānadiṭṭhivicikicchābhavarāgāvijjānaṃ etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sampayuttadhammānaṃ attano ākārānuvidhānaṭṭhena mūlā; akhemaṭṭhena akusalā; dhammānaṃ patiṭṭhābhūtātipi mūlā; sāvajjadukkhavipākaṭṭhena akusalā; ubhayampetaṃ lobhadosamohānaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Te hi “lobho, bhikkhave, akusalañca akusalamūlañcā”tiādinā nayena evaṃ niddiṭṭhā. Evamete anusayā tena tena maggena pahīnattā yassa keci na santi, ete ca akusalamūlā tatheva samūhatāse, samūhatā icceva attho. Paccattabahuvacanassa hi se-kārāgamaṃ icchanti saddalakkhaṇakovidā. Aṭṭhakathācariyā pana “seti nipāto”ti vaṇṇayanti. Yaṃ ruccati, taṃ gahetabbaṃ. Ettha pana “kiñcāpi so evaṃvidho bhikkhu khīṇāsavo hoti, khīṇāsavo ca neva ādiyati, na pajahati, pajahitvā ṭhito”ti vutto. Tathāpi vattamānasamīpe vattamānavacanalakkhaṇena “jahāti orapāra”nti vuccati. Atha vā anupādisesāya ca nibbānadhātuyā parinibbāyanto attano ajjhattikabāhirāyatanasaṅkhātaṃ jahāti orapāranti veditabbo.

14. Herein, this is the explanation of the meaning: Because they are not abandoned, they lie dormant in the continuity of beings; thus they are called latent tendencies. This is a designation for sensual lust, aversion, conceit, views, doubt, craving for existence, and ignorance. They are called roots because they cause associated states to conform to their own nature; they are unwholesome because they are unsafe. They are also called roots because they serve as the foundation for unwholesome states; they are unwholesome because they are blameworthy and result in suffering. Both these terms are a designation for greed, hatred, and delusion. For they are described in this way: 'Greed, monks, is unwholesome and an unwholesome root,' and so on. Thus, for one for whom these latent tendencies, being abandoned by the respective paths, do not exist at all, and these unwholesome roots are likewise uprooted—'uprooted' is the meaning. Experts in the characteristics of language desire the addition of the syllable 'se' for the nominative plural. The commentators, however, explain that 'se' is a particle. One may adopt whichever interpretation is preferred. Herein, it is said: 'Although such a monk is one whose taints are destroyed, and one whose taints are destroyed neither takes up nor abandons, but stands having abandoned.' Nevertheless, by the characteristic of using the present tense for what is near to the present, the expression 'abandons this shore and the far shore' is used. Alternatively, it should be understood that one who is attaining final Nibbāna in the Nibbāna-element without remainder abandons what is designated as the internal and external sense bases, which are 'this shore and the far shore'.

Tattha kilesapaṭipāṭiyā maggapaṭipāṭiyā cāti dvidhā anusayānaṃ abhāvo veditabbo. Kilesapaṭipāṭiyā hi kāmarāgānusayapaṭighānusayānaṃ tatiyamaggena abhāvo hoti, mānānusayassa catutthamaggena, diṭṭhānusayavicikicchānusayānaṃ paṭhamamaggena, bhavarāgānusayāvijjānusayānaṃ catutthamaggeneva. Maggapaṭipāṭiyā [P 1.0024] pana paṭhamamaggena diṭṭhānusayavicikicchānusayānaṃ abhāvo hoti. Dutiyamaggena kāmarāgānusayapaṭighānusayānaṃ tanubhāvo, tatiyamaggena sabbaso abhāvo, catutthamaggena mānānusayabhavarāgānusayāvijjānusayānaṃ abhāvo hoti. Tattha yasmā na sabbe anusayā akusalamūlā; kāmarāgabhavarāgānusayā eva hi lobhākusalamūlena saṅgahaṃ gacchanti. Paṭighānusayāvijjānusayā ca “doso akusalamūlaṃ, moho akusalamūlaṃ” icceva saṅkhaṃ gacchanti, diṭṭhimānavicikicchānusayā [V 1.0021] pana na kiñci akusalamūlaṃ honti, yasmā vā anusayābhāvavasena ca akusalamūlasamugghātavasena ca kilesappahānaṃ paṭṭhapesi, tasmā –

Here, the absence of latent tendencies should be understood in two ways: according to the sequence of defilements and according to the sequence of paths. According to the sequence of defilements, the latent tendencies of sensual lust and aversion are eliminated by the third path; the latent tendency of conceit by the fourth path; the latent tendencies of views and doubt by the first path; and the latent tendencies of craving for existence and ignorance by the fourth path alone. According to the sequence of paths, however, the latent tendencies of views and doubt are eliminated by the first path. By the second path, the latent tendencies of sensual lust and aversion are attenuated; by the third path, they are completely eliminated; by the fourth path, the latent tendencies of conceit, craving for existence, and ignorance are eliminated. Here, since not all latent tendencies are unwholesome roots—for only the latent tendencies of sensual lust and craving for existence are included under the unwholesome root of greed, while the latent tendencies of aversion and ignorance are classified respectively as 'hatred is an unwholesome root' and 'delusion is an unwholesome root,' and the latent tendencies of views, conceit, and doubt are not any unwholesome root—and because the abandonment of defilements was set forth both by way of the absence of latent tendencies and by way of the uprooting of unwholesome roots, therefore:

“Yassānusayā [M 1.0022] na santi keci, mūlā ca akusalā samūhatāse”. –

“For whom no latent tendencies whatsoever exist, and the unwholesome roots are uprooted.”

Iti bhagavā āha.

Thus said the Blessed One.

15. Yassa darathajāti ettha pana paṭhamuppannā kilesā pariḷāhaṭṭhena darathā nāma, aparāparuppannā pana tehi darathehi jātattā darathajā nāma. Oranti sakkāyo vuccati. Yathāha – “orimaṃ tīranti kho, bhikkhu, sakkāyassetaṃ adhivacana”nti (saṃ. ni. 4.238). Āgamanāyāti uppattiyā. Paccayāseti paccayā eva. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yassa pana upādānakkhandhaggahaṇāya paccayabhūtā ariyamaggena pahīnattā, keci darathajavevacanā kilesā na santi, pubbe vuttanayeneva so bhikkhu jahāti orapāranti.

15. Here, in the phrase 'born of torment' (darathajā), the defilements that first arise are called 'torment' (darathā) in the sense of burning, while those that arise subsequently are called 'born of torment' (darathajā) because they are born from those torments. 'The near shore' (oraṃ) is said to be personality-view (sakkāyo). As it is said: '“The near shore,” monk, is a designation for this personality-view.' 'For coming' (āgamanāya) means for arising. 'As a condition' (paccayāse) means simply 'conditions'. What is meant? For a certain one, because the conditions for grasping the aggregates of clinging have been abandoned by the noble path, no defilements synonymous with 'born of torment' exist. In the manner previously stated, that monk abandons the near and the far shore.

16. Yassa vanathajāti etthapi darathajā viya vanathajā veditabbā. Vacanatthe pana ayaṃ viseso – vanute, vanotīti vā vanaṃ yācati sevati bhajatīti attho. Taṇhāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sā hi visayānaṃ patthanato sevanato ca “vana”nti vuccati. Taṃ pariyuṭṭhānavasena vanaṃ tharati tanotīti vanatho, taṇhānusayassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Vanathā jātāti vanathajāti. Keci panāhu “sabbepi kilesā gahanaṭṭhena vanathoti vuccanti, aparāparuppannā pana vanathajā”ti. Ayameva [P 1.0025] cettha uragasutte attho adhippeto, itaro pana dhammapadagāthāyaṃ. Vinibandhāya bhavāyāti bhavavinibandhāya. Atha vā cittassa visayesu vinibandhāya āyatiṃ uppattiyā cāti attho. Hetuyeva hetukappā.

16. Here too, in 'born of craving' (vanathajā), it should be understood in a similar way to 'born of torment' (darathajā). In the verbal meaning, however, there is this distinction: it is called 'craving' (vana) because one desires it (vanute) or serves it (vanoti), meaning one requests, frequents, or indulges in it. This is a designation for craving (taṇhā). For it is called 'vana' because of longing for and frequenting sense objects. That which, by way of obsession, spreads or extends that 'vana' is 'vanatha'; this is a designation for the latent tendency of craving. 'Born from vanatha' is 'vanathajā'. Some, however, say: 'All defilements are called 'vanatha' in the sense of being a thicket, and those that arise subsequently are 'vanathajā'.' This very meaning is intended here in the Uraga Sutta, while the other meaning is intended in the Dhammapada verse. 'For bondage to existence' (vinibandhāya bhavāya) means for the bondage of existence. Alternatively, the meaning is for the bondage of the mind to sense objects and for future arising. The cause itself is the causal factor.

17. Yo nīvaraṇeti ettha nīvaraṇāti cittaṃ, hitapaṭipattiṃ vā nīvarantīti nīvaraṇā, paṭicchādentīti attho. Pahāyāti chaḍḍetvā. Pañcāti tesaṃ saṅkhyāparicchedo. Īghābhāvato anīgho. Kathaṃkathāya tiṇṇattā tiṇṇakathaṃkatho. Vigatasallattā visallo. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yo bhikkhu kāmacchandādīni pañca nīvaraṇāni samantabhaddake vuttanayena sāmaññato visesato ca nīvaraṇesu ādīnavaṃ disvā tena tena maggena pahāya tesañca pahīnattā eva kilesadukkhasaṅkhātassa īghassābhāvena [M 1.0023] anīgho, “ahosiṃ nu kho ahaṃ atītamaddhāna”ntiādinā (ma. ni. 1.18; saṃ. ni. 2.20) nayena pavattāya kathaṃkathāya tiṇṇattā tiṇṇakathaṃkatho[V 1.0022], “tattha katame pañca sallā? Rāgasallo, dosasallo, mohasallo, mānasallo, diṭṭhisallo”ti vuttānaṃ pañcannaṃ sallānaṃ vigatattā visallo. So bhikkhu pubbe vuttanayeneva jahāti orapāranti.

17. Here, in 'the hindrances' (yo nīvaraṇe), they are called 'hindrances' (nīvaraṇā) because they obstruct (nīvaranti) the mind or the practice conducive to welfare; the meaning is that they cover over. 'Having abandoned' (pahāya) means having discarded. 'Five' (pañca) is the specification of their number. 'Undistressed' (anīgho) is due to the absence of distress (īgha). 'One who has crossed over doubt' (tiṇṇakathaṃkatho) is due to having crossed over perplexity (kathaṃkathā). 'Dartless' (visallo) is due to being without darts (salla). What is meant? A monk who, having seen the danger in the five hindrances—sensual desire and so forth—both generally and specifically according to the method stated in the Samantabhaddaka, abandons them by the respective path, and because of their very abandonment is 'undistressed' through the absence of the distress known as the suffering of defilements; who has 'crossed over doubt' by having surmounted the perplexity that proceeds in the manner of “Did I exist in the past?” and so on; and who is 'dartless' because of being without the five darts spoken of thus: “What are the five darts? The dart of lust, the dart of hatred, the dart of delusion, the dart of conceit, and the dart of views.” That monk, in the manner previously stated, abandons the near and the far shore.

Atrāpi ca kilesapaṭipāṭiyā maggapaṭipāṭiyā cāti dvidhā eva nīvaraṇappahānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Kilesapaṭipāṭiyā hi kāmacchandanīvaraṇassa byāpādanīvaraṇassa ca tatiyamaggena pahānaṃ hoti, thinamiddhanīvaraṇassa uddhaccanīvaraṇassa ca catutthamaggena. “Akataṃ vata me kusala”ntiādinā (ma. ni. 3.248; netti. 120) nayena pavattassa vippaṭisārasaṅkhātassa kukkuccanīvaraṇassa vicikicchānīvaraṇassa [P 1.0026] ca paṭhamamaggena. Maggapaṭipāṭiyā pana kukkuccanīvaraṇassa vicikicchānīvaraṇassa ca paṭhamamaggena pahānaṃ hoti, kāmacchandanīvaraṇassa byāpādanīvaraṇassa ca dutiyamaggena tanubhāvo hoti, tatiyena anavasesappahānaṃ. Thinamiddhanīvaraṇassa uddhaccanīvaraṇassa ca catutthamaggena pahānaṃ hotīti. Evaṃ –

Here too, the abandonment of the hindrances should be understood in two ways: by the sequence of defilements and by the sequence of the path. According to the sequence of defilements, the hindrance of sensual desire and that of ill will are abandoned by the third path; the hindrances of sloth and torpor and of restlessness are abandoned by the fourth path; and the hindrances of remorse—which arises in the manner of, ‘Alas, I have not done what is wholesome’—and of doubt are abandoned by the first path. But according to the sequence of the path, the hindrances of remorse and of doubt are abandoned by the first path; the hindrances of sensual desire and of ill will are attenuated by the second path and completely abandoned by the third; and the hindrances of sloth and torpor and of restlessness are abandoned by the fourth path. Thus—

“Yo nīvaraṇe pahāya pañca, anīgho tiṇṇakathaṃkatho visallo;

So bhikkhu jahāti orapāraṃ, urago jiṇṇamivattacaṃ purāṇa”nti. –

“Having abandoned the five hindrances, without anguish, having crossed beyond doubt, rid of the dart; that monk abandons the near and far shores, like a snake its old, worn-out skin.”

Arahattanikūṭeneva bhagavā desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi. Desanāpariyosāne so bhikkhu arahatte patiṭṭhito. “Ekacce yena yena tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ yā yā gāthā desitā, tena tena tassā tassā gāthāya pariyosāne so so bhikkhu arahatte patiṭṭhito”ti vadanti.

The Blessed One concluded the discourse with the pinnacle of arahantship. At the end of the teaching, that monk was established in arahantship. Some say that for whichever of those monks whichever verse was taught, at the conclusion of that particular verse, that particular monk was established in arahantship.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya uragasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Uraga Sutta in the Commentary on the Suttanipāta is concluded.

2. Dhaniyasuttavaṇṇanā

2. The Explanation of the Dhaniya Sutta

18. Pakkodanoti [M 1.0024][V 1.0023] dhaniyasuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati. Tena samayena dhaniyo gopo mahītīre paṭivasati. Tassāyaṃ pubbayogo – kassapassa bhagavato pāvacane dibbamāne vīsati vassasahassāni divase divase saṅghassa vīsati salākabhattāni adāsi. So tato cuto devesu uppanno. Evaṃ devaloke ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ khepetvā amhākaṃ bhagavato kāle videharaṭṭhamajjhe pabbataraṭṭhaṃ nāma atthi tattha dhammakoraṇḍaṃ nāma nagaraṃ, tasmiṃ nagare seṭṭhiputto hutvā abhinibbatto, goyūthaṃ nissāya jīvati. Tassa hi tiṃsamattāni gosahassāni honti, sattavīsasahassā gāvo khīraṃ duyhanti. Gopā nāma nibaddhavāsino na honti. Vassike cattāromāse thale vasanti, avasese aṭṭhamāse yattha tiṇodakaṃ sukhaṃ labbhati, tattha vasanti. Tañca nadītīraṃ vā jātassaratīraṃ vā hoti. Athāyampi vassakāle attano vasitagāmato nikkhamitvā [P 1.0027] gunnaṃ phāsuvihāratthāya okāsaṃ gavesanto mahāmahī bhijjitvā ekato kālamahī ekato mahāmahicceva saṅkhaṃ gantvā sandamānā puna samuddasamīpe samāgantvā pavattā. Yaṃ okāsaṃ antaradīpaṃ akāsi, taṃ pavisitvā vacchānaṃ sālaṃ attano ca nivesanaṃ māpetvā vāsaṃ kappesi. Tassa satta puttā, satta dhītaro, satta suṇisā, aneke ca kammakārā honti. Gopā nāma vassanimittaṃ jānanti. Yadā sakuṇikā kulāvakāni rukkhagge karonti, kakkaṭakā udakasamīpe dvāraṃ pidahitvā thalasamīpadvārena vaḷañjenti, tadā suvuṭṭhikā bhavissatīti gaṇhanti. Yadā pana sakuṇikā kulāvakāni nīcaṭṭhāne udakapiṭṭhe karonti, kakkaṭakā thalasamīpe dvāraṃ pidahitvā udakasamīpadvārena vaḷañjenti, tadā dubbuṭṭhikā bhavissatīti gaṇhanti.

18. “Pakkodano” is the Dhaniya Sutta. What is its origin? The Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī. At that time, the cowherd Dhaniya lived on the bank of the Mahī River. This was his past meritorious deed: during the resplendent dispensation of the Buddha Kassapa, for twenty thousand years he daily gave twenty ticket-meals to the Saṅgha. Passing away from there, he was reborn among the devas. Thus, having spent one Buddha-interval in a devaloka, during the time of our Blessed One, he was reborn as the son of a wealthy merchant in a city named Dhammakoraṇḍa, in a region named Pabbataraṭṭha in the middle of the Videha country. He made his living by depending on a herd of cattle. He had thirty thousand cows, and twenty-seven thousand of them were milked. Cowherds are not permanent residents. For the four months of the rainy season they live on high ground; for the remaining eight months they live wherever grass and water are easily found, be it on a riverbank or the shore of a natural lake. Then this Dhaniya, too, during the rainy season, left his home village and, while searching for a place for the cattle to live comfortably, entered an island that the great Mahī river had formed where it had split and then flowed together again near the ocean. There he had a shed built for the calves and a dwelling for himself, and took up residence. He had seven sons, seven daughters, seven daughters-in-law, and many workers. Cowherds know the signs of the rain. When birds build their nests high in the trees, and crabs close their waterside burrows and use their landside ones, they take it as a sign that there will be good rain. But when birds build their nests in low places near the water, and crabs close their landside burrows and use their waterside ones, they take it as a sign that there will be little rain.

Atha so dhaniyo suvuṭṭhikanimittāni upasallakkhetvā upakaṭṭhe vassakāle antaradīpā nikkhamitvā mahāmahiyā paratīre sattasattāhampi deve vassante udakena anajjhottharaṇokāse attano vasanokāsaṃ katvā samantā parikkhipitvā, vacchasālāyo māpetvā, tattha nivāsaṃ kappesi. Athassa dārutiṇādisaṅgahe kate sabbesu puttadārakammakaraporisesu [M 1.0025] samāniyesu jātesu nānappakāre khajjabhojje paṭiyatte samantā catuddisā meghamaṇḍalāni uṭṭhahiṃsu. So dhenuyo duhāpetvā[V 1.0024], vacchasālāsu vacche saṇṭhāpetvā, gunnaṃ catuddisā dhūmaṃ kārāpetvā, sabbaparijanaṃ bhojāpetvā, sabbakiccāni kārāpetvā tattha tattha dīpe ujjālāpetvā, sayaṃ khīrena bhattaṃ bhuñjitvā, mahāsayane sayanto attano sirisampattiṃ disvā, tuṭṭhacitto hutvā, aparadisāya meghatthanitasaddaṃ sutvā nipanno imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi “pakkodano duddhakhīrohamasmī”ti.

Then Dhaniya, having observed the signs of good rain, left the island as the rainy season approached. On the far shore of the great Mahī river, he made his dwelling in a place that would not be flooded by water even if it were to rain for seven weeks. Having enclosed it all around and had sheds for the calves built, he took up residence there. Then, when his provisions of firewood, grass, and so on had been gathered, when all his sons, household, and workers were assembled, and when various kinds of food, hard and soft, had been prepared, masses of clouds arose from all four directions. He had the milk-cows milked, had the calves settled in their sheds, had smoke made in the four directions for the cattle, had all his retinue fed, and had all tasks completed. He himself ate rice with milk and, while lying on a great bed, he saw his own glorious fortune and became joyful-minded. Then, hearing the sound of thunder from another direction as he lay there, he uttered this inspired utterance: “My rice is cooked, my milk is milked.”

Tatrāyaṃ atthavaṇṇanā – pakkodanoti siddhabhatto. Duddhakhīroti gāvo duhitvā gahitakhīro. Ahanti attānaṃ nidasseti[P 1.0028], asmīti attano tathābhāvaṃ. Pakkodano duddhakhīro ca ahamasmi bhavāmīti attho. Itīti evamāhāti attho. Niddese pana “itīti padasandhi, padasaṃsaggo, padapāripūri, akkharasamavāyo byañjanasiliṭṭhatā padānupubbatāmeta”nti (cūḷani. ajitamāṇavapucchāniddesa 1) evamassa attho vaṇṇito. Sopi idameva sandhāyāti veditabbo. Yaṃ yaṃ hi padaṃ pubbapadena vuttaṃ, tassa tassa evamāhāti etamatthaṃ pakāsentoyeva itisaddo pacchimena padena metteyyo iti vā bhagavā iti vā evamādinā padasandhi hoti, nāññathā.

Herein is the explanation of the meaning: 'Pakkodano' means one who has cooked rice. 'Duddhakhīro' means one who has taken milk after milking cows. 'Ahaṃ' indicates oneself; 'asmi' indicates one's state of being so. The meaning is: 'I am one who has cooked rice and one who has milked cows.' 'Iti' means 'thus he says.' In the Niddesa, however, its meaning is described thus: '“Iti” is the conjunction of words, the connection of words, the completion of words, the combination of syllables, the fluency of consonants, and the sequence of words.' This, too, should be understood as referring to this very thing. For whatever word is connected with a preceding word, the particle 'iti', while revealing for that word the meaning 'thus he says', forms a conjunction with the subsequent word—as in 'Metteyyo iti' or 'Bhagavā iti', and so on. It is not otherwise.

Dhaniyo gopoti tassa seṭṭhiputtassa nāmasamodhānaṃ. So hi yānimāni thāvarādīni pañca dhanāni, tesu ṭhapetvā dānasīlādianugāmikadhanaṃ, khettavatthu-ārāmādito thāvaradhanatopi, gavassādito jaṅgamadhanatopi hiraññasuvaṇṇādito saṃhārimadhanatopi, sippāyatanādito aṅgasamadhanatopi yaṃ taṃ lokassa pañcagorasānuppadānena bahūpakāraṃ taṃ sandhāya “natthi gosamitaṃ dhana”nti (saṃ. ni. 1.13; netti. 123) evaṃ visesitaṃ godhanaṃ, tena samannāgatattā dhaniyo, gunnaṃ pālanato gopo. Yo hi attano gāvo pāleti, so “gopo”ti vuccati. Yo paresaṃ vetanena bhaṭo hutvā, so gopālako. Ayaṃ pana attanoyeva, tena gopoti vutto.

'Dhaniya the herdsman' is the combination of names for that merchant's son. For, among the five kinds of wealth—setting aside the 'following-after' wealth consisting of generosity, virtue, and so on—that is, from immovable wealth such as fields, estates, and parks; from movable wealth such as cattle and horses; from portable wealth such as gold and silver; and from personal wealth such as skills and crafts—it is the wealth of cattle, which is of great benefit to the world through providing the five products of the cow, that is especially praised with reference to the saying: 'There is no wealth equal to cattle.' Because he was endowed with that, he is 'Dhaniyo' (the wealthy one); from protecting cattle, he is 'gopo' (a herdsman). Indeed, one who protects his own cattle is called a 'gopo'. One who is a hireling and protects the cattle of others for wages is called a 'gopālako' (cowherd). This man, however, protects his own; therefore, he is called a 'gopo'.

Anutīreti [M 1.0026] tīrassa samīpe. Mahiyāti mahāmahīnāmikāya nadiyā. Samānena anukūlavattinā parijanena saddhiṃ vāso yassa so samānavāso, ayañca tathāvidho. Tenāha “samānavāso”ti. Channāti tiṇapaṇṇacchadanehi anovassakā katā. Kuṭīti vasanagharassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Āhitoti ābhato, jālito vā. Ginīti aggi. Tesu tesu ṭhānesu aggi “ginī”ti voharīyati. Atha ce patthayasīti idāni yadi icchasīti vuttaṃ hoti. Pavassāti siñca, pagghara, udakaṃ muñcāti attho. Devāti meghaṃ ālapati. Ayaṃ tāvettha padavaṇṇanā.

'Anutīre' means near the bank. 'Mahiyā' means of the river named Mahāmahī. 'Samānavāso' is one who has a dwelling together with an agreeable and compliant retinue, and this man is of such a kind. Therefore, it is said 'samānavāso'. 'Channā' means made impervious to rain with coverings of grass and leaves. 'Kuṭī' is a term for a dwelling house. 'Āhito' means brought or kindled. 'Ginī' means fire. In various places, fire is referred to as 'ginī'. 'Atha ce patthayasī' means 'if you now desire'. 'Pavassa' means 'sprinkle, pour down, release water'. 'Deva' is an address to the cloud. This, for a start, is the explanation of the words herein.

Ayaṃ [P 1.0029] pana atthavaṇṇanā – evamayaṃ dhaniyo gopo attano sayanaghare mahāsayane nipanno meghatthanitaṃ [V 1.0025] sutvā “pakkodanohamasmī”ti bhaṇanto kāyadukkhavūpasamūpāyaṃ kāyasukhahetuñca attano sannihitaṃ dīpeti. “Duddhakhīrohamasmī”ti bhaṇanto cittadukkhavūpasamūpāyaṃ cittasukhahetuñca. “Anutīre mahiyā”ti nivāsaṭṭhānasampattiṃ, “samānavāso”ti tādise kāle piyavippayogapadaṭṭhānassa sokassābhāvaṃ. “Channā kuṭī”ti kāyadukkhāpagamapaṭighātaṃ. “Āhito ginī”ti yasmā gopālakā parikkhepadhūmadāruaggivasena tayo aggī karonti. Te ca tassa gehe sabbe katā, tasmā sabbadisāsu parikkhepaggiṃ sandhāya “āhito ginī”ti bhaṇanto vāḷamigāgamananivāraṇaṃ dīpeti, gunnaṃ majjhe gomayādīhi dhūmaggiṃ sandhāya ḍaṃsamakasādīhi gunnaṃ anābādhaṃ, gopālakānaṃ sayanaṭṭhāne dāruaggiṃ sandhāya gopālakānaṃ sītābādhapaṭighātaṃ. So evaṃ dīpento attano vā gunnaṃ vā parijanassa vā vuṭṭhipaccayassa kassaci ābādhassa abhāvato pītisomanassajāto āha – “atha ce patthayasī pavassa devā”ti.

This, however, is the explanation of the meaning: Thus this herdsman Dhaniya, lying on a great couch in his own sleeping-house, having heard the sound of thunder, by saying, 'I am one with cooked rice,' indicates that the means for pacifying bodily suffering and the cause of bodily happiness are at hand for him. By saying, 'I am one with milked milk,' he indicates the means for pacifying mental suffering and the cause of mental happiness. By 'On the bank of the Mahī,' he indicates the excellence of his dwelling place. By 'living together in harmony,' he indicates the absence of sorrow, which has separation from loved ones as its proximate cause, at such a time. By 'My hut is roofed,' he indicates the removal of and protection from bodily suffering. By 'My fire is kindled,' since cowherds make three fires—an encircling fire, a smoke fire, and a wood fire—and all these were made in his house, therefore, with reference to the encircling fire in all directions, by saying 'My fire is kindled,' he indicates the prevention of the approach of wild beasts. With reference to the smoke fire made from cow-dung and so on in the midst of the cattle, he indicates the freedom of the cattle from gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like. With reference to the wood fire in the cowherds' sleeping place, he indicates the protection of the cowherds from the affliction of cold. Thus indicating that for himself, his cattle, and his retinue there was an absence of any affliction caused by the rain, he, with joy and gladness arisen, said: 'Therefore, if you so desire, rain on, O deva!'

19. Evaṃ dhaniyassa imaṃ gāthaṃ bhāsamānassa assosi bhagavā dibbāya sotadhātuyā visuddhāya atikkantamānusikāya jetavanamahāvihāre gandhakuṭiyaṃ viharanto. Sutvā ca pana buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ volokento addasa dhaniyañca pajāpatiñcassa “ime ubhopi hetusampannā. Sace ahaṃ gantvā dhammaṃ desessāmi, ubhopi pabbajitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇissanti. No ce gamissāmi, sve udakoghena vinassissantī”ti taṃ khaṇeyeva sāvatthito satta yojanasatāni dhaniyassa nivāsaṭṭhānaṃ ākāsena gantvā tassa kuṭiyā upari aṭṭhāsi. Dhaniyo taṃ gāthaṃ punappunaṃ bhāsatiyeva[M 1.0027], na niṭṭhāpeti, bhagavati gatepi bhāsati. Bhagavā ca taṃ sutvā “na ettakena santuṭṭhā vā vissatthā vā honti, evaṃ pana hontī”ti dassetuṃ –

19. As Dhaniya was speaking this verse, the Blessed One, while dwelling in the Perfumed Chamber in the great Jetavana monastery, heard him with the divine ear-element, which is purified and surpasses the human. And having heard, surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, he saw Dhaniya and his wife and thought: 'These two are endowed with the necessary conditions. If I go and teach them the Dhamma, both will go forth and attain Arahantship. If I do not go, tomorrow they will perish in a flood of water.' In that very moment, traveling seven hundred yojanas from Sāvatthī through the air to Dhaniya's dwelling place, he stood above his hut. Dhaniya was repeating that verse again and again; he did not finish it. Even when the Blessed One had arrived, he was still speaking. And the Blessed One, having heard him, in order to show, 'By this much one is not content or secure, but in this way one is,' prepared to speak.

“Akkodhano vigatakhilohamasmi, anutīre mahiyekarattivāso;

Vivaṭā kuṭi nibbuto gini, atha ce patthayasī pavassa devā”ti. –

I am without anger, without barrenness, dwelling for one night by the Mahī's bank; my hut is open, the fire is quenched; now, if you wish, rain, O deva.

Imaṃ paṭigāthaṃ abhāsi byañjanasabhāgaṃ [P 1.0030] no atthasabhāgaṃ. Na hi “pakkodano”ti, “akkodhano”ti ca ādīni padāni atthato samenti mahāsamuddassa orimapārimatīrāni viya, byañjanaṃ panettha kiñci kiñci sametīti byañjanasabhāgāni honti. Tattha purimagāthāya sadisapadānaṃ vuttanayeneva attho veditabbo.

He spoke this counter-verse, which is similar in phrasing but not in meaning. For words like 'pakkodano' and 'akkodhano' do not correspond in meaning, just as the near and far shores of the great ocean do not meet. But since the phrasing here corresponds somewhat, they are similar in phrasing. Therein, the meaning of the corresponding words in the former verse should be understood in the way already explained.

Visesapadānaṃ panāyaṃ padato atthato ca vaṇṇanā – akkodhanoti akujjhanasabhāvo. Yo [V 1.0026] hi so pubbe vuttappakāraāghātavatthusambhavo kodho ekaccassa suparittopi uppajjamāno hadayaṃ santāpetvā vūpasammati, yena ca tato balavataruppannena ekacco mukhavikuṇanamattaṃ karoti, tato balavatarena ekacco pharusaṃ vattukāmo hanusañcalanamattaṃ karoti, aparo tato balavatarena pharusaṃ bhaṇati, aparo tato balavatarena daṇḍaṃ vā satthaṃ vā gavesanto disā viloketi, aparo tato balavatarena daṇḍaṃ vā satthaṃ vā āmasati, aparo tato balavatarena daṇḍādīni gahetvā upadhāvati, aparo tato balavatarena ekaṃ vā dve vā pahāre deti, aparo tato balavatarena api ñātisālohitaṃ jīvitā voropeti, ekacco tato balavatarena pacchā vippaṭisārī attānampi jīvitā voropeti sīhaḷadīpe kālagāmavāsī amacco viya. Ettāvatā ca kodho paramavepullappatto hoti. So bhagavatā bodhimaṇḍeyeva sabbaso pahīno ucchinnamūlo tālāvatthukato, tasmā bhagavā “akkodhanohamasmī”ti āha.

Now, this is the explanation of the special terms, both by word and by meaning. Akkodhano means the state of being without anger. Indeed, that anger which arises from the previously mentioned grounds for resentment, when it arises even slightly in some, burns the heart and then subsides. When it arises more forcefully, one person makes only a facial contortion. With still greater force, another, wishing to speak harshly, only moves their jaw. Another, with still greater force, speaks harshly. Another, with still greater force, looks around seeking a stick or a weapon. Another, with still greater force, handles a stick or a weapon. Another, with still greater force, takes up a stick or the like and charges. Another, with still greater force, delivers one or two blows. Another, with still greater force, deprives even a relative or blood kin of life. Some, with even greater force, later feel remorse and take their own lives, like the minister in Sri Lanka who lived in Kālagāma village. To this extent, anger reaches its utmost proliferation. That anger was completely abandoned by the Blessed One at the very seat of enlightenment, its root cut off, made like a palmyra stump. Therefore, the Blessed One said, 'I am without anger.'

Vigatakhiloti apagatakhilo. Ye hi te cittabandhabhāvena pañca cetokhilā vuttā, ye hi ca khilabhūte citte seyyathāpi nāma khile bhūmibhāge [M 1.0028] cattāro māse vassantepi deve sassāni na ruhanti, evamevaṃ saddhammassavanādikusalahetuvasse vassantepi kusalaṃ na ruhati te ca bhagavatā bodhimaṇḍeyeva sabbaso pahīnā, tasmā bhagavā “vigatakhilohamasmī”ti āha.

Vigatakhilo means one whose obstacles are gone. Indeed, there are those five mental obstacles that have been spoken of because they bind the mind. Just as on a barren plot of land crops do not grow even when the sky rains for four months, so too in a mind that has become barren, the wholesome does not grow even when the rain of wholesome causes, such as listening to the good Dhamma, falls. Those obstacles have been completely abandoned by the Blessed One at the very seat of enlightenment. Therefore, the Blessed One said, 'I am without obstacles.'

Ekarattiṃ vāso assāti ekarattivāso[P 1.0031]. Yathā hi dhaniyo tattha cattāro vassike māse nibaddhavāsaṃ upagato, na tathā bhagavā. Bhagavā hi taṃyeva rattiṃ tassa atthakāmatāya tattha vāsaṃ upagato. Tasmā “ekarattivāso”ti āha. Vivaṭāti apanītacchadanā. Kuṭīti attabhāvo. Attabhāvo hi taṃ taṃ atthavasaṃ paṭicca kāyotipi guhātipi dehotipi sandehotipi nāvātipi rathotipi vaṇotipi dhajotipi vammikotipi kuṭītipi kuṭikātipi vuccati. Idha pana kaṭṭhādīni paṭicca gehanāmikā kuṭi viya aṭṭhiādīni paṭicca saṅkhyaṃ gatattā “kuṭī”ti vutto. Yathāha –

Ekarattivāso means 'his dwelling is for one night'. For just as Dhaniya had taken up permanent residence there for the four months of the rainy season, the Blessed One was not so. Indeed, the Blessed One had taken up residence there for that very night out of a desire for his welfare. Therefore, he said 'ekarattivāso'. Vivaṭā means 'with the covering removed'. Kuṭī means individual existence. Indeed, individual existence, depending on the context, is called a body, a cave, a dwelling, a mass, a boat, a chariot, a wound, a banner, an anthill, a hut, or a small hut. Here, however, just as a house is called 'kuṭi' with reference to wood and so forth, so too, individual existence is called 'kuṭī' because it is reckoned with reference to bones and so forth. As it is said:

“Seyyathāpi, āvuso, kaṭṭhañca paṭicca, valliñca paṭicca, mattikañca paṭicca, tiṇañca paṭicca, ākāso parivārito agāraṃtveva saṅkhaṃ gacchati; evameva kho, āvuso, aṭṭhiñca paṭicca, nhāruñca paṭicca, maṃsañca paṭicca, cammañca paṭicca, ākāso parivārito rūpantveva saṅkhaṃ gacchatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.306).

"Just as, friend, dependent on wood, creepers, clay, and grass, the space enclosed is reckoned as a house; in the same way, friend, dependent on bones, sinews, flesh, and skin, the space enclosed is reckoned as a form."

Cittamakkaṭassa nivāsato vā kuṭi. Yathāha –

Or, it is a 'kuṭi' because it is the dwelling of the monkey of the mind. As it is said:

“Aṭṭhikaṅkalakuṭi [V 1.0027] ce sā, makkaṭāvasatho iti;

Makkaṭo pañcadvārāya, kuṭikāya pasakkiya;

Dvārena anupariyāti, ghaṭṭayanto punappuna”nti. (theragā. 125);

"If this is a hut made of a skeleton, it is the monkey's dwelling;

The monkey, having entered the small five-doored hut,

Wanders from door to door, striking again and again."

Sā kuṭi yena taṇhāmānadiṭṭhichadanena sattānaṃ channattā punappunaṃ rāgādikilesavassaṃ ativassati. Yathāha –

That hut, because it is covered for beings by the thatch of craving, conceit, and views, is repeatedly deluged by the rain of defilements such as lust. As it is said:

“Channamativassati, vivaṭaṃ nātivassati;

Tasmā channaṃ vivaretha, evaṃ taṃ nātivassatī”ti. (udā. 45; theragā. 447; pari. 339);

“Rain soaks through what is roofed; it does not soak through what is open. Therefore, uncover what is roofed, so it will not soak through.”

Ayaṃ [M 1.0029] gāthā dvīsu ṭhānesu vuttā khandhake theragāthāyañca. Khandhake hi “yo āpattiṃ paṭicchādeti, tassa kilesā ca punappunaṃ āpattiyo ca ativassanti, yo pana na paṭicchādeti, tassa nātivassantī”ti imaṃ atthaṃ paṭicca vuttā. Theragāthāyaṃ “yassa rāgādicchadanaṃ atthi, tassa puna iṭṭhārammaṇādīsu rāgādisambhavato channamativassati[P 1.0032]. Yo vā uppanne kilese adhivāseti, tasseva adhivāsitakilesacchadanacchannā attabhāvakuṭi punappunaṃ kilesavassaṃ ativassati. Yassa pana arahattamaggañāṇavātena kilesacchadanassa viddhaṃsitattā vivaṭā, tassa nātivassatī”ti. Ayamattho idha adhippeto. Bhagavatā hi yathāvuttaṃ chadanaṃ yathāvutteneva nayena viddhaṃsitaṃ, tasmā “vivaṭā kuṭī”ti āha. Nibbutoti upasanto. Ginīti aggi. Yena hi ekādasavidhena agginā sabbamidaṃ ādittaṃ. Yathāha – “ādittaṃ rāgagginā”ti vitthāro. So aggi bhagavato bodhimūleyeva ariyamaggasalilasekena nibbuto, tasmā “nibbuto ginī”ti āha.

This verse is spoken in two places: in the Khandhaka and in the Theragāthā. In the Khandhaka, it is said with reference to this meaning: 'For one who conceals an offense, their defilements and offenses rain down again and again; but for one who does not conceal, they do not rain down.' In the Theragāthā, it is said: 'For one who has the covering of lust and so on, because lust and so on arise again with regard to desirable objects and the like, the covered is excessively rained upon. Or, for one who endures arisen defilements, the hut of their individual existence, covered by the thatch of endured defilements, is again and again excessively rained upon by the rain of defilements. But for one whose covering of defilements has been shattered by the wind of the knowledge of the path to Arahantship, and is thus open, for them it does not rain excessively.' This is the meaning intended here. Indeed, the aforementioned covering was shattered by the Blessed One in the very way described; therefore, it is said, 'the hut is open.' Nibbuto means extinguished. Ginī means fire. For by the elevenfold fire all this is ablaze. As it is said: 'Ablaze with the fire of lust…' and so on. That fire was extinguished for the Blessed One right at the root of the Bodhi tree by the sprinkling of the water of the noble path; therefore, it is said, 'the fire is extinguished.'

Evaṃ vadanto ca dhaniyaṃ atuṭṭhabbena tussamānaṃ aññāpadeseneva paribhāsati, ovadati, anusāsati. Kathaṃ? “Akkodhano”ti hi vadamāno, dhaniya, tvaṃ “pakkodanohamasmī”ti tuṭṭho, odanapāko ca yāvajīvaṃ dhanaparikkhayena kattabbo, dhanaparikkhayo ca ārakkhādidukkhapadaṭṭhāno, evaṃ sante dukkheneva tuṭṭho hosi. Ahaṃ pana “akkodhanohamasmī”ti tussanto sandiṭṭhikasamparāyikadukkhābhāvena tuṭṭho homīti dīpeti. “Vigatakhilo”ti vadamāno tvaṃ “duddhakhīrohamasmī”ti tussanto akatakiccova “katakiccohamasmī”ti mantvā tuṭṭho, ahaṃ pana “vigatakhilohamasmī”ti tussanto katakiccova tuṭṭho homīti dīpeti. “Anutīre [V 1.0028] mahiyekarattivāso”ti vadamāno tvaṃ anutīre mahiyā samānavāsoti tussanto catumāsanibaddhavāsena tuṭṭho. Nibaddhavāso ca āvāsasaṅgena hoti, so ca dukkho, evaṃ sante dukkheneva tuṭṭho hosi. Ahaṃ pana ekarattivāsoti tussanto anibaddhavāsena tuṭṭho, anibaddhavāso ca āvāsasaṅgābhāvena hoti, āvāsasaṅgābhāvo ca sukhoti sukheneva tuṭṭho homīti [P 1.0033] dīpeti.

Speaking thus, the Blessed One reproached, admonished, and instructed Dhaniya—who was pleased with what is not a cause for pleasure—by way of indirect reference. How? When saying, ‘I am without anger,’ Dhaniya, you are pleased, thinking, ‘I have cooked rice.’ But the cooking of rice must be done throughout life by the expenditure of wealth, and the expenditure of wealth is a basis for suffering, such as the need for protection. This being so, you are pleased with suffering itself. I, however, being pleased with ‘I am without anger,’ am pleased due to the absence of suffering in this life and the next, so he showed. When saying, ‘I am without barrenness,’ you are pleased, thinking, ‘I have milked the cows,’ and though your task is unfinished, you consider, ‘My task is finished,’ and are pleased. I, however, being pleased with ‘I am without barrenness,’ am pleased because my task is truly finished, so he showed. When saying, ‘I dwell for one night on the bank of the Mahī,’ you are pleased, thinking, ‘I dwell equally on the bank of the Mahī,’ and are pleased with a fixed residence for four months. A fixed residence involves attachment to the dwelling, and that is suffering. This being so, you are pleased with suffering itself. I, however, being pleased with ‘dwelling for one night,’ am pleased with having no fixed residence. Having no fixed residence comes from the absence of attachment to a dwelling, and the absence of attachment to a dwelling is happiness. Thus, I am pleased with happiness itself, so he showed.

“Vivaṭā [M 1.0030] kuṭī”ti vadamāno tvaṃ channā kuṭīti tussanto channagehatāya tuṭṭho, gehe ca te channepi attabhāvakuṭikaṃ kilesavassaṃ ativassati, yena sañjanitehi catūhi mahoghehi vuyhamāno anayabyasanaṃ pāpuṇeyyāsi, evaṃ sante atuṭṭhabbeneva tuṭṭho hosi. Ahaṃ pana “vivaṭā kuṭī”ti tussanto attabhāvakuṭiyā kilesacchadanābhāvena tuṭṭho. Evañca me vivaṭāya kuṭiyā na taṃ kilesavassaṃ ativassati, yena sañjanitehi catūhi mahoghehi vuyhamāno anayabyasanaṃ pāpuṇeyyaṃ, evaṃ sante tuṭṭhabbeneva tuṭṭho homīti dīpeti. “Nibbuto ginī”ti vadamāno tvaṃ āhito ginīti tussanto akatūpaddavanivāraṇova katūpaddavanivāraṇosmīti mantvā tuṭṭho. Ahaṃ pana nibbuto ginīti tussanto ekādasaggipariḷāhābhāvato katūpaddavanivāraṇatāyeva tuṭṭhoti dīpeti. “Atha ce patthayasī pavassa devā”ti vadamāno evaṃ vigatadukkhānaṃ anuppattasukhānaṃ katasabbakiccānaṃ amhādisānaṃ etaṃ vacanaṃ sobhati, atha ce patthayasi, pavassa deva, na no tayi vassante vā avassante vā vuḍḍhi vā hāni vā atthi, tvaṃ pana kasmā evaṃ vadasīti dīpeti. Tasmā yaṃ vuttaṃ “evaṃ vadanto ca dhaniya atuṭṭhabbeneva tussamānaṃ aññāpadeseneva paribhāsati ovadati, anusāsatī”ti, taṃ sammadeva vuttanti.

When saying, ‘The hut is open,’ you are pleased with a covered hut, pleased by having a roofed house. And even though your house is roofed, upon the hut of your personal existence the rain of defilements pours down heavily, drenched by which and carried away by the four great floods, you would come to ruin and disaster. This being so, you are pleased with what is not a cause for pleasure. I, however, being pleased with ‘the hut is open,’ am pleased by the absence of the roofing of defilements on the hut of my personal existence. And so, in my open hut, that rain of defilements does not pour down heavily, drenched by which and carried away by the four great floods, I would not come to ruin and disaster. This being so, I am pleased with what is truly a cause for pleasure, so he showed. When saying, ‘The fire is extinguished,’ you are pleased with ‘the fire is kindled,’ and though you have not averted dangers, you think, ‘I have averted dangers,’ and are pleased. I, however, being pleased with ‘the fire is extinguished,’ am pleased precisely because I have averted dangers, due to the absence of the blaze of the eleven fires, so he showed. When saying, ‘Then, if you wish, rain, O Deva,’ for those like us who are free from suffering, have attained happiness, and have completed all duties, this statement is fitting. ‘Then, if you wish, rain, O Deva, for us, whether you rain or not, there is neither increase nor decrease.’ But why do you speak thus? so he showed. Therefore, what was said—‘Speaking thus, he reproaches, admonishes, and instructs Dhaniya, who is pleased with what is not a cause for pleasure, by way of indirect reference’—that was rightly said.

20. Evamimaṃ bhagavatā vuttaṃ gāthaṃ sutvāpi dhaniyo gopo “ko ayaṃ gāthaṃ bhāsatī”ti avatvā tena subhāsitena parituṭṭho punapi tathārūpaṃ sotukāmo aparampi gāthamāha “andhakamakasā”ti. Tattha andhakāti kāḷamakkhikānaṃ adhivacanaṃ, piṅgalamakkhikānantipi eke. Makasāti makasāyeva. Na vijjareti natthi. Kaccheti dve kacchā – nadīkaccho ca pabbatakaccho ca. Idha nadīkaccho. Ruḷhatiṇeti sañjātatiṇe. Carantīti bhattakiccaṃ [P 1.0034] karonti. Vuṭṭhimpīti vātavuṭṭhiādikā anekā vuṭṭhiyo, tā āḷavakasutte pakāsayissāma. Idha pana vassavuṭṭhiṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Saheyyunti khameyyuṃ. Sesaṃ pākaṭameva. Ettha dhaniyo ye andhakamakasā sannipatitvā rudhire pivantā muhutteneva gāvo anayabyasanaṃ pāpenti, tasmā vuṭṭhitamatteyeva te gopālakā paṃsunā ca sākhāhi ca [M 1.0031] mārenti, tesaṃ abhāvena gunnaṃ khemataṃ, kacche [V 1.0029] ruḷhatiṇacaraṇena addhānagamanaparissamābhāvaṃ vatvā khudākilamathābhāvañca dīpento “yathā aññesaṃ gāvo andhakamakasasamphassehi dissamānā addhānagamanena kilantā khudāya milāyamānā ekavuṭṭhinipātampi na saheyyuṃ, na me tathā gāvo, mayhaṃ pana gāvo vuttappakārābhāvā dvikkhattuṃ vā tikkhatuṃ vā vuṭṭhimpi saheyyu”nti dīpeti.

20. Having heard this verse spoken by the Blessed One, the cowherd Dhaniya, without saying, “Who is this who speaks a verse?”, was greatly pleased by those well-spoken words and, desiring to hear such again, spoke another verse: “Gadflies and mosquitoes…” Here, `andhakā` is a term for black flies; some say it is for tawny flies. `Makasā` means mosquitoes. `Na vijjare` means they do not exist. `Kacche` refers to two types of marshy ground: river marsh and mountain marsh. Here, it is the river marsh. `Ruḷhatiṇe` means on the grass that has grown. `Caranti` means they do their feeding. `Vuṭṭhimpi` refers to many kinds of rain, such as wind-rain; we will explain these in the Āḷavaka Sutta. Here, however, it is said in reference to the seasonal rain. `Saheyyuṃ` means they could endure. The rest is clear. Here, Dhaniya, explaining that there are gadflies and mosquitoes which, having gathered and drinking blood, in a moment bring cattle to ruin and disaster, and therefore as soon as they appear the cowherds kill them with dust and branches, and that due to their absence there is safety for the cattle, and by their grazing on the grown grass in the marsh there is no weariness from long journeys, and pointing out the absence of hunger and fatigue, illustrates thus: “Just as other cattle, being bitten by the touch of gadflies and mosquitoes, weary from long journeys, and wilting with hunger, could not endure even a single downpour of rain, my cattle are not so. My cattle, however, due to the absence of the aforementioned conditions, could endure the rain even two or three times.”

21. Tato bhagavā yasmā dhaniyo antaradīpe vasanto bhayaṃ disvā, kullaṃ bandhitvā, mahāmahiṃ taritvā, taṃ kacchaṃ āgamma “ahaṃ suṭṭhu āgato, nibbhayeva ṭhāne ṭhito”ti maññamāno evamāha, sabhaye eva ca so ṭhāne ṭhito, tasmā tassa āgamanaṭṭhānā attano āgamanaṭṭhānaṃ uttaritarañca paṇītatarañca vaṇṇento “baddhāsi bhisī”ti imaṃ gāthamabhāsi, atthasabhāgaṃ no byañjanasabhāgaṃ.

21. Then the Blessed One, because Dhaniya—dwelling on an island in the river, having seen danger, bound a raft, crossed the great Mahī, and come to that marshy ground—spoke thus, thinking, “I have come well; I stand in a place free from danger,” while he was in fact standing in a place of danger; therefore, praising his own place of arrival as more superior and more excellent than his place of arrival, spoke this verse beginning, “Bound is the `bhisi`,” which is similar in meaning but not in wording.

Tattha bhisīti pattharitvā puthulaṃ katvā baddhakullo vuccati loke. Ariyassa pana dhammavinaye ariyamaggassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Ariyamaggo hi –

Therein, `bhisi` is said in the world to be a raft that is bound after being spread out and made wide. In the Dhamma and Discipline of the Noble One, however, it is a designation for the Noble Path. For the Noble Path is:

“Maggo pajjo patho pantho, añjasaṃ vaṭumāyanaṃ;

Nāvā uttarasetu ca, kullo ca bhisi saṅkamo”. (cūḷani. pārāyanatthutigāthāniddesa 101);

“The path, the way, the road, the track, the straight path, the route; the boat and the crossing-bridge, the raft and the `bhisi`, the causeway.”

“Addhānaṃ pabhavo ceva, tattha tattha pakāsito”.

“The origin of the journey, and it is revealed in various places.”

Imāyapi gāthāya bhagavā purimanayeneva taṃ ovadanto imaṃ atthaṃ āhāti veditabbo – dhaniya, tvaṃ kullaṃ bandhitvā, mahiṃ taritvā, imaṃ ṭhānamāgato, punapi ca te kullo [P 1.0035] bandhitabbo eva bhavissati, nadī ca taritabbā, na cetaṃ ṭhānaṃ khemaṃ. Mayā pana ekacitte maggaṅgāni samodhānetvā ñāṇabandhanena baddhā ahosi bhisi. Sā ca sattatiṃsabodhipakkhiyadhammaparipuṇṇatāya ekarasabhāvūpagatattā aññamaññaṃ anativattanena puna bandhitabbappayojanābhāvena devamanussesu kenaci mocetuṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya ca susaṅkhatā. Tāya camhi tiṇṇo, pubbe patthitaṃ tīrappadesaṃ gato. Gacchantopi ca na sotāpannādayo viya kañcideva padesaṃ gato. Atha kho pāragato sabbāsavakkhayaṃ sabbadhammapāraṃ paramaṃ khemaṃ nibbānaṃ gato, tiṇṇoti vā sabbaññutaṃ patto, pāragatoti arahattaṃ patto[M 1.0032]. Kiṃ vineyya pāragatoti ce? Vineyya oghaṃ, kāmoghādicatubbidhaṃ oghaṃ taritvā atikkamma taṃ pāraṃ gatoti. Idāni ca [V 1.0030] pana me puna taritabbābhāvato attho bhisiyā na vijjati, tasmā mameva yuttaṃ vattuṃ “atha ce patthayasī pavassa devā”ti.

By this verse too, it should be understood that the Blessed One, advising him in the same manner as before, spoke this meaning: “Dhaniya, you have built a raft, crossed the great river, and arrived at this place. Yet, you will have to build a raft again and cross the river, for this place is not safe. But I, having united the factors of the path within a single mind, have bound a raft with the bond of knowledge. And that raft, being complete with the thirty-seven aids to enlightenment, having attained a single nature, its parts not transgressing one another, having no need to be bound again, and being unable to be loosened by any god or human, is well-constructed. By it, I have crossed over and reached the shore I had previously aspired to. And in going, I did not reach merely some region, as do stream-enterers and others. Rather, having gone beyond, I have reached Nibbāna, which is the destruction of all taints, the further shore of all phenomena, the supreme security. Or, 'crossed over' means having attained omniscience; 'gone beyond' means having attained arahantship. If it is asked, 'Having subdued what has he gone beyond?' Having subdued the flood—having crossed and gone beyond the fourfold flood beginning with the flood of sensuality—he has gone to that further shore. And now, since there is no further need for me to cross, there is no purpose for a raft for me. Therefore, it is fitting for me alone to say, ‘If you wish, let the rain pour down.’”

22. Tampi sutvā dhaniyo purimanayeneva “gopī mama assavā”ti imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi. Tattha gopīti bhariyaṃ niddisati. Assavāti vacanakarā kiṃkārapaṭisāvinī. Alolāti mātugāmo hi pañcahi lolatāhi lolo hoti – āhāralolatāya, alaṅkāralolatāya, parapurisalolatāya, dhanalolatāya, pādalolatāya. Tathā hi mātugāmo bhattapūvasurādibhede āhāre lolatāya antamaso pārivāsikabhattampi bhuñjati, hatthotāpakampi khādati, diguṇaṃ dhanamanuppadatvāpi suraṃ pivati. Alaṅkāralolatāya aññaṃ alaṅkāraṃ alabhamāno antamaso udakatelakenapi kese osaṇḍetvā mukhaṃ parimajjati. Parapurisalolatāya antamaso puttenapi [P 1.0036] tādise padese pakkosiyamāno paṭhamaṃ asaddhammavasena cinteti. Dhanalolatāya “haṃsarājaṃ gahetvāna suvaṇṇā parihāyatha”. Pādalolatāya ārāmādigamanasīlo hutvā sabbaṃ dhanaṃ vināseti. Tattha dhaniyo “ekāpi lolatā mayhaṃ gopiyā natthī”ti dassento alolāti āha.

22. Hearing this, Dhaniya, in the same manner as before, spoke this verse: “My wife is obedient.” Here, gopī indicates his wife. Assavā means she does his bidding, responsive to what is to be done. Alolā means not fickle. For a woman is fickle in five ways: fickleness for food, fickleness for adornments, fickleness for other men, fickleness for wealth, and fickleness of foot. Indeed, a woman, due to fickleness for food such as cooked rice, cakes, and liquor, will eat even stale food from the previous night and will eat scrapings from her hand; even without producing double the wealth, she drinks liquor. Due to fickleness for adornments, if she cannot obtain other ornaments, she will at least comb her hair with water as if it were oil and wipe her face. Due to fickleness for other men, if summoned to a secluded place even by her own son, she first thinks in terms of misconduct. Due to fickleness for wealth, it is as in the saying: 'Having seized the goose king, they were deprived of gold.' Due to fickleness of foot, being disposed to go to parks and so on, she squanders all her wealth. Here, Dhaniya, showing that “not even one fickleness exists in my wife,” says, “She is not fickle.”

Dīgharattaṃ saṃvāsiyāti dīghakālaṃ saddhiṃ vasamānā komārabhāvato pabhuti ekato vaḍḍhitā. Tena parapurise na jānātīti dasseti. Manāpāti evaṃ parapurise ajānantī mameva manaṃ allīyatīti dasseti. Tassā na suṇāmi kiñci pāpanti “itthannāmena nāma saddhiṃ imāya hasitaṃ vā lapitaṃ vā”ti evaṃ tassā na suṇāmi, kañci aticāradosanti dasseti.

Having lived together for a long time means: having lived together for a long time, they have grown up together since her maidenhood. By this he shows: 'She does not know another man.' Pleasing means: thus, not knowing another man, her mind clings only to me—this is shown. I hear no evil of her means: I do not hear, 'She has laughed or spoken with a man of such-and-such a name.' Thus he shows: 'I do not hear of any fault of transgression concerning her.'

23. Atha bhagavā etehi guṇehi gopiyā tuṭṭhaṃ dhaniyaṃ ovadanto purimanayeneva “cittaṃ mama assava”nti imaṃ gāthamabhāsi, atthasabhāgaṃ, byañjanasabhāgañca. Tattha uttānatthāneva padāni. Ayaṃ pana adhippāyo – dhaniya, tvaṃ “gopī mama assavā”ti tuṭṭho, sā pana te assavā [M 1.0033] bhaveyya vā na vā; dujjānaṃ paracittaṃ, visesato mātugāmassa. Mātugāmañhi kucchiyā pariharantāpi rakkhituṃ na sakkonti, evaṃ durakkhacittattā eva na sakkā tumhādisehi itthī alolāti vā saṃvāsiyāti vā manāpāti vā nippāpāti vā jānituṃ. Mayhaṃ pana cittaṃ assavaṃ ovādapaṭikaraṃ mama vase vattati, nāhaṃ tassa vase vattāmi. So cassa assavabhāvo yamakapāṭihāriye channaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ aggidhārāsu ca udakadhārāsu ca pavattamānāsu sabbajanassa pākaṭo ahosi. Agginimmāne hi tejokasiṇaṃ samāpajjitabbaṃ udakanimmāne āpokasiṇaṃ, nīlādinimmāne nīlādikasiṇāni. Buddhānampi hi dve cittāni ekato [V 1.0031] nappavattanti, ekameva pana assavabhāvena evaṃ vasavatti ahosi. Tañca kho pana sabbakilesabandhanāpagamā [P 1.0037] vimuttaṃ, vimuttattā tadeva alolaṃ, na tava gopī. Dīpaṅkarabuddhakālato ca pabhuti dānasīlādīhi dīgharattaṃ paribhāvitattā saṃvāsiyaṃ, na tava gopī. Tadetaṃ anuttarena damathena damitattā sudantaṃ, sudantattā attano vasena chadvāravisevanaṃ pahāya mameva adhippāyamanassa vasenānuvattanato manāpaṃ, na tava gopī.

23. Then the Blessed One, advising Dhaniya, who was pleased by these qualities of his wife, spoke this verse, which was similar in meaning and wording: “My mind is obedient.” Here the words are clear in meaning. But the intention is this: Dhaniya, you are pleased thinking, “My wife is obedient,” but whether she is obedient to you or not, who can say? Another’s mind is difficult to know, especially a woman’s. For a woman cannot be guarded even if one were to carry her in one's own belly; because her mind is so difficult to guard, it is impossible for someone like you to know whether a woman is not fickle, or faithful, or pleasing, or without evil. My mind, however, is obedient, responsive to advice, and acts under my control—I do not act under its control. And this obedient nature of the mind was made manifest to all during the Twin Miracle, when streams of fire and streams of water of six colors were proceeding forth. For in creating fire, the fire kasiṇa must be attained; in creating water, the water kasiṇa; and in creating blue and other colors, the blue and other kasiṇas. For even in Buddhas, two minds do not arise at once, but a single mind, through its obedient nature, was thus under control. Moreover, that mind is liberated, having departed from all the bonds of the defilements. Because it is liberated, it is not fickle—unlike your wife. And because it has been cultivated for a long time since the time of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara through generosity, virtue, and so on, it is faithful—unlike your wife. And this mind, tamed by the unsurpassed taming, is well-tamed. Because it is well-tamed, it has, by its own power, abandoned indulgence through the six doors and follows only in accordance with my own intention; thus it is pleasing—unlike your wife.

Pāpaṃ pana me na vijjatīti iminā pana bhagavā tassa attano cittassa pāpābhāvaṃ dasseti, dhaniyo viya gopiyā. So cassa pāpābhāvo na kevalaṃ sammāsambuddhakāleyeva, ekūnatiṃsa vassāni sarāgādikāle agāramajjhe vasantassāpi veditabbo. Tadāpi hissa agāriyabhāvānurūpaṃ viññupaṭikuṭṭhaṃ kāyaduccaritaṃ vā vacīduccaritaṃ vā manoduccaritaṃ vā na uppannapubbaṃ. Tato paraṃ māropi chabbassāni anabhisambuddhaṃ, ekaṃ vassaṃ abhisambuddhanti satta vassāni tathāgataṃ anubandhi “appeva nāma vālagganitudanamattampissa pāpasamācāraṃ passeyya”nti. So adisvāva nibbinno imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi –

But no evil is found in me—with this statement the Blessed One shows the absence of evil in his own mind, just as Dhaniya did regarding Gopi. And this absence of evil was not only during the time of his perfect enlightenment. Even during the twenty-nine years he lived in the household, amidst sensual desires and so on, it should be understood. Even then, no bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, or mental misconduct—even such as would be censured by the wise—ever arose in him, even in his householder state. After that, Māra followed the Tathāgata for seven years—six years before his enlightenment and one year after—thinking, “Perhaps I might see even a hair’s breadth of evil conduct in him.” Not seeing any, he became disenchanted and spoke this verse:

“Satta vassāni bhagavantaṃ, anubandhiṃ padāpadaṃ;

Otāraṃ nādhigacchissaṃ, sambuddhassa satīmato”ti. (su. ni. 448);

“For seven years I followed the Blessed One closely, footstep by footstep; yet I found no fault in the mindful, fully Awakened One.”

Buddhakālepi naṃ uttaramāṇavo satta māsāni anubandhi ābhisamācārikaṃ daṭṭhukāmo. So kiñci vajjaṃ adisvāva parisuddhasamācāro bhagavāti gato. Cattāri hi tathāgatassa arakkheyyāni. Yathāha –

Even during the Buddha’s time, the young man Uttara followed him for seven months, wishing to observe his refined conduct. Seeing no fault whatsoever, he departed, concluding, “The Blessed One’s conduct is perfectly pure.” For the Tathāgata has four things that need no guarding. As it is said:

“Cattārimāni[M 1.0034], bhikkhave, tathāgatassa arakkheyyāni. Katamāni cattāri? Parisuddhakāyasamācāro, bhikkhave, tathāgato, natthi tathāgatassa kāyaduccaritaṃ, yaṃ tathāgato rakkheyya ‘mā me idaṃ paro aññāsī’ti, parisuddhavacīsamācāro…pe… parisuddhamanosamācāro…pe… parisuddhājīvo, bhikkhave, tathāgato, natthi tathāgatassa micchājīvo, yaṃ tathāgato rakkheyya [P 1.0038] ‘mā me idaṃ paro aññāsī’”ti (a. ni. 7.58).

“Bhikkhus, there are these four things a Tathāgata does not need to guard. What four? A Tathāgata is pure in bodily conduct, bhikkhus. There is no bodily misconduct in a Tathāgata that he would need to guard, thinking, ‘May others not know this about me.’ The Tathāgata is pure in verbal conduct… The Tathāgata is pure in mental conduct… The Tathāgata is pure in livelihood, bhikkhus. There is no wrong livelihood in a Tathāgata that he would need to guard, thinking, ‘May others not know this about me.’”

Evaṃ yasmā tathāgatassa cittassa na kevalaṃ sammāsambuddhakāle, pubbepi pāpaṃ natthi eva, tasmā āha – “pāpaṃ pana me na vijjatī”ti. Tassādhippāyo – mameva cittassa pāpaṃ na sakkā [V 1.0032] suṇituṃ, na tava gopiyā. Tasmā yadi etehi guṇehi tuṭṭhena “atha ce patthayasī pavassa devā”ti vattabbaṃ, mayāvetaṃ vattabbanti.

Thus, because the Tathāgata’s mind has no evil, not only at the time of perfect enlightenment but also previously, he therefore said: “But no evil is found in me.” The meaning of this is: It is of my own mind that evil cannot be heard, unlike in the case of your Gopi. Therefore, if the words, “Then, if you wish, rain, O deva,” are to be said by one pleased with these virtues, it is I who should say them.

24. Tampi sutvā dhaniyo tatuttaripi subhāsitarasāyanaṃ pivitukāmo attano bhujissabhāvaṃ dassento āha “attavetanabhatohamasmī”ti. Tattha attavetanabhatoti attaniyeneva ghāsacchādanena bhato, attanoyeva kammaṃ katvā jīvāmi, na parassa vetanaṃ gahetvā parassa kammaṃ karomīti dasseti. Puttāti dhītaro ca puttā ca, te sabbe puttātveva ekajjhaṃ vuccanti. Samāniyāti sannihitā avippavuṭṭhā. Arogāti nirābādhā, sabbeva ūrubāhubalāti dasseti. Tesaṃ na suṇāmi kiñci pāpanti tesaṃ corāti vā paradārikāti vā dussīlāti vā kiñci pāpaṃ na suṇāmīti.

Hearing this, Dhaniya, wishing to drink still more of the elixir of those well-spoken words and showing his own state of being a free man, said, “I am one who lives on my own earnings.” Here, “one who lives on my own earnings” shows that he is sustained by his own food and clothing, living by doing his own work, not taking wages from another to do another’s work. “Children” refers to both daughters and sons; all are collectively called children. “Living together” means they are present and not separated. “Healthy” means without ailments, showing that they all possess the strength of thigh and arm. “I hear nothing bad about them” means he hears nothing bad about them, such as being called “a thief,” “an adulterer,” or “immoral.”

25. Evaṃ vutte bhagavā purimanayeneva dhaniyaṃ ovadanto imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi – “nāhaṃ bhatako”ti. Atrāpi uttānatthāneva padāni. Ayaṃ pana adhippāyo – tvaṃ “bhujissohamasmī”ti mantvā tuṭṭho, paramatthato ca attano kammaṃ karitvā jīvantopi dāso evāsi taṇhādāsattā, bhatakavādā ca na parimuccasi. Vuttañhetaṃ “ūno loko atitto taṇhādāso”ti (ma. ni. 2.305). Paramatthato pana nāhaṃ bhatakosmi kassaci. Ahañhi kassaci parassa vā attano vā bhatako na homi. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Yasmā [M 1.0035] nibbiṭṭhena carāmi sabbaloke. Ahañhi dīpaṅkarapādamūlato yāva bodhi, tāva sabbaññutaññāṇassa bhatako ahosiṃ. Sabbaññutaṃ patto pana nibbiṭṭho nibbiso rājabhato viya. Teneva nibbiṭṭhena sabbaññubhāvena lokuttarasamādhisukhena ca jīvāmi. Tassa me idāni [P 1.0039] uttarikaraṇīyassa kataparicayassa vā abhāvato appahīnapaṭisandhikānaṃ tādisānaṃ viya pattabbo koci attho bhatiyā na vijjati. “Bhaṭiyā”tipi pāṭho. Tasmā yadi bhujissatāya tuṭṭhena “atha ce patthayasī pavassa devā”ti vattabbaṃ, mayāvetaṃ vattabbanti.

24. When this was said, the Blessed One, advising Dhaniya as before, spoke this verse: “I am no hired servant.” Here too, the words are of obvious meaning. The intention here is this: you, thinking “I am independent,” are content, but in the ultimate sense, even while living by doing your own work, you are a slave due to being a slave to craving, and you are not freed from being called a hired servant. As it is said, “The world is lacking, insatiable, a slave to craving.” But in the ultimate sense, I am no one’s hired servant. For I am not a hired servant of anyone, whether another or myself. Why? Because I wander with my task completed in the whole world. For from the time at the feet of Dīpaṅkara until enlightenment, I was a hired servant to the knowledge of omniscience. But having attained omniscience, I am one whose task is completed, free from obligation, like a royal servant whose term of service is completed. I live by that very state of having completed my task, by omniscience, and by the bliss of supramundane concentration. For me now, since there is no further task to be done nor any completed practice to be accumulated, there is no purpose whatsoever to be attained by way of hire, unlike for those who have not abandoned rebirth-linking. “Bhaṭiyā” is also a reading. Therefore, if the words, “Then, if you wish, rain, O deva,” are to be said by one content with independence, it is I who should say them.

26. Tampi sutvā dhaniyo atittova subhāsitāmatena attano pañcappakāragomaṇḍalaparipuṇṇabhāvaṃ dassento āha “atthi vasā”ti. Tattha vasāti adamitavuḍḍhavacchakā. Dhenupāti dhenuṃ pivantā taruṇavacchakā, khīradāyikā vā gāvo. Godharaṇiyoti gabbhiniyo. Paveṇiyoti vayappattā balībaddehi saddhiṃ methunapatthanakagāvo. Usabhopi gavampatīti yo gopālakehi pāto eva nhāpetvā, bhojetvā, pañcaṅgulaṃ datvā, mālaṃ bandhitvā – “ehi, tāta, gāvo gocaraṃ pāpetvā rakkhitvā ānehī”ti pesīyati, evaṃ pesito [V 1.0033] ca tā gāvo agocaraṃ pariharitvā, gocare cāretvā, sīhabyagghādibhayā parittāyitvā āneti, tathārūpo usabhopi gavampati idha mayhaṃ gomaṇḍale atthīti dassesi.

25. Hearing this, Dhaniya, still unsatisfied with the nectar of well-spoken words, wishing to show the completeness of his fivefold herd of cattle, said, “There are heifers…” Here, ‘vasā’ refers to untamed young bulls. ‘Dhenupā’ refers to young calves drinking from their mothers, or milk-giving cows. ‘Godharaṇī’ refers to pregnant cows. ‘Paveṇī’ refers to cows of breeding age, desiring to mate with bulls. “And a bull, the lord of the herd”—this is one whom the herdsmen bathe in the morning, feed, give the five-finger mark, and garland, saying, “Come, dear one, lead the cows to pasture, guard them, and bring them back.” Thus sent, he avoids taking the cows to non-pasturing ground, grazes them in suitable pasture, protects them from dangers like lions and tigers, and brings them back. Such a bull, the lord of the herd, is also present in my herd of cattle—thus he indicated.

27. Evaṃ vutte bhagavā tatheva dhaniyaṃ ovadanto imaṃ paccanīkagāthaṃ āha “natthi vasā”ti. Ettha cesa adhippāyo – idha amhākaṃ sāsane adamitaṭṭhena vuḍḍhaṭṭhena ca vasāsaṅkhātā pariyuṭṭhānā vā, taruṇavacchake sandhāya vasānaṃ mūlaṭṭhena khīradāyiniyo sandhāya paggharaṇaṭṭhena dhenupāsaṅkhātā anusayā vā, paṭisandhigabbhadhāraṇaṭṭhena godharaṇisaṅkhātā puññāpuññāneñjābhisaṅkhāracetanā vā, saṃyogapatthanaṭṭhena paveṇisaṅkhātā patthanā taṇhā vā, ādhipaccaṭṭhena pubbaṅgamaṭṭhena seṭṭhaṭṭhena ca gavampatiusabhasaṅkhātaṃ abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇaṃ vā natthi, svāhaṃ imāya sabbayogakkhemabhūtāya natthitāya tuṭṭho. Tvaṃ pana sokādivatthubhūtāya atthitāya tuṭṭho[M 1.0036]. Tasmā sabbayogakkhematāya [P 1.0040] tuṭṭhassa mamevetaṃ yuttaṃ vattuṃ “atha ce patthayasī pavassa devā”ti.

27. When this was said, the Blessed One, advising Dhaniya in the same manner, spoke this counter-verse beginning, “There are no ‘vasā’…” Herein, this is the intended meaning: In this Teaching of ours, there are no obsessions, called ‘vasā’ in the sense of being untamed or aged; nor are there underlying tendencies, called ‘dhenupā’, so-called with reference to young calves in the sense of being the root of ‘vasā’ (grease), or with reference to milk-giving cows in the sense of ‘flowing out’; nor are there volitional formations of merit, demerit, or the imperturbable, called ‘godharaṇī’ in the sense of carrying the womb of rebirth-linking; nor is there craving for existence, called ‘paveṇī’ in the sense of desiring union; nor is there volitional consciousness, called ‘usabha, the lord of the herd,’ in the sense of sovereignty, being foremost, and being best. I am content with this state of non-existence, which is security from all yokes. You, however, are content with existence, which is the basis for sorrow and so forth. Therefore, it is fitting for me alone, who is content with security from all yokes, to say, “If you so wish, O deva, let it rain.”

28. Tampi sutvā dhaniyo tatuttaripi subhāsitaṃ amatarasaṃ adhigantukāmo attano gogaṇassa khilabandhanasampattiṃ dassento āha “khilā nikhātā”ti. Tattha khilāti gunnaṃ bandhanatthambhā. Nikhātāti ākoṭetvā bhūmiyaṃ pavesitā khuddakā mahantā khaṇitvā ṭhapitā. Asampavedhīti akampakā. Dāmāti vacchakānaṃ bandhanatthāya katā ganthitapāsayuttā rajjubandhanavisesā. Muñjamayāti muñjatiṇamayā. Navāti acirakatā. Susaṇṭhānāti suṭṭhu saṇṭhānā, suvaṭṭitasaṇṭhānā vā. Na hi sakkhintīti neva sakkhissanti. Dhenupāpi chettunti taruṇavacchakāpi chindituṃ.

28. Hearing this, Dhaniya, desiring to attain still further the deathless nectar of this well-spoken teaching, displayed the excellence of the stakes and tethers for his herd of cattle and said, “The stakes are driven in…” Herein, ‘khilā’ means the posts for tethering cattle. ‘Nikhātā’ means driven in, hammered and inserted into the ground; or, whether small or large, dug in and set up. ‘Asampavedhī’ means unshakeable. ‘Dāmā’ means special rope tethers, fitted with knots and loops, made for the purpose of tying up the calves. ‘Muñjamayā’ means made of muñja grass. ‘Navā’ means newly made. ‘Susaṇṭhānā’ means well-twisted or well-formed. ‘Na hi sakkhinti’ means they will not be able. ‘Dhenupāpi chettuṃ’ means for even the young calves to break.

29. Evaṃ vutte bhagavā dhaniyassa indriya-paripākakālaṃ ñatvā purimanayeneva taṃ ovadanto imaṃ catusaccadīpikaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi “usabhoriva chetvā”ti. Tattha usabhoti gopitā gopariṇāyako goyūthapati balībaddo. Keci pana bhaṇanti “gavasatajeṭṭho usabho, sahassajeṭṭho vasabho, satasahassajeṭṭho nisabho”ti. Apare “ekagāmakhette jeṭṭho usabho, dvīsu jeṭṭho vasabho, sabbattha appaṭihato nisabho”ti. Sabbepete papañcā, apica kho pana usabhoti vā vasabhoti vā nisabhoti vā sabbepete appaṭisamaṭṭhena veditabbā. Yathāha – “nisabho vata bho samaṇo gotamo”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.38). Ra-kāro padasandhikaro. Bandhanānīti rajjubandhanāni kilesabandhanāni ca. Nāgoti hatthī. Pūtilatanti gaḷocīlataṃ. Yathā hi suvaṇṇavaṇṇopi kāyo pūtikāyo, vassasatikopi sunakho kukkuro, tadahujātopi siṅgālo [V 1.0034] “jarasiṅgālo”ti vuccati, evaṃ abhinavāpi gaḷocīlatā asārakattena “pūtilatā”ti vuccati. Dālayitvāti chinditvā. Gabbhañca [P 1.0041] seyyañca gabbhaseyyaṃ. Tattha gabbhaggahaṇena jalābujayoni, seyyaggahaṇena avasesā. Gabbhaseyyamukhena vā sabbāpi tā vuttāti veditabbā. Sesamettha padatthato uttānameva.

29. When this was said, the Blessed One, knowing it was the time for Dhaniya’s spiritual faculties to mature, advised him in the same way as before and uttered this verse that illuminates the Four Truths, beginning, “Having broken them like a bull…” Herein, ‘usabho’ means a bull, a protector of cows, a leader of the herd, a strong ox. Some, however, say: “An ‘usabha’ is the chief of a hundred cattle, a ‘vasabha’ is the chief of a thousand, and a ‘nisabha’ is the chief of a hundred thousand.” Others say: “An ‘usabha’ is the chief in the fields of one village, a ‘vasabha’ in two, and a ‘nisabha’ is one who is unopposed everywhere.” All these are elaborations. But in any case, whether ‘usabha,’ ‘vasabha,’ or ‘nisabha,’ all these should be understood in the sense of ‘unequalled.’ As it is said: “Truly, venerable sir, the ascetic Gotama is a nisabha.” The letter ‘ra’ is for euphonic conjunction. ‘Bandhanāni’ means both rope-tethers and the tethers of the defilements. ‘Nāgo’ means an elephant. ‘Pūtilatā’ means a gaḷocī creeper. For just as a body, though golden-hued, is called a ‘putrid body’; and a dog, though a hundred years old, is called a ‘kukkura’; and a jackal, though born that very day, is called an ‘old jackal’; even so a fresh gaḷocī creeper is called a ‘rotten creeper’ because it is without substance. ‘Dālayitvā’ means having cut. ‘Gabbhaseyyaṃ’ is composed of ‘gabbha’ (womb) and ‘seyya’ (lying down). Herein, by the word ‘gabbha,’ the womb-born are indicated; by the word ‘seyya,’ the remaining types of birth. Or it should be understood that by the term ‘gabbhaseyyaṃ,’ all types of birth are indicated. The rest of the meaning here is clear from the words themselves.

Ayaṃ [M 1.0037] panettha adhippāyo – dhaniya, tvaṃ bandhanena tuṭṭho, ahaṃ pana bandhanena aṭṭīyanto thāmavīriyūpeto mahāusabhoriva bandhanāni pañcuddhambhāgiyasaṃyojanāni catutthaariyamaggathāmavīriyena chetvā, nāgo pūtilataṃva pañcorambhāgiyasaṃyojanabandhanāni heṭṭhāmaggattayathāmavīriyena dālayitvā, atha vā usabhoriva bandhanāni anusaye nāgo pūtilataṃva pariyuṭṭhānāni chetvā dālayitvāva ṭhito. Tasmā na puna gabbhaseyyaṃ upessaṃ. Sohaṃ jātidukkhavatthukehi sabbadukkhehi parimutto sobhāmi – “atha ce patthayasī pavassa devā”ti vadamāno. Tasmā sace tvampi ahaṃ viya vattumicchasi, chinda tāni bandhanānīti. Ettha ca bandhanāni samudayasaccaṃ, gabbhaseyyā dukkhasaccaṃ, “na upessa”nti ettha anupagamo anupādisesavasena, “chetvā dālayitvā”ti ettha chedo padālanañca saupādisesavasena nirodhasaccaṃ, yena chindati padāleti ca, taṃ maggasaccanti.

Herein, this is the intended meaning: Dhaniya, you are content with bonds, but I, being wearied by bonds and endowed with strength and energy, have cut the five higher fetters with the strength and energy of the fourth noble path, like a great bull breaking its bonds; and I have split the five lower fetters with the strength and energy of the three lower paths, like an elephant splitting a rotten creeper. Alternatively, I stand firm, having cut the underlying tendencies as a bull cuts its bonds, and having split the obsessions as an elephant splits a rotten creeper. Therefore, I will not lie in a womb again. I, being liberated from all sufferings that are founded on the suffering of birth, shine forth when I say, “If you so wish, O deva, let it rain.” Therefore, if you too wish to speak as I do, then cut those bonds. Herein, the ‘bonds’ indicate the truth of the origin; the ‘womb-bed,’ the truth of suffering; ‘I will not enter’ indicates, by way of final Nibbāna with no residue remaining, the state of non-return; ‘having cut and split’ indicates, by way of Nibbāna with residue remaining, the truth of cessation; and that by which one cuts and splits is the truth of the path.

Evametaṃ catusaccadīpikaṃ gāthaṃ sutvā gāthāpariyosāne dhaniyo ca pajāpati cassa dve ca dhītaroti cattāro janā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahiṃsu. Atha dhaniyo aveccappasādayogena tathāgate mūlajātāya patiṭṭhitāya saddhāya paññācakkhunā bhagavato dhammakāyaṃ disvā dhammatāya coditahadayo cintesi – “bandhanāni chindiṃ, gabbhaseyyo ca me natthī”ti avīciṃ pariyantaṃ katvā yāva bhavaggā ko añño evaṃ sīhanādaṃ nadissati aññatra bhagavatā, āgato nu kho me satthāti. Tato bhagavā chabbaṇṇarasmijālavicitraṃ suvaṇṇarasasekapiñjaraṃ viya sarīrābhaṃ dhaniyassa nivesane muñci “passa dāni yathāsukha”nti.

Having heard this verse that illuminates the Four Truths, at the end of the verse, four people—Dhaniya, his wife, and his two daughters—were established in the fruit of stream-entry. Then Dhaniya, through his connection with unwavering confidence in the Tathāgata, with faith that was deep-rooted and established, saw the Dhamma-body of the Blessed One with the eye of wisdom. With his heart stirred by the nature of the Dhamma, he reflected: “Who else, from the Avīci hell up to the highest state of existence, could utter such a lion’s roar—‘I have cut the bonds, and for me there is no more lying in a womb’—other than the Blessed One? Surely my Teacher has come.” Then the Blessed One released into Dhaniya’s dwelling the radiance of his body—variegated with a net of six-colored rays, like a cage sprinkled with liquid gold—saying, “Now, see as you wish.”

30. Atha dhaniyo anto paviṭṭhacandimasūriyaṃ viya [P 1.0042] samantā pajjalitapadīpasahassasamujjalitamiva ca nivesanaṃ disvā “āgato bhagavā”ti cittaṃ uppādesi. Tasmiṃyeva ca samaye meghopi pāvassi. Tenāhu saṅgītikārā “ninnañca thalañca pūrayanto”ti. Tattha ninnanti pallalaṃ. Thalanti ukkūlaṃ. Evametaṃ ukkūlavikūlaṃ sabbampi samaṃ katvā pūrayanto mahāmegho pāvassi, vassituṃ ārabhīti vuttaṃ hoti. Tāvadevāti yaṃ khaṇaṃ bhagavā sarīrābhaṃ [V 1.0035] muñci, dhaniyo ca “satthā me āgato”ti saddhāmayaṃ cittābhaṃ [M 1.0038] muñci, taṃ khaṇaṃ pāvassīti. Keci pana “sūriyuggamanampi tasmiṃyeva khaṇe”ti vaṇṇayanti.

30. Then Dhaniya, seeing his dwelling as if the sun and moon had entered within, and blazing on all sides as if with the brilliance of a thousand lamps, generated the thought, 'The Blessed One has come!' At that very moment, a great cloud also poured down. Therefore the compilers of the canon said, 'Filling the lowlands and the highlands.' Here, 'lowland' means a low-lying place; 'highland' means elevated ground. Thus, making all this, the high and the low, level and filling it, the great cloud poured down; it is said that it began to pour. 'At that very moment' means the instant when the Blessed One released the radiance of his body, and Dhaniya, thinking, 'My Teacher has come!', released the radiance of his faith-born mind—at that moment it poured down. Some, however, explain that the sunrise also occurred at that very moment.

31-32. Evaṃ tasmiṃ dhaniyassa saddhuppādatathāgatobhāsapharaṇasūriyuggamanakkhaṇe vassato devassa saddaṃ sutvā dhaniyo pītisomanassajāto imamatthaṃ abhāsatha “lābhā vata no anappakā”ti dve gāthā vattabbā.

Thus, at that moment of Dhaniya's arising of faith, the spreading of the Tathāgata's radiance, and the sunrise, Dhaniya, having heard the sound of the pouring rain, and being filled with joy and gladness, spoke this meaning in two verses: 'Truly, our gain is not insignificant...'

Tattha yasmā dhaniyo saputtadāro bhagavato ariyamaggapaṭivedhena dhammakāyaṃ disvā, lokuttaracakkhunā rūpakāyaṃ disvā, lokiyacakkhunā saddhāpaṭilābhaṃ labhi. Tasmā āha – “lābhā vata no anappakā, ye mayaṃ bhagavantaṃ addasāmā”ti. Tattha vata iti vimhayatthe nipāto. No iti amhākaṃ. Anappakāti vipulā. Sesaṃ uttānameva. Saraṇaṃ taṃ upemāti ettha pana kiñcāpi maggapaṭivedhenevassa siddhaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ, tattha pana nicchayagamanameva gato, idāni vācāya attasanniyyātanaṃ karoti. Maggavasena vā sanniyyātanasaraṇataṃ acalasaraṇataṃ patto, taṃ paresaṃ vācāya pākaṭaṃ karonto paṇipātasaraṇagamanaṃ gacchati.
