Cakkhumāti bhagavā pakatidibbapaññāsamantabuddhacakkhūhi pañcahi cakkhūhi cakkhumā. Taṃ ālapanto āha – “saraṇaṃ taṃ upema cakkhumā”ti. “Satthā no hohi tuvaṃ mahāmunī”ti idaṃ pana vacanaṃ sissabhāvūpagamanenāpi saraṇagamanaṃ pūretuṃ bhaṇati, gopī ca ahañca assavā, brahmacariyaṃ [P 1.0043] sugate carāmaseti idaṃ samādānavasena.

There, because Dhaniya, together with his wife and children, having seen the Dhamma-body of the Blessed One through penetration of the Noble Path, having seen his physical body with the supramundane eye, and having gained the acquisition of faith with the mundane eye, he therefore said: 'Truly, our gain is not insignificant, for we have seen the Blessed One.' Here, 'vata' is a particle expressing wonder. 'No' means 'our.' 'Anappakā' means 'abundant.' The rest is evident. Regarding 'We go for refuge to you,' here, although his going for refuge was accomplished through penetration of the Path, he had already gone for refuge with certainty; now he makes the verbal declaration of self-dedication. Or, by way of the Path, having attained the refuge of self-dedication, the unwavering refuge, he, making it manifest to others by word, goes for refuge with prostration. 'Cakkhumā' (Visionary)—the Blessed One is endowed with five eyes: the natural eye, the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the universal eye, and the Buddha-eye. Addressing him, he says: 'We go for refuge to you, O Visionary.' The statement 'Be our Teacher, O Great Sage' is spoken to complete the going for refuge by accepting the state of a disciple. The statement 'Gopī and I, being compliant, shall live the holy life under the Well-Gone One' is spoken as a commitment.

Tattha brahmacariyanti methunaviratimaggasamaṇadhammasāsanasadārasantosānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. “Brahmacārī”ti evamādīsu (ma. ni. 1.83) hi methunavirati brahmacariyanti vuccati. “Idaṃ kho pana me pañcasikha, brahmacariyaṃ ekantanibbidāyā”ti evamādīsu (dī. ni. 2.329) maggo. “Abhijānāmi kho panāhaṃ, sāriputta, caturaṅgasamannāgataṃ brahmacariyaṃ caritā”ti evamādīsu (ma. ni. 1.155) samaṇadhammo. “Tayidaṃ brahmacariyaṃ iddhañceva phītañcā”ti evamādīsu (dī. ni. 3.174) sāsanaṃ.

Here, 'brahmacariya' is a designation for abstinence from sexual intercourse, the path, the recluse's life, the teaching, and contentment with one's own spouse. For instance, in passages such as 'brahmacārī' (one who lives the holy life), abstinence from sexual intercourse is called 'brahmacariya.' In passages like 'This, Pañcasikha, is the holy life that leads entirely to disenchantment,' it refers to the path. In statements such as 'I recall, Sāriputta, having lived the holy life endowed with four factors,' it denotes the recluse's life. In passages like 'This holy life is prosperous and flourishing,' it signifies the teaching.

“Mayañca [M 1.0039] bhariyā nātikkamāma, amhe ca bhariyā nātikkamanti;

Aññatra tāhi brahmacariyaṃ carāma, tasmā hi amhaṃ daharā na mīyare”ti. (jā. 1.10.97) –

'We do not transgress against our wives, nor do our wives transgress against us; except with them, we live the holy life, therefore our young ones do not die.'

Evamādīsu [V 1.0036] sadārasantoso. Idha pana samaṇadhammabrahmacariyapubbaṅgamaṃ uparimaggabrahmacariyamadhippetaṃ. Sugateti sugatassa santike. Bhagavā hi antadvayamanupaggamma suṭṭhu gatattā, sobhaṇena ca ariyamaggagamanena samannāgatattā, sundarañca nibbānasaṅkhātaṃ ṭhānaṃ gatattā sugatoti vuccati. Samīpatthe cettha bhummavacanaṃ, tasmā sugatassa santiketi attho. Carāmaseti carāma. Yañhi taṃ sakkate carāmasīti vuccati, taṃ idha carāmaseti. Aṭṭhakathācariyā pana “seti nipāto”ti bhaṇanti. Teneva cettha āyācanatthaṃ sandhāya “carema se”tipi pāṭhaṃ vikappenti. Yaṃ ruccati, taṃ gahetabbaṃ.

In such passages, contentment with one's own wife is meant. Here, however, the holy life of the higher path, which is preceded by the holy life of a recluse, is intended. 'Sugate' means 'in the presence of the Sugata.' The Blessed One is called 'Sugata' because he has gone well, not approaching the two extremes; because he is endowed with the excellent going of the noble path; and because he has gone to the beautiful state known as Nibbāna. Here, the locative case is used in the sense of proximity; therefore, the meaning is 'in the presence of the Sugata.' 'Carāmase' means 'we shall live' (carāma). For what is called 'carāmasi' in Sanskrit, that is here 'carāmase.' The commentary teachers, however, say that 'se' is a particle. Therefore, understanding it to be in the sense of a request, they also suggest the reading 'carema se.' One may adopt whichever is preferred.

Evaṃ dhaniyo brahmacariyacaraṇāpadesena bhagavantaṃ pabbajjaṃ yācitvā pabbajjapayojanaṃ dīpento āha “jātīmaraṇassa pāragū, dukkhassantakarā bhavāmase”ti. Jātimaraṇassa pāraṃ nāma nibbānaṃ, taṃ arahattamaggena [P 1.0044] gacchāma. Dukkhassāti vaṭṭadukkhassa. Antakarāti abhāvakarā. Bhavāmaseti bhavāma, atha vā aho vata mayaṃ bhaveyyāmāti. “Carāmase”ti ettha vuttanayeneva taṃ veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ vatvāpi ca puna ubhopi kira bhagavantaṃ vanditvā “pabbājetha no bhagavā”ti evaṃ pabbajjaṃ yāciṃsūti.

Thus, Dhaniya, requesting ordination from the Blessed One by way of his intention to practice the holy life, and explaining the purpose of ordination, said: 'We shall become those who have gone to the far shore of birth and death, makers of an end to suffering.' The 'far shore of birth and death' is Nibbāna; we shall reach it through the path of arahantship. 'Of suffering' means of the suffering of the cycle of existence. 'Makers of an end' means those who cause its cessation. 'Bhavāmase' means 'we shall become' (bhavāma), or 'Oh, may we become!' This should be understood in the same way as explained earlier regarding 'carāmase.' And having spoken thus, it is said that both of them, having paid homage to the Blessed One, again requested ordination, saying, 'May the Blessed One ordain us.'

33. Atha māro pāpimā evaṃ te ubhopi vanditvā pabbajjaṃ yācante disvā – “ime mama visayaṃ atikkamitukāmā, handa nesaṃ antarāyaṃ karomī”ti āgantvā gharāvāse guṇaṃ dassento imaṃ gāthamāha “nandati puttehi puttimā”ti. Tattha nandatīti tussati modati. Puttehīti puttehipi dhītarehipi, sahayogatthe, karaṇatthe vā karaṇavacanaṃ, puttehi saha nandati, puttehi karaṇabhūtehi nandatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Puttimāti puttavā puggalo. Itīti evamāha. Māroti vasavattibhūmiyaṃ aññataro dāmarikadevaputto. So hi saṭṭhānātikkamitukāmaṃ janaṃ [M 1.0040] yaṃ sakkoti, taṃ māreti. Yaṃ na sakkoti, tassapi maraṇaṃ icchati. Tena “māro”ti vuccati. Pāpimāti lāmakapuggalo, pāpasamācāro vā. Saṅgītikārānametaṃ vacanaṃ, sabbagāthāsu ca īdisāni. Yathā ca puttehi puttimā, gopiyo gohi tatheva nandati. Yassa gāvo atthi, sopi gopiyo, gohi saha, gohi vā karaṇabhūtehi tatheva nandatīti attho.

33. Then Māra the Evil One, seeing them both paying homage and requesting ordination, thought, 'These two wish to escape my domain. Come, let me create an obstacle for them.' Approaching, and showing the virtue of the household life, he recited this verse: 'One with children delights in children.' Herein, nandati means 'is pleased,' 'rejoices.' Puttehi means 'with sons' or 'with daughters'; it is the instrumental case in the sense of association, or in the sense of cause. It is said: 'one delights with children,' or 'one delights because of children.' Puttimā means a person who has children. Iti means 'thus he spoke.' Māro refers to a certain malevolent devaputta in the realm of Vasavatti. For he obstructs whomever he can among the people who wish to escape his domain. For whom he cannot obstruct, he desires that one's death. Therefore, he is called 'Māra.' Pāpimā means a base person, or one of evil conduct. This is a saying of the compilers of the scriptures, and such expressions are found in all the verses. And just as one with children delights in children, so too does one who has cows delight in cows. He who has cows is a gopiya; he delights with cows, or because of cows—this is the meaning.

Evaṃ vatvā idāni tassatthassa sādhakakāraṇaṃ niddisati, “upadhī hi narassa nandanā”ti. Tattha upadhīti cattāro upadhayo – kāmūpadhi, khandhūpadhi, kilesūpadhi, abhisaṅkhārūpadhīti. Kāmā hi “yaṃ pañcakāmaguṇe paṭicca uppajjati sukhaṃ somanassaṃ, ayaṃ kāmānaṃ assādo”ti (ma. ni. 1.166) evaṃ vuttassa sukhassa adhiṭṭhānabhāvato upadhīyati [V 1.0037] ettha sukhanti iminā vacanatthena upadhīti vuccanti. Khandhāpi khandhamūlakadukkhassa adhiṭṭhānabhāvato, kilesāpi apāyadukkhassa adhiṭṭhānabhāvato, abhisaṅkhārāpi bhavadukkhassa [P 1.0045] adhiṭṭhānabhāvatoti. Idha pana kāmūpadhi adhippeto. So sattasaṅkhāravasena duvidho. Tattha sattapaṭibaddho padhāno, taṃ dassento “puttehi gohī”ti vatvā kāraṇamāha – “upadhī hi narassa nandanā”ti. Tassattho – yasmā ime kāmūpadhī narassa nandanā, nandayanti naraṃ pītisomanassaṃ upasaṃharantā, tasmā veditabbametaṃ “nandati puttehi puttimā, gopiyo gohi tatheva nandati, tvañca puttimā gopiyo ca, tasmā etehi, nanda, mā pabbajjaṃ pāṭikaṅkhi. Pabbajitassa hi ete upadhayo na santi, evaṃ sante tvaṃ dukkhassantaṃ patthentopi dukkhitova bhavissasī”ti.

Having said this, he now indicates the supporting reason for that meaning with: 'For attachments are a man's delights.' Herein, upadhi refers to the four attachments: the attachment of sensual pleasures, the attachment of the aggregates, the attachment of the defilements, and the attachment of volitional formations. Sensual pleasures are called upadhi because of this explanation: 'Whatever happiness and joy arise in dependence on the five cords of sensual pleasure, this is the gratification of sensual pleasures' (MN 1.166), and since they are the basis for the happiness thus described, happiness is 'placed upon' (upadhīyati) them. The aggregates are also called attachments because they are the basis for suffering rooted in the aggregates; the defilements, because they are the basis for suffering in the lower realms; and volitional formations, because they are the basis for the suffering of existence. Here, however, the attachment of sensual pleasures is intended. It is twofold: by way of beings and by way of conditioned things. Among these, that which is connected with beings is primary. Indicating this by saying 'with sons, with cattle,' he states the reason: 'For attachments are a man's delights.' The meaning of this is: 'Because these attachments of sensual pleasures are a man's delights—they delight a man, bringing him joy and happiness—therefore this should be understood: "One with sons delights in sons, and one with cattle likewise delights in cattle. And you are one with sons and one with cattle. Therefore, rejoice in these things; do not desire to go forth. For one who has gone forth, these attachments do not exist. That being so, even while you seek the end of suffering, you will only be one who suffers."

Idāni tassapi atthassa sādhakakāraṇaṃ niddisati “na hi so nandati, yo nirūpadhī”ti. Tassattho – yasmā yassete upadhayo natthi, so piyehi ñātīhi vippayutto nibbhogūpakaraṇo na nandati, tasmā tvaṃ ime upadhayo vajjetvā pabbajito dukkhitova bhavissasīti.

Now he indicates the supporting reason for that meaning as well: 'For he does not rejoice who is without attachments.' The meaning of this is: 'Because he for whom these attachments do not exist is separated from dear relatives and is without the means for enjoyment, he does not rejoice. Therefore, you, having abandoned these attachments and gone forth, will indeed be one who suffers.'

34. Atha bhagavā “māro ayaṃ pāpimā imesaṃ antarāyāya āgato”ti viditvā phalena phalaṃ pātento viya tāyeva mārenābhatāya upamāya māravādaṃ bhindanto tameva gāthaṃ parivattetvā “upadhi [M 1.0041] sokavatthū”ti dassento āha “socati puttehi puttimā”ti. Tattha sabbaṃ padatthato uttānameva. Ayaṃ pana adhippāyo – mā, pāpima, evaṃ avaca “nandati puttehi puttimā”ti. Sabbeheva hi piyehi, manāpehi nānābhāvo vinābhāvo, anatikkamanīyo ayaṃ vidhi, tesañca piyamanāpānaṃ puttadārānaṃ gavāssavaḷavahiraññasuvaṇṇādīnaṃ vinābhāvena adhimattasokasallasamappitahadayā sattā ummattakāpi honti khittacittā, maraṇampi nigacchanti maraṇamattampi dukkhaṃ. Tasmā evaṃ gaṇha – socati puttehi puttimā. Yathā ca puttehi puttimā, gopiyo gohi tatheva socatīti. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Upadhī hi narassa socanā. Yasmā ca upadhī hi narassa socanā, tasmā eva “na hi so socati, yo nirūpadhi”. Yo upadhīsu saṅgappahānena nirupadhi hoti, so santuṭṭho hoti kāyaparihārikena cīvarena, kucchiparihārikena piṇḍapātena, yena yeneva pakkamati, samādāyeva pakkamati. Seyyathāpi nāma pakkhī sakuṇo [P 1.0046] …pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānāti. Evaṃ sabbasokasamugghātā “na hi so socati, yo nirupadhī”ti. Iti bhagavā arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ vosāpesi. Atha vā yo nirupadhi, yo nikkileso, so na socati. Yāvadeva hi kilesā santi, tāvadeva sabbe [V 1.0038] upadhayo sokapphalāva honti. Kilesappahānā pana natthi sokoti. Evampi arahattanikūṭeneva desanaṃ vosāpesi. Desanāpariyosāne dhaniyo ca gopī ca ubhopi pabbajiṃsu. Bhagavā ākāseneva jetavanaṃ agamāsi. Te pabbajitvā arahattaṃ sacchikariṃsu. Vasanaṭṭhāne ca nesaṃ gopālakā vihāraṃ kāresuṃ. So ajjāpi gopālakavihārotveva paññāyatīti.

34. Then the Blessed One, knowing, 'This Māra the Evil One has come to create an obstacle for them,' shattering Māra's argument with the very simile brought forth by Māra—like knocking down one fruit with another—turned that very verse around and, showing that 'attachment is a basis for sorrow,' said: 'One with sons grieves on account of sons.' Herein, the meaning of every word is self-evident. This, however, is the intended meaning: 'Do not, O Evil One, speak thus: "One with sons delights in sons." For with all that is dear and beloved, there is separation and parting; this law is insurmountable. And through separation from those dear and beloved ones—sons, wives, cattle, horses, mares, gold, silver, and so on—beings whose hearts are pierced by the dart of excessive sorrow become insane and mentally deranged; they go to their death or suffer pain equivalent to death. Therefore, take it thus: "One with sons grieves on account of sons." And just as one with sons grieves, so too does one with cattle grieve on account of cattle. For what reason? Because attachments are a man's source of sorrow. And since attachments are a man's source of sorrow, it is for this very reason that "He does not grieve who is without attachments." He who becomes without attachments by abandoning clinging to them is content with a robe sufficient for his body and almsfood sufficient for his belly. Wherever he goes, he goes taking only these with him. Just as a bird with wings, wherever it flies... he understands: "There is no more of this state of being." Thus, with all sorrow eradicated, "He does not grieve who is without attachments." In this way, the Blessed One concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of Arahantship. Alternatively: he who is without attachments, who is without defilements, does not grieve. For as long as defilements exist, all attachments have sorrow as their only fruit. But for those who have abandoned the defilements, there is no sorrow. In this way, too, he concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of Arahantship. At the end of the teaching, both Dhaniya and Gopī went forth into homelessness. The Blessed One went to Jetavana through the air. They, having gone forth, realized Arahantship. And at their place of residence, the cowherds built a monastery. To this day, it is known as the Gopālaka Vihāra.'

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

This is from the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya.

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya dhaniyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Herein concludes the explanation of the Dhaniya Sutta, from the Commentary on the Suttanipāta.

3. Khaggavisāṇasuttavaṇṇanā

3. The Exposition of the Khaggavisāṇa Sutta

Sabbesu [M 1.0042][V 1.0039] bhūtesūti khaggavisāṇasuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Sabbasuttānaṃ catubbidhā uppatti – attajjhāsayato, parajjhāsayato, aṭṭhuppattito, pucchāvasito cāti. Dvayatānupassanādīnañhi attajjhāsayato uppatti, mettasuttādīnaṃ parajjhāsayato, uragasuttādīnaṃ aṭṭhuppattito, dhammikasuttādīnaṃ pucchāvasito. Tattha khaggavisāṇasuttassa avisesena pucchāvasito uppatti. Visesena pana yasmā ettha kāci gāthā tena tena paccekasambuddhena puṭṭhena vuttā, kāci apuṭṭhena attanā adhigatamagganayānurūpaṃ udānaṃyeva udānentena, tasmā kāyaci gāthāya pucchāvasito, kāyaci attajjhāsayato uppatti.

The sutta beginning 'Sabbesu bhūtesu' is the Khaggavisāṇa Sutta. What is its origin? The origin of all suttas is fourfold: from personal inclination, from the inclination of others, from an incident, and from a question. Indeed, the origin of the Dvayatānupassanā and similar suttas is from personal inclination; the origin of the Mettā Sutta and similar suttas is from the inclination of others; the origin of the Uraga Sutta and similar suttas is from an incident; and the origin of the Dhammika Sutta and similar suttas is from a question. Here, the Khaggavisāṇa Sutta generally originates from a question. Specifically, however, because some verses here were spoken by certain Paccekabuddhas when questioned, while others were uttered as an inspired utterance in accordance with the path they had realized, some verses originate from a question, and some from personal inclination.

Tattha [P 1.0047] yā ayaṃ avisesena pucchāvasito uppatti, sā ādito pabhuti evaṃ veditabbā – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati. Atha kho āyasmato ānandassa rahogatassa paṭisallīnassa evaṃ cetaso parivitakko udapādi – “buddhānaṃ patthanā ca abhinīhāro ca dissati; tathā sāvakānaṃ, paccekabuddhānaṃ na dissati; yaṃnūnāhaṃ bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā puccheyya”nti. So paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā yathākkamena etamatthaṃ pucchi. Athassa bhagavā pubbayogāvacarasuttaṃ abhāsi –

Regarding this origin, which is generally from a question, it should be understood from the beginning as follows: At one time, the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī. Then, while the Venerable Ānanda was alone in seclusion, this thought arose in his mind: "The aspiration and resolution of the Buddhas are seen; likewise those of the disciples are seen, but those of the Paccekabuddhas are not seen. What if I were to approach the Blessed One and ask him about this matter?" So, emerging from seclusion, he approached the Blessed One and asked him about this matter in due order. Then the Blessed One spoke the Pubbayogāvacara Sutta:

“Pañcime, ānanda, ānisaṃsā pubbayogāvacare diṭṭheva dhamme paṭikacceva aññaṃ ārādheti. No ce diṭṭheva dhamme paṭikacceva aññaṃ ārādheti, atha maraṇakāle aññaṃ ārādheti. No ce maraṇakāle aññaṃ ārādheti, atha devaputto samāno aññaṃ ārādheti, atha buddhānaṃ sammukhībhāve khippābhiñño hoti, atha pacchime kāle paccekasambuddho hotī”ti –

"Ānanda, there are these five benefits for one engaged in prior practice. In this very life, he readily attains final knowledge. If he does not readily attain final knowledge in this very life, then at the time of death he attains final knowledge. If he does not attain final knowledge at the time of death, then, having become a deva, he attains final knowledge. If not then, in the presence of the Buddhas he becomes one of quick direct knowledge. If not even then, in his final existence he becomes a Paccekabuddha."

Evaṃ vatvā puna āha –

Having said this, he said further:

“Paccekabuddhā nāma, ānanda, abhinīhārasampannā pubbayogāvacarā honti. Tasmā buddhapaccekabuddhasāvakānaṃ sabbesaṃ patthanā ca abhinīhāro ca icchitabbo”ti.

"Ānanda, Paccekabuddhas are those accomplished in resolve and engaged in prior practice. Therefore, the aspirations and resolves of all—Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples—are to be desired."

So [V 1.0040][M 1.0043] āha – “buddhānaṃ, bhante, patthanā kīva ciraṃ vaṭṭatī”ti? Buddhānaṃ, ānanda, heṭṭhimaparicchedena cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni kappasatasahassañca, majjhimaparicchedena aṭṭha asaṅkhyeyyāni kappasatasahassañca, uparimaparicchedena soḷasa asaṅkhyeyyāni kappasatasahassañca. Ete ca bhedā paññādhikasaddhādhikavīriyādhikavasena ñātabbā. Paññādhikānañhi saddhā mandā hoti, paññā tikkhā. Saddhādhikānaṃ paññā majjhimā hoti, saddhā balavā. Vīriyādhikānaṃ saddhāpaññā mandā, vīriyaṃ balavanti. Appatvā pana cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni kappasatasahassañca divase divase vessantaradānasadisaṃ [P 1.0048] dānaṃ dentopi tadanurūpasīlādisabbapāramidhamme ācinantopi antarā buddho bhavissatīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Kasmā? Ñāṇaṃ gabbhaṃ na gaṇhāti, vepullaṃ nāpajjati, paripākaṃ na gacchatīti. Yathā nāma timāsacatumāsapañcamāsaccayena nipphajjanakaṃ sassaṃ taṃ taṃ kālaṃ appatvā divase divase sahassakkhattuṃ keḷāyantopi udakena siñcantopi antarā pakkhena vā māsena vā nipphādessatīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Kasmā? Sassaṃ gabbhaṃ na gaṇhāti, vepullaṃ nāpajjati, paripākaṃ na gacchatīti. Evamevaṃ appatvā cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni…pe… netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatīti. Tasmā yathāvuttameva kālaṃ pāramipūraṇaṃ kātabbaṃ ñāṇaparipākatthāya. Ettakenapi ca kālena buddhattaṃ patthayato abhinīhārakaraṇe aṭṭha sampattiyo icchitabbā. Ayañhi –

He said: "Venerable sir, how long does the aspiration of the Buddhas last?" "Ananda, the aspiration of the Buddhas lasts, by the lower reckoning, for four incalculable ages and a hundred thousand eons; by the middle reckoning, for eight incalculable ages and a hundred thousand eons; by the higher reckoning, for sixteen incalculable ages and a hundred thousand eons. These distinctions should be understood according to whether wisdom, faith, or energy is predominant. For those in whom wisdom is predominant, faith is weak, but wisdom is sharp. For those in whom faith is predominant, wisdom is moderate, but faith is strong. For those in whom energy is predominant, both faith and wisdom are weak, but energy is strong. However, without having reached four incalculable ages and a hundred thousand eons, even if one were to give gifts similar to those of Vessantara every single day and accumulate all the perfections like morality and so forth, it is not possible that one would become a Buddha in the meantime. Why? Because the knowledge does not form an embryo, does not reach full development, and does not come to maturity. Just as with a crop that ripens after three, four, or five months, without having reached its proper time, it is not possible that one could bring it to fruition in the meantime—within half a month or a month—even if one were to cherish it a thousand times a day or water it. Why? Because the crop does not form an embryo, does not reach full development, and does not come to maturity. In the same way, without attaining four incalculable ages... it is not possible. Therefore, one must fulfill the perfections for the stated period in order to mature the knowledge. Moreover, for one who aspires to Buddhahood and makes the resolution during such a time, eight accomplishments should be desired. For it is said—

“Manussattaṃ liṅgasampatti, hetu satthāradassanaṃ;

Pabbajjā guṇasampatti, adhikāro ca chandatā;

Aṭṭhadhammasamodhānā, abhinīhāro samijjhatī”ti. (bu. vaṃ. 2.59);

"Human existence, accomplishment in gender, the right conditions, the sight of the Teacher;

Going forth, accomplishment in qualities, a decisive act, and zeal;

When these eight factors converge,

The resolution succeeds."

Abhinīhāroti ca mūlapaṇidhānassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tattha manussattanti manussajāti. Aññatra hi manussajātiyā avasesajātīsu devajātiyampi ṭhitassa paṇidhi na ijjhati. Ettha ṭhitena pana buddhattaṃ patthentena dānādīni puññakammāni katvā manussattaṃyeva patthetabbaṃ. Tattha ṭhatvā paṇidhi kātabbo. Evañhi samijjhati. Liṅgasampattīti purisabhāvo. Mātugāmanapuṃsakaubhatobyañjanakānañhi manussajātiyaṃ ṭhitānampi paṇidhi na samijjhati. Tattha ṭhitena pana buddhattaṃ patthentena dānādīni puññakammāni katvā purisabhāvoyeva patthetabbo. Tattha ṭhatvā paṇidhi kātabbo. Evañhi [M 1.0044] samijjhati. Hetūti arahattassa upanissayasampatti. Yo hi tasmiṃ attabhāve vāyamanto [P 1.0049] arahattaṃ pāpuṇituṃ samattho, tassa samijjhati, no itarassa, yathā sumedhapaṇḍitassa. So hi dīpaṅkarapādamūle pabbajitvā tenattabhāvena arahattaṃ pāpuṇituṃ samattho ahosi[V 1.0041]. Satthāradassananti buddhānaṃ sammukhādassanaṃ. Evañhi ijjhati, no aññathā; yathā sumedhapaṇḍitassa. So hi dīpaṅkaraṃ sammukhā disvā paṇidhesi. Pabbajjāti anagāriyabhāvo. So ca kho sāsane vā kammavādikiriyavāditāpasaparibbājakanikāye vā vaṭṭati yathā sumedhapaṇḍitassa. So hi sumedho nāma tāpaso hutvā paṇidhesi. Guṇasampattīti jhānādiguṇapaṭilābho. Pabbajitassāpi hi guṇasampannasseva ijjhati, no itarassa; yathā sumedhapaṇḍitassa. So hi pañcābhiñño aṭṭhasamāpattilābhī ca hutvā paṇidhesi. Adhikāroti adhikakāro, pariccāgoti attho. Jīvitādipariccāgañhi katvā paṇidahatoyeva ijjhati, no itarassa; yathā sumedhapaṇḍitassa. So hi –

The word 'abhinīhāra' is a term for the root aspiration. Herein, 'human existence' means the human species. For, apart from the human species, among the remaining species, even for one established in the divine species, the aspiration does not succeed. But one established thus, aspiring to Buddhahood, should perform meritorious deeds such as giving and aspire only for human existence. Having become established therein, the aspiration should be made. For thus it succeeds. 'Attainment of the right sex' means the male state. For even those established in the human species who are women, neuters, or hermaphrodites, the aspiration does not succeed. But one established thus, aspiring to Buddhahood, should perform meritorious deeds such as giving and aspire only for the male state. Having become established therein, the aspiration should be made. For thus it succeeds. 'Cause' means the attainment of the supporting condition for Arahantship. For whoever, by striving in that very existence, is capable of attaining Arahantship, for him it succeeds, but not for another; as in the case of the wise Sumedha. For he, having gone forth at the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, was capable of attaining Arahantship in that very existence. 'Seeing the Teacher' means seeing the Buddhas face to face. For thus it succeeds, and not otherwise; as in the case of the wise Sumedha. For he, having seen the Buddha Dīpaṅkara face to face, made his aspiration. 'Going forth' means the homeless state. And this is valid either in the Dispensation or among the sects of ascetics and wanderers who are proponents of kamma and action; as in the case of the wise Sumedha. For he, having become an ascetic named Sumedha, made his aspiration. 'Attainment of qualities' means the acquisition of qualities such as the jhānas. For even for one who has gone forth, it succeeds only for one who is endowed with such qualities, but not for another; as in the case of the wise Sumedha. For he, having become one who possessed the five supernormal knowledges and had attained the eight meditative attainments, made his aspiration. 'Extraordinary service' means an extraordinary deed; the meaning is 'sacrifice.' For it succeeds only for one who makes an aspiration after having made a sacrifice of life and so on, but not for another; as in the case of the wise Sumedha. For he—

“Akkamitvāna maṃ buddho, saha sissehi gacchatu;

Mā naṃ kalale akkamittha, hitāya me bhavissatī”ti. (bu. vaṃ. 2.53) –

Having stepped on me, let the Buddha proceed with his disciples; let him not step in the mire—this will be for my welfare.

Evaṃ jīvitapariccāgaṃ katvā paṇidhesi. Chandatāti kattukamyatā. Sā yassa balavatī hoti, tassa ijjhati. Sā ca, sace koci vadeyya “ko cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni satasahassañca kappe niraye paccitvā buddhattaṃ icchatī”ti, taṃ sutvā yo “aha”nti vattuṃ ussahati, tassa balavatīti veditabbā. Tathā yadi koci vadeyya “ko sakalacakkavāḷaṃ vītaccikānaṃ aṅgārānaṃ pūraṃ akkamanto atikkamitvā buddhattaṃ icchati, ko sakalacakkavāḷaṃ sattisūlehi ākiṇṇaṃ akkamanto atikkamitvā buddhattaṃ icchati, ko sakalacakkavāḷaṃ samatittikaṃ udakapuṇṇaṃ uttaritvā buddhattaṃ icchati, ko sakalacakkavāḷaṃ nirantaraṃ veḷugumbasañchannaṃ maddanto atikkamitvā buddhattaṃ icchatī”ti taṃ sutvā yo “aha”nti vattuṃ ussahati, tassa balavatīti veditabbā. Evarūpena ca kattukamyatāchandena samannāgato sumedhapaṇḍito paṇidhesīti.

Thus, having made a sacrifice of his life, he made his aspiration. 'Eagerness' means the will to act. For whom this is strong, for him it succeeds. And if someone were to say, 'Who, after being tormented in hell for four incalculable and one hundred thousand aeons, would desire Buddhahood?'—upon hearing this, whoever is able to say, 'I am,' his will should be known as strong. Likewise, if someone were to say, 'Who, by treading upon and crossing over the entire world-system filled with flameless embers, would desire Buddhahood? Who, by treading upon and crossing over the entire world-system strewn with spears and stakes, would desire Buddhahood? Who, by swimming across the entire world-system filled to the brim with water, would desire Buddhahood? Who, by crushing and crossing over the entire world-system continuously covered with bamboo thickets, would desire Buddhahood?'—upon hearing this, whoever is able to say, 'I am,' his will should be known as strong. Endowed with such a will to act, the wise Sumedha made his aspiration.

Evaṃ [M 1.0045] samiddhābhinīhāro [P 1.0050] ca bodhisatto imāni aṭṭhārasa abhabbaṭṭhānāni na upeti. So hi tato pabhuti na jaccandho hoti, na jaccabadhiro, na ummattako, na eḷamūgo, na pīṭhasappī, na milakkhūsu uppajjati, na dāsikucchiyā nibbattati, na niyatamicchādiṭṭhiko hoti, nāssa liṅgaṃ parivattati, na pañcānantariyakammāni karoti, na kuṭṭhī hoti, na tiracchānayoniyaṃ vaṭṭakato pacchimattabhāvo hoti, na khuppipāsikanijjhāmataṇhikapetesu uppajjati, na kālakañcikāsuresu, na avīciniraye, na lokantarikesu, kāmāvacaresu na māro [V 1.0042] hoti, rūpāvacaresu na asaññībhave, na suddhāvāsabhavesu uppajjati, na arūpabhavesu, na aññaṃ cakkavāḷaṃ saṅkamati.

Thus, a Bodhisatta whose aspiration is successful does not arrive at these eighteen impossible states. From that time onwards, he is not born blind, nor born deaf; he is not insane, nor a deaf-mute, nor a cripple; he is not born among barbarians, nor conceived in a slave’s womb; he does not hold fixed wrong views, nor does his sex change; he does not commit the five deeds with immediate retribution; he is not a leper; when born in the animal realm, his body is never smaller than that of a quail; he is not born among the 'hunger-and-thirst-tormented' petas or the 'parched-with-thirst' petas, nor among the Kālakañjaka asuras; not in the Avīci hell, nor in the interstitial hells; in the sense-sphere realms, he does not become Māra; in the fine-material-sphere realms, he is not born in the sphere of non-percipient beings, nor in the Pure Abodes; he is not born in the immaterial-sphere realms; and he does not transmigrate to another world-system.

Yā cimā ussāho ummaṅgo avatthānaṃ hitacariyā cāti catasso buddhabhūmiyo, tāhi samannāgato hoti. Tattha –

He possesses these four grounds of a Buddha: zeal, ingenuity, steadfastness, and beneficent conduct. Herein—

“Ussāho vīriyaṃ vuttaṃ, ummaṅgo paññā pavuccati;

Avatthānaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ, hitacariyā mettābhāvanā”ti. –

Zeal is said to be energy; ingenuity is declared as wisdom; steadfastness is determination; beneficent conduct is the development of loving-kindness.

Veditabbā. Ye cāpi ime nekkhammajjhāsayo, pavivekajjhāsayo, alobhajjhāsayo, adosajjhāsayo, amohajjhāsayo, nissaraṇajjhāsayoti cha ajjhāsayā bodhiparipākāya saṃvattanti, yehi samannāgatattā nekkhammajjhāsayā ca bodhisattā kāme dosadassāvino, pavivekajjhāsayā ca bodhisattā saṅgaṇikāya dosadassāvino, alobhajjhāsayā ca bodhisattā lobhe dosadassāvino, adosajjhāsayā ca bodhisattā dose dosadassāvino, amohajjhāsayā ca bodhisattā mohe dosadassāvino, nissaraṇajjhāsayā ca bodhisattā sabbabhavesu dosadassāvinoti vuccanti, tehi ca samannāgato hoti.

This should be understood. Furthermore, these six dispositions—the disposition towards renunciation, the disposition towards seclusion, the disposition towards non-greed, the disposition towards non-hatred, the disposition towards non-delusion, and the disposition towards escape—conduce to the maturing of enlightenment. Because of being endowed with these, Bodhisattas with a disposition towards renunciation are said to be those who see the danger in sensual pleasures; Bodhisattas with a disposition towards seclusion are said to be those who see the danger in company; Bodhisattas with a disposition towards non-greed are said to be those who see the danger in greed; Bodhisattas with a disposition towards non-hatred are said to be those who see the danger in hatred; Bodhisattas with a disposition towards non-delusion are said to be those who see the danger in delusion; and Bodhisattas with a disposition towards escape are said to be those who see the danger in all forms of existence. And he is endowed with these.

Paccekabuddhānaṃ pana kīva ciraṃ patthanā vaṭṭatīti? Paccekabuddhānaṃ dve asaṅkhyeyyāni kappasatasahassañca. Tato oraṃ na sakkā. Pubbe vuttanayenevettha kāraṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Ettakenāpi [P 1.0051] ca kālena paccekabuddhattaṃ patthayato abhinīhārakaraṇe pañca sampattiyo icchitabbā. Tesañhi –

For how long is the aspiration of the Paccekabuddhas valid? For the Paccekabuddhas, it is for two incalculable aeons and one hundred thousand aeons. Less than that is not possible. Here, the reason should be understood in the manner previously stated. And even for this length of time, one aspiring to Paccekabuddhahood must desire five accomplishments at the time of making the resolution. For them:

Manussattaṃ [M 1.0046] liṅgasampatti, vigatāsavadassanaṃ;

Adhikāro chandatā ete, abhinīhārakāraṇā.

Human existence, the attainment of the male gender, seeing one who is free from taints, a foundational act of service, and ardent desire—these are the causes for the resolution.

Tattha vigatāsavadassananti buddhapaccekabuddhasāvakānaṃ yassa kassaci dassananti attho. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

Therein, 'seeing one who is free from taints' means seeing any one of the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, or their disciples. The rest is just as has been previously stated.

Atha sāvakānaṃ patthanā kittakaṃ vaṭṭatīti? Dvinnaṃ aggasāvakānaṃ ekaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ kappasatasahassañca, asītimahāsāvakānaṃ kappasatasahassaṃ, tathā buddhassa mātāpitūnaṃ upaṭṭhākassa [V 1.0043] puttassa cāti. Tato oraṃ na sakkā. Vuttanayamevettha kāraṇaṃ. Imesaṃ pana sabbesampi adhikāro chandatāti dvaṅgasampannoyeva abhinīhāro hoti.

Then, for how long is the aspiration of the disciples valid? For the two chief disciples, one incalculable aeon and one hundred thousand aeons; for the eighty great disciples, one hundred thousand aeons; and likewise for the Buddha’s parents, attendant, and son. Less than that is not possible. The reason here is as previously stated. For all of these, however, the resolution is endowed with only two factors: a foundational act of service and ardent desire.

Evaṃ imāya patthanāya iminā ca abhinīhārena yathāvuttappabhedaṃ kālaṃ pāramiyo pūretvā buddhā loke uppajjantā khattiyakule vā brāhmaṇakule vā uppajjanti, paccekabuddhā khattiyabrāhmaṇagahapatikulānaṃ aññatarasmiṃ, aggasāvakā pana khattiyabrāhmaṇakulesveva buddhā iva sabbabuddhā saṃvaṭṭamāne kappe na uppajjanti, vivaṭṭamāne kappe uppajjanti. Paccekabuddhā buddhe appatvā buddhānaṃ uppajjanakāleyeva uppajjanti. Buddhā sayañca bujjhanti, pare ca bodhenti. Paccekabuddhā sayameva bujjhanti, na pare bodhenti. Attharasameva paṭivijjhanti, na dhammarasaṃ. Na hi te lokuttaradhammaṃ paññattiṃ āropetvā desetuṃ sakkonti, mūgena diṭṭhasupino viya vanacarakena nagare sāyitabyañjanaraso viya ca nesaṃ dhammābhisamayo hoti. Sabbaṃ iddhisamāpattipaṭisambhidāpabhedaṃ pāpuṇanti, guṇavisiṭṭhatāya buddhānaṃ heṭṭhā sāvakānaṃ upari honti, aññe pabbājetvā ābhisamācārikaṃ sikkhāpenti, “cittasallekho kātabbo, vosānaṃ nāpajjitabba”nti iminā uddesena uposathaṃ karonti, ‘ajjuposatho’ti [P 1.0052] vacanamattena vā. Uposathaṃ karontā ca gandhamādane mañjūsakarukkhamūle ratanamāḷe sannipatitvā karontīti. Evaṃ bhagavā āyasmato ānandassa paccekabuddhānaṃ sabbākāraparipūraṃ patthanañca abhinīhārañca kathetvā, idāni imāya patthanāya iminā ca abhinīhārena samudāgate te te paccekabuddhe kathetuṃ “sabbesu bhūtesu nidhāya daṇḍa”ntiādinā [M 1.0047] nayena imaṃ khaggavisāṇasuttaṃ abhāsi. Ayaṃ tāva avisesena pucchāvasito khaggavisāṇasuttassa uppatti.

Thus, with this aspiration and this resolution, having fulfilled the perfections over the afore-mentioned period of time, Buddhas, when they arise in the world, arise in either a khattiya family or a brāhmaṇa family. Paccekabuddhas arise in one of the khattiya, brāhmaṇa, or gahapati families. The chief disciples, however, arise only in khattiya or brāhmaṇa families, like the Buddhas. All Buddhas do not arise in a contracting aeon; they arise in an unfolding aeon. Paccekabuddhas arise during an interval between Buddhas. Buddhas awaken by themselves and they cause others to awaken. Paccekabuddhas awaken by themselves, but they do not cause others to awaken. They penetrate only the flavor of the meaning, not the flavor of the Dhamma. For they are unable to teach by formulating the supramundane Dhamma into concepts. Their realization of the Dhamma is like a dream seen by a mute person, or like the flavor of a city curry tasted by a forest-dweller. They attain all the varieties of psychic powers, meditative attainments, and analytical knowledges. Due to the distinction of their qualities, they are below the Buddhas but above the disciples. They give the going forth to others and train them in the proper conduct for recluses, saying, ‘The mind should be effaced; one should not cease striving.’ They perform the Uposatha with this brief instruction, or simply by the statement, ‘Today is the Uposatha.’ And when performing the Uposatha, they gather and do so on Mount Gandhamādana, at the foot of a Mañjūsaka tree, on the Jeweled Terrace. In this way, having explained to the Venerable Ānanda the aspiration and resolution of the Paccekabuddhas, complete in all aspects, the Blessed One, in order to speak of those various Paccekabuddhas who had come to be through this aspiration and this resolution, delivered this Khaggavisāṇa Sutta by the method beginning with, ‘Having laid aside the rod toward all beings…’ This, for now, is the general origin of the Khaggavisāṇa Sutta, which concludes the questioning.

35. Idāni visesena vattabbā. Tattha imissā tāva gāthāya evaṃ uppatti veditabbā – ayaṃ kira paccekabuddho paccekabodhisattabhūmiṃ ogāhanto dve asaṅkhyeyyāni kappasatasahassañca pāramiyo pūretvā kassapassa bhagavato sāsane pabbajitvā āraññiko hutvā gatapaccāgatavattaṃ pūrento samaṇadhammaṃ akāsi. Etaṃ kira vattaṃ aparipūretvā paccekabodhiṃ pāpuṇantā nāma natthi. Kiṃ panetaṃ gatapaccāgatavattaṃ nāma? Haraṇapaccāharaṇanti. Taṃ yathā vibhūtaṃ hoti, tathā kathessāma.

35. Now, this is to be told in detail. Therein, first, the origin of this verse should be understood thus: This Paccekabuddha, it is said, while entering upon the stage of a Paccekabodhisatta, fulfilled the perfections for two incalculable aeons and one hundred thousand aeons. Having gone forth in the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, he became a forest-dweller and, while fulfilling the observance of going and returning, practiced the duties of a recluse. Indeed, it is said that there are none who attain Paccekabodhi without having fulfilled this observance. What, then, is this observance of going and returning? It is carrying forth and bringing back. We shall explain this in such a way that it becomes clear.

Idhekacco bhikkhu harati, na paccāharati; ekacco paccāharati, na harati; ekacco pana neva harati, na paccāharati; ekacco harati ca paccāharati ca. Tattha yo bhikkhu pageva vuṭṭhāya cetiyaṅgaṇabodhiyaṅgaṇavattaṃ katvā, bodhirukkhe udakaṃ āsiñcitvā, pānīyaghaṭaṃ pūretvā [V 1.0044] pānīyamāḷe ṭhapetvā, ācariyavattaṃ upajjhāyavattaṃ katvā, dveasīti khuddakavattāni cuddasa mahāvattāni ca samādāya vattati, so sarīraparikammaṃ katvā, senāsanaṃ pavisitvā, yāva bhikkhācāravelā tāva vivittāsane vītināmetvā, velaṃ ñatvā, nivāsetvā, kāyabandhanaṃ bandhitvā, uttarāsaṅgaṃ karitvā, saṅghāṭiṃ khandhe karitvā, pattaṃ aṃse ālaggetvā, kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasi [P 1.0053] karonto cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ patvā, cetiyañca bodhiñca vanditvā, gāmasamīpe cīvaraṃ pārupitvā, pattamādāya gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pavisati, evaṃ paviṭṭho ca lābhī bhikkhu puññavā upāsakehi sakkatagarukato upaṭṭhākakule vā paṭikkamanasālāyaṃ vā paṭikkamitvā upāsakehi taṃ taṃ pañhaṃ pucchiyamāno tesaṃ pañhavissajjanena dhammadesanāvikkhepena ca taṃ manasikāraṃ chaḍḍetvā nikkhamati, vihāraṃ āgatopi bhikkhūnaṃ pañhaṃ puṭṭho katheti, dhammaṃ bhaṇati, taṃ taṃ byāpāramāpajjati, pacchābhattampi purimayāmampi majjhimayāmampi evaṃ bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ papañcitvā kāyaduṭṭhullābhibhūto pacchimayāmepi sayati, neva kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasi karoti, ayaṃ vuccati harati, na paccāharatīti.

Herein, a certain monk carries forth, but does not bring back; another brings back, but does not carry forth; another neither carries forth nor brings back; and another both carries forth and brings back. Therein, a monk who, having risen early, performs the observances of the cetiya-courtyard and the Bodhi-courtyard, pours water on the Bodhi tree, fills the water pot and places it on the water-stand, performs his duties to his teacher and preceptor, and undertakes and practices the eighty-two minor observances; he, having attended to his body, enters his dwelling place and, until it is time for the alms-round, passes the time on a secluded seat. Knowing the time, he dresses, fastens his belt, puts on his upper robe, places his outer robe on his shoulder, slings his bowl over his shoulder, and, keeping his meditation subject in mind, goes to the cetiya-courtyard. Having paid homage to the cetiya and the Bodhi tree, he puts on his robe near the village and enters the village for alms. Having entered thus, this monk, who is fortunate in receiving requisites and is meritorious, being respected and honored by the lay devotees, goes to the house of his supporters or to a reception hall. Being asked various questions by the lay devotees, he abandons his mental application through answering their questions and the distraction of giving a Dhamma talk, and then departs. Even upon returning to the monastery, when asked questions by the monks, he speaks, teaches the Dhamma, and gets involved in various affairs. After the meal, and also in the first and middle watches of the night, he thus engages in proliferation with the monks and, being overcome by physical sluggishness, he sleeps even in the last watch. He never brings his meditation subject to mind. This one is called: ‘He carries forth, but does not bring back.’

Yo [M 1.0048] pana byādhibahulo hoti, bhuttāhāro paccūsasamaye na sammā pariṇamati, pageva vuṭṭhāya yathāvuttaṃ vattaṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti kammaṭṭhānaṃ vā manasi kātuṃ, aññadatthu yāguṃ vā bhesajjaṃ vā patthayamāno kālasseva pattacīvaramādāya gāmaṃ pavisati. Tattha yāguṃ vā bhesajjaṃ vā bhattaṃ vā laddhā bhattakiccaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā, paññattāsane nisinno kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasi katvā, visesaṃ patvā vā appatvā vā, vihāraṃ āgantvā, teneva manasikārena viharati. Ayaṃ vuccati paccāharati na haratīti. Edisā ca bhikkhū yāguṃ pivitvā, vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā, buddhasāsane arahattaṃ pattā gaṇanapathaṃ vītivattā. Sīhaḷadīpeyeva tesu tesu gāmesu āsanasālāya na taṃ āsanaṃ atthi, yattha yāguṃ pivitvā arahattaṃ patto bhikkhu natthīti.

Now, a certain monk is very sickly; the food he has eaten does not digest well at dawn, and rising early, he is unable to perform the aforementioned duties or to attend to a meditation subject. Instead, desiring gruel or medicine, he takes his bowl and robe early and enters the village. There, having obtained gruel, medicine, or food, and having concluded the meal, he sits on the appointed seat and attends to his meditation subject. Whether he attains a higher state or not, he returns to the monastery and dwells with that very same attention. This one is called 'he brings back but does not carry away.' And such monks, having drunk gruel and undertaken insight meditation, who attained Arahantship in the Buddha's Dispensation, are beyond reckoning. Indeed, in the island of Sri Lanka, in those various villages, there is no seat in the assembly halls where a monk, having drunk gruel, has not attained Arahantship.

Yo pana pamādavihārī hoti nikkhittadhuro, sabbavattāni bhinditvā pañcavidhacetokhilavinibandhanabaddhacitto viharanto kammaṭṭhānamanasikāramananuyutto gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pavisitvā gihipapañcena papañcito tucchako nikkhamati, ayaṃ vuccati neva harati na paccāharatīti.

Now, a certain monk dwells in heedlessness, having cast off the yoke. Having broken all observances, dwelling with a mind bound by the five kinds of mental barrenness and fetters, unyoked from attention to his meditation subject, he enters the village for alms. Having become ensnared in the conceptual proliferation of householders, he departs empty. This one is called 'he neither carries away nor brings back.'

Yo pana pageva [P 1.0054] vuṭṭhāya purimanayeneva sabbavattāni paripūretvā yāva bhikkhācāravelā, tāva pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasi karoti. Kammaṭṭhānaṃ nāma duvidhaṃ – sabbatthakaṃ, pārihāriyañca. Sabbatthakaṃ nāma mettā ca maraṇassati ca. Taṃ sabbattha icchitabbato “sabbatthaka”nti vuccati. Mettā nāma āvāsādīsu sabbattha icchitabbā. Āvāsesu hi mettāvihārī [V 1.0045] bhikkhu sabrahmacārīnaṃ piyo hoti, tena phāsu asaṅghaṭṭho viharati. Devatāsu mettāvihārī devatāhi rakkhitagopito sukhaṃ viharati. Rājarājamahāmattādīsu mettāvihārī, tehi mamāyito sukhaṃ viharati. Gāmanigamādīsu mettāvihārī sabbattha bhikkhācariyādīsu manussehi sakkatagarukato sukhaṃ viharati. Maraṇassatibhāvanāya jīvitanikantiṃ pahāya appamatto viharati.

Now, a certain monk, rising early and fulfilling all duties in the same way as before, sits cross-legged until the time for the alms-round and attends to his meditation subject. A meditation subject is of two kinds: the universal and the one to be maintained. The universal consists of loving-kindness and mindfulness of death. It is called 'universal' because it is desirable everywhere. Loving-kindness is desirable everywhere, in dwellings and so forth. For a monk dwelling with loving-kindness in a dwelling is dear to his companions in the holy life; thus he dwells comfortably and without conflict. Dwelling with loving-kindness towards deities, he dwells happily, protected and guarded by the deities. Dwelling with loving-kindness towards kings, royal ministers, and so forth, he dwells happily, cherished by them. Dwelling with loving-kindness in villages, towns, and so forth, he is respected and honored by people everywhere during his alms-round and so on, and dwells happily. Through the development of mindfulness of death, he abandons craving for life and dwells heedfully.

Yaṃ pana sadā pariharitabbaṃ caritānukūlena gahitattā dasāsubhakasiṇānussatīsu aññataraṃ, catudhātuvavatthānameva vā, taṃ sadā pariharitabbato, rakkhitabbato, bhāvetabbato ca pārihāriyanti vuccati, mūlakammaṭṭhānantipi [M 1.0049] tadeva. Tattha yaṃ paṭhamaṃ sabbatthakakammaṭṭhānaṃ manasi karitvā pacchā pārihāriyakammaṭṭhānaṃ manasi karoti, taṃ catudhātuvavatthānamukhena dassessāma.

Now, that which, having been taken up in accordance with one's temperament—be it any one of the ten kinds of foulness, the ten kasiṇas, or the ten recollections, or the defining of the four elements—should always be maintained, is called the 'one to be maintained' (pārihāriya) because it should always be maintained, protected, and developed. It is also the root meditation subject. Herein, we shall show, by way of the defining of the four elements, how one first attends to the universal meditation subject and afterwards attends to the one to be maintained.

Ayañhi yathāṭhitaṃ yathāpaṇihitaṃ kāyaṃ dhātuso paccavekkhati – yaṃ imasmiṃ sarīre vīsatikoṭṭhāsesu kakkhaḷaṃ kharagataṃ, sā pathavīdhātu. Yaṃ dvādasasu ābandhanakiccakaraṃ snehagataṃ, sā āpodhātu. Yaṃ catūsu paripācanakaraṃ usumagataṃ, sā tejodhātu. Yaṃ pana chasu vitthambhanakaraṃ vāyogataṃ, sā vāyodhātu. Yaṃ panettha catūhi mahābhūtehi asamphuṭṭhaṃ chiddaṃ vivaraṃ, sā ākāsadhātu. Taṃvijānanakaṃ cittaṃ viññāṇadhātu. Tato uttari añño satto vā puggalo vā natthi. Kevalaṃ suddhasaṅkhārapuñjova [P 1.0055] ayanti.

For one reviews this body, however it is placed or disposed, element-wise: Whatever in this body, among the twenty parts, is hard and solid, that is the earth element. Whatever among the twelve parts performs the function of binding and is cohesive, that is the water element. Whatever among the four parts performs the function of maturing and is of the nature of heat, that is the fire element. And whatever among the six parts performs the function of supporting and is of the nature of motion, that is the air element. Whatever here is untouched by the four great elements—the aperture, the space—that is the space element. The consciousness that cognizes this is the consciousness element. Beyond these, there is no other being or person. This is merely a heap of bare formations.

Evaṃ ādimajjhapariyosānato kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasi karitvā, kālaṃ ñatvā, uṭṭhāyāsanā nivāsetvā, pubbe vuttanayeneva gāmaṃ piṇḍāya gacchati. Gacchanto ca yathā andhaputhujjanā abhikkamādīsu “attā abhikkamati, attanā abhikkamo nibbattito”ti vā, “ahaṃ abhikkamāmi, mayā abhikkamo nibbattito”ti vā sammuyhanti, tathā asammuyhanto “abhikkamāmīti citte uppajjamāne teneva cittena saddhiṃ cittasamuṭṭhānā sandhāraṇavāyodhātu uppajjati. Sā imaṃ pathavīdhātvādisannivesabhūtaṃ kāyasammataṃ aṭṭhikasaṅghāṭaṃ vippharati, tato cittakiriyāvāyodhātuvipphāravasena ayaṃ kāyasammato aṭṭhikasaṅghāṭo abhikkamati. Tassevaṃ abhikkamato ekekapāduddhāraṇe catūsu dhātūsu vāyodhātuanugatā tejodhātu adhikā uppajjati, mandā itarā. Atiharaṇavītiharaṇāpaharaṇesu pana tejodhātuanugatā vāyodhātu adhikā uppajjati, mandā itarā. Orohaṇe pana pathavīdhātuanugatā āpodhātu adhikā uppajjati, mandā itarā. Sannikkhepanasamuppīḷanesu āpodhātuanugatā pathavīdhātu adhikā uppajjati, mandā itarā. Iccetā dhātuyo tena tena attano uppādakacittena saddhiṃ tattha tattheva bhijjanti[V 1.0046]. Tattha ko eko abhikkamati, kassa vā ekassa abhikkamana”nti evaṃ ekekapāduddhāraṇādippakāresu ekekasmiṃ pakāre uppannadhātuyo, tadavinibbhuttā ca sesā rūpadhammā, taṃsamuṭṭhāpakaṃ cittaṃ, taṃsampayuttā ca [M 1.0050] sesā arūpadhammāti ete rūpārūpadhammā. Tato paraṃ atiharaṇavītiharaṇādīsu aññaṃ pakāraṃ na sampāpuṇanti, tattha tattheva bhijjanti. Tasmā aniccā. Yañca aniccaṃ, taṃ dukkhaṃ. Yaṃ dukkhaṃ, tadanattāti evaṃ sabbākāraparipūraṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikarontova gacchati. Atthakāmā hi kulaputtā sāsane pabbajitvā dasapi vīsampi tiṃsampi cattālīsampi paññāsampi saṭṭhipi sattatipi satampi ekato vasantā katikavattaṃ katvā viharanti – “āvuso, tumhe na iṇaṭṭhā, na bhayaṭṭhā, na jīvikāpakatā pabbajitā; dukkhā muccitukāmā panettha pabbajitā. Tasmā gamane uppannakilesaṃ gamaneyeva niggaṇhatha, ṭhāne nisajjāya, sayane uppannakilesaṃ gamaneyeva niggaṇhathā”ti. Te evaṃ katikavattaṃ katvā bhikkhācāraṃ gacchantā aḍḍhausabhausabhaaḍḍhagāvutagāvutantaresu pāsāṇā honti, tāya saññāya kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikarontāva gacchanti. Sace kassaci gamane kileso uppajjati, tattheva naṃ niggaṇhāti. Tathā asakkonto tiṭṭhati. Athassa pacchato āgacchantopi tiṭṭhati. So – “ayaṃ bhikkhu tuyhaṃ uppannavitakkaṃ jānāti, ananucchavikaṃ te eta”nti attānaṃ paṭicodetvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā tattheva ariyabhūmiṃ okkamati. Tathā asakkonto nisīdati. Athassa pacchato āgacchantopi nisīdatīti soyeva nayo. Ariyabhūmi okkamituṃ asakkontopi taṃ kilesaṃ vikkhambhetvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikarontova gacchati. Na kammaṭṭhānavippayuttena cittena pādaṃ uddharati. Uddharati ce, paṭinivattitvā purimappadesaṃyeva eti sīhaḷadīpe ālindakavāsī mahāphussadevatthero viya[P 1.0056].

Having thus attended to the meditation subject from beginning, middle, and end, knowing the time, rising from the seat, and dressing, one goes to the village for alms in the manner previously stated. And while walking, unlike blind ordinary people who become confused in movements such as going forward, thinking, 'The self goes forward, the going forward is produced by the self,' or 'I go forward, the going forward is produced by me,' one does not become confused. Instead, when the thought 'I am going forward' arises in the mind, along with that mind, the sustaining wind element arising from the mind arises. It pervades this collection of bones, designated as the body, which is established in the earth element and other elements. Then, by means of the pervasion of the wind element produced by mental activity, this collection of bones, designated as the body, moves forward. As one thus moves forward, with each lifting of a foot, among the four elements, the fire element accompanied by the wind element arises predominantly, while the others are weak. In extending, withdrawing, and placing the foot, the wind element accompanied by the fire element arises predominantly, while the others are weak. In lowering, the water element accompanied by the earth element arises predominantly, while the others are weak. In pressing down and compressing, the earth element accompanied by the water element arises predominantly, while the others are weak. Thus, these elements break apart right there, together with the mind that produces them. Here, who is the one that moves forward? Whose movement is it? In this way, in each instance of lifting and placing the foot, the arisen elements, the remaining material phenomena inseparable from them, the mind that produces them, and the remaining immaterial phenomena associated with them—these are the material and immaterial phenomena. Beyond this, they do not reach another state in extending, withdrawing, and so on; they break apart right there. Therefore, they are impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering. What is suffering is non-self. Thus, one walks while fully attending to the meditation subject in every way. For sons of good families who have gone forth in the dispensation desiring their welfare, living together in groups of ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, sixty, seventy, or a hundred, make a pact and dwell thus: 'Venerable sirs, you have not gone forth because of debt, nor out of fear, nor for the sake of a livelihood; you have gone forth here out of a desire to be freed from suffering. Therefore, when a defilement arises while walking, subdue it right there while walking; when it arises while standing, subdue it right there while standing; when it arises while sitting, subdue it right there while sitting; and when it arises while lying down, subdue it right there while lying down.' Having made such a pact, as they go for alms-round, there are stones at intervals of half an usabha, an usabha, half a gāvuta, and a gāvuta; with the perception of these, they go along attending only to their meditation subject. If a defilement arises in someone while walking, he subdues it right there. Being unable to do so, he stops. Then the one coming from behind him also stops. That bhikkhu, reproaching himself, 'This bhikkhu knows the thought that has arisen in you; this is unbecoming of you,' develops insight and right there enters the noble stage. Being unable to do so, he sits down. Then the one coming from behind him also sits down—this is the method in this case as well. Even one who is unable to enter the noble stage, having suppressed that defilement, goes along attending only to the meditation subject. He does not lift his foot with a mind disconnected from the meditation subject. If he does lift it, he turns back and returns to the very same previous spot, like the Elder Mahāphussadeva, the porch-dweller on the island of Sri Lanka.

So kira ekūnavīsati vassāni gatapaccāgatavattaṃ pūrento eva vihāsi. Manussāpi sudaṃ antarāmagge kasantā ca vapantā ca maddantā ca kammāni karontā theraṃ tathā gacchantaṃ disvā – “ayaṃ thero punappunaṃ nivattitvā gacchati, kiṃ nu kho maggamūḷho, udāhu kiñci pamuṭṭho”ti samullapanti. So taṃ anādiyitvā kammaṭṭhānayutteneva cittena samaṇadhammaṃ karonto vīsativassabbhantare arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Arahattappattadivase cassa caṅkamanakoṭiyaṃ adhivatthā devatā aṅgulīhi dīpaṃ ujjāletvā aṭṭhāsi. Cattāropi mahārājāno sakko ca devānamindo, brahmā ca sahampati upaṭṭhānaṃ āgamaṃsu. Tañca obhāsaṃ disvā vanavāsī mahātissatthero taṃ dutiyadivase pucchi [M 1.0051] “rattibhāge āyasmato santike obhāso ahosi, kiṃ so obhāso”ti? Thero vikkhepaṃ karonto “obhāso nāma dīpobhāsopi hoti, maṇiobhāsopī”ti [V 1.0047] evamādiṃ āha. So “paṭicchādetha tumhe”ti nibaddho “āmā”ti paṭijānitvā ārocesi.

It is said that he spent nineteen years fulfilling the practice of going back and forth. And people, it is said, while plowing, sowing, and threshing along the road, doing their work, seeing the elder going in that manner, would say: 'This elder keeps turning back and forth as he goes. Is he confused about the path, or has he forgotten something?' Disregarding them, with his mind devoted to the meditation subject, he practiced the duty of a recluse and within twenty years attained arahantship. And on the day he attained arahantship, a deity dwelling at the end of his walking path stood there, causing her fingers to shine like a lamp. The Four Great Kings, Sakka the king of the devas, and Brahmā Sahampati also came to attend upon him. Seeing that radiance, the forest-dwelling elder Mahātissa asked him the next day: 'Venerable sir, there was a radiance near you during the night. What was that radiance?' The elder, creating a diversion, said: 'Radiance can be the light of a lamp or the light of a gem,' and so on. When pressed further with 'You are concealing it,' he admitted, 'Yes,' and then explained.

Kāḷavallimaṇḍapavāsī mahānāgatthero viya ca. Sopi kira gatapaccāgatavattaṃ pūrento “paṭhamaṃ tāva bhagavato mahāpadhānaṃ pūjemī”ti satta vassāni ṭhānacaṅkamameva adhiṭṭhāsi. Puna soḷasa vassāni gatapaccāgatavattaṃ pūretvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Evaṃ kammaṭṭhānayutteneva cittena pādaṃ uddharanto vippayuttena cittena uddhaṭe pana paṭinivattanto gāmasamīpaṃ gantvā, “gāvī nu pabbajito nū”ti āsaṅkanīyappadese ṭhatvā, saṅghāṭiṃ pārupitvā pattaṃ gahetvā, gāmadvāraṃ patvā, kacchakantarato udakaṃ gahetvā, gaṇḍūsaṃ katvā gāmaṃ pavisati “bhikkhaṃ dātuṃ vā vandituṃ vā upagate manusse ‘dīghāyukā hothā’ti vacanamattenapi mā me kammaṭṭhānavikkhepo ahosī”ti sace pana “ajja, bhante, kiṃ sattamī, udāhu aṭṭhamī”ti divasaṃ pucchanti, udakaṃ gilitvā āroceti. Sace divasapucchakā na honti, nikkhamanavelāyaṃ [P 1.0057] gāmadvāre niṭṭhubhitvāva yāti.

And like the great elder Mahānāga who dwelt at Kāḷavallimaṇḍapa. It is said that he, fulfilling the practice of going and returning, resolved: “First, I will honor the Blessed One’s great striving,” and for seven years, he maintained standing and walking meditation exclusively. Then, after fulfilling the practice of going and returning for another sixteen years, he attained arahantship. Thus, with a mind devoted to his meditation subject, he would lift his foot, but if his mind became distracted while it was lifted, he would turn back. Upon reaching the vicinity of the village, he would stop in a place where one might be an object of doubt, prompting the question, 'Is that a cow or a monk?'. Then, draping his outer robe and taking his alms bowl, he would approach the village gate. Taking water from under his arm, he would rinse his mouth and enter the village, thinking, 'When people approach to give alms or to pay respects, may there be no disturbance to my meditation subject even by the mere utterance, ‘May you live long.’' But if they asked, “Venerable, is today the seventh or the eighth day?” he would swallow the water and then reply. If no one asked about the day, he would spit at the village gate when leaving and go on his way.

Sīhaḷadīpeyeva kalambatitthavihāre vassūpagatā paññāsabhikkhū viya ca. Te kira vassūpanāyikauposathadivase katikavattaṃ akaṃsu – “arahattaṃ appatvā aññamaññaṃ nālapissāmā”ti. Gāmañca piṇḍāya pavisantā gāmadvāre udakagaṇḍūsaṃ katvā pavisiṃsu, divase pucchite udakaṃ gilitvā ārocesuṃ, apucchite gāmadvāre niṭṭhubhitvā vihāraṃ āgamaṃsu. Tattha manussā niṭṭhubhanaṭṭhānaṃ disvā jāniṃsu “ajja eko āgato, ajja dve”ti. Evañca cintesuṃ “kiṃ nu kho ete amheheva saddhiṃ na sallapanti, udāhu aññamaññampi? Yadi aññamaññampi na sallapanti, addhā vivādajātā bhavissanti, handa nesaṃ aññamaññaṃ khamāpessāmā”ti sabbe vihāraṃ agamaṃsu. Tattha paññāsabhikkhūsu vassaṃ upagatesu dve bhikkhū ekokāse nāddasaṃsu. Tato yo tesu cakkhumā puriso, so evamāha – “na, bho, kalahakārakānaṃ vasanokāso īdiso hoti, susammaṭṭhaṃ cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ bodhiyaṅgaṇaṃ, sunikkhittā sammajjaniyo, sūpaṭṭhapitaṃ pānīyaparibhojanīya”nti. Te tatova [M 1.0052] nivattā. Te bhikkhū antotemāseyeva vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā arahattaṃ patvā mahāpavāraṇāya visuddhipavāraṇaṃ pavāresuṃ.

And like the fifty monks who had entered the rains residence at the Kalamba Landing Monastery in the island of Sri Lanka itself. It is said that on the Uposatha day marking the beginning of the rains, they made a pact: “Until we attain arahantship, we will not speak to one another.” When entering the village for alms, they would rinse their mouths with water at the village gate before entering. If asked about the day, they would swallow the water and reply; if not asked, they would spit at the village gate and return to the monastery. There, people, seeing the place of spitting, realized, “Today one has come, today two.” They then thought, “Why do these monks not converse with us, or even with each other? If they do not speak even among themselves, surely a quarrel has arisen. Let us go and reconcile them.” So they all went to the monastery. There, among the fifty monks who had entered the rains, they did not see two monks together in one place. Then, a discerning person among them said, “No, friends, the dwelling place of quarrel-makers is not like this: the courtyard of the shrine and the Bodhi tree are well-swept, the brooms are neatly placed, and drinking water and water for use are properly arranged.” Hearing this, they turned back. Those monks, within those three months, having begun insight meditation, attained arahantship. On the great Pavāraṇā day, they performed the Pavāraṇā of purity.

Evaṃ kāḷavallimaṇḍapavāsī mahānāgatthero viya kalambatitthavihāre vassūpagatabhikkhū viya ca kammaṭṭhānayutteneva cittena pādaṃ uddharanto gāmasamīpaṃ patvā, udakagaṇḍūsaṃ katvā, vīthiyo sallakkhetvā, yattha surāsoṇḍadhuttādayo kalahakārakā caṇḍahatthiassādayo vā natthi, taṃ [V 1.0048] vīthiṃ paṭipajjati. Tattha ca piṇḍāya caramāno na turitaturito viya javena gacchati, javanapiṇḍapātikadhutaṅgaṃ nāma natthi. Visamabhūmibhāgappattaṃ [P 1.0058] pana udakabharitasakaṭamiva niccalova hutvā gacchati. Anugharaṃ paviṭṭho ca dātukāmaṃ adātukāmaṃ vā sallakkhetuṃ tadanurūpaṃ kālaṃ āgamento bhikkhaṃ gahetvā, patirūpe okāse nisīditvā, kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasi karonto āhāre paṭikūlasaññaṃ upaṭṭhapetvā, akkhabbhañjanavaṇālepanaputtamaṃsūpamāvasena paccavekkhanto aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgataṃ āhāraṃ āhāreti, neva davāya na madāya…pe… bhuttāvī ca udakakiccaṃ katvā, muhuttaṃ bhattakilamathaṃ paṭippassambhetvā, yathā pure bhattaṃ, evaṃ pacchā bhattaṃ purimayāmaṃ pacchimayāmañca kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasi karoti. Ayaṃ vuccati harati ceva paccāharati cāti. Evametaṃ haraṇapaccāharaṇaṃ gatapaccāgatavattanti vuccati.

Thus, like the great elder Mahānāga who dwelt at Kāḷavallimaṇḍapa, and like the monks who spent the rains residence at Kalambatittha monastery, with a mind devoted to his meditation subject, he would lift his foot and, upon reaching the vicinity of the village, rinse his mouth with water, observe the streets, and take a path where there are no drunkards, gamblers, troublemakers, or fierce elephants and horses. While walking for alms there, he does not move hurriedly, for there is no ascetic practice called 'swift alms-gathering.' When he comes to uneven ground, he moves steadily, like a cart laden with water. Going from house to house, observing whether the people wish to give or not, and awaiting a suitable time, he receives alms. Then, sitting in a suitable place and keeping his meditation subject in mind, he establishes the perception of the repulsiveness of food. Reflecting on it by way of the similes of greasing an axle, applying ointment to a wound, and eating the flesh of one's son, he consumes the food endowed with eight factors—neither for amusement nor for intoxication... Having eaten, he performs his duties with water, rests for a moment to calm the fatigue from the meal, and then, just as before the meal, so also after the meal, he applies his mind to the meditation subject during the first and last watches of the night. This is called “taking and bringing back.” Thus, this taking and bringing back is called the practice of “going and returning.”

Etaṃ pūrento yadi upanissayasampanno hoti, paṭhamavaye eva arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. No ce paṭhamavaye pāpuṇāti, atha majjhimavaye pāpuṇāti. No ce majjhimavaye pāpuṇāti, atha maraṇasamaye pāpuṇāti. No ce maraṇasamaye pāpuṇāti, atha devaputto hutvā pāpuṇāti. No ce devaputto hutvā pāpuṇāti, atha paccekasambuddho hutvā parinibbāti. No ce paccekasambuddho hutvā parinibbāti, atha buddhānaṃ santike khippābhiñño hoti; seyyathāpi – thero bāhiyo, mahāpañño vā hoti; seyyathāpi thero sāriputto.

Fulfilling this, if one is endowed with supporting conditions, one attains arahantship in the first period of life. If one does not attain it in the first period, then one attains it in the middle period of life. If one does not attain it in the middle period, then one attains it at the time of death. If one does not attain it at the time of death, then one attains it after becoming a deva. If one does not attain it after becoming a deva, then one attains final Nibbāna as a Paccekabuddha. If one does not attain final Nibbāna as a Paccekabuddha, then one becomes of swift insight in the presence of the Buddhas, just like the Elder Bāhiya; or one becomes of great wisdom, just like the Elder Sāriputta.

Ayaṃ pana paccekabodhisatto kassapassa bhagavato sāsane pabbajitvā, āraññiko hutvā, vīsati vassasahassāni etaṃ gatapaccāgatavattaṃ pūretvā, kālaṃ katvā, kāmāvacaradevaloke uppajji. Tato cavitvā bārāṇasirañño aggamahesiyā kucchimhi paṭisandhiṃ aggahesi. Kusalā itthiyo tadaheva gabbhasaṇṭhānaṃ jānanti, sā ca tāsamaññatarā[M 1.0053], tasmā taṃ gabbhapatiṭṭhānaṃ rañño nivedesi. Dhammatā esā, yaṃ puññavante satte gabbhe uppanne mātugāmo [P 1.0059] gabbhaparihāraṃ labhati. Tasmā rājā tassā gabbhaparihāraṃ adāsi. Sā tato pabhuti nāccuṇhaṃ kiñci ajjhoharituṃ labhati, nātisītaṃ, nātiambilaṃ, nātiloṇaṃ, nātikaṭukaṃ, nātitittakaṃ. Accuṇhe hi mātarā ajjhohaṭe gabbhassa lohakumbhivāso viya hoti, atisīte lokantarikavāso viya, accambilaloṇakaṭukatittakesu bhuttesu satthena phāletvā ambilādīhi sittāni viya gabbhaseyyakassa aṅgāni tibbavedanāni honti. Aticaṅkamanaṭṭhānanisajjāsayanatopi naṃ nivārenti – “kucchigatassa sañcalanadukkhaṃ mā ahosī”ti. Mudukattharaṇatthatāya bhūmiyaṃ caṅkamanādīni mattāya kātuṃ labhati, vaṇṇagandhādisampannaṃ sādusappāyaṃ annapānaṃ labhati. Pariggahetvāva naṃ caṅkamāpenti, nisīdāpenti, vuṭṭhāpenti.

Now, this Paccekabodhisatta, having gone forth in the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, lived as a forest-dweller, and after fulfilling the practice of going back and forth for twenty thousand years, he passed away and was reborn in the sensual heavenly realm. Having departed from there, he took conception in the womb of the chief queen of the king of Bārāṇasī. Skillful women know the formation of the embryo on that very day, and she, being one of them, informed the king of her pregnancy. It is a natural law that when meritorious beings are conceived, women receive special care during pregnancy. Therefore, the king provided her with such care. From then on, she could not consume anything too hot, too cold, too sour, too salty, too pungent, or too bitter. For if a mother consumes something too hot, it is as if the fetus dwells in a copper cauldron; if too cold, it is like dwelling in the Lokantarika hell. If excessively sour, salty, pungent, or bitter things are eaten, the limbs of the fetus lying in the womb feel intense pain, as if slashed with a knife and drenched with sour liquids and the like. They also prevented her from excessive walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, thinking, “May there be no suffering from movement for the one in the womb.” She was allowed to walk and perform other activities in moderation on ground spread with soft coverings. She received delicious and agreeable food and drink, endowed with color, fragrance, and other qualities. They made her walk, sit, or rise only after supporting her.

Sā [V 1.0049] evaṃ parihariyamānā gabbhaparipākakāle sūtigharaṃ pavisitvā paccūsasamaye puttaṃ vijāyi pakkatelamadditamanosilāpiṇḍisadisaṃ dhaññapuññalakkhaṇūpetaṃ. Tato naṃ pañcamadivase alaṅkatappaṭiyattaṃ rañño dassesuṃ, rājā tuṭṭho chasaṭṭhiyā dhātīhi upaṭṭhāpesi. So sabbasampattīhi vaḍḍhamāno na cirasseva viññutaṃ pāpuṇi. Taṃ soḷasavassuddesikameva samānaṃ rājā rajje abhisiñci, vividhanāṭakāni cassa upaṭṭhāpesi. Abhisitto rājaputto rajjaṃ kāresi nāmena brahmadatto sakalajambudīpe vīsatiyā nagarasahassesu. Jambudīpe hi pubbe caturāsīti nagarasahassāni ahesuṃ. Tāni parihāyantāni saṭṭhi ahesuṃ, tato parihāyantāni cattālīsaṃ, sabbaparihāyanakāle pana vīsati honti. Ayañca brahmadatto sabbaparihāyanakāle uppajji. Tenassa vīsati nagarasahassāni ahesuṃ, vīsati pāsādasahassāni, vīsati hatthisahassāni, vīsati assasahassāni, vīsati rathasahassāni[P 1.0060], vīsati pattisahassāni, vīsati itthisahassāni – orodhā ca nāṭakitthiyo ca, vīsati amaccasahassāni. So mahārajjaṃ kārayamāno eva kasiṇaparikammaṃ katvā pañca abhiññāyo, aṭṭha samāpattiyo ca nibbattesi. Yasmā pana abhisittaraññā nāma avassaṃ aṭṭakaraṇe nisīditabbaṃ, tasmā ekadivasaṃ pageva pātarāsaṃ bhuñjitvā vinicchayaṭṭhāne nisīdi. Tattha uccāsaddamahāsaddaṃ akaṃsu. So “ayaṃ saddo samāpattiyā upakkileso”ti pāsādatalaṃ [M 1.0054] abhiruhitvā “samāpattiṃ appemī”ti nisinno nāsakkhi appetuṃ, rajjavikkhepena samāpatti parihīnā. Tato cintesi “kiṃ rajjaṃ varaṃ, udāhu samaṇadhammo”ti. Tato “rajjasukhaṃ parittaṃ anekādīnavaṃ, samaṇadhammasukhaṃ pana vipulamanekānisaṃsaṃ uttamapurisasevitañcā”ti ñatvā aññataraṃ amaccaṃ āṇāpesi – “imaṃ rajjaṃ dhammena samena anusāsa, mā kho adhammakāraṃ akāsī”ti sabbaṃ niyyātetvā pāsādaṃ abhiruhitvā samāpattisukhena viharati, na koci upasaṅkamituṃ labhati aññatra mukhadhovanadantakaṭṭhadāyakabhattanīhārakādīhi.

She, being thus carefully tended, at the time of her pregnancy's maturity entered the lying-in chamber and at dawn gave birth to a son resembling a lump of red arsenic smeared with refined oil, endowed with the marks of prosperity and merit. Then on the fifth day, they showed him, adorned and prepared, to the king. The king, delighted, appointed sixty-six nurses to attend him. Growing up with all prosperity, he soon attained discernment. When he was just sixteen years old, the king consecrated him to the throne and arranged various theatrical performances for him. The consecrated prince ruled the kingdom under the name Brahmadatta over twenty thousand cities in all of Jambudīpa. For in Jambudīpa, there were once eighty-four thousand cities. These dwindled to sixty thousand, then to forty thousand, and at the time of complete decline, there were twenty thousand. This Brahmadatta arose during the time of complete decline. Thus, he had twenty thousand cities, twenty thousand palaces, twenty thousand elephants, twenty thousand horses, twenty thousand chariots, twenty thousand foot soldiers, twenty thousand women—both the harem and dancing girls—and twenty thousand ministers. While ruling this great kingdom, he practiced the preliminary kasina meditation and attained the five higher knowledges and the eight meditative attainments. However, because a consecrated king must inevitably sit in the judgment hall, one day after eating his morning meal early, he sat in the court. There, they made a loud and great noise. Thinking, "This noise is a defilement to my attainment," he ascended to the palace terrace. Sitting there, wishing to enter the meditative attainment, he was unable to do so; his attainment was lost due to the distraction of kingship. Then he reflected, "Which is better: kingship or the life of a recluse?" Realizing that "The happiness of kingship is limited and has many dangers, whereas the happiness of the life of a recluse is vast, has many benefits, and is frequented by the noblest of men," he summoned a minister and commanded, "Rule this kingdom righteously and justly; do not act unrighteously." Having entrusted everything, he ascended the palace and dwelt in the bliss of attainment. No one could approach him except for those bringing water for washing his face, tooth-sticks, or meals.

Tato addhamāsamatte vītikkante mahesī pucchi “rājā uyyānagamanabaladassananāṭakādīsu katthaci na dissati, kuhiṃ gato”ti? Tassā tamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. Sā amaccassa pāhesi “rajje paṭicchite ahampi paṭicchitā homi, etu mayā saddhiṃ saṃvāsaṃ kappetū”ti. So ubho kaṇṇe thaketvā “asavanīyameta”nti paṭikkhipi. Sā punapi dvattikkhattuṃ pesetvā anicchamānaṃ tajjāpesi – “yadi na karosi, ṭhānāpi te cāvemi, jīvitāpi voropemī”ti. So bhīto “mātugāmo nāma daḷhanicchayo, kadāci evampi kārāpeyyā”ti ekadivasaṃ raho gantvā tāya saddhiṃ sirisayane saṃvāsaṃ kappesi. Sā puññavatī [V 1.0050] sukhasamphassā. So tassā samphassarāgena ratto tattha abhikkhaṇaṃ saṅkitasaṅkitova agamāsi. Anukkamena [P 1.0061] attano gharasāmiko viya nibbisaṅko pavisitumāraddho.

Then, when about half a month had passed, the chief queen asked, "The king is not seen anywhere in the pleasure gardens, military reviews, or theatrical performances—where has he gone?" They informed her of the matter. She sent a message to the minister: "When the kingdom is accepted, I too am to be accepted. Come and engage in intimacy with me." Covering both ears, he refused, saying, "This is not to be heard." She sent the message two or three times more, and when he was still unwilling, she threatened him: "If you do not comply, I will remove you from your position and deprive you of your life." Frightened, he thought, "Women are of firm resolve; perhaps she might even have this done." So one day, he went secretly and engaged in intimacy with her on the royal bed. She was a woman of merit and of pleasant touch. Infatuated by the passion for her touch, he went there frequently, though very hesitantly. Gradually, he began to enter without apprehension, as if he were the master of his own house.

Tato rājamanussā taṃ pavattiṃ rañño ārocesuṃ. Rājā na saddahati. Dutiyampi tatiyampi ārocesuṃ. Tato nilīno sayameva disvā sabbāmacce sannipātāpetvā ārocesi. Te – “ayaṃ rājāparādhiko hatthacchedaṃ arahati, pādacchedaṃ arahatī”ti yāva sūle uttāsanaṃ, tāva sabbakammakāraṇāni niddisiṃsu. Rājā – “etassa vadhabandhanatāḷane mayhaṃ vihiṃsā uppajjeyya, jīvitā voropane pāṇātipāto bhaveyya, dhanaharaṇe adinnādānaṃ, alaṃ evarūpehi katehi, imaṃ mama rajjā nikkaḍḍhathā”ti āha. Amaccā taṃ nibbisayaṃ akaṃsu. So attano dhanasārañca puttadārañca gahetvā paravisayaṃ agamāsi. Tattha rājā sutvā “kiṃ āgatosī”ti pucchi. “Deva, icchāmi taṃ upaṭṭhātu”nti. So taṃ sampaṭicchi. Amacco katipāhaccayena laddhavissāso taṃ rājānaṃ etadavoca – “mahārāja, amakkhikamadhuṃ [M 1.0055] passāmi, taṃ khādanto natthī”ti. Rājā “kiṃ etaṃ uppaṇḍetukāmo bhaṇatī”ti na suṇāti. So antaraṃ labhitvā punapi suṭṭhutaraṃ vaṇṇetvā ārocesi. Rājā “kiṃ eta”nti pucchi. “Bārāṇasirajjaṃ, devā”ti. Rājā “maṃ netvā māretukāmosī”ti āha. So “mā, deva, evaṃ avaca, yadi na saddahasi, manusse pesehī”ti. So manusse pesesi. Te gantvā gopuraṃ khaṇitvā rañño sayanaghare uṭṭhahiṃsu.

Then, the king's men reported this matter to the king. The king did not believe it. They reported it a second and a third time. Then the king, hiding himself, saw it with his own eyes. Summoning all his ministers, he informed them. They declared, “This man is guilty of treason; he deserves to have his hands cut off, he deserves to have his feet cut off,” and so on, prescribing all manner of punishments up to impalement. The king said, “Through his execution, imprisonment, or beating, harm would arise for me. By depriving him of life, there would be the destruction of a living being, and by seizing his wealth, there would be taking what is not given. Enough of such actions—banish him from my kingdom.” The ministers banished him from the country. He took his essential wealth, his wife and children, and went to another country. There, the king, hearing of his arrival, asked, “Why have you come?” He replied, “Your Majesty, I wish to serve you.” The king accepted him. After a few days, having gained his trust, the minister said to that king, “Great king, I see honey without flies, and there is no one eating it.” The king, thinking, “What is this he says, wishing to mock me?” paid him no heed. Seizing an opportunity, the minister praised it even more elaborately and informed him again. The king asked, “What is this?” He replied, “The kingdom of Bārāṇasī, sire.” The king said, “Do you wish to take me there to kill me?” The minister replied, “No, sire, do not say so. If you do not believe me, send men.” So the king sent men. They went, dug under the city gate-tower, and rose up in the king’s bedchamber.

Rājā disvā “kissa āgatātthā”ti pucchi. “Corā mayaṃ, mahārājā”ti. Rājā tesaṃ dhanaṃ dāpetvā “mā puna evamakatthā”ti ovaditvā vissajjesi. Te āgantvā tassa rañño ārocesuṃ. So punapi dvattikkhattuṃ tatheva vīmaṃsitvā “sīlavā rājā”ti caturaṅginiṃ senaṃ sannayhitvā sīmantare ekaṃ nagaraṃ upagamma tattha amaccassa pāhesi “nagaraṃ vā me dehi yuddhaṃ vā”ti. So brahmadattassa tamatthaṃ ārocāpesi “āṇāpetu devo kiṃ yujjhāmi, udāhu nagaraṃ demī”ti. Rājā “na yujjhitabbaṃ, nagaraṃ datvā idhāgacchā”ti pesesi. So tathā akāsi. Paṭirājāpi taṃ nagaraṃ gahetvā avasesanagaresupi [P 1.0062] tatheva dūtaṃ pāhesi. Tepi amaccā tatheva brahmadattassa ārocetvā tena “na yujjhitabbaṃ, idhāgantabba”nti vuttā bārāṇasiṃ āgamaṃsu.

The king saw them and asked, “Why have you come?” “We are thieves, great king,” they replied. The king had wealth given to them and, advising them, “Do not do such a thing again,” he sent them away. They returned and reported this to that other king. He, again, having investigated the matter two or three times in the same way and concluding, “The king is virtuous,” assembled a fourfold army. Advancing to a city on the border, he sent a message to the minister there: “Either give me the city or give battle.” That minister had this matter reported to King Brahmadatta: “Let the Lord command—shall I fight, or shall I give the city?” The king sent word: “Do not fight. Give the city and come here.” He did so. The rival king, having taken that city, likewise sent a messenger to the remaining cities. Those ministers also reported the matter to Brahmadatta in the same way, and being told by him, “You are not to fight; you are to come here,” they came to Bārāṇasī.

Tato amaccā brahmadattaṃ āhaṃsu – “mahārāja, tena saha yujjhāmā”ti. Rājā – “mama pāṇātipāto bhavissatī”ti vāresi. Amaccā – “mayaṃ, mahārāja, taṃ jīvaggāhaṃ gahetvā [V 1.0051] idheva ānessāmā”ti nānāupāyehi rājānaṃ saññāpetvā “ehi mahārājā”ti gantuṃ āraddhā. Rājā “sace sattamāraṇappaharaṇavilumpanakammaṃ na karotha, gacchāmī”ti bhaṇati. Amaccā “na, deva, karoma, bhayaṃ dassetvā palāpemā”ti caturaṅginiṃ senaṃ sannayhitvā ghaṭesu dīpe pakkhipitvā rattiṃ gacchiṃsu. Paṭirājā taṃ divasaṃ bārāṇasisamīpe nagaraṃ gahetvā idāni kinti rattiṃ sannāhaṃ mocāpetvā pamatto niddaṃ okkami saddhiṃ balakāyena. Tato amaccā bārāṇasirājānaṃ gahetvā paṭirañño khandhāvāraṃ gantvā sabbaghaṭehi dīpe niharāpetvā ekapajjotāya senāya saddaṃ akaṃsu. Paṭirañño amacco mahābalaṃ disvā bhīto attano rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “uṭṭhehi amakkhikamadhuṃ khādāhī”ti mahāsaddaṃ akāsi. Tathā dutiyopi, tatiyopi. Paṭirājā tena saddena paṭibujjhitvā [M 1.0056] bhayaṃ santāsaṃ āpajji. Ukkuṭṭhisatāni pavattiṃsu.
