So “paravacanaṃ saddahitvā amittahatthaṃ pattomhī”ti sabbarattiṃ taṃ taṃ vippalapitvā dutiyadivase “dhammiko rājā, uparodhaṃ na kareyya, gantvā khamāpemī”ti cintetvā rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā jaṇṇukehi patiṭṭhahitvā “khama, mahārāja, mayhaṃ aparādha”nti āha. Rājā taṃ ovaditvā “uṭṭhehi, khamāmi te”ti āha. So raññā evaṃ vuttamatteyeva paramassāsappatto ahosi, bārāṇasirañño samīpeyeva janapade rajjaṃ labhi. Te aññamaññaṃ sahāyakā ahesuṃ.

Then the ministers said to Brahmadatta, “Great king, let us fight with him.” The king forbade them, saying, “There would be the destruction of life on my part.” The ministers said, “Great king, we will capture him alive and bring him here.” Having persuaded the king with various strategies, they said, “Come, great king,” and prepared to go. The king said, “If you do not commit acts of killing beings, striking, and plundering, I will go.” The ministers replied, “We will not, sire. We will just show them a fearsome sight and make them flee.” They assembled a fourfold army, placed lamps inside pots, and went by night. The rival king, having captured a city near Bārāṇasī that day, had his armor removed at night and, being heedless, fell asleep along with his host. Then the ministers, taking the king of Bārāṇasī, went to the rival king’s camp, had the lamps brought out from all the pots, and with the army lit up as one single flame, they raised a great shout. The rival king’s minister, seeing the great army, was terrified. He approached his own king and shouted loudly, “Arise! Eat the honey without flies!” He did so a second and a third time. The rival king, awakened by that sound, was overcome with fear and terror. Hundreds of cries arose. He lamented the whole night, “Having believed another’s words, I have fallen into the enemy’s hands!” The next day, he thought, “He is a righteous king; he would not cause injury. I will go and ask for his forgiveness.” Approaching the king and kneeling down, he said, “Forgive my offense, great king.” The king advised him and said, “Arise, I forgive you.” As soon as the king had spoken these words, he attained the greatest relief. He received a kingdom in the country near the king of Bārāṇasī. They became friends with one another.

Atha brahmadatto dvepi senā sammodamānā ekato ṭhitā disvā “mamekassa cittānurakkhaṇāya asmiṃ janakāye khuddakamakkhikāya pivanamattampi lohitabindu [P 1.0063] na uppannaṃ. Aho sādhu, aho suṭṭhu, sabbe sattā sukhitā hontu, averā hontu, abyāpajjhā hontū”ti mettājhānaṃ uppādetvā, tadeva pādakaṃ katvā, saṅkhāre sammasitvā, paccekabodhiñāṇaṃ sacchikatvā, sayambhutaṃ pāpuṇi. Taṃ maggasukhena phalasukhena sukhitaṃ hatthikkhandhe nisinnaṃ amaccā paṇipātaṃ katvā āhaṃsu – “yānakālo, mahārāja, vijitabalakāyassa sakkāro kātabbo, parājitabalakāyassa bhattaparibbayo dātabbo”ti. So āha – “nāhaṃ, bhaṇe, rājā, paccekabuddho nāmāha”nti. Kiṃ devo bhaṇati, na edisā paccekabuddhā hontīti? Kīdisā, bhaṇe, paccekabuddhāti? Paccekabuddhā nāma dvaṅgulakesamassu aṭṭhaparikkhārayuttā bhavantīti. So dakkhiṇahatthena sīsaṃ parāmasi, tāvadeva gihiliṅgaṃ antaradhāyi, pabbajitaveso pāturahosi, dvaṅgulakesamassu aṭṭhaparikkhārasamannāgato vassasatikattherasadiso ahosi. So catutthajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā hatthikkhandhato vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā padumapupphe nisīdi. Amaccā vanditvā “kiṃ, bhante, kammaṭṭhānaṃ, kathaṃ adhigatosī”ti pucchiṃsu. So yato assa mettājhānakammaṭṭhānaṃ ahosi[V 1.0052], tañca vipassanaṃ vipassitvā adhigato, tasmā tamatthaṃ dassento udānagāthañca byākaraṇagāthañca imaññeva gāthaṃ abhāsi “sabbesu bhūtesu nidhāya daṇḍa”nti.

Then Brahmadatta, seeing the two armies standing together in harmony, thought: "For the sake of protecting my own mind, not even a drop of blood the size of a small fly’s sip has arisen in this mass of people. Oh, how good! Oh, how excellent! May all beings be happy, free from enmity, free from ill will!" Having aroused the meditation on loving-kindness, making that his foundation, contemplating the formations, and realizing the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha, he attained self-enlightenment. Seated happily on the elephant's back, experiencing the bliss of the path and the fruit, the ministers bowed down to him and said: "It is time to depart, great king. Honor should be paid to the victorious army, and provisions should be given to the defeated army." He replied: "I am not a king, friends. I am a Paccekabuddha." They asked: "What does Your Majesty say? Paccekabuddhas are not like this, are they?" He said: "What are Paccekabuddhas like, friends?" They replied: "Paccekabuddhas have hair and a beard two fingers long and are endowed with the eight requisites." Then he stroked his head with his right hand, and immediately his householder's appearance vanished. The appearance of a renunciant became manifest; endowed with hair and a beard two fingers long and the eight requisites, he resembled an elder of a hundred years. Entering the fourth jhāna, he rose into the air from the elephant's back and sat on a lotus flower. The ministers paid homage and asked: "Venerable sir, what was your meditation subject? How did you attain it?" Since his meditation subject was the meditation on loving-kindness, and he had attained it by contemplating that with insight, he explained the matter by uttering both an inspired utterance and a declaration, speaking this very verse: "Having laid aside the rod in regard to all beings."

Tattha sabbesūti anavasesesu. Bhūtesūti sattesu. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāraṃ pana ratanasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ vakkhāma. Nidhāyāti nikkhipitvā. Daṇḍanti [M 1.0057] kāyavacīmanodaṇḍaṃ, kāyaduccaritādīnametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Kāyaduccaritañhi daṇḍayatīti daṇḍo, bādheti anayabyasanaṃ pāpetīti vuttaṃ hoti. Evaṃ vacīduccaritaṃ manoduccaritaṃ ca. Paharaṇadaṇḍo eva vā daṇḍo, taṃ nidhāyātipi vuttaṃ hoti. Aviheṭhayanti aviheṭhayanto. Aññatarampīti yaṃkiñci ekampi. Tesanti tesaṃ sabbabhūtānaṃ. Na puttamiccheyyāti atrajo, khetrajo, dinnako, antevāsikoti imesu catūsu [P 1.0064] puttesu yaṃ kiñci puttaṃ na iccheyya. Kuto sahāyanti sahāyaṃ pana iccheyyāti kuto eva etaṃ.

Herein, 'all' means without exception. 'Beings' means sentient beings. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation we shall give in the commentary on the Ratana Sutta. 'Having laid aside' means having set aside. 'The rod' means the rod of body, speech, and mind; this is a term for bodily misconduct and the like. For bodily misconduct punishes (daṇḍayati), thus it is a 'rod'; it is said that it oppresses and leads to ruin and calamity. The same applies to verbal misconduct and mental misconduct. Alternatively, 'the rod' is simply the rod used for striking; it is also said in the sense of 'having laid that down'. 'Not harming' means not causing harm. 'Any one of them' means any single one whatsoever. 'Of them' means of all those beings. 'One should not wish for a son' means one should not wish for any kind of son among these four: one born of oneself (atrajo), one born of the field (khetrajo), one who is given (dinnako), or a pupil (antevāsiko). 'How then a companion?' means how could one possibly wish for a companion?

Ekoti pabbajjāsaṅkhātena eko, adutiyaṭṭhena eko, taṇhāpahānena eko, ekantavigatakilesoti eko, eko paccekasambodhiṃ abhisambuddhoti eko. Samaṇasahassassāpi hi majjhe vattamāno gihisaññojanassa chinnattā eko – evaṃ pabbajjāsaṅkhātena eko. Eko tiṭṭhati, eko gacchati, eko nisīdati, eko seyyaṃ kappeti, eko iriyati vattatīti – evaṃ adutiyaṭṭhena eko.

One by the designation of renunciation. One in the sense of having no second. One through the abandoning of craving. One as being with defilements entirely gone. One as being awakened to individual enlightenment. Indeed, even while amidst a thousand monks, he is one because the fetters of a householder are cut off—thus, he is one by the designation of renunciation. He stands alone, walks alone, sits alone, prepares his resting place alone, and conducts himself alone—thus, he is one in the sense of having no second.

“Taṇhādutiyo puriso, dīghamaddhānasaṃsaraṃ;

Itthabhāvaññathābhāvaṃ, saṃsāraṃ nātivattati.

A person with craving as a companion wanders through the long ages; from one state of being to another, they do not pass beyond saṃsāra.

“Evamādīnavaṃ ñatvā, taṇhaṃ dukkhassa sambhavaṃ;

Vītataṇho anādāno, sato bhikkhu paribbaje”ti. (itivu. 15, 105; mahāni. 191; cūḷani. pārāyanānugītigāthāniddesa 107) –

Having thus understood the danger, that craving is the origin of suffering, a monk, free from craving and without grasping, should wander mindfully.

Evaṃ taṇhāpahānaṭṭhena eko. Sabbakilesāssa pahīnā ucchinnamūlā tālāvatthukatā anabhāvaṃkatā āyatiṃ anuppādadhammāti – evaṃ ekantavigatakilesoti eko. Anācariyako hutvā sayambhū sāmaññeva paccekasambodhiṃ abhisambuddhoti – evaṃ eko paccekasambodhiṃ abhisambuddhoti eko.

Thus, in the sense of abandoning craving, he is one. All his defilements are abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, brought to non-existence, and are of a nature not to arise in the future—thus, being one whose defilements are entirely gone, he is one. Having no teacher, being self-awakened, he awakens by himself to individual enlightenment—thus, he is one who is awakened to individual enlightenment.

Careti yā imā aṭṭha cariyāyo; seyyathidaṃ – paṇidhisampannānaṃ catūsu iriyāpathesu iriyāpathacariyā[V 1.0053], indriyesu guttadvārānaṃ ajjhattikāyatanesu āyatanacariyā, appamādavihārīnaṃ catūsu satipaṭṭhānesu saticariyā, adhicittamanuyuttānaṃ catūsu jhānesu samādhicariyā, buddhisampannānaṃ catūsu ariyasaccesu ñāṇacariyā, sammā paṭipannānaṃ catūsu ariyamaggesu maggacariyā, adhigatapphalānaṃ catūsu sāmaññaphalesu [M 1.0058] patticariyā, tiṇṇaṃ buddhānaṃ sabbasattesu lokatthacariyā, tattha padesato paccekabuddhasāvakānanti. Yathāha – “cariyāti aṭṭha cariyāyo iriyāpathacariyā”ti [P 1.0065] (paṭi. ma. 1.197; 3.28) vitthāro. Tāhi cariyāhi samannāgato bhaveyyāti attho. Atha vā yā imā “adhimuccanto saddhāya carati, paggaṇhanto vīriyena carati, upaṭṭhahanto satiyā carati, avikkhitto samādhinā carati, pajānanto paññāya carati, vijānanto viññāṇena carati, evaṃ paṭipannassa kusalā dhammā āyatantīti āyatanacariyāya carati, evaṃ paṭipanno visesamadhigacchatīti visesacariyāya caratī”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.197; 3.29) evaṃ aparāpi aṭṭha cariyā vuttā. Tāhipi samannāgato bhaveyyāti attho. Khaggavisāṇakappoti ettha khaggavisāṇaṃ nāma khaggamigasiṅgaṃ. Kappasaddassa atthaṃ vitthārato maṅgalasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ pakāsayissāma. Idha panāyaṃ “satthukappena vata, bho, kira sāvakena saddhiṃ mantayamānā”ti (ma. ni. 1.260) evamādīsu viya paṭibhāgo veditabbo. Khaggavisāṇakappoti khaggavisāṇasadisoti vuttaṃ hoti. Ayaṃ tāvettha padato atthavaṇṇanā.

The practices (cariyā) are these eight: namely, the practice of deportment in the four postures for those accomplished in aspiration; the practice of the sense-bases in the internal sense-bases for those who guard the doors of their faculties; the practice of mindfulness in the four foundations of mindfulness for those who dwell diligently; the practice of concentration in the four jhānas for those devoted to the higher mind; the practice of knowledge in the four noble truths for those endowed with wisdom; the practice of the path in the four noble paths for those rightly practicing; the practice of attainment in the four fruits of recluseship for those who have attained the fruits; and the practice for the welfare of the world towards all beings by the three types of Buddhas, which applies in part to Paccekabuddhas and disciples. As it is said: 'Practice means the eight practices, such as the practice of deportment' (Patisambhidāmagga 1.197; 3.28)—this is the detailed explanation. The meaning is that one should be endowed with these practices. Alternatively, these other eight practices are also mentioned: 'One practices with faith by being resolved, practices with energy by exerting, practices with mindfulness by being attentive, practices with concentration by being undistracted, practices with wisdom by understanding, practices with consciousness by discerning. For one who practices thus, wholesome qualities are established—thus one practices the practice of establishment. One who practices thus attains distinction—thus one practices the practice of distinction' (Patisambhidāmagga 1.197; 3.29). The meaning is that one should be endowed with these practices as well. 'Like a rhinoceros horn'—here, 'rhinoceros horn' means the horn of a rhinoceros. The meaning of the word 'kappa' will be explained in detail in the commentary on the Maṅgala Sutta. Here, however, its sense of comparison should be understood as in phrases like, 'Indeed, friends, it seems a disciple like the teacher was conversing' (Majjhima Nikāya 1.260). 'Like a rhinoceros horn' means 'similar to a rhinoceros horn.' This, for now, is the word-by-word explanation of the meaning here.

Adhippāyānusandhito pana evaṃ veditabbā – yvāyaṃ vuttappakāro daṇḍo bhūtesu pavattiyamāno ahito hoti, taṃ tesu appavattanena tappaṭipakkhabhūtāya mettāya parahitūpasaṃhārena ca sabbesu bhūtesu nidhāya daṇḍaṃ, nihitadaṇḍattā eva ca. Yathā anihitadaṇḍā sattā bhūtāni daṇḍena vā satthena vā pāṇinā vā leḍḍunā vā viheṭhayanti, tathā aviheṭhayaṃ aññatarampi tesaṃ. Imaṃ mettākammaṭṭhānamāgamma yadeva tattha vedanāgataṃ saññāsaṅkhāraviññāṇagataṃ tañca tadanusāreneva tadaññañca saṅkhāragataṃ vipassitvā imaṃ paccekabodhiṃ adhigatomhīti ayaṃ tāva adhippāyo.

However, from the perspective of the intended meaning and its connection, it should be understood thus: That kind of rod described, when wielded against beings, is harmful. By not wielding it against them, by means of loving-kindness which is its opposite, and by bringing about the welfare of others, one lays down the rod with respect to all beings, and is one who has indeed laid down the rod. Just as beings who have not laid down the rod harm other beings with a stick, a weapon, a hand, or a clod of earth, so one does not harm any one of them. Having undertaken this meditation subject of loving-kindness, and having contemplated with insight whatever there pertains to feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, and, in accordance with that, whatever else pertains to formations, one realizes, 'I have attained this enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha.' This, for now, is the intended meaning.

Ayaṃ pana anusandhi – evaṃ vutte te amaccā āhaṃsu – “idāni, bhante, kuhiṃ gacchathā”ti? Tato tena “pubbapaccekasambuddhā kattha vasantī”ti [P 1.0066] āvajjetvā ñatvā “gandhamādanapabbate”ti vutte punāhaṃsu – “amhe dāni, bhante, pajahatha, na icchathā”ti. Atha paccekabuddho āha – “na puttamiccheyyā”ti sabbaṃ. Tatrādhippāyo – ahaṃ idāni atrajādīsu yaṃ [M 1.0059] kiñci puttampi na iccheyyaṃ, kuto pana tumhādisaṃ sahāyaṃ? Tasmā tumhesupi yo mayā saddhiṃ [V 1.0054] gantuṃ mādiso vā hotuṃ icchati, so eko care khaggavisāṇakappo. Atha vā tehi “amhe dāni, bhante, pajahatha na icchathā”ti vutte so paccekabuddho “na puttamiccheyya kuto sahāya”nti vatvā attano yathāvuttenatthena ekacariyāya guṇaṃ disvā pamudito pītisomanassajāto imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi – “eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”ti. Evaṃ vatvā pekkhamānasseva mahājanassa ākāse uppatitvā gandhamādanaṃ agamāsi.

This, however, is the connection: When this was said, those ministers asked, 'Now, venerable sir, where are you going?' Then, when he, having reflected and known, 'Where do the previous Paccekabuddhas dwell?', said, 'On Gandhamādana mountain,' they said again, 'Now, venerable sir, you are abandoning us! You do not want us!' Then the Paccekabuddha said the entire verse beginning, 'One would not want a son.' The intention there is: 'Now I would not want any son, such as one born of myself; how much less a companion like you? Therefore, whoever among you wishes to go with me or to be like me, let him wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.' Or alternatively, when they said, 'Now, venerable sir, you are abandoning us! You do not want us!', that Paccekabuddha, saying, 'One would not want a son, how much less a companion,' and seeing the virtue of solitary practice in accordance with the meaning he had stated, filled with joy, rapture, and happiness, uttered this inspired utterance: 'Wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.' Having said this, while the great crowd was watching, he rose up into the sky and went to Gandhamādana.

Gandhamādano nāma himavati cūḷakāḷapabbataṃ, mahākāḷapabbataṃ, nāgapaliveṭhanaṃ, candagabbhaṃ, sūriyagabbhaṃ, suvaṇṇapassaṃ, himavantapabbatanti satta pabbate atikkamma hoti. Tattha nandamūlakaṃ nāma pabbhāraṃ paccekabuddhānaṃ vasanokāso. Tisso ca guhāyo – suvaṇṇaguhā, maṇiguhā, rajataguhāti. Tattha maṇiguhādvāre mañjūsako nāma rukkho yojanaṃ ubbedhena, yojanaṃ vitthārena. So yattakāni udake vā thale vā pupphāni, sabbāni tāni pupphayati visesena paccekabuddhāgamanadivase. Tassūparito sabbaratanamāḷo hoti. Tattha sammajjanakavāto kacavaraṃ chaḍḍeti, samakaraṇavāto sabbaratanamayaṃ vālikaṃ samaṃ karoti, siñcanakavāto anotattadahato ānetvā udakaṃ siñcati, sugandhakaraṇavāto himavantato sabbesaṃ gandharukkhānaṃ gandhe āneti, ocinakavāto pupphāni ocinitvā [P 1.0067] pāteti, santharakavāto sabbattha santharati. Sadā paññattāneva cettha āsanāni honti, yesu paccekabuddhuppādadivase uposathadivase ca sabbapaccekabuddhā sannipatitvā nisīdanti. Ayaṃ tattha pakati. Abhisambuddha-paccekabuddho tattha gantvā paññattāsane nisīdati. Tato sace tasmiṃ kāle aññepi paccekabuddhā saṃvijjanti, tepi taṅkhaṇaṃ sannipatitvā paññattāsanesu nisīdanti. Nisīditvā ca kiñcideva samāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhahanti, tato saṅghatthero adhunāgatapaccekabuddhaṃ sabbesaṃ anumodanatthāya “kathamadhigata”nti kammaṭṭhānaṃ pucchati. Tadāpi so tameva attano udānabyākaraṇagāthaṃ bhāsati. Puna bhagavāpi āyasmatā ānandena puṭṭho tameva gāthaṃ bhāsati, ānando ca saṅgītiyanti evamekekā gāthā paccekasambodhiabhisambuddhaṭṭhāne, mañjūsakamāḷe[M 1.0060], ānandena pucchitakāle, saṅgītiyanti catukkhattuṃ bhāsitā hotīti.

Gandhamādana is in the Himalayas, beyond the seven mountains—namely, Cūḷakāḷapabbata, Mahākāḷapabbata, Nāgapaliveṭhana, Candagabbha, Sūriyagabbha, Suvaṇṇapassa, and Himavantapabbata. There, the Nandamūlaka cavern serves as a dwelling place for Paccekabuddhas. There are also three caves: the Suvaṇṇaguhā, Maṇiguhā, and Rajataguhā. At the entrance of the Maṇiguhā stands the Mañjūsaka tree, a yojana in height and a yojana in breadth. This tree blooms with all the flowers that grow in water or on land, especially on the day of a Paccekabuddha's arrival. Above it is a terrace made of all kinds of jewels. There, a sweeping wind clears away rubbish, a leveling wind spreads jeweled sand evenly, a sprinkling wind brings water from Lake Anotatta to moisten the ground, a perfuming wind carries fragrances from all the scented trees of the Himalayas, a gathering wind gathers and drops flowers, and a spreading wind arranges them everywhere. Seats are always prepared there. On the day a Paccekabuddha arises and on Uposatha days, all Paccekabuddhas gather and sit upon these seats. This is the natural order there. A Paccekabuddha who has attained full enlightenment, having arrived there, sits on the prepared seat. Then, if other Paccekabuddhas are present at that time, they too immediately gather and sit on their prepared seats. After sitting, they enter into some attainment and then emerge. Then, the elder of the Saṅgha, so that all may rejoice, asks the newly arrived Paccekabuddha about the meditation subject, saying, 'How was it attained?' At that time, he recites that very inspirational and explanatory verse of his own. Furthermore, when the Blessed One was questioned by the Venerable Ānanda, he too recited the same verse, and Ānanda recited it at the Saṅgīti. Thus, each single verse—spoken at the place of attaining Paccekasambodhi, on the Mañjūsaka terrace, when questioned by Ānanda, and at the Saṅgīti—was declared four times.

Paṭhamagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the first verse is concluded.

36. Saṃsaggajātassāti kā uppatti? Ayampi paccekabodhisatto kassapassa bhagavato sāsane vīsati vassasahassāni purimanayeneva samaṇadhammaṃ karonto kasiṇaparikammaṃ katvā, paṭhamajjhānaṃ nibbattetvā, nāmarūpaṃ vavatthapetvā, lakkhaṇasammasanaṃ katvā, ariyamaggaṃ anadhigamma brahmaloke [V 1.0055] nibbatti. So tato cuto bārāṇasirañño aggamahesiyā kucchimhi uppajjitvā purimanayeneva vaḍḍhamāno yato pabhuti “ayaṃ itthī ayaṃ puriso”ti visesaṃ aññāsi, tatupādāya itthīnaṃ hatthe na ramati, ucchādananhāpanamaṇḍanādimattampi na sahati. Taṃ purisā eva posenti, thaññapāyanakāle dhātiyo kañcukaṃ [P 1.0068] paṭimuñcitvā purisavesena thaññaṃ pāyenti. So itthīnaṃ gandhaṃ ghāyitvā saddaṃ vā sutvā rodati, viññutaṃ pattopi itthiyo passituṃ na icchati, tena taṃ anitthigandhotveva sañjāniṃsu.

36. What is the origin of the verse beginning 'Of one born of association'? This Bodhisatta destined to be a Paccekabuddha, during the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, practiced the duties of a recluse for twenty thousand years in the manner described before. Having performed the preliminary work of kasiṇa, generated the first jhāna, discerned name-and-form, and contemplated the characteristics, but without attaining the noble path, he was reborn in the Brahmā world. Having passed away from there, he was conceived in the womb of the chief queen of the king of Bārāṇasī. Growing up in the manner described before, from the time he recognized the distinction, thinking, 'This is a woman, this is a man,' he took no delight in the hands of women and could not endure even the slightest anointing, bathing, or adornment. Men alone attended to him. At nursing times, the nurses would don bodices and nurse him in the guise of men. If he smelled the scent of women or heard their voices, he would cry. Even when he attained discernment, he did not wish to see women. Thus, they came to know him as Anitthigandha, 'Averse to the Scent of Women'.

Tasmiṃ soḷasavassuddesike jāte rājā “kulavaṃsaṃ saṇṭhapessāmī”ti nānākulehi tassa anurūpā kaññāyo ānetvā aññataraṃ amaccaṃ āṇāpesi “kumāraṃ ramāpehī”ti. Amacco upāyena taṃ ramāpetukāmo tassa avidūre sāṇipākāraṃ parikkhipāpetvā nāṭakāni payojāpesi. Kumāro gītavāditasaddaṃ sutvā – “kasseso saddo”ti āha. Amacco “taveso, deva, nāṭakitthīnaṃ saddo, puññavantānaṃ īdisāni nāṭakāni honti, abhirama, deva, mahāpuññosi tva”nti āha. Kumāro amaccaṃ daṇḍena tāḷāpetvā nikkaḍḍhāpesi. So rañño ārocesi. Rājā kumārassa mātarā saha gantvā, kumāraṃ khamāpetvā, puna amaccaṃ appesi. Kumāro tehi atinippīḷiyamāno seṭṭhasuvaṇṇaṃ datvā suvaṇṇakāre āṇāpesi – “sundaraṃ itthirūpaṃ karothā”ti. Te vissakammunā nimmitasadisaṃ sabbālaṅkāravibhūsitaṃ itthirūpaṃ katvā dassesuṃ. Kumāro disvā vimhayena sīsaṃ cāletvā mātāpitūnaṃ pesesi “yadi īdisiṃ itthiṃ labhissāmi, gaṇhissāmī”ti. Mātāpitaro [M 1.0061] “amhākaṃ putto mahāpuñño, avassaṃ tena saha katapuññā kāci dārikā loke uppannā bhavissatī”ti taṃ suvaṇṇarūpaṃ rathaṃ āropetvā amaccānaṃ appesuṃ “gacchatha, īdisiṃ dārikaṃ gavesathā”ti. Te gahetvā soḷasa mahājanapade vicarantā taṃ taṃ gāmaṃ gantvā udakatitthādīsu yattha yattha janasamūhaṃ passanti, tattha tattha devataṃ viya suvaṇṇarūpaṃ ṭhapetvā nānāpupphavatthālaṅkārehi pūjaṃ katvā, vitānaṃ bandhitvā, ekamantaṃ tiṭṭhanti – “yadi kenaci evarūpā diṭṭhapubbā bhavissati, so kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpessatī”ti? Etenupāyena aññatra maddaraṭṭhā sabbe [P 1.0069] janapade āhiṇḍitvā taṃ “khuddakaraṭṭha”nti avamaññamānā tattha paṭhamaṃ agantvā nivattiṃsu.

When he was about sixteen years of age, the king, thinking, 'I will establish the family line,' brought suitable maidens from various clans for him and ordered a certain minister, 'Entertain the prince.' The minister, wishing to entertain him by some stratagem, had a cloth screen enclosure set up not far from him and arranged for theatrical performances. Hearing the sounds of singing and music, the prince asked, 'Whose sound is this?' The minister replied, 'This, lord, is the sound of your actresses. Those with merit have such performances. Delight yourself, lord, for you are of great merit.' The prince had the minister struck with a stick and driven away. He reported this to the king. The king went with the prince’s mother, appeased the prince, and sent the minister again. Being greatly pressured by them, the prince gave excellent gold to goldsmiths and ordered, 'Make a beautiful female figure.' They crafted a female form resembling one created by Vissakamma, adorned with all ornaments, and showed it to him. Upon seeing it, the prince shook his head in amazement and sent a message to his parents: 'If I can obtain such a woman, I will take her.' His parents thought, 'Our son is of great merit. Surely, some maiden who has made merit together with him must have been born in the world.' They placed the golden figure on a chariot and dispatched the ministers, saying, 'Go and search for such a maiden.' Taking it, they traveled through the sixteen great provinces. Wherever they went to a village, a watering place, or the like, and saw a crowd of people, they would set up the golden figure like a deity, worship it with various flowers, garments, and ornaments, erect a canopy, and stand aside, thinking, 'If anyone has ever seen such a woman, they will bring up the matter.' By this method, they wandered through all the provinces except for the Madda country. Disdaining it as a 'small country,' they did not go there first but turned back.

Tato nesaṃ ahosi “maddaraṭṭhampi tāva gacchāma, mā no bārāṇasiṃ paviṭṭhepi rājā puna pāhesī”ti maddaraṭṭhe sāgalanagaraṃ agamaṃsu. Sāgalanagare ca maddavo nāma rājā. Tassa dhītā soḷasavassuddesikā abhirūpā hoti. Tassā vaṇṇadāsiyo nhānodakatthāya titthaṃ gatā. Tattha amaccehi ṭhapitaṃ taṃ suvaṇṇarūpaṃ dūratova disvā “amhe udakatthāya pesetvā rājaputtī sayameva [V 1.0056] āgatā”ti bhaṇantiyo samīpaṃ gantvā “nāyaṃ sāminī, amhākaṃ sāminī ito abhirūpatarā”ti āhaṃsu. Amaccā taṃ sutvā rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā anurūpena nayena dārikaṃ yāciṃsu, sopi adāsi. Tato bārāṇasirañño pāhesuṃ “laddhā dārikā, sāmaṃ āgacchissati, udāhu amheva ānemā”ti? So ca “mayi āgacchante janapadapīḷā bhavissati, tumheva ānethā”ti pesesi.

Then a thought occurred to them: "Let us go to the Madda country first, lest the king send for us again even after we have entered Bārāṇasī." Thinking thus, they went to the city of Sāgala in the Madda country. Now in the city of Sāgala, there was a king named Maddava. He had a beautiful daughter of about sixteen years of age. Her high-caste maidservants, having gone to the bathing place for water, saw from afar the golden image placed there by the ministers. Saying, "Having sent us for water, the princess has come herself!" they approached and then declared, "This is not our mistress; our mistress is more beautiful than this." Hearing this, the ministers approached the king and requested the girl in a suitable manner, and he gave her to them. Then they sent a message to the king of Bārāṇasī: "The girl has been obtained. Will she come herself, or should we bring her?" He sent back word: "If I come, there will be affliction for the countryfolk. You yourselves bring her."

Amaccā dārikaṃ gahetvā nagarā nikkhamitvā kumārassa pāhesuṃ – “laddhā suvaṇṇarūpasadisī dārikā”ti. Kumāro sutvāva rāgena abhibhūto paṭhamajjhānā parihāyi. So dūtaparamparaṃ pesesi “sīghaṃ ānetha, sīghaṃ ānethā”ti. Te sabbattha ekarattivāseneva bārāṇasiṃ patvā bahinagare ṭhitā rañño pāhesuṃ – “ajja pavisitabbaṃ, no”ti? Rājā “seṭṭhakulā ānītā dārikā, maṅgalakiriyaṃ katvā mahāsakkārena pavesessāma, uyyānaṃ tāva naṃ nethā”ti āṇāpesi. Te tathā akaṃsu. Sā accantasukhumālā yānugghātena ubbāḷhā addhānaparissamena uppannavātarogā milātamālā viya [M 1.0062] hutvā rattiṃyeva kālamakāsi. Amaccā “sakkārā paribhaṭṭhamhā”ti parideviṃsu. Rājā ca nāgarā ca “kulavaṃso vinaṭṭho”ti parideviṃsu. Nagare mahākolāhalaṃ ahosi. Kumārassa sutamatteyeva mahāsoko udapādi. Tato kumāro sokassa mūlaṃ khaṇitumāraddho. So cintesi – “ayaṃ soko nāma na ajātassa hoti, jātassa pana hoti, tasmā jātiṃ paṭicca soko”ti. “Jāti pana kiṃ [P 1.0070] paṭiccā”ti? Tato “bhavaṃ paṭicca jātī”ti evaṃ pubbabhāvanānubhāvena yoniso manasikaronto anulomapaṭilomapaṭiccasamuppādaṃ disvā saṅkhāre sammasanto tattheva nisinno paccekabodhiṃ sacchākāsi. Taṃ maggaphalasukhena sukhitaṃ santindriyaṃ santamānasaṃ nisinnaṃ disvā, paṇipātaṃ katvā, amaccā āhaṃsu – “mā soci, deva, mahanto jambudīpo, aññaṃ tato sundarataraṃ ānessāmā”ti. So āha – “nāhaṃ socako, nissoko paccekabuddho aha”nti. Ito paraṃ sabbaṃ purimagāthāsadisameva ṭhapetvā gāthāvaṇṇanaṃ.

The ministers took the girl, departed from the city, and sent word to the prince: "A girl resembling a golden image has been obtained." Upon hearing this, the prince, overwhelmed by passion, fell from the first jhāna. He sent messengers in succession, saying, "Bring her quickly, bring her quickly!" Traveling by staying only one night in each place, they reached Bārāṇasī. Staying outside the city, they sent word to the king: "Should we enter today or not?" The king ordered: "The girl has been brought from a noble family. After performing the auspicious ceremony, we will have her enter with great honor. First, lead her to the park." They did so. She, being extremely delicate, was afflicted by the jolting of the vehicle and, with a wind-illness that arose from the fatigue of the long journey, became like a withered garland and passed away that very night. The ministers lamented, "We have been deprived of our reward!" The king and the citizens lamented, "The lineage has been destroyed!" A great uproar arose in the city. As soon as the prince heard the news, great sorrow arose in him. Then the prince began to dig up the root of sorrow. He reflected: "This sorrow does not arise for one who is not born, but it does arise for one who is born. Therefore, sorrow is dependent on birth." "And what is birth dependent on?" Then, reflecting with proper attention through the power of his past cultivation, "Birth is dependent on becoming," he saw dependent origination in forward and reverse order. Comprehending the formations, while sitting right there, he realized the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha. Seeing him seated, blissful with the bliss of the path and fruit, with serene faculties and a serene mind, the ministers paid homage and said, "Do not grieve, lord. Jambudīpa is vast; we will bring another, even more beautiful than she." He replied, "I am not one who grieves. I am a sorrowless Paccekabuddha." From this point onward, everything is the same as in the previous verses, setting aside the commentary on the verses.

Gāthāvaṇṇanāyaṃ pana saṃsaggajātassāti jātasaṃsaggassa. Tattha dassana, savana, kāya, samullapana, sambhogasaṃsaggavasena pañcavidho saṃsaggo. Tattha aññamaññaṃ disvā cakkhuviññāṇavīthivasena uppannarāgo dassanasaṃsaggo nāma. Tattha sīhaḷadīpe kāḷadīghavāpīgāme piṇḍāya carantaṃ kalyāṇavihāravāsīdīghabhāṇakadaharabhikkhuṃ disvā paṭibaddhacittā kenaci upāyena taṃ alabhitvā, kālakatā kuṭumbiyadhītā, tassā nivāsanacoḷakhaṇḍaṃ disvā “evarūpavatthadhāriniyā [V 1.0057] nāma saddhiṃ saṃvāsaṃ nālattha”nti hadayaṃ phāletvā kālakato. So eva ca daharo nidassanaṃ.

Now, in the commentary on the verses, the phrase 'for one in whom association has arisen' means for one who has formed an association. Therein, association is of five kinds: by way of seeing, hearing, bodily contact, conversation, and sexual union. Among these, the passion that arises through the process of eye-consciousness upon seeing one another is called association by sight. Herein is an example from the island of Sīhaḷa: In the village of Kāḷadīghavāpī, a daughter of a householder saw a young reciter of the Dīgha Nikāya from Kalyāṇa Vihāra who was walking for alms, and she became infatuated. Unable to obtain him by any means, the householder's daughter died. Later, upon seeing a piece of her lower garment, the young monk's heart broke as he thought, 'I did not get to cohabit with the one who wore such a garment,' and he died. That very young monk is the example.

Parehi pana kathiyamānaṃ rūpādisampattiṃ attanā vā hasitalapitagītasaddaṃ sutvā sotaviññāṇavīthivasena uppanno rāgo savanasaṃsaggo nāma. Tatrāpi girigāmavāsīkammāradhītāya pañcahi kumārīhi saddhiṃ padumassaraṃ gantvā, nhatvā mālaṃ āropetvā, uccāsaddena gāyantiyā ākāsena gacchanto saddaṃ sutvā kāmarāgena visesā parihāyitvā anayabyasanaṃ patto pañcaggaḷaleṇavāsī tissadaharo nidassanaṃ.

Furthermore, the passion that arises through the process of ear-consciousness—either by hearing others speak of the perfection of form and so on, or by oneself hearing the sound of laughter, speech, or song—is called association by hearing. Here too, the young Tissa, a resident of Pañcaggaḷa Cave, is the example. A smith's daughter, a resident of a mountain village, went to a lotus lake with five other maidens, bathed, and placed a garland on her head. While she was singing in a loud voice, he, traveling through the sky, heard the sound and, due to sensual passion, fell away from his spiritual attainment and met with ruin and disaster.

Aññamaññaṃ aṅgaparāmasanena uppannarāgo kāyasaṃsaggo nāma. Dhammagāyanadaharabhikkhu [P 1.0071] cettha nidassanaṃ. Mahāvihāre kira daharabhikkhu dhammaṃ bhāsati[M 1.0063]. Tattha mahājane āgate rājāpi agamāsi saddhiṃ antepurena. Tato rājadhītāya tassa rūpañca saddañca āgamma balavarāgo uppanno, tassa ca daharassāpi. Taṃ disvā rājā sallakkhetvā sāṇipākārena parikkhipāpesi. Te aññamaññaṃ parāmasitvā āliṅgiṃsu. Puna sāṇipākāraṃ apanetvā passantā dvepi kālakateyeva addasaṃsūti.

The passion that arises from touching one another's limbs is called association by body. The young monk who was reciting the Dhamma is the example here. It is said that in the Mahāvihāra, a young monk was preaching the Dhamma. When a great crowd gathered there, the king also came with his harem. Then, for the king's daughter, a very strong passion arose based on the monk's form and voice, and it arose for the young monk as well. The king, seeing and noticing this, had them enclosed with a cloth curtain. They touched one another and embraced. When the cloth curtain was removed and people looked again, they saw that both were already dead.

Aññamaññaṃ ālapanasamullapane uppanno rāgo pana samullapanasaṃsaggo nāma. Bhikkhubhikkhunīhi saddhiṃ paribhogakaraṇe uppannarāgo sambhogasaṃsaggo nāma. Dvīsupi cetesu pārājikappatto bhikkhu ca bhikkhunī ca nidassanaṃ. Maricivaṭṭināmamahāvihāramahe kira duṭṭhagāmaṇi abhayamahārājā mahādānaṃ paṭiyādetvā ubhatosaṅghaṃ parivisati. Tattha uṇhayāguyā dinnāya saṅghanavakasāmaṇerī anādhārakassa saṅghanavakasāmaṇerassa dantavalayaṃ datvā samullāpaṃ akāsi. Te ubhopi upasampajjitvā saṭṭhivassā hutvā paratīraṃ gatā aññamaññaṃ samullāpena pubbasaññaṃ paṭilabhitvā tāvadeva jātasinehā sikkhāpadaṃ vītikkamitvā pārājikā ahesunti.

Lust that arises from mutual conversation and pleasantries is called 'association through pleasantries.' Lust that arises from a monk and nuns partaking together is called 'association through partaking.' An example of a monk and a nun who have committed a pārājika offense in both these cases is as follows. It is said that at the festival of the great monastery named Maricivaṭṭi, the great King Duṭṭhagāmaṇi Abhaya prepared a great offering and served the twofold Saṅgha. There, when hot gruel was given, a junior novice nun, giving an ivory bowl-stand to a junior novice monk who was without one, engaged in pleasant conversation. Both of them, after receiving higher ordination and having sixty years of seniority, went to the further shore. Through mutual pleasant conversation, they regained their former recognition, and with affection arising at that very moment, they transgressed the training rule and committed a pārājika offense.

Evaṃ pañcavidhe saṃsagge yena kenaci saṃsaggena jātasaṃsaggassa bhavati sneho, purimarāgapaccayā balavarāgo uppajjati. Tato snehanvayaṃ dukkhamidaṃ pahoti tameva snehaṃ anugacchantaṃ sandiṭṭhikasamparāyikasokaparidevādinānappakārakaṃ dukkhamidaṃ pahoti, nibbattati, bhavati, jāyati. Apare pana “ārammaṇe cittassa vossaggo saṃsaggo”ti bhaṇanti. Tato sneho, snehā dukkhamidanti.

Thus, in the five kinds of association, affection arises for one who has formed an association through any of these means, and due to previous lust as a condition, strong passion arises. From that, this suffering that follows from affection comes to be. For one who follows that very affection, this suffering of various kinds—such as sorrow and lamentation, in the present and in the future—arises, is produced, comes to be, and is born. Others, however, say, 'The giving over of the mind to an object is association.' From that comes affection, and from affection comes this suffering.

Evamatthappabhedaṃ [P 1.0072][V 1.0058] imaṃ aḍḍhagāthaṃ vatvā so paccekabuddho āha – “svāhaṃ yamidaṃ snehanvayaṃ sokādidukkhaṃ pahoti, tassa dukkhassa mūlaṃ khananto paccekasambodhimadhigato”ti. Evaṃ vutte te amaccā āhaṃsu – “amhehi dāni, bhante, kiṃ kātabba”nti? Tato so āha – “tumhe vā aññe vā yo imamhā dukkhā muccitukāmo, so sabbopi ādīnavaṃ snehajaṃ pekkhamāno, eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”ti. Ettha ca yaṃ “snehanvayaṃ dukkhamidaṃ pahotī”ti vuttaṃ “tadeva sandhāya ādīnavaṃ snehajaṃ pekkhamāno”ti idaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Atha vā yathāvuttena saṃsaggena saṃsaggajātassa bhavati sneho, snehanvayaṃ dukkhamidaṃ pahoti, etaṃ yathābhūtaṃ ādīnavaṃ snehajaṃ pekkhamāno ahaṃ adhigatoti. Evaṃ abhisambandhitvā catutthapādo pubbe vuttanayeneva [M 1.0064] udānavasena vuttopi veditabbo. Tato paraṃ sabbaṃ purimagāthāya vuttasadisamevāti.

Having thus spoken this half-verse explaining the various meanings, that Paccekabuddha said: 'I, while digging up the root of this suffering—namely, the sorrow and so on that follows from affection—attained solitary enlightenment.' When this was said, those ministers asked: 'Venerable sir, what should we do now?' Then he said: 'Whether you or others, whoever wishes to be freed from this suffering, seeing the danger born of affection, should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.' And here, it should be understood that the statement 'seeing the danger born of affection' was said with reference to what was stated as 'this suffering that follows from affection comes to be.' Alternatively: 'Through association as described, affection arises for one born of that association; this suffering follows from affection. Seeing this danger born of affection as it truly is, I have attained.' Thus connecting the meaning, the fourth line should be understood as having been spoken as an inspired utterance, in the same way as stated before. Thereafter, everything is similar to what was said in the previous verse.

Saṃsaggagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Verse on Association is complete.

37. Mitte suhajjeti kā uppatti? Ayaṃ paccekabodhisatto purimagāthāya vuttanayeneva uppajjitvā bārāṇasiyaṃ rajjaṃ kārento paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ nibbattetvā “kiṃ samaṇadhammo varo, rajjaṃ vara”nti vīmaṃsitvā catunnaṃ amaccānaṃ hatthe rajjaṃ niyyātetvā samaṇadhammaṃ karoti. Amaccā “dhammena samena karothā”ti vuttāpi lañjaṃ gahetvā adhammena karonti. Te lañjaṃ gahetvā sāmike parājentā ekadā aññataraṃ rājavallabhaṃ parājesuṃ. So rañño bhattahārakena saddhiṃ pavisitvā sabbaṃ ārocesi. Rājā dutiyadivase sayaṃ vinicchayaṭṭhānaṃ agamāsi. Tato mahājanakāyā – “amaccā sāmike asāmike karontī”ti mahāsaddaṃ karontā mahāyuddhaṃ viya akaṃsu. Atha rājā vinicchayaṭṭhānā vuṭṭhāya pāsādaṃ abhiruhitvā samāpattiṃ appetuṃ nisinno tena saddena vikkhittacitto [P 1.0073] na sakkoti appetuṃ. So “kiṃ me rajjena, samaṇadhammo varo”ti rajjasukhaṃ pahāya puna samāpattiṃ nibbattetvā pubbe vuttanayeneva vipassanto paccekasambodhiṃ sacchākāsi. Kammaṭṭhānañca pucchito imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi –

37. Regarding the verse beginning 'Mitte suhajje,' what is its origin? This Bodhisatta who was to become a Paccekabuddha, having arisen in the manner described in the previous verse and while ruling the kingdom in Bārāṇasī, produced the first jhāna. Having considered, 'What is superior, the ascetic life or the kingdom?' he entrusted the kingdom into the hands of four ministers and undertook the ascetic life. Although the ministers were told, 'You should rule with justice and impartiality,' they took bribes and ruled unjustly. Taking bribes and causing the rightful owners to lose, they one day caused a certain royal favorite to lose his case. He entered with the king's food-bearer and reported everything. The next day, the king himself went to the place of judgment. Then a great crowd of people, shouting, 'The ministers are making owners into non-owners!' made a great noise as if it were a great battle. Then the king, having risen from the place of judgment and ascended to the palace, sat down to enter into attainment, but being distracted by that noise, he was unable to enter it. He thought, 'What is this kingdom to me? The ascetic life is superior.' Having abandoned the pleasure of kingship, he again produced the attainment and, practicing insight in the manner previously described, he realized solitary enlightenment. And being asked about his meditation subject, he spoke this verse:

“Mitte suhajje anukampamāno, hāpeti atthaṃ paṭibaddhacitto;

Etaṃ bhayaṃ santhave pekkhamāno, eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”ti.

Having compassion for friends and companions, with a mind bound by attachment, one neglects one's true welfare. Seeing this danger in intimacy, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.

Tattha mettāyanavasena mittā. Suhadayabhāvena suhajjā. Keci hi ekantahitakāmatāya mittāva honti, na suhajjā. Keci gamanāgamanaṭṭhānanisajjāsamullāpādīsu hadayasukhajananena suhajjāva honti, na mittā. Keci tadubhayavasena suhajjā ceva mittā ca. Te duvidhā honti [V 1.0059] – agāriyā anagāriyā ca. Tattha agāriyā tividhā honti – upakāro, samānasukhadukkho, anukampakoti. Anagāriyā visesena atthakkhāyino eva. Te catūhi aṅgehi samannāgatā honti. Yathāha –

Therein, they are 'friends' (mittā) by way of loving. They are 'companions' (suhajjā) by way of being good-hearted. For some are only friends out of an exclusive desire for one's welfare, not companions. Some are only companions by generating happiness in the heart through coming and going, standing, sitting, conversing, and so on, not friends. Some, by way of both, are companions and friends. They are of two kinds: householders and the homeless. Among them, householder friends are of three kinds: the helper, the one who is the same in happiness and sorrow, and the compassionate one. The homeless friends are especially those who explain what is beneficial. They are endowed with four characteristics. As it is said:

“Catūhi [M 1.0065] kho, gahapatiputta, ṭhānehi upakāro mitto suhado veditabbo – pamattaṃ rakkhati, pamattassa sāpateyyaṃ rakkhati, bhītassa saraṇaṃ hoti, uppannesu kiccakaraṇīyesu taddiguṇaṃ bhogaṃ anuppadeti” (dī. ni. 3.261).

'Son of a householder, a friend who is a helper and a companion should be understood by four things: he protects one who is heedless, he protects the property of the heedless, he is a refuge to the fearful, and when tasks and duties arise, he provides twice the wealth required.' (Dī. Ni. 3.261)

Tathā –

Likewise:

“Catūhi kho, gahapatiputta, ṭhānehi samānasukhadukkho mitto suhado veditabbo – guyhamassa ācikkhati, guyhamassa parigūhati, āpadāsu na vijahati, jīvitampissa atthāya pariccattaṃ hoti” (dī. ni. 3.262).

'Son of a householder, a friend and companion who is the same in happiness and sorrow should be understood by four things: he reveals his own secrets, he keeps his friend's secrets, he does not abandon him in misfortune, and he would even lay down his life for his sake.' (Dī. Ni. 3.262)

Tathā –

Likewise:

“Catūhi kho, gahapatiputta, ṭhānehi anukampako mitto suhado veditabbo – abhavenassa na nandati, bhavenassa nandati, avaṇṇaṃ bhaṇamānaṃ nivāreti, vaṇṇaṃ bhaṇamānaṃ pasaṃsati” (dī. ni. 3.264).

'Son of a householder, a compassionate friend and companion should be understood by four things: he does not rejoice in his friend's misfortune, he rejoices in his prosperity, he restrains those who speak ill of him, and he commends those who speak well of him.' (Dī. Ni. 3.264)

Tathā –

Likewise:

“Catūhi kho, gahapatiputta, ṭhānehi atthakkhāyī mitto suhado veditabbo – pāpā nivāreti, kalyāṇe niveseti, assutaṃ sāveti, saggassa maggaṃ ācikkhatī”ti (dī. ni. 3.263).

"Householder's son, a friend who speaks for one's welfare, a good-hearted friend, is to be known by four instances: he restrains one from evil, encourages one in the good, makes one hear what has not been heard, and points out the path to heaven." (Dī. Ni. 3.263)

Tesvidha agāriyā adhippetā. Atthato pana sabbepi yujjanti. Te mitte suhajje. Anukampamānoti anudayamāno. Tesaṃ sukhaṃ upasaṃharitukāmo dukkhaṃ [P 1.0074] apaharitukāmo ca.

Herein, among them, householders are intended. But in terms of meaning, all are suitable. They are friends, good-hearted ones. Anukampamāno means being compassionate, desiring to bring them happiness and to remove their suffering.

Hāpeti atthanti diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaparamatthavasena tividhaṃ, tathā attatthaparatthaubhayatthavasenāpi [V 1.0060] tividhaṃ. Atthaṃ laddhavināsanena aladdhānuppādanenāti dvidhāpi hāpeti vināseti. Paṭibaddhacittoti “ahaṃ imaṃ vinā na jīvāmi, esa me gati, esa me parāyaṇa”nti evaṃ attānaṃ nīce ṭhāne ṭhapentopi paṭibaddhacitto hoti. “Ime maṃ vinā na jīvanti, ahaṃ tesaṃ gati, tesaṃ parāyaṇa”nti evaṃ attānaṃ ucce ṭhāne ṭhapentopi paṭibaddhacitto hoti. Idha pana evaṃ paṭibaddhacitto adhippeto. Etaṃ bhayanti etaṃ atthahāpanabhayaṃ, attano samāpattihāniṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Santhaveti [M 1.0066] tividho santhavo – taṇhādiṭṭhimittasanthavavasena. Tattha aṭṭhasatappabhedāpi taṇhā taṇhāsanthavo, dvāsaṭṭhibhedāpi diṭṭhi diṭṭhisanthavo, paṭibaddhacittatāya mittānukampanā mittasanthavo. So idhādhippeto. Tena hissa samāpatti parihīnā. Tenāha – “etaṃ bhayaṃ santhave pekkhamāno ahamadhigato”ti. Sesaṃ vuttasadisamevāti veditabbanti.

Hāpeti atthaṃ means he causes the loss of benefit. This benefit is threefold in terms of the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal; similarly, it is threefold in terms of one's own benefit, another's benefit, and the benefit of both. He causes the loss of, and destroys, benefit in two ways: by the destruction of what has been gained and by the non-arising of what has not been gained. Paṭibaddhacitto means one with a bound mind. One who places oneself in a low position, thinking, 'I cannot live without this person; he is my recourse, he is my final resort,' has a bound mind. And one who places oneself in a high position, thinking, 'They cannot live without me; I am their recourse, their final resort,' also has a bound mind. Here, however, one with such a bound mind is intended. Etaṃ bhayaṃ means 'this danger'—this danger of causing the loss of benefit, spoken with reference to the loss of his own attainment. Santhavo means association, and association is of three kinds: by way of association through craving, association through views, and association through friendship. Therein, craving, of one hundred and eight kinds, is association through craving; views, of sixty-two kinds, are association through views; and compassion for friends due to a bound mind is association through friendship. The latter is intended here. For it was because of this that his attainment was lost. Therefore it is said: 'Seeing this danger in association, I attained.' The rest should be understood as has been said.

Mittasuhajjagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Mittasuhajja Gāthā is complete.

38. Vaṃso visāloti kā uppatti? Pubbe kira kassapassa bhagavato sāsane tayo paccekabodhisattā pabbajitvā vīsati vassasahassāni gatapaccāgatavattaṃ pūretvā devaloke uppannā. Tato cavitvā tesaṃ jeṭṭhako bārāṇasirājakule nibbatto, itare paccantarājakulesu. Te ubhopi kammaṭṭhānaṃ uggaṇhitvā, rajjaṃ pahāya pabbajitvā, anukkamena paccekabuddhā hutvā, nandamūlakapabbhāre vasantā ekadivasaṃ samāpattito vuṭṭhāya “mayaṃ kiṃ kammaṃ katvā imaṃ lokuttarasukhaṃ anuppattā”ti āvajjetvā paccavekkhamānā kassapabuddhakāle attano cariyaṃ addasaṃsu. Tato “tatiyo kuhi”nti āvajjentā bārāṇasiyaṃ rajjaṃ [P 1.0075] kārentaṃ disvā tassa guṇe saritvā “so pakatiyāva appicchatādiguṇasamannāgato ahosi, amhākaññeva ovādako vattā vacanakkhamo pāpagarahī, handa, naṃ ārammaṇaṃ dassetvā mocessāmā”ti okāsaṃ gavesantā taṃ ekadivasaṃ sabbālaṅkāravibhūsitaṃ uyyānaṃ gacchantaṃ disvā ākāsenāgantvā uyyānadvāre veḷugumbamūle aṭṭhaṃsu. Mahājano atitto rājadassanena rājānaṃ oloketi. Tato rājā “atthi nu kho koci mama dassane abyāvaṭo”ti olokento paccekabuddhe addakkhi. Saha dassaneneva cassa tesu sineho uppajji.

38. What is the origin of 'Vaṃso visālo'? It is said that in the past, during the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, three Paccekabodhisattas went forth and, after fulfilling the practice of coming and going for twenty thousand years, arose in the world of the devas. After passing away from there, the eldest of them was reborn in the royal family of Bārāṇasī, while the others were reborn in outlying royal families. Both of them, having learned a meditation subject, renounced their kingdoms and went forth. In due course, they became Paccekabuddhas and were dwelling on the Nandamūlaka mountain slope. One day, emerging from their attainment, they reflected, 'Having done what kamma have we attained this supramundane happiness?' Reviewing thus, they saw their own conduct during the time of the Buddha Kassapa. Then, reflecting, 'Where is the third one?' they saw him ruling in Bārāṇasī. Remembering his virtues, they thought: 'He was naturally endowed with qualities such as having few wishes; he was our advisor, an admonisher, receptive to counsel, and a reprover of evil. Come, let us show him a meditation object and liberate him.' Seeking an opportunity, one day they saw him going to the park, adorned with all his ornaments. Coming through the sky, they stood at the park gate at the foot of a bamboo clump. The great crowd, not having had their fill of seeing the king, gazed upon him. Then the king, looking around and thinking, 'Is there anyone not engaged in seeing me?' saw the Paccekabuddhas. And just upon seeing them, affection for them arose in him.

So hatthikkhandhā oruyha santena upacārena te upasaṅkamitvā “bhante, kiṃ nāmā tumhe”ti pucchi. Te āhaṃsu “mayaṃ, mahārāja, asajjamānā nāmā”ti. “Bhante, ‘asajjamānā’ti etassa ko attho”ti? “Alagganattho, mahārājā”ti. Tato taṃ veḷugumbaṃ dassentā āhaṃsu – “seyyathāpi, mahārāja, imaṃ veḷugumbaṃ sabbaso mūlakhandhasākhānusākhāhi saṃsibbitvā [V 1.0061] ṭhitaṃ asihattho puriso mūle chetvā āviñchanto na sakkuṇeyya uddharituṃ[M 1.0067], evameva tvaṃ anto ca bahi ca jaṭāya jaṭito āsattavisatto tattha laggo. Seyyathāpi vā panassa vemajjhagatopi ayaṃ vaṃsakaḷīro asañjātasākhattā kenaci alaggo ṭhito, sakkā ca pana agge vā mūle vā chetvā uddharituṃ, evameva mayaṃ katthaci asajjamānā sabbadisā gacchāmā”ti tāvadeva catutthajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā passato eva rañño ākāsena nandamūlakapabbhāraṃ agamaṃsu. Tato rājā cintesi – “kadā nu kho ahampi evaṃ asajjamāno bhaveyya”nti tattheva nisīditvā vipassanto paccekabodhiṃ sacchākāsi. Purimanayeneva kammaṭṭhānaṃ pucchito imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi –

He descended from the elephant's back and, with a calm demeanor, approached them and asked, 'Venerable sirs, what are your names?' They replied, 'Great king, we are called the Unattached.' 'Venerable sirs, what is the meaning of "Unattached"?' 'It means not clinging, great king.' Then, pointing to that clump of bamboo, they said: 'Great king, just as this clump of bamboo stands, completely intertwined with all its roots, trunk, branches, and twigs, and a man with a sword in hand, having cut it at the root, would not be able to pull it out and uproot it; in the same way, you are entangled within and without by entanglement, attached, clinging, and stuck there. But just as this bamboo shoot in its midst, having not yet grown branches, stands unattached to anything, and it is possible to cut it at the top or the root and pull it out; so too, we go in all directions without clinging anywhere.' Then and there, having entered the fourth jhāna, they went through the sky to the Nandamūlaka mountain slope, even as the king was watching. Then the king thought: 'When, indeed, will I too be thus unattached?' Sitting right there and developing insight, he realized the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha. When asked about his meditation subject in the same way as before, he spoke this verse:

“Vaṃso visālova yathā visatto, puttesu dāresu ca yā apekkhā;

Vaṃsakkaḷīrova asajjamāno, eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”ti.

“Just as a great bamboo is entangled, so is the longing for sons and wives; like a bamboo shoot, unattached, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.”

Tattha [P 1.0076] vaṃsoti veḷu. Visāloti vitthiṇṇo. Cakāro avadhāraṇattho, evakāro vā ayaṃ, sandhivasenettha ekāro naṭṭho. Tassa parapadena sambandho, taṃ pacchā yojessāma. Yathāti paṭibhāge. Visattoti laggo, jaṭito saṃsibbito. Puttesu dāresu cāti puttadhītubhariyāsu. Yā apekkhāti yā taṇhā yo sneho. Vaṃsakkaḷīrova asajjamānoti vaṃsakaḷīro viya alaggamāno. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yathā vaṃso visālo visatto eva hoti, puttesu dāresu ca yā apekkhā, sāpi evaṃ tāni vatthūni saṃsibbitvā ṭhitattā visattā eva. Svāhaṃ tāya apekkhāya apekkhavā visālo vaṃso viya visattoti evaṃ apekkhāya ādīnavaṃ disvā taṃ apekkhaṃ maggañāṇena chindanto ayaṃ vaṃsakaḷīrova rūpādīsu vā lobhādīsu vā kāmabhavādīsu vā diṭṭhādīsu vā taṇhāmānadiṭṭhivasena asajjamāno paccekabodhiṃ adhigatoti. Sesaṃ purimanayeneva veditabbanti.

Herein, 'vaṃsa' means bamboo. 'Visāla' means broad. The particle 'ca' has the meaning of emphasis, or this is the word 'eva', where the letter 'e' has been lost due to sandhi. Its connection is with the following word; we shall apply it later. 'Yathā' is in the sense of comparison. 'Visatta' means attached, entangled, intertwined. 'Puttesu dāresu ca' means among sons, daughters, and wives. 'Yā apekkhā' means that craving, that affection. 'Vaṃsakkaḷīrova asajjamāno' means like a bamboo shoot, unattached. What is meant? Just as a broad bamboo is indeed entangled, so too is the longing for sons and wives; because it stands intertwined with those objects, it is indeed entangled. I, seeing the danger in that longing and cutting it off with the knowledge of the path, like this bamboo shoot, unattached to forms, etc., or greed, etc., or sensual existence, etc., or views, etc., by way of craving, conceit, and wrong views, have attained Paccekabodhi. The rest should be understood in the same way as before.

Vaṃsakaḷīragāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Vaṃsakaḷīra Gāthā is concluded.

39. Migo [M 1.0068] araññamhīti kā uppatti? Eko kira bhikkhu kassapassa bhagavato sāsane yogāvacaro kālaṃ katvā, bārāṇasiyaṃ seṭṭhikule uppanno aḍḍhe mahaddhane mahābhoge, so subhago ahosi. Tato paradāriko hutvā tattha kālakato niraye nibbatto tattha paccitvā vipākāvasesena seṭṭhibhariyāya kucchimhi itthipaṭisandhiṃ aggahesi. Nirayato āgatānaṃ gattāni uṇhāni honti. Tena seṭṭhibhariyā ḍayhamānena udarena kicchena kasirena taṃ gabbhaṃ dhāretvā [V 1.0062] kālena dārikaṃ vijāyi. Sā jātadivasato pabhuti mātāpitūnaṃ sesabandhuparijanānañca dessā ahosi. Vayappattā ca yamhi kule dinnā, tatthāpi sāmikasassusasurānaṃ dessāva ahosi appiyā amanāpā. Atha nakkhatte ghosite seṭṭhiputto tāya saddhiṃ kīḷituṃ anicchanto vesiṃ ānetvā kīḷati. Sā taṃ dāsīnaṃ santikā sutvā seṭṭhiputtaṃ upasaṅkamitvā nānappakārehi anunayitvā āha – “ayyaputta, itthī nāma sacepi dasannaṃ rājūnaṃ kaniṭṭhā hoti, cakkavattino vā dhītā, tathāpi sāmikassa pesanakarā hoti. Sāmike anālapante sūle āropitā viya dukkhaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti. Sace [P 1.0077] ahaṃ anuggahārahā, anuggahetabbā. No ce, vissajjetabbā, attano ñātikulaṃ gamissāmī”ti. Seṭṭhiputto – “hotu, bhadde, mā soci, kīḷanasajjā hohi, nakkhattaṃ kīḷissāmā”ti āha. Seṭṭhidhītā tāvatakenapi sallāpamattena ussāhajātā “sve nakkhattaṃ kīḷissāmī”ti bahuṃ khajjabhojjaṃ paṭiyādeti. Seṭṭhiputto dutiyadivase anārocetvāva kīḷanaṭṭhānaṃ gato. Sā “idāni pesessati, idāni pesessatī”ti maggaṃ olokentī nisinnā ussūraṃ disvā manusse pesesi. Te paccāgantvā “seṭṭhiputto gato”ti ārocesuṃ. Sā sabbaṃ taṃ paṭiyāditaṃ ādāya yānaṃ abhiruhitvā uyyānaṃ gantuṃ āraddhā.

39. What is the origin of “A deer in the forest”? It is said that a certain monk in the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, a meditator, passed away and was reborn in a wealthy merchant family in Bārāṇasī, a family that was prosperous, of great wealth, and with many possessions. He was handsome. Later, having become an adulterer, he died and was reborn in hell. Having been tormented there, due to the residual effect of his karma, he took rebirth as a female in the womb of the merchant's wife. The bodies of those who come from hell are hot. Therefore, the merchant's wife, with her belly burning, carried that fetus with difficulty and hardship, and in due time gave birth to a girl. From the day of her birth, she was detested by her parents and by her other relatives and attendants. When she came of age and was given in marriage into a certain family, there too she was detested by her husband, mother-in-law, and father-in-law, being unloved and disagreeable. Then, when a festival was announced, the merchant's son, not wanting to celebrate with her, brought a courtesan and celebrated with her. Having heard this from the female servants, she approached the merchant's son and, after persuading him in various ways, said: “Noble son, even if a woman is the youngest sister of ten kings, or the daughter of a wheel-turning monarch, she is still a servant to her husband. When her husband does not speak to her, she experiences suffering as if she were impaled on a stake. If I am worthy of favor, I should be favored. If not, I should be sent away, and I will go to my own relatives' family.” The merchant's son said: “So be it, good lady. Do not grieve. Get ready for the celebration; we will celebrate the festival.” The merchant's daughter, encouraged by even that little bit of conversation, thinking, “Tomorrow I will celebrate the festival,” prepared much edible and non-edible food. The next day, without informing her, the merchant's son went to the place of celebration. She sat watching the road, thinking, “Now he will send for me, now he will send for me,” and seeing it was late, she sent some people. They returned and reported, “The merchant's son has gone.” Taking all that she had prepared, she mounted a vehicle and set out to go to the park.

Atha nandamūlakapabbhāre paccekasambuddho sattame divase nirodhā vuṭṭhāya anotatte mukhaṃ dhovitvā nāgalatādantapoṇaṃ khāditvā “kattha ajja bhikkhaṃ carissāmī”ti āvajjento taṃ seṭṭhidhītaraṃ disvā “imissā mayi sakkāraṃ karitvā taṃ kammaṃ parikkhayaṃ gamissatī”ti ñatvā pabbhārasamīpe [M 1.0069] saṭṭhiyojanaṃ manosilātalaṃ, tattha ṭhatvā nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya abhiññāpādakajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā ākāsenāgantvā tassā paṭipathe oruyha bārāṇasībhimukho agamāsi. Taṃ disvā dāsiyo seṭṭhidhītāya ārocesuṃ. Sā yānā oruyha sakkaccaṃ vanditvā, pattaṃ gahetvā, sabbarasasampannena khādanīyabhojanīyena pūretvā, padumapupphena paṭicchādetvā heṭṭhāpi padumapupphaṃ katvā, pupphakalāpaṃ hatthena gahetvā, paccekabuddhaṃ upasaṅkamitvā, tassa hatthe pattaṃ datvā, vanditvā, pupphakalāpahatthā patthesi “bhante, yathā idaṃ pupphaṃ, evāhaṃ yattha yattha uppajjāmi, tattha tattha mahājanassa piyā bhaveyyaṃ manāpā”ti. Evaṃ patthetvā dutiyaṃ patthesi “bhante, dukkho gabbhavāso, taṃ anupagamma padumapupphe evaṃ paṭisandhi bhaveyyā”ti. Tatiyampi patthesi “bhante, jigucchanīyo mātugāmo, cakkavattidhītāpi paravasaṃ gacchati, tasmā ahaṃ itthibhāvaṃ anupagamma puriso bhaveyya”nti. Catutthampi [P 1.0078] patthesi “bhante, imaṃ saṃsāradukkhaṃ atikkamma pariyosāne tumhehi pattaṃ amataṃ pāpuṇeyya”nti.

Then, a Paccekabuddha at the Nandamūla slope, having emerged from cessation on the seventh day, washed his face at Anotatta lake, chewed a nāgalatā tooth-stick, and while considering, "Where shall I go for alms today?" he saw the merchant’s daughter. Knowing, "By her making an offering to me, that karma of hers will come to exhaustion," he stood on a sixty-yojana-wide platform of red arsenic near the slope, donned his robes, took his bowl and robe, entered the meditative attainment that is the basis for supernormal powers, traveled through the sky, descended onto her path, and proceeded toward Bārāṇasī. Seeing him, the maids informed the merchant’s daughter. She descended from her vehicle, respectfully paid homage, took his bowl, filled it with edible and non-edible food endowed with all flavors, covered it with a lotus flower, placed a lotus flower beneath it as well, took a cluster of flowers in her hand, approached the Paccekabuddha, placed the bowl into his hands, paid homage, and with the cluster of flowers in hand, she made a wish: "Venerable sir, just as this flower is, so may I be dear and pleasing to the great multitude wherever I am reborn." Having made this wish, she made a second: "Venerable sir, dwelling in the womb is painful; without undergoing that, may my rebirth be in a lotus flower." She also made a third wish: "Venerable sir, the female state is repulsive; even a wheel-turning monarch’s daughter becomes dependent on another. Therefore, may I not undergo the female state but be a man." She also made a fourth wish: "Venerable sir, having transcended this suffering of saṃsāra, may I, in the end, attain the deathless state attained by you."

Evaṃ [V 1.0063] caturo paṇidhayo katvā, taṃ padumapupphakalāpaṃ pūjetvā, paccekabuddhassa pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā “pupphasadiso eva me gandho ceva vaṇṇo ca hotū”ti imaṃ pañcamaṃ paṇidhiṃ akāsi. Tato paccekabuddho pattaṃ pupphakalāpañca gahetvā ākāse ṭhatvā –

Having thus made four aspirations, she offered that cluster of lotus flowers to the Paccekabuddha and paid homage with the fivefold prostration. She then made this fifth aspiration: "May my fragrance and complexion be just like a flower." Then the Paccekabuddha, taking the bowl and the cluster of flowers, stood in the sky and—

“Icchitaṃ patthitaṃ tuyhaṃ, khippameva samijjhatu;

Sabbe pūrentu saṅkappā, cando pannaraso yathā”ti. –

“May what you have wished and longed for be quickly fulfilled for you; may all your aspirations be fulfilled, like the moon on the fifteenth day.”

Imāya gāthāya seṭṭhidhītāya anumodanaṃ katvā “seṭṭhidhītā maṃ gacchantaṃ passatū”ti adhiṭṭhahitvā nandamūlakapabbhāraṃ agamāsi. Seṭṭhidhītāya taṃ disvā mahatī pīti uppannā. Bhavantare kataṃ akusalakammaṃ anokāsatāya parikkhīṇaṃ, ciñcambiladhotatambabhājanamiva suddhā jātā. Tāvadeva cassā patikule ñātikule ca sabbo jano tuṭṭho “kiṃ karomā”ti piyavacanāni paṇṇākārāni ca pesesi. Seṭṭhiputto manusse pesesi “sīghaṃ sīghaṃ ānetha seṭṭhidhītaraṃ, ahaṃ vissaritvā uyyānaṃ āgato”ti. Tato pabhuti ca naṃ ure vilittacandanaṃ viya āmuttamuttāhāraṃ viya pupphamālaṃ viya ca piyāyanto parihari.

Having given thanks to the merchant's daughter with this verse, he resolved, "May the merchant's daughter see me as I go," and went to the Nandamūla slope. When the merchant's daughter saw him, great joy arose in her. The unwholesome kamma done in a previous existence, having found no opportunity, was exhausted, and she became pure, like a copper pot washed with tamarind. Immediately, all the people in her husband's family and her own family were delighted, sending affectionate words and gifts, saying, "What shall we do for you?" The merchant's son sent men, saying, "Quickly, quickly bring the merchant's daughter; I came to the park, having forgotten her." From then on, cherishing her, he cared for her as if she were sandalwood smeared on his chest, a pearl necklace he wore, or a garland of flowers.

Sā [M 1.0070] tattha yāvatāyukaṃ issariyabhogasukhaṃ anubhavitvā kālaṃ katvā purisabhāvena devaloke padumapupphe uppajji. So devaputto gacchantopi padumapupphagabbheyeva gacchati, tiṭṭhantopi, nisīdantopi, sayantopi padumagabbheyeva sayati. Mahāpadumadevaputtoti cassa nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Evaṃ so tena iddhānubhāvena anulomapaṭilomaṃ chadevaloke eva saṃsarati.

She, having experienced the pleasures of sovereignty and wealth there for as long as her life lasted, passed away and was reborn in a male state in the deva world, in a lotus flower. That devaputta, even when going, went within the lotus womb; even when standing, sitting, or lying down, he lay down within the lotus womb. They gave him the name Mahāpadumadevaputta. Thus, by that supernormal power, he transmigrated only within the six deva worlds, in direct and reverse order.

Tena [P 1.0079] ca samayena bārāṇasirañño vīsati itthisahassāni honti. Rājā ekissāpi kucchiyaṃ puttaṃ na labhati. Amaccā rājānaṃ viññāpesuṃ “deva, kulavaṃsānupālako putto icchitabbo, atraje avijjamāne khetrajopi kulavaṃsadharo hotī”ti. Rājā “ṭhapetvā mahesiṃ avasesā nāṭakitthiyo sattāhaṃ dhammanāṭakaṃ karothā”ti yathākāmaṃ bahi carāpesi, tathāpi puttaṃ nālattha. Puna amaccā āhaṃsu – “mahārāja, mahesī nāma puññena ca paññāya ca sabbitthīnaṃ aggā, appeva nāma devo mahesiyāpi kucchismiṃ puttaṃ labheyyā”ti. Rājā mahesiyā etamatthaṃ ārocesi. Sā āha – “mahārāja, yā itthī saccavādinī sīlavatī, sā puttaṃ labheyya, hirottapparahitāya kuto putto”ti pāsādaṃ abhiruhitvā pañca sīlāni samādiyitvā punappunaṃ anumajjati. Sīlavatiyā rājadhītāya pañca sīlāni anumajjantiyā puttapatthanācitte uppannamatte sakkassa āsanaṃ santappi.

At that time, the king of Bārāṇasī had twenty thousand women. The king did not obtain a son from the womb of even one. The ministers advised the king, "Your Majesty, a son who upholds the lineage should be sought. If there is no son of one's own, even a field-born child can carry on the lineage." The king commanded, "Except for the chief queen, let the remaining dancing women perform a righteous drama for seven days," and had them wander outside as they wished. Still, he did not obtain a son. Again, the ministers said, "Great king, the chief queen is foremost among all women in merit and wisdom. Perhaps Your Majesty may obtain a son in the chief queen's womb." The king informed the chief queen of this matter. She said, "Great king, a woman who is truthful and virtuous may obtain a son. How can one without shame and moral dread have a son?" Ascending the palace, she undertook the five precepts and repeatedly reflected upon them. As the virtuous princess reflected upon the five precepts, just as the wish for a son arose in her mind, Sakka's throne grew hot.

Atha [V 1.0064] sakko āsanatāpakāraṇaṃ āvajjento etamatthaṃ viditvā “sīlavatiyā rājadhītāya puttavaraṃ demī”ti ākāsenāgantvā deviyā sammukhe ṭhatvā “kiṃ patthesi devī”ti pucchi. “Puttaṃ, mahārājā”ti. “Dammi te, devi, puttaṃ, mā cintayī”ti vatvā devalokaṃ gantvā “atthi nu kho ettha khīṇāyuko”ti āvajjento “ayaṃ mahāpadumo uparidevaloke uppajjituṃ ito cavatī”ti ñatvā tassa vimānaṃ gantvā “tāta mahāpaduma, manussalokaṃ gacchāhī”ti yāci. So āha – “mahārāja, mā evaṃ bhaṇi, jeguccho manussaloko”ti. “Tāta, tvaṃ manussaloke puññaṃ katvā idhūpapanno, tattheva ṭhatvā pāramiyo pūretabbā, gaccha, tātā”ti. “Dukkho, mahārāja, gabbhavāso, na sakkomi tattha vasitu”nti. “Kiṃ te, tāta, gabbhavāsena, tathā hi tvaṃ kammamakāsi, yathā [M 1.0071] padumagabbheyeva nibbattissasi, gaccha, tātā”ti punappunaṃ vuccamāno adhivāsesi.

Then Sakka, considering the reason for his seat being hot, understood the matter. Thinking, “I shall grant the boon of a son to the virtuous princess,” he came through the air, stood before the queen, and asked, “What do you desire, O queen?” “A son, great king,” she replied. “I grant you a son, O queen; do not worry,” he said, and went to the deva world. Considering, “Is there anyone here whose life is exhausted?” he knew, “This Mahāpaduma is passing away from here to be reborn in an upper deva world.” Going to his celestial mansion, he requested, “Dear Mahāpaduma, go to the human world.” He replied, “Great king, do not say so; the human world is repulsive.” “Dear one, you performed merit in the human world and were reborn here. Remaining there, you should fulfill the perfections. Go, dear one.” “Great king, dwelling in the womb is painful; I cannot endure living there.” “What is dwelling in the womb to you, dear one? For you have performed such kamma that you will be born right in a lotus womb. Go, dear one.” Being repeatedly urged, he consented.

Tato mahāpadumo devalokā cavitvā bārāṇasirañño [P 1.0080] uyyāne silāpaṭṭapokkharaṇiyaṃ padumagabbhe nibbatto. Tañca rattiṃ mahesī paccūsasamaye supinantena vīsatiitthisahassaparivutā uyyānaṃ gantvā silāpaṭṭapokkharaṇiyaṃ padumassare puttaṃ laddhā viya ahosi. Sā pabhātāya rattiyā sīlāni rakkhamānā tatheva tattha gantvā ekaṃ padumapupphaṃ addasa. Taṃ neva tīre hoti na gambhīre. Saha dassaneneva cassā tattha puttasineho uppajji. Sā sāmaṃyeva pavisitvā taṃ pupphaṃ aggahesi. Pupphe gahitamatteyeva pattāni vikasiṃsu. Tattha taṭṭake āsittasuvaṇṇapaṭimaṃ viya dārakaṃ addasa. Disvāva “putto me laddho”ti saddaṃ nicchāresi. Mahājano sādhukārasahassāni muñci, rañño ca pesesi. Rājā sutvā “kattha laddho”ti pucchitvā laddhokāsañca sutvā “uyyānañca pokkharaṇiyaṃ padumañca amhākaññeva khettaṃ, tasmā amhākaṃ khette jātattā khetrajo nāmāyaṃ putto”ti vatvā nagaraṃ pavesetvā vīsatisahassaitthiyo dhātikiccaṃ kārāpesi. Yā yā kumārassa ruciṃ ñatvā patthitapatthitaṃ khādanīyaṃ khādāpeti, sā sā sahassaṃ labhati. Sakalabārāṇasī calitā, sabbo jano kumārassa paṇṇākārasahassāni pesesi. Kumāro taṃ taṃ atinetvā “imaṃ khāda, imaṃ bhuñjā”ti vuccamāno bhojanena ubbāḷho ukkaṇṭhito hutvā, gopuradvāraṃ gantvā, lākhāguḷakena kīḷati.

Then Mahāpaduma, having passed away from the deva world, was born in a lotus womb in the stone-slab pond in the park of the king of Bārāṇasī. And that night, at dawn, the queen had a dream in which, surrounded by twenty thousand women, she went to the park and it was as if she had obtained a son in the lotus pond of the stone-slab pond. When the night had dawned, while observing the precepts, she went there just as in her dream and saw a single lotus flower. It was neither near the shore nor in the deep water. Merely upon seeing it, maternal affection arose in her. She entered the water herself and took hold of the flower. The moment she grasped it, the petals opened, and there she saw a child like a cast golden image. Upon seeing him, she exclaimed, “I have obtained a son!” The great multitude uttered thousands of acclamations and sent word to the king. Hearing this, the king asked, “Where was he found?” Upon learning the place, he declared, “The park, the pond, and the lotus are all our own property. Therefore, since he was born in our field, this son is named ‘Born of the Field.’” He then had the child brought into the city and appointed twenty thousand women to nurse him. Whichever woman understood the prince’s liking and fed him the desired delicacies received a thousand. The whole of Bārāṇasī was stirred, and all the people sent thousands of gifts to the prince. The prince, being constantly urged, “Eat this, consume that,” as they brought him various foods, became overwhelmed and distressed. He went to the city gate and played with a lac ball.

Tadā aññataro paccekabuddho bārāṇasiṃ nissāya isipatane vasati. So kālasseva vuṭṭhāya senāsanavattasarīraparikammamanasikārādīni sabbakiccāni katvā, paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito “ajja kattha bhikkhaṃ gahessāmī”ti āvajjento kumārassa sampattiṃ disvā “esa pubbe kiṃ kammaṃ karī”ti vīmaṃsanto “mādisassa piṇḍapātaṃ datvā, catasso patthanā patthesi tattha tisso [V 1.0065] siddhā, ekā tāva na sijjhati, tassa upāyena ārammaṇaṃ dassemī”ti bhikkhācariyavasena [P 1.0081] kumārassa santikaṃ agamāsi. Kumāro taṃ disvā “samaṇa, mā idha āgacchi, ime hi tampi ‘idaṃ khāda, idaṃ bhuñjā’ti vadeyyu”nti āha. So ekavacaneneva tato nivattitvā [M 1.0072] attano senāsanaṃ pāvisi. Kumāro parijanaṃ āha – “ayaṃ samaṇo mayā vuttamattova nivatto, kuddho, nu, kho mamā”ti. Tato tehi “pabbajitā nāma, deva, na kodhaparāyaṇā honti, parena pasannamanena yaṃ dinnaṃ hoti, tena yāpentī”ti vuccamānopi “kuddho eva mamāyaṃ samaṇo, khamāpessāmi na”nti mātāpitūnaṃ ārocetvā hatthiṃ abhiruhitvā, mahatā rājānubhāvena isipatanaṃ gantvā, migayūthaṃ disvā, pucchi “kiṃ nāma ete”ti? “Ete, sāmi, migā nāmā”ti. Etesaṃ “imaṃ khādatha, imaṃ bhuñjatha, imaṃ sāyathā”ti vatvā paṭijaggantā atthīti. Natthi sāmi, yattha tiṇodakaṃ sulabhaṃ, tattha vasantīti.

At that time, a certain Paccekabuddha was dwelling near Bārāṇasī in Isipatana. Rising early, he completed all his duties, such as the observances of the lodging, care of the body, and mental application. Emerging from seclusion, he considered, “Where shall I go for alms today?” Noticing the prince’s prosperity, he wondered, “What deed did this one perform in the past?” Investigating, he thought, “Having given almsfood to one like me, he made four aspirations. Of these, three have been fulfilled, but one is not yet fulfilled. By a skillful means, I shall give him an object for reflection.” Thus, in the course of his alms-round, he approached the prince. Seeing him, the prince said, “Ascetic, do not come here, for these people might say even to you, ‘Eat this, consume that.’” With just that one word, the Paccekabuddha turned back and entered his own dwelling. The prince said to his attendants, “This ascetic turned back as soon as I spoke. Could he be angry with me?” Then, although they said, “Lord, those who have gone forth are not prone to anger. They sustain themselves with what is given by another with a serene mind,” he thought, “This ascetic is indeed angry with me. I shall ask for his forgiveness.” Having informed his parents, he mounted an elephant and, with great royal splendor, went to Isipatana. Seeing a herd of deer, he asked, “What are these called?” “Lord, these are called deer.” “Are there any who look after them, saying, ‘Eat this, consume this, taste this’?” “There are not, lord. They dwell where grass and water are easily found.”

Kumāro “yathā ime arakkhiyamānāva yattha icchanti, tattha vasanti, kadā nu, kho, ahampi evaṃ vaseyya”nti etamārammaṇaṃ aggahesi. Paccekabuddhopi tassa āgamanaṃ ñatvā senāsanamaggañca caṅkamañca sammajjitvā, maṭṭhaṃ katvā, ekadvikkhattuṃ caṅkamitvā, padanikkhepaṃ dassetvā, divāvihārokāsañca paṇṇasālañca sammajjitvā, maṭṭhaṃ katvā, pavisanapadanikkhepaṃ dassetvā, nikkhamanapadanikkhepaṃ adassetvā, aññatra agamāsi. Kumāro tattha gantvā taṃ padesaṃ sammajjitvā maṭṭhaṃ kataṃ disvā “vasati maññe ettha so paccekabuddho”ti parijanena bhāsitaṃ sutvā āha – “pātopi so samaṇo kuddho, idāni hatthiassādīhi attano okāsaṃ akkantaṃ disvā, suṭṭhutaraṃ kujjheyya, idheva tumhe tiṭṭhathā”ti hatthikkhandhā oruyha ekakova senāsanaṃ paviṭṭho vattasīsena susammaṭṭhokāse [P 1.0082] padanikkhepaṃ disvā, “ayaṃ samaṇo ettha caṅkamanto na vaṇijjādikammaṃ cintesi, addhā attano hitameva cintesi maññe”ti pasannamānaso caṅkamaṃ āruhitvā, dūrīkataputhuvitakko gantvā, pāsāṇaphalake nisīditvā, sañjātaekaggo hutvā, paṇṇasālaṃ pavisitvā, vipassanto paccekabodhiñāṇaṃ adhigantvā, purimanayeneva purohitena kammaṭṭhāne pucchite gaganatale nisinno imaṃ gāthamāha –

The prince took this as his object of reflection: “Just as these deer, unguarded, dwell wherever they wish, when, I wonder, will I too dwell in such a way?” The Paccekabuddha, knowing of his arrival, swept the path to his dwelling and the walking path, making them smooth. He walked up and down once or twice, leaving his footprints. He swept the place for daytime abiding and the leaf-hut, making them smooth. He left footprints showing his entry, but not his exit, and went elsewhere. When the prince arrived there, he saw that the area was swept and made smooth. Hearing his attendants say, “I think that Paccekabuddha dwells here,” he replied, “That ascetic was angry this morning; now, seeing his place trampled by elephants, horses, and so on, he would be even more angry. You all stay right here.” Descending from the elephant’s back, he entered the dwelling alone. Seeing the footprints on the well-swept ground, he thought, “While walking here, this ascetic did not think of commerce or other such activities; surely, I think, he thought only of his own welfare.” With a serene mind, he went up to the walking path. Having put aside worldly thoughts, he went and sat on a stone slab and, becoming one-pointed in mind, he entered the leaf-hut. Practicing insight meditation, he attained the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha. Then, when questioned by the chaplain about his object of meditation, just as before, he sat in the sky and spoke this verse:

“Migo [M 1.0073] araññamhi yathā abaddho, yenicchakaṃ gacchati gocarāya;

Viññū naro seritaṃ pekkhamāno, eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”ti.

“As a deer in the forest, unbound, goes wherever it desires for pasture; so the wise person, seeing freedom, should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.”

Tattha migoti dve migā eṇīmigo, pasadamigo cāti. Apica sabbesaṃ āraññikānaṃ catuppadānametaṃ [V 1.0066] adhivacanaṃ. Idha pana pasadamigo adhippeto. Araññamhīti gāmañca [P 1.0083] gāmūpacārañca ṭhapetvā avasesaṃ araññaṃ, idhaṃ pana uyyānamadhippetaṃ, tasmā uyyānamhīti vuttaṃ hoti. Yathāti paṭibhāge. Abaddhoti rajjubandhanādīhi abaddho, etena vissatthacariyaṃ dīpeti. Yenicchakaṃ gacchati gocarāyati yena yena disābhāgena gantumicchati, tena tena disābhāgena gocarāya gacchati. Vuttampi cetaṃ bhagavatā –

Therein, 'miga' refers to two kinds of deer: the eṇī-deer and the pasada-deer. Moreover, this is a designation for all four-footed forest creatures. Here, however, the pasada-deer is intended. 'In the forest' means that when the village and the village outskirts are excluded, the remainder is the forest. Here, however, a park is intended; therefore, it is said as 'in the park.' 'Yathā' (as) is in the sense of a comparison. 'Unbound' means not bound by ropes and so forth; by this is shown its free-roaming conduct. 'Goes for pasture wherever it wishes' means that it goes to graze in whatever direction it wishes to go. And this was also stated by the Blessed One:

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, āraññako migo araññe pavane caramāno vissattho gacchati, vissattho tiṭṭhati, vissattho nisīdati, vissattho seyyaṃ kappeti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Anāpāthagato, bhikkhave, luddassa; evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi…pe… paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, bhikkhu andhamakāsi māraṃ apadaṃ, vadhitvā māracakkhuṃ adassanaṃ gato pāpimato”ti (ma. ni. 1.287; cūḷani. khaggavisāṇasuttaniddesa 125) vitthāro.

“Just as, monks, a forest deer wandering in a forest grove moves confidently, stands confidently, sits confidently, and lies down confidently. For what reason? Because, monks, it is out of the hunter’s range. In the same way, monks, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures… having entered and abided in the first jhāna. This monk, monks, is said to have blinded Māra, to have made him trackless, and, having destroyed Māra’s eye, to have passed from the sight of the Evil One.”

Viññū [M 1.0074] naroti paṇḍitapuriso. Seritanti sacchandavuttitaṃ aparāyattataṃ. Pekkhamānoti paññācakkhunā olokayamāno. Atha vā dhammaseritaṃ puggalaseritañca. Lokuttaradhammā hi kilesavasaṃ agamanato serino tehi samannāgatā puggalā ca, tesaṃ bhāvaniddeso seritā. Taṃ pekkhamānoti. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? “Yathā migo araññamhi abaddho yenicchakaṃ gacchati gocarāya, kadā nu kho ahampi evaṃ gaccheyya”nti iti me tumhehi ito cito ca parivāretvā ṭhitehi baddhassa yenicchakaṃ gantuṃ alabhantassa [P 1.0084] tasmiṃ yenicchakagamanābhāvena yenicchakagamane cānisaṃsaṃ disvā anukkamena samathavipassanā pāripūriṃ agamaṃsu. Tato paccekabodhiṃ adhigatomhi. Tasmā aññopi viññū paṇḍito naro seritaṃ pekkhamāno eko care khaggavisāṇakappoti. Sesaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbanti.

A wise person is an intelligent man. 'Serita' means living according to one's own will, independence. 'Pekkhamāno' means observing with the eye of wisdom. Alternatively, it refers to the freedom of the Dhamma and the freedom of the person. For supramundane Dhammas are free, not falling under the sway of defilements, and the individuals endowed with them are likewise free; their state is 'seritā'.
