'Observing that' means this: What is said? 'Just as a deer in the forest, unbound, goes for pasture wherever it wishes, when indeed shall I too go thus?' Thus, for me, who was bound by you standing and surrounding me here and there, unable to go as I wished, upon seeing the benefit of going as one wishes through the lack thereof, serenity and insight gradually reached fulfillment. Then I attained Paccekabodhi. Therefore, any other wise and intelligent person, observing such freedom, should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros. The rest should be understood in the manner already explained.

Migaaraññagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Migaarañña-gāthā is complete.

40. Āmantanā hotīti kā uppatti? Atīte kira ekavajjikabrahmadatto nāma rājā ahosi mudukajātiko. Yadā amaccā tena saha yuttaṃ vā ayuttaṃ vā mantetukāmā honti, tadā naṃ pāṭiyekkaṃ pāṭiyekkaṃ ekamantaṃ nenti. Taṃ ekadivasaṃ divāseyyaṃ upagataṃ aññataro amacco “deva, mama sotabbaṃ atthī”ti ekamantaṃ gamanaṃ yāci. So uṭṭhāya agamāsi. Puna eko mahāupaṭṭhāne nisinnaṃ varaṃ yāci, eko hatthikkhandhe, eko assapiṭṭhiyaṃ[V 1.0067], eko suvaṇṇarathe, eko sivikāya nisīditvā uyyānaṃ gacchantaṃ yāci. Rājā tato orohitvā ekamantaṃ agamāsi. Aparo janapadacārikaṃ gacchantaṃ yāci, tassāpi vacanaṃ sutvā hatthito oruyha ekamantaṃ agamāsi. Evaṃ so tehi nibbinno hutvā pabbaji. Amaccā issariyena vaḍḍhanti. Tesu eko gantvā rājānaṃ āha – “amukaṃ, mahārāja, janapadaṃ mayhaṃ dehī”ti. Rājā “taṃ itthannāmo bhuñjatī”ti bhaṇati. So rañño vacanaṃ anādiyitvā “gacchāmahaṃ taṃ janapadaṃ gahetvā bhuñjāmī”ti tattha gantvā, kalahaṃ katvā, puna ubhopi rañño santikaṃ āgantvā, aññamaññassa dosaṃ ārocenti. Rājā “na sakkā ime tosetu”nti tesaṃ [M 1.0075] lobhe ādīnavaṃ disvā vipassanto paccekasambodhiṃ sacchākāsi. So purimanayeneva imaṃ udānagāthaṃ abhāsi –

40. What is the origin of the verse beginning, 'Āmantanā hoti'? In the past, it is said, there was a king named Brahmadatta, who was of a gentle nature and was addressed individually. Whenever his ministers wished to discuss with him what was proper or improper, they would take him aside one by one. One day, while he was taking his daytime rest, a certain minister said, 'Your Majesty, I have something that must be heard,' and requested to go aside with him. The king rose and went aside. Then another requested a boon while he was seated in the great assembly; another, while he was on an elephant's back; another, on horseback; another, in a golden chariot; and another, while seated in a palanquin going to the park. The king descended from each and went aside. Yet another minister made a request while the king was touring the countryside; hearing his words as well, the king dismounted from his elephant and went aside. Thus, having become disenchanted with them, he went forth into homelessness. The ministers grew in power. One of them went to the king and said, 'Great king, give me such-and-such a district.' The king replied, 'So-and-so enjoys that.' Disregarding the king's words, he thought, 'I will go, take that district, and enjoy it.' He went there, started a quarrel, and then both returned to the king's presence and reported each other's faults. The king, thinking, 'It is not possible to satisfy these men,' and seeing the danger in their greed, practiced insight meditation and realized Paccekabodhi. In the same manner as before, he uttered this inspired verse:

“Āmantanā hoti sahāyamajjhe, vāse ṭhāne gamane cārikāya;

Anabhijjhitaṃ seritaṃ pekkhamāno, eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”ti.

There is solicitation among companions, in dwelling, in standing, in going, and on tour. Observing that uncoveted freedom, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.

Tassattho [P 1.0085] – sahāyamajjhe ṭhitassa divāseyyasaṅkhāte vāse ca, mahāupaṭṭhānasaṅkhāte ṭhāne ca, uyyānagamanasaṅkhāte gamane ca, janapadacārikasaṅkhātāya cārikāya ca “idaṃ me suṇa, idaṃ me dehī”tiādinā nayena tathā tathā āmantanā hoti, tasmā ahaṃ tattha nibbijjitvā yāyaṃ ariyajanasevitā anekānisaṃsā ekantasukhā, evaṃ santepi lobhābhibhūtehi sabbakāpurisehi anabhijjhitā anabhipatthitā pabbajjā, taṃ anabhijjhitaṃ paresaṃ avasavattanena dhammapuggalavasena ca seritaṃ pekkhamāno vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā anukkamena paccekasambodhiṃ adhigatomhīti. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti.

Its meaning is this: For one who is in the midst of companions—whether in an abode called a daytime rest, a station called the great assembly, on a journey to the park, or on a tour of the countryside—there is solicitation in various ways, such as, 'Listen to this of mine,' or 'Give this to me.' Therefore, I, having become disenchanted with that, and observing that uncoveted freedom—which is the renunciation resorted to by noble ones, of many benefits, and of exclusive bliss, and yet is not coveted or desired by base persons overcome by greed; a freedom that comes from not being subject to the will of others and from being a person of the Dhamma—began insight meditation and gradually attained Paccekabodhi. The rest is as has been explained.

Āmantanāgāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Āmantanā-gāthā is complete.

41. Khiḍḍā ratīti kā uppatti? Bārāṇasiyaṃ ekaputtakabrahmadatto nāma rājā ahosi. So cassa ekaputtako piyo ahosi manāpo pāṇasamo. So sabbiriyāpathesu puttaṃ gahetvāva vattati. So ekadivasaṃ uyyānaṃ gacchanto taṃ ṭhapetvā gato. Kumāropi taṃ divasaṃyeva uppannena byādhinā mato. Amaccā “puttasinehena rañño hadayampi phaleyyā”ti anārocetvāva naṃ jhāpesuṃ. Rājā uyyāne surāmadena matto puttaṃ neva sari, tathā dutiyadivasepi nhānabhojanavelāsu. Atha bhuttāvī nisinno saritvā “puttaṃ me ānethā”ti āha. Tassa anurūpena vidhānena taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesuṃ. Tato sokābhibhūto nisinno evaṃ yoniso manasākāsi “imasmiṃ sati idaṃ hoti, imassuppādā idaṃ uppajjatī”ti. So evaṃ anukkamena [V 1.0068] anulomapaṭilomaṃ [P 1.0086] paṭiccasamuppādaṃ sammasanto paccekabodhiṃ sacchākāsi. Sesaṃ saṃsaggagāthāya vuttasadisameva ṭhapetvā gāthāyatthavaṇṇanaṃ.

41. What is the origin of 'Mirth and Delight'? In Benares, there was a king named Brahmadatta, who had only one son. That only son was dear to him, pleasing, and as dear as his own life. He always went about taking his son with him in all his postures. One day, while going to the park, he left him behind. That very day, the prince died from an illness that had arisen. The ministers, fearing that the king’s heart would break from affection for his son, did not inform him and had him cremated. The king, intoxicated with strong drink in the park, did not remember his son, nor did he the next day during the times of bathing and eating. Then, after eating, as he sat down, he remembered and said, “Bring my son to me.” They informed him of what had happened in a manner fitting the occasion. Overcome by sorrow, he sat reflecting wisely thus: “When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises.” Thus, gradually contemplating dependent origination in forward and reverse order, he realized Paccekabodhi. The remainder is similar to what was stated in the verse on association, setting aside the explanation of the verse's meaning.

Atthavaṇṇanāyaṃ [M 1.0076] pana khiḍḍāti kīḷanā. Sā duvidhā hoti – kāyikā, vācasikā ca. Tattha kāyikā nāma hatthīhipi kīḷanti, assehipi, rathehipi, dhanūhipi, tharūhipīti evamādi. Vācasikā nāma gītaṃ, silokabhaṇanaṃ, mukhabherīti evamādi. Ratīti pañcakāmaguṇarati. Vipulanti yāva aṭṭhimiñjaṃ āhacca ṭhānena sakalattabhāvabyāpakaṃ. Sesaṃ pākaṭameva. Anusandhiyojanāpi cettha saṃsaggagāthāya vuttanayeneva veditabbā, tato parañca sabbanti.

In the explanation of the meaning, 'play' (khiḍḍā) means sport. It is of two kinds: bodily and verbal. Among these, bodily play includes playing with elephants, horses, chariots, bows, swords, and so on. Verbal play includes singing, reciting verses, playing the mouth-drum, and the like. 'Delight' (rati) refers to delight in the five strands of sensual pleasure. 'Abundant' (vipula) means pervading the entire body, affecting one even to the bone marrow. The remainder is evident. The linking of context here should also be understood in the same way as explained in the verse on association, and everything thereafter.

Khiḍḍāratigāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Khiḍḍā-rati-gāthā is complete.

42. Cātuddisoti kā uppatti? Pubbe kira kassapassa bhagavato sāsane pañca paccekabodhisattā pabbajitvā vīsati vassasahassāni gatapaccāgatavattaṃ pūretvā devaloke uppannā. Tato cavitvā tesaṃ jeṭṭhako bārāṇasiyaṃ rājā ahosi, sesā pākatikarājāno. Te cattāropi kammaṭṭhānaṃ uggaṇhitvā, rajjaṃ pahāya pabbajitvā, anukkamena paccekabuddhā hutvā nandamūlakapabbhāre vasantā ekadivasaṃ samāpattito vuṭṭhāya vaṃsakaḷīragāthāyaṃ vuttanayeneva attano kammañca sahāyañca āvajjetvā ñatvā bārāṇasirañño upāyena ārammaṇaṃ dassetuṃ okāsaṃ gavesanti. So ca rājā tikkhattuṃ rattiyā ubbijjati, bhīto vissaraṃ karoti, mahātale dhāvati. Purohitena kālasseva vuṭṭhāya sukhaseyyaṃ pucchitopi “kuto me, ācariya, sukha”nti sabbaṃ taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesi. Purohitopi “ayaṃ rogo na sakkā yena kenaci uddhaṃvirecanādinā bhesajjakammena vinetuṃ[P 1.0087], mayhaṃ pana khādanūpāyo uppanno”ti cintetvā “rajjahānijīvitantarāyādīnaṃ pubbanimittaṃ etaṃ mahārājā”ti rājānaṃ suṭṭhutaraṃ ubbejetvā tassa vūpasamanatthaṃ “ettake ca ettake ca hatthiassarathādayo hiraññasuvaṇṇañca dakkhiṇaṃ datvā yañño yajitabbo”ti taṃ yaññayajane samādapesi.

42. What is the origin of 'Cātuddisa'? In the past, it is said, during the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, five Paccekabodhisattas went forth. After fulfilling the practice of going and returning for twenty thousand years, they were reborn in the deva-world. After passing away from there, the eldest of them became king in Bārāṇasī, while the rest became ordinary kings. These four, having learned a meditation subject, renounced their kingdoms and went forth. In due course, they became Paccekabuddhas and dwelled in the Nandamūlaka mountain cave. One day, arising from absorption, in the way described in the Vaṃsakaḷīra verses, they considered their own karma and their companion and, knowing this, sought an opportunity to show an object of meditation to the king of Bārāṇasī by some means. That king was startled three times during the night; terrified, he cried out and ran about on the upper floor of the palace. When the chaplain rose early and asked if he had slept well, the king replied, "How can there be comfort for me, teacher?" and recounted all that had happened. The chaplain thought, "This sickness cannot be remedied by any medicinal treatment such as purgatives. But a means of getting a meal has occurred to me." He then thoroughly alarmed the king, saying, "Great king, this is an ill omen of the loss of your kingdom, danger to your life, and so on." To pacify this, he persuaded the king to perform a sacrifice, saying, "After giving such and such elephants, horses, chariots, gold, and silver as a gift, a sacrifice must be performed."

Tato paccekabuddhā anekāni pāṇasahassāni yaññatthāya sampiṇḍiyamānāni disvā “etasmiṃ kamme kate dubbodhaneyyo bhavissati, handa naṃ paṭikacceva gantvā pekkhāmā”ti vaṃsakaḷīragāthāyaṃ vuttanayeneva āgantvā piṇḍāya caramānā rājaṅgaṇe paṭipāṭiyā agamaṃsu. Rājā sīhapañjare ṭhito rājaṅgaṇaṃ olokayamāno te addakkhi[M 1.0077], saha dassaneneva cassa sineho uppajji. Tato te pakkosāpetvā ākāsatale paññattāsane nisīdāpetvā sakkaccaṃ bhojetvā [V 1.0069] katabhattakicce “ke tumhe”ti pucchi. “Mayaṃ, mahārāja, cātuddisā nāmā”ti. “Bhante, cātuddisāti imassa ko attho”ti? “Catūsu disāsu katthaci kutoci bhayaṃ vā cittutrāso vā amhākaṃ natthi, mahārājā”ti. “Bhante, tumhākaṃ taṃ bhayaṃ kiṃ kāraṇā na hotī”ti? “Mayañhi, mahārāja, mettaṃ bhāvema, karuṇaṃ bhāvema, muditaṃ bhāvema, upekkhaṃ bhāvema, tena no taṃ bhayaṃ na hotī”ti vatvā uṭṭhāyāsanā attano vasatiṃ agamaṃsu.

Then, seeing many thousands of living beings being gathered for the sacrifice, the Paccekabuddhas thought, "If this deed is done, he will be difficult to instruct. Come, let us go beforehand and see him." Following the method described in the Vaṃsakaḷīragāthā, they came and, while wandering for alms, entered the royal courtyard in succession. The king, standing in a lion-window and looking over the royal courtyard, saw them. At the very sight of them, affection arose in him. Then, having them summoned, he had them seated on seats prepared in the open air, respectfully served them a meal, and after they had finished eating, asked, "Who are you?" “We, great king, are called 'Cātuddisā' (of the Four Directions).” “Venerable sirs, what is the meaning of 'Cātuddisā'?” “In the four directions, great king, from anywhere or from any cause, there is no fear or mental terror for us.” “Venerable sirs, for what reason is there no such fear for you?” “Great king, we cultivate loving-kindness, we cultivate compassion, we cultivate sympathetic joy, we cultivate equanimity. Therefore, that fear does not exist for us.” Having spoken thus, they rose from their seats and returned to their dwelling.

Tato rājā cintesi “ime samaṇā mettādibhāvanāya bhayaṃ na hotīti bhaṇanti, brāhmaṇā pana anekasahassapāṇavadhaṃ vaṇṇayanti, kesaṃ nu kho vacanaṃ sacca”nti. Athassa etadahosi – “samaṇā suddhena asuddhaṃ dhovanti, brāhmaṇā pana asuddhena asuddhaṃ. Na ca sakkā asuddhena asuddhaṃ dhovituṃ, pabbajitānaṃ eva vacanaṃ sacca”nti. So “sabbe sattā sukhitā hontū”tiādinā nayena mettādayo cattāropi brahmavihāre bhāvetvā hitapharaṇacittena amacce [P 1.0088] āṇāpesi “sabbe pāṇe muñcatha, sītāni pānīyāni pivantu, haritāni tiṇāni khādantu, sīto ca nesaṃ vāto upavāyatū”ti. Te tathā akaṃsu.

Then the king thought, "These ascetics say that through the cultivation of loving-kindness and the like, there is no fear, but the brahmins praise the slaughter of many thousands of beings. Whose words, I wonder, are true?" Then it occurred to him, "The ascetics wash the impure with the pure, but the brahmins wash the impure with the impure. And it is not possible to wash the impure with the impure; the words of the renunciants alone are true." So, having developed the four divine abodes—loving-kindness and the rest—in the way beginning with, "May all beings be happy," and with a mind suffusing them with welfare, he commanded his ministers: "Release all the creatures. Let them drink cool water, eat green grass, and may a cool breeze blow upon them." They did so.

Tato rājā “kalyāṇamittānaṃ vacaneneva pāpakammato muttomhī”ti tattheva nisinno vipassitvā paccekasambodhiṃ sacchākāsi. Amaccehi ca bhojanavelāyaṃ “bhuñja, mahārāja, kālo”ti vutte “nāhaṃ rājā”ti purimanayeneva sabbaṃ vatvā imaṃ udānabyākaraṇagāthaṃ abhāsi –

Then the king thought, 'By the very words of my good friends I have been freed from an evil deed.' Sitting right there, he developed insight and realized the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha. And when his ministers said to him at mealtime, 'Eat, great king, it is time,' he replied, 'I am not a king.' Following the previous manner, he explained the whole matter and uttered this verse of inspired utterance and explanation:

“Cātuddiso appaṭigho ca hoti, santussamāno itarītarena;

Parissayānaṃ sahitā achambhī, eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”ti.

“He is of the four directions and unresisting, content with whatever he obtains; enduring dangers, fearless, one should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.”

Tattha cātuddisoti catūsu disāsu yathāsukhavihārī, “ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharatī”tiādinā (dī. ni. 3.308; a. ni. 4.125; cūḷani. khaggavisāṇasuttaniddesa 128) vā nayena brahmavihārabhāvanāpharitā catasso disā assa santītipi cātuddiso. Tāsu disāsu katthaci satte [M 1.0078] vā saṅkhāre vā bhayena na paṭihaññatīti appaṭigho. Santussamānoti dvādasavidhassa santosassavasena santussako, itarītarenāti uccāvacena paccayena. Parissayānaṃ sahitā achambhīti ettha parissayanti kāyacittāni, parihāpenti vā tesaṃ sampattiṃ, tāni vā paṭicca sayantīti parissayā, bāhirānaṃ sīhabyagghādīnaṃ abbhantarānañca kāmacchandādīnaṃ kāyacittupaddavānaṃ etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Te parissaye adhivāsanakhantiyā [V 1.0070] ca vīriyādīhi dhammehi ca sahatīti parissayānaṃ sahitā. Thaddhabhāvakarabhayābhāvena achambhī. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yathā te cattāro samaṇā, evaṃ itarītarena paccayena santussamāno ettha paṭipattipadaṭṭhāne santose ṭhito catūsu disāsu mettādibhāvanāya cātuddiso, sattasaṅkhāresu paṭihananabhayābhāvena appaṭigho ca hoti. So cātuddisattā vuttappakārānaṃ parissayānaṃ sahitā, appaṭighattā achambhī ca hotīti evaṃ paṭipattiguṇaṃ disvā yoniso paṭipajjitvā paccekabodhiṃ adhigatomhīti. Atha vā te samaṇā viya santussamāno [P 1.0089] itarītarena vuttanayeneva cātuddiso hotīti ñatvā evaṃ cātuddisabhāvaṃ patthayanto yoniso paṭipajjitvā adhigatomhi. Tasmā aññopi īdisaṃ ṭhānaṃ patthayamāno cātuddisatāya parissayānaṃ sahitā appaṭighatāya ca achambhī hutvā eko care khaggavisāṇakappoti. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti.

Herein, `cātuddiso` means one who dwells comfortably in the four directions; or, according to the method beginning with, “dwelling having pervaded one direction” (Dī. Ni. 3.308; A. Ni. 4.125; Cūḷani. Khaggavisāṇasuttaniddesa 128), he is one for whom the four directions are pervaded by the development of the divine abidings, and thus he is `cātuddiso`. In those directions, he does not strike against any beings or formations out of fear; therefore, he is `appaṭigho` (non-conflicting). `Santussamāno` means being content by way of the twelve kinds of contentment; `itarītarena` means with requisites high or low. Regarding `parissayānaṃ sahitā achambhī` (an endurer of dangers, unfrightened): herein, `parissayā` (dangers) are so called because they encompass (`parissayanti`) body and mind, or because they cause the decline (`parihāpenti`) of their well-being, or because they lie (`sayanti`) in dependence (`paṭicca`) on them. This is a term for external dangers such as lions and tigers, and for internal calamities for the body and mind such as sensual desire. He endures (`sahati`) those dangers with enduring patience and with qualities such as energy; thus he is `parissayānaṃ sahitā` (an endurer of dangers). Because of the absence of fear that causes rigidity, he is `achambhī` (unfrightened). What is meant by this? Just as those four ascetics, so too, being content with whatever requisites, established in contentment as the basis for the practice, he becomes `cātuddiso` through developing loving-kindness and so forth in the four directions, and he is `appaṭigho` due to the absence of the fear of striking against beings or formations. Because he is `cātuddiso`, he is an endurer of dangers of the aforementioned kind, and because he is `appaṭigho`, he is unfrightened. Thus, having seen this virtue of the practice and having practiced wisely, I have attained Paccekabodhi. Alternatively: knowing, ‘Like those ascetics, being content with whatever requisites, one becomes `cātuddiso` in the way described,’ and thus aspiring to this state of being `cātuddiso`, I practiced wisely and have attained it. Therefore, another who aspires to such a state, by being `cātuddiso` becomes an endurer of dangers, and by being `appaṭigho` becomes unfrightened, and so should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn. The rest is as previously explained.

Cātuddisagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The explanation of the Cātuddisa Gāthā is concluded.

43. Dussaṅgahāti kā uppatti? Bārāṇasirañño kira aggamahesī kālamakāsi. Tato vītivattesu sokadivasesu ekaṃ divasaṃ amaccā “rājūnaṃ nāma tesu tesu kiccesu aggamahesī avassaṃ icchitabbā, sādhu, devo, aññaṃ deviṃ ānetū”ti yāciṃsu. Rājā“tena hi, bhaṇe, jānāthā”ti āha. Te pariyesantā sāmantarajje rājā mato. Tassa devī rajjaṃ anusāsati. Sā ca gabbhinī hoti. Amaccā “ayaṃ rañño anurūpā”ti ñatvā taṃ yāciṃsu. Sā “gabbhinī nāma manussānaṃ amanāpā hoti, sace āgametha, yāva vijāyāmi, evaṃ hotu, no ce, aññaṃ pariyesathā”ti āha. Te raññopi etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. Rājā “gabbhinīpi hotu ānethā”ti. Te ānesuṃ. Rājā taṃ abhisiñcitvā sabbaṃ mahesībhogaṃ adāsi. Tassā parijanañca nānāvidhehi [M 1.0079] paṇṇākārehi saṅgaṇhāti. Sā kālena puttaṃ vijāyi. Tampi rājā attano jātaputtamiva sabbiriyāpathesu aṅke ca ure ca katvā viharati. Tato deviyā parijano cintesi “rājā ativiya saṅgaṇhāti kumāraṃ, ativissāsaniyāni rājahadayāni, handa naṃ paribhedemā”ti.

43. What is the origin of the verse beginning `Dussaṅgahā`? It is said that the chief queen of the king of Bārāṇasī passed away. After the days of mourning had passed, one day the ministers requested, “For kings, in various matters, a chief queen is absolutely necessary. It would be good, Your Majesty, for you to bring another queen.” The king replied, “In that case, sirs, find one.” While they were searching, the king in a neighboring kingdom died. His queen was ruling the kingdom, and she was pregnant. The ministers, thinking, “She is suitable for the king,” requested her. She said, “A pregnant woman is undesirable to people. If you will wait until I give birth, so be it. If not, seek another.” They reported this matter to the king. The king said, “Even if she is pregnant, bring her.” They brought her. The king consecrated her and gave her all the privileges of a chief queen. He also favored her retinue with various gifts. In due time, she gave birth to a son. The king treated him like his own born son, holding him on his lap and chest in all postures. Then the queen's retinue thought, “The king favors the prince exceedingly. The hearts of kings are not to be trusted. Come, let us cause a division.”

Tato kumāraṃ – “tvaṃ, tāta, amhākaṃ rañño putto, na imassa rañño, mā ettha vissāsaṃ āpajjī”ti āhaṃsu. Atha kumāro “ehi puttā”ti raññā vuccamānopi hatthe gahetvā ākaḍḍhiyamānopi pubbe viya rājānaṃ na allīyati. Rājā “kiṃ eta”nti vīmaṃsanto taṃ pavattiṃ ñatvā “are, ete mayā evaṃ saṅgahitāpi [P 1.0090] paṭikūlavuttino evā”ti nibbijjitvā rajjaṃ pahāya pabbajito. “Rājā pabbajito”ti amaccaparijanāpi bahū pabbajitā[V 1.0071], “saparijano rājā pabbajito”ti manussā paṇīte paccaye upanenti. Rājā paṇīte paccaye yathāvuḍḍhaṃ dāpeti. Tattha ye sundaraṃ labhanti, te tussanti. Itare ujjhāyanti “mayaṃ pariveṇasammajjanādīni sabbakiccāni karontā lūkhabhattaṃ jiṇṇavatthañca labhāmā”ti. So tampi ñatvā “are, yathāvuḍḍhaṃ diyyamānepi nāma ujjhāyanti, aho, ayaṃ parisā dussaṅgahā”ti pattacīvaraṃ ādāya eko araññaṃ pavisitvā vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā paccekabodhiṃ sacchākāsi. Tattha āgatehi ca kammaṭṭhānaṃ pucchito imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi –

Then they told the prince, “Dear boy, you are the son of our king, not of this king. Do not place your trust here.” Thereafter, even when the king called, “Come, son,” and took his hand and pulled him, the prince did not draw near to the king as before. The king, wondering, “What is this?” investigated and learned of the matter. Becoming disenchanted, he thought, “Alas! Even though they have been treated so well by me, they are still hostile in their conduct.” He renounced the kingdom and went forth. Hearing, “The king has gone forth,” many ministers and attendants also went forth. People, thinking, “The king has gone forth with his retinue,” brought excellent requisites. The king had the excellent requisites distributed according to seniority. Therein, those who received fine things were satisfied, but the others complained, “We do all the duties, such as sweeping the monastery grounds, yet we receive coarse food and worn-out robes.” He, learning of this too, thought, “Alas! Even when things are given according to seniority, they complain. Truly, this assembly is difficult to support.” Taking his bowl and robe, he entered the forest alone, began insight meditation, and realized Paccekabodhi. And when asked by those who came to him for a meditation subject, he spoke this verse:

“Dussaṅgahā pabbajitāpi eke, atho gahaṭṭhā gharamāvasantā;

Appossukko paraputtesu hutvā, eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”ti.

“Some who have gone forth are difficult to support, and so are householders living at home. Being unconcerned for the children of others, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.”

Sā atthato pākaṭā eva. Ayaṃ pana yojanā – dussaṅgahā pabbajitāpi eke, ye asantosābhibhūtā, tathāvidhā eva ca atho gahaṭṭhā gharamāvasantā. Etamahaṃ dussaṅgahabhāvaṃ jigucchanto vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā paccekabodhiṃ adhigatomhīti. Sesaṃ purimanayeneva veditabbanti.

Its meaning is indeed clear. This, however, is the construction: some who have gone forth are difficult to support, those who are overcome by discontent; and householders dwelling at home are also of such a nature. I, being disgusted by this state of being difficult to support, began insight meditation and have attained Paccekabodhi. The rest should be understood in the same way as before.

Dussaṅgahagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The explanation of the Dussaṅgaha Gāthā is concluded.

44. Oropayitvāti [M 1.0080] kā uppatti? Bārāṇasiyaṃ kira cātumāsikabrahmadatto nāma rājā gimhānaṃ paṭhame māse uyyānaṃ gato. Tattha ramaṇīye bhūmibhāge nīlaghanapattasañchannaṃ koviḷārarukkhaṃ disvā “koviḷāramūle mama sayanaṃ paññāpethā”ti vatvā uyyāne kīḷitvā sāyanhasamayaṃ tattha seyyaṃ kappesi. Puna gimhānaṃ majjhime māse uyyānaṃ gato. Tadā koviḷāro pupphito hoti, tadāpi tatheva akāsi. Puna gimhānaṃ pacchime māse gato. Tadā koviḷāro sañchinnapatto sukkharukkho viya hoti. Tadāpi so adisvāva taṃ rukkhaṃ pubbaparicayena tattheva seyyaṃ āṇāpesi. Amaccā jānantāpi “raññā āṇatta”nti bhayena tattha sayanaṃ paññāpesuṃ. So uyyāne kīḷitvā sāyanhasamayaṃ [P 1.0091] tattha seyyaṃ kappento taṃ rukkhaṃ disvā “are, ayaṃ pubbe sañchannapatto maṇimayo viya abhirūpadassano ahosi. Tato maṇivaṇṇasākhantare ṭhapitapavāḷaṅkurasadisehi pupphehi sassirikacārudassano ahosi. Muttādalasadisavālikākiṇṇo cassa heṭṭhā bhūmibhāgo bandhanā pamuttapupphasañchanno rattakambalasanthato viya ahosi. So nāmajja sukkharukkho viya sākhāmattāvaseso ṭhito. ‘Aho, jarāya upahato koviḷāro’”ti cintetvā “anupādinnampi tāva jarā haññati, kimaṅga pana upādinna”nti aniccasaññaṃ paṭilabhi. Tadanusāreneva sabbasaṅkhāre dukkhato anattato ca vipassanto “aho vatāhampi [V 1.0072] sañchinnapatto koviḷāro viya apetagihibyañjano bhaveyya”nti patthayamāno anupubbena tasmiṃ sayanatale dakkhiṇena passena nipannoyeva paccekabodhiṃ sacchākāsi. Tato gamanakāle amaccehi “kālo gantuṃ, mahārājā”ti vutte “nāhaṃ rājā”tiādīni vatvā purimanayeneva imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi –

44. What is the origin of 'Oropayitvā'? It is said that in Bārāṇasī, a king named Cātumāsika Brahmadatta went to a park in the first month of summer. There, in a delightful area, he saw a koviḷāra tree covered with dense, dark leaves and said, 'Prepare my bed at the foot of the koviḷāra tree.' After enjoying the park, he rested there in the evening. Again, in the middle month of summer, he went to the park. At that time, the koviḷāra tree was in bloom, and he did the same as before. Again, in the last month of summer, he went. By then, the koviḷāra tree had shed its leaves and was like a withered tree. Even without seeing the tree, out of previous habit, he ordered his bed to be prepared in that same place. The ministers, though they knew, prepared the bed there out of fear of the king's command. After enjoying the park, while resting there in the evening, he saw the tree and thought: 'Ah, this tree was previously covered with leaves, as if made of jewels, beautiful to behold. Then, with flowers like coral sprouts set among its gem-colored branches, it was glorious and lovely to see. The ground beneath it, strewn with sand like pearl dust and covered with flowers released from their stalks, was as if spread with a red blanket. That very tree now stands with only its branches remaining, like a withered tree. Alas, the koviḷāra tree is afflicted by old age!' Reflecting thus, he thought, 'Even that which is not appropriated is struck by decay; what then of that which is appropriated?' and he gained the perception of impermanence. In accordance with that, contemplating all conditioned things as suffering and as non-self, he aspired, 'Ah, may I too, like this koviḷāra tree that has shed its leaves, be free from the signs of a householder!' Gradually, while lying on his right side on that very bed, he realized Paccekabodhi. Then, when it was time to depart, the ministers said, 'It is time to go, great king.' He replied, 'I am not a king,' and so forth, and in the manner previously described, spoke this verse:

“Oropayitvā gihibyañjanāni, sañchinnapatto yathā koviḷāro;

Chetvāna vīro gihibandhanāni, eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”ti.

“Having laid aside the signs of a householder, like a koviḷāra tree with its leaves shed; the hero, having severed the bonds of household life, should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.”

Tattha oropayitvāti apanetvā. Gihibyañjanānīti kesamassuodātavatthālaṅkāramālāgandhavilepanaitthiputtadāsidāsādīni. Etāni hi gihibhāvaṃ [M 1.0081] byañjayanti, tasmā “gihibyañjanānī”ti vuccanti. Sañchinnapattoti patitapatto. Chetvānāti maggañāṇena chinditvā. Vīroti maggavīriyasamannāgato. Gihibandhanānīti kāmabandhanāni. Kāmā hi gihīnaṃ bandhanāni. Ayaṃ tāva padattho.

Therein, 'having laid aside' (oropayitvā) means having removed. 'The signs of a householder' (gihibyañjanāni) are such as hair and beard, white clothes, ornaments, garlands, perfumes, unguents, wife, son, male and female slaves, and so forth. For these signify the state of a householder; hence they are called 'the signs of a householder'. 'With leaves shed' (sañchinnapatto) means with fallen leaves. 'Having cut' (chetvāna) means having severed with path-knowledge. 'A hero' (vīro) means one endowed with the energy of the path. 'The bonds of a householder' (gihibandhanāni) are the bonds of sensual pleasures. For sensual pleasures are indeed the bonds of householders. This, for now, is the meaning of the words.

Ayaṃ pana adhippāyo – “aho vatāhampi oropayitvā gihibyañjanāni sañchinnapatto yathā koviḷāro bhaveyya”nti evañhi cintayamāno vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā paccekabodhiṃ adhigatomhīti. Sesaṃ purimanayeneva veditabbanti.

This, however, is the intention: 'Oh, that I too, having laid aside the signs of a householder, might be like a koviḷāra tree with its leaves shed!' Thinking thus, having undertaken insight, I attained Paccekabodhi. The rest should be understood in accordance with the previous method.

Koviḷāragāthāvaṇṇanā samattā. Paṭhamo vaggo niṭṭhito.

The commentary on the Koviḷāra Verse is concluded. The First Chapter is finished.

45-46. Sace [P 1.0092] labhethāti kā uppatti? Pubbe kira kassapassa bhagavato sāsane dve paccekabodhisattā pabbajitvā vīsati vassasahassāni gatapaccāgatavattaṃ pūretvā devaloke uppannā. Tato cavitvā tesaṃ jeṭṭhako bārāṇasirañño putto ahosi, kaniṭṭho purohitassa putto ahosi. Te ekadivasaṃyeva paṭisandhiṃ gahetvā ekadivasameva mātukucchito nikkhamitvā sahapaṃsukīḷitasahāyakā ahesuṃ. Purohitaputto paññavā ahosi. So rājaputtaṃ āha – “samma, tvaṃ pituno accayena rajjaṃ labhissasi, ahaṃ purohitaṭṭhānaṃ, susikkhitena ca sukhaṃ rajjaṃ anusāsituṃ sakkā, ehi sippaṃ uggahessāmā”ti. Tato ubhopi pubbopacitakammā hutvā [V 1.0073] gāmanigamādīsu bhikkhaṃ caramānā paccantajanapadagāmaṃ gatā. Tañca gāmaṃ paccekabuddhā bhikkhācāravelāya pavisanti. Atha manussā paccekabuddhe disvā ussāhajātā āsanāni paññāpenti, paṇītaṃ khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyaṃ upanāmenti, mānenti, pūjenti. Tesaṃ etadahosi – “amhehi sadisā uccākulikā nāma natthi, atha ca panime manussā yadi icchanti, amhākaṃ bhikkhaṃ denti, yadi ca nicchanti, na denti, imesaṃ pana pabbajitānaṃ evarūpaṃ sakkāraṃ karonti, addhā ete kiñci sippaṃ jānanti, handa nesaṃ santike sippaṃ uggaṇhāmā”ti.

What is the origin of the verse beginning 'Sace labhetha'? It is said that in the past, during the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, two Bodhisattas destined for Paccekabuddhahood went forth and, for twenty thousand years, fulfilled the practice of going and returning, and were then reborn in the deva world. Passing away from there, the elder became the son of the king of Bārāṇasī, and the younger became the son of the royal chaplain. They were conceived on the same day, were born from their mothers' wombs on the same day, and became friends who played together in the dust. The chaplain's son was wise. He said to the prince: 'Friend, upon your father's passing, you will obtain the kingdom, and I will obtain the position of royal chaplain; for with proper training, it is easy to govern the kingdom. Come, let us learn a craft.' Then, both having accumulated wholesome kamma in the past, they wandered for alms in villages, towns, and so forth, and came to a village in a border region. Paccekabuddhas would enter that village at the time for the alms-round. Seeing the Paccekabuddhas, the people became inspired, prepared seats, offered choice hard and soft foods, and paid them honor and reverence. This thought occurred to them: 'There are none of such high birth as us, yet these people give us alms only if they wish, and if they do not wish, they do not give. But for these renunciants, they perform such honors. Surely, they must know some craft. Come, let us learn this craft from them.'

Te [M 1.0082] manussesu paṭikkantesu okāsaṃ labhitvā “yaṃ, bhante, tumhe sippaṃ jānātha, taṃ amhepi sikkhāpethā”ti yāciṃsu. Paccekabuddhā “na sakkā apabbajitena sikkhitu”nti āhaṃsu. Te pabbajjaṃ yācitvā pabbajiṃsu. Tato nesaṃ paccekabuddhā “evaṃ vo nivāsetabbaṃ, evaṃ pārupitabba”ntiādinā nayena ābhisamācārikaṃ ācikkhitvā “imassa sippassa ekībhāvābhirati nipphatti, tasmā ekeneva nisīditabbaṃ, ekena caṅkamitabbaṃ, ṭhātabbaṃ, sayitabba”nti pāṭiyekkaṃ paṇṇasālamadaṃsu. Tato te attano attano paṇṇasālaṃ pavisitvā nisīdiṃsu. Purohitaputto nisinnakālato [P 1.0093] pabhuti cittasamādhānaṃ laddhā jhānaṃ labhi. Rājaputto muhutteneva ukkaṇṭhito tassa santikaṃ āgato. So taṃ disvā “kiṃ, sammā”ti pucchi. “Ukkaṇṭhitomhī”ti āha. “Tena hi idha nisīdā”ti. So tattha muhuttaṃ nisīditvā āha – “imassa kira, samma, sippassa ekībhāvābhirati nipphattī”ti purohitaputto “evaṃ, samma, tena hi tvaṃ attano nisinnokāsaṃ eva gaccha, uggahessāmi imassa sippassa nipphatti”nti āha. So gantvā punapi muhutteneva ukkaṇṭhito purimanayeneva tikkhattuṃ āgato.

When the people had departed, they obtained an opportunity and requested, 'Venerable sirs, please teach us the craft that you know.' The Paccekabuddhas replied, 'It is not possible for one who has not gone forth to learn this.' They then requested ordination and were ordained. Then the Paccekabuddhas instructed them in the proper conduct, saying, 'This is how you should wear your lower robe, this is how you should wear your upper robe,' and so forth. They explained, 'The fulfillment of this craft comes from delighting in solitude. Therefore, one should sit alone, walk alone, stand alone, and lie down alone.' Then they gave each a separate leaf hut. Entering their respective leaf huts, they sat down. From the moment he sat down, the chaplain's son attained concentration of mind and gained jhāna. The prince, however, became restless in a moment and went to him. Seeing him, the chaplain's son asked, 'What is it, friend?' 'I am restless,' he replied. 'Then sit here,' said the chaplain's son. After sitting there for a moment, the prince said, 'Friend, it is said that the fulfillment of this craft comes from delighting in solitude.' The chaplain's son replied, 'Yes, friend. In that case, you should return to your own sitting place. I will master the fulfillment of this craft.' He left but soon became restless again. Three times he returned in the same manner as before.

Tato naṃ purohitaputto tatheva uyyojetvā tasmiṃ gate cintesi “ayaṃ attano ca kammaṃ hāpeti, mama ca idhābhikkhaṇaṃ āgacchanto”ti. So paṇṇasālato nikkhamma araññaṃ paviṭṭho. Itaro attano paṇṇasālāyeva nisinno punapi muhutteneva ukkaṇṭhito hutvā tassa paṇṇasālaṃ āgantvā ito cito ca maggantopi taṃ adisvā cintesi – “yo gahaṭṭhakāle paṇṇākārampi ādāya āgato maṃ daṭṭhuṃ na labhati, so nāma mayi āgate dassanampi adātukāmo pakkāmi, aho, re citta, na lajjasi, yaṃ maṃ catukkhattuṃ idhānesi, sodāni te vase na vattissāmi, aññadatthu taṃyeva mama vase vattāpessāmī”ti attano senāsanaṃ pavisitvā vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā paccekabodhiṃ sacchikatvā ākāsena nandamūlakapabbhāraṃ agamāsi. Itaropi araññaṃ pavisitvā vipassanaṃ [V 1.0074] ārabhitvā paccekabodhiṃ sacchikatvā tattheva agamāsi. Te ubhopi manosilātale nisīditvā pāṭiyekkaṃ pāṭiyekkaṃ imā udānagāthāyo abhāsiṃsu –

Then the chaplain's son, having dismissed him in the same way, thought when he had gone: 'This man ruins his own work and mine as well by coming here frequently.' He left his leaf hut and entered the forest. The other, sitting in his own leaf hut, became restless again in a moment and went to the chaplain's son's leaf hut. Not seeing him, though searching here and there, he thought: 'He who in household life would come carrying a gift but could not get to see me, now that I have come, is unwilling to grant even a sight of himself and has departed. Oh, mind, are you not ashamed that you brought me here for the fourth time? From now on, I will not be under your control; on the contrary, I will make you submit to my control!' Entering his dwelling, he began insight meditation, realized Paccekabodhi, and went through the air to the Nandamūlaka mountainside. The other also entered the forest, began insight meditation, realized Paccekabodhi, and went to the same place. Both of them, sitting on the red-arsenic rock slab, each uttered these inspired verses:

“Sace [M 1.0083] labhetha nipakaṃ sahāyaṃ, saddhiṃ caraṃ sādhuvihāri dhīraṃ;

Abhibhuyya sabbāni parissayāni, careyya tenattamano satīmā.

If one should obtain a prudent companion, a fellow traveler, virtuous in living, and steadfast; overcoming all dangers, one should wander with him, joyous and mindful.

“No ce labhetha nipakaṃ sahāyaṃ, saddhiṃ caraṃ sādhuvihāri dhīraṃ;

Rājāva raṭṭhaṃ vijitaṃ pahāya, eko care mātaṅgaraññeva nāgo”ti.

If one should not obtain a prudent companion, a fellow traveler, virtuous in living, and steadfast; one should wander alone like a king who has abandoned a conquered kingdom, like a lone elephant in the Mātanga forest.

Tattha nipakanti pakatinipuṇaṃ paṇḍitaṃ kasiṇaparikammādīsu kusalaṃ. Sādhuvihārinti appanāvihārena vā upacārena vā samannāgataṃ. Dhīranti dhitisampannaṃ. Tattha nipakattena dhitisampadā vuttā. Idha pana dhitisampannamevāti attho. Dhiti nāma asithilaparakkamatā, “kāmaṃ taco [P 1.0094] ca nhāru cā”ti (ma. ni. 2.184; a. ni. 2.5; mahāni. 196) evaṃ pavattavīriyassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Apica dhikatapāpotipi dhīro. Rājāva raṭṭhaṃ vijitaṃ pahāyāti yathā paṭirājā “vijitaṃ raṭṭhaṃ anatthāvaha”nti ñatvā rajjaṃ pahāya eko carati, evaṃ bālasahāyaṃ pahāya eko care. Atha vā rājāva raṭṭhanti yathā sutasomo rājā vijitaṃ raṭṭhaṃ pahāya eko cari, yathā ca mahājanako, evaṃ eko careti ayampi tassattho. Sesaṃ vuttānusārena sakkā jānitunti na vitthāritanti.

Therein, 'prudent' (nipakaṃ) means naturally astute, wise, skilled in kasiṇa-preparations and so forth. 'Virtuous in living' (sādhuvihāri) means endowed with either absorption abiding (appanāvihāra) or access abiding (upacāravihāra). 'Steadfast' (dhīraṃ) means possessed of steadfastness. Therein, by 'prudence', the accomplishment of steadfastness is stated. Here, however, the meaning is precisely 'being endowed with steadfastness'. Steadfastness (dhiti) is unrelaxing effort; this is a designation for the energy that proceeds as in 'Let only skin, sinews, and bone remain' (M.ii.184; A.ii.5; Mahānid. 196). Moreover, one who has dispelled evil (dhikatapāpo) is also 'steadfast' (dhīra). 'Like a king abandoning a conquered kingdom' (Rājāva raṭṭhaṃ vijitaṃ pahāya): just as an opposing king, knowing 'a conquered kingdom brings no benefit,' abandons the kingdom and wanders alone, so too should one abandon a foolish companion and wander alone. Alternatively, 'like a king... the kingdom' (rājāva raṭṭhaṃ): just as King Sutasoma abandoned his conquered kingdom and wandered alone, and as did Mahājanaka, so should one wander alone — this too is its meaning. The rest can be understood in accordance with what has been said; thus it has not been elaborated.

Sahāyagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Verses on Companionship is concluded.

47. Addhā pasaṃsāmāti imissā gāthāya yāva ākāsatale paññattāsane paccekabuddhānaṃ nisajjā, tāva cātuddisagāthāya uppattisadisā eva uppatti. Ayaṃ pana viseso – yathā so rājā rattiyā tikkhattuṃ ubbijji, na tathā ayaṃ, nevassa yañño paccupaṭṭhito ahosi. So ākāsatale paññattesu āsanesu paccekabuddhe nisīdāpetvā “ke tumhe”ti pucchi. “Mayaṃ, mahārāja, anavajjabhojino nāmā”ti. “Bhante, ‘anavajjabhojino’ti imassa ko attho”ti? “Sundaraṃ vā asundaraṃ vā laddhā nibbikārā bhuñjāma, mahārājā”ti. Taṃ sutvā rañño etadahosi “yaṃnūnāhaṃ ime upaparikkheyyaṃ edisā vā no vā”ti. Taṃ divasaṃ kaṇājakena [M 1.0084] bilaṅgadutiyena parivisi. Paccekabuddhā amataṃ bhuñjantā viya nibbikārā bhuñjiṃsu. Rājā “honti nāma ekadivasaṃ paṭiññātattā nibbikārā, sve jānissāmī”ti svātanāyapi [V 1.0075] nimantesi. Tato dutiyadivasepi tathevākāsi. Tepi tatheva paribhuñjiṃsu. Atha rājā “idāni sundaraṃ datvā vīmaṃsissāmī”ti punapi nimantetvā, dve divase mahāsakkāraṃ katvā, paṇītena ativicitrena khādanīyena bhojanīyena parivisi. Tepi tatheva nibbikārā bhuñjitvā rañño maṅgalaṃ vatvā pakkamiṃsu. Rājā acirapakkantesu tesu “anavajjabhojinova ete samaṇā, aho vatāhampi anavajjabhojī [P 1.0095] bhaveyya”nti cintetvā mahārajjaṃ pahāya pabbajjaṃ samādāya vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā, paccekabuddho hutvā, mañjūsakarukkhamūle paccekabuddhānaṃ majjhe attano ārammaṇaṃ vibhāvento imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi –

47. The origin story for this verse, 'Addhā pasaṃsāma,' up to the Paccekabuddhas' sitting on the seats arranged in the sky, is similar to the origin story of the Cātuddisa verse. However, there is this difference: while that king was startled three times during the night, this one was not; nor was a sacrifice being prepared for him. Having seated the Paccekabuddhas on the seats prepared in the sky, he asked, 'Who are you?' 'We, great king, are called the Blameless Eaters.' 'Venerable sirs, what is the meaning of "Blameless Eaters"?' 'We eat whatever we receive, whether fine or coarse, without reaction, great king.' Hearing this, the king thought, 'Let me test them to see whether they are like that or not.' That day, he served them broken rice with sour rice-gruel as a second dish. The Paccekabuddhas ate without reaction, as if consuming ambrosia. The king thought, 'Perhaps they are impartial for one day because they have made a promise; I shall know tomorrow,' and invited them again for the next day. On the second day, he did the same, and they partook in the same way. Then the king thought, 'Now I shall test them by giving them fine food,' and after inviting them again, having made a great offering for two days, he served them with excellent and very diverse hard and soft foods. They ate without reaction as before, pronounced a blessing on the king, and departed. Soon after their departure, the king reflected, 'These ascetics are indeed Blameless Eaters. Oh, that I too might become a Blameless Eater!' Having given up his great kingdom, he undertook the ascetic life, began to develop insight, and became a Paccekabuddha. Seated at the foot of the Mañjūsaka tree among the Paccekabuddhas, while clarifying the reason for his attainment, he uttered this verse:

“Addhā pasaṃsāma sahāyasampadaṃ, seṭṭhā samā sevitabbā sahāyā;

Ete aladdhā anavajjabhojī, eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”ti.

Truly, we praise the blessing of companionship; superior and equal friends are to be associated with. Not obtaining these, one who eats blamelessly should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.

Sā padatthato uttānā eva. Kevalaṃ pana sahāyasampadanti ettha asekhehi sīlādikkhandhehi sampannā sahāyā eva sahāyasampadāti veditabbā. Ayaṃ panettha yojanā – yāyaṃ vuttā sahāyasampadā, taṃ sahāyasampadaṃ addhā pasaṃsāma, ekaṃseneva thomemāti vuttaṃ hoti. Kathaṃ? Seṭṭhā samā sevitabbā sahāyāti. Kasmā? Attano hi sīlādīhi seṭṭhe sevamānassa sīlādayo dhammā anuppannā uppajjanti, uppannā vuddhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ pāpuṇanti. Same sevamānassa aññamaññaṃ samadhāraṇena kukkuccassa vinodanena ca laddhā na parihāyanti. Ete pana sahāyake seṭṭhe ca same ca aladdhā kuhanādimicchājīvaṃ vajjetvā dhammena samena uppannaṃ bhojanaṃ bhuñjanto tattha ca paṭighānunayaṃ anuppādento anavajjabhojī hutvā atthakāmo kulaputto eko care khaggavisāṇakappo. Ahampi hi evaṃ caranto imaṃ sampattiṃ adhigatomhīti.

The verse is straightforward in its word-meaning. However, here, 'the blessing of companionship' should be understood as companions who are perfected ones, endowed with the aggregates of virtue and so forth. This is the construction here: that which is called the blessing of companionship, that blessing of companionship we truly praise; it means, 'we praise it unequivocally.' How so? 'Superior and equal companions are to be associated with.' Why? For one who associates with those superior to oneself in virtue and so on, unarisen wholesome qualities arise, and those already arisen reach growth, increase, and abundance. For one who associates with equals, through mutual support and the dispelling of scruples, what has been gained does not decline. But not finding such companions—whether superior or equal—then, avoiding wrong livelihood such as deceit, eating food that has arisen righteously and impartially, not giving rise to aversion or attachment thereto, and being one who eats blamelessly, a clansman who desires his welfare should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn. For I too, having wandered thus, have attained this accomplishment.

Anavajjabhojigāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the verse on blameless eating is complete.

48. Disvā [M 1.0085] suvaṇṇassāti kā uppatti? Aññataro bārāṇasirājā gimhasamaye divāseyyaṃ upagato. Santike cassa vaṇṇadāsī gosītacandanaṃ pisati. Tassā ekabāhāyaṃ ekaṃ suvaṇṇavalayaṃ, ekabāhāyaṃ dve, tāni saṅghaṭṭanti itaraṃ na saṅghaṭṭati. Rājā taṃ disvā “evameva gaṇavāse saṅghaṭṭanā, ekavāse asaṅghaṭṭanā”ti punappunaṃ taṃ dāsiṃ olokayamāno cintesi. Tena ca samayena sabbālaṅkārabhūsitā devī taṃ bījayantī ṭhitā hoti. Sā “vaṇṇadāsiyā paṭibaddhacitto maññe rājā”ti cintetvā taṃ dāsiṃ uṭṭhāpetvā sayameva pisitumāraddhā[V 1.0076]. Tassā ubhosu bāhāsu aneke suvaṇṇavalayā, te saṅghaṭṭantā mahāsaddaṃ janayiṃsu. Rājā suṭṭhutaraṃ nibbinno dakkhiṇena passena nipannoyeva vipassanaṃ [P 1.0096] ārabhitvā paccekabodhiṃ sacchākāsi. Taṃ anuttarena sukhena sukhitaṃ nipannaṃ candanahatthā devī upasaṅkamitvā “ālimpāmi, mahārājā”ti āha. Rājā – “apehi, mā ālimpāhī”ti āha. Sā “kissa, mahārājā”ti āha. So “nāhaṃ rājā”ti. Evametesaṃ taṃ kathāsallāpaṃ sutvā amaccā upasaṅkamiṃsu. Tehipi mahārājavādena ālapito “nāhaṃ, bhaṇe, rājā”ti āha. Sesaṃ paṭhamagāthāya vuttasadisameva.

48. Regarding 'Having seen the golden...': what is its origin? A certain king of Bārāṇasī, during the hot season, retired for his daytime rest. Near him, a handmaiden was grinding gosīta sandalwood. On one of her arms was a single golden bracelet, and on the other arm were two; these two clashed together, but the single one did not. The king, seeing this, thought, 'Even so, in communal living there is friction, but in solitary living there is none,' and he reflected while looking at the handmaiden again and again. At that time, the queen, adorned with all her ornaments, stood fanning him. She thought, 'I believe the king's mind is attached to the handmaiden,' and so, having made the handmaiden rise, she herself began to grind. On both her arms were many golden bracelets, and as they clashed, they made a great noise. The king, becoming exceedingly disenchanted, while still lying on his right side, began to develop insight and realized Paccekabodhi. As he lay there, blissful with unsurpassed happiness, the queen, with sandalwood in her hand, approached and said, 'Let me anoint you, great king.' The king said, 'Go away, do not anoint me.' She asked, 'Why, great king?' He replied, 'I am not a king.' Hearing this conversation of theirs, the ministers approached. When they too addressed him with the words 'great king,' he said, 'Sirs, I am not a king.' The rest is just as was said in the first verse.

Ayaṃ pana gāthāvaṇṇanā – disvāti oloketvā. Suvaṇṇassāti kañcanassa “valayānī”ti pāṭhaseso. Sāvasesapāṭho hi ayaṃ attho. Pabhassarānīti pabhāsanasīlāni, jutimantānīti vuttaṃ hoti. Sesaṃ uttānatthameva. Ayaṃ pana yojanā – disvā bhujasmiṃ suvaṇṇassa valayāni “gaṇavāse sati saṅghaṭṭanā, ekavāse asaṅghaṭṭanā”ti evaṃ cintento vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā paccekabodhiṃ adhigatomhīti. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti.

This, then, is the commentary on the verse. 'Disvā' means having seen. 'Suvaṇṇassa' means of gold; 'valayāni' (bracelets) is the rest of the phrase to be supplied. Indeed, this is an elliptical reading. 'Pabhassarāni' means having a shining nature; that is to say, radiant. The rest is clear in meaning. This, then, is the construction: 'Having seen the golden bracelets on the arm, and thinking, "When living in a group, there is clashing; when living alone, there is no clashing," I began to develop insight and attained Paccekabodhi.' The rest is as has been explained.

Suvaṇṇavalayagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Suvaṇṇavalayagāthā is complete.

49. Evaṃ dutiyenāti kā uppatti? Aññataro bārāṇasirājā daharova pabbajitukāmo amacce āṇāpesi “deviṃ gahetvā rajjaṃ pariharatha, ahaṃ pabbajissāmī”ti. Amaccā “na, mahārāja, arājakaṃ rajjaṃ amhehi sakkā rakkhituṃ, sāmantarājāno āgamma vilumpissanti, yāva ekaputtopi uppajjati, tāva āgamehī”ti saññāpesuṃ. Muducitto rājā [M 1.0086] adhivāsesi. Atha devī gabbhaṃ gaṇhi. Rājā punapi te āṇāpesi – “devī gabbhinī, puttaṃ jātaṃ rajje abhisiñcitvā rajjaṃ pariharatha, ahaṃ pabbajissāmī”ti. Amaccā “dujjānaṃ, mahārāja, etaṃ devī puttaṃ vā vijāyissati dhītaraṃ vā, vijāyanakālaṃ tāva āgamehī”ti punapi saññāpesuṃ. Atha sā puttaṃ vijāyi. Tadāpi rājā tatheva amacce āṇāpesi. Amaccā punapi rājānaṃ “āgamehi, mahārāja, yāva, paṭibalo hotī”ti bahūhi kāraṇehi saññāpesuṃ. Tato kumāre paṭibale [P 1.0097] jāte amacce sannipātāpetvā “paṭibalo ayaṃ, taṃ rajje abhisiñcitvā paṭipajjathā”ti amaccānaṃ okāsaṃ adatvā antarāpaṇā kāsāyavatthādayo sabbaparikkhāre āharāpetvā antepure eva pabbajitvā mahājanako viya nikkhami. Sabbaparijano nānappakārakaṃ paridevamāno rājānaṃ anubandhi.

49. What is the origin of the verse beginning 'Evaṃ dutiyena'? A certain king of Bārāṇasī, while still young, desired to go forth and commanded his ministers: 'Take the queen and govern the kingdom; I shall go forth.' The ministers informed him, saying: 'No, great king, we cannot protect a kingdom without a king. The neighboring kings will come and plunder it. Wait until at least one son is born.' The soft-hearted king agreed. Then the queen conceived. The king again commanded them: 'The queen is with child. When a son is born, having consecrated him to the throne, govern the kingdom; I shall go forth.' The ministers again informed him, saying: 'It is hard to know, great king, whether the queen will give birth to a son or a daughter. Wait until the time of birth.' Then she gave birth to a son. Even then, the king gave the same command to the ministers. The ministers once more persuaded the king with many reasons, saying: 'Wait, great king, until he is capable.' Then, when the prince became capable, the king had the ministers assemble, and without giving them an opportunity to object, he said: 'This one is capable; having consecrated him to the throne, you must govern.' Then, having arranged for the saffron robes and all the other requisites to be brought from the market, he went forth right there in the inner palace and departed like Mahājanaka. His entire retinue followed the king, lamenting in various ways.

Rājā [V 1.0077] yāva attano rajjasīmā, tāva gantvā kattaradaṇḍena lekhaṃ katvā “ayaṃ lekhā nātikkamitabbā”ti āha. Mahājano lekhāya sīsaṃ katvā, bhūmiyaṃ nipanno paridevamāno “tuyhaṃ dāni, tāta, rañño āṇā, kiṃ karissatī”ti kumāraṃ lekhaṃ atikkamāpesi. Kumāro “tāta, tātā”ti dhāvitvā rājānaṃ sampāpuṇi. Rājā kumāraṃ disvā “etaṃ mahājanaṃ pariharanto rajjaṃ kāresiṃ, kiṃ dāni ekaṃ dārakaṃ pariharituṃ na sakkhissa”nti kumāraṃ gahetvā araññaṃ paviṭṭho, tattha pubbapaccekabuddhehi vasitapaṇṇasālaṃ disvā vāsaṃ kappesi saddhiṃ puttena. Tato kumāro varasayanādīsu kataparicayo tiṇasanthārake vā rajjumañcake vā sayamāno rodati. Sītavātādīhi phuṭṭho samāno “sītaṃ, tāta, uṇhaṃ, tāta, makkhikā, tāta, khādanti, chātomhi, tāta, pipāsitomhi, tātā”ti vadati. Rājā taṃ saññāpentoyeva rattiṃ vītināmeti. Divāpissa piṇḍāya caritvā bhattaṃ upanāmeti, taṃ hoti missakabhattaṃ kaṅguvarakamuggādibahulaṃ. Kumāro acchādentampi taṃ jighacchāvasena bhuñjamāno katipāheneva uṇhe ṭhapitapadumaṃ viya milāyi. Paccekabodhisatto pana paṭisaṅkhānabalena nibbikāroyeva bhuñjati.

The king went as far as the boundary of his kingdom, and having drawn a line with a stick, he declared: 'This line must not be crossed.' The great crowd, bowing their heads to the line and lying on the ground, lamented, and saying, 'Dear child, what can your father the king's command do now?' they had the prince cross the line. The prince, crying 'Father, father!' ran and reached the king. Seeing the prince, the king thought: 'I governed the kingdom while caring for this great crowd; why should I not be able to care for a single child now?' So, taking the prince, he entered the forest. There, seeing a leaf-hut once inhabited by past Paccekabuddhas, he took up residence with his son. Then the prince, who was accustomed to fine beds, wept while lying on a pallet of grass or a rope bedstead. Afflicted by cold winds and the like, he would say: 'It is cold, father! It is hot, father! The flies are biting, father! I am hungry, father! I am thirsty, father!' The king would spend the night comforting him. During the day, he would go for alms and bring back food for him. It was a mixed meal, plentiful with millet, varaka beans, mung beans, and the like. Although it was unappealing to the prince, he ate it out of hunger, and within a few days he withered like a lotus placed in the sun. The Paccekabodhisatta, however, ate without any aversion, sustained by the power of reflection.

Tato so kumāraṃ saññāpento āha – “nagarasmiṃ, tāta, paṇītāhāro labbhati, tattha gacchāmā”ti. Kumāro “āma, tātā”ti āha. Tato naṃ purakkhatvā āgatamaggeneva nivatti. Kumāramātāpi devī [M 1.0087] “na dāni rājā kumāraṃ gahetvā araññe ciraṃ vasissati, katipāheneva nivattissatī”ti [P 1.0098] cintetvā raññā kattaradaṇḍena likhitaṭṭhāneyeva vatiṃ kārāpetvā vāsaṃ kappesi. Tato rājā tassā vatiyā avidūre ṭhatvā “ettha te, tāta, mātā nisinnā, gacchāhī”ti pesesi. Yāva ca so taṃ ṭhānaṃ pāpuṇāti, tāva udikkhanto aṭṭhāsi “mā heva naṃ koci viheṭheyyā”ti. Kumāro mātu santikaṃ dhāvanto agamāsi. Ārakkhakapurisā ca naṃ disvā deviyā ārocesuṃ. Devī vīsatināṭakitthisahassaparivutā gantvā paṭiggahesi, rañño ca pavattiṃ pucchi. Atha “pacchato āgacchatī”ti sutvā manusse pesesi. Rājāpi tāvadeva sakavasatiṃ agamāsi. Manussā rājānaṃ adisvā nivattiṃsu. Tato devī nirāsāva hutvā, puttaṃ gahetvā, nagaraṃ gantvā, taṃ rajje abhisiñci. Rājāpi attano vasatiṃ patvā, tattha nisinno vipassitvā, paccekabodhiṃ sacchikatvā, mañjūsakarukkhamūle paccekabuddhānaṃ majjhe imaṃ udānagāthaṃ abhāsi –

Then, persuading the prince, he said: 'Dear son, fine food is available in the city; let us go there.' The prince replied: 'Yes, father.' Then, placing him in front, he turned back by the very path they had come. The prince's mother, the queen, thinking, 'The king will not now stay long in the forest with the prince; he will return in a few days,' had an enclosure built at the very place marked by the king's stick and took up residence there. Then the king, standing not far from her enclosure, sent the prince, saying: 'Go, dear son, your mother is seated there.' And he stood watching until the prince reached that place, thinking: 'May no one harm him.' The prince ran to his mother. The guards saw him and informed the queen. The queen, surrounded by twenty thousand dancing women, went and received him, and asked for news of the king. Then, hearing that he was coming behind, she sent men. The king, however, had just then gone to his own dwelling. The men, not seeing the king, turned back. Then the queen, having lost hope, took her son, went to the city, and consecrated him to the throne. The king, too, having reached his own dwelling, sat there practicing insight, realized Paccekabodhi, and at the foot of the Mañjūsaka tree, in the midst of Paccekabuddhas, uttered this inspired verse:

“Evaṃ dutiyena saha mamassa, vācābhilāpo abhisajjanā vā;

Etaṃ bhayaṃ āyatiṃ pekkhamāno, eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”ti.

Thus, with a companion, there would be for me conversation or attachment; Foreseeing this future danger, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.

Sā [V 1.0078] padatthato uttānā eva. Ayaṃ panettha adhippāyo – yvāyaṃ etena dutiyena kumārena sītuṇhādīni nivedentena sahavāsena taṃ saññāpentassa mama vācābhilāpo, tasmiṃ sinehavasena abhisajjanā ca jātā, sace ahaṃ imaṃ na pariccajāmi, tato āyatimpi hessati yatheva idāni; evaṃ dutiyena saha mamassa vācābhilāpo abhisajjanā vā. Ubhayampi cetaṃ antarāyakaraṃ visesādhigamassāti etaṃ bhayaṃ āyatiṃ pekkhamāno taṃ chaḍḍetvā yoniso paṭipajjitvā paccekabodhiṃ adhigatomhīti. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti.

The meaning of its words is clear. Herein, this is the intention: Due to living together with this companion, the prince, who would report the cold, the heat, and so on, there arose for me, while I was comforting him, conversation; and due to affection for him, attachment also arose. If I do not abandon him, then in the future it will be just as it is now; thus, with a companion, there would be for me conversation or attachment. Both of these are an obstacle to the attainment of distinction. Foreseeing this future danger, I abandoned him, practiced with proper attention, and have attained Paccekabodhi. The rest is as has been explained.

Āyatibhayagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Verse of Future Danger is concluded.

50. Kāmā hi citrāti kā uppatti? Bārāṇasiyaṃ kira seṭṭhiputto daharova seṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ labhi. Tassa tiṇṇaṃ utūnaṃ tayo pāsādā honti[M 1.0088]. So tattha sabbasampattīhi devakumāro viya paricāreti. So daharova samāno “pabbajissāmī”ti mātāpitaro yāci. Te naṃ vārenti. So tatheva nibandhati. Punapi naṃ mātāpitaro “tvaṃ, tāta, sukhumālo, dukkarā pabbajjā, khuradhārāya upari caṅkamanasadisā”ti nānappakārehi vārenti. So tatheva nibandhati. Te cintesuṃ “sacāyaṃ [P 1.0099] pabbajati, amhākaṃ domanassaṃ hoti. Sace naṃ nivārema, etassa domanassaṃ hoti. Apica amhākaṃ domanassaṃ hotu, mā ca etassā”ti anujāniṃsu. Tato so sabbaparijanaṃ paridevamānaṃ anādiyitvā isipatanaṃ gantvā paccekabuddhānaṃ santike pabbaji. Tassa uḷārasenāsanaṃ na pāpuṇāti, mañcake taṭṭikaṃ pattharitvā sayi. So varasayane kataparicayo sabbarattiṃ atidukkhito ahosi. Pabhātepi sarīraparikammaṃ katvā, pattacīvaramādāya paccekabuddhehi saddhiṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Tattha vuḍḍhā aggāsanañca aggapiṇḍañca labhanti, navakā yaṃkiñcideva āsanaṃ lūkhabhojanañca. So tena lūkhabhojanenāpi atidukkhito ahosi. So katipāhaṃyeva kiso dubbaṇṇo hutvā nibbijji yathā taṃ aparipākagate samaṇadhamme. Tato mātāpitūnaṃ dūtaṃ pesetvā uppabbaji. So katipāhaṃyeva balaṃ gahetvā punapi pabbajitukāmo ahosi. Tato teneva kamena pabbajitvā punapi uppabbajitvā tatiyavāre pabbajitvā sammā paṭipanno paccekasambodhiṃ sacchikatvā imaṃ udānagāthaṃ vatvā puna paccekabuddhānaṃ majjhe imameva byākaraṇagāthaṃ abhāsi –

50. What is the origin of the verse beginning, 'Sensual pleasures are indeed variegated'? In Bārāṇasī, it is said, a merchant’s son, while still young, obtained the position of a merchant. He had three mansions appropriate for the three seasons. There, he enjoyed all luxuries like a divine prince. While still a youth, he asked his parents, 'I will go forth.' They tried to prevent him. He persisted in the same way. Again, his parents tried to prevent him in various ways, saying, 'Dear child, you are delicate. Going forth is difficult; it is like walking on the edge of a razor.' He persisted in the same way. They thought, 'If he goes forth, it will cause us sorrow. If we prevent him, it will cause him sorrow. Let the sorrow be ours, but not his.' And so they gave their consent. Disregarding the lamentations of his entire household, he went to Isipatana and went forth in the presence of the Paccekabuddhas. He did not receive a magnificent dwelling; he slept on a mat spread over a cot. Accustomed to fine beds, he was greatly distressed all night. At dawn, after attending to his bodily needs, he took his bowl and robe and entered the village for alms with the Paccekabuddhas. There, the elder monks received the foremost seats and the choicest alms, while the new monks received whatever seat and coarse food was available. He was greatly distressed even by that coarse food. Within just a few days, he became thin and pale and grew disenchanted, as is the case when the ascetic practice has not matured. Then, sending a messenger to his parents, he disrobed. After regaining his strength in just a few days, he again became desirous of going forth. Then, in that same sequence, having gone forth and disrobed again, he went forth for a third time, practiced rightly, realized Paccekasambodhi, and after uttering this inspired utterance, he spoke this very same verse of declaration amidst the Paccekabuddhas:

“Kāmā hi citrā madhurā manoramā, virūparūpena mathenti cittaṃ;

Ādīnavaṃ kāmaguṇesu disvā, eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”ti.

Sensual pleasures are indeed variegated, sweet, and delightful; they churn the mind with their diverse forms. Having seen the danger in sensual qualities, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.

Tattha [V 1.0079] kāmāti dve kāmā vatthukāmā ca kilesakāmā ca. Tattha vatthukāmā manāpiyarūpādayo dhammā, kilesakāmā chandādayo sabbepi rāgappabhedā. Idha pana vatthukāmā adhippetā. Rūpādianekappakāravasena citrā. Lokassādavasena madhurā. Bālaputhujjanānaṃ manaṃ ramentīti manoramā. Virūparūpenāti virūpena rūpena, anekavidhena sabhāvenāti vuttaṃ hoti. Te hi rūpādivasena citrā, rūpādīsupi nīlādivasena vividharūpā. Evaṃ tena virūparūpena tathā tathā assādaṃ dassetvā [M 1.0089] mathenti cittaṃ pabbajjāya abhiramituṃ na dentīti. Sesamettha pākaṭameva. Nigamanampi dvīhi tīhi vā padehi yojetvā purimagāthāsu vuttanayeneva veditabbanti.

Therein, regarding 'sensual pleasures' (kāmā), there are two kinds: sensual objects (vatthukāmā) and sensual defilements (kilesakāmā). Of these, sensual objects are phenomena such as pleasing forms. Sensual defilements are all the varieties of lust. Here, however, sensual objects are intended. They are 'variegated' (citrā) by way of many kinds of sense objects, such as forms. They are 'sweet' (madhurā) by way of worldly gratification. Because they delight the minds of foolish worldlings, they are 'delightful' (manoramā). 'With diverse forms' (virūparūpena) means with a diverse form, that is to say, with a manifold nature. For they are variegated by way of forms and so on, and even within forms, they are of diverse kinds, such as blue and so on. Thus, by displaying gratification in such and such a way through those diverse forms, they churn the mind and do not allow it to delight in the life of renunciation. The rest here is self-evident. The conclusion should also be understood by connecting it with two or three terms in the same way as stated in the previous verses.

Kāmagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the verse concerning sensual pleasure is concluded.

51. Ītī [P 1.0100] cāti kā uppatti? Bārāṇasiyaṃ kira rañño gaṇḍo udapādi. Bāḷhā vedanā vattanti. Vejjā “satthakammena vinā phāsu na hotī”ti bhaṇanti. Rājā tesaṃ abhayaṃ datvā satthakammaṃ kārāpesi. Te phāletvā, pubbalohitaṃ nīharitvā, nibbedanaṃ katvā, vaṇaṃ paṭṭena bandhiṃsu, āhārācāresu ca naṃ sammā ovadiṃsu. Rājā lūkhabhojanena kisasarīro ahosi, gaṇḍo cassa milāyi. So phāsukasaññī hutvā siniddhāhāraṃ bhuñji. Tena ca sañjātabalo visaye paṭisevi. Tassa gaṇḍo puna purimasabhāvameva sampāpuṇi. Evaṃ yāva tikkhattuṃ satthakammaṃ kārāpetvā, vejjehi parivajjito nibbijjitvā, rajjaṃ pahāya pabbajitvā, araññaṃ pavisitvā, vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā, sattahi vassehi paccekabodhiṃ sacchikatvā, imaṃ udānagāthaṃ bhāsitvā nandamūlakapabbhāraṃ agamāsi.

51. What is the origin of the verse beginning, 'A calamity and...'? It is said that in Bārāṇasī, a boil arose on the king. Severe pains occurred. The physicians said, 'Without surgery, there will be no relief.' The king, granting them immunity, had the surgery performed. They lanced it, removed the pus and blood, made it painless, bandaged the wound with a cloth, and advised him properly on matters of diet. The king, by eating coarse food, became thin, and his boil subsided. Perceiving himself to be well, he ate rich food. And because of that, having regained his strength, he indulged in sensual pleasures. His boil returned to its former state. Thus, after having surgery performed three times, he was given up by the physicians. Becoming disenchanted, he renounced the kingdom, went forth, entered the forest, began insight meditation, and after seven years realized Paccekabodhi. He uttered this inspired utterance and went to the Nandamūlaka mountain slope.

“Ītī ca gaṇḍo ca upaddavo ca, rogo ca sallañca bhayañca metaṃ;

Etaṃ bhayaṃ kāmaguṇesu disvā, eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”ti.

A calamity, a boil, an affliction, a disease, a dart, and a fear—this is what is mine. Seeing this fear in sensual qualities, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.

Tattha etīti īti, āgantukānaṃ akusalabhāgiyānaṃ byasanahetūnaṃ etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tasmā kāmaguṇāpi ete anekabyasanāvahaṭṭhena daḷhasannipātaṭṭhena ca īti. Gaṇḍopi asuciṃ paggharati, uddhumātaparipakkaparibhinno hoti. Tasmā ete kilesāsucipaggharaṇato uppādajarābhaṅgehi uddhumātaparipakkaparibhinnabhāvato ca gaṇḍo. Upaddavatīti upaddavo; anatthaṃ janento abhibhavati; ajjhottharatīti attho, rājadaṇḍādīnametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tasmā kāmaguṇāpete aviditanibbānatthāvahahetutāya sabbupaddavavatthutāya ca upaddavo. Yasmā panete kilesāturabhāvaṃ janentā sīlasaṅkhātamārogyaṃ, loluppaṃ vā [M 1.0090] uppādentā pākatikameva ārogyaṃ vilumpanti, tasmā iminā [V 1.0080] ārogyavilumpanaṭṭheneva rogo. Abbhantaramanuppaviṭṭhaṭṭhena pana antotudakaṭṭhena dunniharaṇīyaṭṭhena ca sallaṃ. Diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikabhayāvahanato [P 1.0101] bhayaṃ. Me etanti metaṃ. Sesamettha pākaṭameva. Nigamanaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbanti.

Therein, 'calamity' (īti) is so called because 'it comes' (eti); it is a designation for adventitious, unwholesome causes of ruin. Therefore, these sensual qualities are also a 'calamity' because they bring many kinds of ruin and are a firm accumulation. A 'boil' (gaṇḍa) also oozes impurity; it becomes swollen, ripe, and bursts. Therefore, these defilements are a 'boil' because they ooze the impurity of defilements and because, through arising, aging, and dissolution, they have the nature of being swollen, ripe, and burst. 'It afflicts' (upaddavati), hence it is an 'affliction' (upaddavo); it overwhelms by generating what is not beneficial; the meaning is 'it oppresses.' Therefore, these sensual qualities are an 'affliction' because they are a cause that prevents the knowing of Nibbāna's benefit and because they are the basis for all afflictions. Furthermore, since these defilements, by generating a state of sickness, destroy the health known as virtue, or by producing greed, plunder even natural health, they are a 'disease' (rogo) for this very reason of destroying health. Then, because it has penetrated within, because it pierces inwardly, and because it is difficult to extract, it is a 'dart' (sallaṃ). Because it brings fear both in this present life and in the next, it is 'fear' (bhayaṃ). 'This is mine' (me etaṃ) becomes 'metaṃ'. The rest here is self-evident. The conclusion should be understood in the very way that has been stated.

Ītigāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the 'Īti' verse is concluded.

52. Sītañcāti kā uppatti? Bārāṇasiyaṃ kira sītālukabrahmadatto nāma rājā ahosi. So pabbajitvā araññakuṭikāya viharati. Tasmiñca padese sīte sītaṃ, uṇhe uṇhameva ca hoti abbhokāsattā padesassa. Gocaragāme bhikkhā yāvadatthāya na labbhati. Pivanakapānīyampi dullabhaṃ, vātātapaḍaṃsasarīsapāpi bādhenti. Tassa etadahosi – “ito aḍḍhayojanamatte sampanno padeso, tattha sabbepi ete parissayā natthi. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ tattha gaccheyyaṃ; phāsukaṃ viharantena sakkā visesaṃ adhigantu”nti. Tassa puna ahosi – “pabbajitā nāma na paccayavasikā honti, evarūpañca cittaṃ vase vattenti, na cittassa vase vattenti, nāhaṃ gamissāmī”ti paccavekkhitvā na agamāsi. Evaṃ yāvatatiyakaṃ uppannacittaṃ paccavekkhitvā nivattesi. Tato tattheva satta vassāni vasitvā, sammā paṭipajjamāno paccekasambodhiṃ sacchikatvā, imaṃ udānagāthaṃ bhāsitvā nandamūlakapabbhāraṃ agamāsi.

52. What is the origin of 'Sītañca'? It is said that in Bārāṇasī there was a king named Sītāluka Brahmadatta. He went forth and lived in a forest hut. In that region, it was cold in the cold season and hot in the hot season, for the area was open to the sky. In the alms-village, almsfood could not be obtained as needed. Even drinking water was scarce, and he was afflicted by wind, sun, gadflies, and creeping creatures. The thought occurred to him: 'About half a yojana from here, there is a well-provided region where none of these hardships exist. What if I were to go there? Dwelling in comfort, it would be possible to attain a higher state.' Then it occurred to him again: 'Those who have gone forth are not dependent on conditions. They bring the mind under their control; they do not fall under the control of the mind. I will not go.' Having reflected thus, he did not go. In this way, up to the third time, he reflected upon the thought that had arisen and rejected it. Then, having lived right there for seven years and practicing rightly, he realized paccekasambodhi. Having uttered this inspired verse, he went to the Nandamūlaka mountain slope.

“Sītañca uṇhañca khudaṃ pipāsaṃ, vātātape ḍaṃsasarīsape ca;

Sabbānipetāni abhisambhavitvā, eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”ti.

“Cold and heat, hunger and thirst, wind and sun, gadflies and creeping creatures; having overcome all these, one should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.”

Tattha sītañcāti sītaṃ nāma duvidhaṃ abbhantaradhātukkhobhapaccayañca, bāhiradhātukkhobhapaccayañca; tathā uṇhaṃ. Ḍaṃsāti piṅgalamakkhikā. Sarīsapāti ye keci dīghajātikā saritvā gacchanti. Sesaṃ pākaṭameva. Nigamanampi vuttanayeneva veditabbanti.

Here, 'cold' refers to two types: that caused by internal elemental disturbance and that caused by external elemental disturbance; similarly for 'heat'. 'Ḍaṃsa' means reddish-brown flies. 'Sarīsapa' refers to any long-bodied creatures that crawl. The rest is clear. The conclusion should be understood in the same way as explained.

Sītālukagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Sītāluka Gāthā is concluded.

53. Nāgovāti [M 1.0091] kā uppatti? Bārāṇasiyaṃ kira aññataro rājā vīsati vassāni rajjaṃ kāretvā kālakato niraye vīsati eva vassāni paccitvā himavantappadese hatthiyoniyaṃ uppajjitvā [P 1.0102] sañjātakkhandho padumavaṇṇasakalasarīro uḷāro yūthapati mahānāgo ahosi. Tassa obhaggobhaggaṃ sākhābhaṅgaṃ hatthichāpāva khādanti. Ogāhepi naṃ hatthiniyo kaddamena limpanti[V 1.0081], sabbaṃ pālileyyakanāgasseva ahosi. So yūthā nibbijjitvā pakkami. Tato naṃ padānusārena yūthaṃ anubandhi. Evaṃ yāvatatiyaṃ pakkanto anubaddhova. Tato cintesi – “idāni mayhaṃ nattako bārāṇasiyaṃ rajjaṃ kāreti, yaṃnūnāhaṃ attano purimajātiyā uyyānaṃ gaccheyyaṃ, tatra maṃ so rakkhissatī”ti. Tato rattiṃ niddāvasaṃ gate yūthe yūthaṃ pahāya tameva uyyānaṃ pāvisi. Uyyānapālo disvā rañño ārocesi. Rājā “hatthiṃ gahessāmī”ti senāya parivāresi. Hatthī rājānaṃ eva abhimukho gacchati. Rājā “maṃ abhimukho etī”ti khurappaṃ sannayhitvā aṭṭhāsi. Tato hatthī “vijjheyyāpi maṃ eso”ti mānusikāya vācāya “brahmadatta, mā maṃ vijjha, ahaṃ te ayyako”ti āha. Rājā “kiṃ bhaṇasī”ti sabbaṃ pucchi. Hatthīpi rajje ca narake ca hatthiyoniyañca pavattiṃ sabbaṃ ārocesi. Rājā “sundaraṃ, mā bhāyi, mā ca kañci bhiṃsāpehī”ti hatthino vaṭṭañca ārakkhake ca hatthibhaṇḍe ca upaṭṭhāpesi.

53. What is the origin of 'Nāgo'? It is said that a certain king in Bārāṇasī ruled for twenty years and, upon his death, having been tormented in hell for twenty years, was reborn in the elephant realm in the Himalayan region. Having developed a massive body, with his entire body the color of a lotus, he became a magnificent great elephant, the leader of a herd. The young elephants would eat the branches he had broken. Even when he entered the water, the female elephants would smear him with mud—everything was just as it was for the elephant Pālileyyaka. He grew weary of the herd and departed. Then the herd followed him by his footprints. In this way, though he departed up to a third time, he was still followed. Then he thought: 'Now my grandson rules in Bārāṇasī. What if I were to go to the park of my former birth? He will protect me there.' So, at night, when the herd was overcome by sleep, he abandoned the herd and entered that very park. The park keeper saw him and reported it to the king. The king, thinking, 'I will capture the elephant,' surrounded him with his army. The elephant walked straight toward the king. The king, thinking, 'He is coming straight at me,' fitted his razor-arrow and stood ready. Then the elephant, thinking, 'This one might shoot me,' spoke in a human voice: 'Brahmadatta, do not shoot me—I am your grandfather.' The king asked, 'What are you saying?' and questioned him about everything. The elephant recounted the whole story: his reign, his time in hell, and his existence in the elephant realm. The king said, 'Excellent! Do not fear, and do not cause fear in anyone.' He then had provisions, guards, and elephant-trappings supplied for the elephant.

Athekadivasaṃ rājā hatthikkhandhagato “ayaṃ vīsati vassāni rajjaṃ katvā niraye pakko, vipākāvasesena ca tiracchānayoniyaṃ uppanno, tatthapi gaṇavāsasaṅghaṭṭanaṃ asahanto idhāgato. Aho dukkho gaṇavāso, ekībhāvo eva ca pana sukho”ti cintetvā tattheva vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā paccekabodhiṃ sacchākāsi. Taṃ lokuttarasukhena sukhitaṃ amaccā upasaṅkamitvā, paṇipātaṃ katvā “yānakālo mahārājā”ti āhaṃsu. Tato “nāhaṃ rājā”ti vatvā purimanayeneva imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi –

Then one day, while seated on the elephant's back, the king reflected: 'This one ruled for twenty years and then was tormented in hell; due to the remainder of his kamma-result, he was reborn in the animal realm. Even there, unable to endure the friction of living in a group, he came here. Alas, living in a group is suffering! The state of being alone, however, is happiness.' Thinking thus, he began insight meditation right there and realized paccekabodhi. As he was experiencing the bliss of the supramundane, his ministers approached, paid homage, and said, 'It is time to depart, great king.' Then, saying, 'I am no king,' he uttered this verse in the same manner as before:

“Nāgova yūthāni vivajjayitvā, sañjātakhandho padumī uḷāro;

Yathābhirantaṃ viharaṃ araññe, eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”ti.

“Like an elephant, noble, avoiding the herds, with a massive body, lotus-like; wandering at will in the forest, one should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.”

Sā [M 1.0092][P 1.0103] padatthato pākaṭā eva. Ayaṃ panettha adhippāyayojanā. Sā ca kho yuttivaseneva, na anussavavasena. Yathā ayaṃ hatthī manussakantesu sīlesu dantattā adantabhūmiṃ nāgacchatīti vā, sarīramahantatāya vā nāgo, evaṃ kudāssu nāmāhampi ariyakantesu sīlesu dantattā adantabhūmiṃ nāgamanena āguṃ akaraṇena puna itthattaṃ anāgamanena ca guṇasarīramahantatāya vā nāgo bhaveyyaṃ. Yathā cesa yūthāni vivajjetvā ekacariyasukhena yathābhirantaṃ viharaṃ araññe eko care khaggavisāṇakappo, kudāssu nāmāhampi evaṃ gaṇaṃ vivajjetvā ekavihārasukhena jhānasukhena yathābhirantaṃ viharaṃ araññe attano yathā yathā sukhaṃ, tathā tathā yattakaṃ vā icchāmi, tattakaṃ araññe nivāsaṃ eko care khaggavisāṇakappo careyyanti attho. Yathā cesa susaṇṭhitakkhandhatāya [V 1.0082] sañjātakkhandho, kudāssu nāmāhampi evaṃ asekhasīlakkhandhamahantatāya sañjātakkhandho bhaveyyaṃ. Yathā cesa padumasadisagattatāya vā padumakule uppannatāya vā padumī, kudāssu nāmāhampi evaṃ padumasadisaujugattatāya vā ariyajātipadume uppannatāya vā padumī bhaveyyaṃ. Yathā cesa thāmabalajavādīhi uḷāro, kudāssu nāmāhampi evaṃ parisuddhakāyasamācāratādīhi sīlasamādhinibbedhikapaññādīhi vā uḷāro bhaveyyanti evaṃ cintento vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā paccekabodhiṃ adhigatomhīti.

The meaning of the verse is evident from the words themselves. This, however, is the application of the intended meaning, which is based on reasoning, not on mere tradition. Just as this elephant, being tamed in virtues pleasing to humans, does not go to the untamed region—or is called a 'nāga' because of its massive body—so too, when will I, by being tamed in virtues pleasing to the noble ones, by not going to the untamed region, by not committing a fault, and by not returning to this state of existence again, become a 'nāga' due to the greatness of my virtuous qualities? And just as this one, having abandoned its herds, dwells happily enjoying solitude in the forest, wandering alone like a rhinoceros horn—so too, when will I, having abandoned the crowd, dwell happily enjoying solitary dwelling and the bliss of jhāna, in the forest, according to my pleasure, as I please, and for as long as I wish, living in the forest, wandering alone like a rhinoceros horn? And just as this one is 'sañjātakkhandha' because of its well-formed shoulders—so too, when will I become 'sañjātakkhandha' due to the greatness of the aggregate of the morality of an adept? And just as this one is 'padumī' because of its lotus-like body or because it is born in a lotus family—so too, when will I become 'padumī' because of my lotus-like uprightness or because I am born in the noble lotus lineage? And just as this one is magnificent in strength, power, speed, and so forth—so too, when will I become magnificent through purified bodily conduct and so forth, or by morality, concentration, and penetrating wisdom, and so forth? Thus reflecting, having initiated insight, I attained Paccekabodhi.

Nāgagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Nāga Verses is concluded.

54. Aṭṭhāna tanti kā uppatti? Bārāṇasirañño kira putto daharo eva samāno pabbajitukāmo mātāpitaro yāci. Mātāpitaro naṃ vārenti. So vāriyamānopi nibandhatiyeva “pabbajissāmī”ti. Tato naṃ pubbe vuttaseṭṭhiputtaṃ [P 1.0104] viya sabbaṃ vatvā anujāniṃsu. Pabbajitvā ca uyyāneyeva vasitabbanti paṭijānāpesuṃ, so tathā akāsi. Tassa mātā pātova vīsatisahassanāṭakitthiparivutā uyyānaṃ gantvā, puttaṃ yāguṃ pāyetvā, antarā khajjakādīni ca khādāpetvā, yāva majjhanhikasamayaṃ tena saddhiṃ samullapitvā, nagaraṃ pavisati. Pitā ca majjhanhike āgantvā, taṃ bhojetvā attanāpi bhuñjitvā, divasaṃ tena saddhiṃ samullapitvā, sāyanhasamaye [M 1.0093] jagganapurise ṭhapetvā nagaraṃ pavisati. So evaṃ rattindivaṃ avivitto viharati. Tena kho pana samayena ādiccabandhu nāma paccekabuddho nandamūlakapabbhāre viharati. So āvajjento taṃ addasa – “ayaṃ kumāro pabbajituṃ asakkhi, jaṭaṃ chindituṃ na sakkotī”ti. Tato paraṃ āvajji “attano dhammatāya nibbijjissati, no”ti. Atha “dhammatāya nibbindanto aticiraṃ bhavissatī”ti ñatvā “tassa ārammaṇaṃ dassessāmī”ti pubbe vuttanayeneva manosilātalato āgantvā uyyāne aṭṭhāsi. Rājapuriso disvā “paccekabuddho āgato, mahārājā”ti rañño ārocesi. Rājā “idāni me putto paccekabuddhena saddhiṃ anukkaṇṭhito vasissatī”ti pamuditamano hutvā paccekabuddhaṃ sakkaccaṃ upaṭṭhahitvā tattheva vāsaṃ yācitvā paṇṇasālādivāvihāraṭṭhānacaṅkamādisabbaṃ kāretvā vāsesi.

54. What is the origin of the Aṭṭhāna verse? It is said that the young son of the king of Bārāṇasī, while still a child, wished to go forth into homelessness and asked his parents. His parents tried to dissuade him, but though dissuaded, he insisted, saying, “I will go forth.” Then, after saying everything, they granted him permission, just as was said previously concerning the merchant’s son.
