After his going forth, they made him promise to stay only in the park, and he did so. His mother, early in the morning, surrounded by twenty thousand dancing women, would go to the park, give him rice gruel, have him eat snacks and other foods in between, converse with him until midday, and then enter the city. His father, arriving at midday, would feed him, eat himself, spend the day conversing with him, and at evening, leaving guards behind, would enter the city. Thus, he lived without being secluded day and night. At that time, a Paccekabuddha named Ādiccabandhu was dwelling on the slopes of Mount Nandamūla. Reflecting, he saw him: “This young man was able to go forth but cannot cut off his fetters.” Then he reflected further: “Will he become disenchanted by his own nature or not?” Knowing that “one who becomes disenchanted by nature will take a very long time,” he thought, “I will give him an object of contemplation.” As previously described, he came from the Manosilā plateau and stood in the park. A royal servant saw him and reported to the king, “A Paccekabuddha has come, great king.” The king, thinking, “Now my son will live without discontent in the company of the Paccekabuddha,” joyfully attended to the Paccekabuddha with reverence. He requested him to stay right there, had a leaf hut and other dwelling places, walking paths, and everything else prepared, and settled him there.

So tattha vasanto ekadivasaṃ okāsaṃ labhitvā kumāraṃ pucchi “kosi tva”nti? So āha “ahaṃ pabbajito”ti. “Pabbajitā nāma na edisā hontī”ti. “Atha bhante, kīdisā honti, kiṃ mayhaṃ ananucchavika”nti vutte “tvaṃ attano ananucchavikaṃ na pekkhasi[V 1.0083], nanu te mātā vīsatisahassaitthīhi saddhiṃ pubbaṇhasamaye āgacchantī uyyānaṃ avivittaṃ karoti, pitā mahatā balakāyena sāyanhasamaye, jagganapurisā sakalarattiṃ; pabbajitā nāma tava sadisā na honti, ‘edisā pana hontī’”ti tatra ṭhitasseva iddhiyā himavante aññataraṃ vihāraṃ dassesi. So tattha paccekabuddhe ālambanabāhaṃ [P 1.0105] nissāya ṭhite ca caṅkamante ca rajanakammasūcikammādīni karonte ca disvā āha – “tumhe idha, nāgacchatha, pabbajjā nāma tumhehi anuññātā”ti. “Āma, pabbajjā anuññātā, pabbajitakālato paṭṭhāya samaṇā nāma attano nissaraṇaṃ kātuṃ icchitapatthitañca padesaṃ gantuṃ labhanti, ettakaṃva vaṭṭatī”ti vatvā ākāse ṭhatvā –

Living there, one day he found an opportunity and asked the prince, 'Who are you?' He replied, 'I am a renunciant.' 'Renunciants are not like this,' he said. 'Then, venerable sir, what are they like? What about me is unsuitable?' When this was said, he replied, 'Do you not see what is unsuitable about yourself? Does not your mother, coming to the garden in the morning with twenty thousand women, make it unsecluded? And your father with a large army in the evening, and the watchmen throughout the entire night? Renunciants are not like you; rather, they are like this.' Standing right there, he displayed through his psychic power a certain monastery in the Himalayas. Seeing the Paccekabuddhas there—some standing leaning on an armrest, some walking back and forth, and some doing tasks like dyeing robes and needlework—the prince said: 'You do not come here. Is this what is sanctioned as "renunciation"?' The Paccekabuddha replied: 'Yes, renunciation is sanctioned. From the time of renunciation, ascetics are permitted to bring about their own liberation and to go to any place they wish and desire. This much is proper.' Having said this, he stood in the air—

“Aṭṭhāna taṃ saṅgaṇikāratassa, yaṃ phassaye sāmayikaṃ vimutti”nti. –

“It is impossible for one who delights in company to experience temporary liberation.”

Imaṃ [M 1.0094] upaḍḍhagāthaṃ vatvā, dissamāneneva kāyena nandamūlakapabbhāraṃ agamāsi. Evaṃ gate paccekabuddhe so attano paṇṇasālaṃ pavisitvā nipajji. Ārakkhakapurisopi “sayito kumāro, idāni kuhiṃ gamissatī”ti pamatto niddaṃ okkami. So tassa pamattabhāvaṃ ñatvā pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā araññaṃ pāvisi. Tatra ca vivitto vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā, paccekabodhiṃ sacchikatvā, paccekabuddhaṭṭhānaṃ gato. Tatra ca “kathamadhigata”nti pucchito ādiccabandhunā vuttaṃ upaḍḍhagāthaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ katvā abhāsi.

Having spoken this half-verse, he went to the Nandamūlaka Slope in his visible form. When the Paccekabuddha had thus departed, he entered his leaf-hut and lay down. The guard, thinking, “The prince is asleep, where will he go now?” became negligent and fell asleep. Knowing his negligence, he took his bowl and robe and entered the forest. There, in seclusion, having undertaken insight meditation, he realized Paccekabodhi and went to the abode of the Paccekabuddhas. And there, when asked, “How was it attained?” he completed the half-verse spoken by Ādiccabandhu and recited it.

Tassattho – aṭṭhāna tanti. Aṭṭhānaṃ taṃ, akāraṇaṃ tanti vuttaṃ hoti, anunāsikalopo kato “ariyasaccāna dassana”ntiādīsu (khu. pā. 5.11; su. ni. 270) viya. Saṅgaṇikāratassāti gaṇābhiratassa. Yanti karaṇavacanametaṃ “yaṃ hirīyati hirīyitabbenā”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 30) viya. Phassayeti adhigacche. Sāmayikaṃ vimuttinti lokiyasamāpattiṃ. Sā hi appitappitasamaye eva paccanīkehi vimuccanato “sāmayikā vimuttī”ti vuccati. Taṃ sāmayikaṃ vimuttiṃ. Aṭṭhānaṃ taṃ, na taṃ kāraṇaṃ vijjati saṅgaṇikāratassa, yena kāraṇena phassayeti etaṃ ādiccabandhussa paccekabuddhassa vaco nisamma saṅgaṇikāratiṃ pahāya yoniso paṭipajjanto adhigatomhīti āha. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti.

Its meaning is as follows: Aṭṭhānaṃ taṃ. This means: That is not the right condition, that is not the cause. The elision of the nasal is made, as in such phrases as ariyasaccāna dassana. Saṅgaṇikāratassa means: for one who delights in company. Yaṃ is a word indicating reason, as in such phrases as yaṃ hirīyati hirīyitabbena. Phassaye means: one might attain. Sāmayikaṃ vimuttiṃ means: worldly attainment. For it is called ‘temporary liberation’ because one is liberated from opposing states only at the time of absorption. That temporary liberation—that is not the right condition, that cause does not exist for one who delights in company, by which cause one might attain it. Having reflected upon this word of the Paccekabuddha Ādiccabandhu, having abandoned delight in company and practicing rightly, I have attained—thus he says. The rest is as has been explained.

Aṭṭhānagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Aṭṭhāna verse is completed.

Dutiyo vaggo niṭṭhito.

The second chapter is finished.

55. Diṭṭhīvisūkānīti [P 1.0106][V 1.0084] kā uppatti? Bārāṇasiyaṃ kira aññataro rājā rahogato cintesi – “yathā sītādīnaṃ paṭighātakāni uṇhādīni atthi, atthi nu kho evaṃ vaṭṭapaṭighātakaṃ vinaṭṭaṃ, no”ti. So amacce pucchi – “vivaṭṭaṃ jānāthā”ti? Te “jānāma, mahārājā”ti āhaṃsu. Rājā – “kiṃ ta”nti? Tato “antavā loko”tiādinā nayena sassatucchedaṃ kathesuṃ. Atha rājā “ime na jānanti, sabbepime diṭṭhigatikā”ti sayameva tesaṃ vilomatañca ayuttatañca disvā “vaṭṭapaṭighātakaṃ vivaṭṭaṃ atthi, taṃ gavesitabba”nti cintetvā rajjaṃ pahāya pabbajitvā vipassanto paccekabodhiṃ sacchākāsi. Imañca udānagāthaṃ abhāsi paccekabuddhamajjhe byākaraṇagāthañca –

55. Regarding Diṭṭhivisūkāni: what is its origin? It is said that in Bārāṇasī a certain king, having gone into seclusion, reflected: ‘Just as there are counteragents for cold and so on, such as heat and so on, is there likewise that which counteracts the round of existence, an unrolling, or not?’ He asked his ministers: ‘Do you know of the unrolling?’ They replied: ‘We know, great king.’ The king asked: ‘What is it?’ Then, in the manner beginning with ‘the world is finite,’ they spoke of eternalism and annihilationism. Then the king, thinking, ‘These do not know; all of them are adherents of wrong views,’ and seeing for himself their perversity and irrationality, reflected: ‘There is that which counteracts the round of existence, an unrolling; it must be sought.’ Having renounced his kingdom and gone forth, while developing insight he realized Paccekabodhi. And he uttered this inspired utterance and a verse of declaration in the midst of the Paccekabuddhas:

“Diṭṭhīvisūkāni [M 1.0095] upātivatto, patto niyāmaṃ paṭiladdhamaggo;

Uppannañāṇomhi anaññaneyyo, eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”ti.

“Having transcended the darts of views, having reached the fixed order, attained the path; arisen is knowledge, not to be led by others, let one wander alone like a rhinoceros.”

Tassattho – diṭṭhīvisūkānīti dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhigatāni. Tāni hi maggasammādiṭṭhiyā visūkaṭṭhena vijjhanaṭṭhena vilomaṭṭhena ca visūkāni. Evaṃ diṭṭhiyā visūkāni, diṭṭhi eva vā visūkāni diṭṭhivisūkāni. Upātivattoti dassanamaggena atikkanto. Patto niyāmanti avinipātadhammatāya sambodhiparāyaṇatāya ca niyatabhāvaṃ adhigato, sammattaniyāmasaṅkhātaṃ vā paṭhamamagganti. Ettāvatā paṭhamamaggakiccanipphatti ca tassa paṭilābho ca vutto. Idāni paṭiladdhamaggoti iminā sesamaggapaṭilābhaṃ dasseti. Uppannañāṇomhīti uppannapaccekabodhiñāṇo amhi. Etena phalaṃ dasseti. Anaññaneyyoti aññehi “idaṃ saccaṃ, idaṃ sacca”nti na netabbo. Etena sayambhutaṃ dīpeti, patte vā paccekabodhiñāṇe aneyyatāya abhāvā sayaṃvasitaṃ. Samathavipassanāya vā diṭṭhivisūkāni upātivatto, ādimaggena patto niyāmaṃ, sesehi [P 1.0107] paṭiladdhamaggo, phalañāṇena uppannañāṇo, taṃ sabbaṃ attanāva adhigatoti anaññaneyyo. Sesaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbanti.

The meaning is this: Diṭṭhivisūkāni refers to the sixty-two bases of wrong view. For they are visūka (barbs) in relation to the right view of the path, in the sense of piercing and in the sense of being contrary. Thus, they are the barbs of view, or the views themselves are barbs; hence diṭṭhivisūkāni. Upātivatto means: he has transcended by the path of vision. Patto niyāmaṃ means: he has attained the state of certainty by being of a nature not to fall into a lower state and by having enlightenment as his destination; or, he has attained the first path, known as the rightly-fixed course. By this much, the accomplishment of the function of the first path and its attainment are stated. Now, by paṭiladdhamaggo, he shows the attainment of the remaining paths. Uppannañāṇomhi means: I am one in whom the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha has arisen. By this, he shows the fruition. Anaññaneyyo means: not to be led by others saying, ‘This is the truth, this is the truth.’ By this, he indicates that he is self-originating. Alternatively: by serenity and insight he has transcended the barbs of views; by the initial path he has reached the fixed course; by the remaining paths he has attained the path; by the knowledge of fruition he is one in whom knowledge has arisen; all this he has attained by himself, and therefore he is anaññaneyyo. The rest should be understood in the manner already stated.

Diṭṭhivisūkagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Diṭṭhivisūka verse is completed.

56. Nillolupoti kā uppatti? Bārāṇasirañño kira sūdo antarabhattaṃ pacitvā upanāmesi manuññadassanaṃ sādurasaṃ “appeva nāma me rājā dhanamanuppadeyyā”ti. Taṃ rañño gandheneva bhottukāmataṃ janesi mukhe kheḷaṃ uppādentaṃ. Paṭhamakabaḷe pana mukhe pakkhittamatte sattarasaharaṇisahassāni amateneva phuṭṭhāni ahesuṃ. Sūdo “idāni me dassati, idāni me dassatī”ti [V 1.0085] cintesi. Rājāpi “sakkārāraho sūdo”ti cintesi – “rasaṃ sāyitvā pana sakkarontaṃ maṃ pāpako kittisaddo abbhuggaccheyya – ‘lolo ayaṃ rājā rasagaruko’”ti na kiñci abhaṇi. Evaṃ yāva bhojanapariyosānaṃ, tāva sūdopi “idāni dassati, idāni dassatī”ti cintesi. Rājāpi avaṇṇabhayena na kiñci abhaṇi. Tato [M 1.0096] sūdo “natthi imassa rañño jivhāviññāṇa”nti dutiyadivase arasabhattaṃ upanāmesi. Rājā bhuñjanto “niggahāraho ajja sūdo”ti jānantopi pubbe viya paccavekkhitvā avaṇṇabhayena na kiñci abhaṇi. Tato sūdo “rājā neva sundaraṃ nāsundaraṃ jānātī”ti cintetvā sabbaṃ paribbayaṃ attanā gahetvā yaṃkiñcideva pacitvā rañño deti. Rājā “aho vata lobho, ahaṃ nāma vīsati nagarasahassāni bhuñjanto imassa lobhena bhattamattampi na labhāmī”ti nibbijjitvā, rajjaṃ pahāya pabbajitvā, vipassanto paccekabodhiṃ sacchākāsi, purimanayeneva ca imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi –

56. What is the origin of 'Not Greedy'? It is said that the cook of the king of Bārāṇasī, having prepared a midday meal, presented it—pleasing to the eye and delicious in taste—thinking, 'Perhaps the king will bestow wealth upon me.' By its aroma alone, it aroused the king's desire to eat, causing saliva to form in his mouth. As soon as the first morsel was placed in his mouth, seven thousand taste-conducting nerves were touched as if with nectar. The cook thought, 'Now he will give to me, now he will give to me.' The king also thought, 'The cook is worthy of honor,' but thinking, 'If I were to honor him after tasting the flavor, a bad reputation would arise about me: “This king is greedy; he gives importance to taste,”' he said nothing. Thus, until the meal was finished, the cook kept thinking, 'Now he will give, now he will give.' The king, too, fearing blame, said nothing. Then the cook, thinking, 'This king has no sense of taste,' served a tasteless meal on the second day. The king, while eating, though knowing, 'Today the cook deserves punishment,' reflected as before and, fearing blame, said nothing. Then the cook, thinking, 'The king knows neither what is good nor what is not good,' took all the provisions for himself, cooked whatever he pleased, and gave it to the king. The king, becoming disenchanted, thought, 'Alas, what greed! I, who enjoy the revenue of twenty thousand cities, do not receive even a proper meal because of this man's greed!' Disenchanted, he renounced his kingdom, went forth, and while developing insight, realized individual enlightenment. Then, in the same manner as before, he spoke this verse:

“Nillolupo nikkuho nippipāso, nimmakkho niddhantakasāvamoho;

Nirāsayo sabbaloke bhavitvā, eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”ti.

“Free from greed, without deceit, thirstless, without disparagement, with delusion’s stain washed away; having become without longing in the whole world, one should wander alone like a rhinoceros.”

Tattha nillolupoti alolupo. Yo hi rasataṇhābhibhūto hoti, so bhusaṃ luppati punappunañca luppati, tena lolupoti vuccati. Tasmā esa taṃ paṭikkhipanto āha “nillolupo”ti. Nikkuhoti ettha kiñcāpi yassa tividhaṃ kuhanavatthu natthi, so nikkuhoti vuccati. Imissā pana gāthāya manuññabhojanādīsu vimhayamanāpajjanato nikkuhoti ayamadhippāyo[P 1.0108]. Nippipāsoti ettha pātumicchā pipāsā, tassā abhāvena nippipāso, sādurasalobhena bhottukamyatāvirahitoti attho. Nimmakkhoti ettha paraguṇavināsanalakkhaṇo makkho, tassa abhāvena nimmakkho. Attano gahaṭṭhakāle sūdassa guṇamakkhanābhāvaṃ sandhāyāha. Niddhantakasāvamohoti ettha rāgādayo tayo, kāyaduccaritādīni ca tīṇīti cha dhammā yathāsambhavaṃ appasannaṭṭhena sakabhāvaṃ vijahāpetvā parabhāvaṃ gaṇhāpanaṭṭhena kasaṭaṭṭhena ca kasāvāti veditabbā. Yathāha –

Therein, 'not greedy' means uncovetous. For one who is overcome by craving for flavors is greatly agitated and repeatedly agitated; thus he is called 'greedy.' Therefore, rejecting that, he said, 'not greedy.' Herein, regarding 'without deceit': although one for whom the threefold ground of deceit does not exist is called 'without deceit,' in this verse the intended meaning is being without the pretense of being amazed or delighted by pleasing food and so on. Herein, regarding 'thirstless': the desire to drink is thirst; due to its absence, one is 'thirstless.' The meaning is being free from the desire to eat out of greed for tasty flavors. Herein, regarding 'without disparagement': disparagement has the characteristic of destroying the virtues of others; due to its absence, one is 'without disparagement.' This is said with reference to the absence of disparaging the cook's virtues during his time as a householder. Herein, regarding 'with delusion's stain washed away': the three things beginning with lust, and the three things beginning with bodily misconduct—these six things, as may be the case, are to be known as 'stains' in the sense of being impure, in the sense of causing one to abandon one's own nature and adopt another's, and in the sense of being dregs. As it is said:

“Tattha, katame tayo kasāvā? Rāgakasāvo, dosakasāvo, mohakasāvo, ime tayo kasāvā. Tattha, katame aparepi tayo kasāvā? Kāyakasāvo, vacīkasāvo, manokasāvo”ti (vibha. 924).

“Herein, what are the three stains? The stain of lust, the stain of hate, the stain of delusion—these are the three stains. Herein, what are the other three stains? The bodily stain, the verbal stain, the mental stain.”

Tesu [M 1.0097][V 1.0086] mohaṃ ṭhapetvā pañcannaṃ kasāvānaṃ tesañca sabbesaṃ mūlabhūtassa mohassa niddhantattā niddhantakasāvamoho, tiṇṇaṃ eva vā kāyavacīmanokasāvānaṃ mohassa ca niddhantattā niddhantakasāvamoho. Itaresu nillolupatādīhi rāgakasāvassa, nimmakkhatāya dosakasāvassa niddhantabhāvo siddho eva. Nirāsayoti nittaṇho. Sabbaloketi sakalaloke, tīsu bhavesu dvādasasu vā āyatanesu bhavavibhavataṇhāvirahito hutvāti attho. Sesaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Atha vā tayopi pāde vatvā eko careti eko carituṃ sakkuṇeyyāti evampi ettha sambandho kātabboti.

Among these, one is called 'with delusion's stain washed away' because the five stains—setting aside delusion—and delusion itself, which is the root of all of them, have been washed away. Or, one is called 'with delusion's stain washed away' because the three stains of body, speech, and mind, and delusion, have been washed away. Among the other terms, the washing away of the stain of lust is established by 'not being greedy' and so on, and the washing away of the stain of hate is established by 'not being disparaging.' 'Without longing' means without craving. 'In the whole world' means in the entire world; that is, having become free from craving for existence and for non-existence in the three planes of existence or in the twelve sense bases—this is the meaning. The rest should be understood in the manner already stated. Alternatively, a connection can also be made here in this way: having stated the three lines, 'one should wander alone' implies 'one would be able to wander alone.'

Nillolupagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the 'Not Greedy' verse is concluded.

57. Pāpaṃ sahāyanti kā uppatti? Bārāṇasiyaṃ kira aññataro rājā mahaccarājānubhāvena nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ karonto manusse koṭṭhāgārato purāṇadhaññāni bahiddhā nīharante disvā “kiṃ, bhaṇe, ida”nti amacce pucchi. “Idāni, mahārāja, navadhaññāni uppajjissanti, tesaṃ okāsaṃ kātuṃ ime manussā purāṇadhaññādīni chaḍḍentī”ti. Rājā – “kiṃ, bhaṇe, itthāgārabalakāyādīnaṃ vaṭṭaṃ paripuṇṇa”nti[P 1.0109]? “Āma, mahārāja, paripuṇṇanti”. “Tena hi, bhaṇe, dānasālaṃ kārāpetha, dānaṃ dassāmi, mā imāni dhaññāni anupakārāni vinassiṃsū”ti. Tato naṃ aññataro diṭṭhigatiko amacco “mahārāja, natthi dinna”nti ārabbha yāva “bālā ca paṇḍitā ca sandhāvitvā saṃsaritvā dukkhassantaṃ karissantī”ti vatvā nivāresi. So dutiyampi tatiyampi koṭṭhāgāre vilumpante disvā tatheva āṇāpesi. Tatiyampi naṃ “mahārāja, dattupaññattaṃ yadidaṃ dāna”ntiādīni vatvā nivāresi. So “are, ahaṃ attano santakampi na labhāmi dātuṃ, kiṃ me imehi pāpasahāyehī”ti nibbinno rajjaṃ pahāya pabbajitvā vipassanto paccekabodhiṃ sacchākāsi. Tañca pāpaṃ sahāyaṃ garahanto imaṃ udānagāthaṃ abhāsi –

57. What is the origin of 'an evil companion'? It is said that in Bārāṇasī, a certain king, while circumambulating the city with great royal majesty, saw people removing old grains from the granary. He asked his ministers, 'Sirs, what is this?' They replied, 'Great king, new grains will soon be harvested. To make room for them, these people are discarding the old grains and so on.' The king asked, 'Sirs, are the provisions for the women's quarters, the army, and so on, complete?' 'Yes, great king, they are complete.' 'In that case, sirs, have a hall for giving built. I will give alms. Let not these grains perish without being of use.' Then a certain minister who held wrong views restrained him, saying, 'Great king, there is no fruit of giving,' and so on, up to, 'Both fools and the wise, having transmigrated and wandered on, will make an end of suffering.' A second and a third time, seeing the granaries being emptied, he gave the same order. And for a third time, the minister restrained him, saying things like, 'Great king, this so-called giving is merely a convention.' Disgusted, the king thought, 'Indeed, I am not able to give even what is my own. What use are these evil companions to me?' Becoming disenchanted, he renounced the kingdom and went forth. Developing insight, he realized individual enlightenment. And, censuring that evil companion, he uttered this inspired verse:

“Pāpaṃ sahāyaṃ parivajjayetha, anatthadassiṃ visame niviṭṭhaṃ;

Sayaṃ na seve pasutaṃ pamattaṃ, eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”ti.

One should avoid an evil companion, one who sees what is unbeneficial, established in what is wrong. One should not personally associate with one who is attached and heedless; one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.

Tassāyaṃ [M 1.0098] saṅkhepattho – yvāyaṃ dasavatthukāya pāpadiṭṭhiyā samannāgatattā pāpo, paresampi anatthaṃ passatīti anatthadassī, kāyaduccaritādimhi ca visame niviṭṭho, taṃ atthakāmo kulaputto pāpaṃ sahāyaṃ parivajjayetha anatthadassiṃ visame niviṭṭhaṃ. Sayaṃ na seveti attano vasena na seve. Yadi pana paravaso hoti, kiṃ sakkā kātunti vuttaṃ hoti. Pasutanti pasaṭaṃ[V 1.0087], diṭṭhivasena tattha tattha lagganti attho. Pamattanti kāmaguṇesu vossaṭṭhacittaṃ, kusalabhāvanārahitaṃ vā. Taṃ evarūpaṃ na seve, na bhaje, na payirupāse, aññadatthu eko care khaggavisāṇakappoti.

This is its concise meaning: Whosoever, being endowed with the tenfold wrong view, is evil; and because he sees what is unbeneficial for others, he is called 'one who sees what is unbeneficial'; and he is established in what is wrong, such as bodily misconduct. A clansman who desires his own welfare should avoid such an evil companion, one who sees what is unbeneficial, one established in what is wrong. 'One should not personally associate' means one should not associate of one's own accord. But if one is under another's control, what can be done? Thus it is said. 'Attached' means clinging here and there by way of their views. 'Heedless' means one whose mind is given over to sensual pleasures, or one who is devoid of the development of what is wholesome. One should not associate with, serve, or attend upon such a person; on the contrary, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.

Pāpasahāyagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the verse concerning the evil companion is concluded.

58. Bahussutanti kā uppatti? Pubbe kira kassapassa bhagavato sāsane aṭṭha paccekabodhisattā pabbajitvā gatapaccāgatavattaṃ pūretvā devaloke uppannāti sabbaṃ anavajjabhojīgāthāya vuttasadisameva. Ayaṃ pana viseso – paccekabuddhe nisīdāpetvā rājā āha “ke tumhe”ti? Te āhaṃsu – “mayaṃ, mahārāja, bahussutā nāmā”ti. Rājā [P 1.0110] – “ahaṃ sutabrahmadatto nāma, sutena tittiṃ na gacchāmi, handa, nesaṃ santike vicitranayaṃ saddhammadesanaṃ sossāmī”ti attamano dakkhiṇodakaṃ datvā, parivisitvā, bhattakiccapariyosāne saṅghattherassa pattaṃ gahetvā, vanditvā, purato nisīdi “dhammakathaṃ, bhante, karothā”ti. So “sukhito hotu, mahārāja, rāgakkhayo hotū”ti vatvā uṭṭhito. Rājā “ayaṃ na bahussuto, dutiyo bahussuto bhavissati, sve dāni vicitradhammadesanaṃ sossāmī”ti svātanāya nimantesi. Evaṃ yāva sabbesaṃ paṭipāṭi gacchati, tāva nimantesi. Te sabbepi “dosakkhayo hotu, mohakkhayo, gatikkhayo, vaṭṭakkhayo, upadhikkhayo, taṇhakkhayo hotū”ti evaṃ ekekaṃ padaṃ visesetvā sesaṃ paṭhamasadisameva vatvā uṭṭhahiṃsu.

58. Regarding 'the very learned': what is its origin? It is said that formerly, in the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, eight Paccekabodhisattas went forth, and having fulfilled the duty of going and returning, they arose in the world of the devas—all this is just as was said in the verse on blameless food. This, however, is the distinction: Having had the Paccekabuddhas take their seats, the king said, 'Who are you?' They replied, 'Mahārāja, we are called the Very Learned.' The king said, 'I am named Sutabrahmadatta, and I do not find satisfaction through learning. Come now, I shall hear a teaching on the true Dhamma of varied method from them.' Being pleased, he gave the dedicatory water, served them, and at the conclusion of the meal, he took the bowl of the elder of the Sangha, paid homage, and sat down before him, saying, 'Venerable sir, please give a talk on the Dhamma.' The elder, having said, 'May you be happy, Mahārāja; may there be a destruction of lust,' arose. The king thought, 'This one is not very learned; the second one will be very learned. Tomorrow I shall hear a Dhamma teaching of varied method,' and so he invited them for the next day. In this way, he went to all of them in succession and invited them. All of them, making each word distinct, said, 'May there be a destruction of hatred; a destruction of delusion; a destruction of destinations; a destruction of the round of existence; a destruction of the substrata of existence,' and having said the rest just as the first had, they arose.

Tato rājā “ime ‘bahussutā maya’nti bhaṇanti, na ca tesaṃ vicitrakathā, kimetehi vutta”nti tesaṃ vacanatthaṃ upaparikkhitumāraddho. Atha “rāgakkhayo hotū”ti upaparikkhanto “rāge khīṇe dosopi mohopi [M 1.0099] aññataraññatarepi kilesā khīṇā hontī”ti ñatvā attamano ahosi – “nippariyāyabahussutā ime samaṇā. Yathā hi purisena mahāpathaviṃ vā ākāsaṃ vā aṅguliyā niddisantena na aṅgulimattova padeso niddiṭṭho hoti, apica, kho, pana pathavīākāsā eva niddiṭṭhā honti, evaṃ imehi ekamekaṃ atthaṃ niddisantehi aparimāṇā atthā niddiṭṭhā hontī”ti. Tato so “kudāssu nāmāhampi evaṃ bahussuto bhavissāmī”ti tathārūpaṃ bahussutabhāvaṃ patthento rajjaṃ pahāya pabbajitvā, vipassanto paccekabodhiṃ sacchikatvā, imaṃ udānagāthaṃ abhāsi –

Then the king began to examine the meaning of their words, thinking, 'These men say, "We are very learned," yet their talk is not varied. What have they said?' Then, while examining the phrase, 'May there be a destruction of lust,' he understood, 'When lust is destroyed, hatred and delusion, and also the various other defilements, are destroyed.' Realizing this, he was pleased and thought: 'These ascetics are directly and truly very learned. For it is as when a man, pointing with his finger to the great earth or to the sky, does not point out a region merely the size of his finger, but rather the earth and the sky themselves are pointed out. In the same way, by these ascetics pointing out a single meaning, immeasurable meanings are pointed out.' Then, aspiring to such a state of great learning, he thought, 'When, indeed, shall I also become so learned?' Renouncing his kingdom, he went forth, and while developing insight, he realized the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha and uttered this inspired verse:

“Bahussutaṃ dhammadharaṃ bhajetha, mittaṃ uḷāraṃ paṭibhānavantaṃ;

Aññāya atthāni vineyya kaṅkhaṃ, eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”ti.

One should associate with a friend who is very learned, an upholder of the Dhamma, noble and endowed with ready wit. Having understood the benefits and dispelled doubt, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.

Tatthāyaṃ [V 1.0088] saṅkhepattho – bahussutanti duvidho bahussuto tīsu piṭakesu atthato nikhilo pariyattibahussuto ca, maggaphalavijjābhiññānaṃ paṭividdhattā paṭivedhabahussuto ca. Āgatāgamo dhammadharo. Uḷārehi pana kāyavacīmanokammehi samannāgato uḷāro. Yuttapaṭibhāno ca muttapaṭibhāno [P 1.0111] ca yuttamuttapaṭibhāno ca paṭibhānavā. Pariyattiparipucchādhigamavasena vā tidhā paṭibhānavā veditabbo. Yassa hi pariyatti paṭibhāti, so pariyattipaṭibhānavā. Yassa atthañca ñāṇañca lakkhaṇañca ṭhānāṭṭhānañca paripucchantassa paripucchā paṭibhāti, so paripucchāpaṭibhānavā. Yena maggādayo paṭividdhā honti, so adhigamapaṭibhānavā. Taṃ evarūpaṃ bahussutaṃ dhammadharaṃ bhajetha mittaṃ uḷāraṃ paṭibhānavantaṃ. Tato tassānubhāvena attatthaparatthaubhayatthabhedato vā diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaparamatthabhedato vā anekappakārāni aññāya atthāni. Tato – “ahosiṃ nu kho ahaṃ atītamaddhāna”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.18; saṃ. ni. 2.20) kaṅkhaṭṭhānesu vineyya kaṅkhaṃ, vicikicchaṃ vinetvā vināsetvā evaṃ katasabbakicco eko care khaggavisāṇakappoti.

Herein, this is the concise meaning: 'Very learned'—one who is very learned is twofold: one very learned in the scriptures, who is complete in the meaning of the three Piṭakas; and one very learned in penetration, due to having penetrated the paths, fruits, true knowledges, and supernormal powers. One who has mastered the transmitted scriptures is a 'bearer of the Dhamma.' One endowed with noble bodily, verbal, and mental actions is 'noble.' One endowed with ready wit has wit that is appropriate, wit that is spontaneous, and wit that is both appropriate and spontaneous. Or, one endowed with ready wit should be understood as threefold, by way of scriptures, questioning, and attainment. For one to whom the scriptures are clear is one with wit regarding the scriptures. One to whom, when questioned, the meaning and the reason become clear, is one with wit regarding questioning. One by whom the paths and so on have been penetrated is one with wit regarding attainment. One should associate with such a friend who is very learned, a bearer of the Dhamma, noble, and endowed with ready wit. Then, through that one's power, having understood the many kinds of benefits—classified as for one's own welfare, for the welfare of others, and for the welfare of both; or classified as pertaining to the present life, to the future life, and to the ultimate goal—and then, in matters of doubt such as, 'Did I exist in the past?', having dispelled doubt, having removed and destroyed perplexity, and having thus completed all that was to be done, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.

Bahussutagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the verse concerning the very learned is concluded.

59. Khiḍḍaṃ [M 1.0100] ratinti kā uppatti? Bārāṇasiyaṃ vibhūsakabrahmadatto nāma rājā pātova yāguṃ vā bhattaṃ vā bhuñjitvā nānāvidhavibhūsanehi attānaṃ vibhūsāpetvā mahāādāse sakalasarīraṃ disvā yaṃ na icchati taṃ apanetvā aññena vibhūsanena vibhūsāpeti. Tassa ekadivasaṃ evaṃ karoto bhattavelā majjhanhikasamayo patto. Atha avibhūsitova dussapaṭṭena sīsaṃ veṭhetvā, bhuñjitvā, divāseyyaṃ upagacchi. Punapi uṭṭhahitvā tatheva karoto sūriyo atthaṅgato. Evaṃ dutiyadivasepi tatiyadivasepi. Athassa evaṃ maṇḍanappasutassa piṭṭhirogo udapādi. Tassetadahosi – “aho re, ahaṃ sabbathāmena vibhūsantopi imasmiṃ kappake vibhūsane asantuṭṭho lobhaṃ uppādesiṃ. Lobho ca nāmesa apāyagamanīyo dhammo, handāhaṃ, lobhaṃ niggaṇhāmī”ti rajjaṃ pahāya pabbajitvā vipassanto paccekabodhiṃ sacchikatvā imaṃ udānagāthaṃ abhāsi –

59. What is the origin of the verse beginning, 'Khiḍḍaṃ ratiṃ'? In Bārāṇasī, it is said, there was a king named Vibhūsaka Brahmadatta. Early in the morning, after eating rice gruel or a meal, he would have himself adorned with various ornaments. Seeing his whole body in a large mirror, he would have what he did not like removed and have himself adorned with other ornaments. One day, while he was doing so, the time for the midday meal arrived. Then, still unadorned, he wrapped his head with a cloth strip, ate, and went to his day-rest. Rising again, he continued in the same way until the sun set. The same happened on the second day and on the third day. Then, as he was thus intent on adornment, a backache arose in him. It occurred to him: 'Alas, though I am having myself adorned with all my might, I am dissatisfied with this trifling adornment and have given rise to greed. And this thing called greed is a state that leads to the lower realms. Come now, I shall restrain greed!' Having abandoned the kingdom, he went forth and, practicing insight, realized the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha and uttered this inspired utterance:

“Khiḍḍaṃ ratiṃ kāmasukhañca loke, analaṅkaritvā anapekkhamāno;

Vibhūsanaṭṭhānā virato saccavādī, eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”ti.

Not adorning play, delight, and sensual pleasure in the world, being unconcerned; having abstained from the occasion for adornment, a speaker of truth, one should wander alone like a rhinoceros.

Tattha [P 1.0112] khiḍḍā ca rati ca pubbe vuttāva. Kāmasukhanti vatthukāmasukhaṃ. Vatthukāmāpi hi sukhassa visayādibhāvena sukhanti vuccanti. Yathāha – “atthi rūpaṃ sukhaṃ sukhānupatita”nti (saṃ. ni. 3.60). Evametaṃ [V 1.0089] khiḍḍaṃ ratiṃ kāmasukhañca imasmiṃ okāsaloke analaṅkaritvā alanti akatvā, etaṃ tappakanti vā sārabhūtanti vā evaṃ aggahetvā. Anapekkhamānoti tena alaṅkaraṇena anapekkhaṇasīlo, apihāluko, nittaṇho, vibhūsanaṭṭhānā virato saccavādī eko careti. Tattha vibhūsā duvidhā – agārikavibhūsā, anagārikavibhūsā ca. Tattha agārikavibhūsā sāṭakaveṭhanamālāgandhādi, anagārikavibhūsā pattamaṇḍanādi. Vibhūsā eva vibhūsanaṭṭhānaṃ. Tasmā vibhūsanaṭṭhānā tividhāya viratiyā virato. Avitathavacanato saccavādīti evamattho daṭṭhabbo.

Herein, 'play' (khiḍḍā) and 'delight' (rati) are as stated before. By 'sensual pleasure' (kāmasukha) is meant pleasure related to sensual objects (vatthukāmasukha). For sensual objects themselves are called 'pleasure' because they are the objective basis of pleasure. As it is said: 'There is form that is pleasant, accompanied by pleasure.' Thus, 'not adorning' these—play, delight, and sensual pleasure—in this physical world, means not considering them sufficient, or not grasping them as being of that nature or as being essential. By 'being unconcerned' (anapekkhamāno) is meant one whose nature is to be unconcerned with such adornment, not covetous, free from thirst. 'Having abstained from the occasion for adornment, a speaker of truth, one should wander alone.' Here, adornment (vibhūsā) is twofold: the householder's adornment and the homeless one's adornment. The householder's adornment consists of garments, head-wraps, garlands, perfumes, and so forth; the homeless one's adornment consists of decorating the bowl, and so forth. Adornment itself is the 'occasion for adornment'. Therefore, one has abstained from the occasion for adornment by means of the threefold abstinence. Because of speaking what is not untrue, one is a 'speaker of truth'—thus the meaning should be understood.

Vibhūsanaṭṭhānagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the verse concerning the occasion for adornment is concluded.

60. Puttañca [M 1.0101] dāranti kā uppatti? Bārāṇasirañño kira putto daharakāle eva abhisitto rajjaṃ kāresi. So paṭhamagāthāya vuttapaccekabodhisatto viya rajjasirimanubhavanto ekadivasaṃ cintesi – “ahaṃ rajjaṃ kārento bahūnaṃ dukkhaṃ karomi. Kiṃ me ekabhattatthāya iminā pāpena, handa sukhamuppādemī”ti rajjaṃ pahāya pabbajitvā vipassanto paccekabodhiṃ sacchikatvā imaṃ udānagāthaṃ abhāsi –

60. What is the origin of the verse beginning, 'Puttañca dāraṃ'? It is said that the son of the king of Bārāṇasī was anointed while still young and ruled the kingdom. While enjoying the splendor of kingship, like the Paccekabodhisatta mentioned in the first verse, one day he thought: 'By ruling the kingdom, I cause suffering to many. What use to me is this evil for the sake of a single meal? Come now, I shall bring about happiness!' Having abandoned the kingdom, he went forth and, practicing insight, realized the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha and uttered this inspired utterance:

“Puttañca dāraṃ pitarañca mātaraṃ, dhanāni dhaññāni ca bandhavāni;

Hitvāna kāmāni yathodhikāni, eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”ti.

Having abandoned son and wife, father and mother, wealth, grain, and kinsmen; having abandoned sensual pleasures in their various spheres, one should wander alone like a rhinoceros.

Tattha dhanānīti muttāmaṇiveḷuriyasaṅkhasilāpavāḷarajatajātarūpādīni ratanāni. Dhaññānīti sālivīhiyavagodhumakaṅkuvarakakudrūsakapabhedāni satta sesāparaṇṇāni ca. Bandhavānīti ñātibandhugottabandhumittabandhusippabandhuvasena [P 1.0113] catubbidhe bandhave. Yathodhikānīti sakasakaodhivasena ṭhitāneva. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti.

Herein, 'wealth' (dhanāni) means gems such as pearls, jewels, beryl, conch-shells, crystal, coral, silver, gold, and so forth. 'Grains' (dhaññāni) means the seven kinds of grain—such as fine rice, paddy, barley, wheat, common millet, panic grass, and kudrūsaka—and other remaining pulses. 'Kinsmen' (bandhavāni) means the four kinds of relations: relations by blood, relations by clan, relations by friendship, and relations by craft. 'In their various spheres' (yathodhikāni) means just as they are established according to their respective limits. The rest is as has been explained.

Puttadāragāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the verse concerning son and wife is concluded.

61. Saṅgo esoti kā uppatti? Bārāṇasiyaṃ kira pādalolabrahmadatto nāma rājā ahosi. So pātova yāguṃ vā bhattaṃ vā bhuñjitvā tīsu pāsādesu tividhanāṭakāni passati. Tividhanāṭakānīti kira pubbarājato āgataṃ, anantararājato āgataṃ, attano kāle uṭṭhitanti. So ekadivasaṃ pātova daharanāṭakapāsādaṃ gato. Tā nāṭakitthiyo “rājānaṃ [V 1.0090] ramāpessāmā”ti sakkassa devānamindassa accharāyo viya atimanoharaṃ naccagītavāditaṃ payojesuṃ. Rājā – “anacchariyametaṃ daharāna”nti asantuṭṭho hutvā majjhimanāṭakapāsādaṃ gato. Tāpi nāṭakitthiyo tatheva akaṃsu. So tatthāpi tatheva asantuṭṭho hutvā mahānāṭakapāsādaṃ gato. Tāpi nāṭakitthiyo tatheva akaṃsu. Rājā dve tayo rājaparivaṭṭe atītānaṃ tāsaṃ mahallakabhāvena aṭṭhikīḷanasadisaṃ naccaṃ disvā gītañca amadhuraṃ sutvā punadeva daharanāṭakapāsādaṃ, puna majjhimanāṭakapāsādanti evaṃ vicaritvā katthaci asantuṭṭho cintesi – “imā nāṭakitthiyo sakkaṃ [M 1.0102] devānamindaṃ accharāyo viya maṃ ramāpetukāmā sabbathāmena naccagītavāditaṃ payojesuṃ, svāhaṃ katthaci asantuṭṭho lobhameva vaḍḍhemi, lobho ca nāmesa apāyagamanīyo dhammo, handāhaṃ lobhaṃ niggaṇhāmī”ti rajjaṃ pahāya pabbajitvā vipassanto paccekabodhiṃ sacchikatvā imaṃ udānagāthaṃ abhāsi –

61. What is the origin of the verse beginning, 'Saṅgo eso'? In Bārāṇasī, it is said, there was a king named Pādalola Brahmadatta. Early in the morning, after eating rice gruel or a meal, he would watch three kinds of theatrical troupes in three palaces. The three kinds of troupes, it is said, were those inherited from a former king, those from the immediately preceding king, and those established in his own time. One day, early in the morning, he went to the palace of the young performers. Those actresses, thinking, 'We will delight the king,' put on an exceedingly charming performance of dance, song, and music, like the nymphs of Sakka, lord of the devas. The king, thinking, 'This is nothing extraordinary for the young,' was dissatisfied and went to the palace of the middle-aged performers. Those actresses also performed in the same way. Still dissatisfied there, he went to the palace of the elderly performers. Those actresses also performed in the same way. The king, seeing that their dance, on account of their old age and having passed through two or three reigns, resembled a play of skeletons, and hearing their unmelodious songs, went back again to the palace of the young performers, and then again to the palace of the middle-aged performers. Wandering about in this way and dissatisfied everywhere, he thought: 'These actresses, wishing to delight me like the nymphs of Sakka, performed their dance, song, and music with all their might, yet I am dissatisfied everywhere and only increase my greed. And this thing called greed is a state that leads to the lower realms. Come now, I shall restrain greed!' Having abandoned the kingdom, he went forth and, practicing insight, realized the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha and uttered this inspired utterance:

“Saṅgo eso parittamettha sokhyaṃ, appassādo dukkhamettha bhiyyo;

Gaḷo eso iti ñatvā matimā, eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”ti.

This is an attachment; little is the happiness here, scant the gratification, and the suffering is greater. Knowing this to be a fish-hook, the wise one should wander alone like a rhinoceros.

Tassattho – saṅgo esoti attano upabhogaṃ niddisati. So hi sajjanti tattha pāṇino kaddame paviṭṭho hatthī viyāti saṅgo. Parittamettha sokhyanti ettha pañcakāmaguṇūpabhogakāle viparītasaññāya uppādetabbato kāmāvacaradhammapariyāpannato vā lāmakaṭṭhena sokhyaṃ parittaṃ, vijjuppabhāya obhāsitanaccadassanasukhaṃ viya ittaraṃ[P 1.0114], tāvakālikanti vuttaṃ hoti. Appassādo dukkhamettha bhiyyoti ettha ca yvāyaṃ “yaṃ kho, bhikkhave, ime pañca kāmaguṇe paṭicca uppajjati sukhaṃ somanassaṃ, ayaṃ kāmānaṃ assādo”ti (ma. ni. 1.166) vutto. So yadidaṃ “ko ca, bhikkhave, kāmānaṃ ādīnavo? Idha, bhikkhave, kulaputto yena sippaṭṭhānena jīvikaṃ kappeti, yadi muddāya, yadi gaṇanāyā”ti evamādinā (ma. ni. 1.167) nayenettha dukkhaṃ vuttaṃ. Taṃ upanidhāya appo udakabindumatto hoti. Atha kho dukkhameva bhiyyo bahu, catūsu samuddesu udakasadisaṃ hoti. Tena vuttaṃ “appassādo dukkhamettha bhiyyo”ti. Gaḷo esoti assādaṃ dassetvā ākaḍḍhanavasena baḷiso viya eso yadidaṃ pañca kāmaguṇā. Iti ñatvā matimāti evaṃ ñatvā buddhimā paṇḍito puriso sabbampetaṃ pahāya eko care khaggavisāṇakappoti.

The meaning is this: 'This is an attachment' refers to one's own enjoyment. For beings are attached thereto, like an elephant that has entered mud—thus it is an attachment. 'Little happiness is here' means that the happiness here is limited in the sense of being inferior, either because it must be produced by distorted perception while enjoying the five strands of sensual pleasure, or because it is included among the phenomena of the sensual sphere; it is momentary, like the fleeting pleasure of seeing a dance illuminated by a flash of lightning—this is what is meant. 'Scant is the gratification; more suffering is here': And here, the gratification spoken of as, 'Whatever pleasure and joy arises, bhikkhus, in dependence on these five strands of sensual pleasure, this is the gratification of sensual pleasures,' when compared with the suffering spoken of in the passage beginning, 'And what, bhikkhus, is the danger in sensual pleasures? Herein, bhikkhus, a clansman earns his living by some craft, whether by accounting or by calculation...', is small, the measure of a drop of water. But the suffering is indeed much, abundant, like the water in the four oceans. Therefore it is said, 'Scant is the gratification; more suffering is here.' 'This is a hook' means that these five strands of sensual pleasure are like a fish-hook that, having shown the gratification, drags one in. 'Knowing this, the discerning one': thus knowing, the intelligent, wise person, having abandoned all this, should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.

Saṅgagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the verse concerning attachment is concluded.

62. Sandālayitvānāti kā uppatti? Bārāṇasiyaṃ kira anivattabrahmadatto nāma rājā ahosi[V 1.0091]. So saṅgāmaṃ otiṇṇo ajinitvā aññaṃ vā kiccaṃ āraddho aniṭṭhapetvā na nivattati, tasmā naṃ evaṃ sañjāniṃsu. So [M 1.0103] ekadivasaṃ uyyānaṃ gacchati. Tena ca samayena vanadāho uṭṭhāsi. So aggi sukkhāni ca haritāni ca tiṇādīni dahanto anivattamāno eva gacchati. Rājā taṃ disvā tappaṭibhāganimittaṃ uppādesi. “Yathāyaṃ vanadāho, evameva ekādasavidho aggi sabbasatte dahanto anivattamānova gacchati mahādukkhaṃ uppādento, kudāssu nāmāhampi imassa dukkhassa nivattanatthaṃ ayaṃ aggi viya ariyamaggañāṇagginā kilese dahanto anivattamāno gaccheyya”nti? Tato muhuttaṃ gantvā kevaṭṭe addasa nadiyaṃ macche gaṇhante[P 1.0115]. Tesaṃ jālantaraṃ paviṭṭho eko mahāmaccho jālaṃ bhetvā palāyi. Te “maccho jālaṃ bhetvā gato”ti saddamakaṃsu. Rājā tampi vacanaṃ sutvā tappaṭibhāganimittaṃ uppādesi – “kudāssu nāmāhampi ariyamaggañāṇena taṇhādiṭṭhijālaṃ bhetvā asajjamāno gaccheyya”nti. So rajjaṃ pahāya pabbajitvā vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā paccekabodhiṃ sacchākāsi, imañca udānagāthaṃ abhāsi –

62. What is the origin of 'Sandālayitvāna'? It is said that in Bārāṇasī there was a king named Anivattabrahmadatta. He, having gone to battle, would not turn back without conquering, or having undertaken another task, would not turn back without completing it; therefore they knew him by that name. One day, he went to a park. At that time, a forest fire broke out. The fire, burning dry and green grass and such, advanced without turning back. Seeing this, the king conceived a corresponding sign: 'Just as this forest fire, so too the elevenfold fire, burning all beings, advances without turning back, producing great suffering. When, I wonder, will I too, for the cessation of this suffering, like this fire, burning defilements with the fire of noble path knowledge, advance without turning back?' Then, after traveling for a short while, he saw fishermen catching fish in a river. A large fish that had entered their net broke through the net and escaped. They made a noise, shouting, 'The fish has broken the net and gone!' Hearing this statement as well, the king conceived a corresponding sign: 'When, I wonder, will I too, with noble path knowledge, having broken the net of craving and views, go forth unattached?' He then renounced his kingdom, went forth, undertook insight meditation, and realized paccekabodhi. He uttered this inspired verse:

“Sandālayitvāna saṃyojanāni, jālaṃva bhetvā salilambucārī;

Aggīva daḍḍhaṃ anivattamāno, eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”ti.

Having shattered the fetters, like a water-dweller breaking through a net; like a fire not returning to what it has burned, one should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.

Tassā dutiyapāde jālanti suttamayaṃ vuccati. Ambūti udakaṃ, tattha caratīti ambucārī, macchassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Salile ambucārī salilambucārī, tasmiṃ nadīsalile jālaṃ bhetvā ambucārīvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tatiyapāde daḍḍhanti daḍḍhaṭṭhānaṃ vuccati. Yathā aggi daḍḍhaṭṭhānaṃ puna na nivattati, na tattha bhiyyo āgacchati, evaṃ maggañāṇagginā daḍḍhaṃ kāmaguṇaṭṭhānaṃ anivattamāno tattha bhiyyo anāgacchantoti vuttaṃ hoti. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti.

In the second line of the verse, 'jāla' is said to be a net made of thread. 'Ambū' is water, and one who moves therein is an 'ambucārī'; this is a designation for a fish. 'Salile ambucārī' becomes 'salilambucārī'. The meaning is: like a water-dweller having broken the net in that flowing water. In the third line, 'daḍḍhaṃ' refers to a place that has been burned. Just as fire does not return to a place it has burned, nor does it come there again, so too, it is meant that one, not returning to the place of sensual pleasures burned by the fire of path-knowledge, does not come there again. The rest is as has been explained.

Sandālanagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Sandālana verse is complete.

63. Okkhittacakkhūti kā uppatti? Bārāṇasiyaṃ kira cakkhulolabrahmadatto nāma rājā pādalolabrahmadatto viya nāṭakadassanamanuyutto hoti. Ayaṃ pana viseso – so asantuṭṭho tattha tattha gacchati, ayaṃ taṃ taṃ nāṭakaṃ disvā ativiya abhinanditvā nāṭakaparivattadassanena taṇhaṃ vaḍḍhento vicarati. So kira nāṭakadassanāya āgataṃ aññataraṃ [M 1.0104] kuṭumbiyabhariyaṃ disvā rāgaṃ uppādesi. Tato saṃvegamāpajjitvā puna “ahaṃ imaṃ taṇhaṃ vaḍḍhento apāyaparipūrako bhavissāmi, handa naṃ niggaṇhāmī”ti pabbajitvā vipassanto paccekabodhiṃ [V 1.0092] sacchikatvā attano purimapaṭipattiṃ garahanto tappaṭipakkhaguṇadīpikaṃ imaṃ udānagāthaṃ abhāsi –

63. What is the origin of 'Okkhittacakkhū'? It is said that in Bārāṇasī there was a king named Cakkhulola Brahmadatta who was devoted to watching plays, just as Pādalola Brahmadatta was. But this was the distinction: that one, being unsatisfied, would go here and there; this one, however, seeing various plays, would become excessively delighted and wander about, increasing his craving by watching the performances repeatedly. It is said that upon seeing a certain householder's wife who had come to watch a play, he developed lust. Then, feeling a sense of urgency, he thought, 'By increasing this craving, I will become a filler of the woeful states. Come, let me restrain it.' So he went forth, and while practicing insight, he realized Paccekabodhi. Then, censuring his own former conduct, he uttered this inspired verse, which illuminates the qualities opposed to it:

“Okkhittacakkhū na ca pādalolo, guttindriyo rakkhitamānasāno;

Anavassuto apariḍayhamāno, eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”ti.

With downcast eyes and not restless of foot, with faculties guarded and mind well-restrained; untainted, unconsumed, one should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.

Tattha [P 1.0116] okkhittacakkhūti heṭṭhākhittacakkhu, satta gīvaṭṭhīni paṭipāṭiyā ṭhapetvā parivajjagahetabbadassanatthaṃ yugamattaṃ pekkhamānoti vuttaṃ hoti. Na tu hanukaṭṭhinā hadayaṭṭhiṃ saṅghaṭṭento. Evañhi okkhittacakkhutā na samaṇasāruppā hotī. Na ca pādaloloti ekassa dutiyo, dvinnaṃ tatiyoti evaṃ gaṇamajjhaṃ pavisitukāmatāya kaṇḍūyamānapādo viya abhavanto, dīghacārikaanavaṭṭhitacārikavirato vā. Guttindriyoti chasu indriyesu idha visuṃvuttāvasesavasena gopitindriyo. Rakkhitamānasānoti mānasaṃ yeva mānasānaṃ, taṃ rakkhitamassāti rakkhitamānasāno. Yathā kilesehi na viluppati, evaṃ rakkhitacittoti vuttaṃ hoti. Anavassutoti imāya paṭipattiyā tesu tesu ārammaṇesu kilesaanvāssavavirahito. Apariḍayhamānoti evaṃ anvāssavavirahāva kilesaggīhi apariḍayhamāno. Bahiddhā vā anavassuto, ajjhattaṃ apariḍayhamāno. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti.

Herein, 'with downcast eyes' means having the eyes cast downwards. It is said to mean: having placed the seven neck-bones in sequence, one looks a yoke’s length ahead for the purpose of seeing while abandoning turning the head. It does not mean pressing the jawbone against the breastbone, for in that way, having downcast eyes is not suitable for a recluse. 'And not restless of foot' means not rushing about like one with itching feet, with the desire to enter the midst of a group—a second after the first, a third after the second—and refraining from long and aimless wandering. 'With guarded senses' means having the senses guarded, in this context, with respect to what remains apart from what has been separately mentioned among the six senses. 'With a guarded mind' (rakkhitamānasāno): the mind (mānasaṃ) itself is mānasānaṃ; his mind is guarded (rakkhitaṃ), thus he is rakkhitamānasāno. It is said to mean having a guarded mind so that it is not defiled by the corruptions. 'Without influx' means that through this practice, one is devoid of the influx of corruptions with regard to those various sense-objects. 'Not being burned' means that, being thus devoid of influx, one is not burned by the fires of the corruptions. Or, externally without influx, internally unburned. The remainder is just as has been explained.

Okkhittacakkhugāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Okkhittacakkhu verse is concluded.

64. Ohārayitvāti kā uppatti? Bārāṇasiyaṃ kira ayaṃ aññopi cātumāsikabrahmadatto nāma rājā catumāse catumāse uyyānakīḷaṃ gacchati. So ekadivasaṃ gimhānaṃ majjhime māse uyyānaṃ pavisanto uyyānadvāre [M 1.0105] pattasañchannaṃ pupphālaṅkataviṭapaṃ pāricchattakakoviḷāraṃ disvā ekaṃ pupphaṃ gahetvā uyyānaṃ pāvisi. Tato “raññā aggapupphaṃ gahita”nti aññataropi amacco hatthikkhandhe ṭhito eva ekaṃ pupphaṃ aggahesi. Eteneva upāyena sabbo balakāyo aggahesi. Pupphaṃ anassādentā [P 1.0117] pattampi gaṇhiṃsu. So rukkho nippattapuppho khandhamattova ahosi. Taṃ rājā sāyanhasamaye uyyānā nikkhamanto disvā “kiṃ kato ayaṃ rukkho, mama āgamanavelāyaṃ maṇivaṇṇasākhantaresu pavāḷasadisapupphālaṅkato ahosi, idāni nippattapuppho jāto”ti cintento tassevāvidūre apupphitaṃ rukkhaṃ sañchannapalāsaṃ addasa. Disvā cassa etadahosi – “ayaṃ rukkho pupphabharitasākhattā bahujanassa lobhanīyo ahosi, tena muhutteneva byasanaṃ patto, ayaṃ panañño alobhanīyattā tatheva ṭhito. Idampi rajjaṃ pupphitarukkho [V 1.0093] viya lobhanīyaṃ, bhikkhubhāvo pana apupphitarukkho viya alobhanīyo. Tasmā yāva idampi ayaṃ rukkho viya na viluppati, tāva ayamañño sañchannapatto yathā pāricchattako, evaṃ kāsāvena parisañchannena hutvā pabbajitabba”nti. So rajjaṃ pahāya pabbajitvā vipassanto paccekabodhiṃ sacchikatvā imaṃ udānagāthaṃ abhāsi –

64. What is the origin of 'Having laid aside'? It is said that in Bārāṇasī there was another king named Cātumāsika Brahmadatta who would go to the pleasure garden every four months. One day, during the middle month of summer, as he was entering the garden, he saw at the garden gate a Pāricchattaka Koviḷāra tree with branches adorned with flowers and covered with leaves. He plucked one flower and entered the garden. Then, thinking, 'The king has taken the first flower,' a certain minister, while still standing on the elephant's back, also took one flower. In this same way, the entire army took them. Not being satisfied with the flowers, they also took the leaves. That tree became bereft of leaves and flowers, and was just a trunk. In the evening, as the king was leaving the garden, he saw it and thought, 'What has been done to this tree? At the time of my arrival, it was adorned with flowers like coral amidst its branches the color of gems, but now it has become bereft of leaves and flowers.' While thinking thus, not far from it he saw another tree, covered with foliage but without flowers. And upon seeing it, this thought occurred to him: 'This tree, because its branches were laden with flowers, was desirable to many people, and for that reason it met with ruin in a mere moment. This other one, however, being undesirable, remains as it was. This kingship, too, is desirable like a flowering tree, but the state of a bhikkhu is undesirable like a flowerless tree. Therefore, before this kingship is plundered like that tree, just as this other Pāricchattaka is covered with leaves, so should I go forth, having become covered with the saffron-dyed robe.' Having renounced the kingdom and gone forth, while practicing insight he realized the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha and uttered this inspired verse:

“Ohārayitvā gihibyañjanāni, sañchannapatto yathā pārichatto;

Kāsāyavattho abhinikkhamitvā, eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”ti.

“Having laid aside the marks of a householder, like a Pāricchattaka tree covered with leaves; clad in the saffron robe, having gone forth, one should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.”

Tattha kāsāyavattho abhinikkhamitvāti imassa pādassa gehā abhinikkhamitvā kāsāyavattho hutvāti evamattho veditabbo. Sesaṃ vuttanayeneva sakkā jānitunti na vitthāritanti.

Herein, the meaning of the line 'clad in the saffron robe, having gone forth' should be understood thus: 'having gone forth from the home and become one clad in the saffron robe.' The remainder can be known in the way already explained, thus it is not elaborated upon.

Pāricchattakagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Pāricchattaka verse is concluded.

Tatiyo vaggo niṭṭhito.

The Third Chapter is concluded.

65. Rasesūti kā uppatti? Aññataro kira bārāṇasirājā uyyāne amaccaputtehi parivuto silāpaṭṭapokkharaṇiyaṃ kīḷati. Tassa sūdo [M 1.0106] sabbamaṃsānaṃ rasaṃ gahetvā atīva susaṅkhataṃ amatakappaṃ antarabhattaṃ pacitvā upanāmesi. So tattha gedhamāpanno kassaci kiñci adatvā attanāva bhuñji. Udakakīḷato ca ativikāle nikkhanto sīghaṃ sīghaṃ bhuñji. Yehi saddhiṃ pubbe bhuñjati, na tesaṃ kañci sari. Atha pacchā paṭisaṅkhānaṃ uppādetvā “aho, mayā pāpaṃ kataṃ, yvāhaṃ rasataṇhāya abhibhūto sabbajanaṃ visaritvā [P 1.0118] ekakova bhuñjiṃ. Handa rasataṇhaṃ niggaṇhāmī”ti rajjaṃ pahāya pabbajitvā vipassanto paccekabodhiṃ sacchikatvā attano purimapaṭipattiṃ garahanto tappaṭipakkhaguṇadīpikaṃ imaṃ udānagāthaṃ abhāsi –

65. What is the origin of 'Regarding flavors'? It is said that a certain king of Bārāṇasī, surrounded by the sons of his ministers, was playing in a park in a pond with a stone platform. His cook, having extracted the essence of all kinds of meat, prepared an exceedingly well-made intermediate meal, like ambrosia, and served it to him. Having become overcome by greed for it, he ate it all by himself without giving anything to anyone. And having emerged from playing in the water at a very late hour, he ate very quickly. He did not remember anyone with whom he had previously eaten. Then, afterwards, arousing reflection, he thought: 'Alas, I have done an evil thing, in that I, overpowered by craving for flavors, forgot everyone and ate all alone. Well then, I shall restrain this craving for flavors!' Having renounced his kingdom and gone forth, while practicing insight he realized the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha. Censuring his own former conduct, he uttered this inspired verse which illuminates the qualities that are the opposite of that conduct:

“Rasesu gedhaṃ akaraṃ alolo, anaññaposī sapadānacārī;

Kule kule appaṭibaddhacitto, eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”ti.

“Not given to greed for flavors, not covetous, not supported by any other, practicing the uninterrupted alms-round; with a mind unattached to family after family, one should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.”

Tattha rasesūti ambilamadhuratittakakaṭukaloṇikakhārikakasāvādibhedesu sāyanīyesu. Gedhaṃ akaranti giddhiṃ akaronto, taṇhaṃ anuppādentoti vuttaṃ hoti. Aloloti “idaṃ sāyissāmi, idaṃ sāyissāmī”ti evaṃ rasavisesesu anākulo. Anaññaposīti posetabbakasaddhivihārikādivirahito[V 1.0094], kāyasandhāraṇamattena santuṭṭhoti vuttaṃ hoti. Yathā vā pubbe uyyāne rasesu gedhakaraṇalolo hutvā aññaposī āsiṃ, evaṃ ahutvā yāya taṇhāya lolo hutvā rasesu gedhaṃ karoti. Taṃ taṇhaṃ hitvā āyatiṃ taṇhāmūlakassa aññassa attabhāvassa anibbattanena anaññaposīti dasseti. Atha vā atthabhañjanakaṭṭhena aññeti kilesā vuccanti. Tesaṃ aposanena anaññaposīti ayampettha attho. Sapadānacārīti avokkammacārī anupubbacārī, gharapaṭipāṭiṃ achaḍḍetvā aḍḍhakulañca daliddakulañca nirantaraṃ piṇḍāya pavisamānoti attho. Kule kule appaṭibaddhacittoti khattiyakulādīsu yattha katthaci kilesavasena alaggacitto, candūpamo niccanavako hutvāti attho. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti.

Herein, 'in flavors' (rasesu) refers to those things which are to be tasted, distinguished by such flavors as sour, sweet, bitter, pungent, salty, alkaline, astringent, and so on. 'Not making greed' (gedhaṃ akaraṃ) means not creating greed, not arousing craving; this is what is said. 'Not greedy' (alolo) means not being agitated regarding various flavors with thoughts such as, “I will taste this, I will taste that.” 'Not nourishing another' (anaññaposī) means being without co-residents and others who must be supported, being content with the mere sustenance of the body; this is what is said. Or, it indicates that, unlike in the past when, in the park, I was greedy for flavors and nourished by another, I am not so now; having abandoned that craving by which one becomes greedy and creates attachment to flavors, I am 'not nourishing another' by not bringing into existence in the future another state of being rooted in craving. Alternatively, 'another' (añña) refers to defilements, in the sense of destroying welfare. By not nourishing them, one is 'not nourishing another'; this is also the meaning here. 'Going on an uninterrupted alms round' (sapadānacārī) means one who walks without skipping, proceeding in order; one who enters for alms continuously among both wealthy and poor families, not neglecting the order of houses; this is the meaning. 'With mind unattached to any family' (kule kule appaṭibaddhacitto) means having a mind not attached through defilements to anyone anywhere among families of the warrior caste and others, being ever new like the moon; this is the meaning. The rest is as has been explained.

Rasagedhagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the verse concerning craving for flavors is concluded.

66. Pahāya [M 1.0107] pañcāvaraṇānīti kā uppatti? Bārāṇasiyaṃ kira aññataro rājā paṭhamajjhānalābhī ahosi. So jhānānurakkhaṇatthaṃ rajjaṃ pahāya pabbajitvā vipassanto paccekabodhiṃ sacchikatvā attano paṭipattisampadaṃ dīpento imaṃ udānagāthaṃ abhāsi –

66. What is the origin of the verse beginning 'Having abandoned the five hindrances'? It is said that in Bārāṇasī a certain king was an obtainer of the first jhāna. For the sake of protecting his jhāna, he renounced his kingdom, went forth, and while practicing insight, he realized paccekabodhi. Revealing his own accomplishment in the practice, he uttered this inspired verse:

“Pahāya pañcāvaraṇāni cetaso, upakkilese byapanujja sabbe;

Anissito chetva sinehadosaṃ, eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”ti.

Having abandoned the five hindrances of the mind, having dispelled all defilements, unattached, having cut off affection and hatred, one should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.

Tattha āvaraṇānīti nīvaraṇāneva. Tāni atthato uragasutte [P 1.0119] vuttāni. Tāni pana yasmā abbhādayo viya candasūriye ceto āvaranti, tasmā “āvaraṇāni cetaso”ti vuttāni. Tāni upacārena vā appanāya vā pahāya. Upakkileseti upagamma cittaṃ vibādhente akusale dhamme, vatthopamādīsu vutte abhijjhādayo vā. Byapanujjāti panuditvā vināsetvā, vipassanāmaggena pajahitvāti attho. Sabbeti anavasese. Evaṃ samathavipassanāsampanno paṭhamamaggena diṭṭhinissayassa pahīnattā anissito. Sesamaggehi chetvā tedhātukaṃ sinehadosaṃ, taṇhārāganti vuttaṃ hoti. Sineho eva hi guṇapaṭipakkhato sinehadosoti vutto. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti.

Herein, 'hindrances' (āvaraṇāni) are the very hindrances (nīvaraṇāni). In terms of meaning, they have been spoken of in the Uraga Sutta. And since they cover the mind just as clouds and so forth cover the moon and sun, they are called 'hindrances of the mind'. These are abandoned by means of access concentration or absorption concentration. 'Defilements' (upakkilese) refers to unwholesome states that approach and afflict the mind, or to covetousness and others spoken of in the Simile of the Cloth and so on. 'Having dispelled' (byapanujja) means having driven away and destroyed them; that is, having abandoned them by means of the path of insight; this is the meaning. 'All' (sabbe) means without remainder. Thus, one who is accomplished in serenity and insight is 'unattached' (anissito) because reliance on views has been abandoned by means of the first path. With the remaining paths, having cut off the taint of affection belonging to the three realms—which is to say, craving and lust. For affection itself, being contrary to virtue, is called the 'taint of affection'. The rest is as has been explained.

Āvaraṇagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the verse concerning the hindrances is concluded.

67. Vipiṭṭhikatvānāti kā uppatti? Bārāṇasiyaṃ kira aññataro rājā catutthajjhānalābhī [V 1.0095] ahosi. So jhānānurakkhaṇatthaṃ rajjaṃ pahāya pabbajitvā vipassanto paccekabodhiṃ sacchikatvā attano paṭipattisampadaṃ dīpento imaṃ udānagāthaṃ abhāsi –

What is the origin of the verse beginning 'Having turned one's back on'? It is said that in Bārāṇasī, a certain king was an obtainer of the fourth jhāna. For the sake of protecting his jhāna, he renounced his kingdom and went forth. While practicing insight, he realized paccekabodhi, and revealing the accomplishment of his own practice, he spoke this inspired verse:

“Vipiṭṭhikatvāna sukhaṃ dukhañca, pubbeva ca somanassadomanassaṃ;

Laddhānupekkhaṃ samathaṃ visuddhaṃ, eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”ti.

Having put pleasure and pain behind, and mental joy and sorrow as before, having attained pure equanimity and calm, one should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.

Tattha [M 1.0108] vipiṭṭhikatvānāti piṭṭhito katvā, chaḍḍetvā jahitvāti attho. Sukhaṃ dukhañcāti kāyikaṃ sātāsātaṃ. Somanassadomanassanti cetasikaṃ sātāsātaṃ. Upekkhanti catutthajjhānupekkhaṃ. Samathanti catutthajjhānasamathameva. Visuddhanti pañcanīvaraṇavitakkavicārapītisukhasaṅkhātehi navahi paccanīkadhammehi vimuttattā visuddhaṃ, niddhantasuvaṇṇamiva vigatūpakkilesanti attho.

67. Herein, 'having turned one's back on' (vipiṭṭhikatvāna) means having put behind, having discarded, having abandoned; this is the meaning. 'Pleasure and pain' (sukhaṃ dukhañca) refers to bodily pleasant and unpleasant feeling. 'Joy and sorrow' (somanassadomanassaṃ) refers to mental pleasant and unpleasant feeling. 'Equanimity' (upekkhā) is the equanimity of the fourth jhāna. 'Calm' (samatha) is the calm of the fourth jhāna itself. 'Pure' (visuddhaṃ) means pure because it is freed from the nine opposing states—namely, the five hindrances, initial application, sustained application, rapture, and happiness—like refined gold from which impurities have been removed; this is the meaning.

Ayaṃ pana yojanā – vipiṭṭhikatvāna sukhaṃ dukkhañca pubbeva paṭhamajjhānupacārabhūmiyaṃyeva dukkhaṃ, tatiyajjhānupacārabhūmiyaṃ sukhanti adhippāyo. Puna ādito vuttaṃ cakāraṃ parato netvā “somanassaṃ domanassañca [P 1.0120] vipiṭṭhikatvāna pubbevā”ti adhikāro. Tena somanassaṃ catutthajjhānupacāre, domanassañca dutiyajjhānupacāreyevāti dīpeti. Etāni hi etesaṃ pariyāyato pahānaṭṭhānāni. Nippariyāyato pana dukkhassa paṭhamajjhānaṃ, domanassassa dutiyajjhānaṃ, sukhassa tatiyajjhānaṃ, somanassassa catutthajjhānaṃ pahānaṭṭhānaṃ. Yathāha – “paṭhamajjhānaṃ upasampajja viharati etthuppannaṃ dukkhindriyaṃ aparisesaṃ nirujjhatī”tiādi (saṃ. ni. 5.510). Taṃ sabbaṃ aṭṭhasāliniyā dhammasaṅgahaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 165) vuttaṃ. Yato pubbeva tīsu paṭhamajjhānādīsu dukkhadomanassasukhāni vipiṭṭhikatvā ettheva catutthajjhāne somanassaṃ vipiṭṭhikatvā imāya paṭipadāya laddhānupekkhaṃ samathaṃ visuddhaṃ eko careti. Sesaṃ sabbattha pākaṭamevāti.

This, however, is the construction: 'Having turned one's back on pleasure and pain' means that pain is abandoned 'earlier', in the access sphere of the first jhāna, and pleasure in the access sphere of the third jhāna; this is the intention. Furthermore, by taking the particle 'ca' mentioned at the beginning and applying it to what follows, the reading is: 'and earlier having turned one's back on joy and sorrow.' By this, it is shown that joy is abandoned in the access sphere of the fourth jhāna, and sorrow in the access sphere of the second jhāna. For these are their places of abandonment indirectly. Directly, however, the first jhāna is the place for abandoning pain, the second jhāna for sorrow, the third jhāna for pleasure, and the fourth jhāna for joy. As it is said: 'He attains and abides in the first jhāna; the faculty of pain that has arisen there ceases without remainder,' and so on. All this is stated in the Aṭṭhasālinī, the commentary on the Dhammasaṅgaṇī. Since pain, sorrow, and pleasure are turned back on 'earlier' in the three jhānas beginning with the first, and joy is turned back on right here in the fourth jhāna, it is by this practice that 'having attained pure, calm equanimity, one wanders alone.' The rest is clear in every respect.

Vipiṭṭhikatvāgāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the verse beginning 'Having turned one's back on' is concluded.

68. Āraddhavīriyoti kā uppatti? Aññataro kira paccantarājā sahassayodhaparimāṇabalakāyo rajjena khuddako, paññāya mahanto ahosi. So ekadivasaṃ “kiñcāpi ahaṃ khuddako, paññavatā ca pana sakkā sakalajambudīpaṃ gahetu”nti cintetvā sāmantarañño dūtaṃ pāhesi – “sattadivasabbhantare me rajjaṃ vā detu yuddhaṃ vā”ti. Tato so attano [V 1.0096] amacce samodhānetvā āha – “mayā tumhe anāpucchāyeva sāhasaṃ kataṃ, amukassa rañño evaṃ pahitaṃ, kiṃ kātabba”nti? Te āhaṃsu – “sakkā, mahārāja, so dūto nivattetu”nti? “Na sakkā, gato bhavissatī”ti. “Yadi evaṃ vināsitamhā tayā, tena hi dukkhaṃ [M 1.0109] aññassa satthena marituṃ. Handa, mayaṃ aññamaññaṃ paharitvā marāma, attānaṃ paharitvā marāma, ubbandhāma, visaṃ khādāmā”ti. Evaṃ tesu ekameko maraṇameva saṃvaṇṇeti. Tato rājā – “kiṃ me, imehi, atthi, bhaṇe, mayhaṃ yodhā”ti āha. Atha “ahaṃ, mahārāja, yodho, ahaṃ, mahārāja, yodho”ti taṃ yodhasahassaṃ uṭṭhahi.

68. What is the origin of 'Āraddhavīriyo'? It is said that there was a certain border king whose army consisted of a thousand warriors. His dominion was small, but he was great in wisdom. One day, he thought, 'Though I am small, with wisdom it is possible to conquer all of Jambudīpa.' So he sent a messenger to a neighboring king with the message: 'Within seven days, either surrender your kingdom to me or prepare for battle.' Then, he gathered his ministers and said, 'Without consulting you, I have acted rashly. Such a message has been sent to such-and-such a king. What should be done now?' They replied, 'Great king, is it possible to recall the messenger?' 'No, he must have already gone,' said the king. 'If that is the case, then we are ruined by you. Therefore, it is a misery to die by another's weapon. Come, let us strike each other and die, or strike ourselves and die, or hang ourselves, or take poison.' Thus, each of them extolled only death. Then the king said, 'What use are these to me? Tell me, do I have any warriors?' At that moment, the thousand warriors rose up, declaring, 'Great king, I am a warrior! Great king, I am a warrior!'

Rājā “ete upaparikkhissāmī”ti mantvā [P 1.0121] citakaṃ sajjetvā āha – “mayā, bhaṇe, idaṃ nāma sāhasaṃ kataṃ, taṃ me amaccā paṭikkosanti, sohaṃ citakaṃ pavisissāmi, ko mayā saddhiṃ pavisissati, kena mayhaṃ jīvitaṃ pariccatta”nti? Evaṃ vutte pañcasatā yodhā uṭṭhahiṃsu – “mayaṃ, mahārāja, pavisāmā”ti. Tato rājā apare pañcasate yodhe āha – “tumhe idāni, tātā, kiṃ karissathā”ti? Te āhaṃsu – “nāyaṃ, mahārāja, purisakāro, itthikiriyā esā, apica mahārājena paṭirañño dūto pesito, tena mayaṃ raññā saddhiṃ yujjhitvā marissāmā”ti. Tato rājā “pariccattaṃ tumhehi mama jīvita”nti caturaṅginiṃ senaṃ sannayhitvā tena yodhasahassena parivuto gantvā rajjasīmāya nisīdi.

The king, thinking, 'I will examine them,' had a pyre prepared and said: 'Friends, I have committed this rash act, and my ministers rebuke me for it. I will enter the pyre. Who will enter with me? Who will sacrifice their life for me?' When this was said, five hundred warriors rose up: 'Great king, we will enter.' Then the king addressed the other five hundred warriors: 'Now, my dear ones, what will you do?' They replied: 'Great king, this is not a manly act; it is a woman's action. Moreover, the great king has sent a messenger to the rival king; we shall fight with that king and die.' Then the king said, 'You have relinquished your lives for me,' and marshaled his fourfold army. Surrounded by those thousand warriors, he went and sat down at the border of the kingdom.

Sopi paṭirājā taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā “are, so khuddakarājā mama dāsassāpi nappahotī”ti kujjhitvā sabbaṃ balakāyaṃ ādāya yujjhituṃ nikkhami. Khuddakarājā taṃ abbhuyyātaṃ disvā balakāyaṃ āha – “tātā, tumhe na bahukā; sabbe sampiṇḍitvā, asicammaṃ gahetvā, sīghaṃ imassa rañño purato ujukaṃ eva gacchathā”ti. Te tathā akaṃsu. Atha sā senā dvidhā bhijjitvā antaramadāsi. Te taṃ rājānaṃ jīvaggāhaṃ gaṇhiṃsu, aññe yodhā palāyiṃsu. Khuddakarājā “taṃ māremī”ti purato dhāvati, paṭirājā taṃ abhayaṃ yāci. Tato tassa abhayaṃ datvā, sapathaṃ kārāpetvā, taṃ attano manussaṃ katvā, tena saha aññaṃ rājānaṃ abbhuggantvā, tassa rajjasīmāya ṭhatvā pesesi – “rajjaṃ vā me detu yuddhaṃ vā”ti. So “ahaṃ ekayuddhampi na sahāmī”ti rajjaṃ niyyātesi. Eteneva upāyena sabbarājāno gahetvā ante bārāṇasirājānampi aggahesi.

Hearing this news, the opposing king became angry, saying, 'Ah, that petty king is not even fit to be my slave!' and marched out with his entire army to fight. Seeing them approach, the petty king addressed his troops: 'My friends, you are few in number. Gather together, take up your swords and shields, and quickly advance straight to the front of that king.' They did so. Then that army split in two and left a gap. They captured that king alive, while the other warriors fled. The petty king ran forward, intending to kill him, but the opposing king begged for safety. Then, granting him safety and making him swear an oath, he made him his own man. Together with him, he marched against another king, stood at the border of his kingdom, and sent a message: 'Either give me the kingdom or fight.' That king replied, 'I cannot endure even a single battle,' and handed over his kingdom. By this very strategy, he took all the kings and finally captured even the king of Bārāṇasī.

So [M 1.0110] ekasatarājaparivuto sakalajambudīpe rajjaṃ anusāsanto cintesi – “ahaṃ pubbe khuddako ahosiṃ, somhi attano ñāṇasampattiyā sakalajambudīpassa issaro jāto. Taṃ [P 1.0122] kho pana [V 1.0097] me ñāṇaṃ lokiyavīriyasampayuttaṃ, neva nibbidāya na virāgāya saṃvattati, sādhu vatassa svāhaṃ iminā ñāṇena lokuttaradhammaṃ gaveseyya”nti. Tato bārāṇasirañño rajjaṃ datvā, puttadārañca sakajanapadameva pesetvā, pabbajjaṃ samādāya vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā, paccekabodhiṃ sacchikatvā attano vīriyasampattiṃ dīpento imaṃ udānagāthaṃ abhāsi –

Surrounded by one hundred and one kings, ruling over the whole of Jambudīpa, he reflected: 'Before, I was insignificant, but through the accomplishment of my own wisdom, I have become lord of all Jambudīpa. But this wisdom of mine, connected with worldly effort, does not lead to disenchantment or dispassion. It would be good if I, with this wisdom, should seek the supramundane Dhamma.' Then, having given the kingdom to the king of Bārāṇasī, and having sent his son and wife back to his own country, he undertook the ascetic life. Having initiated insight meditation and realized Paccekabodhi, and revealing his own accomplishment of effort, he uttered this inspired verse:

“Āraddhaviriyo paramatthapattiyā, alīnacitto akusītavutti;

Daḷhanikkamo thāmabalūpapanno, eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”ti.

With energy roused for the attainment of the highest goal, with mind unshrinking and of unslothful conduct; firm in purpose, endowed with strength and power, one should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.

Tattha āraddhaṃ vīriyamassāti āraddhaviriyo. Etena attano vīriyārambhaṃ ādivīriyaṃ dasseti. Paramattho vuccati nibbānaṃ, tassa pattiyā paramatthapattiyā. Etena vīriyārambhena pattabbaphalaṃ dasseti. Alīnacittoti etena balavīriyūpatthambhānaṃ cittacetasikānaṃ alīnataṃ dasseti. Akusītavuttīti etena ṭhānaāsanacaṅkamanādīsu kāyassa anavasīdanaṃ. Daḷhanikkamoti etena “kāmaṃ taco ca nhāru cā”ti (ma. ni. 2.184; a. ni. 2.5; mahāni. 196) evaṃ pavattaṃ padahanavīriyaṃ dasseti, yaṃ taṃ anupubbasikkhādīsu padahanto “kāyena ceva paramasaccaṃ sacchikaroti, paññāya ca naṃ ativijjha passatī”ti vuccati. Atha vā etena maggasampayuttavīriyaṃ dasseti. Tañhi daḷhañca bhāvanāpāripūriṃ gatattā, nikkamo ca sabbaso paṭipakkhā nikkhantattā, tasmā taṃsamaṅgīpuggalopi daḷho nikkamo assāti “daḷhanikkamo”ti vuccati. Thāmabalūpapannoti maggakkhaṇe kāyathāmena ñāṇabalena ca upapanno, atha vā thāmabhūtena balena upapannoti thāmabalūpapanno, thirañāṇabalūpapannoti vuttaṃ hoti. Etena tassa vīriyassa vipassanāñāṇasampayogaṃ dīpento yoniso padahanabhāvaṃ sādheti. Pubbabhāgamajjhimaukkaṭṭhavīriyavasena vā tayopi pādā yojetabbā. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti.

Herein, 'one with aroused energy' means one in whom energy is aroused. This shows the undertaking of one's own energy, the initial energy. The ultimate goal is called Nibbāna; for its attainment is 'for the attainment of the ultimate goal' (paramatthapattiyā). This shows the fruit to be attained through the undertaking of energy. 'With an unsluggish mind' shows the unsluggishness of the mind and mental factors supported by strong energy. 'Of un-idle conduct' shows the non-languishing of the body in standing, sitting, walking, and so on. 'With firm exertion' shows the striving-energy, as described: 'Let skin and sinews...'—that which, when one strives in the progressive trainings, is said to 'realize the ultimate truth with the body and, having penetrated it, see it with wisdom.' Alternatively, this shows the energy associated with the path. For that energy is firm, having reached the fulfillment of development, and it is an exertion, having completely gone forth from all adversaries. Therefore, a person endowed with it is called 'one with firm exertion.' 'Endowed with strength and power' means that at the moment of the path, one is endowed with bodily strength and the power of knowledge. Or, it means being endowed with strength that is stamina, hence 'endowed with strength-power,' which is to say, 'endowed with firm knowledge-power.' By this, demonstrating the association of that energy with insight-knowledge, the state of wise striving is established. Alternatively, all three phrases may be applied according to preliminary, middle, and supreme energy. The rest is just as has been explained.

Āraddhavīriyagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the verse concerning aroused energy is concluded.

69. Paṭisallānanti [M 1.0111] kā uppatti? Imissā gāthāya āvaraṇagāthāya uppattisadisā eva uppatti, natthi koci viseso. Atthavaṇṇanāyaṃ panassā paṭisallānanti tehi tehi sattasaṅkhārehi [P 1.0123] paṭinivattitvā sallīnaṃ ekattasevitā ekībhāvo, kāyavivekoti attho. Jhānanti paccanīkajhāpanato ārammaṇalakkhaṇūpanijjhānato ca cittaviveko vuccati. Tattha aṭṭhasamāpattiyo nīvaraṇādipaccanīkajhāpanato ārammaṇūpanijjhānato ca jhānanti vuccati, vipassanāmaggaphalāni sattasaññādipaccanīkajhāpanato, lakkhaṇūpanijjhānatoyeva cettha phalāni. Idha [V 1.0098] pana ārammaṇūpanijjhānameva adhippetaṃ. Evametaṃ paṭisallānañca jhānañca ariñcamāno, ajahamāno, anissajjamāno. Dhammesūti vipassanūpagesu pañcakkhandhādidhammesu. Niccanti satataṃ, samitaṃ, abbhokiṇṇaṃ. Anudhammacārīti te dhamme ārabbha pavattamānena anugataṃ vipassanādhammaṃ caramāno. Atha vā dhammāti nava lokuttaradhammā, tesaṃ dhammānaṃ anulomo dhammoti anudhammo, vipassanāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tattha “dhammānaṃ niccaṃ anudhammacārī”ti vattabbe gāthābandhasukhatthaṃ vibhattibyattayena “dhammesū”ti vuttaṃ siyā. Ādīnavaṃ sammasitā bhavesūti tāya anudhammacaritāsaṅkhātāya vipassanāya aniccākārādidosaṃ tīsu bhavesu samanupassanto evaṃ imaṃ kāyavivekacittavivekaṃ ariñcamāno sikhāppattavipassanāsaṅkhātāya paṭipadāya adhigatoti vattabbo eko careti evaṃ yojanā veditabbā.

69. What is the origin of 'seclusion'? The origin of this verse is similar to that of the Āvaraṇa verse; there is no particular difference. In the explanation of the meaning, however, 'seclusion' means withdrawing from the various constituents of beings and dwelling in solitude, a state of oneness cultivated in isolation; this is the meaning of bodily seclusion. 'Meditation' (jhāna) refers to mental seclusion, from the burning up of adversaries and from the close contemplation of the object and of characteristics. Herein, the eight attainments are called 'meditation' because they burn up adversaries such as the hindrances and because of the close contemplation of the object. Insight, paths, and fruits are so called because they burn up adversaries such as the perception of a being; and here, the fruits are so called only because of the close contemplation of characteristics. In this context, however, only the close contemplation of the object is intended. Thus, not abandoning, not giving up, not relinquishing this seclusion and meditation. 'In phenomena' refers to phenomena such as the five aggregates, which are conducive to insight. 'Constantly' means continuously, uninterruptedly, without a break. 'Practicing in accordance with the Dhamma' means practicing the insight-Dhamma that proceeds in dependence on those phenomena. Alternatively, 'Dhamma' refers to the nine supramundane Dhammas; 'in accordance with the Dhamma' means the Dhamma conforming to those Dhammas—this is a term for insight. Here, though it should be said 'constantly practicing in accordance with the Dhammas' (dhammānaṃ niccaṃ anudhammacārī), for the sake of metrical ease, it may have been said as 'in phenomena' (dhammesu) by a change of case ending. 'Having comprehended the danger in existences' means: by means of that insight called 'practice in accordance with the Dhamma,' perceiving the fault of the characteristic of impermanence and so on in the three existences, thus not abandoning this bodily and mental seclusion, it is to be understood that one has attained this through the path of practice called 'insight that has reached its peak.' The connection 'one should wander alone' should be understood in this way.

Paṭisallānagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the verse concerning seclusion is concluded.

70. Taṇhakkhayanti kā uppatti? Aññataro kira bārāṇasirājā mahaccarājānubhāvena nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ karoti. Tassa sarīrasobhāya āvaṭṭitahadayā sattā purato gacchantāpi nivattitvā tameva ullokenti, pacchato gacchantāpi, ubhohi passehi gacchantāpi.
