Pakatiyā eva hi buddhadassane puṇṇacandasamuddarājadassane ca atitto loko. Atha aññatarā kuṭumbiyabhariyāpi uparipāsādagatā sīhapañjaraṃ vivaritvā olokayamānā aṭṭhāsi. Rājā taṃ disvāva paṭibaddhacitto hutvā amaccaṃ āṇāpesi – “jānāhi tāva, bhaṇe, ayaṃ itthī sasāmikā vā [M 1.0112] asāmikā vā”ti. So gantvā [P 1.0124] “sasāmikā”ti ārocesi. Atha rājā cintesi – “imā vīsatisahassanāṭakitthiyo devaccharāyo viya maṃyeva ekaṃ abhiramenti, so dānāhaṃ etāpi atusitvā parassa itthiyā taṇhaṃ uppādesiṃ, sā uppannā apāyameva ākaḍḍhatī”ti taṇhāya ādīnavaṃ disvā “handa naṃ niggaṇhāmī”ti rajjaṃ pahāya pabbajitvā vipassanto paccekabodhiṃ sacchikatvā imaṃ udānagāthaṃ abhāsi –

70. What is the origin of 'the destruction of craving'? It is said that a certain king of Bārāṇasī, with the great majesty of a king, was circumambulating the city. Beings whose hearts were captivated by the splendor of his body, even while walking ahead, turned back to gaze at him; those walking behind and those walking on both sides did likewise. Indeed, by nature, the world is never satisfied with seeing a Buddha, a full moon, the ocean, or a king. Then, a certain householder’s wife, having gone to an upper palace terrace, opened a lion-window and stood looking out. The king, upon seeing her, became infatuated and ordered his minister: “Go, my friend, and find out whether this woman has a husband or not.” He went and reported, “She has a husband.” Then the king reflected: “These twenty thousand dancing women, like celestial nymphs, delight me alone. Yet now, unsatisfied even with them, I have aroused craving for another’s wife. This craving, once arisen, drags one only to the planes of misery.” Seeing the danger in craving, he thought, “Come, I shall restrain it.” Renouncing the kingdom, he went forth and, practicing insight, realized the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha and uttered this inspired verse:

“Taṇhakkhayaṃ patthayamappamatto, aneḷamūgo sutavā satīmā;

Saṅkhātadhammo niyato padhānavā, eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”ti.

“Seeking the destruction of craving, heedful, not stammering, not dull, learned, mindful, one who has comprehended the Dhamma, certain of liberation, endowed with effort, one should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.”

Tattha taṇhakkhayanti nibbānaṃ, evaṃ diṭṭhādīnavāya taṇhāya eva appavattiṃ. Appamattoti sātaccakārī sakkaccakārī. Aneḷamūgoti alālāmukho. Atha vā aneḷo ca amūgo ca, paṇḍito byattoti vuttaṃ hoti. Hitasukhasampāpakaṃ sutamassa atthīti sutavā āgamasampannoti vuttaṃ [V 1.0099] hoti. Satīmāti cirakatādīnaṃ anussaritā. Saṅkhātadhammoti dhammupaparikkhāya pariññātadhammo. Niyatoti ariyamaggena niyāmaṃ patto. Padhānavāti sammappadhānavīriyasampanno. Uppaṭipāṭiyā esa pāṭho yojetabbo. Evametehi appamādādīhi samannāgato niyāmasampāpakena padhānena padhānavā, tena padhānena pattaniyāmattā niyato, tato arahattappattiyā saṅkhātadhammo. Arahā hi puna saṅkhātabbābhāvato “saṅkhātadhammo”ti vuccati. Yathāha “ye ca saṅkhātadhammāse, ye ca sekhā puthū idhā”ti (su. ni. 1044; cūḷani. ajitamāṇavapucchāniddesa 7). Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti.

Therein, 'the destruction of craving' is Nibbāna, the very non-arising of craving, the danger of which has been thus seen. 'Heedful' means one who acts continuously and carefully. 'Not stammering, not dull' means one whose mouth does not drool. Alternatively, it means one who is neither stammering nor dull, that is to say, wise and eloquent. 'Learned' means one who has heard what leads to welfare and happiness; it is said to be one endowed with the sacred texts. 'Mindful' means one who recollects what was done long ago and so forth. 'One who has comprehended the Dhamma' means one who has fully understood the Dhamma through investigation of the Dhamma. 'Certain of liberation' means one who has attained certainty through the Noble Path. 'Endowed with effort' means one endowed with the energy of right effort. This passage should be connected in reverse order. Thus, endowed with these qualities—heedfulness and so on—one is 'endowed with effort' by means of the effort that brings certainty; by reaching certainty through that effort, one is 'certain of liberation'; and then, by attaining Arahantship, one is 'one who has comprehended the Dhamma'. For an Arahant, since there is nothing further to be comprehended, is called 'one who has comprehended the Dhamma'. As it is said: 'Those who have comprehended the Dhamma, and the various trainees here.' The rest is to be understood in the same way as explained.

Taṇhakkhayagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the verse on the destruction of craving is concluded.

71. Sīho vāti kā uppatti? Aññatarassa kira bārāṇasirañño dūre uyyānaṃ hoti. So pageva vuṭṭhāya uyyānaṃ gacchanto antarāmagge yānā oruyha udakaṭṭhānaṃ upagato “mukhaṃ [P 1.0125] dhovissāmī”ti. Tasmiñca padese sīhī potakaṃ janetvā gocarāya gatā. Rājapuriso taṃ disvā “sīhapotako devā”ti ārocesi. Rājā “sīho kira [M 1.0113] na kassaci bhāyatī”ti taṃ upaparikkhituṃ bheriādīni ākoṭāpesi. Sīhapotako taṃ saddaṃ sutvāpi tatheva sayi. Rājā yāvatatiyakaṃ ākoṭāpesi, so tatiyavāre sīsaṃ ukkhipitvā sabbaṃ parisaṃ oloketvā tatheva sayi. Atha rājā “yāvassa mātā nāgacchati, tāva gacchāmā”ti vatvā gacchanto cintesi – “taṃ divasaṃ jātopi sīhapotako na santasati na bhāyati, kudāssu nāmāhampi taṇhādiṭṭhiparitāsaṃ chetvā na santaseyyaṃ na bhāyeyya”nti. So taṃ ārammaṇaṃ gahetvā, gacchanto puna kevaṭṭehi macche gahetvā sākhāsu bandhitvā pasārite jāle vātaṃ alaggaṃyeva gacchamānaṃ disvā, tampi nimittaṃ aggahesi – “kudāssu nāmāhampi taṇhādiṭṭhijālaṃ mohajālaṃ vā phāletvā evaṃ asajjamāno gaccheyya”nti.

71. What is the origin of 'like a lion'? It is said that a certain king of Bārāṇasī had a distant park. Rising early, as he was going to the park, he descended from his chariot on the way and approached a watering place, thinking, 'I will wash my face.' At that very spot, a lioness had given birth to a cub and gone off to hunt. A royal servant saw it and reported, 'Your Majesty, a lion cub!' The king, thinking, 'They say a lion fears no one,' had drums and so forth beaten to test it. Hearing the sound, the lion cub remained lying still. The king had the drums beaten up to a third time. On the third occasion, the cub raised its head, looked around at the whole assembly, and lay back down. Then the king said, 'Let us go before its mother returns.' As he went, he reflected: 'Even on the very day of its birth, this lion cub does not tremble or fear. When will I too, having cut through the trembling of craving and wrong view, live without trembling or fear?' Taking this as his theme, he went on. Then, seeing the wind passing unhindered and not getting caught in a net spread out by fishermen who had caught fish and tied them to branches, he took that too as a sign: 'When will I too, having torn through the net of craving and wrong view, or the net of delusion, go forth thus unentangled?'

Atha uyyānaṃ gantvā silāpaṭṭapokkharaṇitīre nisinno vātabbhāhatāni padumāni onamitvā udakaṃ phusitvā vātavigame puna yathāṭhāne ṭhitāni udakena anupalittāni disvā tampi nimittaṃ aggahesi – “kudāssu nāmāhampi yathā etāni udake jātāni udakena anupalittāni tiṭṭhanti, evamevaṃ loke jāto lokena anupalitto tiṭṭheyya”nti. So punappunaṃ “yathā sīhavātapadumāni, evaṃ asantasantena asajjamānena anupalittena bhavitabba”nti cintetvā, rajjaṃ pahāya pabbajitvā, vipassanto paccekabodhiṃ sacchikatvā imaṃ udānagāthaṃ abhāsi –

Then, having gone to the park, he sat on the bank of the stone-slab pond. Seeing the lotuses battered by the wind bending down and touching the water, and when the wind subsided, standing upright again, unsoiled by the water, he grasped this sign: 'When indeed will I, just as these lotuses born in water stand unsoiled by the water, in the same way, born in the world, stand unsoiled by the world?' Again and again, he reflected: 'Just like the lion, the wind, and the lotuses, so must one be—unperturbed, unattached, unsoiled.' Having renounced the kingdom and gone forth, through insight he realized Paccekabodhi and uttered this inspired verse:

“Sīhova [V 1.0100] saddesu asantasanto, vātova jālamhi asajjamāno;

Padumaṃva toyena alippamāno, eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”ti.

“Like a lion not trembling at sounds, like the wind not caught in a net, like a lotus unstained by water, one should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.”

Tattha sīhoti cattāro sīhā – tiṇasīho, paṇḍusīho, kāḷasīho, kesarasīhoti. Kesarasīho tesaṃ aggamakkhāyati. Sova idha adhippeto. Vāto puratthimādivasena anekavidho, padumaṃ rattasetādivasena. Tesu yo koci vāto yaṃkiñci padumañca vaṭṭatiyeva. Tattha yasmā santāso attasinehena hoti, attasineho ca taṇhālepo, sopi diṭṭhisampayuttena vā diṭṭhivippayuttena vā lobhena [M 1.0114] hoti, so ca taṇhāyeva. Sajjanaṃ pana tattha upaparikkhāvirahitassa mohena hoti, moho [P 1.0126] ca avijjā. Tattha samathena taṇhāya pahānaṃ hoti, vipassanāya, avijjāya. Tasmā samathena attasinehaṃ pahāya sīhova saddesu aniccādīsu asantasanto, vipassanāya mohaṃ pahāya vātova jālamhi khandhāyatanādīsu asajjamāno, samatheneva lobhaṃ lobhasampayuttaṃ eva diṭṭhiñca pahāya, padumaṃva toyena sabbabhavabhogalobhena alippamāno. Ettha ca samathassa sīlaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ, samatho samādhi, vipassanā paññāti. Evaṃ tesu dvīsu dhammesu siddhesu tayopi khandhā siddhā honti. Tattha sīlakkhandhena surato hoti. So sīhova saddesu āghātavatthūsu kujjhitukāmatāya na santasati. Paññākkhandhena paṭividdhasabhāvo vātova jālamhi khandhādidhammabhede na sajjati, samādhikkhandhena vītarāgo padumaṃva toyena rāgena na lippati. Evaṃ samathavipassanāhi sīlasamādhipaññākkhandhehi ca yathāsambhavaṃ avijjātaṇhānaṃ tiṇṇañca akusalamūlānaṃ pahānavasena asantasanto asajjamāno alippamāno ca veditabbo. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti.

Here, 'lion' refers to four kinds of lions: the grass-lion, the pale-lion, the black-lion, and the maned-lion. The maned-lion is said to be the foremost among them. It is this one that is intended here. The wind is of many kinds, such as the east wind and others, just as the lotus is of many kinds, like the red lotus and the white lotus. Among them, any kind of wind and any kind of lotus is applicable. Here, agitation arises from self-affection, and self-affection is a defilement of craving. And that arises from greed, whether associated with views or dissociated from views; and that is indeed craving. Clinging, however, arises there in one devoid of investigation due to delusion, and delusion is ignorance. Here, the abandoning of craving occurs through serenity, and the abandoning of ignorance through insight. Therefore, having abandoned self-affection through serenity, like a lion not trembling at sounds, one does not tremble when contemplating impermanence and so forth; and having abandoned delusion through insight, like the wind not clinging to the net of aggregates, sense bases, and so forth, one abandons greed, and views associated with greed, through serenity alone—just as a lotus is untainted by water, so one remains unstained by all greed for existence and enjoyment. And in this context, virtue is the proximate cause for serenity, serenity has concentration as its proximate cause, and insight has wisdom as its proximate cause. Thus, when these two qualities are accomplished, the three aggregates are also accomplished. Here, through the aggregate of virtue, one becomes courageous. Like a lion not trembling at sounds, one does not tremble with the desire to become angry at the grounds for resentment. Through the aggregate of wisdom, one has penetrated the true nature of things and, like the wind in a net, does not cling to the diversity of phenomena such as the aggregates and so forth. Through the aggregate of concentration, one is free from lust and, like a lotus untainted by water, is not stained by lust. Thus, through serenity and insight, and through the aggregates of virtue, concentration, and wisdom, by way of abandoning ignorance, craving, and the three unwholesome roots as is appropriate, one should be understood as not trembling, not clinging, and not stained. The rest should be understood in the same way as previously stated.

Asantasantagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the verse on not trembling is complete.

72. Sīho yathāti kā uppatti? Aññataro kira bārāṇasirājā paccantaṃ kuppitaṃ vūpasametuṃ gāmānugāmimaggaṃ chaḍḍetvā, ujuṃ aṭavimaggaṃ gahetvā, mahatiyā senāya gacchati. Tena ca samayena aññatarasmiṃ pabbatapāde sīho bālasūriyātapaṃ tappamāno nipanno hoti. Taṃ disvā rājapuriso rañño ārocesi. Rājā “sīho kira saddena na santasatī”ti bherisaṅkhapaṇavādīhi saddaṃ kārāpesi. Sīho tatheva nipajji. Dutiyampi kārāpesi. Sīho tatheva nipajji. Tatiyampi kārāpesi. Sīho “mama paṭisattu atthī”ti catūhi pādehi suppatiṭṭhitaṃ patiṭṭhahitvā sīhanādaṃ nadi. Taṃ sutvāva hatthārohādayo hatthiādīhi orohitvā [P 1.0127] tiṇagahanāni paviṭṭhā, hatthiassagaṇā disāvidisā palātā. Rañño hatthīpi rājānaṃ gahetvā vanagahanāni [V 1.0101] pothayamāno palāyi. So taṃ sandhāretuṃ asakkonto rukkhasākhāya olambitvā[M 1.0115], pathaviṃ patitvā, ekapadikamaggena gacchanto paccekabuddhānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ pāpuṇitvā tattha paccekabuddhe pucchi – “api, bhante, saddamassutthā”ti? “Āma, mahārājā”ti. “Kassa saddaṃ, bhante”ti? “Paṭhamaṃ bherisaṅkhādīnaṃ, pacchā sīhassā”ti. “Na bhāyittha, bhante”ti? “Na mayaṃ, mahārāja, kassaci saddassa bhāyāmā”ti. “Sakkā pana, bhante, mayhampi edisaṃ kātu”nti? “Sakkā, mahārāja, sace pabbajasī”ti. “Pabbajāmi, bhante”ti. Tato naṃ pabbājetvā pubbe vuttanayeneva ābhisamācārikaṃ sikkhāpesuṃ. Sopi pubbe vuttanayeneva vipassanto paccekabodhiṃ sacchikatvā imaṃ udānagāthaṃ abhāsi –

72. How did the verse 'Like a lion' originate? It is said that a certain king of Bārāṇasī, in order to quell a rebellion in a border region, abandoned the village-to-village route and took a direct forest path, traveling with a large army. At that time, a lion lay basking in the warmth of the morning sun at the foot of a certain mountain. Seeing this, a king's man informed the king. The king, thinking, 'It is said that a lion does not tremble at sound,' had drums, conches, and kettledrums sounded. The lion remained lying just as it was. A second time he had them sounded. The lion still lay just as it was. A third time he had them sounded. The lion, thinking, 'I have an adversary,' stood firmly on all four feet and roared a lion's roar. Upon hearing it, elephant riders and others dismounted from their elephants and other mounts and entered the thickets of grass, while troops of elephants and horses scattered in all directions. Even the king's own elephant, carrying the king, crashed through the jungle thickets and fled. Unable to control it, he clung to a tree branch, fell to the ground, and proceeding by a single-file path, reached the dwelling place of the Paccekabuddhas. There he asked the Paccekabuddhas, 'Venerable sirs, did you hear a sound?' 'Yes, great king.' 'Whose sound, venerable sirs?' 'First that of the drums, conches, and the like, then the lion's.' 'Were you not afraid, venerable sirs?' 'We, great king, are not afraid of any sound.' 'Is it possible for me too, venerable sirs, to achieve such a state?' 'It is possible, great king, if you go forth.' 'I will go forth, venerable sirs.' Then they gave him the going forth and instructed him in the proper conduct, as previously described. He too, practicing insight as before, realized Paccekabodhi and uttered this inspired verse:

“Sīho yathā dāṭhabalī pasayha, rājā migānaṃ abhibhuyya cārī;

Sevetha pantāni senāsanāni, eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”ti.

As a lion, strong of fang, the king of beasts, roams having overcome by force; so should one frequent secluded lodgings, and wander alone, like a rhinoceros horn.

Tattha sahanā ca hananā ca sīghajavattā ca sīho. Kesarasīhova idha adhippeto. Dāṭhā balamassa atthīti dāṭhabalī. Pasayha abhibhuyyāti, ubhayaṃ cārīsaddena saha yojetabbaṃ pasayhacārī abhibhuyyacārīti tattha pasayha niggahetvā caraṇena pasayhacārī, abhibhavitvā, santāsetvā, vasīkatvā, caraṇena abhibhuyyacārī. Svāyaṃ kāyabalena pasayhacārī, tejasā abhibhuyyacārī. Tattha sace koci vadeyya – “kiṃ pasayha abhibhuyya cārī”ti, tato migānanti sāmivacanaṃ upayogavacanaṃ katvā “mige pasayha abhibhuyya cārī”ti paṭivattabbaṃ. Pantānīti dūrāni. Senāsanānīti vasanaṭṭhānāni. Sesaṃ pubbe vuttanayeneva sakkā jānitunti na vitthāritanti.

Therein, a 'sīha' (lion) is so called because of its endurance (sahanā), its killing (hananā), and its swiftness (sīghajavattā). It is the maned lion that is intended here. 'Dāṭhabalī' (strong of fang) means one for whom fangs are its strength. As for 'pasayha abhibhuyya' (by force, having overcome), both should be combined with the word 'cārī' (roaming), thus forming 'pasayhacārī' (roaming by force) and 'abhibhuyyacārī' (roaming by overcoming). Therein, 'pasayhacārī' means roaming by restraining and subduing; 'abhibhuyyacārī' means roaming by overpowering, terrifying, and mastering. This lion is 'pasayhacārī' by bodily strength, and 'abhibhuyyacārī' by majesty. Therein, if someone were to ask, 'What does it roam overcoming by force?' then, taking 'migānaṃ' (of beasts) from the genitive case to the objective case, one should reply, 'It roams overcoming the beasts by force.' 'Pantāni' means distant. 'Senāsanāni' means dwelling places. The rest can be understood in the same way as previously explained and is therefore not elaborated upon.

Dāṭhabalīgāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Dāṭhabalī verse is complete.

73. Mettaṃ upekkhanti kā uppatti? Aññataro kira rājā mettādijhānalābhī ahosi. So “jhānasukhantarāyakaraṃ rajja”nti jhānānurakkhaṇatthaṃ [P 1.0128] rajjaṃ pahāya pabbajitvā vipassanto paccekabodhiṃ sacchikatvā, imaṃ udānagāthaṃ abhāsi –

73. How did the verse 'Loving-kindness, equanimity' originate? It is said that a certain king was an attainer of the jhānas beginning with loving-kindness. Thinking, 'Kingship is an obstacle to the bliss of jhāna,' he renounced his kingdom to protect his jhāna, went forth, and while practicing insight, realized Paccekabodhi. Then he uttered this inspired verse:

Mettaṃ [M 1.0116] upekkhaṃ karuṇaṃ vimuttiṃ, āsevamāno muditañca kāle;

Sabbena lokena avirujjhamāno, eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”ti.

Cultivating loving-kindness, equanimity, compassion, and liberation, and sympathetic joy at the proper time; not conflicting with the entire world, one should wander alone, like a rhinoceros horn.

Tattha “sabbe sattā sukhitā hontū”tiādinā nayena hitasukhupanayanakāmatā mettā. “Aho [V 1.0102] vata imamhā dukkhā vimucceyyu”ntiādinā nayena ahitadukkhāpanayanakāmatā karuṇā. “Modanti vata bhonto sattā modanti sādhu suṭṭhū”tiādinā nayena hitasukhāvippayogakāmatā muditā. “Paññāyissanti sakena kammenā”ti sukhadukkhesu ajjhupekkhanatā upekkhā. Gāthābandhasukhatthaṃ pana uppaṭipāṭiyā mettaṃ vatvā upekkhā vuttā, muditā pacchā. Vimuttinti catassopi hi etā attano paccanīkadhammehi vimuttattā vimuttiyo. Tena vuttaṃ “mettaṃ upekkhaṃ karuṇaṃ, vimuttiṃ, āsevamāno muditañca kāle”ti.

Therein, mettā (loving-kindness) is the desire to bring about welfare and happiness, in the manner of 'May all beings be happy.' Karuṇā (compassion) is the desire to remove what is not welfare and is suffering, in the manner of 'Oh, may they be freed from this suffering!' Muditā (sympathetic joy) is the desire for non-separation from welfare and happiness, in the manner of 'Sirs, beings are rejoicing! They rejoice! It is good, it is excellent!' Upekkhā (equanimity) is looking on with neutrality at happiness and suffering, thinking, 'They will be known by their own kamma.' However, for the sake of ease in composing the verse, after stating loving-kindness, equanimity is stated out of order, and sympathetic joy afterwards. As for 'vimutti' (liberation): all four of these are indeed liberations because they are liberated from their opposing states. Therefore it was said: 'Cultivating loving-kindness, equanimity, compassion, and liberation, and sympathetic joy at the proper time.'

Tattha āsevamānoti tisso tikacatukkajjhānavasena, upekkhaṃ catutthajjhānavasena bhāvayamāno. Kāleti mettaṃ āsevitvā tato vuṭṭhāya karuṇaṃ, tato vuṭṭhāya muditaṃ, tato itarato vā nippītikajhānato vuṭṭhāya upekkhaṃ āsevamāno “kāle āsevamāno”ti vuccati, āsevituṃ phāsukāle vā. Sabbena lokena avirujjhamānoti dasasu disāsu sabbena sattalokena avirujjhamāno. Mettādīnañhi bhāvitattā sattā appaṭikūlā honti. Sattesu ca virodhabhūto paṭigho vūpasammati. Tena vuttaṃ – “sabbena lokena avirujjhamāno”ti. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthārena pana mettādikathā aṭṭhasāliniyā dhammasaṅgahaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 251) vuttā. Sesaṃ pubbavuttasadisamevāti.

Therein, 'cultivating' means developing the three states by means of the jhānas of the three-fold and four-fold systems, and equanimity by means of the fourth jhāna. 'At the proper time' refers to one who, having cultivated loving-kindness, then arises from that and cultivates compassion, then arises from that and cultivates sympathetic joy, or arises from that other jhāna devoid of joy and cultivates equanimity; such a one is called 'one who cultivates at the proper time.' Alternatively, it means at a time convenient for cultivation. 'Not conflicting with the entire world' means not conflicting with the entire world of beings in the ten directions. For when loving-kindness and the other states have been developed, beings become non-repulsive. And towards beings, aversion, which is the basis of conflict, subsides. Therefore it was said: 'not conflicting with the entire world.' This is the summary here. The discussion of loving-kindness and the other states, however, is given in detail in the Aṭṭhasālinī, the commentary on the Dhammasaṅgaṇī. The rest is just as stated before.

Appamaññāgāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the verse on the illimitables is complete.

74. Rāgañca dosañcāti kā uppatti? Rājagahaṃ kira upanissāya mātaṅgo nāma paccekabuddho viharati sabbapacchimo [P 1.0129] paccekabuddhānaṃ. Atha amhākaṃ bodhisatte uppanne devatāyo bodhisattassa pūjanatthāya āgacchantiyo taṃ disvā “mārisā, mārisā, buddho loke uppanno”ti bhaṇiṃsu[M 1.0117]. So nirodhā vuṭṭhahanto taṃ saddaṃ sutvā, attano ca jīvitakkhayaṃ disvā, himavante mahāpapāto nāma pabbato paccekabuddhānaṃ parinibbānaṭṭhānaṃ, tattha ākāsena gantvā pubbe parinibbutapaccekabuddhassa aṭṭhisaṅghātaṃ papāte pakkhipitvā, silātale nisīditvā imaṃ udānagāthaṃ abhāsi –

74. What is the origin of [the verse beginning,] 'Lust and hatred...'? It is said that near Rājagaha there lived a Paccekabuddha named Mātaṅga, the very last of the Paccekabuddhas. Then, when our Bodhisatta had arisen, deities, coming for the purpose of honoring the Bodhisatta, saw him and said, 'Sirs, sirs, a Buddha has arisen in the world!' He, while rising from cessation, having heard that sound and having seen the exhaustion of his own life, went through the sky to the Himavanta, to a mountain named Mahāpapāta, the place of the final Nibbāna of Paccekabuddhas. There, having cast the collection of bones of a previously passed-away Paccekabuddha into the precipice, he sat on a stone slab and uttered this inspired verse:

“Rāgañca dosañca pahāya mohaṃ, sandālayitvāna saṃyojanāni;

Asantasaṃ jīvitasaṅkhayamhi, eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”ti.

Having abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion, having shattered the fetters; not trembling at the exhaustion of life, one should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.

Tattha rāgadosamohā uragasutte vuttā. Saṃyojanānīti dasa saṃyojanāni. Tāni ca tena tena [V 1.0103] maggena sandālayitvā. Asantasaṃ jīvitasaṅkhayamhīti jīvitasaṅkhayo vuccati cuticittassa paribhedo, tasmiñca jīvitasaṅkhaye jīvitanikantiyā pahīnattā asantasanti. Ettāvatā sopādisesaṃ nibbānadhātuṃ attano dassetvā gāthāpariyosāne anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbāyīti.

Therein, lust, hatred, and delusion are as spoken of in the Uraga Sutta. 'Fetters' means the ten fetters. And these are shattered by their respective paths. As for 'not trembling at the exhaustion of life': the exhaustion of life is said to be the breaking up of the death-consciousness. And in that exhaustion of life, because craving for life has been abandoned, one is said to be 'not trembling'. By this much, having shown his own Nibbāna-element with residue remaining, at the conclusion of the verse, he attained final Nibbāna with the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining.

Jīvitasaṅkhayagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the verse on the exhaustion of life is complete.

75. Bhajantīti kā uppatti? Bārāṇasiyaṃ kira aññataro rājā ādigāthāya vuttappakārameva phītaṃ rajjaṃ samanusāsati. Tassa kharo ābādho uppajji, dukkhā vedanā vattanti. Vīsatisahassitthiyo parivāretvā hatthapādasambāhanādīni karonti. Amaccā “na dānāyaṃ rājā jīvissati, handa mayaṃ attano saraṇaṃ gavesāmā”ti cintetvā aññassa rañño santikaṃ gantvā upaṭṭhānaṃ yāciṃsu. Te tattha upaṭṭhahantiyeva, na kiñci labhanti. Rājāpi ābādhā vuṭṭhahitvā pucchi “itthannāmo ca itthannāmo ca kuhi”nti? Tato taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā sīsaṃ cāletvā tuṇhī ahosi. Tepi amaccā “rājā vuṭṭhito”ti sutvā tattha kiñci alabhamānā paramena pārijuññena samannāgatā punadeva āgantvā rājānaṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhaṃsu. Tena ca raññā [P 1.0130] “kuhiṃ, tātā, tumhe gatā”ti vuttā āhaṃsu – “devaṃ dubbalaṃ disvā ājīvikabhayenamhā asukaṃ nāma janapadaṃ gatā”ti. Rājā [M 1.0118] sīsaṃ cāletvā cintesi – “yaṃnūnāhaṃ ime vīmaṃseyyaṃ, kiṃ punapi evaṃ kareyyuṃ no”ti? So pubbe ābādhikarogena phuṭṭho viya bāḷhavedanaṃ attānaṃ dassento gilānālayaṃ akāsi. Itthiyo samparivāretvā pubbasadisameva sabbaṃ akaṃsu. Tepi amaccā tatheva puna bahutaraṃ janaṃ gahetvā pakkamiṃsu. Evaṃ rājā yāvatatiyaṃ sabbaṃ pubbasadisaṃ akāsi. Tepi tatheva pakkamiṃsu. Tato catutthampi te āgate disvā “aho ime dukkaraṃ akaṃsu, ye maṃ byādhitaṃ pahāya anapekkhā pakkamiṃsū”ti nibbinno rajjaṃ pahāya pabbajitvā vipassanto paccekabodhiṃ sacchikatvā imaṃ udānagāthaṃ abhāsi –

75. What is the origin of [the verse beginning,] 'Bhajanti...'? It is said that in Bārāṇasī, a certain king ruled a prosperous kingdom just as described in the first verse. A severe illness arose in him, and painful feelings afflicted him. Twenty thousand women surrounded him, massaging his hands and feet and so on. The ministers thought, 'This king will not live now. Come, let us seek a refuge for ourselves.' Thinking thus, they went to another king and requested to serve him. While they were serving there, they received nothing. The king, having recovered from his illness, asked, 'Where are so-and-so and so-and-so?' Then, having heard what had happened, he shook his head and became silent. Those ministers, too, hearing 'The king has recovered,' and receiving nothing there, being overcome with the utmost dejection, came back again, paid homage to the king, and stood to one side. When they were asked by the king, 'Where did you go, my good sirs?' they said, 'Your Majesty, seeing you were weak, we went to such-and-such a country out of fear for our livelihood.' The king shook his head and thought, 'What if I were to test them? Would they do so again or not?' So, showing himself to have intense feelings of pain as if afflicted by his former illness, he took to his sickbed. The women surrounded him and did everything just as before. Those ministers, too, just as before, taking even more people, departed again. In this way, the king did everything just as before up to a third time. They too departed just as before. Then, seeing them when they had come for a fourth time, he thought, 'Ah, these men have done a difficult thing! They abandoned me when I was sick and departed without concern.' Becoming disenchanted, he renounced the kingdom, went forth, and while practicing insight meditation, he realized Paccekabodhi and uttered this inspired verse:

“Bhajanti sevanti ca kāraṇatthā, nikkāraṇā dullabhā ajja mittā;

Attaṭṭhapaññā asucī manussā, eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”ti.

They associate and they serve for a reason; friends without a reason are rare today. Humans have wisdom for their own benefit and are impure; one should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.

Tattha bhajantīti sarīrena allīyitvā payirupāsanti. Sevantīti añjalikammādīhi kiṃ kārapaṭissāvitāya ca paricaranti. Kāraṇaṃ attho etesanti kāraṇatthā, bhajanāya sevanāya ca nāññaṃ kāraṇamatthi, attho eva nesaṃ kāraṇaṃ, atthahetu sevantīti vuttaṃ hoti. Nikkāraṇā [V 1.0104] dullabhā ajja mittāti “ito kiñci lacchāmā”ti evaṃ attapaṭilābhakāraṇena nikkāraṇā, kevalaṃ –

Therein, 'bhajanti' means they attend upon by clinging with their bodies. 'Sevanti' means they serve with gestures such as the añjali and by being responsive to what is to be done. 'Kāraṇatthā' means those for whom a reason is a benefit. For their associating and serving there is no other reason; benefit alone is their reason. It is said that they serve for the sake of benefit. As for 'friends without a reason are rare today': `nikkāraṇā` means being without the reason of gaining for oneself, such as thinking, 'We shall obtain something from this.' Only—

“Upakāro ca yo mitto,

Sukhe dukkhe ca yo sakhā;

Atthakkhāyī ca yo mitto,

Yo ca mittānukampako”ti. (dī. ni. 3.265) –

A friend who is a helper, a companion in happiness and suffering, a friend who explains what is beneficial, and one who is compassionate towards friends.

Evaṃ vuttena ariyena mittabhāvena samannāgatā dullabhā ajja mittā. Attani ṭhitā etesaṃ paññā, attānaṃyeva olokenti, na aññanti attaṭṭhapaññā. Diṭṭhatthapaññāti ayampi [P 1.0131] kira porāṇapāṭho, sampati diṭṭhiyeva atthe etesaṃ paññā, āyatiṃ na pekkhantīti vuttaṃ hoti. Asucīti [M 1.0119] asucinā anariyena kāyavacīmanokammena samannāgatā. Sesaṃ pubbe vuttanayeneva veditabbanti.

Friends endowed with such a noble state of friendship as has been described are rare today. As for 'wisdom for their own benefit' (`attaṭṭhapaññā`): their wisdom is established in themselves; they look only to themselves, not to another. 'Wisdom for the visible benefit' (`diṭṭhatthapaññā`) is also, it seems, an ancient reading; this means their wisdom is only in the present, visible benefit; they do not regard the future. 'Impure' (`asucī`) means they are endowed with impure, ignoble bodily, verbal, and mental action. The rest should be understood in the same way as previously stated.

Kāraṇatthagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Kāraṇattha verse is complete.

Catuttho vaggo niṭṭhito ekādasahi gāthāhi.

The fourth chapter, with eleven verses, is finished.

Evametaṃ ekacattālīsagāthāparimāṇaṃ khaggavisāṇasuttaṃ katthacideva vuttena yojanānayena sabbattha yathānurūpaṃ yojetvā anusandhito atthato ca veditabbaṃ. Ativitthārabhayena pana amhehi na sabbattha yojitanti.

Thus this Khaggavisāṇa Sutta, measuring forty-one verses, should be understood in terms of its sequence and meaning by applying it appropriately everywhere according to the method of application stated in certain places. However, out of fear of excessive detail, it has not been applied by us everywhere.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the commentary on the Khuddaka Collection,

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya khaggavisāṇasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

in the commentary on the Suttanipāta, the explanation of the Khaggavisāṇa Sutta is finished.

4. Kasibhāradvājasuttavaṇṇanā

4. The Explanation of the Kasibhāradvāja Sutta

Evaṃ [V 1.0105] me sutanti kasibhāradvājasuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Bhagavā magadhesu viharanto dakkhiṇāgirismiṃ ekanālāyaṃ brāhmaṇagāme purebhattakiccaṃ pacchābhattakiccanti imesu dvīsu buddhakiccesu purebhattakiccaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā pacchābhattakiccāvasāne buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ volokento kasibhāradvājaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ arahattassa upanissayasampannaṃ disvā “tattha mayi gate yathā pavattissati, tato kathāvasāne dhammadesanaṃ sutvā esa brāhmaṇo pabbajitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇissatī”ti ca ñatvā, tattha gantvā, kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā, imaṃ suttaṃ abhāsi.

Thus have I heard: the Kasibhāradvāja Sutta. What is its origin? The Blessed One, while dwelling in the Magadha country, in the southern hills, in the brahmin village of Ekanālā, having completed the forenoon duty, at the conclusion of the after-meal duty—these being the two duties of a Buddha—surveying the world with the Buddha’s eye, saw the brahmin Kasibhāradvāja, who was endowed with the supporting conditions for arahantship. He considered, “When I go there, a conversation will arise; then, at the end of the conversation, after hearing the Dhamma teaching, this brahmin will go forth and attain arahantship.” And knowing this, he went there, initiated the conversation, and delivered this sutta.

Tattha siyā “katamaṃ buddhānaṃ purebhattakiccaṃ, katamaṃ pacchābhattakicca”nti? Vuccate – buddho bhagavā pāto eva uṭṭhāya upaṭṭhākānuggahatthaṃ sarīraphāsukatthañca mukhadhovanādisarīraparikammaṃ katvā yāva bhikkhācāravelā, tāva vivittāsane vītināmetvā, bhikkhācāravelāya [P 1.0132] nivāsetvā, kāyabandhanaṃ bandhitvā, cīvaraṃ pārupitvā, pattamādāya kadāci ekakova kadāci bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā piṇḍāya pavisati, kadāci pakatiyā, kadāci anekehi [M 1.0120] pāṭihāriyehi vattamānehi. Seyyathidaṃ – piṇḍāya pavisato lokanāthassa purato purato gantvā mudugatiyo vātā pathaviṃ sodhenti; valāhakā udakaphusitāni muñcantā magge reṇuṃ vūpasametvā upari vitānaṃ hutvā tiṭṭhanti. Apare vātā pupphāni upasaṃharitvā magge okiranti, unnatā bhūmippadesā onamanti, onatā unnamanti, pādanikkhepasamaye samāva bhūmi hoti, sukhasamphassāni rathacakkamattāni padumapupphāni vā pāde sampaṭicchanti, indakhīlassa anto ṭhapitamatte dakkhiṇapāde sarīrā chabbaṇṇarasmiyo niccharitvā suvaṇṇarasapiñjarāni viya citrapaṭaparikkhittāni viya ca pāsādakūṭāgārādīni karontiyo ito cito ca vidhāvanti, hatthiassavihaṅgādayo sakasakaṭṭhānesu ṭhitāyeva madhurenākārena saddaṃ karonti, tathā bherivīṇādīni tūriyāni manussānaṃ kāyūpagāni ca ābharaṇāni, tena saññāṇena manussā jānanti “ajja bhagavā idha piṇḍāya paviṭṭho”ti. Te sunivatthā supārutā gandhapupphādīni ādāya gharā nikkhamitvā antaravīthiṃ paṭipajjitvā bhagavantaṃ gandhapupphādīhi sakkaccaṃ pūjetvā vanditvā – “amhākaṃ[V 1.0106], bhante, dasa bhikkhū, amhākaṃ vīsati, amhākaṃ bhikkhusataṃ dethā”ti yācitvā bhagavatopi pattaṃ gahetvā, āsanaṃ paññāpetvā sakkaccaṃ piṇḍapātena paṭimānenti.

Here, one might ask: "What are the duties of the Buddhas before the meal, and what are those after?" It is said—the Blessed One, the Buddha, rises early in the morning and, for the sake of attending to his attendants and for bodily comfort, performs the morning routines such as washing his face and tending to his body. Then, until the time for the almsround arrives, he spends time in seclusion on his seat. When the time for the almsround comes, he puts on his lower robe, fastens his belt, drapes his upper robe, takes his bowl, and sometimes enters the village or town alone for alms, sometimes surrounded by the Sangha of monks. Occasionally, he goes in the usual manner, and at other times, with many miracles occurring. For example—when the Protector of the World enters for alms, gentle winds go before him, sweeping the ground clean. Clouds sprinkle water droplets, settling the dust on the path, while above, they form a canopy. Other winds gather flowers and scatter them along the path. High ground lowers, and low ground rises; wherever he places his foot, the earth becomes even. Lotus flowers the size of chariot wheels, pleasant to the touch, receive his feet. When his right foot is placed within the threshold, six-colored rays emanate from his body, making the palaces, pinnacles, and houses appear as if smeared with liquid gold or covered with painted cloths, as they dart here and there. Elephants, horses, birds, and other creatures, though remaining in their places, produce sweet sounds. Likewise, drums, lutes, and other musical instruments, as well as the ornaments on people’s bodies, resound. By these signs, people know: "Today, the Blessed One has entered here for alms." Well-dressed and well-covered, they take perfumes and flowers, leave their homes, and go to the street. They reverently honor the Blessed One with perfumes and flowers, pay homage, and request: "Venerable sir, give us ten monks, give us twenty, give us a hundred monks!" Then, taking the Blessed One’s bowl, they prepare a seat and respectfully honor him with almsfood.

Bhagavā katabhattakicco tesaṃ santānāni oloketvā tathā dhammaṃ deseti, yathā keci saraṇagamane patiṭṭhahanti, keci pañcasu sīlesu, keci sotāpattisakadāgāmianāgāmiphalānaṃ aññatarasmiṃ, keci pabbajitvā aggaphale arahatteti. Evaṃ tathā tathā janaṃ anuggahetvā uṭṭhāyāsanā vihāraṃ gacchati. Tattha maṇḍalamāḷe paññattavarabuddhāsane nisīdati bhikkhūnaṃ bhattakiccapariyosānaṃ āgamayamāno. Tato bhikkhūnaṃ bhattakiccapariyosāne upaṭṭhāko [P 1.0133] bhagavato nivedeti. Atha bhagavā gandhakuṭiṃ pavisati. Idaṃ tāva purebhattakiccaṃ. Yañcettha na vuttaṃ, taṃ brahmāyusutte vuttanayeneva gahetabbaṃ.

The Blessed One, having finished His meal, observes their dispositions and teaches the Dhamma accordingly—so that some are established in taking refuge, some in the five precepts, some in one of the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, or non-returning, and some, having gone forth, in the supreme fruit, that is, arahantship. Thus, having benefited people in these various ways, He rises from His seat and goes to the monastery. There, in the circular pavilion, He sits on the prepared excellent Buddha-seat, waiting for the monks to finish their meal. When the monks have finished their meal, the attendant informs the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One enters the Fragrant Cottage. This, for now, is the forenoon duty. Whatever is not mentioned here should be understood in the way explained in the Brahmāyu Sutta.

Atha bhagavā evaṃ katapurebhattakicco gandhakuṭiyā upaṭṭhāne nisīditvā, pāde pakkhāletvā, pādapīṭhe ṭhatvā, bhikkhusaṅghaṃ ovadati – “bhikkhave, appamādena sampādetha, buddhuppādo dullabho lokasmiṃ, manussapaṭilābho dullabho, saddhāsampatti dullabhā, pabbajjā dullabhā, saddhammassavanaṃ dullabhaṃ [M 1.0121] lokasmi”nti. Tato bhikkhū bhagavantaṃ vanditvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ pucchanti. Atha bhagavā bhikkhūnaṃ cariyavasena kammaṭṭhānaṃ deti. Te kammaṭṭhānaṃ uggahetvā, bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā, attano attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gacchanti; keci araññaṃ, keci rukkhamūlaṃ, keci pabbatādīnaṃ aññataraṃ, keci cātumahārājikabhavanaṃ…pe… keci vasavattibhavananti. Tato bhagavā gandhakuṭiṃ pavisitvā sace ākaṅkhati, dakkhiṇena passena sato sampajāno muhuttaṃ sīhaseyyaṃ kappeti. Atha samassāsitakāyo uṭṭhahitvā dutiyabhāge lokaṃ voloketi. Tatiyabhāge yaṃ gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā upanissāya viharati, tattha jano purebhattaṃ dānaṃ datvā pacchābhattaṃ sunivattho supāruto gandhapupphādīni ādāya vihāre sannipatati. Tato bhagavā sampattaparisāya anurūpena pāṭihāriyena gantvā dhammasabhāyaṃ paññattavarabuddhāsane nisajja dhammaṃ deseti kālayuttaṃ pamāṇayuttaṃ. Atha kālaṃ viditvā parisaṃ uyyojeti.

Then the Blessed One, having completed his forenoon duties, sat down in the assembly hall of the fragrant cottage. Having washed his feet and standing on the footstool, he exhorted the Sangha of monks: “Monks, strive with heedfulness! The arising of a Buddha is rare in the world, obtaining a human birth is rare, attainment of faith is rare, going forth is rare, and hearing the true Dhamma is rare in the world.” Then the monks paid homage to the Blessed One and asked for meditation subjects. Thereupon the Blessed One gave the monks meditation subjects according to their dispositions. Having taken up their meditation subjects, they paid homage to the Blessed One and went to their respective dwelling places—some to the forest, some to the foot of a tree, some to one of the mountains and so on, some to the realm of the Four Great Kings... up to... some to the realm of Vasavatti. Then the Blessed One entered the fragrant cottage and, if he wished, mindfully and with clear comprehension, he adopted the lion’s posture on his right side for a short while. Then, his body refreshed, he would rise and survey the world in the second part of the day. In the third part, in whatever village or town he was residing near, the people, having given alms in the forenoon, would gather at the monastery in the afternoon, well-dressed and well-covered, bringing perfumes and flowers. Then the Blessed One would go to the Dhamma hall for the assembled congregation by means of a suitable miracle. Seated on the prepared excellent Buddha-seat, he would teach the Dhamma, suitable to the time and in due measure. Then, knowing the time, he would dismiss the assembly.

Tato sace gattāni osiñcitukāmo hoti. Atha buddhāsanā uṭṭhāya upaṭṭhākena udakapaṭiyāditokāsaṃ gantvā, upaṭṭhākahatthato udakasāṭikaṃ gahetvā, nhānakoṭṭhakaṃ pavisati. Upaṭṭhākopi buddhāsanaṃ ānetvā gandhakuṭipariveṇe paññāpeti. Bhagavā gattāni osiñcitvā, surattadupaṭṭaṃ nivāsetvā[P 1.0134], kāyabandhanaṃ bandhitvā, uttarāsaṅgaṃ katvā, tattha āgantvā, nisīdati ekakova muhuttaṃ paṭisallīno. Atha bhikkhū tato tato āgamma bhagavato upaṭṭhānaṃ gacchanti. Tattha [V 1.0107] ekacce pañhaṃ pucchanti, ekacce kammaṭṭhānaṃ, ekacce dhammassavanaṃ yācanti. Bhagavā tesaṃ adhippāyaṃ sampādento paṭhamaṃ yāmaṃ vītināmeti.

Thereafter, if he wishes to bathe his limbs, he rises from the Buddha-seat, goes to the place prepared with water by the attendant, takes the bathing cloth from the attendant’s hand, and enters the bathing chamber. The attendant also brings the Buddha-seat and prepares it in the enclosure of the fragrant hut. The Blessed One, having bathed his limbs, puts on a well-dyed double-cloth, fastens the waistband, arranges the upper robe, and having come there, sits alone in seclusion for a moment. Then monks come from various places to attend upon the Blessed One. There, some ask questions, some request meditation subjects, and some ask to hear the Dhamma. The Blessed One, fulfilling their intentions, passes the first watch of the night.

Majjhimayāme sakaladasasahassilokadhātudevatāyo okāsaṃ labhamānā bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā pañhaṃ pucchanti yathābhisaṅkhataṃ antamaso caturakkharampi. Bhagavā tāsaṃ devatānaṃ pañhaṃ vissajjento majjhimayāmaṃ vītināmeti. Tato pacchimayāmaṃ cattāro bhāge katvā ekaṃ bhāgaṃ caṅkamaṃ adhiṭṭhāti, dutiyabhāgaṃ gandhakuṭiṃ pavisitvā dakkhiṇena passena sato sampajāno sīhaseyyaṃ kappeti, tatiyabhāgaṃ phalasamāpattiyā vītināmeti, catutthabhāgaṃ mahākaruṇāsamāpattiṃ pavisitvā buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ voloketi apparajakkhamahārajakkhādisattadassanatthaṃ. Idaṃ pacchābhattakiccaṃ.

In the middle watch, deities from the entire ten-thousandfold world system, obtaining an opportunity, approach the Blessed One and ask questions as they have prepared, even if only of four syllables. The Blessed One, answering the questions of those deities, passes the middle watch. Then, having divided the last watch into four parts, for one part he undertakes walking meditation; for the second part, having entered the fragrant hut, he assumes the lion's posture on his right side, mindful and fully aware; he passes the third part in the attainment of fruition; and for the fourth part, having entered the attainment of great compassion, he surveys the world with the Buddha-eye for the purpose of seeing beings with little dust, with much dust, and so on. This is the after-meal duty.

Evamimassa [M 1.0122] pacchābhattakiccassa lokavolokanasaṅkhāte catutthabhāgāvasāne buddhadhammasaṅghesu dānasīlauposathakammādīsu ca akatādhikāre katādhikāre ca anupanissayasampanne upanissayasampanne ca satte passituṃ buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ volokento kasibhāradvājaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ arahattassa upanissayasampannaṃ disvā “tattha mayi gate kathā pavattissati, tato kathāvasāne dhammadesanaṃ sutvā esa brāhmaṇo pabbajitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇissatī”ti ca ñatvā, tattha gantvā, kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā imaṃ suttamabhāsi.

Thus, at the end of the fourth part of this after-meal duty, designated as 'surveying the world,' while surveying the world with the Buddha-eye to see beings—those who have and have not made a meritorious aspiration with regard to the Buddha, Dhamma, and Sangha, and in giving, virtue, observance day duties, and so on, and those who are and are not endowed with the supporting condition—he saw the brahmin Kasibhāradvāja, who was endowed with the supporting condition for Arahantship. Having seen him, and knowing, 'When I have gone there, a conversation will take place. Then, at the end of the conversation, having heard the Dhamma teaching, this brahmin will go forth and attain Arahantship,' he went there, initiated a conversation, and spoke this Sutta.

Tattha evaṃ me sutantiādi āyasmatā ānandena paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikāle dhammasaṅgītiṃ karontena āyasmatā mahākassapattherena puṭṭhena pañcannaṃ arahantasatānaṃ vuttaṃ, “ahaṃ, kho, samaṇa kasāmi ca vapāmi cā”ti kasibhāradvājena vuttaṃ, “ahampi kho brāhmaṇa kasāmi [P 1.0135] ca vapāmi cā”tiādi bhagavatā vuttaṃ. Tadetaṃ sabbampi samodhānetvā “kasibhāradvājasutta”nti vuccati.

Therein, 'Thus have I heard,' and so on, was spoken by the Venerable Ānanda at the time of the First Great Council—while he was reciting the Dhamma, being questioned by the Venerable Mahākassapa Thera—to the five hundred Arahants. 'I, recluse, plow and sow,' was spoken by Kasibhāradvāja. 'I too, brahmin, plow and sow,' and so on, was spoken by the Blessed One. Having combined all this, it is called the 'Kasibhāradvāja Sutta.'

Tattha evanti ayaṃ ākāranidassanāvadhāraṇattho evaṃ-saddo. Ākāratthena hi etena etamatthaṃ dīpeti – nānānayanipuṇamanekajjhāsayasamuṭṭhānaṃ atthabyañjanasampannaṃ vividhapāṭihāriyaṃ dhammatthadesanāpaṭivedhagambhīraṃ sabbasattehi sakasakabhāsānurūpamupalakkhaṇiyasabhāvaṃ tassa bhagavato vacanaṃ, taṃ sabbākārena ko samattho viññātuṃ; atha, kho, “evaṃ me sutaṃ, mayāpi ekenākārena suta”nti. Nidassanatthena “nāhaṃ sayambhū, na mayā idaṃ sacchikata”nti attānaṃ parimocento “evaṃ me sutaṃ, mayā evaṃ suta”nti idāni vattabbaṃ sakalasuttaṃ nidasseti. Avadhāraṇatthena [V 1.0108] “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ bahussutānaṃ yadidaṃ ānando, gatimantānaṃ, satimantānaṃ, dhitimantānaṃ, upaṭṭhākānaṃ yadidaṃ ānando”ti (a. ni. 1.219-223) evaṃ bhagavatā pasatthabhāvānurūpaṃ attano dhāraṇabalaṃ dassento sattānaṃ sotukamyataṃ janeti “evaṃ me sutaṃ tañca atthato vā byañjanato vā anūnamanadhikaṃ, evameva, na aññathā daṭṭhabba”nti. Me sutanti ettha mayāsaddattho me-saddo, sotadvāraviññāṇattho sutasaddo. Tasmā evaṃ me sutanti evaṃ mayā sotaviññāṇapubbaṅgamāya viññāṇavīthiyā upadhāritanti vuttaṃ hoti.

Therein, this word 'evaṃ' has the meanings of manner, demonstration, and emphasis. By the meaning of 'manner', it reveals this meaning: The Blessed One's speech—skillful in diverse approaches, arising from varied inclinations, complete in meaning and phrasing, displaying manifold wonders, profound in Dhamma, meaning, teaching, and penetration, and of a nature to be understood by all beings according to their own languages—who is able to understand it in all its aspects? Rather, it means, 'Thus have I heard; I, too, have heard it in one particular manner.' By the meaning of 'demonstration', freeing himself with 'I am not self-originated, nor have I realized this myself,' he points to the entire Sutta now to be recited with 'Thus have I heard; thus was it heard by me.' By the meaning of 'emphasis', showing his own power of retention in accordance with the praise given by the Blessed One—'Monks, among my monk disciples who are learned, Ānanda is foremost; among those with good deportment, mindfulness, resolution, and among attendants, Ānanda is foremost' (a. ni. 1.219-223)—he generates in beings a desire to listen, implying: 'Thus have I heard, and it should be regarded as neither deficient nor excessive in meaning or phrasing, just so and not otherwise.' Herein, in 'me sutaṃ,' the word 'me' has the meaning of 'mayā' (by me), and the word 'suta' has the meaning of ear-door consciousness. Therefore, 'evaṃ me sutaṃ' is said to mean, 'Thus was it retained by me through a cognitive process-path preceded by ear-consciousness.'

Ekaṃ [M 1.0123] samayanti ekaṃ kālaṃ. Bhagavāti bhāgyavā, bhaggavā, bhattavāti vuttaṃ hoti. Magadhesu viharatīti magadhā nāma janapadino rājakumārā, tesaṃ nivāso ekopi janapado ruḷhīsaddena “magadhā”ti vuccati. Tasmiṃ magadhesu janapade. Keci pana “yasmā cetiyarājā musāvādaṃ bhaṇitvā bhūmiṃ pavisanto ‘mā gadhaṃ pavisā’ti vutto, yasmā vā taṃ rājānaṃ maggantā bhūmiṃ khanantā purisā ‘mā gadhaṃ karothā’ti vuttā, tasmā magadhā”ti evamādīhi nayehi bahudhā [P 1.0136] papañcenti. Yaṃ ruccati, taṃ gahetabbanti. Viharatīti ekaṃ iriyāpathabādhanaṃ aparena iriyāpathena vicchinditvā aparipatantaṃ attabhāvaṃ harati, pavattetīti vuttaṃ hoti. Dibbabrahmaariyavihārehi vā sattānaṃ vividhaṃ hitaṃ haratīti viharati. Haratīti upasaṃharati, upaneti, janeti, uppādetīti vuttaṃ hoti. Tathā hi yadā sattā kāmesu vippaṭipajjanti, tadā kira bhagavā dibbena vihārena viharati tesaṃ alobhakusalamūluppādanatthaṃ – “appeva nāma imaṃ paṭipattiṃ disvā ettha ruciṃ uppādetvā kāmesu virajjeyyu”nti. Yadā pana issariyatthaṃ sattesu vippaṭipajjanti, tadā brahmavihārena viharati tesaṃ adosakusalamūluppādanatthaṃ – “appeva nāma imaṃ paṭipattiṃ disvā ettha ruciṃ uppādetvā adosena dosaṃ vūpasameyyu”nti. Yadā pana pabbajitā dhammādhikaraṇaṃ vivadanti, tadā ariyavihārena viharati tesaṃ amohakusalamūluppādanatthaṃ – “appeva nāma imaṃ paṭipattiṃ disvā ettha ruciṃ uppādetvā amohena mohaṃ vūpasameyyu”nti. Iriyāpathavihārena pana na kadāci na viharati taṃ vinā attabhāvapariharaṇābhāvatoti. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāraṃ pana maṅgalasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ vakkhāma.

At one time means on one occasion. The Blessed One (Bhagavā)—he is so called because he is fortunate (bhāgyavā), has broken (bhaggavā) the defilements, and has distributed (bhattavā) the Dhamma. Dwelling among the Magadhans—the princes who rule the country are called Magadhans. Their residence, though a single country, is also conventionally called 'Magadha.' In that country of the Magadhans. Some, however, elaborate in various ways, saying: 'Because King Cetiya, having spoken falsely, was entering the earth and was told, "Do not enter the deep place (mā gadhaṃ pavisā)," or because the men searching for that king while digging the earth were told, "Do not make a deep place (mā gadhaṃ karothā)," therefore it is called Magadha.' Whatever is preferred, that should be accepted. Dwelling (viharati) means that having relieved the strain of one posture with another, he carries on (harati) his bodily existence without it collapsing; he maintains it, so it is said. Or, he brings (harati) various benefits to beings through the divine, brahma, and noble dwellings (vihāra). Brings (harati) means he conveys, leads to, generates, produces; so it is said. Indeed, when beings misconduct themselves in sensual pleasures, the Blessed One, it is said, dwells in the divine dwelling to generate in them the wholesome root of non-greed, thinking: 'Perhaps, having seen this practice, they might generate interest in it and become dispassionate towards sensual pleasures.' When they misconduct themselves towards beings for the sake of power, he dwells in the brahma-dwelling to generate in them the wholesome root of non-hatred, thinking: 'Perhaps, having seen this practice, they might generate interest in it and pacify hatred with non-hatred.' And when renunciants dispute over a point of Dhamma, he dwells in the noble dwelling to generate in them the wholesome root of non-delusion, thinking: 'Perhaps, having seen this practice, they might generate interest in it and pacify delusion with non-delusion.' He always dwells, however, by means of the postures, because without that, the body cannot be sustained. This is the summary here; we will speak of the details in the commentary on the Maṅgala Sutta.

Dakkhiṇāgirisminti yo so rājagahaṃ parivāretvā ṭhito giri, tassa dakkhiṇapasse janapado “dakkhiṇāgirī”ti vuccati, tasmiṃ janapadeti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha vihārassāpi tadeva nāmaṃ. Ekanāḷāyaṃ brāhmaṇagāmeti ekanāḷāti tassa gāmassa nāmaṃ. Brāhmaṇā cettha sambahulā paṭivasanti, brāhmaṇabhogo vā so, tasmā “brāhmaṇagāmo”ti vuccati.

In the southern hills—that hill which surrounds Rājagaha, the country on its southern side is called 'Dakkhiṇāgiri'; thus it is said of that country. There, the monastery also has the same name. In the brahmin village of Ekanāḷa—Ekanāḷa is the name of that village. And many brahmins reside here, or it is a fief enjoyed by brahmins; therefore it is called 'the brahmin village.'

Tena [V 1.0109] kho pana samayenāti yaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā aparājitapallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambujjhitvā pavattitavaradhammacakko magadharaṭṭhe [M 1.0124] ekanāḷaṃ brāhmaṇagāmaṃ upanissāya dakkhiṇāgirimahāvihāre [P 1.0137] brāhmaṇassa indriyaparipākaṃ āgamayamāno viharati, tena samayena karaṇabhūtenāti vuttaṃ hoti. Kho panāti idaṃ panettha nipātadvayaṃ padapūraṇamattaṃ, adhikārantaradassanatthaṃ vāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kasibhāradvājassa brāhmaṇassāti so brāhmaṇo kasiyā jīvati, bhāradvājoti cassa gottaṃ, tasmā evaṃ vuccati. Pañcamattānīti yathā – “bhojane mattaññū”ti ettha mattasaddo pamāṇe vattati, evamidhāpi, tasmā pañcapamāṇāni anūnāni anadhikāni, pañcanaṅgalasatānīti vuttaṃ hoti. Payuttānīti payojitāni, balibaddānaṃ khandhesu ṭhapetvā yuge yottehi yojitāni hontīti attho.

At that time means: at the time which was the occasion when the Blessed One—having sat cross-legged on the unconquered seat, having fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, and having set rolling the excellent Wheel of Dhamma—was dwelling near the brahmin village of Ekanāḷa in the country of Magadha, in the great monastery on the southern mountain, awaiting the maturing of the brahmin's faculties. The words 'kho pana' here are a pair of particles that are merely for filling out the verse, or it should be seen that they are for indicating a transition to another topic. Of the brahmin Kasibhāradvāja: that brahmin lived by farming (kasi), and Bhāradvāja was his clan name (gotta); therefore he is called thus. Five measures (pañcamattāni): just as in the phrase 'knows the measure in eating' (bhojane mattaññū), the word 'matta' is used in the sense of 'measure' (pamāṇa), so too here. Therefore, it means five measures, no less and no more; that is, five hundred ploughs. Yoked (payuttāni) means harnessed. That is, yokes having been placed on the shoulders of the oxen, they are harnessed with straps.

Vappakāleti vapanakāle, bījanikkhipakāleti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha dve vappāni kalalavappañca, paṃsuvappañca. Paṃsuvappaṃ idha adhippetaṃ. Tañca kho paṭhamadivase maṅgalavappaṃ. Tatthāyaṃ upakaraṇasampadā – tīṇi balibaddasahassāni upaṭṭhāpitāni honti, sabbesaṃ suvaṇṇamayāni siṅgāni paṭimukkāni, rajatamayā khurā, sabbe setamālāhi sabbagandhasugandhehi pañcaṅgulikehi ca alaṅkatā paripuṇṇaṅgapaccaṅgā sabbalakkhaṇasampannā, ekacce kāḷā añjanavaṇṇāyeva, ekacce setā phalikavaṇṇā, ekacce rattā pavāḷavaṇṇā, ekacce kammāsā masāragallavaṇṇā. Pañcasatā kassakapurisā sabbe ahatasetavatthanivatthā mālālaṅkatā dakkhiṇaaṃsakūṭesu ṭhapitapupphacumbaṭakā haritālamanosilālañchanujjalitagattabhāgā dasa dasa naṅgalā ekekagumbā hutvā gacchanti. Naṅgalānaṃ sīsañca yugañca patodā ca suvaṇṇavinaddhā. Paṭhamanaṅgale aṭṭha balibaddā yuttā, sesesu cattāro cattāro, avasesā kilantaparivattanatthaṃ ānītā. Ekekagumbe ekamekaṃ bījasakaṭaṃ ekeko kasati, ekeko vapati.

At the time of sowing (vappakāle) means at the time of planting, that is, at the time of casting the seeds. In this regard, there are two kinds of sowing: sowing in mud and sowing in dust. Here, sowing in dust is intended. And that is the auspicious sowing on the first day. Herein is the perfection of the equipment: three thousand oxen are provided. All have their horns fitted with gold and their hooves are made of silver. All are adorned with white garlands, all kinds of fragrant scents, and marked with five-finger imprints; they are complete in their major and minor limbs and endowed with all the auspicious marks. Some are black, the color of kohl; some are white, the color of crystal; some are red, the color of coral; some are dappled, the color of masāragalla gems. Five hundred ploughmen, all dressed in new white garments, adorned with garlands, with bunches of flowers placed on their right shoulder-tips, with parts of their bodies shining with markings of yellow orpiment and realgar, go in groups of ten ploughs each. The heads of the ploughs, the yokes, and the goads are bound with gold. To the first plough, eight oxen are yoked; to the others, four each. The remaining oxen are brought for replacing the tired ones. In each group there is one seed cart; one person ploughs, and another sows.

Brāhmaṇo pana pageva massukammaṃ kārāpetvā nhatvā sugandhagandhehi vilitto pañcasatagghanakaṃ [P 1.0138] vatthaṃ nivāsetvā sahassagghanakaṃ ekaṃsaṃ karitvā ekamekissā aṅguliyā dve dve katvā vīsati aṅgulimuddikāyo, kaṇṇesu sīhakuṇḍalāni, sīse ca brahmaveṭhanaṃ paṭimuñcitvā suvaṇṇamālaṃ kaṇṭhe [M 1.0125] katvā brāhmaṇagaṇaparivuto kammantaṃ vosāsati. Athassa brāhmaṇī anekasatabhājanesu pāyāsaṃ pacāpetvā mahāsakaṭesu āropetvā gandhodakena nhāyitvā sabbālaṅkāravibhūsitā brāhmaṇīgaṇaparivutā kammantaṃ agamāsi. Gehampissa sabbattha gandhehi suvilittaṃ pupphehi sukatabalikammaṃ, khettañca tesu tesu ṭhānesu samussitapaṭākaṃ ahosi. Parijanakammakārehi [V 1.0110] saha kammantaṃ osaṭaparisā aḍḍhateyyasahassā ahosi. Sabbe ahatavatthanivatthā, sabbesañca pāyāsabhojanaṃ paṭiyattaṃ ahosi.

The brahmin, however, having beforehand had his hair and beard trimmed, bathed and anointed himself with fragrant scents, dressed in a garment worth five hundred, draped a shawl worth a thousand over one shoulder, wearing twenty finger-rings, two on each finger, lion-faced earrings in his ears, and having fastened a brahmin's turban on his head, wearing a golden garland around his neck, surrounded by a company of brahmins, supervised the work. Then his brahmin wife, having had milk-rice cooked in many hundreds of vessels, loaded them onto large carts, bathed with scented water, and adorned with all ornaments, went to the work site surrounded by a company of brahmin women. His house, too, was everywhere well-anointed with scents, with offerings well-made with flowers; and the field had banners raised in various places. The assembly gathered for the work, together with the servants and workers, numbered two thousand five hundred. All were dressed in new garments, and a milk-rice meal was prepared for all.

Atha brāhmaṇo yattha sāmaṃ bhuñjati, taṃ suvaṇṇapātiṃ dhovāpetvā pāyāsassa pūretvā sappimadhuphāṇitādīni abhisaṅkharitvā naṅgalabalikammaṃ kārāpesi. Brāhmaṇī pañca kassakasatāni suvaṇṇarajatakaṃsatambamayāni bhājanāni gahetvā nisinnāni suvaṇṇakaṭacchuṃ gahetvā pāyāsena parivisantī gacchati. Brāhmaṇo pana balikammaṃ kārāpetvā rattasuvaṇṇabandhūpāhanāyo ārohitvā rattasuvaṇṇadaṇḍaṃ gahetvā “idha pāyāsaṃ detha, idha sappiṃ, idha sakkharaṃ dethā”ti vosāsamāno vicarati. Atha bhagavā gandhakuṭiyaṃ nisinnova brāhmaṇassa parivesanaṃ vattamānaṃ ñatvā “ayaṃ kālo brāhmaṇaṃ dametu”nti nivāsetvā, kāyabandhanaṃ bandhitvā, saṅghāṭiṃ pārupitvā, pattaṃ gahetvā, gandhakuṭito nikkhami yathā taṃ anuttaro purisadammasārathi. Tenāha āyasmā ānando “atha kho bhagavā pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā”ti.

Then the brahmin had the golden bowl in which he himself ate washed, filled it with milk-rice, prepared it with ghee, honey, molasses, and so forth, and had the plowing ceremony performed. The brahmin’s wife took a golden ladle and went about serving milk-rice to the five hundred seated plowmen who held vessels of gold, silver, bronze, and copper. The brahmin, for his part, having had the offering ceremony performed, put on sandals bound with red-gold, took a red-gold staff, and walked about directing, “Give milk-rice here, give ghee here, give sugar here.” Then the Blessed One, seated in the perfumed chamber, knowing that the brahmin’s distribution of food was taking place, thought, “This is the time to tame the brahmin.” Having dressed, fastened his belt, put on his outer robe, and taken his bowl, he left the perfumed chamber, as is the way of the unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed. For that reason, the Venerable Ānanda said: “Then, indeed, the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning…”

Tattha atha iti nipāto aññādhikāravacanārambhe khoti [P 1.0139] padapūraṇe. Bhagavāti vuttanayameva. Pubbaṇhasamayanti divasassa pubbabhāgasamayaṃ, pubbaṇhasamayeti attho, pubbaṇhe vā samayaṃ pubbaṇhasamayaṃ, pubbaṇhe ekaṃ khaṇanti vuttaṃ hoti. Evaṃ accantasaṃyoge upayogavacanaṃ labbhati. Nivāsetvāti paridahitvā, vihāranivāsanaparivattanavasenetaṃ veditabbaṃ. Na hi bhagavā tato pubbe anivattho āsi. Pattacīvaramādāyāti pattaṃ hatthehi, cīvaraṃ kāyena ādiyitvā, sampaṭicchitvā dhāretvāti attho. Bhagavato kira piṇḍāya pavisitukāmassa bhamaro viya vikasitapadumadvayamajjhaṃ, indanīlamaṇivaṇṇaṃ [M 1.0126] selamayaṃ pattaṃ hatthadvayamajjhaṃ āgacchati. Tasmā evamāgataṃ pattaṃ hatthehi sampaṭicchitvā cīvarañca parimaṇḍalaṃ pārutaṃ kāyena dhāretvāti evamassa attho veditabbo. Yena vā tena vā hi pakārena gaṇhanto ādāya icceva vuccati yathā “samādāyeva pakkamatī”ti.

‘Herein, the particle `atha` is used to begin a statement on a different topic, and `kho` is a particle for filling out the phrase. `Bhagavā` is to be understood in the same way as previously explained. `Pubbaṇhasamayaṃ` means 'the early part of the day,' that is, 'the morning time.' Alternatively, `pubbaṇhasamayaṃ` means 'a time in the morning,' or 'a single moment in the morning' is what is meant. In this way, the accusative case is used in the sense of continuous duration. `Nivāsetvā` means 'having dressed,' and this should be understood as a change of dwelling-robe. For the Blessed One was not unclothed before that. `Pattacīvaramādāya` means 'having taken the bowl with his hands and the robe on his body'—that is, 'having received and worn them.' It is said that when the Blessed One wished to enter for alms, a stone bowl the color of an indanīla gem would come into the midst of his two hands, like a bee into the midst of two blossoming lotuses. Therefore, its meaning should be understood as 'receiving with his hands such a bowl that has come, and wearing the robe neatly wrapped around his body.' For taking in any manner whatsoever is expressed by `ādāya`, as in the phrase 'he departs only after taking up' (samādāyeva pakkamatī).

Yenāti yena maggena. Kammantoti kammakaraṇokāso. Tenāti tena maggena. Upasaṅkamīti gato, yena maggena kasibhāradvājassa brāhmaṇassa kammanto gammati, tena maggena gatoti vuttaṃ hoti. Atha kasmā, bhikkhū, bhagavantaṃ nānubandhiṃsūti? Vuccate – yadā bhagavā ekakova katthaci upasaṅkamitukāmo hoti, bhikkhācāravelāyaṃ dvāraṃ pidahitvā antogandhakuṭiṃ pavisati. Tato bhikkhū tāya saññāya jānanti – “ajja bhagavā ekakova gāmaṃ pavisitukāmo, addhā kañci eva vinetabbapuggalaṃ addasā”ti. Te attano pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā, gandhakuṭiṃ padakkhiṇaṃ [V 1.0111] katvā, bhikkhācāraṃ gacchanti. Tadā ca bhagavā evamakāsi. Tasmā bhikkhū bhagavantaṃ nānubandhiṃsūti.

‘Yena’ means ‘by which path.’ ‘Kammanto’ means ‘the place of work.’ ‘Tena’ means ‘by that path.’ ‘Upasaṅkamī’ means ‘he went’; it is said that he went by the path by which the brahmin Kasibhāradvāja’s work-place was reached. But why did the monks not follow the Blessed One? It is said: When the Blessed One wished to go somewhere alone, at the time for the alms round, he would close the door and enter the inner perfumed chamber. Then the monks, recognizing this sign, would know, “Today the Blessed One wishes to enter the village alone; surely he must have seen some person to be tamed.” Taking their bowls and robes, they would circumambulate the perfumed chamber and go for alms. And on that day, the Blessed One acted thus. Therefore, the monks did not follow the Blessed One.

Tena [P 1.0140] kho pana samayenāti yena samayena bhagavā kammantaṃ upasaṅkami, tena samayena tassa brāhmaṇassa parivesanā vattati, bhattavissaggo vattatīti attho. Yaṃ pubbe avocumha – “brāhmaṇī pañca kassakasatāni suvaṇṇarajatakaṃsatambamayāni bhājanāni gahetvā nisinnāni suvaṇṇakaṭacchuṃ gahetvā pāyāsena parivisantī gacchatī”ti. Atha kho bhagavā yena parivesanā tenupasaṅkami. Kiṃ kāraṇāti? Brāhmaṇassa anuggahakaraṇatthaṃ. Na hi bhagavā kapaṇapuriso viya bhottukāmatāya parivesanaṃ upasaṅkamati. Bhagavato hi dve asītisahassasaṅkhyā sakyakoliyarājāno ñātayo, te attano sampattiyā nibaddhabhattaṃ dātuṃ ussahanti. Na pana bhagavā bhattatthāya pabbajito, apica kho pana “anekāni asaṅkhyeyyāni pañca mahāpariccāge pariccajanto pāramiyo pūretvā mutto mocessāmi, danto damessāmi; santo samessāmi, parinibbuto parinibbāpessāmī”ti pabbajito. Tasmā attano muttattā…pe… parinibbutattā ca paraṃ mocento…pe… parinibbāpento ca loke vicaranto brāhmaṇassa anuggahakaraṇatthaṃ yena parivesanā tenupasaṅkamīti veditabbaṃ.

‘Now at that time’ means that at the time the Blessed One approached the workplace, at that time the brahmin’s serving was taking place, the distribution of food was occurring. As we previously said: ‘The brahmin woman, with five hundred farmers seated holding golden, silver, bronze, and copper vessels, took a golden ladle and went around serving the milk-rice.’ Then the Blessed One approached the place where the food was being distributed. For what reason? For the sake of showing favor to the brahmin. For the Blessed One does not approach the meal distribution like a poor man desiring food. Indeed, the Blessed One has eighty-two thousand Sakyan and Koliyan kings as relatives, who are able to offer him regular provisions from their own wealth. But the Blessed One did not go forth for the sake of food; rather, having made countless and immeasurable great sacrifices, fulfilling the perfections, he went forth thinking, ‘Freed, I will free; tamed, I will tame; calmed, I will calm; fully extinguished, I will lead to full extinguishment.’ Therefore, it should be understood that, being himself freed… and fully extinguished, and freeing others… and leading others to full extinguishment, while wandering the world, he approached the meal distribution for the sake of showing favor to the brahmin.

Upasaṅkamitvā [M 1.0127] ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsīti evaṃ upasaṅkamitvā ca ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Ekamantanti bhāvanapuṃsakaniddeso, ekokāsaṃ ekapassanti vuttaṃ hoti. Bhummatthe vā upayogavacanaṃ, tassa dassanūpacāre kathāsavanaṭṭhāne, yattha ṭhitaṃ brāhmaṇo passati, tattha uccaṭṭhāne aṭṭhāsi. Ṭhatvā ca suvaṇṇarasapiñjaraṃ sahassacandasūriyobhāsātibhāsayamānaṃ sarīrābhaṃ muñci samantato asītihatthaparimāṇaṃ, yāya ajjhottharitattā brāhmaṇassa kammantasālābhittirukkhakasitamattikāpiṇḍādayo suvaṇṇamayā viya ahesuṃ. Atha manussā pāyāsaṃ bhuttā asītianubyañjanaparivāradvattiṃsavaralakkhaṇapaṭimaṇḍitasarīraṃ byāmappabhāparikkhepavibhūsitabāhuyugaḷaṃ ketumālāsamujjalitasassirikadassanaṃ [P 1.0141] jaṅgamamiva padumassaraṃ, raṃsijālujjalitatārāgaṇamiva gaganatalaṃ, ādittamiva ca kanakagirisikharaṃ siriyā jalamānaṃ sammāsambuddhaṃ ekamantaṃ ṭhitaṃ disvā hatthapāde dhovitvā añjaliṃ paggayha samparivāretvā aṭṭhaṃsu. Evaṃ tehi samparivāritaṃ addasa kho kasibhāradvājo brāhmaṇo bhagavantaṃ piṇḍāya ṭhitaṃ. Disvāna bhagavantaṃ etadavoca “ahaṃ kho, samaṇa, kasāmi ca vapāmi cā”ti.

‘Having approached, he stood to one side’ means that having thus approached, he stood to one side. ‘Ekamantaṃ’ is a designation in the adverbial neuter, meaning ‘a single place, a single side.’ Alternatively, it is an accusative case used in the sense of the locative, meaning he stood in a high place, in a place within sight and suitable for hearing his discourse, where the brahmin could see him standing. And standing there, he released a bodily radiance, golden-hued like molten gold, outshining the radiance of a thousand moons and suns, extending eighty cubits all around. Because of being overwhelmed by this radiance, the brahmin’s work-hall, walls, trees, plowed clods of earth, and so on, appeared as if made of gold. Then, the men who had eaten the milk-rice saw the Perfectly Enlightened One standing to one side, his body adorned with the thirty-two excellent marks of a great man and surrounded by the eighty minor characteristics, his pair of arms beautified by the surrounding fathom-long aura, his appearance glorious to behold, resplendent with a garland of rays, like a moving lotus pond, like the celestial sphere with its host of stars blazing with a net of rays, and like a blazing golden mountain peak, shining with glory. Seeing him, they washed their hands and feet, raised their joined palms in reverence, and stood surrounding him. Thus surrounded by them, the brahmin Kasibhāradvāja saw the Blessed One standing for alms. Having seen him, he said this to the Blessed One: “I, ascetic, plow and sow.”

Kasmā panāyaṃ evamāha? Kiṃ samantapāsādike pasādanīye uttamadamathasamathamanuppattepi bhagavati [V 1.0112] appasādena, udāhu aḍḍhateyyānaṃ janasahassānaṃ pāyāsaṃ paṭiyādetvāpi kaṭacchubhikkhāya maccherenāti? Ubhayathāpi no, apica khvāssa bhagavato dassanena atittaṃ nikkhittakammantaṃ janaṃ disvā “kammabhaṅgaṃ me kātuṃ āgato”ti anattamanatā ahosi. Tasmā evamāha. Bhagavato ca lakkhaṇasampattiṃ disvā “sacāyaṃ kammante payojayissa, sakalajambudīpe manussānaṃ sīse cūḷāmaṇi viya abhavissa, ko nāmassa attho na sampajjissa, evamevaṃ alasatāya kammante appayojetvā vappamaṅgalādīsu piṇḍāya caritvā bhuñjanto kāyadaḷhībahulo vicaratī”tipissa ahosi. Tenāha – “ahaṃ kho, samaṇa, kasāmi ca vapāmi ca, kasitvā ca vapitvā ca bhuñjāmī”ti. Na me kammantā byāpajjanti, na camhi yathā tvaṃ evaṃ lakkhaṇasampannoti adhippāyo. Tvampi samaṇa…pe… bhuñjassu, ko te attho na sampajjeyya evaṃ lakkhaṇasampannassāti adhippāyo.

But why did he speak thus? Was it due to lack of faith in the Blessed One, who is all-around pleasant, inspiring confidence, and has attained supreme taming and tranquility? Or was it out of miserliness over a spoonful of alms, despite having prepared milk-rice for two and a half thousand people? In both cases, no. Rather, seeing the people who had put down their work, unsatisfied with seeing the Blessed One, he became displeased, thinking, ‘He has come to cause the ruin of my work.’ That is why he spoke thus. And seeing the perfection of the Blessed One’s marks, this thought also occurred to him: ‘If this man were to apply himself to work, he would be like a crest-jewel on the heads of the people of all Jambudīpa. What need of his would not be fulfilled? Yet, due to laziness, not applying himself to work, he wanders about for alms at the plowing festival and so on, eating, and is of robust body.’ Therefore he said: ‘I, ascetic, plow and sow, and having plowed and sown, I eat.’ The intention is: ‘My work is not obstructed, and I am not endowed with marks as you are.’ And also: ‘You too, ascetic… eat. What need would not be fulfilled for one so endowed with marks?’

Apicāyaṃ [M 1.0128] assosi – “sakyarājakule kira kumāro uppanno, so cakkavattirajjaṃ pahāya pabbajito”ti. Tasmā “idāni ayaṃ so”ti ñatvā “cakkavattirajjaṃ kira pahāya kilantosī”ti upārambhaṃ karonto āha “ahaṃ kho samaṇā”ti. Apicāyaṃ tikkhapañño brāhmaṇo, na bhagavantaṃ avakkhipanto [P 1.0142] bhaṇati, bhagavato pana rūpasampattiṃ disvā paññāsampattiṃ sambhāvayamāno kathāpavattanatthampi evamāha – “ahaṃ kho samaṇā”ti. Tato bhagavā veneyyavasena sadevake loke aggakassakavappakabhāvaṃ attano dassento āha “ahampi kho brāhmaṇā”ti.

Moreover, he had heard this: ‘Indeed, a prince has been born in the Sakyan royal family, and he has renounced universal sovereignty to go forth.’ Therefore, knowing, ‘Now, this is he,’ and making a reproach, thinking, ‘Having renounced universal sovereignty, you are now toiling,’ he said, ‘I, ascetic…’ Moreover, this brahmin was sharp-witted; he did not speak disparagingly of the Blessed One, but, seeing the Blessed One’s physical perfection, he surmised his perfection of wisdom and also spoke thus to initiate conversation: ‘I, ascetic…’ Then the Blessed One, displaying his own state as the foremost farmer and sower in the world with its gods, according to the disposition of those to be trained, said, ‘I too, brahmin…’

Atha brāhmaṇassa cintā udapādi – “ayaṃ samaṇo ‘kasāmi ca vapāmi cā’ti āha. Na cassa oḷārikāni yuganaṅgalādīni kasibhaṇḍāni passāmi, so musā nu kho bhaṇati, no”ti bhagavantaṃ pādatalā paṭṭhāya yāva upari kesantā sammālokayamāno aṅgavijjāya katādhikārattā dvattiṃsavaralakkhaṇasampattimassa ñatvā “aṭṭhānametaṃ anavakāso, yaṃ evarūpo musā bhaṇeyyā”ti tāvadeva sañjātabahumāno bhagavati samaṇavādaṃ pahāya gottena bhagavantaṃ samudācaramāno āha “na kho pana mayaṃ passāma bhoto gotamassā”ti.

Then this thought arose in the brahmin: ‘This ascetic says, “I plow and I sow.” But I do not see any of his coarse farming implements like yokes and plows. Is he speaking falsely, or not?’ Scrutinizing the Blessed One from the soles of his feet up to the tips of his hair, and because of his expertise in the science of bodily marks, he recognized his possession of the thirty-two excellent marks and thought, ‘It is impossible, there is no occasion, that such a one would speak falsely.’ At that very moment, great respect arose in him for the Blessed One. Abandoning the address ‘ascetic’ and addressing the Blessed One by his clan name, he said, ‘But we do not see Master Gotama’s farming implements.’

Evañca pana vatvā tikkhapañño brāhmaṇo “gambhīratthaṃ sandhāya iminā etaṃ vutta”nti ñatvā pucchitvā tamatthaṃ ñātukāmo bhagavantaṃ gāthāya ajjhabhāsi. Tenāha āyasmā ānando “atha kho kasibhāradvājo brāhmaṇo bhagavantaṃ gāthāya ajjhabhāsī”ti. Tattha gāthāyāti akkharapadaniyamitena vacanena. Ajjhabhāsīti abhāsi.

Having spoken thus, the sharp-witted brahmin, knowing, 'This was said by him with a profound meaning in mind,' and wishing to understand that meaning by questioning, addressed the Blessed One with a verse. Therefore, the Venerable Ānanda said: 'Then the brahmin Kasibhāradvāja addressed the Blessed One with a verse.' Herein, 'with a verse' means with speech regulated by syllables and words. 'Addressed' means spoke.

76-77. Tattha [V 1.0113] brāhmaṇo “kasi”nti yuganaṅgalādikasisambhārasamāyogaṃ vadati. Bhagavā pana yasmā pubbadhammasabhāgena ropetvā kathanaṃ nāma buddhānaṃ ānubhāvo, tasmā buddhānubhāvaṃ dīpento pubbadhammasabhāgena ropento āha – “saddhā bīja”nti. Ko panettha pubbadhammasabhāgo, nanu brāhmaṇena bhagavā yuganaṅgalādikasisambhārasamāyogaṃ pucchito atha ca pana apucchitassa bījassa sabhāgena ropento āha – “saddhā bīja”nti, evañca sati ananusandhikāva ayaṃ kathā hotīti? Vuccate – na buddhānaṃ [M 1.0129] ananusandhikā nāma kathā atthi, nāpi buddhā pubbadhammasabhāgaṃ anāropetvā kathenti. Evañcettha [P 1.0143] anusandhi veditabbā – anena hi brāhmaṇena bhagavā yuganaṅgalādikasisambhāravasena kasiṃ pucchito. So tassa anukampāya “idaṃ apucchita”nti aparihāpetvā samūlaṃ saupakāraṃ sasambhāraṃ saphalaṃ kasiṃ ñāpetuṃ mūlato paṭṭhāya kasiṃ dassento āha – “saddhā bīja”nti. Bījañhi kasiyā mūlaṃ tasmiṃ sati kattabbato, asati akattabbato, tappamāṇena ca kattabbato. Bīje hi sati kasiṃ karonti, asati na karonti. Bījappamāṇena ca kusalā kassakā khettaṃ kasanti, na ūnaṃ “mā no sassaṃ parihāyī”ti, na adhikaṃ “mā no mogho vāyāmo ahosī”ti. Yasmā ca bījameva mūlaṃ, tasmā bhagavā mūlato paṭṭhāya kasiṃ dassento tassa brāhmaṇassa kasiyā pubbadhammassa bījassa sabhāgena attano kasiyā pubbadhammaṃ ropento āha – “saddhā bīja”nti. Evamettha pubbadhammasabhāgo veditabbo.

Herein, the brahmin, by 'cultivation,' speaks of the combination of farming equipment such as the yoke and plough. But as for the Blessed One, because speaking by superimposing a similar previous topic is the power of the Buddhas, He, therefore, revealing the Buddha's power and superimposing a similar previous topic, said: 'Faith is the seed.' What, here, is the similar previous topic? Was not the Blessed One asked by the brahmin about the combination of farming equipment such as the yoke and plough? And yet, superimposing by way of similarity to the unasked-for seed, He said: 'Faith is the seed.' This being so, is this talk not disconnected? It is said: There is no talk of the Buddhas that is disconnected, nor do the Buddhas speak without superimposing a similar previous topic. And here the connection should be understood thus: this brahmin asked the Blessed One about cultivation by way of farming equipment such as the yoke and plough. Out of compassion for him, not omitting this unasked-for matter, in order to make known the cultivation that is with root, with support, with equipment, and with fruit, showing cultivation starting from the root, He said: 'Faith is the seed.' For the seed is the root of cultivation, because when it is present, cultivation is to be done; when it is absent, it is not to be done; and it is to be done according to its measure. For when there is seed, they cultivate; when there is not, they do not cultivate. And skilled farmers plough the field according to the measure of the seed, not less, thinking, 'May our crop not diminish,' and not more, thinking, 'May our effort not be in vain.' And because the seed itself is the root, the Blessed One, therefore, showing cultivation starting from the root, and superimposing the preliminary element of His own cultivation by way of its similarity to the seed, the preliminary element of that brahmin's cultivation, said: 'Faith is the seed.' Thus should the similar previous topic be understood herein.

Pucchitaṃyeva vatvā apucchitaṃ pacchā kiṃ na vuttanti ce? Tassa upakārabhāvato dhammasambandhasamatthabhāvato ca. Ayañhi brāhmaṇo paññavā, micchādiṭṭhikule pana jātattā saddhāvirahito. Saddhāvirahito ca paññavā paresaṃ saddhāya attano visaye apaṭipajjamāno visesaṃ nādhigacchati, kilesakālussiyabhāvāpagamappasādamattalakkhaṇāpi cassa dubbalā saddhā balavatiyā paññāya saha vattamānā atthasiddhiṃ na karoti, hatthinā saha ekadhure yuttagoṇo viya. Tasmā tassa saddhā upakārikā. Evaṃ tassa brāhmaṇassa saupakārabhāvato taṃ brāhmaṇaṃ saddhāya patiṭṭhāpentena pacchāpi vattabbo ayamattho pubbe vutto desanākusalatāya yathā aññatrāpi “saddhā bandhati pātheyya”nti (saṃ. ni. 1.79) ca, “saddhā dutiyā purisassa hotī”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.59) ca, “saddhīdha vittaṃ purisassa seṭṭha”nti (saṃ. ni. 1.73, 246; su. ni. 184) ca, “saddhāya tarati ogha”nti (saṃ. ni. 1.246) ca, “saddhāhattho mahānāgo”ti (a. ni. 6.43; theragā. 694) ca, “saddhesiko kho, bhikkhave, ariyasāvakoti cā”ti (a. ni. 7.67). Bījassa ca upakārikā [V 1.0114] vuṭṭhi, sā tadanantaraññeva vuccamānā samatthā hoti[P 1.0144]. Evaṃ dhammasambandhasamatthabhāvato [M 1.0130] pacchāpi vattabbo ayamattho pubbe vutto, añño ca evaṃvidho īsāyottādi.

If it is asked: 'Having stated only what was asked, why was the unasked-for matter not stated afterwards?' It was stated because of its helpfulness and its capacity for connection with the Dhamma. For this brahmin was wise, but having been born in a family of wrong view, he was devoid of faith. And a wise person devoid of faith, not practicing in his own domain concerning the faith of others, does not attain distinction. And for him, even the weak faith which has the characteristic of mere serenity from the removal of the state of defilement and turbidity, when occurring together with strong wisdom, does not accomplish the goal, like an ox yoked in a single harness with an elephant. Therefore, faith was helpful for him. Thus, because it was helpful for that brahmin, this meaning, which should have been spoken later, was spoken before by the one establishing that brahmin in faith, due to skill in teaching, as has been said previously elsewhere: 'Faith binds provisions for the journey,' and, 'Faith is a person's second companion,' and, 'Herein, faith is a person's best wealth,' and, 'By faith one crosses the flood,' and, 'Mahānāma has faith as his hand,' and, 'Monks, a noble disciple is one who has faith.' And rain is helpful to the seed; being spoken of immediately after it, it is effective. Thus, because of its capacity for connection with the Dhamma, this meaning, which should have been spoken later, was spoken before; and so too for other such things like the plough-pole, the rope, and so on.
