Tattha sampasādanalakkhaṇā saddhā, okappanalakkhaṇā vā, pakkhandanarasā, adhimuttipaccupaṭṭhānā, akālussiyapaccupaṭṭhānā vā, sotāpattiyaṅgapadaṭṭhānā, saddahitabbadhammapadaṭṭhānā vā, ādāsajalatalādīnaṃ pasādo viya cetaso pasādabhūtā, udakappasādakamaṇi viya udakassa, sampayuttadhammānaṃ pasādikā. Bījanti pañcavidhaṃ – mūlabījaṃ, khandhabījaṃ, phalubījaṃ, aggabījaṃ, bījabījameva pañcamanti. Taṃ sabbampi viruhanaṭṭhena bījaṃtveva saṅkhaṃ gacchati. Yathāha – “bījañcetaṃ viruhanaṭṭhenā”ti.

Herein, faith has the characteristic of complete serenity, or the characteristic of conviction. Its function is to surge forward. Its manifestation is resolve, or non-turbidity. Its proximate cause is the factors of stream-entry, or the states in which faith should be placed. Like the clarity of a mirror, the surface of water, and so on, it is the clarity of the mind. Like a water-clarifying gem for water, it is what clarifies associated states. 'Seed' is of five kinds: root-seed, stem-seed, joint-seed, tip-seed, and seed-seed as the fifth. All of this comes to be reckoned as 'seed' in the sense of sprouting. As it is said: 'And this is seed in the sense of sprouting.'

Tattha yathā brāhmaṇassa kasiyā mūlabhūtaṃ bījaṃ dve kiccāni karoti, heṭṭhā mūlena patiṭṭhāti, upari aṅkuraṃ uṭṭhāpeti; evaṃ bhagavato kasiyā mūlabhūtā saddhā heṭṭhā sīlamūlena patiṭṭhāti, upari samathavipassanaṅkuraṃ uṭṭhāpeti. Yathā ca taṃ mūlena pathavirasaṃ āporasaṃ gahetvā nāḷena dhaññaparipākagahaṇatthaṃ vaḍḍhati; evamayaṃ sīlamūlena samathavipassanārasaṃ gahetvā ariyamagganāḷena ariyaphaladhaññaparipākagahaṇatthaṃ vaḍḍhati. Yathā ca taṃ subhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhahitvā mūlaṅkurapaṇṇanāḷakaṇḍappasavehi vuḍḍhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ patvā, khīraṃ janetvā, anekasāliphalabharitaṃ sālisīsaṃ nipphādeti; evamayaṃ cittasantāne patiṭṭhahitvā sīlacittadiṭṭhikaṅkhāvitaraṇamaggāmaggañāṇadassanapaṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhīhi vuḍḍhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ patvā ñāṇadassanavisuddhikhīraṃ janetvā anekapaṭisambhidābhiññābharitaṃ arahattaphalaṃ nipphādeti. Tenāha bhagavā – “saddhā bīja”nti.

Herein, just as for a brahmin's cultivation, the seed that is the root performs two functions: below, it is established by the root, and above, it raises a sprout; even so, for the Blessed One's cultivation, faith which is the root is established below by the root of virtue, and above, it raises the sprout of serenity and insight. And just as that seed, having absorbed the essence of earth and the essence of water through its root, grows by its stalk for the purpose of attaining the ripening of the grain; even so, this faith, having absorbed the essence of serenity and insight through the root of virtue, grows by the stalk of the Noble Path for the purpose of attaining the ripening of the grain of the Noble Fruit. And just as that seed, having been established in fertile soil, attains growth, development, and abundance through its roots, shoots, leaves, stalks, sections, and offshoots, produces sap, and yields a head of rice laden with many grains; even so, this faith, having been established in the continuum of the mind, attains growth, development, and abundance through the purifications of virtue, mind, view, the overcoming of doubt, knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path, and knowledge and vision of the way, produces the sap of the purification of knowledge and vision, yielding the fruit of arahantship laden with many analytical insights and supernormal knowledges. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Faith is the seed."

Tattha siyā “paropaññāsakusaladhammesu ekato uppajjamānesu kasmā saddhāva bījanti vuttā”ti? Vuccate – bījakiccakaraṇato. Yathā hi tesu viññāṇaṃyeva vijānanakiccaṃ karoti, evaṃ saddhā bījakiccaṃ, sā ca sabbakusalānaṃ mūlabhūtā. Yathāha –

Herein, one might ask: "When more than fifty wholesome states arise together, why is faith alone called the seed?" It is said: Because it performs the function of a seed. For just as among them, consciousness alone performs the function of cognizing, so faith performs the function of a seed, and it is the root of all wholesome states. As it is said:

“Saddhājāto upasaṅkamati, upasaṅkamanto payirupāsati, payirupāsanto sotaṃ odahati[P 1.0145], ohitasoto dhammaṃ suṇāti, sutvā dhammaṃ dhāreti, dhatānaṃ dhammānaṃ atthaṃ upaparikkhati[M 1.0131], atthaṃ upaparikkhato dhammā nijjhānaṃ khamanti, dhammanijjhānakkhantiyā sati chando jāyati, chandajāto ussahati, ussāhetvā tulayati, tulayitvā padahati, pahitatto [V 1.0115] samāno kāyena ceva paramasaccaṃ sacchikaroti, paññāya ca naṃ ativijjhapassatī”ti (ma. ni. 2.183, 432).

"Having been born of faith, one approaches; approaching, one attends upon; attending upon, one lends an ear; with ear lent, one hears the Dhamma; having heard the Dhamma, one remembers it; of the remembered teachings, one examines the meaning; when one examines the meaning, the teachings are reflectively accepted; with the reflective acceptance of the teachings, zeal is born; having been born of zeal, one makes an effort; having made an effort, one weighs it up; having weighed it up, one strives; being self-resolute, one realizes the ultimate truth with the body and sees it by penetrating it with wisdom."

Tapati akusale dhamme kāyañcāti tapo; indriyasaṃvaravīriyadhutaṅgadukkarakārikānaṃ etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Idha pana indriyasaṃvaro adhippeto. Vuṭṭhīti vassavuṭṭhivātavuṭṭhītiādinā anekavidhā. Idha vassavuṭṭhi adhippetā. Yathā hi brāhmaṇassa vassavuṭṭhisamanuggahitaṃ bījaṃ bījamūlakañca sassaṃ viruhati na milāyati nipphattiṃ gacchati, evaṃ bhagavato indriyasaṃvarasamanuggahitā saddhā saddhāmūlā ca sīlādayo dhammā viruhanti na milāyanti nipphattiṃ gacchanti. Tenāha – “tapo vuṭṭhī”ti. “Paññā me”ti ettha ca vutto me-saddo imesupi padesu yojetabbo “saddhā me bījaṃ, tapo me vuṭṭhī”ti. Tena kiṃ dīpeti? Yathā, brāhmaṇa, tayā vapite bīje sace vuṭṭhi atthi, sādhu, no ce atthi, udakampi dātabbaṃ hoti, tathā mayā hiri-īse paññāyuganaṅgale manoyottena ekābaddhe kate vīriyabalibadde yojetvā satipācanena vijjhitvā attano cittasantānakhette saddhābīje vapite vuṭṭhi-abhāvo nāma natthi. Ayaṃ pana me satataṃ samitaṃ tapo vuṭṭhīti.

It burns up unwholesome states and the body, thus it is austerity (tapo); this is a designation for restraint of the senses, energy, ascetic practices, and the undertaking of difficult tasks. Here, however, restraint of the senses is intended. Rainfall (vuṭṭhi) is of many kinds, such as rain-fall, wind-fall, and so on. Here, rain-fall is intended. For just as for a brahmin, a seed and the crop rooted in it, supported by rainfall, grow, do not wither, and reach maturity, so too for the Blessed One, faith and the qualities, such as virtue, that are rooted in faith, supported by restraint of the senses, grow, do not wither, and reach maturity. Therefore, He said: "Austerity is the rainfall." And in 'wisdom is mine,' the word 'mine' mentioned here should be applied in these contexts as well: 'Faith is my seed, austerity is my rainfall.' What does this illustrate? Just as, O brahmin, when you have sown a seed, if there is rainfall, it is good; if not, water must still be given, so too, for me, when the pole of moral shame, the yoke and plow of wisdom, and the rein of the mind are bound as one, and having yoked the oxen of energy and prodded them with the goad of mindfulness, the seed of faith is sown in the field of my own mental continuum—there is no lack of rainfall. Moreover, this austerity is my constant and perpetual rainfall.

Pajānāti etāya puggalo, sayaṃ vā pajānātīti paññā, sā kāmāvacarādibhedato anekavidhā. Idha pana saha vipassanāya maggapaññā adhippetā. Yuganaṅgalanti yugañca naṅgalañca. Yathā hi brāhmaṇassa yuganaṅgalaṃ, evaṃ [P 1.0146] bhagavato duvidhāpi paññā. Tattha yathā yugaṃ īsāya upanissayaṃ hoti, purato hoti, īsābaddhaṃ hoti, yottānaṃ nissayaṃ hoti, balibaddānaṃ ekato gamanaṃ dhāreti, evaṃ paññā hiripamukhānaṃ dhammānaṃ upanissayā hoti. Yathāha – “paññuttarā sabbe kusalā dhammā”ti (a. ni. 8.83) ca, “paññā hi seṭṭhā kusalā vadanti, nakkhattarājāriva tārakāna”nti (jā. 2.17.81) ca. Kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pubbaṅgamaṭṭhena purato ca hoti. Yathāha – “sīlaṃ hirī cāpi satañca dhammo, anvāyikā paññavato bhavantī”ti. Hirivippayogena [M 1.0132] anuppattito īsābaddhā hoti, manosaṅkhātassa samādhiyottassa nissayapaccayato yottānaṃ nissayo hoti, accāraddhātilīnabhāvapaṭisedhanato vīriyabalibaddānaṃ ekato gamanaṃ dhāreti. Yathā ca naṅgalaṃ phālayuttaṃ kasanakāle pathavighanaṃ bhindati, mūlasantānakāni padāleti, evaṃ satiyuttā paññā vipassanākāle dhammānaṃ santatisamūhakiccārammaṇaghanaṃ bhindati, sabbakilesamūlasantānakāni padāleti. Sā ca kho lokuttarāva itarā pana lokiyāpi siyā. Tenāha – “paññā me yuganaṅgala”nti.

A person understands through this, or one understands by oneself—this is wisdom (paññā). It is of many kinds, distinguished as that pertaining to the sense-sphere and so on. Here, however, the path wisdom together with insight is intended. Yoke and plow (yuganaṅgala) means both the yoke and the plow. For just as a brahmin has a yoke and plow, so too does the Blessed One possess twofold wisdom. In this regard, just as the yoke is a support for the pole, is in front, is bound to the pole, is a support for the straps, and maintains the unified movement of the oxen, so too is wisdom the support for qualities headed by moral shame. As it is said: "All wholesome qualities are surpassed by wisdom" and "The wise declare wisdom to be the best of wholesome things, like the king of stars among the constellations." It is also in front in the sense of being the forerunner of wholesome qualities. As it is said: "Virtue, moral shame, and the Dhamma of the good are followers of one who has wisdom." Because it does not arise in separation from moral shame, it is bound to the pole. It serves as a support for the straps by being a support-condition for the 'strap' of concentration, which is designated as mind. By preventing the state of being overly energetic or too lax, it maintains the unified movement of the oxen of energy. And just as the plow, fitted with a blade, breaks up the compact earth during plowing and severs the root systems, so too does wisdom, coupled with mindfulness, break up the dense mass of the continuity, grouping, function, and object of phenomena during insight meditation, and severs all the root systems of defilements. And that wisdom is indeed supramundane, while the other may be mundane. Hence He said: "Wisdom is my yoke and plow."

Hirīyati [V 1.0116] etāya puggalo, sayaṃ vā hirīyati akusalappavattiṃ jigucchatīti hirī. Taggahaṇena sahacaraṇabhāvato ottappaṃ gahitaṃyeva hoti. Īsāti yuganaṅgalasandhārikā dāruyaṭṭhi. Yathā hi brāhmaṇassa īsā yuganaṅgalaṃ sandhāreti, evaṃ bhagavatopi hirī lokiyalokuttarapaññāsaṅkhātaṃ yuganaṅgalaṃ sandhāreti hiriyā asati paññāya abhāvato. Yathā ca īsāpaṭibaddhaṃ yuganaṅgalaṃ kiccakaraṃ hoti acalaṃ asithilaṃ, evaṃ hiripaṭibaddhā ca paññā kiccakārī hoti acalā asithilā abbokiṇṇā ahirikena. Tenāha “hirī īsā”ti.

A person is ashamed because of this, or one is ashamed oneself and is disgusted by the occurrence of unwholesome states—this is moral shame (hirī). By its inclusion, moral dread (ottappa) is also included, due to their being companions. The pole (īsā) is the wooden shaft that holds together the yoke and plow. Just as the pole holds together the yoke and plow, so too does the Blessed One's moral shame hold together the yoke-and-plow reckoned as worldly and supramundane wisdom; for when moral shame is absent, wisdom is absent. And just as a yoke-and-plow connected to the pole is effective, unshaken, and firm, so too is wisdom connected to moral shame effective, unshaken, firm, and unmixed with shamelessness. Therefore, He said, 'Moral shame is the pole.'

Munātīti mano, cittassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Idha pana manosīsena [P 1.0147] taṃsampayutto samādhi adhippeto. Yottanti rajjubandhanaṃ. Taṃ tividhaṃ īsāya saha yugassa bandhanaṃ, yugena saha balibaddānaṃ bandhanaṃ, sārathinā saha balibaddānaṃ bandhananti. Tattha yathā brāhmaṇassa yottaṃ īsāyugabalibadde ekābaddhe katvā sakakicce paṭipādeti, evaṃ bhagavato samādhi sabbeva te hiripaññāvīriyadhamme ekārammaṇe avikkhepabhāvena bandhitvā sakakicce paṭipādeti. Tenāha – “mano yotta”nti.

It knows, thus it is mind (mano); this is a designation for consciousness. Here, however, concentration associated with it, with the mind as its head, is intended. The rein (yotta) is a rope-binding. It is threefold: the binding of the yoke with the pole, the binding of the oxen with the yoke, and the binding of the oxen with the driver. In this context, just as a brahmin's rein, having made the pole, yoke, and oxen into a single unit, accomplishes his tasks, so too does the Blessed One's concentration, having bound all those states of moral shame, wisdom, and energy to a single object with non-distraction, accomplish His tasks. Hence, He said, 'The mind is the rein.'

Sarati etāya cirakatādimatthaṃ puggalo, sayaṃ vā saratīti sati, sā asammussanalakkhaṇā. Phāletīti phālo. Pājeti etenāti pājanaṃ. Taṃ idha “pācana”nti vuccati, patodassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Phālo ca pācanañca phālapācanaṃ. Yathā hi brāhmaṇassa phālapācanaṃ, evaṃ bhagavato vipassanāyuttā maggayuttā ca sati. Tattha yathā phālo naṅgalamanurakkhati, purato cassa gacchati, evaṃ sati kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ gatiyo samanvesamānā ārammaṇe vā upaṭṭhāpayamānā paññānaṅgalaṃ rakkhati, tathā hi “satārakkhena [M 1.0133] cetasā viharatī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 10.20) “ārakkhā”ti vuttā. Asammussanavasena cassa purato hoti. Satiparicite hi dhamme paññā pajānāti, no sammuṭṭhe. Yathā ca pācanaṃ balibaddānaṃ vijjhanabhayaṃ dassentaṃ saṃsīdanaṃ na deti, uppathagamanañca vāreti, evaṃ sati vīriyabalibaddānaṃ apāyabhayaṃ dassentī kosajjasaṃsīdanaṃ na deti, kāmaguṇasaṅkhāte agocare cāraṃ nivāretvā kammaṭṭhāne niyojentī uppathagamanañca vāreti. Tenāha – “sati me phālapācana”nti.

A person remembers with this things done long ago, etc., or one remembers by oneself—thus it is mindfulness (sati); its characteristic is non-forgetfulness. It splits, thus it is a plowshare (phālo). One drives with this, thus it is a goad (pājanaṃ). Here it is called a pācana; this is a synonym for a goad (patoda). The plowshare and the goad are the plowshare-and-goad. Just as a brahmin has a plowshare and a goad, so the Blessed One has mindfulness connected with insight and with the path. Therein, just as the plowshare protects the plow and goes before it, so mindfulness, by investigating the courses of wholesome states or by establishing itself in the object, protects the plow of wisdom. Indeed, it is called a 'guard' in passages such as, 'He dwells with a mind guarded by mindfulness.' And by way of non-forgetfulness, it goes before wisdom. For wisdom understands states familiarized by mindfulness, not those that are forgotten. And just as the goad, by showing the danger of being struck to the oxen, does not allow them to sink back and prevents them from going on the wrong path, so mindfulness, by showing the danger of the lower realms to the oxen of energy, does not allow sinking back into laziness, and by preventing them from roaming in the unsuitable pasture of sensual pleasures, it yokes them to the meditation subject and prevents them from going on the wrong path. Therefore, He said, 'Mindfulness is my plowshare and goad.'

78. Kāyaguttoti tividhena kāyasucaritena gutto. Vacīguttoti catubbidhena vacīsucaritena gutto. Ettāvatā pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlaṃ vuttaṃ. Āhāre udare yatoti ettha āhāramukhena sabbapaccayānaṃ saṅgahitattā catubbidhepi paccaye [P 1.0148] yato saṃyato nirupakkilesoti attho. Iminā ājīvapārisuddhisīlaṃ vuttaṃ. Udare yatoti udare yato saṃyato mitabhojī, āhāre [V 1.0117] mattaññūti vuttaṃ hoti. Iminā bhojane mattaññutāmukhena paccayapaṭisevanasīlaṃ vuttaṃ. Tena kiṃ dīpeti? Yathā tvaṃ, brāhmaṇa, bījaṃ vapitvā sassaparipālanatthaṃ kaṇṭakavatiṃ vā rukkhavatiṃ vā pākāraparikkhepaṃ vā karosi, tena te gomahiṃsamigagaṇā pavesaṃ alabhantā sassaṃ na vilumpanti, evamahampi saddhābījaṃ vapitvā nānappakārakusalasassaparipālanatthaṃ kāyavacīāhāraguttimayaṃ tividhaparikkhepaṃ karomi. Tena me rāgādiakusaladhammagomahiṃsamigagaṇā pavesaṃ alabhantā nānappakārakusalasassaṃ na vilumpantīti.

78. 'Guarded in body' means guarded by the threefold good conduct of the body. 'Guarded in speech' means guarded by the fourfold good conduct of speech. By this much, the virtue of Pātimokkha restraint is stated. In the phrase 'restrained in the belly regarding food,' since all requisites are included by way of food, the meaning is that one is restrained, controlled, and without defilement in regard to all four requisites. By this, the virtue of purity of livelihood is stated. 'Restrained in the belly' means one is restrained and controlled in the belly, eats in moderation; it is said one knows the proper measure in food. By this, through knowing the measure in food, the virtue pertaining to the use of requisites is stated. What does this illustrate? Just as you, brahmin, having sown a seed, make a fence of thorns, a wooden fence, or a surrounding wall to protect the crop, so that herds of cattle, buffaloes, and deer, being unable to enter, do not destroy the crop; in the same way, I too, having sown the seed of faith, make a threefold enclosure consisting of guarding the body, speech, and food to protect the crop of various wholesome states. Because of this, for me, the herds of cattle, buffaloes, and deer—which are unwholesome states such as lust—being unable to enter, do not destroy the crop of various wholesome states.

Saccaṃ karomi niddānanti ettha dvīhi dvārehi avisaṃvādanaṃ saccaṃ. Niddānanti chedanaṃ lunanaṃ uppāṭanaṃ, karaṇatthe cetaṃ upayogavacanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Ayañhi ettha attho “saccena karomi niddāna”nti. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yathā tvaṃ bāhiraṃ kasiṃ kasitvā sassadūsakānaṃ tiṇānaṃ hatthena vā asitena vā niddānaṃ karosi; evamahampi ajjhattikaṃ kasiṃ kasitvā kusalasassadūsakānaṃ visaṃvādanatiṇānaṃ saccena niddānaṃ karomi. Ñāṇasaccaṃ vā ettha saccanti veditabbaṃ, yaṃ taṃ yathābhūtañāṇanti vuccati. Tena attasaññādīnaṃ tiṇānaṃ niddānaṃ karomīti evaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Atha vā niddānanti chedakaṃ lāvakaṃ, uppāṭakanti attho. Evaṃ sante yathā tvaṃ dāsaṃ vā kammakaraṃ [M 1.0134] vā niddānaṃ karosi, “niddehi tiṇānī”ti tiṇānaṃ chedakaṃ lāvakaṃ uppāṭakaṃ karosi; evamahaṃ saccaṃ karomīti upayogavacaneneva vattuṃ yujjati. Atha vā saccanti diṭṭhisaccaṃ. Tamahaṃ niddānaṃ karomi, chinditabbaṃ lunitabbaṃ uppāṭetabbaṃ karomīti evampi upayogavacaneneva vattuṃ yujjati.

In the phrase 'I make truth my weeding,' truth (sacca) is non-deception in two ways. 'Weeding' (niddāna) means cutting, reaping, and uprooting. And this accusative case should be understood in the instrumental sense. For this is the meaning here: 'I do the weeding with truth.' What is being said? Just as you, having plowed an external field, weed the tares that spoil the crop with your hand or a sickle; so I too, having plowed the internal field, weed the tares of deception that spoil the wholesome crop with truth. Or, truth here should be understood as the truth of knowledge, which is called the knowledge of things as they really are. With that, it should be construed thus: 'I weed the tares of the perception of self and so on.' Alternatively, 'weeding' means a cutter, a reaper, an uprooter. In that case, just as you make a slave or a worker into a weeder—that is, you make them a cutter, reaper, and uprooter of tares, saying, 'Weed the tares!'—so too it is fitting to say, 'I make truth the weeder,' using the accusative case. Or again, 'truth' can mean the truth of views. 'I make that into something to be weeded'—meaning, 'I make it something to be cut, reaped, and uprooted.' This too is fitting to say using the accusative case.

Soraccaṃ me pamocananti ettha yaṃ taṃ “kāyiko avītikkamo, vācasiko avītikkamo”ti, evaṃ [P 1.0149] sīlameva “soracca”nti vuttaṃ, na taṃ idha adhippetaṃ, vuttameva etaṃ “kāyagutto”tiādinā nayena, arahattaphalaṃ pana adhippetaṃ. Tampi hi sundare nibbāne ratabhāvato “soracca”nti vuccati. Pamocananti yoggavissajjanaṃ. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yathā tava pamocanaṃ punapi sāyanhe vā dutiyadivase vā anāgatasaṃvacchare vā yojetabbato appamocanameva hoti, na mama evaṃ. Na hi mama antarā mocanaṃ nāma atthi. Ahañhi dīpaṅkaradasabalakālato pabhuti paññānaṅgale vīriyabalibadde yojetvā cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni kappasatasahassañca mahākasiṃ kasanto tāva na muñciṃ, yāva na sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambujjhi. Yadā ca me sabbaṃ taṃ kālaṃ khepetvā bodhirukkhamūle aparājitapallaṅke nisinnassa sabbaguṇaparivāraṃ arahattaphalaṃ udapādi, tadā mayā taṃ sabbussukkapaṭippassaddhippattiyā [V 1.0118] pamuttaṃ, na dāni puna yojetabbaṃ bhavissatīti. Etamatthaṃ sandhāyāha bhagavā – “soraccaṃ me pamocana”nti.

In 'Gentleness is my release,' that which is called 'gentleness' as 'no transgression in body, no transgression in speech'—that virtue is not intended here, for it has already been stated by way of 'guarded in body,' and so on. Rather, the fruit of arahantship is intended. For that too is called 'gentleness' because of delighting in the beautiful Nibbāna. 'Release' means the unyoking. What is being said? Just as your release, since the yoke must be applied again in the evening, or on the next day, or in a coming year, is indeed no release, it is not so for me. For me, there is no such thing as an intermittent release. Indeed, from the time of Dīpaṅkara, the Ten-Powered One, having yoked the oxen of energy to the plow of wisdom, I cultivated the great cultivation for four incalculable ages and a hundred thousand great eons, and did not unyoke until I attained supreme enlightenment. And when, after having spent all that time, while seated at the foot of the Bodhi tree on the unconquered throne, the fruit of arahantship, surrounded by all virtues, arose in me, then I was released by attaining the complete calming of all striving, and it will not need to be yoked again. With this meaning in mind, the Blessed One said: 'Gentleness is my release.'

79. Vīriyaṃ me dhuradhorayhanti ettha vīriyanti “kāyiko vā, cetasiko vā vīriyārambho”tiādinā nayena vuttapadhānaṃ. Dhurāyaṃ dhorayhaṃ dhuradhorayhaṃ, dhuraṃ vahatīti attho. Yathā hi brāhmaṇassa dhurāyaṃ dhorayhākaḍḍhitaṃ naṅgalaṃ bhūmighanaṃ bhindati, mūlasantānakāni ca padāleti, evaṃ bhagavato vīriyākaḍḍhitaṃ paññānaṅgalaṃ yathāvuttaṃ ghanaṃ bhindati, kilesasantānakāni ca padāleti. Tenāha – “vīriyaṃ me dhuradhorayha”nti. Atha vā purimadhuraṃ vahantā dhurā, mūladhuraṃ vahantā dhorayhā; dhurā ca dhorayhā ca dhuradhorayhā. Tattha yathā brāhmaṇassa ekamekasmiṃ naṅgale catubalibaddappabhedaṃ dhuradhorayhaṃ vahantaṃ uppannānuppannatiṇamūlaghātaṃ sassasampattiñca sādheti, evaṃ bhagavato catusammappadhānavīriyappabhedaṃ dhuradhorayhaṃ vahantaṃ uppannānuppannākusalamūlaghātaṃ kusalasampattiñca [P 1.0150] sādheti. Tenāha – “vīriyaṃ me dhuradhorayha”nti.

79. In 'Energy is my burden-bearer,' 'energy' refers to the effort that has been spoken of by way of 'bodily or mental exertion,' etc., namely, the right exertions. A bearer (dhorayha) for the burden (dhura) is a dhuradhorayha; the meaning is 'it bears the burden.' For just as a brahmin’s plow, drawn by a burden-bearing team, breaks up the hard earth and shatters the root networks, so too the Blessed One’s plow of wisdom, drawn by energy, breaks up the hard mass of defilements as described and shatters the networks of defilements. Therefore, he said: 'Energy is my burden-bearer.' Alternatively, those that bear the front yoke are the dhurā, and those that bear the main yoke are the dhorayhā; the dhurā and the dhorayhā together are the dhuradhorayhā. Therein, just as for a brahmin, a team of four oxen bearing the yoke for a single plow accomplishes the destruction of arisen and unarisen weeds and the success of the crop, so too for the Blessed One, the burden-bearer consisting of the four right efforts accomplishes the destruction of arisen and unarisen unwholesome roots and the success of the wholesome. Therefore, he said: 'Energy is my burden-bearer.'

Yogakkhemādhivāhananti [M 1.0135] ettha yogehi khemattā “yogakkhema”nti nibbānaṃ vuccati, taṃ adhikatvā vāhīyati, abhimukhaṃ vā vāhīyatīti adhivāhanaṃ. Yogakkhemassa adhivāhanaṃ yogakkhemādhivāhanaṃ. Tena kiṃ dīpeti? Yathā tava dhuradhorayhaṃ puratthimaṃ disaṃ pacchimādīsu vā aññataraṃ abhimukhaṃ vāhīyati, tathā mama dhuradhorayhaṃ nibbānābhimukhaṃ vāhīyati.

In 'the vehicle leading to security from bondage,' Nibbāna is called 'security from bondage' because it is security from the bonds. That which carries with reference to it, or carries facing towards it, is a 'vehicle leading.' The vehicle leading to security from bondage is yogakkhemādhivāhana. What does this show? Just as your burden-bearer is driven toward the eastern direction, or the western and other directions, so too my burden-bearer is driven toward Nibbāna.

Evaṃ vāhiyamānañca gacchati anivattantaṃ. Yathā tava naṅgalaṃ vahantaṃ dhuradhorayhaṃ khettakoṭiṃ patvā puna nivattati, evaṃ anivattantaṃ dīpaṅkarakālato pabhuti gacchateva. Yasmā vā tena tena maggena pahīnā kilesā punappunaṃ pahātabbā na honti, yathā tava naṅgalena chinnāni tiṇāni punapi aparasmiṃ samaye chinditabbāni honti, tasmāpi etaṃ paṭhamamaggavasena diṭṭhekaṭṭhe kilese, dutiyavasena oḷārike, tatiyavasena anusahagate kilese, catutthavasena sabbakilese pajahantaṃ gacchati anivattantaṃ. Atha vā gacchati anivattanti nivattanarahitaṃ hutvā gacchatīti attho. Nti taṃ dhuradhorayhaṃ. Evampettha padacchedo veditabbo. Evaṃ gacchantañca yathā tava dhuradhorayhaṃ na taṃ ṭhānaṃ gacchati, yattha gantvā kassako asoko nissoko virajo hutvā na socati, etaṃ pana taṃ ṭhānaṃ gacchati, yattha gantvā na socati. Yattha satipācanena etaṃ vīriyadhuradhorayhaṃ codento gantvā mādiso kassako asoko nissoko virajo hutvā na socati, taṃ sabbasokasallasamugghātabhūtaṃ nibbānāmatasaṅkhātaṃ ṭhānaṃ gacchatīti.

And so, being carried along, it goes without turning back. Just as your burden-bearer, pulling the plow, reaches the field’s edge and then turns back, so this goes without turning back, ever since the time of Dīpaṅkara. Or, because the defilements abandoned by each respective path do not need to be abandoned again and again—unlike the grass cut by your plow, which needs to be cut again at another time—therefore it also goes without turning back, abandoning the defilements: by the first path, those connected with wrong view; by the second path, the coarse ones; by the third path, the subtle ones; and by the fourth path, all defilements. Alternatively, 'it goes without turning back' (gacchati anivattaṃ) means it goes having become free from returning. The word division here should be understood as 'anivattaṃ iti'. 'Taṃ' refers to that burden-bearer. And as it goes, unlike your burden-bearer, it reaches that place where your burden-bearer does not go—the place where, having gone, the farmer becomes free from sorrow, griefless, and stainless, and does not grieve. This, however, reaches that place where, having gone, one does not grieve. Urged on by the goad of mindfulness, this burden-bearer of energy goes to where a farmer such as I, having gone, becomes free from sorrow, griefless, and stainless, and does not grieve. It goes to that place called the deathless Nibbāna, which is the uprooting of all the darts of sorrow.

80. Idāni [V 1.0119] nigamanaṃ karonto bhagavā imaṃ gāthamāha –

80. Now, making a conclusion, the Blessed One spoke this verse:

“Evamesā kasī kaṭṭhā, sā hoti amatapphalā;

Etaṃ kasiṃ kasitvāna, sabbadukkhā pamuccatī”ti.

"Thus this plowing is arduous, it bears the deathless fruit; Having plowed this plowing, one is freed from all suffering."

Tassāyaṃ saṅkhepattho – mayā brāhmaṇa esā saddhābījā tapovuṭṭhiyā anuggahitā kasi, paññāmayaṃ yuganaṅgalaṃ, hirimayañca īsaṃ, manomayena yottena, ekābaddhaṃ [P 1.0151] katvā, paññānaṅgale satiphālaṃ ākoṭetvā, satipācanaṃ gahetvā, kāyavacīāhāraguttiyā gopetvā, saccaṃ niddānaṃ katvā, soraccaṃ pamocanaṃ vīriyaṃ dhuradhorayhaṃ yogakkhemābhimukhaṃ anivattantaṃ vāhentena kaṭṭhā, kasikammapariyosānaṃ catubbidhaṃ sāmaññaphalaṃ pāpitā, sā [M 1.0136] hoti amatapphalā, sā esā kasi amatapphalā hoti. Amataṃ vuccati nibbānaṃ, nibbānānisaṃsā hotīti attho. Sā kho panesā kasi na mamevekassa amatapphalā hoti, apica, kho, pana yo koci khattiyo vā brāhmaṇo vā vesso vā suddo vā gahaṭṭho vā pabbajito vā etaṃ kasiṃ kasati, so sabbopi etaṃ kasiṃ kasitvāna, sabbadukkhā pamuccati, sabbasmā vaṭṭadukkhadukkhadukkhasaṅkhāradukkhavipariṇāmadukkhā pamuccatīti. Evaṃ bhagavā brāhmaṇassa arahattanikūṭena nibbānapariyosānaṃ katvā desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi.

This is its concise meaning: 'O Brahmin, this cultivation of mine has faith as its seed, and is supported by the rain of austerity. Wisdom is the yoke and plow, conscience the plow-pole. Having bound them together with the mind as the rope, and having fixed the plowshare of mindfulness onto the plow of wisdom; taking up the goad of mindfulness; guarding it with restraint of body, speech, and food; making truth the weeding; gentleness the unyoking; and energy the beast of burden, carrying it towards security from bondage, without turning back—thus it is cultivated. It has been brought to the culmination of the farmer's work, the fourfold fruit of recluseship. That cultivation has the deathless as its fruit. That cultivation yields the deathless fruit. The deathless is called Nibbāna; this means it has Nibbāna as its benefit. Moreover, this cultivation does not yield the deathless fruit for me alone. Indeed, whoever—be it a noble, a brahmin, a merchant, a laborer, a householder, or a renunciant—cultivates this cultivation, having so cultivated, is freed from all suffering: from all the suffering of the round, suffering as suffering, the suffering of formations, and the suffering of change.' Thus, the Blessed One concluded his teaching for the brahmin, making Nibbāna its culmination with the pinnacle of arahantship.

Tato brāhmaṇo gambhīratthaṃ desanaṃ sutvā “mama kasiphalaṃ bhuñjitvā aparajju eva chāto hoti, imassa pana kasi amatapphalā, tassā phalaṃ bhuñjitvā sabbadukkhā pamuccatī”ti ca viditvā pasanno pasannākāraṃ kātuṃ pāyāsaṃ dātumāraddho. Tenāha “atha kho kasibhāradvājo”ti. Tattha mahatiyāti mahatiyanti attho. Kaṃsapātiyāti suvaṇṇapātiyaṃ, satasahassagghanake attano suvaṇṇathāle. Vaḍḍhetvāti chupitvā, ākiritvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Bhagavato upanāmesīti sappimadhuphāṇitādīhi vicitraṃ katvā, dukūlavitānena paṭicchādetvā, ukkhipitvā, sakkaccaṃ tathāgatassa abhihari. Kinti? “Bhuñjatu bhavaṃ gotamo pāyāsaṃ, kassako bhava”nti. Tato kassakabhāvasādhakaṃ kāraṇamāha “yañhi…pe… kasatī”ti, yasmā bhavaṃ…pe… kasatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Atha bhagavā “gāthābhigītaṃ me”ti āha.

Then the brahmin, having heard the teaching of profound meaning, understood: 'Having eaten the fruit of my cultivation, on the very next day I am hungry again. But this one's cultivation has the deathless as its fruit; having eaten its fruit, one is freed from all suffering.' Being pleased, and wishing to show his pleasure, he began to offer milk-rice. Therefore it is said: 'Then Kasibhāradvāja...' Here, `mahatiyā` means 'in a great one.' `Kaṃsapātiyā` means in a golden bowl, in his own golden bowl worth a hundred thousand. `Vaḍḍhetvā` means having filled it to the brim and poured it; thus it is said. 'He presented it to the Blessed One' means he prepared it exquisitely with ghee, honey, molasses, and so on, covered it with a canopy of fine cloth, lifted it up, and respectfully brought it to the Tathāgata, saying: 'May the venerable Gotama partake of the milk-rice, for the venerable one is a farmer.' Then, to establish his status as a farmer, he stated the reason: 'For indeed... he plows...' which means, 'because the venerable one... plows.' Then the Blessed One said: 'What is gained by verses...'

81. Tattha gāthābhigītanti gāthāhi abhigītaṃ, gāthāyo bhāsitvā laddhanti vuttaṃ hoti. Meti mayā. Abhojaneyyanti bhuñjanārahaṃ na hoti. Sampassatanti sammā ājīvasuddhiṃ passataṃ[P 1.0152], samantā vā passataṃ sampassataṃ, buddhānanti vuttaṃ hoti. Nesa dhammoti “gāthābhigītaṃ bhuñjitabba”nti [V 1.0120] esa dhammo etaṃ cārittaṃ na hoti, tasmā gāthābhigītaṃ panudanti buddhā paṭikkhipanti na bhuñjantīti. Kiṃ pana bhagavatā pāyāsatthaṃ gāthā abhigītā, yena evamāhāti? Na etadatthaṃ abhigītā, apica, kho, pana pāto paṭṭhāya khettasamīpe ṭhatvā kaṭacchubhikkhampi alabhitvā puna sakalabuddhaguṇe pakāsetvā laddhaṃ tadetaṃ naṭanaccakādīhi naccitvā gāyitvā ca laddhasadisaṃ hoti, tena “gāthābhigīta”nti vuttaṃ. Tādisañca yasmā [M 1.0137] buddhānaṃ na kappati, tasmā “abhojaneyya”nti vuttaṃ. Appicchatānurūpañcetaṃ na hoti, tasmāpi pacchimaṃ janataṃ anukampamānena ca evaṃ vuttaṃ. Yatra ca nāma parappakāsitenāpi attano guṇena uppannaṃ lābhaṃ paṭikkhipanti seyyathāpi appiccho ghaṭikāro kumbhakāro, tatra kathaṃ koṭippattāya appicchatāya samannāgato bhagavā attanāva attano guṇappakāsanena uppannaṃ lābhaṃ sādiyissati, yato yuttameva etaṃ bhagavato vattunti.

81. There, `gāthābhigītaṃ` means 'sung over with verses'; it means what is obtained by reciting verses. `Me` means 'by me.' `Abhojaneyyaṃ` means it is not fit to be eaten. `Sampassataṃ` means 'of those who see,' that is, of those who rightly see the purity of livelihood, or of those who see all around; this refers to the Buddhas. `Nesa dhammo` means: 'That one should eat what is gained by verses'—this is not the Dhamma, this is not the practice. Therefore, the Buddhas spurn what is gained by verses; they reject it and do not eat it. But were the verses sung by the Blessed One for the sake of the milk-rice, that he spoke thus? They were not sung for this purpose. Rather, from early morning, having stood near the field and not having received even a ladleful of alms, it was then obtained by proclaiming all the virtues of the Buddha. That which was thus obtained is similar to what is obtained by dancers, acrobats, and so on, through dancing and singing. Hence, it is called `gāthābhigītaṃ`. And because such a thing is not allowable for Buddhas, it is called `abhojaneyyaṃ`. Moreover, this is not in conformity with having few wishes, and so it was also said out of compassion for future generations. For where even gain that arises from another proclaiming one's own virtues is rejected—as in the case of Ghaṭikāra the potter, who had few wishes—how then would the Blessed One, who is endowed with the highest degree of having few wishes, consent to gain that arises from his own proclamation of his own virtues? Therefore, it is indeed proper for the Blessed One to say this.

Ettāvatā “appasannaṃ adātukāmaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ gāthāgāyanena dātukāmaṃ katvā, samaṇo gotamo bhojanaṃ paṭiggahesi, āmisakāraṇā imassa desanā”ti imamhā lokāpavādā attānaṃ mocento desanāpārisuddhiṃ dīpetvā, idāni ājīvapārisuddhiṃ dīpento āha “dhamme satī brāhmaṇa vuttiresā”ti tassattho – ājīvapārisuddhidhamme vā dasavidhasucaritadhamme vā buddhānaṃ cārittadhamme vā sati saṃvijjamāne anupahate vattamāne vuttiresā ekantavodātā ākāse pāṇippasāraṇakappā esanā pariyesanā jīvitavutti buddhānaṃ brāhmaṇāti.

Thus far, having freed himself from this worldly slander—"The ascetic Gotama accepted food after making an unwilling and reluctant brahmin willing to give by singing verses; his teaching is for the sake of material gain"—and having illuminated the purity of his teaching, now illuminating the purity of livelihood, he says, "Brahmin, this is the livelihood when the Dhamma exists." The meaning is this: When the purity of livelihood Dhamma, or the tenfold wholesome conduct Dhamma, or the conduct Dhamma of the Buddhas exists, unbroken, and continues, this is the livelihood—utterly pure, like extending one's hand into the sky—the search, the quest, the way of life of the Buddhas, O brahmin.

82. Evaṃ vutte brāhmaṇo “pāyāsaṃ me paṭikkhipati, akappiyaṃ kiretaṃ bhojanaṃ, adhañño vatasmiṃ, dānaṃ dātuṃ [P 1.0153] na labhāmī”ti domanassaṃ uppādetvā “appeva nāma aññaṃ paṭiggaṇheyyā”ti ca cintesi. Taṃ ñatvā bhagavā “ahaṃ bhikkhācāravelaṃ paricchinditvā āgato – ‘ettakena kālena imaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ pasādessāmī’ti, brāhmaṇo ca domanassaṃ akāsi. Idāni tena domanassena mayi cittaṃ pakopetvā amatavaradhammaṃ paṭivijjhituṃ na sakkhissatī”ti brāhmaṇassa pasādajananatthaṃ tena patthitamanorathaṃ pūrento āha “aññena ca kevalina”nti. Tattha kevalinanti sabbaguṇaparipuṇṇaṃ, sabbayogavisaṃyuttaṃ vāti attho. Mahantānaṃ sīlakkhandhādīnaṃ guṇānaṃ esanato mahesiṃ. Parikkhīṇasabbāsavattā khīṇāsavaṃ. Hatthapādakukkuccamādiṃ katvā vūpasantasabbakukkuccattā kukkuccavūpasantaṃ. Upaṭṭhahassūti parivisassu paṭimānayassu. Evaṃ brāhmaṇena citte uppāditepi pariyāyameva bhaṇati, na tu bhaṇati “dehi, āharāhī”ti. Sesamettha uttānameva.

82. When this was said, the brahmin, generating sorrow, thought, “He refuses my milk-rice. This food is surely unsuitable. Alas, I am unfortunate; I am unable to give a gift.” And he also thought, “Perhaps he might accept something else.” Knowing this, the Blessed One thought, “I came after determining the time for the alms-round, thinking, ‘Within this much time, I will inspire faith in this brahmin.’ But the brahmin has become sorrowful. Now, with that sorrow, having corrupted his mind towards me, he will not be able to penetrate the excellent, deathless Dhamma.” To inspire faith in the brahmin and to fulfill his wished-for desire, He said, “And to another who is complete.” Therein, “complete” means endowed with all virtues, or else free from all yokes. Because he seeks the great virtues, such as the aggregates of morality, he is a great seer. Due to the utter destruction of all taints, he is one whose taints are destroyed. Due to all scruples being calmed, beginning with those concerning hands and feet, he is one whose scruples are calmed. “You should attend” means you should serve, you should honor. Thus, even when this thought had arisen in the brahmin’s mind, the Blessed One spoke only indirectly; he did not say, “Give,” or “Bring it.” The rest here is self-evident.

Atha [V 1.0121][M 1.0138] brāhmaṇo “ayaṃ pāyāso bhagavato ānīto nāhaṃ arahāmi taṃ attano chandena kassaci dātu”nti cintetvā āha “atha kassa cāha”nti. Tato bhagavā “taṃ pāyāsaṃ ṭhapetvā tathāgataṃ tathāgatasāvakañca aññassa ajīraṇadhammo”ti ñatvā āha – “na khvāhaṃ ta”nti. Tattha sadevakavacanena pañcakāmāvacaradevaggahaṇaṃ, samārakavacanena chaṭṭhakāmāvacaradevaggahaṇaṃ, sabrahmakavacanena rūpāvacarabrahmaggahaṇaṃ arūpāvacarā pana bhuñjeyyunti asambhāvaneyyā. Sassamaṇabrāhmaṇivacanena sāsanapaccatthikapaccāmittasamaṇabrāhmaṇaggahaṇaṃ samitapāpabāhitapāpasamaṇabrāhmaṇaggahaṇañca. Pajāvacanena sattalokaggahaṇaṃ, sadevamanussavacanena sammutidevaavasesamanussaggahaṇaṃ. Evamettha tīhi vacanehi okāsaloko, dvīhi pajāvasena sattaloko gahitoti veditabbo. Esa saṅkhepo, vitthāraṃ pana āḷavakasutte [P 1.0154] vaṇṇayissāma.

Then the brahmin, thinking, “This milk-rice was brought for the Blessed One; it is not right for me to give it to anyone according to my own wish,” said, “Then to whom shall I give it?” Then the Blessed One, knowing, “Setting aside the Tathāgata and a disciple of the Tathāgata, this milk-rice is indigestible for any other,” said, “I do not see…” Herein, by the word “with the devas,” the devas of the five sense-sphere realms are included. By the word “with Māra,” the devas of the sixth sense-sphere realm are included. By the word “with Brahmā,” the brahmās of the form realm are included; but that those of the formless realm might eat is not to be considered. By the phrase “with its ascetics and brahmins,” hostile ascetics and brahmins who are opponents of the teaching are included, as well as ascetics and brahmins who have pacified evil and banished evil. By the word “progeny,” the world of beings is included. By the phrase “with its devas and humans,” conventional devas and the remaining humans are included. Thus it should be understood that herein, by three phrases the spatial world is included, and by two, by means of the word ‘progeny,’ the world of beings is included. This is a summary; we shall explain it in detail in the commentary on the Āḷavaka Sutta.

Kasmā pana sadevakādīsu kassaci na sammā pariṇāmaṃ gaccheyyāti? Oḷārike sukhumojāpakkhipanato. Imasmiñhi pāyāse bhagavantaṃ uddissa gahitamatteyeva devatāhi ojā pakkhittā yathā sujātāya pāyāse, cundassa ca sūkaramaddave paccamāne, verañjāyañca bhagavatā gahitagahitālope, bhesajjakkhandhake ca kaccānassa guḷhakumbhasmiṃ avasiṭṭhaguḷhe. So oḷārike sukhumojāpakkhipanato devānaṃ na pariṇamati. Devā hi sukhumasarīrā, tesaṃ oḷāriko manussāhāro na sammā pariṇamati. Manussānampi na pariṇamati. Manussā hi oḷārikasarīrā, tesaṃ sukhumā dibbojā na sammā pariṇamati. Tathāgatassa pana pakatiaggināva pariṇamati, sammā jīrati. Kāyabalañāṇabalappabhāvenāti eke tathāgatasāvakassa khīṇāsavassetaṃ samādhibalena mattaññutāya ca pariṇamati, itaresaṃ iddhimantānampi na pariṇamati. Acintanīyaṃ vā ettha kāraṇaṃ, buddhavisayo esoti.

But why would it not be properly digested by anyone among the devas and so forth? Because subtle essence was infused into the coarse food. For in this milk-rice, as soon as it was taken with the Blessed One in mind, the deities infused essence into it, just as in Sujātā’s milk-rice, in Cunda’s pork dish while it was being prepared, in the lumps of food taken by the Blessed One at Verañjā, and in the leftover molasses in Kaccāna’s pot in the Section on Medicines. Because of the infusion of subtle essence into the coarse food, it is not digested by the devas. For devas have subtle bodies, and coarse human food is not properly digested by them. It is also not digested by humans. For humans have coarse bodies, and the subtle divine essence is not properly digested by them. For the Tathāgata, however, it is digested by his natural digestive fire and digests well. Some say this is due to the power of his bodily strength and knowledge. For a disciple of the Tathāgata who is an arahant, it is digested through the power of concentration and through knowing the proper measure, but it is not digested by others, even those with psychic powers. Or else, the reason here is inconceivable; this is the domain of the Buddhas.

Tena hi tvanti yasmā aññaṃ na passāmi, mama na kappati, mama akappantaṃ sāvakassāpi me na kappati, tasmā tvaṃ brāhmaṇāti vuttaṃ hoti. Appahariteti parittaharitatiṇe, apparuḷharitatiṇe vā pāsāṇapiṭṭhisadise. Appāṇaketi nippāṇake, pāyāsajjhottharaṇakāraṇena maritabbapāṇarahite vā mahāudakakkhandhe. Saha tiṇanissitehi pāṇehi tiṇānaṃ pāṇakānañca anurakkhaṇatthāya etaṃ vuttaṃ. Cicciṭāyati ciṭiciṭāyatīti [M 1.0139] evaṃ saddaṃ karoti. Saṃdhūpāyatīti samantā dhūpāyati. Sampadhūpāyatīti tatheva adhimattaṃ dhūpāyati. Kasmā evaṃ ahosīti? Bhagavato ānubhāvena, na udakassa, na pāyāsassa, na brāhmaṇassa, na aññesaṃ devayakkhādīnaṃ. Bhagavā hi brāhmaṇassa dhammasaṃvegatthaṃ tathā adhiṭṭhāsi. Seyyathāpi nāmāti opammanidassanamattametaṃ, yathā phāloti ettakameva [P 1.0155] vuttaṃ hoti. Saṃviggo cittena, lomahaṭṭhajāto [V 1.0122] sarīrena. Sarīre kirassa navanavutilomakūpasahassāni suvaṇṇabhittiyā āhatamaṇināgadantā viya uddhaggā ahesuṃ. Sesaṃ pākaṭameva.

The phrase ‘Therefore, you…’ means: ‘Because I see no other, and it is not suitable for me, and what is not suitable for me is also not suitable for my disciple, therefore it was said to you, “Brahmin.”’ ‘In a place with little green grass’ means on ground with sparse green grass, or on ground with no green grass grown, like a stone slab. ‘In a place without living beings’ means in a great mass of water that is without creatures, or that is free of creatures that would die from being covered by the milk-rice. This was said for the protection of both the grass and the creatures dependent on the grass. ‘It sizzles’ means it makes a sound like ‘cicciṭa, ciṭiciṭa.’ ‘It steams’ means it gives off steam all around. ‘It steams profusely’ means it gives off an exceedingly great amount of steam in the same way. Why did this happen? It happened through the power of the Blessed One, not of the water, not of the milk-rice, not of the brahmin, nor of other devas, yakkhas, and so on. For the Blessed One made this resolution for the sake of inspiring spiritual urgency in the brahmin. The phrase ‘Just as…’ is merely for the purpose of showing a simile; it means only this much has been said: ‘like a ploughshare.’ He was stirred in mind, and the hairs of his body stood on end. It is said that on his body, ninety-nine thousand hair-pores stood erect, like ivory pegs inlaid with jewels driven into a golden wall. The rest is self-evident.

Pādesu pana nipatitvā bhagavato dhammadesanaṃ abbhanumodamāno bhagavantaṃ etadavoca “abhikkantaṃ, bho gotama, abhikkantaṃ, bho gotamā”ti. Abbhanumodane hi ayamidha abhikkanta saddo. Vitthārato panassa maṅgalasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ atthavaṇṇanā āvi bhavissati. Yasmā ca abbhanumodanatthe, tasmā sādhu sādhu bho gotamāti vuttaṃ hotīti veditabbaṃ.

Then, having fallen at the feet of the Blessed One and greatly rejoicing in his teaching of the Dhamma, he said this to the Blessed One: “Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama!” For here, this word ‘excellent’ is used in the sense of great rejoicing. A detailed explanation of its meaning will become clear in the commentary on the Maṅgala Sutta. And because it is in the sense of great rejoicing, it should be understood to mean, “It is good, it is good, Master Gotama!”

“Bhaye kodhe pasaṃsāyaṃ, turite kotūhalacchare;

Hāse soke pasāde ca, kare āmeḍitaṃ budho”ti. –

“In fear, in anger, in praise, in haste, in excitement and wonder, in laughter, in sorrow, and in faith, a wise person makes a repetition.”

Iminā ca lakkhaṇena idha pasādavasena pasaṃsāvasena cāyaṃ dvikkhattuṃ vuttoti veditabbo. Atha vā abhikkantanti abhikantaṃ atiiṭṭhaṃ, atimanāpaṃ, atisundaranti vuttaṃ hoti.

By this characteristic, it should be understood that here, by way of confidence and by way of praise, this word 'abhikkanta' is spoken twice. Alternatively, 'abhikkanta' means excellent, most desired, most pleasing, and most beautiful—thus it is said.

Tattha ekena abhikkantasaddena desanaṃ thometi, ekena attano pasādaṃ. Ayañhi ettha adhippāyo – abhikkantaṃ, bho gotama, yadidaṃ bhoto gotamassa dhammadesanā, abhikkantaṃ yadidaṃ bhoto gotamassa dhammadesanaṃ āgamma mama pasādoti. Bhagavato eva vā vacanaṃ dve dve atthe sandhāya thometi – bhoto gotamassa vacanaṃ abhikkantaṃ dosanāsanato, abhikkantaṃ guṇādhigamanato, tathā saddhājananato, paññājananato, sātthato, sabyañjanato, uttānapadato, gambhīratthato, kaṇṇasukhato, hadayaṅgamato, anattukkaṃsanato, aparavambhanato, karuṇāsītalato, paññāvadātato, āpātharamaṇīyato, vimaddakkhamato, suyyamānasukhato, vīmaṃsiyamānahitatoti evamādīhi yojetabbaṃ.

Herein, with one utterance of 'excellent,' he praises the teaching, and with the other, his own confidence. For this is the intended meaning here: 'Excellent, Venerable Gotama, is this teaching of the Venerable Gotama; excellent is the confidence that has arisen in me on account of the Venerable Gotama's teaching.' Alternatively, he praises the words of the Blessed One, referring to two meanings for each—the words of the Venerable Gotama are excellent because they dispel faults, and excellent because they lead to the attainment of virtues; likewise, because they generate faith and generate wisdom; are meaningful and well-phrased; clear in wording and profound in meaning; pleasing to the ear and touching the heart; not self-praising and not disparaging others; cool with compassion and bright with wisdom; delightful upon first hearing and able to withstand scrutiny; pleasant while being heard and beneficial when examined—thus it should be connected in these and other ways.

Tato [M 1.0140] parampi catūhi upamāhi desanaṃyeva thometi. Tattha nikkujjitanti adhomukhaṭṭhapitaṃ, heṭṭhā mukhajātaṃ vā. Ukkujjeyyāti uparimukhaṃ kareyya. Paṭicchannanti tiṇapaṇṇādicchāditaṃ. Vivareyyāti ugghāṭeyya. Mūḷhassāti disāmūḷhassa. Maggaṃ ācikkheyyāti hatthe gahetvā [P 1.0156] “esa maggo”ti vadeyya. Andhakāreti kāḷapakkhacātuddasīaḍḍharattaghanavanasaṇḍameghapaṭalehi caturaṅge tamasi. Ayaṃ tāva padattho.

Furthermore, he praises the teaching with four similes. Herein, 'overturned' means placed face-down, or having its opening downwards. 'Set upright' means to make it face upwards. 'Covered' means concealed by grass, leaves, and so forth. 'Uncovered' means to open up. 'For one who is lost' means for one who has lost their direction. 'Would point out the path' means taking one by the hand and saying, 'This is the path.' 'In the darkness' means in the fourfold darkness of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, midnight, a dense forest grove, and a layer of clouds. This, for now, is the meaning of the words.

Ayaṃ pana adhippāyayojanā – yathā koci nikkujjitaṃ ukkujjeyya, evaṃ saddhammavimukhaṃ [V 1.0123] asaddhammapatitaṃ maṃ asaddhammā vuṭṭhāpentena, yathā paṭicchannaṃ vivareyya; evaṃ kassapassa bhagavato sāsanantaradhānā pabhuti micchādiṭṭhigahanapaṭicchannaṃ sāsanaṃ vivarantena, yathā mūḷhassa maggaṃ ācikkheyya, evaṃ kummaggamicchāmaggapaṭipannassa me saggamokkhamaggaṃ ācikkhantena, yathā andhakāre telapajjotaṃ dhāreyya, evaṃ mohandhakāranimuggassa me buddhādiratanarūpāni apassato tappaṭicchādakamohandhakāraviddhaṃsakadesanāpajjotadhāraṇena mayhaṃ bhotā gotamena etehi pariyāyehi desitattā anekapariyāyena dhammo pakāsito.

Now, this is the application of the intended meaning: Just as one might set upright what has been overturned, so too, for me, who was turned away from the true Dhamma and had fallen into false teachings, the Venerable Gotama has raised me up from those false teachings. Just as one might uncover what is hidden, so too has he revealed the teaching that had been obscured by the thicket of wrong views since the disappearance of the dispensation of the Blessed Kassapa. Just as one might show the path to one who is lost, so too, for me, who had embarked on the wrong path, the false path, has the Venerable Gotama shown the path to heaven and liberation. And just as one might hold up an oil lamp in the darkness, so too, for me, who was immersed in the darkness of delusion and unable to see the treasures of the Buddha and so on, has the Venerable Gotama, by holding up the lamp of his teaching that destroys the concealing darkness of delusion, illuminated the Dhamma. Because it was taught by the Venerable Gotama in these various ways, the Dhamma has been illuminated in many ways.

Atha vā ekacciyena mattena yasmā ayaṃ dhammo dukkhadassanena asubhe “subha”nti vipallāsappahānena ca nikkujjitukkujjitasadiso, samudayadassanena dukkhe “sukha”nti vipallāsappahānena ca paṭicchannavivaraṇasadiso, nirodhadassanena anicce “nicca”nti vipallāsappahānena ca mūḷhassa maggācikkhaṇasadiso, maggadassanena anattani “attā”ti vipallāsappahānena ca andhakāre pajjotasadiso, tasmā seyyathāpi nāma nikkujjitaṃ vā ukkujjeyya…pe… pajjotaṃ dhāreyya “cakkhumanto rūpāni dakkhantī”ti, evaṃ pakāsito hoti.

Alternatively, according to one opinion: because this Dhamma, through the seeing of suffering and the abandoning of the distortion of perceiving the foul as 'fair,' is like setting upright what was overturned; and through the seeing of the origin and the abandoning of the distortion of perceiving suffering as 'pleasure,' is like uncovering what was covered; and through the seeing of cessation and the abandoning of the distortion of perceiving the impermanent as 'permanent,' is like showing the path to one who is lost; and through the seeing of the path and the abandoning of the distortion of perceiving what is not-self as 'self,' is like a lamp in the darkness—therefore, just as one might set upright what was overturned... or hold up a lamp so that 'those with eyes might see forms,' even so has the Dhamma been illuminated.

Yasmā panettha saddhātapakāyaguttatādīhi sīlakkhandho pakāsito hoti, paññāya paññākkhandho, hirimanādīhi samādhikkhandho, yogakkhemena nirodhoti evaṃ tikkhandho ariyamaggo nirodho cāti sarūpeneva dve ariyasaccāni pakāsitāni. Tattha maggo paṭipakkho samudayassa, nirodho dukkhassāti paṭipakkhena dve. Iti iminā pariyāyena cattāri saccāni pakāsitāni. Tasmā anekapariyāyena pakāsito hotīti veditabbo[P 1.0157].

Because herein the aggregate of virtue is illuminated through faith, austerity, guarding of the body, and so forth; the aggregate of wisdom is illuminated through wisdom; and the aggregate of concentration is illuminated through moral shame, mindfulness, and so forth; and through security from bondage, cessation is illuminated—thus the noble path of three aggregates and cessation, two noble truths, are illuminated in their own form. Therein, the path is the opponent of the origin, and cessation is the opponent of suffering—thus two more are illuminated by way of opposition. In this way, the four noble truths are illuminated. Therefore, it should be understood that the Dhamma is illuminated in many ways.

Esāhantiādīsu [M 1.0141] eso ahanti esāhaṃ. Saraṇaṃ gacchāmīti pādesu nipatitvā paṇipātena saraṇagamanena gatopi idāni vācāya samādiyanto āha. Atha vā paṇipātena buddhaṃyeva saraṇaṃ gatoti idāni taṃ ādiṃ katvā sese dhammasaṅghepi gantuṃ āha. Ajjataggeti ajjataṃ ādiṃ katvā, ajjadaggeti vā pāṭho, da-kāro padasandhikaro, ajja aggaṃ katvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Pāṇehi upetaṃ pāṇupetaṃ, yāva me jīvitaṃ pavattati, tāva upetaṃ, anaññasatthukaṃ tīhi saraṇagamanehi saraṇaṃ gataṃ maṃ bhavaṃ gotamo dhāretu jānātūti vuttaṃ hoti. Ettāvatā anena sutānurūpā paṭipatti dassitā hoti. Nikkujjitādīhi vā satthusampattiṃ dassetvā iminā “esāha”ntiādinā sissasampatti dassitā. Tena vā paññāpaṭilābhaṃ dassetvā iminā saddhāpaṭilābho dassito. Idāni evaṃ paṭiladdhasaddhena paññavatā yaṃ [V 1.0124] kattabbaṃ, taṃ kattukāmo bhagavantaṃ yācati “labheyyāha”nti. Tattha bhagavato iddhiyādīhi abhippasāditacitto “bhagavāpi cakkavattirajjaṃ pahāya pabbajito, kimaṅgaṃ panāha”nti saddhāya pabbajjaṃ yācati, tattha paripūrakāritaṃ patthento paññāya upasampadaṃ. Sesaṃ pākaṭameva.

In phrases such as `esāhaṃ`, the division of the words is `eso ahaṃ` (this I am). Regarding 'I go for refuge': although he had already gone for refuge by prostrating at the feet with a gesture of reverence, he now says this, undertaking it verbally. Alternatively, having gone for refuge only to the Buddha with a gesture of reverence, he now speaks, intending to go for refuge in the remaining Dhamma and Saṅgha as well, taking that as the starting point. Regarding `ajjatagge`: this means 'taking today as the beginning.' Or the reading is `ajjadagge`, where the letter 'd' is for euphonic connection, meaning 'making today the foremost.' `Pāṇupetaṃ` means 'endowed with life'; for as long as my life continues, so long am I endowed. 'May the Venerable Gotama regard me as one who has gone for refuge through the three refuges, having no other teacher'—this is what is said. By this much, the practice suitable to what was heard is shown by him. Alternatively, having shown the Teacher's accomplishment through the similes of the overturned, etc., by this phrase 'This I am,' etc., the disciple's accomplishment is shown. Or, having shown the attainment of wisdom by the former, the attainment of faith is shown by the latter. Now, having thus acquired faith and wisdom, desiring to do what ought to be done, he requests of the Blessed One, 'May I receive...' Herein, his mind greatly inspired by the Blessed One's psychic powers and so on, he thinks, 'The Blessed One himself renounced the sovereignty of a universal monarch and went forth; what then of me?' and with faith requests the going forth. Therein, aspiring for its fulfillment, he requests the higher ordination through wisdom. The rest is self-evident.

Eko vūpakaṭṭhotiādīsu pana eko kāyavivekena, vūpakaṭṭho cittavivekena, appamatto kammaṭṭhāne satiavijahanena, ātāpī kāyikacetasikavīriyasaṅkhātena ātāpena, pahitatto kāye ca jīvite ca anapekkhatāya viharanto aññatarairiyāpathavihārena. Na cirassevāti pabbajjaṃ upādāya vuccati. Kulaputtāti duvidhā kulaputtā, jātikulaputtā, ācārakulaputtā ca. Ayaṃ pana ubhayathāpi kulaputto. Agārasmāti gharā. Agārānaṃ hitaṃ agāriyaṃ kasigorakkhādikuṭumbaposanakammaṃ vuccati. Natthi ettha agāriyanti anagāriyaṃ, pabbajjāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ pabbajantīti upagacchanti upasaṅkamanti. Tadanuttaranti taṃ anuttaraṃ. Brahmacariyapariyosānanti maggabrahmacariyassa pariyosānaṃ, arahattaphalanti [P 1.0158] vuttaṃ hoti. Tassa hi atthāya kulaputtā pabbajanti. Diṭṭheva dhammeti tasmiṃyeva attabhāve. Sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvāti attanāyeva paññāya paccakkhaṃ katvā, aparappaccayaṃ ñatvāti attho. Upasampajja vihāsīti pāpuṇitvā sampādetvā vā vihāsi. Evaṃ viharanto ca khīṇā jāti…pe… abbhaññāsi. Etenassa paccavekkhaṇabhūmiṃ dasseti.

Now, in such phrases as 'alone, withdrawn': 'alone' means through seclusion of the body; 'withdrawn' means through seclusion of the mind; 'diligent' means by not abandoning mindfulness on the meditation subject; 'ardent' means with the ardour known as bodily and mental energy; 'with a resolute mind' means by being unconcerned for body and life, while dwelling in one or another posture. 'Not long after' is said with reference to his going forth. 'A clansman': there are two kinds of clansmen, a clansman by birth and a clansman by conduct. This one, however, was a clansman in both ways. 'From the home' means from the house. The work of farming, cattle-tending, and supporting a family is called 'agāriyaṃ', that which pertains to the household. Because there is no 'agāriyaṃ' here, it is 'anagāriyaṃ'; this is a synonym for the going forth. 'They go forth' means they approach, they draw near. 'That unsurpassed' means that is unsurpassed. 'The culmination of the holy life' means the culmination of the holy life of the path, which is to say, the fruit of arahantship. For it is for the sake of this that clansmen go forth. 'In this very life' means in this very existence. 'Having realized it for himself through direct knowledge' means having made it manifest with his own wisdom, knowing it without reliance on another. 'Having attained it, he dwelled' means having reached or having accomplished it, he dwelled. And dwelling thus, he understood: 'Birth is destroyed…' By this, the text shows his stage of reviewing.

Katamā [M 1.0142] panassa jāti khīṇā, kathañca naṃ abbhaññāsīti? Vuccate – na tāvassa atītā jāti khīṇā pubbeva khīṇattā, na anāgatā anāgate vāyāmābhāvato, na paccuppannā vijjamānattā. Yā pana maggassa abhāvitattā uppajjeyya ekacatupañcavokārabhavesu ekacatupañcakkhandhappabhedā jāti, sā maggassa bhāvitattā anuppādadhammataṃ āpajjanena khīṇā. Taṃ so maggabhāvanāya pahīnakilese paccavekkhitvā kilesābhāve vijjamānampi kammaṃ āyatiṃ apaṭisandhikaṃ hotīti jānanto jānāti.

But which birth of his is destroyed, and how did he understand it? It is said: To begin with, his past birth is not what is destroyed, for it was already destroyed. Not the future birth, because there is no effort concerning the future. Not the present birth, because it is currently existing. But that birth—differentiated into one, four, or five aggregates in the one-, four-, or five-constituent existences—which might have arisen because the path had not been developed, that birth is destroyed because, through the development of the path, it has attained the nature of non-arising. He knows this by reviewing the defilements that were abandoned through the development of the path, knowing with certainty that in the absence of defilements, even existing kamma does not lead to a future relinking.

Vusitanti vutthaṃ parivutthaṃ, kataṃ caritaṃ niṭṭhāpitanti attho. Brahmacariyanti maggabrahmacariyaṃ. Kataṃ karaṇīyanti catūsu saccesu catūhi maggehi pariññāpahānasacchikiriyabhāvanāvasena soḷasavidhampi kiccaṃ niṭṭhāpitanti attho. Nāparaṃ itthattāyāti idāni puna itthabhāvāya evaṃ soḷasakiccabhāvāya kilesakkhayāya vā maggabhāvanā natthīti. Atha vā itthattāyāti itthabhāvato, imasmā evaṃpakārā idāni vattamānakkhandhasantānā aparaṃ khandhasantānaṃ natthi. Ime pana pañcakkhandhā pariññātā tiṭṭhanti chinnamūlako rukkho viyāti abbhaññāsi. Aññataroti [V 1.0125] eko. Arahatanti arahantānaṃ. Mahāsāvakānaṃ abbhantaro āyasmā bhāradvājo ahosīti ayaṃ kirettha adhippāyoti.

'The holy life has been lived' means it has been lived, done, practiced, and brought to completion—this is the meaning. 'The holy life' means the holy life of the path. 'What was to be done has been done' means that the sixteenfold task—by way of full understanding, abandoning, realizing, and developing with respect to the four truths by means of the four paths—has been brought to completion; this is the meaning. 'There is nothing further for this state' means that now there is no further development of the path for this state of being, or for the state of the sixteen tasks, or for the destruction of defilements. Or alternatively, 'for this state' means from this state of being; from this present continuum of aggregates of this kind, there is no other continuum of aggregates. He understood: 'These five aggregates, having been fully understood, remain like a tree with its root cut.' 'One of' means one. 'Of the Arahants' means among the Arahants. The Venerable Bhāradvāja became one included among the great disciples—this, it is said, is the intention here.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

Of the Paramatthajotikā, a commentary on a text of the Khuddaka Nikāya,

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya kasibhāradvājasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

In the Commentary on the Suttanipāta, the explanation of the Kasibhāradvāja Sutta is finished.

5. Cundasuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Explanation of the Cunda Sutta

83. Pucchāmi [V 1.0126][P 1.0159] muniṃ pahūtapaññanti cundasuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Saṅkhepato tāva attajjhāsayaparajjhāsayaaṭṭhuppattipucchāvasikabhedato catūsu uppattīsu imassa suttassa pucchāvasikā uppatti. Vitthārato pana ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā mallesu cārikaṃ caramāno mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ yena pāvā tadavasari. Tatra sudaṃ bhagavā pāvāyaṃ viharati cundassa kammāraputtassa ambavane. Ito pabhuti yāva “atha kho bhagavā pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghena yena cundassa [M 1.0143] kammāraputtassa nivesanaṃ tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā paññatte āsane nisīdī”ti (dī. ni. 2.189), tāva sutte āgatanayeneva vitthāretabbaṃ.

83. 'I ask the sage of great wisdom'—this is the Cunda Sutta. What is its origin? Briefly, to begin with, among the four kinds of origin—namely, that based on personal inclination, on the inclination of others, on an incident, and on a question—the origin of this sutta is that based on a question. In detail, however: at one time the Blessed One, while wandering on tour among the Mallas with a great Sangha of monks, arrived at Pāvā. There, it is said, the Blessed One dwelt in Pāvā in the mango grove of Cunda the smith's son. From this point up to 'Then, in the morning, the Blessed One, having dressed, taking his bowl and robe, went together with the Sangha of monks to the residence of Cunda the smith's son; having approached, he sat down on the prepared seat,' it should be elaborated according to the method that has come down in the Sutta.

Evaṃ bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ nisinne bhagavati cundo kammāraputto buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ parivisanto byañjanasūpādigahaṇatthaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ suvaṇṇabhājanāni upanāmesi. Apaññatte sikkhāpade keci bhikkhū suvaṇṇabhājanāni paṭicchiṃsu keci na paṭicchiṃsu. Bhagavato pana ekameva bhājanaṃ attano selamayaṃ pattaṃ, dutiyabhājanaṃ buddhā na gaṇhanti. Tattha aññataro pāpabhikkhu sahassagghanakaṃ suvaṇṇabhājanaṃ attano bhojanatthāya sampattaṃ theyyacittena kuñcikatthavikāya pakkhipi. Cundo parivisitvā hatthapādaṃ dhovitvā bhagavantaṃ namassamāno bhikkhusaṅghaṃ olokento taṃ bhikkhuṃ addasa, disvā ca pana apassamāno viya hutvā na naṃ kiñci abhaṇi bhagavati theresu ca gāravena, apica “micchādiṭṭhikānaṃ vacanapatho mā ahosī”ti. So “kiṃ nu kho saṃvarayuttāyeva samaṇā, udāhu bhinnasaṃvarā īdisāpi samaṇā”ti ñātukāmo sāyanhasamaye bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā āha “pucchāmi muni”nti.

Thus, while the Blessed One was seated together with the Sangha of monks, Cunda the smith's son, while serving the Sangha of monks headed by the Buddha, offered golden vessels to the monks for receiving curries, soups, and so on. As a training rule had not yet been laid down, some monks accepted the golden vessels, while others did not. The Blessed One, however, had only one vessel, his own stone bowl; Buddhas do not take a second vessel. There, a certain evil monk, with a thieving mind, put a golden vessel worth a thousand that had come to him for his meal into his key-pouch. Cunda, having finished serving, washed his hands and feet, and while paying homage to the Blessed One and looking over the Sangha of monks, saw that monk. But having seen him, pretending not to see, he said nothing to him out of respect for the Blessed One and the elders, and also thinking, 'Let there not be an opportunity for the speech of those with wrong views.' He, wishing to know, 'Are recluses only those endowed with restraint, or are there also recluses of this sort whose restraint is broken?' approached the Blessed One in the evening and said, 'I ask the sage...'

Tattha pucchāmīti idaṃ “tisso pucchā adiṭṭhajotanā pucchā”tiādinā [P 1.0160] (cūḷani. puṇṇakamāṇavapucchāniddesa 12) nayena niddese vuttanayameva. Muninti etampi “monaṃ vuccati ñāṇaṃ. Yā paññā pajānanā…pe… sammādiṭṭhi, tena ñāṇena samannāgato muni, monappattoti, tīṇi moneyyāni kāyamoneyya”ntiādinā (mahāni. 14) nayena tattheva vuttanayameva[V 1.0127]. Ayampanettha saṅkhepo. Pucchāmīti okāsaṃ kārento muninti munimuniṃ bhagavantaṃ ālapati. Pahūtapaññantiādīni thutivacanāni, tehi taṃ muniṃ thunāti. Tattha pahūtapaññanti vipulapaññaṃ. Ñeyyapariyantikattā cassa vipulatā veditabbā. Iti cundo kammāraputtoti idaṃ dvayaṃ dhaniyasutte vuttanayameva. Ito paraṃ pana ettakampi avatvā sabbaṃ vuttanayaṃ chaḍḍetvā avuttanayameva vaṇṇayissāma.

Therein, ‘I ask’ is in the manner stated in the Niddesa, by the method beginning, ‘Three questions: the question illuminating the unseen…’ ‘The Sage’ is also in the manner stated in that very Niddesa, by the method beginning, ‘Sagacity is called knowledge. That wisdom which is understanding… right view. One endowed with such knowledge is a sage, one who has attained sagacity. There are three kinds of sagacity: bodily sagacity…’ and so on. Here, however, is a summary. Saying ‘I ask,’ he requests permission and addresses the Blessed One as ‘the Sage.’ The words of praise, such as ‘of abundant wisdom,’ are used to extol that Sage. Therein, ‘of abundant wisdom’ means of vast wisdom. Its vastness should be understood as having the knowable as its limit. ‘Thus, Cunda, the smith’s son’—this pair is in the manner stated in the Dhaniya Sutta. From here onward, however, without saying even this much, we will abandon all previously stated methods and explain only what has not been stated before.

Buddhanti tīsu buddhesu tatiyabuddhaṃ. Dhammassāminti maggadhammassa janakattā puttasseva pitaraṃ attanā uppāditasippāyatanādīnaṃ viya ca ācariyaṃ dhammassa sāmiṃ, dhammissaraṃ dhammarājaṃ dhammavasavattinti attho. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

‘The Buddha’ means the third Buddha among the three kinds of Buddhas. ‘Lord of the Dhamma’ means that because he is the originator of the path-Dhamma—like a father to his own son, and like a teacher in regard to the crafts and fields of knowledge he himself has brought forth—he is the lord of the Dhamma, the sovereign of the Dhamma, the king of the Dhamma, one with mastery over the Dhamma. This is the meaning. And this has been said:

“So [M 1.0144] hi, brāhmaṇa, bhagavā anuppannassa maggassa uppādetā, asañjātassa maggassa sañjanetā, anakkhātassa maggassa akkhātā, maggaññū, maggavidū, maggakovido. Maggānugā ca pana etarahi sāvakā viharanti pacchā samannāgatā”ti (ma. ni. 3.79).

“Indeed, brahmin, the Blessed One is the originator of the unarisen path, the producer of the unproduced path, the declarer of the undeclared path. He is the knower of the path, the discoverer of the path, the one skilled in the path. And now his disciples are followers of the path, endowed with it afterwards.”

Vītataṇhanti vigatakāmabhavavibhavataṇhaṃ. Dvipaduttamanti dvipadānaṃ uttamaṃ. Tattha kiñcāpi bhagavā na kevalaṃ dvipaduttamo eva, atha kho yāvatā sattā apadā vā dvipadā vā…pe… nevasaññīnāsaññino vā, tesaṃ sabbesaṃ uttamo. Atha kho ukkaṭṭhaparicchedavasena dvipaduttamotveva vuccati. Dvipadā hi sabbasattānaṃ ukkaṭṭhā cakkavattimahāsāvakapaccekabuddhānaṃ tattha uppattito, tesañca uttamoti vutte sabbasattuttamoti [P 1.0161] vuttoyeva hoti. Sārathīnaṃ pavaranti sāretīti sārathi, hatthidamakādīnametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tesañca bhagavā pavaro anuttarena damanena purisadamme dametuṃ samatthabhāvato. Yathāha –

‘Free from craving’ means devoid of craving for sensual pleasure, existence, and non-existence. ‘The best of bipeds’ means the supreme among bipeds. Therein, although the Blessed One is not only the best of bipeds, but is indeed the supreme among all beings—whether footless, two-footed… or with neither perception nor non-perception—he is nevertheless called ‘the best of bipeds’ by way of a superlative distinction. For bipeds are the highest among all beings, since wheel-turning monarchs and great disciples arise among them. And when he is called their supreme, it is as if he is said to be the supreme of all beings. ‘The foremost of charioteers’: one who guides is a charioteer; this is a designation for elephant-tamers and the like. And the Blessed One is their foremost because of his ability to tame with unsurpassed taming those men who are fit to be tamed. As it is said:

“Hatthidamakena, bhikkhave, hatthidammo sārito ekaṃ eva disaṃ dhāvati puratthimaṃ vā pacchimaṃ vā uttaraṃ vā dakkhiṇaṃ vā. Assadamakena, bhikkhave, assadammo…pe… godamakena, bhikkhave, godammo…pe… dakkhiṇaṃ vā. Tathāgatena hi, bhikkhave, arahatā sammāsambuddhena purisadammo sārito aṭṭha disā vidhāvati, rūpī rūpāni passati, ayamekā disā…pe… saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ upasampajja viharati, ayaṃ aṭṭhamī disā”ti (ma. ni. 3.312).

“Monks, an elephant trained by an elephant-tamer, when guided, runs in only one direction—east, west, north, or south. A horse trained by a horse-tamer… a bull trained by a bull-tamer… when guided, runs in only one direction—east, west, north, or south. But, monks, a person trained by the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, when guided, runs in eight directions. Possessed of form, he sees forms; this is one direction… Having entered upon and abiding in the cessation of perception and feeling; this is the eighth direction.”

Katīti [V 1.0128] atthappabhedapucchā. Loketi sattaloke. Samaṇāti pucchitabbaatthanidassanaṃ. Iṅghāti yācanatthe nipāto. Tadiṅghāti te iṅgha. Brūhīti ācikkha kathayassūti.

‘How many?’ is a question inquiring about the classification of meaning. ‘In the world’ means in the world of beings. ‘Ascetics’ is a pointing out of the meaning to be asked about. ‘Please’ is a particle in the sense of a request. ‘So please’ means ‘therefore, please.’ ‘Tell’ means ‘explain, speak.’

84. Evaṃ vutte bhagavā cundaṃ kammāraputtaṃ “kiṃ, bhante, kusalaṃ, kiṃ akusala”ntiādinā (ma. ni. 3.296) nayena gihipañhaṃ apucchitvā samaṇapañhaṃ pucchantaṃ disvā āvajjento “taṃ pāpabhikkhuṃ sandhāya ayaṃ pucchatī”ti ñatvā tassa aññatra vohāramattā assamaṇabhāvaṃ dīpento āha “caturo samaṇā”ti. Tattha caturoti saṅkhyāparicchedo. Samaṇāti kadāci [M 1.0145] bhagavā titthiye samaṇavādena vadati; yathāha – “yāni tāni puthusamaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ vatakotūhalamaṅgalānī”ti (ma. ni. 1.407). Kadāci puthujjane; yathāha – “samaṇā samaṇāti kho, bhikkhave, jano sañjānātī”ti (ma. ni. 1.435). Kadāci sekkhe; yathāha – “idheva, bhikkhave, samaṇo, idha dutiyo samaṇo”ti (ma. ni. 1.139; dī. ni. 2.214; a. ni. 4.241). Kadāci khīṇāsave; yathāha – “āsavānaṃ khayā samaṇo hotī”ti (ma. ni. 1.438). Kadāci attānaṃyeva; yathāha – “samaṇoti kho, bhikkhave, tathāgatassetaṃ adhivacana”nti (a. ni. 8.85). Idha pana tīhi padehi sabbepi ariye sīlavantaṃ puthujjanañca[P 1.0162], catutthena itaraṃ assamaṇampi bhaṇḍuṃ kāsāvakaṇṭhaṃ kevalaṃ vohāramattakena samaṇoti saṅgaṇhitvā “caturo samaṇā”ti āha. Na pañcamatthīti imasmiṃ dhammavinaye vohāramattakena paṭiññāmattakenāpi pañcamo samaṇo nāma natthi.

When this was said, the Blessed One, seeing Cunda the smith’s son asking a question about ascetics instead of a householder’s question in the manner of “What, venerable sir, is wholesome, what is unwholesome?”, reflected and understood, “He is asking this with reference to that wicked monk.” Then, revealing that, apart from mere designation, he was not an ascetic, the Blessed One said, “There are four ascetics.” Herein, ‘four’ is a numerical determination. ‘Ascetics’—sometimes the Blessed One refers to sectarians with the term ‘ascetic’; as it is said: “Those various observances, rites, and auspicious ceremonies of the many ascetics and brahmins.” Sometimes he refers to ordinary people; as it is said: “Monks, people recognize them as ‘ascetics, ascetics.’” Sometimes he refers to trainees; as it is said: “Here, monks, is the ascetic, here is the second ascetic.” Sometimes he refers to one whose taints are destroyed; as it is said: “Through the destruction of the taints, one is an ascetic.” Sometimes he refers to himself; as it is said: “Monks, ‘ascetic’ is a designation for the Tathāgata.” Here, however, with three terms he includes all the noble ones and the virtuous ordinary person; and with the fourth, he includes the other who, though not an ascetic, is a shaven-headed man with a yellow robe around his neck, including him as an ‘ascetic’ by mere designation only, and so he said, “There are four ascetics.” ‘There is no fifth’ means that in this Dhamma and Discipline, there is no fifth kind of ascetic, not even by mere designation or by mere claim.

Te te āvikaromīti te caturo samaṇe tava pākaṭe karomi. Sakkhipuṭṭhoti sammukhā pucchito. Maggajinoti maggena sabbakilese vijitāvīti attho. Maggadesakoti paresaṃ maggaṃ desetā. Magge jīvatīti sattasu sekkhesu yo koci sekkho apariyositamaggavāsattā lokuttare, sīlavantaputhujjano ca lokiye magge jīvati nāma, sīlavantaputhujjano vā lokuttaramagganimittaṃ jīvanatopi magge jīvatīti veditabbo. Yo ca maggadūsīti yo ca dussīlo micchādiṭṭhi maggapaṭilomāya paṭipattiyā maggadūsakoti attho.

"I shall make them manifest to you" means: I shall make those four ascetics clear to you. "Questioned in person" means: asked face-to-face. "The Path-Conqueror" means: one who has conquered all defilements by the path. "The Path-Indicator" means: one who points out the path to others. "One who lives in the path" means: among the seven trainees, any trainee, because of dwelling in the unfinished path, is said to live in the supramundane path; and the virtuous worldling is said to live in the mundane path. Or, it should be understood that the virtuous worldling also lives in the path by living on account of the supramundane path. "And the Path-Corrupter" means: whichever immoral one, through the practice contrary to the path, which is wrong view, is a corrupter of the path.

85. “Ime te caturo samaṇā”ti evaṃ bhagavatā saṅkhepena uddiṭṭhe caturo samaṇe “ayaṃ nāmettha maggajino, ayaṃ maggadesako, ayaṃ magge jīvati, ayaṃ maggadūsī”ti evaṃ paṭivijjhituṃ asakkonto puna pucchituṃ cundo āha “kaṃ maggajina”nti. Tattha magge jīvati meti yo so magge jīvati, taṃ me brūhi puṭṭhoti. Sesaṃ pākaṭameva.

85. When the Blessed One had thus pointed out in brief the four ascetics, saying, "These are the four ascetics," Cunda, being unable to penetrate it thus: "This one here is the Path-Conqueror, this one is the Path-Indicator, this one lives in the path, this one is the Path-Corrupter," in order to ask again, said, "Whom do you call the Path-Conqueror?". Therein, "one who lives in the path to me" means: "He who lives in the path, explain him to me who asks." The rest is clear.

86. Idānissa bhagavā [V 1.0129] caturopi samaṇe catūhi gāthāhi niddisanto āha “yo tiṇṇakathaṃkatho visallo”ti. Tattha tiṇṇakathaṃkatho visalloti etaṃ uragasutte vuttanayameva. Ayaṃ pana viseso. Yasmā imāya gāthāya maggajinoti buddhasamaṇo adhippeto, tasmā sabbaññutaññāṇena [M 1.0146] kathaṃkathāpatirūpakassa sabbadhammesu aññāṇassa tiṇṇattāpi “tiṇṇakathaṃkatho”ti veditabbo. Pubbe vuttanayena hi tiṇṇakathaṃkathāpi sotāpannādayo paccekabuddhapariyosānā sakadāgāmivisayādīsu buddhavisayapariyosānesu paṭihatañāṇappabhāvattā pariyāyena atiṇṇakathaṃkathāva [P 1.0163] honti. Bhagavā pana sabbappakārena tiṇṇakathaṃkathoti. Nibbānābhiratoti nibbāne abhirato, phalasamāpattivasena sadā nibbānaninnacittoti attho. Tādiso ca bhagavā. Yathāha –

86. Now the Blessed One, indicating all four ascetics with four verses, said: "He who has crossed over doubt, is dartless." Therein, the phrase "has crossed over doubt, is dartless" is in the same manner as was stated in the Uraga Sutta. This, however, is the distinction: since by this verse "the Path-Conqueror" is intended to mean the Buddha-ascetic, therefore, because of having crossed over, by the knowledge of omniscience, the ignorance in all things which has the nature of doubt, he should be understood as "one who has crossed over doubt." For, in the manner previously stated, even those who have crossed over doubt—from the stream-enterer up to the Paccekabuddha—because their knowledge is obstructed in the domains of the once-returner and so on, up to the domain of a Buddha, are, in a relative sense, ones who have not crossed over doubt. The Blessed One, however, has in every way crossed over doubt. "Delighting in Nibbāna" means delighting in Nibbāna; the meaning is that, by way of the attainment of fruition, his mind is ever inclined towards Nibbāna. And such is the Blessed One. As it is said:

“So kho ahaṃ, aggivessana, tassā eva kathāya pariyosāne, tasmiṃyeva purimasmiṃ samādhinimitte ajjhattameva cittaṃ saṇṭhapemi, sannisādemi, ekodiṃ karomi, samādahāmī”ti (ma. ni. 1.387).

"Then I, Aggivessana, at the very conclusion of that talk, establish my mind right on that former sign of concentration, I settle it down, I make it one-pointed, and I concentrate it."

Anānugiddhoti kañci dhammaṃ taṇhāgedhena ananugijjhanto. Lokassa sadevakassa netāti āsayānusayānulomena dhammaṃ desetvā pārāyanamahāsamayādīsu anekesu suttantesu aparimāṇānaṃ devamanussānaṃ saccapaṭivedhasampādanena sadevakassa lokassa netā, gamayitā, tāretā, pāraṃ sampāpetāti attho. Tādinti tādisaṃ yathāvuttappakāralokadhammehi nibbikāranti attho. Sesamettha pākaṭameva.

"Not greedy" means: not being greedy for any phenomenon with the greed of craving. "Leader of the world with its devas" means: having taught the Dhamma in accordance with dispositions and latent tendencies, and in many discourses such as the Pārāyana and the Mahāsamaya, by bringing about the penetration of the truths for countless devas and humans, he is the leader of the world with its devas, the one who makes them go, the one who takes them across, the one who brings them to the further shore. This is the meaning. "Such a one" means: such, unperturbed by worldly conditions of the aforesaid kind. This is the meaning. The rest here is clear.

87. Evaṃ bhagavā imāya gāthāya “maggajina”nti buddhasamaṇaṃ niddisitvā idāni khīṇāsavasamaṇaṃ niddisanto āha “paramaṃ paramantī”ti. Tattha paramaṃ nāma nibbānaṃ, sabbadhammānaṃ aggaṃ uttamanti attho. Paramanti yodha ñatvāti taṃ paramaṃ paramamicceva yo idha sāsane ñatvā paccavekkhaṇañāṇena. Akkhāti vibhajate idheva dhammanti nibbānadhammaṃ akkhāti, attanā paṭividdhattā paresaṃ pākaṭaṃ karoti “idaṃ nibbāna”nti, maggadhammaṃ vibhajati “ime cattāro satipaṭṭhānā…pe… ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo”ti. Ubhayampi vā ugghaṭitaññūnaṃ saṅkhepadesanāya ācikkhati, vipañcitaññūnaṃ vitthāradesanāya vibhajati. Evaṃ ācikkhanto vibhajanto ca “idheva sāsane ayaṃ dhammo, na ito bahiddhā”ti sīhanādaṃ nadanto akkhāti ca vibhajati ca. Tena vuttaṃ “akkhāti vibhajate idheva dhamma”nti. Taṃ kaṅkhachidaṃ muniṃ anejanti taṃ evarūpaṃ catusaccapaṭivedhena [P 1.0164] attano, desanāya ca paresaṃ kaṅkhacchedanena kaṅkhacchidaṃ[M 1.0147], moneyyasamannāgamena muniṃ, ejāsaṅkhātāya taṇhāya abhāvato anejaṃ dutiyaṃ bhikkhunamāhu maggadesinti.
