87. Thus the Blessed One, having indicated the Buddha-ascetic as the "Path-Conqueror" with this verse, now, indicating the ascetic whose cankers are destroyed, said, "The supreme, as 'supreme'…". Therein, "supreme" is Nibbāna; the meaning is that it is the highest, the most excellent of all things. "Having known here as 'supreme'" means: he who, having known that supreme Nibbāna here in this Dispensation with the knowledge of reviewing, as "it is indeed supreme." "He declares and analyzes the Dhamma right here" means: he declares the Dhamma of Nibbāna; because he has penetrated it himself, he makes it clear to others, saying, "This is Nibbāna." He analyzes the path-Dhamma, saying, "These are the four foundations of mindfulness… the Noble Eightfold Path." Or, for both, he explains with a brief teaching to those of quick understanding, and he analyzes with a detailed teaching for those who require elaboration. Thus explaining and analyzing, roaring the lion's roar, "This Dhamma is only here in this Dispensation, not outside of it," he both declares and analyzes. Therefore it is said, "He declares and analyzes the Dhamma right here." "That doubt-cutter, sage, unperturbed one" means: such a one is a "doubt-cutter" by cutting through his own doubts by penetrating the Four Noble Truths, and the doubts of others by his teaching; he is a "sage" through being endowed with sagacity; he is "unperturbed" due to the absence of craving, which is called "agitation." They call him the second of the bhikkhus, the Path-Indicator.

88. Evaṃ [V 1.0130] imāya gāthāya sayaṃ anuttaraṃ maggaṃ uppādetvā desanāya anuttaro maggadesī samānopi dūtamiva lekhavācakamiva ca rañño attano sāsanaharaṃ sāsanajotakañca “maggadesi”nti khīṇāsavasamaṇaṃ niddisitvā idāni sekkhasamaṇañca sīlavantaputhujjanasamaṇañca niddisanto āha “yo dhammapade”ti. Tattha padavaṇṇanā pākaṭāyeva. Ayaṃ panettha atthavaṇṇanā – yo nibbānadhammassa padattā dhammapade, ubho ante anupagamma desitattā āsayānurūpato vā satipaṭṭhānādinānappakārehi desitattā sudesite, maggasamaṅgīpi anavasitamaggakiccattā magge jīvati, sīlasaṃyamena saññato, kāyādīsu sūpaṭṭhitāya cirakatādisaraṇāya vā satiyā satimā, aṇumattassāpi vajjassa abhāvato anavajjattā, koṭṭhāsabhāvena ca padattā sattatiṃsabodhipakkhiyadhammasaṅkhātāni anavajjapadāni bhaṅgañāṇato pabhuti bhāvanāsevanāya sevamāno, taṃ bhikkhunaṃ tatiyaṃ maggajīvinti āhūti.

88. Thus, with this verse, having indicated the ascetic with cankers destroyed as the "Path-Indicator"—who, although the unsurpassed Path-Indicator by his teaching, having himself brought into being the unsurpassed path, is like a king's messenger or a scribe who reads a letter, a bearer and illuminator of his own Dispensation—now, indicating the trainee-ascetic and the virtuous worldling-ascetic, he said, "He who in the Dhamma-path...". Therein, the explanation of the words is clear. This is the explanation of the meaning here: "in the Dhamma-path," because it is the cause of the Nibbāna-Dhamma; "well-taught," because it is taught without approaching either of the two extremes, or because it is taught in various ways, such as the foundations of mindfulness, according to the dispositions of beings; even one endowed with the path lives in the path because the task of the path is not yet concluded; he is "restrained" by the restraint of virtue; he is "mindful" through mindfulness that is well-established in body and so on, or that can recall things done long ago; "blamelessness," due to the absence of even a minute fault; cultivating the blameless paths—called the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, which are also causes of Nibbāna by being its components—by means of developing and practicing them from the knowledge of dissolution onwards; they call him the third of the bhikkhus, the "Path-Liver."

89. Evaṃ bhagavā imāya gāthāya “maggajīvi”nti sekkhasamaṇaṃ sīlavantaputhujjanasamaṇañca niddisitvā idāni taṃ bhaṇḍuṃ kāsāvakaṇṭhaṃ kevalaṃ vohāramattasamaṇaṃ niddisanto āha “chadanaṃ katvānā”ti. Tattha chadanaṃ katvānāti patirūpaṃ karitvā, vesaṃ gahetvā, liṅgaṃ dhāretvāti attho. Subbatānanti buddhapaccekabuddhasāvakānaṃ. Tesañhi sundarāni vatāni, tasmā te subbatāti vuccanti. Pakkhandīti pakkhandako, anto pavisakoti attho. Dussīlo hi gūthapaṭicchādanatthaṃ tiṇapaṇṇādicchadanaṃ viya attano dussīlabhāvaṃ paṭicchādanatthaṃ subbatānaṃ chadanaṃ [P 1.0165] katvā “ahampi bhikkhū”ti bhikkhumajjhe pakkhandati, “ettakavassena bhikkhunā gahetabbaṃ eta”nti lābhe dīyamāne “ahaṃ ettakavasso”ti gaṇhituṃ pakkhandati, tena vuccati “chadanaṃ katvāna subbatānaṃ pakkhandī”ti. Catunnampi khattiyādikulānaṃ uppannaṃ pasādaṃ ananurūpapaṭipattiyā dūsetīti kuladūsako. Pagabbhoti aṭṭhaṭṭhānena kāyapāgabbhiyena, catuṭṭhānena vacīpāgabbhiyena, anekaṭṭhānena manopāgabbhiyena ca samannāgatoti attho. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāraṃ pana mettasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ vakkhāma.

89. Thus the Blessed One, having with this verse pointed out the 'one who lives by the path' as the ascetic in training and the virtuous worldling ascetic, now, indicating that shaven-headed one with the ochre robe around his neck who is merely an ascetic by designation, said the verse beginning 'Having made a covering.' Therein, 'having made a covering' means having adopted a suitable guise, having taken on the appearance, having worn the sign. 'Of those of good conduct' refers to the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and their disciples. For their practices are excellent; therefore, they are called 'those of good conduct.' 'He rushes in' means one who rushes in, one who enters within. For an immoral one, just as one might use a covering of grass, leaves, and so on to cover excrement, so too, to cover his own immorality, he makes a 'covering' of those of good conduct and rushes into the midst of bhikkhus, thinking, 'I too am a bhikkhu.' When a gain is being given, with the thought, 'This should be taken by a bhikkhu of so many years' seniority,' he rushes in to take it, saying, 'I am of so many years' seniority.' Therefore it is said, 'Having made a covering of those of good conduct, he rushes in.' He is a 'corrupter of families' because he corrupts the arisen confidence of the four classes, khattiyas and so on, by his unsuitable practice. 'Bold' means endowed with the eight kinds of bodily boldness, the four kinds of verbal boldness, and the many kinds of mental boldness. This is the summary here; we shall state the detailed explanation in the commentary on the Metta Sutta.

Katapaṭicchādanalakkhaṇāya [M 1.0148] māyāya samannāgatattā māyāvī. Sīlasaṃyamābhāvena asaññato. Palāpasadisattā palāpo. Yathā hi palāpo anto taṇḍularahitopi bahi thusena vīhi viya dissati, evamidhekacco anto sīlādiguṇasāravirahitopi bahi subbatacchadanena samaṇavesena samaṇo viya dissati. So evaṃ palāpasadisattā “palāpo”ti vuccati. Ānāpānassatisutte pana “apalāpāyaṃ, bhikkhave, parisā, nippalāpāyaṃ, bhikkhave, parisā, suddhā sāre patiṭṭhitā”ti (ma. ni. 3.146) evaṃ puthujjanakalyāṇopi “palāpo”ti vutto[V 1.0131]. Idha pana kapilasutte ca “tato palāpe vāhetha, assamaṇe samaṇamānine”ti (su. ni. 284) evaṃ parājitako “palāpo”ti vutto. Patirūpena caraṃ samaggadūsīti taṃ subbatānaṃ chadanaṃ katvā yathā carantaṃ “āraññiko ayaṃ rukkhamūliko, paṃsukūliko, piṇḍapātiko, appiccho, santuṭṭho”ti jano jānāti, evaṃ patirūpena yuttarūpena bāhiramaṭṭhena ācārena caranto puggalo attano lokuttaramaggassa, paresaṃ sugatimaggassa ca dūsanato “maggadūsī”ti veditabbo.

He is a deceiver because he is endowed with deceit, which is characterized by covering up what has been done. He is unrestrained due to the absence of virtue and self-control. He is chaff because of his resemblance to chaff. For just as chaff, though devoid of rice grains within, appears outwardly like paddy because of the husk, so too here a certain person, though devoid of the essence of the qualities of virtue and so on within, appears outwardly like an ascetic by the covering of good conduct and the appearance of an ascetic. Thus, because of his resemblance to chaff, he is called 'chaff.' In the Ānāpānassati Sutta, however, it is said: 'This assembly, monks, is without chaff; this assembly, monks, is free from chaff, pure, established in the essence.' In that context, even a virtuous worldling is called 'chaff.' But here and in the Kapila Sutta, where it is said: 'Therefore, drive out the chaff, the non-ascetics who consider themselves ascetics,' one who is defeated is called 'chaff.' As for 'one who behaves with outward propriety, a corrupter of the path': when he behaves in a certain way, adopting the covering of those with good conduct, people know him thus: 'This is a forest-dweller, a tree-root-dweller, a rag-robe-wearer, an alms-food-goer, of few wishes, content.' In this way, a person who behaves with a suitable, fitting, and outwardly polished conduct should be known as a 'corrupter of the path' because he corrupts his own supramundane path and the path to a good destination for others.

90. Evaṃ imāya gāthāya “maggadūsī”ti dussīlaṃ vohāramattakasamaṇaṃ niddisitvā idāni tesaṃ aññamaññaṃ abyāmissībhāvaṃ dīpento āha “ete ca paṭivijjhī”ti. Tassattho – ete caturo samaṇe yathāvuttena [P 1.0166] lakkhaṇena paṭivijjhi aññāsi sacchākāsi yo gahaṭṭho khattiyo vā brāhmaṇo vā añño vā koci, imesaṃ catunnaṃ samaṇānaṃ lakkhaṇassavanamattena sutavā, tasseva lakkhaṇassa ariyānaṃ santike sutattā ariyasāvako, teyeva samaṇe “ayañca ayañca evaṃlakkhaṇo”ti pajānanamattena sappañño, yādiso ayaṃ pacchā vutto maggadūsī, itarepi sabbe netādisāti ñatvā iti disvā evaṃ pāpaṃ karontampi etaṃ pāpabhikkhuṃ disvā. Tatthāyaṃ yojanā – ete ca paṭivijjhi yo gahaṭṭho sutavā ariyasāvako sappañño, tassa tāya paññāya sabbe “netādisā”ti ñatvā viharato iti disvā na hāpeti saddhā, evaṃ pāpakammaṃ karontaṃ pāpabhikkhuṃ disvāpi na hāpeti, na hāyati, na nassati saddhāti.

90. Thus, with this verse, having pointed out the immoral, merely nominal ascetic as the 'corrupter of the path,' now, explaining their state of not being mixed with one another, he said, 'And these he penetrated.' Its meaning is this: whoever—be it a householder, a khattiya, a brahmin, or anyone else—penetrated, knew, and realized these four ascetics by their aforementioned characteristics. He is 'learned' merely by hearing the characteristics of these four ascetics. He is a 'noble disciple' because he has heard these very characteristics in the presence of the noble ones. He is 'wise' merely by knowing of those ascetics, 'This one and that one have such-and-such a characteristic.' Knowing, 'Just as this one mentioned last is a corrupter of the path, all the others are not like this,' and seeing thus, even seeing this evil bhikkhu doing such evil... Herein, this is the construction of the meaning: Whoever, being a householder, learned, a noble disciple, and wise, has penetrated these—for him, dwelling with that wisdom, knowing 'not all are like this,' and seeing thus, his faith is not lost. Even seeing an evil bhikkhu performing an evil deed, he does not abandon his faith; it is not diminished, it does not perish.

Evaṃ [M 1.0149] imāya gāthāya tesaṃ abyāmissībhāvaṃ dīpetvā idāni iti disvāpi “sabbe netādisā”ti jānantaṃ ariyasāvakaṃ pasaṃsanto āha “kathañhi duṭṭhenā”ti. Tassa sambandho – etadeva ca yuttaṃ sutavato ariyasāvakassa, yadidaṃ ekaccaṃ pāpaṃ karontaṃ iti disvāpi sabbe “netādisā”ti jānanaṃ. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Kathañhi duṭṭhena asampaduṭṭhaṃ, suddhaṃ asuddhena samaṃ kareyyāti? Tassattho – kathañhi sutavā ariyasāvako sappañño, sīlavipattiyā duṭṭhena maggadūsinā aduṭṭhaṃ itaraṃ samaṇattayaṃ, suddhaṃ samaṇattayamevaṃ aparisuddhakāyasamācāratādīhi asuddhena pacchimena vohāramattakasamaṇena samaṃ kareyya sadisanti jāneyyāti. Suttapariyosāne upāsakassa maggo vā phalaṃ vā na kathitaṃ. Kaṅkhāmattameva hi tassa pahīnanti.

Thus, with this verse, having explained their state of not being mixed, now, praising the noble disciple who, even seeing this, knows 'Not all are like this,' he said the verse beginning, 'How indeed with the corrupt?' Its connection is this: this indeed is fitting for a learned noble disciple, that even upon seeing a certain one doing evil, he knows, 'Not all are like this.' For what reason? 'How indeed could one make the uncorrupted equal with the corrupted, the pure with the impure?' Its meaning is: How indeed could a learned, wise, noble disciple make the other three uncorrupted types of ascetics equal with the path-corrupter who is corrupted by the failure of virtue? How could he know the pure three types of ascetics to be the same as the last one, the merely nominal ascetic who is impure due to unpurified bodily conduct and so on? At the conclusion of the sutta, it is not stated that the lay follower attained the path or the fruit. For only his doubt was abandoned.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya cundasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

In the Commentary on the Suttanipāta, the exposition of the Cunda Sutta is concluded.

6. Parābhavasuttavaṇṇanā

6. The Exposition of the Parābhava Sutta

Evaṃ [V 1.0132] me sutanti parābhavasuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Maṅgalasuttaṃ kira sutvā devānaṃ etadahosi – “bhagavatā maṅgalasutte sattānaṃ vuḍḍhiñca sotthiñca kathayamānena ekaṃsena bhavo eva kathito, no parābhavo. Handa dāni yena sattā parihāyanti vinassanti, taṃ nesaṃ parābhavampi [P 1.0167] pucchāmā”ti. Atha maṅgalasuttaṃ kathitadivasato dutiyadivase dasasahassacakkavāḷesu devatāyo parābhavasuttaṃ sotukāmā imasmiṃ ekacakkavāḷe sannipatitvā ekavālaggakoṭiokāsamatte dasapi vīsampi tiṃsampi cattālīsampi paññāsampi saṭṭhipi sattatipi asītipi sukhumattabhāve nimminitvā sabbadevamārabrahmāno siriyā ca tejena ca adhigayha virocamānaṃ paññattavarabuddhāsane nisinnaṃ bhagavantaṃ parivāretvā aṭṭhaṃsu. Tato sakkena devānamindena āṇatto aññataro devaputto bhagavantaṃ parābhavapañhaṃ pucchi. Atha bhagavā pucchāvasena imaṃ suttamabhāsi.

Thus have I heard. This is the Parābhavasutta. What is its origin? It is said that after hearing the Maṅgalasutta, the gods thought: “While the Blessed One, in the Maṅgalasutta, spoke of the growth and welfare of beings, he spoke only of prosperity, not of decline. Now let us ask about that by which beings decline and perish.” Then, on the second day after the Maṅgalasutta was taught, deities from ten thousand world-systems, desiring to hear the Parābhavasutta, gathered in this single world-system. Having created subtle forms, so that ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, sixty, seventy, or eighty could occupy a space the size of a hair-tip, all the gods, Māras, and Brahmās surrounded the Blessed One, who, surpassing them in glory and splendor, was shining forth, seated on the prepared excellent Buddha-seat, and they stood. Then, commanded by Sakka, king of the gods, a certain devaputta asked the Blessed One the question about decline. Thereupon, the Blessed One spoke this sutta in response to the question.

Tattha [M 1.0150] “evaṃ me suta”ntiādi āyasmatā ānandena vuttaṃ. “Parābhavantaṃ purisa”ntiādinā nayena ekantarikā gāthā devaputtena vuttā, “suvijāno bhavaṃ hotī”tiādinā nayena ekantarikā eva avasānagāthā ca bhagavatā vuttā, tadetaṃ sabbampi samodhānetvā “parābhavasutta”nti vuccati. Tattha “evaṃ me suta”ntiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ maṅgalasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ vakkhāma.

Herein, “Thus have I heard,” and so on, was spoken by the Venerable Ānanda. The alternating verses beginning “A man heading for ruin,” and so on, were spoken by the devaputta, while the alternating verses beginning “The prosperous one is easily known,” and so on, and the concluding verse, were spoken by the Blessed One. Combining all of this, it is called the “Parābhavasutta.” As for what should be said regarding “Thus have I heard,” and so on, all that we will explain in the commentary on the Maṅgala Sutta.

91. Parābhavantaṃ purisantiādīsu pana parābhavantanti parihāyantaṃ vinassantaṃ. Purisanti yaṃkiñci sattaṃ jantuṃ. Mayaṃ pucchāma gotamāti sesadevehi saddhiṃ attānaṃ nidassetvā okāsaṃ kārento so devaputto gottena bhagavantaṃ ālapati. Bhavantaṃ puṭṭhumāgammāti mayañhi bhavantaṃ pucchissāmāti tato tato cakkavāḷā āgatāti attho. Etena ādaraṃ dasseti. Kiṃ parābhavato mukhanti evaṃ āgatānaṃ amhākaṃ brūhi parābhavato purisassa kiṃ mukhaṃ, kiṃ dvāraṃ, kā yoni, kiṃ kāraṇaṃ, yena mayaṃ parābhavantaṃ purisaṃ jāneyyāmāti attho. Etena “parābhavantaṃ purisa”nti ettha vuttassa parābhavato purisassa parābhavakāraṇaṃ pucchati. Parābhavakāraṇe hi ñāte tena kāraṇasāmaññena sakkā yo koci parābhavapuriso jānitunti[P 1.0168].

91. In the passage beginning with “A man heading for ruin,” “heading for ruin” means declining, perishing. “Man” refers to any being, any creature. “We ask Gotama”—that devaputta, presenting himself along with the other deities and creating an opportunity, addresses the Blessed One by his clan name. “We have come to question you, the Blessed One”—the meaning is, “We have come from various world-systems to question the Blessed One.” “What is the gateway to ruin?”—the meaning is, “Tell us who have come thus: what is the gateway, what is the door, what is the origin, what is the cause of a man’s ruin, by which we may know a man heading for ruin?” By this, he asks about the cause of ruin for the man heading for ruin mentioned in “a man heading for ruin.” For when the cause of ruin is known, then by that commonality of cause, it is possible to know any man destined for ruin.

92. Athassa [V 1.0133] bhagavā suṭṭhu pākaṭīkaraṇatthaṃ paṭipakkhaṃ dassetvā puggalādhiṭṭhānāya desanāya parābhavamukhaṃ dīpento āha “suvijāno bhava”nti. Tassattho – yvāyaṃ bhavaṃ vaḍḍhanto aparihāyanto puriso, so suvijāno hoti, sukhena akasirena akicchena sakkā vijānituṃ. Yopāyaṃ parābhavatīti parābhavo, parihāyati vinassati, yassa tumhe parābhavato purisassa mukhaṃ maṃ pucchatha, sopi suvijāno. Kathaṃ? Ayañhi dhammakāmo bhavaṃ hoti dasakusalakammapathadhammaṃ kāmeti, piheti, pattheti, suṇāti, paṭipajjati, so taṃ paṭipattiṃ disvā sutvā ca jānitabbato suvijāno hoti. Itaropi dhammadessī parābhavo, tameva dhammaṃ dessati, na kāmeti, na piheti, na pattheti, na suṇāti, na paṭipajjati, so taṃ vippaṭipattiṃ disvā sutvā ca jānitabbato suvijāno hotīti. Evamettha bhagavā paṭipakkhaṃ dassento atthato dhammakāmataṃ bhavato mukhaṃ dassetvā dhammadessitaṃ parābhavato mukhaṃ dassetīti veditabbaṃ.

92. Then, to make it very clear for him, the Blessed One, showing the opposite and illuminating the gateway to ruin by means of a teaching based on individuals, said, “The prosperous one is easily known.” The meaning is: That man who is prosperous, growing, not declining—he is easily known; it is possible to know him with ease, without hardship, without trouble. And that one who is subject to ruin—he declines, he perishes, he whose gateway to ruin you ask me about—he too is easily known. How? This prosperous one is a lover of the Dhamma; he desires, yearns for, aspires to, listens to, and practices the Dhamma of the ten wholesome paths of action. Because he is to be known from seeing and hearing that practice, he is easily known. The other, the one subject to ruin, is a hater of the Dhamma; he hates that very Dhamma, does not desire it, does not yearn for it, does not aspire to it, does not listen to it, does not practice it. Because he is to be known from seeing and hearing that wrong practice, he too is easily known. Thus, it should be understood that here the Blessed One, by showing the opposite, in essence shows that love for the Dhamma is the gateway to prosperity and hatred for the Dhamma is the gateway to ruin.

93. Atha [M 1.0151] sā devatā bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandamānā āha “iti heta”nti. Tassattho – iti hi yathā vutto bhagavatā, tatheva etaṃ vijānāma, gaṇhāma, dhārema, paṭhamo so parābhavo so dhammadessitālakkhaṇo paṭhamo parābhavo. Yāni mayaṃ parābhavamukhāni vijānituṃ āgatamhā, tesu idaṃ tāva ekaṃ parābhavamukhanti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha viggaho, parābhavanti etenāti parābhavo. Kena ca parābhavanti? Yaṃ parābhavato mukhaṃ, kāraṇaṃ, tena. Byañjanamattena eva hi ettha nānākaraṇaṃ, atthato pana parābhavoti vā parābhavato mukhanti vā nānākaraṇaṃ natthi. Evamekaṃ parābhavato mukhaṃ vijānāmāti abhinanditvā tato paraṃ ñātukāmatāyāha “dutiyaṃ bhagavā brūhi, kiṃ parābhavato mukha”nti. Ito parañca tatiyaṃ catutthantiādīsupi imināva nayenattho veditabbo.

93. Then that deity, delighting in the Blessed One’s words, said, “So it is.” The meaning is: “Indeed, just as the Blessed One has said, so we understand, accept, and hold it: that is the first downfall, the first downfall characterized by hatred of the Dhamma. Of the gateways to downfall that we have come to learn, this, for now, is one gateway to downfall.” Here, the term “downfall” (parābhavo) is analyzed as “that by which one falls.” And by what does one fall? By that which is the gateway, the cause of downfall. For here there is a difference merely in the wording, but in meaning there is no difference between “downfall” and “gateway to downfall.” Thus, having rejoiced, saying, “We understand one gateway to downfall,” she then asked, out of a desire to know more, “Blessed One, speak of the second—what is the gateway to downfall?” From here onward, the meaning of the third, fourth, and so on should be understood in this same way.

94. Byākaraṇapakkhepi ca yasmā [P 1.0169] te te sattā tehi tehi parābhavamukhehi samannāgatā, na ekoyeva sabbehi, na ca sabbe ekeneva, tasmā tesaṃ tesaṃ tāni tāni parābhavamukhāni dassetuṃ “asantassa piyā hontī”tiādinā nayena puggalādhiṭṭhānāya eva desanāya nānāvidhāni parābhavamukhāni byākāsīti veditabbā.

94. And in the section of explanation, it should be understood that because those various beings are endowed with those various gateways to downfall—for not one person is endowed with all of them, nor are all persons endowed with only one—therefore, to show their respective gateways to downfall, the Blessed One explained the various gateways to downfall by means of a teaching based on individuals, in the manner beginning, 'The unvirtuous are dear to him...'

Tatrāyaṃ saṅkhepato atthavaṇṇanā – asanto nāma cha satthāro, ye vā panaññepi avūpasantena kāyavacīmanokammena samannāgatā, te asanto assapiyā honti sunakkhattādīnaṃ acelakakorakhattiyādayo viya. Santo nāma buddhapaccekabuddhasāvakā. Ye vā panaññepi vūpasantena [V 1.0134] kāyavacīmanokammena samannāgatā, te sante na kurute piyaṃ, attano piye iṭṭhe kante manāpe na kuruteti attho. Veneyyavasena hettha vacanabhedo katoti veditabbo. Atha vā sante na kuruteti sante na sevatīti attho, yathā “rājānaṃ sevatī”ti etasmiñhi atthe rājānaṃ piyaṃ kuruteti saddavidū mantenti. Piyanti piyamāno, tussamāno, modamānoti attho. Asataṃ [M 1.0152] dhammo nāma dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhigatāni, dasākusalakammapathā vā. Taṃ asataṃ dhammaṃ roceti, piheti, pattheti, sevati. Evametāya gāthāya asantapiyatā, santaappiyatā, asaddhammarocanañcāti tividhaṃ parābhavato mukhaṃ vuttaṃ. Etena hi samannāgato puriso parābhavati parihāyati, neva idha na huraṃ vuḍḍhiṃ pāpuṇāti, tasmā “parābhavato mukha”nti vuccati. Vitthāraṃ panettha “asevanā ca bālānaṃ, paṇḍitānañca sevanā”ti gāthāvaṇṇanāyaṃ vakkhāma.

Herein is the brief explanation of the meaning: The unvirtuous are the six teachers, or any others who are endowed with unpacified conduct of body, speech, and mind. To such a person, the unvirtuous are dear, just as the naked ascetic Korakhattiya and others were dear to Sunakkhatta and others. The virtuous are the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and their disciples, or any others who are endowed with pacified conduct of body, speech, and mind. The phrase 'sante na kurute piyaṃ' means that one does not make the virtuous beloved, desired, liked, or pleasing to oneself. It should be understood that the variation in wording here is made for the sake of those to be taught. Alternatively, 'sante na kurute' means one does not associate with the virtuous; just as in the sense of 'rājānaṃ sevati' (he serves the king), those skilled in grammar consider it to mean 'rājānaṃ piyaṃ kurute' (he holds the king dear). 'Piyaṃ' means being fond, being satisfied, and being delighted. The teaching of the unvirtuous refers to the sixty-two wrong views or the ten unwholesome courses of action. One approves of, yearns for, desires, and follows that teaching of the unvirtuous. Thus, in this verse, three causes of downfall are stated: affection for the unvirtuous, lack of affection for the virtuous, and delighting in the false teaching. For a person endowed with these falls into ruin and decline, attaining no growth either in this world or the next. Therefore, it is called 'a cause of downfall.' We will explain this in detail in the commentary on the verse: 'Not associating with fools, but associating with the wise.'

96. Niddāsīlī nāma yo gacchantopi, nisīdantopi, tiṭṭhantopi, sayānopi niddāyatiyeva. Sabhāsīlī nāma saṅgaṇikārāmataṃ, bhassārāmatamanuyutto. Anuṭṭhātāti vīriyatejavirahito uṭṭhānasīlo na hoti, aññehi codiyamāno gahaṭṭho vā samāno gahaṭṭhakammaṃ[P 1.0170], pabbajito vā pabbajitakammaṃ ārabhati. Alasoti jātialaso, accantābhibhūto thinena ṭhitaṭṭhāne ṭhito eva hoti, nisinnaṭṭhāne nisinno eva hoti, attano ussāhena aññaṃ iriyāpathaṃ na kappeti. Atīte araññe aggimhi uṭṭhite apalāyanaalasā cettha nidassanaṃ. Ayamettha ukkaṭṭhaparicchedo, tato lāmakaparicchedenāpi pana alaso alasotveva veditabbo. Dhajova rathassa, dhūmova aggino, kodho paññāṇamassāti kodhapaññāṇo. Dosacarito khippakopī arukūpamacitto puggalo evarūpo hoti. Imāya gāthāya niddāsīlatā, sabhāsīlatā, anuṭṭhānatā, alasatā, kodhapaññāṇatāti pañcavidhaṃ parābhavamukhaṃ vuttaṃ. Etena hi samannāgato neva gahaṭṭho gahaṭṭhavuḍḍhiṃ, na pabbajito pabbajitavuḍḍhiṃ pāpuṇāti, aññadatthu parihāyatiyeva parābhavatiyeva, tasmā “parābhavato mukha”nti vuccati.

96. One who is given to sleep is a person who is drowsy whether walking, sitting, standing, or lying down. One who is fond of company is one who delights in society and is devoted to chatter. One who is inactive is devoid of the power of energy and is not of an energetic disposition; only when urged by others does a householder undertake the work of a householder, or one who has gone forth undertake the work of one who has gone forth. One who is lazy is lazy by nature, utterly overcome by sloth; he remains standing in a place for standing, he remains sitting in a place for sitting, and does not by his own effort adopt another posture. An example of this is the lazy person who did not flee when a fire broke out in the forest in the past. This is the highest classification; below that, even by a lesser classification, a lazy person should be understood simply as lazy. Just as a banner is the sign of a chariot, and smoke is the sign of a fire, so anger is his sign; hence he is called 'one whose sign is anger.' A person of hateful disposition, quick to anger, with a mind like a festering sore, is of such a nature. By this verse, a fivefold cause of downfall is stated: being given to sleep, being fond of company, being inactive, being lazy, and being one whose sign is anger. For one endowed with these, neither a householder attains the growth of a householder, nor one who has gone forth attains the growth of one who has gone forth; on the contrary, he only declines and meets with ruin. Therefore, it is called 'a cause of downfall.'

98. Mātāti janikā veditabbā. Pitāti janakoyeva. Jiṇṇakaṃ sarīrasithilatāya. Gatayobbanaṃ yobbanātikkamena āsītikaṃ vā nāvutikaṃ vā sayaṃ kammāni kātumasamatthaṃ. Pahu santoti samattho samāno sukhaṃ jīvamāno. Na bharatīti na poseti. Imāya gāthāya mātāpitūnaṃ abharaṇaṃ, aposanaṃ, anupaṭṭhānaṃ ekaṃyeva parābhavamukhaṃ vuttaṃ. Etena hi samannāgato yaṃ taṃ –

98. 'Mother' should be understood as she who gives birth. 'Father' is the progenitor. 'Aged' means due to the body's frailty. 'Past their youth' means having passed beyond youth, being eighty or ninety years old and unable to do their own work. 'Being able' means being capable and living in comfort. 'Does not support' means does not provide for. In this verse, not supporting, not providing for, and not attending to one's parents is stated as the one cause of downfall. For one endowed with this...

“Tāya [M 1.0153][V 1.0135] naṃ pāricariyāya, mātāpitūsu paṇḍitā;

Idheva naṃ pasaṃsanti, pecca sagge pamodatī”ti. (itivu. 106; a. ni. 4.63) –

'For that service to his mother and father, the wise praise him here in this world; and after death, he rejoices in heaven.'

Mātāpitubharaṇe ānisaṃsaṃ vuttaṃ. Taṃ na pāpuṇāti, aññadatthu “mātāpitaropi na bharati, kaṃ aññaṃ bharissatī”ti nindañca vajjanīyatañca duggatiñca pāpuṇanto parābhavatiyeva, tasmā “parābhavato mukha”nti vuccati.

The benefit of supporting one's parents has been stated. He does not attain that; on the contrary, incurring blame, reproach, and a bad destination, with people thinking, "He does not even support his parents—who else will he support?" he is certainly ruined. Therefore, it is called "a cause of downfall."

100. Pāpānaṃ bāhitattā brāhmaṇaṃ, samitattā samaṇaṃ. Brāhmaṇakulappabhavampi vā brāhmaṇaṃ, pabbajjupagataṃ [P 1.0171] samaṇaṃ, tato aññaṃ vāpi yaṃkiñci yācanakaṃ. Musāvādena vañcetīti “vada, bhante, paccayenā”ti pavāretvā yācito vā paṭijānitvā pacchā appadānena tassa taṃ āsaṃ visaṃvādeti. Imāya gāthāya brāhmaṇādīnaṃ musāvādena vañcanaṃ ekaṃyeva parābhavamukhaṃ vuttaṃ. Etena hi samannāgato idha nindaṃ, samparāye duggatiṃ sugatiyampi adhippāyavipattiñca pāpuṇāti. Vuttañhetaṃ –

100. Because he has banished evil, he is a brahmin; because he is pacified, he is a recluse. Or one born of a brahmin family is a brahmin; one who has gone forth is a recluse; or any other mendicant whatsoever. He deceives with false speech: having invited with, "Speak, venerable sir, as to your need," and then, when asked or having promised, later by not giving, he deceives that hope of his. In this verse, deceiving brahmins and others with false speech is stated as a single cause of downfall. For one endowed with this, he incurs blame in this life, a bad destination in the next, and even in a good destination encounters the failure of his intentions. As it is said:

“Dussīlassa sīlavipannassa pāpako kittisaddo abbhuggacchatī”ti (dī. ni. 2.149; a. ni. 5.213; mahāva. 285).

"For the immoral one, one who has failed in virtue, a bad reputation arises."

Tathā –

Furthermore—

“Catūhi, bhikkhave, dhammehi samannāgato yathābhataṃ nikkhitto evaṃ niraye. Katamehi catūhi? Musāvādī hotī”tiādi (a. ni. 4.82).

"Monks, one possessed of four qualities is cast into hell as if brought there. What four? He is a liar..."

Tathā –

Furthermore—

“Idha, sāriputta, ekacco samaṇaṃ vā brāhmaṇaṃ vā upasaṅkamitvā pavāreti, ‘vada, bhante, paccayenā’ti, so yena pavāreti, taṃ na deti. So ce tato cuto itthattaṃ āgacchati. So yaṃ yadeva vaṇijjaṃ payojeti, sāssa hoti chedagāminī. Idha pana sāriputta…pe… so yena pavāreti, na taṃ yathādhippāyaṃ deti. So ce tato cuto [V 1.0136] itthattaṃ āgacchati. So yaṃ yadeva vaṇijjaṃ payojeti, sāssa na hoti yathādhippāyā”ti (a. ni. 4.79).

"Here, Sāriputta, someone approaches a recluse or brahmin and invites them, saying, ‘Speak, venerable sir, as to your need.’ But what he invites them for, that he does not give. If, after dying, he is reborn into this state, whatever trade he undertakes leads to ruin. But here, Sāriputta… what he invites them for, that he does not give according to their wish. If, after dying, he is reborn into this state, whatever trade he undertakes does not succeed as he intended."

Evamimāni [M 1.0154] nindādīni pāpuṇanto parābhavatiyeva, tasmā “parābhavato mukha”nti vuttaṃ.

Thus, incurring these reproaches and the like, he is certainly ruined. Therefore, it is said to be "a cause of downfall."

102. Pahūtavittoti pahūtajātarūparajatamaṇiratano. Sahiraññoti sakahāpaṇo. Sabhojanoti anekasūpabyañjanabhojanasampanno. Eko bhuñjati sādūnīti sādūni bhojanāni attano puttānampi adatvā paṭicchannokāse bhuñjatīti eko bhuñjati sādūni. Imāya gāthāya bhojanagiddhatāya bhojanamacchariyaṃ ekaṃyeva parābhavamukhaṃ vuttaṃ. Etena hi samannāgato nindaṃ vajjanīyaṃ duggatinti evamādīni pāpuṇanto parābhavatiyeva, tasmā “parābhavato mukha”nti vuttaṃ. Vuttanayeneva sabbaṃ suttānusārena yojetabbaṃ, ativitthārabhayena pana idāni yojanānayaṃ adassetvā atthamattameva bhaṇāma.

102. "Abundant in wealth" means possessing much gold, silver, gems, and jewels. "With money" means possessing currency. "With food" means being endowed with many soups, curries, and foods. "He eats delicacies alone" means that, not giving even to his own children, he eats delicious foods in a concealed place; thus, "he eats delicacies alone." In this verse, on account of greed for food, stinginess with food is stated as the one cause of downfall. For one endowed with this, upon encountering blame, fault, a bad destination, and so on, certainly comes to ruin; therefore, it is called "a cause of downfall." Everything should be connected according to the method already stated and in accordance with the sutta. However, due to fear of excessive expansion, we shall now state only the meaning without showing the method of connection.

104. Jātitthaddho nāma yo “ahaṃ jātisampanno”ti mānaṃ janetvā tena thaddho vātapūritabhastā viya uddhumāto hutvā na kassaci [P 1.0172] onamati. Esa nayo dhanagottatthaddhesu. Saññātiṃ atimaññetīti attano ñātimpi jātiyā atimaññati sakyā viya viṭaṭūbhaṃ. Dhanenāpi ca “kapaṇo ayaṃ daliddo”ti atimaññati, sāmīcimattampi na karoti, tassa te ñātayo parābhavameva icchanti. Imāya gāthāya vatthuto catubbidhaṃ, lakkhaṇato ekaṃyeva parābhavamukhaṃ vuttaṃ.

104. One who is arrogant due to birth is one who, having generated the conceit, "I am of noble birth," becomes arrogant on account of it. Inflated like a leather bag filled with wind, he does not bow to anyone. This is the way also for those arrogant due to wealth or lineage. "He scorns his own kinsmen" means he scorns even his own relatives on account of birth, just as the Sakyans did Viṭaṭūbha. And on account of wealth, he also scorns others, thinking, "This one is wretched and poor," and does not perform even a small act of respect. Those relatives of his wish only for his ruin. In this verse, a cause of downfall that is fourfold in substance but single in characteristic is stated.

106. Itthidhuttoti itthīsu sāratto, yaṃkiñci atthi, taṃ sabbampi datvā aparāparaṃ itthiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Tathā sabbampi attano santakaṃ nikkhipitvā surāpānapayutto surādhutto. Nivatthasāṭakampi nikkhipitvā jūtakīḷanamanuyutto akkhadhutto. Etehi tīhi ṭhānehi yaṃkiñcipi laddhaṃ hoti, tassa vināsanato laddhaṃ laddhaṃ vināsetīti veditabbo. Evaṃvidho parābhavatiyeva, tenassetaṃ imāya gāthāya tividhaṃ parābhavamukhaṃ vuttaṃ.

106. A debauchee with women is one who is infatuated with women; giving away all that he has, he takes up with one woman after another. Likewise, a debauchee with liquor is one who, devoted to drinking liquor, squanders all his own possessions. A debauchee with dice is one who, constantly engaged in playing at dice, discards even the cloth he is wearing. Because of these three situations, whatever is gained is destroyed; thus it should be understood that he destroys whatever is gained. Such a person certainly comes to ruin. Therefore, for him, this threefold cause of downfall is stated in this verse.

108. Sehi dārehīti attano dārehi. Yo attano dārehi asantuṭṭho hutvā vesiyāsu padussati, tathā paradāresu, so [M 1.0155] yasmā vesīnaṃ dhanappadānena paradārasevanena ca rājadaṇḍādīhi parābhavatiyeva, tenassetaṃ imāya gāthāya duvidhaṃ parābhavamukhaṃ vuttaṃ.

108. "With his own wives" means with one's own wives. The man who, being dissatisfied with his own wives, transgresses with courtesans and likewise with the wives of others—since he certainly comes to ruin by giving wealth to courtesans and, through consorting with the wives of others, by royal punishment and so on—therefore, for him, this twofold cause of downfall is stated in this verse.

110. Atītayobbanoti [V 1.0137] yobbanamaticca āsītiko vā nāvutiko vā hutvā āneti pariggaṇhāti. Timbarutthaninti timbaruphalasadisatthaniṃ taruṇadārikaṃ. Tassā issā na supatīti “daharāya mahallakena saddhiṃ rati ca saṃvāso ca amanāpo, mā heva kho taruṇaṃ pattheyyā”ti issāya taṃ rakkhanto na supati. So yasmā kāmarāgena ca issāya ca ḍayhanto bahiddhā kammante ca appayojento parābhavatiyeva, tenassetaṃ imāya gāthāya imaṃ issāya asupanaṃ ekaṃyeva parābhavamukhaṃ vuttaṃ.

110. "Past his youth" means one who, having surpassed youth, being eighty or ninety years old, brings home and takes possession of a young girl. "With breasts like the Timbaru fruit" means a young girl with breasts resembling the Timbaru fruit. "Out of jealousy for her, he does not sleep" means that, thinking, "For a young woman, delight and living together with an old man are not pleasing; lest she should desire a young man," he guards her out of jealousy and does not sleep. Since, being burned by sensual lust and jealousy, and not applying himself to external work, he certainly comes to ruin, therefore, for him, in this verse, this not sleeping due to jealousy is stated as the one cause of downfall.

112. Soṇḍinti macchamaṃsādīsu lolaṃ gedhajātikaṃ. Vikiraṇinti tesaṃ atthāya dhanaṃ paṃsukaṃ viya vikiritvā nāsanasīlaṃ. Purisaṃ vāpi tādisanti puriso vāpi yo evarūpo hoti, taṃ yo issariyasmiṃ ṭhapeti, lañchanamuddikādīni datvā gharāvāse kammante [P 1.0173] vā vaṇijjādivohāresu vā tadeva vāvaṭaṃ kāreti. So yasmā tassa dosena dhanakkhayaṃ pāpuṇanto parābhavatiyeva, tenassetaṃ imāya gāthāya tathāvidhassa issariyasmiṃ ṭhapanaṃ ekaṃyeva parābhavamukhaṃ vuttaṃ.

112. "A spendthrift" means one who is fickle and of a gluttonous nature regarding fish, meat, and so on. "A squanderer" means one of a destructive habit who, for the sake of these things, scatters wealth like dust. "Or a man of such a kind" means a man who is also of such a nature. One who places him in a position of authority, giving emblems, seals, and so on, and puts him in charge of household affairs, work, or commerce and trade—since he (the appointer), due to the fault of that one (the appointee), encounters the destruction of wealth and certainly comes to ruin, therefore, for such a person, this act of placing another in authority is stated in this verse as the one cause of downfall.

114. Appabhogo nāma sannicitānañca bhogānaṃ āyamukhassa ca abhāvato. Mahātaṇhoti mahatiyā bhogataṇhāya samannāgato, yaṃ laddhaṃ, tena asantuṭṭho. Khattiye jāyate kuleti khattiyānaṃ kule jāyati. So ca rajjaṃ patthayatīti so etāya mahātaṇhatāya anupāyena uppaṭipāṭiyā attano dāyajjabhūtaṃ alabbhaneyyaṃ vā parasantakaṃ rajjaṃ pattheti, so evaṃ patthento yasmā tampi appakaṃ bhogaṃ yodhājīvādīnaṃ datvā rajjaṃ apāpuṇanto parābhavatiyeva, tenassetaṃ imāya gāthāya rajjapatthanaṃ ekaṃyeva parābhavamukhaṃ vuttaṃ.

114. "Of little wealth" means due to the absence of accumulated wealth and sources of income. "Of great craving" means endowed with a great craving for wealth, being dissatisfied with what has been obtained. "Is born in a noble family" means he is born in a family of khattiyas. "And he aspires to sovereignty" means that he, with this great craving, through improper means and out of turn, desires the kingdom that is his inheritance or the unattainable property of another. Since, in aspiring thus, he gives even that little wealth he has to soldiers and their like and, not attaining the kingdom, certainly comes to ruin, therefore, for him, this aspiration for sovereignty is stated in this verse as the one cause of downfall.

115. Ito [M 1.0156] paraṃ yadi sā devatā “terasamaṃ bhagavā brūhi…pe… satasahassimaṃ bhagavā brūhī”ti puccheyya, tampi bhagavā katheyya. Yasmā pana sā devatā “kiṃ imehi pucchitehi, ekamettha vuḍḍhikaraṃ natthī”ti tāni parābhavamukhāni asuyyamānā ettakampi pucchitvā vippaṭisārī hutvā tuṇhī ahosi, tasmā bhagavā tassāsayaṃ viditvā desanaṃ niṭṭhāpento imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi “ete parābhave loke”ti.

115. Further, if that devatā had asked, "Blessed One, speak of the thirteenth... Blessed One, speak of the hundred-thousandth," the Blessed One would have spoken that as well. However, since that devatā, not wishing to hear those causes of downfall and thinking, "What is the use of asking about these? There is not one among them that brings growth," became remorseful after asking only this much and fell silent, therefore the Blessed One, knowing her intention and concluding the teaching, spoke this verse: "These are the causes of ruin in the world..."

Tattha paṇḍitoti parivīmaṃsāya samannāgato. Samavekkhiyāti paññācakkhunā upaparikkhitvā. Ariyoti na maggena, na phalena, apica kho, pana etasmiṃ parābhavasaṅkhāte anaye na iriyatīti ariyo. Yena dassanena yāya paññāya parābhave disvā vivajjeti, tena [V 1.0138] sampannattā dassanasampanno. Sa lokaṃ bhajate sivanti so evarūpo sivaṃ khemamuttamamanupaddavaṃ devalokaṃ bhajati, allīyati, upagacchatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Desanāpariyosāne parābhavamukhāni sutvā uppannasaṃvegānurūpaṃ yoniso padahitvā sotāpattisakadāgāmianāgāmiphalāni pattā devatā gaṇanaṃ vītivattā. Yathāha –

Herein, "a wise person" means one endowed with thorough investigation. "Having well considered" means having examined with the eye of wisdom. "Noble" means not an ariya by path, nor an ariya by fruit; but rather, because one does not fare in this wrong way called 'ruin,' one is 'noble.' Because one is endowed with that vision, with that wisdom, by which, having seen the causes of ruin, one avoids them, one is 'endowed with vision.' "He resorts to a blissful world" means that such a person resorts to, cleaves to, and approaches the blissful, secure, supreme, untroubled world of the devas. At the conclusion of the discourse, having heard the causes of downfall, devatās for whom spiritual urgency had arisen, striving wisely in accordance with it, attained the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, and non-returning, in numbers beyond calculation. As it is said:

“Mahāsamayasutte [P 1.0174] ca, atho maṅgalasuttake;

Samacitte rāhulovāde, dhammacakke parābhave.

In the Mahāsamaya Sutta, and also in the Maṅgala Sutta; in the Samacitta Sutta, the Rāhulovāda Sutta, the Dhammacakka Sutta, and the Parābhava Sutta.

“Devatāsamitī tattha, appameyyā asaṅkhiyā;

Dhammābhisamayo cettha, gaṇanāto asaṅkhiyo”ti.

An immeasurable, countless assembly of deities was there; and here, the realization of the Dhamma was beyond calculation.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

In the commentary named Paramatthajotikā,

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya parābhavasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

the explanation of the Parābhava Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary is concluded.

7. Aggikabhāradvājasuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Explanation of the Aggikabhāradvāja Sutta

Evaṃ [V 1.0139] me sutanti aggikabhāradvājasuttaṃ, “vasalasutta”ntipi vuccati. Kā uppatti? Bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Kasibhāradvājasutte vuttanayena pacchābhattakiccāvasāne buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ [M 1.0157] volokento aggikabhāradvājaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ saraṇasikkhāpadānaṃ upanissayasampannaṃ disvā “tattha mayi gate kathā pavattissati, tato kathāvasāne dhammadesanaṃ sutvā esa brāhmaṇo saraṇaṃ gantvā sikkhāpadāni samādiyissatī”ti ñatvā, tattha gantvā, pavattāya kathāya brāhmaṇena dhammadesanaṃ yācito imaṃ suttaṃ abhāsi. Tattha “evaṃ me suta”ntiādiṃ maṅgalasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ vaṇṇayissāma, “atha kho bhagavā pubbaṇhasamaya”ntiādi kasibhāradvājasutte vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

Thus have I heard. This is the Aggikabhāradvāja Sutta, which is also called the 'Vasala Sutta.' What is its origin? The Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's park. In the manner described in the Kasibhāradvāja Sutta, at the conclusion of the duties after the meal, the Blessed One surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye and saw the brahmin Aggikabhāradvāja, who was endowed with the supporting condition for taking refuge and the training rules. Knowing that 'when I go there, a conversation will arise, and at the end of that conversation, after hearing the Dhamma teaching, this brahmin will go for refuge and undertake the training rules,' he went there. On account of the conversation that arose, having been requested for a Dhamma teaching by the brahmin, the Blessed One delivered this discourse. Therein, 'Thus have I heard' and so on we shall explain in the commentary on the Maṅgala Sutta. 'Then the Blessed One, in the morning...' and so on should be understood in the same way as described in the Kasibhāradvāja Sutta.

Tena kho pana samayena aggikabhāradvājassāti yaṃ yaṃ avuttapubbaṃ, taṃ tadeva vaṇṇayissāma. Seyyathidaṃ – so hi brāhmaṇo aggiṃ juhati paricaratīti katvā aggikoti nāmena pākaṭo ahosi, bhāradvājoti gottena. Tasmā vuttaṃ “aggikabhāradvājassā”ti. Nivesaneti ghare. Tassa kira brāhmaṇassa nivesanadvāre antaravīthiyaṃ aggihutasālā ahosi. Tato “nivesanadvāre”ti vattabbe tassapi padesassa nivesaneyeva pariyāpannattā “nivesane”ti vuttaṃ. Samīpatthe vā bhummavacanaṃ, nivesanasamīpeti attho. Aggi pajjalito hotīti aggiyādhāne ṭhito aggi katabbhuddharaṇo samidhāpakkhepaṃ bījanavātañca labhitvā [P 1.0175] jalito uddhaṃ samuggataccisamākulo hoti. Āhuti paggahitāti sasīsaṃ nhāyitvā mahatā sakkārena pāyāsasappimadhuphāṇitādīni abhisaṅkhatāni hontīti attho. Yañhi kiñci aggimhi juhitabbaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ “āhutī”ti vuccati. Sapadānanti anugharaṃ. Bhagavā hi sabbajanānuggahatthāya āhārasantuṭṭhiyā ca uccanīcakulaṃ avokkamma piṇḍāya carati. Tena vuttaṃ “sapadānaṃ piṇḍāya caramāno”ti.

Concerning the phrase 'At that time, to Aggika Bhāradvāja...': whatever has not been said before, that very thing we shall explain. To wit: that brahmin was known by the name Aggika because he offers to and tends the fire, and by the clan name Bhāradvāja. Therefore, it is said, 'to Aggika Bhāradvāja.' 'In the residence' means in his home. It is said that at the entrance to that brahmin’s residence, in the middle of the street, there was a fire-offering hall. Therefore, though it should have been said 'at the entrance to the residence,' since that place was included within the residence itself, it is said 'in the residence.' Or, the locative case is used in the sense of proximity, meaning 'near the residence.' 'The fire was blazing' means: the fire, standing in the fire-receptacle, with wood piled on it, having received the addition of fuel-sticks and wind from a fan, blazed, filled with flames rising upwards. 'The offering was held ready' means: having bathed including his head, with great reverence, offerings such as milk-rice, ghee, honey, and molasses were prepared. For whatever is to be offered into the fire is called an 'offering.' 'Sequentially' means from house to house. For the Blessed One, for the welfare of all people and being content with almsfood, wanders for alms without skipping over any family, whether high or low. Therefore, it is said, 'wandering sequentially for alms.'

Atha kimatthaṃ sabbākārasampannaṃ samantapāsādikaṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā brāhmaṇassa cittaṃ nappasīdati? Kasmā ca evaṃ pharusena vacanena bhagavantaṃ samudācaratīti? Vuccate – ayaṃ kira [V 1.0140] brāhmaṇo “maṅgalakiccesu samaṇadassanaṃ avamaṅgala”nti evaṃdiṭṭhiko, tato “mahābrahmuno bhuñjanavelāya kāḷakaṇṇī muṇḍakasamaṇako mama nivesanaṃ upasaṅkamatī”ti mantvā cittaṃ nappasādesi, aññadatthu dosavasaṃyeva agamāsi. Atha kuddho anattamano anattamanavācaṃ nicchāresi “tatreva muṇḍakā”tiādi. Tatrāpi [M 1.0158] ca yasmā “muṇḍo asuddho hotī”ti brāhmaṇānaṃ diṭṭhi, tasmā “ayaṃ asuddho, tena devabrāhmaṇapūjako na hotī”ti jigucchanto “muṇḍakā”ti āha. Muṇḍakattā vā ucchiṭṭho esa, na imaṃ padesaṃ arahati āgacchitunti samaṇo hutvāpi īdisaṃ kāyakilesaṃ na vaṇṇetīti ca samaṇabhāvaṃ jigucchanto “samaṇakā”ti āha. Na kevalaṃ dosavaseneva, vasale vā pabbājetvā tehi saddhiṃ ekato sambhogaparibhogakaraṇena patito ayaṃ vasalatopi pāpataroti jigucchanto “vasalakā”ti āha – “vasalajātikānaṃ vā āhutidassanamattasavanena pāpaṃ hotī”ti maññamānopi evamāha.

Then why, upon seeing the Blessed One—perfect in all aspects and inspiring confidence all around—did the brahmin's mind not become serene? And why did he address the Blessed One with such harsh words? It is said: This brahmin, it seems, held the view that 'seeing an ascetic during auspicious ceremonies is inauspicious.' Therefore, thinking, 'At the time of the great brahma's meal, this ill-omened, shaven-headed ascetic approaches my residence,' he did not allow his mind to become serene; on the contrary, he fell under the sway of anger. Then, angry and displeased, he uttered words of displeasure: 'Stay right there, you shaveling,' and so on. Therein, because brahmins hold the view that 'a shaven-headed one is impure,' he said 'shaveling' in disgust, thinking, 'This one is impure; therefore, he is not worthy of worship by gods and brahmins.' Or, 'Because he is a shaveling, he is refuse; he is not worthy to approach this place.' And despising the state of being an ascetic, thinking, 'Even though he is an ascetic, he does not commend this kind of bodily defilement,' he said 'little ascetic.' It was not only due to anger; despising him, thinking, 'Having given the going-forth to outcasts, and by associating and sharing with them, this one has fallen and is more wicked than an outcast,' he said 'outcast.' Or, he spoke thus thinking, 'For those of outcast birth, evil arises merely by seeing or hearing of an offering.'

Bhagavā tathā vuttopi vippasanneneva mukhavaṇṇena madhurena sarena brāhmaṇassa upari anukampāsītalena cittena attano sabbasattehi asādhāraṇatādibhāvaṃ pakāsento āha “jānāsi pana, tvaṃ brāhmaṇā”ti. Atha brāhmaṇo bhagavato [P 1.0176] mukhappasādasūcitaṃ tādibhāvaṃ ñatvā anukampāsītalena cittena nicchāritaṃ madhurassaraṃ sutvā amateneva abhisittahadayo attamano vippasannindriyo nihatamāno hutvā taṃ jātisabhāvaṃ visauggirasadisaṃ samudācāravacanaṃ pahāya “nūna yamahaṃ hīnajaccaṃ vasalanti paccemi, na so paramatthato vasalo, na ca hīnajaccatā eva vasalakaraṇo dhammo”ti maññamāno “na khvāhaṃ, bho gotamā”ti āha. Dhammatā hesā, yaṃ hetusampanno paccayālābhena pharusopi samāno laddhamatte paccaye muduko hotīti.

Even though addressed in this way, the Blessed One, with a perfectly serene facial expression and a sweet voice, with a mind cooled by compassion for the brahmin, revealing his own state of equanimity which is not shared by all beings, said: 'But do you know, brahmin, who an outcast is?' Then the brahmin, recognizing that state of equanimity indicated by the Blessed One's serene countenance, and hearing the sweet voice uttered with a mind cooled by compassion, his heart as if sprinkled with ambrosia, became pleased, with serene faculties and humbled pride. Abandoning that innate manner of speech, which was like spitting poison, he thought, 'Surely, I consider one of low birth to be an outcast, but in the ultimate sense, he is not an outcast, nor is low birth itself the principle that makes one an outcast.' Thinking thus, the brahmin said, 'Indeed, I do not know, good Gotama.' For this is the nature of things: a person endowed with the cause, though harsh from not obtaining a supporting condition, becomes gentle the moment they obtain that condition.

Tattha sādhūti ayaṃ saddo āyācanasampaṭicchanasampahaṃsanasundaradaḷhīkammādīsu dissati. “Sādhu me, bhante, bhagavā saṃkhittena dhammaṃ desetū”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 4.95; a. ni. 7.83) hi āyācane. “Sādhu, bhanteti kho so bhikkhu bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinanditvā anumoditvā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.86) sampaṭicchane. “Sādhu, sādhu, sāriputtā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 3.349) sampahaṃsane.

Here, the word "sādhu" is seen in contexts of requesting, receiving, praising, being good, strengthening, and so on. For example, in requesting: "Venerable sir, may the Blessed One kindly teach me the Dhamma in brief," and so on (Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.95; Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.83). In receiving: "Very well, venerable sir," said that monk, delighting and rejoicing in the Blessed One’s words (Majjhima Nikāya 3.86). In praise: "Good, good, Sāriputta," and so on (Dīgha Nikāya 3.349).

“Sādhu dhammarucī rājā, sādhu paññāṇavā naro;

Sādhu mittānamaddubbho, pāpassākaraṇaṃ sukha”nti. (jā. 2.18.101) –

Good is the king who delights in the Dhamma; good is the person of wisdom. Good is a friend who is not treacherous; not doing evil is happiness.

Ādīsu [M 1.0159][V 1.0141] sundare. “Taṃ suṇātha, sādhukaṃ manasi karothā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.1) daḷhīkamme. Idha pana āyācane.

In such verses, it is used in the sense of 'good'. In passages such as ‘Listen to that, attend carefully!’ (MN 1), it is for strengthening. Here, however, it is an entreaty.

Tena hīti tassādhippāyanidassanaṃ, sace ñātukāmosīti vuttaṃ hoti. Kāraṇavacanaṃ vā, tassa yasmā ñātukāmosi, tasmā, brāhmaṇa, suṇāhi, sādhukaṃ manasi karohi, tathā te bhāsissāmi, yathā tvaṃ jānissasīti evaṃ parapadehi saddhiṃ sambandho veditabbo. Tatra ca suṇāhīti sotindriyavikkhepavāraṇaṃ, sādhukaṃ manasi karohīti manasikāre daḷhīkammaniyojanena manindriyavikkhepavāraṇaṃ. Purimañcettha byañjanavipallāsaggāhavāraṇaṃ, pacchimaṃ atthavipallāsaggāhavāraṇaṃ[P 1.0177]. Purimena ca dhammassavane niyojeti, pacchimena sutānaṃ dhammānaṃ dhāraṇatthūpaparikkhādīsu. Purimena ca “sabyañjano ayaṃ dhammo, tasmā savanīyo”ti dīpeti, pacchimena “sāttho, tasmā manasi kātabbo”ti. Sādhukapadaṃ vā ubhayapadehi yojetvā “yasmā ayaṃ dhammo dhammagambhīro ca desanāgambhīro ca, tasmā suṇāhi sādhukaṃ. Yasmā atthagambhīro paṭivedhagambhīro ca, tasmā sādhukaṃ manasi karohī”ti etamatthaṃ dīpento āha – “suṇāhi sādhukaṃ manasi karohī”ti.

‘Then, brahmin’ (tena hi) is an indication of his intention, meaning, ‘if you wish to know.’ Or it is a statement of reason: ‘Since you wish to know, therefore, brahmin, listen, attend carefully, and I will speak to you in such a way that you will understand.’ Thus, its connection with the subsequent words should be understood. Here, ‘listen’ (suṇāhi) prevents distraction of the ear faculty, and ‘attend carefully’ (sādhukaṃ manasi karohi) prevents distraction of the mind faculty by enjoining firm application of attention. The former here prevents misapprehension due to distortion of the words, the latter prevents misapprehension due to distortion of the meaning. By the former, one is enjoined to hear the Dhamma; by the latter, to retain, examine, etc., the Dhamma that has been heard. By the former, it is shown that ‘this Dhamma is complete with its expressions, therefore it should be listened to’; by the latter, that ‘it is meaningful, therefore it should be kept in mind.’ Alternatively, connecting the word ‘carefully’ (sādhukaṃ) with both phrases, he spoke, illuminating this meaning: ‘Since this Dhamma is profound in the Dhamma and profound in its exposition, therefore listen carefully. Since it is profound in meaning and profound in penetration, therefore attend carefully.’ Thus he said, ‘Listen carefully, attend carefully.’

Tato “evaṃ gambhīre kathamahaṃ patiṭṭhaṃ labhissāmī”ti visīdantamiva taṃ brāhmaṇaṃ samussāhento āha – “bhāsissāmī”ti. Tattha “yathā tvaṃ ñassasi, tathā parimaṇḍalehi padabyañjanehi uttānena nayena bhāsissāmī”ti evamadhippāyo veditabbo. Tato ussāhajāto hutvā “evaṃ bho”ti kho aggikabhāradvājo brāhmaṇo bhagavato paccassosi, sampaṭicchi paṭiggahesīti vuttaṃ hoti, yathānusiṭṭhaṃ vā paṭipajjanena abhimukho assosīti. Athassa “bhagavā etadavocā”ti idāni vattabbaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “kodhano upanāhī”ti evamādikaṃ.

Then, encouraging that brahmin who was, as it were, sinking in despair, thinking, ‘How shall I find a footing in such a profound teaching?’ he said, ‘I will speak.’ Here, the meaning should be understood as: ‘I will speak with well-rounded words and syllables, in an accessible manner, so that you can comprehend.’ Then, filled with enthusiasm, the brahmin Aggikabhāradvāja responded to the Blessed One, saying, ‘Yes, sir,’ accepted, and received it—meaning, he listened attentively, ready to follow the instruction given. Now, with reference to what was to be said, ‘The Blessed One said this to him,’ the passage beginning ‘One who is angry, resentful…’ was spoken.

116. Tattha kodhanoti kujjhanasīlo. Upanāhīti tasseva kodhassa daḷhīkammena upanāhena samannāgato. Paresaṃ guṇe makkheti puñchatīti makkhī, pāpo ca so makkhī cāti pāpamakkhī. Vipannadiṭṭhīti vinaṭṭhasammādiṭṭhi, vipannāya vā virūpaṃ gatāya dasavatthukāya micchādiṭṭhiyā samannāgato. Māyāvīti attani vijjamānadosapaṭicchādanalakkhaṇāya māyāya [M 1.0160] samannāgato. Taṃ jaññā vasalo itīti taṃ evarūpaṃ puggalaṃ etesaṃ hīnadhammānaṃ vassanato siñcanato anvāssavanato “vasalo”ti jāneyyāti, etehi sabbehi brāhmaṇamatthake jāto. Ayañhi paramatthato vasalo eva, attano [P 1.0178] hadayatuṭṭhimattaṃ, na paranti. Evamettha bhagavā ādipadeneva tassa brāhmaṇassa kodhaniggahaṃ katvā “kodhādidhammo hīnapuggalo”ti puggalādhiṭṭhānāya [V 1.0142] ca desanāya kodhādidhamme desento ekena tāva pariyāyena vasalañca vasalakaraṇe ca dhamme desesi. Evaṃ desento ca “tvaṃ aha”nti paravambhanaṃ attukkaṃsanañca akatvā dhammeneva samena ñāyena taṃ brāhmaṇaṃ vasalabhāve, attānañca brāhmaṇabhāve ṭhapesi.

116. Here, ‘angry’ (kodhano) means one prone to anger. ‘Resentful’ (upanāhī) means one who is endowed with resentment, which is the strengthening of that very anger by way of holding a grudge. ‘Makkhī’ (one who denigrates) means one who smears or wipes away the virtues of others; and ‘pāpamakkhī’ (a wicked denigrator) means one who is evil and also a denigrator. ‘Corrupt in view’ (vipannadiṭṭhī) means one who has lost right view, or is endowed with a distorted, tenfold wrong view that has gone astray. ‘Deceitful’ (māyāvī) means one who is endowed with deceit, characterized by concealing faults existing within oneself. ‘Know him as an outcast’ (taṃ jaññā vasalo iti): one should recognize such a person as an ‘outcast’ (vasalo) due to his being a dwelling place for, being sprinkled with, and leaking these inferior qualities. Though born a brahmin in all respects, in the ultimate sense, this person is an outcast, concerned only with his own heart’s satisfaction, not that of others. Thus, here, the Blessed One, with the very first word, having restrained the brahmin’s anger, taught that ‘a person with angry and other base qualities is an inferior person.’ By a teaching based on the individual, explaining the qualities beginning with anger, he taught, in one way, both the outcast and the qualities that make one an outcast. In teaching thus, without disparaging others or exalting himself, he placed that brahmin in the state of an outcast and himself in the state of a brahmin through just and fair means based on the Dhamma.

117. Idāni yāyaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ diṭṭhi “kadāci pāṇātipātaadinnādānādīni karontopi brāhmaṇo evā”ti. Taṃ diṭṭhiṃ paṭisedhento, ye ca sattavihiṃsādīsu akusaladhammesu tehi tehi samannāgatā ādīnavaṃ apassantā te dhamme uppādenti, tesaṃ “hīnā ete dhammā vasalakaraṇā”ti tattha ādīnavañca dassento aparehipi pariyāyehi vasalañca vasalakaraṇe ca dhamme desetuṃ “ekajaṃ vā dvijaṃ vā”ti evamādigāthāyo abhāsi.

117. Now, to refute the view held by brahmins that ‘even if one occasionally commits acts like killing living beings and taking what is not given, one is still a brahmin,’ the Teacher spoke the verses beginning, ‘Whether once-born or twice-born…’. He did so to show the danger for those who, being endowed with various unwholesome qualities such as harming beings, do not see the danger and so give rise to those qualities, showing them that ‘these qualities are base, they make one an outcast,’ and to teach, by other methods as well, about the outcast and the qualities that make one an outcast.

Tattha ekajoti ṭhapetvā aṇḍajaṃ avasesayonijo. So hi ekadā eva jāyati. Dvijoti aṇḍajo. So hi mātukucchito aṇḍakosato cāti dvikkhattuṃ jāyati. Taṃ ekajaṃ vā dvijaṃ vāpi. Yodha pāṇanti yo idha sattaṃ. Vihiṃsatīti kāyadvārikacetanāsamuṭṭhitena vā vacīdvārikacetanāsamuṭṭhitena vā payogena jīvitā voropeti. “Pāṇāni hiṃsatī”tipi pāṭho. Tattha ekajaṃ vā dvijaṃ vāti evaṃpabhedāni yodha pāṇāni hiṃsatīti evaṃ sambandho veditabbo. Yassa pāṇe dayā natthīti etena manasā anukampāya abhāvaṃ āha. Sesamettha vuttanayameva. Ito parāsu ca gāthāsu, yato ettakampi avatvā ito paraṃ uttānatthāni padāni pariharantā avaṇṇitapadavaṇṇanāmattameva karissāma.

Herein, ‘single-born’ (ekaja) refers to those of the remaining origins, excluding the egg-born. For they are born only once. ‘Twice-born’ (dvija) refers to the egg-born. For they are born twice: once from the mother’s womb and once from the eggshell. ‘Whether single-born or twice-born, whoever here harms living beings’ (taṃ ekajaṃ vā dvijaṃ vāpi yo idha pāṇaṃ vihiṃsati)—this means one who deprives them of life through an effort arisen from bodily intention or verbal intention. The reading ‘harms living beings’ (pāṇāni hiṃsati) is also found. Herein, the connection should be understood as: ‘whoever here harms living beings of such distinctions as single-born or twice-born.’ ‘For whom there is no compassion for living beings’ (yassa pāṇe dayā natthi)—by this, the absence of compassion in the mind is stated. The rest here follows the same method. In the subsequent verses, without saying even this much, we will henceforth omit words with obvious meanings and provide explanations only for words not yet commented upon.

118. Hantīti [M 1.0161] hanati vināseti. Parirundhatīti senāya parivāretvā tiṭṭhati. Gāmāni nigamāni cāti ettha ca-saddena nagarānītipi vattabbaṃ. Niggāhako samaññātoti iminā hananaparirundhanena gāmanigamanagaraghātakoti loke vidito.

118. ‘Kills’ (hanti) means he strikes, he destroys. ‘Besieges’ (parirundhati) means he surrounds with an army and remains stationed. In ‘villages and towns’ (gāmāni nigamāni ca), the word ‘cities’ (nagarāni) should also be understood by the particle ‘ca’. ‘Known as an oppressor’ (niggāhako samaññāto)—by this killing and besieging, he is known in the world as a destroyer of villages, towns, and cities.

119. Gāme vā yadi vāraññeti [P 1.0179] gāmopi nigamopi nagarampi sabbova idha gāmo saddhiṃ upacārena, taṃ ṭhapetvā sesaṃ araññaṃ. Tasmiṃ gāme vā yadi vāraññe yaṃ paresaṃ mamāyitaṃ, yaṃ parasattānaṃ pariggahitamapariccattaṃ satto vā saṅkhāro vā. Theyyā adinnamādetīti tehi adinnaṃ ananuññātaṃ theyyacittena ādiyati, yena kenaci payogena yena kenaci avahārena attano gahaṇaṃ sādheti.

119. In ‘in the village or in the wilderness’ (gāme vā yadi vāraññe), here ‘village’ (gāma) includes every village, market town, and city, together with its environs, by extension; what remains, excluding that, is the wilderness. In that village or in the wilderness, ‘whatever is claimed by others’ (yaṃ paresaṃ mamāyitaṃ) is that which is possessed by other beings and not relinquished, whether a living being or a conditioned thing. ‘Takes what is not given with thievish intent’ (theyyā adinnamādeti) means he takes with a thieving intention what is not given or permitted by them, accomplishing its seizure for himself by whatever means, by whatever act of removal.

120. Iṇamādāyāti attano santakaṃ kiñci nikkhipitvā nikkhepaggahaṇena vā, kiñci [V 1.0143] anikkhipitvā “ettakena kālena ettakaṃ vaḍḍhiṃ dassāmī”ti vaḍḍhiggahaṇena vā, “yaṃ ito udayaṃ bhavissati, taṃ mayhaṃ mūlaṃ taveva bhavissatī”ti vā “udayaṃ ubhinnampi sādhāraṇa”nti vā evaṃ taṃtaṃāyogaggahaṇena vā iṇaṃ gahetvā. Cujjamāno palāyati na hi te iṇamatthīti tena iṇāyikena “dehi me iṇa”nti codiyamāno “na hi te iṇamatthi, mayā gahitanti ko sakkhī”ti evaṃ bhaṇanena ghare vasantopi palāyati.

120. ‘Having taken a loan’ (iṇaṃ ādāya) means having taken a loan either by depositing something of one’s own as collateral, or by taking a loan for interest without depositing anything, saying, ‘I will give this much interest by this time,’ or by taking a loan through various such agreements, saying, ‘Whatever profit arises from this will be mine, and the principal will be yours,’ or ‘The profit will be shared between us.’ ‘When pressed, he flees, saying, “I owe you nothing”’ (cujjamāno palāyati na hi te iṇamatthīti)—when pressed by the lender, saying, ‘Give me the loan,’ he flees even while living at home, saying, ‘You have no loan from me; who is the witness that I took it?’

121. Kiñcikkhakamyatāti appamattakepi kismiñcideva icchāya. Panthasmiṃ vajantaṃ jananti magge gacchantaṃ yaṃkiñci itthiṃ vā purisaṃ vā. Hantvā kiñcikkhamādetīti māretvā koṭṭetvā taṃ bhaṇḍakaṃ gaṇhāti.

121. ‘For the sake of some trifle’ (kiñcikkhakamyatā) means because of a desire for even some small thing. ‘A person traveling on the road’ (panthasmiṃ vajantaṃ janaṃ) means any woman or man going along the path. ‘Having killed, he takes some trifle’ (hantvā kiñcikkhamādeti) means having killed or beaten them, he takes that property.

122. Attahetūti attano jīvitakāraṇā, tathā parahetu. Dhanahetūti sakadhanassa vā paradhanassa vā kāraṇā. Ca-kāro sabbattha vikappanattho. Sakkhipuṭṭhoti yaṃ jānāsi, taṃ vadehīti pucchito. Musā brūtīti jānanto vā “na jānāmī”ti ajānanto vā “jānāmī”ti bhaṇati, sāmike asāmike, asāmike ca sāmike karoti.

122. ‘For one’s own sake’ (attahetu) means for the sake of one’s own life; likewise for another’s sake. ‘For wealth’s sake’ (dhanahetu) means for the sake of one’s own wealth or another’s wealth. The particle ‘ca’ (and) serves everywhere to indicate alternatives. ‘When asked as a witness’ (sakkhipuṭṭho) means when questioned with ‘What do you know? Speak that.’ ‘He speaks falsely’ (musā brūti) means, knowing, he says ‘I do not know,’ or not knowing, he says ‘I know,’ making an owner into a non-owner, and a non-owner into an owner.

123. Ñātīnanti [M 1.0162] sambandhīnaṃ. Sakhīnanti vayassānaṃ dāresūti parapariggahitesu. Paṭidissatīti paṭikūlena dissati, aticaranto dissatīti attho. Sāhasāti balakkārena anicchaṃ. Sampiyenāti tehi tesaṃ dārehi patthiyamāno sayañca patthayamāno, ubhayasinehavasenāpīti vuttaṃ hoti.

123. Of relatives (ñātīnaṃ): of kinsmen. Of friends (sakhīnaṃ): of companions. In wives (dāresu): in those possessed by others. Is seen among them (paṭidissatīti): he is seen in a hostile manner; the meaning is, he is seen transgressing. By force (sāhasā): by violence, against their will. With consent (sampiyena): being desired by their wives and desiring them himself, it is said to be due to mutual affection.

124. Mātaraṃ pitaraṃ vāti evaṃ mettāya padaṭṭhānabhūtampi, jiṇṇakaṃ gatayobbananti evaṃ karuṇāya padaṭṭhānabhūtampi[P 1.0180]. Pahu santo na bharatīti atthasampanno upakaraṇasampanno hutvāpi na poseti.

124. ‘Mother or father’ (mātaraṃ pitaraṃ vā): even they who are a basis for loving-kindness; ‘the aged, past their youth’ (jiṇṇakaṃ gatayobbanaṃ): even they who are a basis for compassion. ‘Though capable, he does not support’ (pahu santo na bharati): though wealthy and having resources, he does not provide for them.

125. Sasunti sassuṃ. Hantīti pāṇinā vā leḍḍunā vā aññena vā kenaci paharati. Rosetīti kodhamassa sañjaneti vācāya pharusavacanena.

125. ‘Mother-in-law’ (sasuṃ): his mother-in-law. ‘Strikes’ (hanti): hits with the hand, a clod, or any other thing. ‘Provokes’ (roseti): arouses her anger with harsh speech.

126. Atthanti sandiṭṭhikasamparāyikaparamatthesu yaṃkiñci. Pucchito santoti puṭṭho samāno. Anatthamanusāsatīti tassa ahitameva ācikkhati. Paṭicchannena mantetīti atthaṃ ācikkhantopi [V 1.0144] yathā so na jānāti, tathā apākaṭehi padabyañjanehi paṭicchannena vacanena manteti, ācariyamuṭṭhiṃ vā katvā dīgharattaṃ vasāpetvā sāvasesameva manteti.

126. ‘Benefit’ (atthaṃ): anything pertaining to visible, future, or ultimate welfare. ‘When asked’ (pucchito santo): being questioned. ‘He advises what is not beneficial’ (anatthamanusāsati): he points out only what is detrimental to him. ‘He advises in a concealed manner’ (paṭicchannena manteti): even when pointing out something beneficial, he does so in a concealed manner with obscure words and phrases so that the other does not understand; or, making a ‘teacher's fist,’ he makes them stay for a long time and advises them while holding something back.

127. Yo katvāti ettha mayā pubbabhāge pāpicchatā vuttā. Yā sā “idhekacco kāyena duccaritaṃ caritvā, vācāya duccaritaṃ caritvā, manasā duccaritaṃ caritvā, tassa paṭicchādanahetu pāpikaṃ icchaṃ paṇidahati, mā maṃ jaññāti icchatī”ti evaṃ āgatā. Yathā aññe na jānanti, tathā karaṇena katānañca avivaraṇena paṭicchannā assa kammantāti paṭicchannakammanto.

127. Regarding ‘Whoever, having done’ (yo katvā), herein evil desire was spoken of by me in a previous section. That is as follows: ‘Here, some person, having engaged in misconduct by body, speech, and mind, harbors an evil desire for the sake of concealing it, wishing, “May no one know me.”’ Because his deeds are concealed by acting in such a way that others do not know and by not disclosing what has been done, he is ‘one with concealed deeds’ (paṭicchannakammanto).

128. Parakulanti ñātikulaṃ vā mittakulaṃ vā. Āgatanti yassa tena kule bhuttaṃ, taṃ attano gehamāgataṃ pānabhojanādīhi nappaṭipūjeti, na vā deti, avabhuttaṃ vā detīti adhippāyo.

128. ‘To another’s family’ (parakulaṃ): to a relative's family or a friend’s family. ‘Having gone’ (āgataṃ): one who has been fed in that household, when that person comes to his own home, he does not honor them in return with drinks, food, and so on; he either does not give at all, or gives leftovers—this is the intention.

129. Yo brāhmaṇaṃ vāti parābhavasutte vuttanayameva.

129. ‘Whoever a brahmin…’ (yo brāhmaṇaṃ vā): this is by the same method as stated in the Parābhava Sutta.

130. Bhattakāle [M 1.0163] upaṭṭhiteti bhojanakāle jāte. Upaṭṭhitantipi pāṭho, bhattakāle āgatanti attho. Roseti vācā na ca detīti “atthakāmo me ayaṃ balakkārena maṃ puññaṃ kārāpetuṃ āgato”ti acintetvā appatirūpena pharusavacanena roseti, antamaso sammukhabhāvamattampi cassa na deti, pageva bhojananti adhippāyo.

130. ‘When mealtime is at hand’ (bhattakāle upaṭṭhite): when the time for the meal has come. There is also the reading ‘upaṭṭhitaṃ,’ meaning ‘one who arrives at mealtime.’ ‘He provokes with speech and does not give’ (roseti vācāya na ca deti): without considering, ‘This person wishes me well and has come to make me perform a meritorious deed by force,’ he provokes with inappropriate, harsh speech; he does not give him even so much as a direct glance, let alone food—this is the intention.

131. Asataṃ yodha pabrūtīti yo idha yathā nimittāni dissanti “asukadivase idañcidañca te bhavissatī”ti evaṃ asajjanānaṃ vacanaṃ pabrūti. “Asanta”ntipi pāṭho, abhūtanti attho. Pabrūtīti bhaṇati “amukasmiṃ nāma gāme mayhaṃ īdiso gharavibhavo, ehi tattha gacchāma, gharaṇī [P 1.0181] me bhavissasi, idañcidañca te dassāmī”ti parabhariyaṃ paradāsiṃ vā vañcento dhutto viya. Nijigīsānoti nijigīsamāno maggamāno, taṃ vañcetvā yaṃkiñci gahetvā palāyitukāmoti adhippāyo.

131. Asataṃ yodha pabrūtīti: one who here speaks the words of the unvirtuous, saying things like, 'On such and such a day, this and that will happen to you,' based on perceived signs. Another reading is 'asantaṃ,' meaning untrue. Pabrūti: he speaks, like a rogue deceiving another’s wife or female slave, saying, 'In such and such a village, I have such wealth; come, let us go there, you will be my wife, and I will give you this and that.' Nijigīsāno: desiring to conquer, searching; the intention is that, having deceived her and taken whatever he can, he desires to flee.

132. Yo cattānanti yo ca attānaṃ. Samukkaṃseti jātiādīhi samukkaṃsati uccaṭṭhāne ṭhapeti. Pare ca mavajānātīti tehiyeva pare avajānāti, nīcaṃ karoti. Ma-kāro padasandhikaro[V 1.0145]. Nihīnoti guṇavuḍḍhito parihīno, adhamabhāvaṃ vā gato. Sena mānenāti tena ukkaṃsanāvajānanasaṅkhātena attano mānena.

132. Yo cattānaṃ: and one who exalts himself. Samukkaṃseti: he exalts himself with reference to things like birth and places himself in a high position. Pare ca mavajānāti: he looks down on others with those very things, belittling them. The letter 'm' serves as a euphonic consonant. Nihīna: deficient in virtue, or fallen into a low state. Sena mānena: by his own pride, characterized as exaltation and contempt.

133. Rosakoti kāyavācāhi paresaṃ rosajanako. Kadariyoti thaddhamaccharī, yo pare paresaṃ dente aññaṃ vā puññaṃ karonte vāreti, tassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Pāpicchoti asantaguṇasambhāvanicchāya samannāgato. Maccharīti āvāsādimacchariyayutto. Saṭhoti asantaguṇappakāsanalakkhaṇena sāṭheyyena samannāgato, asammābhāsī vā akātukāmopi “karomī”tiādivacanena. Nāssa pāpajigucchanalakkhaṇā hirī, nāssa uttāsanato ubbegalakkhaṇaṃ ottappanti ahiriko anottappī.

133. Rosako: one who provokes anger in others through body and speech. Kadariyo: a stubborn miser who prevents others from giving to others or from making merit; this is a designation for such a person. Pāpiccho: one endowed with the desire to be esteemed for qualities one does not possess. Maccharī: one possessed of stinginess regarding dwellings and the like. Saṭho: one endowed with deceit, characterized by the display of nonexistent virtues, or one who speaks falsely, for example, saying, 'I will do it,' even when not wanting to. He lacks shame (hirī), which is characterized by disgust toward evil, and he lacks moral dread (ottappa), which is characterized by trepidation arising from fear; thus he is shameless and without moral dread.

134. Buddhanti sammāsambuddhaṃ. Paribhāsatīti “asabbaññū”tiādīhi apavadati, sāvakañca “duppaṭipanno”tiādīhi. Paribbājaṃ gahaṭṭhaṃ vāti sāvakavisesanamevetaṃ [M 1.0164] pabbajitaṃ vā tassa sāvakaṃ, gahaṭṭhaṃ vā paccayadāyakanti attho. Bāhirakaṃ vā paribbājakaṃ yaṃkiñci gahaṭṭhaṃ vā abhūtena dosena paribhāsatīti evampettha atthaṃ icchanti porāṇā.

134. Buddha: the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. Paribhāsati: he disparages Him with words like, 'He is not omniscient,' and so on, and His disciples with words like, 'They are of wrong practice,' and so on. Paribbājaṃ gahaṭṭhaṃ vā: this is a qualifier for His disciples, whether an ordained one or a lay supporter. Alternatively, the ancients hold the meaning here to be that he disparages an external wanderer or any householder with a false accusation.

135. Anarahaṃ santoti akhīṇāsavo samāno. Arahaṃ paṭijānātīti “ahaṃ arahā”ti paṭijānāti, yathā naṃ “arahā aya”nti jānanti, tathā vācaṃ nicchāreti, kāyena parakkamati, cittena icchati adhivāseti. Coroti theno. Sabrahmake loketi ukkaṭṭhavasena āha – sabbaloketi vuttaṃ hoti[P 1.0182]. Loke hi sandhicchedananillopaharaṇaekāgārikakaraṇaparipanthatiṭṭhanādīhi paresaṃ dhanaṃ vilumpantā corāti vuccanti. Sāsane pana parisasampattiādīhi paccayādīni vilumpantā. Yathāha –

135. Anarahaṃ santo: one who is not an arahant, being one whose taints are not destroyed. Arahaṃ paṭijānāti: he claims, 'I am an arahant,' or utters speech in such a way that others would know him as an arahant, or strives with the body, or desires and consents with the mind. Coro: a thief. Sabrahmake loke: 'in the world with its Brahmā' is said in an elevated sense—meaning 'in the entire world.' For in the world, those who steal others' wealth by house-breaking, plundering, robbing a single house, highway robbery, and so on, are called thieves. But in the Dispensation, there are those who plunder requisites by means of gaining a following and so on. As it is said:

“Pañcime, bhikkhave, mahācorā santo saṃvijjamānā lokasmiṃ. Katame pañca? Idha, bhikkhave, ekaccassa mahācorassa evaṃ hoti ‘kudāssu nāmāhaṃ satena vā sahassena vā parivuto gāmanigamarājadhānīsu āhiṇḍissāmi hananto, ghātento, chindanto, chedāpento, pacanto pācentoti, so aparena samayena satena vā sahassena vā parivuto gāmanigamarājadhānīsu āhiṇḍati hananto…pe… pācento. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, idhekaccassa pāpabhikkhuno evaṃ hoti ‘kudāssu nāmāhaṃ satena vā…pe… rājadhānīsu cārikaṃ carissāmi sakkato, garukato, mānito, pūjito, apacito, gahaṭṭhānañceva pabbajitānañca lābhī cīvara…pe… parikkhārāna’nti. So aparena [V 1.0146] samayena satena vā sahassena vā parivuto gāmanigamarājadhānīsu cārikaṃ carati sakkato…pe… parikkhārānaṃ. Ayaṃ, bhikkhave, paṭhamo mahācoro santo saṃvijjamāno lokasmiṃ.

“Monks, there are these five great thieves existing in the world. Which five? Here, monks, a certain great thief thinks: ‘Oh, when will I wander through villages, towns, and royal cities, surrounded by a hundred or a thousand men, killing, causing to kill, cutting, causing to cut, tormenting, and causing to torment?’ Then, after some time, he wanders through villages, towns, and royal cities, surrounded by a hundred or a thousand men, killing… causing to torment. In the same way, monks, a certain wicked monk thinks: ‘Oh, when will I wander through villages… royal cities, honored, respected, revered, worshipped, and venerated by both householders and monastics, receiving robes… and other requisites?’ Then, after some time, he wanders through villages… royal cities, honored… receiving requisites. This, monks, is the first great thief existing in the world.

“Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, idhekacco pāpabhikkhu tathāgatappaveditaṃ dhammavinayaṃ pariyāpuṇitvā attano dahati, ayaṃ, bhikkhave, dutiyo…pe… lokasmiṃ.

“Furthermore, monks, here a certain wicked monk, having learned the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, claims it as his own. This, monks, is the second great thief existing in the world.

“Puna [M 1.0165] caparaṃ, bhikkhave, idhekacco pāpabhikkhu suddhaṃ brahmacāriṃ parisuddhaṃ brahmacariyaṃ carantaṃ amūlakena abrahmacariyena anuddhaṃseti. Ayaṃ, bhikkhave, tatiyo…pe… lokasmiṃ.

“Furthermore, monks, here a certain wicked monk groundlessly accuses a pure spiritual practitioner, who is living a perfectly pure spiritual life, of unchastity. This, monks, is the third great thief existing in the world.

“Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, idhekacco, pāpabhikkhu yāni tāni saṅghassa garubhaṇḍāni garuparikkhārāni, seyyathidaṃ – ārāmo, ārāmavatthu, vihāro, vihāravatthu, mañco, pīṭhaṃ, bhisi, bimbohanaṃ, lohakumbhī, lohabhāṇakaṃ, lohavārako, lohakaṭāhaṃ, vāsi, pharasu, kuṭhārī, kudālo, nikhādanaṃ, valli, veḷu, muñjaṃ, pabbajaṃ, tiṇaṃ, mattikā, dārubhaṇḍaṃ, mattikābhaṇḍaṃ, tehi gihiṃ saṅgaṇhāti upalāpeti. Ayaṃ, bhikkhave, catuttho…pe… lokasmiṃ.

“Furthermore, monks, here a certain wicked monk takes the Sangha’s heavy goods and heavy requisites—such as a monastery, monastery grounds, a dwelling, dwelling grounds, a bed, a chair, a mattress, a cushion, a metal pot, a metal bowl, a metal basin, a metal cauldron, an adze, an axe, a hatchet, a spade, a digging tool, vines, bamboo, muñja grass, pabbaja grass, common grass, clay, wooden articles, and clay articles—and with these he wins over and flatters laypeople. This, monks, is the fourth great thief existing in the world.

“Sadevake, bhikkhave, loke…pe… sadevamanussāya ayaṃ aggo mahācoro, yo asantaṃ abhūtaṃ uttarimanussadhammaṃ ullapatī”ti (pārā. 195).

“Monks, in the world with its devas… with its devas and humans, this is the foremost great thief: one who lays claim to a superior human state that is nonexistent and untrue.”

Tattha lokiyacorā lokiyameva dhanadhaññādiṃ thenenti. Sāsane vuttacoresu paṭhamo tathārūpameva cīvarādipaccayamattaṃ, dutiyo pariyattidhammaṃ, tatiyo parassa brahmacariyaṃ, catuttho saṅghikagarubhaṇḍaṃ, pañcamo jhānasamādhisamāpattimaggaphalappabhedaṃ lokiyalokuttaraguṇadhanaṃ, lokiyañca cīvarādipaccayajātaṃ. Yathāha – “theyyāya vo, bhikkhave, raṭṭhapiṇḍo bhutto”ti. Tattha yvāyaṃ pañcamo mahācoro, taṃ sandhāyāha bhagavā “coro sabrahmake loke”ti. So hi “sadevake, bhikkhave, loke…pe… sadevamanussāya ayaṃ aggo mahācoro, yo asantaṃ abhūtaṃ uttarimanussadhammaṃ ullapatī”ti (pārā. 195) evaṃ lokiyalokuttaradhanathenanato aggo mahācoroti vutto, tasmā taṃ idhāpi “sabrahmake loke”ti iminā ukkaṭṭhaparicchedena pakāsesi.

Therein, worldly thieves steal only worldly wealth, such as money and grain. Among the thieves described in the Dispensation, the first steals mere requisites like robes; the second, the Dhamma of learning; the third, another’s holy life; the fourth, the Saṅgha’s heavy goods; and the fifth steals the wealth of mundane and supramundane qualities—distinguished as jhāna, concentration, attainments, paths, and fruits—as well as mundane requisites like robes.
