As it is said: “Monks, the country's almsfood is eaten by you through theft.” Therein, referring to this fifth great thief, the Blessed One said, “a thief in the world with its Brahmās.” For he is called the foremost great thief because of stealing the wealth of mundane and supramundane qualities, as stated: “In the world with its devas, monks… among devas and humans, this is the foremost great thief: one who lays claim to a superhuman state that is non-existent and untrue.” Therefore, here too, He indicated him by this supreme designation: “in the world with its Brahmās.”

Eso kho vasalādhamoti. Ettha khoti avadhāraṇattho, tena eso eva vasalādhamo. Vasalānaṃ [V 1.0147] hīno sabbapacchimakoti avadhāreti. Kasmā? Visiṭṭhavatthumhi theyyadhammavassanato, yāva taṃ paṭiññaṃ na vissajjeti, tāva avigatavasalakaraṇadhammato cāti.

This, indeed, is the lowest of outcasts. Herein, `kho` is for emphasis; thus, “this very one is the lowest outcast.” It defines him as the lowest, the very last, of outcasts. Why? Because of his thievish nature with respect to a distinguished object, and because, as long as he does not abandon that claim, the quality that makes one an outcast has not departed.

Ete [M 1.0166] kho vasalāti. Idāni ye te paṭhamagāthāya āsayavipattivasena [P 1.0183] kodhanādayo pañca, pāpamakkhiṃ vā dvidhā katvā cha, dutiyagāthāya payogavipattivasena pāṇahiṃsako eko, tatiyāya payogavipattivaseneva gāmanigamaniggāhako eko, catutthāya theyyāvahāravasena eko, pañcamāya iṇavañcanavasena eko, chaṭṭhāya pasayhāvahāravasena panthadūsako eko, sattamāya kūṭasakkhivasena eko, aṭṭhamāya mittadubbhivasena eko, navamāya akataññuvasena eko, dasamāya katanāsanavihesanavasena eko, ekādasamāya hadayavañcanavasena eko, dvādasamāya paṭicchannakammantavasena dve, terasamāya akataññuvasena eko, cuddasamāya vañcanavasena eko, pannarasamāya vihesanavasena eko, soḷasamāya vañcanavasena eko, sattarasamāya attukkaṃsanaparavambhanavasena dve, aṭṭhārasamāya payogāsayavipattivasena rosakādayo satta, ekūnavīsatimāya paribhāsanavasena dve, vīsatimāya aggamahācoravasena ekoti evaṃ tettiṃsa catuttiṃsa vā vasalā vuttā. Te niddisanto āha “ete kho vasalā vuttā, mayā ye te pakāsitā”ti. Tassattho – ye te mayā pubbe “jānāsi pana tvaṃ, brāhmaṇa, vasala”nti evaṃ saṅkhepato vasalā vuttā, te vitthārato ete kho pakāsitāti. Atha vā ye te mayā puggalavasena vuttā, te dhammavasenāpi ete kho pakāsitā. Atha vā ete kho vasalā vuttā ariyehi kammavasena, na jātivasena, mayā ye te pakāsitā “kodhano upanāhī”tiādinā nayena.

These, indeed, are outcasts. Now, those who were mentioned: in the first verse, five due to failure of intention, such as the angry and others—or the one with malice, divided into two, making six; in the second verse, one due to failure of action, the killer of living beings; in the third verse, again due to failure of action, the oppressor of villages and towns; in the fourth verse, one due to theft; in the fifth verse, one due to deceit in debt; in the sixth verse, one due to highway robbery; in the seventh verse, one due to false testimony; in the eighth verse, one due to betraying friends; in the ninth verse, one due to ingratitude; in the tenth verse, one due to destroying a good deed done and causing vexation; in the eleventh verse, one due to deceitfulness; in the twelfth verse, two due to hidden deeds; in the thirteenth verse, one due to ingratitude; in the fourteenth verse, one due to deceit; in the fifteenth verse, one due to harassment; in the sixteenth verse, one due to deceit; in the seventeenth verse, two due to self-praise and disparaging others; in the eighteenth verse, seven due to failure of action and intention, the quarrelsome and others; in the nineteenth verse, two due to abuse; in the twentieth verse, one as the foremost great thief—thus, thirty-three or thirty-four outcasts have been described. Pointing them out, He said: “These, indeed, are the outcasts declared, those whom I have revealed.” The meaning is this: those whom I previously mentioned in brief, saying, “Do you know, Brahmin, an outcast?”—these very ones I have now revealed in detail. Alternatively, those whom I described in terms of individuals are also revealed here in terms of principles. Or again, these are the outcasts declared by the noble ones based on action, not by birth—those whom I have revealed by the method beginning with “the angry, the resentful.”

136. Evaṃ bhagavā vasalaṃ dassetvā idāni yasmā brāhmaṇo sakāya diṭṭhiyā atīva abhiniviṭṭho hoti, tasmā taṃ diṭṭhiṃ paṭisedhento āha “na jaccā vasalo hotī”ti. Tassattho – paramatthato hi na jaccā vasalo hoti, na jaccā hoti brāhmaṇo, apica kho kammunā vasalo hoti, kammunā hoti brāhmaṇo, aparisuddhakammavassanato vasalo hoti, parisuddhena kammunā aparisuddhavāhanato brāhmaṇo hoti. Yasmā vā tumhe hīnaṃ vasalaṃ ukkaṭṭhaṃ [M 1.0167] brāhmaṇaṃ [P 1.0184] maññittha, tasmā hīnena kammunā vasalo hoti, ukkaṭṭhena kammunā brāhmaṇo hotīti evampi atthaṃ ñāpento evamāha.

136. Having thus shown the outcast, and because the brahmin was now extremely attached to his own view, the Blessed One, refuting that view, said: “Not by birth is one an outcast.” The meaning of this is: in the ultimate sense, one is not an outcast by birth, nor is one a brahmin by birth. Rather, one is an outcast by action, and one is a brahmin by action. One is an outcast (vasala) because of being overcome by impure action; one is a brahmin because of having carried away the impure by means of pure action. Or, since you consider the lowly to be an outcast and the superior to be a brahmin, therefore one is an outcast by lowly action and a brahmin by superior action—thus, making the meaning known, He spoke in this way.

137-139. Idāni tamevatthaṃ nidassanena sādhetuṃ “tadamināpi jānāthā”tiādikā tisso gāthāyo āha. Tāsu dve catuppādā, ekā chappādā, tāsaṃ attho – yaṃ mayā vuttaṃ “na jaccā vasalo hotī”tiādi, tadamināpi jānātha, yathā medaṃ nidassanaṃ, taṃ imināpi pakārena [V 1.0148] jānātha, yena me pakārena yena sāmaññena idaṃ nidassananti vuttaṃ hoti. Katamaṃ nidassananti ce? Caṇḍālaputto sopāko…pe… brahmalokūpapattiyāti.

Now, to establish that very meaning with an example, He spoke three verses beginning, “Know that also by this.” Among them, two have four lines and one has six. Their meaning is: That which was spoken by me, beginning with “Not by birth is one an outcast,” know that also by this example. As this example of mine is, know it by this manner, by which method and by which general principle of mine this is said to be an example. If it is asked, “What is the example?”: “The caṇḍāla’s son, Sopāka… up to attainment of the Brahma-world.”

Caṇḍālassa putto caṇḍālaputto. Attano khādanatthāya mate sunakhe labhitvā pacatīti sopāko. Mātaṅgoti evaṃnāmo vissutoti evaṃ hīnāya jātiyā ca jīvikāya ca nāmena ca pākaṭo.

The son of a caṇḍāla is a caṇḍāla's son. He is called Sopāka because, having obtained dead dogs for his own consumption, he cooks them. Mātaṅga was his name. He was renowned, that is, he was well-known for his low birth, livelihood, and name.

Soti purimapadena sambandhitvā so mātaṅgo yasaṃ paramaṃ patto, abbhutaṃ uttamaṃ ativisiṭṭhaṃ yasaṃ kittiṃ pasaṃsaṃ patto. Yaṃ sudullabhanti yaṃ uḷārakulūpapannenāpi dullabhaṃ, hīnakulūpapannena sudullabhaṃ. Evaṃ yasappattassa ca āgacchuṃ tassupaṭṭhānaṃ, khattiyā brāhmaṇā bahū, tassa mātaṅgassa pāricariyatthaṃ khattiyā ca brāhmaṇā ca aññe ca bahū vessasuddādayo jambudīpamanussā yebhuyyena upaṭṭhānaṃ āgamiṃsūti attho.

Connecting the word `so` with the preceding word: that Mātaṅga attained supreme glory; he attained wonderful, excellent, and most distinguished glory, fame, and praise. ‘That which is very hard to obtain’ means: that which is hard to obtain even for one born into a high family is exceedingly hard to obtain for one born into a low family. And many khattiyas and brahmins came to attend upon him who had thus attained glory. The meaning is that for the service of that Mātaṅga, many khattiyas, brahmins, and others—vessas, suddas, and the people of Jambudīpa—for the most part, came into his attendance.

Evaṃ upaṭṭhānasampanno so mātaṅgo vigatakilesarajattā virajaṃ, mahantehi buddhādīhi paṭipannattā mahāpathaṃ, brahmalokasaṅkhātaṃ devalokaṃ yāpetuṃ samatthattā devalokayānasaññitaṃ aṭṭhasamāpattiyānaṃ abhiruyha, tāya paṭipattiyā kāmarāgaṃ virājetvā, kāyassa bhedā brahmalokūpago ahu, sā tathā hīnāpi na naṃ jāti nivāresi brahmalokūpapattiyā, brahmalokūpapattitoti vuttaṃ hoti.

Thus endowed with attendance, that Mātaṅga, having mounted the vehicle of the eight attainments—which is dustless, as he was free from the dust of the defilements; which is the great path, as it is trodden by the great ones such as the Buddhas; and which is known as the vehicle to the Brahma-world, as it is capable of conveying one to the celestial world called the Brahma-world—and by that practice having become dispassionate towards sensual desire, upon the breaking up of the body, he became one who goes to the Brahma-world. Thus, even though his birth was so low, it did not prevent him from attaining rebirth in the Brahma-world. This is what is meant by 'rebirth in the Brahma-world'.

Ayaṃ panattho evaṃ veditabbo – atīte kira mahāpuriso tena tenupāyena sattahitaṃ karonto sopākajīvike caṇḍālakule uppajji. So nāmena mātaṅgo[P 1.0185], rūpena duddasiko hutvā bahinagare cammakuṭikāya vasati, antonagare bhikkhaṃ caritvā jīvikaṃ kappeti. Athekadivasaṃ [M 1.0168] tasmiṃ nagare surānakkhatte ghosite dhuttā yathāsakena parivārena kīḷanti. Aññatarāpi brāhmaṇamahāsāladhītā pannarasasoḷasavassuddesikā devakaññā viya rūpena dassanīyā pāsādikā “attano kulavaṃsānurūpaṃ kīḷissāmī”ti pahūtaṃ khajjabhojjādikīḷanasambhāraṃ sakaṭesu āropetvā sabbasetavaḷavayuttaṃ yānamāruyha mahāparivārena uyyānabhūmiṃ gacchati diṭṭhamaṅgalikāti nāmena. Sā kira “dussaṇṭhitaṃ rūpaṃ avamaṅgala”nti daṭṭhuṃ na icchati, tenassā diṭṭhamaṅgalikātveva saṅkhā udapādi.

This meaning, however, should be understood thus: In the past, it is said, the Great Being, while working for the welfare of beings by this and that means, was born in a caṇḍāla family that lived by being dog-cookers. His name was Mātaṅga, and being unsightly in appearance, he lived in a hut made of hides outside the city. He sustained his life by going for alms within the city. Then one day, when a drinking festival was announced in that city, profligates were amusing themselves with their respective retinues. A certain daughter of a very wealthy brahmin, about fifteen or sixteen years of age, as lovely and pleasing to see as a celestial maiden, thinking, 'I will amuse myself in a manner befitting my family lineage,' loaded many requisites for amusement, such as various foods, onto carts, mounted a vehicle yoked with all-white bullocks, and went to the pleasure garden with a large retinue. Her name was Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā. It is said that she did not wish to see any ill-formed shape, considering it to be inauspicious; for that reason, the designation 'Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā' arose for her.

Tadā so mātaṅgo kālasseva vuṭṭhāya paṭapilotikaṃ nivāsetvā, kaṃsatāḷaṃ hatthe bandhitvā, bhājanahattho [V 1.0149] nagaraṃ pavisati, manusse disvā dūrato eva kaṃsatāḷaṃ ākoṭento. Atha diṭṭhamaṅgalikā “ussaratha, ussarathā”ti purato purato hīnajanaṃ apanentehi purisehi nīyamānā nagaradvāramajjhe mātaṅgaṃ disvā “ko eso”ti āha. Ahaṃ mātaṅgacaṇḍāloti. Sā “īdisaṃ disvā gatānaṃ kuto vuḍḍhī”ti yānaṃ nivattāpesi. Manussā “yaṃ mayaṃ uyyānaṃ gantvā khajjabhojjādiṃ labheyyāma, tassa no mātaṅgena antarāyo kato”ti kupitā “gaṇhatha caṇḍāla”nti leḍḍūhi paharitvā “mato”ti pāde gahetvā ekamante chaḍḍetvā kacavarena paṭicchādetvā agamaṃsu. So satiṃ paṭilabhitvā uṭṭhāya manusse pucchi – “kiṃ, ayyā, dvāraṃ nāma sabbasādhāraṇaṃ, udāhu brāhmaṇānaṃyeva kata”nti? Manussā āhaṃsu – “sabbesaṃ sādhāraṇa”nti. “Evaṃ sabbasādhāraṇadvārena pavisitvā bhikkhāhārena yāpentaṃ maṃ diṭṭhamaṅgalikāya manussā imaṃ anayabyasanaṃ pāpesu”nti rathikāya rathikaṃ āhiṇḍanto manussānaṃ ārocetvā brāhmaṇassa gharadvāre nipajji – “diṭṭhamaṅgalikaṃ aladdhā na vuṭṭhahissāmī”ti.

At that time, Mātaṅga rose early, put on a patched garment, tied a bronze clapper to his hand, and, holding a bowl, entered the city, striking the bronze clapper from afar upon seeing people. Then Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, being led by men who were clearing the low-born people from her path ahead, crying, 'Make way, make way!', saw Mātaṅga in the middle of the city gate and asked, 'Who is that?' When it was said, 'That is Mātaṅga the caṇḍāla,' she had her vehicle turned back, saying, 'Whence is there prosperity for those who have gone on after seeing such a one?' The people became angry, thinking, 'The food and drink we would have received by going to the pleasure garden—Mātaṅga has created an obstacle to that for us!' Shouting, 'Seize the caṇḍāla!', they struck him with clods of earth. Thinking he was dead, they seized him by the feet, cast him aside in a certain place, covered him with rubbish, and departed. He, having regained consciousness, got up and asked the people: 'Sirs, is the gate common to all, or was it made only for brahmins?' The people said: 'It is common to all.' He then said, 'Though I entered by this gate common to all and was sustaining myself on alms-food, the people of Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā have brought me to this ruin and disaster!' Wandering from street to street and announcing this to the people, he lay down at the brahmin’s door, declaring: 'I will not get up until I get Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā!'

Brāhmaṇo “gharadvāre mātaṅgo nipanno”ti sutvā “tassa kākaṇikaṃ detha, telena aṅgaṃ makkhetvā gacchatū”ti āha. So taṃ na icchati, “diṭṭhamaṅgalikaṃ [P 1.0186] aladdhā na vuṭṭhahissāmi”cceva āha. Tato brāhmaṇo “dve kākaṇikāyo detha, kākaṇikāya pūvaṃ khādatu, kākaṇikāya [M 1.0169] telena aṅgaṃ makkhetvā gacchatū”ti āha. So taṃ na icchati, tatheva vadati. Brāhmaṇo sutvā “māsakaṃ detha, pādaṃ, upaḍḍhakahāpaṇaṃ, kahāpaṇaṃ dve tīṇī”ti yāva sataṃ āṇāpesi. So na icchati, tatheva vadati. Evaṃ yācantānaṃyeva sūriyo atthaṅgato. Atha brāhmaṇī pāsādā oruyha sāṇipākāraṃ parikkhipāpetvā taṃ upasaṅkamitvā yāci – “tāta mātaṅga, diṭṭhamaṅgalikāya aparādhaṃ khama, sahassaṃ gaṇhāhi, dve tīṇī”ti yāva “satasahassaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti āha. So tuṇhībhūto nipajjiyeva.

The brahmin, hearing, 'Mātaṅga is lying at the house door,' said: 'Give him a kākaṇika, anoint his limbs with oil, and let him go.' But he did not want it, saying only: 'I will not get up until I get Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā.' Then the brahmin said: 'Give him two kākaṇikas; let him eat a cake for one kākaṇika and anoint his limbs with oil for the other, and let him go.' He did not want it and said the same thing. The brahmin, hearing this, gave orders: 'Give him a māsaka, a pāda, half a kahāpaṇa, one kahāpaṇa, two, three,' and so on up to a hundred. He did not want it and said the same thing. While they were thus pleading, the sun set. Then the brahmin's wife, descending from the upper story of the house, had an enclosure of coarse cloth set up around him, approached him, and pleaded: 'Dear Mātaṅga, forgive Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā's offense. Take a thousand,' and so on up to 'Take a hundred thousand.' But he, having become silent, just remained lying there.

Evaṃ catūhapañcāhe vītivatte bahumpi paṇṇākāraṃ datvā diṭṭhamaṅgalikaṃ alabhantā khattiyakumārādayo mātaṅgassa upakaṇṇake ārocāpesuṃ – “purisā nāma anekānipi saṃvaccharāni vīriyaṃ katvā icchitatthaṃ pāpuṇanti, mā kho tvaṃ nibbijji, addhā dvīhatīhaccayena diṭṭhamaṅgalikaṃ lacchasī”ti. So tuṇhībhūto nipajjiyeva. Atha sattame divase samantā paṭivissakā uṭṭhahitvā “tumhe mātaṅgaṃ vā uṭṭhāpetha, dārikaṃ vā detha, mā amhe sabbe nāsayitthā”ti āhaṃsu. Tesaṃ kira ayaṃ diṭṭhi “yassa gharadvāre evaṃ nipanno caṇḍālo marati, tassa gharena saha samantā sattasattagharavāsino caṇḍālā hontī”ti. Tato diṭṭhamaṅgalikaṃ nīlapaṭapilotikaṃ nivāsāpetvā uḷuṅkakaḷopikādīni datvā paridevamānaṃ tassa santikaṃ [V 1.0150] netvā “gaṇha dārikaṃ, uṭṭhāya gacchāhī”ti adaṃsu. Sā passe ṭhatvā “uṭṭhāhī”ti āha, so “hatthena maṃ gahetvā uṭṭhāpehī”ti āha. Sā naṃ uṭṭhāpesi. So nisīditvā āha – “mayaṃ antonagare vasituṃ na labhāma, ehi maṃ bahinagare cammakuṭiṃ nehī”ti. Sā naṃ hatthe gahetvā tattha nesi. “Piṭṭhiyaṃ āropetvā”ti jātakabhāṇakā. Netvā [P 1.0187] cassa sarīraṃ telena makkhetvā, uṇhodakena nhāpetvā, yāguṃ pacitvā adāsi. So “brāhmaṇakaññā ayaṃ mā vinassī”ti jātisambhedaṃ akatvāva aḍḍhamāsamattaṃ balaṃ gahetvā “ahaṃ vanaṃ gacchāmi, ‘aticirāyatī’ti mā tvaṃ ukkaṇṭhī”ti vatvā gharamānusakāni ca “imaṃ mā pamajjitthā”ti āṇāpetvā gharā nikkhamma tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā, kasiṇaparikammaṃ katvā, katipāheneva aṭṭha samāpattiyo pañca ca abhiññāyo nibbattetvā “idānāhaṃ diṭṭhamaṅgalikāya [M 1.0170] manāpo bhavissāmī”ti ākāsenāgantvā nagaradvāre orohitvā diṭṭhamaṅgalikāya santikaṃ pesesi.

Thus, after four or five days had passed, though they gave many kinds of gifts, the young noblemen and others, unable to obtain Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, informed Mātaṅga at his ear: 'Men, indeed, striving for many years, attain their desired goal. Do not be disheartened; surely in two or three days you will obtain Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā.' He remained silent and just lay there. Then, on the seventh day, the neighbors all around rose up and said: 'Either make Mātaṅga rise or give the girl, lest you destroy us all.' Their belief was this: 'If such an outcaste dies lying at the doorway of someone’s house, then the inhabitants of that house, along with all the seven neighboring households all around, will become outcastes.' Then, dressing Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā in a blue cloth garment and giving her a pot, a ladle, and other things, they brought her, lamenting, to his presence and said: 'Take the girl, rise up and go.' She stood by and said: 'Get up.' He replied: 'Take me by the hand and make me rise.' She lifted him up. Sitting down, he said: 'We cannot live inside the city; come, lead me to a leather hut outside the city.' Taking him by the hand, she led him there. The narrators of the Jātaka say: 'Having placed him on her back.' Having led him there, she massaged his body with oil, bathed him with warm water, cooked gruel, and gave it to him. Thinking: 'This brahmin girl must not be ruined,' without transgressing caste, he regained strength in about half a month. Then he said: 'I will go to the forest; do not grieve thinking, "He is taking too long."' Giving orders to the neighbors: 'Do not neglect her,' he left the house. Taking up the ascetic life, he practiced kasiṇa meditation and in just a few days attained the eight meditative attainments and the five higher knowledges. Thinking: 'Now I shall be pleasing to Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā,' he came through the air, descended at the city gate, and sent word to Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā.

Sā sutvā “koci maññe mama ñātako pabbajito maṃ dukkhitaṃ ñatvā daṭṭhuṃ āgato bhavissatī”ti cintayamānā gantvā, taṃ ñatvā, pādesu nipatitvā “kissa maṃ anāthaṃ tumhe akatthā”ti āha. Mahāpuriso “mā tvaṃ diṭṭhamaṅgalike dukkhinī ahosi, sakalajambudīpavāsīhi te sakkāraṃ kāressāmī”ti vatvā etadavoca – “gaccha tvaṃ ghosanaṃ karohi – ‘mahābrahmā mama sāmiko na mātaṅgo, so candavimānaṃ bhinditvā sattame divase mama santikaṃ āgamissatī’”ti. Sā āha – “ahaṃ, bhante, brāhmaṇamahāsāladhītā hutvā attano pāpakammena imaṃ caṇḍālabhāvaṃ pattā, na sakkomi evaṃ vattu”nti. Mahāpuriso “na tvaṃ mātaṅgassa ānubhāvaṃ jānāsī”ti vatvā yathā sā saddahati, tathā anekāni pāṭihāriyāni dassetvā tatheva taṃ āṇāpetvā attano vasatiṃ agamāsi. Sā tathā akāsi.

Hearing this, she thought: 'Perhaps some relative of mine has gone forth and, knowing I am suffering, has come to see me.' Reflecting thus, she went, recognized him, fell at his feet, and said: 'Why have you made me helpless?' The Great Being replied: 'Do not grieve, Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā. I will ensure that all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa honor you.' Then he instructed her: 'Go and proclaim: "My husband is not Mātaṅga, but the Great Brahmā. He will shatter the lunar mansion and come to me on the seventh day."' She said: 'Venerable sir, though I was born as the daughter of a wealthy brahmin, my own evil deeds have led me to this outcaste state. I cannot speak thus.' The Great Being said: 'You do not know the power of Mātaṅga.' Having inspired her faith by displaying many miracles, he commanded her to do as he said and returned to his dwelling. She did as instructed.

Manussā ujjhāyanti hasanti – “kathañhi nāmāyaṃ attano pāpakammena caṇḍālabhāvaṃ patvā puna taṃ mahābrahmānaṃ karissatī”ti. Sā adhimānā eva hutvā divase divase ghosantī nagaraṃ āhiṇḍati “ito chaṭṭhe divase, pañcame, catutthe, tatiye, suve, ajja āgamissatī”ti. Manussā [P 1.0188] tassā vissatthavācaṃ sutvā “kadāci evampi siyā”ti attano attano gharadvāresu maṇḍapaṃ kārāpetvā, sāṇipākāraṃ sajjetvā, vayappattā dārikāyo alaṅkaritvā “mahābrahmani āgate kaññādānaṃ dassāmā”ti ākāsaṃ ullokentā nisīdiṃsu. Atha mahāpuriso puṇṇamadivase gaganatalaṃ upārūḷhe cande candavimānaṃ phāletvā passato mahājanassa mahābrahmarūpena niggacchi. Mahājano “dve candā jātā”ti atimaññi. Tato anukkamena āgataṃ disvā “saccaṃ diṭṭhamaṅgalikā āha, mahābrahmāva ayaṃ diṭṭhamaṅgalikaṃ dametuṃ [V 1.0151] pubbe mātaṅgavesenāgacchī”ti niṭṭhaṃ agamāsi. Evaṃ so mahājanena dissamāno diṭṭhamaṅgalikāya vasanaṭṭhāne eva otari. Sā ca tadā utunī ahosi. So tassā nābhiṃ aṅguṭṭhakena parāmasi. Tena phassena gabbho patiṭṭhāsi. Tato naṃ “gabbho te saṇṭhito[M 1.0171], puttamhi jāte taṃ nissāya jīvāhī”ti vatvā passato mahājanassa puna candavimānaṃ pāvisi.

People grumbled and laughed, saying: 'How could this woman, having fallen to the state of an outcaste due to her own evil deeds, now make him the Great Brahmā?' Filled with great pride, she wandered through the city day after day, proclaiming: 'Six days from now, five, four, three, tomorrow, today, he will come!' Hearing her confident words, the people thought: 'Perhaps it might be so,' and they built pavilions at their own doorways, prepared enclosures of cloth, adorned marriageable girls, and sat gazing at the sky, saying: 'When the Great Brahmā comes, we will offer him these maidens.' Then, on the full moon day, when the moon had ascended to the sky, the Great Being, shattering the moon's orb, appeared before the great multitude in the form of the Great Brahmā. The great multitude, astonished, thought: 'Two moons have appeared!' Then, seeing him gradually approach, they concluded: 'Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā spoke the truth. This is indeed the Great Brahmā, who previously came disguised as Mātaṅga to subdue Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā.' Thus, visible to the great multitude, he descended right where Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā lived. At that time, she was in her fertile period. He touched her navel with his thumb, and by that touch, conception took place. Then he said to her: 'Your pregnancy is established. When the son is born, live dependent on him.' Having spoken, he re-entered the moon's orb in full view of the great multitude.

Brāhmaṇā “diṭṭhamaṅgalikā mahābrahmuno pajāpati amhākaṃ mātā jātā”ti vatvā tato tato āgacchanti. Taṃ sakkāraṃ kātukāmānaṃ manussānaṃ sampīḷanena nagaradvārāni anokāsāni ahesuṃ. Te diṭṭhamaṅgalikaṃ hiraññarāsimhi ṭhapetvā, nhāpetvā, maṇḍetvā, rathaṃ āropetvā, mahāsakkārena nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ kārāpetvā, nagaramajjhe maṇḍapaṃ kārāpetvā, tatra naṃ “mahābrahmuno pajāpatī”ti diṭṭhaṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā vasāpenti “yāvassā patirūpaṃ vasanokāsaṃ karoma, tāva idheva vasatū”ti. Sā maṇḍape eva puttaṃ vijāyi. Taṃ visuddhadivase saddhiṃ puttena sasīsaṃ nhāpetvā maṇḍape jātoti dārakassa “maṇḍabyakumāro”ti nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Tato pabhuti ca naṃ brāhmaṇā “mahābrahmuno putto”ti parivāretvā caranti. Tato anekasatasahassappakārā paṇṇākārā āgacchanti, te brāhmaṇā kumārassārakkhaṃ [P 1.0189] ṭhapesuṃ, āgatā lahuṃ kumāraṃ daṭṭhuṃ na labhanti.

The brahmins, saying, "Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, the consort of Mahābrahmā, has been born as our mother," came from various places. The city gates became impassable due to the crowding of people who wished to pay her homage. They placed Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā on a pile of gold, bathed her, adorned her, placed her on a chariot, and with great honor had her circumambulate the city. In the city center, they built a pavilion and installed her there, declaring, "She is the consort of Mahābrahmā," and settled her in that prominent place, saying, "Let her dwell here until we prepare a suitable dwelling for her." There in the pavilion, she gave birth to a son. On the day of her purification, they bathed her together with the son, head and all, and since he was born in the pavilion, they named the boy "Maṇḍabyakumāra." From then on, the brahmins surrounded him, proclaiming, "He is the son of Mahābrahmā." Then, gifts of many hundreds of thousands of kinds arrived, and the brahmins appointed guards for the prince, so that those who arrived could not easily see the boy.

Kumāro anupubbena vuḍḍhimanvāya dānaṃ dātuṃ āraddho. So sālāya sampattānaṃ kapaṇaddhikānaṃ adatvā brāhmaṇānaṃyeva deti. Mahāpuriso “kiṃ mama putto dānaṃ detī”ti āvajjetvā brāhmaṇānaṃyeva dānaṃ dentaṃ disvā “yathā sabbesaṃ dassati, tathā karissāmī”ti cīvaraṃ pārupitvā pattaṃ gahetvā ākāsena āgamma puttassa gharadvāre aṭṭhāsi. Kumāro taṃ disvā “kuto ayaṃ evaṃ virūpaveso vasalo āgato”ti kuddho imaṃ gāthamāha –

The prince, gradually growing up, began to give alms. However, he gave only to brahmins, not to the poor and needy who had arrived at the hall. The Great Being, reflecting, "What alms does my son give?" and seeing him giving only to brahmins, thought, "I will arrange it so that he will give to all." So he donned a robe, took a bowl, and came through the air to stand at his son's door. When the prince saw him, he became angry, thinking, "From where has this outcast of unsightly appearance come?" and spoke this verse:

“Kuto nu āgacchasi dummavāsī, otallako paṃsupisācakova;

Saṅkāracoḷaṃ paṭimuñca kaṇṭhe, ko re tuvaṃ hosi adakkhiṇeyyo”ti.

"From where do you come, ill-clad one, impudent, like a dust-demon? Hang that rag from the rubbish heap around your neck! Who are you, unworthy of offerings?"

Brāhmaṇā “gaṇhatha gaṇhathā”ti taṃ gahetvā ākoṭetvā anayabyasanaṃ pāpesuṃ. So ākāsena gantvā bahinagare paccaṭṭhāsi[M 1.0172]. Devatā kupitā kumāraṃ gale gahetvā uddhaṃpādaṃ adhosiraṃ ṭhapesuṃ. So akkhīhi niggatehi mukhena kheḷaṃ paggharantena gharugharupassāsī dukkhaṃ vedayati. Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā sutvā “koci āgato atthī”ti pucchi. “Āma, pabbajito āgacchī”ti. “Kuhiṃ gato”ti? “Evaṃ gato”ti. Sā tattha gantvā “khamatha, bhante, attano [V 1.0152] dāsassā”ti yācantī tassa pādamūle bhūmiyā nipajji. Tena ca samayena mahāpuriso piṇḍāya caritvā, yāguṃ labhitvā, taṃ pivanto tattha nisinno hoti, so avasiṭṭhaṃ thokaṃ yāguṃ diṭṭhamaṅgalikāya adāsi. “Gaccha imaṃ yāguṃ udakakumbhiyā āloletvā yesaṃ bhūtavikāro atthi, tesaṃ akkhimukhakaṇṇanāsābilesu āsiñca, sarīrañca paripphosehi, evaṃ nibbikārā bhavissantī”ti. Sā tathā akāsi. Tato [P 1.0190] kumāre pakatisarīre jāte “ehi, tāta maṇḍabya, taṃ khamāpessāmā”ti puttañca sabbe brāhmaṇe ca tassa pādamūle nikkujjitvā nipajjāpetvā khamāpesi.

The brahmins, crying, "Seize him, seize him!" seized him, beat him, and brought him to ruin and disaster. He went through the air and stood outside the city. The angry deities grabbed the boy by the neck and hung him upside down with his head downwards. With his eyes bulging out, saliva dripping from his mouth, and breathing with a gurgling sound, he experienced great suffering. Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā heard this and asked, "Has someone arrived?" "Yes, a renunciate has come." "Where has he gone?" "He has gone that way." She went there and, begging, said, "Venerable sir, forgive this slave of yours," and she lay down on the ground at his feet. At that time, the Great Being had gone for alms, received rice gruel, and was sitting there drinking it. He gave the remaining little gruel to Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, saying, "Go, mix this gruel with water in a pot, and for those who have a disturbance of the elements, pour it into the openings of their eyes, mouths, ears, and noses, and sprinkle their bodies. Thus they will be free from disorder." She did so. Then, when the boy's body was restored to normal, she said, "Come, dear Maṇḍabya, I will have him forgive you." She then made her son and all the brahmins bow down and lie prostrate at his feet and ask for his forgiveness.

So “sabbajanassa dānaṃ dātabba”nti ovaditvā, dhammakathaṃ katvā, attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃyeva gantvā, cintesi “itthīsu pākaṭā diṭṭhamaṅgalikā damitā, purisesu pākaṭo maṇḍabyakumāro, idāni ko dametabbo”ti. Tato jātimantatāpasaṃ addasa bandhumatīnagaraṃ nissāya kumbhavatīnadītīre viharantaṃ. So “ahaṃ jātiyā visiṭṭho, aññehi paribhuttodakaṃ na paribhuñjāmī”ti uparinadiyā vasati. Mahāpuriso tassa uparibhāge vāsaṃ kappetvā tassa udakaparibhogavelāyaṃ dantakaṭṭhaṃ khāditvā udake pakkhipi. Tāpaso taṃ udakena vuyhamānaṃ disvā “kenidaṃ khitta”nti paṭisotaṃ gantvā mahāpurisaṃ disvā “ko etthā”ti āha. “Mātaṅgacaṇḍālo, ācariyā”ti. “Apehi, caṇḍāla, mā uparinadiyā vasī”ti. Mahāpuriso “sādhu, ācariyā”ti heṭṭhānadiyā vasati, paṭisotampi dantakaṭṭhaṃ tāpasassa santikaṃ āgacchati. Tāpaso puna gantvā “apehi, caṇḍāla, mā heṭṭhānadiyaṃ vasa, uparinadiyāyeva vasā”ti āha. Mahāpuriso “sādhu, ācariyā”ti tathā akāsi, punapi tatheva ahosi. Tāpaso punapi “tathā karotī”ti duṭṭho mahāpurisaṃ sapi “sūriyassa te uggamanavelāya sattadhā muddhā phalatū”ti. Mahāpurisopi “sādhu, ācariya, ahaṃ pana sūriyuṭṭhānaṃ na demī”ti vatvā sūriyuṭṭhānaṃ nivāresi[M 1.0173]. Tato ratti na vibhāyati, andhakāro jāto, bhītā bandhumatīvāsino tāpasassa santikaṃ gantvā “atthi nu kho, ācariya, amhākaṃ sotthibhāvo”ti pucchiṃsu. Te hi taṃ “arahā”ti maññanti. So tesaṃ sabbamācikkhi. Te mahāpurisaṃ upasaṅkamitvā [P 1.0191] “sūriyaṃ, bhante, muñcathā”ti yāciṃsu. Mahāpuriso “yadi tumhākaṃ arahā āgantvā maṃ khamāpeti, muñcāmī”ti āha.

Having advised, "Alms should be given to all people," and having delivered a Dhamma talk, he went to his own dwelling place and reflected: "Among women, the renowned Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā has been tamed; among men, the renowned Maṇḍabyakumāra. Now, who is to be tamed next?" Then he saw a high-born ascetic dwelling on the bank of the Kumbhavati River near the city of Bandhumati. That ascetic, thinking, "I am superior by birth; I will not use water used by others," lived upstream. The Great Being took up residence upstream from him. At the time when the ascetic was using the water, the Great Being chewed a toothstick and threw it into the water. Seeing it being carried downstream by the water, the ascetic went upstream, asking, "By whom was this thrown?" and seeing the Great Being, he asked, "Who is here?" "Mātaṅga, an outcaste, teacher." "Go away, outcaste! Do not live upstream!" The Great Being replied, "Very well, teacher," and went to live downstream. But the toothstick went against the current and came to the ascetic. The ascetic went again and said, "Go away, outcaste! Do not live downstream—live upstream!" The Great Being replied, "Very well, teacher," and did so, but the same thing happened again. The ascetic, angered that he kept doing this, cursed the Great Being: "At the time of sunrise, may your head split into seven pieces!" The Great Being replied, "Very well, teacher, but I will not let the sun rise." And he prevented the sun from rising. Then the night did not dawn, and it became dark. The frightened inhabitants of Bandhumati went to the ascetic and asked, "Teacher, is there any well-being for us?" For they considered him to be an arahant. He told them everything. They approached the Great Being and pleaded, "Venerable sir, release the sun!" The Great Being said, "If your arahant comes and asks me for forgiveness, I will release it."

Manussā gantvā tāpasaṃ āhaṃsu – “ehi, bhante, mātaṅgapaṇḍitaṃ khamāpehi, mā tumhākaṃ kalahakāraṇā mayaṃ nassimhā”ti. So “nāhaṃ caṇḍālaṃ khamāpemī”ti āha. Manussā “amhe tvaṃ nāsesī”ti taṃ hatthapādesu gahetvā mahāpurisassa santikaṃ nesuṃ. Mahāpuriso “mama pādamūle [V 1.0153] kucchiyā nipajjitvā khamāpente khamāmī”ti āha. Manussā “evaṃ karohī”ti āhaṃsu. Tāpaso “nāhaṃ caṇḍālaṃ vandāmī”ti. Manussā “tava chandena na vandissasī”ti hatthapādamassugīvādīsu gahetvā mahāpurisassa pādamūle sayāpesuṃ. So “khamāmahaṃ imassa, apicāhaṃ tassevānukampāya sūriyaṃ na muñcāmi, sūriye hi uggatamatte muddhā assa sattadhā phalissatī”ti āha. Manussā “idāni, bhante, kiṃ kātabba”nti āhaṃsu. Mahāpuriso “tena hi imaṃ galappamāṇe udake ṭhapetvā mattikāpiṇḍenassa sīsaṃ paṭicchādetha, sūriyarasmīhi phuṭṭho mattikāpiṇḍo sattadhā phalissati. Tasmiṃ phalite esa aññatra gacchatū”ti āha. Te tāpasaṃ hatthapādādīsu gahetvā tathā akaṃsu. Sūriye muñcitamatte mattikāpiṇḍo sattadhā phalitvā pati, tāpaso bhīto palāyi. Manussā disvā “passatha, bho, samaṇassa ānubhāva”nti dantakaṭṭhapakkhipanamādiṃ katvā sabbaṃ vitthāretvā “natthi īdiso samaṇo”ti tasmiṃ pasīdiṃsu. Tato pabhuti sakalajambudīpe khattiyabrāhmaṇādayo gahaṭṭhapabbajitā mātaṅgapaṇḍitassa upaṭṭhānaṃ agamaṃsu. So yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā kāyassa bhedā brahmaloke uppajji. Tenāha bhagavā “tadamināpi jānātha…pe… brahmalokūpapattiyā”ti.

The people went and said to the ascetic, 'Come, venerable sir, ask Mātaṅga the Wise for forgiveness, lest we perish because of your quarrel.' He replied, 'I will not ask an outcaste for forgiveness.' The people said, 'You will destroy us,' and seizing him by his hands and feet, they took him to the Great Being. The Great Being said, 'I will forgive him if he lies down on his belly at my feet and asks for forgiveness.' The people said, 'Do so!' The ascetic replied, 'I will not bow to an outcaste.' The people said, 'You will bow whether you wish to or not,' and seizing him by his hands, feet, beard, neck, and so on, they made him lie down at the feet of the Great Being. He said, 'I forgive him, but out of compassion for him, I will not release the sun. For as soon as the sun rises, his head will split into seven pieces.' The people asked, 'What should be done now, venerable sir?' The Great Being said, 'Then place him in water up to his neck and cover his head with a lump of clay. When struck by the sun's rays, the lump of clay will split into seven pieces. When that happens, let him go elsewhere.' They seized the ascetic by his hands, feet, and so on, and did so. As soon as the sun was released, the lump of clay split into seven pieces and fell. The terrified ascetic fled. Seeing this, the people said, 'See, friends, the power of the recluse!' They recounted everything, starting from the throwing of the toothstick, saying, 'There is no recluse like this one,' and they placed their faith in him. From then on, throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, khattiyas, brahmins, and others, whether householders or renunciants, attended upon Mātaṅga the Wise. He lived out his lifespan, and after the breaking up of the body, he was reborn in the Brahma-world. Therefore, the Blessed One said, 'Know this also... rebirth in the Brahma-world.'

140-141. Evaṃ “na jaccā vasalo hoti, kammunā vasalo hotī”ti sādhetvā [P 1.0192] idāni “na jaccā hoti brāhmaṇo, kammunā hoti brāhmaṇo”ti etaṃ sādhetuṃ āha “ajjhāyakakule jātā [M 1.0174] …pe… duggatyā garahāya vā”ti. Tattha ajjhāyakakule jātāti mantajjhāyake brāhmaṇakule jātā. “Ajjhāyakākuḷe jātā”tipi pāṭho. Mantānaṃ ajjhāyake anupakuṭṭhe ca brāhmaṇakule jātāti attho. Mantā bandhavā etesanti mantabandhavā. Vedabandhū vedapaṭissaraṇāti vuttaṃ hoti. Te ca pāpesu kammesu abhiṇhamupadissareti te evaṃ kule jātā mantabandhavā ca samānāpi yadi pāṇātipātādīsu pāpakammesu punappunaṃ upadissanti, atha diṭṭheva dhamme gārayhā samparāye ca duggati te evamupadissamānā imasmiṃyeva attabhāve mātāpitūhipi “nayime amhākaṃ puttā, dujjātā ete kulassa aṅgārabhūtā, nikkaḍḍhatha ne”ti, brāhmaṇehipi “gahapatikā ete, na ete brāhmaṇā, mā nesaṃ saddhayaññathālipākādīsu pavesaṃ detha, mā nehi saddhiṃ sallapathā”ti, aññehipi manussehi “pāpakammantā ete, na ete brāhmaṇā”ti evaṃ gārayhā honti. Samparāye ca nesaṃ duggati nirayādibhedā, duggati etesaṃ paraloke hotīti attho. Samparāye vātipi pāṭho. Paraloke etesaṃ dukkhassa gati duggati, dukkhappattiyeva hotīti attho. Na ne jāti nivāreti, duggatyā garahāya vāti sā tathā ukkaṭṭhāpi yaṃ tvaṃ sārato paccesi, jāti ete pāpakammesu padissante brāhmaṇe “samparāye [V 1.0154] ca duggatī”ti ettha vuttappakārāya duggatiyā vā, “diṭṭheva dhamme gārayhā”ti ettha vuttappakārāya garahāya vā na nivāreti.

Having thus established that 'one is not an outcast by birth, but by deeds,' now to establish that 'one is not a brahmin by birth, but by deeds,' it is said: 'Born in a family of reciters... or [liable to] wretched destiny [and] blame.' Herein, 'born in a family of reciters' means born in a brahmin family devoted to reciting mantras. There is also a variant reading: 'born in a family of reciters.' It means born in a brahmin family devoted to reciting mantras, and irreproachable. 'Bound by mantras' means those whose bonds are mantras. It is said that they rely on the Vedas as their kin. And if they are frequently seen engaged in evil deeds, such as killing living beings, then, even though born in such a family and bound by mantras, if they are repeatedly seen committing evil deeds like killing, then in this very life they are blameworthy, and in the future, they face a wretched destiny. Thus, even though they are seen in this way, in this very existence, their parents say, 'These are not our sons; they are ill-born, mere embers of the family. Cast them out!' The brahmins say, 'These are householders, not brahmins. Do not allow them to participate in offerings supported by faith, sacrifices, or the like. Do not converse with them.' Other people say, 'These are evildoers, not brahmins.' Thus, they are blameworthy. In the future, their wretched destiny takes the form of hell, etc. It means they will have a miserable fate in the next world. There is also a variant reading: 'or in the future.' It means in the next world, their suffering and fate is wretched—they will meet with misery. Birth does not prevent this. 'Or [liable to] wretched destiny [and] blame'—even if that birth is so exalted, which you accept as essential, birth does not prevent these brahmins, who are seen engaged in evil deeds, from facing a wretched destiny in the future as described, nor from being blameworthy in this very life as described.

142. Evaṃ bhagavā ajjhāyakakule jātānampi brāhmaṇānaṃ gārayhādikammavasena diṭṭheva dhamme patitabhāvaṃ dīpento duggatigamanena ca samparāye brāhmaṇajātiyā abhāvaṃ dīpento “na jaccā hoti brāhmaṇo, kammunā hoti brāhmaṇo”ti etampi atthaṃ sādhetvā idāni duvidhampi atthaṃ nigamento āha, evaṃ brāhmaṇa –

142. Thus, the Blessed One, revealing the downfall in this very life of even those brahmins born into families of reciters, due to blameworthy actions, and revealing the disappearance of the brahmin status in the next life due to going to a bad destination, having also established the meaning that 'not by birth is one a brahmin, but by action is one a brahmin,' now concluding both meanings, said thus, O Brahmin:

“Na jaccā vasalo hoti, na jaccā hoti brāhmaṇo;

Kammunā vasalo hoti, kammunā hoti brāhmaṇo”ti.

Not by birth is one an outcast; not by birth is one a Brahmin. By action one becomes an outcast; by action one becomes a Brahmin.

Sesaṃ [P 1.0193] kasibhāradvājasutte vuttanayameva. Visesato vā ettha nikkujjitaṃ vātiādīnaṃ evaṃ yojanā veditabbā – yathā koci nikkujjitaṃ vā [M 1.0175] ukkujjeyya, evaṃ maṃ kammavimukhaṃ jātivāde patitaṃ “jātiyā brāhmaṇavasalabhāvo hotī”ti diṭṭhito vuṭṭhāpentena, yathā paṭicchannaṃ vivareyya, evaṃ jātivādapaṭicchannaṃ kammavādaṃ vivarantena, yathā mūḷhassa maggaṃ ācikkheyya, evaṃ brāhmaṇavasalabhāvassa asambhinnaujumaggaṃ ācikkhantena, yathā andhakāre vā telapajjotaṃ dhāreyya, evaṃ mātaṅgādinidassanapajjotadhāraṇena mayhaṃ bhotā gotamena etehi pariyāyehi pakāsitattā anekapariyāyena dhammo pakāsitoti.

The rest is as explained in the Kasibhāradvāja Sutta. Specifically here, the application of the phrases such as 'what is overturned' should be understood thus: 'Just as someone might set upright what is overturned, so has the venerable Gotama raised me—who was averse to action and had fallen into the doctrine of birth—from the view that "one's status as a brahmin or an outcast is by birth"; just as one might uncover what is hidden, so has he revealed the doctrine of action concealed by the doctrine of birth; just as one might show the path to one who is lost, so has he pointed out the unconfused, straight path regarding the state of being a brahmin or an outcast; and just as one might hold up an oil lamp in the darkness, so has he held up the lamp of examples such as Mātaṅga. In these many ways, the Dhamma has been made clear to me by the venerable Gotama.'

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the commentary on the Khuddaka collection,

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya aggikabhāradvājasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Here ends the explanation of the Aggikabhāradvāja Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary.

8. Mettasuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Explanation of the Discourse on Loving-Kindness

Karaṇīyamatthakusalenāti [V 1.0155] mettasuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Himavantapassato kira devatāhi ubbāḷhā bhikkhū bhagavato santikaṃ sāvatthiṃ āgacchiṃsu. Tesaṃ bhagavā parittatthāya kammaṭṭhānatthāya ca imaṃ suttaṃ abhāsi. Ayaṃ tāva saṅkhepo.

This is the Discourse on Loving-kindness, which begins with the words 'Karaṇīyamatthakusalena.' What is its origin? It is said that from the slopes of the Himalayas, monks who were harassed by deities came to the Blessed One in Sāvatthī. For their protection and as a subject of meditation, the Blessed One delivered this discourse. This, for now, is the summary.

Ayaṃ pana vitthāro – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati upakaṭṭhāya vassūpanāyikāya. Tena kho pana samayena sambahulā nānāverajjakā bhikkhū bhagavato santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā tattha tattha vassaṃ upagantukāmā bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamanti. Tatra sudaṃ bhagavā rāgacaritānaṃ saviññāṇakāviññāṇakavasena ekādasavidhaṃ asubhakammaṭṭhānaṃ, dosacaritānaṃ catubbidhaṃ mettādikammaṭṭhānaṃ, mohacaritānaṃ maraṇassatikammaṭṭhānādīni, vitakkacaritānaṃ ānāpānassatipathavīkasiṇādīni, saddhācaritānaṃ buddhānussatikammaṭṭhānādīni, buddhicaritānaṃ catudhātuvavatthanādīnīti iminā nayena caturāsītisahassappabhedacaritānukūlāni kammaṭṭhānāni katheti.

This, however, is the detailed account: At one time, the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī as the time for the rains-residence was approaching. At that time, many monks from various regions, having received subjects of meditation from the Blessed One and wishing to enter the rains-residence in various places, approached him. There, it is said, the Blessed One taught subjects of meditation suitable for the eighty-four thousand types of temperaments in this manner: for those of a lustful temperament, the eleven kinds of meditation on foulness, in terms of animate and inanimate objects; for those of a hateful temperament, the fourfold meditation beginning with loving-kindness; for those of a deluded temperament, mindfulness of death and other subjects; for those of a speculative temperament, mindfulness of breathing, the earth kasiṇa, and other subjects; for those of a faithful temperament, recollection of the Buddha and other subjects; and for those of an intellectual temperament, the analysis of the four elements and other subjects.

Atha kho pañcamattāni bhikkhusatāni bhagavato santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ uggahetvā sappāyasenāsanañca gocaragāmañca pariyesamānāni anupubbena gantvā [M 1.0176] paccante himavantena saddhiṃ ekābaddhaṃ nīlakācamaṇisannibhasilātalaṃ sītalaghanacchāyanīlavanasaṇḍamaṇḍitaṃ muttātalarajatapaṭṭasadisavālukākiṇṇabhūmibhāgaṃ sucisātasītalajalāsayaparivāritaṃ pabbatamaddasaṃsu. Atha kho te bhikkhū tatthekarattiṃ vasitvā pabhātāya rattiyā sarīraparikammaṃ katvā tassa avidūre aññataraṃ gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pavisiṃsu. Gāmo ghananivesasanniviṭṭhakulasahassayutto, manussā cettha saddhā pasannā, te paccante pabbajitadassanassa dullabhatāya bhikkhū disvā eva pītisomanassajātā hutvā te bhikkhū bhojetvā “idheva, bhante, temāsaṃ vasathā”ti yācitvā pañcapadhānakuṭisatāni kārāpetvā tattha mañcapīṭhapānīyaparibhojanīyaghaṭādīni sabbūpakaraṇāni paṭiyādesuṃ.

Then, five hundred monks, having received a subject of meditation from the Blessed One and seeking suitable lodgings and an alms-resort village, journeyed in due course and arrived at a remote region connected with the Himalayas. There they saw a mountain with a continuous rock-surface resembling a blue gem, adorned with cool, dense shade and groves of blue forest, having a ground covered with sand like a surface of pearls or a silver sheet, and surrounded by reservoirs of pure, pleasant, and cool water. Having dwelt there for one night, when the night had dawned, the monks attended to their bodily needs and entered a certain village nearby for alms. The village was comprised of a thousand families, densely and well-established, and the people there were faithful and devout. Due to the rarity of seeing renunciants in that remote area, upon the very sight of the monks, they were filled with joy and happiness. They fed the monks and requested, 'Venerable sirs, please dwell right here for the three months of the rains.' Then they had five hundred meditation huts built and prepared all the necessary furnishings therein—beds, seats, pots for drinking and washing water, and other requisites.

Bhikkhū dutiyadivase aññaṃ gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pavisiṃsu. Tatthāpi manussā tatheva upaṭṭhahitvā vassāvāsaṃ yāciṃsu. Bhikkhū “asati antarāye”ti adhivāsetvā taṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ pavisitvā sabbarattindivaṃ āraddhavīriyā hutvā yāmagaṇḍikaṃ koṭṭetvā yonisomanasikārabahulā viharantā rukkhamūlāni upagantvā nisīdiṃsu. Sīlavantānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ tejena vihatatejā rukkhadevatā [V 1.0156] attano attano vimānā oruyha dārake gahetvā ito cito ca vicaranti. Seyyathāpi nāma rājūhi vā rājamahāmattehi vā gāmakāvāsaṃ gatehi gāmavāsīnaṃ gharesu okāse gahite gharamānusakā gharā nikkhamitvā aññatra vasantā “kadā nu kho gamissantī”ti dūrato olokenti; evameva devatā attano attano vimānāni chaḍḍetvā ito cito ca vicarantiyo dūratova olokenti – “kadā nu kho bhadantā gamissantī”ti. Tato evaṃ samacintesuṃ “paṭhamavassūpagatā bhikkhū avassaṃ temāsaṃ vasissanti. Mayaṃ pana tāva ciraṃ dārake gahetvā okkamma vasituṃ na sakkhissāma. Handa mayaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ bhayānakaṃ ārammaṇaṃ dassemā”ti. Tā rattiṃ bhikkhūnaṃ samaṇadhammakaraṇavelāya bhiṃsanakāni yakkharūpāni nimminitvā purato purato tiṭṭhanti, bheravasaddañca karonti. Bhikkhūnaṃ tāni rūpāni passantānaṃ tañca saddaṃ suṇantānaṃ hadayaṃ phandi, dubbaṇṇā ca ahesuṃ uppaṇḍupaṇḍukajātā. Tena te cittaṃ ekaggaṃ kātuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu. Tesaṃ anekaggacittānaṃ bhayena ca punappunaṃ saṃviggānaṃ sati sammussi. Tato nesaṃ muṭṭhassatīnaṃ duggandhāni ārammaṇāni payojesuṃ. Tesaṃ tena [M 1.0177] duggandhena nimmathiyamānamiva matthaluṅgaṃ ahosi, bāḷhā sīsavedanā uppajjiṃsu, na ca taṃ pavattiṃ aññamaññassa ārocesuṃ.

On the second day, the monks entered another village for alms. There too, the people attended to them in the same way and requested them to take up the rains-residence. The monks, saying, 'If there is no impediment,' consented and entered that forest grove. Exerting themselves energetically day and night, striking the time-gong, and dwelling with abundant wise attention, they approached the roots of trees and sat down. The radiance of the tree deities was overcome by the spiritual power of the virtuous monks, so they descended from their celestial mansions, took their children, and wandered here and there. Just as when kings or royal ministers, having gone to reside in a village, occupy the homes of the villagers, the householders leave their homes and dwell elsewhere, watching from afar and thinking, 'When will they leave?'—so too, the deities, having abandoned their own mansions and wandering here and there, watched from afar, thinking, 'When will the venerable ones depart?' Then they considered thus: 'These monks who have come for the first rains-residence will surely stay for three months. We, however, will not be able to take our children and dwell apart for so long. Come, let us show the monks a frightening object.' At night, at the time for the monks' ascetic practices, they created terrifying forms of yakkhas and stood right before them, making dreadful sounds. As the monks saw those forms and heard those sounds, their hearts trembled, and they became discolored, turning utterly pale and yellowish. Because of this, they were unable to make their minds one-pointed. For them, with their minds unconcentrated and repeatedly agitated by fear, mindfulness was lost. Then, for them whose mindfulness was lost, the deities presented foul-smelling objects. From that foul smell, their brains felt as if they were being churned, severe headaches arose, and they did not report this occurrence to one another.

Athekadivasaṃ saṅghattherassa upaṭṭhānakāle sabbesu sannipatitesu saṅghatthero pucchi – “tumhākaṃ, āvuso, imaṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ paviṭṭhānaṃ katipāhaṃ ativiya parisuddho chavivaṇṇo ahosi pariyodāto, vippasannāni ca indriyāni etarahi panattha kisā dubbaṇṇā uppaṇḍupaṇḍukajātā, kiṃ vo idha asappāya”nti? Tato eko bhikkhu āha – “ahaṃ, bhante, rattiṃ īdisañca īdisañca bheravārammaṇaṃ passāmi ca suṇāmi ca, īdisañca gandhaṃ ghāyāmi, tena me cittaṃ na samādhiyatī”ti. Eteneva upāyena sabbe taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesuṃ. Saṅghatthero āha – “bhagavatā āvuso dve vassūpanāyikā paññattā, amhākañca idaṃ senāsanaṃ asappāyaṃ, āyāmāvuso bhagavato santikaṃ, gantvā aññaṃ sappāyaṃ senāsanaṃ pucchāmā”ti. “Sādhu bhante”ti te bhikkhū therassa paṭissuṇitvā sabbe senāsanaṃ saṃsāmetvā pattacīvaramādāya anupalittattā kulesu kañci anāmantetvā eva yena sāvatthi tena cārikaṃ pakkamiṃsu. Anupubbena sāvatthiṃ gantvā bhagavato santikaṃ agamiṃsu.

Then one day, when all had gathered to attend upon the Saṅgha-elder, the Saṅgha-elder asked, “Friends, when you entered this forest grove, for a few days your complexion was exceedingly pure, bright, and clear, and your faculties were serene? But now you are thin, discolored, and pale. What here is unsuitable for you?” Then one monk said, “Venerable sir, at night I see and hear such and such terrifying objects, and I smell such and such odors, so my mind does not become composed.” In the same way, all of them related their experiences. The Saṅgha-elder said, “Friends, the Blessed One has prescribed two rainy season retreats, and this dwelling place is unsuitable for us. Come, friends, let us go to the presence of the Blessed One. Having gone, we will ask for another suitable dwelling place.” “Very well, venerable sir,” those monks replied to the elder. Then, having put their lodging in order and taken their bowls and robes, without taking leave of any families—being unattached—they set out on a journey toward Sāvatthī. Gradually, they reached Sāvatthī and approached the presence of the Blessed One.

Bhagavā te bhikkhū disvā etadavoca – “na, bhikkhave, antovassaṃ cārikā caritabbāti mayā sikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ, kissa tumhe cārikaṃ carathā”ti. Te bhagavato sabbaṃ ārocesuṃ. Bhagavā āvajjento sakalajambudīpe antamaso catuppādapīṭhakaṭṭhānamattampi tesaṃ sappāyaṃ senāsanaṃ nāddasa. Atha te bhikkhū āha – “na, bhikkhave, tumhākaṃ aññaṃ sappāyaṃ senāsanaṃ atthi, tattheva tumhe viharantā āsavakkhayaṃ pāpuṇeyyātha. Gacchatha, bhikkhave, tameva senāsanaṃ [V 1.0157] upanissāya viharatha. Sace pana devatāhi abhayaṃ icchatha, imaṃ parittaṃ uggaṇhatha, etañhi vo parittañca kammaṭṭhānañca bhavissatī”ti imaṃ suttamabhāsi.

The Blessed One saw those monks and said: “Monks, I have laid down the training rule that one should not wander during the rainy season. Why are you wandering?” They told the Blessed One everything. The Blessed One, reflecting, did not see in the whole of Jambudīpa even a space for a four-legged stool that was suitable as lodging for them. Then the Blessed One said to those monks: “Monks, there is no other suitable lodging for you. By staying right there, you might attain the destruction of the taints. Go, monks, dwell relying on that very lodging. If you wish for safety from deities, learn this protective recitation. For this will be both your protection and meditation subject.” He spoke this discourse.

Apare panāhu – “gacchatha, bhikkhave, tameva senāsanaṃ upanissāya viharathā”ti idañca vatvā bhagavā āha – “apica kho āraññakena pariharaṇaṃ ñātabbaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ – sāyaṃpātaṃ karaṇavasena dve mettā, dve parittā, dve asubhā, dve maraṇassatī aṭṭha mahāsaṃvegavatthusamāvajjanañca. Aṭṭha mahāsaṃvegavatthūni nāma jāti jarā byādhi maraṇaṃ cattāri apāyadukkhānīti[M 1.0178]. Atha vā jātijarābyādhimaraṇāni cattāri, apāyadukkhaṃ pañcamaṃ, atīte vaṭṭamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ, anāgate vaṭṭamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ, paccuppanne āhārapariyeṭṭhimūlakaṃ dukkha”nti. Evaṃ bhagavā pariharaṇaṃ ācikkhitvā tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ mettatthañca parittatthañca vipassanāpādakajhānatthañca imaṃ suttaṃ abhāsīti.

Others, however, say: “Go, monks, dwell depending on that very dwelling.” Having said this, the Blessed One further said: “Moreover, the forest dweller should know the practice. Namely: in the evening and morning, by way of doing, two practices of loving-kindness, two practices of protection, two practices of foulness, two practices of mindfulness of death, and the recollection of the eight great causes for spiritual urgency. The eight great causes for spiritual urgency are: birth, aging, sickness, death—these four—and the sufferings of the states of woe. Or alternatively: birth, aging, sickness, death—these four; the suffering of the states of woe as the fifth; past suffering rooted in the round of existence, future suffering rooted in the round of existence, and present suffering rooted in the search for food.” Thus, having explained the practice, the Blessed One spoke this discourse to those monks for the purpose of loving-kindness, protection, and the jhānas that are the basis for insight.

143. Tattha karaṇīyamatthakusalenāti imissā paṭhamagāthāya tāva ayaṃ padavaṇṇanā – karaṇīyanti kātabbaṃ, karaṇārahanti attho. Atthoti paṭipadā, yaṃ vā kiñci attano hitaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ araṇīyato atthoti vuccati, araṇīyato nāma upagantabbato. Atthe kusalena atthakusalena, atthachekenāti vuttaṃ hoti. Yanti aniyamitapaccattaṃ. Nti niyamitaupayogaṃ. Ubhayampi vā yaṃ tanti paccattavacanaṃ. Santaṃ padanti upayogavacanaṃ. Tattha lakkhaṇato santaṃ, pattabbato padaṃ, nibbānassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Abhisameccāti abhisamāgantvā. Sakkotīti sakko, samattho paṭibaloti vuttaṃ hoti. Ujūti ajjavayutto. Suṭṭhu ujūti suhuju. Sukhaṃ vaco asminti suvaco. Assāti bhaveyya. Mudūti maddavayutto. Na atimānīti anatimānī.

143. Herein, concerning the first verse beginning ‘karaṇīyamatthakusalena,’ this, firstly, is the explanation of the words: ‘Karaṇīyaṃ’ means what should be done, what is worthy of being done. ‘Attha’ means the path; or, whatever is for one’s own welfare, all that is called ‘attha’ because it is to be approached. ‘By one skilled in the good’ means by one clever in the good. ‘Yaṃ’ is an indefinite term in the nominative case. ‘Santaṃ padaṃ’ is a term in the accusative case. Therein, ‘santaṃ’ is, by characteristic, peaceful; ‘padaṃ’ is to be attained—this is a designation for Nibbāna. ‘Abhisamecca’ means having fully realized. ‘Sakko’ means capable, competent, powerful. ‘Uju’ means straight, upright. ‘Suhuju’ means very straight. ‘Suvaco’ means pleasant in speech. ‘Assa’ means should be. ‘Mudu’ means gentle. ‘Anatimānī’ means not conceited.

Ayaṃ panettha atthavaṇṇanā – karaṇīyamatthakusalena yanta santaṃ padaṃ abhisameccāti. Ettha tāva atthi karaṇīyaṃ, atthi akaraṇīyaṃ. Tattha saṅkhepato sikkhattayaṃ karaṇīyaṃ, sīlavipatti, diṭṭhivipatti, ācāravipatti, ājīvavipattīti evamādi akaraṇīyaṃ. Tathā atthi atthakusalo, atthi anatthakusalo.

This is the meaning explanation here: “By one skilled in the good, desiring to attain the peaceful state.” Herein, first, there is what should be done, and there is what should not be done. Briefly, the threefold training is what should be done; failure in virtue, failure in view, failure in conduct, failure in livelihood, and so on, are what should not be done. Likewise, there is one skilled in the good, and one unskilled in the good.

Tattha yo imasmiṃ sāsane pabbajitvā na attānaṃ sammā payojeti, khaṇḍasīlo hoti, ekavīsatividhaṃ anesanaṃ nissāya jīvikaṃ kappeti. Seyyathidaṃ – veḷudānaṃ, pattadānaṃ, pupphadānaṃ, phaladānaṃ, dantakaṭṭhadānaṃ, mukhodakadānaṃ, sinānadānaṃ, cuṇṇadānaṃ, mattikādānaṃ, cāṭukamyataṃ, muggasūpyataṃ, pāribhaṭutaṃ, jaṅghapesaniyaṃ, vejjakammaṃ, dūtakammaṃ, pahiṇagamanaṃ, piṇḍapaṭipiṇḍadānānuppadānaṃ, vatthuvijjaṃ, nakkhattavijjaṃ, aṅgavijjanti. Chabbidhe ca agocare carati[M 1.0179]. Seyyathidaṃ – vesiyagocare vidhavāthullakumārikapaṇḍakabhikkhunipānāgāragocareti. Saṃsaṭṭho ca [V 1.0158] viharati rājūhi rājamahāmattehi titthiyehi titthiyasāvakehi ananulomikena gihisaṃsaggena. Yāni vā pana tāni kulāni asaddhāni appasannāni anopānabhūtāni akkosakaparibhāsakāni anatthakāmāni ahitaaphāsukaayogakkhemakāmāni bhikkhūnaṃ…pe… upāsikānaṃ, tathārūpāni kulāni sevati bhajati payirupāsati. Ayaṃ anatthakusalo.

Herein, a certain bhikkhu, having gone forth in this Dispensation, does not apply himself rightly, is of broken virtue, and makes a living by relying on twenty-one kinds of wrong livelihood. What are these? Giving bamboo, giving leaves, giving flowers, giving fruits, giving tooth-wood, giving water for rinsing the mouth, giving bathing items, giving powder, giving clay, employing flattery, speaking half-truths, acting as a children's attendant, acting as a leg-messenger, practicing medicine, acting as a messenger, going on errands, giving a gift in hopes of a greater one, practicing the science of building sites, practicing astrology, and practicing prognostication from bodily marks. And he resorts to the six kinds of improper resorts. What are these? Resorts of courtesans, widows, mature unmarried women, eunuchs, bhikkhunīs, and taverns. He dwells in association with kings, royal ministers, sectarians, and disciples of sectarians, engaging in improper socializing with householders. Or he frequents, associates with, and attends upon those families who are faithless, lacking confidence, abusive and reproachful, wishing no good, benefit, comfort, or safety from bondage for the bhikkhus... for the female lay disciples. This one is skilled in what is unbeneficial.

Yo pana imasmiṃ sāsane pabbajitvā attānaṃ sammā payojeti, anesanaṃ pahāya catupārisuddhisīle patiṭṭhātukāmo saddhāsīsena pātimokkhasaṃvaraṃ, satisīsena indriyasaṃvaraṃ, vīriyasīsena ājīvapārisuddhiṃ, paññāsīsena paccayapaṭisevanaṃ pūreti ayaṃ atthakusalo.

But one who, having gone forth in this Dispensation, rightly applies himself, abandoning wrong livelihood and desiring to be established in the fourfold purity of virtue, fulfills the Pātimokkha restraint headed by faith, the restraint of the senses headed by mindfulness, purity of livelihood headed by effort, and the proper use of requisites headed by wisdom—this one is skilled in what is beneficial.

Yo vā sattāpattikkhandhasodhanavasena pātimokkhasaṃvaraṃ, chadvāre ghaṭṭitārammaṇesu abhijjhādīnaṃ anuppattivasena indriyasaṃvaraṃ, anesanaparivajjanavasena viññupasatthabuddhabuddhasāvakavaṇṇitapaccayapaṭisevanena ca ājīvapārisuddhiṃ, yathāvuttapaccavekkhaṇavasena paccayapaṭisevanaṃ, catuiriyāpathaparivattane sātthakādīnaṃ paccavekkhaṇavasena sampajaññañca sodheti, ayampi atthakusalo.

Or one who purifies the Pātimokkha restraint by means of cleansing the seven classes of offenses; the restraint of the senses by means of preventing the arising of covetousness and so forth at the six doors when objects impinge; the purity of livelihood by means of avoiding wrong livelihood and by using requisites praised by the wise, the Buddha, and the Buddha's disciples; the proper use of requisites by means of reflecting as has been stated; and clear comprehension by means of reflecting on the purposefulness and so forth of the four postures when changing them—this one, too, is skilled in what is beneficial.

Yo vā yathā ūsodakaṃ paṭicca saṃkiliṭṭhaṃ vatthaṃ pariyodāyati, chārikaṃ paṭicca ādāso, ukkāmukhaṃ paṭicca jātarūpaṃ, tathā ñāṇaṃ paṭicca sīlaṃ vodāyatīti ñatvā ñāṇodakena dhovanto sīlaṃ pariyodāpeti. Yathā ca kikī sakuṇikā aṇḍaṃ, camarīmigo vāladhiṃ, ekaputtikā nārī piyaṃ ekaputtakaṃ, ekanayano puriso taṃ ekanayanaṃ rakkhati, tathā ativiya appamatto attano sīlakkhandhaṃ rakkhati, sāyaṃpātaṃ paccavekkhamāno aṇumattampi vajjaṃ na passati, ayampi atthakusalo.

Or one who, knowing that 'Just as a soiled cloth is cleansed by lye, a mirror by ash, and gold by a furnace, so too is virtue purified by knowledge,' washes one's virtue with the water of knowledge and makes it perfectly pure. And just as a partridge hen guards her egg, a yak its tail, a mother with one son her dear only son, and a one-eyed man his one eye, so too one guards one's aggregate of virtue with extreme heedfulness. Reflecting morning and evening, one sees not even the slightest fault. This one, too, is skilled in what is beneficial.

Yo vā pana avippaṭisārakarasīle patiṭṭhāya kilesavikkhambhanapaṭipadaṃ paggaṇhāti, taṃ paggahetvā kasiṇaparikammaṃ karoti, kasiṇaparikammaṃ katvā samāpattiyo nibbatteti, ayampi atthakusalo. Yo vā pana samāpattito [M 1.0180] vuṭṭhāya saṅkhāre sammasitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, ayaṃ atthakusalānaṃ aggo.

Furthermore, one who, established in virtue that causes no remorse, undertakes the practice for the suppression of the defilements; and having undertaken it, performs the preliminary work on a kasiṇa; and having performed the preliminary work on a kasiṇa, brings forth the meditative attainments—this one, too, is skilled in what is beneficial. But one who, emerging from a meditative attainment, comprehends the conditioned formations and attains Arahantship—this one is the foremost among those skilled in what is beneficial.

Tattha ye ime yāva avippaṭisārakarasīle patiṭṭhānena, yāva vā kilesavikkhambhanapaṭipadāya paggahaṇena maggaphalena vaṇṇitā atthakusalā, te imasmiṃ atthe atthakusalāti adhippetā. Tathāvidhā ca te bhikkhū. Tena bhagavā te bhikkhū sandhāya ekapuggalādhiṭṭhānāya desanāya “karaṇīyamatthakusalenā”ti āha.

Herein, those skilled in what is beneficial who were praised—by means of their establishment in virtue that causes no remorse, or by means of their undertaking the practice leading to the suppression of defilements, up to the attainment of the path and its fruit—are intended as 'skilled in what is beneficial' in this context. And such were those bhikkhus. Therefore, the Blessed One, with reference to those bhikkhus, spoke in a teaching established on a single individual: 'What is to be done by one skilled in what is beneficial.'

Tato [V 1.0159] “kiṃ karaṇīya”nti tesaṃ sañjātakaṅkhānaṃ āha “yanta santaṃ padaṃ abhisameccā”ti. Ayamettha adhippāyo – taṃ buddhānubuddhehi vaṇṇitaṃ santaṃ nibbānapadaṃ paṭivedhavasena abhisamecca viharitukāmena yaṃ karaṇīyanti. Ettha ca yanti imassa gāthāpādassa ādito vuttameva karaṇīyanti. Adhikārato anuvattati taṃ santaṃ padaṃ abhisameccāti. Ayaṃ pana yasmā sāvasesapāṭho attho, tasmā “viharitukāmenā”ti vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

Then, to those in whom the doubt 'What is to be done?' had arisen, He said: 'Having comprehended that peaceful state.' Herein, this is the intended meaning: what is to be done by one who wishes to dwell having comprehended, by way of penetration, that peaceful state of Nibbāna praised by the Buddhas and the enlightened ones. And here, the word 'what' (yaṃ) refers back to 'what is to be done' (karaṇīyaṃ), stated at the beginning of this verse line, due to the governing context. 'Having comprehended that peaceful state' follows. However, since this meaning is based on an elliptical reading, it should be understood that 'by one who wishes to dwell' is stated to complete the sense.

Atha vā santaṃ padaṃ abhisameccāti anussavādivasena lokiyapaññāya nibbānapadaṃ santanti ñatvā taṃ adhigantukāmena yantaṃ karaṇīyanti adhikārato anuvattati, taṃ karaṇīyamatthakusalenāti evampettha adhippāyo veditabbo. Atha vā “karaṇīyamatthakusalenā”ti vutte “ki”nti cintentānaṃ āha “yanta santaṃ padaṃ abhisameccā”ti. Tassevaṃ adhippāyo veditabbo – lokiyapaññāya santaṃ padaṃ abhisamecca yaṃ karaṇīyaṃ, tanti. Yaṃ kātabbaṃ, taṃ karaṇīyaṃ, karaṇārahameva tanti vuttaṃ hoti.

Alternatively, 'having comprehended the peaceful state' means: having known through tradition and so forth, by means of worldly wisdom, that the state of Nibbāna is peaceful, for one who desires to attain it, 'that which is to be done' follows from the context. That is to be done by one skilled in what is beneficial—thus the intended meaning should be understood here. Alternatively, when 'What is to be done by one skilled in what is beneficial' was said, to those who were considering 'What?', He said: 'Having comprehended that peaceful state.' Its intended meaning should be understood thus: having comprehended the peaceful state with worldly wisdom, that which is to be done, that is it. What is to be done, that is to be done; it is said to be simply what is worthy of being done.

Kiṃ pana tanti? Kimaññaṃ siyā aññatra tadadhigamūpāyato. Kāmañcetaṃ karaṇārahatthena sikkhattayadīpakena ādipadeneva vuttaṃ. Tathā hi tassa atthavaṇṇanāyaṃ avocumhā “atthi karaṇīyaṃ atthi akaraṇīyaṃ. Tattha saṅkhepato sikkhattayaṃ karaṇīya”nti. Atisaṅkhepadesitattā pana tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ kehici viññātaṃ, kehici na viññātaṃ. Tato yehi na viññātaṃ, tesaṃ viññāpanatthaṃ yaṃ visesato āraññakena bhikkhunā kātabbaṃ, taṃ vitthārento [M 1.0181] “sakko ujū ca suhujū ca, suvaco cassa mudu anatimānī”ti imaṃ tāva upaḍḍhagāthaṃ āha.

But what is it? What else could it be other than the means to its attainment? Indeed, this was stated by the very first word, which signifies what is worthy of doing and illuminates the threefold training. For in the explanation of its meaning, we said: "There is what is to be done, and there is what is not to be done. There, in brief, the threefold training is what is to be done." However, because it was taught too concisely, some monks understood it, while others did not. Therefore, for the sake of making it understood by those who did not understand, elaborating on what should be specifically done by a forest-dwelling monk, he first spoke this half-verse: "Capable, upright, exceedingly upright, easy to admonish, gentle, and without conceit..."

Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Santaṃ padaṃ abhisamecca viharitukāmo lokiyapaññāya vā taṃ abhisamecca tadadhigamāya paṭipajjamāno āraññako bhikkhu dutiyacatutthapadhāniyaṅgasamannāgamena kāye ca jīvite ca anapekkho hutvā saccapaṭivedhāya paṭipajjituṃ sakko assa, tathā kasiṇaparikammavattasamādānādīsu, attano pattacīvarapaṭisaṅkharaṇādīsu ca yāni tāni sabrahmacārīnaṃ uccāvacāni kiṃ karaṇīyāni, tesu aññesu ca evarūpesu sakko assa dakkho analaso samattho. Sakko hontopi ca tatiyapadhāniyaṅgasamannāgamena uju assa. Uju hontopi ca sakiṃ ujubhāvena santosaṃ anāpajjitvā yāvajīvaṃ punappunaṃ asithilakaraṇena suṭṭhutaraṃ uju assa. Asaṭhatāya vā uju, amāyāvitāya suhuju. Kāyavacīvaṅkappahānena vā uju, manovaṅkappahānena suhuju. Asantaguṇassa vā anāvikaraṇena uju, asantaguṇena uppannassa lābhassa anadhivāsanena suhuju. Evaṃ ārammaṇalakkhaṇūpanijjhānehi purimadvayatatiyasikkhāhi payogāsayasuddhīhi ca uju ca suhuju ca assa.

What is meant? A forest-dwelling monk, wishing to dwell having comprehended the peaceful state, or one who, having comprehended it by means of worldly wisdom, practices for its attainment—such a monk should be able to practice for the penetration of the truths by being endowed with the second and fourth factors of striving, unconcerned with body and life. Likewise, in undertaking the preliminary work and observances for the kasiṇas, in repairing his own bowl and robes, and in whatever other duties, high or low, are to be done for his companions in the holy life, and in other such matters, he should be able, skilled, not lazy, and competent. Though able, he should also be upright by being endowed with the third factor of striving. Though upright, he should not be content with a single instance of uprightness, but by repeatedly not slackening as long as he lives, he should be perfectly upright. Or, by being without deceit, he is upright; by being without fraudulence, he is perfectly upright. By abandoning crookedness of body and speech, he is upright; by abandoning crookedness of mind, he is perfectly upright. Or, by not making manifest non-existent qualities, he is upright; by not tolerating the gain that has arisen from non-existent qualities, he is perfectly upright. Thus, through contemplation of the object and of the characteristics, through the three trainings, and through purity of effort and disposition, he should be both upright and perfectly upright.

Na [V 1.0160] kevalañca uju ca suhuju ca, apica pana subbaco ca assa. Yo hi puggalo “idaṃ na kātabba”nti vutto “kiṃ te diṭṭhaṃ, kiṃ te sutaṃ, ko me hutvā vadasi, kiṃ upajjhāyo ācariyo sandiṭṭho sambhatto vā”ti vadati, tuṇhībhāvena vā taṃ viheṭheti, sampaṭicchitvā vā na tathā karoti, so visesādhigamassa dūre hoti. Yo pana ovadiyamāno “sādhu, bhante, suṭṭhu vuttaṃ, attano vajjaṃ nāma duddasaṃ hoti, punapi maṃ evarūpaṃ disvā vadeyyātha anukampaṃ upādāya, cirassaṃ me tumhākaṃ santikā ovādo laddho”ti vadati, yathānusiṭṭhañca paṭipajjati, so visesādhigamassa avidūre hoti. Tasmā evaṃ parassa vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā karonto subbaco ca assa.

And not only should he be upright and perfectly upright, but he should also be easy to admonish. For a person who, when told, 'This should not be done,' replies, 'What have you seen? What have you heard? Who are you to speak to me? Are you my preceptor? My teacher? A close friend? An intimate companion?'—or who vexes the speaker with silence, or who, having accepted the advice, does not act accordingly—such a one is far from the attainment of distinction. But one who, when being admonished, says, 'Good, venerable sir, well spoken. One’s own fault is indeed hard to see. Again, upon seeing such a thing in me, please speak out of compassion. It has been a long time since I received instruction from you'—and who practices as instructed—such a one is not far from the attainment of distinction. Therefore, by accepting another’s words and acting accordingly, he should be easy to admonish.

Yathā ca suvaco, evaṃ mudu assa. Mudūti gahaṭṭhehi dūtagamanappahiṇagamanādīsu niyuñjiyamāno tattha mudubhāvaṃ akatvā thaddho hutvā vattapaṭipattiyaṃ sakalabrahmacariye ca mudu assa suparikammakatasuvaṇṇaṃ viya tattha tattha viniyogakkhamo. Atha vā mudūti abhākuṭiko uttānamukho sukhasambhāso [M 1.0182] paṭisanthāravutti sutitthaṃ viya sukhāvagāho assa. Na kevalañca mudu, apica pana anatimānī assa, jātigottādīhi atimānavatthūhi pare nātimaññeyya, sāriputtatthero viya caṇḍālakumārakasamena cetasā vihareyyāti.

And just as he is easy to admonish, so should he be gentle. ‘Gentle’ means this: when being engaged by householders for such tasks as running errands or carrying messages, he should not show gentleness in that regard but should be firm; yet in the practice of his duties and in the entire holy life, he should be gentle, like well-refined gold, fit to be used in any way. Or, ‘gentle’ means he is without a frown, has a bright face, is pleasant in conversation, and has a welcoming disposition; he should be easy to approach, like a good river-ford. And not only should he be gentle, but he should also be without conceit. He should not despise others on grounds for conceit such as birth or clan. Like the Elder Sāriputta, he should dwell with a mind that is the same towards even a boy of an outcaste family.

144. Evaṃ bhagavā santaṃ padaṃ abhisamecca viharitukāmassa tadadhigamāya vā paṭipajjamānassa visesato āraññakassa bhikkhuno ekaccaṃ karaṇīyaṃ vatvā puna tatuttaripi vattukāmo “santussako cā”ti dutiyaṃ gāthamāha.

144. Thus the Blessed One, having stated a certain duty for a monk—especially a forest-dwelling monk—who wishes to dwell having comprehended the peaceful state, or who is practicing for its attainment, and then wishing to speak of what is even further, spoke the second verse beginning, 'Contented too...'

Tattha “santuṭṭhī ca kataññutā”ti ettha vuttappabhedena dvādasavidhena santosena santussatīti santussako. Atha vā tussatīti tussako, sakena tussako, santena tussako, samena tussakoti santussako. Tattha sakaṃ nāma “piṇḍiyālopabhojanaṃ nissāyā”ti (mahāva. 73) evaṃ upasampadamāḷake uddiṭṭhaṃ attanā ca sampaṭicchitaṃ catupaccayajātaṃ. Tena sundarena vā asundarena vā sakkaccaṃ vā asakkaccaṃ vā dinnena paṭiggahaṇakāle paribhogakāle ca vikāramadassetvā yāpento “sakena tussako”ti vuccati. Santaṃ nāma yaṃ laddhaṃ hoti attano vijjamānaṃ, tena santeneva tussanto tato paraṃ na patthento atricchataṃ pajahanto “santena tussako”ti vuccati. Samaṃ nāma iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu anunayapaṭighappahānaṃ. Tena samena sabbārammaṇesu tussanto “samena tussako”ti vuccati.

Herein, regarding the phrase 'contentment and gratitude': one is content (santussati) with the twelve kinds of contentment as they have been explained, thus one is called santussako (contented). Alternatively, one is pleased (tussati), thus tussako; santussako means one who is pleased with what is one's own (sakena), pleased with what is available (santena), and pleased with what is balanced (samena). Therein, 'what is one's own' refers to the four kinds of requisites pointed out in the ordination enclosure and accepted by oneself, as in the passage beginning, 'relying on alms-food...' (Mahāvagga 73). One who maintains himself without showing any sign of displeasure at the time of receiving or using them—whether they are fine or coarse, given respectfully or disrespectfully—is called 'one pleased with what is one's own.' 'What is available' means what one has received and what is presently in one's possession. One who is content with just that, not longing for anything more and abandoning excessive desire, is called 'one pleased with what is available.' 'What is balanced' means the abandoning of attraction and aversion towards desirable and undesirable things. One who is pleased in a balanced manner with regard to all objects is called 'one pleased with what is balanced.'

Sukhena bharīyatīti subharo, suposoti vuttaṃ hoti. Yo hi bhikkhu sālimaṃsodanādīnaṃ patte pūretvā dinnepi dummukhabhāvaṃ anattamanabhāvameva ca dasseti, tesaṃ vā sammukhāva taṃ piṇḍapātaṃ [V 1.0161] “kiṃ tumhehi dinna”nti apasādento sāmaṇeragahaṭṭhādīnaṃ deti, esa dubbharo. Etaṃ disvā manussā dūratova parivajjenti “dubbharo bhikkhu na sakkā positu”nti. Yo pana yaṃkiñci lūkhaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā appaṃ vā bahuṃ vā labhitvā attamano vippasannamukho hutvā yāpeti, esa subharo. Etaṃ disvā manussā ativiya vissatthā honti – “amhākaṃ bhadanto subharo thokathokenapi [M 1.0183] tussati, mayameva naṃ posessāmā”ti paṭiññaṃ katvā posenti. Evarūpo idha subharoti adhippeto.

He is easily supported (sukhena bharīyati), thus he is subharo (easy to support); this means he is 'easy to nourish' (suposo). For there is the monk who, even when given a bowl filled with things like fine rice with meat, shows only a sullen face and displeasure; or, right in front of the donors, he disparages the alms-food, saying, 'What is this you have given?' and gives it to novices, householders, or others. Such a one is hard to support (dubbharo). Seeing him, people avoid him from afar, thinking, 'This monk is hard to support; he cannot be nourished.' But there is another monk who, upon receiving anything at all—whether coarse or fine, little or much—maintains himself, pleased at heart and with a serene face. Such a one is easy to support (subharo). Seeing him, people become very trusting and, making a pledge—'Our venerable sir is easy to support; he is satisfied even with a little. We ourselves shall nourish him'—they nourish him. Such a one is intended here by 'easy to support'.

Appaṃ kiccamassāti appakicco, na kammārāmatābhassārāmatāsaṅgaṇikārāmatādianekakiccabyāvaṭo. Atha vā sakalavihāre navakammasaṅghabhogasāmaṇeraārāmikavosāsanādikiccavirahito, attano kesanakhacchedanapattacīvaraparikammādiṃ katvā samaṇadhammakiccaparo hotīti vuttaṃ hoti.

He has few duties (appaṃ kiccamassa), thus he is appakicco (one of few duties); he is not busy with numerous duties such as delighting in work, delighting in talk, or delighting in company. Alternatively, he is free from duties concerning the entire monastery, such as new construction work, managing the Sangha's property, or giving instructions to novices and monastery attendants. Having done his own personal tasks, such as cutting his hair and nails and attending to his bowl and robes, he is devoted to the duties of the ascetic life—this is the meaning.

Sallahukā vutti assāti sallahukavutti. Yathā ekacco bahubhaṇḍo bhikkhu disāpakkamanakāle bahuṃ pattacīvarapaccattharaṇatelaguḷādiṃ mahājanena sīsabhārakaṭibhārādīhi uccārāpetvā pakkamati, evaṃ ahutvā yo appaparikkhāro hoti, pattacīvarādiaṭṭhasamaṇaparikkhāramattameva pariharati, disāpakkamanakāle pakkhī sakuṇo viya samādāyeva pakkamati, evarūpo idha sallahukavuttīti adhippeto. Santāni indriyāni assāti santindriyo, iṭṭhārammaṇādīsu rāgādivasena anuddhatindriyoti vuttaṃ hoti. Nipakoti viññū vibhāvī paññavā, sīlānurakkhaṇapaññāya cīvarādivicāraṇapaññāya āvāsādisattasappāyaparijānanapaññāya ca samannāgatoti adhippāyo.

He has a light livelihood (sallahukā vutti assā), thus he is called one of light livelihood (sallahukavutti). Just as a certain monk with many belongings, when departing for another region, has a large quantity of bowls, robes, bedding, oil, molasses, and so forth, carried by many people as head-loads, waist-loads, and the like, and then departs; not being like that, one who has few requisites, who carries only the measure of the eight monastic requisites such as the bowl and robes, and who, when departing for another region, departs taking them up himself like a winged bird—such a one is intended here as 'one of light livelihood'. He has tranquil faculties (santāni indriyāni assā), thus he is called one with tranquil faculties (santindriyo); it is said that his faculties are unagitated by the power of lust and so forth in regard to desirable objects and the like. 'Nipako' means wise, discerning, and endowed with wisdom; the meaning is that he is endowed with the wisdom of guarding virtue, the wisdom of managing robes and other requisites, and the wisdom of knowing the seven suitable conditions, such as a dwelling.

Na pagabbhoti appagabbho, aṭṭhaṭṭhānena kāyapāgabbhiyena, catuṭṭhānena vacīpāgabbhiyena, anekaṭṭhānena manopāgabbhiyena ca virahitoti attho.

Not insolent (na pagabbho), thus unpresumptuous (appagabbho). The meaning is: devoid of bodily presumption on eight grounds, verbal presumption on four grounds, and mental presumption on many grounds.

Aṭṭhaṭṭhānaṃ kāyapāgabbhiyaṃ (mahāni. 87) nāma saṅghagaṇapuggalabhojanasālājantāgharanhānatitthabhikkhācāramaggaantaragharapavesanesu kāyena appatirūpakaraṇaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ – idhekacco saṅghamajjhe pallatthikāya vā nisīdati, pāde pādamodahitvā vāti evamādi, tathā gaṇamajjhe, gaṇamajjheti catuparisasannipāte, tathā vuḍḍhatare puggale. Bhojanasālāyaṃ pana vuḍḍhānaṃ āsanaṃ na deti, navānaṃ āsanaṃ paṭibāhati, tathā jantāghare. Vuḍḍhe cettha anāpucchā aggijālanādīni karoti. Nhānatitthe ca yadidaṃ “daharo vuḍḍhoti pamāṇaṃ akatvā āgatapaṭipāṭiyā nhāyitabba”nti vuttaṃ[M 1.0184], tampi anādiyanto pacchā āgantvā udakaṃ otaritvā vuḍḍhe ca nave ca bādheti. Bhikkhācāramagge pana aggāsanaaggodakaaggapiṇḍatthaṃ vuḍḍhānaṃ purato purato yāti bāhāya [V 1.0162] bāhaṃ paharanto, antaragharappavesane vuḍḍhānaṃ paṭhamataraṃ pavisati, daharehi kāyakīḷanaṃ karotīti evamādi.

Bodily presumption on eight grounds (Mahāni. 87) is improper bodily conduct in the midst of the Sangha, a group, an individual, a dining hall, a steam-bath house, a bathing place, on the alms-round path, or when entering a household.
