For example: here a certain one sits in the midst of the Sangha with his legs crossed, or with one foot placed on the other, and so forth; likewise in the midst of a group—and by 'in the midst of a group' is meant in an assembly of the fourfold assembly—and likewise in the presence of a more senior individual. In the dining hall, he does not give a seat to the elders and obstructs the new monks from their seats; likewise in the steam-bath house. There, without asking the elders, he does things like lighting the fire. And at the bathing place, disregarding the stated rule that 'one should bathe in the order of arrival, making no distinction between junior and senior,' he arrives later, enters the water, and harasses both the elders and the new monks. On the alms-round path, for the sake of the first seat, the first water, or the first alms-food, he walks ahead of the elders, striking his arm against theirs. When entering a household, he enters before the elders and engages in physical play with the junior monks, and so on.

Catuṭṭhānaṃ vacīpāgabbhiyaṃ nāma saṅghagaṇapuggalaantaragharesu appatirūpavācānicchāraṇaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ – idhekacco saṅghamajjhe anāpucchā dhammaṃ bhāsati, tathā pubbe vuttappakāre gaṇe vuḍḍhatare puggale ca. Tattha manussehi pañhaṃ puṭṭho vuḍḍhataraṃ anāpucchā vissajjeti. Antaraghare pana “itthannāme kiṃ atthi, kiṃ yāgu udāhu khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyaṃ, kiṃ me dassasi, kimajja khādissāmi, kiṃ bhuñjissāmi, kiṃ pivissāmī”ti edamādiṃ bhāsati.

Verbal presumption on four grounds is the uttering of improper speech in the midst of the Sangha, a group, an individual, or within a household. For example: here a certain one speaks the Dhamma in the midst of the Sangha without having asked permission; likewise in a group of the aforementioned type, and in the presence of a more senior individual. There, when asked a question by laypeople, he answers without asking permission from a more senior monk. Within a household, he says such things as: 'So-and-so, what is there? Is it gruel, or is it hard food? What will you give me? What shall I eat today? What shall I consume? What shall I drink?' and so on.

Anekaṭṭhānaṃ manopāgabbhiyaṃ nāma tesu tesu ṭhānesu kāyavācāhi ajjhācāraṃ anāpajjitvāpi manasā eva kāmavitakkādinānappakāraappatirūpavitakkanaṃ.

Mental presumption on many grounds is, in those various situations, even without having committed a transgression with body and speech, to think with the mind alone various kinds of improper thoughts, such as thoughts of sensual desire and so forth.

Kulesvananugiddhoti yāni kulāni upasaṅkamati, tesu paccayataṇhāya vā ananulomiyagihisaṃsaggavasena vā ananugiddho, na sahasokī, na sahanandī, na sukhitesu sukhito, na dukkhitesu dukkhito, na uppannesu kiccakaraṇīyesu attanā vā yogamāpajjitāti vuttaṃ hoti. Imissā ca gāthāya yaṃ “suvaco cassā”ti ettha vuttaṃ “assā”ti vacanaṃ, taṃ sabbapadehi saddhiṃ “santussako ca assa, subharo ca assā”ti evaṃ yojetabbaṃ.

'Not attached to families' (kulesvananugiddho) means that in whatever families one approaches, one is not attached, either through craving for requisites or through unsuitable association with householders. It is said that one is not sorrowful with them, not joyful with them, not happy when they are happy, not pained when they are in pain, nor does one personally apply oneself when their duties and obligations arise. Furthermore, in this stanza, the word 'assa' (he should be), which is stated in the phrase 'suvaco cassa' (and he should be easy to correct), should be connected with all the terms, thus: 'santussako ca assa' (and he should be content), 'subharo ca assā' (and he should be easy to support), and so on.

145. Evaṃ bhagavā santaṃ padaṃ abhisamecca viharitukāmassa tadadhigamāya vā paṭipajjitukāmassa visesato āraññakassa bhikkhuno tatuttaripi karaṇīyaṃ ācikkhitvā idāni akaraṇīyampi ācikkhitukāmo “na ca khuddamācare kiñci, yena viññū pare upavadeyyu”nti imaṃ upaḍḍhagāthamāha. Tassattho – evamimaṃ karaṇīyaṃ karonto yaṃ taṃ kāyavacīmanoduccaritaṃ khuddaṃ lāmakanti vuccati, taṃ na ca khuddaṃ samācare. Asamācaranto ca na kevalaṃ oḷārikaṃ, kiṃ pana kiñci na samācare, appamattakaṃ aṇumattampi na samācareti vuttaṃ hoti.

145. Thus the Blessed One, having explained what is to be done even beyond that for a monk—especially a forest-dweller—who desires to dwell having realized the peaceful state, or who desires to practice for its attainment, now, desiring to explain also what is not to be done, spoke this half-verse: 'And one should not commit any slight wrong for which other wise ones might censure him.' Its meaning is this: While undertaking what is to be done, one should not practice that bodily, verbal, or mental misconduct which is called 'slight' or 'inferior'. And in not practicing it, it is said that one should not practice not only what is gross, but anything whatsoever; one should not practice even the slightest, most minute thing.

Tato [M 1.0185] tassa samācāre sandiṭṭhikamevādīnavaṃ dasseti “yena viññū pare upavadeyyu”nti. Ettha ca yasmā aviññū pare appamāṇaṃ. Te hi anavajjaṃ vā sāvajjaṃ karonti, appasāvajjaṃ vā mahāsāvajjaṃ. Viññū eva pana pamāṇaṃ. Te hi anuvicca pariyogāhetvā avaṇṇārahassa avaṇṇaṃ bhāsanti, vaṇṇārahassa ca vaṇṇaṃ bhāsanti, tasmā “viññū pare”ti vuttaṃ.

Then, with the phrase 'for which other wise ones might censure him,' He shows the immediately visible danger in practicing it. And here, the reason is that other unwise people are no standard. For they make the blameless blameworthy, or what is slightly blameworthy greatly blameworthy. But the wise alone are the standard. For they, having investigated and scrutinized, speak dispraise of one who deserves dispraise and praise of one who deserves praise. Therefore, it was said, 'other wise ones'.

Evaṃ bhagavā imāhi aḍḍhateyyāhi gāthāhi santaṃ padaṃ abhisamecca viharitukāmassa, tadadhigamāya [V 1.0163] vā paṭipajjitukāmassa visesato āraññakassa āraññakasīsena ca sabbesampi kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā viharitukāmānaṃ karaṇīyākaraṇīyabhedaṃ kammaṭṭhānūpacāraṃ vatvā idāni tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ tassa devatābhayassa paṭighātāya parittatthaṃ vipassanāpādakajjhānavasena kammaṭṭhānatthañca “sukhino va khemino hontū”tiādinā nayena mettakathaṃ kathetumāraddho.

Thus the Blessed One, with these two and a half verses, having explained the preliminary practice for the meditation subject—distinguishing between what should and should not be done—for one who desires to dwell having realized the peaceful state, or who desires to practice for its attainment (especially for a forest-dweller, and, taking the forest-dweller as the primary example, for all who desire to dwell having taken up a meditation subject), now began to deliver the discourse on loving-kindness. He did so for those monks in order to dispel the fear caused by that deity, for the purpose of protection, and for the purpose of the meditation subject by means of the absorption that is a basis for insight, in the manner of 'May they be happy and secure,' and so on.

Tattha sukhinoti sukhasamaṅgino. Kheminoti khemavanto, abhayā nirupaddavāti vuttaṃ hoti. Sabbeti anavasesā. Sattāti pāṇino. Sukhitattāti sukhitacittā. Ettha ca kāyikena sukhena sukhino, mānasena sukhitattā, tadubhayenāpi sabbabhayūpaddavavigamena vā kheminoti veditabbā. Kasmā pana evaṃ vuttaṃ? Mettābhāvanākāradassanatthaṃ. Evañhi mettā bhāvetabbā “sabbe sattā sukhino hontū”ti vā, “khemino hontū”ti vā, “sukhitattā hontū”ti vā.

Here, "sukhino" means possessing happiness. "Khemino" means possessing security; that is, being free from fear and calamity. "Sabbe" means without exception. "Sattā" refers to living beings. "Sukhitattā" means happy in mind. And here, with physical happiness they are "sukhino," with mental happiness they are "sukhitattā," and by means of both, or by the removal of all fear and calamity, they are to be understood as "khemino." But why is it said thus? To show the manner of developing loving-kindness. For loving-kindness should be developed thus: "May all beings be happy," or "May they be secure," or "May they be happy-hearted."

146. Evaṃ yāva upacārato appanākoṭi, tāva saṅkhepena mettābhāvanaṃ dassetvā idāni vitthāratopi taṃ dassetuṃ “ye kecī”ti gāthādvayamāha. Atha vā yasmā puthuttārammaṇe paricitaṃ cittaṃ na ādikeneva ekatte saṇṭhāti, ārammaṇappabhedaṃ pana anugantvā kamena saṇṭhāti, tasmā tassa tasathāvarādidukatikappabhede ārammaṇe anugantvā anugantvā saṇṭhānatthampi “ye kecī”ti gāthādvayamāha. Atha vā yasmā yassa yaṃ ārammaṇaṃ vibhūtaṃ hoti, tassa tattha cittaṃ sukhaṃ tiṭṭhati. Tasmā tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ yassa yaṃ vibhūtaṃ ārammaṇaṃ, tassa tattha cittaṃ saṇṭhāpetukāmo tasathāvarādidukattikaārammaṇappabhedadīpakaṃ “ye kecī”ti imaṃ gāthādvayamāha.

146. Thus, having briefly shown the development of loving-kindness from access concentration up to the culmination of absorption, now, to show it in detail as well, he speaks the two verses beginning with "Whatever beings." Alternatively, because a mind accustomed to diverse objects does not settle on a single one right away, but gradually settles by following the distinctions of the object, therefore, for the purpose of settling that mind by repeatedly following the distinctions of the object—such as the twofold and threefold classifications of beings like the trembling and the firm—he speaks the two verses beginning with "Whatever beings." Or, because for whomever a particular object is clear, the mind dwells happily there. Therefore, desiring to establish the minds of those monks wherever their clear object may be, he speaks these two verses illuminating the distinctions of the object, such as the twofold and threefold classifications of beings like the trembling and the firm, beginning with "Whatever beings."

Ettha [M 1.0186] hi tasathāvaradukaṃ diṭṭhādiṭṭhadukaṃ dūrasantikadukaṃ bhūtasambhavesidukanti cattāri dukāni, dīghādīhi ca chahi padehi majjhimapadassa tīsu, aṇukapadassa ca dvīsu tikesu atthasambhavato dīgharassamajjhimattikaṃ mahantāṇukamajjhimattikaṃ thūlāṇukamajjhimattikanti tayo tike dīpeti. Tattha ye kecīti anavasesavacanaṃ. Pāṇā eva bhūtā pāṇabhūtā. Atha vā pāṇantīti pāṇā. Etena assāsapassāsapaṭibaddhe pañcavokārasatte gaṇhāti. Bhavantīti bhūtā. Etena ekavokāracatuvokārasatte gaṇhāti. Atthīti santi, saṃvijjanti.

Here, indeed, are four pairs: the pair of the trembling and the steadfast, the pair of the seen and the unseen, the pair of the far and the near, and the pair of the born and those seeking birth. And by means of the six terms beginning with 'long', it elucidates three triads—the triad of long, short, and medium; the triad of great, subtle, and medium; and the triad of gross, subtle, and medium—since a meaning is possible in the triads by combining with the medium term in three cases and with the subtle term in two. Here, 'whatever' is a term of non-omission. 'Living beings' (pāṇabhūtā) means beings that breathe (pāṇā) are beings (bhūtā). Alternatively, because they breathe (pāṇanti), they are 'pāṇā'. By this, it includes five-constituent beings connected with inhalation and exhalation. Because they have come to be (bhavanti), they are 'bhūtā'. By this, it includes one-constituent and four-constituent beings. 'They are' (atthi) means they exist, they are present.

Evaṃ “ye keci pāṇabhūtatthī”ti iminā vacanena dukattikehi saṅgahetabbe sabbe satte ekajjhaṃ dassetvā idāni sabbepi te tasā vā thāvarā vā anavasesāti iminā dukena saṅgahetvā dasseti.

Thus, having shown all beings who are to be included by the dyads and triads gathered into one by means of the phrase 'whatever living beings there are,' he now shows all of them, without exception, whether trembling or steadfast, included by means of this dyad.

Tattha tasantīti tasā, sataṇhānaṃ sabhayānañcetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tiṭṭhantīti thāvarā, pahīnataṇhābhayānaṃ arahataṃ etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Natthi tesaṃ avasesanti anavasesā, sabbepīti vuttaṃ [V 1.0164] hoti. Yañca dutiyagāthāya ante vuttaṃ, taṃ sabbadukatikehi sambandhitabbaṃ – ye keci pāṇabhūtatthi tasā vā thāvarā vā anavasesā, imepi sabbe sattā bhavantu sukhitattā. Evaṃ yāva bhūtā vā sambhavesī vā imepi sabbe sattā bhavantu sukhitattāti.

Here, 'the trembling' (tasā) means 'those who tremble'; this is a designation for those with craving and fear. 'The steadfast' (thāvarā) means 'those who stand firm'; this is a designation for arahants who have abandoned craving and fear. 'Without remainder' (anavasesā) is so called because nothing of them is left out; this is said to mean 'all'. And what was stated at the end of the second verse should be connected with all the dyads and triads: 'Whatever living beings there are, whether trembling or steadfast, without remainder, may all these beings be happy-minded.' Thus, up to 'whether born or seeking birth, may all these beings be happy-minded.'

Idāni dīgharassamajjhimāditikattayadīpakesu dīghā vātiādīsu chasu padesu dīghāti dīghattabhāvā nāgamacchagodhādayo. Anekabyāmasatappamāṇāpi hi mahāsamudde nāgānaṃ attabhāvā anekayojanappamāṇāpi macchagodhādīnaṃ attabhāvā honti. Mahantāti mahantattabhāvā jale macchakacchapādayo, thale hatthināgādayo, amanussesu dānavādayo. Āha ca – “rāhuggaṃ attabhāvīna”nti (a. ni. 4.15). Tassa hi attabhāvo ubbedhena cattāri yojanasahassāni aṭṭha ca yojanasatāni, bāhū dvādasayojanasataparimāṇā, paññāsayojanaṃ bhamukantaraṃ, tathā aṅgulantarikā, hatthatalāni dve yojanasatānīti. Majjhimāti assagoṇamahiṃsasūkarādīnaṃ attabhāvā. Rassakāti tāsu tāsu jātīsu vāmanādayo dīghamajjhimehi omakappamāṇā sattā. Aṇukāti maṃsacakkhussa [M 1.0187] agocarā, dibbacakkhuvisayā udakādīsu nibbattā sukhumattabhāvā sattā, ūkādayo vā. Apica ye tāsu tāsu jātīsu mahantamajjhimehi thūlamajjhimehi ca omakappamāṇā sattā, te aṇukāti veditabbā. Thūlāti parimaṇḍalattabhāvā macchakummasippikasambukādayo sattā.

Now, in the exposition of the three triads beginning with long, short, and medium, among the six terms beginning with 'long,' etc., 'long' (dīghā) refers to beings with long forms, such as nāgas, fish, and monitor lizards. For in the great ocean, the forms of nāgas can measure many hundreds of fathoms, and the forms of fish, monitor lizards, and others can measure many yojanas. 'Great' (mahantā) refers to beings with great forms, such as fish and turtles in water, elephants and nāgas on land, and dānavas among non-humans. And it is said: 'Rāhu is foremost among those with a body' (AN 4.50). For his body is four thousand eight hundred yojanas in height, his arms measure twelve hundred yojanas, the space between his eyebrows is fifty yojanas, similarly the space between his fingers, and his palms are two hundred yojanas. 'Medium' (majjhimā) refers to the forms of horses, cattle, buffaloes, pigs, etc. 'Short' (rassakā) refers to dwarfs and other beings of lesser size than the long and medium ones in their respective species. 'Subtle' (aṇukā) refers to beings whose subtle forms are not within the range of the physical eye but are within the range of the divine eye, born in water and other such places, or beings such as lice. Furthermore, those beings of lesser size than the great and medium, and the gross and medium, in their respective species, should be understood as 'subtle'. 'Gross' (thūlā) refers to beings with rounded forms, such as fish, tortoises, shellfish, conches, etc.

147. Evaṃ tīhi tikehi anavasesato satte dassetvā idāni “diṭṭhā vā yeva adiṭṭhā”tiādīhi tīhi dukehipi te saṅgahetvā dasseti.

147. Having thus shown beings exhaustively through these three triads, he now shows them included through the three dyads beginning with 'seen or unseen,' etc.

Tattha diṭṭhāti ye attano cakkhussa āpāthamāgatavasena diṭṭhapubbā. Adiṭṭhāti ye parasamuddaparaselaparacakkavāḷādīsu ṭhitā. “Yeva dūre vasanti avidūre”ti iminā pana dukena attano attabhāvassa dūre ca avidūre ca vasante satte dasseti. Te upādāyupādāvasena veditabbā. Attano hi kāye vasantā sattā avidūre, bahikāye vasantā dūre. Tathā antoupacāre vasantā avidūre, bahiupacāre vasantā dūre. Attano vihāre gāme janapade dīpe cakkavāḷe vasantā avidūre, paracakkavāḷe vasantā dūre vasantīti vuccanti.

Here, 'seen' (diṭṭhā) refers to those who have been seen before, having come within the range of one's own eye. 'Unseen' (adiṭṭhā) refers to those dwelling in other oceans, other mountains, other world-systems, etc. By the dyad 'dwelling far or near,' beings dwelling far and near in relation to one's own form are shown. They should be understood by way of what is grasped and ungrasped. For beings dwelling within one's own body are near, while those dwelling outside the body are far. Similarly, those dwelling within one's own vicinity are near, while those dwelling outside one's vicinity are far. Beings dwelling in one's own monastery, village, country, island, or world-system are near, while those dwelling in another world-system are said to be dwelling far.

Bhūtāti jātā, abhinibbattā. Ye bhūtā eva, na puna bhavissantīti saṅkhyaṃ gacchanti, tesaṃ khīṇāsavānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sambhavamesantīti sambhavesī. Appahīnabhavasaṃyojanattā āyatimpi sambhavaṃ esantānaṃ sekkhaputhujjanānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Atha vā catūsu yonīsu aṇḍajajalābujā sattā yāva aṇḍakosaṃ vatthikosañca na bhindanti, tāva sambhavesī nāma. Aṇḍakosaṃ vatthikosañca bhinditvā bahi nikkhantā bhūtā nāma. Saṃsedajā opapātikā ca paṭhamacittakkhaṇe [V 1.0165] sambhavesī nāma. Dutiyacittakkhaṇato pabhuti bhūtā nāma. Yena vā iriyāpathena jāyanti, yāva tato aññaṃ na pāpuṇanti, tāva sambhavesī nāma. Tato paraṃ bhūtāti.

‘Beings’ (bhūtā) means those who are born, who have come into being. Those who are truly ‘beings’ and will not come to be again are thus reckoned; this is a designation for those whose taints are destroyed. ‘Those seeking to become’ (sambhavesī) are so called because they seek to become. Because they have not abandoned the fetter of existence, this is a designation for trainees and ordinary persons who seek to become in the future. Alternatively, among the four kinds of birth, egg-born and womb-born beings are called ‘those seeking to become’ as long as they have not broken the eggshell or the womb-sac. Having broken the eggshell and the womb-sac and emerged, they are called ‘beings’. Moisture-born and spontaneously arisen beings are called ‘those seeking to become’ at the first moment of consciousness. From the second moment of consciousness onwards, they are called ‘beings’. Or, by whatever posture they are born, as long as they have not yet attained another, they are called ‘those seeking to become.’ Thereafter, they are called ‘beings’.

148. Evaṃ bhagavā “sukhino vā”tiādīhi aḍḍhateyyāhi gāthāhi nānappakārato tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ hitasukhāgamapatthanāvasena sattesu mettābhāvanaṃ [M 1.0188] dassetvā idāni ahitadukkhānāgamapatthanāvasenāpi taṃ dassento āha “na paro paraṃ nikubbethā”ti. Esa porāṇapāṭho, idāni pana “paraṃ hī”tipi paṭhanti, ayaṃ na sobhano.

148. Thus, the Blessed One, with the two and a half verses beginning ‘sukhino vā,’ having shown in various ways the cultivation of loving-kindness towards beings by way of wishing for the arrival of their welfare and happiness, now, showing it also by way of wishing for the non-arrival of harm and suffering, said: ‘Let no one deceive another.’ This is the ancient reading, but now some also recite ‘paraṃ hi,’ which is not a good reading.

Tattha paroti parajano. Paranti parajanaṃ. Na nikubbethāti na vañceyya. Nātimaññethāti na atikkamitvā maññeyya. Katthacīti katthaci okāse, gāme vā nigame vā khette vā ñātimajjhe vā pūgamajjhe vātiādi. Nanti etaṃ. Kañcīti yaṃ kañci khattiyaṃ vā brāhmaṇaṃ vā gahaṭṭhaṃ vā pabbajitaṃ vā sugataṃ vā duggataṃ vātiādi. Byārosanā paṭighasaññāti kāyavacīvikārehi byārosanāya ca, manovikārena paṭighasaññāya ca. “Byārosanāya paṭighasaññāyā”ti hi vattabbe “byārosanā paṭighasaññā”ti vuccati yathā “samma daññāya vimuttā”ti vattabbe “samma daññā vimuttā”ti, yathā ca “anupubbasikkhāya anupubbakiriyāya anupubbapaṭipadāyā”ti vattabbe “anupubbasikkhā anupubbakiriyā anupubbapaṭipadā”ti (a. ni. 8.19; udā. 45; cūḷava. 385). Nāññamaññassa dukkhamiccheyyāti aññamaññassa dukkhaṃ na iccheyya. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Na kevalaṃ “sukhino vā khemino vā hontū”tiādi manasikāravaseneva mettaṃ bhāveyya. Kiṃ pana “aho vata yo koci parapuggalo yaṃ kañci parapuggalaṃ vañcanādīhi nikatīhi na nikubbetha, jātiādīhi ca navahi mānavatthūhi katthaci padese yaṃ kañci parapuggalaṃ nātimaññeyya, aññamaññassa ca byārosanāya vā paṭighasaññāya vā dukkhaṃ na iccheyyā”ti evampi manasi karonto bhāveyyāti.

Herein, ‘another’ (paro) means another person. ‘Another’ (paraṃ) means another person. ‘Should not deceive’ (na nikubbetha) means one should not cheat. ‘Should not despise’ (nātimaññetha) means one should not, having overcome them, hold them in contempt. ‘Anywhere’ (katthaci) means in any place, whether in a village, a town, a field, in the midst of relatives, or in the midst of a group, and so on. ‘Them’ (naṃ) means this one. ‘Anyone’ (kañci) means any person whatsoever, whether a khattiya, a brahmin, a householder, one gone forth, one faring well, or one faring ill, and so on. ‘Through provocation and a perception of hostility’ (byārosanā paṭighasaññā) means through provocation by way of bodily and verbal misdeeds, and through a perception of hostility by way of a mental misdeed. For when it should be said ‘byārosanāya paṭighasaññāya’ (by provocation and by a perception of hostility), it is said ‘byārosanā paṭighasaññā,’ just as when it should be said ‘samma-d-aññāya vimuttā’ (liberated through perfect direct knowledge), it is said ‘samma-d-aññā vimuttā’; and just as when it should be said ‘anupubbasikkhāya anupubbakiriyāya anupubbapaṭipadāya’ (through gradual training, through gradual practice, through gradual progress), it is said ‘anupubbasikkhā anupubbakiriyā anupubbapaṭipadā.’ ‘One should not wish for another’s suffering’ (nāññamaññassa dukkhamiccheyya) means one should not wish suffering for one another. What is meant? One should not cultivate loving-kindness merely by way of the reflection, ‘May they be happy, may they be secure,’ and so on. Rather, one should cultivate it by reflecting thus: ‘Oh, may no person whatsoever deceive any other person with cheating and other such wiles! May no one, in any place, despise any other person on account of the nine grounds for conceit, such as birth! And may they not, through provocation or a perception of hostility, wish suffering for one another!’

149. Evaṃ ahitadukkhānāgamapatthanāvasena atthato mettābhāvanaṃ dassetvā idāni tameva upamāya dassento āha “mātā yathā niyaṃ putta”nti.

149. Thus, having shown the cultivation of loving-kindness in terms of its meaning—by way of wishing for the non-arrival of harm and suffering—now, showing that very thing by means of a simile, he said: ‘mātā yathā niyaṃ puttaṃ’ (As a mother her own son).

Tassattho – yathā mātā niyaṃ puttaṃ attani jātaṃ orasaṃ puttaṃ, tañca ekaputtameva āyusā anurakkhe, tassa dukkhāgamapaṭibāhanatthaṃ attano āyumpi cajitvā taṃ anurakkhe, evampi sabbabhūtesu idaṃ mettamānasaṃ bhāvaye, punappunaṃ janaye vaḍḍhaye, tañca aparimāṇasattārammaṇavasena ekasmiṃ vā satte anavasesapharaṇavasena aparimāṇaṃ bhāvayeti.

The meaning of this is: Just as a mother would protect with her life her own son, the son born of her, her own flesh and blood, and an only son at that—protecting him by giving up even her own life in order to ward off the coming of suffering for him—even so, towards all beings should one cultivate this mind of loving-kindness. One should generate it again and again, and increase it. And one should cultivate it as boundless, either by way of taking limitless beings as its object, or by way of pervading a single being without remainder.

150. Evaṃ [M 1.0189][V 1.0166] sabbākārena mettābhāvanaṃ dassetvā idāni tasseva vaḍḍhanaṃ dassento āha “mettañca sabbalokasmī”ti.

150. Thus, having shown the cultivation of loving-kindness in all its aspects, now, showing its development, he said: ‘mettañca sabbalokasmiṃ’ (And loving-kindness toward the entire world).

Tattha mijjati tāyati cāti mitto, hitajjhāsayatāya siniyhati, ahitāgamato rakkhati cāti attho. Mittassa bhāvo mettaṃ. Sabbasminti anavasese. Lokasminti sattaloke. Manasi bhavanti mānasaṃ. Tañhi cittasampayuttattā evaṃ vuttaṃ. Bhāvayeti vaḍḍhaye. Nāssa parimāṇanti aparimāṇaṃ, appamāṇasattārammaṇatāya evaṃ vuttaṃ. Uddhanti upari. Tena arūpabhavaṃ gaṇhāti. Adhoti heṭṭhā. Tena kāmabhavaṃ gaṇhāti. Tiriyanti vemajjhaṃ. Tena rūpabhavaṃ gaṇhāti. Asambādhanti sambādhavirahitaṃ, bhinnasīmanti vuttaṃ hoti. Sīmā nāma paccatthiko vuccati, tasmimpi pavattanti attho. Averanti veravirahitaṃ, antarantarāpi veracetanāpātubhāvavirahitanti vuttaṃ hoti. Asapattanti vigatapaccatthikaṃ. Mettāvihārī hi puggalo manussānaṃ piyo hoti, amanussānaṃ piyo hoti, nāssa koci paccatthiko hoti, tenassa taṃ mānasaṃ vigatapaccatthikattā “asapatta”nti vuccati. Pariyāyavacanañhi etaṃ, yadidaṃ paccatthiko sapattoti. Ayaṃ anupadato atthavaṇṇanā.

Herein, a ‘friend’ (mitto) is one who is affectionate (mijjati) and protects (tāyati). The meaning is that one is affectionate due to an intention for welfare, and one protects from the arrival of what is not welfare. The state of a friend is loving-kindness (mettā). ‘In the entire’ (sabbasmiṃ) means without remainder. ‘World’ (lokasmiṃ) means in the world of beings. ‘Mental’ (mānasaṃ) means it arises in the mind. It is called this because it is associated with consciousness. ‘One should cultivate’ (bhāvaye) means one should develop it. ‘Limitless’ (aparimāṇaṃ) means it has no measure; it is called this because it has limitless beings as its object. ‘Above’ (uddhaṃ) means upwards; by this, one takes in the formless existence. ‘Below’ (adho) means downwards; by this, one takes in the sense-sphere existence. ‘Across’ (tiriyaṃ) means in the middle; by this, one takes in the fine-material existence. ‘Unrestricted’ (asambādhaṃ) means free from constriction; this means it is said to have its boundaries broken. A ‘boundary’ is said to be an enemy; the meaning is that loving-kindness extends even to him. ‘Without enmity’ (averaṃ) means free from enmity; this means it is said to be free from the arising of a hostile intention, even intermittently. ‘Without a rival’ (asapattaṃ) means with adversaries departed. For a person who abides in loving-kindness is dear to human beings and dear to non-human beings; they have no enemy. Therefore, because that mind of theirs is devoid of enemies, it is called ‘without a rival.’ For this is a synonym, that is, ‘enemy’ (paccatthiko) and ‘rival’ (sapatto). This is the explanation of the meaning, word by word.

Ayaṃ panettha adhippetatthavaṇṇanā – yadetaṃ “evampi sabbabhūtesu mānasaṃ bhāvaye aparimāṇa”nti vuttaṃ. Tañcetaṃ aparimāṇaṃ mettaṃ mānasaṃ sabbalokasmiṃ bhāvaye vaḍḍhaye, vuḍḍhiṃ, virūḷhiṃ, vepullaṃ gamaye. Kathaṃ? Uddhaṃ adho ca tiriyañca, uddhaṃ yāva bhavaggā, adho yāva avīcito, tiriyaṃ yāva avasesadisā. Uddhaṃ vā āruppaṃ, adho kāmadhātuṃ, tiriyaṃ rūpadhātuṃ anavasesaṃ pharanto. Evaṃ bhāventopi ca taṃ yathā asambādhaṃ, averaṃ, asapattañca, hoti tathā sambādhaverasapattābhāvaṃ karonto bhāvaye. Yaṃ vā taṃ bhāvanāsampadaṃ pattaṃ sabbattha okāsalābhavasena asambādhaṃ. Attano paresu āghātapaṭivinayena averaṃ, attani ca paresaṃ āghātapaṭivinayena asapattaṃ hoti, taṃ asambādhaṃ averaṃ asapattaṃ aparimāṇaṃ mettaṃ mānasaṃ uddhaṃ adho tiriyañcāti tividhaparicchede sabbalokasmiṃ bhāvaye vaḍḍhayeti.

Herein, this is the explanation of the intended meaning: that which was stated, 'Thus should one develop an immeasurable mind towards all beings.' And that immeasurable mind of loving-kindness should be developed and increased in the entire world; it should be brought to growth, expansion, and abundance. How? Upwards, downwards, and across: upwards as far as the summit of existence, downwards as far as Avīci, and across as far as the remaining directions. Or, pervading the formless realm upwards, the sense-sphere realm downwards, and the form realm across, without remainder. And even while developing it thus, one should cultivate it while making it free from confinement, enmity, and rivalry, so that it becomes unconfined, without enmity, and without rivalry. Or, that which has attained the accomplishment of development is unconfined everywhere by way of gaining the world of space. It is without enmity through the removal of one's own animosity towards others, and it is without rivalry through the removal of others' animosity towards oneself. That unconfined, enmity-free, rivalry-free, immeasurable mind of loving-kindness should be developed and increased in the entire world in its threefold division: upwards, downwards, and across.

151. Evaṃ [M 1.0190] mettābhāvanāya vaḍḍhanaṃ dassetvā idāni taṃ bhāvanamanuyuttassa viharato iriyāpathaniyamābhāvaṃ dassento āha “tiṭṭhaṃ caraṃ…pe… adhiṭṭheyyā”ti.

151. Having thus shown the increase of the development of loving-kindness, now, to show the absence of restriction regarding postures for one who dwells devoted to that development, He said: 'Standing, walking... one should resolve.'

Tassattho – evametaṃ mettaṃ mānasaṃ bhāvento so “nisīdati pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā, ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāyā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.374; ma. ni. 1.107; vibha. 508) viya iriyāpathaniyamaṃ akatvā yathāsukhaṃ aññataraññatarairiyāpathabādhanavinodanaṃ karonto tiṭṭhaṃ vā caraṃ vā nisinno vā sayāno vā yāvatā vigatamiddho assa, atha etaṃ mettājhānassatiṃ adhiṭṭheyya.

Its meaning is this: One who develops such a mind of loving-kindness should, without making a fixed rule for postures as in 'sitting cross-legged, keeping the body upright,' and so on, but instead relieving discomfort in any one or another posture as one pleases—whether standing, walking, sitting, or lying down—for as long as one is free from drowsiness, then establish this mindfulness that is the jhāna of loving-kindness.

Atha [V 1.0167] vā evaṃ mettābhāvanāya vaḍḍhanaṃ dassetvā idāni vasībhāvaṃ dassento āha “tiṭṭhaṃ cara”nti. Vasippatto hi tiṭṭhaṃ vā caraṃ vā nisinno vā sayāno vā yāvatā iriyāpathena etaṃ mettājhānassatiṃ adhiṭṭhātukāmo hoti. Atha vā tiṭṭhaṃ vā caraṃ vāti na tassa ṭhānādīni antarāyakarāni honti, apica kho so yāvatā etaṃ mettājhānassatiṃ adhiṭṭhātukāmo hoti, tāvatā vitamiddho hutvā adhiṭṭhāti, natthi tassa tattha dandhāyitattaṃ. Tenāha “tiṭṭhaṃ caraṃ nisinno va sayāno, yāvatāssa vitamiddho. Etaṃ satiṃ adhiṭṭheyyā”ti.

Alternatively, having thus shown the increase of the development of loving-kindness, now, indicating mastery, He said: 'Standing, walking...' For one who has attained mastery, in whatever posture—whether standing, walking, sitting, or lying down—he wishes to establish this mindfulness that is the jhāna of loving-kindness, he is able to do so. Or, for him, standing or walking and so on are not obstacles; rather, to whatever extent he wishes to establish this mindfulness that is the jhāna of loving-kindness, to that extent, being free from drowsiness, he establishes it. There is no sluggishness for him in this. Therefore, He said: 'Whether standing, walking, sitting, or lying down, for as long as he is free from drowsiness, he should resolve upon this mindfulness.'

Tassāyamadhippāyo – yaṃ taṃ “mettañca sabbalokasmi, mānasaṃ bhāvaye”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ tathā bhāvaye, yathā ṭhānādīsu yāvatā iriyāpathena, ṭhānādīni vā anādiyitvā yāvatā etaṃ mettājhānassatiṃ adhiṭṭhātukāmo assa, tāvatā vitamiddho hutvā etaṃ satiṃ adhiṭṭheyyāti.

This is its intention: That which was stated, 'And one should develop a mind of loving-kindness toward the entire world,' should be developed in such a way that, in any posture such as standing, or without regard to posture, for as long as one may wish to resolve upon this mindfulness that is the jhāna of loving-kindness, for that long, being free from drowsiness, one should resolve upon this mindfulness.

Evaṃ mettābhāvanāya vasībhāvaṃ dassento “etaṃ satiṃ adhiṭṭheyyā”ti tasmiṃ mettāvihāre niyojetvā idāni taṃ vihāraṃ thunanto āha “brahmametaṃ vihāramidhamāhū”ti.

Having thus shown mastery in the development of loving-kindness and, saying, 'one should establish this mindfulness,' having directed one to that abode of loving-kindness, now praising that abode, He said: 'This is called the divine abode here.'

Tassattho – yvāyaṃ “sukhinova khemino hontū”tiādiṃ katvā yāva “etaṃ satiṃ adhiṭṭheyyā”ti saṃvaṇṇito mettāvihāro, etaṃ catūsu dibbabrahmaariyairiyāpathavihāresu niddosattā attanopi paresampi atthakarattā ca idha ariyassa dhammavinaye brahmavihāramāhu, seṭṭhavihāramāhūti. Yato satataṃ samitaṃ abbokiṇṇaṃ tiṭṭhaṃ caraṃ nisinno [M 1.0191] vā sayāno vā yāvatāssa vitamiddho, etaṃ satiṃ adhiṭṭheyyāti.

Its meaning is this: This abiding in loving-kindness, which was described beginning with 'May they be happy and secure' and continuing up to 'he should resolve upon this mindfulness,' is called a divine abiding, a supreme abiding, here in the Dhamma and Discipline of the Noble One because, among the four abodes—the divine, the brahma-like, the noble, and the postural—it is faultless and because it is beneficial to oneself and others. Therefore, constantly, continually, and uninterruptedly, whether standing, walking, sitting, or lying down, for as long as he is free from drowsiness, he should resolve upon this mindfulness.

152. Evaṃ bhagavā tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ nānappakārato mettābhāvanaṃ dassetvā idāni yasmā mettā sattārammaṇattā attadiṭṭhiyā āsannā hoti tasmā diṭṭhigahaṇanisedhanamukhena tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ tadeva mettājhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā ariyabhūmippattiṃ dassento āha “diṭṭhiñca anupaggammā”ti. Imāya gāthāya desanaṃ samāpesi.

152. Thus, the Blessed One, having shown the monks the development of loving-kindness in various ways, now, because loving-kindness, having beings as its object, is close to self-view, therefore, by way of prohibiting the grasping of views, making that very jhāna of loving-kindness the basis for those monks and showing the attainment of the noble stage, He said: 'And not taking up views.' With this verse, He concluded the discourse.

Tassattho – yvāyaṃ “brahmametaṃ vihāramidhamāhū”ti saṃvaṇṇito mettājhānavihāro, tato vuṭṭhāya ye tattha vitakkavicārādayo dhammā, te, tesañca vatthādianusārena rūpadhamme pariggahetvā iminā nāmarūpaparicchedena “suddhasaṅkhārapuñjoyaṃ, na idha sattūpalabbhatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.171) evaṃ diṭṭhiñca anupaggamma anupubbena lokuttarasīlena sīlavā hutvā lokuttarasīlasampayutteneva sotāpattimaggasammādiṭṭhisaṅkhātena dassanena sampanno. Tato paraṃ yopāyaṃ vatthukāmesu gedho kilesakāmo appahīno hoti, tampi sakadāgāmianāgāmimaggehi tanubhāvena anavasesappahānena ca kāmesu gedhaṃ vineyya vinayitvā vūpasametvā na hi jātu gabbhaseyya puna reti [V 1.0168] ekaṃseneva puna gabbhaseyyaṃ na eti, suddhāvāsesu nibbattitvā tattheva arahattaṃ pāpuṇitvā parinibbātīti.

Its meaning is this: Regarding this abiding in the jhāna of loving-kindness praised as 'This they call the divine abiding here,' one emerges from that jhāna. Having comprehended the mental phenomena therein, such as initial and sustained thought, and the material phenomena according to their bases, by means of this delimitation of name-and-form, and not taking up the view that 'This is a mere heap of formations; no being is found here,' one gradually becomes virtuous with supramundane virtue. One becomes endowed with the vision designated as the right view of the stream-entry path, which is itself associated with supramundane virtue. Thereafter, whatever greed for sensual pleasures, the defilement of sensual desire, remains unabandoned, one removes that greed for sensual pleasures through the paths of the once-returner and the non-returner—by way of attenuation and then complete abandonment. Having removed and appeased it, 'he surely never again goes to a womb-bed.' He certainly does not go to a womb-bed again; being reborn in the Pure Abodes and having attained Arahantship right there, he attains final Nibbāna.

Evaṃ bhagavā desanaṃ samāpetvā te bhikkhū āha – “gacchatha, bhikkhave, tasmiṃyeva vanasaṇḍe viharatha. Imañca suttaṃ māsassa aṭṭhasu dhammassavanadivasesu gaṇḍiṃ ākoṭetvā ussāretha, dhammakathaṃ karotha, sākacchatha, anumodatha, idameva kammaṭṭhānaṃ āsevatha, bhāvetha, bahulīkarotha. Tepi vo amanussā taṃ bheravārammaṇaṃ na dassessanti, aññadatthu atthakāmā hitakāmā bhavissantī”ti. Te “sādhū”ti bhagavato paṭissuṇitvā uṭṭhāyāsanā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā, padakkhiṇaṃ katvā, tattha gantvā, tathā akaṃsu. Devatāyo ca “bhadantā amhākaṃ atthakāmā hitakāmā”ti pītisomanassajātā hutvā sayameva senāsanaṃ sammajjanti, uṇhodakaṃ paṭiyādenti, piṭṭhiparikammapādaparikammaṃ karonti, ārakkhaṃ saṃvidahanti. Te bhikkhū tatheva mettaṃ bhāvetvā tameva [M 1.0192] ca pādakaṃ katvā vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā sabbeva tasmiṃyeva antotemāse aggaphalaṃ arahattaṃ pāpuṇitvā mahāpavāraṇāya visuddhipavāraṇaṃ pavāresunti.

Having concluded the teaching, the Blessed One addressed those monks: "Go, monks, dwell in that very grove. And on the eight days for listening to the Dhamma each month, strike the gong, recite this discourse, give Dhamma talks, discuss, rejoice, cultivate this very meditation subject, develop it, and make much of it. Those non-humans will not show you that terrifying spectacle; on the contrary, they will desire your benefit and welfare." Responding "Very well" to the Blessed One, they rose from their seats, paid homage to him, circumambulated him, and went there to do as instructed. The deities, filled with joy and happiness, thinking, "The venerable ones desire our benefit and welfare," themselves swept the lodgings, prepared hot water, attended to the back and foot massages, and arranged for protection. Those monks, having cultivated loving-kindness in the same way and made that their basis, began insight meditation. All of them attained the supreme fruit of arahantship within that very three-month period and, at the great Pavāraṇā, declared their purity.

Evañhi atthakusalena tathāgatena,

Dhammissarena kathitaṃ karaṇīyamatthaṃ;

Katvānubhuyya paramaṃ hadayassa santiṃ,

Santaṃ padaṃ abhisamenti samattapaññā.

Thus indeed, by the Tathāgata, the Lord of the Dhamma, skilled in the goal, was taught what ought to be done; having accomplished this and experienced the supreme peace of the heart, those of perfected wisdom realize the peaceful state.

Tasmā hi taṃ amatamabbhutamariyakantaṃ,

Santaṃ padaṃ abhisamecca viharitukāmo;

Viññū jano vimalasīlasamādhipaññā,

Bhedaṃ kareyya satataṃ karaṇīyamatthanti.

Therefore, a wise person desiring to dwell, having realized that deathless, wondrous, peaceful state, delightful to the noble ones, should constantly perform the task to be done, which is distinguished by stainless virtue, concentration, and wisdom.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya.

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya mettasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the Mettasutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary is concluded.

9. Hemavatasuttavaṇṇanā

9. The Exposition of the Hemavatasutta

Ajja [V 1.0169] pannarasoti hemavatasuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Pucchāvasikā uppatti. Hemavatena hi puṭṭho bhagavā “chasu loko samuppanno”tiādīni abhāsi. Tattha “ajja pannaraso”tiādi sātāgirena vuttaṃ, “iti sātāgiro”tiādi saṅgītikārehi, “kaccimano”tiādi hemavatena, “chasu loko”tiādi bhagavatā, taṃ sabbampi samodhānetvā [P 1.0194] “hemavatasutta”nti vuccati. “Sātāgirisutta”nti ekaccehi.

“Today is the fifteenth”—thus begins the Hemavatasutta. What is its origin? It originates from a question. For when questioned by Hemavata, the Blessed One spoke the verses beginning, “The world has arisen in the six.” Herein, the lines “Today is the fifteenth” and so forth were spoken by Sātāgira; “Thus Sātāgira” and so forth by the compilers of the canon; “I trust your mind” and so forth by Hemavata; and “The world has arisen in the six” and so forth by the Blessed One. All of these are combined and called the “Hemavatasutta.” By some, it is called the “Sātāgirisutta.”

Tattha yāyaṃ “ajja pannaraso”tiādi gāthā. Tassā uppatti – imasmiṃyeva bhaddakappe vīsativassasahassāyukesu purisesu uppajjitvā soḷasavassasahassāyukāni ṭhatvā parinibbutassa bhagavato kassapasammāsambuddhassa mahatiyā pūjāya sarīrakiccaṃ akaṃsu. Tassa dhātuyo avikiritvā [M 1.0193] suvaṇṇakkhandho viya ekagghanā hutvā aṭṭhaṃsu. Dīghāyukabuddhānañhi esā dhammatā. Appāyukabuddhā pana yasmā bahutarena janena adiṭṭhā eva parinibbāyanti, tasmā dhātupūjampi katvā “tattha tattha janā puññaṃ pasavissantī”ti anukampāya “dhātuyo vikirantū”ti adhiṭṭhahanti. Tena tesaṃ suvaṇṇacuṇṇāni viya dhātuyo vikiranti, seyyathāpi amhākaṃ bhagavato.

Herein, this is the origin of the verse beginning “Today is the fifteenth.” In this very auspicious aeon, when the lifespan of human beings was twenty thousand years, the Blessed One Kassapa, the Perfectly Enlightened One, arose and, after living for sixteen thousand years, attained final Nibbāna. They performed the bodily rites for him with great ceremony. His relics did not scatter but remained as a single solid mass, like a block of gold. For this is the nature of long-lived Buddhas. Short-lived Buddhas, however, pass into final Nibbāna unseen by the majority of people. Therefore, out of compassion, thinking, “By performing worship of the relics, people in various places will generate merit,” they resolve, “May the relics scatter.” Because of this, their relics scatter like gold dust, just as with our Blessed One.

Manussā tassa bhagavato ekaṃyeva dhātugharaṃ katvā cetiyaṃ patiṭṭhāpesuṃ yojanaṃ ubbedhena parikkhepena ca. Tassa ekekagāvutantarāni cattāri dvārāni ahesuṃ. Ekaṃ dvāraṃ kikī rājā aggahesi; ekaṃ tasseva putto pathavindharo nāma; ekaṃ senāpatipamukhā amaccā; ekaṃ seṭṭhipamukhā jānapadā rattasuvaṇṇamayā ekagghanā suvaṇṇarasapaṭibhāgā ca nānāratanamayā iṭṭhakā ahesuṃ ekekā satasahassagghanikā. Te haritālamanosilāhi mattikākiccaṃ surabhitelena udakakiccañca katvā taṃ cetiyaṃ patiṭṭhāpesuṃ.

People built a single relic chamber for that Blessed One and established a cetiya one yojana in height and in circumference. It had four gateways, each a gāvuta apart. King Kikī took charge of one gateway; his son, named Pathavindhara, took another; the ministers headed by the general took another; and the people of the district headed by the wealthy merchants took the last. The bricks were of solid red gold, like portions of molten gold, and of various jewels, each worth a hundred thousand. Using orpiment and realgar for mortar and fragrant oil for water, they established that cetiya.

Evaṃ patiṭṭhite cetiye dve kulaputtā sahāyakā nikkhamitvā sammukhasāvakānaṃ therānaṃ santike pabbajiṃsu. Dīghāyukabuddhānañhi sammukhasāvakāyeva pabbājenti, upasampādenti, nissayaṃ [V 1.0170] denti, itare na labhanti. Tato te kulaputtā “sāsane, bhante, kati dhurānī”ti pucchiṃsu. Therā “dve dhurānī”ti kathesuṃ – “vāsadhuraṃ, pariyattidhurañcā”ti. Tattha pabbajitena kulaputtena ācariyupajjhāyānaṃ santike pañca vassāni vasitvā, vattapaṭivattaṃ pūretvā, pātimokkhaṃ dve tīṇi bhāṇavārasuttantāni ca paguṇaṃ [P 1.0195] katvā, kammaṭṭhānaṃ uggahetvā, kule vā gaṇe vā nirālayena araññaṃ pavisitvā, arahattasacchikiriyāya ghaṭitabbaṃ vāyamitabbaṃ, etaṃ vāsadhuraṃ. Attano thāmena pana ekaṃ vā nikāyaṃ pariyāpuṇitvā dve vā pañca vā nikāye pariyattito ca atthato ca suvisadaṃ sāsanaṃ anuyuñjitabbaṃ, etaṃ pariyattidhuranti. Atha te kulaputtā “dvinnaṃ dhurānaṃ vāsadhurameva seṭṭha”nti vatvā “mayaṃ panamhā daharā, vuḍḍhakāle vāsadhuraṃ paripūressāma, pariyattidhuraṃ tāva pūremā”ti pariyattiṃ ārabhiṃsu. Te pakatiyāva paññavanto nacirasseva sakale buddhavacane pakataññano vinaye ca ativiya vinicchayakusalā ahesuṃ. Tesaṃ pariyattiṃ nissāya parivāro uppajji, parivāraṃ nissāya [M 1.0194] lābho, ekamekassa pañcasatapañcasatā bhikkhū parivārā ahesuṃ. Te satthusāsanaṃ dīpentā vihariṃsu, puna buddhakālo viya ahosi.

When the shrine was thus established, two young men of good family, who were friends, went forth and were ordained in the presence of the elders who were direct disciples of the Buddha. For it is only the direct disciples of the long-lived Buddhas who give the going forth, the full ordination, and dependence; others do not receive this. Then those young men of good family asked, “Venerable sirs, how many duties are there in the Dispensation?” The elders replied, “There are two duties: the duty of meditative dwelling and the duty of study.” In this regard, a young man of good family who has gone forth should live in the presence of his teachers and preceptors for five years, fulfill his duties and reciprocal duties, become proficient in the two Pātimokkhas and two or three recitation sections of the Suttas, learn a meditation subject, and then, being without attachment to family or group, enter the wilderness. There he should strive and exert himself for the realization of Arahantship—this is the duty of meditative dwelling. Alternatively, according to one's own ability, one should learn one Nikāya, or two, or five, and then engage with the very clear Dispensation in terms of both the letter and the meaning—this is the duty of study. Then those young men of good family said, “Of the two duties, the duty of meditative dwelling is indeed the best,” but added, “We, however, are young; in our old age we will fulfill the duty of meditative dwelling. For now, let us fulfill the duty of study.” So they began their study. Being wise by nature, before long they became thoroughly acquainted with all the Buddha's words and were exceedingly skilled in making judgments in the Vinaya. Due to their learning, a following arose for them, and due to their following, material gain arose. Each had a retinue of five hundred monks. They lived illuminating the Teacher's Dispensation, and it was as if the time of a Buddha had come again.

Tadā dve bhikkhū gāmakāvāse viharanti dhammavādī ca adhammavādī ca. Adhammavādī caṇḍo hoti pharuso, mukharo, tassa ajjhācāro itarassa pākaṭo hoti. Tato naṃ “idaṃ te, āvuso, kammaṃ sāsanassa appatirūpa”nti codesi. So “kiṃ te diṭṭhaṃ, kiṃ suta”nti vikkhipati. Itaro “vinayadharā jānissantī”ti āha. Tato adhammavādī “sace imaṃ vatthuṃ vinayadharā vinicchinissanti, addhā me sāsane patiṭṭhā na bhavissatī”ti ñatvā attano pakkhaṃ kātukāmo tāvadeva parikkhāre ādāya te dve there upasaṅkamitvā samaṇaparikkhāre datvā tesaṃ nissayena viharitumāraddho. Sabbañca nesaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ karonto sakkaccaṃ vattapaṭivattaṃ pūretukāmo viya akāsi. Tato ekadivasaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā vanditvā tehi vissajjiyamānopi aṭṭhāsiyeva. Therā “kiñci vattabbamatthī”ti taṃ pucchiṃsu. So “āma, bhante, ekena me bhikkhunā saha ajjhācāraṃ paṭicca vivādo atthi. So yadi taṃ vatthuṃ idhāgantvā āroceti, yathāvinicchayaṃ na vinicchinitabba”nti. Therā “osaṭaṃ [P 1.0196] vatthuṃ yathāvinicchayaṃ na vinicchinituṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti āhaṃsu. So “evaṃ kariyamāne, bhante, mama sāsane patiṭṭhā natthi, mayhetaṃ pāpaṃ hotu, mā tumhe vinicchinathā”ti. Te tena nippīḷiyamānā sampaṭicchiṃsu. So tesaṃ paṭiññaṃ gahetvā puna taṃ āvāsaṃ gantvā “sabbaṃ vinayadharānaṃ santike niṭṭhita”nti taṃ dhammavādiṃ suṭṭhutaraṃ avamaññanto pharusena samudācarati. Dhammavādī “nissaṅko ayaṃ jāto”ti tāvadeva nikkhamitvā therānaṃ parivāraṃ bhikkhusahassaṃ upasaṅkamitvā āha [V 1.0171] – “nanu, āvuso, osaṭaṃ vatthu yathādhammaṃ vinicchinitabbaṃ, anosarāpetvā eva vā aññamaññaṃ accayaṃ desāpetvā sāmaggī kātabbā. Ime pana therā neva vatthuṃ vinicchiniṃsu, na sāmaggiṃ akaṃsu. Kiṃ nāmeta”nti? Tepi sutvā tuṇhī ahesuṃ – “nūna kiñci ācariyehi ñāta”nti. Tato adhammavādī okāsaṃ labhitvā “tvaṃ pubbe ‘vinayadharā jānissantī’ti bhaṇasi. Idāni tesaṃ vinayadharānaṃ ārocehi taṃ [M 1.0195] vatthu”nti dhammavādiṃ pīḷetvā “ajjatagge parājito tvaṃ, mā taṃ āvāsaṃ āgacchī”ti vatvā pakkāmi. Tato dhammavādī there upasaṅkamitvā “tumhe sāsanaṃ anapekkhitvā ‘amhe upaṭṭhesi paritosesī’ti puggalameva apekkhittha, sāsanaṃ arakkhitvā puggalaṃ rakkhittha, ajjatagge dāni tumhākaṃ vinicchayaṃ vinicchinituṃ na vaṭṭati, ajja parinibbuto kassapo bhagavā”ti mahāsaddena kanditvā “naṭṭhaṃ satthu sāsana”nti paridevamāno pakkāmi.

At that time, two monks were dwelling in a village residence: a proponent of the Dhamma and a proponent of non-Dhamma. The proponent of non-Dhamma was fierce, rough, and abusive; his transgression was evident to the other. The other monk then charged him, saying, “Friend, this action of yours is unbecoming of the Dispensation.” He deflected it, saying, “What have you seen? What have you heard?” The other replied, “The experts in the Vinaya will know.” Then the proponent of non-Dhamma, realizing, “If the experts in the Vinaya decide this matter, surely I will have no standing in the Dispensation,” and wishing to form his own faction, immediately took his requisites and approached the two elders. He offered them monastic requisites and began to dwell in dependence on them. He attended to all their needs, acting as if he wished to fulfill his duties and reciprocal duties with reverence. Then one day, after attending to them and paying respects, he remained standing even when dismissed. The elders asked him, “Is there something to be said?” He replied, “Yes, venerable sirs. I have a dispute with a certain monk concerning a transgression. If he comes here and reports the matter, it should not be decided according to the rule.” The elders said, “It is not proper not to decide a matter that has been brought up according to the rule.” He insisted, “If this is done, venerable sirs, I will have no standing in the Dispensation. Let that evil be on me; do not you decide it!” Being pressed by him, they consented. Having secured their promise, he returned to that residence and, despising the proponent of the Dhamma even more, treated him harshly, saying, “Everything has been settled in the presence of the experts in the Vinaya.” The proponent of the Dhamma, thinking, “This one has become fearless,” immediately left and approached the elders’ retinue of a thousand monks and said: “Friends, should not a matter that has been brought up be decided according to the Dhamma? Or, without bringing it to a formal hearing, should harmony not be made by having the parties confess their offense to each other? But these elders neither decided the matter nor made harmony. What kind of decision is this?” Hearing this, they too remained silent, thinking, “Surely the teachers must know something.” Then the proponent of non-Dhamma, having found his opportunity, harassed the proponent of the Dhamma, saying, “You said before, ‘The experts in the Vinaya will know.’ Now, report that matter to those experts in the Vinaya!” Then, saying, “From this day forward you are defeated; do not come to this residence!” he departed. Thereupon, the proponent of the Dhamma approached the elders and said, “You, disregarding the Dispensation, considered only the individual, thinking, ‘He served us, he pleased us.’ You protected the individual, not the Dispensation. From this day forward, it is not proper for you to make a judgment. Today, the Blessed One Kassapa has attained Parinibbāna!” Crying out with a loud voice, he departed, lamenting, “The Teacher’s Dispensation is lost!”

Atha kho te bhikkhū saṃviggamānasā “mayaṃ puggalamanurakkhantā sāsanaratanaṃ sobbhe pakkhipimhā”ti kukkuccaṃ uppādesuṃ[P 1.0197]. Te teneva kukkuccena upahatāsayattā kālaṃ katvā sagge nibbattitumasakkontā ekācariyo himavati hemavate pabbate nibbatti hemavato yakkhoti nāmena. Dutiyācariyo majjhimadese sātapabbate sātāgiroti nāmena. Tepi nesaṃ parivārā bhikkhū tesaṃyeva anuvattitvā sagge nibbattitumasakkontā tesaṃ parivārā yakkhāva hutvā nibbattiṃsu. Tesaṃ pana paccayadāyakā gahaṭṭhā devaloke nibbatiṃsu. Hemavatasātāgirā aṭṭhavīsatiyakkhasenāpatīnamabbhantarā mahānubhāvā yakkharājāno ahesuṃ.

Then those monks, with agitated minds, produced remorse, thinking, "While protecting an individual, we have thrown the jewel of the Dispensation into a pit." Their minds being afflicted by that very remorse, they were unable to be reborn in a heavenly world after dying. One teacher was reborn on Hemavata mountain in the Himalayas, by the name of Hemavata the yakkha. The second teacher was reborn in the Middle Country on Sātapabbata mountain, by the name of Sātāgira. And those monks who were their followers, having followed them and also being unable to be reborn in a heavenly world, were reborn as yakkhas in their retinue. Their lay supporters, however, who had provided them with requisites, were reborn in the world of the devas. Hemavata and Sātāgira became yakkha kings of great power among the twenty-eight yakkha commanders.

Yakkhasenāpatīnañca ayaṃ dhammatā – māse māse aṭṭha divasāni dhammavinicchayatthaṃ himavati manosilātale nāgavatimaṇḍape devatānaṃ sannipāto hoti, tattha sannipatitabbanti. Atha sātāgirahemavatā tasmiṃ samāgame aññamaññaṃ disvā sañjāniṃsu – “tvaṃ, samma, kuhiṃ uppanno, tvaṃ kuhi”nti attano attano uppattiṭṭhānañca pucchitvā vippaṭisārino ahesuṃ. “Naṭṭhā mayaṃ, samma, pubbe vīsati vassasahassāni samaṇadhammaṃ katvā ekaṃ pāpasahāyaṃ nissāya yakkhayoniyaṃ uppannā, amhākaṃ pana paccayadāyakā kāmāvacaradevesu nibbattā”ti. Atha sātāgiro āha – “mārisa, himavā nāma acchariyabbhutasammato, kiñci acchariyaṃ disvā vā sutvā vā mamāpi āroceyyāsī”ti. Hemavatopi āha – “mārisa, majjhimadeso nāma acchariyabbhutasammato, kiñci acchariyaṃ disvā vā sutvā vā mamāpi āroceyyāsī”ti. Evaṃ tesu dvīsu sahāyesu aññamaññaṃ katikaṃ katvā, tameva uppattiṃ avivajjetvā vasamānesu ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ vītivattaṃ, mahāpathavī ekayojanatigāvutamattaṃ ussadā.

And this is the custom of the yakkha commanders: every month, for eight days, there is an assembly of devas on the Manosilā plateau in the Himalayas at the Nāgavatī pavilion for the purpose of judging matters of Dhamma. There they must assemble. Then, Sātāgira and Hemavata, seeing each other at that gathering, recognized one another. Having asked about each other's place of rebirth, saying, "Friend, where were you reborn? And you, where?" they became remorseful. "We are lost, friend! Having practiced the ascetic's life for twenty thousand years, we have been reborn in the yakkha realm because we relied on one evil companion. Our supporters who provided requisites, however, have been reborn among the devas of the sense-sphere." Then Sātāgira said, "Friend, the Himalayas are considered wonderful and marvelous. If you see or hear anything wonderful, please tell me also." Hemavata also said, "Friend, the Middle Country is considered wonderful and marvelous. If you see or hear anything wonderful, please tell me also." Thus, while those two friends, having made this agreement with each other, were living on without leaving that state of existence, one Buddha-interval passed, and the great earth rose up by one yojana and three gāvutas.

Athamhākaṃ [M 1.0196][V 1.0172][P 1.0198] bodhisatto dīpaṅkarapādamūle katapaṇidhāno yāva vessantarajātakaṃ, tāva pāramiyo pūretvā, tusitabhavane uppajjitvā, tattha yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā, dhammapadanidāne vuttanayena devatāhi āyācito pañca mahāvilokanāni viloketvā, devatānaṃ ārocetvā, dvattiṃsāya pubbanimittesu vattamānesu idha paṭisandhiṃ aggahesi dasasahassilokadhātuṃ kampetvā. Tāni disvāpi ime rājayakkhā “iminā kāraṇena nibbattānī”ti na jāniṃsu. “Khiḍḍāpasutattā nevāddasaṃsū”ti eke. Esa nayo jātiyaṃ abhinikkhamane bodhiyañca. Dhammacakkappavattane pana pañcavaggiye āmantetvā bhagavati tiparivaṭṭaṃ dvādasākāraṃ varadhammacakkaṃ pavattente mahābhūmicālaṃ pubbanimittaṃ pāṭihāriyāni ca etesaṃ eko sātāgiroyeva paṭhamaṃ addasa. Nibbattikāraṇañca tesaṃ ñatvā sapariso bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamma dhammadesanaṃ assosi, na ca kiñci visesaṃ adhigacchi. Kasmā? So hi dhammaṃ suṇanto hemavataṃ anussaritvā “āgato nu kho me sahāyako, no”ti parisaṃ oloketvā taṃ apassanto “vañcito me sahāyo, yo evaṃ vicitrapaṭibhānaṃ bhagavato dhammadesanaṃ na suṇātī”ti vikkhittacitto ahosi. Bhagavā ca atthaṅgatepi ca sūriye desanaṃ na niṭṭhāpesi.

Then our Bodhisatta, having made his aspiration at the feet of Dīpaṅkara, fulfilled the perfections up to the Vessantara Jātaka. After that, he was reborn in the Tusita abode. Having remained there for the duration of his life, in the manner stated in the Dhammapada Nidāna, he was entreated by the devas. Having surveyed the five great considerations, he announced it to the devas. While the thirty-two premonitory signs were occurring, he took conception here, shaking the ten-thousandfold world-system. Even seeing these signs, these royal yakkhas did not know, 'They have arisen for this reason.' Some say, 'Being absorbed in play, they did not see.' This was the way of things at his birth, his renunciation, and his enlightenment. However, at the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, when the Blessed One addressed the group of five monks and set in motion the noble Wheel of Dhamma, with its three rounds and twelve aspects, of the two yakkhas, Sātāgira alone was the first to see the great earthquake and the premonitory miracles. And knowing the reason for their occurrence, he approached the Blessed One with his retinue and listened to the Dhamma teaching, yet he did not attain any special insight. Why? For while listening to the Dhamma, recollecting Hemavata, he thought, 'Has my friend come or not?' Looking around the assembly and not seeing him, his mind became distracted, thinking, 'My friend has been deprived, who does not hear the Blessed One’s Dhamma teaching of such varied brilliance.' And the Blessed One did not conclude the teaching, even after the sun had set.

Atha sātāgiro “sahāyaṃ gahetvā tena sahāgamma dhammadesanaṃ sossāmī”ti hatthiyānaassayānagaruḷayānādīni māpetvā pañcahi yakkhasatehi parivuto himavantābhimukho pāyāsi, tadā hemavatopi. Yasmā paṭisandhijāti-abhinikkhamana-bodhiparinibbānesveva dvattiṃsa pubbanimittāni hutvāva pativigacchanti, na ciraṭṭhitikāni honti, dhammacakkapavattane pana tāni savisesāni hutvā, cirataraṃ ṭhatvā nirujjhanti, tasmā himavati taṃ acchariyapātubhāvaṃ disvā “yato ahaṃ jāto, na kadāci ayaṃ pabbato evaṃ abhirāmo bhūtapubbo, handa dāni mama sahāyaṃ gahetvā āgamma tena saha imaṃ pupphasiriṃ anubhavissāmī”ti tatheva majjhimadesābhimukho āgacchati. Te ubhopi rājagahassa [P 1.0199] upari samāgantvā aññamaññassa āgamanakāraṇaṃ pucchiṃsu. Hemavato āha – “yato ahaṃ, mārisa, jāto, nāyaṃ pabbato evaṃ akālakusumitehi rukkhehi abhirāmo bhūtapubbo, tasmā etaṃ pupphasiriṃ tayā saddhiṃ anubhavissāmīti āgatomhī”ti[M 1.0197]. Sātāgiro āha – “jānāsi, pana, tvaṃ mārisa, yena kāraṇena imaṃ akālapupphapāṭihāriyaṃ jāta”nti? “Na jānāmi, mārisā”ti. “Imaṃ, mārisa, pāṭihāriyaṃ na kevala himavanteyeva, apica kho pana dasasahassilokadhātūsu nibbattaṃ, sammāsambuddho loke uppanno, ajja dhammacakkaṃ pavattesi, tena kāraṇenā”ti. Evaṃ sātāgiro hemavatassa buddhuppādaṃ kathetvā, taṃ bhagavato santikaṃ ānetukāmo imaṃ gāthamāha. Keci pana gotamake cetiye viharante bhagavati ayamevamāhāti bhaṇanti “ajja pannaraso”ti.

Then Sātāgira, thinking, 'Taking my friend, I will go with him and listen to the teaching of the Dhamma,' having conjured elephant-vehicles, horse-vehicles, Garuḷa-vehicles, and so on, and surrounded by five hundred yakkhas, set out towards the Himālaya. At that time, Hemavata also... Because the thirty-two premonitory signs appear only at the moments of conception, birth, renunciation, enlightenment, and Parinibbāna, and then vanish—they do not last long. However, at the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, these signs appear with special distinction, remain for a longer time, and then cease. Therefore, seeing this marvelous manifestation in the Himālaya, Hemavata thought, 'Since I was born, this mountain has never been so delightful. Come now, I will take my friend and go to enjoy this floral splendor together with him.' Thus, he too set out towards the Middle Country. The two met above Rājagaha and asked each other the reason for their coming. Hemavata said, 'Friend, since I was born, this mountain has never been so beautifully adorned with trees flowering out of season. Therefore, I have come to enjoy this floral splendor with you.' Sātāgira replied, 'But do you know, friend, the reason why this miraculous display of unseasonal flowers has occurred?' 'I do not know, friend,' said Hemavata. 'Friend, this miracle has appeared not only in the Himālaya but throughout the ten-thousandfold world-system. A Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddha has arisen in the world, and today he has set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma. That is the reason.' Thus, Sātāgira explained to Hemavata about the arising of the Buddha and, wishing to bring him to the presence of the Blessed One, spoke this verse. Some, however, say that when the Blessed One was dwelling at the Gotamaka Shrine, he himself spoke thus: 'Today is the fifteenth.'

153. Tattha [V 1.0173] ajjāti ayaṃ rattindivo pakkhagaṇanato pannaraso, upavasitabbato uposatho. Tīsu vā uposathesu ajja pannaraso uposatho, na cātuddasī uposatho, na sāmaggīuposatho. Yasmā vā pātimokkhuddesaaṭṭhaṅgaupavāsapaññattidivasādīsu sambahulesu atthesu uposathasaddo vattati. “Āyāmāvuso, kappina, uposathaṃ gamissāmā”tiādīsu hi pātimokkhuddese uposathasaddo. “Evaṃ aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgato kho visākhe uposatho upavuttho”tiādīsu (a. ni. 8.43) pāṇātipātā veramaṇiādikesu aṭṭhaṅgesu. “Suddhassa ve sadā phaggu, suddhassuposatho sadā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.79) upavāse. “Uposatho nāma nāgarājā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.246; ma. ni. 3.258) paññattiyaṃ. “Tadahuposathe pannarase sīsaṃnhātassā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 3.85; ma. ni. 3.256) divase. Tasmā avasesatthaṃ paṭikkhipitvā āsāḷhīpuṇṇamadivasaṃyeva niyāmento āha – “ajja pannaraso uposatho”ti. Pāṭipado dutiyoti evaṃ gaṇiyamāne ajja pannaraso divasoti attho.

153. Herein, 'today' (ajja) means this day and night is the fifteenth, reckoned by the fortnightly count, and it is the Uposatha because it is to be observed (upavasitabba). Or, among the three kinds of Uposatha, today is the fifteenth Uposatha; it is not the fourteenth Uposatha, nor the Uposatha of harmony. For the word 'Uposatha' is used in many senses, such as the recitation of the Pātimokkha, the eight-factored observance, fasting, a designation, a day, and so on. For instance, in statements like, 'Come, friend Kappina, let us go to the Uposatha,' the word 'Uposatha' refers to the recitation of the Pātimokkha. In statements like, 'Visākha, the Uposatha observed is endowed with eight factors,' it refers to the eight factors beginning with abstaining from the destruction of life. In statements like, 'For the pure, every day is indeed Phaggu; for the pure, every day is Uposatha,' it refers to fasting. In statements like, 'Uposatha is the name of a Nāga king,' it refers to a designation. In statements like, 'On that Uposatha, the fifteenth day, after washing his head,' it refers to a day. Therefore, having excluded the other meanings and specifically referring to the full moon day of Āsāḷhī, he says, 'Today is the fifteenth Uposatha.' When counting thus, 'the first day, the second day,' the meaning is that today is the fifteenth day.

Divi bhavāni dibbāni, dibbāni ettha atthīti dibbā. Kāni tāni? Rūpāni. Tañhi [P 1.0200] rattiṃ devānaṃ dasasahassilokadhātuto sannipatitānaṃ sarīravatthābharaṇavimānappabhāhi abbhādiupakkilesavirahitāya candappabhāya ca sakalajambudīpo alaṅkato ahosi. Visesālaṅkato ca paramavisuddhidevassa bhagavato sarīrappabhāya. Tenāha “dibbā ratti upaṭṭhitā”ti.

That which is in heaven (divi) is divine (dibbāni); because divine things are present here, the night is called 'divine.' What are those things? Forms. For on that night, the gods having assembled from the ten-thousandfold world-system, the entire Jambudīpa was adorned with the radiance of their bodies, garments, ornaments, and celestial mansions, and with the moonlight, free from impurities such as clouds. And it was especially adorned by the bodily radiance of the Blessed One, the supremely pure deity. Therefore, it is said: 'The divine night has arrived.'

Evaṃ [M 1.0198] rattiguṇavaṇṇanāpadesenāpi sahāyassa cittappasādaṃ janento buddhuppādaṃ kathetvā āha “anomanāmaṃ satthāraṃ, handa passāma gotama”nti. Tattha anomehi alāmakehi sabbākāraparipūrehi guṇehi nāmaṃ assāti anomanāmo. Tathā hissa “bujjhitā saccānīti buddho, bodhetā pajāyāti buddho”tiādinā (mahāni. 192; cūḷani. pārāyanatthutigāthāniddesa 97; paṭi. ma. 1.162) nayena buddhoti anomehi guṇehi nāmaṃ, “bhaggarāgoti bhagavā, bhaggadosoti bhagavā”tiādinā (mahāni. 84) nayena ca anomehi guṇehi nāmaṃ. Esa nayo “arahaṃ sammāsambuddho vijjācaraṇasampanno”tiādīsu. Diṭṭhadhammikādīsu atthesu devamanusse anusāsati “imaṃ pajahatha, imaṃ samādāya vattathā”ti satthā. Apica “satthā bhagavā satthavāho, yathā satthavāho satte kantāraṃ tāretī”tiādinā (mahāni. 190) niddese vuttanayenāpi satthā. Taṃ anomanāmaṃ satthāraṃ. Handāti byavasānatthe nipāto. Passāmāti tena attānaṃ saha saṅgahetvā paccuppannavacanaṃ. Gotamanti gotamagottaṃ. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti[V 1.0174]? “Satthā, na satthā”ti mā vimatiṃ akāsi, ekantabyavasito hutvāva ehi passāma gotamanti.

Thus, by means of describing the qualities of the night, generating confidence in his companion's mind and having spoken of the arising of the Buddha, he said, 'The Teacher of peerless name—come, let us see Gotama.' Herein, 'of peerless name' (anomanāmo) means his name is endowed with peerless (anoma), faultless, and perfectly complete qualities. For indeed, his name 'Buddha' is endowed with peerless qualities, according to the method: 'He has awakened to the truths, thus he is the Buddha; he awakens beings, thus he is the Buddha.' Similarly, his name 'Bhagavā' is endowed with peerless qualities, according to the method: 'He has destroyed lust (bhagga-rāgo), thus he is the Bhagavā; he has destroyed hatred (bhagga-doso), thus he is the Bhagavā.' This same method should be understood for terms like 'Arahant, Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, accomplished in knowledge and conduct,' and so on. He is the Teacher (Satthā) because he instructs gods and humans in matters pertaining to this life and beyond, saying, 'Abandon this; undertake this and practice.' Moreover, as stated in the Niddesa, the Blessed One is the Teacher (Satthā) because he is a caravan leader (satthavāho), just as a caravan leader guides beings across a wilderness. That is the Teacher of peerless name. 'Come' (handa) is a particle in the sense of resolve. 'Let us see' (passāma) is a present-tense verb, including himself with the other. 'Gotama' refers to the Gotama clan. What is meant by this? 'Do not have the doubt, "Is he the Teacher or not?" Being fully resolved, come! Let us see Gotama.'

154. Evaṃ vutte hemavato “ayaṃ sātāgiro ‘anomanāmaṃ satthāra’nti bhaṇanto tassa sabbaññutaṃ pakāseti, sabbaññuno ca dullabhā loke, sabbaññupaṭiññehi pūraṇādisadiseheva loko upadduto. So pana yadi sabbaññū, addhā tādilakkhaṇappatto bhavissati, tena taṃ evaṃ pariggaṇhissāmī”ti cintetvā tādilakkhaṇaṃ pucchanto āha – “kacci mano”ti.

154. When this was said, Hemavata thought: "This Sātāgira, by saying, 'The Teacher of peerless name,' proclaims his omniscience. Omniscient ones are rare in the world, and the world is afflicted by those like Pūraṇa and others who profess omniscience. But if he is truly omniscient, assuredly he will have attained the characteristics of one who is 'such.' Therefore, I will examine him thus." Thinking thus, and asking about the characteristics of one who is 'such,' he said: 'Is the mind...?'

Tattha kaccīti pucchā. Manoti cittaṃ. Supaṇihitoti suṭṭhu ṭhapito, acalo asampavedhī. Sabbesu bhūtesu sabbabhūtesu. Tādinoti tādilakkhaṇappattasseva [P 1.0201] sato. Pucchā eva vā ayaṃ “so te satthā sabbabhūtesu tādī, udāhu no”ti. Iṭṭhe aniṭṭhe cāti evarūpe ārammaṇe. Saṅkappāti vitakkā. Vasīkatāti vasaṃ gamitā. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yaṃ tvaṃ satthāraṃ vadasi, tassa te satthuno kacci tādilakkhaṇappattassa sato sabbabhūtesu mano supaṇihito, udāhu yāva calanapaccayaṃ na labhati, tāva supaṇihito viya khāyati. So vā te satthā kacci sabbabhūtesu samacittena tādī, udāhu no, ye ca kho iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu [M 1.0199] ārammaṇesu rāgadosavasena saṅkappā uppajjeyyuṃ, tyāssa kacci vasīkatā, udāhu kadāci tesampi vasena vattatīti.

Herein, 'kacci' is a particle of interrogation. 'Mano' means mind. 'Supaṇihito' means well-established, unmoving, undisturbed. 'Sabbesu bhūtesu' refers to all beings. 'Tādī' means one who is steadfast, one who has attained the characteristic of steadfastness. Or this is simply a question: 'Is your teacher steadfast towards all beings, or not?' 'Iṭṭhe aniṭṭhe ca' refers to agreeable and disagreeable objects. 'Saṅkappā' means thoughts, or deliberations. 'Vasīkatā' means brought under control. What is meant? When you speak of your teacher, is his mind, being one who has attained the characteristic of steadfastness, well-established towards all beings, or does it only appear well-established until it encounters a condition for wavering? Or is your teacher steadfast with an even mind towards all beings, or not? And when thoughts of desire and aversion arise towards agreeable and disagreeable objects, are those thoughts under his control, or does he sometimes act under their influence?

155. Tato sātāgiro bhagavato sabbaññubhāve byavasitattā sabbe sabbaññuguṇe anujānanto āha “mano cassa supaṇihito”tiādi. Tattha supaṇihitoti suṭṭhu ṭhapito, pathavīsamo avirujjhanaṭṭhena, sinerusamo suppatiṭṭhitācalanaṭṭhena, indakhīlasamo catubbidhamāraparavādigaṇehi akampiyaṭṭhena. Anacchariyañcetaṃ, bhagavato idāni sabbākārasampannattā sabbaññubhāve ṭhitassa mano supaṇihito acalo bhaveyya. Yassa tiracchānabhūtassāpi sarāgādikāle chaddantanāgakule uppannassa savisena sallena viddhassa acalo ahosi, vadhakepi tasmiṃ nappadussi, aññadatthu tasseva attano dante chetvā adāsi; tathā mahākapibhūtassa mahatiyā silāya sīse pahaṭassāpi tasseva ca maggaṃ dassesi; tathā vidhurapaṇḍitabhūtassa pādesu gahetvā saṭṭhiyojane kāḷapabbatapapāte pakkhittassāpi aññadatthu tasseva yakkhassatthāya dhammaṃ desesi. Tasmā sammadeva āha sātāgiro – “mano cassa supaṇihito”ti.

155. Then Sātāgira, having ascertained the Blessed One’s omniscience and approving of all the qualities of an omniscient one, said: 'His mind is well-established,' and so on. Here, 'supaṇihito' means well-established: like the earth in its non-resistance; like Mount Meru in its firmly established immovability; like an Indakhīla pillar in its unshakeability by the fourfold Māras and opposing disputants. And this is not surprising, for the Blessed One, now perfect in all aspects and established in omniscience, his mind would be well-established and unmoving. Even when he was an animal—in a time when he still had passion and so on, born into the Chaddanta elephant clan—though struck by a poisoned arrow, he remained unmoving. He bore no malice toward the hunter; on the contrary, he broke off his own tusks and gave them to him. Similarly, when he was a great monkey, though his head was struck with a large rock, he still showed the way to that very person. Likewise, when he was the wise Vidhura, though seized by the feet and thrown into the sixty-yojana-deep precipice of the Kāḷa Mountain, he on the contrary taught the Dhamma for the sake of that very yakkha. Therefore, Sātāgira rightly said: 'His mind is well-established.'

Sabbabhūtesu [V 1.0175] tādinoti sabbasattesu tādilakkhaṇappattasseva sato mano supaṇihito, na yāva paccayaṃ na labhatīti attho[P 1.0202]. Tattha bhagavato tādilakkhaṇaṃ pañcadhā veditabbaṃ. Yathāha –

Regarding 'steadfast towards all beings': this means that the mind of one who possesses the characteristic of steadfastness is well-established towards all beings, not just for as long as a cause for wavering is not encountered. Herein, the Blessed One’s characteristic of steadfastness should be understood in five ways, as it is said:

“Bhagavā pañcahākārehi tādī, iṭṭhāniṭṭhe tādī, cattāvīti tādī, muttāvīti tādī, tiṇṇāvīti tādī, tanniddesāti tādī. Kathaṃ bhagavā iṭṭhāniṭṭhe tādī? Bhagavā lābhepi tādī”ti (mahāni. 38).

The Blessed One is steadfast in five ways: he is steadfast in the face of the agreeable and disagreeable; he is steadfast as one who has abandoned; he is steadfast as one who is liberated; he is steadfast as one who has crossed over; and he is steadfast in that he can explain it. How is the Blessed One steadfast in the face of the agreeable and disagreeable? The Blessed One is steadfast even in gain... (Mahāniddesa 38).

Evamādi sabbaṃ niddese vuttanayeneva gahetabbaṃ. Lābhādayo ca tassa mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vitthāritanayena veditabbā. “Pucchā eva vā ayaṃ. So te satthā sabbabhūtesu tādī, udāhu no”ti imasmimpi vikappe sabbabhūtesu samacittatāya tādī amhākaṃ satthāti attho. Ayañhi bhagavā sukhūpasaṃhārakāmatāya dukkhāpanayanakāmatāya ca sabbasattesu samacitto, yādiso attani, tādiso paresu, yādiso [M 1.0200] mātari mahāmāyāya, tādiso ciñcamāṇavikāya, yādiso pitari suddhodane, tādiso suppabuddhe, yādiso putte rāhule, tādiso vadhakesu devadattadhanapālakaaṅgulimālādīsu. Sadevake lokepi tādī. Tasmā sammadevāha sātāgiro – “sabbabhūtesu tādino”ti.

All such points should be understood in the manner explained in the Niddesa. And terms like 'gain' should be understood in detail as expounded in the Great Commentary. In the alternative interpretation, 'Is this indeed a question: Is your Teacher steadfast toward all beings, or not?', the meaning is that our Teacher is steadfast toward all beings due to his equal-mindedness. For this Blessed One is even-minded toward all beings, desiring to bring about happiness and to remove suffering. As he is toward himself, so he is toward others; as he is toward his mother, Mahāmāyā, so he is toward Ciñcamāṇavikā; as he is toward his father, Suddhodana, so he is toward Suppabuddha; as he is toward his son, Rāhula, so he is toward the murderers Devadatta, Dhanapāla, Aṅgulimāla, and others. He is steadfast even toward the world with its devas. Therefore, Sātāgira rightly declared: 'steadfast toward all beings.'

Atho iṭṭhe aniṭṭhe cāti. Ettha pana evaṃ attho daṭṭhabbo – yaṃ kiñci iṭṭhaṃ vā aniṭṭhaṃ vā ārammaṇaṃ, sabbappakārehi tattha ye rāgadosavasena saṅkappā uppajjeyyuṃ, tyāssa anuttarena maggena rāgādīnaṃ pahīnattā vasīkatā, na kadāci tesaṃ vase vattati. So hi bhagavā anāvilasaṅkappo suvimuttacitto suvimuttapaññoti. Ettha ca supaṇihitamanatāya ayonisomanasikārābhāvo vutto. Sabbabhūtesu iṭṭhāniṭṭhehi so yattha bhaveyya, taṃ sattasaṅkhārabhedato duvidhamārammaṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Saṅkappavasībhāvena tasmiṃ ārammaṇe tassa manasikārābhāvato kilesappahānaṃ vuttaṃ. Supaṇihitamanatāya ca manosamācārasuddhi, sabbabhūtesu tāditāya kāyasamācārasuddhi, saṅkappavasībhāvena vitakkamūlakattā vācāya vacīsamācārasuddhi. Tathā supaṇihitamanatāya lobhādisabbadosābhāvo[P 1.0203], sabbabhūtesu tāditāya mettādiguṇasabbhāvo, saṅkappavasībhāvena paṭikūle appaṭikūlasaññitādibhedā ariyiddhi, tāya cassa sabbaññubhāvo vutto hotīti veditabbo.

Furthermore, regarding 'in the agreeable and disagreeable.' Here, the meaning should be understood thus: whatever object there may be, whether agreeable or disagreeable, in all its aspects, any thoughts that might arise there due to lust or hatred have been brought under his control, because defilements such as lust have been abandoned through the unsurpassed path; he never comes under their sway. For that Blessed One is one whose thoughts are untainted, whose mind is well liberated, and whose wisdom is well liberated. Herein, the absence of unwise attention is stated by way of his mind being well-established. The agreeable and disagreeable things that may exist in relation to all beings—that object is spoken of as twofold, distinguished as beings and formations. Because he is master of his thoughts, the abandoning of defilements is stated by way of the absence of his mental engagement with that object. Through his mind being well-established, purity of mental conduct is stated; through his steadfastness toward all beings, purity of bodily conduct is stated; and because he is master of his thoughts, which are rooted in thinking, purity of verbal conduct is stated. Likewise, through his mind being well-established, the absence of all faults such as greed is stated; through his steadfastness toward all beings, the presence of qualities like loving-kindness is stated; and because he is master of his thoughts, the noble power, of which perceiving the repulsive as non-repulsive is one type, is stated. And through that, his omniscience is declared to be stated—thus it should be understood.

156. Evaṃ hemavato pubbe manodvāravaseneva tādibhāvaṃ pucchitvā tañca paṭijānantamimaṃ sutvā daḷhīkammatthaṃ idāni dvārattayavasenāpi, pubbe vā saṅkhepena kāyavacīmanodvārasuddhiṃ pucchitvā tañca paṭijānantamimaṃ sutvā daḷhīkammatthameva vitthārenāpi pucchanto [V 1.0176] āha “kacci adinna”nti. Tattha gāthābandhasukhatthāya paṭhamaṃ adinnādānaviratiṃ pucchati. Ārā pamādamhāti pañcasu kāmaguṇesu cittavossaggato dūrībhāvena abrahmacariyaviratiṃ pucchati. “Ārā pamadamhā”tipi paṭhanti, ārā mātugāmāti vuttaṃ hoti. Jhānaṃ na riñcatīti iminā pana tassāyeva tividhāya kāyaduccaritaviratiyā balavabhāvaṃ pucchati. Jhānayuttassa hi virati balavatī hotīti.

156. Thus Hemavata, having previously asked about the state of being 'such' by way of the mind-door alone and having heard his acknowledgement, now for the sake of making it firm, asks also by way of the three doors. Or, having previously asked briefly about the purity of the doors of body, speech, and mind and having heard his acknowledgement, for the very sake of making it firm, wishing to ask in detail, he said: 'I hope he does not take what is not given?' Therein, for the sake of ease in composing the verse, he first asks about abstinence from taking what is not given. By 'Far from negligence,' he asks about abstinence from unchastity, through being far from the mind's release upon the five strands of sensual pleasure. They also read the text as 'Far from women,' which is to say, 'far from womenfolk.' By 'He does not forsake jhāna,' he asks about the strength of that very threefold abstinence from bodily misconduct. For the abstinence of one endowed with jhāna is indeed strong.

157. Atha [M 1.0201] sātāgiro yasmā bhagavā na kevalaṃ etarahi, atītepi addhāne dīgharattaṃ adinnādānādīhi paṭivirato, tassā tassāyeva ca viratiyā ānubhāvena taṃ taṃ mahāpurisalakkhaṇaṃ paṭilabhi, sadevako cassa loko “adinnādānā paṭivirato samaṇo gotamo”tiādinā nayena vaṇṇaṃ bhāsati. Tasmā vissaṭṭhāya vācāya sīhanādaṃ nadanto āha “na so adinnaṃ ādiyatī”ti. Taṃ atthato pākaṭameva. Imissāpi gāthāya tatiyapāde “pamādamhā pamadamhā”ti dvidhā pāṭho. Catutthapāde ca jhānaṃ na riñcatīti jhānaṃ rittakaṃ suññakaṃ na karoti, na pariccajatīti attho veditabbo.

157. Then Sātāgira, because the Blessed One not only now but also in past times has for a long time abstained from taking what is not given and so on, and through the power of that very abstinence has obtained the various marks of a Great Man, and the world with its devas proclaims his praise, saying, 'The ascetic Gotama abstains from taking what is not given,' therefore, uttering a lion’s roar with unhesitating speech, he says, 'He does not take what is not given.' The meaning of that is self-evident. In the third line of this verse also, there are two readings for the phrase. In the fourth line, 'he does not forsake jhāna' means he does not make jhāna empty or void, he does not abandon it—this is the meaning to be understood.

158. Evaṃ kāyadvāre suddhiṃ sutvā idāni vacīdvāre suddhiṃ pucchanto [P 1.0204] āha – “kacci musā na bhaṇatī”ti. Ettha khīṇātīti khīṇo, vihiṃsati badhatīti attho. Vācāya patho byappatho, khīṇo byappatho assāti khīṇabyappatho. Taṃ na-kārena paṭisedhetvā pucchati “na khīṇabyappatho”ti, na pharusavācoti vuttaṃ hoti. “Nākhīṇabyappatho”tipi pāṭho, na akhīṇavacanoti attho. Pharusavacanañhi paresaṃ hadaye akhīyamānaṃ tiṭṭhati. Tādisavacano kacci na soti vuttaṃ hoti. Vibhūtīti vināso, vibhūtiṃ kāsati karoti vāti vibhūtikaṃ, vibhūtikameva vebhūtikaṃ, vebhūtiyantipi vuccati, pesuññassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tañhi sattānaṃ aññamaññato bhedanena vināsaṃ karoti. Sesaṃ uttānatthameva.

158. Having thus heard about purity in the body-door, now, questioning about purity in the speech-door, he said: 'I hope he does not speak falsely?'
