Herein, `khīṇa` means 'harsh'; the meaning is 'it harms, it oppresses.' `Byappatho` is a path of speech; `khīṇabyappatho` is one who has a harsh path of speech. Negating this with the particle `na`, he asks: `na khīṇabyappatho`? This means, 'Is he not one of harsh speech?' There is also the reading `nākhīṇabyappatho`, which means 'he is not one of imperishable speech.' For harsh speech remains in the hearts of others without perishing. This is to say, 'I hope he is not one who speaks in such a way.' `Vibhūti` is destruction; `vibhūtikaṃ` is what causes destruction. `Vibhūtikaṃ` itself is `vebhūtikaṃ`, which is also called `vebhūtiyaṃ`. This is a synonym for slander. For it causes the destruction of beings by creating division among them. The rest has an obvious meaning.

159. Atha sātāgiro yasmā bhagavā na kevalaṃ etarahi, atītepi addhāne dīgharattaṃ musāvādādīhi paṭivirato, tassā tassāyeva ca viratiyā ānubhāvena taṃ taṃ mahāpurisalakkhaṇaṃ paṭilabhi, sadevako cassa loko “musāvādā paṭivirato samaṇo gotamo”ti vaṇṇaṃ bhāsati. Tasmā vissaṭṭhāya vācāya sīhanādaṃ nadanto āha, “musā ca so na bhaṇatī”ti. Tattha musāti vinidhāya diṭṭhādīni paravisaṃvādanavacanaṃ. Taṃ so na bhaṇati. Dutiyapāde pana paṭhamatthavasena na khīṇabyappathoti, dutiyatthavasena nākhīṇabyappathoti pāṭho. Catutthapāde mantāti paññā vuccati. Bhagavā yasmā tāya mantāya paricchinditvā atthameva [V 1.0177] bhāsati atthato anapetavacanaṃ, na samphaṃ[M 1.0202]. Aññāṇapurekkhārañhi niratthakavacanaṃ buddhānaṃ natthi. Tasmā āha – “mantā atthaṃ so bhāsatī”ti. Sesamettha pākaṭameva.

159. Then Sātāgira, because the Blessed One not only now but also in past times has for a long time abstained from false speech and so on, and by the power of that very abstinence has obtained the various marks of a Great Man, and the world with its devas proclaims his praise, saying, 'The ascetic Gotama abstains from false speech,' therefore, uttering a lion’s roar with unhesitating speech, he said, 'And he does not speak falsely.' Herein, 'false' means speech that deceives others by misrepresenting what has been seen and so on. He does not speak it. In the second line, the reading is `na khīṇabyappatho` according to the first meaning, and `nākhīṇabyappatho` according to the second meaning. In the fourth line, `mantā` is said to be wisdom. Because the Blessed One, having discerned with that wisdom, speaks only what is meaningful—speech that is not devoid of meaning, not idle chatter. For the Buddhas have no meaningless speech that is preceded by ignorance. Therefore, it is said: 'With wisdom he speaks what is meaningful.' The rest here is self-evident.

160. Evaṃ vacīdvārasuddhimpi sutvā idāni manodvārasuddhiṃ [P 1.0205] pucchanto āha “kacci na rajjati kāmesū”ti. Tattha kāmāti vatthukāmā. Tesu kilesakāmena na rajjatīti pucchanto anabhijjhālutaṃ pucchati. Anāvilanti pucchanto byāpādena āvilabhāvaṃ sandhāya abyāpādataṃ pucchati. Mohaṃ atikkantoti pucchanto yena mohena mūḷho micchādiṭṭhiṃ gaṇhāti, tassātikkamena sammādiṭṭhitaṃ pucchati. Dhammesu cakkhumāti pucchanto sabbadhammesu appaṭihatassa ñāṇacakkhuno, pañcacakkhuvisayesu vā dhammesu pañcannampi cakkhūnaṃ vasena sabbaññutaṃ pucchati “dvārattayapārisuddhiyāpi sabbaññū na hotī”ti cintetvā.

160. Having thus heard about the purity of the speech-door, now, questioning the purity of the mind-door, he said: 'I hope he is not impassioned for sensual pleasures?' Herein, `kāma` refers to both objective sensual pleasures and defiling sensual pleasures. By asking whether he is not impassioned for the objective pleasures by means of the defiling pleasures, he inquires about non-covetousness. By asking 'Is his mind unclouded?' he inquires about non-ill will, with reference to the state of being clouded by ill will. By asking 'Has he overcome delusion?' he inquires about the state of right view, through the overcoming of that delusion by which a deluded person takes up wrong view. By asking 'Is he one with the eye regarding phenomena?' he inquires about omniscience, either by way of the unobstructed eye of knowledge regarding all phenomena, or by way of all five eyes regarding the phenomena that are the domain of the five eyes, having considered that 'one does not become omniscient merely through the purity of the three doors.'

161. Atha sātāgiro yasmā bhagavā appatvāva arahattaṃ anāgāmimaggena kāmarāgabyāpādānaṃ pahīnattā neva kāmesu rajjati, na byāpādena āvilacitto, sotāpattimaggeneva ca micchādiṭṭhipaccayassa saccapaṭicchādakamohassa pahīnattā mohaṃ atikkanto, sāmañca saccāni abhisambujjhitvā buddhoti vimokkhantikaṃ nāmaṃ yathāvuttāni ca cakkhūni paṭilabhi, tasmā tassa manodvārasuddhiṃ sabbaññutañca ugghosento āha “na so rajjati kāmesū”ti.

161. Then Sātāgira, because the Blessed One, even before attaining arahantship, had abandoned sensual lust and ill will by means of the non-returner's path, and thus is neither impassioned for sensual pleasures nor is his mind clouded by ill will; and because by the stream-entry path he had overcome delusion, having abandoned the delusion that conceals the truths and is the condition for wrong view; and because he had fully awakened to the truths by himself and is thus called 'Buddha'—a name that culminates in liberation—and had obtained the eyes as previously described; therefore, proclaiming the purity of his mind-door and his omniscience, he declared, 'He is not impassioned for sensual pleasures.'

162. Evaṃ hemavato bhagavato dvārattayapārisuddhiṃ sabbaññutañca sutvā haṭṭho udaggo atītajātiyaṃ bāhusaccavisadāya paññāya asajjamānavacanappatho hutvā acchariyabbhutarūpe sabbaññuguṇe sotukāmo āha “kacci vijjāya sampanno”ti. Tattha vijjāya sampannoti iminā dassanasampattiṃ pucchati, saṃsuddhacāraṇoti iminā gamanasampattiṃ. Chandavasena cettha dīghaṃ katvā cākāramāha, saṃsuddhacaraṇoti attho. Āsavā khīṇāti iminā etāya dassanagamanasampattiyā pattabbāya āsavakkhayasaññitāya paṭhamanibbānadhātuyā pattiṃ pucchati, natthi punabbhavoti iminā dutiyanibbānadhātupattisamatthataṃ, paccavekkhaṇañāṇena vā paramassāsappattiṃ ñatvā ṭhitabhāvaṃ.

162. Thus, having heard of the Blessed One's purity in the three doors and his omniscience, Hemavata, delighted and uplifted, having an unhindered path of speech due to his extensive learning and clear wisdom from a past birth, and eager to hear the marvelous and extraordinary qualities of omniscience, asked, 'Is he accomplished in knowledge?' Herein, 'accomplished in knowledge' inquires about the perfection of vision, while 'of pure conduct' inquires about the perfection of conduct. Due to metrical reasons, the 'ca' is lengthened here, with the meaning 'of pure conduct' (saṃsuddhacaraṇo). 'The taints are destroyed'—herein, he inquires about the attainment of the first Nibbāna-element, known as the destruction of the taints, which is to be reached through this perfection of vision and conduct. 'There is no renewed existence'—herein, he inquires about the capability to attain the second Nibbāna-element, or about the state of abiding, having known the attainment of the highest peace through reviewing knowledge.

163. Tato [M 1.0203] yā esā “so anekavihitaṃ [P 1.0206] pubbenivāsa”ntiādinā (ma. ni. 1.52) nayena bhayabheravādīsu tividhā, “so evaṃ samāhite citte…pe… āneñjappatte ñāṇadassanāya cittaṃ abhinīharatī”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.279) nayena ambaṭṭhādīsu aṭṭhavidhā vijjā vuttā, tāya yasmā sabbāyapi sabbākārasampannāya bhagavā upeto. Yañcetaṃ “idha, mahānāma, ariyasāvako sīlasampanno hoti, indriyesu guttadvāro hoti, bhojane mattaññū hoti[V 1.0178], jāgariyaṃ anuyutto hoti, sattahi saddhammehi samannāgato hoti, catunnaṃ jhānānaṃ ābhicetasikānaṃ diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārānaṃ nikāmalābhī hotī”ti evaṃ uddisitvā “kathañca, mahānāma, ariyasāvako sīlasampanno hotī”tiādinā (ma. ni. 2.24) nayena sekhasutte niddiṭṭhaṃ pannarasappabhedaṃ caraṇaṃ. Tañca yasmā sabbūpakkilesappahānena bhagavato ativiya saṃsuddhaṃ. Yepime kāmāsavādayo cattāro āsavā, tepi yasmā sabbe saparivārā savāsanā bhagavato khīṇā. Yasmā ca imāya vijjācaraṇasampadāya khīṇāsavo hutvā tadā bhagavā “natthi dāni punabbhavo”ti paccavekkhitvā ṭhito, tasmā sātāgiro bhagavato sabbaññubhāve byavasāyena samussāhitahadayo sabbepi guṇe anujānanto āha “vijjāya ceva sampanno”ti.

163. Then, as for the threefold knowledge described in the way beginning with 'He recollects his manifold past lives...' in the Bhayabherava Sutta and others, and the eightfold knowledge described in the way beginning with 'When his mind is thus concentrated...' in the Ambaṭṭha Sutta and others—because the Blessed One is endowed with all of these, which are complete in all aspects. And as for the fifteenfold conduct described in the Sekha Sutta, after stating, 'Here, Mahānāma, a noble disciple is accomplished in virtue, guards the sense doors, is moderate in eating, devoted to wakefulness, possesses the seven good qualities, and is a gainer at will of the four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life,' and then explaining, 'And how, Mahānāma, is a noble disciple accomplished in virtue?'—because this conduct is supremely purified in the Blessed One through the abandoning of all corruptions. And as for these four taints, such as the taint of sensual pleasure—because all of them, along with their retinue and underlying tendencies, have been destroyed in the Blessed One. And because, through this perfection of knowledge and conduct, the Blessed One, having destroyed the taints, then reflected, 'Now there is no renewed existence,' and remained thus—therefore, Sātāgira, with his heart uplifted by firm conviction in the Blessed One's omniscience, acknowledging all these qualities, said, 'He is accomplished in knowledge and conduct...'

164. Tato hemavato “sammāsambuddho bhagavā”ti bhagavati nikkaṅkho hutvā ākāse ṭhitoyeva bhagavantaṃ pasaṃsanto sātāgirañca ārādhento āha “sampannaṃ munino citta”nti. Tassattho – sampannaṃ munino cittaṃ, “mano cassa supaṇihito”ti ettha vuttatādibhāvena puṇṇaṃ sampuṇṇaṃ, “na so adinnaṃ ādiyatī”ti ettha vuttakāyakammunā, “na so rajjati kāmesū”ti ettha vuttamanokammunā ca puṇṇaṃ sampuṇṇaṃ, “musā ca so na bhaṇatī”ti ettha vuttabyappathena ca vacīkammunāti [P 1.0207] vuttaṃ hoti. Evaṃ sampannacittañca anuttarāya vijjācaraṇasampadāya sampannattā vijjācaraṇasampannañca imehi guṇehi “mano cassa supaṇihito”tiādinā nayena dhammato naṃ pasaṃsasi, sabhāvato tacchato bhūtato eva naṃ pasaṃsasi, na kevalaṃ saddhāmattakenāti dasseti.

164. Then Hemavata, having no doubt regarding the Blessed One, thinking, 'The Blessed One is a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One,' while standing in the sky, praising the Blessed One and gratifying Sātāgira, said, 'The mind of the sage is perfected.' The meaning is this: 'The mind of the sage is perfected' means it is full and complete by virtue of the steadfast quality mentioned in 'and his mind is well-directed'; it is full and complete by virtue of the bodily action mentioned in 'he does not take what is not given,' by virtue of the mental action mentioned in 'he is not passionate in sensual pleasures,' and by virtue of the verbal action mentioned in 'and he does not speak falsely'—thus it is said. And thus, with his mind perfected, and being accomplished in the unsurpassed perfection of knowledge and conduct, he is indeed accomplished in knowledge and conduct. With these qualities, in the manner of 'and his mind is well-directed' and so on, you praise him according to the Dhamma; you praise him from his true nature, from what is factual, from what is real, not merely out of faith alone—this is what is shown.

165-166. Tato [M 1.0204] sātāgiropi “evametaṃ, mārisa, suṭṭhu tayā ñātañca anumoditañcā”ti adhippāyena tameva saṃrādhento āha – “sampannaṃ munino…pe… dhammato anumodasī”ti. Evañca pana vatvā puna bhagavato dassane taṃ abhitthavayamāno āha “sampannaṃ…pe… handa passāma gotama”nti.

Then Sātāgira, with the intention, 'Indeed, friend, you have well understood and rejoiced in this,' gratifying him, said, 'The sage is endowed... you rejoice according to the Dhamma...' And having spoken thus, again extolling the Blessed One with a view to seeing him, he said, 'Endowed... Come, let us see Gotama.'

167. Atha hemavato attano abhirucitaguṇehi purimajātibāhusaccabalena bhagavantaṃ abhitthunanto sātāgiraṃ āha – “eṇijaṅghaṃ…pe… ehi passāma gotama”nti. Tassattho – eṇimigasseva jaṅghā assāti eṇijaṅgho. Buddhānañhi eṇimigasseva anupubbavaṭṭā jaṅghā honti, na purato nimmaṃsā pacchato susumārakucchi viya uddhumātā. Kisā ca buddhā honti dīgharassasamavaṭṭitayuttaṭṭhānesu tathārūpāya aṅgapaccaṅgasampattiyā, na vaṭharapurisā viya thūlā. Paññāya vilikhitakilesattā vā kisā. Ajjhattikabāhirasapattaviddhaṃsanato vīrā. Ekāsanabhojitāya parimitabhojitāya ca appāhārā, na dvattimattālopabhojitāya. Yathāha –

167. Then Hemavata, extolling the Blessed One with qualities pleasing to himself and with the power of extensive learning from a past birth, said to Sātāgira, 'With legs like an antelope... come, let us see Gotama.' The meaning is this: 'Eṇijaṅgha' means one who has legs like an antelope's. For the Buddhas have legs that are gradually rounded like those of an antelope, not fleshless in front nor swollen behind like a crocodile's belly. And the Buddhas are lean, with a perfection of major and minor limbs of such a kind in places that should be long, short, even, and round; they are not thick like other men. Or they are lean because their defilements have been scraped away by wisdom. They are heroic because of having destroyed internal and external enemies. They are of little food because of eating in one session and eating a limited amount, not greedily eating two or three mouthfuls. As it is said:

“Ahaṃ [V 1.0179] kho pana, udāyi, appekadā iminā pattena samatittikampi bhuñjāmi, bhiyyopi bhuñjāmi. ‘Appāhāro samaṇo gotamo appāhāratāya ca vaṇṇavādī’ti iti ce maṃ, udāyi, sāvakā sakkareyyuṃ, garuṃ kareyyuṃ, māneyyuṃ, pūjeyyuṃ, sakkatvā, garuṃ katvā, upanissāya vihareyyuṃ. Ye te, udāyi, mama sāvakā kosakāhārāpi aḍḍhakosakāhārāpi beluvāhārāpi aḍḍhabeluvāhārāpi, na maṃ te iminā dhammena sakkareyyuṃ…pe… upanissāya vihareyyu”nti (ma. ni. 2.242).

“But sometimes, Udāyi, I eat a full bowl, and even more. If my disciples were to honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me for this reason, thinking, ‘The ascetic Gotama eats little and praises eating little,’ and having honored and respected me, they were to live in dependence on me—well, Udāyi, those disciples of mine who eat a kosaka-measure, or half a kosaka-measure, or a beluva-measure, or half a beluva-measure, would not honor me… or live in dependence on me for this quality.”

Āhāre chandarāgābhāvena [P 1.0208] alolupā aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgataṃ āhāraṃ āhārenti moneyyasampattiyā munino. Anagārikatāya vivekaninnamānasatāya ca vane jhāyanti. Tenāha hemavato yakkho “eṇijaṅghaṃ…pe… ehi passāma gotama”nti.

Free from desire and lust for food, ungreedy, they consume food endowed with eight factors for the sake of the sage’s attainment of sagehood. With minds inclined to seclusion due to their homeless state, they meditate in the forest. Thus spoke the yakkha Hemavata: “With legs like an antelope… come, let us see Gotama.”

168. Evañca vatvā puna tassa bhagavato santike dhammaṃ sotukāmatāya “sīhaṃvekacara”nti imaṃ gāthamāha. Tassattho – sīhaṃvāti durāsadaṭṭhena [M 1.0205] khamanaṭṭhena nibbhayaṭṭhena ca kesarasīhasadisaṃ. Yāya taṇhāya “taṇhādutiyo puriso”ti vuccati, tassā abhāvena ekacaraṃ, ekissā lokadhātuyā dvinnaṃ buddhānaṃ anuppattitopi ekacaraṃ. Khaggavisāṇasutte vuttanayenāpi cettha taṃ taṃ attho daṭṭhabbo. Nāganti punabbhavaṃ neva gantāraṃ nāgantāraṃ. Atha vā āguṃ na karotītipi nāgo. Balavātipi nāgo. Taṃ nāgaṃ. Kāmesu anapekkhinanti dvīsupi kāmesu chandarāgābhāvena anapekkhinaṃ. Upasaṅkamma pucchāma, maccupāsappamocananti taṃ evarūpaṃ mahesiṃ upasaṅkamitvā tebhūmakavaṭṭassa maccupāsassa pamocanaṃ vivaṭṭaṃ nibbānaṃ pucchāma. Yena vā upāyena dukkhasamudayasaṅkhātā maccupāsā pamuccati, taṃ maccupāsappamocanaṃ pucchāmāti. Imaṃ gāthaṃ hemavato sātāgirañca sātāgiraparisañca attano parisañca sandhāya āha.

168. Having said this, and desiring to hear the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One, he then spoke this verse: “Like a lion, solitary…” The meaning is this: “Like a lion” refers to being difficult to approach, forbearing, and fearless, thus resembling a maned lion. “Solitary” means being without craving, by which one is called “a person with craving as a companion.” It also means solitary because two Buddhas do not arise in a single world-system. Herein, the respective meanings should also be understood in the way explained in the Khaggavisāṇa Sutta. “The nāga” refers to one who does not go to renewed existence, one who does not return. Alternatively, a nāga is one who does no evil. Or, a nāga is one who is powerful. That nāga. “Unconcerned with sensual pleasures” means without desire and lust for both kinds of sensual pleasures. “Having approached, we shall ask about release from the snare of death” means: having approached such a great sage, we shall ask about release from the snare of death of the three-realmed cycle of existence, which is the unbinding, Nibbāna. Or, we shall ask about that release from the snare of death, the means by which one is freed from the snare of death which is designated as the origin of suffering. Hemavata spoke this verse with reference to Sātāgira, Sātāgira’s assembly, and his own assembly.

Tena kho pana samayena āsāḷhīnakkhattaṃ ghositaṃ ahosi. Atha samantato alaṅkatapaṭiyatte devanagare siriṃ paccanubhontī viya rājagahe kāḷī nāma kuraragharikā upāsikā pāsādamāruyha sīhapañjaraṃ vivaritvā [P 1.0209] gabbhaparissamaṃ vinodentī savātappadese utuggahaṇatthaṃ ṭhitā tesaṃ yakkhasenāpatīnaṃ taṃ buddhaguṇapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ kathaṃ ādimajjhapariyosānato assosi. Sutvā ca “evaṃ vividhaguṇasamannāgatā buddhā”ti buddhārammaṇaṃ pītiṃ uppādetvā tāya nīvaraṇāni vikkhambhetvā tattheva ṭhitā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāsi. Tato eva bhagavatā “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvikānaṃ upāsikānaṃ anussavappasannānaṃ, yadidaṃ kāḷī upāsikā kuraragharikā”ti (a. ni. 1.267) etadagge ṭhapitā.

Now, at that time, the Āsāḷhī festival had been proclaimed. Then, in Rājagaha, which was like a celestial city, decorated and prepared all around, a lay disciple named Kāḷī of the Kurara household, as if experiencing its splendor, ascended her mansion, opened the lion-window, and while dispelling the weariness of being confined indoors, she heard from beginning, middle, to end that talk of the yakkha generals connected with the virtues of the Buddha. Having heard it, and thinking, “Indeed, the Buddhas are endowed with such diverse virtues,” she generated joy with the Buddha as its object. Through that joy, she suppressed the hindrances and, while standing right there, became established in the fruit of stream-entry. It was for this very reason that the Blessed One placed her in the foremost position, saying: “Monks, foremost among my female lay disciples who have gained confidence through hearsay is this one, that is, the lay disciple Kāḷī of the Kurara household.”

169. Tepi [V 1.0180] yakkhasenāpatayo sahassayakkhaparivārā majjhimayāmasamaye isipatanaṃ patvā, dhammacakkappavattitapallaṅkeneva nisinnaṃ bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamma vanditvā, imāya gāthāya bhagavantaṃ abhitthavitvā okāsamakārayiṃsu “akkhātāraṃ pavattāra”nti. Tassattho – ṭhapetvā taṇhaṃ tebhūmake dhamme “idaṃ kho pana, bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ ariyasacca”ntiādinā (saṃ. ni. 5.1081; mahāva. 14) nayena saccānaṃ vavatthānakathāya akkhātāraṃ, “‘taṃ kho panidaṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ pariññeyya’nti me bhikkhave”tiādinā nayena tesu kiccañāṇakatañāṇappavattanena pavattāraṃ. Ye vā dhammā yathā voharitabbā, tesu tathā [M 1.0206] vohārakathanena akkhātāraṃ, tesaṃyeva dhammānaṃ sattānurūpato pavattāraṃ. Ugghaṭitaññuvipañcitaññūnaṃ vā desanāya akkhātāraṃ, neyyānaṃ paṭipādanena pavattāraṃ. Uddesena vā akkhātāraṃ, vibhaṅgena tehi tehi pakārehi vacanato pavattāraṃ. Bodhipakkhiyānaṃ vā salakkhaṇakathanena akkhātāraṃ, sattānaṃ cittasantāne pavattanena pavattāraṃ. Saṅkhepato vā tīhi parivaṭṭehi [P 1.0210] saccānaṃ kathanena akkhātāraṃ, vitthārato pavattāraṃ. “Saddhindriyaṃ dhammo, taṃ dhammaṃ pavattetīti dhammacakka”nti (paṭi. ma. 2.40) evamādinā paṭisambhidānayena vitthāritassa dhammacakkassa pavattanato pavattāraṃ.

169. Those yakkha generals, too, with their retinue of a thousand yakkhas, approached the Blessed One, who was seated on the very seat where he had set in motion the Wheel of the Dhamma, paid homage, and after praising the Blessed One with this verse, they requested an opportunity, saying: “The Proclaimer, the Setter in Motion.” The meaning of this is: He is the ‘Proclaimer’ because, with regard to the phenomena of the three realms (excluding craving), he proclaims the truths by way of definition with the teaching beginning, “This, monks, is the noble truth of suffering.” He is the ‘Setter in Motion’ because he sets forth the knowledge of the task to be done and the knowledge of what has been done regarding those truths, with the teaching beginning, “‘This noble truth of suffering is to be fully understood,’ monks.” Or, he is the ‘Proclaimer’ by explaining phenomena as they are to be designated, and the ‘Setter in Motion’ by setting them forth in a way that is suitable for beings. Or, for those of quick understanding and those who understand through explanation, he is the ‘Proclaimer’ through his teaching, and for those who are to be guided, he is the ‘Setter in Motion’ through his training. Or, he is the ‘Proclaimer’ by way of summary, and the ‘Setter in Motion’ by way of analysis according to the various methods. Or, he is the ‘Proclaimer’ by explaining the characteristics of the factors of enlightenment, and the ‘Setter in Motion’ by causing them to arise in the mental continuum of beings. Or, he is the ‘Proclaimer’ by briefly teaching the truths with their three turnings, and the ‘Setter in Motion’ by teaching them in detail. Or, he is the ‘Setter in Motion’ by setting in motion the Wheel of the Dhamma, which is explained in detail according to the method of the Paṭisambhidāmagga, beginning with: “The faculty of faith is a dhamma; he sets that dhamma in motion, thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.”

Sabbadhammānanti catubhūmakadhammānaṃ. Pāragunti chahākārehi pāraṃ gataṃ abhiññāya, pariññāya, pahānena, bhāvanāya, sacchikiriyāya, samāpattiyā. So hi bhagavā sabbadhamme abhijānanto gatoti abhiññāpāragū, pañcupādānakkhandhe parijānanto gatoti pariññāpāragū, sabbakilese pajahanto gatoti pahānapāragū, cattāro magge bhāvento gatoti bhāvanāpāragū, nirodhaṃ sacchikaronto gatoti sacchikiriyāpāragū, sabbā samāpattiyo samāpajjanto gatoti samāpattipāragū. Evaṃ sabbadhammānaṃ pāraguṃ. Buddhaṃ verabhayātītanti aññāṇasayanato paṭibuddhattā buddhaṃ, sabbena vā saraṇavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttenatthena buddhaṃ, pañcaverabhayānaṃ atītattā verabhayātītaṃ. Evaṃ bhagavantaṃ atitthavantā “mayaṃ pucchāma gotama”nti okāsamakārayiṃsu.

“Of all phenomena” means of the phenomena of the four planes. “One who has gone to the far shore” means one who has gone to the far shore in six ways: through direct knowledge, full understanding, abandoning, development, realization, and meditative attainment. For the Blessed One, by directly knowing all phenomena, has gone to the far shore; thus he is a ‘master of direct knowledge.’ By fully understanding the five aggregates subject to clinging, he has gone to the far shore; thus he is a ‘master of full understanding.’ By abandoning all defilements, he has gone to the far shore; thus he is a ‘master of abandoning.’ By developing the four paths, he has gone to the far shore; thus he is a ‘master of development.’ By realizing cessation, he has gone to the far shore; thus he is a ‘master of realization.’ By attaining all meditative attainments, he has gone to the far shore; thus he is a ‘master of meditative attainment.’ In this way, he is one who has gone to the far shore of all phenomena. “The Buddha, who is beyond enmity and fear” means: he is the ‘Buddha’ because he has awakened from the sleep of ignorance, or because of the meaning given in the explanation of the refuges. He is ‘beyond enmity and fear’ because he has gone beyond the five kinds of enmity and fear. Thus praising the Blessed One, they requested an opportunity, saying: “We shall ask you, Gotama.”

170. Atha nesaṃ yakkhānaṃ tejena ca paññāya ca aggo hemavato yathādhippetaṃ pucchitabbaṃ pucchanto “kismiṃ loko”ti imaṃ gāthamāha. Tassādipāde kisminti bhāvenabhāvalakkhaṇe bhummavacanaṃ, kismiṃ uppanne loko samuppanno hotīti ayañhettha adhippāyo. Sattalokasaṅkhāraloke sandhāya pucchati. Kismiṃ kubbati santhavanti ahanti vā mamanti vā taṇhādiṭṭhisanthavaṃ kismiṃ kubbati, adhikaraṇatthe bhummavacanaṃ. Kissa lokoti upayogatthe sāmivacanaṃ, kiṃ upādāya lokoti saṅkhyaṃ gacchatīti ayañhettha adhippāyo. Kismiṃ lokoti bhāvenabhāvalakkhaṇakāraṇatthesu [V 1.0181] bhummavacanaṃ. Kismiṃ [P 1.0211] sati kena kāraṇena loko vihaññati pīḷīyati bādhīyatīti ayañhettha adhippāyo.

170. Then Hemavata, chief among those yakkhas in power and wisdom, wishing to ask what was to be asked as he desired, spoke this verse beginning, “In what is the world…?” In its first line, the word “in what” is a locative expression in the sense of a locative absolute. The meaning here is this: “When what has arisen is the world well-arisen?” He asks with reference to the world of beings and the world of formations. Regarding “In what does one make intimacy?”: in what does one make the intimacy of craving and views, such as “I” or “mine”? Here, it is a locative expression in the sense of a basis. Regarding “Of what is the world?”: this is a genitive expression in the sense of relation. The meaning here is this: “Clinging to what is it designated ‘the world’?” Regarding “In what is the world afflicted?”: this is a locative expression in the senses of the locative absolute and of cause. The meaning here is this: “When what exists, for what reason is the world afflicted, oppressed, and tormented?”

171. Atha [M 1.0207] bhagavā yasmā chasu ajjhattikabāhiresu āyatanesu uppannesu sattaloko ca dhanadhaññādivasena saṅkhāraloko ca uppanno hoti, yasmā cettha sattaloko tesveva chasu duvidhampi santhavaṃ karoti. Cakkhāyatanaṃ vā hi “ahaṃ mama”nti gaṇhāti avasesesu vā aññataraṃ. Yathāha – “cakkhu attāti yo vadeyya, taṃ na upapajjatī”tiādi (ma. ni. 3.422). Yasmā ca etāniyeva cha upādāya duvidhopi lokoti saṅkhyaṃ gacchati, yasmā ca tesveva chasu sati sattaloko dukkhapātubhāvena vihaññati. Yathāha –

171. Then the Blessed One [thought]: Because when the six internal and external sense bases have arisen, both the world of beings and the world of formations (by way of wealth, grain, and so on) have arisen; and because, herein, the world of beings makes intimacy of both kinds with those very six. For one grasps the eye-base as “I” or “mine,” or any of the remaining ones. As it is said: “Whoever would say, ‘The eye is the self,’ that would not be tenable,” and so on (MN 148). And because, by clinging to these very six, both kinds come to be designated ‘world’; and because, when these very six exist, the world of beings is afflicted by the manifestation of suffering. As it is said:

“Hatthesu, bhikkhave, sati ādānanikkhepanaṃ hoti, pādesu sati abhikkamapaṭikkamo hoti, pabbesu sati samiñjanapasāraṇaṃ hoti, kucchismiṃ sati jighacchāpipāsā hoti; evameva kho, bhikkhave, cakkhusmiṃ sati cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati ajjhattaṃ sukhaṃ dukkha”ntiādi (saṃ. ni. 4.237).

“Bhikkhus, when there are hands, there is taking up and putting down; when there are feet, there is going forward and returning; when there are joints, there is bending and stretching; when there is a belly, there is hunger and thirst. In the same way, bhikkhus, when there is the eye, conditioned by eye-contact, internal pleasure and pain arise,” and so on (SN 35.248).

Tathā tesu ādhārabhūtesu paṭihato saṅkhāraloko vihaññati. Yathāha –

Likewise, when those [sense bases] have become the foundation, the world of formations, being impinged upon, is afflicted. As it is said:

“Cakkhusmiṃ anidassane sappaṭighe paṭihaññi vā”iti (dha. sa. 597-8) ca.

“And: ‘…or it was impinged upon in the eye, which is invisible and resistant’” (Dhs §597-8).

“Cakkhu, bhikkhave, paṭihaññati manāpāmanāpesu rūpesū”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.238) evamādi.

“Bhikkhus, the eye is impinged upon by agreeable and disagreeable forms,” and so on (SN 35.249).

Tathā tehiyeva kāraṇabhūtehi duvidhopi loko vihaññati. Yathāha –

Likewise, by those very same causal factors, the world of both kinds is afflicted. As it is said:

“Cakkhu vihaññati manāpāmanāpesu rūpesū”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.238) ca.

“And: ‘The eye is afflicted by agreeable and disagreeable forms’” (SN 35.249).

“Cakkhu, bhikkhave, ādittaṃ, rūpā ādittā. Kena ādittaṃ? Rāgagginā”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.28; mahāva. 54) evamādi.

“Bhikkhus, the eye is ablaze; forms are ablaze. With what are they ablaze? With the fire of passion,” and so on (SN 35.28; Vin Mv 1.21).

Tasmā [V 1.0182] chaajjhattikabāhirāyatanavasena taṃ pucchaṃ vissajjento āha “chasu loko samuppanno”ti.

Therefore, answering that question by way of the six internal and external sense bases, he said: “In the six the world arises.”

172. Atha so yakkho attanā vaṭṭavasena puṭṭhapañhaṃ bhagavatā dvādasāyatanavasena saṅkhipitvā vissajjitaṃ na [P 1.0212] suṭṭhu upalakkhetvā tañca atthaṃ [M 1.0208] tappaṭipakkhañca ñātukāmo saṅkhepeneva vaṭṭavivaṭṭaṃ pucchanto āha “katamaṃ ta”nti. Tattha upādātabbaṭṭhena upādānaṃ, dukkhasaccassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Yattha loko vihaññatīti “chasu loko vihaññatī”ti evaṃ bhagavatā yattha chabbidhe upādāne loko vihaññatīti vutto, taṃ katamaṃ upādānanti? Evaṃ upaḍḍhagāthāya sarūpeneva dukkhasaccaṃ pucchi. Samudayasaccaṃ pana tassa kāraṇabhāvena gahitameva hoti. Niyyānaṃ pucchitoti imāya pana upaḍḍhagāthāya maggasaccaṃ pucchi. Maggasaccena hi ariyasāvako dukkhaṃ parijānanto, samudayaṃ pajahanto, nirodhaṃ sacchikaronto, maggaṃ bhāvento lokamhā niyyāti, tasmā niyyānanti vuccati. Kathanti kena pakārena. Dukkhā pamuccatīti “upādāna”nti vuttā vaṭṭadukkhā pamokkhaṃ pāpuṇāti. Evamettha sarūpeneva maggasaccaṃ pucchi, nirodhasaccaṃ pana tassa visayabhāvena gahitameva hoti.

172. Then that yakkha, not having properly understood the answer—given concisely by the Blessed One in terms of the twelve sense bases—to the question he had asked regarding the round of existence, and wishing to know that meaning and its opposite, asked briefly about the round and the escape from the round, saying, “What is that…?” Therein, ‘clinging’ (upādāna) is so called in the sense of that which is to be clung to; this is a synonym for the truth of suffering. Regarding the statement “Wherein the world is afflicted,” the Blessed One had said, “In the six the world is afflicted,” meaning that the world is afflicted in the sixfold clinging. So the question is, “What is that clinging?” Thus, with half a verse, he asked about the truth of suffering in its own nature. The truth of the origin, however, is included by way of being its cause. With the half-verse beginning, “He asked about the escape,” he asked about the truth of the path. For by means of the truth of the path, a noble disciple—fully understanding suffering, abandoning the origin, realizing cessation, and developing the path—goes forth from the world; therefore, it is called ‘the escape.’ ‘How?’ means by what method. ‘Is freed from suffering’ means: how does one attain freedom from the suffering of the round, which is called ‘clinging’? Thus, here he asked about the truth of the path in its own nature; the truth of cessation, however, is included by way of being its object.

173. Evaṃ yakkhena sarūpena dassetvā ca adassetvā ca catusaccavasena pañhaṃ puṭṭho bhagavā teneva nayena vissajjento āha “pañca kāmaguṇā”ti. Tattha pañcakāmaguṇasaṅkhātagocaraggahaṇena taggocarāni pañcāyatanāni gahitāneva honti. Mano chaṭṭho etesanti manochaṭṭhā. Paveditāti pakāsitā. Ettha ajjhattikesu chaṭṭhassa manāyatanassa gahaṇena tassa visayabhūtaṃ dhammāyatanaṃ gahitameva hoti. Evaṃ “katamaṃ taṃ upādāna”nti imaṃ pañhaṃ vissajjento punapi dvādasāyatanānaṃ vaseneva dukkhasaccaṃ pakāsesi. Manogahaṇena vā sattannaṃ viññāṇadhātūnaṃ gahitattā tāsu purimapañcaviññāṇadhātuggahaṇena tāsaṃ vatthūni pañca cakkhādīni āyatanāni, manodhātumanoviññāṇadhātuggahaṇena tāsaṃ vatthugocarabhedaṃ dhammāyatanaṃ gahitamevāti evampi dvādasāyatanavasena dukkhasaccaṃ pakāsesi. Lokuttaramanāyatanadhammāyatanekadeso [P 1.0213] panettha yattha loko vihaññati, taṃ sandhāya niddiṭṭhattā na saṅgayhati.

173. Thus, the Blessed One, having been asked a question by the yakkha in terms of the four truths—some shown in their own nature and some not—answered in that same way, saying, “The five strands of sensual pleasure…” Therein, by taking the objects called the five strands of sensual pleasure, the five sense bases that have them as objects are thereby included. “Mind is the sixth of these,” thus they are “with mind as the sixth.” ‘Declared’ means made known. Herein, by taking the sixth of the internal bases, the mind-base, its object, the dhamma-base, is thereby included. Thus, in answering the question, “What is that clinging?” he again explained the truth of suffering by way of the twelve sense bases. Alternatively, by taking ‘mind,’ the seven consciousness elements are included. Among these, by taking the first five consciousness elements, their bases—the five sense bases beginning with the eye—are included. By taking the mind-element and the mind-consciousness-element, their base and object without distinction, the dhamma-base, is thereby included. In this way also, he explained the truth of suffering by way of the twelve sense bases. Herein, a portion of the supramundane mind-base and dhamma-base is not included, because the context was indicated with reference to “wherein the world is afflicted.”

Ettha chandaṃ virājetvāti ettha dvādasāyatanabhede dukkhasacce tānevāyatanāni khandhato dhātuto nāmarūpatoti tathā tathā vavatthapetvā, tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā, vipassanto arahattamaggapariyosānāya vipassanāya taṇhāsaṅkhātaṃ chandaṃ sabbaso virājetvā vinetvā viddhaṃsetvāti attho. Evaṃ dukkhā pamuccatīti iminā pakārena etasmā [M 1.0209] vaṭṭadukkhā pamuccatīti[V 1.0183]. Evamimāya upaḍḍhagāthāya “niyyānaṃ pucchito brūhi, kathaṃ dukkhā pamuccatī”ti ayaṃ pañho vissajjito hoti, maggasaccañca pakāsitaṃ samudayanirodhasaccāni panettha purimanayeneva saṅgahitattā pakāsitāneva hontīti veditabbāni. Upaḍḍhagāthāya vā dukkhasaccaṃ, chandena samudayasaccaṃ, “virājetvā”ti ettha virāgena nirodhasaccaṃ, “virāgāvimuccatī”ti vacanato vā maggasaccaṃ. “Eva”nti upāyanidassanena maggasaccaṃ, dukkhanirodhanti vacanato vā. “Dukkhā pamuccatī”ti dukkhapamokkhena nirodhasaccanti evamettha cattāri saccāni pakāsitāni hontīti veditabbāni.

Here, in 'having dispelled desire', the meaning is this: in the truth of suffering, which is divided into the twelve sense bases, one determines those very sense bases in various ways—as aggregates, as elements, and as name-and-form—and applies the three characteristics. Practicing insight, with an insight that culminates in the path of arahantship, one completely dispels, removes, and destroys desire, which is known as craving. 'Thus one is freed from suffering' means that in this manner one is freed from the suffering of the cycle of existence. In this way, by this half-verse, the question, 'Being asked about the escape, tell me, how is one freed from suffering?' is answered, and the truth of the path is also revealed. The truths of origin and cessation, however, are to be understood as already revealed here, since they are included by the previous method. Alternatively, by the half-verse, the truth of suffering is shown; by 'desire', the truth of origin; in 'having dispelled', the truth of cessation is shown through dispassion; or, according to the statement 'one is liberated through dispassion', the truth of the path. By 'thus', indicating the means, the truth of the path is shown; or according to the statement 'the cessation of suffering'. In 'one is freed from suffering', the truth of cessation is shown through liberation from suffering. In this way, it should be understood that the four truths are revealed here.

174. Evaṃ catusaccagabbhāya gāthāya lakkhaṇato niyyānaṃ pakāsetvā puna tadeva sakena niruttābhilāpena nigamento āha “etaṃ lokassa niyyāna”nti. Ettha etanti pubbe vuttassa niddeso, lokassāti tedhātukalokassa. Yathātathanti aviparītaṃ. Etaṃ vo ahamakkhāmīti sacepi maṃ sahassakkhattuṃ puccheyyātha, etaṃ vo ahamakkhāmi, na aññaṃ. Kasmā? Yasmā evaṃ dukkhā pamuccati, na aññathāti adhippāyo. Atha vā etena niyyānena ekadvattikkhatuṃ niggatānampi etaṃ vo ahamakkhāmi, uparivisesādhigamāyapi etadeva ahamakkhāmīti attho. Kasmā? Yasmā evaṃ dukkhā pamuccati asesanissesāti arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi. Desanāpariyosāne dvepi yakkhasenāpatayo sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahiṃsu saddhiṃ yakkhasahassena.

174. Thus, having shown the way out through its characteristics in the verse embodying the four truths, he then, concluding in his own expression, declared the same again: 'This is the escape from the world.' Here, 'this' refers to what was previously stated, and 'of the world' means of the world of the three realms. 'As it truly is' means without perversion. 'This I declare to you' means: even if you were to ask me a thousand times, I would declare this to you, and nothing else. Why? Because it is only in this way that one is freed from suffering, not otherwise—this is the intended meaning. Alternatively, even for those who have escaped once, twice, or thrice by this means of escape, 'this I declare to you'—this is the meaning. Why? Because it is only in this way that one is freed from suffering completely, without remainder—thus, he concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of arahantship. At the end of the teaching, both commanders of the yakkha armies, along with a thousand yakkhas, were established in the fruit of stream-entry.

175. Atha hemavato pakatiyāpi dhammagaru idāni ariyabhūmiyaṃ [P 1.0214] patiṭṭhāya suṭṭhutaraṃ atitto bhagavato vicitrapaṭibhānāya desanāya bhagavantaṃ sekkhāsekkhabhūmiṃ pucchanto “ko sūdha taratī”ti gāthamabhāsi. Tattha ko sūdha tarati oghanti iminā caturoghaṃ ko taratīti sekkhabhūmiṃ pucchati avisesena. Yasmā aṇṇavanti na vitthatamattaṃ nāpi gambhīramattaṃ apica pana yaṃ vitthatatarañca gambhīratarañca, taṃ vuccati. Tādiso ca saṃsāraṇṇavo. Ayañhi samantato pariyantābhāvena vitthato, heṭṭhā patiṭṭhābhāvena upari ālambanābhāvena ca gambhīro, tasmā “ko idha tarati aṇṇavaṃ, tasmiñca appatiṭṭhe anālambe gambhīre aṇṇave ko na sīdatī”ti asekkhabhūmiṃ pucchati.

175. Then Hemavata, who by nature revered the Dhamma and now stood firmly on the noble ground, being even more insatiate with the Blessed One's brilliant exposition, asked the Blessed One about the stages of learners and non-learners with the verse beginning, 'Who here crosses over?' Here, with 'Who here crosses over the flood?', he asks generally about the stage of a learner, regarding who crosses the four floods. For what is called an 'ocean' is not merely a matter of breadth or depth, but rather that which is vaster and deeper. Such is the ocean of saṃsāra. For it is vast because it has no boundaries all around, and deep because it has no footing below nor support above. Therefore, with 'Who here crosses the ocean?' and 'In that ocean which is without footing, without support, and deep, who does not sink?', he asks about the stage of one beyond training.

176. Atha [M 1.0210] bhagavā yo bhikkhu jīvitahetupi vītikkamaṃ akaronto sabbadā sīlasampanno lokiyalokuttarāya ca paññāya paññavā, upacārappanāsamādhinā iriyāpathaheṭṭhimamaggaphalehi ca susamāhito, tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā vipassanāya niyakajjhattacintanasīlo, sātaccakiriyāvahāya [V 1.0184] appamādasatiyā ca samannāgato. Yasmā so catutthena maggena imaṃ suduttaraṃ oghaṃ anavasesaṃ tarati, tasmā sekkhabhūmiṃ vissajjento “sabbadā sīlasampanno”ti imaṃ tisikkhāgabbhaṃ gāthamāha. Ettha hi sīlasampadāya adhisīlasikkhā, satisamādhīhi adhicittasikkhā, ajjhattacintitāpaññāhi adhipaññāsikkhāti tisso sikkhā saupakārā sānisaṃsā ca vuttā. Upakāro hi sikkhānaṃ lokiyapaññā sati ca, anisaṃso sāmaññaphalānīti.

176. Then the Blessed One, explaining the stage of a trainee, spoke this verse which encompasses the threefold training: 'Always perfect in virtue...' For a monk who, not transgressing even for the sake of his life, is always perfect in virtue; who is wise with mundane and supramundane wisdom; who is well-composed through access and attainment concentration, and through the postures and the lower paths and fruits; who is accustomed to contemplating his own internal nature through insight after applying the three characteristics; and who is endowed with heedful mindfulness that brings continuous effort—such a one crosses this very difficult flood completely with the fourth path. Herein, by perfection in virtue, the higher training in virtue is stated; by mindfulness and concentration, the higher training in mind; by wisdom from internal contemplation, the higher training in wisdom. Thus the three trainings are stated with their supports and their benefits. The support for the trainings is mundane wisdom and mindfulness, while the benefits are the fruits of recluseship.

177. Evaṃ paṭhamagāthāya sekkhabhūmiṃ dassetvā idāni asekkhabhūmiṃ dassento dutiyagāthamāha. Tassattho virato kāmasaññāyāti yā kāci kāmasaññā, tato sabbato catutthamaggasampayuttāya samucchedaviratiyā virato. “Viratto”tipi pāṭho. Tadā “kāmasaññāyā”ti bhummavacanaṃ hoti, sagāthāvagge pana “kāmasaññāsū”tipi (saṃ. ni. 1.96) pāṭho. Catūhipi maggehi dasannaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ atītattā sabbasaṃyojanātigo, catuttheneva vā uddhambhāgiyasabbasaṃyojanātigo[P 1.0215], tatratatrābhinandinītaṇhāsaṅkhātāya nandiyā tiṇṇañca bhavānaṃ parikkhīṇattā nandībhavaparikkhīṇo so tādiso khīṇāsavo bhikkhu gambhīre saṃsāraṇṇave na sīdati nandīparikkhayena saupādisesaṃ, bhavaparikkhayena ca anupādisesaṃ nibbānathalaṃ samāpajja paramassāsappattiyāti.

177. Having thus shown the stage of a trainee in the first verse, now, to show the stage of one beyond training, he speaks the second verse. Its meaning is: 'Detached from perceptions of sensual pleasure'—that is, detached entirely from any perception of sensual pleasure through the detachment by eradication associated with the fourth path. There is also the reading 'viratto' (dispassionate). In that case, 'kāmasaññāya' would be in the locative case; but in the Sagāthāvagga, there is also the reading 'kāmasaññāsu'. Having transcended the ten fetters through the four paths, he has overcome all fetters; or, having transcended all the higher fetters through the fourth path alone. Because delight—which is craving that rejoices here and there—and the three kinds of existence are exhausted, he is one whose delight and existence are exhausted. Such a monk, whose taints are destroyed, does not sink in the deep ocean of saṃsāra. Through the exhaustion of delight, he attains Nibbāna with residue remaining; and through the exhaustion of existence, Nibbāna without residue remaining, thus attaining the ground of Nibbāna and reaching ultimate relief.

178. Atha hemavato sahāyañca yakkhaparisañca oloketvā pītisomanassajāto “gambhīrapañña”nti evamādīhi gāthāhi bhagavantaṃ abhitthavitvā sabbāvatiyā parisāya sahāyena ca saddhiṃ abhivādetvā, padakkhiṇaṃ katvā, attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ agamāsi.

178. Then Hemavata, having observed his friend and the assembly of yakkhas, filled with joy and gladness, extolled the Blessed One with verses such as 'of deep wisdom.' Together with his friend and the entire assembly, he paid homage, circumambulated him respectfully, and returned to his own dwelling place.

Tāsaṃ pana gāthānaṃ ayaṃ atthavaṇṇanā – gambhīrapaññanti gambhīrāya paññāya samannāgataṃ. Tattha paṭisambhidāyaṃ vuttanayena gambhīrapaññā veditabbā. Vuttañhi tattha [M 1.0211] “gambhīresu khandhesu ñāṇaṃ pavattatīti gambhīrapaññā”tiādi (paṭi. ma. 3.4). Nipuṇatthadassinti nipuṇehi khattiyapaṇḍitādīhi abhisaṅkhatānaṃ pañhānaṃ atthadassiṃ atthānaṃ vā yāni nipuṇāni kāraṇāni duppaṭivijjhāni aññehi tesaṃ dassanena nipuṇatthadassiṃ. Rāgādikiñcanābhāvena akiñcanaṃ. Duvidhe kāme tividhe ce bhave alagganena kāmabhave asattaṃ. Khandhādibhedesu sabbārammaṇesu chandarāgabandhanābhāvena sabbadhi vippamuttaṃ. Dibbe pathe kamamānanti aṭṭhasamāpattibhede dibbe pathe samāpajjanavasena caṅkamantaṃ. Tattha kiñcāpi na tāya velāya bhagavā dibbe pathe kamati, apica kho pubbe kamanaṃ upādāya kamanasattisabbhāvena tattha laddhavasībhāvatāya evaṃ vuccati. Atha vā ye te visuddhidevā arahanto, tesaṃ pathe santavihāre kamanenāpetaṃ vuttaṃ. Mahantānaṃ guṇānaṃ esanena mahesiṃ.

This is the explanation of the meaning of those verses: Gambhīrapaññan’ti means endowed with profound wisdom. Here, profound wisdom should be understood according to the method stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga. For it is said there: “Wisdom operates in the profound aggregates, thus it is profound wisdom,” and so on (Paṭi. Ma. 3.4). Nipuṇatthadassin’ti means one who sees the meaning of subtle questions devised by clever khattiya scholars and others, or who sees the subtle reasons that are difficult for others to comprehend. Akiñcanaṃ means without possessions, due to the absence of hindrances such as lust. Kāmabhave asattaṃ means unattached to the two kinds of sensual pleasures and the three kinds of existence through non-clinging. Sabbadhi vippamuttaṃ means liberated in every way, free from the bonds of desire and lust regarding all objects, such as the aggregates. Dibbe pathe kamamānan’ti means journeying by way of entering the divine path, which consists of the eight attainments. Although the Blessed One was not journeying on the divine path at that time, this is said with reference to his previous journeying, due to his power of journeying and the mastery gained therein. Alternatively, it refers to those pure deities who are arahants, and thus it is said that he journeys in their path, which is a peaceful abiding. Mahesiṃ means a great sage, from seeking great qualities.

179. Dutiyagāthāya [V 1.0185] aparena pariyāyena thuti āraddhāti katvā puna nipuṇatthadassiggahaṇaṃ nidasseti. Atha vā nipuṇatthe dassetāranti attho. Paññādadanti paññāpaṭilābhasaṃvattanikāya [P 1.0216] paṭipattiyā kathanena paññādāyakaṃ. Kāmālaye asattanti yvāyaṃkāmesu taṇhādiṭṭhivasena duvidho ālayo, tattha asattaṃ. Sabbavidunti sabbadhammaviduṃ, sabbaññunti vuttaṃ hoti. Sumedhanti tassa sabbaññubhāvassa maggabhūtāya pāramīpaññāsaṅkhātāya medhāya samannāgataṃ. Ariye patheti aṭṭhaṅgike magge, phalasamāpattiyaṃ vā. Kamamānanti paññāya ajjhogāhamānaṃ maggalakkhaṇaṃ ñatvā desanato, pavisamānaṃ vā khaṇe khaṇe phalasamāpattisamāpajjanato, catubbidhamaggabhāvanāsaṅkhātāya kamanasattiyā kamitapubbaṃ vā.

179. With the second verse, praise is begun in another way, thus it indicates the taking up again of the term nipuṇatthadassī. Alternatively, the meaning is ‘one who shows the subtle meaning.’ Paññādadaṃ (giver of wisdom) means a giver of wisdom by speaking of the practice that conduces to the acquisition of wisdom. Kāmālaye asattaṃ (unattached in the abode of sensuality) means not clinging to the twofold attachment of craving and views in regard to sensual pleasures. Sabbaviduṃ (all-knowing) means knowing all phenomena, which is to say, omniscient. Sumedhaṃ (wise) means endowed with the intelligence, reckoned as the perfection of wisdom, that is the path to that omniscience. Ariye pathe (on the noble path) means on the eightfold path or in the attainment of fruition. Kamamānaṃ (advancing) means knowing the characteristic of the path by penetrating it with wisdom and teaching it; or entering moment by moment into the attainment of fruition; or one who has previously advanced by the power of advancement, reckoned as the development of the fourfold path.

180. Sudiṭṭhaṃ vata no ajjāti. Ajja amhehi sundaraṃ diṭṭhaṃ, ajja vā amhākaṃ sundaraṃ diṭṭhaṃ, dassananti attho. Suppabhātaṃ suhuṭṭhitanti ajja amhākaṃ suṭṭhu pabhātaṃ sobhanaṃ vā pabhātaṃ ahosi. Ajja ca no sundaraṃ uṭṭhitaṃ ahosi, anuparodhena sayanato uṭṭhitaṃ. Kiṃ kāraṇaṃ? Yaṃ addasāma sambuddhaṃ, yasmā sambuddhaṃ addasāmāti attano lābhasampattiṃ ārabbha pāmojjaṃ pavedeti.

180. Sudiṭṭhaṃ vata no ajjā’ti (Truly, it is well seen by us today). This means: ‘Today something beautiful has been seen by us,’ or ‘Today a beautiful sight has been seen by us’—such is the meaning. Suppabhātaṃ suhuṭṭhitan’ti (A splendid dawn, a well-risen morning). This means: ‘Today our dawn was excellent,’ or ‘a beautiful dawn arose for us.’ And ‘today we rose beautifully,’ meaning we rose from sleep without being troubled. What is the reason? Yaṃ addasāma sambuddhaṃ (Because we saw the Fully Enlightened One); because they have seen the Fully Enlightened One, they express their joy concerning their own attainment of gain.

181. Iddhimantoti [M 1.0212] kammavipākajiddhiyā samannāgatā. Yasassinoti lābhaggaparivāraggasampannā. Saraṇaṃ yantīti kiñcāpi maggeneva gatā, tathāpi sotāpannabhāvaparidīpanatthaṃ pasādadassanatthañca vācaṃ bhindati.

181. Iddhimanto’ti (endowed with psychic power) means endowed with psychic power born of karmic result. Yasassino’ti (glorious) means endowed with supreme gain and retinue. Saraṇaṃ yantī’ti (They go for refuge)—although they have already gone for refuge by means of the path, still, to reveal their state of stream-entry and to show their faith, they utter these words.

182. Gāmā gāmanti devagāmā devagāmaṃ. Nagā naganti devapabbatā devapabbataṃ. Namassamānā sambuddhaṃ, dhammassa ca sudhammatanti “sammāsambuddho vata bhagavā, svākkhāto vata bhagavato dhammo”tiādinā nayena buddhasubodhitañca dhammasudhammatañca. “Suppaṭipanno vata bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho”tiādinā saṅgha-suppaṭipattiñca abhitthavitvā abhitthavitvā namassamānā dhammaghosakā hutvā vicarissāmāti vuttaṃ hoti. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti.

182. Gāmā gāman’ti means from deva-village to deva-village. Nagā nagan’ti means from deva-mountain to deva-mountain. Namassamānā sambuddhaṃ, dhammassa ca sudhammatan’ti: praising the Buddha's excellent enlightenment and the Dhamma's sublime excellence with the words, “Truly, the Blessed One is a Perfectly Enlightened Buddha, the Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One,” and so on; and praising the Sangha's good practice with the words, “Truly, the Blessed One’s Sangha practices well,” and so on—having repeatedly praised them, it is said that they declared: “While paying homage, we will wander forth as proclaimers of the Dhamma.” The rest here is clear in meaning.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Collection,

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya hemavatasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Hemavata Sutta in the Sutta Nipāta Commentary is completed.

10. Āḷavakasuttavaṇṇanā

10. The Explanation of the Āḷavaka Sutta

Evaṃ [P 1.0217][V 1.0186] me sutanti āḷavakasuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Atthavaṇṇanānayenevassa uppatti āvibhavissati. Atthavaṇṇanāya ca “evaṃ me sutaṃ, ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā”ti etaṃ vuttatthameva. Āḷaviyaṃ viharati āḷavakassa yakkhassa bhavaneti ettha pana kā āḷavī, kasmā ca bhagavā tassa yakkhassa bhavane viharatīti? Vuccate – āḷavīti raṭṭhampi nagarampi vuccati, tadubhayampi idha vaṭṭati. Āḷavīnagarassa hi samīpe viharantopi “āḷaviyaṃ viharatī”ti vuccati. Tassa ca nagarassa samīpe avidūre gāvutamatte taṃ bhavanaṃ, āḷavīraṭṭhe viharantopi “āḷaviyaṃ viharatī”ti vuccati, āḷavīraṭṭhe cetaṃ bhavanaṃ.

The Āḷavaka Sutta begins, “Thus have I heard.” What is its origin? Its origin will become apparent through the method of explaining the meaning. And in the explanation of the meaning, the phrase “Thus have I heard; at one time the Blessed One…” has the meaning already stated. “Dwelling at Āḷavī, in the abode of the yakkha Āḷavaka”—here, what is Āḷavī, and why did the Blessed One dwell in the abode of that yakkha? It is said: Āḷavī refers to both a country and a city; both are applicable here. For even one dwelling near the city of Āḷavī is said to be “dwelling at Āḷavī.” And near that city, not far away, about a gāvuta's distance, was that abode. Even one dwelling in the country of Āḷavī is said to be “dwelling at Āḷavī,” and this abode was in the country of Āḷavī.

Yasmā pana āḷavako rājā vividhanāṭakūpabhogaṃ chaḍḍetvā corapaṭibāhanatthaṃ paṭirājanisedhanatthaṃ byāyāmakaraṇatthañca sattame sattame divase migavaṃ gacchanto ekadivasaṃ balakāyena saddhiṃ katikaṃ akāsi – “yassa passena [M 1.0213] migo palāyati, tasseva so bhāro”ti. Atha tasseva passena migo palāyi, javasampanno rājā dhanuṃ gahetvā pattikova tiyojanaṃ taṃ migaṃ anubandhi. Eṇimigā ca tiyojanavegā eva honti. Atha parikkhīṇajavaṃ taṃ migaṃ udakaṃ pavisitvā, ṭhitaṃ vadhitvā, dvidhā chetvā, anatthikopi maṃsena “nāsakkhi migaṃ gahetu”nti apavādamocanatthaṃ kājenādāya āgacchanto nagarassāvidūre bahalapattapalāsaṃ mahānigrodhaṃ disvā parissamavinodanatthaṃ tassa mūlamupagato. Tasmiñca nigrodhe āḷavako yakkho mahārājasantikā varaṃ labhitvā majjhanhikasamaye tassa rukkhassa chāyāya phuṭṭhokāsaṃ paviṭṭhe pāṇino khādanto paṭivasati. So taṃ disvā [P 1.0218] khādituṃ upagato. Atha rājā tena saddhiṃ katikaṃ akāsi – “muñca maṃ, ahaṃ te divase divase manussañca thālipākañca pesessāmī”ti. Yakkho “tvaṃ rājūpabhogena pamatto sammussasi, ahaṃ pana bhavanaṃ anupagatañca ananuññātañca khādituṃ na labhāmi, svāhaṃ bhavantampi jīyeyya”nti na muñci. Rājā “yaṃ divasaṃ na pesemi, taṃ divasaṃ maṃ gahetvā khādāhī”ti attānaṃ anujānitvā tena mutto nagarābhimukho agamāsi.

Now, King Āḷavaka, having abandoned the various pleasures of plays and entertainments, went hunting every seventh day to suppress thieves, ward off rival kings, and for the purpose of exercise. One day, he made an agreement with his troops: 'The burden falls on the one from whose side the deer escapes.' Then, a deer fled from his side. The swift-footed king took his bow and pursued that deer on foot for three leagues. For Eṇī deer have a speed of three leagues. When the deer’s speed was exhausted, it entered the water and stood still. The king killed it, cut it in two, and though he had no need for the meat, he took it, carrying it on a pole, to avoid the blame, 'He could not catch the deer.' As he was returning near the city, he saw a great banyan tree with dense leaves and foliage. To relieve his exhaustion, he went to its root. Now, in that banyan tree lived the yakkha Āḷavaka, who had obtained a boon from the Great Kings. At midday, he would devour any living being that entered the space touched by the shade of that tree. Seeing the king, he approached to eat him. The king then made an agreement with him: 'Release me, and I will send you a human and a pot of cooked rice every day.' The yakkha, thinking, 'You, being heedless with royal enjoyments, will forget. As for me, I am not permitted to eat anyone who has not come to my dwelling or is not authorized. Thus I would be deprived even of you,' did not release him. The king, offering himself as a pledge, said, 'On any day I fail to send someone, you may seize and eat me that day.' Released by him on this condition, he went toward the city.

Balakāyo [V 1.0187] magge khandhāvāraṃ bandhitvā ṭhito rājānaṃ disvā – “kiṃ, mahārāja, ayasamattabhayā evaṃ kilantosī”ti vadanto paccuggantvā paṭiggahesi. Rājā taṃ pavattiṃ anārocetvā nagaraṃ gantvā, katapātarāso nagaraguttikaṃ āmantetvā etamatthaṃ ārocesi. Nagaraguttiko – “kiṃ, deva, kālaparicchedo kato”ti āha. Rājā “na kato, bhaṇe”ti āha. “Duṭṭhu kataṃ, deva, amanussā hi paricchinnamattameva labhanti, aparicchinne pana janapadassa ābādho bhavissati. Hotu, deva, kiñcāpi evamakāsi, appossukko tvaṃ rajjasukhaṃ anubhohi, ahamettha kātabbaṃ karissāmī”ti. So kālasseva vuṭṭhāya bandhanāgāraṃ gantvā ye ye vajjhā honti, te te sandhāya – “yo jīvitatthiko hoti, so [M 1.0214] nikkhamatū”ti bhaṇati. Yo paṭhamaṃ nikkhamati taṃ gehaṃ netvā, nhāpetvā, bhojetvā ca, “imaṃ thālipākaṃ yakkhassa dehī”ti peseti. Taṃ rukkhamūlaṃ paviṭṭhamattaṃyeva yakkho bheravaṃ attabhāvaṃ nimminitvā mūlakandaṃ viya khādati[P 1.0219]. Yakkhānubhāvena kira manussānaṃ kesādīni upādāya sakalasarīraṃ navanītapiṇḍo viya hoti. Yakkhassa bhattaṃ gāhāpettuṃ gatapurisā taṃ disvā bhītā yathāmittaṃ ārocesuṃ. Tato pabhuti “rājā core gahetvā yakkhassa detī”ti manussā corakammato paṭiviratā. Tato aparena samayena navacorānaṃ abhāvena purāṇacorānañca parikkhayena bandhanāgārāni suññāni ahesuṃ.

His army, having set up camp on the road, saw the king and, saying, 'Why, great king, are you so weary from fear of disgrace?' went forth to meet and receive him. The king, explaining the situation to them, went to the city. After finishing his morning meal, he summoned the city guard and informed him of the matter. The city guard asked, 'Lord, has a time limit been set?' The king replied, 'It was not set, my friend.' 'That was poorly done, lord,' he said. 'For non-humans only receive what is specified; without a specified limit, there will be an affliction for the country. But let it be, lord. Even though you have acted thus, remain without anxiety and enjoy the bliss of kingship. I will do what needs to be done here.' He rose early in the morning, went to the prison, and addressing those who were condemned to death, he announced, 'Whoever wishes to live, let him come out.' The first one to come out he took to a house, had him bathed and fed, and then sent him, saying, 'Give this pot of cooked rice to the yakkha.' As soon as the man entered the base of the tree, the yakkha, creating a terrifying form, devoured him like a root bulb. It is said that by the yakkha’s power, a human’s entire body, from the hair downwards, becomes like a lump of fresh butter. The men who had gone to have the yakkha’s meal delivered saw this and, terrified, reported it to their companions. From then on, thinking, 'The king captures thieves and gives them to the yakkha,' people refrained from theft. Then, at a later time, due to the absence of new thieves and the elimination of the old ones, the prisons became empty.

Atha nagaraguttiko rañño ārocesi. Rājā attano dhanaṃ nagararacchāsu chaḍḍāpesi – “appeva nāma koci lobhena gaṇheyyā”ti. Taṃ pādenapi na koci chupi. So core alabhanto amaccānaṃ ārocesi. Amaccā “kulapaṭipāṭiyā ekamekaṃ jiṇṇakaṃ pesema, so pakatiyāpi maccumukhe vattatī”ti āhaṃsu. Rājā “‘amhākaṃ pitaraṃ, amhākaṃ pitāmahaṃ pesetī’ti manussā khobhaṃ karissanti, mā vo etaṃ ruccī”ti nivāresi. “Tena hi, deva, dārakaṃ pesema uttānaseyyakaṃ, tathāvidhassa hi ‘mātā me pitā me’ti sineho natthī”ti āhaṃsu. Rājā anujāni. Te tathā akaṃsu. Nagare dārakamātaro ca dārake gahetvā gabbhiniyo ca palāyitvā parajanapade dārake saṃvaḍḍhetvā ānenti. Evaṃ sabbānipi dvādasa vassāni gatāni.

Then the city guard reported to the king. The king had his wealth scattered in the city streets, thinking, 'Perhaps someone might take it out of greed.' But no one touched it even with a foot. Failing to find any thieves, he informed his ministers. The ministers said, 'Let us send, one by one according to family lineage, an elderly man; he is, by nature, already in the mouth of death.' The king forbade them, saying, 'People will become agitated, saying, "He is sending our father, our grandfather." Let this not be your preference.' 'In that case, Your Majesty,' they said, 'let us send an infant lying on its back, for such a one has no affection, thinking, "my mother, my father."' The king consented. They did so. In the city, mothers with young children, as well as pregnant women, took their children and fled. They raised their children in other regions and then brought them back. In this manner, twelve full years passed.

Tato ekadivasaṃ sakalanagaraṃ vicinitvā ekampi dārakaṃ alabhitvā rañño ārocesuṃ – “natthi, deva, nagare dārako ṭhapetvā antepure tava puttaṃ āḷavakakumāra”nti. Rājā “yathā mama putto piyo, evaṃ sabbalokassa, attanā pana piyataraṃ natthi, gacchatha, tampi datvā mama jīvitaṃ rakkhathā”ti āha. Tena ca samayena āḷavakakumārassa mātā puttaṃ [V 1.0188] nhāpetvā, maṇḍetvā, dukūlacumbaṭake katvā, aṅke sayāpetvā, nisinnā hoti. Rājapurisā rañño āṇāya tattha gantvā vippalapantiyā tassā soḷasannañca itthisahassānaṃ saddhiṃ dhātiyā taṃ ādāya pakkamiṃsu “sve yakkhabhakkho bhavissatī”ti. Taṃ divasañca bhagavā paccūsasamaye [M 1.0215] paccuṭṭhāya jetavanamahāvihāre [P 1.0220] gandhakuṭiyaṃ mahākaruṇāsamāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā puna buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ volokento addasa āḷavakassa kumārassa anāgāmiphaluppattiyā upanissayaṃ, yakkhassa ca sotāpattiphaluppattiyā upanissayaṃ desanāpariyosāne ca caturāsītiyā pāṇasahassānaṃ dhammacakkhupaṭilābhassāti. Tasmā vibhātāya rattiyā purebhattakiccaṃ katvā aniṭṭhitapacchābhattakiccova kāḷapakkhauposathadivase vattamāne oggate sūriye ekakova adutiyo pattacīvaramādāya pādagamaneneva sāvatthito tiṃsa yojanāni gantvā tassa yakkhassa bhavanaṃ pāvisi. Tena vuttaṃ “āḷavakassa yakkhassa bhavane”ti.

Then one day, after searching the entire city and not finding even a single child, they reported to the king: 'Your Majesty, there is no child in the city except for your own son in the palace, Prince Āḷavaka.' The king said: 'Just as my son is dear to me, so it is for all the world; however, there is none dearer than oneself. Go, give him also and protect my life.' At that time, the mother of Prince Āḷavaka had bathed her son, adorned him, placed him in a fine cloth wrap, and was sitting with him sleeping on her lap. The king’s men, by the king’s order, went there and, while she, along with the nurse and sixteen thousand women, was lamenting, they took the child and departed, thinking, 'Tomorrow he will be the yakkha’s meal.' That very day, at dawn, the Blessed One arose and, in the Gandhakuṭī in the Jetavana Great Monastery, entered into the attainment of great compassion. Then, surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, he saw the supporting condition for Prince Āḷavaka to attain the fruit of non-returning, the supporting condition for the yakkha to attain the fruit of stream-entry, and, at the conclusion of the teaching, for eighty-four thousand beings to attain the Dhamma-eye. Therefore, when the night had passed, after completing his pre-meal duties and without having finished his post-meal duties—it being the observance day of the dark fortnight and the sun having risen—he set out alone, without a companion, took his bowl and robe, and traveling thirty yojanas from Sāvatthī on foot, he entered the dwelling of that yakkha. Hence it is said: 'in the dwelling of the yakkha Āḷavaka.'

Kiṃ pana bhagavā yasmiṃ nigrodhe āḷavakassa bhavanaṃ, tassa mūle vihāsi, udāhu bhavaneyevāti? Vuccate – bhavaneyeva. Yatheva hi yakkhā attano bhavanaṃ passanti, tathā bhagavāpi. So tattha gantvā bhavanadvāre aṭṭhāsi. Tadā āḷavako himavante yakkhasamāgamaṃ gato hoti. Tato āḷavakassa dvārapālo gadrabho nāma yakkho bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā, vanditvā – “kiṃ, bhante, bhagavā vikāle āgato”ti āha. “Āma, gadrabha, āgatomhi. Sace te agaru, vihareyyāmekarattiṃ āḷavakassa bhavane”ti. “Na me, bhante, garu, apica kho so yakkho kakkhaḷo pharuso, mātāpitūnampi abhivādanādīni na karoti, mā rucci bhagavato idha vāso”ti. “Jānāmi, gadrabha, tassa kakkhaḷattaṃ, na koci mamantarāyo bhavissati, sace te agaru, vihareyyāmekaratti”nti[P 1.0221].

Now, did the Blessed One stay at the foot of the banyan tree where Āḷavaka's dwelling was, or in the dwelling itself? It is said: in the dwelling itself. For just as yakkhas see their own dwellings, so too does the Blessed One. He went there and stood at the door of the dwelling. At that time, Āḷavaka had gone to a gathering of yakkhas in the Himalayas. Then Āḷavaka's gatekeeper, a yakkha named Gadrabha, approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and said, 'Venerable Sir, why has the Blessed One come at an untimely hour?' 'Yes, Gadrabha, I have come. If it is not a burden to you, I would stay one night in Āḷavaka's dwelling.' 'It is no burden to me, Venerable Sir, but that yakkha is harsh and cruel. He does not perform acts of respect, such as bowing, even to his own parents. May the Blessed One not approve of staying here.' 'I know, Gadrabha, of his harshness. No harm will come to me. If it is not a burden to you, I would stay for one night.'

Dutiyampi gadrabho yakkho bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “aggitattakapālasadiso, bhante, āḷavako, ‘mātāpitaro’ti vā ‘samaṇabrāhmaṇā’ti vā ‘dhammo’ti vā na jānāti, idhāgatānaṃ cittakkhepampi karoti, hadayampi phāleti, pādepi gahetvā parasamudde vā paracakkavāḷe vā khipatī”ti. Dutiyampi bhagavā āha – “jānāmi, gadrabha, sace te agaru, vihareyyāmekaratti”nti. Tatiyampi gadrabho yakkho bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “aggitattakapālasadiso, bhante, āḷavako, ‘mātāpitaro’ti vā ‘samaṇabrāhmaṇā’ti vā ‘dhammo’ti vā na jānāti, idhāgatānaṃ cittakkhepampi karoti, hadayampi phāleti, pādepi gahetvā parasamudde [M 1.0216] vā paracakkavāḷe vā khipatī”ti. Tatiyampi bhagavā āha – “jānāmi, gadrabha, sace te agaru, vihareyyāmekaratti”nti. “Na me, bhante, garu, apica kho so yakkho attano anārocetvā [V 1.0189] anujānantaṃ maṃ jīvitā voropeyya, ārocemi, bhante, tassā”ti. “Yathāsukhaṃ, gadrabha, ārocehī”ti. “Tena hi, bhante, tvameva jānāhī”ti bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā himavantābhimukho pakkāmi. Bhavanadvārampi sayameva bhagavato vivaramadāsi. Bhagavā antobhavanaṃ pavisitvā yattha abhilakkhitesu maṅgaladivasādīsu nisīditvā āḷavako siriṃ anubhoti, tasmiṃyeva dibbaratanapallaṅke nisīditvā suvaṇṇābhaṃ muñci. Taṃ disvā yakkhassa itthiyo āgantvā, bhagavantaṃ vanditvā, samparivāretvā nisīdiṃsu. Bhagavā “pubbe tumhe dānaṃ datvā, sīlaṃ samādiyitvā, pūjaneyyaṃ pūjetvā, imaṃ sampattiṃ pattā, idānipi tatheva karotha, mā aññamaññaṃ issāmacchariyābhibhūtā viharathā”tiādinā nayena tāsaṃ pakiṇṇakadhammakathaṃ kathesi. Tā ca bhagavato madhuranigghosaṃ sutvā, sādhukārasahassāni datvā, bhagavantaṃ parivāretvā nisīdiṃsuyeva. Gadrabhopi himavantaṃ gantvā āḷavakassa ārocesi – “yagghe, mārisa, jāneyyāsi, vimāne te bhagavā nisinno”ti. So gadrabhassa saññamakāsi “tuṇhī hohi, gantvā kattabbaṃ karissāmī”ti. Purisamānena kira lajjito ahosi, tasmā “mā koci parisamajjhe suṇeyyā”ti vāresi.

A second time, the yakkha Gadrabha said this to the Blessed One: 'Venerable Sir, Āḷavaka is like a red-hot iron pan. He does not recognize "mother and father," or "ascetics and brahmins," or "Dhamma." For those who come here, he causes distraction of mind, he splits their hearts, and seizing them by the feet, he hurls them to the far shore of the ocean or to another world-system.' A second time, the Blessed One said: 'I know, Gadrabha. If it is not a burden to you, I would stay for one night.' A third time, the yakkha Gadrabha said this to the Blessed One: 'Venerable Sir, Āḷavaka is like a red-hot iron pan. He does not recognize "mother and father," or "ascetics and brahmins," or "Dhamma." For those who come here, he causes distraction of mind, he splits their hearts, and seizing them by the feet, he hurls them to the far shore of the ocean or to another world-system.' A third time, the Blessed One said: 'I know, Gadrabha. If it is not a burden to you, I would stay for one night.' 'It is no burden to me, Venerable Sir. But that yakkha would deprive me of my life for giving permission without having informed him. Venerable Sir, I will inform him.' 'Inform him as you see fit, Gadrabha.' 'In that case, Venerable Sir, you yourself must know what to do.' Having paid homage to the Blessed One, he departed, facing the Himalayas. The door of the dwelling also opened by itself for the Blessed One. The Blessed One entered the dwelling and, seating himself on the very divine jeweled couch where Āḷavaka would sit and enjoy his splendor on auspicious days and other such occasions, he emitted a golden radiance. Seeing this, the yakkha's women came, paid homage to the Blessed One, surrounded him, and sat down. The Blessed One gave them a miscellaneous Dhamma talk in this manner: 'In the past, you gave alms, undertook the moral precepts, and honored those worthy of honor, and thus you attained this prosperity. Now, too, you should act in the same way. Do not dwell overcome by mutual envy and avarice.' Hearing the sweet, resonant voice of the Blessed One, they uttered thousands of cries of 'Sādhu!' and sat surrounding him. Gadrabha, for his part, went to the Himalayas and informed Āḷavaka: 'My good sir, I pray you know, the Blessed One is seated in your dwelling.' He made a sign to Gadrabha, saying, 'Be silent. I will go and do what must be done.' It is said that he was ashamed out of manly pride; therefore, he stopped him, thinking, 'Let no one in the midst of the assembly hear of this.'

Tadā sātāgirahemavatā bhagavantaṃ jetavaneyeva vanditvā “yakkhasamāgamaṃ gamissāmā”ti saparivārā nānāyānehi ākāsena gacchanti. Ākāse ca yakkhānaṃ na sabbattha [P 1.0222] maggo atthi, ākāsaṭṭhāni vimānāni pariharitvā maggaṭṭhāneneva maggo hoti. Āḷavakassa pana vimānaṃ bhūmaṭṭhaṃ suguttaṃ pākāraparikkhittaṃ susaṃvihitadvāraṭṭālakagopuraṃ, upari kaṃsajālasañchannaṃ mañjūsasadisaṃ tiyojanaṃ ubbedhena. Tassa upari maggo hoti. Te taṃ padesamāgamma gantuṃ asamatthā ahesuṃ. Buddhānañhi nisinnokāsassa uparibhāgena yāva bhavaggā, tāva koci gantuṃ asamattho. Te “kimida”nti āvajjetvā bhagavantaṃ disvā ākāse khittaleḍḍu viya oruyha vanditvā, dhammaṃ sutvā, padakkhiṇaṃ katvā “yakkhasamāgamaṃ gacchāma bhagavā”ti tīṇi vatthūni pasaṃsantā yakkhasamāgamaṃ agamaṃsu. Āḷavako te disvā “idha nisīdathā”ti paṭikkamma okāsamadāsi. Te [M 1.0217] āḷavakassa nivedesuṃ “lābhā te, āḷavaka, yassa te bhavane bhagavā viharati, gacchāvuso bhagavantaṃ payirupāsassū”ti. Evaṃ bhagavā bhavaneyeva vihāsi, na yasmiṃ nigrodhe āḷavakassa bhavanaṃ, tassa mūleti. Tena vuttaṃ “ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā āḷaviyaṃ viharati āḷavakassa yakkhassa bhavane”ti.

Then Sātāgira and Hemavata, having paid homage to the Blessed One at Jetavana, set out through the sky with their retinues in various vehicles, saying, 'We will go to the gathering of yakkhas.' Now, in the sky, there is not a path for yakkhas everywhere; a path exists only by avoiding the celestial mansions. But Āḷavaka’s mansion stood on the ground, well-guarded, surrounded by walls, with well-arranged gates, watchtowers, and gatehouses. Above, it was covered with a bronze netting, resembling a chest, three leagues in height. The path lay above it. Reaching that place, they were unable to proceed. For no one is able to go above the place where a Buddha is seated, up to the highest realm of existence. They reflected, 'What is this?' Then, seeing the Blessed One, they descended like a clod of earth thrown into the sky, paid homage, listened to the Dhamma, circumambulated him, and said, 'Blessed One, we are going to the gathering of yakkhas.' Praising the Three Jewels, they went to the yakkha assembly. Āḷavaka, seeing them, stepped back and offered them a place to sit. They informed Āḷavaka, 'You are fortunate, Āḷavaka, that the Blessed One dwells in your mansion. Go, friend, and attend upon the Blessed One.' Thus, the Blessed One remained in the mansion itself, not at the foot of the banyan tree where Āḷavaka’s dwelling was. Therefore, it is said: 'At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Āḷavī in the mansion of the yakkha Āḷavaka.'

Atha kho āḷavako…pe… bhagavantaṃ etadavoca “nikkhama samaṇā”ti. “Kasmā panāyaṃ etadavocā”ti? Vuccate – rosetukāmatāya. Tatrevaṃ ādito pabhuti sambandho veditabbo [V 1.0190] – ayañhi yasmā assaddhassa saddhākathā dukkathā hoti dussīlādīnaṃ sīlādikathā viya, tasmā tesaṃ yakkhānaṃ santikā bhagavato pasaṃsaṃ sutvā eva aggimhi pakkhittaloṇasakkharā viya abbhantarakopena taṭataṭāyamānahadayo hutvā “ko so bhagavā nāma, yo mama bhavanaṃ paviṭṭho”ti āha. Te āhaṃsu – “na tvaṃ, āvuso, jānāsi bhagavantaṃ amhākaṃ satthāraṃ, yo tusitabhavane ṭhito pañca mahāvilokanāni viloketvā”tiādinā nayena yāva dhammacakkappavattanaṃ kathentā paṭisandhiādinā dvattiṃsa pubbanimittāni vatvā “imānipi tvaṃ, āvuso[P 1.0223], acchariyāni nāddasā”ti codesuṃ. So disvāpi kodhavasena “nāddasa”nti āha. Āvuso āḷavaka passeyyāsi vā tvaṃ, na vā, ko tayā attho passatā vā apassatā vā, kiṃ tvaṃ karissasi amhākaṃ satthuno, yo tvaṃ taṃ upanidhāya calakkakudhamahāusabhasamīpe tadahujātavacchako viya, tidhāpabhinnamattavāraṇasamīpe bhiṅkapotako viya, bhāsuravilambakesaraupasobhitakkhandhassa migarañño samīpe jarasiṅgālo viya, diyaḍḍhayojanasatappavaḍḍhakāyasupaṇṇarājasamīpe chinnapakkhakākapotako viya khāyasi, gaccha yaṃ te karaṇīyaṃ, taṃ karohīti. Evaṃ vutte kuddho āḷavako uṭṭhahitvā manosilātale vāmapādena ṭhatvā “passatha dāni tumhākaṃ vā satthā mahānubhāvo, ahaṃ vā”ti dakkhiṇapādena saṭṭhiyojanamattaṃ kelāsapabbatakūṭaṃ akkami, taṃ ayokūṭapahaṭo niddhantaayopiṇḍo viya papaṭikāyo muñci. So tatra ṭhatvā “ahaṃ āḷavako”ti ghosesi, sakalajambudīpaṃ saddo phari.

Then Āḷavaka… addressed the Blessed One, saying, 'Get out, ascetic!' 'But why did he say this?' It is said—out of a desire to provoke. From the very beginning, the connection should be understood thus: just as talk of virtue is unpleasant to the immoral, so talk of faith is unpleasant to the faithless. Therefore, having heard praise of the Blessed One from those yakkhas, his heart crackled with inner rage, like salt crystals thrown into a fire. He said, 'Who is this so-called Blessed One who has entered my dwelling?' They replied, 'Friend, do you not know the Blessed One, our teacher, who, while in the Tusita heaven, surveyed the five great observations?'—and so on, recounting up to the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma. They described the thirty-two portents, beginning with his conception, and reproached him, saying, 'Friend, have you not seen these wonders?' Though he had seen them, out of anger he said, 'I have not seen them!' 'Friend Āḷavaka, whether you have seen or not, what use is it to you, seeing or not seeing? What can you do to our teacher? Compared to him, you appear like a newborn calf beside a mighty bull with a shaking hump; like an elephant calf beside a great elephant in full, threefold musth; like an old jackal beside the king of beasts, whose shoulders are adorned with a splendid, flowing mane; like a young crow with clipped wings beside the king of the Supaṇṇas, whose body is one hundred and fifty leagues long. Go, do what you must do!' Enraged by these words, Āḷavaka rose up, stood on a slab of red arsenic with his left foot, and said, 'Now you shall see whether your teacher is of great power, or I am!' With his right foot, he stamped on the sixty-league peak of Mount Kelāsa. Like a smelted lump of iron struck by an iron hammer, it broke into pieces. Standing there, he roared, 'I am Āḷavaka!' The sound spread throughout the entire Jambudīpa.

Cattāro [M 1.0218] kira saddā sakalajambudīpe suyyiṃsu – yañca puṇṇako yakkhasenāpati dhanañcayakorabyarājānaṃ jūte jinitvā apphoṭetvā “ahaṃ jini”nti ugghosesi, yañca sakko devānamindo kassapassa bhagavato sāsane parihāyamāne vissakammaṃ devaputtaṃ sunakhaṃ kāretvā “ahaṃ pāpabhikkhū ca pāpabhikkhuniyo ca upāsake ca upāsikāyo ca sabbeva adhammavādino khādāmī”ti ugghosāpesi, yañca kusajātake pabhāvatihetu sattahi rājūhi nagare uparuddhe pabhāvatiṃ attanā saha hatthikkhandhaṃ āropetvā nagarā nikkhamma “ahaṃ sīhassarakusamahārājā”ti mahāpuriso ugghosesi, yañca āḷavako kelāsamuddhani ṭhatvā “ahaṃ āḷavako”ti. Tadā hi sakalajambudīpe dvāre dvāre ṭhatvā ugghositasadisaṃ ahosi, tiyojanasahassavitthato [P 1.0224] ca himavāpi saṅkampi yakkhassa ānubhāvena.

Four sounds, it is said, were heard throughout all of Jambudīpa: the sound when Puṇṇaka, the yakkha commander, having defeated King Dhanañjaya Korabya in a game of dice, clapped his arms and proclaimed, 'I have won!'; the sound when Sakka, king of the devas, during the decline of the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, had the deva Vissakamma create a dog and caused it to be proclaimed, 'I will devour the wicked monks, wicked nuns, wicked laymen, and wicked laywomen—all who teach what is not the Dhamma!'; the sound in the Kusa Jātaka when, the city being besieged by seven kings on account of Pabhāvatī, the great being placed Pabhāvatī together with himself on an elephant’s back, went forth from the city and proclaimed, 'I am the Great King Kusa, of the lion-like voice!'; and the sound when Āḷavaka stood atop Mount Kelāsa and proclaimed, 'I am Āḷavaka!' At that time, it was as if that sound were proclaimed while standing at every door in all of Jambudīpa. And the Himavanta, three thousand leagues in breadth, also trembled by the yakkha’s power.

So vātamaṇḍalaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi – “eteneva samaṇaṃ palāpessāmī”ti. Te puratthimādibhedā vātā samuṭṭhahitvā aḍḍhayojanayojanadviyojanatiyojanappamāṇāni pabbatakūṭāni padāletvā vanagaccharukkhādīni ummūletvā āḷavīnagaraṃ pakkhantā jiṇṇahatthisālādīni cuṇṇentā chadaniṭṭhakā [V 1.0191] ākāse bhamentā. Bhagavā “mā kassaci uparodho hotū”ti adhiṭṭhāsi. Te vātā dasabalaṃ patvā cīvarakaṇṇamattampi cāletuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu. Tato mahāvassaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi “udakena ajjhottharitvā samaṇaṃ māressāmī”ti. Tassānubhāvena uparūpari satapaṭalasahassapaṭalādibhedā valāhakā uṭṭhahitvā vassiṃsu, vuṭṭhidhārāvegena pathavī chiddā ahosi, vanarukkhādīnaṃ upari mahogho āgantvā dasabalassa cīvare ussāvabindumattampi temetuṃ nāsakkhi. Tato pāsāṇavassaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi, mahantāni mahantāni pabbatakūṭāni dhūmāyantāni pajjalantāni ākāsenāgantvā dasabalaṃ patvā dibbamālāguḷāni sampajjiṃsu. Tato paharaṇavassaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi, ekatodhārāubhatodhārā asisattikhurappādayo dhūmāyantā pajjalantā ākāsenāgantvā dasabalaṃ patvā dibbapupphāni ahesuṃ. Tato aṅgāravassaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi, kiṃsukavaṇṇā aṅgārā ākāsenāgantvā dasabalassa pādamūle dibbapupphāni hutvā vikiriṃsu. Tato kukkulavassaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi, accuṇho kukkulo ākāsenāgantvā dasabalassa pādamūle candanacuṇṇaṃ hutvā nipati. Tato vālukāvassaṃ [M 1.0219] samuṭṭhāpesi, atisukhumā vālukā dhūmāyantā pajjalantā ākāsenāgantvā dasabalassa pādamūle dibbapupphāni hutvā nipatiṃsu. Tato kalalavassaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi, taṃ kalalavassaṃ dhūmāyantaṃ pajjalantaṃ ākāsenāgantvā dasabalassa pādamūle dibbagandhaṃ hutvā nipati. Tato andhakāraṃ samuṭṭhāpesi “bhiṃsetvā samaṇaṃ palāpessāmī”ti. Taṃ caturaṅgasamannāgatandhakārasadisaṃ hutvā dasabalaṃ patvā sūriyappabhāvihatamivandhakāraṃ antaradhāyi.

He raised a whirlwind, thinking, 'With this alone, I will drive away the ascetic.' Winds arose from the east and other directions, shattering mountain peaks measuring half a yojana, one yojana, two yojanas, and three yojanas. They uprooted forest trees and groves, and upon entering the city of Āḷavī, crushed dilapidated elephant sheds and sent roof tiles whirling into the sky. The Blessed One resolved, 'May no one be harmed.' Those winds, upon reaching the One of Ten Powers, could not stir even the corner of his robe. Then he conjured a great rainstorm, thinking, 'I will kill the ascetic by overwhelming him with water.' By his power, clouds arose layer upon layer—hundreds and thousands of layers—and poured down rain. The force of the downpour split the earth, and though a great flood came over the forest trees, it could not moisten even a dewdrop on the robe of the One of Ten Powers. Next, he conjured a shower of stones. Massive mountain peaks, smoking and blazing, descended from the sky, but upon reaching the One of Ten Powers, they turned into divine garlands and bouquets. Then he conjured a shower of weapons. Single-edged and double-edged weapons such as swords, spears, and razors, smoking and blazing, descended from the sky, but upon reaching the One of Ten Powers, they became divine flowers. Then he conjured a shower of embers. Embers the color of the kiṃsuka flower descended from the sky and, upon becoming divine flowers at the feet of the One of Ten Powers, scattered about. Next, he conjured a shower of hot ashes. Extremely hot ashes descended from the sky but, upon becoming sandalwood powder at the feet of the One of Ten Powers, fell there. Then he conjured a shower of sand. Very fine sand, smoking and blazing, descended from the sky but, upon becoming divine flowers at the feet of the One of Ten Powers, fell there.
