Then he conjured a shower of mud. That shower of mud, smoking and blazing, descended from the sky but, upon becoming a divine fragrance at the feet of the One of Ten Powers, fell there. Finally, he conjured darkness, thinking, 'I will frighten the ascetic and drive him away.' That darkness, like the impenetrable darkness of the four factors, reached the One of Ten Powers but vanished like darkness dispelled by the light of the sun.

Evaṃ yakkho imāhi navahi vātavassapāsāṇapaharaṇaṅgārakukkulavālukakalalandhakāravuṭṭhīhi [P 1.0225] bhagavantaṃ palāpetuṃ asakkonto nānāvidhapaharaṇahatthāya anekappakārarūpabhūtagaṇasamākulāya caturaṅginiyā senāya sayameva bhagavantaṃ abhigato. Te bhūtagaṇā anekappakāre vikāre katvā “gaṇhatha hanathā”ti bhagavato upari āgacchantā viya honti, apica te niddhantalohapiṇḍaṃ viya makkhikā, bhagavantaṃ allīyituṃ asamatthā evaṃ ahesuṃ. Evaṃ santepi yathā bodhimaṇḍe māro āgatavelāyameva nivatto, tathā anivattitvā upaḍḍharattimattaṃ byākulamakaṃsu. Evaṃ upaḍḍharattimattaṃ anekappakāravibhiṃsanadassanenapi bhagavantaṃ cāletumasakkonto āḷavako cintesi – “yaṃnūnāhaṃ kenaci ajeyyaṃ dussāvudhaṃ muñceyya”nti.

Thus, the yakkha, unable to drive the Blessed One away with these nine deluges—of wind, rain, stones, weapons, embers, hot ashes, sand, mud, and darkness—approached the Blessed One himself with a fourfold army, teeming with a host of beings of manifold forms, with various weapons in hand. Those hosts of beings, creating various terrifying transformations, appeared to come upon the Blessed One shouting, 'Seize him! Kill him!' Yet, like flies on a molten lump of iron, they were unable to so much as touch the Blessed One. Even so, unlike Māra, who retreated at the very moment of his arrival at the Bodhi throne, they did not retreat but created turmoil for about half the night. Thus, for about half the night, unable to stir the Blessed One even by the mere showing of many kinds of terrifying sights, Āḷavaka the yakkha thought, 'What if I were to release the Dussāvudha, the cloth-weapon, which is invincible by anyone?'

Cattāri kira āvudhāni loke seṭṭhāni – sakkassa vajirāvudhaṃ, vessavaṇassa gadāvudhaṃ, yamassa nayanāvudhaṃ, āḷavakassa dussāvudhanti. Yadi hi sakko kuddho vajirāvudhaṃ sinerumatthake pahareyya aṭṭhasaṭṭhisahassādhikayojanasatasahassaṃ sineruṃ vinivijjhitvā heṭṭhato gaccheyya[V 1.0192]. Vessavaṇassa puthujjanakāle vissajjitagadā bahūnaṃ yakkhasahassānaṃ sīsaṃ pātetvā puna hatthapāsaṃ āgantvā tiṭṭhati. Yamena kuddhena nayanāvudhena olokitamatte anekāni kumbhaṇḍasahassāni tattakapāle tilā viya vipphurantāni vinassanti. Āḷavako kuddho sace ākāse dussāvudhaṃ muñceyya, dvādasa vassāni devo na vasseyya. Sace pathaviyaṃ muñceyya, sabbarukkhatiṇādīni sussitvā dvādasavassantaraṃ na puna ruheyyuṃ. Sace samudde muñceyya, tattakapāle udakabindu viya sabbamudakaṃ susseyya. Sace sinerusadisepi pabbate muñceyya, khaṇḍākhaṇḍaṃ hutvā vikireyya. So evaṃ mahānubhāvaṃ dussāvudhaṃ uttarīyakataṃ muñcitvā aggahesi[M 1.0220][P 1.0226]. Yebhuyyena dasasahassilokadhātudevatā vegena sannipatiṃsu – “ajja bhagavā āḷavakaṃ damessati, tattha dhammaṃ sossāmā”ti. Yuddhadassanakāmāpi devatā sannipatiṃsu. Evaṃ sakalampi ākāsaṃ devatāhi puripuṇṇamahosi.

It is said that there are four supreme weapons in the world: the thunderbolt-weapon of Sakka, the club-weapon of Vessavaṇa, the eye-weapon of Yama, and the cloth-weapon of Āḷavaka. If Sakka, in his anger, were to strike the peak of Mount Sineru with his thunderbolt-weapon, it would pierce through the one hundred sixty-eight thousand yojanas of Sineru and pass out the bottom. The club-weapon that Vessavaṇa released when he was a worldling would fell the heads of many thousands of yakkhas and then return to his hand. When Yama, in his anger, merely looks with his eye-weapon, many thousands of kumbhaṇḍas perish, sputtering like sesame seeds on a hot pan. If Āḷavaka, in his anger, were to release his cloth-weapon into the sky, the gods would not send rain for twelve years. If he were to release it upon the earth, all trees, grass, and so on would wither and not grow again for twelve years. If he were to release it into the ocean, all the water would dry up like a drop of water on a hot pan. If he were to release it upon a mountain like Sineru, it would be shattered into fragments and scattered. So Āḷavaka unfastened and grasped that cloth-weapon of such immense power, which he wore as an upper garment. Then, for the most part, the deities from the ten-thousandfold world-system swiftly gathered, thinking, 'Today the Blessed One will subdue Āḷavaka, and there we shall hear the Dhamma.' Deities desiring to witness the battle also assembled. Thus, the entire sky became completely filled with deities.

Atha āḷavako bhagavato samīpe uparūpari vicaritvā vatthāvudhaṃ muñci. Taṃ asanivicakkaṃ viya ākāse bheravasaddaṃ karontaṃ dhūmāyantaṃ pajjalantaṃ bhagavantaṃ patvā yakkhassa mānamaddanatthaṃ pādamuñchanacoḷakaṃ hutvā pādamūle nipati. Āḷavako taṃ disvā chinnavisāṇo viya usabho, uddhaṭadāṭho viya sappo, nittejo nimmado nipatitamānaddhajo hutvā cintesi – “dussāvudhampi samaṇaṃ nabhibhosi, kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa”nti? Idaṃ kāraṇaṃ, mettāvihārayutto samaṇo, handa naṃ rosetvā mettāya viyojemīti. Iminā sambandhenetaṃ vuttaṃ – “atha kho āḷavako yakkho yena bhagavā…pe… nikkhama samaṇā”ti. Tatrāyamadhippāyo – kasmā mayā ananuññāto mama bhavanaṃ pavisitvā gharasāmiko viya itthāgārassa majjhe nisinnosi, nanu ayuttametaṃ samaṇassa yadidaṃ adinnapaṭibhogo itthisaṃsaggo ca, tasmā yadi tvaṃ samaṇadhamme ṭhito, nikkhama samaṇāti. Eke pana “etāni aññāni ca pharusavacanāni vatvā evāyaṃ etadavocā”ti bhaṇanti.

Then the yakkha Āḷavaka, having paced up and down near the Blessed One, released his cloth-weapon. That weapon, like a thunderbolt-wheel in the sky, making a terrifying sound, smoking and blazing, upon reaching the Blessed One, for the purpose of crushing the yakkha's pride, became a foot-wiping cloth and fell at his feet. Seeing this, Āḷavaka, like a bull with broken horns, like a snake with fangs extracted, became strengthless, without pride, his banner of pride fallen, and thought: 'Not even the cloth-weapon could harm the ascetic. What could be the reason?' This is the reason: the ascetic abides endowed with loving-kindness. Come, let me anger him and separate him from loving-kindness. In this connection, it is said: 'Then the yakkha Āḷavaka approached the Blessed One... Get out, ascetic!' Herein, this is the meaning: 'Why, unpermitted by me, have you entered my dwelling and are seated in the midst of the women's quarters like the master of the house? Is it not indeed improper for an ascetic, this which is enjoying what is not given and association with women? Therefore, if you are established in the ascetic's code, get out, ascetic!' Some, however, say that he said this only after speaking these and other harsh words.

Atha bhagavā “yasmā thaddho paṭithaddhabhāvena vinetuṃ na sakkā, so hi paṭithaddhabhāve kariyamāne seyyathāpi caṇḍassa kukkurassa nāsāya pittaṃ bhindeyya, so bhiyyoso mattāya caṇḍataro assa, evaṃ thaddhataro hoti, mudunā pana so sakkā vinetu”nti ñatvā “sādhāvuso”ti piyavacanena tassa vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā nikkhami[P 1.0227]. Tena vuttaṃ “sādhāvusoti bhagavā nikkhamī”ti.

Then the Blessed One, knowing that 'one who is stubborn cannot be tamed by stubbornness, for if stubbornness is applied to him, it would be as if one were to break the gall bladder on the nose of a fierce dog—he would become exceedingly fiercer and thus more stubborn. But with gentleness, he can be tamed,' accepted his words with pleasant speech, saying, 'Good, friend,' and departed. Therefore, it is said: 'The Blessed One departed, saying, “Good, friend.”'

Tato āḷavako “suvaco vatāyaṃ samaṇo ekavacaneneva nikkhanto, evaṃ nāma nikkhametuṃ [V 1.0193] sukhaṃ samaṇaṃ akāraṇenevāhaṃ sakalarattiṃ yuddhena abbhuyyāsi”nti muducitto hutvā puna cintesi “idānipi na sakkā jānituṃ, kiṃ nu kho suvacatāya nikkhanto, udāhu kodhena, handa naṃ vīmaṃsāmī”ti. Tato “pavisa samaṇā”ti āha. Atha “suvaco”ti mudubhūtacittavavatthānakaraṇatthaṃ punapi piyavacanaṃ vadanto sādhāvusoti bhagavā pāvisi. Āḷavako punappunaṃ tameva suvacabhāvaṃ vīmaṃsanto [M 1.0221] dutiyampi tatiyampi “nikkhama pavisā”ti āha. Bhagavāpi tathā akāsi. Yadi na kareyya, pakatiyāpi thaddhayakkhassa cittaṃ thaddhataraṃ hutvā dhammakathāya bhājanaṃ na bhaveyya. Tasmā yathā nāma mātā rodantaṃ puttakaṃ yaṃ so icchati, taṃ datvā vā katvā vā saññāpeti, tathā bhagavā kilesarodanena rodantaṃ yakkhaṃ saññāpetuṃ yaṃ so bhaṇati, taṃ akāsi. Yathā ca dhātī thaññaṃ apivantaṃ dārakaṃ kiñci datvā upalāḷetvā pāyeti, tathā bhagavā yakkhaṃ lokuttaradhammakhīraṃ pāyetuṃ tassa patthitavacanakaraṇena upalāḷento evamakāsi. Yathā ca puriso lābumhi catumadhuraṃ pūretukāmo tassabbhantaraṃ sodheti, evaṃ bhagavā yakkhassa citte lokuttaracatumadhuraṃ pūretukāmo tassa abbhantare kodhamalaṃ sodhetuṃ yāva tatiyaṃ nikkhamanapavesanaṃ akāsi.

Then Āḷavaka thought: 'This ascetic is indeed easy to speak to; he departed with just one word. It is easy to make such an ascetic depart! For no reason, I assailed him with battle all night long.' With a softened heart, he pondered again: 'Even now, it is not possible to know—did he depart out of compliance, or out of anger? Come, let me test him.' Then he said, 'Enter, ascetic.' Then, for the purpose of establishing the state of his softened mind, the Blessed One, again speaking pleasant words, said, 'Very well, friend,' and entered. Āḷavaka, repeatedly testing that very quality of being easy to speak to, a second and a third time said, 'Leave! Enter!' The Blessed One also did so. If he had not done so, the yakkha’s naturally stubborn mind would have become even more stubborn and would not have been a vessel for a Dhamma discourse. Therefore, just as a mother pacifies her crying child by giving or doing what it wants, so the Blessed One, to pacify the yakkha crying with the crying of defilements, did as he was told. And just as a wet nurse, coaxing a child who is not drinking milk by giving it something, persuades it to drink, so too the Blessed One, to make the yakkha drink the milk of the supramundane Dhamma, coaxed him by doing as he requested. And just as a man wishing to fill a gourd with the fourfold sweetness first cleans its interior, so too the Blessed One, desiring to fill the yakkha's mind with the supramundane fourfold sweetness, cleansed the inner stain of anger by leaving and entering up to the third time.

Atha āḷavako “suvaco ayaṃ samaṇo, ‘nikkhamā’ti vutto nikkhamati, ‘pavisā’ti vutto pavisati, yaṃnūnāhaṃ imaṃ samaṇaṃ evamevaṃ sakalarattiṃ kilametvā, pāde gahetvā, pāragaṅgāya khipeyya”nti pāpakaṃ citaṃ uppādetvā catutthavāraṃ āha – “nikkhama samaṇā”ti. Taṃ ñatvā bhagavā “na khvāhaṃ ta”nti āha. “Evaṃ vutte taduttariṃ karaṇīyaṃ pariyesamāno pañhaṃ pucchitabbaṃ maññissati, taṃ dhammakathāya mukhaṃ bhavissatī”ti ñatvā [P 1.0228] “na khvāhaṃ ta”nti āha. Tattha naiti paṭikkhepe, khoiti avadhāraṇe. Ahanti attanidassanaṃ, nti hetuvacanaṃ. Tenettha “yasmā tvaṃ evaṃ cintesi, tasmā ahaṃ āvuso neva nikkhamissāmi, yaṃ te karaṇīyaṃ, taṃ karohī”ti evamattho daṭṭhabbo.

Then the yakkha Āḷavaka thought: 'This ascetic is compliant: when told, “Go out,” he goes out; when told, “Come in,” he comes in. What if I were to wear out this ascetic all night long in this very way, and then, grabbing him by the feet, throw him to the far bank of the Ganges?' Having given rise to this evil thought, he spoke for the fourth time: 'Go out, ascetic!' Knowing this, the Blessed One said, 'I will not go out.' Knowing that, 'When this is said, seeking what to do next, he will think that a question should be asked, and that will become an opening for a Dhamma discourse,' the Blessed One said, 'I will not go out.' Herein, `na` is a particle of negation, `kho` is a particle of emphasis, `ahaṃ` is a self-reference, and the word `taṃ` indicates a reason. By that, the meaning here should be understood thus: 'Because you have thought thus, friend, I will not go out. Do what you must do.'

Tato āḷavako yasmā pubbepi ākāsenāgamanavelāyaṃ “kiṃ nu kho, etaṃ suvaṇṇavimānaṃ, udāhu rajatamaṇivimānānaṃ aññataraṃ, handa naṃ passāmā”ti evaṃ attano vimānaṃ āgate iddhimante tāpasaparibbājake pañhaṃ pucchitvā vissajjetumasakkonte cittakkhepādīhi viheṭheti. Kathaṃ? Amanussā hi bhiṃsanakarūpadassanena vā hadayavatthuparimaddanena vāti dvīhākārehi cittakkhepaṃ karonti. Ayaṃ pana yasmā “iddhimanto bhiṃsanakarūpadassanena na tasantī”ti ñatvā attano iddhippabhāvena sukhumattabhāvaṃ nimminitvā, tesaṃ anto pavisitvā hadayavatthuṃ parimaddati, tato cittasantati na saṇṭhāti, tassā asaṇṭhamānāya [V 1.0194] ummattakā honti [M 1.0222] khittacittā. Evaṃ khittacittānaṃ etesaṃ urampi phāleti, pādepi ne gahetvā pāragaṅgāya khipati “māssu me puna evarūpā bhavanamāgamiṃsū”ti, tasmā te pañhe saritvā “yaṃnūnāhaṃ imaṃ samaṇaṃ idāni evaṃ viheṭheyya”nti cintetvā āha “pañhaṃ taṃ samaṇā”tiādi.

Therefore, Āḷavaka—because in the past, whenever ascetics and wanderers possessed of psychic power came to his celestial palace through the sky, thinking, 'What is this? Is it a golden palace, or is it one of silver or jewels? Come, let us see it!'—would question them, and when they were unable to answer, he would torment them with mental derangement and the like. How so? Non-humans, indeed, cause mental derangement in two ways: either by showing a terrifying form or by crushing the heart-base. But this yakkha, knowing, 'Those with psychic power are not frightened by the sight of a terrifying form,' would create a subtle physical form by his own psychic power, enter into them, and crush their heart-base. Consequently, their stream of consciousness would become unstable, and with it being unstable, they would become mad, their minds deranged. When their minds were thus deranged, he would even split their chests, and seizing them by the feet, he would hurl them to the far side of the Ganges, thinking, 'May such beings never again come to my abode!' Therefore, recalling those questions and thinking, 'What if I were to torment this ascetic now in the same way?' he said, 'Ascetic, I will ask you a question,' and so on.

Kuto panassa te pañhāti? Tassa kira mātāpitaro kassapaṃ bhagavantaṃ payirupāsitvā aṭṭha pañhe savissajjane uggahesuṃ. Te daharakāle āḷavakaṃ pariyāpuṇāpesuṃ. So kālaccayena vissajjanaṃ sammussi. Tato “ime pañhāpi mā vinassantū”ti suvaṇṇapaṭṭe jātihiṅgulakena likhāpetvā vimāne nikkhipi. Evamete buddhapañhā buddhavisayā eva honti. Bhagavā taṃ sutvā yasmā buddhānaṃ pariccattalābhantarāyo vā jīvitantarāyo vā sabbaññutaññāṇabyāmappabhānaṃ paṭighāto vā na sakkā kenaci kātuṃ, tasmā taṃ loke asādhāraṇaṃ buddhānubhāvaṃ dassento āha [P 1.0229] “na khvāhaṃ taṃ, āvuso, passāmi sadevake loke”ti.

From where, then, did these questions of his come? It is said that his parents, having attended upon the Blessed One Kassapa, learned eight questions together with their answers. When Āḷavaka was young, they had him master them. In the course of time, he forgot the answers. Then, thinking, 'May these questions not be lost,' he had them inscribed on a golden plate with natural vermilion and placed it in his celestial palace. Thus, these are Buddha-questions, truly the domain of a Buddha. The Blessed One, having heard this, and because it is not possible for anyone to create an obstacle to a Buddha's gains, or a danger to his life, or an obstruction to the fathom-wide radiance of his knowledge of omniscience, demonstrated that power of a Buddha which is unparalleled in the world, saying: 'Friend, I do not see one in this world with its gods...'

Tattha “sadevakavacanena pañcakāmāvacaradevaggahaṇa”ntiādinā nayena etesaṃ padānaṃ atthamattadassanena saṅkhepo vutto, na anusandhiyojanākkamena vitthāro. Svāyaṃ vuccati – sadevakavacanena hi ukkaṭṭhaparicchedato sabbadevesu gahitesupi yesaṃ tattha sannipatite devagaṇe vimati ahosi “māro mahānubhāvo chakāmāvacarissaro vasavattī paccanīkasāto dhammadessī kururakammanto, kiṃ nu kho, sopissa cittakkhepādīni na kareyyā”ti, tesaṃ vimatipaṭibāhanatthaṃ “samārake”ti āha. Tato yesaṃ ahosi – “brahmā mahānubhāvo ekaṅguliyā ekacakkavāḷasahasse ālokaṃ karoti, dvīhi…pe… dasahi aṅgulīhi dasasu cakkavāḷasahassesu, anuttarañca jhānasamāpattisukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti, kiṃ sopi na kareyyā”ti, tesaṃ vimatipaṭibāhanatthaṃ “sabrahmake”ti āha. Atha yesaṃ ahosi “puthu samaṇabrāhmaṇā sāsanassa paccatthikā paccāmittā mantādibalasamannāgatā, kiṃ tepi na kareyyu”nti, tesaṃ vimatipaṭibāhanatthaṃ “sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiyā pajāyā”ti āha. Evaṃ ukkaṭṭhaṭṭhānesu kassaci abhāvaṃ dassetvā idāni sadevamanussāyāti vacanena [M 1.0223] sammutideve avasesamanusse ca upādāya ukkaṭṭhaparicchedavaseneva sesasattalokepi kassaci abhāvaṃ dassesīti evamettha anusandhiyojanākkamo veditabbo.

Herein, by the method beginning with 'by the word sadevake is meant the inclusion of the devas of the five sense-spheres,' a summary is given by showing only the meaning of these terms, not an elaboration according to the method of sequential connection. This is as follows: Although by the word sadevake, through the principle of including the highest category, all devas are included, for those in the assembled company of devas who had this doubt: 'Māra is of great power, lord of the six sense-spheres, the sovereign Vasavattī, hostile, a hater of the Dhamma, a doer of cruel deeds—might he not be able to cause mental derangement and the like?'—to dispel their doubt, the words 'with its Māra' were spoken. Then, for those who had this doubt: 'Brahmā is of great power; with one finger he illuminates a thousand world-systems, with two... with ten fingers he illuminates ten thousand world-systems, and he experiences the unsurpassed bliss of jhāna-attainment—might he not be able to do so?'—to dispel their doubt, the words 'with its Brahmās' were spoken. Then, for those who had this doubt: 'Many ascetics and brahmins are opponents and enemies of the Teaching, possessed of the power of mantras and so on—might they not be able to do so?'—to dispel their doubt, the words 'with its ascetics and brahmins' were spoken. Thus, having shown the absence of anyone in the highest stations, now by the words 'with its devas and humans'—including conventional devas and the remaining human beings—he showed, by this same principle of including the highest category, the absence of anyone in the remaining world of beings. In this way, the method of sequential connection should be understood here.

Evaṃ bhagavā tassa bādhanacittaṃ paṭisedhetvā pañhapucchane ussāhaṃ janento āha “apica tvaṃ, āvuso, puccha yadākaṅkhasī”ti. Tassattho – puccha, yadi ākaṅkhasi, na me pañhavissajjane [V 1.0195] bhāro atthi. Atha vā “puccha yaṃ ākaṅkhasi, te sabbaṃ vissajjessāmī”ti sabbaññupavāraṇaṃ pavāresi asādhāraṇaṃ paccekabuddhaaggasāvakamahāsāvakehi. Te hi “pucchāvuso sutvā vedissāmā”ti vadanti. Buddhā pana “pucchāvuso yadākaṅkhasī”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.237, 246) vā,

Thus the Blessed One, having prevented his intention to harm and seeking to generate his enthusiasm for asking questions, said: 'Furthermore, friend, ask what you desire.' Its meaning is: 'Ask, if you desire; for me there is no burden in answering questions.' Or, 'Ask what you desire, and I will answer it all for you.' In this way, he extended the invitation of the Omniscient One, one not shared with Paccekabuddhas, chief disciples, and great disciples. For they indeed say, 'Ask, friend; having heard, we shall know.' The Buddhas, however, say, 'Ask, friend, what you desire,' or,

“Puccha vāsava maṃ pañhaṃ, yaṃ kiñci manasicchasī”ti vā. (dī. ni. 2.356);

'Ask of me a question, Vāsava, whatever you desire in your mind,' or,

“Bāvarissa [P 1.0230] ca tuyhaṃ vā, sabbesaṃ sabbasaṃsayaṃ;

Katāvakāsā pucchavho, yaṃ kiñci manasicchathā”ti vā. (su. ni. 1036) –

'For Bāvari, and for you, and for all,

Regarding every single doubt;

The opportunity is granted, you may ask

Whatever you desire in your mind,' or,

Evamādinā nayena devamanussānaṃ sabbaññupavāraṇaṃ pavārenti. Anacchariyañcetaṃ, yaṃ bhagavā buddhabhūmiṃ patvā evaṃ pavāraṇaṃ pavāreyya, yo bodhisattabhūmiyaṃ padesañāṇe vattamānopi –

By this and other such methods, they extend the invitation of omniscience to devas and humans. And it is no wonder that the Blessed One, having attained the stage of a Buddha, should extend such an invitation, for he, even while abiding in the Bodhisattva-stage with only partial knowledge—

“Koṇḍañña pañhāni viyākarohi, yācanti taṃ isayo sādhurūpā;

Koṇḍañña eso manujesu dhammo, yaṃ vuddhamāgacchati esa bhāro”ti. (jā. 2.17.60) –

'Koṇḍañña, do explain the questions;

The seers of virtuous form entreat you.

Koṇḍañña, this is the custom among humans:

This burden falls to one who is senior.'

Evaṃ isīhi yācito –

Thus entreated by the seers—

“Katāvakāsā pucchantu bhonto, yaṃ kiñci pañhaṃ manasābhipatthitaṃ;

Ahañhi taṃ taṃ vo viyākarissaṃ, ñatvā sayaṃ lokamimaṃ parañcā”ti. –

'An opportunity is granted, sirs, please ask

Whatever question is desired in your mind;

For I shall explain each one to you,

Having myself known this world and the next.'

Evaṃ [M 1.0224] sarabhaṅgakāle sambhavajātake ca sakalajambudīpe tikkhattuṃ vicaritvā pañhānaṃ antakaraṃ adisvā jātiyā sattavassiko rathikāya paṃsukīḷikaṃ kīḷanto suciratena brāhmaṇena puṭṭho –

Thus, at the time of the Sarabhaṅga Jātaka and the Sambhava Jātaka; and also when, having wandered throughout the whole of Jambudīpa three times without finding anyone who could make an end of questions, he was playing a dust-game in the street at seven years of age, he was asked by the brahmin Sucirata—

“Taggha te ahamakkhissaṃ, yathāpi kusalo tathā;

Rājā ca kho naṃ jānāti, yadi kāhati vā na vā”ti. (jā. 1.16.172) –

“Indeed, I shall explain it to you, just as a skilled one would. And the king knows him, whether he will act or not.”

Evaṃ [V 1.0196] sabbaññupavāraṇaṃ pavāresi. Evaṃ bhagavatā āḷavakassa sabbaññupavāraṇāya pavāritāya atha kho āḷavako yakkho bhagavantaṃ gāthāya ajjhabhāsi “kiṃ sūdha vitta”nti.

Thus He made the invitation of omniscience. When the invitation of omniscience had thus been made by the Blessed One to Āḷavaka, then the yakkha Āḷavaka addressed the Blessed One with the verse beginning, ‘What, indeed, is wealth here?’

183. Tattha kinti pucchāvacanaṃ. Sūti padapūraṇamatte nipāto. Idhāti imasmiṃ loke. Vittanti vidati, pītiṃ karotīti vittaṃ, dhanassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Suciṇṇanti sukataṃ. Sukhanti [P 1.0231] kāyikacetasikaṃ sātaṃ. Āvahātīti āvahati, āneti, deti, appetīti vuttaṃ hoti haveti daḷhatthe nipāto. Sādutaranti atisayena sāduṃ. “Sādhutara”ntipi pāṭho. Rasānanti rasasaññitānaṃ dhammānaṃ. Kathanti kena pakārena, kathaṃjīvino jīvitaṃ kathaṃjīvijīvitaṃ, gāthābandhasukhatthaṃ pana sānunāsikaṃ vuccati. “Kathaṃjīviṃ jīvata”nti vā pāṭho. Tassa jīvantānaṃ kathaṃjīvinti attho. Sesamettha pākaṭameva. Evamimāya gāthāya “kiṃ su idha loke purisassa vittaṃ seṭṭhaṃ, kiṃ su suciṇṇaṃ sukhamāvahāti, kiṃ rasānaṃ sādutaraṃ, kathaṃjīvino jīvitaṃ seṭṭhamāhū”ti ime cattāro pañhe pucchi.

183. Herein, `kiṃ` is an interrogative word. `Sū` is a particle used merely to fill the line. `Idha` means ‘in this world.’ `Vittaṃ` (wealth) is so called because `vidati` (it is found) or `pītiṃ karoti` (it creates joy); it is a synonym for riches. `Suciṇṇaṃ` means ‘well-done.’ `Sukhaṃ` is bodily and mental pleasure. `Āvahāti` means it brings, fetches, gives, or conveys; this is what is said. `Have` is a particle in the sense of emphasis. `Sādutaraṃ` means ‘exceedingly sweet.’ Another reading is `sādhutaraṃ`. `Rasānaṃ` means ‘of things designated as flavors.’ `Kathaṃ` means ‘in what manner.’ `Kathaṃjīvino jīvitaṃ` means ‘the life of one living how.’ The form `kathaṃjīvijīvitaṃ` with a nasal is used for the sake of metrical ease. Alternatively, the reading is `kathaṃjīviṃ jīvataṃ`, which means ‘how do the living live?’ The rest here is self-evident. Thus, with this verse, he asked these four questions: ‘What, indeed, is the best wealth for a person in this world? What, well-practiced, brings happiness? What, indeed, is the sweetest of flavors? The life of one living in what manner do they call the best?’

184. Athassa bhagavā kassapadasabalena vissajjitanayeneva vissajjento imaṃ gāthamāha “saddhīdha vitta”nti. Tattha yathā hiraññasuvaṇṇādi vittaṃ upabhogaparibhogasukhaṃ āvahati, khuppipāsādidukkhaṃ paṭibāhati, dāliddiyaṃ vūpasameti, muttādiratanapaṭilābhahetu hoti, lokasanthutiñca āvahati, evaṃ lokiyalokuttarā saddhāpi yathāsambhavaṃ lokiyalokuttaravipākasukhamāvahati, saddhādhurena paṭipannānaṃ jātijarādidukkhaṃ paṭibāhati, guṇadāliddiyaṃ vūpasameti, satisambojjhaṅgādiratanapaṭilābhahetu hoti.

184. Then the Blessed One, answering in the very manner of the answer given by the Ten-Powered Kassapa, spoke this verse: ‘Faith is the wealth here.’ Herein, just as wealth such as gold and silver brings the happiness of enjoyment and use, wards off the suffering of hunger, thirst, and so on, alleviates poverty, is the cause for obtaining jewels such as pearls, and brings worldly praise, so too does mundane and supramundane faith, as is appropriate, bring the happiness of mundane and supramundane results, ward off the suffering of birth, aging, and so on for those who practice with faith at the forefront, alleviate the poverty of virtue, and become the cause for obtaining jewels such as the enlightenment factor of mindfulness.

“Saddho [M 1.0225] sīlena sampanno, yaso bhogasamappito;

Yaṃ yaṃ padesaṃ bhajati, tattha tattheva pūjito”ti. (dha. pa. 303) –

“One who is faithful and endowed with virtue, possessed of fame and wealth, whatever place one resorts to, right there one is revered.”

Vacanato lokasanthutiñca āvahatīti katvā “vitta”nti vuttā. Yasmā panetaṃ saddhāvittaṃ anugāmikaṃ anaññasādhāraṇaṃ sabbasampattihetu, lokiyassa hiraññasuvaṇṇādivittassāpi nidānaṃ. Saddhoyeva hi dānādīni puññāni katvā vittaṃ adhigacchati, assaddhassa pana vittaṃ yāvadeva anatthāya hoti, tasmā “seṭṭha”nti vuttaṃ. Purisassāti ukkaṭṭhaparicchedadesanā; tasmā na kevalaṃ purisassa[P 1.0232], itthiādīnampi saddhāvittameva seṭṭhanti veditabbaṃ.

Because of the saying that it brings worldly praise, it is called ‘wealth.’ For this wealth of faith is that which follows one, is not shared with others, is the cause of all attainments, and is the source even of mundane wealth such as gold and silver. Indeed, it is a faithful person who performs meritorious deeds such as giving and thereby acquires wealth; for a faithless person, however, wealth leads only to ruin. Therefore, it is called ‘the best.’ The word `purisassa` (‘of a person’) is a teaching that defines by way of the superior case; therefore, it should be understood that the wealth of faith is the best not only for a man, but also for women and others.

Dhammoti dasakusalakammapathadhammo, dānasīlabhāvanādhammo vā. Suciṇṇoti sukato sucarito[V 1.0197]. Sukhamāvahātīti soṇaseṭṭhiputtaraṭṭhapālādīnaṃ viya manussasukhaṃ, sakkādīnaṃ viya dibbasukhaṃ, pariyosāne ca mahāpadumādīnaṃ viya nibbānasukhañca āvahatīti.

‘Dhamma’ means the dhamma of the ten wholesome courses of action, or the dhamma of giving, virtue, and meditation. ‘Well-practiced’ means well-done, well-conducted. ‘Brings happiness’ means that it brings human happiness, like that of the son of the treasurer Soṇa, Raṭṭhapāla, and others; divine happiness, like that of Sakka and others; and finally, the happiness of Nibbāna, like that of Mahāpaduma and others.

Saccanti ayaṃ saccasaddo anekesu atthesu dissati. Seyyathidaṃ – “saccaṃ bhaṇe na kujjheyyā”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 224) vācāsacce. “Sacce ṭhitā samaṇabrāhmaṇā cā”tiādīsu (jā. 2.21.433) viratisacce. “Kasmā nu saccāni vadanti nānā, pavādiyāse kusalāvadānā”tiādīsu (su. ni. 891) diṭṭhisacce. “Cattārimāni, bhikkhave, brāhmaṇasaccānī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.185) brāhmaṇasacce. “Ekañhi saccaṃ na dutīyamatthī”tiādīsu (su. ni. 890) paramatthasacce. “Catunnaṃ saccānaṃ kati kusalā”tiādīsu (vibha. 216) ariyasacce. Idha pana paramatthasaccaṃ nibbānaṃ, viratisaccaṃ vā abbhantaraṃ katvā vācāsaccaṃ adhippetaṃ, yassānubhāvena udakādīni vase vattenti jātijarāmaraṇapāraṃ taranti. Yathāha –

‘Truth’: this word ‘truth’ is seen in many senses. For instance: in passages such as ‘One should speak the truth, one should not be angry’ (Dhp. 224), it is seen in the sense of verbal truth. In passages such as ‘Ascetics and brahmins established in truth’ (Jā. 2.21.433), it is seen in the sense of the truth of abstinence. In passages such as ‘Why do they, skilled debaters, speak of various truths?’ (Sn. 891), it is seen in the sense of the truth of views. In passages such as ‘These four, monks, are the brahmin-truths’ (AN 4.185), it is seen in the sense of brahmin-truth. In passages such as ‘There is only one truth, there is no second’ (Sn. 890), it is seen in the sense of ultimate truth. In passages such as ‘Of the four truths, how many are wholesome?’ (Vibh. 216), it is seen in the sense of the Noble Truths. Here, however, while including the ultimate truth (Nibbāna) or the truth of abstinence, it is verbal truth that is primarily intended, by the power of which they make things like water conform to their will and cross beyond birth, aging, and death. As it is said:

“Saccena vācenudakampi dhāvati, visampi saccena hananti paṇḍitā;

Saccena devo thanayaṃ pavassati, sacce ṭhitā nibbutiṃ patthayanti.

“By truthful speech, one can hold back even water; by truth, the wise neutralize poison. By truth, the deity sends thundering rain; established in truth, they long for Nibbāna.”

“Ye [M 1.0226] kecime atthi rasā pathabyā, saccaṃ tesaṃ sādutaraṃ rasānaṃ;

Sacce ṭhitā samaṇabrāhmaṇā ca, taranti jātimaraṇassa pāra”nti. (jā. 2.21.433);

“Of whatever flavors there are on earth, truth is the sweetest flavor of them all. Ascetics and brahmins who are established in truth cross to the far shore of birth and death.”

Sādutaranti madhurataraṃ, paṇītataraṃ. Rasānanti ye ime “mūlaraso, khandharaso”tiādinā (dha. sa. 628-630) nayena sāyanīyadhammā, ye cime “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, sabbaṃ phalarasaṃ [P 1.0233] (mahāva. 300) arasarūpo bhavaṃ gotamo, ye te, brāhmaṇa, rūparasā, saddarasā (a. ni. 8.11; pārā. 3), anāpatti rasarase (pāci. 607-609), ayaṃ dhammavinayo ekaraso vimuttiraso (a. ni. 8.19; cūḷava. 385), bhāgī vā bhagavā attharasassa dhammarasassā”tiādinā (mahāni. 149; cūḷani. ajitamāṇavapucchāniddesa 2) nayena vācārasūpavajjā avasesabyañjanādayo dhammā “rasā”ti vuccanti, tesaṃ rasānaṃ saccaṃ have sādutaraṃ saccameva sādutaraṃ, sādhutaraṃ vā seṭṭhataraṃ, uttamataraṃ. Mūlarasādayo hi sarīraṃ upabrūhenti, saṃkilesikañca sukhamāvahanti. Saccarase viratisaccavācāsaccarasā samathavipassanādīhi cittamupabrūhenti, asaṃkilesikañca sukhamāvahanti, vimuttiraso [V 1.0198] paramatthasaccarasaparibhāvitattā sādu, attharasadhammarasā ca tadadhigamūpāyabhūtaṃ atthañca dhammañca nissāya pavattitoti.

“Sweeter” means more delicious, more excellent. By “flavors” it refers to those things to be tasted in the manner of “the taste of roots, the taste of stems,” and so on (Dhs. 628-630), and also those things such as condiments, excluding the flavor of speech, which are called “flavors” in the manner of “I allow, monks, all fruit flavors” (Mahāvagga 300); “The venerable Gotama is devoid of flavor; these are the flavors of form, sound” (AN 8.11; Pārā. 3); “There is no offense regarding flavors” (Pāc. 607-609); “This Dhamma-Vinaya has a single flavor—the flavor of liberation” (AN 8.19; Cūḷavagga 385); “The Blessed One is a partaker of the flavor of meaning and the flavor of Dhamma” and so on (Mahāniddesa 149; Cūḷaniddesa, Ajitamāṇavapucchāniddesa 2). Of these flavors, truth is indeed sweeter; truth itself is sweeter, or rather, more excellent, supreme. For the flavors of roots and so on nourish the body and bring defiled pleasure. The flavor of truth—namely the flavor of the truth of abstinence and the flavor of verbal truth—nourishes the mind through serenity, insight, and so on, bringing undefiled happiness. The flavor of liberation is sweet because it is pervaded by the flavor of the ultimate truth. The flavors of meaning and Dhamma arise in dependence on the meaning and the Dhamma, which are the means for its attainment.

Paññājīvinti ettha pana yvāyaṃ andhekacakkhudvicakkhukesu dvicakkhupuggalo gahaṭṭho vā kammantānuṭṭhānasaraṇagamanadānasaṃvibhāgasīlasamādānauposathakammādigahaṭṭhapaṭipadaṃ, pabbajito vā avippaṭisārakarasīlasaṅkhātaṃ taduttaricittavisuddhiādibhedaṃ vā pabbajitapaṭipadaṃ paññāya ārādhetvā jīvati, tassa paññājīvino jīvitaṃ, taṃ vā paññājīviṃ jīvitaṃ seṭṭhamāhūti evamattho daṭṭhabbo.

Here, regarding 'one who lives by wisdom,' it should be understood thus: whoever is the 'two-eyed person' among the blind, the one-eyed, and the two-eyed—whether a householder who lives by accomplishing with wisdom the householder's practice, such as engaging in work, taking refuge, giving and sharing, undertaking precepts, and Uposatha duties; or a renunciate who lives by accomplishing with wisdom the renunciate's practice, described as virtue that brings no remorse or distinguished by purity of mind beyond that—the wise say that the life of such a one who lives by wisdom is best, or that a life lived by wisdom is best. This is the meaning to be understood.

185-6. Evaṃ bhagavatā vissajjite cattāropi pañhe sutvā attamano yakkho avasesepi cattāro pañhe pucchanto “kathaṃ su tarati ogha”nti gāthamāha. Athassa bhagavā purimanayeneva vissajjento “saddhāya taratī”ti [P 1.0234] gāthamāha. Tattha kiñcāpi yo catubbidhaṃ oghaṃ tarati, so saṃsāraṇṇavampi tarati, vaṭṭadukkhampi acceti, kilesamalāpi parisujjhati, evaṃ [M 1.0227] santepi pana yasmā assaddho oghataraṇaṃ asaddahanto na pakkhandati, pañcasu kāmaguṇesu cittavossaggena pamatto tattheva sattavisattatāya saṃsāraṇṇavaṃ na tarati, kusīto dukkhaṃ viharati vokiṇṇo akusalehi dhammehi, appañño suddhimaggaṃ ajānanto na parisujjhati, tasmā tappaṭipakkhaṃ dassentena bhagavatā ayaṃ gāthā vuttā.

Thus, having heard the four questions answered by the Blessed One, the yakkha, delighted in mind, asked the remaining four questions by speaking the verse: “How does one cross the flood?” Then the Blessed One, replying in the same way as before, spoke the verse: “One crosses by faith.” Herein, although one who crosses the fourfold flood also crosses the ocean of saṃsāra, overcomes the suffering of the round, and is purified from the stains of defilements, it is nevertheless the case that: one without faith, not believing in crossing the flood, does not embark upon it; being heedless by releasing the mind into the five strands of sensual pleasure, and being attached and entangled right there, one does not cross the ocean of saṃsāra; a lazy person dwells in suffering, intermingled with unwholesome states; and an unwise person, not knowing the path to purity, is not purified. Therefore, this verse was spoken by the Blessed One to show the opposite of these things.

Evaṃ vuttāya cetāya yasmā sotāpattiyaṅgapadaṭṭhānaṃ saddhindriyaṃ, tasmā “saddhāya tarati ogha”nti iminā padena diṭṭhoghataraṇaṃ sotāpattimaggaṃ sotāpannañca pakāseti. Yasmā pana sotāpanno kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ bhāvanāya sātaccakiriyāsaṅkhātena appamādena samannāgato dutiyamaggaṃ ārādhetvā ṭhapetvā sakideva imaṃ lokaṃ āgamanamattaṃ avasesaṃ sotāpattimaggena atiṇṇaṃ bhavoghavatthuṃ saṃsāraṇṇavaṃ tarati, tasmā “appamādena aṇṇava”nti iminā padena bhavoghataraṇaṃ sakadāgāmimaggaṃ sakadāgāmiñca pakāseti. Yasmā sakadāgāmī vīriyena tatiyamaggaṃ ārādhetvā sakadāgāmimaggena anatītaṃ kāmoghavatthuṃ; kāmoghasaññitañca kāmadukkhamacceti, tasmā “vīriyena dukkhamaccetī”ti iminā padena kāmoghataraṇaṃ anāgāmimaggaṃ anāgāmiñca pakāseti. Yasmā pana anāgāmī vigatakāmapaṅkatāya parisuddhāya paññāya ekantaparisuddhaṃ catutthamaggapaññaṃ ārādhetvā anāgāmimaggena appahīnaṃ avijjāsaṅkhātaṃ paramamalaṃ pajahati, tasmā “paññāya parisujjhatī”ti iminā padena avijjoghataraṇaṃ [V 1.0199] arahattamaggaṃ arahantañca pakāseti. Imāya ca arahattanikūṭena kathitāya gāthāya pariyosāne yakkho sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāsi.

This having been said, because the faculty of faith is the proximate cause for the factors of stream-entry, therefore the phrase “one crosses the flood by faith” reveals the path of stream-entry, which is the crossing of the flood of views, and the stream-enterer. Furthermore, because the stream-enterer, endowed with diligence—defined as continuous application in developing wholesome states—having cultivated the second path, crosses the ocean of saṃsāra, the basis for the flood of becoming, which was not crossed by the path of stream-entry (except for the fact of returning to this world just once more), therefore the phrase “by diligence, the ocean” reveals the path of once-returning, which is the crossing of the flood of becoming, and the once-returner. Because the once-returner, through energy, having cultivated the third path, overcomes the basis for the flood of sensual pleasure, which was not surpassed by the path of once-returning, and the suffering related to sensual desire, designated as the flood of sensual pleasure, therefore the phrase “by energy one overcomes suffering” reveals the path of non-returning, which is the crossing of the flood of sensual pleasure, and the non-returner. And because the non-returner, with wisdom purified by being free from the mire of sensual desire, having cultivated the utterly pure wisdom of the fourth path, abandons the supreme stain called ignorance, which was not abandoned by the path of non-returning, therefore the phrase “by wisdom one is purified” reveals the path of arahantship, which is the crossing of the flood of ignorance, and the arahant. And at the conclusion of this verse, spoken with arahantship as its pinnacle, the yakkha was established in the fruit of stream-entry.

187. Idāni tameva “paññāya parisujjhatī”ti ettha vuttaṃ paññāpadaṃ gahetvā attano paṭibhānena lokiyalokuttaramissakaṃ pañhaṃ pucchanto “kathaṃ su labhate pañña”nti [P 1.0235] imaṃ chappadagāthamāha. Tattha kathaṃ sūti sabbattheva atthayuttipucchā hoti. Ayañhi paññādiatthaṃ ñatvā tassa yuttiṃ pucchati “kathaṃ kāya yuttiyā kena kāraṇena paññaṃ labhatī”ti. Esa nayo dhanādīsu.

187. Now, taking up that very word 'wisdom' from the phrase 'by wisdom one is purified,' and with his own ready insight, he asks a question mixing worldly and supramundane matters, speaking this six-part verse beginning: “How indeed does one obtain wisdom?” Therein, “how indeed” is in every case a question about the proper method. For this one, having understood the meaning of wisdom and so on, asks for its proper method: “How, by what method, for what reason, does one obtain wisdom?” This same principle applies to wealth and the other topics.

188. Athassa [M 1.0228] bhagavā catūhi kāraṇehi paññālābhaṃ dassento “saddahāno”tiādimāha. Tassattho – yena pubbabhāge kāyasucaritādibhedena, aparabhāge ca sattatiṃsabodhipakkhiyabhedena dhammena arahanto buddhapaccekabuddhasāvakā nibbānaṃ pattā, taṃ saddahāno arahataṃ dhammaṃ nibbānappattiyā lokiyalokuttaraṃ paññaṃ labhati. Tañca kho na saddhāmattakeneva, yasmā pana saddhājāto upasaṅkamati, upasaṅkamanto payirupāsati, payirupāsanto sotaṃ odahati, ohitasoto dhammaṃ suṇāti, tasmā upasaṅkamanato pabhuti yāva dhammassavanena sussūsaṃ labhati. Ki vuttaṃ hoti – taṃ dhammaṃ saddahitvāpi ācariyupajjhāye kālena upasaṅkamitvā vattakaraṇena payirupāsitvā yadā payirupāsanāya ārādhitacittā kiñci vattukāmā honti. Atha adhigatāya sotukāmatāya sotaṃ odahitvā suṇanto labhatīti. Evaṃ susūsampi ca satiavippavāsena appamatto subhāsitadubbhāsitaññutāya vicakkhaṇo eva labhati, na itaro. Tenāha “appamatto vicakkhaṇo”ti.

188. Then the Blessed One, wishing to show the four reasons for gaining wisdom, spoke the verse beginning with 'saddahāno' (one who has faith). The meaning is this: One who has faith in the Dhamma of the Arahants—the Dhamma by which the Arahants, the Buddhas, the Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples have attained Nibbāna, whether in the preliminary stage through such things as good bodily conduct, or in the later stage through the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—gains worldly and supramundane wisdom for the attainment of Nibbāna. And yet, this is not gained by mere faith alone. For one who has faith approaches; approaching, one attends upon them; attending, one lends an ear; with ear lent, one hears the Dhamma. Therefore, from the act of approaching up to the hearing of the Dhamma, one gains the desire to listen. What is meant by this? Having faith in that Dhamma, one approaches the teacher or preceptor at the proper time and serves them by performing their duties. When their minds are pleased by such service and they are willing to speak something, then, having acquired the desire to listen, one lends an ear and, while listening, gains wisdom. Thus, even with the desire to listen, it is only one who is not separated from mindfulness, is diligent, and is discerning with the knowledge of what is well-spoken and ill-spoken who gains wisdom—not another. Therefore He said, 'diligent and discerning.'

Evaṃ yasmā saddhāya paññālābhasaṃvattanikaṃ paṭipadaṃ paṭipajjati, sussūsāya sakkaccaṃ paññādhigamūpāyaṃ suṇāti, appamādena gahitaṃ na sammussati, vicakkhaṇatāya anūnādhikaṃ aviparītañca gahetvā vitthārikaṃ karoti. Sussūsāya vā ohitasoto paññāpaṭilābhahetuṃ dhammaṃ suṇāti, appamādena sutvā dhammaṃ dhāreti[P 1.0236], vicakkhaṇatāya dhatānaṃ dhammānaṃ atthamupaparikkhati, athānupubbena paramatthasaccaṃ sacchikaroti, tasmāssa bhagavā “kathaṃ su labhate pañña”nti puṭṭho imāni cattāri kāraṇāni dassento imaṃ gāthamāha – “saddahāno…pe… vicakkhaṇo”ti.

Thus, since through faith one undertakes the practice conducive to gaining wisdom; through the desire to listen, one respectfully hears the means for attaining wisdom; through diligence, one does not forget what has been grasped; and through discernment, having grasped it without deficiency, excess, or distortion, one elaborates upon it. Alternatively, through the desire to listen, one with an attentive ear hears the Dhamma that is a cause for the attainment of wisdom; through diligence, having heard, one retains the Dhamma; through discernment, one investigates the meaning of the teachings that have been retained; and then, sequentially, one realizes the ultimate truth. Therefore, the Blessed One, when asked, 'How indeed does one gain wisdom?', wishing to show these four reasons, spoke this verse: 'One who has faith... discerning.'

189. Idāni tato pare tayo pañhe vissajjento “patirūpakārī”ti imaṃ gāthamāha. Tattha [V 1.0200] desakālādīni ahāpetvā lokiyassa lokuttarassa vā dhanassa patirūpaṃ adhigamūpāyaṃ karotīti patirūpakārī. Dhuravāti cetasikavīriyavasena anikkhittadhuro. Uṭṭhātāti “yo ca sītañca uṇhañca, tiṇā bhiyyo na maññatī”tiādinā (theragā. 232; dī. ni. 3.253) nayena kāyikavīriyavasena uṭṭhānasampanno asithilaparakkamo. Vindate [M 1.0229] dhananti ekamūsikāya na cirasseva dvesatasahassasaṅkhaṃ cūḷantevāsī viya lokiyadhanañca, mahallakamahātissatthero viya lokuttaradhanañca labhati. So hi “tīhi iriyāpathehi viharissāmī”ti vattaṃ katvā thinamiddhāgamanavelāya palālacumbaṭakaṃ temetvā, sīse katvā, galappamāṇaṃ udakaṃ pavisitvā, thinamiddhaṃ paṭibāhento dvādasahi vassehi arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Saccenāti vacīsaccenāpi “saccavādī bhūtavādī”ti, paramatthasaccenāpi “buddho paccekabuddho ariyasāvako”ti evaṃ kittiṃ pappoti. Dadanti yaṃkiñci icchitapatthitaṃ dadanto mittāni ganthati, sampādeti karotīti attho. Duddadaṃ vā dadaṃ ganthati, dānamukhena vā cattāripi saṅgahavatthūni gahitānīti veditabbāni. Tehi mittāni karotīti vuttaṃ hoti.

189. Now, answering the three questions that follow, He speaks this verse beginning with 'patirūpakārī' (a proper doer). Herein, 'a proper doer' is one who, without neglecting such things as time and place, creates a suitable means for attaining worldly or supramundane wealth. 'Dhuravā' (steadfast) means one who has not laid down the burden, by way of mental energy. 'Uṭṭhātā' (energetic) means one endowed with energy, with unslackened exertion, by way of physical energy, according to the method stated: 'Who does not regard cold and heat more than grass,' and so on. 'Vindate dhanaṃ' (one finds wealth) means one obtains worldly wealth, like the young apprentice who in no long time gained two hundred thousand from a single dead mouse, and supramundane wealth, like the elder Mahā-Mahātissa. For that elder, having made a vow, 'I will dwell in only three postures,' would, at the time of the onset of sloth and torpor, wet a bundle of straw, place it on his head, enter water up to his neck, and, while warding off sloth and torpor, attained arahantship in twelve years. 'Saccena' (by truth): by verbal truth one attains fame as 'a speaker of truth, a speaker of what is'; and by ultimate truth one attains fame as 'a Buddha, a Paccekabuddha, or a noble disciple.' 'Dadanti' (by giving): by giving whatever is desired and wished for, one binds friends; the meaning is one accomplishes or makes them. Or, by giving what is difficult to give, one binds them. Or, it should be understood that through the gateway of giving, all four bases of sympathy are included. By these, it is said, one makes friends.

190. Evaṃ gahaṭṭhapabbajitānaṃ sādhāraṇena lokiyalokuttaramissakena nayena cattāro pañhe vissajjetvā idāni “kathaṃ pecca na socatī”ti imaṃ pañcamaṃ pañhaṃ gahaṭṭhavasena vissajjento āha “yassete”ti. Tassattho – yassa “saddahāno arahata”nti ettha vuttāya sabbakalyāṇadhammuppādikāya saddhāya samannāgatattā saddhassa [P 1.0237] gharamesino gharāvāsaṃ pañca vā kāmaguṇe esantassa gavesantassa kāmabhogino gahaṭṭhassa “saccena kittiṃ pappotī”ti ettha vuttappakāraṃ saccaṃ, “sussūsaṃ labhate pañña”nti ettha sussūsapaññānāmena vutto dhammo, “dhuravā uṭṭhātā”ti ettha dhuranāmena uṭṭhānanāmena ca vuttā dhīti, “dadaṃ mittāni ganthatī”ti ettha vuttappakāro cāgo cāti ete caturo dhammā santi. Sa ve pecca na socatīti idhalokā paralokaṃ gantvā sa ve na socatīti.

190. Thus, having answered four questions in a manner common to householders and renunciants, with a method blending the worldly and the supramundane, He now answers this fifth question, 'How does one not grieve after death?', by way of the householder, saying: 'For whom these...' The meaning is this: For whichever faithful householder—one endowed with the faith mentioned in the phrase 'one who has faith in the Arahants,' the faith that gives rise to all wholesome qualities; one who, as a house-seeker, desires, seeks, and enjoys the five strands of sensual pleasure—for such a one, these four qualities are present: truth, of the kind mentioned in 'by truth one attains fame'; the Dhamma, spoken of by the names 'listening' and 'wisdom' in 'by listening one gains wisdom'; fortitude, spoken of by the names 'steadfastness' and 'energy' in 'one who is steadfast, energetic'; and generosity, of the kind mentioned in 'by giving one binds friends.' 'That one indeed does not grieve after death' means: having gone from this world to the next, that one truly does not grieve.

191. Evaṃ bhagavā pañcamampi pañhaṃ vissajjetvā taṃ yakkhaṃ codento āha – “iṅgha aññepī”ti. Tattha iṅghāti codanatthe nipāto. Aññepīti aññepi dhamme puthū samaṇabrāhmaṇe pucchassu, aññepi vā pūraṇādayo sabbaññupaṭiññe puthū samaṇabrāhmaṇe pucchassu. Yadi amhehi “saccena kittiṃ pappotī”ti ettha vuttappakārā saccā bhiyyo kittippattikāraṇaṃ vā, “sussūsaṃ labhate pañña”nti ettha sussūsanapaññāpadesena vuttā damā bhiyyo [M 1.0230] lokiyalokuttarapaññāpaṭilābhakāraṇaṃ vā. “Dadaṃ mittāni ganthatī”ti ettha vuttappakārā cāgā bhiyyo mittaganthanakāraṇaṃ vā, “dhuravā uṭṭhātā”ti ettha taṃ taṃ atthavasaṃ paṭicca dhuranāmena uṭṭhānanāmena [V 1.0201] ca vuttāya mahābhārasahanaṭṭhena ussoḷhībhāvappattāya vīriyasaṅkhātāya khantyā bhiyyo lokiyalokuttaradhanavindanakāraṇaṃ vā, “saccaṃ dhammo dhiti cāgo”ti evaṃ vuttehi imeheva catūhi dhammehi bhiyyo asmā lokā paraṃ lokaṃ pecca asocanakāraṇaṃ vā idha vijjatīti ayamettha saddhiṃ saṅkhepayojanāya atthavaṇṇanā. Vitthārato pana ekamekaṃ padaṃ atthuddhārapaduddhāravaṇṇanānayehi vibhajitvā veditabbā.

191. Having answered the fifth question, the Blessed One then challenged the yakkha, saying, 'Come now, ask others as well!' Herein, ‘iṅgha’ is a particle used in the sense of urging. ‘Aññepi’ means ‘ask other ascetics and brahmins,’ or ‘ask other ascetics and brahmins like Pūraṇa and others who claim omniscience,’ whether there is a cause for gaining fame greater than the truth spoken of in ‘one attains fame through truth’; or a cause for acquiring worldly and supramundane wisdom greater than the qualities described by way of listening in ‘one gains wisdom through listening’; or a cause for forming friendships greater than the generosity spoken of in ‘giving binds friends’; or a cause for attaining worldly and supramundane wealth greater than the patience known as energy—which, in relation to various objectives, is described as ‘bearing a burden’ and ‘striving,’ and which has attained a state of great exertion by its nature of bearing a heavy load—as stated in ‘the steadfast worker finds wealth’; or whether there is a cause for not grieving after passing from this world to the next greater than these four qualities spoken of thus: ‘truth, Dhamma, fortitude, and generosity.’ This is the explanation of the meaning here, together with a concise analysis. For a detailed explanation, however, each word should be analyzed and understood by way of semantic and lexical analysis.

192. Evaṃ vutte yakkho yena saṃsayena aññe puccheyya, tassa pahīnattā “kathaṃ nu dāni puccheyyaṃ, puthū samaṇabrāhmaṇeti vatvā yepissa apucchanakāraṇaṃ na jānanti, tepi jānāpento “yohaṃ ajja pajānāmi, yo attho samparāyiko”ti [P 1.0238] āha. Tattha ajjāti ajjādiṃ katvāti adhippāyo. Pajānāmīti yathāvuttena pakārena jānāmi. Yo atthoti ettāvatā “sussūsaṃ labhate pañña”ntiādinā nayena vuttaṃ diṭṭhadhammikaṃ dasseti samparāyikoti iminā “yassete caturo dhammā”ti vuttaṃ pecca sokābhāvakaraṃ samparāyikaṃ. Atthoti ca kāraṇassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Ayañhi atthasaddo “sātthaṃ sabyañjana”nti evamādīsu (pārā. 1; dī. ni. 1.255) pāṭhatthe vattati. “Attho me, gahapati, hiraññasuvaṇṇenā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.250; ma. ni. 3.258) kiccatthe “hoti sīlavataṃ attho”tiādīsu (jā. 1.1.11) vuḍḍhimhi. “Bahujano bhajate atthahetū”tiādīsu (jā. 1.15.89) dhane. “Ubhinnamatthaṃ caratī”tiādīsu (jā. 1.7.66; saṃ. ni. 1.250; theragā. 443) hite. “Atthe jāte ca paṇḍita”ntiādīsu (jā. 1.1.92) kāraṇe. Idha pana kāraṇe. Tasmā yaṃ paññādilābhādīnaṃ kāraṇaṃ diṭṭhadhammikaṃ, yañca pecca sokābhāvassa kāraṇaṃ samparāyikaṃ, taṃ yohaṃ ajja bhagavatā vuttanayena sāmaṃyeva pajānāmi, so kathaṃ nu dāni puccheyyaṃ puthū samaṇabrāhmaṇeti evamettha saṅkhepato attho veditabbo.

192. When this was said, the yakkha, since the doubt by which he might have questioned others was abandoned, said, 'How now should I question the many ascetics and brahmins?' And, wishing to make it known even to those who did not know his reason for not questioning, he spoke the line: 'Today I understand the benefit that pertains to the future life.' Herein, ‘ajja’ means ‘from today onwards’; this is the intention. ‘Pajānāmi’ means ‘I understand in the way that has been described.’ By the words `yo attho`, he indicates the benefit visible in this life, spoken of in the manner of 'one gains wisdom through listening,' and so on. By `samparāyiko`, he indicates the cause for the absence of sorrow after death, which pertains to the future life, spoken of in 'for whom these four qualities.' And `attha` is a synonym for 'cause.' Indeed, this word `attha` is used in the sense of 'text' in such phrases as 'with the meaning and the phrasing.' In 'I have need, householder, of gold and silver,' it is used in the sense of 'need.' In 'there is prosperity for the virtuous,' it is used in the sense of 'growth.' In 'many people associate for the sake of wealth,' it is used in the sense of 'wealth.' In 'he practices for the welfare of both,' it is used in the sense of 'welfare.' In 'and a wise one when a cause has arisen,' it is used in the sense of 'cause.' Here, however, it is used in the sense of 'cause.' Therefore, the meaning here should be understood briefly in this way: 'That cause for gaining wisdom and so forth, which pertains to this life, and that cause for the absence of sorrow after death, which pertains to the future life—that I myself now understand today through the method taught by the Blessed One. So how, then, should I now question the many ascetics and brahmins?'

193. Evaṃ [M 1.0231] yakkho “pajānāmi yo attho samparāyiko”ti vatvā tassa ñāṇassa bhagavaṃmūlakattaṃ dassento “atthāya vata me buddho”ti āha. Tattha atthāyāti hitāya, vuḍḍhiyā vā. Yattha dinnaṃ mahapphalanti “yassete caturo dhammā”ti (jā. 1.1.97) ettha vuttacāgena yattha dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ hoti, taṃ aggadakkhiṇeyyaṃ buddhaṃ pajānāmīti attho. Keci pana “saṅghaṃ sandhāya evamāhā”ti bhaṇanti.

193. Thus the yakkha, having said, ‘I understand the benefit that pertains to the future life,’ showing that this knowledge has the Blessed One as its root, said: ‘Truly, for my benefit the Buddha came to Āḷavī to dwell!’ Herein, ‘atthāya’ means ‘for my welfare,’ or ‘for my growth.’ The phrase ‘where a gift given is of great fruit’ means: ‘I understand the Buddha to be the foremost recipient of offerings, to whom a gift given is of great fruit, by means of the generosity spoken of in the verse “for whom these four qualities...”’ Some, however, say that he spoke this with reference to the Saṅgha.

194. Evaṃ imāya gāthāya attano hitādhigamaṃ dassetvā idāni parahitāya paṭipattiṃ dīpento āha “so ahaṃ vicarissāmī”ti. Tassattho hemavatasutte vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

194. Having thus shown his own attainment of welfare through this verse, he now reveals the practice for the welfare of others, saying: ‘Therefore, I will wander…’ Its meaning should be understood in the same way as explained in the Hemavata Sutta.

Evamimāya [V 1.0202][P 1.0239] gāthāya pariyosānañca rattivibhāyanañca sādhukārasadduṭṭhānañca āḷavakakumārassa yakkhassa bhavanaṃ ānayanañca ekakkhaṇeyeva ahosi. Rājapurisā sādhukārasaddaṃ sutvā “evarūpo sādhukārasaddo ṭhapetvā buddhe na aññesaṃ abbhuggacchati, āgato nu kho bhagavā”ti āvajjentā bhagavato sarīrappabhaṃ disvā, pubbe viya bahi aṭṭhatvā, nibbisaṅkā antoyeva pavisitvā, addasaṃsu bhagavantaṃ yakkhassa bhavane nisinnaṃ, yakkhañca añjaliṃ paggahetvā ṭhitaṃ. Disvāna yakkhaṃ āhaṃsu – “ayaṃ te, mahāyakkha, rājakumāro balikammāya ānīto, handa naṃ khāda vā bhuñja vā, yathāpaccayaṃ vā karohī”ti. So sotāpannattā lajjito visesato ca bhagavato purato evaṃ vuccamāno, atha taṃ kumāraṃ ubhohi hatthehi paṭiggahetvā bhagavato upanāmesi – “ayaṃ bhante kumāro mayhaṃ pesito, imāhaṃ bhagavato dammi, hitānukampakā buddhā, paṭiggaṇhātu, bhante, bhagavā imaṃ dārakaṃ imassa hitatthāya sukhatthāyā”ti. Imañca gāthamāha –

Thus, the conclusion of this verse, the breaking of dawn, the rising of the sound of approval, and the bringing of the prince to the yakkha Āḷavaka’s dwelling—all happened in a single moment. The royal attendants, hearing the sound of approval, thought: ‘Such a sound of approval, apart from the Buddha, does not arise for others. Has the Blessed One arrived?’ Turning their attention, seeing the radiance of the Blessed One’s body, they did not stand outside as before, but entered inside fearlessly, and saw the Blessed One seated in the yakkha’s dwelling, and the yakkha standing with hands reverently joined. Seeing this, they said to the yakkha: ‘O great yakkha, this prince has been brought to you for sacrifice. Come now, devour him, eat him, or do as you please.’ But he, being a stream-enterer and ashamed, especially at being addressed thus in the presence of the Blessed One, then took the prince with both hands and presented him to the Blessed One, saying: ‘Venerable sir, this prince was sent for me. I give him to the Blessed One. The Buddhas are compassionate for the welfare of beings. Please, Venerable Sir, accept this child for his benefit and happiness.’ And he spoke this verse:

“Imaṃ kumāraṃ satapuññalakkhaṇaṃ, sabbaṅgupetaṃ paripuṇṇabyañjanaṃ;

Udaggacitto sumano dadāmi te, paṭiggaha lokahitāya cakkhumā”ti.

‘This prince, possessing the marks of a hundred merits, complete in all his limbs, with perfect features, with uplifted mind and joyful heart, I give to you; accept him, O Seer, for the good of the world.’

Paṭiggahesi bhagavā kumāraṃ, paṭiggaṇhanto ca yakkhassa ca kumārassa ca maṅgalakaraṇatthaṃ pādūnagāthaṃ abhāsi. Taṃ yakkho kumāraṃ saraṇaṃ gamento tikkhattuṃ catutthapādena pūreti. Seyyathidaṃ –

The Blessed One accepted the prince, and upon accepting him, for the blessing of both the yakkha and the prince, he spoke a verse lacking one line. The yakkha, wishing to guide the prince to the refuges, completed the verse three times with a fourth line. It is as follows:

“Dīghāyuko [M 1.0232] hotu ayaṃ kumāro,

Tuvañca yakkha sukhito bhavāhi;

Abyādhitā lokahitāya tiṭṭhatha,

Ayaṃ kumāro saraṇamupeti buddhaṃ…pe… dhammaṃ…pe… saṅgha”nti.

‘May this prince be long-lived, and may you, yakkha, be happy; may you both abide without affliction for the welfare of the world. This prince goes for refuge to the Buddha… to the Dhamma… to the Saṅgha.’

Bhagavā kumāraṃ rājapurisānaṃ adāsi – “imaṃ vaḍḍhetvā puna mameva dethā”ti. Evaṃ so kumāro rājapurisānaṃ hatthato yakkhassa hatthaṃ yakkhassa hatthato bhagavato [P 1.0240] hatthaṃ, bhagavato hatthato puna rājapurisānaṃ hatthaṃ gatattā nāmato “hatthako āḷavako”ti jāto. Taṃ ādāya paṭinivatte rājapurise disvā kassakavanakammikādayo “kiṃ yakkho kumāraṃ atidaharattā na icchatī”ti bhītā pucchiṃsu. Rājapurisā “mā bhāyatha, khemaṃ kataṃ bhagavatā”ti sabbamārocesuṃ. Tato “sādhu sādhū”ti [V 1.0203] sakalaṃ āḷavīnagaraṃ ekakolāhalena yakkhābhimukhaṃ ahosi. Yakkhopi bhagavato bhikkhācārakāle anuppatte pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā upaḍḍhamaggaṃ āgantvā nivatti.

The Blessed One gave the prince to the royal attendants, saying, ‘Raise this one and then give him back to me.’ Thus, because the prince had gone from the hands of the royal attendants to the hand of the yakkha, from the yakkha’s hand to the Blessed One’s hand, and from the Blessed One’s hand back to the hands of the royal attendants, he became known by the name ‘Hatthaka Āḷavaka.’ Seeing the royal attendants returning with him, farmers, forest workers, and others, being frightened, asked, ‘Is it that the yakkha does not want the prince because he is too young?’ The royal attendants said, ‘Do not be afraid; safety has been created by the Blessed One,’ and they related the entire matter. Then, with cries of ‘Excellent, excellent!’ the entire city of Āḷavī became one great uproar facing the yakkha. The yakkha, too, when the time for the Blessed One’s alms round arrived, took his bowl and robe, came halfway along the road, and turned back.

Atha bhagavā nagare piṇḍāya caritvā katabhattakicco nagaradvāre aññatarasmiṃ vivitte rukkhamūle paññattavarabuddhāsane nisīdi. Tato mahājanakāyena saddhiṃ rājā ca nāgarā ca ekato sampiṇḍitvā bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamma vanditvā parivāretvā nisinnā “kathaṃ, bhante, evaṃ dāruṇaṃ yakkhaṃ damayitthā”ti pucchiṃsu. Tesaṃ bhagavā yuddhamādiṃ katvā “evaṃ navavidhavassaṃ vassi, evaṃ vibhiṃsanakaṃ akāsi, evaṃ pañhaṃ pucchi, tassāhaṃ evaṃ vissajjesi”nti tamevāḷavakasuttaṃ kathesi. Kathāpariyosāne caturāsītipāṇasahassānaṃ dhammābhisamayo ahosi. Tato rājā ca nāgarā ca vessavaṇamahārājassa bhavanasamīpe yakkhassa bhavanaṃ katvā pupphagandhādisakkārūpetaṃ niccaṃ baliṃ pavattesuṃ. Tañca kumāraṃ viññutaṃ pattaṃ “tvaṃ bhagavantaṃ nissāya jīvitaṃ labhi, gaccha, bhagavantaṃyeva payirupāsassu bhikkhusaṅghañcā”ti vissajjesuṃ. So bhagavantañca bhikkhusaṅghañca payirupāsamāno na cirasseva anāgāmiphale patiṭṭhāya sabbaṃ buddhavacanaṃ uggahetvā pañcasataupāsakaparivāro ahosi. Bhagavā ca naṃ etadagge niddisi “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ upāsakānaṃ catūhi [M 1.0233] saṅgahavatthūhi parisaṃ saṅgaṇhantānaṃ yadidaṃ hatthako āḷavako”ti (a ni. 1.251).

Then the Blessed One, having walked for alms in the city and finished his meal, sat down on the excellent, prepared Buddha-seat at the foot of a certain secluded tree near the city gate. Then the king and the citizens, having gathered together with a great multitude, approached the Blessed One, paid homage, surrounded him, and sat down. They asked, ‘Venerable sir, how did you tame such a dreadful yakkha?’ The Blessed One, beginning with the battle, recounted that very Āḷavaka Sutta, saying: ‘Thus he rained down a ninefold rain, thus he performed a terrifying act, thus he asked questions, and thus I answered him.’ At the conclusion of the talk, the comprehension of the Dhamma arose in eighty-four thousand living beings. Then the king and the citizens, having built a dwelling for the yakkha near the mansion of the great king Vessavaṇa, established a constant tribute endowed with honors such as flowers and fragrances. And when that prince had reached the age of discretion, they sent him forth, saying, ‘You received your life on account of the Blessed One. Go, attend upon the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.’ As he was attending upon the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, it was not long before he was established in the fruit of non-returning. Having learned the entire word of the Buddha, he came to have a following of five hundred lay disciples. And the Blessed One designated him as the foremost, saying: ‘Bhikkhus, foremost among my lay disciples who gather a following by means of the four bases of sympathy is this Hatthaka Āḷavaka.’

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya,

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya āḷavakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Āḷavaka Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary is concluded.

11. Vijayasuttavaṇṇanā

11. The Explanation of the Vijaya Sutta

Caraṃ [V 1.0204][P 1.0241] vā yadi vā tiṭṭhanti nandasuttaṃ. “Vijayasuttaṃ kāyavicchandanikasutta”ntipi vuccati. Kā uppatti? Idaṃ kira suttaṃ dvīsu ṭhānesu vuttaṃ, tasmā assa duvidhā uppatti. Tattha bhagavatā anupubbena kapilavatthuṃ anuppatvā, sākiye vinetvā nandādayo pabbājetvā, anuññātāya mātugāmassa pabbajjāya ānandattherassa bhaginī nandā, khemakasakkarañño dhītā abhirūpanandā, janapadakalyāṇī nandāti tisso nandāyo pabbajiṃsu. Tena ca samayena bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati. Abhirūpanandā abhirūpā eva ahosi dassanīyā pāsādikā, tenevassā abhirūpanandāti nāmamakaṃsu. Janapadakalyāṇī nandāpi rūpena attanā sadisaṃ na passati. Tā ubhopi rūpamadamattā “bhagavā rūpaṃ vivaṇṇeti, garahati, anekapariyāyena rūpe ādīnavaṃ dassetī”ti bhagavato upaṭṭhānaṃ na gacchanti, daṭṭhumpi na icchanti. Evaṃ appasannā kasmā pabbajitāti ce? Agatiyā. Abhirūpanandāya hi vāreyyadivaseyeva sāmiko sakyakumāro kālamakāsi. Atha naṃ mātāpitaro akāmakaṃ pabbājesuṃ. Janapadakalyāṇī nandāpi āyasmante nande arahattaṃ patte nirāsā hutvā “mayhaṃ sāmiko ca mātā ca mahāpajāpati aññe ca ñātakā pabbajitā, ñātīhi vinā dukkho gharāvāso”ti gharāvāse assādamalabhantī pabbajitā, na saddhāya.

The sutta beginning ‘Caraṃ vā yadi vā tiṭṭhaṃ’ is the Nanda Sutta. It is also called the Vijaya Sutta and the Kāyavicchandanika Sutta. What is its origin? This sutta was spoken in two places; therefore, its origin is twofold. In this regard: the Blessed One, having gradually arrived at Kapilavatthu, disciplined the Sakyans and gave the going forth to Nanda and others. After the going forth was permitted for women, three Nandās went forth: Nandā, the sister of the Elder Nanda; Abhirūpanandā, the daughter of the Sakyan king Khemaka; and Janapadakalyāṇī Nandā. At that time, the Blessed One was dwelling in Sāvatthī. Abhirūpanandā was indeed beautiful, lovely, and pleasing, for which reason they gave her the name Abhirūpanandā. Janapadakalyāṇī Nandā, too, did not see anyone equal to herself in beauty. Both of them, intoxicated by their physical beauty, did not go to attend upon the Blessed One, thinking, ‘The Blessed One disparages physical form, he censures it, and in many ways he shows the danger in physical form.’ They did not even wish to see him. If it is asked why they went forth, being so lacking in faith, it was due to having no other recourse. In the case of Abhirūpanandā, on the very day she was to be wed, her husband-to-be, a Sakyan prince, died. Then her parents had her go forth against her will. As for Janapadakalyāṇī Nandā, when the Venerable Nanda attained arahantship, she became hopeless and went forth because she could find no satisfaction in the household life, thinking, ‘My husband, my mother Mahāpajāpati, and my other relatives have gone forth. Without relatives, the household life is suffering.’ She did not go forth out of faith.

Atha bhagavā tāsaṃ ñāṇaparipākaṃ viditvā mahāpajāpatiṃ āṇāpesi “sabbāpi bhikkhuniyo paṭipāṭiyā ovādaṃ āgacchantū”ti[P 1.0242]. Tā attano vāre sampatte aññaṃ pesenti. Tato bhagavā “sampatte vāre attanāva [M 1.0234] āgantabbaṃ, na aññā pesetabbā”ti āha. Athekadivasaṃ abhirūpanandā agamāsi. Taṃ bhagavā nimmitarūpena saṃvejetvā “aṭṭhīnaṃ nagaraṃ kata”nti imāya dhammapadagāthāya –

Then the Blessed One, knowing the maturity of their knowledge, instructed Mahāpajāpatī, saying, ‘Let all the bhikkhunīs come in succession to receive instruction.’ When their own turn arrived, they would send another. Then the Blessed One said, ‘When one’s turn arrives, one must come oneself; another is not to be sent.’ Then one day, Abhirūpanandā came. The Blessed One, having stirred a sense of urgency in her by means of a created form, taught with this Dhammapada verse:

“Āturaṃ asuciṃ pūtiṃ, passa nande samussayaṃ;

Uggharantaṃ paggharantaṃ, bālānaṃ abhipatthitaṃ. (therīgā. 19);

‘Behold, Nanda, this afflicted, impure, putrid body, oozing and dripping, which is longed for by fools.’

“Animittañca [V 1.0205] bhāvehi, mānānusayamujjaha;

Tato mānābhisamayā, upasantā carissasī”ti. (su. ni. 344; therīgā. 20) –

‘Develop the signless, abandon the underlying tendency to conceit; then, through the full understanding of conceit, you will go about at peace.’

Imāhi therīgāthāhi ca anupubbena arahatte patiṭṭhāpesi. Athekadivasaṃ sāvatthivāsino purebhattaṃ dānaṃ datvā samādinnuposathā sunivatthā supārutā gandhapupphādīni ādāya dhammassavanatthāya jetavanaṃ gantvā dhammassavanapariyosāne bhagavantaṃ vanditvā nagaraṃ pavisanti. Bhikkhunisaṅghopi dhammakathaṃ sutvā bhikkhuniupassayaṃ gacchati. Tattha manussā ca bhikkhuniyo ca bhagavato vaṇṇaṃ bhāsanti. Catuppamāṇike hi lokasannivāse sammāsambuddhaṃ disvā appasīdanto nāma natthi. Rūpappamāṇikā hi puggalā bhagavato lakkhaṇakhacitamanubyañjanavicitraṃ samujjalitaketumālābyāmappabhāvinaddhamalaṅkāratthamiva lokassa samuppannaṃ rūpaṃ disvā pasīdanti, ghosappamāṇikā anekasatesu jātakesu kittighosaṃ aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgataṃ karavīkamadhuranigghosaṃ brahmassarañca sutvā, lūkhappamāṇikā pattacīvarādilūkhataṃ dukkarakārikalūkhataṃ vā disvā, dhammappamāṇikā sīlakkhandhādīsu yaṃkiñci dhammakkhandhaṃ upaparikkhitvā. Tasmā sabbaṭṭhānesu bhagavato vaṇṇaṃ bhāsanti. Janapadakalyāṇī nandā bhikkhunipassayaṃ patvāpi anekapariyāyena bhagavato vaṇṇaṃ bhāsantānaṃ [P 1.0243] tesaṃ sutvā bhagavantaṃ upagantukāmā hutvā bhikkhunīnaṃ ārocesi. Bhikkhuniyo taṃ gahetvā bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamiṃsu.

Then one day, the residents of Sāvatthī, having given alms before noon, undertaking the Uposatha observance, well-dressed and well-adorned, took perfumes and flowers, and went to Jetavana to listen to the Dhamma. At the end of the Dhamma talk, they paid homage to the Blessed One and entered the city. The community of bhikkhunīs also, having listened to the Dhamma talk, went to the bhikkhunīs’ dwelling. There, both the people and the bhikkhunīs praised the virtues of the Blessed One. For in this world assembly measured by four standards, there is none who, having seen the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, is not pleased. Those whose measure is form, seeing the Blessed One’s body, inlaid with the major characteristics and variegated with the minor characteristics, radiant with a crown of light and a fathom-long aura, as if an ornament arisen for the world, are pleased. Those whose measure is voice, hearing the sound of his fame in hundreds of Jātakas, his voice endowed with eight qualities, sweet as the call of the karavīka bird, and like the voice of Brahmā, are pleased. Those whose measure is austerity, seeing the austerity of his bowl and robes or the austerity of his difficult practices, are pleased. Those whose measure is Dhamma, examining any of the aggregates of the Dhamma, such as the aggregate of virtue, are pleased. Therefore, in all places, they praise the virtues of the Blessed One. Janapadakalyāṇī Nandā, having reached the bhikkhunīs’ dwelling, also heard them praising the Blessed One in many ways. Hearing this, she became desirous of approaching the Blessed One and informed the bhikkhunīs. The bhikkhunīs, taking her along, approached the Blessed One.

Bhagavā paṭikacceva tassāgamanaṃ viditvā kaṇṭakena kaṇṭakaṃ, āṇiyā ca āṇiṃ nīharitukāmo puriso viya rūpeneva rūpamadaṃ vinetuṃ attano iddhibalena pannarasasoḷasavassuddesikaṃ atidassanīyaṃ itthiṃ passe ṭhatvā bījamānaṃ abhinimmini. Nandā bhikkhunīhi saddhiṃ upasaṅkamitvā, bhagavantaṃ vanditvā, bhikkhunisaṅghassa antare nisīditvā, pādatalā pabhuti yāva kesaggā bhagavato [M 1.0235] rūpasampattiṃ disvā puna taṃ bhagavato passe ṭhitaṃ nimmatarūpañca disvā “aho ayaṃ itthī rūpavatī”ti attano rūpamadaṃ jahitvā tassā rūpe abhirattabhāvā ahosi. Tato bhagavā taṃ itthiṃ vīsativassappamāṇaṃ katvā dassesi. Mātugāmo hi soḷasavassuddesikoyeva sobhati, na tato uddhaṃ. Atha tassā rūpaparihāniṃ disvā nandāya tasmiṃ rūpe chandarāgo tanuko ahosi. Tato bhagavā avijātavaṇṇaṃ, sakiṃvijātavaṇṇaṃ, majjhimitthivaṇṇaṃ, mahitthivaṇṇanti evaṃ yāva vassasatikaṃ obhaggaṃ daṇḍaparāyaṇaṃ tilakāhatagattaṃ katvā, dassetvā passamānāyeva nandāya tassā maraṇaṃ uddhumātakādibhedaṃ kākādīhi samparivāretvā khajjamānaṃ duggandhaṃ jegucchapaṭikūlabhāvañca dassesi[V 1.0206]. Nandāya taṃ kamaṃ disvā “evamevaṃ mamapi aññesampi sabbasādhāraṇo ayaṃ kamo”ti aniccasaññā saṇṭhāsi, tadanusārena ca dukkhanattasaññāpi, tayo bhavā ādittamiva agāraṃ appaṭisaraṇā hutvā upaṭṭhahiṃsu. Atha bhagavā “kammaṭṭhāne pakkhantaṃ nandāya citta”nti ñatvā tassā sappāyavasena imā gāthāyo abhāsi –

The Blessed One, knowing beforehand of her arrival, like a man wishing to remove a thorn with a thorn, or a peg with a peg, desired to tame her intoxication with beauty by means of beauty itself. Through his psychic power, he created a woman of surpassing beauty, estimated to be fifteen or sixteen years old, standing and fanning beside him. Nandā approached the Blessed One together with the nuns, paid homage to him, and sat down among the assembly of nuns. From the soles of his feet up to the tip of his hair, she observed the perfection of the Blessed One’s form. Then, seeing the created form standing beside the Blessed One, she thought, “Ah, this woman is beautiful!” Abandoning her own intoxication with beauty, she became infatuated with that woman’s form. Then the Blessed One made that woman appear as if she were twenty years old. For a woman shines most when estimated to be sixteen years of age, not beyond that. Seeing the decline in her beauty, Nandā’s desire and lust for that form diminished. Next, the Blessed One made her appear as a woman who has not yet given birth, then as one who has given birth once, then as a middle-aged woman, then as an elderly woman, and so on up to a hundred-year-old woman—bent over, relying on a stick, her body covered with spots. As Nandā watched, he showed her death, her corpse bloated and in other stages of decay, being devoured by crows and other creatures, foul-smelling, and in a disgusting and repulsive state. Seeing this process, Nandā thought, “Even so, this process is common to me and to all others.” The perception of impermanence was established in her, and in accordance with that, the perceptions of suffering and non-self also arose. The three states of existence appeared to her like a burning house, offering no refuge. Then the Blessed One, knowing that Nandā’s mind had entered upon the meditation subject, spoke these verses suitable for her:

“Āturaṃ [P 1.0244] asuciṃ pūtiṃ, passa nande samussayaṃ;

Uggharantaṃ paggharantaṃ, bālānaṃ abhipatthitaṃ. (therīgā. 19);

“See, Nanda, this body, diseased, impure, and foul, oozing and dripping, desired by fools.”

“Yathā idaṃ tathā etaṃ, yathā etaṃ tathā idaṃ;

Dhātuso suññato passa, mā lokaṃ punarāgami;

Bhave chandaṃ virājetvā, upasantā carissasī”ti. (su. ni. 205);

“As this is, so is that; as that is, so is this. See it as elemental, as empty. Do not come again to the world. Having become dispassionate towards desire for becoming, you will fare on, calmed.”

Gāthāpariyosāne nandā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāsi. Athassā bhagavā uparimaggādhigamatthaṃ suññataparivāraṃ vipassanākammaṭṭhānaṃ kathento imaṃ suttamabhāsi. Ayaṃ tāvassa ekā uppatti.

At the conclusion of the verses, Nandā was established in the fruit of stream-entry. Then, for her to attain the higher paths, the Blessed One, teaching the meditation subject of insight accompanied by emptiness, spoke this discourse. This, for now, was one origin of it.

Bhagavati pana rājagahe viharante yā sā cīvarakkhandhake (mahāva. 326) vitthārato vuttasamuṭṭhānāya sālavatiyā gaṇikāya dhītā jīvakassa kaniṭṭhā sirimā nāma mātu accayena taṃ ṭhānaṃ labhitvā “akkodhena jine kodha”nti (dha. pa. 223; jā. 1.2.1) imissā gāthāya vatthumhi puṇṇakaseṭṭhidhītaraṃ avamaññitvā, bhagavantaṃ khamāpentī dhammadesanaṃ sutvā, sotāpannā hutvā aṭṭha niccabhattāni [M 1.0236] pavattesi. Taṃ ārabbha aññataro niccabhattiko bhikkhu rāgaṃ uppādesi. Āhārakiccampi ca kātuṃ asakkonto nirāhāro nipajjīti dhammapadagāthāvatthumhi vuttaṃ. Tasmiṃ tathānipanneyeva sirimā kālaṃ katvā yāmabhavane suyāmassa devī ahosi. Atha tassā sarīrassa aggikiccaṃ nivāretvā āmakasusāne raññā nikkhipāpitaṃ sarīraṃ dassanāya bhagavā bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto agamāsi, tampi bhikkhuṃ ādāya, tathā nāgarā ca rājā ca. Tattha manussā bhaṇanti “pubbe sirimāya aṭṭhuttarasahassenāpi dassanaṃ dullabhaṃ[P 1.0245], taṃ dānajja kākaṇikāyāpi daṭṭhukāmo natthī”ti. Sirimāpi devakaññā pañcahi rathasatehi parivutā tatrāgamāsi. Tatrāpi bhagavā sannipatitānaṃ dhammadesanatthaṃ imaṃ suttaṃ tassa bhikkhuno ovādatthaṃ “passa cittakataṃ bimba”nti (dha. pa. 147) imañca dhammapadagāthaṃ abhāsi. Ayamassa dutiyā uppatti.

When the Blessed One was residing in Rājagaha, Sirimā, the younger sister of Jīvaka and daughter of the courtesan Sālavatī (the detailed account of whose origin is told in the Cīvarakkhandhaka (Mahāvagga 326)), inherited her mother’s position after her death. In the story of the verse, “Conquer anger with non-anger” (Dhammapada 223; Jātaka 1.2.1), having disdained the daughter of the merchant Puṇṇaka, she sought forgiveness from the Blessed One, listened to his Dhamma teaching, became a stream-enterer, and established eight perpetual meals. In connection with this, a certain monk who received perpetual alms developed lust. Unable to perform even the task of eating, he lay down without food—as is told in the story of the Dhammapada verse. While he was thus lying down, Sirimā passed away and became the consort of Suyāma in the Yāma realm. Then, preventing the cremation of her body, the king had it placed in the charnel ground. Accompanied by the Saṅgha of monks, the Blessed One went to see the body, taking that monk along, as did the citizens and the king. There, people remarked, “Previously, a glimpse of Sirimā was difficult to obtain even for one thousand and eight, but now no one desires to see her even for a kākaṇikā.” Sirimā, now a celestial maiden, also arrived there surrounded by five hundred chariots. There, for the sake of teaching the Dhamma to the assembled crowd and to admonish that monk, the Blessed One spoke this discourse and this Dhammapada verse, “Behold this decorated image…” (Dhammapada 147). This was the second occasion for its arising.

195. Tattha [V 1.0207] caraṃ vāti sakalarūpakāyassa gantabbadisābhimukhenābhinīhārena gacchanto vā. Yadi vā tiṭṭhanti tasseva ussāpanabhāvena tiṭṭhanto vā. Nisinno uda vā sayanti tasseva heṭṭhimabhāgasamiñjanauparimabhāgasamussāpanabhāvena nisinno vā, tiriyaṃ pasāraṇabhāvena sayanto vā. Samiñjeti pasāretīti tāni tāni pabbāni samiñjeti ca pasāreti ca.

195. There, 'moving about' means going, directing the entire physical body with intention toward the destination to be reached. Or, 'standing' means standing, by the state of being held erect. 'Sitting' or 'lying down' means sitting, by bending the lower part and raising the upper part, or lying down, by extending horizontally. 'Drawing in' and 'stretching out' means one draws in and stretches out those various joints.

Esā kāyassa iñjanāti sabbāpesā imasseva saviññāṇakassa kāyassa iñjanā calanā phandanā, natthettha añño koci caranto vā pasārento vā, apica kho pana “carāmī”ti citte uppajjante taṃsamuṭṭhānā vāyodhātu kāyaṃ pharati, tenassa gantabbadisābhimukho abhinīhāro hoti, desantare rūpantarapātubhāvoti attho. Tena “cara”nti vuccati. Tathā “tiṭṭhāmī”ti citte uppajjante taṃsamuṭṭhānā vāyodhātu kāyaṃ pharati, tenassa samussāpanaṃ hoti, uparūpariṭṭhānena rūpapātubhāvoti attho. Tena “tiṭṭha”nti vuccati. Tathā “nisīdāmī”ti citte uppajjante taṃsamuṭṭhānā vāyodhātu kāyaṃ pharati, tenassa heṭṭhimabhāgasamiñjanañca uparimabhāgasamussāpanañca hoti, tathābhāvena rūpapātubhāvoti attho. Tena “nisinno”ti vuccati. Tathā “sayāmī”ti citte uppajjante taṃsamuṭṭhānā [M 1.0237] vāyodhātu kāyaṃ pharati, tenassa tiriyaṃ pasāraṇaṃ hoti, tathābhāvena rūpapātubhāvoti attho. Tena “saya”nti vuccati.

This is the agitation of the body. All this is the agitation, movement, and trembling of just this conscious body. There is no other being here that walks or stretches out. Rather, when the thought 'I will walk' arises, the wind element originating from that pervades the body, by which there is for him an inclination towards the direction to be gone to; the meaning is the appearance of a different form in a different place. Therefore, it is called 'walking.' Similarly, when the thought 'I will stand' arises, the wind element originating from that pervades the body, by which there is for him an erecting; the meaning is the appearance of a form in an upright standing position. Therefore, it is called 'standing.' Likewise, when the thought 'I will sit' arises, the wind element originating from that pervades the body, by which there is for him a bending of the lower part and an erecting of the upper part; the meaning is the appearance of a form in that state. Therefore, it is called 'sitting.' Similarly, when the thought 'I will lie down' arises, the wind element originating from that pervades the body, by which there is for him a horizontal extension; the meaning is the appearance of a form in that state. Therefore, it is called 'lying down.'

Evaṃ cāyamāyasmā yo koci itthannāmo caraṃ vā yadi vā tiṭṭhaṃ, nisinno uda vā sayaṃ yametaṃ [P 1.0246] tattha tattha iriyāpathe tesaṃ tesaṃ pabbānaṃ samiñjanappasāraṇavasena samiñjeti pasāretīti vuccati. Tampi yasmā samiñjanappasāraṇacitte uppajjamāne yathāvutteneva nayena hoti, tasmā esā kāyassa iñjanā, natthettha añño koci, suññamidaṃ kenaci carantena vā pasārentena vā sattena vā puggalena vā. Kevalaṃ pana –

Thus, this venerable one, whoever he may be, of such a name, whether walking or standing, sitting or lying down—in whatever posture, it is said that one bends and stretches those various joints by way of drawing them in and stretching them out. And since that too occurs in the manner just described when the thought to draw in and stretch out arises, therefore this is the agitation of the body. There is no other being here; this is empty of anyone who walks or stretches, of any sentient being or person. It is merely—

“Cittanānattamāgamma, nānattaṃ hoti vāyuno;

Vāyunānattato nānā, hoti kāyassa iñjanā”ti. –

“Depending on the diversity of mind, there is diversity of the wind element; from the diversity of the wind element, diverse agitations of the body arise.”
