Ayamettha paramattho.

This is the ultimate meaning here.

Evametāya gāthāya bhagavā yasmā ekasmiṃ iriyāpathe ciraviniyogena kāyapīḷanaṃ hoti, tassa ca vinodanatthaṃ iriyāpathaparivattanaṃ karīyati, tasmā “caraṃ vā”tiādīhi iriyāpathapaṭicchannaṃ dukkhalakkhaṇaṃ dīpeti, tathā caraṇakāle ṭhānādīnamabhāvato sabbametaṃ caraṇādibhedaṃ [V 1.0208] “esā kāyassa iñjanā”ti bhaṇanto santatipaṭicchannaṃ aniccalakkhaṇaṃ. Tāya tāya sāmaggiyā pavattāya “esā kāyassa iñjanā”ti ca attapaṭikkhepena bhaṇanto attasaññāghanapaṭicchannaṃ anattalakkhaṇaṃ dīpeti.

Thus, with this verse, the Blessed One shows that because remaining long in one posture causes bodily affliction, a change of posture is made for the purpose of dispelling it. Therefore, with 'walking or...' and so on, he reveals the characteristic of suffering concealed by the postures. Likewise, because at the time of walking there is an absence of standing and so on, by saying 'this is the agitation of the body' regarding all these distinctions of walking and so on, he reveals the characteristic of impermanence concealed by continuity. And by saying 'this is the agitation of the body'—which proceeds from the harmony of those various factors—and by rejecting a self, he reveals the characteristic of not-self concealed by the compactness of the perception of self.

196. Evaṃ lakkhaṇattayadīpanena suññatakammaṭṭhānaṃ kathetvā puna saviññāṇakāviññāṇakaasubhadassanatthaṃ “aṭṭhinahārusaṃyutto”ti ārabhi. Tassattho – yassa cesā kāyassa iñjanā, svāyaṃ kāyo visuddhimagge dvattiṃsākāravaṇṇanāyaṃ vaṇṇasaṇṭhānadisokāsaparicchedabhedena abyāpāranayena ca pakāsitehi saṭṭhādhikehi tīhi aṭṭhisatehi navahi nhārusatehi ca saṃyuttattā aṭṭhinahārusaṃyutto. Tattheva pakāsitena aggapādaṅgulitacādinā [P 1.0247] tacena ca navapesisatappabhedena ca maṃsena avalittattā tacamaṃsāvalepano paramaduggandhajegucchapaṭikūloti veditabbo[M 1.0238]. Kiñcettha veditabbaṃ siyā, yadi esa yā sā majjhimassa purisassa sakalasarīrato saṃkaḍḍhitā badaraṭṭhippamāṇā bhaveyya, tāya makkhikāpattasukhumacchaviyā nīlādiraṅgajātena gehabhitti viya paṭicchanno na bhaveyya, ayaṃ pana evaṃ sukhumāyapi chaviyā kāyo paṭicchanno paññācakkhuvirahitehi bālaputhujjanehi yathābhūtaṃ na dissati. Chavirāgarañjito hissa paramajegucchapaṭikūladhammasaṅkhāto tacopi tacapaliveṭhitaṃ yaṃ taṃ pabhedato –

196. Having thus elucidated by means of the three characteristics and spoken on the meditation of emptiness, he then began with “composed of bones and sinews” in order to show the foulness of the body with and without consciousness. The meaning thereof is this: this body, which possesses such movement, is, as described in the Path of Purification in the exposition of the thirty-two parts—in terms of the distinctions of color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation, and by the principle of non-agency—connected with three hundred and sixty-odd bones and nine hundred sinews; hence, it is “composed of bones and sinews.” Furthermore, as explained therein, it is smeared with skin—from the skin of the toes and fingers onwards—and with flesh divided into nine hundred portions; hence, it is “smeared with skin and flesh.” It should be understood as exceedingly foul-smelling, disgusting, and repulsive. Moreover, what should be understood here is this: this skin, if gathered from the whole body of an average person, would be the size of a jujube seed. Because the body is covered by this skin, as fine as a fly’s wing and tinted with blue and other colors like a house wall, it is not seen as it truly is by foolish ordinary people who lack the eye of wisdom. For to one whose mind is dyed with lust for the skin, even the skin itself—which is reckoned as a thing exceedingly disgusting and repulsive—and that which is wrapped in skin, is not seen as it truly is when analyzed by its components—

“Navapesisatā maṃsā, avalittā kaḷevare;

Nānākimikulākiṇṇaṃ, miḷhaṭṭhānaṃva pūtikā”ti. –

“Nine hundred portions of flesh, smeared on the body, infested with various kinds of worms, putrid like a place of excrement.”

Evaṃ vuttaṃ navamaṃsasatampi, maṃsāvalittā ye te –

Thus it is said of the nine hundred portions of flesh, with which it is smeared—

“Navanhārusatā honti, byāmamatte kaḷevare;

Bandhanti aṭṭhisaṅghātaṃ, agāramiva valliyā”ti. –

“There are nine hundred sinews in a body measuring a fathom; they bind the framework of bones, like vines binding a house.”

Tepi, nhārusamuṭṭhitāni paṭipāṭiyā avaṭṭhitāni pūtīni duggandhāni tīṇi saṭṭhādhikāni aṭṭhisatānipi yathābhūtaṃ na dissanti yato anādiyitvā taṃ makkhikāpattasukhumacchaviṃ. Yāni panassa chavirāgarattena tacena paliveṭhitattā sabbalokassa apākaṭāni nānappakārāni abbhantarakuṇapāni paramāsuciduggandhajegucchanīyapaṭikūlāni, tānipi paññācakkhunā paṭivijjhitvā evaṃ passitabbo “antapūro udarapūro…pe… pittassa ca vasāya cā”ti.

And these three hundred and sixty-odd bones—upheld by sinews, arranged in sequence, putrid, and foul-smelling—are also not seen as they truly are, because that delicate skin like a fly's wing is not properly comprehended. And those various internal corpses—supremely impure, foul-smelling, disgusting, and repulsive—which are concealed from the whole world because they are wrapped in skin dyed with the lust for complexion, these too should be penetrated by the eye of wisdom and seen thus: “Full of intestines, full of the stomach… and of bile and of fat.”

197. Tattha [V 1.0209] antassa pūro antapūro. Udarassa pūro udarapūro. Udaranti ca udariyassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tañhi ṭhānanāmena “udara”nti vuttaṃ. Yakanapeḷassāti yakanapiṇḍassa. Vatthinoti muttassa. Ṭhānūpacārena panetaṃ “vatthī”ti [P 1.0248] vuttaṃ. Pūroti adhikāro, tasmā yakanapeḷassa pūro vatthino pūroti evaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Esa nayo hadayassātiādīsu. Sabbāneva cetāni antādīni vaṇṇasaṇṭhānadisokāsaparicchedabhedena abyāpāranayena ca visuddhimagge vuttanayavaseneva veditabbāni.

197. Herein, ‘full of intestines’ means full of the intestines. ‘Full of the stomach’ means full of the stomach. And ‘stomach’ (udara) is a designation for the stomach’s contents (udariya); for it is called ‘stomach’ by the name of its place. ‘Of the liver-lump’ means of the mass of the liver. ‘Of the bladder’ means of urine; it is called ‘bladder’ (vatthi) by way of a metonymy for its location. ‘Full’ is a governing term; therefore, it should be construed thus: ‘full of the liver-lump,’ ‘full of the bladder.’ This same method should be understood for ‘of the heart,’ and so on. All these—the intestines and the rest—should be understood according to the method described in the Visuddhimagga, in terms of the distinctions of their color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation, and by the principle of non-agency.

199-200. Evaṃ bhagavā “na kiñcettha ekampi gayhūpagaṃ muttāmaṇisadisaṃ atthi, aññadatthu asuciparipūrovāyaṃ kāyo”ti abbhantarakuṇapaṃ dassetvā [M 1.0239] idāni tameva abbhantarakuṇapaṃ bahinikkhamanakuṇapena pākaṭaṃ katvā dassento pubbe vuttañca saṅgaṇhitvā “athassa navahi sotehī”ti gāthādvayamāha.

Thus, the Blessed One, having shown the internal corpse by stating, “There is nothing here, not even a single thing worth taking hold of, comparable to a pearl or gem; indeed, this body is utterly filled with impurities,” now, revealing that same internal corpse, makes it manifest through the externally issuing corpse. Summarizing what was previously said, he then speaks the following two verses beginning with, “And from its nine openings...”

Tattha athāti pariyāyantaranidassanaṃ, aparenāpi pariyāyena asucibhāvaṃ passāti vuttaṃ hoti. Assāti imassa kāyassa. Navahi sotehīti ubhoakkhicchiddakaṇṇacchiddanāsāchiddamukhavaccamaggapassāvamaggehi. Asuci savatīti sabbalokapākaṭanānappakāraparamaduggandhajegucchaasuciyeva savati, sandati, paggharati, na aññaṃ kiñci agarucandanādigandhajātaṃ vā maṇimuttādiratanajātaṃ vā. Sabbadāti tañca kho sabbadā rattimpi divāpi pubbaṇhepi sāyanhepi tiṭṭhatopi gacchatopīti. Kiṃ taṃ asucīti ce? “Akkhimhā akkhigūthako”tiādi. Etassa hi dvīhi akkhicchiddehi apanītatacamaṃsasadiso akkhigūthako, kaṇṇacchiddehi rajojallasadiso kaṇṇagūthako, nāsāchiddehi pubbasadisā siṅghāṇikā ca savati, mukhena ca vamati. Kiṃ vamatīti ce? Ekadā pittaṃ, yadā abaddhapittaṃ kuppitaṃ hoti, tadā taṃ vamatīti adhippāyo. Semhañcāti na kevalañca pittaṃ, yampi udarapaṭale ekapatthapūrappamāṇaṃ semhaṃ tiṭṭhati, tampi ekadā vamati. Taṃ panetaṃ vaṇṇādito visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.203-204, 210-211) vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. “Semhañcā”ti ca-saddena semhañca aññañca evarūpaṃ udariyalohitādiasuciṃ vamatīti dasseti. Evaṃ sattahi dvārehi asucivamanaṃ dassetvā kālaññū puggalaññū parisaññū ca bhagavā taduttari [P 1.0249] dve dvārāni visesavacanena anāmasitvā aparena pariyāyena sabbasmāpi kāyā asucisavanaṃ dassento āha “kāyamhā sedajallikā”ti. Tattha sedajallikāti sedo ca loṇapaṭalamalabhedā jallikā ca, tassa “savati sabbadā”ti iminā saddhiṃ sambandho.

Herein, ‘atha’ indicates another method, meaning it is said: ‘See the impurity in yet another way.’ ‘Assa’ refers to this body. ‘Navahi sotehi’ means through the nine openings: the two eye-orifices, the two ear-orifices, the two nostril-orifices, the mouth, the passage for feces, and the passage for urine. ‘Asuci savati’ means that only impurity—manifest to the whole world, of various kinds, exceedingly foul-smelling and disgusting—flows, oozes, and trickles forth; not any other thing, no fragrant substance such as aloe or sandalwood, nor any precious substance such as gems or pearls. ‘Sabbadā’ means always: at night and in the day, in the morning and in the evening, while standing and while walking. If it is asked, ‘What is that impurity?’: “From the eyes, eye-discharge,” and so on. Indeed, from this one’s two eye-orifices, eye-discharge resembling removed skin and flesh flows; from the ear-orifices, earwax resembling dust and grime; from the nostril-orifices, snot resembling pus flows; and from the mouth, one vomits. If it is asked, ‘What does one vomit?’: Sometimes bile—when the unbound bile is agitated, then one vomits it; this is the intention. ‘Semhañcā’ (and phlegm): not only bile, but also the phlegm that sits on the surface of the stomach, about a bowlful in quantity, is sometimes vomited. This should be understood according to the method explained in the Visuddhimagga regarding its color and so on. By the word ‘ca’ in ‘semhañcā,’ it is shown that one vomits phlegm and other such impurities like stomach contents, blood, and so on. Having thus shown the vomiting of impurity from seven doors, the Blessed One—knower of time, knower of individuals, and knower of assemblies—without referring to the remaining two doors with a specific statement, shows in another way the flowing of impurity from the entire body, saying: “from the body, sweat and grime.” Herein, ‘sedajallikā’ means sweat and grime, which is a kind of salty film-like dirt. Its connection is with the phrase “flows always.”

201. Evaṃ [V 1.0210] bhagavā yathā nāma bhatte paccamāne taṇḍulamalañca udakamalañca pheṇena saddhiṃ uṭṭhahitvā ukkhalimukhaṃ makkhetvā bahi gaḷati, tathā asitapītādibhede āhāre kammajena agginā paccamāne yaṃ asitapītādimalaṃ uṭṭhahitvā “akkhimhā akkhigūthako”tiādinā bhedena nikkhamantaṃ akkhiādīni makkhetvā bahi gaḷati, tassāpi vasena imassa kāyassa [M 1.0240] asucibhāvaṃ dassetvā idāni yaṃ loke uttamaṅgasammataṃ sīsaṃ ativisiṭṭhabhāvato paccentā vandaneyyānampi vandanaṃ na karonti, tassāpi nissāratāya asucitāya cassa asucibhāvaṃ dassento “athassa susiraṃ sīsa”nti imaṃ gāthamāha.

201. Thus, the Blessed One, having shown the impure nature of this body by means of that impurity—just as when rice is being cooked, the scum of the rice and the scum of the water rise up with the foam, smear the rim of the pot, and flow outside; so too, when food of various kinds, such as that which is eaten and drunk, is being digested by the fire born of kamma, the impurity from what was eaten and drunk rises up and, exiting in various ways such as 'eye-discharge from the eye,' smears the eyes and so forth and flows outside—now, wishing to show the worthlessness and impurity of even the head, which is considered the most excellent part in the world, and which, due to its exceedingly special nature, people do not bow even to those worthy of reverence, He spoke this verse: 'And his head is hollow.'

Tattha susiranti chiddaṃ. Matthaluṅgassa pūritanti dadhibharitaalābukaṃ viya matthaluṅgabharitaṃ. Tañca panetaṃ matthaluṅgaṃ visuddhimagge vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Subhato naṃ maññati bāloti tamenaṃ evaṃ nānāvidhakuṇapabharitampi kāyaṃ duccintitacintī bālo subhato maññati, subhaṃ suciṃ iṭṭhaṃ kantaṃ manāpanti tīhipi taṇhādiṭṭhimānamaññanāhi maññati. Kasmā? Yasmā avijjāya purakkhato catusaccapaṭicchādakena mohena purakkhato, codito, pavattito, “evaṃ ādiya, evaṃ abhinivisa evaṃ maññāhī”ti gāhitoti adhippāyo. Passa yāva anatthakarā cāyaṃ avijjāti.

Herein, 'hollow' means having an opening. 'Filled with brain-matter' means it is filled with brain-matter like a gourd filled with curds. And that brain-matter should be understood in the way described in the Visuddhimagga. 'A fool considers it beautiful': thus, a fool who thinks wrong thoughts considers this body, though filled with various kinds of carrion, as beautiful. He considers it beautiful, pure, desirable, lovely, and agreeable with the three conceivings of craving, wrong view, and conceit. Why? Because, being placed foremost by ignorance, placed foremost by the delusion that conceals the Four Truths, he is urged on, set in motion, and seized by the thought: 'Grasp it thus, adhere to it thus, conceive it thus!' This is the meaning. See how harmful this ignorance is!

202. Evaṃ bhagavā saviññāṇakavasena asubhaṃ dassetvā idāni aviññāṇakavasena dassetuṃ, yasmā vā cakkavattiraññopi kāyo yathāvuttakuṇapabharitoyeva hoti, tasmā sabbappakārenapi [P 1.0250] sampattibhave asubhaṃ dassetvā idāni vipattibhave dassetuṃ “yadā ca so mato setī”ti gāthamāha.

202. Thus, the Blessed One, having shown the foulness by way of the conscious body, now, in order to show it by way of the non-conscious body—or, because even the body of a wheel-turning king is indeed filled with carrion as described, therefore, having shown the foulness in a state of prosperity in every way, now, in order to show it in a state of adversity—He spoke the verse, 'And when he is dead, he lies.'

Tassattho – svāyamevaṃvidho kāyo yadā āyuusmāviññāṇāpagamena mato vātabharitabhastā viya uddhumātako vaṇṇaparibhedena vinīlako susānasmiṃ niratthaṃva kaliṅgaraṃ chaḍḍitattā apaviddho seti, atha “na dānissa puna uṭṭhānaṃ bhavissatī”ti ekaṃsatoyeva anapekkhā honti ñātayo. Tattha matoti aniccataṃ dasseti, setīti nirīhakattaṃ. Tadubhayena ca jīvitabalamadappahāne niyojeti. Uddhumātoti saṇṭhānavipattiṃ dasseti, vinīlakoti chavirāgavipattiṃ. Tadubhayena ca rūpamadappahāne vaṇṇapokkharataṃ paṭicca mānappahāne ca niyojeti. Apaviddhoti gahetabbābhāvaṃ dasseti, susānasminti anto adhivāsetumanarahaṃ jigucchanīyabhāvaṃ. Tadubhayenapi “mama”nti gāhassa subhasaññāya ca pahāne niyojeti. Anapekkhā honti ñātayoti paṭikiriyābhāvaṃ dasseti, tena ca parivāramadappahāne niyojeti.

Its meaning is as follows: When this very body, dead with the departure of life, heat, and consciousness, lies cast away in a charnel ground—bloated like a wind-filled bellows, discolored and turned blueish due to the change of complexion, discarded like a useless log—then the relatives are utterly without concern, thinking, 'Surely, there will be no rising up for it again.' Herein, 'dead' shows impermanence; 'lies' shows inertness. By both, He directs one to the abandoning of the pride of vital strength. 'Bloated' shows the destruction of its form; 'discolored' shows the destruction of the skin's radiance. By both, He directs one to the abandoning of the pride of form and to the abandoning of conceit based on perfection of complexion. 'Cast away' shows its unworthiness of being taken up; 'in a charnel ground' shows its repulsive nature, unfit to be kept indoors. By both, He directs one to the abandoning of the grasping 'mine' and of the perception of beauty. 'The relatives are without concern' shows the absence of any further care, and by that, He directs one to the abandoning of the pride of retinue.

203. Evamimāya [M 1.0241][V 1.0211] gāthāya aparibhinnāviññāṇakavasena asubhaṃ dassetvā idāni paribhinnavasenāpi dassetuṃ “khādanti na”nti gāthamāha. Tattha ye caññeti ye ca aññepi kākakulalādayo kuṇapabhakkhā pāṇino santi, tepi naṃ khādantīti attho. Sesaṃ uttānameva.

203. Thus, having shown the foulness by this verse by way of the non-conscious body that is not yet broken up, now, in order to show it also by way of the broken-up state, He spoke the verse beginning, 'They devour it.' Herein, 'and others' means that whatever other carrion-eating creatures there are, such as crows and hawks, they too devour it. This is the meaning. The rest is self-evident.

204. Evaṃ “caraṃ vā”tiādinā nayena suññatakammaṭṭhānavasena, “aṭṭhinahārusaṃyutto”tiādinā saviññāṇakāsubhavasena “yadā ca so mato setī”tiādinā aviññāṇakāsubhavasena kāyaṃ dassetvā evaṃ niccasukhattabhāvasuññe ekantaasubhe cāpi kāyasmiṃ “subhato naṃ maññati bālo, avijjāya purakkhato”ti iminā bālassa vuttiṃ pakāsetvā avijjāmukhena ca vaṭṭaṃ dassetvā idāni tattha paṇḍitassa vuttiṃ pariññāmukhena ca vivaṭṭaṃ dassetuṃ “sutvāna buddhavacana”nti ārabhi.

204. Thus, having shown the body by way of the meditation subject of emptiness with the method beginning 'while walking'; by way of the foulness of the conscious body with the method beginning 'bound by bones and sinews'; and by way of the foulness of the non-conscious body with the method beginning 'and when he is dead, he lies'—the body being thus empty of permanence, happiness, and self, and also utterly foul—and having declared the conduct of the fool with the words 'the fool considers it beautiful, being placed foremost by ignorance,' and having shown the round of existence through the entrance of ignorance, now, in order to show the conduct of the wise regarding it and the escape from the round through the entrance of full understanding, He began with 'having heard the Buddha's word.'

Tattha sutvānāti yoniso nisāmetvā. Buddhavacananti kāyavicchandanakaraṃ [P 1.0251] buddhavacanaṃ. Bhikkhūti sekkho vā puthujjano vā. Paññāṇavāti paññāṇaṃ vuccati vipassanā aniccādippakāresu pavattattā, tāya samannāgatoti attho. Idhāti sāsane. So kho naṃ parijānātīti so imaṃ kāyaṃ tīhi pariññāhi parijānāti. Kathaṃ? Yathā nāma kusalo vāṇijo idañcidañcāti bhaṇḍaṃ oloketvā “ettakena gahite ettako nāma udayo bhavissatī”ti tulayitvā tathā katvā puna saudayaṃ mūlaṃ gaṇhanto taṃ bhaṇḍaṃ chaḍḍeti, evamevaṃ “aṭṭhinhāruādayo ime kesalomādayo cā”ti ñāṇacakkhunā olokento ñātapariññāya parijānāti, “aniccā ete dhammā dukkhā anattā”ti tulayanto tīraṇapariññāya parijānāti, evaṃ tīrayitvā ariyamaggaṃ pāpuṇanto tattha chandarāgappahānena pahānapariññāya parijānāti. Saviññāṇakāviññāṇakaasubhavasena vā passanto ñātapariññāya parijānāti, aniccādivasena passanto tīraṇapariññāya, arahattamaggena tato chandarāgaṃ apakaḍḍhitvā taṃ pajahanto pahānapariññāya parijānāti.

Herein, 'having heard' means having attended carefully. 'The Buddha's word' refers to the Buddha's teaching that causes disenchantment with the body. 'A bhikkhu' refers to either a trainee or a worldling. 'With wisdom': wisdom is called insight because it proceeds in aspects such as impermanence; 'with wisdom' means one is endowed with that. 'Here' means in this Dispensation. 'He fully understands it' means he fully understands this body through three kinds of full understanding. How? Just as a skilled merchant, examining goods and thinking, 'If I buy this for such a price, the profit will be so much,' weighs the matter, acts accordingly, and then, taking back the profit with the original capital, discards the goods; even so, one who looks with the eye of wisdom at 'these bones and sinews, this hair of the head and hair of the body,' understands through the full understanding of knowledge. By weighing, 'these phenomena are impermanent, suffering, and not-self,' one understands through the full understanding by scrutinizing. Having thus scrutinized, upon reaching the noble path, one understands through the full understanding by abandoning, by means of the abandoning of desire and lust for those things. Or, by seeing by way of the foulness of the conscious and non-conscious body, one understands through the full understanding of knowledge. By seeing by way of impermanence and so forth, one understands through the full understanding by scrutinizing. Through the path of arahantship, by drawing away desire and lust from that and abandoning it, one understands through the full understanding by abandoning.

Kasmā so evaṃ parijānātīti ce? Yathābhūtañhi passati, yasmā yathābhūtaṃ passatīti attho. “Paññāṇavā”tiādinā eva ca etasmiṃ atthe [M 1.0242] siddhe yasmā buddhavacanaṃ sutvā tassa paññāṇavattaṃ hoti, yasmā ca sabbajanassa pākaṭopāyaṃ kāyo asutvā buddhavacanaṃ na sakkā parijānituṃ, tasmā tassa ñāṇahetuṃ ito bāhirānaṃ evaṃ daṭṭhuṃ asamatthatañca dassetuṃ “sutvāna buddhavacana”nti āha. Nandābhikkhuniṃ tañca vipallatthacittaṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha desanāpavattito aggaparisato tappaṭipattippattānaṃ bhikkhubhāvadassanato ca “bhikkhū”ti āha.

If it is asked, ‘Why does he fully understand thus?’—Because he sees things as they truly are; the meaning is that he sees things as they truly are. And although this meaning is established by 'one with wisdom,' etc., because it is by having heard the Buddha's word that one becomes wise, and because it is not possible for all people to fully understand the body, a manifest means, without having heard the Buddha's word, therefore, to show the cause of his knowledge and the inability of those outside this teaching to see in this way, he said, ‘having heard the Buddha’s word.’ Because the discourse was set in motion concerning the nun Nandā and that monk with a perverted mind, and because of showing the state of a bhikkhu to those in the foremost assembly who have attained that practice, he said 'bhikkhu'.

205. Idāni [V 1.0212][P 1.0252] “yathābhūtañhi passatī”ti ettha yathā passanto yathābhūtaṃ passati, taṃ dassetuṃ āha “yathā idaṃ tathā etaṃ, yathā etaṃ tathā ida”nti. Tassattho – yathā idaṃ saviññāṇakāsubhaṃ āyuusmāviññāṇānaṃ anapagamā carati, tiṭṭhati, nisīdati, sayati; tathā etaṃ etarahi susāne sayitaṃ aviññāṇakampi pubbe tesaṃ dhammānaṃ anapagamā ahosi. Yathā ca etaṃ etarahi matasarīraṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ apagamā na carati, na tiṭṭhati, na nisīdati, na seyyaṃ kappeti, tathā idaṃ saviññāṇakampi tesaṃ dhammānaṃ apagamā bhavissati. Yathā ca idaṃ saviññāṇakaṃ etarahi na susāne mataṃ seti, na uddhumātakādibhāvamupagataṃ, tathā etaṃ etarahi matasarīrampi pubbe ahosi. Yathā panetaṃ etarahi aviññāṇakāsubhaṃ mataṃ susāne seti, uddhumātakādibhāvañca upagataṃ, tathā idaṃ saviññāṇakampi bhavissatīti.

205. Now, regarding the statement ‘he sees it as it truly is,’ to show how one who is seeing sees it as it truly is, he says: ‘As this is, so is that; as that is, so is this.’ Its meaning is as follows: Just as this foul thing with consciousness moves, stands, sits, and lies down due to the non-departure of life, heat, and consciousness; so too was that lifeless thing now lying in the charnel ground formerly, due to the non-departure of those qualities. And just as that dead body now, due to the departure of those qualities, does not move, does not stand, does not sit, and does not assume a lying posture; so too will this thing with consciousness be, with the departure of those qualities. And just as this thing with consciousness now does not lie dead in the charnel ground, nor has it reached the state of being bloated and so forth, so too was that dead body formerly. But just as that lifeless, foul thing now lies dead in the charnel ground and has reached the state of being bloated and so forth, so too will this thing with consciousness be.

Tattha yathā idaṃ tathā etanti attanā matassa sarīrassa samānabhāvaṃ karonto bāhire dosaṃ pajahati. Yathā etaṃ tathā idanti matasarīrena attano samānabhāvaṃ karonto ajjhattike rāgaṃ pajahati. Yenākārena ubhayaṃ sabhaṃ karoti, taṃ pajānanto ubhayattha mohaṃ pajahati. Evaṃ yathābhūtadassanena pubbabhāgeyeva akusalamūlappahānaṃ sādhetvā, yasmā evaṃ paṭipanno bhikkhu anupubbena arahattamaggaṃ patvā sabbaṃ chandarāgaṃ virājetuṃ samattho hoti, tasmā āha “ajjhattañca bahiddhā ca, kāye chandaṃ virājaye”ti. Evaṃ paṭipanno bhikkhu anupubbenāti pāṭhaseso.

Therein, by making one's own body equal to a dead body, reflecting 'as this is, so is that,' one abandons fault-finding with the external. By making one's own body equal to the dead body, reflecting 'as that is, so is this,' one abandons internal lust. Knowing the manner in which one makes both equal, one abandons delusion in both respects. Thus, by seeing things as they truly are, having accomplished the abandoning of unwholesome roots even in the preliminary stage, because a bhikkhu who practices thus gradually attains the path of arahantship and becomes capable of dispelling all desire and lust, it is said: ‘He should dispel desire for the body, both internally and externally.’ The remainder of the text is: 'A bhikkhu who practices thus, gradually...'

206. Evaṃ sekkhabhūmiṃ dassetvā idāni asekkhabhūmiṃ dassento āha “chandarāgaviratto so”ti. Tassattho – so bhikkhu arahattamaggañāṇena paññāṇavā maggānantaraṃ phalaṃ pāpuṇāti, atha sabbaso chandarāgassa [M 1.0243] pahīnattā “chandarāgaviratto”ti ca, maraṇābhāvena paṇītaṭṭhena [P 1.0253] vā amataṃ sabbasaṅkhāravūpasamanato santiṃ taṇhāsaṅkhātavānābhāvato nibbānaṃ, cavanābhāvato accutanti saṃvaṇṇitaṃ padamajjhagāti ca vuccati. Atha vā so bhikkhu arahattamaggañāṇena paññāṇavā maggānantaraphale ṭhito chandarāgaviratto nāma hoti, vuttappakārañca padamajjhagāti veditabbo. Tena “idamassa pahīnaṃ, idañcānena laddha”nti dīpeti.

206. Having thus shown the stage of a trainee, now, showing the stage of one beyond training, he says: ‘He is detached from desire and lust.’ Its meaning is as follows: That bhikkhu, being wise with the knowledge of the path of arahantship, attains the fruit immediately after the path. Then, because of the complete abandonment of desire and lust, he is called ‘one detached from desire and lust.’ And he is said to have attained the state described as the deathless, due to the absence of death or its sublime nature; as peace, due to the stilling of all formations; as Nibbāna, due to the absence of that which is called craving; and as the imperishable, due to the absence of passing away. Alternatively, that bhikkhu, being wise with the knowledge of the path of arahantship and established in the fruit immediately following the path, is called ‘one detached from desire and lust,’ and the state described should be understood as ‘the state he has attained.’ By this, it is shown: ‘This has been abandoned by him, and this has been attained by him.’

207-208. Evaṃ saviññāṇakāviññāṇakavasena asubhakammaṭṭhānaṃ saha nipphattiyā kathetvā puna saṅkhepadesanāya evaṃ mahato ānisaṃsassa antarāyakaraṃ pamādavihāraṃ garahanto “dvipādakoya”nti gāthādvayamāha. Tattha kiñcāpi apādakādayopi kāyā asucīyeva, idhādhikāravasena pana ukkaṭṭhaparicchedavasena vā, yasmā vā aññe asucibhūtāpi kāyā loṇambilādīhi [V 1.0213] abhisaṅkharitvā manussānaṃ bhojanepi upanīyanti, na tveva manussakāyo, tasmā asucitarabhāvamassa dassentopi “dvipādako”ti āha.

Having thus explained the meditation on foulness in terms of bodies with and without consciousness, together with its accomplishment, and then, by way of a brief teaching, censuring the heedless dwelling that is an obstacle to such a great benefit, he spoke the pair of verses beginning, 'This two-footed one.' Therein, although bodies without feet and so on are also impure, he spoke of 'the two-footed one' either due to the main subject matter here, or by way of delimiting the supreme case. Or, because other bodies, although impure, are prepared with salt, sour liquids, and so on, and are even offered as food to humans—but never the human body—therefore, also to show its state of being more impure, he said 'the two-footed one.'

Ayanti manussakāyaṃ dasseti. Duggandho parihīratīti duggandho samāno pupphagandhādīhi abhisaṅkharitvā parihīrati. Nānākuṇapaparipūroti kesādianekappakārakuṇapabharito. Vissavanto tato tatoti pupphagandhādīhi paṭicchādetuṃ ghaṭentānampi taṃ vāyāmaṃ nipphalaṃ katvā navahi dvārehi kheḷasiṅghāṇikādīni, lomakūpehi ca sedajallikaṃ vissavantoyeva. Tattha dāni passatha – etādisena kāyena yo puriso vā itthī vā koci bālo maññe uṇṇametave taṇhādiṭṭhimānamaññanāhi “aha”nti vā “mama”nti vā “nicco”ti vātiādinā nayena yo uṇṇamituṃ maññeyya, paraṃ vā jātiādīhi avajāneyya attānaṃ ucce ṭhāne ṭhapento, kimaññatra adassanā ṭhapetvā ariyamaggena ariyasaccadassanābhāvaṃ kimaññaṃ tassa evaṃ uṇṇamāvajānanakāraṇaṃ siyāti.

'This' indicates the human body. 'It is carried about foul-smelling' means: being foul-smelling, it is maintained by being embellished with the scents of flowers and so on. 'Filled with various corpses' means it is filled with many kinds of corpses, such as hair and so on. 'Oozing from here and there' means that, rendering futile the effort of those who try to conceal it with scents of flowers and the like, it is always oozing saliva, mucus, and so on from the nine orifices, and sweat and grime from the pores. Now then, consider: with such a body, what foolish man or woman might think to be exalted through the notions of craving, views, and conceit, thinking 'I,' or 'mine,' or 'permanent,' and so on; or, placing themselves on high, might disparage another based on birth and so on? What could be the reason for such exalting and disparaging, other than not seeing? That is, apart from the absence of seeing the Noble Truths by means of the Noble Path, what other cause could there be?

Desanāpariyosāne nandā bhikkhunī saṃvegamāpādi – “aho vata re, ahaṃ bālā, yā maṃyeva ārabbha evaṃ vividhadhammadesanāpavattakassa bhagavato upaṭṭhānaṃ [P 1.0254] nāgamāsi”nti. Evaṃ saṃviggā ca tameva dhammadesanaṃ samannāharitvā [M 1.0244] teneva kammaṭṭhānena katipayadivasabbhantare arahattaṃ sacchākāsi. Dutiyaṭṭhānepi kira desanāpariyosāne caturāsītiyā pāṇasahassānaṃ dhammābhisamayo ahosi, sirimā devakaññā anāgāmiphalaṃ pattā, so ca bhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahīti.

At the end of the teaching, the bhikkhunī Nandā was overcome with spiritual urgency—'Alas, friends, how foolish I am, that I did not attend upon the Blessed One, who sets in motion such a diverse teaching concerning me myself!' Thus overcome with urgency, and having reflected well upon that very Dhamma teaching, by means of that same meditation subject, within a few days she realized Arahantship. It is said that on the second occasion as well, at the end of the teaching, the comprehension of the Dhamma occurred for eighty-four thousand beings. The celestial maiden Sirimā attained the fruit of non-returning, and that monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Minor Collection:

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya vijayasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the Vijaya Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary is completed.

12. Munisuttavaṇṇanā

12. The Exposition of the Muni Sutta

209. Santhavāto [V 1.0214] bhayaṃ jātanti munisuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Na sabbasseva suttassa ekā uppatti, apicettha ādito tāva catunnaṃ gāthānaṃ ayamuppatti – bhagavati kira sāvatthiyaṃ viharante gāmakāvāse aññatarā duggatitthī matapatikā puttaṃ bhikkhūsu pabbājetvā attanāpi bhikkhunīsu pabbaji. Te ubhopi sāvatthiyaṃ vassaṃ upagantvā abhiṇhaṃ aññamaññassa dassanakāmā ahesuṃ. Mātā kiñci labhitvā puttassa harati, puttopi mātu. Evaṃ sāyampi pātopi aññamaññaṃ samāgantvā laddhaṃ laddhaṃ saṃvibhajamānā, sammodamānā, sukhadukkhaṃ pucchamānā, nirāsaṅkā ahesuṃ. Tesaṃ evaṃ abhiṇhadassanena saṃsaggo uppajji, saṃsaggā vissāso, vissāsā otāro, rāgena otiṇṇacittānaṃ pabbajitasaññā ca mātuputtasaññā ca antaradhāyi. Tato mariyādavītikkamaṃ katvā asaddhammaṃ paṭiseviṃsu, ayasappattā ca vibbhamitvā agāramajjhe vasiṃsu. Bhikkhū bhagavato ārocesuṃ. “Kiṃ nu so, bhikkhave, moghapuriso maññati na mātā putte sārajjati, putto vā pana mātarī”ti garahitvā “nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, aññaṃ [P 1.0255] ekarūpampi samanupassāmī”tiādinā (a. ni. 5.55) avasesasuttenapi bhikkhū saṃvejetvā “tasmātiha, bhikkhave –

209. 'From intimacy, fear is born'—this is the Muni Sutta. What is its origin? Not every sutta has a single origin, but here, to begin with, is the origin of the first four verses. It is said that while the Blessed One was dwelling in a village near Sāvatthī, a certain poor woman, a widow, had her son go forth among the monks and she herself went forth among the nuns. Both of them, having entered the rains retreat in Sāvatthī, frequently desired to see each other. When the mother received anything, she would bring it to her son, and the son likewise to his mother. Thus, meeting in the morning and evening, sharing whatever they had received, greeting each other, and inquiring about each other’s well-being and hardship, they became uninhibited. From their frequent seeing, association arose; from association, intimacy; from intimacy, a lapse occurred. With their minds overcome by lust, the perception of being monastics and the perception of being mother and son disappeared. Then, transgressing the boundary, they engaged in improper conduct. Having fallen into disrepute, they disrobed and lived together in a household. The monks reported this to the Blessed One. He rebuked them, saying, 'What, monks, does that worthless man think? That a mother does not feel passion for her son, or a son for his mother?' and having stirred a sense of urgency in the monks with the teaching beginning, 'Monks, I do not see even one other form...', he said: 'Therefore, monks—'

“Visaṃ yathā halāhalaṃ, telaṃ pakkuthitaṃ yathā;

Tambalohavilīnaṃva, mātugāmaṃ vivajjaye”ti ca. –

'A woman should be avoided like halāhala poison, like boiling oil, and like molten copper.'

Vatvā [M 1.0245] puna bhikkhūnaṃ dhammadesanatthaṃ – “santhavāto bhayaṃ jāta”nti imā attupanāyikā catasso gāthā abhāsi.

Having spoken thus, again, for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma to the monks, he uttered these four verses that apply to oneself, beginning with: 'From intimacy, fear is born.'

Tattha santhavo taṇhādiṭṭhimittabhedena tividhoti pubbe vutto. Idha taṇhādiṭṭhisanthavo adhippeto. Taṃ sandhāya bhagavā āha – “passatha, bhikkhave, yathā idaṃ tassa moghapurisassa santhavāto bhayaṃ jāta”nti. Tañhi tassa abhiṇhadassanakāmatāditaṇhāya balavakilesabhayaṃ jātaṃ, yena saṇṭhātuṃ asakkonto mātari vippaṭipajji. Attānuvādādikaṃ vā mahābhayaṃ, yena sāsanaṃ [V 1.0215] chaḍḍetvā vibbhanto. Niketāti “rūpanimittaniketavisāravinibandhā kho, gahapati, ‘niketasārī’ti vuccatī”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 3.3) nayena vuttā ārammaṇappabhedā. Jāyate rajoti rāgadosamoharajo jāyate. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Na kevalañca tassa santhavāto bhayaṃ jātaṃ, apica kho pana yadetaṃ kilesānaṃ nivāsaṭṭhena sāsavārammaṇaṃ “niketa”nti vuccati, idānissa bhinnasaṃvarattā atikkantamariyādattā suṭṭhutaraṃ tato niketā jāyate rajo, yena saṃkiliṭṭhacitto anayabyasanaṃ pāpuṇissati. Atha vā passatha, bhikkhave, yathā idaṃ tassa moghapurisassa santhavāto bhayaṃ jātaṃ, yathā ca sabbaputhujjanānaṃ niketā jāyate rajoti evampetaṃ padadvayaṃ yojetabbaṃ.

Herein, santhava (intimacy), as was stated previously, is threefold, distinguished as craving, wrong view, and friendship. Here, intimacy through craving and wrong view is intended. It was with reference to this that the Blessed One said: 'See, monks, how fear was born from this worthless man’s intimacy.' For from his craving, such as the desire to see her frequently, the powerful fear of the defilements was born, because of which, being unable to establish himself, he misconducted himself with his mother. Or else, the great fear of self-reproach and the like was born, because of which he abandoned the teaching and disrobed. Niketa (abode) refers to the various kinds of objects spoken of in the manner of the passage beginning: 'Householder, one who is bound by attachment spreading from the abode of the sign of form is called a "dweller in an abode."' Rajo jāyate (dust is born) means the dust of lust, hatred, and delusion is born. What is meant by this? Not only was fear born from his intimacy, but furthermore—since his restraint was broken and he had transgressed the boundary—all the more intensely from that niketa, which is so called because it is an abode for the defilements and a support for the taints, dust is born. Because of this, with a defiled mind, he will reach ruin and disaster. Alternatively, the two phrases should be connected thus: 'See, monks, how this fear was born from that worthless man’s intimacy, and how from the niketa of all ordinary people, dust is born.'

Sabbathā pana iminā purimaddhena bhagavā puthujjanadassanaṃ garahitvā attano dassanaṃ pasaṃsanto “aniketa”nti pacchimaddhamāha. Tattha yathāvuttaniketapaṭikkhepena aniketaṃ, santhavapaṭikkhepena [P 1.0256] ca asanthavaṃ veditabbaṃ. Ubhayampetaṃ nibbānassādhivacanaṃ. Etaṃ ve munidassananti etaṃ aniketamasanthavaṃ buddhamuninā diṭṭhanti attho. Tattha veti vimhayatthe nipāto daṭṭhabbo. Tena ca yaṃ nāma niketasanthavavasena mātāputtesu vippaṭipajjamānesu aniketamasanthavaṃ, etaṃ muninā diṭṭhaṃ aho abbhutanti ayamadhippāyo siddho hoti. Atha vā munino dassanantipi munidassanaṃ, dassanaṃ nāma khanti ruci, khamati ceva ruccati cāti attho.

In every way, however, with this first half of the verse, the Blessed One, having censured the vision of ordinary people and wishing to praise his own vision, spoke the second half, beginning with aniketa. Therein, aniketa (without abode) should be understood as the rejection of the abode as described, and asanthava (without intimacy) as the rejection of intimacy. Both of these terms are synonyms for Nibbāna. Etaṃ ve munidassanaṃ ('This, indeed, is the sage's vision') means: this state without abode and without intimacy has been seen by the sage, the Buddha. Here, the particle ve should be understood as being in the sense of wonder. By this, the following intention is established: 'How wonderful it is that while a mother and son misconduct themselves on account of an abode and intimacy, this state without abode and without intimacy has been seen by the sage!' Alternatively, munidassanaṃ is the vision of the sage (munino dassanaṃ). Vision, in this sense, means forbearance and approval (khanti ruci); that is, he both forbears and approves.

210. Dutiyagāthāya yo jātamucchijjāti yo kismiñcideva vatthusmiṃ jātaṃ bhūtaṃ nibbattaṃ kilesaṃ yathā uppannākusalappahānaṃ hoti, tathā [M 1.0246] vāyamanto tasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ puna anibbattanavasena ucchinditvā yo anāgatopi kileso tathārūpappaccayasamodhāne nibbattituṃ abhimukhībhūtattā vattamānasamīpe vattamānalakkhaṇena “jāyanto”ti vuccati, tañca na ropayeyya jāyantaṃ, yathā anuppannākusalānuppādo hoti, tathā vāyamanto na nibbatteyyāti attho. Kathañca na nibbatteyya? Assa nānuppavecche, yena paccayena so nibbatteyya taṃ nānuppaveseyya na samodhāneyya. Evaṃ sambhāravekallakaraṇena taṃ na ropayeyya jāyantaṃ. Atha vā yasmā maggabhāvanāya atītāpi kilesā ucchijjanti āyatiṃ vipākābhāvena vattamānāpi na ropīyanti tadabhāvena, anāgatāpi cittasantatiṃ nānuppavesīyanti uppattisāmatthiyavighātena, tasmā yo ariyamaggabhāvanāya jātamucchijja na ropayeyya jāyantaṃ, anāgatampi cassa jāyantassa nānuppavecche, tamāhu ekaṃ muninaṃ carantaṃ, so ca addakkhi santipadaṃ mahesīti evampettha yojanā veditabbā. Ekantanikkilesatāya ekaṃ, seṭṭhaṭṭhena vā ekaṃ. Muninanti muniṃ, munīsu vā ekaṃ. Carantanti sabbākāraparipūrāya lokatthacariyāya avasesacariyāhi [V 1.0216] ca [P 1.0257] carantaṃ. Addakkhīti addasa. Soti yo jātamucchijja aropane ananuppavesane ca samatthatāya “na ropayeyya jāyantamassa nānuppavecche”ti vutto buddhamuni. Santipadanti santikoṭṭhāsaṃ, dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhigatavipassanānibbānabhedāsu tīsu sammutisanti, tadaṅgasanti, accantasantīsu seṭṭhaṃ evaṃ anupasante loke accantasantiṃ addasa mahesīti evamattho veditabbo.

210. In the second verse, 'one who would cut off what has arisen' means: whatever defilement has arisen, come into being, or been produced in any object whatsoever, one, striving just as there is the abandoning of arisen unwholesome states, would cut it off in that object by means of non-re-arising. And whatever future defilement is said to be 'arising' by the characteristic of the present, being near the present, because it is facing arising when there is a conjunction of suitable conditions—that arising defilement one should not foster. The meaning is that, striving just as there is the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states, one should not produce it. And how should one not produce it? One should not allow it entry. One should not let enter, should not bring together, the condition by which it would be produced. Thus, by creating a deficiency of supporting factors, one does not foster that which is arising. Alternatively, because through the development of the path, past defilements are cut off by the absence of future results, present ones are not fostered due to that absence, and future ones do not enter the continuity of consciousness due to the destruction of their capacity to arise. Therefore, one who, through the development of the Noble Path, having cut off what has arisen, does not foster what is arising, and does not allow entry to what is arising in the future—'him they call the one sage who walks; and that great seer has seen the state of peace.' Thus should the connection be understood here. 'One' (ekaṃ) due to being utterly without defilements, or 'one' in the sense of 'supreme'. 'Of the sage' (muninaṃ) means 'the sage', or 'one among sages'. 'Walking' (carantaṃ) means walking with conduct for the welfare of the world, complete in all aspects, and with the remaining forms of conduct. 'He saw' (addakkhi) means he perceived. 'He' (so) is the Buddha-sage who is spoken of as 'he should not foster what is arising, nor should he allow it entry' due to his capability in not fostering and not allowing entry, having cut off what has arisen. 'The state of peace' (santipadaṃ) means the portion of peace; among the three—conventional peace, peace by suppression, and absolute peace, which are distinguished by the sixty-two views, insight, and Nibbāna—it is the supreme. Thus, in an unpeaceful world, the great seer saw the absolute peace. Thus should the meaning be understood.

211. Tatiyagāthāya saṅkhāyāti gaṇayitvā, paricchinditvā vīmaṃsitvā yathābhūtato ñatvā, dukkhapariññāya parijānitvāti attho. Vatthūnīti yesu evamayaṃ loko sajjati, tāni khandhāyatanadhātubhedāni kilesaṭṭhānāni. Pamāya bījanti yaṃ tesaṃ vatthūnaṃ bījaṃ abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇaṃ, taṃ pamāya hiṃsitvā, bādhitvā, samucchedappahānena pajahitvāti attho. Sinehamassa nānuppaveccheti yena taṇhādiṭṭhisinehena sinehitaṃ taṃ bījaṃ āyatiṃ paṭisandhivasena taṃ yathāvuttaṃ vatthusassaṃ viruheyya, taṃ sinehamassa nānuppavecche, tappaṭipakkhāya maggabhāvanāya taṃ nānuppaveseyyāti attho. Sa ve muni jātikhayantadassīti so evarūpo buddhamuni nibbānasacchikiriyāya jātiyā ca maraṇassa ca antabhūtassa nibbānassa diṭṭhattā jātikkhayantadassī [M 1.0247] takkaṃ pahāya na upeti saṅkhaṃ. Imāya catusaccabhāvanāya navappabhedampi akusalavitakkaṃ pahāya saupādisesanibbānadhātuṃ patvā lokatthacariyaṃ karonto anupubbena carimaviññāṇakkhayā anupādisesanibbānadhātuppattiyā “devo vā manusso vā”ti na upeti saṅkhaṃ. Aparinibbuto eva vā yathā kāmavitakkādino vitakkassa appahīnattā “ayaṃ puggalo ratto”ti vā “duṭṭho”ti vā saṅkhaṃ upeti, evaṃ takkaṃ pahāya na upeti saṅkhanti evampettha attho daṭṭhabbo[P 1.0258].

211. In the third verse, 'having reckoned' (saṅkhāya) means having calculated, defined, examined, and known as it truly is; the meaning is 'having fully understood by means of the full understanding of suffering.' 'Grounds' (vatthūni) refers to those things distinguished as aggregates, sense bases, and elements, which are the bases of defilements, wherein this world becomes attached. 'Having measured the seed' (pamāya bījaṃ) means having harmed, suppressed, and abandoned the seed of those grounds—the formational consciousness—through abandonment by eradication; this is the meaning. 'He should not let moisture enter him' (sinehamassa nānuppavecche) means that he should not let that moisture of craving and views enter him, by which that moistened seed would cause the crop of those aforementioned grounds to sprout in the future through rebirth-linking; the meaning is that through the development of the path that is its opposite, he should not let it enter. 'That sage, indeed, is a seer of the end of birth' (sa ve muni jātikhayantadassī) means such a Buddha-sage, being a seer of the end of birth because he has seen Nibbāna, which is the end of birth and death, through its realization, abandons thought and is not subject to reckoning. Through this cultivation of the Four Noble Truths, having abandoned even the ninefold unwholesome thought and attained the Nibbāna-element with residue remaining, while performing conduct for the welfare of the world, he gradually, with the cessation of the final consciousness and the attainment of the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining, is not subject to the reckoning 'a deva or a human.' Alternatively, just as one who is not yet fully extinguished, because thought such as sensual thought has not been abandoned, is subject to the reckoning 'this person is lustful' or 'hateful', so he, having abandoned thought, is not subject to reckoning—this is how the meaning should be understood here.

212. Catutthagāthāya aññāyāti aniccādinayena jānitvā. Sabbānīti anavasesāni, nivesanānīti kāmabhavādike bhave. Nivasanti hi tesu sattā, tasmā “nivesanānī”ti vuccanti. Anikāmayaṃ aññatarampi tesanti evaṃ diṭṭhādīnavattā tesaṃ nivesanānaṃ ekampi apatthento so evarūpo buddhamuni maggabhāvanābalena taṇhāgedhassa vigatattā vītagedho, vītagedhattā eva ca agiddho, na yathā eke avītagedhā eva samānā “agiddhamhā”ti paṭijānanti, evaṃ. Nāyūhatīti tassa tassa nivesanassa nibbattakaṃ kusalaṃ vā akusalaṃ vā na karoti. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Pāragato hi hoti, yasmā evarūpo sabbanivesanānaṃ pāraṃ nibbānaṃ gato hotīti attho.

212. In the fourth verse, 'having known' (aññāya) means knowing through the method of impermanence, etc. 'All' (sabbāni) means without remainder. 'Abodes' (nivesanāni) refers to states of existence such as the sense-sphere existence and others. For beings dwell in them; hence, they are called 'abodes.' 'Not desiring any of them' (anikāmayaṃ aññatarampi tesaṃ) means that, having seen the danger, such a Buddha-sage does not wish for even one of those abodes. Through the power of the development of the path, being free from the greed of craving, he is without greed; and just because of being without greed, he is not greedy—not like some who, while not being free from greed, claim, 'We are not greedy.' 'He does not accumulate' (nāyūhati) means he does not perform wholesome or unwholesome kamma that produces this or that abode. For what reason? Because he has gone to the far shore. The meaning is that such a one has gone to Nibbāna, the far shore of all abodes.

Evaṃ [V 1.0217] paṭhamagāthāya puthujjanadassanaṃ garahitvā attano dassanaṃ pasaṃsanto dutiyagāthāya yehi kilesehi puthujjano anupasanto hoti, tesaṃ abhāvena attano santipadādhigamaṃ pasaṃsanto tatiyagāthāya yesu vatthūsu puthujjano takkaṃ appahāya tathā tathā saṅkhaṃ upeti, tesu catusaccabhāvanāya takkaṃ pahāya attano saṅkhānupagamanaṃ pasaṃsanto catutthagāthāya āyatimpi yāni nivesanāni kāmayamāno puthujjano bhavataṇhāya āyūhati, tesu taṇhābhāvena attano anāyūhanaṃ pasaṃsanto catūhi gāthāhi arahattanikūṭeneva ekaṭṭhuppattikaṃ desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi.

Thus, with the first verse, having criticized the view of the ordinary person, he praised his own view. With the second verse, he praised his own attainment of the state of peace through the absence of those defilements by which the ordinary person is unpeaceful. With the third verse, he praised his own not being subject to reckoning, having abandoned thought in those things through the cultivation of the Four Noble Truths, whereas the ordinary person, not abandoning thought, is subject to reckoning in various ways. With the fourth verse, he praised his own non-accumulation through the absence of craving for those abodes which the ordinary person, desiring them, accumulates in the future with craving for existence. With these four verses, he concluded the teaching, which has a single purpose and culminates in arahantship.

213. Sabbābhibhunti kā uppatti? Mahāpuriso mahābhinikkhamanaṃ katvā anupubbena sabbaññutaṃ patvā dhammacakkappavattanatthāya bārāṇasiṃ gacchanto [M 1.0248] bodhimaṇḍassa ca gayāya ca antare upakenājīvakena samāgacchi. Tena ca “vippasannāni kho te, āvuso, indriyānī”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.285; mahāva. 11) nayena puṭṭho “sabbābhibhū”tiādīni āha. Upako “hupeyyāvuso”ti vatvā, sīsaṃ okampetvā, ummaggaṃ gahetvā pakkāmi[P 1.0259]. Anukkamena ca vaṅkahārajanapade aññataraṃ māgavikagāmaṃ pāpuṇi. Tamenaṃ māgavikajeṭṭhako disvā – “aho appiccho samaṇo vatthampi na nivāseti, ayaṃ loke arahā”ti gharaṃ netvā maṃsarasena parivisitvā bhuttāviñca naṃ saputtadāro vanditvā “idheva, bhante, vasatha, ahaṃ paccayena upaṭṭhahissāmī”ti nimantetvā, vasanokāsaṃ katvā adāsi. So tattha vasati.

213. What is the origin of the verse 'Sabbābhibhū'? The Great Man, having made the great renunciation and gradually attained omniscience, was on his way to Bārāṇasī to set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma when he met the Ājīvaka Upaka between the site of enlightenment and Gayā. When questioned by him in the manner of, 'Friend, your faculties are serene...' and so on (Majjhima Nikāya 1.285; Mahāvagga 11), he replied with the words 'Sabbābhibhū' and others. Upaka said, 'It may be so, friend,' shook his head, took a side path, and departed. In due course, he reached a certain hunter's village in the Vaṅga country. Seeing him, the chief hunter thought, 'Oh, this ascetic has few wishes; he does not even wear a lower garment. He must be an arahant in this world!' He led him to his home, served him with meat broth, and after he had eaten, he, along with his wife and children, paid homage to him. He then invited him, saying, 'Venerable sir, please stay right here. I will support you with the requisites.' Having prepared a dwelling place, he gave it to him. So he dwelt there.

Māgaviko gimhakāle udakasampanne sītale padese carituṃ dūraṃ apakkantesu migesu tattha gacchanto “amhākaṃ arahantaṃ sakkaccaṃ upaṭṭhahassū”ti chāvaṃ nāma dhītaraṃ āṇāpetvā agamāsi saddhiṃ puttabhātukehi. Sā cassa dhītā dassanīyā hoti koṭṭhāsasampannā. Dutiyadivase upako gharaṃ āgato taṃ dārikaṃ sabbaṃ upacāraṃ katvā, parivisituṃ upagataṃ disvā, rāgena abhibhūto bhuñjitumpi asakkonto bhājanena bhattaṃ ādāya vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā, bhattaṃ ekamante nikkhipitvā – “sace chāvaṃ labhāmi, jīvāmi, no ce, marāmī”ti nirāhāro sayi. Sattame divase māgaviko āgantvā dhītaraṃ upakassa pavattiṃ pucchi. Sā – “ekadivasameva āgantvā puna nāgatapubbo”ti āha. Māgaviko “āgataveseneva naṃ upasaṅkamitvā pucchissāmī”ti taṅkhaṇaññeva gantvā – “kiṃ, bhante, aphāsuka”nti pāde parāmasanto pucchi. Upako nitthunanto parivattatiyeva. So “vada, bhante, yaṃ mayā sakkā kātuṃ, sabbaṃ karissāmī”ti āha. Upako – “sace chāvaṃ labhāmi, jīvāmi, no ce, idheva maraṇaṃ seyyo”ti āha. “Jānāsi pana, bhante, kiñci sippa”nti? “Na jānāmī”ti[V 1.0218]. “Na, bhante, kiñci sippaṃ ajānantena sakkā gharāvāsaṃ adhiṭṭhātu”nti? So āha – “nāhaṃ kiñci sippaṃ jānāmi, apica tumhākaṃ maṃsahārako bhavissāmi, maṃsañca vikkiṇissāmī”ti. Māgavikopi “amhākaṃ etadeva ruccatī”ti uttarasāṭakaṃ [P 1.0260] datvā, gharaṃ ānetvā dhītaraṃ adāsi. Tesaṃ saṃvāsamanvāya putto [M 1.0249] vijāyi. Subhaddotissa nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Chāvā puttatosanagītena upakaṃ uppaṇḍesi. So taṃ asahanto “bhadde, ahaṃ anantajinassa santikaṃ gacchāmī”ti majjhimadesābhimukho pakkāmi.

During the hot season, as the hunter was going to a distant, cool place abundant with water where the deer had gone to roam, he instructed his daughter named Chāvā, saying, 'Attend respectfully to our Arahant,' and departed with his sons and younger brothers. And that daughter of his was lovely to see and well-proportioned. On the second day, when Upaka came to the house, he saw the girl, who had performed all the services and had approached to serve him, and was overcome by lust. Unable even to eat, he took his bowl of food, went to his dwelling place, set the food aside, and lay down without eating, thinking, 'If I obtain Chāvā, I will live; if not, I will die.' On the seventh day, the hunter returned and asked his daughter about Upaka's condition. She replied, 'He came only on one day and has not come again.' The hunter thought, 'I will approach and question him, pretending to have just arrived.' He went at that very moment and, stroking Upaka’s feet, asked, 'Venerable sir, are you unwell?' Upaka, groaning, just kept turning over. The hunter said, 'Speak, venerable sir. Whatever I can do, I will do it all.' Upaka replied, 'If I obtain Chāvā, I will live; otherwise, death right here would be better.' 'But, venerable sir, do you know any craft?' 'I do not know any.' 'Venerable sir, can one who knows no craft maintain a household life?' He replied, 'I do not know any craft, but I will be your meat-carrier and I will sell meat.' The hunter, saying, 'This is agreeable to us,' gave him an upper garment, brought him home, and gave him his daughter. As a result of their living together, a son was born. They gave him the name Subhadda. Chāvā taunted Upaka with a song for delighting her son. Unable to bear it, he said, 'Good lady, I am going to the presence of the Anantajina,' and set out toward the Middle Country.

Bhagavā ca tena samayena sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavanamahāvihāre. Atha kho bhagavā paṭikacceva bhikkhū āṇāpesi – “yo, bhikkhave, anantajinoti pucchamāno āgacchati, tassa maṃ dasseyyāthā”ti. Upakopi kho anupubbeneva sāvatthiṃ āgantvā vihāramajjhe ṭhatvā “imasmiṃ vihāre mama sahāyo anantajino nāma atthi, so kuhiṃ vasatī”ti pucchi. Taṃ bhikkhū bhagavato santikaṃ nayiṃsu. Bhagavā tassānurūpaṃ dhammaṃ desesi. So desanāpariyosāne anāgāmiphale patiṭṭhāsi. Bhikkhū tassa pubbappavattiṃ sutvā kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “bhagavā paṭhamaṃ nissirikassa naggasamaṇassa dhammaṃ desesī”ti. Bhagavā taṃ kathāsamuṭṭhānaṃ viditvā gandhakuṭito nikkhamma taṅkhaṇānurūpena pāṭihāriyena buddhāsane nisīditvā bhikkhū āmantesi – “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti? Te sabbaṃ kathesuṃ. Tato bhagavā – “na, bhikkhave, tathāgato ahetuappaccayā dhammaṃ deseti, nimmalā tathāgatassa dhammadesanā, na sakkā tattha dosaṃ daṭṭhuṃ. Tena, bhikkhave, dhammadesanūpanissayena upako etarahi anāgāmī jāto”ti vatvā attano desanāmalābhāvadīpikaṃ imaṃ gāthamabhāsi.

And at that time, the Blessed One was dwelling in Sāvatthī at the great monastery in Jeta's Grove. Then the Blessed One instructed the monks in advance: 'Monks, if someone comes asking for the Anantajina, you should show him to me.' Upaka, too, gradually arrived in Sāvatthī and, standing in the middle of the monastery, asked, 'In this monastery is my friend named Anantajina; where does he dwell?' The monks led him to the presence of the Blessed One. The Blessed One taught him the Dhamma in a way suitable for him. At the end of the discourse, he was established in the fruit of non-returning. The monks, having heard his previous story, raised a topic of conversation: 'The Blessed One first taught the Dhamma to a luckless, naked ascetic.' The Blessed One, knowing that this topic of conversation had arisen, came out of the Perfumed Chamber and, with a miracle suitable for the occasion, sat down on the Buddha-seat and addressed the monks: 'Monks, for what topic of conversation are you now assembled?' They told him everything. Then the Blessed One said: 'Monks, the Tathāgata does not teach the Dhamma without cause, without condition. The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma is stainless; no fault can be seen in it. Monks, with that teaching of the Dhamma as a strong supporting condition, Upaka has now become a non-returner.' Having said this, to illuminate the stainless nature of his teaching, he spoke this verse.

Tassattho – sāsavesu sabbakhandhāyatanadhātūsu chandarāgappahānena tehi anabhibhūtattā sayañca te dhamme sabbe abhibhuyya pavattattā sabbābhibhuṃ. Tesañca aññesañca sabbadhammānaṃ sabbākārena viditattā sabbaviduṃ. Sabbadhammadesanasamatthāya sobhanāya medhāya samannāgatattā sumedhaṃ. Yesaṃ taṇhādiṭṭhilepānaṃ [P 1.0261] vasena sāsavakhandhādibhedesu sabbadhammesu upalimpati, tesaṃ lepānaṃ abhāvā tesu sabbesu dhammesu anupalittaṃ. Tesu ca sabbadhammesu chandarāgābhāvena sabbe te dhamme jahitvā ṭhitattā sabbañjahaṃ. Upadhivivekaninnena cittena taṇhakkhaye nibbāne visesena muttattā taṇhakkhaye vimuttaṃ, adhimuttanti vuttaṃ hoti. Taṃ vāpi dhīrā muni vedayantīti tampi paṇḍitā sattā muniṃ vedayanti jānanti. Passatha yāva paṭivisiṭṭhovāyaṃ muni, tassa kuto desanāmalanti attānaṃ vibhāveti[M 1.0250]. Vibhāvanattho hi ettha vāsaddoti. Keci pana vaṇṇayanti – “upako tadā tathāgataṃ disvāpi ‘ayaṃ buddhamunī’ti na saddahī”ti evaṃ bhikkhū kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ[V 1.0219], tato bhagavā “saddahatu vā mā vā, dhīrā pana taṃ muniṃ vedayantī”ti dassento imaṃ gāthamabhāsīti.

The meaning of this is as follows: Because he has abandoned desire and lust for all aggregates, sense bases, and elements that are subject to the taints, is not overcome by them, and has himself overcome and prevailed over all those phenomena, he is the All-Overcomer. Because he has known in every aspect all phenomena, both these and others, he is the All-Knower. Because he is endowed with a beautiful wisdom capable of teaching all phenomena, he is one of Good Wisdom. Because of the absence of those defilements of craving and wrong view, by the power of which one is stained in all phenomena classified as tainted aggregates and so on, he is unstained by all those phenomena. And because, through the absence of desire and lust for all those phenomena, he abides having abandoned them all, he is the All-Abandoner. With a mind inclined toward seclusion from the substrates of existence, and being especially liberated in Nibbāna, the destruction of craving, he is 'liberated in the destruction of craving'; it is said he is 'intent upon it'. 'The wise, too, know him as a sage' means that wise beings know and understand him as a sage. 'Behold how distinguished this sage is! Whence could there be any stain in his teaching?'—thus he reveals himself. For here, the word 'vā' has the meaning of clarification. Some, however, explain it thus: The monks raised a discussion, saying, 'At that time, even though Upaka saw the Tathāgata, he did not have faith that "This is the Buddha, the sage."' Then the Blessed One, to show that 'Whether he has faith or not, the wise still know him as a sage,' spoke this verse.

214. Paññābalanti kā uppatti? Ayaṃ gāthā revatattheraṃ ārabbha vuttā. Tattha “gāme vā yadi vāraññe”ti imissā gāthāya vuttanayeneva revatattherassa ādito pabhuti pabbajjā, pabbajitassa khadiravane vihāro, tattha viharato visesādhigamo, bhagavato tattha gamanapaccāgamanañca veditabbaṃ. Paccāgate pana bhagavati yo so mahallakabhikkhu upāhanaṃ sammussitvā paṭinivatto khadirarukkhe ālaggitaṃ disvā sāvatthiṃ anuppatto visākhāya upāsikāya “kiṃ, bhante, revatattherassa vasanokāso ramaṇīyo”ti bhikkhū pucchamānāya yehi bhikkhūhi pasaṃsito, te apasādento “upāsike, ete tucchaṃ bhaṇanti, na sundaro bhūmippadeso, atilūkhakakkhaḷaṃ khadiravanamevā”ti āha. So visākhāya āgantukabhattaṃ bhuñjitvā pacchābhattaṃ maṇḍalamāḷe sannipatite bhikkhū ujjhāpento āha – “kiṃ, āvuso, revatattherassa senāsane ramaṇīyaṃ tumhehi diṭṭha”nti[P 1.0262]. Bhagavā taṃ ñatvā gandhakuṭito nikkhamma taṅkhaṇānurūpena pāṭihāriyena parisamajjhaṃ patvā, buddhāsane nisīditvā bhikkhū āmantesi – “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti? Te āhaṃsu – “revataṃ, bhante, ārabbha kathā uppannā ‘evaṃ navakammiko kadā samaṇadhammaṃ karissatī’”ti. “Na, bhikkhave, revato navakammiko, arahā revato khīṇāsavo”ti vatvā taṃ ārabbha tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ dhammadesanatthaṃ imaṃ gāthamabhāsi.

214. What is the origin of the verse beginning 'With the power of wisdom'? This verse was spoken concerning the Elder Revata. In this connection, the story of the Elder Revata—from his going forth at the beginning, his dwelling in the acacia forest after going forth, his attainment of distinction while dwelling there, and the Blessed One's journey there and back—should be understood in the same way as it was told in connection with the verse, 'Whether in the village or in the forest.' Now, when the Blessed One had returned, a certain elderly monk, who had forgotten his sandals and turned back, saw them caught on an acacia tree. Upon arriving in Sāvatthī, when the female lay disciple Visākhā was asking the monks, 'Venerable sirs, is the Elder Revata's dwelling place delightful?', he disparaged those monks who had praised it, saying, 'Laywoman, they speak empty words. The plot of land is not beautiful; it is just an extremely rough and harsh acacia forest.' Having eaten the meal for newcomers offered by Visākhā, he, after the meal, criticized the monks gathered in the assembly hall, saying: 'Friends, what did you see that was delightful in the Elder Revata's lodging?' The Blessed One, knowing this, came out from the Fragrant Chamber and, by a miracle appropriate for the occasion, arrived in the midst of the assembly. Seating himself on the Buddha-seat, he addressed the monks: 'Monks, for the sake of what discussion are you now gathered together?' They replied: 'Venerable Sir, a discussion has arisen concerning Revata: "Being so engaged in new work, when will he practice the ascetic's duties?"' The Blessed One said: 'Monks, Revata is not one engaged in new work; Revata is an Arahant, one whose taints are destroyed.' Having said this, he spoke this verse concerning him for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma to those monks.

Tassattho – dubbalakarakilesappahānasādhakena vikubbanaadhiṭṭhānappabhedena vā paññābalena samannāgatattā paññābalaṃ, catupārisuddhisīlena dhutaṅgavatena ca upapannattā sīlavatūpapannaṃ, maggasamādhinā phalasamādhinā iriyāpathasamādhinā ca samāhitaṃ, upacārappanābhedena jhānena jhāne vā ratattā jhānarataṃ, sativepullappattattā satimaṃ, rāgādisaṅgato pamuttatā saṅgā pamuttaṃ, pañcacetokhilacatuāsavābhāvena akhilaṃ anāsavaṃ taṃ vāpi dhīrā muniṃ vedayanti. Tampi evaṃ paññādiguṇasaṃyuttaṃ saṅgādidosavisaṃyuttaṃ paṇḍitā sattā muniṃ vā vedayanti. Passatha yāva paṭivisiṭṭhovāyaṃ [M 1.0251] khīṇāsavamuni, so “navakammiko”ti vā “kadā samaṇadhammaṃ karissatī”ti vā kathaṃ vattabbo. So hi paññābalena taṃ vihāraṃ niṭṭhāpesi, na navakammakaraṇena, katakiccova so, na idāni samaṇadhammaṃ karissatīti revatattheraṃ vibhāveti. Vibhāvanattho hi ettha vā-saddoti.

The meaning of this is as follows: He is 'one with the power of wisdom' because he is endowed with the power of wisdom that accomplishes the abandoning of defilements that cause weakness, or which has the varieties of transformation-power and determination-power. He is 'endowed with virtue' because he possesses the fourfold purity of virtue and the ascetic observances. He is 'composed' through path-concentration, fruition-concentration, and posture-concentration. He is 'delighting in jhāna' because he delights in jhāna, which is distinguished as access and absorption. He is 'mindful' because he has attained fullness of mindfulness. He is 'liberated from association' because he is freed from the association of lust and other defilements. He is 'without wilderness' and 'taintless' because he is devoid of the five mental wildernesses and the four taints. 'The wise, too, know him as a sage.' Wise beings know him, who is thus endowed with qualities such as wisdom and free from faults such as attachment, as a sage. Behold how distinguished this taint-destroyed sage is! How could he be called 'one engaged in new work' or be asked, 'When will he practice the ascetic's duties?' For he completed that monastery by the power of wisdom, not by performing construction work. He is one whose task is done; it is not that he has yet to practice the ascetic's duties. Thus he makes the Elder Revata plain. For the word 'vā' here has the meaning of clarification.

215. Ekaṃ carantanti kā uppatti? Bodhimaṇḍato pabhuti yathākkamaṃ kapilavatthuṃ anuppatte [V 1.0220] bhagavati pitāputtasamāgame vattamāne bhagavā sammodamānena raññā suddhodanena “tumhe, bhante, gahaṭṭhakāle gandhakaraṇḍake vāsitāni kāsikādīni dussāni nivāsetvā idāni kathaṃ chinnakāni paṃsukūlāni dhārethā”ti evamādinā vutto rājānaṃ anunayamāno –

215. What is the origin of the verse beginning 'Wandering alone'? When the Blessed One, having journeyed from the seat of enlightenment, arrived in due course at Kapilavatthu, and while the meeting between father and son was taking place, the rejoicing King Suddhodana spoke to the Blessed One. Having been addressed by him thus: 'Venerable Sir, in your time as a householder, you wore fine cloths from Kāsi and other regions, perfumed in scent-caskets. How is it that you now wear cut-up rag-robes?', the Blessed One, conciliating the king—

“Yaṃ [P 1.0263] tvaṃ tāta vade mayhaṃ, paṭṭuṇṇaṃ dukūlakāsikaṃ;

Paṃsukūlaṃ tato seyyaṃ, etaṃ me abhipatthita”nti. –

‘That which you, dear father, speak of to me—fine woven cloth, linen, and silks of Kāsi—a rag-robe is superior to that; this is what I have longed for.’

Ādīni vatvā lokadhammehi attano avikampabhāvaṃ dassento rañño dhammadesanatthaṃ imaṃ sattapadagāthamabhāsi.

Having spoken these and other words, and showing his own unshaken nature in the face of worldly conditions, he uttered this seven-line verse for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma to the king.

Tassattho – pabbajjāsaṅkhātādīhi ekaṃ, iriyāpathādīhi cariyāhi carantaṃ. Moneyyadhammasamannāgamena muniṃ. Sabbaṭṭhānesu pamādābhāvato appamattaṃ. Akkosanagarahanādibhedāya nindāya vaṇṇanathomanādibhedāya pasaṃsāya cāti imāsu nindāpasaṃsāsu paṭighānunayavasena avedhamānaṃ. Nindāpasaṃsāmukhena cettha aṭṭhapi lokadhammā vuttāti veditabbā. Sīhaṃva bherisaddādīsu saddesu aṭṭhasu lokadhammesu pakativikārānupagamena asantasantaṃ, pantesu vā senāsanesu santāsābhāvena. Vātaṃva suttamayādibhede jālamhi catūhi maggehi taṇhādiṭṭhijāle asajjamānaṃ, aṭṭhasu vā lokadhammesu paṭighānunayavasena asajjamānaṃ. Padumaṃva toyena loke jātampi yesaṃ taṇhādiṭṭhilepānaṃ vasena sattā lokena lippanti, tesaṃ lepānaṃ pahīnattā lokena alippamānaṃ, nibbānagāmimaggaṃ uppādetvā tena maggena netāramaññesaṃ devamanussānaṃ. Attano pana aññena kenaci maggaṃ dassetvā anetabbattā anaññaneyyaṃ taṃ vāpi dhīrā muni vedayanti buddhamuniṃ vedayantīti attānaṃ vibhāveti. Sesamettha vuttanayameva.

Its meaning is this: 'alone' refers to one who is alone by way of renunciation and so on, and 'wandering' refers to conduct by way of the postures and so on. He is a sage through the possession of the qualities of sagacity. He is heedful due to the absence of negligence in all situations. He is unshaken by blame and praise, not moved by aversion or approval in the face of criticism—such as abuse and reproach—or praise—such as commendation and acclaim. Here, it should be understood that the eight worldly conditions are also spoken of through the medium of blame and praise. Like a lion unperturbed by sounds such as the beating of a drum, so too is he untrembling amidst the eight worldly conditions, not undergoing any unnatural alteration; or, this is due to his absence of fear in remote lodgings. Like the wind in a net made of thread and so on, he is not caught in the net of craving and views, not clinging to it by means of the four paths; or, not clinging to the eight worldly conditions by way of aversion or approval. Like a lotus, though born in the world, he is unstained by the world; for although beings are stained by the world through the defilements of craving and views, he is unstained by the world because those defilements have been abandoned. He is one who generates the path leading to Nibbāna and guides others—gods and humans—along that path. But as for himself, being unleadable, not needing to be shown the path by anyone else, the wise know that sage as the Buddha-sage. Thus he reveals himself. The rest here is as has been explained.

216. Yo [M 1.0252] ogahaṇeti kā uppatti? Bhagavato paṭhamābhisambuddhassa cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni kappasatasahassañca pūritadasapāramidasaupapāramidasaparamatthapāramippabhedaṃ [P 1.0264] abhinīhāraguṇapāramiyo pūretvā tusitabhavane abhinibbattiguṇaṃ tattha nivāsaguṇaṃ mahāvilokanaguṇaṃ gabbhavokkantiṃ gabbhavāsaṃ gabbhanikkhamanaṃ padavītihāraṃ disāvilokanaṃ brahmagajjanaṃ mahābhinikkhamanaṃ mahāpadhānaṃ abhisambodhiṃ dhammacakkappavattanaṃ catubbidhaṃ maggañāṇaṃ phalañāṇaṃ aṭṭhasu parisāsu akampanañāṇaṃ, dasabalañāṇaṃ, catuyoniparicchedakañāṇaṃ, pañcagatiparicchedakañāṇaṃ, chabbidhaṃ asādhāraṇañāṇaṃ, aṭṭhavidhaṃ sāvakasādhāraṇabuddhañāṇaṃ, cuddasavidhaṃ buddhañāṇaṃ, aṭṭhārasabuddhaguṇaparicchedakañāṇaṃ, ekūnavīsatividhapaccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ, sattasattatividhañāṇavatthu [V 1.0221] evamiccādiguṇasatasahasse nissāya pavattaṃ mahālābhasakkāraṃ asahamānehi titthiyehi uyyojitāya ciñcamāṇavikāya “ekaṃ dhammaṃ atītassā”ti imissā gāthāya vatthumhi vuttanayena catuparisamajjhe bhagavato ayase uppādite tappaccayā bhikkhū kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “evarūpepi nāma ayase uppanne na bhagavato cittassa aññathattaṃ atthī”ti. Taṃ ñatvā bhagavā gandhakuṭito nikkhamma taṅkhaṇānurūpena pāṭihāriyena parisamajjhaṃ patvā, buddhāsane nisīditvā, bhikkhū āmantesi – “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti? Te sabbaṃ ārocesuṃ. Tato bhagavā – “buddhā nāma, bhikkhave, aṭṭhasu lokadhammesu tādino hontī”ti vatvā tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ dhammadesanatthaṃ imaṃ gāthamabhāsi.

216. What is the origin of the verse beginning 'Yo ogahaṇe'? The Blessed One first attained full enlightenment after fulfilling the perfections—the ten perfections, the ten higher perfections, and the ten ultimate perfections—along with the quality of the great aspiration, for four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons. Relying on these and hundreds of thousands of other qualities—such as the quality of his rebirth in the Tusita heaven, the quality of his dwelling there, the quality of the great survey, the descent into the womb, the abiding in the womb, the emergence from the womb, the seven steps, the surveying of the directions, the bull-like roar, the great renunciation, the great striving, the supreme enlightenment, the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, the fourfold knowledge of the path, the knowledge of the fruits, the unshaken knowledge in the eight assemblies, the ten powers, the knowledge that defines the four types of birth, the knowledge that defines the five destinations, the six kinds of unique knowledge, the eight kinds of Buddha-knowledge shared with disciples, the fourteen kinds of Buddha-knowledge, the knowledge that defines the eighteen qualities of a Buddha, the nineteen kinds of reflective knowledge, and the seventy-seven bases of knowledge—great gain and honor arose for him. Unable to bear this, the sectarians incited the woman Ciñcamāṇavikā. When dishonor was brought upon the Blessed One in the midst of the fourfold assembly, in the manner described in the backstory to the verse beginning, 'Ekaṃ dhammaṃ atītassa,' the monks began a discussion on account of it: 'Even when such dishonor has arisen, there is no alteration in the Blessed One’s mind.' Knowing this, the Blessed One emerged from his perfumed chamber and, by a miracle suitable for the occasion, went to the midst of the assembly. Seated on the Buddha's seat, he addressed the monks: 'Monks, for what discussion are you now assembled?' They told him everything. Then the Blessed One said, 'Monks, Buddhas are imperturbable amidst the eight worldly conditions,' and in order to teach the Dhamma to those monks, he spoke this verse.

Tassattho [P 1.0265] – yathā nāma ogahaṇe manussānaṃ nhānatitthe aṅgaghaṃsanatthāya caturasse vā aṭṭhaṃse vā thambhe nikhāte uccakulīnāpi nīcakulīnāpi aṅgaṃ ghaṃsanti, na tena thambhassa unnati vā onati vā hoti. Evamevaṃ yo ogahaṇe thambhorivābhijāyati yasmiṃ pare vācāpariyantaṃ vadanti. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ pare titthiyā vā aññe vā vaṇṇavasena uparimaṃ vā avaṇṇavasena heṭṭhimaṃ vā vācāpariyantaṃ vadanti, tasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ anunayaṃ vā paṭighaṃ vā anāpajjamāno tādibhāvena yo ogahaṇe thambhoriva bhavatīti. Taṃ vītarāgaṃ susamāhitindriyanti taṃ iṭṭhārammaṇe rāgābhāvena vītarāgaṃ, aniṭṭhārammaṇe ca dosamohābhāvena susamāhitindriyaṃ, suṭṭhu vā samodhānetvā ṭhapitindriyaṃ, rakkhitindriyaṃ, gopitindriyanti [M 1.0253] vuttaṃ hoti. Taṃ vāpi dhīrā muni vedayanti buddhamuniṃ vedayanti, tassa kathaṃ cittassa aññathattaṃ bhavissatīti attānaṃ vibhāveti. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

The meaning is this: Just as at a bathing place, a ford for bathing, people of high or low birth rub their limbs against a four-sided or eight-sided post fixed there for scrubbing, yet the post does not rise up or sink down because of this. In the same way, one stands firm like a post at a bathing place, against whom others speak a torrent of words. What is meant by this? On whatever matter others—sectarians or anyone else—speak a torrent of words, whether praise from above by way of commendation or blame from below by way of condemnation, on that matter one who does not give rise to approval or aversion remains like a post at a bathing place through their imperturbability. 'Him, free from lust, with well-composed faculties' means: he is free from lust through the absence of lust for desirable objects, and with well-composed faculties through the absence of aversion and delusion towards undesirable objects. Or, it means his faculties are well-composed, well-established, guarded, and protected. The wise know such a one as a sage, as the Buddha-sage. 'How could there be any alteration in his mind?'—thus he reveals himself. The remainder is as has been explained.

217. Yo ve ṭhitattoti kā uppatti? Sāvatthiyaṃ kira aññatarā seṭṭhidhītā pāsādā oruyha heṭṭhāpāsāde tantavāyasālaṃ gantvā tasaraṃ vaṭṭente disvā tassa ujubhāvena tappaṭibhāganimittaṃ aggahesi – “aho vata sabbe sattā kāyavacīmanovaṅkaṃ pahāya tasaraṃ viya ujucittā bhaveyyu”nti. Sā pāsādaṃ abhiruhitvāpi punappunaṃ tadeva nimittaṃ āvajjentī nisīdi. Evaṃ paṭipannāya cassā na cirasseva aniccalakkhaṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ ahosi, tadanusāreneva ca dukkhānattalakkhaṇānipi. Athassā tayopi bhavā ādittā viya upaṭṭhahiṃsu. Taṃ tathā vipassamānaṃ ñatvā bhagavā gandhakuṭiyaṃ nisinnova obhāsaṃ muñci. Sā taṃ disvā “kiṃ ida”nti āvajjentī bhagavantaṃ passe nisinnamiva [P 1.0266] disvā uṭṭhāya pañjalikā aṭṭhāsi. Athassā bhagavā sappāyaṃ viditvā dhammadesanāvasena imaṃ gāthamabhāsi.

217. What is the origin of 'Yo ve ṭhitatto'? In Sāvatthī, it is said that a certain merchant's daughter, descending from her mansion, went to the weaver's workshop below. Seeing a shuttle being moved, she grasped a corresponding sign through its straightness, thinking: 'Oh, if only all beings could abandon crookedness in body, speech, and mind and become straight-minded like this shuttle!' Even after ascending to the mansion, she repeatedly reflected on that very sign and sat down. Practicing thus, before long the characteristic of impermanence became clear to her, and in accordance with that, the characteristics of suffering and non-self also became evident. Then, all three existences appeared to her as if on fire. Knowing she was contemplating thus with insight, the Blessed One, while seated in his fragrant hut, emitted a radiance. Seeing it, and reflecting 'What is this?', she perceived the Blessed One as if seated nearby. Rising, she stood with hands clasped in reverence. Then the Blessed One, knowing what was suitable for her, spoke this verse by way of a teaching.

Tassattho [V 1.0222] – yo ve ekaggacittatāya akuppavimuttitāya ca vuḍḍhihānīnaṃ abhāvato vikkhīṇajātisaṃsārattā bhavantarūpagamanābhāvato ca ṭhitatto, pahīnakāyavacīmanovaṅkatāya agatigamanābhāvena vā tasaraṃva uju, hirottappasampannattā jigucchati kammehi pāpakehi, pāpakāni kammāni gūthagataṃ viya muttagataṃ viya ca jigucchati, hirīyatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Yogavibhāgena hi upayogatthe karaṇavacanaṃ saddasatthe sijjhati. Vīmaṃsamāno visamaṃ samañcāti kāyavisamādivisamaṃ kāyasamādisamañca pahānabhāvanākiccasādhanena maggapaññāya vīmaṃsamāno upaparikkhamāno. Taṃ vāpi khīṇāsavaṃ dhīrā muniṃ vedayantīti. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yathāvuttanayena maggapaññāya vīmaṃsamāno visamaṃ samañca yo ve ṭhitatto hoti, so evaṃ tasaraṃva uju hutvā kiñci vītikkamaṃ anāpajjanto jigucchati kammehi pāpakehi. Taṃ vāpi dhīrā muniṃ vedayanti. Yato īdiso hotīti khīṇāsavamuniṃ dassento arahattanikūṭena gāthaṃ desesi. Desanāpariyosāne seṭṭhidhītā sotāpattiphale [M 1.0254] patiṭṭhahi. Ettha ca vikappe vā samuccaye vā vāsaddo daṭṭhabbo.

Its meaning is this: one who, through one-pointedness of mind and unshakable liberation, due to the absence of growth and decline, whose cycle of rebirth is exhausted, and who does not go to another existence, is steadfast; or, due to the abandonment of bodily, verbal, and mental crookedness and the absence of going to wrong destinations, is straight as a shuttle. Endowed with moral shame and fear of wrongdoing, he loathes evil deeds; he loathes evil actions as if they were excrement or urine, and it is said he is ashamed. Indeed, by analysis of usage, the instrumental case is established in grammar in the sense of application. 'Examining the uneven and the even' means examining and scrutinizing the unevenness of body, etc., and the evenness of body, etc., by accomplishing the task of abandoning and developing through the wisdom of the path. The wise know even such a one, whose cankers are destroyed, as a sage. What is meant by this? As described, one who examines the uneven and the even with the wisdom of the path, who is indeed steadfast, being straight as a shuttle and not falling into any transgression, loathes evil deeds. The wise also know him as a sage. Because he is such, showing the sage whose cankers are destroyed, he taught the verse with the pinnacle of Arahantship. At the end of the teaching, the merchant’s daughter became established in the fruit of stream-entry. Here, the word 'vā' should be understood in the sense of alternation or combination.

218. Yo saññatattoti kā uppatti? Bhagavati kira āḷaviyaṃ viharante āḷavīnagare aññataro tantavāyo sattavassikaṃ dhītaraṃ āṇāpesi – “amma, hiyyo avasiṭṭhatasaraṃ na bahu, tasaraṃ vaṭṭetvā lahuṃ tantavāyasālaṃ āgaccheyyāsi, mā kho cirāyī”ti. Sā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchi. So sālaṃ gantvā tantaṃ vinento aṭṭhāsi. Taṃ divasañca bhagavā mahākaruṇāsamāpattito vuṭṭhāya lokaṃ volokento tassā dārikāya sotāpattiphalūpanissayaṃ desanāpariyosāne [P 1.0267] caturāsītiyā pāṇasahassānañca dhammābhisamayaṃ disvā pageva sarīrapaṭijagganaṃ katvā pattacīvaramādāya nagaraṃ pāvisi. Manussā bhagavantaṃ disvā – “addhā ajja koci anuggahetabbo atthi, pageva paviṭṭho bhagavā”ti bhagavantaṃ upagacchiṃsu. Bhagavā yena maggena sā dārikā pitusantikaṃ gacchati, tasmiṃ aṭṭhāsi. Nagaravāsino taṃ padesaṃ sammajjitvā, paripphositvā, pupphūpahāraṃ katvā, vitānaṃ bandhitvā, āsanaṃ paññāpesuṃ. Nisīdi bhagavā paññatte āsane, mahājanakāyo parivāretvā aṭṭhāsi. Sā dārikā taṃ padesaṃ pattā mahājanaparivutaṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā pañcapatiṭṭhitena vandi. Taṃ bhagavā āmantetvā – “dārike kuto āgatāsī”ti pucchi. “Na jānāmi bhagavā”ti. “Kuhiṃ gamissasī”ti? “Na jānāmi bhagavā”ti. “Na jānāsī”ti? “Jānāmi bhagavā”ti. “Jānāsī”ti? “Na jānāmi bhagavā”ti.

218. What is the origin of 'Yo saññatatto'? It is said that while the Blessed One was residing in Āḷavī, in the city of Āḷavī, a certain weaver instructed his seven-year-old daughter: 'Dear, the remaining thread from yesterday is not much; after spinning the thread, come quickly to the weaving shed; do not delay.'
