She agreed, saying, 'Very well.' He went to the shed and stood there weaving. That same day, the Blessed One arose from the attainment of great compassion and surveyed the world. Seeing that the girl had the potential to attain the fruit of stream-entry and that at the end of the teaching eighty-four thousand beings would gain understanding of the Dhamma, he attended to his bodily needs early and, taking his bowl and robe, entered the city. People, upon seeing the Blessed One, approached him, thinking, 'Surely today there is someone to be helped, since the Blessed One has entered so early.' The Blessed One stood on the path by which the girl was going to her father. The city dwellers swept that spot, sprinkled it with water, made flower offerings, hung up a canopy, and prepared a seat. The Blessed One sat on the prepared seat, and a great crowd gathered around and stood there. The girl, arriving at that place, saw the Blessed One surrounded by the large crowd and paid homage with the fivefold prostration. The Blessed One addressed her and asked, 'Girl, where have you come from?' 'I do not know, Blessed One.' 'Where will you go?' 'I do not know, Blessed One.' 'You do not know?' 'I know, Blessed One.' 'You know?' 'I do not know, Blessed One.'

Taṃ sutvā manussā ujjhāyanti – “passatha, bho, ayaṃ dārikā attano gharā āgatāpi bhagavatā [V 1.0223] pucchiyamānā ‘na jānāmī’ti āha, tantavāyasālaṃ gacchantī cāpi pucchiyamānā ‘na jānāmī’ti āha, ‘na jānāsī’ti vuttā ‘jānāmī’ti āha, ‘jānāsī’ti vuttā ‘na jānāmī’ti āha, sabbaṃ paccanīkameva karotī”ti. Bhagavā manussānaṃ tamatthaṃ pākaṭaṃ kātukāmo taṃ pucchi – “kiṃ mayā pucchitaṃ, kiṃ tayā vutta”nti? Sā āha – “na maṃ, bhante, koci na jānāti, gharato āgatā tantavāyasālaṃ gacchatī”ti; apica maṃ tumhe paṭisandhivasena pucchatha, “kuto āgatāsī”ti, cutivasena pucchatha, “kuhiṃ gamissasī”ti ahañca na jānāmi. “Kuto camhi āgatā; nirayā vā devalokā vā”ti, na hi jānāmi, “kuhimpi gamissāmi nirayaṃ vā devalokaṃ vā”ti, tasmā “na jānāmī”ti [M 1.0255] avacaṃ. Tato maṃ bhagavā maraṇaṃ sandhāya pucchi – “na [P 1.0268] jānāsī”ti, ahañca jānāmi. “Sabbesaṃ maraṇaṃ dhuva”nti, tenāvocaṃ “jānāmī”ti. Tato maṃ bhagavā maraṇakālaṃ sandhāya pucchi “jānāsī”ti, ahañca na jānāmi “kadā marissāmi kiṃ ajja vā udāhu sve vā”ti, tenāvocaṃ “na jānāmī”ti. Bhagavā tāya vissajjitaṃ pañhaṃ “sādhu sādhū”ti anumodi. Mahājanakāyopi “yāva paṇḍitā ayaṃ dārikā”ti sādhukārasahassāni adāsi. Atha bhagavā dārikāya sappāyaṃ viditvā dhammaṃ desento –

Hearing this, the people grumbled: “Look, friends, this girl, even though she came from her own house and was questioned by the Blessed One, said, ‘I do not know.’ Even when she was going to the weaver’s shed and was questioned, she said, ‘I do not know.’ When told, ‘You do not know,’ she said, ‘I know.’ When told, ‘You know,’ she said, ‘I do not know.’ She does everything contrary!” The Blessed One, wishing to make the matter clear to the people, asked her: “What did I ask, and what did you say?” She replied: “Venerable sir, everyone knows that I have come from my house and am going to the weaver’s shed. But you asked me about rebirth, ‘Where have you come from?’ and about decease, ‘Where will you go?’ And I do not know. ‘Where have I come from—from hell or the heavenly realm?’ I truly do not know. ‘Where will I go—to hell or the heavenly realm?’ Therefore, I said, ‘I do not know.’ Then the Blessed One asked me regarding death, ‘Do you not know?’ And I do know. ‘Death is certain for all.’ Therefore, I said, ‘I know.’ Then the Blessed One asked me regarding the time of death, ‘Do you know?’ And I do not know, ‘When will I die—today or tomorrow?’ Therefore, I said, ‘I do not know.’” The Blessed One approved of the answer she gave to the question, saying, “Good, good!” The great crowd also exclaimed, “How wise this girl is!” and gave thousands of cheers. Then the Blessed One, knowing what was suitable for the girl, taught the Dhamma, saying:

“Andhabhūto ayaṃ loko, tanukettha vipassati;

Sakuṇo jālamuttova, appo saggāya gacchatī”ti. (dha. pa. 174) –

“This world is blind; few here have insight. Like a bird escaped from the net, few go to heaven.”

Imaṃ gāthamāha. Sā gāthāpariyosāne sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāsi, caturāsītiyā pāṇasahassānañca dhammābhisamayo ahosi.

He spoke this verse. At the end of the verse, she was established in the fruit of stream-entry, and a realization of the Dhamma arose in eighty-four thousand beings.

Sā bhagavantaṃ vanditvā pitu santikaṃ agamāsi. Pitā taṃ disvā “cirenāgatā”ti kuddho vegena tante vemaṃ pakkhipi. Taṃ nikkhamitvā dārikāya kucchiṃ bhindi. Sā tattheva kālamakāsi. So disvā – “nāhaṃ mama dhītaraṃ pahariṃ, apica kho imaṃ vemaṃ vegasā nikkhamitvā imissā kucchiṃ bhindi. Jīvati nu kho nanu kho”ti vīmaṃsanto mataṃ disvā cintesi – “manussā maṃ ‘iminā dhītā māritā’ti ñatvā upakkoseyyuṃ, tena rājāpi garukaṃ daṇḍaṃ paṇeyya, handāhaṃ paṭikacceva palāyāmī”ti. So daṇḍabhayena palāyanto bhagavato santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā araññe vasantānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ vasanokāsaṃ pāpuṇi. Te ca bhikkhū upasaṅkamitvā pabbajjaṃ yāci. Te taṃ pabbājetvā tacapañcakakammaṭṭhānaṃ adaṃsu. So taṃ uggahetvā vāyamanto na cirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi, te cassa ācariyupajjhāyā. Atha mahāpavāraṇāya [V 1.0224] sabbeva bhagavato santikaṃ agamaṃsu [P 1.0269] – “visuddhipavāraṇaṃ pavāressāmā”ti. Bhagavā pavāretvā vutthavasso bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto gāmanigamādīsu cārikaṃ caramāno anupubbena āḷaviṃ agamāsi. Tattha manussā bhagavantaṃ nimantetvā dānādīni karontā taṃ bhikkhuṃ disvā “dhītaraṃ māretvā idāni kaṃ māretuṃ āgatosī”tiādīni vatvā uppaṇḍesuṃ. Bhikkhū taṃ sutvā upaṭṭhānavelāyaṃ upasaṅkamitvā bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. Bhagavā – “na, bhikkhave[M 1.0256], ayaṃ bhikkhu dhītaraṃ māresi, sā attano kammena matā”ti vatvā tassa bhikkhuno manussehi dubbijānaṃ khīṇāsavamunibhāvaṃ pakāsento bhikkhūnaṃ dhammadesanatthaṃ imaṃ gāthamabhāsi.

She paid homage to the Blessed One and went to her father. Upon seeing her, her father, angry that she had come after a long time, swiftly threw a shuttle. It shot out and pierced the girl’s belly. She died right there. Seeing this, he thought: “I did not strike my daughter, but this shuttle, flying swiftly, shot out and pierced her belly. Is she alive or not?” Investigating and seeing she was dead, he reflected: “People, knowing that I killed my daughter, would accuse me, and the king would impose a severe punishment. Therefore, I should flee beforehand.” Fearing punishment, he fled and, after taking a meditation subject from the Blessed One, came to the dwelling place of monks living in the forest. Approaching those monks, he requested ordination. They ordained him and gave him the meditation subject on the five parts of the body. Mastering it and striving diligently, he soon attained arahantship, and they became his teachers and preceptors. Then, on the occasion of the great Pavāraṇā, they all went to the Blessed One, intending, “We will perform the Pavāraṇā of purity.” The Blessed One, having performed the Pavāraṇā and completed the rains retreat, surrounded by the Sangha of monks, was traveling through villages and towns and gradually arrived at Āḷavī. There, people who had invited the Blessed One and were making offerings saw that monk and taunted him, saying, “After killing your daughter, whom have you come to kill now?” Hearing this, the monks approached the Blessed One during the time of attendance and reported the matter. The Blessed One said: “Monks, this monk did not kill his daughter; she died by her own kamma.” Then, to reveal to the people the state of that monk as a sage with defilements destroyed—a state difficult to discern—and to teach the Dhamma to the monks, he spoke this verse.

Tassattho – yo tīsupi kammadvāresu sīlasaṃyamena saṃyatatto kāyena vā vācāya vā cetasā vā hiṃsādikaṃ na karoti pāpaṃ, tañca kho pana daharo vā daharavaye ṭhito, majjhimo vā majjhimavaye ṭhito, eteneva nayena thero vā pacchimavaye ṭhitoti kadācipi na karoti. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Yatatto, yasmā anuttarāya viratiyā sabbapāpehi uparatacittoti vuttaṃ hoti.

Its meaning is this: one whose self is restrained in the three doors of action by the restraint of virtue, who does no evil such as harming with body, speech, or mind, and who—whether young or established in youth, middle-aged or established in middle age, or likewise old or established in old age—never does so at any time. What is the reason? Because they are self-controlled; because their mind has turned away from all evil through the unsurpassed abstinence, so it is said.

Idāni muni arosaneyyo na so roseti kañcīti etesaṃ padānaṃ ayaṃ yojanā ca adhippāyo ca – so khīṇāsavamuni arosaneyyo “dhītumārako”ti vā “pesakāro”ti vā evamādinā nayena kāyena vā vācāya vā rosetuṃ, ghaṭṭetuṃ, bādhetuṃ araho na hoti. Sopi hi na roseti kañci, “nāhaṃ mama dhītaraṃ māremi, tvaṃ māresi, tumhādiso vā māretī”tiādīni vatvā kañci na roseti, na ghaṭṭeti, na bādheti, tasmā sopi na rosaneyyo. Apica kho pana “tiṭṭhatu nāgo, mā nāgaṃ ghaṭṭesi, namo karohi nāgassā”ti (ma. ni. 1.249) vuttanayena namassitabboyeva hoti. Taṃ vāpi dhīrā muni vedayantīti ettha pana tampi dhīrāva muniṃ vedayantīti evaṃ padavibhāgo veditabbo. Adhippāyo cettha – taṃ “ayaṃ arosaneyyo”ti ete bālamanussā [P 1.0270] ajānitvā rosenti. Ye pana dhīrā honti, te dhīrāva tampi muniṃ vedayanti, ayaṃ khīṇāsavamunīti jānantīti.

Now, as for ‘the sage is not to be provoked, nor does he provoke anyone,’ this is the construction and meaning of these words: That sage, who has destroyed the taints, is not fit to be provoked, harassed, or troubled by anyone through body or speech, whether by calling him ‘daughter-killer’ or ‘weaver’ or in any similar way. For he himself does not provoke anyone, nor does he harass or trouble anyone, by saying such things as, ‘I did not kill my daughter, you killed her, or someone like you killed her.’ Therefore, he too is not to be provoked. Moreover, as it is said, ‘Let the nāga be, do not disturb the nāga, pay homage to the nāga’ (MN 29), he should indeed be revered. As for ‘the wise, too, recognize him as a sage,’ here the division of words should be understood as ‘the wise indeed recognize him as a sage.’ The meaning here is this: foolish people, not knowing that ‘this one is not to be provoked,’ provoke him. But those who are wise, they indeed recognize that sage, knowing, ‘This is a sage who has destroyed the taints.’”

219. Yadaggatoti kā uppatti? Sāvatthiyaṃ kira pañcaggadāyako nāma brāhmaṇo ahosi. So nipphajjamānesu sassesu khettaggaṃ, rāsaggaṃ, koṭṭhaggaṃ, kumbhiaggaṃ, bhojanagganti imāni pañca aggāni deti. Tattha paṭhamapakkāniyeva sāli-yava-godhūma-sīsāni āharāpetvā yāgupāyāsaputhukādīni paṭiyādetvā “aggassa dātā medhāvī, aggaṃ so adhigacchatī”ti evaṃdiṭṭhiko hutvā buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa dānaṃ [M 1.0257] deti, idamassa khettaggadānaṃ. Nipphannesu pana sassesu lāyitesu madditesu ca varadhaññāni gahetvā tatheva dānaṃ deti, idamassa rāsaggadānaṃ[V 1.0225]. Puna tehi dhaññehi koṭṭhāgārāni pūrāpetvā paṭhamakoṭṭhāgāravivaraṇe paṭhamanīhaṭāni dhaññāni gahetvā tatheva dānaṃ deti, idamassa koṭṭhaggadānaṃ. Yaṃ yadeva panassa ghare randheti, tato aggaṃ anuppattapabbajitānaṃ adatvā antamaso dārakānampi na kiñci deti, idamassa kumbhiaggadānaṃ. Puna attano bhojanakāle paṭhamūpanītaṃ bhojanaṃ purebhattakāle saṅghassa, pacchābhattakāle sampattayācakānaṃ, tadabhāve antamaso sunakhānampi adatvā na bhuñjati, idamassa bhojanaggadānaṃ. Evaṃ so pañcaggadāyakotveva abhilakkhito ahosi.

219. What is the origin of the verse beginning 'Yadaggato'? It is said that in Sāvatthī there was a brahmin named Pañcaggadāyaka. When the crops were ripening, he would give these five foremost offerings: the foremost of the field, the foremost of the heap, the foremost of the granary, the foremost of the pot, and the foremost of the meal. In that regard, having had the very first-ripened heads of rice, barley, and wheat brought, and having prepared rice-gruel, milk-rice, parched grain, and the like, with the view, 'The wise one, a giver of the foremost, attains the foremost,' he would give alms to the community of monks headed by the Buddha—this was his offering of the foremost of the field. Then, when the crops were harvested, reaped, and threshed, he would take the choice grains and give alms in the same way—this was his offering of the foremost of the heap. Again, having filled the granaries with those grains, upon the first opening of a granary, he would take the grains that were first brought out and give alms in the same way—this was his offering of the foremost of the granary. Furthermore, whatever was cooked in his house, he would not give even a little, even to his own children, without first giving the foremost portion to the mendicants who had arrived—this was his offering of the foremost of the pot. Again, at his own mealtime, he would not eat without first giving the food that was first served to him to the Sangha in the forenoon, to any beggars who had arrived in the afternoon, or, in their absence, even to the dogs—this was his offering of the foremost of the meal. Thus, he became known as 'Pañcaggadāyaka,' the Giver of the Five Foremost Offerings.

Athekadivasaṃ bhagavā paccūsasamaye buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ volokento tassa brāhmaṇassa brāhmaṇiyā ca sotāpattimaggaupanissayaṃ disvā sarīrapaṭijagganaṃ katvā [P 1.0271] atippageva gandhakuṭiṃ pāvisi. Bhikkhū pihitadvāraṃ gandhakuṭiṃ disvā – “ajja bhagavā ekakova gāmaṃ pavisitukāmo”ti ñatvā bhikkhācāravelāya gandhakuṭiṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā piṇḍāya pavisiṃsu. Bhagavāpi brāhmaṇassa bhojanavelāyaṃ nikkhamitvā sāvatthiṃ pāvisi. Manussā bhagavantaṃ disvā evaṃ – “nūnajja koci satto anuggahetabbo atthi, tathā hi bhagavā ekakova paviṭṭho”ti ñatvā na bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamiṃsu nimantanatthāya. Bhagavāpi anupubbena brāhmaṇassa gharadvāraṃ sampatvā aṭṭhāsi. Tena ca samayena brāhmaṇo bhojanaṃ gahetvā nisinno hoti, brāhmaṇī panassa bījaniṃ gahetvā ṭhitā. Sā bhagavantaṃ disvā “sacāyaṃ brāhmaṇo passeyya, pattaṃ gahetvā sabbaṃ bhojanaṃ dadeyya, tato me puna pacitabbaṃ bhaveyyā”ti cintetvā appasādañca maccherañca uppādetvā yathā brāhmaṇo bhagavantaṃ na passati, evaṃ tālavaṇṭena paṭicchādesi. Bhagavā taṃ ñatvā sarīrābhaṃ muñci. Taṃ brāhmaṇo suvaṇṇobhāsaṃ disvā “kimeta”nti ullokento addasa bhagavantaṃ dvāre ṭhitaṃ. Brāhmaṇīpi “diṭṭhonena bhagavā”ti tāvadeva tālavaṇṭaṃ nikkhipitvā bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā pañcapatiṭṭhitena vandi, vanditvā cassā uṭṭhahantiyā sappāyaṃ viditvā –

Then one day, at dawn, the Blessed One, surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, saw the supporting condition for the path of stream-entry in that brahmin and his wife. After attending to his bodily needs, he entered the perfumed chamber very early. The monks, seeing the perfumed chamber with its door closed, knew, 'Today the Blessed One wishes to enter the village alone.' At the time for the almsround, they circumambulated the perfumed chamber and entered the village for alms. The Blessed One, for his part, left at the brahmin’s mealtime and entered Sāvatthī. The people, seeing the Blessed One, thought, 'Surely today there is some being to be helped, for the Blessed One has entered alone,' and knowing this, they did not approach the Blessed One to invite him for a meal. The Blessed One, proceeding in due course, arrived at the brahmin’s door and stood there. At that moment, the brahmin was seated with his meal before him, and his wife stood holding a fan. Seeing the Blessed One, she thought, 'If this brahmin sees him, he will take the bowl and give away all the food, and then I will have to cook again.' Generating displeasure and stinginess, she blocked the view of the Blessed One with the palm-leaf fan so that the brahmin would not see him. The Blessed One, knowing this, emitted a bodily radiance. The brahmin, seeing the golden glow, wondered, 'What is this?' and looking up, he saw the Blessed One standing at the door. The brahmin’s wife, thinking, 'The Blessed One has been seen by him,' immediately put down the palm-leaf fan, approached the Blessed One, and paid homage with the five-point prostration. And as she was rising after paying homage, the Blessed One, knowing what was suitable for her, spoke:

“Sabbaso nāmarūpasmiṃ, yassa natthi mamāyitaṃ;

Asatā ca na socati, sa ve bhikkhūti vuccatī”ti. (dha. pa. 367) –

For whom there is no sense of 'mine' in regard to all name-and-form, and who does not grieve for what is non-existent, he, indeed, is called a bhikkhu.

Imaṃ [M 1.0258] gāthamabhāsi. Sā gāthāpariyosāneyeva sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāsi. Brāhmaṇopi [P 1.0272] bhagavantaṃ antogharaṃ pavesetvā, varāsane nisīdāpetvā, dakkhiṇodakaṃ datvā, attano upanītabhojanaṃ upanāmesi – “tumhe, bhante, sadevake loke aggadakkhiṇeyyā, sādhu, me taṃ bhojanaṃ attano patte [V 1.0226] patiṭṭhāpethā”ti. Bhagavā tassa anuggahatthaṃ paṭiggahetvā paribhuñji. Katabhattakicco ca brāhmaṇassa sappāyaṃ viditvā imaṃ gāthamabhāsi.

At the very conclusion of the verse, she was established in the fruit of stream-entry. The brahmin, for his part, led the Blessed One into the house, seated him on an excellent seat, gave the water of dedication, and offered his own meal, saying, 'Venerable sir, in this world with its gods, you are the foremost recipient of offerings. It would be good if you would establish this food of mine in your bowl.' The Blessed One, to show his favor to him, accepted it and partook of the meal. Having finished the meal, and knowing what was suitable for the brahmin, he spoke this verse:

Tassattho – yaṃ kumbhito paṭhamameva gahitattā aggato, addhāvasesāya kumbhiyā āgantvā tato gahitattā majjhato, ekadvikaṭacchumattāvasesāya kumbhiyā āgantvā tato gahitattā sesato vā piṇḍaṃ labhetha. Paradattūpajīvīti pabbajito. So hi udakadantapoṇaṃ ṭhapetvā avasesaṃ pareneva dattaṃ upajīvati, tasmā “paradattūpajīvī”ti vuccati. Nālaṃ thutuṃ nopi nipaccavādīti aggato laddhā attānaṃ vā dāyakaṃ vā thometumpi nārahati pahīnānunayattā. Sesato laddhā “kiṃ etaṃ iminā dinna”ntiādinā nayena dāyakaṃ nipātetvā appiyavacanāni vattāpi na hoti pahīnapaṭighattā. Taṃ vāpi dhīrā muni vedayantīti tampi pahīnānunayapaṭighaṃ dhīrāva muniṃ vedayantīti brāhmaṇassa arahattanikūṭena gāthaṃ desesi. Gāthāpariyosāne brāhmaṇo sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahīti.

Its meaning is this: whether one might receive an alms-lump from the top, because it was taken from the pot first; or from the middle, because one came when the pot was half-remaining and took from it; or from the leftovers, because one came when only a spoonful or two remained and took from it. 'One who lives on what is given by others' refers to a mendicant. For, excepting water and a tooth-cleaner, he lives on what is given by others; therefore he is called 'one who lives on what is given by others.' 'Not one to praise, nor a disparager' means that having received from the top portion, he is not fit to praise either himself or the donor, because attachment has been abandoned. Having received from the leftovers, he is not one to speak unpleasant words, disparaging the donor in ways such as, 'What is this that has been given by him?', because aversion has been abandoned. 'And the wise know him as a sage' means that the wise know even such a person—one who has abandoned attachment and aversion—to be a sage. Thus, he taught the verse to the brahmin, culminating in arahantship. At the conclusion of the verse, the brahmin was established in the fruit of stream-entry.

220. Muniṃ carantanti kā uppatti? Sāvatthiyaṃ kira aññataro seṭṭhiputto utuvasena tīsu pāsādesu sabbasampattīhi paricārayamāno daharova pabbajitukāmo hutvā, mātāpitaro yācitvā, khaggavisāṇasutte “kāmā hi citrā”ti (su. ni. 50) imissā gāthāya aṭṭhuppattiyaṃ vuttanayeneva tikkhattuṃ pabbajitvā ca uppabbajitvā ca catutthavāre arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Taṃ pubbaparicayena bhikkhū bhaṇanti – “samayo, āvuso, uppabbajitu”nti. So “abhabbo dānāhaṃ, āvuso, vibbhamitu”nti āha. Taṃ sutvā bhikkhū bhagavato ārocesuṃ. Bhagavā “evametaṃ, bhikkhave, abhabbo so [P 1.0273] dāni vibbhamitu”nti tassa khīṇāsavamunibhāvaṃ āvikaronto imaṃ gāthamāha.

220. What is the origin of [the verse beginning] 'Muniṃ carantaṃ'? It is said that in Sāvatthī, a certain merchant's son, being attended with all prosperity in three palaces according to the seasons, desired to go forth while still young. Having requested his parents, in the manner described in the origin story of the verse 'For sensual pleasures are diverse' in the Khaggavisāṇa Sutta, he went forth and disrobed three times, and on the fourth occasion, he attained Arahantship. Due to his former habit, the monks would say to him, 'Friend, it is time to disrobe.' He would reply, 'Friends, I am now incapable of falling away.' Having heard this, the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said, 'Monks, it is so; he is now incapable of falling away,' and making manifest his state as a Muni whose taints are destroyed, He spoke this verse.

Tassattho [M 1.0259] – moneyyadhammasamannāgamena muniṃ, ekavihāritāya, pubbe vuttappakārāsu vā cariyāsu yāya kāyaci cariyāya carantaṃ, pubbe viya methunadhamme cittaṃ akatvā anuttarāya viratiyā virataṃ methunasmā. Dutiyapādassa sambandho – kīdisaṃ muniṃ carantaṃ virataṃ methunasmāti ce? Yo yobbane nopanibajjhate kvaci, yo bhadrepi yobbane vattamāne kvaci itthirūpe yathā pure, evaṃ methunarāgena na upanibajjhati. Atha vā kvaci attano vā parassa vā yobbane “yuvā tāvamhi, ayaṃ vā yuvāti paṭisevāmi tāva kāme”ti evaṃ yo rāgena na upanibajjhatīti ayampettha attho. Na kevalañca virataṃ methunasmā, apica kho pana jātimadādibhedā madā, kāmaguṇesu sativippavāsasaṅkhātā pamādāpi ca virataṃ, evaṃ madappamādā viratattā [V 1.0227] eva ca vippamuttaṃ sabbakilesabandhanehi. Yathā vā eko lokikāyapi viratiyā virato hoti, na evaṃ, kiṃ pana vippamuttaṃ virataṃ, sabbakilesabandhanehi vippamuttattā lokuttaraviratiyā viratantipi attho. Taṃ vāpi dhīrā muni vedayantīti tampi dhīrā eva muniṃ vedayanti, tumhe pana naṃ na vedayatha, tena naṃ evaṃ bhaṇathāti dasseti.

Its meaning is this: he is a muni through being endowed with the qualities of a sage; by dwelling alone, or by practicing in any of the ways previously described, he abstains from sexual intercourse with supreme restraint, not setting his mind on sexual activity as before. The connection of the second line is: If it is asked, 'What kind of muni, practicing, abstains from sexual intercourse?' It is one who is not bound by youth anywhere; who, even when in the prime of youth, is not bound by sexual lust for the form of a woman as he was before. Or, the meaning here is this: one who is not bound by lust, thinking, 'I am still young,' or 'This one is young, so I will indulge in sensual pleasures for now,' with regard to his own youth or another's. And not only does he abstain from sexual intercourse, but he also abstains from intoxications distinguished by pride of birth and so on, and from heedlessness, which is described as the absence of mindfulness regarding sensual pleasures. Thus, being abstinent from intoxication and heedlessness, he is liberated from all bonds of defilements. And it is not that he is abstinent merely through worldly restraint, as one might be; rather, what is his liberated abstinence? It means he is abstinent through supramundane restraint because of being liberated from all bonds of defilements. [The verse says,] 'The wise, indeed, know him as a muni,' which shows that the wise know him as a muni, but you do not know him, and therefore you speak to him thus.

221. Aññāya lokanti kā uppatti? Bhagavā kapilavatthusmiṃ viharati. Tena samayena nandassa ābharaṇamaṅgalaṃ, abhisekamaṅgalaṃ, āvāhamaṅgalanti tīṇi maṅgalāni akaṃsu. Bhagavāpi tattha nimantito pañcahi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ tattha gantvā bhuñjitvā nikkhamanto nandassa hatthe pattaṃ adāsi. Taṃ nikkhamantaṃ disvā janapadakalyāṇī “tuvaṭṭaṃ kho, ayyaputta, āgaccheyyāsī”ti [P 1.0274] āha. So bhagavato gāravena “handa bhagavā patta”nti vattuṃ asakkonto vihārameva gato. Bhagavā gandhakuṭipariveṇe ṭhatvā “āhara, nanda, patta”nti gahetvā “pabbajissasī”ti āha. So bhagavato gāravena paṭikkhipituṃ asakkonto “pabbajāmi, bhagavā”ti āha. Taṃ bhagavā pabbājesi. So pana janapadakalyāṇiyā vacanaṃ punappunaṃ saranto ukkaṇṭhi. Bhikkhū bhagavato ārocesuṃ. Bhagavā nandassa anabhiratiṃ vinodetukāmo “tāvatiṃsabhavanaṃ gatapubbosi, nandā”ti āha. Nando “nāhaṃ, bhante, gatapubbo”ti avoca.

221. What is the origin of [the verse beginning] 'Aññāya lokaṃ'? The Blessed One was dwelling in Kapilavatthu. At that time, they performed three ceremonies for Nanda: the ornament ceremony, the consecration ceremony, and the marriage ceremony. The Blessed One, having been invited there, went with five hundred monks, ate, and upon leaving, gave His bowl into Nanda's hand. Seeing him departing, Janapadakalyāṇī said, 'Noble son, please return quickly.' He, out of reverence for the Blessed One, unable to say, 'Blessed One, please take the bowl,' went right to the monastery. The Blessed One, standing in the precincts of the perfumed chamber, took the bowl and said, 'Nanda, will you go forth?' He, out of reverence for the Blessed One, unable to refuse, said, 'I will go forth, Blessed One.' The Blessed One then ordained him. But he, repeatedly recalling the words of Janapadakalyāṇī, became discontented. The monks reported this to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, wishing to dispel Nanda's discontent, said, 'Nanda, have you ever been to the Tāvatiṃsa realm?' Nanda replied, 'Venerable Sir, I have never been there before.'

Tato naṃ bhagavā attano ānubhāvena tāvatiṃsabhavanaṃ netvā vejayantapāsādadvāre aṭṭhāsi. Bhagavato āgamanaṃ viditvā sakko accharāgaṇaparivuto [M 1.0260] pāsādā orohi. Tā sabbāpi kassapassa bhagavato sāvakānaṃ pādamakkhanatelaṃ datvā kakuṭapādiniyo ahesuṃ. Atha bhagavā nandaṃ āmantesi – “passasi no, tvaṃ nanda, imāni pañca accharāsatāni kakuṭapādānī”ti sabbaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ. Mātugāmassa nāma nimittānubyañjanaṃ gahetabbanti sakalepi buddhavacane etaṃ natthi. Atha ca panettha bhagavā upāyakusalatāya āturassa dose uggiletvā nīharitukāmo vejjo subhojanaṃ viya nandassa rāgaṃ uggiletvā nīharitukāmo nimittānubyañjanaggahaṇaṃ anuññāsi yathā taṃ anuttaro purisadammasārathi. Tato bhagavā accharāhetu nandassa brahmacariye abhiratiṃ disvā bhikkhū āṇāpesi – “bhatakavādena nandaṃ codethā”ti. So tehi codiyamāno lajjito yoniso manasi karonto paṭipajjitvā na cirasseva arahattaṃ sacchākāsi. Tassa caṅkamanakoṭiyaṃ rukkhe adhivatthā devatā bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesi. Bhagavatopi ñāṇaṃ udapādi. Bhikkhū ajānantā [P 1.0275] tathevāyasmantaṃ codenti. Bhagavā “na, bhikkhave, idāni nando evaṃ codetabbo”ti tassa khīṇāsavamunibhāvaṃ dīpento tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ dhammadesanatthaṃ imaṃ gāthamabhāsi.

Then the Blessed One, by his own power, took him to the Tāvatiṃsa realm and stood at the gate of the Vejayanta Palace. Knowing of the Blessed One’s arrival, Sakka, surrounded by a host of nymphs, descended from the palace. All those nymphs, having offered foot-anointing oil to the disciples of the Blessed One Kassapa, had feet like a cock's. Then the Blessed One addressed Nanda: 'Do you see, Nanda, these five hundred nymphs with feet like a cock's?' (This should be elaborated in full.) Nowhere in the entire word of the Buddha is it said that one should grasp the signs and features of a woman. Yet here, the Blessed One, out of skill in means—like a physician who wishes to make an afflicted person vomit out and expel his afflictions—wishing to make Nanda vomit out and expel his lust, permitted the grasping of signs and features, as befits the Incomparable Tamer of Men to be Tamed. Then the Blessed One, seeing Nanda’s delight in the holy life on account of the nymphs, instructed the monks: 'Reprove Nanda by calling him a hireling.' Being reproved by them, he became ashamed, reflected wisely, and practiced accordingly. Before long, he realized Arahantship. A deity dwelling in a tree at the end of his walking path reported this matter to the Blessed One. Knowledge of this also arose for the Blessed One. The monks, not knowing, continued to reprove the venerable one in the same way. The Blessed One said, 'Monks, Nanda should not be reproved in this way now,' and pointing out his state as a Muni with taints destroyed, He spoke this verse for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma to those monks.

Tassattho [V 1.0228] – dukkhasaccavavatthānakaraṇena khandhādilokaṃ aññāya jānitvā vavatthapetvā nirodhasaccasacchikiriyāya paramatthadassiṃ, samudayappahānena catubbidhampi oghaṃ, pahīnasamudayattā rūpamadādivegasahanena cakkhādiāyatanasamuddañca atitariya atitaritvā atikkamitvā maggabhāvanāya, “tanniddesā tādī”ti imāya tādilakkhaṇappattiyā tādiṃ. Yo vāyaṃ kāmarāgādikilesarāsiyeva avahananaṭṭhena ogho, kucchitagatipariyāyena samuddanaṭṭhena samuddo, samudayappahāneneva taṃ oghaṃ samuddañca atitariya atitiṇṇoghattā idāni tumhehi evaṃ vuccamānepi vikāramanāpajjanatāya tādimpi evampettha attho ca adhippāyo ca veditabbo. Taṃ chinnaganthaṃ asitaṃ anāsavanti idaṃ panassa thutivacanameva, imāya catusaccabhāvanāya catunnaṃ ganthānaṃ chinnattā chinnaganthaṃ, diṭṭhiyā taṇhāya vā katthaci anissitattā asitaṃ, catunnaṃ āsavānaṃ abhāvena anāsavanti vuttaṃ hoti. Taṃ vāpi dhīrā muni vedayantīti tampi dhīrāva khīṇāsavamuniṃ vedayanti tumhe pana avedayamānā evaṃ bhaṇathāti dasseti.

The meaning is this: by discerning the truth of suffering, having known and defined the world of aggregates and so forth, and by realizing the truth of cessation, one is a seer of the ultimate reality. By abandoning the origin, one crosses over the fourfold flood; and because the origin is abandoned, by enduring the force of pride in form and so forth, and by developing the path, one has crossed over and transcended the ocean of sense bases like the eye and so forth. By attaining the characteristic of steadfastness, as indicated by 'that is the steadfast one,' one is steadfast. Or, that very flood is the mass of defilements such as sensual desire, in the sense of sweeping away; and the ocean is the same, in the sense of being a place of bad destinations. By abandoning the origin, one crosses over that flood and ocean. Because one has crossed over the flood, even when addressed thus by you now, one remains unshaken and unagitated—this is the meaning and intention to be understood here regarding the steadfast one. 'He has cut the bonds, is unattached, taintless'—this is a statement of praise for him. Because through the cultivation of the four truths, the four bonds are cut, he is 'one whose bonds are cut.' Because he is not dependent on views or craving anywhere, he is 'unattached.' Because there is an absence of the four taints, he is 'taintless'—this is said. 'The wise know him as a sage'—this shows that the wise indeed know him as a sage whose taints are destroyed, but you, not knowing, speak thus.

222. Asamā [M 1.0261] ubhoti kā uppatti? Aññataro bhikkhu kosalaraṭṭhe paccantagāmaṃ nissāya araññe viharati. Tasmiñca gāme migaluddako tassa bhikkhuno vasanokāsaṃ gantvā mige bandhati. So araññaṃ pavisanto theraṃ gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pavisantampi passati, araññā āgacchanto gāmato nikkhamantampi [P 1.0276] passati. Evaṃ abhiṇhadassanena there jātasineho ahosi. So yadā bahuṃ maṃsaṃ labhati, tadā therassāpi rasapiṇḍapātaṃ deti. Manussā ujjhāyanti – “ayaṃ bhikkhu ‘amukasmiṃ padese migā tiṭṭhanti, caranti, pānīyaṃ pivantī’ti luddakassa āroceti. Tato luddako mige māreti, tena ubho saṅgamma jīvikaṃ kappentī”ti. Atha bhagavā janapadacārikaṃ caramāno taṃ janapadaṃ agamāsi. Bhikkhū gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pavisantā taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā bhagavato ārocesuṃ. Bhagavā luddakena saddhiṃ samānajīvikābhāvasādhakaṃ tassa bhikkhuno khīṇāsavamunibhāvaṃ dīpento tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ dhammadesanatthaṃ imaṃ gāthamabhāsi.

222. What is the origin of the expression 'unequal pair'? A certain monk, relying on a border village in the Kosala country, lived in a forest. In that same village, a deer hunter would go to the monk’s dwelling place and trap deer. He would see the elder entering the village for alms, and also see him coming from the forest, leaving the village. Through this frequent seeing, the hunter developed affection for the elder. Whenever he obtained a large amount of meat, he would also give a choice portion of alms food to the elder. People began to complain: 'This monk informs the hunter, “In such and such a place, deer stand, graze, and drink water.” Then the hunter kills the deer, and the two of them, colluding, maintain their livelihood together.' Later, while the Blessed One was traveling through the countryside, he arrived at that region. The monks, going for alms in the village, heard about this incident and reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, revealing that the monk was a sage with taints destroyed and therefore did not share a livelihood with the hunter, delivered this verse to teach the monks the Dhamma.

Tassattho – yo ca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu, yo ca luddako, ete asamā ubho. Yaṃ manussā bhaṇanti “samānajīvikā”ti, taṃ micchā. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Dūravihāravuttino, dūre vihāro ca vutti ca nesanti dūravihāravuttino. Vihāroti vasanokāso, so ca bhikkhuno araññe, luddakassa ca gāme. Vuttīti jīvikā, sā ca bhikkhuno gāme sapadānabhikkhācariyā, luddakassa ca araññe migasakuṇamāraṇā. Puna caparaṃ gihī dāraposī, so luddako tena kammena puttadāraṃ poseti. Amamo ca subbato, puttadāresu taṇhādiṭṭhimamattavirahito sucivatattā sundaravatattā ca subbato so khīṇāsavabhikkhu. Puna caparaṃ parapāṇarodhāya gihī asaññato, so luddako gihī parapāṇarodhāya [V 1.0229] tesaṃ pāṇānaṃ jīvitindriyupacchedāya kāyavācācittehi asaṃyato. Niccaṃ munī rakkhati pāṇine yato, itaro pana khīṇāsavamuni kāyavācācittehi niccaṃ yato saṃyato pāṇino rakkhati. Evaṃ sante te kathaṃ samānajīvikā bhavissantīti?

Its meaning is as follows: 'Monks, a monk and a hunter are not alike. What people say—"They live the same way"—is wrong. Why is that? They are far-dwelling and far-living, meaning their dwelling and way of life are far apart. "Dwelling" means a place to live: for a monk, it is the forest; for a hunter, it is the village. "Way of life" means livelihood: for a monk, it is going for alms from house to house in the village; for a hunter, it is killing animals and birds in the forest. Furthermore, a householder supports his family; the hunter does so through that action, maintaining his wife and children. But the monk is unselfish and of good observances, free from craving, views, and possessiveness regarding wife and children, well-behaved because of his pure conduct and beautiful practice—he is a monk whose taints are destroyed. Moreover, a householder is unrestrained in harming other beings; the hunter, as a householder, is unrestrained in body, speech, and mind for the destruction of other beings, for cutting off the life-faculty of those beings. The sage, being diligent, always protects living beings; that is, the other one, the sage whose taints are destroyed, being ever diligent and restrained in body, speech, and mind, protects living beings. This being so, how can they be said to live the same way?'

223. Sikhī yathāti kā uppatti? Bhagavati kapilavatthusmiṃ viharante sākiyānaṃ kathā udapādi – “paṭhamakasotāpanno pacchā sotāpattiṃ pattassa dhammena vuḍḍhataro hoti, tasmā pacchā sotāpannena bhikkhunā paṭhamasotāpannassa gihino [P 1.0277] abhivādanādīni kattabbānī”ti taṃ kathaṃ aññataro [M 1.0262] piṇḍacāriko bhikkhu sutvā bhagavato ārocesi. Bhagavā “aññā eva hi ayaṃ jāti, pūjaneyyavatthu liṅga”nti sandhāya “anāgāmīpi ce, bhikkhave, gihī hoti, tena tadahupabbajitassāpi sāmaṇerassa abhivādanādīni kattabbānevā”ti vatvā puna pacchā sotāpannassāpi bhikkhuno paṭhamasotāpannagahaṭṭhato atimahantaṃ visesaṃ dassento bhikkhūnaṃ dhammadesanatthaṃ imaṃ gāthamabhāsi.

223. How did the incident concerning Sikhī arise? While the Blessed One was dwelling at Kapilavatthu, a discussion arose among the Sakyans: "One who first became a stream-enterer is senior in the Dhamma to one who attained stream-entry later. Therefore, a monk who attained stream-entry later should perform acts of salutation and so forth to a householder who first became a stream-enterer." Hearing this discussion, a certain alms-going monk reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, referring to the fact that "birth is one thing, but the mark (of a monk) is the basis for veneration," said, "Even if, monks, a householder is a Non-returner, he should still perform acts of salutation and so forth to a novice monk ordained that very day." Then, to further show the great distinction between a monk who attained stream-entry later and a householder who first became a stream-enterer, the Blessed One spoke this verse for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma to the monks.

Tassattho – yvāyaṃ matthake jātāya sikhāya sabbhāvena sikhī, maṇidaṇḍasadisāya gīvāya nīlagīvoti ca mayūravihaṅgamo vuccati. So yathā haritahaṃsatambahaṃsakhīrahaṃsakāḷahaṃsapākahaṃsasuvaṇṇahaṃsesu yvāyaṃ suvaṇṇahaṃso, tassa haṃsassa javena soḷasimpi kalaṃ na upeti. Suvaṇṇahaṃso hi muhuttakena yojanasahassampi gacchati, yojanampi asamattho itaro. Dassanīyatāya pana ubhopi dassanīyā honti, evaṃ gihī paṭhamasotāpannopi kiñcāpi maggadassanena dassanīyo hoti. Atha kho so pacchā sotāpannassāpi maggadassanena tulyadassanīyabhāvassāpi bhikkhuno javena nānukaroti. Katamena javena? Uparimaggavipassanāñāṇajavena. Gihino hi taṃ ñāṇaṃ dandhaṃ hoti puttadārādijaṭāya jaṭitattā, bhikkhuno pana tikkhaṃ hoti tassā jaṭāya vijaṭitattā. Svāyamattho bhagavatā “munino vivittassa vanamhi jhāyato”ti iminā pādena dīpito. Ayañhi sekkhamuni bhikkhu kāyacittavivekena ca vivitto hoti, lakkhaṇārammaṇūpanijjhānena ca niccaṃ vanasmiṃ jhāyati. Kuto gihino evarūpo viveko ca jhānañcāti ayañhettha adhippāyoti?

Its meaning is as follows: The peacock is called 'crested one' because it naturally has a crest born on its head, and 'blue-necked' because its neck resembles a jeweled staff. Just as among green geese, copper-colored geese, milk-white geese, black geese, mature geese, and golden geese, the other geese do not attain even a sixteenth part of the speed of the golden goose. For the golden goose can travel a thousand yojanas in a moment, while the other (the peacock) is incapable of even a single yojana. Yet, in terms of attractiveness, both are attractive. Similarly, although a householder who first became a stream-enterer is attractive by the sight of the path, he still cannot imitate the speed of a monk who attained stream-entry later, even though both are equally attractive by the sight of the path. By what speed? By the swiftness of the insight-knowledge of the higher paths. For a householder, that knowledge is slow, being entangled in the tangle of children, wives, and so on. But for a monk, it is sharp, being disentangled from that tangle. This meaning was illuminated by the Blessed One with this line: 'of the sage, secluded, meditating in the forest.' For this monk, a sage-in-training, is secluded through bodily and mental seclusion, and constantly meditates in the forest by close contemplation upon the characteristics as his object. How could a householder have such seclusion and meditation? This is the intended meaning here.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya,

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya munisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

in the Commentary on the Sutta Nipāta, the exposition of the Muni Sutta is completed.

Niṭṭhito ca paṭhamo vaggo atthavaṇṇanānayato, nāmena

And the first chapter, according to the method of explaining the meaning, is completed, by name,

Uragavaggoti.

The Serpent Chapter.

2. Cūḷavaggo

2. The Minor Division

1. Ratanasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Ratana Sutta

Yānīdha [V 1.0230][M 1.0263][P 1.0278] bhūtānīti ratanasuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Atīte kira vesāliyaṃ dubbhikkhādayo upaddavā uppajjiṃsu. Tesaṃ vūpasamanatthāya licchavayo rājagahaṃ gantvā, yācitvā, bhagavantaṃ vesālimānayiṃsu. Evaṃ ānīto bhagavā tesaṃ upaddavānaṃ vūpasamanatthāya idaṃ suttamabhāsi. Ayamettha saṅkhepo. Porāṇā panassa vesālivatthuto pabhuti uppattiṃ vaṇṇayanti. Sā evaṃ veditabbā – bārāṇasirañño kira aggamahesiyā kucchimhi gabbho saṇṭhāsi. Sā taṃ ñatvā rañño nivedesi. Rājā gabbhaparihāraṃ adāsi. Sā sammā parihariyamānagabbhā gabbhaparipākakāle vijāyanagharaṃ pāvisi. Puññavatīnaṃ paccūsasamaye gabbhavuṭṭhānaṃ hoti, sā ca tāsaṃ aññatarā, tena paccūsasamaye alattakapaṭalabandhujīvakapupphasadisaṃ maṃsapesiṃ vijāyi. Tato “aññā deviyo suvaṇṇabimbasadise putte vijāyanti, aggamahesī maṃsapesinti rañño purato mama avaṇṇo uppajjeyyā”ti cintetvā tena avaṇṇabhayena taṃ maṃsapesiṃ ekasmiṃ bhājane pakkhipitvā aññena paṭikujjitvā rājamuddikāya lañchetvā gaṅgāya sote pakkhipāpesi. Manussehi chaḍḍitamatte devatā ārakkhaṃ saṃvidahiṃsu. Suvaṇṇapaṭṭikañcettha jātihiṅgulakena “bārāṇasirañño aggamahesiyā pajā”ti likhitvā bandhiṃsu. Tato taṃ bhājanaṃ ūmibhayādīhi anupaddutaṃ gaṅgāya sotena pāyāsi.

The Ratana Sutta begins, 'Yānīdha bhūtāni…'. What is its origin? In the past, it is said that in Vesālī calamities such as famine arose. To pacify them, the Licchavis went to Rājagaha and, having requested him, brought the Blessed One to Vesālī. Thus brought, the Blessed One spoke this sutta to pacify those calamities. This is the summary here. However, the ancients describe its origin starting from the Vesālī story. It should be understood as follows: It is said that the chief queen of the king of Bārāṇasī conceived in her womb. Knowing this, she informed the king. The king provided protection for the pregnancy. Being well cared for during her pregnancy, she entered the delivery room when the time came for delivery. For meritorious women, the birth occurs at dawn. She was one of them, and at that dawn, she gave birth to a lump of flesh resembling a bandhujīvaka flower like a mass of lac. Then she thought, "Other queens give birth to sons resembling golden images, but the chief queen gives birth to a lump of flesh. Disrepute may arise for me before the king." Fearing this disrepute, she placed that lump of flesh in a vessel, covered it with another, sealed it with the royal signet, and had it cast into the stream of the Ganges. As soon as it was discarded by the people, the deities arranged for its protection. There, they tied on a golden plate on which they had written with native cinnabar, "The offspring of the chief queen of the king of Bārāṇasī." Then, that vessel, undisturbed by waves or other dangers, floated along the current of the Ganges.

Tena ca samayena aññataro tāpaso gopālakulaṃ nissāya gaṅgāya tīre vasati. So pātovagaṅgaṃ otiṇṇo taṃ bhājanaṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā paṃsukūlasaññāya aggahesi. Tato tattha taṃ akkharapaṭṭikaṃ rājamuddikālañchanañca disvā muñcitvā taṃ maṃsapesiṃ addasa. Disvānassa etadahosi – “siyā gabbho, tathā hissa duggandhapūtibhāvo natthī”ti taṃ assamaṃ netvā suddhe okāse ṭhapesi. Atha aḍḍhamāsaccayena dve maṃsapesiyo ahesuṃ. Tāpaso disvā sādhukataraṃ ṭhapesi. Tato puna addhamāsaccayena ekamekissā pesiyā hatthapādasīsānamatthāya pañca pañca piḷakā [V 1.0231] uṭṭhahiṃsu. Atha tato addhamāsaccayena ekā [M 1.0264] maṃsapesi suvaṇṇabimbasadiso dārako; ekā dārikā ahosi. Tesu tāpasassa puttasineho uppajji, aṅguṭṭhato cassa khīraṃ nibbatti, tato pabhuti ca khīrabhattaṃ labhati. So bhattaṃ bhuñjitvā khīraṃ dārakānaṃ mukhe āsiñcati. Tesaṃ yaṃ yaṃ udaraṃ pavisati, taṃ sabbaṃ maṇibhājanagataṃ viya dissati. Evaṃ nicchavī ahesuṃ. Apare pana āhu – “sibbitvā ṭhapitā viya nesaṃ aññamaññaṃ līnā chavi ahosī”ti. Evaṃ te nicchavitāya vā līnacchavitāya vā licchavīti paññāyiṃsu.

At that time, a certain ascetic lived on the bank of the Ganges, depending on a cowherd family. One morning, having descended into the Ganges, he saw that vessel coming and, with the perception of it being a discarded robe, he seized it. Then, seeing there the letter-tablet and the impression of the royal seal, he untied it and saw the lump of flesh. Seeing it, this thought occurred to him: "It might be a fetus, for there is no foul or putrid quality about it." He took it to his hermitage and placed it in a clean place. After half a month, there were two lumps of flesh. The ascetic, seeing this, placed them even more carefully. Then, after another half-month, on each lump five protuberances arose for the purpose of hands, feet, and a head. Then, after another half-month, one lump of flesh became a boy like a golden image; the other became a girl. Affection for them as his own children arose in the ascetic, and milk flowed from his thumb; and from then on, he obtained milk-rice. Having eaten his meal, he would pour milk into the children’s mouths. Whatever entered their stomachs appeared as if it were placed in a jeweled vessel. Thus, they were 'skinless' (nicchavī). Others, however, said, "Their skin was attached to each other as if stitched." In this way, whether because of being 'skinless' (nicchavitā) or having 'attached skin' (līnacchavitā), they became known as the Licchavis.

Tāpaso dārake posento ussūre gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pavisati, atidivā paṭikkamati. Tassa taṃ byāpāraṃ ñatvā gopālakā āhaṃsu – “bhante, pabbajitānaṃ dārakaposanaṃ palibodho, amhākaṃ dārake detha, mayaṃ posessāma, tumhe attano kammaṃ karothā”ti. Tāpaso “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇi. Gopālakā dutiyadivase maggaṃ samaṃ katvā, pupphehi okiritvā; dhajapaṭākā ussāpetvā tūriyehi vajjamānehi assamaṃ āgatā. Tāpaso “mahāpuññā dārakā, appamādena vaḍḍhetha, vaḍḍhetvā ca aññamaññaṃ āvāhavivāhaṃ karotha, pañcagorasena rājānaṃ tosetvā bhūmibhāgaṃ gahetvā nagaraṃ māpetha, tatra kumāraṃ abhisiñcathā”ti vatvā dārake adāsi. Te “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇitvā dārake netvā posesuṃ.

The ascetic, while raising the children, would enter the village for alms when the sun was high and return late in the day. Knowing of this preoccupation of his, the cowherds said to him, 'Venerable sir, raising children is an encumbrance for those who have gone forth. Give the children to us; we will raise them. You should attend to your own duties.' The ascetic agreed, saying, 'Very well.' The next day, the cowherds leveled the path, scattered it with flowers, raised banners and flags, and, with musical instruments playing, came to the hermitage. The ascetic said, 'These children are of great merit. Raise them with diligence, and when they are grown, arrange marriages with one another. Please the king with the five products of the cow, receive a portion of land, establish a city, and consecrate the prince there.' Having spoken thus, he gave them the children. They agreed, saying, 'Very well,' took the children, and raised them.

Dārakā vaḍḍhimanvāya kīḷantā vivādaṭṭhānesu aññe gopāladārake hatthenapi pādenapi paharanti, te rodanti. “Kissa rodathā”ti ca mātāpitūhi vuttā “ime nimmātāpitikā tāpasapositā amhe atīva paharantī”ti vadanti. Tato tesaṃ mātāpitaro “ime dārakā aññe dārake viheṭhenti dukkhāpenti, na ime saṅgahetabbā, vajjetabbā ime”ti āhaṃsu. Tato pabhuti kira so padeso “vajjī”ti vuccati yojanasataṃ parimāṇena. Atha taṃ padesaṃ gopālakā rājānaṃ tosetvā aggahesuṃ. Tattheva nagaraṃ māpetvā soḷasavassuddesikaṃ kumāraṃ abhisiñcitvā rājānaṃ akaṃsu. Tāya cassa dārikāya saddhiṃ vāreyyaṃ katvā katikaṃ akaṃsu – “na bāhirato dārikā ānetabbā, ito dārikā na kassaci dātabbā”ti. Tesaṃ paṭhamasaṃvāsena dve dārakā jātā dhītā ca putto ca, evaṃ soḷasakkhattuṃ dve dve jātā. Tato tesaṃ [M 1.0265] dārakānaṃ yathākkamaṃ vaḍḍhantānaṃ ārāmuyyānanivāsanaṭṭhānaparivārasampattiṃ gahetuṃ appahontaṃ taṃ nagaraṃ tikkhattuṃ gāvutantarena gāvutantarena pākārena parikkhipiṃsu. Tassa punappunaṃ visālīkatattā vesālītveva nāmaṃ jātaṃ. Idaṃ vesālīvatthu.

The children, upon reaching maturity, would, while playing, strike the other cowherd children with their hands and feet in places of dispute, and those children would cry. When asked by their parents, 'Why do you cry?' they would say, 'These motherless and fatherless children, raised by the ascetic, strike us excessively.' Then their parents said, 'These children harass and cause suffering to the other children; they are to be avoided.' From that time on, it is said, that region, measuring one hundred yojanas, came to be called 'Vajji'. Then the cowherds, having pleased the king, took possession of that region. There they established a city and consecrated the prince, who was about sixteen years of age. They surrounded it three times with a wall, with an interval of a gāvuta between each. Because that city was repeatedly made extensive, its name became 'Vesālī'. This is the story of Vesālī.

Ayaṃ pana vesālī bhagavato uppannakāle iddhā vepullappattā ahosi. Tattha hi rājūnaṃyeva satta sahassāni satta ca satāni satta ca rājāno ahesuṃ, tathā yuvarājasenāpatibhaṇḍāgārikappabhutīnaṃ. Yathāha –

At the time when the Blessed One arose, this Vesālī was prosperous and had reached a state of abundance. For there were seven thousand, seven hundred, and seven kings; and likewise for the crown princes, generals, treasurers, and so forth. As it is said:

“Tena [V 1.0232] kho pana samayena vesālī iddhā ceva hoti phītā ca bahujanā ākiṇṇamanussā subhikkhā ca, satta ca pāsādasahassāni, satta ca pāsādasatāni, satta ca pāsādā, satta ca kūṭāgārasahassāni, satta ca kūṭāgārasatāni, satta ca kūṭāgārāni, satta ca ārāmasahassāni, satta ca ārāmasatāni, satta ca ārāmā, satta ca pokkharaṇisahassāni, satta ca pokkharaṇisatāni, satta ca pokkharaṇiyo”ti (mahāva. 326).

“Now at that time Vesālī was prosperous and flourishing, populous, crowded with people, and with abundant food. There were seven thousand, seven hundred, and seven palaces; seven thousand, seven hundred, and seven gabled halls; seven thousand, seven hundred, and seven parks; and seven thousand, seven hundred, and seven lotus ponds.” (Mahāvagga 326).

Sā aparena samayena dubbhikkhā ahosi dubbuṭṭhikā dussassā. Paṭhamaṃ duggatamanussā maranti, te bahiddhā chaḍḍenti. Matamanussānaṃ kuṇapagandhena amanussā nagaraṃ pavisiṃsu. Tato bahutarā mīyanti, tāya paṭikūlatāya ca sattānaṃ ahivātakarogo uppajji. Iti tīhi dubbhikkhaamanussarogabhayehi upaddutāya vesāliyā nagaravāsino upasaṅkamitvā rājānamāhaṃsu – “mahārāja, imasmiṃ nagare tividhaṃ bhayamuppannaṃ, ito pubbe yāva sattamā rājakulaparivaṭṭā evarūpaṃ anuppannapubbaṃ, tumhākaṃ maññe adhammikattena etarahi uppanna”nti. Rājā sabbe santhāgāre sannipātāpetvā, “mayhaṃ adhammikabhāvaṃ vicinathā”ti āha. Te sabbaṃ paveṇiṃ vicinantā na kiñci addasaṃsu.

At a later time, that city suffered from famine, drought, and poor harvests. First, the destitute died, and their bodies were thrown outside. Due to the stench of the corpses, non-human beings entered the city. Then, many more people died, and from that foulness, a pestilence arose. Thus, the inhabitants of Vesālī, afflicted by the three fears of famine, non-human beings, and disease, approached the king and said: 'Great King, a threefold terror has arisen in this city. Before this, for seven generations of the royal line, such a thing has never occurred. We believe it has now arisen due to your unrighteousness.' The king had everyone assemble in the council hall and said, 'Investigate my unrighteousness.' They examined the entire royal tradition but found nothing amiss.

Tato rañño dosaṃ adisvā “idaṃ bhayaṃ amhākaṃ kathaṃ vūpasameyyā”ti cintesuṃ. Tattha ekacce cha satthāro apadisiṃsu – “etehi okkantamatte vūpasamissatī”ti. Ekacce āhaṃsu – “buddho kira loke uppanno, so bhagavā sabbasattahitāya dhammaṃ deseti mahiddhiko [M 1.0266] mahānubhāvo, tena okkantamatte sabbabhayāni vūpasameyyu”nti. Tena te attamanā hutvā “kahaṃ pana so bhagavā etarahi viharati, amhehi vā pesite āgaccheyyā”ti āhaṃsu. Athāpare āhaṃsu – “buddhā nāma anukampakā, kissa nāgaccheyyuṃ, so pana bhagavā etarahi rājagahe viharati, rājā ca bimbisāro taṃ upaṭṭhahati, kadāci so āgantuṃ na dadeyyā”ti. “Tena hi rājānaṃ saññāpetvā ānessāmā”ti dve licchavirājāno mahatā balakāyena pahūtaṃ paṇṇākāraṃ datvā rañño santikaṃ pesesuṃ – “bimbisāraṃ saññāpetvā bhagavantaṃ ānethā”ti. Te gantvā rañño paṇṇākāraṃ datvā taṃ pavattiṃ nivedetvā “mahārāja, bhagavantaṃ amhākaṃ nagaraṃ pesehī”ti āhaṃsu. Rājā na sampaṭicchi – “tumhe eva jānāthā”ti āha. Te bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā evamāhaṃsu – “bhante, amhākaṃ nagare tīṇi bhayāni uppannāni. Sace bhagavā āgaccheyya, sotthi no bhaveyyā”ti. Bhagavā āvajjetvā “vesāliyaṃ ratanasutte vutte sā rakkhā koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷāni pharissati, suttapariyosāne caturāsītiyā pāṇasahassānaṃ dhammābhisamayo bhavissatī”ti adhivāsesi. Atha rājā bimbisāro bhagavato adhivāsanaṃ sutvā “bhagavatā vesāligamanaṃ adhivāsita”nti nagare ghosanaṃ kārāpetvā bhagavantaṃ [V 1.0233] upasaṅkamitvā āha – “kiṃ, bhante, sampaṭicchittha vesāligamana”nti? “Āma, mahārājā”ti. “Tena hi, bhante, āgametha, yāva maggaṃ paṭiyādemī”ti.

Then, not seeing any fault in the king, they thought, “How can this danger of ours be pacified?” There, some pointed to the six teachers, saying, “Upon their arrival, it will be pacified.” Others said, “It is said that a Buddha has arisen in the world. That Blessed One teaches the Dhamma for the welfare of all beings; he is of great power and might. Upon his arrival, all dangers would be pacified.” Delighted by this, they said, “But where does that Blessed One dwell now? Would he come if we sent for him?” Then others said, “Buddhas are compassionate—why would they not come? That Blessed One now dwells in Rājagaha, and King Bimbisāra attends upon him. Perhaps the king might not allow him to come.” “In that case, let us persuade the king and bring him.” So they sent two Licchavi princes with a great army and abundant gifts to the king, saying, “Persuade Bimbisāra and bring the Blessed One.” They went, gave the gifts to the king, explained the situation, and said, “Great king, send the Blessed One to our city.” The king did not consent, saying, “You yourselves should know.” They approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and said, “Venerable sir, three dangers have arisen in our city. If the Blessed One were to come, there would be safety for us.” The Blessed One reflected, “When the Ratana Sutta is recited in Vesālī, its protection will spread throughout a hundred thousand koṭis of world-systems, and at the conclusion of the sutta, eighty-four thousand beings will attain the Dhamma,” and he consented. Then King Bimbisāra, hearing of the Blessed One’s consent, had it proclaimed in the city: “The Blessed One has agreed to go to Vesālī.” He approached the Blessed One and asked, “Venerable sir, have you consented to go to Vesālī?” “Yes, great king.” “Then, venerable sir, please wait until I prepare the road.”

Atha kho rājā bimbisāro rājagahassa ca gaṅgāya ca antarā pañcayojanaṃ bhūmiṃ samaṃ katvā, yojane yojane vihāraṃ māpetvā, bhagavato gamanakālaṃ paṭivedesi. Bhagavā pañcahi bhikkhusatehi parivuto pāyāsi. Rājā pañcayojanaṃ maggaṃ pañcavaṇṇehi pupphehi jāṇumattaṃ okirāpetvā dhajapaṭākāpuṇṇaghaṭakadaliādīni ussāpetvā bhagavato dve setacchattāni, ekekassa ca bhikkhussa ekamekaṃ ukkhipāpetvā saddhiṃ attano parivārena pupphagandhādīhi pūjaṃ karonto ekekasmiṃ vihāre bhagavantaṃ vasāpetvā mahādānāni datvā pañcahi divasehi gaṅgātīraṃ nesi. Tattha sabbālaṅkārehi nāvaṃ alaṅkaronto vesālikānaṃ sāsanaṃ pesesi – “āgato bhagavā, maggaṃ paṭiyādetvā sabbe bhagavato paccuggamanaṃ [M 1.0267] karothā”ti. Te “diguṇaṃ pūjaṃ karissāmā”ti vesāliyā ca gaṅgāya ca antarā tiyojanaṃ bhūmiṃ samaṃ katvā bhagavato cattāri, ekekassa ca bhikkhuno dve dve setacchattāni sajjetvā pūjaṃ kurumānā gaṅgātīre āgantvā aṭṭhaṃsu.

Then King Bimbisāra, having leveled the ground for five yojanas between Rājagaha and the Ganges, built a monastery at every yojana and informed the Blessed One of the time for his departure. The Blessed One set out, accompanied by five hundred monks. The king had the five-yojana-long path strewn knee-deep with flowers of five colors; had banners, flags, full water pots, banana trees, and so on, raised; and had two white parasols held over the Blessed One and one over each monk. Together with his retinue, he paid homage with flowers, perfumes, and so on, lodging the Blessed One in each monastery along the way and giving great gifts. In five days, he escorted them to the bank of the Ganges. There, while adorning a boat with all kinds of ornaments, he sent a message to the Vesālians: “The Blessed One has arrived; prepare the road and all come out to welcome him.” They, intending, “We will offer double the honors,” leveled the ground for three yojanas between Vesālī and the Ganges, arranged four white parasols for the Blessed One and two for each monk, and, while performing these honors, came to the bank of the Ganges and waited.

Bimbisāro dve nāvāyo saṅghāṭetvā, maṇḍapaṃ katvā, pupphadāmādīhi alaṅkaritvā tattha sabbaratanamayaṃ buddhāsanaṃ paññāpesi. Bhagavā tasmiṃ nisīdi. Pañcasatā bhikkhūpi nāvaṃ abhiruhitvā yathānurūpaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Rājā bhagavantaṃ anugacchanto galappamāṇaṃ udakaṃ orohitvā “yāva, bhante, bhagavā āgacchati, tāvāhaṃ idheva gaṅgātīre vasissāmī”ti vatvā nivatto. Upari devatā yāva akaniṭṭhabhavanā pūjamakaṃsu, heṭṭhā gaṅgānivāsino kambalassatarādayo nāgā pūjamakaṃsu. Evaṃ mahatiyā pūjāya bhagavā yojanamattaṃ addhānaṃ gaṅgāya gantvā vesālikānaṃ sīmantaraṃ paviṭṭho.

King Bimbisāra had two boats fastened together, built a pavilion, adorned it with flower garlands and the like, and prepared a Buddha-seat made entirely of precious gems there. The Blessed One sat upon it. Five hundred monks also boarded the boat and sat in their appropriate places. The king, following the Blessed One, descended into the water up to his neck and said, “Venerable sir, until the Blessed One returns, I will stay right here on the bank of the Ganges.” Having said this, he turned back. Above, deities from as far as the Akaniṭṭha realm paid homage. Below, the nāgas dwelling in the Ganges, such as Kambala and Assatara, paid homage. Thus, with such great honor, the Blessed One traveled about a yojana along the Ganges and entered the territory of the Vesālians.

Tato licchavirājāno tena bimbisārena katapūjāya diguṇaṃ karontā galappamāṇe udake bhagavantaṃ paccuggacchiṃsu. Teneva khaṇena tena muhuttena vijjuppabhāvinaddhandhakāravisaṭakūṭo gaḷagaḷāyanto catūsu disāsu mahāmegho vuṭṭhāsi. Atha bhagavatā paṭhamapāde gaṅgātīre nikkhittamatte pokkharavassaṃ vassi. Ye temetukāmā, te eva tementi, atemetukāmā na tementi. Sabbattha jāṇumattaṃ ūrumattaṃ kaṭimattaṃ galappamāṇaṃ udakaṃ vahati, sabbakuṇapāni udakena gaṅgaṃ pavesitāni parisuddho bhūmibhāgo ahosi.

Then the Licchavi kings, doubling the honor Bimbisāra had shown, went forth to meet the Blessed One in water up to their necks. At that very moment, in that instant, a great cloud arose in the four directions, its peak of darkness interwoven with flashes of lightning, and it roared. Then, as soon as the Blessed One placed his first foot on the bank of the Ganges, a lotus-rain fell. Those who wished to be wet were drenched, but those who did not wish to be wet were not. Everywhere, water flowed knee-deep, thigh-deep, waist-deep, and neck-deep. All the corpses were carried by the water into the Ganges, and the ground became perfectly clean.

Licchavirājāno bhagavantaṃ antarā yojane yojane vāsāpetvā mahādānāni datvā tīhi divasehi diguṇaṃ pūjaṃ karontā vesāliṃ nayiṃsu. Vesāliṃ sampatte bhagavati sakko devānamindo [V 1.0234] devasaṅghapurakkhato āgacchi, mahesakkhānaṃ devānaṃ sannipātena amanussā yebhuyyena palāyiṃsu. Bhagavā nagaradvāre ṭhatvā ānandattheraṃ āmantesi – “imaṃ ānanda, ratanasuttaṃ uggahetvā balikammūpakaraṇāni gahetvā licchavikumārehi saddhiṃ vesāliyā tīsu pākārantaresu vicaranto parittaṃ karohī”ti ratanasuttaṃ abhāsi. Evaṃ “kena panetaṃ suttaṃ, kadā, kattha, kasmā ca vutta”nti etesaṃ pañhānaṃ vissajjanā vitthārena vesālivatthuto pabhuti porāṇehi vaṇṇiyati.

The Licchavi kings, having had the Blessed One stay at intervals of a yojana along the way and having given great gifts, led him to Vesālī in three days, performing worship of double measure. When the Blessed One arrived in Vesālī, Sakka, the lord of the devas, approached, preceded by the host of devas. At the gathering of the powerful devas, most of the non-human beings fled. Standing at the city gate, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, having learned this Ratana Sutta and taken the implements for the protective ritual, wander between the three ramparts of Vesālī together with the Licchavi princes and perform the protection.” Thus he spoke the Ratana Sutta. In this way, the answer to these questions—‘By whom was this sutta spoken? When, where, and for what reason was it spoken?’—is described in detail by the ancients, beginning from the account of Vesālī.

Evaṃ [M 1.0268] bhagavato vesāliṃ anuppattadivaseyeva vesālinagaradvāre tesaṃ upaddavānaṃ paṭighātatthāya vuttamidaṃ ratanasuttaṃ uggahetvā āyasmā ānando parittatthāya bhāsamāno bhagavato pattena udakaṃ ādāya sabbanagaraṃ abbhukkiranto anuvicari. “Yaṃ kiñcī”ti vuttamatteyeva ca therena ye pubbe apalātā saṅkārakūṭabhittippadesādinissitā amanussā, te catūhi dvārehi palāyiṃsu, dvārāni anokāsāni ahesuṃ. Tato ekacce dvāresu okāsaṃ alabhamānā pākāraṃ bhinditvā palātā. Amanussesu gatamattesu manussānaṃ gattesu rogo vūpasanto, te nikkhamitvā sabbagandhapupphādīhi theraṃ pūjesuṃ. Mahājano nagaramajjhe santhāgāraṃ sabbagandhehi limpitvā vitānaṃ katvā sabbālaṅkārehi alaṅkaritvā tattha buddhāsanaṃ paññāpetvā bhagavantaṃ ānesi.

Thus, on the very day the Blessed One arrived in Vesālī, this Ratana Sutta was spoken at the city gate of Vesālī for the purpose of warding off those afflictions. Having learned it, the Venerable Ānanda, reciting it for the purpose of protection, took water with the Blessed One’s bowl and went about the entire city sprinkling it. At the mere utterance of “Yaṃ kiñci” by the Elder, those non-human beings who had not fled before and were resorting to places like garbage heaps and walls, fled through the four gates; the gates afforded no space. Then some, not finding an opportunity at the gates, broke through the city wall and fled. As soon as the non-human beings had departed, the diseases in people’s bodies subsided. They came out and honored the Elder with all kinds of perfumes, flowers, and so forth. The great populace, in the middle of the city, smeared the assembly hall with all kinds of perfumes, set up a canopy, adorned it with all ornaments, prepared a Buddha-seat there, and brought the Blessed One.

Bhagavā santhāgāraṃ pavisitvā paññatte āsane nisīdi. Bhikkhusaṅghopi kho rājāno manussā ca patirūpe okāse nisīdiṃsu. Sakkopi devānamindo dvīsu devalokesu devaparisāya saddhiṃ upanisīdi aññe ca devā. Ānandattheropi sabbaṃ vesāliṃ anuvicaranto ārakkhaṃ katvā vesālinagaravāsīhi saddhiṃ āgantvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Tattha bhagavā sabbesaṃ tadeva ratanasuttaṃ abhāsīti.

The Blessed One entered the assembly hall and sat down on the prepared seat. The community of monks, the kings, and the people also sat down in suitable places. Sakka, the lord of the devas, together with his divine assembly from the two deva worlds, also sat down nearby, as did other devas. The Elder Ānanda, too, having wandered throughout all of Vesālī providing protection, came together with the inhabitants of the city of Vesālī and sat down to one side. There, the Blessed One spoke that very Ratana Sutta to them all.

224. Tattha yānīdha bhūtānīti paṭhamagāthāyaṃ yānīti yādisāni appesakkhāni vā mahesakkhāni vā. Idhāti imasmiṃ padese, tasmiṃ khaṇe sannipatitaṭṭhānaṃ sandhāyāha. Bhūtānīti kiñcāpi bhūtasaddo “bhūtasmiṃ pācittiya”nti evamādīsu (pāci. 69) vijjamāne, “bhūtamidanti, bhikkhave, samanupassathā”ti evamādīsu (ma. ni. 1.401) khandhapañcake, “cattāro kho, bhikkhu, mahābhūtā hetū”ti evamādīsu (ma. ni. 3.86) catubbidhe pathavīdhātvādirūpe, “yo ca kālaghaso bhūto”ti evamādīsu (jā. 1.2.190) khīṇāsave, “sabbeva nikkhipissanti, bhūtā loke samussaya”nti evamādīsu (dī. ni. 2.220) sabbasatte, “bhūtagāmapātabyatāyā”ti evamādīsu (pāci. 90) rukkhādike, “bhūtaṃ bhūtato sañjānātī”ti evamādīsu (ma. ni. 1.3) cātumahārājikānaṃ heṭṭhā sattanikāyaṃ upādāya vattati. Idha pana avisesato amanussesu daṭṭhabbo.

224. Therein, in the first verse, yānīdha bhūtāni: yāni means of whatever kind, whether of little power or of great power. Idha means in this place; he spoke referring to the place of assembly at that moment. As for bhūtāni: although the word bhūta is used in the sense of ‘what exists’ in passages such as “a pācittiya offense concerning what is” (Pāci. 69); in the sense of the five aggregates in passages such as “Monks, you should see this as what has come to be” (MN 1.401); in the sense of the fourfold matter, such as the earth element, in passages such as “Monk, the four great elements are a cause” (MN 3.86); in the sense of one whose cankers are destroyed in passages such as “the being who is a devourer of time” (Jā. 1.2.190); in the sense of all beings in passages such as “all beings in the world will lay down their bodies” (DN 2.220); in the sense of trees and so on in passages such as “on account of destroying plant life” (Pāci. 90); and referring to the host of beings below the Four Great Kings in passages such as “one cognizes a being as a being” (MN 1.3)—here, however, it should be understood as referring generally to non-human beings.

Samāgatānīti [V 1.0235][M 1.0269] sannipatitāni. Bhummānīti bhūmiyaṃ nibbattāni. Vāti vikappane. Tena yānīdha bhummāni vā bhūtāni samāgatānīti imamekaṃ vikappaṃ katvā puna dutiyaṃ vikappaṃ kātuṃ “yāni vā antalikkhe”ti āha. Antalikkhe vā yāni bhūtāni nibbattāni, tāni sabbāni idha samāgatānīti attho. Ettha ca yāmato yāva akaniṭṭhaṃ, tāva nibbattāni bhūtāni ākāse pātubhūtavimānesu nibbattattā “antalikkhe bhūtānī”ti veditabbāni. Tato heṭṭhā sineruto pabhuti yāva bhūmiyaṃ rukkhalatādīsu adhivatthāni pathaviyañca nibbattāni bhūtāni, tāni sabbāni bhūmiyaṃ bhūmipaṭibaddhesu ca rukkhalatāpabbatādīsu nibbattattā “bhummāni bhūtānī”ti veditabbāni.

Samāgatāni means gathered together. Bhummāni means born on the earth. Vā is used in the sense of alternation. Therefore, having made one alternative—“whatever earth-dwelling beings are gathered here”—he then spoke the words “or whatever in the sky” to make a second alternative. The meaning is: or whatever beings are born in the sky, they are all gathered here. And in this context, beings born from the Yāma realm up to the Akaniṭṭha realm should be understood as “beings in the sky” because they are born in celestial mansions that have appeared in the sky. Below that, from Mount Sineru downwards, the beings that dwell in trees, vines, and so on, as far as the earth, and those born on the earth itself—all of them should be understood as “earth-dwelling beings” because they are born on the earth and in things connected to the earth, such as trees, vines, and mountains.

Evaṃ bhagavā sabbāneva amanussabhūtāni “bhummāni vā yāni va antalikkhe”ti dvīhi padehi vikappetvā puna ekena padena pariggahetvā “sabbeva bhūtā sumanā bhavantū”ti āha. Sabbeti anavasesā. Evāti avadhāraṇe, ekampi anapanetvāti adhippāyo. Bhūtāti amanussā. Sumanā bhavantūti sukhitamanā, pītisomanassajātā bhavantūti attho. Athopīti kiccantarasanniyojanatthaṃ vākyopādāne nipātadvayaṃ. Sakkacca suṇantu bhāsitanti aṭṭhiṃ katvā, manasi katvā, sabbacetaso samannāharitvā dibbasampattilokuttarasukhāvahaṃ mama desanaṃ suṇantu.

Thus the Blessed One, having first distinguished all the non-human beings with the two phrases “earth-dwelling or those in the sky,” then encompassed them with a single phrase, saying: “May all beings be of glad mind.” Here, sabbe means without exception. Eva is a particle of emphasis; the intention is “not excluding even one.” Bhūtā refers to non-humans. Sumanā bhavantu means: may they be of happy mind, may they be ones in whom joy and gladness have arisen. Athopi is a pair of particles used when introducing a statement in order to connect another matter. Sakkacca suṇantu bhāsitaṃ means: paying close attention, applying the mind, directing the whole mind, let them listen to my teaching which brings celestial attainment and supramundane happiness.

Evamettha bhagavā “yānīdha bhūtāni samāgatānī”ti aniyamitavacanena bhūtāni pariggahetvā puna “bhummāni vā yāni va antalikkhe”ti dvidhā vikappetvā tato “sabbeva bhūtā”ti puna ekajjhaṃ katvā “sumanā bhavantū”ti iminā vacanena āsayasampattiyaṃ niyojento “sakkacca suṇantu bhāsita”nti payogasampattiyaṃ, tathā yonisomanasikārasampattiyaṃ paratoghosasampattiyañca, tathā attasammāpaṇidhisappurisūpanissayasampattīsu samādhipaññāhetusampattīsu ca niyojento gāthaṃ samāpesi.

Thus, herein, the Blessed One, having included the beings with the unspecified statement, 'Whatever beings are assembled here,' and then having distinguished them in two ways with, 'Whether on the earth or in the sky,' and thereafter having again brought them together as one with, 'All beings,' established the stanza, directing them with the words, 'May they be of joyful mind,' to the perfection of disposition; with, 'Listen attentively to what is spoken,' to the perfection of application; likewise, to the perfection of wise attention and the perfection of hearing from another; and similarly, to the perfections of right self-application, reliance on a virtuous person, and the perfections that are the causes for concentration and wisdom.

225. Tasmā hi bhūtāti dutiyagāthā. Tattha tasmāti kāraṇavacanaṃ. Bhūtāti āmantanavacanaṃ. Nisāmethāti suṇātha. Sabbeti anavasesā[M 1.0270]. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yasmā tumhe dibbaṭṭhānāni tattha upabhogasampadañca pahāya dhammassavanatthaṃ idha samāgatā, na naṭanaccanādidassanatthaṃ, tasmā hi bhūtā nisāmetha sabbeti. Atha vā “sumanā bhavantu sakkacca suṇantū”ti vacanena tesaṃ sumanabhāvaṃ sakkaccaṃ sotukamyatañca disvā āha – yasmā tumhe sumanabhāvena attasammāpaṇidhiyonisomanasikārāsayasuddhīhi sakkaccaṃ sotukamyatāya sappurisūpanissayaparatoghosapadaṭṭhānato payogasuddhīhi ca yuttā, tasmā hi bhūtā nisāmetha sabbeti. Atha vā yaṃ purimagāthāya ante “bhāsita”nti vuttaṃ, taṃ kāraṇabhāvena apadisanto āha – “yasmā mama bhāsitaṃ nāma atidullabhaṃ aṭṭhakkhaṇaparivajjitassa khaṇassa [V 1.0236] dullabhattā, anekānisaṃsañca paññākaruṇāguṇena pavattattā, tañcāhaṃ vattukāmo ‘suṇantu bhāsita’nti avocaṃ. Tasmā hi bhūtā nisāmetha sabbe”ti idaṃ iminā gāthāpadena vuttaṃ hoti.

225. 'Therefore, O beings' is the second stanza. Therein, 'therefore' (tasmā) is a word indicating a reason. 'O beings' (bhūtā) is a term of address. 'Listen' (nisāmetha) means 'hear' (suṇātha). 'All' (sabbe) means 'without remainder' (anavasesā). What is said? 'Because you have gathered here to hear the Dhamma, having left behind divine abodes and their wealth of enjoyments, and not for the sake of seeing dancers, actors, and the like, therefore, O beings, listen, all of you.' Alternatively, seeing their joyful state and eagerness to listen attentively from the words, 'May they be joyful, listen attentively,' he said: 'Because you are endowed with a joyful mind, with purity in right self-application, wise attention, and disposition, and with purity in application due to your eagerness to listen attentively, which has reliance on a virtuous person and the voice of another as its proximate cause, therefore, O beings, listen, all of you.' Or alternatively, pointing to what was said at the end of the previous stanza, 'what is spoken,' as the reason, he said: 'Because my speech is exceedingly rare—due to the rarity of the opportune moment for one who has avoided the eight inopportune times—and has many benefits, as it proceeds from the qualities of wisdom and compassion, and I desire to speak it, I said, "Let them listen to what is spoken." Therefore, O beings, listen, all of you.' This is what is said by this line of the stanza.

Evametaṃ kāraṇaṃ niropento attano bhāsitanisāmane niyojetvā nisāmetabbaṃ vattumāraddho “mettaṃ karotha mānusiyā pajāyā”ti. Tassattho – yāyaṃ tīhi upaddavehi upaddutā mānusī pajā, tassā mānusiyā pajāya mittabhāvaṃ hitajjhāsayataṃ paccupaṭṭhāpethāti. Keci pana “mānusiyaṃ paja”nti paṭhanti, taṃ bhummatthāsambhavā na yujjati. Yampi caññe atthaṃ vaṇṇayanti, sopi na yujjati. Adhippāyo panettha – nāhaṃ buddhoti issariyabalena vadāmi, apica pana tumhākañca imissā ca mānusiyā pajāya hitatthaṃ vadāmi – “mettaṃ karotha mānusiyā pajāyā”ti. Ettha ca –

Thus, having established this reason and having directed them to listen to his speech, he began to speak what was to be listened to: 'Cultivate loving-kindness for the human race.' Its meaning is: 'For this human race, which is afflicted by three calamities, you should establish a friendly disposition, an inclination for their welfare.' Some, however, read 'mānusiyaṃ pajaṃ,' but that is not suitable as a locative sense is not possible. And whatever other meaning others may explain, that too is not suitable. The intention here is this: 'I do not speak out of the power of my authority as a Buddha; rather, I speak for the welfare of both you and this human race—"Cultivate loving-kindness for the human race."' And in this connection—

“Ye sattasaṇḍaṃ pathaviṃ vijetvā, rājisayo yajamānā anupariyagā;

Assamedhaṃ purisamedhaṃ, sammāpāsaṃ vājapeyyaṃ niraggaḷaṃ.

'Those royal sages who, having conquered the earth abounding in beings, went about performing sacrifices as patrons—the horse sacrifice, the human sacrifice, the sammāpāsa, the vājapeyya, and the niraggaḷa—'

“Mettassa cittassa subhāvitassa, kalampi te nānubhavanti soḷasiṃ.

'—they do not experience even a sixteenth part of the value of a mind of well-cultivated loving-kindness.'

“Ekampi [M 1.0271] ce pāṇamaduṭṭhacitto, mettāyati kusalī tena hoti;

Sabbe ca pāṇe manasānukampī, pahūtamariyo pakaroti puñña”nti. (a. ni. 8.1) –

'If, with a mind free from ill will, one extends loving-kindness to even a single living being, one becomes skillful thereby. And the noble one, being compassionate in mind toward all beings, makes abundant merit.'

Evamādīnaṃ suttānaṃ ekādasānisaṃsānañca vasena ye mettaṃ karonti, tesaṃ mettā hitāti veditabbā.

In accordance with such suttas and the eleven benefits, it should be understood that for those who cultivate loving-kindness, this loving-kindness is for their welfare.

“Devatānukampito poso, sadā bhadrāni passatī”ti. (dī. ni. 2.153; udā. 76; mahāva. 286) –

'A person shown compassion by the deities always sees what is auspicious.'

Evamādīnaṃ vasena yesu karīyati, tesampi hitāti veditabbā.

In accordance with such teachings, it should be understood that it is also for the welfare of those towards whom it is cultivated.

Evaṃ ubhayesampi hitabhāvaṃ dassento “mettaṃ karotha mānusiyā pajāyā”ti vatvā idāni upakārampi dassento āha “divā ca ratto ca haranti ye baliṃ, tasmā hi ne rakkhatha appamattā”ti. Tassattho – ye manussā cittakammakaṭṭhakammādīhipi devatā katvā cetiyarukkhādīni [V 1.0237] ca upasaṅkamitvā devatā uddissa divā baliṃ karonti, kāḷapakkhādīsu ca rattiṃ baliṃ karonti. Salākabhattādīni vā datvā ārakkhadevatā upādāya yāva brahmadevatānaṃ pattidānaniyyātanena divā baliṃ karonti, chattāropanadīpamālā sabbarattikadhammassavanādīni kārāpetvā pattidānaniyyātanena ca rattiṃ baliṃ karonti, te kathaṃ na rakkhitabbā. Yato evaṃ divā ca ratto ca tumhe uddissa karonti ye baliṃ, tasmā hi ne rakkhatha. Tasmā balikammakāraṇāpi te manusse rakkhatha gopayatha, ahitaṃ tesaṃ apanetha, hitaṃ upanetha appamattā hutvā taṃ kataññubhāvaṃ hadaye katvā niccamanussarantāti.

Thus, showing that it is for the welfare of both parties, after saying, 'Cultivate loving-kindness for the human race,' he now also showed the service they render, saying: 'Those who bring offerings by day and by night—therefore, protect them diligently.' The meaning of this is: Those humans who, by making images of deities through painting, woodwork, and so on, and by approaching shrines, trees, and the like, make offerings to the deities by day, and who make offerings by night during the dark fortnight and at other times; or who, having given ticket-food and other alms, make offerings by day through the dedication and bestowal of merit, beginning with their guardian deities up to the Brahma deities; and who, having arranged for the raising of parasols, the lighting of lamps, the offering of garlands, and the hearing of the Dhamma throughout the night, make offerings by night through the dedication and bestowal of merit—how should they not be protected? Since they thus make offerings for you by day and by night, therefore, protect them. Therefore, also for the reason of their making these offerings, protect and guard those humans. Remove what is not for their welfare and bring about what is for their welfare. Being diligent, placing that gratitude in your hearts, you should be ever mindful of it.

226. Evaṃ devatāsu manussānaṃ upakārakabhāvaṃ dassetvā tesaṃ upaddavavūpasamanatthaṃ buddhādiguṇappakāsanena ca devamanussānaṃ dhammassavanatthaṃ “yaṃkiñci vitta”ntiādinā nayena saccavacanaṃ payujjitumāraddho. Tattha yaṃkiñcīti aniyamitavasena anavasesaṃ pariyādiyati yaṃkiñci tattha tattha vohārūpagaṃ[M 1.0272]. Vittanti dhanaṃ. Tañhi vittiṃ janetīti vittaṃ. Idha vāti manussalokaṃ niddisati, huraṃ vāti tato paraṃ avasesalokaṃ. Tena ca ṭhapetvā manusse sabbalokaggahaṇe patte “saggesu vā”ti parato vuttattā ṭhapetvā manusse ca sagge ca avasesānaṃ nāgasupaṇṇādīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ imehi dvīhi padehi yaṃ manussānaṃ vohārūpagaṃ alaṅkāraparibhogūpagañca jātarūparajatamuttāmaṇiveḷuriyapavāḷalohitaṅkamasāragallādikaṃ, yañca muttāmaṇivālukatthatāya bhūmiyā ratanamayavimānesu anekayojanasatavitthatesu bhavanesu uppannānaṃ nāgasupaṇṇādīnaṃ vittaṃ, taṃ niddiṭṭhaṃ hoti.

226. Having thus shown the beneficial nature of deities towards humans, and for the purpose of alleviating their distress, as well as for the sake of enabling gods and humans to hear the Dhamma by proclaiming the virtues of the Buddha and others, he began to employ a statement of truth with the method beginning, 'Whatever wealth…' Therein, by 'whatever' (yaṃkiñci), in an unspecified manner, everything without exception is included—whatever is suitable for trade in various places. 'Wealth' (vitta) means riches. Indeed, because it generates delight (vitti), it is called 'wealth'. By 'here' (idha vā), it indicates the human world. By 'or elsewhere' (huraṃ vā), it indicates the remaining world beyond that. And by this, although the taking of all worlds, excluding humans, is implied, because 'or in the heavens' (saggesu vā) is stated later, it should be understood as the taking of the remaining nāgas, supaṇṇas, and so forth, excluding both humans and celestial beings. Thus, by these two phrases, whatever wealth of humans is suitable for trade and suitable for adornment and use—such as gold, silver, pearls, gems, beryl, coral, rubies, and cat's-eye gems—is indicated; as is the wealth of the nāgas, supaṇṇas, and others, which has arisen in their abodes—jeweled mansions hundreds of yojanas wide, situated on ground strewn with pearls and gems for sand.

Saggesu vāti kāmāvacararūpāvacaradevalokesu. Te hi sobhanena kammena ajīyanti gammantīti saggā, suṭṭhu vā aggātipi saggā. Yanti yaṃ sassāmikaṃ vā assāmikaṃ vā. Ratananti ratiṃ nayati, vahati, janayati, vaḍḍhetīti ratanaṃ, yaṃkiñci cittīkataṃ mahagghaṃ atulaṃ dullabhadassanaṃ anomasattaparibhogañca, tassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Yathāha –

'Or in the heavens' (saggesu vā) refers to the celestial worlds of the sense-sphere and form-sphere. Indeed, they are called 'heavens' (saggā) because they are attained or gone to (ajīyanti gammanti) through beautiful deeds (sobhanena kammena); or, they are 'heavens' because they are exceedingly (suṭṭhu) excellent (aggā). 'That which' (yaṃ) refers to that which is either owned or unowned. 'Jewel' (ratana) is so called because it leads to (nayati), brings (vahati), generates (janayati), or increases (vaḍḍheti) delight (ratiṃ). It is a designation for whatever is cherished, of great value, incomparable, rare to behold, and an item of use for noble beings. As it is said:

“Cittīkataṃ mahagghañca, atulaṃ dullabhadassanaṃ;

Anomasattaparibhogaṃ, ratanaṃ tena vuccatī”ti.

“That which is cherished and of great value, incomparable and rare to behold, an item of use for noble beings—for that reason it is called a ‘jewel’.”

Paṇītanti uttamaṃ, seṭṭhaṃ, atappakaṃ.
