Evaṃ iminā gāthāpadena yaṃ saggesu anekayojanasatappamāṇasabbaratanamayavimānesu sudhammavejayantappabhutīsu sassāmikaṃ, yañca buddhuppādavirahena apāyameva paripūrentesu sattesu suññavimānapaṭibaddhaṃ assāmikaṃ, yaṃ vā panaññampi pathavīmahāsamuddahimavantādinissitaṃ assāmikaṃ ratanaṃ, taṃ niddiṭṭhaṃ hoti.

'Excellent' (paṇīta) means supreme (uttamaṃ), best (seṭṭhaṃ), unsurpassed (atappakaṃ). Thus, by this phrase of the verse, the following are indicated: whatever owned jewel exists in the heavens—in mansions made entirely of jewels measuring many hundreds of yojanas, such as the Sudhammā hall and the Vejayanta palace; and whatever unowned jewel is connected with an empty mansion, at a time when, in the absence of a Buddha's arising, beings are only filling the lower realms; or whatever other unowned jewel exists, relying on the earth, the great ocean, the Himavanta, and so forth.

Na [V 1.0238] no samaṃ atthi tathāgatenāti na-iti paṭisedhe, no-iti avadhāraṇe. Samanti tulyaṃ. Atthīti vijjati. Tathāgatenāti buddhena. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yaṃ etaṃ vittañca ratanañca pakāsitaṃ, ettha ekampi buddharatanena sadisaṃ ratanaṃ nevatthi. Yampi hi taṃ cittīkataṭṭhena ratanaṃ, seyyathidaṃ – rañño cakkavattissa cakkaratanaṃ maṇiratanañca, yamhi uppanne mahājano na aññattha cittīkāraṃ karoti, na koci pupphagandhādīni gahetvā yakkhaṭṭhānaṃ vā bhūtaṭṭhānaṃ vā gacchati, sabbopi jano cakkaratanamaṇiratanameva cittiṃ karoti pūjeti, taṃ taṃ varaṃ pattheti, patthitapatthitañcassa ekaccaṃ samijjhati, tampi [M 1.0273] ratanaṃ buddharatanena samaṃ natthi. Yadi hi cittīkataṭṭhena ratanaṃ, tathāgatova ratanaṃ. Tathāgate hi uppanne ye keci mahesakkhā devamanussā, na te aññatra cittīkāraṃ karonti, na kañci aññaṃ pūjenti. Tathā hi brahmā sahampati sinerumattena ratanadāmena tathāgataṃ pūjesi, yathābalañca aññe devā manussā ca bimbisārakosalarājaanāthapiṇḍikādayo. Parinibbutampi ca bhagavantaṃ uddissa channavutikoṭidhanaṃ vissajjetvā asokamahārājā sakalajambudīpe caturāsīti vihārasahassāni patiṭṭhāpesi, ko pana vādo aññesaṃ cittīkārānaṃ. Apica kassaññassa parinibbutassāpi jātibodhidhammacakkappavattanaparinibbānaṭṭhānāni paṭimācetiyādīni vā uddissa evaṃ cittīkāragarukāro vattati yathā bhagavato. Evaṃ cittīkataṭṭhenāpi tathāgatasamaṃ ratanaṃ natthi.

Regarding 'There is nothing equal to the Tathāgata' (Na no samaṃ atthi tathāgatena): 'na' is a particle of negation; 'no' is a particle of emphasis. 'Equal' (samaṃ) means comparable (tulyaṃ). 'There is' (atthi) means it exists (vijjati). 'To the Tathāgata' (tathāgatena) means with the Buddha. What is meant? Of all this wealth and these jewels that have been declared, not even one jewel is equal to the Buddha-jewel. For even that which is a jewel by virtue of being cherished—for instance, the wheel-jewel and the gem-jewel of a wheel-turning monarch—when it appears, the great populace shows reverence to nothing else. No one, taking flowers, fragrances, and so on, goes to a shrine of a yakkha or a spirit. All people cherish and worship only the wheel-jewel and the gem-jewel; they pray for this or that boon, and some of their various prayers are fulfilled. Yet even that jewel is not equal to the Buddha-jewel. For if something is a jewel by virtue of being cherished, then the Tathāgata alone is the jewel. Indeed, when the Tathāgata has appeared, whatever powerful devas and humans there are, they show reverence to no other; they worship no one else. Thus, Brahmā Sahampati worshipped the Tathāgata with a jeweled garland the size of Sineru, and other devas and humans—such as King Bimbisāra, the King of Kosala, Anāthapiṇḍika, and others—did so according to their ability. And even after the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna, King Asoka the Great, dedicating it to him, spent ninety-six crores of wealth and established eighty-four thousand monasteries throughout all of Jambudīpa. What, then, needs to be said of the reverence of others? Furthermore, for what other person, even after their parinibbāna, does such reverence and honor continue towards the sites of their birth, enlightenment, the turning of the Dhamma-wheel, and parinibbāna, or towards images and cetiyas, as it does for the Blessed One? Thus, even by the standard of being cherished, there is no jewel equal to the Tathāgata.

Tathā yampi taṃ mahagghaṭṭhena ratanaṃ, seyyathidaṃ – kāsikaṃ vatthaṃ. Yathāha – “jiṇṇampi, bhikkhave, kāsikaṃ vatthaṃ vaṇṇavantañceva hoti sukhasamphassañca mahagghañcā”ti, tampi buddharatanena samaṃ natthi. Yadi hi mahagghaṭṭhena ratanaṃ, tathāgatova ratanaṃ. Tathāgato hi yesaṃ paṃsukampi paṭiggaṇhāti, tesaṃ taṃ mahapphalaṃ hoti mahānisaṃsaṃ, seyyathāpi asokassa rañño. Idamassa mahagghatāya. Evaṃ mahagghatāvacane cettha dosābhāvasādhakaṃ idaṃ tāva suttapadaṃ veditabbaṃ –

Likewise, consider that which is a jewel by virtue of its great value—for instance, cloth from Kāsi. As it is said: 'Monks, even when old, cloth from Kāsi is beautiful, pleasant to the touch, and of great value.' Yet even that is not equal to the Buddha-jewel. For if something is a jewel by virtue of its great value, then the Tathāgata alone is the jewel. Indeed, for those from whom the Tathāgata accepts even a dust-heap robe, for them it becomes of great fruit and great benefit, as was the case for King Asoka. This is on account of his great value. Thus, in this context of speaking of his great value, the following Sutta passage should be understood as that which establishes the absence of fault:

“Yesaṃ kho pana so paṭiggaṇhāti cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānappaccayabhesajjaparikkhāraṃ, tesaṃ taṃ mahapphalaṃ hoti mahānisaṃsaṃ. Idamassa mahagghatāya vadāmi. Seyyathāpi taṃ, bhikkhave, kāsikaṃ vatthaṃ mahagghaṃ, tathūpamāhaṃ, bhikkhave, imaṃ puggalaṃ vadāmī”ti (a. ni. 3.100).

“Moreover, from whomever he accepts the requisites of robes, alms-food, lodging, and medicine for the sick, for them that is of great fruit, of great benefit. I say this on account of his great value. Just as, monks, cloth from Kāsi is of great value, I say, monks, that this person is comparable to that.”

Evaṃ mahagghaṭṭhenāpi tathāgatasamaṃ ratanaṃ natthi.

Thus, even by the standard of great value, there is no jewel equal to the Tathāgata.

Tathā yampi taṃ atulaṭṭhena ratanaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ – rañño cakkavattissa cakkaratanaṃ uppajjati indanīlamaṇimayanābhi sattaratanamayasahassāraṃ pavāḷamayanemi, rattasuvaṇṇamayasandhi, yassa [V 1.0239] dasannaṃ dasannaṃ arānaṃ upari ekaṃ muṇḍāraṃ hoti [M 1.0274] vātaṃ gahetvā saddakaraṇatthaṃ, yena kato saddo sukusalappatāḷitapañcaṅgikatūriyasaddo viya hoti. Yassa nābhiyā ubhosu passesu dve sīhamukhāni honti, abbhantaraṃ sakaṭacakkasseva susiraṃ, tassa kattā vā kāretā vā natthi, kammapaccayena ututo samuṭṭhāti. Yaṃ rājā dasavidhaṃ cakkavattivattaṃ pūretvā tadahuposathe pannarase puṇṇamadivase sīsaṃnhāto uposathiko uparipāsādavaragato sīlāni sodhento nisinno puṇṇacandaṃ viya sūriyaṃ viya ca uṭṭhentaṃ passati, yassa dvādasayojanato saddo suyyati, yojanato vaṇṇo dissati, yaṃ mahājanena “dutiyo maññe cando sūriyo vā uṭṭhito”ti ativiya kotūhalajātena dissamānaṃ nagarassa upari āgantvā rañño antepurassa pācīnapasse nātiuccaṃ nātinīcaṃ hutvā mahājanassa gandhapupphādīhi pūjetuṃ yuttaṭṭhāne akkhāhataṃ viya tiṭṭhati.

Furthermore, that which is a jewel by virtue of its incomparability. To wit: for a wheel-turning monarch, the wheel-jewel arises. It has a hub made of sapphire, a thousand spokes made of the seven gems, a rim made of coral, and joints made of red gold. Above each set of ten spokes is one ornamental knob for catching the wind to produce a sound, and the sound it makes is like that of a five-part orchestra skillfully played. At its hub on both sides are two lion-faces, and the interior is hollow like that of a cart-wheel. It has no maker or one who caused it to be made, but arises from the season due to karmic cause. When the king, having fulfilled the tenfold duties of a wheel-turning monarch, on the Uposatha day, the fifteenth day of the full moon, having bathed his head and observing the Uposatha, is seated in his excellent upper palace purifying his precepts, he sees it rising like the full moon or the sun. Its sound is heard from twelve yojanas away. The great populace, seeing it, becomes exceedingly curious, thinking, 'It seems a second moon or sun has arisen!' It comes above the city and, arriving at the eastern side of the king's inner palace, stands neither too high nor too low, as if fixed on an axle, in a place suitable for the great populace to worship with perfumes, flowers, and the like.

Tadeva anubandhamānaṃ hatthiratanaṃ uppajjati, sabbaseto rattapādo sattappatiṭṭho iddhimā vehāsaṅgamo uposathakulā vā chaddantakulā vā āgacchati. Uposathakulā āgacchanto hi sabbajeṭṭho āgacchati, chaddantakulā sabbakaniṭṭho sikkhitasikkho damathūpeto. So dvādasayojanaṃ parisaṃ gahetvā sakalajambudīpaṃ anusaṃyāyitvā purepātarāsameva sakaṃ rājadhāniṃ āgacchati.

Following that, the elephant-jewel arises: all white, red-footed, firm on seven points, possessed of psychic power, and able to travel through the air. It comes from either the Uposatha clan or the Chaddanta clan. When coming from the Uposatha clan, it is the eldest of all; when from the Chaddanta clan, it is the youngest of all, thoroughly trained and endowed with discipline. Taking a retinue of twelve yojanas, it travels around the whole of Jambudīpa and returns to its own royal capital before the morning meal.

Tampi anubandhamānaṃ assaratanaṃ uppajjati, sabbaseto rattapādo kākasīso muñjakeso valāhakassa rājakulā āgacchati. Sesamettha hatthiratanasadisameva.

Following that, the horse-jewel arises: all white, red-footed, with a head the color of a crow, and a mane like muñja grass; it comes from the royal clan of Valāhaka horses. The rest is the same as the elephant-jewel.

Tampi anubandhamānaṃ maṇiratanaṃ uppajjati. So hoti maṇi veḷuriyo subho jātimā aṭṭhaṃso suparikammakato āyāmato cakkanābhisadiso, vepullapabbatā āgacchati, so caturaṅgasamannāgatepi andhakāre rañño dhajaggato yojanaṃ obhāseti, yassobhāsena manussā “divā”ti maññamānā kammante payojenti, antamaso kunthakipillikaṃ upādāya passanti.

Following that, the gem-jewel arises. That gem is a beryl, brilliant, of fine quality, eight-faceted, and perfectly finished. In length, it is like a wheel-hub. It comes from Mount Vepulla. Placed at the tip of the king's banner, it illuminates a yojana even in the four-fold darkness. By its radiance, people, thinking it is daytime, apply themselves to their work; they can see everything down to the smallest insects and ants.

Tampi [M 1.0275] anubandhamānaṃ itthiratanaṃ uppajjati. Pakatiaggamahesī vā hoti, uttarakuruto vā āgacchati maddarājakulato vā, atidīghādichadosavivajjitā atikkantā mānusaṃ vaṇṇaṃ appattā dibbaṃ vaṇṇaṃ, yassā rañño sītakāle uṇhāni gattāni honti, uṇhakāle sītāni, satadhā phoṭitatūlapicuno viya samphasso hoti, kāyato candanagandho vāyati, mukhato uppalagandho, pubbuṭṭhāyitādianekaguṇasamannāgatā ca hoti.

Following that, the woman-jewel arises. She is either the natural chief queen, or she comes from Uttarakuru or from the royal family of Madda. She is free from faults such as being too tall, and so on. She has surpassed human beauty but has not attained divine beauty. For the king, in the cold season her limbs are warm, and in the hot season they are cool. Her touch is like a ball of cotton carded a hundred times. From her body wafts the fragrance of sandalwood, and from her mouth, the fragrance of the blue lotus. She is also endowed with many virtues, such as rising before him.

Tampi anubandhamānaṃ gahapatiratanaṃ uppajjati rañño pakatikammakaro seṭṭhi, yassa cakkaratane [V 1.0240] uppannamatte dibbaṃ cakkhu pātubhavati, yena samantato yojanamatte nidhiṃ passati sassāmikampi assāmikampi. So rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā pavāreti “appossukko tvaṃ, deva, hohi, ahaṃ te dhanena dhanakaraṇīyaṃ karissāmī”ti.

Following that, the householder-jewel arises: the king's regular treasurer. As soon as the wheel-jewel has arisen, the divine eye manifests for him, by which he sees treasure for a yojana all around, both that with an owner and that without an owner. He approaches the king and makes an offer: 'Your Majesty, be untroubled. I shall do for you what needs to be done with wealth.'

Tampi anubandhamānaṃ pariṇāyakaratanaṃ uppajjati rañño pakatijeṭṭhaputto, cakkaratane uppannamatte atirekapaññāveyyattiyena samannāgato hoti, dvādasayojanāya parisāya cetasā cittaṃ parijānitvā niggahapaggahasamattho hoti. So rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā pavāreti – “appossukko tvaṃ, deva, hohi, ahaṃ te rajjaṃ anusāsissāmī”ti. Yaṃ vā panaññampi evarūpaṃ atulaṭṭhena ratanaṃ, yassa na sakkā tulayitvā tīrayitvā aggho kātuṃ “sataṃ vā sahassaṃ vā agghati koṭiṃ vā”ti. Tattha ekaratanampi buddharatanena samaṃ natthi. Yadi hi atulaṭṭhena ratanaṃ, tathāgatova ratanaṃ. Tathāgato hi na sakkā sīlato vā samādhito vā paññādīnaṃ vā aññatarato kenaci tulayitvā tīrayitvā “ettakaguṇo vā iminā samo vā sappaṭibhāgo vā”ti paricchindituṃ. Evaṃ atulaṭṭhenāpi tathāgatasamaṃ ratanaṃ natthi.

Following that, the counselor-jewel arises: the king's natural eldest son. As soon as the wheel-jewel has arisen, he becomes endowed with surpassing wisdom and discernment, capable of restraining and uplifting the twelve-yojana-wide assembly, having comprehended their minds with his own mind. He approaches the king and makes an offer: 'Your Majesty, be untroubled. I shall govern the kingdom for you.' Or whatever other such jewel there may be that is a jewel by virtue of its incomparability, whose value cannot be determined by weighing or measuring, saying, 'It is worth a hundred, a thousand, or a koṭi.' Among them, not one jewel is equal to the Buddha-jewel. For if there is a jewel by virtue of incomparability, it is the Tathāgata alone. Indeed, the Tathāgata cannot be defined by anyone through weighing or measuring in terms of virtue, concentration, wisdom, or any other such qualities, so as to say, 'He has such and such qualities,' or 'He is equal to this one,' or 'He has a counterpart.' Thus, even in the sense of incomparability, there is no jewel equal to the Tathāgata.

Tathā yampi taṃ dullabhadassanaṭṭhena ratanaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ – dullabhapātubhāvo rājā cakkavatti cakkādīni ca tassa ratanāni, tampi buddharatanena samaṃ natthi. Yadi hi dullabhadassanaṭṭhena ratanaṃ, tathāgatova ratanaṃ, kuto cakkavattiādīnaṃ ratanattaṃ, yāni ekasmiṃyeva kappe anekāni uppajjanti. Yasmā pana asaṅkhyeyyepi kappe tathāgatasuñño loko [M 1.0276] hoti, tasmā tathāgato eva kadāci karahaci uppajjanato dullabhadassano. Vuttaṃ cetaṃ bhagavatā parinibbānasamaye –

Furthermore, that which is a jewel by virtue of its rarity of appearance. To wit: the wheel-turning monarch, whose appearance is rare, and his jewels such as the wheel-jewel—even these are not equal to the Buddha-jewel. For if there is a jewel by virtue of rarity of appearance, it is the Tathāgata alone. How then could the wheel-turning monarch and his retinue be jewels, when many of them arise in a single eon? But since the world is void of a Tathāgata for even an incalculable number of eons, the Tathāgata is therefore rare to behold, arising only now and then, from time to time. And this was said by the Blessed One at the time of his final passing away:

“Devatā, ānanda, ujjhāyanti – ‘dūrā ca vatamha āgatā tathāgataṃ dassanāya, kadāci karahaci tathāgatā loke uppajjanti arahanto sammāsambuddhā, ajjeva rattiyā pacchime yāme tathāgatassa parinibbānaṃ bhavissati, ayañca mahesakkho bhikkhu bhagavato purato ṭhito ovārento, na mayaṃ labhāma pacchime kāle tathāgataṃ dassanāyā’”ti (dī. ni. 2.200).

“The deities, Ānanda, are complaining: ‘We have come from afar to see the Tathāgata, for only rarely do Tathāgatas, Arahants, Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones, arise in the world. And now, in the last watch of this very night, the Tathāgata's final Parinibbāna will occur. And this mighty monk is standing in front of the Blessed One, obstructing the way, so we cannot obtain the opportunity to see the Tathāgata at this final time!’”

Evaṃ dullabhadassanaṭṭhenapi tathāgatasamaṃ ratanaṃ natthi.

Thus, even in terms of rarity of appearance, there is no treasure equal to the Tathāgata.

Tathā yampi taṃ anomasattaparibhogaṭṭhena ratanaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ – rañño cakkavattissa cakkaratanādi. Tañhi koṭisatasahassadhanānampi sattabhūmikapāsādavaratale vasantānampi caṇḍālavenanesādarathakārapukkusādīnaṃ nīcakulikānaṃ omakapurisānaṃ supinantepi paribhogatthāya na [V 1.0241] nibbattati. Ubhato sujātassa pana rañño khattiyasseva paripūritadasavidhacakkavattivattassa paribhogatthāya nibbattanato anomasattaparibhogaṃyeva hoti, tampi buddharatanena samaṃ natthi. Yadi hi anomasattaparibhogaṭṭhena ratanaṃ, tathāgatova ratanaṃ. Tathāgato hi loke anomasattasammatānampi anupanissayasampannānaṃ viparītadassanānaṃ pūraṇakassapādīnaṃ channaṃ satthārānaṃ aññesañca evarūpānaṃ supinantepi aparibhogo, upanissayasampannānaṃ pana catuppadāyapi gāthāya pariyosāne arahattamadhigantuṃ samatthānaṃ nibbedhikañāṇadassanānaṃ bāhiyadārucīriyappabhutīnaṃ aññesañca mahākulappasutānaṃ mahāsāvakānaṃ paribhogo. Te hi taṃ dassanānuttariyasavanānuttariyapāricariyānuttariyādīni sādhentā tathā tathā paribhuñjanti. Evaṃ anomasattaparibhogaṭṭhenāpi tathāgatasamaṃ ratanaṃ natthi.

Likewise, that which is a treasure in the sense of being enjoyed only by a noble being. For example, the wheel-treasure of a wheel-turning monarch. For even if those of low birth—outcastes, bamboo-workers, hunters, chariot-makers, and scavengers—were to dwell in a seven-tiered palace, though they possess wealth worth hundreds of thousands of crores, such a treasure would not appear even in their dreams for their enjoyment. It manifests for the enjoyment only of a well-born noble king, a Wheel-Turning Monarch who has fulfilled the ten royal duties; thus, it is enjoyed only by a noble being. Even so, it is not equal to the Buddha-treasure. For if there is a treasure in the sense of being enjoyed by a noble being, then the Tathāgata alone is that treasure. Indeed, the Tathāgata is not to be enjoyed, even in a dream, by those in the world who are considered noble beings yet lack the supporting conditions and hold perverse views—such as the six teachers like Pūraṇa Kassapa and others of that kind. But he is to be enjoyed by those endowed with supporting conditions, who possess penetrating knowledge and vision and are capable of attaining arahantship at the end of even a four-line verse—such as Bāhiya Dārucīriya and others—and by other great disciples born into great families. For they, by accomplishing the unsurpassed seeing, unsurpassed hearing, unsurpassed service, and so forth, enjoy him in various ways. Thus, even in terms of being enjoyed only by a noble being, there is no treasure equal to the Tathāgata.

Yampi taṃ avisesato ratijananaṭṭhena ratanaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ – rañño cakkavattissa cakkaratanaṃ. Tañhi disvā rājā cakkavatti attamano hoti, evampi taṃ rañño ratiṃ janeti. Puna caparaṃ rājā cakkavatti vāmena hatthena suvaṇṇabhiṅkāraṃ gahetvā dakkhiṇena hatthena cakkaratanaṃ abbhukkirati “pavattatu [M 1.0277] bhavaṃ cakkaratanaṃ, abhivijinātu bhavaṃ cakkaratana”nti. Tato cakkaratanaṃ pañcaṅgikaṃ viya tūriyaṃ madhurassaraṃ niccharantaṃ ākāsena puratthimaṃ disaṃ gacchati, anvadeva rājā cakkavatti cakkānubhāvena dvādasayojanavitthiṇṇāya caturaṅginiyā senāya nātiuccaṃ nātinīcaṃ uccarukkhānaṃ heṭṭhābhāgena, nīcarukkhānaṃ uparibhāgena, rukkhesu pupphaphalapallavādipaṇṇākāraṃ gahetvā āgatānaṃ hatthato paṇṇākārañca gaṇhanto “ehi kho mahārājā”tievamādinā paramanipaccakārena āgate paṭirājāno “pāṇo na hantabbo”tiādinā nayena anusāsanto gacchati. Yattha pana rājā bhuñjitukāmo vā divāseyyaṃ vā kappetukāmo hoti, tattha cakkaratanaṃ ākāsā otaritvā udakādisabbakiccakkhame same bhūmibhāge akkhāhataṃ viya tiṭṭhati. Puna rañño gamanacitte uppanne purimanayeneva saddaṃ karontaṃ gacchati, yaṃ sutvā dvādasayojanikāpi parisā ākāsena gacchati. Cakkaratanaṃ anupubbena puratthimaṃ samuddaṃ ajjhogāhati, tasmiṃ ajjhogāhante udakaṃ yojanappamāṇaṃ apagantvā bhittīkataṃ viya tiṭṭhati. Mahājano yathākāmaṃ satta ratanāni gaṇhāti. Puna rājā suvaṇṇabhiṅkāraṃ gahetvā “ito paṭṭhāya mama rajja”nti udakena abbhukkiritvā nivattati. Senā purato hoti, cakkaratanaṃ pacchato, rājā majjhe. Cakkaratanassa osakkitosakkitaṭṭhānaṃ udakaṃ paripūrati. Eteneva upāyena dakkhiṇapacchimauttarepi samudde gacchati.

Likewise, that which is a treasure in the sense of generating delight without distinction. For example, the wheel-treasure of a wheel-turning monarch. Upon seeing it, the wheel-turning monarch becomes delighted; thus it generates joy for the king. Furthermore, the wheel-turning monarch, taking a golden pitcher in his left hand, sprinkles the wheel-treasure with his right hand, saying, “Roll forth, noble wheel-treasure! Conquer, noble wheel-treasure!” Then the wheel-treasure, emitting a sweet sound like a five-part orchestra, moves through the sky toward the eastern direction. Following right behind, the wheel-turning monarch proceeds by the power of the wheel with his fourfold army spanning twelve yojanas, traveling neither too high nor too low, passing beneath the tall trees and above the short trees. As he goes, he receives gifts from the hands of those who have come bearing offerings of flowers, fruits, and new leaves, and he also receives gifts from the rival kings who have approached with utmost humility, saying, “Come, great king!” He instructs them with principles such as, “Living beings should not be killed.” Wherever the king wishes to eat or to take his midday rest, the wheel-treasure descends from the sky and stands on level ground suitable for all purposes, such as providing water, as if fixed by an axle. When the king’s intention to travel arises again, it proceeds as before, making its sound. Hearing it, the entire assembly spanning twelve yojanas travels through the sky. The wheel-treasure gradually plunges into the eastern ocean. As it plunges, the water recedes for a yojana, standing as if it were a wall. The great multitude takes the seven kinds of treasures as they wish. Then the king, taking the golden pitcher and sprinkling water, declares, “From here onward, this is my kingdom,” and turns back. The army goes in front, the wheel-treasure is behind, and the king is in the middle. The water fills back into the place from which the wheel-treasure had receded. In this same way, it proceeds to the southern, western, and northern oceans.

Evaṃ catuddisaṃ anusaṃyāyitvā cakkaratanaṃ tiyojanappamāṇaṃ ākāsaṃ ārohati. Tattha ṭhito rājā cakkaratanānubhāvena vijitaṃ pañcasataparittadīpapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ sattayojanasahassaparimaṇḍalaṃ pubbavidehaṃ, tathā aṭṭhayojanasahassaparimaṇḍalaṃ uttarakuruṃ, sattayojanasahassaparimaṇḍalaṃyeva [V 1.0242] aparagoyānaṃ, dasayojanasahassaparimaṇḍalaṃ jambudīpañcāti evaṃ catumahādīpadvisahassaparittadīpapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ ekaṃ cakkavāḷaṃ suphullapuṇḍarīkavanaṃ viya oloketi. Evaṃ olokayato cassa anappikā rati uppajjati. Evampi taṃ cakkaratanaṃ rañño ratiṃ janeti, tampi buddharatanasamaṃ natthi. Yadi hi ratijananaṭṭhena ratanaṃ, tathāgatova ratanaṃ. Kiṃ karissati etaṃ cakkaratanaṃ? Tathāgato hi yassā dibbāya ratiyā cakkaratanādīhi sabbehipi janitā cakkavattirati saṅkhampi kalampi kalabhāgampi na [M 1.0278] upeti, tatopi ratito uttaritarañca paṇītatarañca attano ovādappatikarānaṃ asaṅkhyeyyānampi devamanussānaṃ paṭhamajjhānaratiṃ, dutiyatatiyacatutthapañcamajjhānaratiṃ, ākāsānañcāyatanaratiṃ, viññāṇañcāyatanaākiñcaññāyatananevasaññānāsaññāyatanaratiṃ, sotāpattimaggaratiṃ, sotāpattiphalaratiṃ, sakadāgāmianāgāmiarahattamaggaphalaratiñca janeti. Evaṃ ratijananaṭṭhenāpi tathāgatasamaṃ ratanaṃ natthīti.

Having thus surveyed the four directions, the Wheel-Treasure ascends into the sky to a height of three yojanas. Standing there, the king, by the power of the Wheel-Treasure, surveys the conquered lands adorned with five hundred minor islands—Pubbavideha, measuring seven thousand yojanas in circumference; similarly, Uttarakuru, measuring eight thousand yojanas; Aparagoyāna, also measuring seven thousand yojanas; and Jambudīpa, measuring ten thousand yojanas. Thus he surveys a single world-system, encompassing the four great continents adorned with two thousand minor islands, as if it were a grove of fully bloomed white lotuses. As he gazes upon this, immeasurable joy arises in him. In this way, the Wheel-Treasure brings joy to the king, yet even this is not equal to the Buddha-gem. For if a treasure is defined by its ability to bring joy, then the Tathāgata is the true treasure. What can this Wheel-Treasure accomplish? Indeed, the joy produced for a wheel-turning monarch by the Wheel-Treasure and all other such treasures does not amount to a count, a fraction, or a division of a fraction of the divine joy of which the Tathāgata is the source. Beyond that joy, he generates an even higher and more sublime joy for countless devas and humans who act according to his advice: the joy of the first jhāna; the joy of the second, third, fourth, and fifth jhānas; the joy of the base of infinite space; the joy of the base of infinite consciousness, the base of nothingness, and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; the joy of the path of stream-entry; the joy of the fruit of stream-entry; and the joy of the paths and fruits of the once-returner, non-returner, and arahant. Thus, even in terms of generating joy, there is no treasure equal to the Tathāgata.

Apica ratanaṃ nāmetaṃ duvidhaṃ hoti saviññāṇakaṃ aviññāṇakañca. Tattha aviññāṇakaṃ cakkaratanaṃ maṇiratanaṃ, yaṃ vā panaññampi anindriyabaddhaṃ suvaṇṇarajatādi, saviññāṇakaṃ hatthiratanādi pariṇāyakaratanapariyosānaṃ, yaṃ vā panaññampi evarūpaṃ indriyabaddhaṃ. Evaṃ duvidhe cettha saviññāṇakaratanaṃ aggamakkhāyati. Kasmā? Yasmā aviññāṇakaṃ suvaṇṇarajatamaṇimuttādiratanaṃ, saviññāṇakānaṃ hatthiratanādīnaṃ alaṅkāratthāya upanīyati.

Furthermore, that which is called a treasure is of two kinds: animate and inanimate. Among these, the Wheel-Treasure and the Jewel-Treasure, or any other treasure not bound to the sense faculties, such as gold and silver, are inanimate. Animate treasures include the Elephant-Treasure and so on, ending with the Counselor-Treasure, or any other such treasure bound to the sense faculties. Of these two kinds, the animate treasure is declared to be supreme. Why? Because inanimate treasures such as gold, silver, gems, and pearls are used for the adornment of animate treasures such as the Elephant-Treasure and others.

Saviññāṇakaratanampi duvidhaṃ tiracchānagataratanaṃ, manussaratanañca. Tattha manussaratanaṃ aggamakkhāyati. Kasmā? Yasmā tiracchānagataratanaṃ manussaratanassa opavayhaṃ hoti. Manussaratanampi duvidhaṃ itthiratanaṃ, purisaratanañca. Tattha purisaratanaṃ aggamakkhāyati. Kasmā? Yasmā itthiratanaṃ purisaratanassa paricārikattaṃ āpajjati. Purisaratanampi duvidhaṃ agārikaratanaṃ, anagārikaratanañca. Tattha anagārikaratanaṃ aggamakkhāyati. Kasmā? Yasmā agārikaratanesu aggo cakkavattīpi sīlādiguṇayuttaṃ anagārikaratanaṃ pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā upaṭṭhahitvā payirupāsitvā ca dibbamānusikā sampattiyo pāpuṇitvā ante nibbānasampattiṃ pāpuṇāti.

Animate treasures are also of two kinds: the treasure of animals and the treasure of humans. Among these, the treasure of humans is declared supreme. Why? Because the treasure of animals serves as a mount for the treasure of humans. The treasure of humans is also of two kinds: the treasure of women and the treasure of men. Among these, the treasure of men is declared supreme. Why? Because the treasure of women takes on the role of an attendant to the treasure of men. The treasure of men is also of two kinds: the treasure of householders and the treasure of the homeless. Among these, the treasure of the homeless is declared supreme. Why? Because even the highest among householder-treasures, the wheel-turning monarch, attains divine and human prosperity, and ultimately attains the fulfillment of Nibbāna, by venerating with the five-point prostration, attending upon, and waiting upon the homeless treasure, who is endowed with virtues such as morality.

Evaṃ anagārikaratanampi duvidhaṃ – ariyaputhujjanavasena. Ariyaratanampi duvidhaṃ sekkhāsekkhavasena. Asekkharatanampi duvidhaṃ sukkhavipassakasamathayānikavasena, samathayānikaratanampi duvidhaṃ sāvakapāramippattaṃ, appattañca. Tattha sāvakapāramippattaṃ aggamakkhāyati. Kasmā? Guṇamahantatāya. Sāvakapāramippattaratanatopi paccekabuddharatanaṃ aggamakkhāyati. Kasmā? Guṇamahantatāya. Sāriputtamoggallānasadisāpi hi anekasatā sāvakā [V 1.0243] ekassa paccekabuddhassa guṇānaṃ satabhāgampi na upenti. Paccekabuddharatanatopi sammāsambuddharatanaṃ aggamakkhāyati. Kasmā? Guṇamahantatāya. Sakalampi hi jambudīpaṃ pūretvā pallaṅkena pallaṅkaṃ ghaṭṭentā nisinnā paccekabuddhā ekassa sammāsambuddhassa guṇānaṃ neva saṅkhaṃ na kalaṃ na [M 1.0279] kalabhāgaṃ upenti. Vuttampi cetaṃ bhagavatā – “yāvatā, bhikkhave, sattā apadā vā…pe… tathāgato tesaṃ aggamakkhāyatī”tiādi (saṃ. ni. 5.139; a. ni. 4.34; 5.32; itivu. 90). Evaṃ kenacipi pariyāyena tathāgatasamaṃ ratanaṃ natthi. Tenāha bhagavā “na no samaṃ atthi tathāgatenā”ti.

The treasure of the homeless is also of two kinds: noble ones and worldlings. The noble treasure is also of two kinds: trainees and those beyond training. The treasure of those beyond training is also of two kinds: dry-insight practitioners and serenity-vehicle practitioners. The serenity-vehicle treasure is also of two kinds: those who have attained the perfection of a disciple and those who have not. Among them, those who have attained the perfection of a disciple are declared supreme. Why? Because of the greatness of their qualities. Even compared to the treasure of disciples who have attained perfection, the treasure of Paccekabuddhas is declared supreme. Why? Because of the greatness of their qualities. For even many hundreds of disciples like Sāriputta and Moggallāna do not attain even a hundredth part of the qualities of a single Paccekabuddha. Even compared to the treasure of Paccekabuddhas, the treasure of a Sammāsambuddha is declared supreme. Why? Because of the greatness of his qualities. For even if Paccekabuddhas were to fill the entire continent of Jambudīpa, seated cross-legged so that their knees touched, they would not approach a count, a fraction, or a division of a fraction of the qualities of a single Sammāsambuddha. And this was stated by the Blessed One: 'Monks, of all beings, whether footless... the Tathāgata is declared supreme among them,' and so on. Thus, in no way is there any treasure equal to the Tathāgata. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'There is nothing equal to the Tathāgata.'

Evaṃ bhagavā buddharatanassa aññehi ratanehi asamataṃ vatvā idāni tesaṃ sattānaṃ uppannaupaddavavūpasamanatthaṃ neva jātiṃ na gottaṃ na kolaputtiyaṃ na vaṇṇapokkharatādiṃ nissāya, apica kho avīcimupādāya bhavaggapariyante loke sīlasamādhikkhandhādīhi guṇehi buddharatanassa asadisabhāvaṃ nissāya saccavacanaṃ payuñjati “idampi buddhe ratanaṃ paṇītaṃ, etena saccena suvatthi hotū”ti.

Thus, the Blessed One, having declared the Buddha-jewel incomparable to other jewels, now, for the sake of pacifying the arisen dangers for those beings, relies not on birth, clan, noble birth, or excellence of complexion and the like; but rather, within the world that extends from Avīci hell up to the peak of existence, he utters a statement of truth based on the incomparable nature of the Buddha-jewel, which is due to virtues such as the aggregates of moral conduct, concentration, and so on: 'This, too, is the exquisite jewel in the Buddha; by this truth, may there be well-being.'

Tassattho – idampi idha vā huraṃ vā saggesu vā yaṃkiñci atthi vittaṃ vā ratanaṃ vā, tena saddhiṃ tehi tehi guṇehi asamattā buddharatanaṃ paṇītaṃ. Yadi etaṃ saccaṃ, etena saccena imesaṃ pāṇīnaṃ sotthi hotu, sobhanānaṃ atthitā hotu, arogatā nirupaddavatāti. Ettha ca yathā “cakkhuṃ kho, ānanda, suññaṃ attena vā attaniyena vā”tievamādīsu (saṃ. ni. 4.85) attabhāvena vā attaniyabhāvena vāti attho. Itarathā hi cakkhu attā vā attaniyaṃ vāti appaṭisiddhameva siyā. Evaṃ ratanaṃ paṇītanti ratanattaṃ paṇītaṃ, ratanabhāvo paṇītoti ayamattho veditabbo. Itarathā hi buddho neva ratananti sijjheyya. Na hi yattha ratanaṃ atthi, taṃ ratananti sijjhati. Yattha pana cittīkatādiatthasaṅkhātaṃ yena vā tena vā vidhinā sambandhagataṃ ratanattaṃ atthi, yasmā taṃ ratanattamupādāya ratananti paññāpīyati, tasmā tassa ratanattassa atthitāya ratananti sijjhati. Atha vā idampi buddhe ratananti imināpi kāraṇena buddhova ratananti evampettha attho veditabbo. Vuttamattāya ca bhagavatā imāya gāthāya rājakulassa sotthi jātā, bhayaṃ vūpasantaṃ. Imissā gāthāya āṇā koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷesu amanussehi paṭiggahitāti.

The meaning of this is as follows: Whatever wealth or jewel exists, whether here or elsewhere or in the heavens, the Buddha-jewel is sublime, being incomparable with that by means of these various qualities. If this is true, by this truth may there be safety for these beings; may there be prosperity, health, and freedom from danger. Here, as in the passage, 'Indeed, Ānanda, the eye is empty of self or what belongs to self,' (SN 35.85) the meaning is that it is empty of selfhood or belonging to self. Otherwise, it would not be denied that the eye is self or belongs to self. Thus, 'the jewel is sublime' means that the state of being a jewel is sublime; the nature of a jewel is sublime – this is the meaning to be understood. Otherwise, it would follow that the Buddha is not a jewel. For it is not the case that where a jewel exists, that entity is thereby established as a 'jewel'. But where there is the state of being a jewel—defined as that which is cherished and so on, connected in some way or another—it is designated as a 'jewel' on account of that state of being a jewel. Therefore, because of the existence of that state of being a jewel, it is established as a 'jewel'. Or alternatively, by the reasoning 'this too is a jewel in the Buddha,' the Buddha himself is the jewel – this is the meaning to be understood here. And by the mere utterance of this verse by the Blessed One, well-being arose for the royal family, and fear was pacified. The command of this verse was received by non-human beings in a hundred thousand koṭis of world-systems.

227. Evaṃ buddhaguṇena saccaṃ vatvā idāni nibbānadhammaguṇena vattumāraddho “khayaṃ virāga”nti. Tattha yasmā nibbānasacchikiriyāya rāgādayo khīṇā honti parikkhīṇā, yasmā vā taṃ tesaṃ anuppādanirodhakkhayamattaṃ, yasmā ca [M 1.0280] taṃ rāgādiviyuttaṃ sampayogato ca ārammaṇato ca, yasmā vā tamhi sacchikate rāgādayo accantaṃ virattā honti vigatā viddhastā[V 1.0244], tasmā “khaya”nti ca “virāga”nti ca vuccati. Yasmā panassa na uppādo paññāyati, na vayo na ṭhitassa aññathattaṃ, tasmā taṃ na jāyati na jīyati na mīyatīti katvā “amata”nti vuccati, uttamaṭṭhena pana atappakaṭṭhena ca paṇītanti. Yadajjhagāti yaṃ ajjhagā vindi, paṭilabhi, attano ñāṇabalena sacchākāsi. Sakyamunīti sakyakulappasutattā sakyo, moneyyadhammasamannāgatattā muni, sakyo eva muni sakyamuni. Samāhitoti ariyamaggasamādhinā samāhitacitto. Na tena dhammena samatthi kiñcīti tena khayādināmakena sakyamuninā adhigatena dhammena samaṃ kiñci dhammajātaṃ natthi. Tasmā suttantarepi vuttaṃ “yāvatā, bhikkhave, dhammā saṅkhatā vā asaṅkhatā vā, virāgo tesaṃ dhammānaṃ aggamakkhāyatī”tiādi (a. ni. 4.34; itivu. 90).

227. Having thus spoken the truth by means of the Buddha's qualities, he now begins to speak by means of the qualities of the Dhamma of Nibbāna with the words 'destruction, dispassion.' Herein, because lust and so on are destroyed and completely eradicated by the realization of Nibbāna, or because it is the mere destruction which is their non-arising and cessation, and because it is disjoined from lust and so on, both by way of association and as object, and because when it is realized, lust and so on become utterly dispassionate, departed, and dispersed—therefore it is called 'destruction' and 'dispassion.' Further, because its arising is not discerned, nor its passing away, nor any alteration while it persists, it does not come to be, does not age, and does not die, and is thus called 'the Deathless'; and it is called 'sublime' in the sense of being supreme and in the sense of being excellent. What he attained (yadajjhagā) means: what he attained, found, gained, and realized by the power of his own knowledge. The Sakyan Sage (Sakyamuni): he is a Sakyan because he was born in the Sakyan clan; a sage because he is endowed with the qualities of sagehood; a Sakyan who is a sage is the Sakyan Sage. Composed (samāhito) means: with a mind composed by the concentration of the noble path. There is nothing equal to that Dhamma (na tena dhammena samatthi kiñci) means: there is no kind of phenomenon equal to that Dhamma attained by the Sakyan Sage, which is named 'destruction,' etc. Therefore, it is also said in another sutta: 'Bhikkhus, as far as conditioned or unconditioned phenomena go, dispassion is declared the highest among them,' and so on (AN 4.34; It 90).

Evaṃ bhagavā nibbānadhammassa aññehi dhammehi asamataṃ vatvā idāni tesaṃ sattānaṃ uppannaupaddavavūpasamanatthaṃ khayavirāgāmatapaṇītatāguṇehi nibbānadhammaratanassa asadisabhāvaṃ nissāya saccavacanaṃ payuñjati “idampi dhamme ratanaṃ paṇītaṃ etena saccena suvatthi hotū”ti. Tassattho purimagāthāya vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Imissāpi gāthāya āṇā koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷesu amanussehi paṭiggahitāti.

Thus, having spoken of the unequalled nature of the Dhamma of Nibbāna in comparison with other dhammas, the Blessed One now, for the purpose of pacifying the arisen dangers for those beings, relying on the matchless nature of the jewel of the Dhamma of Nibbāna with its qualities of destruction, dispassion, deathlessness, and sublimity, employs a statement of truth: 'This too is the sublime jewel in the Dhamma. By this truth, may there be well-being.' Its meaning should be understood in the way stated for the preceding verse. The command of this verse too was accepted by non-human beings in a hundred thousand koṭis of world-systems.

228. Evaṃ nibbānadhammaguṇena saccaṃ vatvā idāni maggadhammaguṇena vattumāraddho “yaṃ buddhaseṭṭho”ti. Tattha “bujjhitā saccānī”tiādinā (mahāni. 192; cūḷani. pārāyanatthutigāthāniddesa 97; paṭi. ma. 1.162) nayena buddho, uttamo pasaṃsanīyo cāti seṭṭho, buddho ca so seṭṭho cāti buddhaseṭṭho. Anubuddhapaccekabuddhasaṅkhātesu vā buddhesu seṭṭhoti buddhaseṭṭho. So buddhaseṭṭho yaṃ parivaṇṇayī, “aṭṭhaṅgiko ca maggānaṃ, khemaṃ nibbānappattiyā”ti (ma. ni. 2.215) ca “ariyaṃ vo, bhikkhave, sammāsamādhiṃ desessāmi saupanisaṃ saparikkhāra”nti (ma. ni. 3.136) ca evamādinā nayena tattha tattha pasaṃsi pakāsayi. Sucinti kilesamalasamucchedakaraṇato accantavodānaṃ. Samādhimānantarikaññamāhūti yañca attano pavattisamanantaraṃ niyameneva phaladānato “ānantarikasamādhī”ti āhu. Na hi maggasamādhiñhi uppanne tassa phaluppattinisedhako koci antarāyo atthi. Yathāha –

228. Having thus spoken the truth by means of the qualities of the Dhamma of Nibbāna, he now begins to speak by means of the qualities of the Dhamma of the Path with the words 'Which the Buddha Supreme....' Herein, he is a Buddha in the sense of 'he has understood the truths,' etc.; he is supreme (seṭṭho) because he is the highest and praiseworthy. He is a Buddha and he is supreme, thus the Buddha Supreme (buddhaseṭṭho). Or, he is the Buddha Supreme because he is supreme among the buddhas designated as disciple-buddhas and paccekabuddhas. That Buddha Supreme praised and proclaimed it in various places in such ways as: 'And the eightfold among paths is for security, for the attainment of Nibbāna'; and 'Bhikkhus, I will teach you noble right concentration with its basis and accessories.' Pure (suciṃ) means utterly pure because it effects the eradication of the stain of the defilements. The concentration they call 'the immediate' (samādhimānantarikaññamāhu) refers to that which they call 'the immediate concentration' because it invariably gives its fruit immediately after its own occurrence. For when path-concentration has arisen, there is no obstacle at all that can prevent the arising of its fruit. As it is said:

“Ayañca [M 1.0281] puggalo sotāpattiphalasacchikiriyāya paṭipanno assa, kappassa ca uḍḍayhanavelā assa, neva tāva kappo uḍḍayheyya, yāvāyaṃ puggalo na sotāpattiphalaṃ sacchikaroti, ayaṃ vuccati puggalo ṭhitakappī. Sabbepi maggasamaṅgino puggalā ṭhitakappino”ti (pu. pa. 17).

'Suppose this person is practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, and it is the time for the conflagration of the aeon. The aeon would not burn up so long as this person has not realized the fruit of stream-entry. This person is called one who makes the aeon stand still. All persons endowed with the path are persons who make the aeon stand still' (Pug 17).

Samādhinā [V 1.0245] tena samo na vijjatīti tena buddhaseṭṭhaparivaṇṇitena sucinā ānantarikasamādhinā samo rūpāvacarasamādhi vā arūpāvacarasamādhi vā koci na vijjati. Kasmā? Tesaṃ bhāvitattā tattha tattha brahmaloke uppannassāpi puna nirayādīsu uppattisambhavato, imassa ca arahattasamādhissa bhāvitattā ariyapuggalassa sabbuppattisamugghātasambhavato. Tasmā suttantarepi vuttaṃ “yāvatā, bhikkhave, dhammā saṅkhatā, ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo tesaṃ aggamakkhāyatī”tiādi (a. ni. 4.34; itivu. 90).

“No concentration is found equal to that concentration” means: no concentration of the fine-material sphere or the immaterial sphere whatsoever is found equal to that pure, immediate concentration praised by the Supreme Buddha. Why is that? Because when those other concentrations have been developed, it is still possible for one who has been reborn in this or that brahma world to be reborn again in the hells and other such states; but when this concentration of arahantship has been developed, it is possible for the noble person to eradicate all rebirth. Therefore, it is also said in another sutta: “Bhikkhus, of all conditioned phenomena, the noble eightfold path is declared the chief,” and so on (AN 4.34; It 90).

Evaṃ bhagavā ānantarikasamādhissa aññehi samādhīhi asamataṃ vatvā idāni purimanayeneva maggadhammaratanassa asadisabhāvaṃ nissāya saccavacanaṃ payuñjati “idampi dhamme…pe… hotū”ti. Tassattho pubbe vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Imissāpi gāthāya āṇā koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷesu amanussehi paṭiggahitāti.

Thus, having spoken of the unequalled nature of the immediate concentration in comparison with other concentrations, the Blessed One now, in the same way as before, relying on the matchless nature of the jewel of the Dhamma of the Path, employs a statement of truth: “This too is the sublime jewel in the Dhamma… By this truth, may there be well-being.” Its meaning should be understood in the way stated before. The command of this verse too was accepted by non-human beings in a hundred thousand crores of world-systems.

229. Evaṃ maggadhammaguṇenāpi saccaṃ vatvā idāni saṅghaguṇenāpi vattumāraddho “ye puggalā”ti. Tattha yeti aniyametvā uddeso. Puggalāti sattā. Aṭṭhāti tesaṃ gaṇanaparicchedo. Te hi cattāro ca paṭipannā cattāro ca phale ṭhitāti aṭṭha honti. Sataṃ pasatthāti sappurisehi buddhapaccekabuddhasāvakehi aññehi ca devamanussehi pasatthā. Kasmā? Sahajātasīlādiguṇayogā. Tesañhi campakavakulakusumādīnaṃ sahajātavaṇṇagandhādayo viya sahajātasīlasamādhiādayo guṇā. Tena te vaṇṇagandhādisampannāni viya pupphāni devamanussānaṃ sataṃ piyā manāpā pasaṃsanīyā ca honti. Tena vuttaṃ “ye puggalā aṭṭhasataṃ pasatthā”ti.

229. Having thus spoken the truth by means of the qualities of the Dhamma of the Path, he now begins to speak by means of the qualities of the Sangha with the words “Those persons....” Herein, “those” (ye) is an unspecified indication. “Persons” (puggalā) means beings. “Eight” (aṭṭha) is their numerical determination. For they are eight, being four practicing for the fruit and four established in the fruit. “Praised by the good” (sataṃ pasatthā) means praised by the good persons—by the Buddhas, paccekabuddhas, disciples, and other devas and human beings. Why? Because of their connection with the qualities of virtue and so on that are co-nascent with them. For them, the qualities of virtue, concentration, and so on are co-nascent, like the co-nascent color, fragrance, etc., of campaka, bakula, and other flowers. Therefore, like flowers endowed with color and fragrance, they are dear, pleasing, and praiseworthy to the good among devas and human beings. Hence it is said: “Those persons, eight, praised by the good.”

Atha vā yeti aniyametvā uddeso. Puggalāti sattā. Aṭṭhasatanti tesaṃ gaṇanaparicchedo. Te hi ekabījī kolaṃkolo sattakkhattuparamoti [M 1.0282] tayo sotāpannā, kāmarūpārūpabhavesu adhigatapphalā tayo sakadāgāmino, te sabbepi catunnaṃ paṭipadānaṃ vasena catuvīsati, antarāparinibbāyī, upahaccaparinibbāyī, sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī, asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī, uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmīti, avihesu pañca, tathā atappasudassasudassīsu. Akaniṭṭhesu pana uddhaṃsotavajjā cattāroti catuvīsati anāgāmino, sukkhavipassako samathayānikoti dve arahanto, cattāro maggaṭṭhāti catupaññāsa. Te sabbepi saddhādhurapaññādhurānaṃ vasena diguṇā hutvā aṭṭhasataṃ honti. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

Alternatively: “those” (ye) is an unspecified indication. “Persons” (puggalā) means beings. “One hundred and eight” (aṭṭhasataṃ) is their numerical determination. They are: three kinds of stream-enterers—the one-seeder, the clan-to-clanner, and the one who is reborn at most seven times; three kinds of once-returners who have attained the fruit in the sense-sphere, fine-material, and immaterial existences; all these, by way of the four modes of practice, are twenty-four. Then, one who attains Nibbāna in the interim, one who attains Nibbāna upon landing, one who attains Nibbāna with exertion, one who attains Nibbāna without exertion, and one who is heading upstream, bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm; there are five such in the Aviha realm, and similarly in the Atappa, Sudassa, and Sudassī realms; in the Akaniṭṭha realm, however, there are four, excluding the one heading upstream; thus there are twenty-four non-returners. Then, two kinds of arahants—the bare-insight practitioner and the one who uses serenity as a vehicle; and four on the path. Thus there are fifty-four. All of them, being doubled by way of being faith-dominant and wisdom-dominant, become one hundred and eight. The rest is in the way already stated.

Cattāri etāni yugāni hontīti te sabbepi aṭṭha vā aṭṭhasataṃ vāti vitthāravasena uddiṭṭhapuggalā, saṅkhepavasena sotāpattimaggaṭṭho phalaṭṭhoti ekaṃ yugaṃ, evaṃ yāva arahattamaggaṭṭho phalaṭṭhoti ekaṃ yuganti cattāri yugāni honti. Te dakkhiṇeyyāti ettha teti pubbe aniyametvā [V 1.0246] uddiṭṭhānaṃ niyametvā niddeso. Ye puggalā vitthāravasena aṭṭha vā aṭṭhasataṃ vā, saṅkhepavasena cattāri yugāni hontīti vuttā, sabbepi te dakkhiṇaṃ arahantīti dakkhiṇeyyā. Dakkhiṇā nāma kammañca kammavipākañca saddahitvā “esa me idaṃ vejjakammaṃ vā jaṅghapesanikaṃ vā karissatī”ti evamādīni anapekkhitvā dīyamāno deyyadhammo, taṃ arahanti nāma sīlādiguṇayuttā puggalā. Ime ca tādisā, tena vuccanti te “dakkhiṇeyyā”ti.

“These are four pairs” means: all those persons indicated in detail as eight or one hundred and eight are indicated in brief as four pairs—the one on the path to stream-entry and the one established in its fruit forming one pair, and so on up to the one on the path to arahantship and the one established in its fruit forming one pair. “They are worthy of offerings”: here “they” (te) is a specific designation for those previously indicated without specification. Those persons who have been spoken of in detail as eight or one hundred and eight, or in brief as four pairs—all of them are worthy of offerings (dakkhiṇeyyā) because they are worthy of (arahanti) an offering (dakkhiṇaṃ). An “offering” (dakkhiṇā) is a gift given with faith in kamma and its result, without expecting such things as, “This person will do this medical service or run this errand for me.” Persons endowed with qualities like virtue are worthy of it. Since these are such, they are called “worthy of offerings.”

Sugatassa sāvakāti bhagavā sobhanena gamanena yuttattā, sobhanañca ṭhānaṃ gatattā, suṭṭhu ca gatattā suṭṭhu eva ca gadattā sugato, tassa sugatassa. Sabbepi te vacanaṃ suṇantīti sāvakā. Kāmañca aññepi suṇanti, na pana sutvā kattabbakiccaṃ karonti. Ime pana sutvā kattabbaṃ dhammānudhammapaṭipattiṃ katvā maggaphalāni pattā, tasmā “sāvakā”ti vuccanti. Etesu dinnāni mahapphalānīti etesu sugatasāvakesu appakānipi dānāni dinnāni paṭiggāhakato dakkhiṇāvisuddhibhāvaṃ upagatattā mahapphalāni honti. Tasmā suttantarepi vuttaṃ –

“Disciples of the Well-Gone One”: the Blessed One is the Well-Gone One (sugato) because he is endowed with a good going, because he has gone to a good place, and because he speaks rightly; they are disciples of that Well-Gone One. They are “disciples” (sāvakā) because they all listen (suṇanti) to his word. It is true that others also listen, but having listened they do not perform the task that should be done. These, however, having listened, have undertaken the practice in accordance with the Dhamma, which is what should be done, and have attained the paths and fruits; therefore they are called “disciples.” “Gifts given to them bear great fruit” means: even small gifts given to these disciples of the Well-Gone One become of great fruit because the offering has attained purity on account of the recipient. Therefore it is also said in a sutta:

“Yāvatā, bhikkhave, saṅghā vā gaṇā vā, tathāgatasāvakasaṅgho tesaṃ aggamakkhāyati, yadidaṃ cattāri purisayugāni aṭṭha purisapuggalā, esa bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho…pe… aggo vipāko hotī”ti (a. ni. 4.34; 5.32; itivu. 90).

“Bhikkhus, whatever assemblies or groups there are, the Sangha of the Tathāgata’s disciples is declared the foremost among them, that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight individual persons. This Sangha of the Blessed One’s disciples… the result is supreme.” (AN 4.34; 5.32; It 90).

Evaṃ [M 1.0283] bhagavā sabbesampi maggaṭṭhaphalaṭṭhānaṃ vasena saṅgharatanassa guṇaṃ vatvā idāni tameva guṇaṃ nissāya saccavacanaṃ payuñjati “idampi saṅghe”ti. Tassattho pubbe vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Imissāpi gāthāya āṇā koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷesu amanussehi paṭiggahitāti.

Thus, the Blessed One, having described the virtues of the Sangha-jewel by way of all those established in the path and fruit, now, relying on that very virtue, employs a declaration of truth: “This sublime jewel is also in the Sangha…” Its meaning should be understood in the way previously stated. The command of this verse, too, was accepted by non-human beings throughout a hundred thousand crores of world systems.

230. Evaṃ maggaṭṭhaphalaṭṭhānaṃ vasena saṅghaguṇena saccaṃ vatvā idāni tato ekacciyānaṃ phalasamāpattisukhamanubhavantānaṃ khīṇāsavapuggalānaṃyeva guṇena vattumāraddho “ye suppayuttā”ti. Tattha yeti aniyamituddesavacanaṃ. Suppayuttāti suṭṭhu payuttā, anekavihitaṃ anesanaṃ pahāya suddhājīvitaṃ nissāya vipassanāya attānaṃ payuñjitumāraddhāti attho. Atha vā suppayuttāti parisuddhakāyavacīpayogasamannāgatā. Tena tesaṃ sīlakkhandhaṃ dasseti. Manasā daḷhenāti daḷhena manasā, thirasamādhiyuttena cetasāti attho. Tena tesaṃ samādhikkhandhaṃ dasseti. Nikkāminoti kāye ca jīvite ca anapekkhā hutvā paññādhurena vīriyena sabbakilesehi katanikkamanā. Tena tesaṃ vīriyasampannaṃ paññākkhandhaṃ dasseti.

230. Having thus spoken a truth by means of the Sangha’s virtue, in terms of those established in the path and fruit, he now begins to speak by means of the virtue of only those particular individuals who have destroyed the taints and are experiencing the bliss of the attainment of fruition, with the phrase “Those who are well-devoted.” Herein, “those” is an indefinite term of reference. “Well-devoted” means thoroughly devoted; the meaning is that, having abandoned various kinds of wrong livelihood and relying on a pure livelihood, they have begun to devote themselves to insight meditation. Or alternatively, “well-devoted” means endowed with purified application in body and speech. Thereby he shows their aggregate of virtue. “With steadfast mind” means with a firm mind, with a mind endowed with stable concentration; this is the meaning. Thereby he shows their aggregate of concentration. “Free from longing” means that, being unconcerned about body and life, they have departed from all defilements with energy yoked to wisdom. Thereby he shows their aggregate of wisdom endowed with energy.

Gotamasāsanamhīti [V 1.0247] gottato gotamassa tathāgatasseva sāsanamhi. Tena ito bahiddhā nānappakārampi amaratapaṃ karontānaṃ suppayogādiguṇābhāvato kilesehi nikkamanābhāvaṃ dīpeti. Teti pubbe uddiṭṭhānaṃ niddesavacanaṃ. Pattipattāti ettha pattabbāti patti, pattabbā nāma pattuṃ arahā, yaṃ patvā accantayogakkhemino honti, arahattaphalassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ, taṃ pattiṃ pattāti pattipattā. Amatanti nibbānaṃ. Vigayhāti ārammaṇavasena vigāhitvā. Laddhāti labhitvā. Mudhāti abyayena kākaṇikamattampi byayaṃ akatvā. Nibbutinti paṭippassaddhakilesadarathaṃ phalasamāpattiṃ. Bhuñjamānāti anubhavamānā. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Ye imasmiṃ gotamasāsanamhi sīlasampannattā suppayuttā, samādhisampannattā manasā daḷhena, paññāsampannattā nikkāmino, te imāya sammāpaṭipadāya amataṃ vigayha mudhā laddhā phalasamāpattisaññitaṃ nibbutiṃ bhuñjamānā pattipattā nāma hontīti.

“In the dispensation of Gotama” means in the dispensation of the Tathāgata named Gotama by clan. Thereby it is shown that for those outside this dispensation who practice various kinds of asceticism for immortality, there is no departure from the defilements because they lack the qualities of being well-devoted and so on. “They” is a term specifying those previously indicated. Regarding “they have attained the attainable”: here “the attainable” (patti) is what should be attained (pattabba). What is worthy of being attained is that by attaining which one becomes completely secure from the yokes; this is a synonym for the fruit of arahantship. Those who have attained that attainment are “those who have attained the attainable” (pattipattā). “The Deathless” (amata) means Nibbāna. “Having plunged into” (vigayha) means having plunged into it by way of its being an object. “Having obtained” (laddhā) means having received. “Freely” (mudhā) means without cost, without spending even as much as a small coin. “Extinguishment” (nibbuti) means the attainment of fruition in which the torment of the defilements is allayed. “Enjoying” (bhuñjamānā) means experiencing. What is being said? It is this: Those in this dispensation of Gotama who are well-devoted because they are accomplished in virtue, steadfast in mind because they are accomplished in concentration, and free from longing because they are accomplished in wisdom—they, by this right practice, having plunged into the Deathless and obtained it freely, enjoying the extinguishment called the attainment of fruition, are called “those who have attained the attainable.”

Evaṃ bhagavā phalasamāpattisukhamanubhavantānaṃ khīṇāsavapuggalānaṃyeva vasena saṅgharatanassa guṇaṃ vatvā idāni tameva guṇaṃ nissāya saccavacanaṃ payuñjati [M 1.0284] “idampi saṅghe”ti. Tassattho pubbe vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Imissāpi gāthāya āṇā koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷesu amanussehi paṭiggahitāti.

Thus, the Blessed One, having described the virtue of the Sangha-jewel by way of only those individuals with taints destroyed who are experiencing the bliss of the attainment of fruition, now, relying on that very virtue, employs a declaration of truth: “This excellent quality is also in the Sangha.” Its meaning should be understood in the way previously stated. The command of this verse, too, was accepted by non-human beings throughout a hundred thousand crores of world systems.

231. Evaṃ khīṇāsavapuggalānaṃ guṇena saṅghādhiṭṭhānaṃ saccaṃ vatvā idāni bahujanapaccakkhena sotāpannasseva guṇena vattumāraddho “yathindakhīlo”ti. Tattha yathāti upamāvacanaṃ. Indakhīloti nagaradvāranivāraṇatthaṃ ummārabbhantare aṭṭha vā dasa vā hatthe pathaviṃ khaṇitvā ākoṭitassa sāradārumayathambhassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Pathavinti bhūmiṃ. Sitoti anto pavisitvā nissito. Siyāti bhaveyya. Catubbhi vātehīti catūhi disāhi āgatavātehi. Asampakampiyoti kampetuṃ vā cāletuṃ vā asakkuṇeyyo. Tathūpamanti tathāvidhaṃ. Sappurisanti uttamapurisaṃ. Vadāmīti bhaṇāmi. Yo ariyasaccāni avecca passatīti yo cattāri ariyasaccāni paññāya ajjhogāhetvā passati. Tattha ariyasaccāni visuddhimagge vuttanayeneva veditabbāni.

231. Thus, having spoken a truth based on the Sangha by means of the virtue of those with taints destroyed, he now begins to speak by means of the virtue of a stream-enterer, which is directly perceptible to many people, with the words “Just as an Indra’s pillar.” Herein, “just as” is a word of comparison. “An Indra’s pillar” is a designation for a post made of heartwood, hammered into the ground eight or ten cubits deep inside a city-gate’s threshold for the purpose of blocking it. “In the earth” means on the ground. “Set” (sito) means entered into and established. “Would be” (siyā) means might be. “By the four winds” means by the winds coming from the four directions. “Unshakeable” means it cannot be shaken or moved. “Comparable to that” means of such a kind. “A true person” means a supreme person. “I say” means I declare. “Who sees by penetrating the noble truths” means one who sees the four noble truths by having plunged into them with wisdom. Herein, the noble truths are to be understood in the way stated in the Visuddhimagga.

Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepattho – yathā hi indakhīlo gambhīranematāya pathavissito catubbhi vātehi asampakampiyo siyā, imampi sappurisaṃ tathūpamameva vadāmi, yo ariyasaccāni avecca passati. Kasmā? Yasmā sopi indakhīlo viya catūhi vātehi sabbatitthiyavādavātehi asampakampiyo hoti, tamhā dassanā kenaci kampetuṃ vā cāletuṃ vā asakkuṇeyyo. Tasmā suttantarepi vuttaṃ –

This is the concise meaning here: Just as an Indra’s pillar, set in the earth with a deep foundation, would be unshakeable by the four winds, so too, I say, is that true person comparable to it, the one who sees by penetrating the noble truths. Why? Because he, like that Indra’s pillar, is unshakeable by the four winds—that is, by the winds of all the sectarians’ doctrines. Therefore, he cannot be shaken or moved from that seeing by anyone. Thus it is also said in another sutta:

“Seyyathāpi[V 1.0248], bhikkhave, ayokhīlo vā indakhīlo vā gambhīranemo sunikhāto acalo asampakampī, puratthimāya cepi disāya āgaccheyya bhusā vātavuṭṭhi, neva naṃ saṅkampeyya na sampakampeyya na sampacāleyya. Pacchimāya…pe… dakkhiṇāya… uttarāya cepi…pe… na sampacāleyya. Taṃ kissa hetu? Gambhīrattā, bhikkhave, nemassa sunikhātattā indakhīlassa. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, ye ca kho keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā ‘idaṃ dukkhanti…pe… paṭipadā’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānanti, te na aññassa samaṇassa [M 1.0285] vā brāhmaṇassa vā mukhaṃ olokenti ‘ayaṃ nūna bhavaṃ jānaṃ jānāti passaṃ passatī’ti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Sudiṭṭhattā, bhikkhave, catunnaṃ ariyasaccāna”nti (saṃ. ni. 5.1109).

“Monks, suppose there was an iron post or an Indra’s pillar with a deep foundation, well-dug-in, immovable, and unshakeable. If a fierce wind and rain storm came from the east, it would not shake, tremble, or quake. If it came from the west… from the south… from the north, it would not shake, tremble, or quake. For what reason? Because, monks, the foundation is deep and the Indra’s pillar is well-dug-in. So too, monks, whatever ascetics or brahmins understand as it really is: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering,’ they do not look to the face of another ascetic or brahmin, thinking, ‘Surely this venerable one knows what we do not know, sees what we do not see.’ For what reason? Because, monks, the four noble truths have been well seen by them.”

Evaṃ bhagavā bahujanapaccakkhassa sotāpannasseva vasena saṅgharatanassa guṇaṃ vatvā idāni tameva guṇaṃ nissāya saccavacanaṃ payuñjati “idampi saṅghe”ti. Tassattho pubbe vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Imissāpi gāthāya āṇā koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷesu amanussehi paṭiggahitāti.

Thus, the Blessed One, having described the virtue of the Sangha-jewel by way of a stream-enterer who is directly perceptible to many people, now, relying on that very virtue, employs a declaration of truth: “This excellent quality is also in the Sangha.” Its meaning should be understood in the way previously stated. The command of this verse, too, was accepted by non-human beings throughout a hundred thousand crores of world systems.

232. Evaṃ avisesato sotāpannassa guṇena saṅghādhiṭṭhānaṃ saccaṃ vatvā idāni ye te tayo sotāpannā ekabījī kolaṃkolo sattakkhattuparamoti. Yathāha –

232. Having thus spoken a truth based on the Sangha by means of the virtue of a stream-enterer in general, now the text speaks of the three types of stream-enterers: the one-seeder, the clan-to-clansman, and the seven-times-at-most. As it is said:

“Idhekacco puggalo tiṇṇaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ parikkhayā sotāpanno hoti…pe… so ekaṃyeva bhavaṃ nibbattitvā dukkhassantaṃ karoti, ayaṃ ekabījī. Tathā dve vā tīṇi vā kulāni sandhāvitvā saṃsaritvā dukkhassantaṃ karoti, ayaṃ kolaṃkolo. Tathā sattakkhattuṃ devesu ca manussesu ca sandhāvitvā saṃsaritvā dukkhassantaṃ karoti, ayaṃ sattakkhattuparamo”ti (pu. pa. 31-33).

“Here, with the destruction of the three fetters, a certain person becomes a stream-enterer… After being reborn only one more time, he makes an end of suffering: this is the one-seeder. Similarly, one who, after running and wandering through two or three families, makes an end of suffering: this is the clan-to-clan. Similarly, one who, after running and wandering among devas and humans for seven times at most, makes an end of suffering: this is the seven-times-at-most.”

Tesaṃ sabbakaniṭṭhassa sattakkhattuparamassa guṇena vattumāraddho “ye ariyasaccānī”ti. Tattha ye ariyasaccānīti etaṃ vuttanayameva. Vibhāvayantīti paññāobhāsena saccapaṭicchādakaṃ kilesandhakāraṃ vidhamitvā attano pakāsāni pākaṭāni karonti. Gambhīrapaññenāti appameyyapaññatāya sadevakassapi lokassa ñāṇena alabbhaneyyapatiṭṭhapaññena, sabbaññunāti vuttaṃ hoti. Sudesitānīti samāsabyāsasākalyavekalyādīhi tehi tehi nayehi suṭṭhu desitāni. Kiñcāpi te honti bhusaṃ pamattāti te vibhāvitaariyasaccā puggalā kiñcāpi devarajjacakkavattirajjādippamādaṭṭhānaṃ āgamma bhusaṃ pamattā honti, tathāpi sotāpattimaggañāṇena abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇassa nirodhā ṭhapetvā satta [M 1.0286] bhave anamatagge saṃsāre ye uppajjeyyuṃ nāmañca rūpañca[V 1.0249], tesaṃ niruddhattā atthaṅgatattā na aṭṭhamaṃ bhavaṃ ādiyanti, sattamabhave eva pana vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇantīti.

He begins to speak of the virtue of the seven-times-at-most, the lowest of them all, with the verse beginning, “Those who make manifest the noble truths.” Herein, “those who make manifest the noble truths” is as explained before. “They make manifest” (vibhāvayanti) means that with the light of wisdom they dispel the darkness of the defilements that conceals the truths, and make them manifest and evident to themselves. “By the one of profound wisdom” (gambhīrapaññena) means by the Omniscient One, whose wisdom is immeasurable, a wisdom whose basis cannot be found even by the world with its gods. “Well-taught” (sudesitāni) means perfectly taught by various methods such as the concise and the extensive, the complete and the partial, and so on. “Though they are very heedless”: although those persons who have made the noble truths manifest may become very heedless, having come to a basis for heedlessness such as divine kingship or universal sovereignty, still, because the consciousness conditioned by formations has been stopped by the knowledge of the stream-entry path, they do not take up an eighth existence, since the name-and-form that would have arisen in the beginningless round of rebirths—apart from seven existences—has been stopped and has ceased. Rather, having initiated insight meditation in the seventh existence itself, they attain arahantship.

Evaṃ bhagavā sattakkhattuparamavasena saṅgharatanassa guṇaṃ vatvā idāni tameva guṇaṃ nissāya saccavacanaṃ payuñjati “idampi saṅghe”ti. Tassattho pubbe vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Imissāpi gāthāya āṇā koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷesu amanussehi paṭiggahitāti.

Thus, the Blessed One, having described the virtue of the Sangha-jewel by way of the seven-times-at-most stream-enterer, now, relying on that very virtue, employs a declaration of truth: “This excellent quality is also in the Sangha.” Its meaning should be understood in the way previously stated. The command of this verse, too, was accepted by non-human beings throughout a hundred thousand crores of world systems.

233. Evaṃ sattakkhattuparamassa aṭṭhamaṃ bhavaṃ anādiyanaguṇena saṅghādhiṭṭhānaṃ saccaṃ vatvā idāni tasseva satta bhave ādiyatopi aññehi appahīnabhavādānehi puggalehi visiṭṭhena guṇena vattumāraddho “sahāvassā”ti. Tattha sahāvāti saddhiṃyeva. Assāti “na te bhavaṃ aṭṭhamamādiyantī”ti vuttesu aññatarassa. Dassanasampadāyāti sotāpattimaggasampattiyā. Sotāpattimaggo hi nibbānaṃ disvā kattabbakiccasampadāya sabbapaṭhamaṃ nibbānadassanato “dassana”nti vuccati. Tassa attani pātubhāvo dassanasampadā, tāya dassanasampadāya saha eva. Tayassu dhammā jahitā bhavantīti ettha suiti padapūraṇamatte nipāto. “Idaṃsu me, sāriputta, mahāvikaṭabhojanasmiṃ hotī”tievamādīsu (ma. ni. 1.156) viya. Yato sahāvassa dassanasampadāya tayo dhammā jahitā bhavanti pahīnā bhavantīti ayamevettha attho.

233. Thus, having stated the truth that is the basis of the Sangha by way of the quality of not taking up an eighth existence on the part of one who is at most a seven-times-returner, he now begins to speak of the special quality of that same person who takes up seven existences—a quality that distinguishes him from other persons who have not abandoned the taking up of existence—saying, 'Along with his…' Herein, sahāva means 'together with.' Assa refers to one of those mentioned in 'they do not take up an eighth existence.' 'With the accomplishment of vision' means with the attainment of the path of stream-entry. For the path of stream-entry is called 'vision' (dassana) because it is the very first seeing of Nibbāna, by which one sees Nibbāna and accomplishes the task to be done. Its manifestation in oneself is the accomplishment of vision (dassanasampadā); it is just along with this accomplishment. In 'For him three things are abandoned,' the word su is merely an expletive particle, as in such passages as: 'This, Sāriputta, is what happens to me in the case of a great untimely meal.' The meaning here is just this: that along with his accomplishment of vision, three things are abandoned, are given up.

Idāni jahitadhammadassanatthaṃ āha “sakkāyadiṭṭhī vicikicchitañca, sīlabbataṃ vāpi yadatthi kiñcī”ti. Tattha sati kāye vijjamāne upādānakkhandhapañcakasaṅkhāte kāye vīsativatthukā diṭṭhi sakkāyadiṭṭhi, satī vā tattha kāye diṭṭhītipi sakkāyadiṭṭhi, yathāvuttappakāre kāye vijjamānā diṭṭhīti attho. Satiyeva vā kāye diṭṭhītipi sakkāyadiṭṭhi, yathāvuttappakāre kāye vijjamāne rūpādisaṅkhāto attāti evaṃ pavattā diṭṭhīti attho. Tassā ca pahīnattā sabbadiṭṭhigatāni pahīnāniyeva honti. Sā hi nesaṃ mūlaṃ. Sabbakilesabyādhivūpasamanato paññā “cikicchita”nti vuccati, taṃ paññācikicchitaṃ ito vigataṃ, tato vā paññācikicchitā idaṃ vigatanti vicikicchitaṃ, “satthari kaṅkhatī”tiādinā (dha. sa. 1008; vibha. 915) nayena [M 1.0287] vuttāya aṭṭhavatthukāya vimatiyā etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tassā pahīnattā sabbavicikicchitāni pahīnāni honti. Tañhi nesaṃ mūlaṃ. “Ito bahiddhā samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ sīlena suddhi vatena suddhī”tievamādīsu (dha. sa. 1222; vibha. 938) āgataṃ gosīlakukkurasīlādikaṃ sīlaṃ govatakukkuravatādikañca vataṃ “sīlabbata”nti vuccati. Tassa pahīnattā sabbampi naggiyamuṇḍikādi amaratapaṃ pahīnaṃ hoti. Tañhi tassa mūlaṃ. Tena sabbāvasāne vuttaṃ “yadatthi kiñcī”ti. Dukkhadassanasampadāya [V 1.0250] cettha sakkāyadiṭṭhi, samudayadassanasampadāya vicikicchitaṃ, maggadassananibbānadassanasampadāya sīlabbataṃ pahīyatīti viññātabbaṃ.

Now, to show the things that are abandoned, it is said: 'Identity view and doubt, and whatever rule and observance there might be.' Herein, when there is the body—the existing body, that is, the body designated as the five aggregates subject to clinging—the twenty-grounded view regarding this body is identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi). Or, it is identity view in the sense of 'a view regarding the existing body'; the meaning is a view existing in regard to the body as described. Or again, it is identity view in the sense of 'a view in the existing body'; the meaning is a view that proceeds by holding that in the existing body, described as form, etc., there is a self. By its abandonment, all wrong views are abandoned, for it is their root. Wisdom is called 'treatment' (cikicchita) because it allays the sickness of all defilements. One is devoid of that wisdom-treatment, or has departed from it; hence 'doubt' (vicikicchita). This is a term for the eight-based perplexity stated in the way beginning 'one doubts the Teacher…' By its abandonment, all doubts are abandoned, for it is their root. The rules such as cow-practice and dog-practice, and the observances such as cow-duty and dog-duty, mentioned in such passages as 'Outside of this, some ascetics and brahmins claim purity through rules, purity through observances…', are called 'rules and observances' (sīlabbata). By its abandonment, all such other austerities as nakedness and shaven-headedness are abandoned, for this is their root. Therefore, at the very end it is said, 'whatever there might be.' Here, it should be understood that identity view is abandoned through the accomplishment of seeing suffering, doubt is abandoned through the accomplishment of seeing the origin, and rules and observances are abandoned through the accomplishment of seeing the path and Nibbāna.

234. Evamassa kilesavaṭṭappahānaṃ dassetvā idāni tasmiṃ kilesavaṭṭe sati yena vipākavaṭṭena bhavitabbaṃ, tappahānā tassāpi pahānaṃ dīpento āha “catūhapāyehi ca vippamutto”ti. Tattha cattāro apāyā nāma nirayatiracchānapettivisayaasurakāyā, tehi esa satta bhave upādiyantopi vippamuttoti attho.

234. Having thus shown the abandonment of the round of defilements, now, to clarify that when the round of defilements is present there must be a round of results, and that with the abandonment of the former the latter is also abandoned, he says: 'and he is freed from the four planes of misery.' Herein, the four planes of misery are the hells, the animal realm, the sphere of afflicted spirits, and the host of asuras. The meaning is that although this person still takes up seven existences, he is freed from these.

Evamassa vipākavaṭṭappahānaṃ dassetvā idāni yaṃ imassa vipākavaṭṭassa mūlabhūtaṃ kammavaṭṭaṃ, tassāpi pahānaṃ dassento āha “chaccābhiṭhānāni abhabba kātu”nti. Tattha abhiṭhānānīti oḷārikaṭṭhānāni, tāni esa cha abhabbo kātuṃ. Tāni ca “aṭṭhānametaṃ, bhikkhave, anavakāso, yaṃ diṭṭhisampanno puggalo mātaraṃ jīvitā voropeyyā”tiādinā (a. ni. 1.271; ma. ni. 3.128; vibha. 809) nayena ekakanipāte vuttāni mātughātapitughātaarahantaghātalohituppādasaṅghabhedaaññasatthāruddesakammāni veditabbāni. Tāni hi kiñcāpi diṭṭhisampanno ariyasāvako kunthakipillikampi jīvitā na voropeti, apica kho pana puthujjanabhāvassa vigarahaṇatthaṃ vuttāni. Puthujjano hi adiṭṭhisampannattā evaṃmahāsāvajjāni abhiṭhānānipi karoti, dassanasampanno pana abhabbo tāni kātunti. Abhabbaggahaṇañcettha bhavantarepi akaraṇadassanatthaṃ. Bhavantarepi hi esa attano ariyasāvakabhāvaṃ ajānantopi dhammatāya eva etāni vā cha, pakatipāṇātipātādīni vā pañca verāni aññasatthāruddesena saha cha ṭhānāni na karoti, yāni sandhāya ekacce “chachābhiṭhānānī”ti paṭhanti. Matamacchaggāhādayo cettha ariyasāvakagāmadārakānaṃ nidassanaṃ.

Having thus shown the abandonment of the round of results, now, to show the abandonment of the round of kamma, which is the root of this round of results, the Blessed One says: 'and is incapable of committing the six heinous deeds.' Herein, abhiṭhānāni means gross offenses; he is incapable of committing these six. These are to be understood as the acts of matricide, patricide, the murder of an arahant, the shedding of a Buddha's blood, causing a schism in the Sangha, and taking another teacher, which are mentioned in the Book of Ones in the way beginning: 'It is impossible, bhikkhus, it cannot happen that a person accomplished in view would deprive his mother of life…' (AN 1.268-72; MN 115; Vibh 378). For although a noble disciple accomplished in view would not deprive even an ant or a termite of life, these are mentioned to censure the status of a worldling. For a worldling, being unaccomplished in view, commits even such highly blameworthy heinous deeds, but one accomplished in vision is incapable of committing them. And the word 'incapable' is used here to show that he does not commit them even in a future existence. For even in a future existence, though unaware of his status as a noble disciple, by the very nature of things he does not commit these six deeds, or the five transgressions beginning with the taking of life, which along with taking another teacher make six deeds. It is with reference to these that some recite 'the six heinous deeds.' Herein, the taking of dead fish and so on by the village children of noble disciples is an illustration.

Evaṃ [M 1.0288] bhagavā satta bhave ādiyatopi ariyasāvakassa aññehi appahīnabhavādānehi puggalehi visiṭṭhaguṇavasena saṅgharatanassa guṇaṃ vatvā idāni tameva guṇaṃ nissāya saccavacanaṃ payuñjati “idampi saṅghe”ti. Tassattho pubbe vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Imissāpi gāthāya āṇā koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷesu amanussehi paṭiggahitāti.

Thus the Blessed One, having spoken of the quality of the Sangha gem by way of the special quality of a noble disciple who still takes up seven existences—a quality that distinguishes him from other persons who have not abandoned the taking up of existence—now, relying on that very quality, utters a statement of truth: 'This sublime quality too is in the Sangha.' Its meaning should be understood in the way previously explained. The command of this verse too was accepted by non-human beings throughout a hundred thousand crore world-systems.

235. Evaṃ satta bhave ādiyatopi aññehi appahīnabhavādānehi puggalehi visiṭṭhaguṇavasena saṅghādhiṭṭhānaṃ saccaṃ vatvā idāni “na kevalaṃ dassanasampanno cha abhiṭhānāni abhabbo kātuṃ, kiṃ pana appamattakampi pāpaṃ kammaṃ katvā tassa paṭicchādanāyapi abhabbo”ti pamādavihārinopi dassanasampannassa katapaṭicchādanābhāvaguṇena vattumāraddho “kiñcāpi so kammaṃ karoti pāpaka”nti.

235. Thus, having stated the truth that is the basis of the Sangha by way of the special quality of one who takes up seven existences—a quality that distinguishes him from other persons who have not abandoned the taking up of existence—now, in order to speak of the quality of non-concealment of what has been done on the part of one accomplished in vision even if he dwells heedlessly—to the effect that 'Not only is one accomplished in vision incapable of committing the six heinous deeds, but he is also incapable of concealing even a minor evil deed that he has done'—the Blessed One has begun with the words: 'Though he might do an evil deed…'

Tassattho [V 1.0251] – so dassanasampanno kiñcāpi satisammosena pamādavihāraṃ āgamma yaṃ taṃ bhagavatā lokavajjasañciccānatikkamanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “yaṃ mayā sāvakānaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ, taṃ mama sāvakā jīvitahetupi nātikkamantī”ti (cūḷava. 385; a. ni. 8.19; udā. 45), taṃ ṭhapetvā aññaṃ kuṭikārasahaseyyādiṃ vā paṇṇattivajjavītikkamasaṅkhātaṃ buddhapaṭikuṭṭhaṃ kāyena pāpakammaṃ karoti, padasodhammauttarichappañcavācādhammadesanāsamphappalāpapharusavacanādiṃ vā vācāya, uda cetasā vā katthaci lobhadosuppādanajātarūpādisādiyanaṃ cīvarādiparibhogesu apaccavekkhaṇādiṃ vā pāpakammaṃ karoti. Abhabbo so tassa paṭicchadāya, na so taṃ “idaṃ akappiyamakaraṇīya”nti jānitvā muhuttampi paṭicchādeti, taṅkhaṇaññeva pana satthari vā viññūsu vā sabrahmacārīsu āvi katvā yathādhammaṃ paṭikaroti, “na puna karissāmī”ti evaṃ saṃvaritabbaṃ vā saṃvarati. Kasmā? Yasmā abhabbatā diṭṭhapadassa vuttā, evarūpaṃ pāpakammaṃ katvā tassa paṭicchādāya diṭṭhanibbānapadassa dassanasampannassa puggalassa abhabbatā vuttāti attho.

Its meaning is this: Suppose that one accomplished in vision, through a lapse of mindfulness, having lapsed into heedless living, commits some evil deed. Leaving aside that which was spoken by the Blessed One with reference to the intentional transgression of what is blameworthy in the world—'Whatever training rule has been laid down by me for my disciples, my disciples do not transgress it even for the sake of their lives' (Vin II 99; AN 8:19; Ud 5.5)—he commits by body some other evil deed censured by the Buddha, reckoned as a transgression of a formulated rule, such as building a hut for oneself or sleeping together with an unordained person; or by speech, such as harsh speech, idle chatter, or teaching the Dhamma word-by-word for gain; or by mind, such as arousing greed and hate, accepting gold and silver, or not reflecting when using robes and other requisites. He is incapable of concealing it. Knowing 'This is unallowable and should not be done,' he does not conceal it even for a moment. Rather, at that very instant he reveals it to the Teacher or to wise spiritual companions, makes amends in accordance with the Dhamma, and undertakes restraint, resolving, 'I will not do so again.' Why? Because it is said that one who has seen the state is incapable. The meaning is that a person accomplished in vision, who has seen the state of Nibbāna, is said to be incapable of concealing such an evil deed after having done it.

Kathaṃ –

How so?

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, daharo kumāro mando uttānaseyyako hatthena vā pādena vā aṅgāraṃ akkamitvā khippameva paṭisaṃharati[M 1.0289], evameva kho, bhikkhave, ghammatā esā diṭṭhisampannassa puggalassa, kiñcāpi tathārūpiṃ āpattiṃ āpajjati, yathārūpāya āpattiyā vuṭṭhānaṃ paññāyati, atha kho naṃ khippameva satthari vā viññūsu vā sabrahmacārīsu deseti vivarati uttānīkaroti, desetvā vivaritvā uttānīkatvā āyatiṃ saṃvaraṃ āpajjatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.496).

‘Just as, bhikkhus, a young, tender infant lying on its back, having touched a live coal with its hand or foot, quickly withdraws it; so too, bhikkhus, this is the nature of a person accomplished in view: though he might fall into such an offense for which an emergence is prescribed, he quickly confesses it, reveals it, and discloses it to the Teacher or to wise spiritual companions. Having confessed, revealed, and disclosed it, he undertakes restraint for the future’ (MN 65).

Evaṃ bhagavā pamādavihārinopi dassanasampannassa katapaṭicchādanābhāvaguṇena saṅgharatanassa guṇaṃ vatvā idāni tameva guṇaṃ nissāya saccavacanaṃ payuñjati “idampi saṅghe”ti. Tassattho pubbe vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Imissāpi gāthāya āṇā koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷesu amanussehi paṭiggahitāti.

Thus the Blessed One, having spoken of the quality of the Sangha gem by way of the quality of non-concealment of what has been done on the part of one accomplished in vision even if he dwells heedlessly, now, relying on that very quality, utters a statement of truth: 'This sublime quality too is in the Sangha.' Its meaning should be understood in the way previously explained. The command of this verse too was accepted by non-human beings throughout a hundred thousand crore world-systems.

236. Evaṃ saṅghapariyāpannānaṃ puggalānaṃ tena tena guṇappakārena saṅghādhiṭṭhānaṃ saccaṃ vatvā idāni yvāyaṃ bhagavatā ratanattayaguṇaṃ dīpentena idha saṅkhepena aññatra ca vitthārena pariyattidhammo desito, tampi nissāya puna buddhādhiṭṭhānaṃ saccaṃ vattumāraddho “vanappagumbe yatha phussitagge”ti. Tattha āsannasannivesavavatthitānaṃ rukkhānaṃ samūho vanaṃ, mūlasārapheggutacasākhāpalāsehi pavuḍḍho gumbo pagumbo, vane pagumbo vanappagumbo, svāyaṃ “vanappagumbe”ti vutto[V 1.0252].
