Evampi hi vattuṃ labbhati “atthi savitakkasavicāre, atthi avitakkavicāramatte, sukhe dukkhe jīve”tiādīsu viya. Yathāti opammavacanaṃ. Phussitāni aggāni assāti phussitaggo, sabbasākhāpasākhāsu sañjātapupphoti attho. So pubbe vuttanayeneva “phussitagge”ti vutto. Gimhāna māse paṭhamasmiṃ gimheti ye cattāro gimhamāsā, tesaṃ catunnaṃ gimhānaṃ ekasmiṃ māse. Katamasmiṃ māse iti ce? Paṭhamasmiṃ gimhe, citramāseti attho. So hi “paṭhamagimho”ti ca “bālavasanto”ti ca vuccati. Tato paraṃ padatthato pākaṭameva.

236. Thus, having spoken a truthful statement based on the Sangha concerning the individuals included in it by way of their various qualities, now, relying also on that scriptural teaching taught by the Blessed One—who was illuminating the qualities of the Triple Gem here in brief and elsewhere in detail—he begins again to declare a truthful statement based on the Buddha, saying: “As in a forest grove when the treetops are in bloom.” Here, a collection of trees established in close proximity is a forest. A shrub with developed roots, heartwood, sapwood, bark, branches, and leaves is a pagumbo; a pagumbo in a forest is a vanappagumbo, a forest grove. This is expressed by the locative “in a forest grove” (vanappagumbe). For it can also be expressed this way, as in such passages as: “there is that with initial and sustained thought; there is that without initial thought but with sustained thought only; in pleasure; in pain; in a living being.” The word “as” (yathā) indicates a simile. “With flowering treetops” (phussitagge) means one whose tops are flowering; the meaning is that flowers have appeared on all its branches and sub-branches. This is expressed by the locative “with flowering treetops” (phussitagge) in the way explained before. “In a month of the summer, in the first summer”: of the four summer months, in one of them. Which month? The first summer, meaning the month of Citra. For this is called both “the first summer” and “the early spring.” Beyond this, the meaning of the words is clear.

Ayaṃ panettha piṇḍattho – yathā paṭhamagimhanāmake bālavasante nānāvidharukkhagahane vane supupphitaggasākho taruṇarukkhagacchapariyāyanāmo pagumbo ativiya sassiriko hoti, evamevaṃ khandhāyatanādīhi satipaṭṭhānasammappadhānādīhi [M 1.0290] sīlasamādhikkhandhādīhi vā nānappakārehi atthappabhedapupphehi ativiya sassirikattā tathūpamaṃ nibbānagāmimaggadīpanato nibbānagāmiṃ pariyattidhammavaraṃ neva lābhahetu na sakkārādihetu, kevalañhi mahākaruṇāya abbhussāhitahadayo sattānaṃ paramaṃhitāya adesayīti. Paramaṃhitāyāti ettha ca gāthābandhasukhatthaṃ anunāsiko, ayaṃ panattho “paramahitāya nibbānāya adesayī”ti.

Here is the summary meaning: Just as in the first summer month, the early spring, in a forest thicket of various trees, a young tree or shrub (pagumbo) with its branch-tips in full bloom becomes exceedingly splendid, so too, the excellent scriptural teaching (pariyattidhammavaraṃ) is comparable to that. Because it is exceedingly splendid with the various kinds of flowers that are its different kinds of meanings—such as the aggregates and sense bases, the foundations of mindfulness and right strivings, or the aggregates of virtue and concentration—and because it illuminates the path leading to Nibbāna, he taught this teaching that leads to Nibbāna. He taught it not for the sake of gain, honor, or the like, but solely because his heart was impelled by great compassion, for the supreme welfare of beings. In the phrase paramaṃhitāya (“for the supreme welfare”), the nasal is for metrical ease; the meaning is: “He taught for the supreme welfare, for Nibbāna.”

Evaṃ bhagavā imaṃ supupphitaggavanappagumbasadisaṃ pariyattidhammaṃ vatvā idāni tameva nissāya buddhādhiṭṭhānaṃ saccavacanaṃ payuñjati “idampi buddhe”ti. Tassattho pubbe vuttanayeneva veditabbo, kevalaṃ pana idampi yathāvuttappakārapariyattidhammasaṅkhātaṃ buddhe ratanaṃ paṇītanti yojetabbaṃ. Imissāpi gāthāya āṇā koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷesu amanussehi paṭiggahitāti.

Thus, the Blessed One, having spoken of this Dhamma of learning which resembles a forest grove with flowering treetops, now, relying on that very teaching, utters a truthful statement based on the Buddha: “This too in the Buddha is a sublime jewel.” Its meaning should be understood in the way previously stated. However, it should be connected thus: this sublime jewel in the Buddha is what is reckoned as the Dhamma of learning of the kind described above. The command of this verse too was accepted by non-human beings in a hundred thousand koṭi of world-systems.

237. Evaṃ bhagavā pariyattidhammena buddhādhiṭṭhānaṃ saccaṃ vatvā idāni lokuttaradhammena vattumāraddho “varo varaññū”ti. Tattha varoti paṇītādhimuttikehi icchito “aho vata mayampi evarūpā assāmā”ti, varaguṇayogato vā varo, uttamo seṭṭhoti attho. Varaññūti nibbānaññū. Nibbānañhi sabbadhammānaṃ uttamaṭṭhena varaṃ, tañcesa bodhimūle sayaṃ paṭivijjhitvā aññāsi. Varadoti pañcavaggiyabhaddavaggiyajaṭilādīnaṃ aññesañca devamanussānaṃ nibbedhabhāgiyavāsanābhāgiyavaradhammadāyīti attho. Varāharoti varassa maggassa āhaṭattā varāharoti vuccati. So hi bhagavā dīpaṅkarato pabhuti samatiṃsa pāramiyo pūrento pubbakehi sammāsambuddhehi anuyātaṃ purāṇaṃ maggavaraṃ āhari, tena varāharoti vuccati. Apica sabbaññutaññāṇapaṭilābhena varo, nibbānasacchikiriyāya varaññū, sattānaṃ vimuttisukhadānena varado, uttamapaṭipadāharaṇena varāharo, etehi lokuttaraguṇehi adhikassa kassaci abhāvato anuttaro.

237. Thus, the Blessed One, having spoken a truthful statement based on the Buddha by means of the scriptural teaching, now begins to speak by means of the supramundane Dhamma with the words: “The Excellent One, Knower of the Excellent.” Herein, “the Excellent One” (varo) is desired by those resolved on the sublime, thinking: “Oh, may we too become such!” Or, he is the Excellent One due to being endowed with excellent qualities—supreme, the best. “Knower of the Excellent” (varaññū) means the Knower of Nibbāna. For Nibbāna is the excellent (varaṃ) among all things by virtue of being the highest; and He, having directly realized it at the foot of the Bodhi tree, knew it Himself. “Giver of the Excellent” (varado) means the Giver of the excellent Dhamma, which partakes of penetration and of the right conditions, to beings such as the group of five, the Bhaddavaggiya group, the matted-hair ascetics, and other devas and humans. “Bringer of the Excellent” (varāharo) is so called because He brought the excellent Path. For this Blessed One, fulfilling the thirty perfections from the time of Dīpaṅkara, brought forth the ancient, excellent Path followed by previous Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones—thus He is called the Bringer of the Excellent. Furthermore, through the attainment of the knowledge of omniscience, He is the Excellent One; through the realization of Nibbāna, He is the Knower of the Excellent; through granting beings the happiness of liberation, He is the Giver of the Excellent; through bringing the supreme practice, He is the Bringer of the Excellent. Due to the absence of anyone superior to Him in these supramundane qualities, He is the Unsurpassed One.

Aparo [V 1.0253] nayo – varo upasamādhiṭṭhānaparipūraṇena, varaññū paññādhiṭṭhānaparipūraṇena, varado cāgādhiṭṭhānaparipūraṇena, varāharo saccādhiṭṭhānaparipūraṇena, varaṃ maggasaccamāharīti. Tathā varo puññussayena, varaññū paññussayena, varado buddhabhāvatthikānaṃ tadupāyasampadānena, varāharo [M 1.0291] paccekabuddhabhāvatthikānaṃ tadupāyāharaṇena, anuttaro tattha tattha asadisatāya, attanā vā anācariyako hutvā paresaṃ ācariyabhāvena, dhammavaraṃ adesayi sāvakabhāvatthikānaṃ tadatthāya svākhātatādiguṇayuttassa varadhammassa desanato. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti.

Another method: He is the Excellent One through the fulfillment of the determination on peace; the Knower of the Excellent through the fulfillment of the determination on wisdom; the Giver of the Excellent through the fulfillment of the determination on relinquishment; the Bringer of the Excellent through the fulfillment of the determination on truth, for he brought the excellent truth of the path. Likewise, he is the Excellent One through his abundance of merit; the Knower of the Excellent through his abundance of wisdom; the Giver of the Excellent by bestowing the means on those who desire the state of a Buddha; the Bringer of the Excellent by bringing the means to those who desire the state of a Paccekabuddha. He is the Unsurpassed One because of being unequalled in every respect, or because, having no teacher himself, he became a teacher to others. He taught the excellent Dhamma: because he taught the excellent Dhamma endowed with such qualities as being well-expounded for the benefit of those who desire the state of a disciple. The rest is as has been said.

Evaṃ bhagavā navavidhena lokuttaradhammena attano guṇaṃ vatvā idāni tameva guṇaṃ nissāya buddhādhiṭṭhānaṃ saccavacanaṃ payuñjati “idampi buddhe”ti. Tassattho pubbe vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Kevalaṃ pana yaṃ varaṃ navalokuttaradhammaṃ esa aññāsi, yañca adāsi, yañca āhari, yañca adesayi, idampi buddhe ratanaṃ paṇītanti evaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Imissāpi gāthāya āṇā koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷesu amanussehi paṭiggahitāti.

Thus, the Blessed One, having spoken of his own qualities by means of the ninefold supramundane Dhamma, now, relying on those very qualities, utters a truthful statement based on the Buddha: “This too in the Buddha is a sublime jewel.” Its meaning should be understood in the way previously stated. However, it should be connected thus: whatever excellent ninefold supramundane Dhamma He knew, and gave, and brought, and taught—this too in the Buddha is a sublime jewel. The command of this verse too was accepted by non-human beings in a hundred thousand koṭi of world-systems.

238. Evaṃ bhagavā pariyattidhammaṃ lokuttaradhammañca nissāya dvīhi gāthāhi buddhādhiṭṭhānaṃ saccaṃ vatvā idāni ye taṃ pariyattidhammaṃ assosuṃ sutānusārena ca paṭipajjitvā navappakārampi lokuttaradhammaṃ adhigamiṃsu, tesaṃ anupādisesanibbānappattiguṇaṃ nissāya puna saṅghādhiṭṭhānaṃ saccaṃ vattumāraddho “khīṇaṃ purāṇa”nti. Tattha khīṇanti samucchinnaṃ. Purāṇanti purātanaṃ. Navanti sampati vattamānaṃ. Natthisambhavanti avijjamānapātubhāvaṃ. Virattacittāti vigatarāgacittā. Āyatike bhavasminti anāgatamaddhānaṃ punabbhave. Teti yesaṃ khīṇaṃ purāṇaṃ navaṃ natthisambhavaṃ, ye ca āyatike bhavasmiṃ virattacittā, te khīṇāsavā bhikkhū. Khīṇabījāti ucchinnabījā. Avirūḷhichandāti virūḷhichandavirahitā. Nibbantīti vijjhāyanti. Dhīrāti dhitisampannā. Yathāyaṃ padīpoti ayaṃ padīpo viya.

238. Thus, the Blessed One, relying on both the scriptural teaching and the supramundane Dhamma, having spoken a truth-statement established on the Buddha in two verses, now, relying on the quality of attaining Nibbāna without residue of those who heard that scriptural teaching, practiced in accordance with what they heard, and attained the ninefold supramundane Dhamma, began to speak a truth-statement established on the Sangha, beginning with: 'The old is destroyed.' Herein, 'destroyed' means completely eradicated. 'The old' means ancient. 'New' means presently occurring. 'There is no arising' means the non-existence of a future appearance. 'With detached minds' means with minds devoid of lust. 'In future existence' means in a future time, in a new becoming. 'They' refers to those bhikkhus with cankers destroyed for whom the old is destroyed, for whom the new has no arising, and whose minds are detached from future existence. 'With seeds destroyed' means with seeds cut off. 'Without desire that has sprouted' means devoid of sprouted desire. 'They are extinguished' means they are quenched. 'The steadfast' means those endowed with fortitude. 'Just as this lamp' means like this lamp.

Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yaṃ taṃ sattānaṃ uppajjitvā niruddhampi purāṇaṃ atītakālikaṃ kammaṃ taṇhāsinehassa appahīnattā paṭisandhiāharaṇasamatthatāya akhīṇaṃyeva hoti, taṃ purāṇaṃ kammaṃ yesaṃ arahattamaggena taṇhāsinehassa sositattā agginā daḍḍhabījamiva āyatiṃ vipākadānāsamatthatāya khīṇaṃ. Yañca nesaṃ buddhapūjādivasena idāni pavattamānaṃ kammaṃ navanti vuccati, tañca taṇhāpahāneneva chinnamūlapādapapupphamiva āyatiṃ phaladānāsamatthatāya yesaṃ natthisambhavaṃ, ye ca taṇhāpahāneneva āyatike bhavasmiṃ virattacittā, te khīṇāsavā bhikkhū “kammaṃ khettaṃ viññāṇaṃ [M 1.0292] bīja”nti (a. ni. 3.77) ettha vuttassa paṭisandhiviññāṇassa kammakkhayeneva khīṇattā khīṇabījā. Yopi pubbe punabbhavasaṅkhātāya virūḷhiyā chando ahosi, tassāpi samudayappahāneneva pahīnattā pubbe viya cutikāle asambhavena avirūḷhichandā [V 1.0254] dhitisampannattā dhīrā carimaviññāṇanirodhena yathāyaṃ padīpo nibbuto, evaṃ nibbanti, puna “rūpino vā arūpino vā”ti evamādiṃ paññattipathaṃ accentīti. Tasmiṃ kira samaye nagaradevatānaṃ pūjanatthāya jālitesu padīpesu eko padīpo vijjhāyi, taṃ dassento āha – “yathāyaṃ padīpo”ti.

What is meant? That old, past-time kamma of beings, which, though it has arisen and ceased, remains unexhausted because the adhesive of craving has not been abandoned, and is thus capable of bringing about rebirth—that old kamma is exhausted for those in whom the adhesive of craving has been dried up by the path of arahantship, so that, like a seed scorched by fire, it is incapable of giving a result in the future. And that kamma of theirs which is occurring now, such as through honoring the Buddha, is called ‘new’; but for them, because craving has been abandoned, this too has no future arising, being incapable of giving a fruit in the future, like a flower from a plant with its root cut. Those bhikkhus with cankers destroyed, whose minds are detached from future existence because craving has been abandoned, are ‘those with destroyed seeds’ because the rebirth-linking consciousness mentioned in the passage, “Kamma is the field, consciousness the seed,” has been destroyed through the destruction of kamma. And as for the desire for the growth called renewed existence which they formerly had, that too has been abandoned with the abandoning of its origin; thus, not arising at the time of death as it did before, they are ‘without desire that has sprouted.’ Being endowed with fortitude, they are steadfast. With the cessation of the final consciousness, they are extinguished just as this lamp is extinguished; they transcend the range of designation such as ‘one with form or one without form.’ It is said that at that time, among the lamps lit for the worship of the city deities, one lamp went out. Pointing to it, he said: “Just as this lamp.”

Evaṃ bhagavā ye taṃ purimāhi dvīhi gāthāhi vuttaṃ pariyattidhammaṃ assosuṃ, sutānusāreneva paṭipajjitvā navappakārampi lokuttaradhammaṃ adhigamiṃsu, tesaṃ anupādisesanibbānappattiguṇaṃ vatvā idāni tameva guṇaṃ nissāya saṅghādhiṭṭhānaṃ saccavacanaṃ payuñjanto desanaṃ samāpesi “idampi saṅghe”ti. Tassattho pubbe vuttanayeneva veditabbo, kevalaṃ pana idampi yathāvuttena pakārena khīṇāsavabhikkhūnaṃ nibbānasaṅkhātaṃ saṅghe ratanaṃ paṇītanti evaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Imissāpi gāthāya āṇā koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷesu amanussehi paṭiggahitāti.

Thus the Blessed One, having spoken of the quality of attaining Nibbāna without residue for those who had heard the scriptural teaching as stated in the two previous verses, practiced in accordance with what they had heard, and attained the ninefold supramundane Dhamma, then, relying on that very quality, concluded the teaching by employing an asseveration of truth based on the Sangha, beginning with 'This too in the Sangha...' Its meaning should be understood in the same way as previously stated. However, it should be construed thus: This sublime treasure in the Sangha, designated as Nibbāna for the bhikkhus whose cankers are destroyed in the manner described, is also excellent. The command of this verse, too, was accepted by non-human beings in a hundred thousand koṭis of world-systems.

Desanāpariyosāne rājakulassa sotthi ahosi, sabbūpaddavā vūpasamiṃsu caturāsītiyā pāṇasahassānaṃ dhammābhisamayo ahosi.

At the conclusion of the discourse, there was well-being for the royal family. All calamities subsided, and a realization of the Dhamma arose in eighty-four thousand beings.

239-241. Atha sakko devānamindo “bhagavatā ratanattayaguṇaṃ nissāya saccavacanaṃ payuñjamānena nāgarassa sotthi katā, mayāpi nāgarassa sotthitthaṃ ratanattayaguṇaṃ nissāya kiñci vattabba”nti cintetvā avasāne gāthāttayaṃ abhāsi “yānīdha bhūtānī”ti. Tattha yasmā buddho yathā lokahitatthāya ussukkaṃ āpannehi āgantabbaṃ, tathā āgatato, yathā ca etehi gantabbaṃ, tathā gatato, yathā vā etehi ājānitabbaṃ, tathā ājānanato, yathā ca jānitabbaṃ, tathā jānanato, yañca tatheva hoti, tassa gadanato ca “tathāgato”ti vuccati. Yasmā ca so devamanussehi pupphagandhādinā bahinibbattena upakaraṇena, dhammānudhammappaṭipattādinā ca attani nibbattena ativiya pūjito, tasmā sakko devānamindo sabbadevaparisaṃ attanā saddhiṃ sampiṇḍetvā [M 1.0293] āha “tathāgataṃ devamanussapūjitaṃ, buddhaṃ namassāma suvatthi hotū”ti.

Then Sakka, lord of the devas, thought: 'The Blessed One, by employing an asseveration of truth relying on the qualities of the Triple Gem, has brought about the well-being of the city. I too should say something for the well-being of the city, relying on the qualities of the Triple Gem.' Having reflected thus, at the end he recited three verses. Herein, the Buddha is called 'Tathāgata' because he has come as one should come for the welfare of the world; because he has gone as one should go; because he understands as one should understand; because he knows what should be known; and because he speaks what is so. And because he is exceedingly honored by devas and humans with external requisites such as flowers and incense, and with the internal practice in accordance with the Dhamma, therefore Sakka, lord of the devas, gathering the entire assembly of devas together with himself, said: 'We pay homage to the Tathāgata, the Buddha, honored by devas and humans. May there be well-being!'

Yasmā pana dhamme maggadhammo yathā yuganandha samathavipassanābalena gantabbaṃ kilesapakkhaṃ samucchindantena, tathā gatoti tathāgato. Nibbānadhammopi yathā gato paññāya paṭividdho sabbadukkhavighātāya sampajjati, buddhādīhi tathā avagato, tasmā “tathāgato”ti vuccati. Yasmā ca saṅghopi yathā attahitāya paṭipannehi gantabbaṃ tena tena maggena, tathā gato, tasmā “tathāgato” tveva vuccati. Tasmā avasesagāthādvayepi tathāgataṃ dhammaṃ namassāma suvatthi hotu, tathāgataṃ saṅghaṃ namassāma suvatthi hotūti vuttaṃ. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti.

Because the path-Dhamma is 'thus gone' (tathā gato) with the balanced strength of serenity and insight that cuts off the faction of defilements, it is called 'Tathāgata.' The Dhamma of Nibbāna, too, is 'thus gone' (tathā gato) in that it is penetrated by wisdom and leads to the destruction of all suffering, and is 'thus understood' (tathā avagato) by the Buddhas and others; therefore, it is called 'Tathāgata.' And because the Sangha has 'thus gone' (tathā gato) along the respective paths for their own welfare, they too are called 'Tathāgata.' Therefore, in the remaining two verses, it is said: 'We pay homage to the Dhamma that is "thus gone," may there be well-being. We pay homage to the Sangha that is "thus gone," may there be well-being.' The rest is as said before.

Evaṃ [V 1.0255] sakko devānamindo imaṃ gāthāttayaṃ bhāsitvā bhagavantaṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā devapurameva gato saddhiṃ devaparisāya. Bhagavā pana tadeva ratanasuttaṃ dutiyadivasepi desesi, puna caturāsītiyā pāṇasahassānaṃ dhammābhisamayo ahosi. Evaṃ bhagavā yāva sattamaṃ divasaṃ desesi, divase divase tatheva dhammābhisamayo ahosi. Bhagavā aḍḍhamāsameva vesāliyaṃ viharitvā rājūnaṃ “gacchāmā”ti paṭivedesi. Tato rājāno diguṇena sakkārena puna tīhi divasehi bhagavantaṃ gaṅgātīraṃ nayiṃsu. Gaṅgāyaṃ nibbattā nāgarājāno cintesuṃ – “manussā tathāgatassa sakkāraṃ karonti, mayaṃ kiṃ na karissāmā”ti suvaṇṇarajatamaṇimayā nāvāyo māpetvā suvaṇṇarajatamaṇimaye eva pallaṅke paññāpetvā pañcavaṇṇapadumasañchannaṃ udakaṃ karitvā “amhākaṃ anuggahaṃ karothā”ti bhagavantaṃ upagatā. Bhagavā adhivāsetvā ratananāvamārūḷho pañca ca bhikkhusatāni sakaṃ sakaṃ nāvaṃ. Nāgarājāno bhagavantaṃ saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghena nāgabhavanaṃ pavesesuṃ. Tatra sudaṃ bhagavā sabbarattiṃ nāgaparisāya dhammaṃ desesi. Dutiyadivase dibbehi khādanīyabhojanīyehi mahādānaṃ adaṃsu. Bhagavā anumoditvā nāgabhavanā nikkhami.

Thus, Sakka, the lord of the devas, having spoken these three verses, circumambulated the Blessed One and returned to the deva realm together with the assembly of devas. The Blessed One then taught the same Ratana Sutta on the second day as well, and again a realization of the Dhamma arose in eighty-four thousand beings. In this way, the Blessed One taught for seven days, and each day the same realization of the Dhamma arose. The Blessed One stayed in Vesālī for half a month and then informed the kings, 'We shall depart.' Thereupon, the kings, with double the honor, led the Blessed One to the bank of the Ganges over three days. The nāga kings born in the Ganges thought, 'Humans pay homage to the Tathāgata—why should we not?' They had golden, silver, and jeweled boats created, set up golden, silver, and jeweled couches, covered the water with five-colored lotuses, and approached the Blessed One, saying, 'Grant us your favor.' The Blessed One consented and boarded the jeweled boat, as did the five hundred monks, each to his own boat. The nāga kings led the Blessed One together with the Sangha of monks into the nāga realm. There, the Blessed One spent the entire night teaching the Dhamma to the assembly of nāgas. The next day, they made a great offering of divine hard and soft foods. The Blessed One expressed his appreciation and departed from the nāga realm.

Bhūmaṭṭhā devā “manussā ca nāgā ca tathāgatassa sakkāraṃ karonti, mayaṃ kiṃ na karissāmā”ti cintetvā vanagumbarukkhapabbatādīsu chattātichattāni ukkhipiṃsu. Eteneva upāyena yāva akaniṭṭhabrahmabhavanaṃ, tāva mahāsakkāraviseso [M 1.0294] nibbatti. Bimbisāropi licchavīhi āgatakāle katasakkārato diguṇamakāsi, pubbe vuttanayeneva pañcahi divasehi bhagavantaṃ rājagahaṃ ānesi.

The earth-dwelling deities thought, 'Humans and nāgas honor the Tathāgata, why should we not do the same?' and raised canopies upon canopies over forest thickets, trees, mountains, and so on. By this means, a great and exceptional honoring arose, extending up to the Akaniṭṭha Brahma realm. King Bimbisāra also rendered double the honor that had been performed by the Licchavis when they came; as previously mentioned, he brought the Blessed One to Rājagaha in five days.

Rājagahamanuppatte bhagavati pacchābhattaṃ maṇḍalamāḷe sannipatitānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ ayamantarakathā udapādi – “aho buddhassa bhagavato ānubhāvo, yaṃ uddissa gaṅgāya orato ca pārato ca aṭṭhayojano bhūmibhāgo ninnañca thalañca samaṃ katvā vālukāya okiritvā pupphehi sañchanno, yojanappamāṇaṃ gaṅgāya udakaṃ nānāvaṇṇehi padumehi sañchannaṃ, yāva akaniṭṭhabhavanā chattātichattāni ussitānī”ti. Bhagavā taṃ pavattiṃ ñatvā gandhakuṭito nikkhamitvā taṅkhaṇānurūpena pāṭihāriyena gantvā maṇḍalamāḷe paññattavarabuddhāsane nisīdi. Nisajja kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti? Bhikkhū sabbaṃ ārocesuṃ. Bhagavā etadavoca – “na, bhikkhave, ayaṃ pūjāviseso mayhaṃ buddhānubhāvena nibbatto, na nāgadevabrahmānubhāvena, apica kho pubbe appamattakapariccāgānubhāvena nibbatto”ti. Bhikkhū āhaṃsu – “na mayaṃ, bhante, taṃ appamattakaṃ pariccāgaṃ jānāma, sādhu no bhagavā tathā kathetu, yathā mayaṃ taṃ jāneyyāmā”ti.

When the Blessed One arrived in Rājagaha, after his meal the monks gathered in the assembly hall. This discussion arose among them: 'Ah, the power of the Blessed One, the Buddha! On his account, the land on both the near and far banks of the Ganges—a stretch of eight yojanas—was leveled, covered with sand, and strewn with flowers. The water of the Ganges, for a yojana, was covered with lotuses of various colors, and canopies upon canopies were raised as high as the Akaniṭṭha realm.' Knowing of this discussion, the Blessed One emerged from his fragrant chamber and, performing a miracle appropriate to the occasion, went to the assembly hall and sat down on the excellent Buddha-seat that had been prepared. Seated there, the Blessed One addressed the monks: 'For what discussion, monks, have you now gathered here?' The monks told him everything. The Blessed One said: 'Monks, this special honor has not come about through my power as a Buddha, nor through the power of nāgas, devas, or brahmās. Rather, it has come about through the power of a small act of giving in the past.' The monks said: 'Venerable sir, we do not know of that small act of giving. It would be good if the Blessed One would tell it to us so that we might know it.'

Bhagavā āha – bhūtapubbaṃ, bhikkhave, takkasilāyaṃ saṅkho nāma brāhmaṇo ahosi. Tassa [V 1.0256] putto susīmo nāma māṇavo soḷasavassuddesiko vayena, so ekadivasaṃ pitaraṃ upasaṅkamitvā abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Taṃ pitā āha – “kiṃ, tāta susīmā”ti? So āha – “icchāmahaṃ, tāta, bārāṇasiṃ gantvā sippaṃ uggahetu”nti. “Tena hi, tāta susīma, asuko nāma brāhmaṇo mama sahāyako, tassa santikaṃ gantvā uggaṇhāhī”ti kahāpaṇasahassaṃ adāsi. So taṃ gahetvā mātāpitaro abhivādetvā anupubbena bārāṇasiṃ gantvā upacārayuttena vidhinā ācariyaṃ upasaṅkamitvā abhivādetvā attānaṃ nivedesi. Ācariyo “mama sahāyakassa putto”ti māṇavaṃ sampaṭicchitvā sabbaṃ pāhuneyyamakāsi. So addhānakilamathaṃ paṭivinodetvā taṃ kahāpaṇasahassaṃ ācariyassa pādamūle ṭhapetvā sippaṃ uggahetuṃ okāsaṃ yāci. Ācariyo okāsaṃ katvā uggaṇhāpesi.

The Blessed One said: 'Once in the past, monks, in Takkasilā there was a brahmin named Saṅkha. He had a son, a young man named Susīma, about sixteen years of age. One day, Susīma approached his father, paid homage, and stood to one side. His father asked him, 'What is it, dear Susīma?' He replied, 'Father, I wish to go to Bārāṇasī to learn a craft.' 'In that case, dear Susīma,' his father said, 'a certain brahmin there is a friend of mine. Go to him and learn.' He then gave him a thousand kahāpaṇas. Taking them, Susīma paid homage to his parents and in due course arrived in Bārāṇasī. Following proper etiquette, he approached the teacher, paid homage, and introduced himself. The teacher, recognizing him as his friend’s son, welcomed the young man and treated him with all due hospitality. After recovering from the fatigue of his journey, Susīma placed the thousand kahāpaṇas at the teacher’s feet and asked for the opportunity to learn the craft. The teacher gave his consent and had him taught.'

So [M 1.0295] lahuñca gaṇhanto bahuñca gaṇhanto gahitagahitañca suvaṇṇabhājane pakkhittamiva sīhatelaṃ avinassamānaṃ dhārento dvādasavassikaṃ sippaṃ katipayamāseneva pariyosāpesi. So sajjhāyaṃ karonto ādimajjhaṃyeva passati, no pariyosānaṃ. Atha ācariyaṃ upasaṅkamitvā āha – “imassa sippassa ādimajjhameva passāmi, pariyosānaṃ na passāmī”ti. Ācariyo āha – “ahampi, tāta, evamevā”ti. “Atha ko, ācariya, imassa sippassa pariyosānaṃ jānātī”ti? “Isipatane, tāta, isayo atthi, te jāneyyu”nti. Te upasaṅkamitvā “pucchāmi, ācariyā”ti. “Puccha, tāta, yathāsukha”nti. So isipatanaṃ gantvā paccekabuddhe upasaṅkamitvā pucchi – “ādimajjhapariyosānaṃ jānāthā”ti? “Āmāvuso, jānāmā”ti. “Taṃ mampi sikkhāpethā”ti. “Tena, hāvuso, pabbajāhi, na sakkā apabbajitena sikkhitu”nti. “Sādhu, bhante, pabbājetha vā maṃ, yaṃ vā icchatha, taṃ katvā pariyosānaṃ jānāpethā”ti. Te taṃ pabbājetvā kammaṭṭhāne niyojetuṃ asamatthā “evaṃ te nivāsetabbaṃ, evaṃ pārupitabba”ntiādinā nayena ābhisamācārikaṃ sikkhāpesuṃ. So tattha sikkhanto upanissayasampannattā na cireneva paccekabodhiṃ abhisambujjhi. Sakalabārāṇasiyaṃ “susīmapaccekabuddho”ti pākaṭo ahosi lābhaggayasaggappatto sampannaparivāro. So appāyukasaṃvattanikassa kammassa katattā na cireneva parinibbāyi. Tassa paccekabuddhā ca mahājanakāyo ca sarīrakiccaṃ katvā dhātuto gahetvā nagaradvāre thūpaṃ patiṭṭhāpesuṃ.

He quickly grasped much and retained what he had grasped, like the oil of a lion placed in a golden vessel that does not spoil, and completed the twelve-year craft in just a few months. While reciting, he saw only the beginning and middle, not the end. Then he approached his teacher and said, "I see only the beginning and middle of this craft, not the end." The teacher replied, "I too, my dear, see only that much." "Then who, teacher, knows the end of this craft?" "At Isipatana, my dear, there are sages; they might know." He approached them and said, "I wish to ask you, teachers." "Ask, my dear, as you wish." He went to Isipatana, approached the Paccekabuddhas, and asked, "Do you know the beginning, middle, and end?" "Yes, friend, we know." "Then teach me too." "Then, friend, you must go forth. One cannot learn this while still a layman." "Very well, venerable sirs, ordain me or do as you wish, but teach me the end." They ordained him and, unable to instruct him in meditation, taught him the basic rules of conduct, saying: "This is how you should wear your lower robe, this is how you should wear your outer robe," and so on. Practicing there, due to being endowed with supportive conditions, he soon awakened to Paccekabodhi. Throughout all of Bārāṇasī, he became known as "Susīma the Paccekabuddha," attaining the highest gains and honors, with a complete following. Due to having performed a deed that leads to a short life, he soon attained final Nibbāna. The Paccekabuddhas and a great multitude performed the funeral rites for his body, collected his relics, and erected a stupa at the city gate.

Atha kho saṅkho brāhmaṇo “putto me ciragato, na cassa pavattiṃ jānāmī”ti puttaṃ daṭṭhukāmo takkasilāya nikkhamitvā anupubbena bārāṇasiṃ patvā mahājanakāyaṃ sannipatitaṃ disvā “addhā bahūsu ekopi me puttassa pavattiṃ jānissatī”ti cintento upasaṅkamitvā pucchi – “susīmo nāma māṇavo idha āgato atthi, api nu tassa pavattiṃ jānāthā”ti? Te “āma, brāhmaṇa, jānāma, asmiṃ nagare brāhmaṇassa santike tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ pāragū hutvā paccekabuddhānaṃ [V 1.0257] santike pabbajitvā paccekabuddho hutvā anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbāyi, ayamassa thūpo patiṭṭhāpito”ti āhaṃsu. So bhūmiṃ hatthena [M 1.0296] paharitvā, roditvā ca paridevitvā ca taṃ cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ gantvā tiṇāni uddharitvā uttarasāṭakena vālukaṃ ānetvā, paccekabuddhacetiyaṅgaṇe ākiritvā, kamaṇḍaluto udakena samantato bhūmiṃ paripphositvā vanapupphehi pūjaṃ katvā uttarasāṭakena paṭākaṃ āropetvā thūpassa upari attano chattaṃ bandhitvā pakkāmīti.

Then Saṅkha the Brahmin, thinking, "My son has been gone a long time, and I do not know his news," desiring to see his son, left Takkasilā and gradually arrived at Bārāṇasī. Seeing a great crowd gathered, he thought, "Surely among so many, even one might know news of my son." Approaching, he asked, "Has a young man named Susīma come here? Do you know anything about him?" They replied, "Yes, brahmin, we know. In this city, having mastered the three Vedas under a brahmin, he went forth in the presence of the Paccekabuddhas, became a Paccekabuddha, and attained final Nibbāna with no residue remaining. This is his stupa, which has been erected." Striking the ground with his hand, weeping and lamenting, he went to that stupa's enclosure, cleared away the grass, brought sand in his upper garment, scattered it over the Paccekabuddha's stupa enclosure, sprinkled water all around from his water pot, made offerings with forest flowers, hoisted a banner with his upper garment, and tied his own parasol atop the stupa before departing.

Evaṃ atītaṃ dassetvā taṃ jātakaṃ paccuppannena anusandhento bhikkhūnaṃ dhammakathaṃ kathesi – “siyā kho pana vo, bhikkhave, evamassa añño nūna tena samayena saṅkho brāhmaṇo ahosī”ti, na kho panetaṃ evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, ahaṃ tena samayena saṅkho brāhmaṇo ahosiṃ, mayā susīmassa paccekabuddhassa cetiyaṅgaṇe tiṇāni uddhaṭāni, tassa me kammassa nissandena aṭṭhayojanamaggaṃ vigatakhāṇukaṇṭakaṃ katvā samaṃ suddhamakaṃsu, mayā tattha vālukā okiṇṇā, tassa me nissandena aṭṭhayojanamagge vālukaṃ okiriṃsu. Mayā tattha vanakusumehi pūjā katā, tassa me nissandena navayojanamagge thale ca udake ca nānāpupphehi pupphasantharaṃ akaṃsu. Mayā tattha kamaṇḍaludakena bhūmi paripphositā, tassa me nissandena vesāliyaṃ pokkharavassaṃ vassi. Mayā tasmiṃ cetiye paṭākā āropitā, chattañca baddhaṃ, tassa me nissandena yāva akaniṭṭhabhavanā paṭākā ca āropitā, chattātichattāni ca ussitāni. Iti kho, bhikkhave, ayaṃ mayhaṃ pūjāviseso neva buddhānubhāvena nibbatto, na nāgadevabrahmānubhāvena, apica kho appamattakapariccāgānubhāvena nibbatto”ti. Dhammakathāpariyosāne imaṃ gāthamabhāsi –

Having thus shown the past, connecting that Jātaka to the present, he gave a Dhamma talk to the monks: "Monks, you might think, 'Surely someone else was the brahmin Saṅkha at that time.' But you should not see it thus. I was the brahmin Saṅkha at that time. I uprooted the grass from the Paccekabuddha Susīma's shrine courtyard; as a result of that deed, an eight-yojana road was made free of stumps and thorns, smooth and clean for me. I scattered sand there; as a result of that, sand was strewn along an eight-yojana road for me. I made offerings with forest flowers there; as a result of that, a layer of various flowers was spread over a nine-yojana road, on land and water for me. I sprinkled the ground with water from my water pot; as a result of that, a rain of lotuses fell in Vesālī for me. I hoisted a flag and tied a parasol at that shrine; as a result of that, flags were hoisted up to the Akaniṭṭha realm, and parasols upon parasols were raised for me. Thus, monks, this special honor of mine did not arise from the power of a Buddha, nor from the power of nāgas, devas, or brahmās, but rather from the power of even a small offering." At the end of the Dhamma talk, he spoke this verse:

“Mattāsukhapariccāgā, passe ce vipulaṃ sukhaṃ;

Caje mattāsukhaṃ dhīro, sampassaṃ vipulaṃ sukha”nti. (dha. pa. 290);

If by giving up a lesser happiness, one might see an abundant happiness, the wise one should forsake the lesser happiness, in consideration of the abundant happiness.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, a commentary of the Khuddaka collection,

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya ratanasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Ratana Sutta in the commentary to the Suttanipāta is concluded.

2. Āmagandhasuttavaṇṇanā

2. The Explanation of the Āmagandha Sutta

Sāmākaciṅgūlakacīnakāni [M 1.0297][V 1.0258] cāti āmagandhasuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Anuppanne bhagavati āmagandho nāma brāhmaṇo pañcahi māṇavakasatehi saddhiṃ tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā himavantaṃ pavisitvā pabbatantare assamaṃ kārāpetvā vanamūlaphalāhāro hutvā tattha paṭivasati, na kadāci macchamaṃsaṃ khādati. Atha tesaṃ tāpasānaṃ loṇambilādīni aparibhuñjantānaṃ paṇḍurogo uppajji. Tato te “loṇambilādisevanatthāya manussapathaṃ gacchāmā”ti paccantagāmaṃ sampattā. Tattha manussā tesu pasīditvā nimantetvā bhojesuṃ, katabhattakiccānaṃ nesaṃ mañcapīṭhaparibhogabhājanapādamakkhanādīni upanetvā “ettha, bhante, vasatha, mā ukkaṇṭhitthā”ti vasanaṭṭhānaṃ dassetvā pakkamiṃsu. Dutiyadivasepi nesaṃ dānaṃ datvā puna gharapaṭipāṭiyā ekekadivasaṃ dānamadaṃsu. Tāpasā catumāsaṃ tattha vasitvā loṇambilādisevanāya thirabhāvappattasarīrā hutvā “mayaṃ, āvuso, gacchāmā”ti [P 1.0279] manussānaṃ ārocesuṃ. Manussā tesaṃ telataṇḍulādīni adaṃsu. Te tāni ādāya attano assamameva agamaṃsu. Tañca gāmaṃ tatheva saṃvacchare saṃvacchare āgamiṃsu. Manussāpi tesaṃ āgamanakālaṃ viditvā dānatthāya taṇḍulādīni sajjetvāva acchanti, āgate ca ne tatheva sammānenti.

The Āmagandha Sutta. What is its origin? Before the Blessed One appeared, there was a brahmin named Āmagandha who, along with five hundred young men, took up the ascetic life and entered the Himalayas. There, in a mountain ravine, he had a hermitage built and lived on roots and fruits of the forest, never eating fish or meat. Then, because those ascetics did not consume salt, sour foods, and other seasonings, they developed a pale sickness. So they thought, “Let us go to a human settlement to obtain salt, sour foods, and other seasonings.” They arrived at a border village. There, the people, pleased with them, invited them and offered food. After their meal, they provided them with beds, seats, utensils, foot-wiping cloths, and other necessities, saying, “Stay here, venerable sirs, do not be troubled,” and showed them a place to stay before departing. The next day, they again gave them alms and continued to offer alms daily, house by house. The ascetics stayed there for four months, and by consuming salt, sour foods, and other seasonings, their bodies regained strength. Then they announced to the people, “Friends, we shall now depart.” The people gave them oil, rice, and other provisions. Taking these, they returned to their own hermitage. And year after year, they would come to that village in the same way. The people, too, knowing their time of arrival, would prepare rice and other offerings in advance and wait. When they arrived, they honored them just as before.

Atha bhagavā loke uppajjitvā pavattitavaradhammacakko anupubbena sāvatthiṃ gantvā tattha viharanto tesaṃ tāpasānaṃ upanissayasampattiṃ disvā tato nikkhamma bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto cārikaṃ caramāno anupubbena taṃ gāmaṃ anuppatto. Manussā bhagavantaṃ disvā mahādānāni adaṃsu. Bhagavā tesaṃ dhammaṃ desesi. Te tāya dhammadesanāya appekacce sotāpannā, ekacce sakadāgāmino, ekacce anāgāmino ahesuṃ, ekacce pabbajitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Bhagavā punadeva sāvatthiṃ paccāgamāsi. Atha te tāpasā taṃ gāmaṃ āgamiṃsu. Manussā tāpase disvā na pubbasadisaṃ kotūhalamakaṃsu. Tāpasā taṃ pucchiṃsu – “kiṃ, āvuso, ime manussā na pubbasadisā, kiṃ nu kho ayaṃ gāmo rājadaṇḍena upadduto, udāhu dubbhikkhena, udāhu amhehi sīlādiguṇehi sampannataro koci pabbajito imaṃ gāmamanuppatto”ti? Te āhaṃsu – “na, bhante, rājadaṇḍena, na dubbhikkhenāyaṃ gāmo upadduto, apica buddho loke [M 1.0298] uppanno, so bhagavā bahujanahitāya dhammaṃ desento idhāgato”ti.

Then the Blessed One, having arisen in the world and set rolling the supreme Wheel of Dhamma, gradually journeyed to Sāvatthī and dwelt there. Seeing the ascetics’ attainment of supporting conditions, he departed from there and, surrounded by the community of monks, traveled on tour until he eventually arrived at that village. The people, upon seeing the Blessed One, offered great alms. The Blessed One taught them the Dhamma. Through that Dhamma teaching, some became stream-enterers, some once-returners, and some non-returners; and some, having gone forth, attained arahantship. The Blessed One then returned to Sāvatthī. Then those ascetics came to that village. The people, seeing the ascetics, did not show the same enthusiasm as before. The ascetics asked them, “Why, friends, are these people not as they were before? Has this village been afflicted by royal punishment, or by famine, or has some renunciant more accomplished than us in virtue and other qualities arrived here?” They replied, “No, venerable sirs, this village has not been afflicted by royal punishment or by famine. Rather, a Buddha has arisen in the world. That Blessed One, teaching the Dhamma for the welfare of many, came here.”

Taṃ [V 1.0259] sutvā āmagandhatāpaso “buddhoti, gahapatayo, vadethā”ti? “Buddhoti, bhante, vadāmā”ti tikkhattuṃ vatvā “ghosopi kho eso dullabho lokasmiṃ, yadidaṃ buddho”ti attamano attamanavācaṃ nicchāretvā pucchi – “kiṃ nu kho so buddho āmagandhaṃ bhuñjati, na bhuñjatī”ti? “Ko, bhante, āmagandho”ti? “Āmagandho nāma macchamaṃsaṃ, gahapatayo”ti. “Bhagavā, bhante, macchamaṃsaṃ paribhuñjatī”ti. Taṃ sutvā tāpaso vippaṭisārī ahosi – “māheva kho pana buddho siyā”ti[P 1.0280]. Puna cintesi – “buddhānaṃ pātubhāvo nāma dullabho, gantvā buddhaṃ disvā pucchitvā jānissāmī”ti. Tato yena bhagavā gato, taṃ maggaṃ manusse pucchitvā vacchagiddhinī gāvī viya turitaturito sabbattha ekarattivāsena sāvatthiṃ anuppatvā jetavanameva pāvisi saddhiṃ sakāya parisāya. Bhagavāpi tasmiṃ samaye dhammadesanatthāya āsane nisinno eva hoti. Tāpasā bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamma tuṇhībhūtā anabhivādetvāva ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Bhagavā “kacci vo isayo khamanīya”ntiādinā nayena tehi saddhiṃ paṭisammodi. Tepi “khamanīyaṃ, bho gotamā”tiādimāhaṃsu. Tato āmagandho bhagavantaṃ pucchi – “āmagandhaṃ, bho gotama, bhuñjasi, na bhuñjasī”ti? “Ko so, brāhmaṇa, āmagandho nāmā”ti? “Macchamaṃsaṃ, bho gotamā”ti. Bhagavā “na, brāhmaṇa, macchamaṃsaṃ āmagandho. Apica kho āmagandho nāma sabbe kilesā pāpakā akusalā dhammā”ti vatvā “na, brāhmaṇa, idāni tvameva āmagandhaṃ pucchi, atītepi tisso nāma brāhmaṇo kassapaṃ bhagavantaṃ pucchi. Evañca so pucchi, evañcassa bhagavā byākāsī”ti tissena ca brāhmaṇena kassapena ca bhagavatā vuttagāthāyo eva ānetvā tāhi gāthāhi brāhmaṇaṃ saññāpento āha – “sāmākaciṅgūlakacīnakāni cā”ti. Ayaṃ tāva imassa suttassa idha uppatti.

Hearing that, the ascetic Āmagandha asked, “Householders, do you say ‘Buddha’?” “We say ‘Buddha,’ venerable sir.” After this was said three times, he became joyful, and uttering words of joy, he said, “Indeed, such a sound is rare in the world—that is, ‘Buddha,’” and then asked, “But does that Buddha consume āmagandha or not?” “What, venerable sir, is āmagandha?” “Householders, āmagandha is fish and meat.” “Venerable sir, the Blessed One consumes fish and meat.” Hearing this, the ascetic became remorseful, thinking, “Surely, he cannot be a Buddha.” Then he reflected further, “The appearance of Buddhas is rare. I will go, see the Buddha, ask him, and find out.” Then, asking people for the path by which the Blessed One had gone, he hurried swiftly, like a cow yearning for her calf. Spending only one night in each place, he arrived at Sāvatthī and entered Jetavana along with his retinue. At that time, the Blessed One was seated on his seat for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma. The ascetics approached the Blessed One, but remained silent and sat to one side without greeting him. The Blessed One exchanged courteous greetings with them, asking, “I hope you seers are well?” They replied, “We are well, Master Gotama.” Then Āmagandha asked the Blessed One, “Master Gotama, do you consume āmagandha or not?” “Brahmin, what is this thing called āmagandha?” “Fish and meat, Master Gotama.” The Blessed One said, “No, brahmin, fish and meat are not āmagandha. Rather, āmagandha refers to all defilements, which are evil, unwholesome states.” Having said this, he continued, “Brahmin, it is not only you who now asks about āmagandha; in the past, a brahmin named Tissa also asked the Blessed One Kassapa. He asked in this way, and the Blessed One answered him in that way.” Then, bringing forth the verses spoken by the brahmin Tissa and the Blessed One Kassapa, he instructed the brahmin with those verses, beginning with: “Sāmāka millet, ciṅgūlaka, and cīnakā grains…” This, for now, is the origin of this discourse here.

Atīte pana kassapo kira bodhisatto aṭṭhāsaṅkhyeyyāni kappasatasahassañca pāramiyo pūretvā bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadattassa brāhmaṇassa dhanavatī nāma brāhmaṇī, tassā kucchimhi paṭisandhiṃ aggahesi. Aggasāvakopi taṃ divasaṃyeva devalokā cavitvā anupurohitabrāhmaṇassa pajāpatiyā kucchimhi nibbatti. Evaṃ tesaṃ ekadivasameva paṭisandhiggahaṇañca [M 1.0299] gabbhavuṭṭhānañca ahosi, ekadivasameva [P 1.0281] etesaṃ ekassa kassapo, ekassa tissoti nāmamakaṃsu. Te sahapaṃsukīḷanakā dve sahāyā anupubbena vuḍḍhiṃ agamiṃsu. Tissassa pitā puttaṃ āṇāpesi – “ayaṃ, tāta, kassapo nikkhamma pabbajitvā buddho bhavissati, tvampissa santike pabbajitvā bhavanissaraṇaṃ kareyyāsī”ti. So “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇitvā bodhisattassa santikaṃ gantvā “ubhopi, samma, pabbajissāmā”ti āha. Bodhisatto “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇi. Tato vuḍḍhiṃ [V 1.0260] anuppattakālepi tisso bodhisattaṃ āha – “ehi, samma, pabbajissāmā”ti bodhisatto na nikkhami. Tisso “na tāvassa ñāṇaṃ paripākaṃ gata”nti sayaṃ nikkhamma isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā araññe pabbatapāde assamaṃ kārāpetvā vasati. Bodhisattopi aparena samayena ghare ṭhitoyeva ānāpānassatiṃ pariggahetvā cattāri jhānāni abhiññāyo ca uppādetvā pāsādena bodhimaṇḍasamīpaṃ gantvā “puna pāsādo yathāṭhāneyeva patiṭṭhātū”ti adhiṭṭhāsi, so sakaṭṭhāneyeva patiṭṭhāsi. Apabbajitena kira bodhimaṇḍaṃ upagantuṃ na sakkāti. So pabbajitvā bodhimaṇḍaṃ patvā nisīditvā satta divase padhānayogaṃ katvā sattahi divasehi sammāsambodhiṃ sacchākāsi.

In the past, it is said that the Bodhisatta Kassapa fulfilled the perfections for eight incalculable aeons and one hundred thousand aeons. He took rebirth in the womb of a Brahmin woman named Dhanavatī, the wife of the Brahmin Brahmadatta in Benares. On that very same day, his chief disciple also passed away from the deva world and was born in the womb of the wife of the junior chaplain brahmin. Thus, their conception and emergence from the womb occurred on the same day. On that same day, they were named—one Kassapa and the other Tissa. These two friends, who played together in the dust, gradually grew up. Tissa’s father instructed his son, saying, 'Dear son, this Kassapa will go forth, become an ascetic, and attain Buddhahood. You too should go forth under him and achieve liberation from existence.' He agreed, saying, 'Very well,' and went to the Bodhisatta, saying, 'Friend, let us both go forth.' The Bodhisatta replied, 'Very well.' Later, when they had reached the age of maturity, Tissa said to the Bodhisatta, 'Come, friend, let us go forth.' But the Bodhisatta did not go forth. Tissa thought, 'His knowledge has not yet matured,' and he himself went forth, embraced the ascetic life of a sage, had a hermitage built at the foot of a mountain in the forest, and lived there. Meanwhile, the Bodhisatta, while still at home, cultivated mindfulness of breathing, developed the four jhānas and the higher knowledges, and then, by means of a palace, approached the vicinity of the Bodhi-seat. He resolved, 'May this palace return to its original place,' and it did so. It is said that one cannot approach the Bodhi-seat without having gone forth. Having gone forth, he reached the Bodhi-seat, sat down, and practiced intense striving for seven days. Within seven days, he realized perfect enlightenment.

Tadā isipatane vīsatisahassā pabbajitā paṭivasanti. Atha kassapo bhagavā te āmantetvā dhammacakkaṃ pavattesi. Suttapariyosāne sabbeva arahanto ahesuṃ. So sudaṃ bhagavā vīsatibhikkhusahassaparivuto tattheva isipatane vasati. Kikī ca naṃ kāsirājā catūhi paccayehi upaṭṭhāti. Athekadivasaṃ bārāṇasivāsī eko puriso pabbate candanasārādīni gavesanto tissassa tāpasassa assamaṃ patvā taṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Tāpaso taṃ disvā “kuto [P 1.0282] āgatosī”ti pucchi. “Bārāṇasito, bhante”ti. “Kā tattha pavattī”ti? “Tattha, bhante, kassapo nāma sammāsambuddho uppanno”ti. Tāpaso dullabhavacanaṃ sutvā pītisomanassajāto pucchi – “kiṃ so āmagandhaṃ bhuñjati, na bhuñjatī”ti? “Ko bhante, āmagandho”ti? “Macchamaṃsaṃ āvuso”ti. “Bhagavā, bhante, macchamaṃsaṃ bhuñjatī”ti. Taṃ sutvā tāpaso vippaṭisārī hutvā puna cintesi – “gantvā taṃ pucchissāmi, sace ‘āmagandhaṃ paribhuñjāmī’ti vakkhati, tato naṃ ‘tumhākaṃ, bhante, jātiyā ca kulassa ca gottassa ca ananucchavikameta’nti nivāretvā tassa santike pabbajitvā bhavanissaraṇaṃ karissāmī”ti sallahukaṃ upakaraṇaṃ [M 1.0300] gahetvā sabbattha ekarattivāsena sāyanhasamaye bārāṇasiṃ patvā isipatanameva pāvisi. Bhagavāpi tasmiṃ samaye dhammadesanatthāya āsane nisinnoyeva hoti. Tāpaso bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamma anabhivādetvā tuṇhībhūto ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Bhagavā taṃ disvā pubbe vuttanayeneva paṭisammodi. Sopi “khamanīyaṃ, bho kassapā”tiādīni vatvā ekamantaṃ nisīditvā bhagavantaṃ pucchi – “āmagandhaṃ, bho kassapa, bhuñjasi, na bhuñjasī”ti? “Nāhaṃ, brāhmaṇa, āmagandhaṃ bhuñjāmī”ti. “Sādhu, sādhu, bho kassapa, parakuṇapaṃ akhādanto sundaramakāsi, yuttametaṃ bhoto kassapassa jātiyā ca kulassa ca gottassa cā”ti. Tato bhagavā “ahaṃ kilese sandhāya ‘āmagandhaṃ na bhuñjāmī’ti vadāmi, brāhmaṇo macchamaṃsaṃ pacceti, yaṃnūnāhaṃ sve gāmaṃ piṇḍāya apavisitvā kikīrañño gehā ābhataṃ [V 1.0261] piṇḍapātaṃ paribhuñjeyyaṃ, evaṃ āmagandhaṃ ārabbha kathā pavattissati. Tato brāhmaṇaṃ dhammadesanāya saññāpessāmī”ti dutiyadivase kālasseva sarīraparikammaṃ katvā gandhakuṭiṃ pāvisi. Bhikkhū gandhakuṭidvāraṃ pihitaṃ disvā “na [P 1.0283] bhagavā ajja bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ pavisitukāmo”ti ñatvā gandhakuṭiṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā piṇḍāya pavisiṃsu.

At that time, twenty thousand ascetics were dwelling in Isipatana. Then the Blessed One Kassapa addressed them and set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma. At the conclusion of the discourse, all became arahants. Thus, the Blessed One, surrounded by twenty thousand bhikkhus, continued to dwell there in Isipatana. King Kikī of Kāsi attended to him with the four requisites. One day, a man from Bārāṇasī, while searching for sandalwood and other materials on the mountain, arrived at the hermitage of the ascetic Tissa. He paid homage to the ascetic and stood to one side. Seeing him, the ascetic asked, 'Where have you come from?' 'From Bārāṇasī, venerable sir.' 'What news is there?' 'There, venerable sir, a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One named Kassapa has arisen.' Hearing these rare words, the ascetic was filled with joy and asked, 'Does he consume āmagandha or not?' 'What, venerable sir, is āmagandha?' 'Fish and meat, friend.' 'The Blessed One, venerable sir, consumes fish and meat.' Hearing this, the ascetic became remorseful and then thought, 'I will go and ask him. If he says, "I consume āmagandha," then I will dissuade him, saying, "Venerable sir, this is unbecoming of your birth, clan, and lineage." Having forbidden him, I will go forth in his presence and strive for deliverance from existence.' Taking his simple requisites, staying only one night in any place, he arrived at Bārāṇasī in the evening and entered Isipatana. At that time, the Blessed One was seated on his seat, intending to teach the Dhamma. The ascetic approached the Blessed One and, without paying homage, stood silently to one side. The Blessed One saw him and greeted him in the manner previously mentioned. The ascetic, in turn, after saying, 'Are you well, good Kassapa?' and other pleasantries, sat to one side and asked the Blessed One, 'Good Kassapa, do you consume āmagandha or not?' 'I do not consume āmagandha, brahmin.' 'Good, good, good Kassapa! By not eating another's corpse, you have done well. This is fitting for your birth, clan, and lineage.' Then the Blessed One thought, 'I speak of not consuming āmagandha with reference to defilements, but the brahmin understands it to mean fish and meat. Suppose tomorrow, without entering the village for alms, I partake of the almsfood brought from King Kikī’s house. Then a discussion about āmagandha will arise, and I will make the brahmin understand by teaching him the Dhamma.' The next day, early in the morning, after attending to his bodily needs, he entered his fragrant chamber. The bhikkhus, seeing the door of the fragrant chamber closed, understood, 'The Blessed One does not wish to go for alms with the bhikkhus today,' and after circumambulating the fragrant chamber, they entered the village for alms.

Bhagavāpi gandhakuṭito nikkhamma paññattāsane nisīdi. Tāpasopi kho pattasākaṃ pacitvā khāditvā bhagavato santike nisīdi. Kikī kāsirājā bhikkhū piṇḍāya carante disvā “kuhiṃ bhagavā, bhante”ti pucchitvā “vihāre, mahārājā”ti ca sutvā nānābyañjanarasamanekamaṃsavikatisampannaṃ bhojanaṃ bhagavato pāhesi. Amaccā vihāraṃ netvā bhagavato ārocetvā dakkhiṇodakaṃ datvā parivisantā paṭhamaṃ nānāmaṃsavikatisampannaṃ yāguṃ adaṃsu, tāpaso disvā “khādati nu kho no”ti cintento aṭṭhāsi. Bhagavā tassa passatoyeva yāguṃ pivanto maṃsakhaṇḍaṃ mukhe pakkhipi. Tāpaso disvā kuddho. Puna yāgupītassa nānārasabyañjanaṃ bhojanamadaṃsu, tampi gahetvā bhuñjantaṃ disvā ativiya kuddho “macchamaṃsaṃ khādantoyeva ‘na khādāmī’ti bhaṇatī”ti. Atha bhagavantaṃ katabhattakiccaṃ hatthapāde dhovitvā nisinnaṃ upasaṅkamma “bho kassapa, musā tvaṃ bhaṇasi, netaṃ paṇḍitakiccaṃ. Musāvādo hi garahito buddhānaṃ, yepi te pabbatapāde vanamūlaphalādīhi yāpentā isayo vasanti, tepi musā na bhaṇantī”ti vatvā puna isīnaṃ guṇe gāthāya vaṇṇento āha “sāmākaciṅgūlakacīnakāni cā”ti.

The Blessed One also came out from the fragrant chamber and sat on the prepared seat. The ascetic, having cooked and eaten his leafy greens, also sat near the Blessed One. King Kikī of Kāsi, seeing the monks going for alms, asked, "Where is the Blessed One, venerable sirs?" Hearing, "In the monastery, great king," he sent a meal with various sauces and flavors, complete with many kinds of meat preparations, to the Blessed One. The ministers, bringing it to the monastery, informed the Blessed One, poured the water of dedication, and while serving, first gave a gruel complete with various meat preparations. The ascetic, seeing this, stood thinking, "Will he eat it or not?" The Blessed One, while the ascetic was watching, drank the gruel and placed a piece of meat in his mouth. The ascetic, seeing this, became angry. Again, after he had drunk the gruel, they served him a meal with various flavors and sauces. Seeing him take and eat that too, the ascetic became extremely angry, thinking, "He eats fish and meat yet says, 'I do not eat!'" Then, when the Blessed One had finished his meal, washed his hands and feet, and sat down, the ascetic approached and said, "O Kassapa, you speak falsely; this is not the act of a wise one. False speech is indeed condemned by the Buddhas. Even those sages who sustain themselves on wild roots and fruits at the foot of mountains do not speak falsely." Then, praising the virtues of the sages in a verse, he said, "Sāmāka, ciṅgūlaka, and cīnaka grains..."

242. Tattha [M 1.0301] sāmākāti dhunitvā vā sīsāni uccinitvā vā gayhūpagā tiṇadhaññajāti. Tathā ciṅgūlakā kaṇavīrapupphasaṇṭhānasīsā honti. Cīnakānīti aṭavipabbatapādesu aropitajātā cīnamuggā. Pattapphalanti yaṃkiñci haritapaṇṇaṃ. Mūlaphalanti yaṃkiñci kandamūlaṃ. Gavipphalanti yaṃkiñci rukkhavalliphalaṃ. Mūlaggahaṇena vā kandamūlaṃ, phalaggahaṇena rukkhavalliphalaṃ, gavipphalaggahaṇena [P 1.0284] udake jātasiṅghātakakaserukādiphalaṃ veditabbaṃ. Dhammena laddhanti dūteyyapahiṇagamanādimicchājīvaṃ pahāya vane uñchācariyāya laddhaṃ. Satanti santo ariyā. Asnamānāti bhuñjamānā. Na kāmakāmā alikaṃ bhaṇantīti te evaṃ amamā apariggahā etāni sāmākādīni bhuñjamānā isayo yathā tvaṃ sādurasādike kāme patthayanto āmagandhaṃ bhuñjantoyeva “nāhaṃ, brāhmaṇa, āmagandhaṃ bhuñjāmī”ti bhaṇanto alikaṃ bhaṇasi, tathā na kāmakāmā alikaṃ bhaṇanti, kāme kāmayantā musā na bhaṇantīti isīnaṃ pasaṃsāya bhagavato nindaṃ dīpeti.

242. Herein, sāmāka refers to a species of grass-grain that can be obtained by threshing or by gathering the heads. Likewise, ciṅgūlaka have heads with the appearance of kaṇavīra flowers. Cīnakāni refers to cīna-beans that grow without being planted at the foot of forests and mountains. Pattapphala means any kind of green leaf. Mūlaphala means any kind of tuberous root. Gavipphala means any kind of fruit from trees and creepers. Alternatively, by the term 'root,' a tuberous root should be understood; by the term 'fruit,' fruit from trees and creepers; and by the term 'gavipphala,' fruit that grows in water, such as siṅghāṭaka and kaseruka, should be understood. 'Obtained righteously' means obtained by the practice of gleaning in the forest, having abandoned wrong livelihood such as acting as a messenger or running errands. 'The good' means the good, the noble ones. Asnamānā means consuming. 'Not desiring sensual pleasures, they do not speak falsely' means: those sages, eating these things such as sāmāka, being unattached and without possessions, do not speak falsely out of desire for sensual pleasures, unlike you who, desiring delicious tastes and the like, eat the foulness of meat and yet say, 'I, brahmin, do not eat foulness,' thus speaking falsely. They do not speak falsely out of desire for sensual pleasures. Thus, by way of praising the sages, he indicates a criticism of the Blessed One.

243. Evaṃ [V 1.0262] isīnaṃ pasaṃsāpadesena bhagavantaṃ ninditvā idāni attanā adhippetaṃ nindāvatthuṃ dassetvā nippariyāyeneva bhagavantaṃ nindanto āha “yadasnamāno”ti tattha da-kāro padasandhikaro. Ayaṃ panattho – yaṃ kiñcideva sasamaṃsaṃ vā tittiramaṃsaṃ vā dhovanacchedanādinā pubbaparikammena sukataṃ, pacanavāsanādinā pacchāparikammena suniṭṭhitaṃ, na mātarā na pitarā, apica kho pana “dakkhiṇeyyo aya”nti maññamānehi dhammakāmehi parehi dinnaṃ, sakkārakaraṇena payataṃ paṇītamalaṅkataṃ, uttamarasatāya ojavantatāya thāmabalabharaṇasamatthatāya ca paṇītaṃ asnamāno āhārayamāno, na kevalañca yaṃkiñci maṃsameva, apica kho pana idampi sālīnamannaṃ vicitakāḷakaṃ sālitaṇḍulodanaṃ paribhuñjamāno so bhuñjasi, kassapa, āmagandhaṃ, so tvaṃ yaṃkiñci maṃsaṃ bhuñjamāno idañca sālīnamannaṃ paribhuñjamāno bhuñjasi, kassapa, āmagandhanti bhagavantaṃ gottena ālapati.

243. Thus, having criticized the Blessed One under the pretext of praising the sages, now, pointing out the object of criticism he himself intended, he directly criticized the Blessed One, saying, 'When eating...' Here, the letter 'd' is a euphonic consonant for sandhi. This is the meaning: eating any kind of meat whatsoever, whether hare's meat or partridge meat, well-prepared by preliminary processes like washing and cutting, and perfectly finished by subsequent processes like cooking and seasoning; not from one's mother or father, but rather given by others who desire the Dhamma, thinking, 'This one is worthy of offerings,' respectfully prepared, exquisite, and adorned; exquisite due to its supreme flavor, its nutritive essence, and its capacity to sustain strength and power—consuming such food, and not only any kind of meat, but also this dish of sāli rice, this cooked rice from choice black-flecked sāli grains, you, Kassapa, consume foulness. You, eating any kind of meat and also consuming this dish of sāli rice, you, Kassapa, consume foulness—thus he addresses the Blessed One by his clan name.

244. Evaṃ [P 1.0285] āhārato bhagavantaṃ ninditvā idāni musāvādaṃ āropetvā nindanto āha “na āmagandho…pe… susaṅkhatehī”ti. Tassattho [M 1.0302] – pubbe mayā pucchito samāno “na āmagandho mama kappatī”ti icceva tvaṃ bhāsasi, evaṃ ekaṃseneva tvaṃ bhāsasi brahmabandhu brāhmaṇaguṇavirahitajātimattabrāhmaṇāti paribhāsanto bhaṇati. Sālīnamannanti sālitaṇḍulodanaṃ. Paribhuñjamānoti bhuñjamāno. Sakuntamaṃsehi susaṅkhatehīti tadā bhagavato abhihaṭaṃ sakuṇamaṃsaṃ niddisanto bhaṇati.

244. Having thus criticized the Blessed One with regard to food, now, attributing false speech to him, he criticizes him, saying, 'Foulness is not... well-prepared.' The meaning is: 'Previously, when asked by me, you said, "Foulness is not suitable for me." You spoke thus, quite definitively.' Speaking mockingly, he says: 'O kinsman of a brahmin, a brahmin by birth only, devoid of the qualities of a brahmin.' 'Sālīnamannaṃ' means cooked sāli rice. 'Paribhuñjamāno' means eating. 'Sakuntamaṃsehi susaṅkhatehī' ('well-prepared with fowl meat')—he says this, referring to the fowl meat that was brought for the Blessed One at that time.

Evaṃ bhaṇanto eva ca bhagavato heṭṭhā pādatalā pabhuti yāva upari kesaggā sarīramullokento dvattiṃsavaralakkhaṇāsītianubyañjanasampadaṃ byāmappabhāparikkhepañca disvā “evarūpo mahāpurisalakkhaṇādipaṭimaṇḍitakāyo na musā bhaṇituṃ arahati. Ayaṃ hissa bhavantarepi saccavācānissandeneva uṇṇā bhamukantare jātā odātā mudu tūlasannibhā, ekekāni ca lomakūpesu lomāni. Svāyaṃ kathamidāni musā bhaṇissati. Addhā añño imassa āmagandho bhavissati, yaṃ sandhāya etadavoca – ‘nāhaṃ, brāhmaṇa, āmagandhaṃ bhuñjāmī’ti, yaṃnūnāhaṃ etaṃ puccheyya”nti cintetvā sañjātabahumāno gotteneva ālapanto imaṃ gāthāsesaṃ āha –

As he was speaking thus, he observed the Blessed One’s body from the soles of his feet up to the tips of the hair on his head, and seeing the perfection of the thirty-two excellent marks and the eighty minor characteristics, and the surrounding fathom-wide aura, he thought: 'A body adorned with such marks of a great man is not one that ought to speak falsely. Indeed, as a result of his truthful speech in a previous existence, this uṇṇā has arisen between his eyebrows, white, soft, and like a cotton ball, and there is but a single hair in each pore. How could such a one now speak falsely? Surely, for him, "foulness" must be something else, referring to which he said, "I, brahmin, do not eat foulness." What if I were to ask him about this?' Thinking thus, and with great respect having arisen in him, addressing him by his clan name, he spoke the remainder of the verse:

“Pucchāmi taṃ kassapa etamatthaṃ, kathaṃpakāro tava āmagandho”ti.

I ask you, Kassapa, about this matter: of what kind is your 'foulness'?

245. Athassa bhagavā āmagandhaṃ vissajjetuṃ “pāṇātipāto”ti evamādimāha. Tattha pāṇātipātoti [V 1.0263] pāṇavadho. Vadhachedabandhananti ettha sattānaṃ daṇḍādīhi ākoṭanaṃ vadho, hatthapādādīnaṃ chedanaṃ chedo, rajjuādīhi bandho bandhanaṃ. Theyyaṃ musāvādoti theyyañca musāvādo ca. Nikatīti “dassāmi, karissāmī”tiādinā nayena āsaṃ [P 1.0286] uppādetvā nirāsākaraṇaṃ. Vañcanānīti asuvaṇṇaṃ suvaṇṇanti gāhāpanādīni. Ajjhenakuttanti niratthakamanekaganthapariyāpuṇanaṃ. Paradārasevanāti parapariggahitāsu cārittāpajjanaṃ. Esāmagandho na hi maṃsabhojananti esa pāṇātipātādiakusaladhammasamudācāro āmagandho vissagandho [M 1.0303] kuṇapagandho. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Amanuññattā kilesaasucimissakattā sabbhi jigucchitattā paramaduggandhabhāvāvahattā ca. Ye hi ussannakilesā sattā, te tehi atiduggandhā honti, nikkilesānaṃ matasarīrampi duggandhaṃ na hoti, tasmā esāmagandho. Maṃsabhojanaṃ pana adiṭṭhamasutamaparisaṅkitañca anavajjaṃ, tasmā na hi maṃsabhojanaṃ āmagandhoti.

245. Then the Blessed One, to resolve the matter of the stench of rawness, spoke, beginning with the words, “The killing of living beings.” Herein, “the killing of living beings” is the destruction of life. In the phrase “destruction, cutting, and binding,” striking beings with sticks and the like is destruction; severing hands, feet, and the like is cutting; and tying with ropes and the like is binding. “Theft and false speech” refers to both stealing and lying. “Deceit” means raising hopes by some means, saying, “I will give, I will do,” and then making them baseless. “Fraud” refers to acts such as making others accept base metal as gold. “Useless learning” is the mastery of many meaningless texts. “Adultery” is misconduct with women under the protection of another. This is the stench of rawness, not the eating of meat. For this unwholesome conduct—the killing of living beings and so on—is the stench of rawness, a foul stench, a corpse-like stench. For what reason? Because it is disagreeable, mixed with the impurity of defilements, despised by the virtuous, and because it brings about an extremely foul stench. Indeed, beings with rampant defilements are exceedingly foul-smelling on account of them, whereas the dead bodies of those without defilements do not have a foul smell. Therefore, this is the stench of rawness. The eating of meat, however, when it is not seen, not heard, and not suspected to have been killed for oneself, is blameless. Therefore, the eating of meat is not the stench of rawness.

246. Evaṃ dhammādhiṭṭhānāya desanāya ekena nayena āmagandhaṃ vissajjetvā idāni yasmā te te sattā tehi tehi āmagandhehi samannāgatā, na eko eva sabbehi, na ca sabbe ekeneva, tasmā nesaṃ te te āmagandhe pakāsetuṃ “ye idha kāmesu asaññatā janā”tiādinā nayena puggalādhiṭṭhānāya tāva desanāya āmagandhe vissajjento dve gāthāyo abhāsi.

246. Having thus, in one way, resolved the matter of the stench of rawness with a discourse founded on the Dhamma, he now spoke two verses. For since various beings are endowed with various stenches of rawness—not one person with all of them, nor all persons with only one—therefore, to reveal these various stenches of rawness for them, he first, while resolving the matter of the stenches of rawness with a discourse founded on the individual, spoke two verses beginning with the words, “Those people here who are unrestrained in sensual pleasures.”

Tattha ye idha kāmesu asaññatā janāti ye keci idha loke kāmapaṭisevanasaṅkhātesu kāmesu mātimātucchādīsupi mariyādāvirahena bhinnasaṃvaratāya asaṃyatā puthujjanā. Rasesu giddhāti jivhāviññeyyesu rasesu giddhā gadhitā mucchitā ajjhosannā anādīnavadassāvino anissaraṇapaññā rase paribhuñjanti. Asucibhāvamassitāti tāya rasagiddhiyā rasapaṭilābhatthāya nānappakāramicchājīvasaṅkhātaasucibhāvamissitā. Natthikadiṭṭhīti “natthi dinna”ntiādidasavatthukamicchādiṭṭhisamannāgatā. Visamāti [P 1.0287] visamena kāyakammādinā samannāgatā. Durannayāti duviññāpayā sandiṭṭhiparāmāsīādhānaggāhīduppaṭinissaggitāsamannāgatā. Esāmagandhoti esa etāya gāthāya puggale adhiṭṭhāya niddiṭṭho “kāmesu asaṃyatatā rasagiddhatā ājīvavipattinatthikadiṭṭhikāyaduccaritādivisamatā durannayabhāvatā”ti aparopi pubbe vuttenevatthena chabbidho āmagandho veditabbo. Na hi maṃsabhojananti maṃsabhojanaṃ pana yathāvuttenevatthena na āmagandhoti.

Therein, 'those people here who are unrestrained in sensual pleasures' refers to any ordinary people in this world who are unrestrained in sensual pleasures—characterized as the partaking of sensual desires—due to a lack of boundaries and broken restraint, even with their mothers, maternal aunts, and others. 'Greedy for flavors' means that, being greedy, rapacious, infatuated, and obsessed with flavors cognizable by the tongue, not seeing the danger, and lacking the wisdom for escape, they indulge in flavors. 'Resorting to impurity' means that, due to that greed for flavors and for the sake of obtaining flavors, they are involved in the impurity known as various kinds of wrong livelihood. 'Holding nihilistic views' means they are endowed with the ten-factored wrong view that begins, “There is nothing in what is given.” 'Unrighteous' means they are endowed with unrighteous bodily conduct and so on. 'Hard to guide' means they are difficult to instruct, clinging to their own views, taking up what is not the true cause, and endowed with an unwillingness to relinquish their views. This is the stench of rawness. This stench of rawness, pointed out in this verse with reference to the individual, is to be understood as the sixfold stench of rawness previously explained: unrestraint in sensual pleasures, greed for flavors, corruption of livelihood, nihilistic views, unrighteousness of bodily misconduct and so on, and being hard to guide. It is not the eating of meat; rather, the eating of meat, for the reason already stated, is not the stench of rawness.

247. Dutiyagāthāyapi ye lūkhasāti ye lūkhā nirasā, attakilamathānuyuttāti attho. Dāruṇāti kakkhaḷā dovacassatāyuttā. Piṭṭhimaṃsikāti [M 1.0304] purato madhuraṃ bhaṇitvā parammukhe avaṇṇabhāsino[V 1.0264]. Ete hi abhimukhaṃ oloketumasakkontā parammukhānaṃ piṭṭhimaṃsakhādakā viya honti, tena “piṭṭhimaṃsikā”ti vuccanti. Mittaddunoti mittadūhakā, dāradhanajīvitesu vissāsamāpannānaṃ mittānaṃ tattha micchāpaṭipajjanakāti vuttaṃ hoti. Nikkaruṇāti karuṇāvirahitā sattānaṃ anatthakāmā. Atimāninoti “idhekacco jātiyā vā…pe… aññataraññatarena vatthunā pare atimaññati, yo evarūpo māno ketukamyatā cittassā”ti (vibha. 880) evaṃ vuttena atimānena samannāgatā. Adānasīlāti adānapakatikā, adānādhimuttā asaṃvibhāgaratāti attho. Na ca denti kassacīti tāya ca pana adānasīlatāya yācitāpi santā kassaci kiñci na denti, adinnapubbakakule manussasadisā nijjhāmataṇhikapetaparāyaṇā honti. Keci pana “ādānasīlā”tipi paṭhanti, kevalaṃ gahaṇasīlā, kassaci pana kiñci na dentīti. Esāmagandho na hi maṃsabhojananti esa etāya gāthāya puggale adhiṭṭhāya niddiṭṭho “lūkhatā, dāruṇatā[P 1.0288], piṭṭhimaṃsikatā, mittadūbhitā, nikkaruṇatā, atimānitā, adānasīlatā, adāna”nti aparopi pubbe vuttenevatthena aṭṭhavidho āmagandho veditabbo, na hi maṃsabhojananti.

247. In the second verse as well, 'those who are harsh' means those who are rough and without sweetness; the meaning is that they are devoted to self-mortification. 'Cruel' means they are harsh and endowed with recalcitrance. 'Backbiters' are those who speak sweetly to one's face but speak dispraise in one's absence. For, being unable to look one in the face, they are like those who eat the flesh from another's back; therefore, they are called 'backbiters.' 'Betrayers of friends' means they are destroyers of friends; it is said that they act wrongly towards friends who have placed trust in them regarding their spouses, wealth, and life. 'Merciless' means they are devoid of compassion and desire what is not for the welfare of beings. 'Exceedingly arrogant' means they are endowed with the excessive arrogance spoken of thus: “Here, a certain person despises others on account of birth… or on account of some other thing. Whatever arrogance is of such a kind is a desire for a banner for the mind” (Vibh 880). 'Of a nature not to give' means they are habitually non-giving; the meaning is that they are intent on not giving and do not delight in sharing. 'And they give nothing to anyone' means that, due to this nature of not giving, though they are good people who are asked, they give nothing to anyone. In a family where nothing has been given before, they are destined for the state of the 'parched with thirst' hungry ghosts. Some, however, also recite this as 'of a nature to take'; they are merely of a nature to grasp, but they give nothing to anyone. This is the stench of rawness, not the eating of meat. This stench of rawness, pointed out in this verse with reference to the individual, is to be understood as the eightfold stench of rawness previously explained: harshness, cruelty, backbiting, betrayal of friends, mercilessness, excessive arrogance, a nature of not giving, and non-giving. It is not the eating of meat.

248. Evaṃ puggalādhiṭṭhānāya desanāya dve gāthāyo vatvā puna tassa tāpasassa āsayānuparivattanaṃ viditvā dhammādhiṭṭhānāyeva desanāya ekaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi. Tattha kodho uragasutte vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Madoti “jātimado, gottamado, ārogyamado”tiādinā (vibha. 832) nayena vibhaṅge vuttappabhedo cittassa majjanabhāvo. Thambhoti thaddhabhāvo. Paccupaṭṭhāpanāti paccanīkaṭṭhāpanā, dhammena nayena vuttassa paṭivirujjhitvā ṭhānaṃ. Māyāti “idhekacco kāyena duccaritaṃ caritvā”tiādinā (vibha. 894) nayena vibhaṅge vibhattā katapāpapaṭicchādanatā. Usūyāti paralābhasakkārādīsu issā. Bhassasamussayoti samussitaṃ bhassaṃ, attukkaṃsanatāti vuttaṃ hoti. Mānātimānoti “idhekacco jātiyā vā…pe… aññataraññatarena vatthunā pubbakālaṃ parehi [M 1.0305] sadisaṃ attānaṃ dahati, aparakālaṃ attānaṃ seyyaṃ dahati, pare hīne dahati, yo evarūpo māno…pe… ketukamyatā cittassā”ti (vibha. 880) vibhaṅge vibhatto. Asabbhi santhavoti asappurisehi santhavo. Esāmagandho na hi maṃsabhojananti esa kodhādi navavidho akusalarāsi pubbe vuttenevatthena āmagandhoti veditabbo, na hi maṃsabhojananti.

248. Having thus spoken two verses based on individuals, the Buddha then, discerning the state of that ascetic's disposition, spoke another verse based on the Dhamma itself. Herein, 'anger' should be understood in the same way as explained in the Uraga Sutta. 'Conceit' refers to the intoxicating state of mind, as classified in the Vibhaṅga under categories such as pride of birth, pride of lineage, pride of health, and so forth. 'Stubbornness' means rigidity. 'Contrariness' is establishing opposition, standing against what has been rightly stated by the Dhamma. 'Deceit' is the concealment of committed evil deeds, as detailed in the Vibhaṅga: "Here, someone engages in misconduct by body..." 'Envy' is jealousy regarding others' gains and honors. 'Boastfulness' means exaggerated talk, which is said to be self-exaltation. 'Pride and arrogance' are explained in the Vibhaṅga: "Here, someone, on account of birth or... any other grounds, considers himself equal to others at one time, superior at a later time, or considers others as inferior—such pride... is the mind's desire for prominence." 'Association with the wicked' means fellowship with the ignoble. 'This is the foulness, not the eating of meat'—this ninefold unwholesome mass of anger and other states should be understood as the foulness in the previously explained sense; it is not, indeed, the eating of meat.

249. Evaṃ dhammādhiṭṭhānāya desanāya navavidhaṃ āmagandhaṃ dassetvā punapi pubbe vuttanayeneva puggalādhiṭṭhānāya desanāya āmagandhe vissajjento tisso gāthāyo abhāsi. Tattha ye [V 1.0265] pāpasīlāti ye pāpasamācāratāya “pāpasīlā”ti [P 1.0289] loke pākaṭā. Iṇaghātasūcakāti vasalasutte vuttanayena iṇaṃ gahetvā tassa appadānena iṇaghātā, pesuññena sūcakā ca. Vohārakūṭā idha pāṭirūpikāti dhammaṭṭaṭṭhāne ṭhitā lañjaṃ gahetvā sāmike parājentā kūṭena vohārena samannāgatattā vohārakūṭā, dhammaṭṭhapaṭirūpakattā pāṭirūpikā. Atha vā idhāti sāsane. Pāṭirūpikāti dussīlā. Te hi yasmā nesaṃ iriyāpathasampadādīhi sīlavantapaṭirūpaṃ atthi, tasmā paṭirūpā, paṭirūpā eva pāṭirūpikā. Narādhamā yedha karonti kibbisanti ye idha loke narādhamā mātāpitūsu buddhapaccekabuddhādīsu ca micchāpaṭipattisaññitaṃ kibbisaṃ karonti. Esāmagandho na hi maṃsabhojananti esa etāya gāthāya puggale adhiṭṭhāya niddiṭṭho “pāpasīlatā, iṇaghātatā, sūcakatā, vohārakūṭatā, pāṭirūpikatā, kibbisakāritā”ti aparopi pubbe vuttenevatthena chabbidho āmagandho veditabbo, na hi maṃsabhojananti.

249. Having thus shown the ninefold foulness in the teaching based on the Dhamma, He then, while explaining the foulness in the teaching based on individuals, as previously mentioned, spoke three verses. Herein, 'those of evil conduct' refers to those who are known in the world as 'of evil conduct' due to their wicked behavior. 'Defaulting on debt, informers' refers to those who, as explained in the Vasala Sutta, take a loan and then default on the debt by not repaying, and who are also informers through slander. 'Deceitful in dealings, hypocrites here' refers to those who, while standing in a place of justice, take bribes and defeat the rightful parties, being endowed with deceitful dealings and thus called 'deceitful in dealings'; and being counterfeits of the righteous, they are called 'hypocrites.' Alternatively, 'here' refers to the Dispensation. 'Hypocrites' means the immoral. For since they have the appearance of virtuous ones through their excellence of deportment and other qualities, they are counterfeits, and precisely because they are counterfeits, they are called 'hypocrites.' 'Wretched men who commit sins here' refers to those wretched men in this world who commit the sin known as wrong conduct toward parents, Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and others. 'This is the foulness, not the eating of meat'—this, pointed out in this verse with reference to the person, is another sixfold foulness to be understood in the same sense as previously explained: the state of evil conduct, defaulting on debt, being an informer, deceitful dealings, hypocrisy, and committing sins. It is not, indeed, the eating of meat.

250. Ye idha pāṇesu asaññatā janāti ye janā idhaloke pāṇesu yathākāmacāritāya satampi sahassampi māretvā anuddayāmattassāpi akaraṇena asaṃyatā. Paresamādāya vihesamuyyutāti paresaṃ santakaṃ ādāya dhanaṃ vā jīvitaṃ vā tato “mā evaṃ karothā”ti yācantānaṃ vā nivārentānaṃ vā pāṇileḍḍudaṇḍādīhi vihesaṃ uyyutā. Pare vā satte samādāya “ajja dasa, ajja vīsa”nti evaṃ samādiyitvā tesaṃ vadhabandhanādīhi vihesamuyyutā. Dussīlaluddāti nissīlā ca durācārattā[M 1.0306], luddā ca kurūrakammantā lohitapāṇitāya, macchaghātakamigabandhakasākuṇikādayo idhādhippetā. Pharusāti pharusavācā. Anādarāti “idāni na karissāma, viramissāma evarūpā”ti evaṃ ādaravirahitā[P 1.0290]. Esāmagandho na hi maṃsabhojananti esa etāya gāthāya puggale adhiṭṭhāya niddiṭṭho “pāṇātipāto vadhachedabandhana”ntiādinā nayena pubbe vutto ca avutto ca “pāṇesu asaṃyatatā paresaṃ vihesatā dussīlatā luddatā pharusatā anādaro”ti chabbidho āmagandho veditabbo, na hi maṃsabhojananti. Pubbe vuttampi hi sotūnaṃ sotukāmatāya avadhāraṇatāya daḷhīkaraṇatāyāti evamādīhi kāraṇehi puna vuccati. Teneva ca parato vakkhati “iccetamatthaṃ bhagavā punappunaṃ, akkhāsi naṃ vedayi mantapāragū”ti.

250. ‘Those who here are unrestrained towards living beings’: This means those people who in this world, by acting as they please towards living beings, are unrestrained, killing even a hundred or a thousand without showing even a measure of compassion. ‘Those intent on harming, having taken from others’: This means those who, having seized what belongs to others, whether wealth or life, are then intent on harming with fists, clods of earth, or sticks, those who beg them, “Do not do this,” or who try to prevent them. Or, having seized other beings, and having resolved, “Today ten, today twenty,” they are intent on harming them by killing, binding, and so on. ‘The immoral and cruel’: This means those who are without virtue due to their wicked conduct, and cruel due to their savage deeds and blood-stained hands; fishermen, deer-stalkers, fowlers, and the like are intended here. ‘Harsh’: This means harsh in speech. ‘Without regard’: This means they are devoid of respect, not thinking, “We will not do this now, we will refrain from such things.” ‘This is the foulness, not the eating of meat’: This sixfold foulness, pointed out in this verse with reference to the person, should be understood as what was previously stated and unstated in the manner of “killing, slaying, cutting, and binding,” and so forth: namely, unrestraint towards living beings, harming others, immorality, cruelty, harshness, and lack of regard. It is not, indeed, the eating of meat. For what was stated before is repeated for such reasons as the listeners’ desire to hear, for emphasis, and for reinforcement. And for that very reason it will be said later: “This meaning the Blessed One repeatedly declared; the one who had gone to the end of the vedas made it known.”

251. Etesu giddhā viruddhātipātinoti etesu pāṇesu gedhena giddhā, dosena viruddhā, mohena ādīnavaṃ apassantā punappunaṃ ajjhācārappattiyā atipātino, etesu vā “pāṇātipāto vadhachedabandhana”ntiādinā nayena vuttesu pāpakammesu yathāsambhavaṃ ye gedhavirodhātipātasaṅkhātā rāgadosamohā, tehi giddhā viruddhā atipātino ca. Niccuyyutāti akusalakaraṇe [V 1.0266] niccaṃ uyyutā, kadāci paṭisaṅkhāya appaṭiviratā. Peccāti asmā lokā paraṃ gantvā. Tamaṃ vajanti ye, patanti sattā nirayaṃ avaṃsirāti ye lokantarikandhakārasaṅkhātaṃ nīcakulatādibhedaṃ vā tamaṃ vajanti, ye ca patanti sattā avīciādibhedaṃ nirayaṃ avaṃsirā adhogatasīsā. Esāmagandhoti tesaṃ sattānaṃ tamavajananirayapatanahetu esa gedhavirodhātipātabhedo sabbāmagandhamūlabhūto yathāvuttenatthena tividho āmagandho. Na hi maṃsabhojananti maṃsabhojanaṃ pana na āmagandhoti.

251. “Greedy for these, hostile, and violent”: This means those who are greedy for these living beings through greed, hostile through hatred, and violent through delusion, not seeing the danger, repeatedly committing transgressions; or, in the evil deeds stated in the manner of “killing, cutting, and binding,” etc., those who are greedy, hostile, and violent through the lust, hatred, and delusion, respectively, known as greed, hostility, and violence. “Always intent”: This means constantly intent on performing unwholesome actions, never abstaining even after reflecting. “After departing”: This means having gone from this world to the next. “Those who go to darkness, beings fall headlong into hell”: This means those who go to darkness, which is the darkness of the inter-world (lokantarika) or of low birth, etc., and those beings who fall headlong, head downwards, into hell, such as Avīci and so forth. “This is the stench”: For those beings, this cause of going to darkness and falling into hell—this stench divided into greed, hostility, and violence, which is the root of all stench—is the threefold stench in the sense explained. “Not the eating of meat”: The eating of meat, however, is not called a stench.

252.
