Evaṃ bhagavā paramatthato āmagandhaṃ vissajjetvā duggatimaggabhāvañcassa pakāsetvā idāni yasmiṃ macchamaṃsabhojane tāpaso āmagandhasaññī duggatimaggasaññī [P 1.0291] ca hutvā tassa abhojanena suddhikāmo hutvā taṃ na bhuñjati, tassa ca aññassa ca tathāvidhassa sodhetuṃ asamatthabhāvaṃ dassento “na macchamaṃsa”nti imaṃ chappadaṃ gāthamāha. Tattha sabbapadāni [M 1.0307] antimapādena yojetabbāni – na macchamaṃsaṃ sodheti maccaṃ avitiṇṇakaṅkhaṃ, na āhutiyaññamutūpasevanā sodheti maccaṃ avitiṇṇakaṅkhanti evaṃ. Ettha ca na macchamaṃsanti akhādiyamānaṃ macchamaṃsaṃ na sodheti, tathā anāsakattanti evaṃ porāṇā vaṇṇenti. Evaṃ pana sundarataraṃ siyā “na macchamaṃsānaṃ anāsakattaṃ na macchamaṃsānānāsakattaṃ, macchamaṃsānaṃ anāsakattaṃ na sodheti, macca”nti athāpi siyā, evaṃ sante anāsakattaṃ ohīyatīti? Tañca na, amaratapena saṅgahitattā. “Ye vāpi loke amarā bahū tapā”ti ettha hi sabbopi vuttāvaseso attakilamatho saṅgahaṃ gacchatīti. Naggiyanti acelakattaṃ. Muṇḍiyanti muṇḍabhāvo. Jaṭājallanti jaṭā ca rajojallañca. Kharājinānīti kharāni ajinacammāni. Aggihuttassupasevanāti aggipāricāriyā. Amarāti amarabhāvapatthanatāya pavattakāyakilesā. Bahūti ukkuṭikappadhānādibhedato aneke. Tapāti sarīrasantāpā. Mantāti vedā. Āhutīti aggihomakammaṃ. Yaññamutūpasevanāti assamedhādiyaññā ca utūpasevanā ca. Utūpasevanā nāma gimhe ātapaṭṭhānasevanā, vasse rukkhamūlasevanā, hemante jalappavesasevanā. Na sodhenti maccaṃ avitiṇṇakaṅkhanti kilesasuddhiyā vā bhavasuddhiyā vā avitiṇṇavicikicchaṃ maccaṃ na sodhenti. Kaṅkhāmale hi sati na visuddho hoti, tvañca sakaṅkhoyevāti. Ettha ca “avitiṇṇakaṅkha”nti etaṃ “na macchamaṃsa”ntiādīni [P 1.0292] sutvā “kiṃ nu kho macchamaṃsānaṃ abhojanādinā siyā visuddhimaggo”ti tāpasassa kaṅkhāya uppannāya bhagavatā vuttaṃ siyāti no adhippāyo. Yā cassa “so macchamaṃsaṃ bhuñjatī”ti sutvāva buddhe kaṅkhā uppannā, taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

252. Thus, having explained the ultimate meaning of āmagandha and revealed its nature as a path to a miserable rebirth, the Blessed One, to show the inability to purify of that ascetic—who, perceiving fish and meat as āmagandha and a path to a miserable rebirth, refrains from eating it out of a desire for purity—and of others of a similar kind, now speaks this six-line verse, “Not fish nor meat.” Here, all terms should be connected with the final phrase, for example: “Not fish nor meat purifies a mortal who has not overcome doubt,” and “Not offerings, sacrifices, and seasonal observances purify a mortal who has not overcome doubt.” And herein, regarding “not fish nor meat,” the ancients explain it thus: “Not eating fish and meat does not purify; likewise, the state of not eating (anāsakattaṃ).” However, it might be more beautiful thus: “It is not the non-eating of fish and meat, nor the eating of fish and meat; the non-eating of fish and meat does not purify a mortal.” And if it were said: “In that case, is the practice of not eating disparaged?” That is not so, because it is included in the austerity for the sake of immortality. For in the passage, “Whatever austerities there are in the world for the sake of immortality,” all remaining self-mortification is included. “Nakedness” means being without clothes. “Shaven head” means the state of being shaven-headed. “Matted hair and grime” means matted hair, and dust and grime. “Rough hides” means rough animal skins. “Tending the sacrificial fire” means serving the fire. “Immortality” refers to defilements that arise from the aspiration for an immortal state. “Many” refers to numerous kinds, such as the practice of squatting and so forth. “Austerities” means torments of the body. “Chants” means the Vedas. “Offerings” means the fire-oblation ceremony. “Sacrifices and seasonal observances” means horse sacrifices and so on, and seasonal observances. Seasonal observances are: in summer, attending to a place in the sun; in the rainy season, attending to the root of a tree; in winter, attending to entering the water. “They do not purify a mortal who has not overcome doubt” means they do not purify a mortal who has not crossed beyond uncertainty regarding either the purity of defilements or the purity of existence. For when the stain of doubt is present, one is not purified; and you are one with doubt. And herein, the phrase “who has not overcome doubt” was not, in our opinion, spoken by the Blessed One in response to the doubt that arose in the ascetic upon hearing “Not fish nor meat,” etc., and wondering, “Could the path to purity be through not eating fish and meat and so on?” Rather, it should be understood that it was spoken with reference to the doubt that arose in him concerning the Buddha upon hearing, “He eats fish and meat.”

253. Evaṃ [V 1.0267] macchamaṃsānāsakattādīnaṃ sodhetuṃ asamatthabhāvaṃ dassetvā idāni sodhetuṃ samatthe dhamme dassento “sotesu gutto”ti imaṃ gāthamāha. Tattha sotesūti chasu indriyesu. Guttoti indriyasaṃvaraguttiyā samannāgato. Ettāvatā indriyasaṃvaraparivārasīlaṃ dasseti. Viditindriyo careti ñātapariññāya chaḷindriyāni viditvā pākaṭāni katvā careyya, vihareyyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Ettāvatā visuddhasīlassa nāmarūpaparicchedaṃ dasseti. Dhamme ṭhitoti ariyamaggena abhisametabbacatusaccadhamme ṭhito. Etena sotāpattibhūmiṃ dasseti. Ajjavamaddave [M 1.0308] ratoti ujubhāve ca mudubhāve ca rato. Etena sakadāgāmibhūmiṃ dasseti. Sakadāgāmī hi kāyavaṅkādikarānaṃ cittathaddhabhāvakarānañca rāgadosānaṃ tanubhāvā ajjavamaddave rato hoti. Saṅgātigoti rāgadosasaṅgātigo. Etena anāgāmibhūmiṃ dasseti. Sabbadukkhappahīnoti sabbassa vaṭṭadukkhassa hetuppahānena pahīnasabbadukkho. Etena arahattabhūmiṃ dasseti. Na lippati diṭṭhasutesu dhīroti so evaṃ anupubbena arahattaṃ patto dhitisampadāya dhīro diṭṭhasutesu dhammesu kenaci kilesena na lippati. Na kevalañca diṭṭhasutesu, mutaviññātesu ca na lippati, aññadatthu paramavisuddhippatto hotīti arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi.

253. Having thus shown the inability of not eating fish and meat and so on to purify, the Blessed One now speaks this verse, “Guarded in the senses,” to reveal the qualities capable of purification. Herein, “in the senses” refers to the six sense faculties. “Guarded” means endowed with the guarding of sense restraint. By this much, he indicates the virtue that has sense restraint as its retinue. “One who knows the senses should fare”: this means that having known the six senses through the full understanding of what is known and having made them manifest, one should fare, one should dwell. By this much, for one of pure virtue, he indicates the defining of name-and-form. “Established in the Dhamma”: this means established in the four-truth Dhamma to be fully realized by the noble path. By this, he indicates the stage of stream-entry. “Delighting in uprightness and gentleness”: this means delighting in a state of straightforwardness and a state of gentleness. By this, he indicates the stage of the once-returner. For a once-returner, due to the attenuation of the greed and hatred that cause bodily crookedness and mental rigidity, delights in uprightness and gentleness. “Having overcome attachment”: this means having overcome the attachment of greed and hatred. By this, he indicates the stage of the non-returner. “One who has abandoned all suffering”: this means one who has abandoned all suffering by abandoning the cause of all the suffering of the round of rebirths. By this, he indicates the stage of arahantship. “The wise one is not smeared by what is seen and heard”: Thus, having gradually attained arahantship, that wise one, endowed with steadfastness, is not smeared by any defilement in things seen and heard. And not only in what is seen and heard, but also in what is sensed and cognized he is not smeared; rather, he has attained supreme purity. Thus, he concludes the teaching with the pinnacle of arahantship.

254-5. Ito paraṃ “iccetamattha”nti dve gāthā saṅgītikārehi vuttā. Tāsamattho – iti bhagavā kassapo etamatthaṃ punappunaṃ anekāhi gāthāhi dhammādhiṭṭhānāya puggalādhiṭṭhānāya ca desanāya yāva tāpaso aññāsi, tāva so akkhāsi [P 1.0293] kathesi vitthāresi. Naṃ vedayi mantapāragūti sopi tañca atthaṃ mantapāragū, vedapāragū, tisso brāhmaṇo vedayi aññāsi. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Yasmā atthato ca padato ca desanānayato ca citrāhi gāthāhi munī pakāsayi. Kīdiso? Nirāmagandho asito durannayo, āmagandhakilesābhāvā nirāmagandho, taṇhādiṭṭhinissayābhāvā asito, bāhiradiṭṭhivasena “idaṃ seyyo idaṃ vara”nti kenaci netuṃ asakkuṇeyyattā durannayo. Evaṃ pakāsitavato cassa sutvāna buddhassa subhāsitaṃ padaṃ sukathitaṃ dhammadesanaṃ sutvā nirāmagandhaṃ nikkilesayogaṃ, sabbadukkhappanūdanaṃ sabbavaṭṭadukkhappanūdanaṃ, nīcamano nīcacitto hutvā vandi tathāgatassa, tisso brāhmaṇo tathāgatassa pāde pañcapatiṭṭhitaṃ katvā vandi. Tattheva pabbajjamarocayitthāti tattheva ca naṃ āsane nisinnaṃ kassapaṃ bhagavantaṃ tisso tāpaso pabbajjamarocayittha, ayācīti vuttaṃ hoti. Taṃ bhagavā “ehi bhikkhū”ti āha. So taṅkhaṇaṃyeva aṭṭhaparikkhārayutto hutvā ākāsenāgantvā vassasatikatthero viya bhagavantaṃ vanditvā katipāheneva sāvakapāramiñāṇaṃ paṭivijjhitvā tisso nāma aggasāvako ahosi, puna dutiyo bhāradvājo nāma. Evaṃ tassa bhagavato tissabhāradvājaṃ nāma sāvakayugaṃ ahosi.

Beyond this, two verses beginning 'Thus this meaning' were spoken by the compilers. Their meaning is as follows: Thus the Blessed One Kassapa repeatedly explained this matter with many verses, teaching with reference to the Dhamma and with reference to individuals, until the ascetic understood. He then declared, explained, and elaborated it. 'And the master of mantras understood it' means that the brahmin Tissa, a master of mantras and a master of the Vedas, also understood that meaning. For what reason? Because the Sage revealed it with diverse verses in terms of meaning, wording, and the method of teaching. What kind of Sage? Free from putridity, unattached, hard to lead—free from putridity due to the absence of the defilements of putridity; unattached due to the absence of reliance on craving and wrong views; hard to lead because no one could lead him with external views like 'this is better, this is superior.' Having heard the Buddha's well-spoken word, the well-taught Dhamma discourse—free from putridity, devoid of defiling bonds, dispelling all suffering, removing all the suffering of the cycle of rebirths—the brahmin Tissa, with a humble mind and humble heart, paid homage to the Tathāgata. He paid homage by prostrating with five points at the Tathāgata’s feet. As for the phrase 'Right there, he took delight in the going forth,' this means that the ascetic Tissa requested the going forth from the Blessed One Kassapa, who was seated there on his seat. The Blessed One said to him, 'Come, bhikkhu!' At that very moment, endowed with the eight requisites, he came through the air and, having paid homage to the Blessed One like a centenarian elder, within a few days he penetrated the knowledge of a disciple's perfection and became the chief disciple named Tissa, and the second was named Bhāradvāja. Thus, that Blessed One had a pair of disciples named Tissa and Bhāradvāja.

Amhākaṃ [V 1.0268][M 1.0309] pana bhagavā yā ca tissena brāhmaṇena ādito tisso gāthā vuttā, yā ca kassapena bhagavatā majjhe nava, yā ca tadā saṅgītikārehi ante dve, tā sabbāpi cuddasa gāthā ānetvā paripuṇṇaṃ katvā imaṃ āmagandhasuttaṃ ācariyappamukhānaṃ pañcannaṃ tāpasasatānaṃ āmagandhaṃ byākāsi. Taṃ sutvā so brāhmaṇo tatheva nīcamano [P 1.0294] hutvā bhagavato pāde vanditvā pabbajjaṃ yāci saddhiṃ parisāya. “Etha bhikkhavo”ti bhagavā avoca. Te tatheva ehibhikkhubhāvaṃ patvā ākāsenāgantvā bhagavantaṃ vanditvā katipāheneva sabbeva aggaphale arahatte patiṭṭhahiṃsūti.

But our Blessed One, having brought together all fourteen verses—the three verses initially spoken by the brahmin Tissa, the nine in the middle by the Blessed One Kassapa, and the two at the end by the compilers—made them complete and explained this Āmagandha Sutta, this teaching on putridity, to the five hundred ascetics led by their teacher. Having heard it, that brahmin, in the same way becoming humble-minded, paid homage at the Blessed One's feet and requested the going forth together with his assembly. 'Come, bhikkhus,' the Blessed One said. They, in that same way, attained the state of an 'ehi bhikkhu' and, having come through the air and paid homage to the Blessed One, within a few days were all established in the highest fruit, Arahantship.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya,

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya āmagandhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

in the Suttanipāta Commentary, the explanation of the Āmagandha Sutta is concluded.

3. Hirisuttavaṇṇanā

3. The Explanation of the Hiri Sutta

Hiriṃ [V 1.0269] tarantanti hirisuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Anuppanne bhagavati sāvatthiyaṃ aññataro brāhmaṇamahāsālo aḍḍho ahosi asītikoṭidhanavibhavo. Tassa ekaputtako ahosi piyo manāpo. So taṃ devakumāraṃ viya nānappakārehi sukhūpakaraṇehi saṃvaḍḍhento taṃ sāpateyyaṃ tassa aniyyātetvāva kālamakāsi saddhiṃ brāhmaṇiyā. Tato tassa māṇavassa mātāpitūnaṃ accayena bhaṇḍāgāriko sāragabbhaṃ vivaritvā sāpateyyaṃ niyyātento āha – “idaṃ te, sāmi, mātāpitūnaṃ santakaṃ, idaṃ ayyakapayyakānaṃ santakaṃ, idaṃ sattakulaparivaṭṭena āgata”nti. Māṇavo dhanaṃ disvā cintesi – “idaṃ dhanaṃyeva dissati, yehi pana idaṃ sañcitaṃ, te na dissanti, sabbeva maccuvasaṃ gatā. Gacchantā ca na ito kiñci ādāya agamaṃsu, evaṃ nāma bhoge pahāya gantabbo paraloko, na sakkā kiñci ādāya gantuṃ aññatra sucaritena. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ imaṃ dhanaṃ pariccajitvā sucaritadhanaṃ gaṇheyyaṃ, yaṃ sakkā ādāya gantu”nti. So divase divase satasahassaṃ vissajjento puna cintesi – “pahūtamidaṃ dhanaṃ, kiṃ iminā evamappakena pariccāgena, yaṃnūnāhaṃ [M 1.0310] mahādānaṃ dadeyya”nti. So rañño ārocesi – “mahārāja, mama ghare ettakaṃ dhanaṃ atthi, icchāmi tena mahādānaṃ dātuṃ. Sādhu, mahārāja, nagare ghosanaṃ kārāpethā”ti. Rājā tathā kārāpesi. So āgatāgatānaṃ bhājanāni pūretvā sattahi divasehi sabbadhanamadāsi[P 1.0295], datvā ca cintesi – “evaṃ mahāpariccāgaṃ katvā ayuttaṃ ghare vasituṃ, yaṃnūnāhaṃ pabbajeyya”nti. Tato parijanassa etamatthaṃ ārocesi. Te “mā, tvaṃ sāmi, ‘dhanaṃ parikkhīṇa’nti cintayi, mayaṃ appakeneva kālena nānāvidhehi upāyehi dhanasañcayaṃ karissāmā”ti vatvā nānappakārehi taṃ yāciṃsu. So tesaṃ yācanaṃ anādiyitvāva tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbaji.

The Hiri Sutta (Discourse on Shame) is so called because it deals with 'overcoming shame' (hiriṃ taranta). What is its origin? Before the Blessed One appeared in Sāvatthī, there was a wealthy brahmin householder, possessing eighty crores of wealth. He had a single son, dear and beloved. Raising him like a divine prince with all kinds of comforts, he passed away without transferring his inheritance to him, along with his brahmin wife. After the parents' death, the treasurer opened the treasury vault and, while handing over the inheritance, said to the young man: 'Master, this is your parents' wealth, this belongs to your grandparents and great-grandparents, and this has come down through seven generations.' Seeing the wealth, the young man reflected: 'This wealth is visible, but those who accumulated it are no longer seen—all have fallen under the sway of death. When they departed, they took nothing with them. Thus, one must leave this world abandoning riches; nothing can be taken except good conduct. Let me then relinquish this wealth and acquire the wealth of good conduct, which can be taken along.' Day by day, he gave away a hundred thousand, but then he thought again: 'This wealth is abundant—what is the use of such small generosity? Let me then give a great donation.' He informed the king: 'Great king, I have such wealth at home. I wish to make a great donation. Please, great king, have it proclaimed in the city.' The king did so. He filled the vessels of those who came and within seven days gave away all his wealth. After giving, he reflected: 'Having made such a great sacrifice, it is not fitting to remain at home. Let me then go forth.' He then informed his household of his intention. They pleaded: 'Master, do not think, "The wealth is exhausted." We will quickly amass wealth again through various means.' Though they entreated him in many ways, he disregarded their pleas and went forth into the life of an ascetic.

Tattha aṭṭhavidhā tāpasā – saputtabhariyā, uñchācārikā, sampattakālikā, anaggipakkikā, asmamuṭṭhikā, dantaluyyakā, pavattaphalikā, vaṇṭamuttikā cāti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.280). Tattha saputtabhariyāti puttadārena saddhiṃ pabbajitvā kasivaṇijjādīhi jīvikaṃ kappayamānā keṇiyajaṭilādayo. Uñchācārikāti nagaradvāre assamaṃ kārāpetvā tattha khattiyabrāhmaṇakumārādayo [V 1.0270] sippādīni sikkhāpetvā hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ paṭikkhipitvā tilataṇḍulādikappiyabhaṇḍapaṭiggāhakā, te saputtabhariyehi seṭṭhatarā. Sampattakālikāti āhāravelāya sampattaṃ āhāraṃ gahetvā yāpentā, te uñchācārikehi seṭṭhatarā. Anaggipakkikāti agginā apakkapattaphalāni khāditvā yāpentā, te sampattakālikehi seṭṭhatarā. Asmamuṭṭhikāti muṭṭhipāsāṇaṃ gahetvā aññaṃ vā kiñci vāsisatthakādiṃ gahetvā vicarantā yadā chātā honti, tadā sampattarukkhato tacaṃ gahetvā khāditvā uposathaṅgāni adhiṭṭhāya cattāro brahmavihāre bhāventi, te anaggipakkikehi seṭṭhatarā. Dantaluyyakāti muṭṭhipāsāṇādīnipi agahetvā carantā khudākāle sampattarukkhato dantehi uppāṭetvā tacaṃ khāditvā uposathaṅgāni adhiṭṭhāya brahmavihāre bhāventi, te asmamuṭṭhikehi seṭṭhatarā. Pavattaphalikāti jātassaraṃ [P 1.0296] vā vanasaṇḍaṃ vā nissāya vasantā yaṃ tattha sare bhisamuḷālādi, yaṃ vā vanasaṇḍe pupphakāle pupphaṃ, phalakāle phalaṃ, tameva khādanti. Pupphaphale asati antamaso tattha rukkhapapaṭikampi khāditvā vasanti, na tveva āhāratthāya aññatra gacchanti. Uposathaṅgādhiṭṭhānaṃ [M 1.0311] brahmavihārabhāvanaṃ ca karonti, te dantaluyyakehi seṭṭhatarā. Vaṇṭamuttikā nāma vaṇṭamuttāni bhūmiyaṃ patitāni paṇṇāniyeva khādanti, sesaṃ purimasadisameva, te sabbaseṭṭhā.

Here, there are eight kinds of ascetics: those with wives and children, gleaners, those who live on what comes at the right time, those who eat uncooked food, those who crush with stones, those who gnaw with their teeth, those who live on available produce, and those who eat what has fallen from the stalk (Dīghanikāya Aṭṭhakathā 1.280). Among them, 'those with wives and children' are those who have gone forth along with their wives and children and make a living by farming, trade, and so on, such as Keṇiya and other matted-hair ascetics. 'Gleaners' are those who have a hermitage built near a city gate, teach skills and the like to young nobles and brahmins, refuse gold and silver, and accept allowable items such as sesame and rice; they are superior to those with wives and children. 'Those who live on what comes at the right time' sustain themselves by taking whatever food is available at mealtime; they are superior to the gleaners. 'Those who eat uncooked food' sustain themselves by eating leaves and fruits that are not cooked by fire; they are superior to those who live on what comes at the right time. 'Those who crush with stones' are those who wander carrying a stone in the fist or some other implement like an axe or a small knife. When they are hungry, they take bark from a tree that is at hand, eat it, undertake the Uposatha observances, and cultivate the four divine abidings; they are superior to those who eat uncooked food. 'Those who gnaw with their teeth' are those who wander without taking a stone for the fist or other such things. At a time of hunger, they tear off bark from a tree that is at hand with their teeth, eat it, undertake the Uposatha observances, and cultivate the divine abidings; they are superior to those who crush with stones. 'Those who live on available produce' are those who dwell relying on a natural lake or a forest grove, eating whatever is there in the lake, such as lotus stalks and roots, or in the forest grove, flowers in the flowering season, or fruits in the fruiting season. If there are no flowers or fruits, they eat even the bark of a tree there and sustain themselves, but they never go elsewhere for food. They undertake the Uposatha observances and the cultivation of the divine abidings; they are superior to those who gnaw with their teeth. Those called 'those who eat what has fallen from the stalk' eat only leaves that have been shed from their stalks and have fallen to the ground. The rest is the same as the previous. They are the best of all.

Ayaṃ pana brāhmaṇakulaputto “tāpasapabbajjāsu aggapabbajjaṃ pabbajissāmī”ti vaṇṭamuttikapabbajjameva pabbajitvā himavante dve tayo pabbate atikkamma assamaṃ kārāpetvā paṭivasati. Atha bhagavā loke uppajjitvā pavattitavaradhammacakko anupubbena sāvatthiṃ gantvā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Tena kho pana samayena sāvatthivāsī eko puriso pabbate candanasārādīni gavesanto tassa assamaṃ patvā abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. So taṃ disvā “kuto āgatosī”ti pucchi. “Sāvatthito, bhante”ti. “Kā tattha pavattī”ti? “Tattha, bhante, manussā appamattā dānādīni puññāni karontī”ti. “Kassa ovādaṃ sutvā”ti? “Buddhassa bhagavato”ti. Tāpaso buddhasaddassavanena vimhito “buddhoti tvaṃ, bho purisa, vadesī”ti āmagandhe vuttanayeneva tikkhattuṃ pucchitvā “ghosopi kho eso dullabho”ti attamano bhagavato santikaṃ gantukāmo hutvā cintesi – “na yuttaṃ buddhassa santikaṃ tucchameva gantuṃ, kiṃ nu kho gahetvā gaccheyya”nti. Puna cintesi – “buddhā nāma āmisagarukā na honti, handāhaṃ dhammapaṇṇākāraṃ gahetvā gacchāmī”ti cattāro pañhe abhisaṅkhari [P 1.0297] –

Now, this young man from a brahmin family, thinking, 'Among the ascetic ordinations, I will undertake the supreme ordination,' undertook the very ordination of one who eats what has fallen from the stalk. Having crossed two or three mountains in the Himalayas, he had a hermitage built and dwelt there. Then the Blessed One, having arisen in the world and set in motion the noble Wheel of Dhamma, in due course arrived at Sāvatthī and was dwelling in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. At that time, a certain man from Sāvatthī, while searching for sandalwood heartwood and other things in the mountains, came to the ascetic's hermitage, paid homage, and stood to one side. Seeing him, the ascetic asked, 'Where have you come from?' 'From Sāvatthī, venerable sir.' 'What is the news there?' 'There, venerable sir, the people are heedful and perform meritorious deeds such as giving.' 'Having heard whose instruction?' 'The Buddha, the Blessed One's.' The ascetic, astonished at hearing the word 'Buddha,' asked three times in the same way as stated in the Āmagandha Sutta, 'Good man, do you say "Buddha"?' Then, delighted, thinking, 'Even this sound is difficult to encounter!', he desired to go to the Blessed One and thought: 'It is not proper to go to the Buddha empty-handed. What should I take with me?' He thought again: 'Buddhas do not hold material things in high esteem. Well now, I will take a gift of the Dhamma.' And he formulated four questions:

“Kīdiso [V 1.0271] mitto na sevitabbo, kīdiso mitto sevitabbo;

Kīdiso payogo payuñjitabbo, kiṃ rasānaṃ agga”nti.

What kind of friend should not be associated with, what kind of friend should be associated with; what kind of effort should be applied, what is the chief among tastes?

So te pañhe gahetvā majjhimadesābhimukho pakkamitvā anupubbena sāvatthiṃ patvā jetavanaṃ paviṭṭho. Bhagavāpi tasmiṃ samaye dhammadesanatthāya āsane nisinnoyeva hoti. So bhagavantaṃ disvā avanditvāva ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Bhagavā “kacci, isi, khamanīya”ntiādinā nayena sammodi. Sopi “khamanīyaṃ, bho gotamā”tiādinā nayena paṭisammoditvā “yadi buddho bhavissati, manasā pucchite pañhe vācāya eva vissajjessatī”ti manasā eva bhagavantaṃ te pañhe pucchi. Bhagavā brāhmaṇena puṭṭho ādipañhaṃ [M 1.0312] tāva vissajjetuṃ hiriṃ tarantanti ārabhitvā aḍḍhateyyā gāthāyo āha.

Taking those questions, he set out towards the Middle Country and gradually reached Sāvatthī, entering Jetavana. At that time, the Blessed One was indeed seated on the seat for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma. Upon seeing the Blessed One, he stood to one side without paying respects. The Blessed One greeted him, saying, “I hope, ascetic, that you are keeping well,” and so on. He, in turn, exchanged pleasantries, saying, “I am keeping well, good Gotama,” and so on. Then he thought, “If he is a Buddha, he will answer with speech the questions I ask in my mind.” So he mentally posed those questions to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, asked by the brahmin, in order to answer the first question, began by reciting two and a half verses, starting with 'hiriṃ tarantam...'

256. Tāsaṃ attho – hiriṃ tarantanti hiriṃ atikkamantaṃ ahirikaṃ nillajjaṃ. Vijigucchamānanti asucimiva passamānaṃ. Ahiriko hi hiriṃ jigucchati asucimiva passati, tena naṃ na bhajati na allīyati. Tena vuttaṃ “vijigucchamāna”nti. Tavāhamasmi iti bhāsamānanti “ahaṃ, samma, tava sahāyo hitakāmo sukhakāmo, jīvitampi me tuyhaṃ atthāya pariccatta”nti evamādinā nayena bhāsamānaṃ. Sayhāni kammāni anādiyantanti evaṃ bhāsitvāpi ca sayhāni kātuṃ sakkānipi tassa kammāni anādiyantaṃ karaṇatthāya asamādiyantaṃ. Atha vā cittena tattha ādaramattampi akarontaṃ, apica kho pana uppannesu kiccesu byasanameva dassentaṃ. Neso mamanti iti naṃ vijaññāti taṃ evarūpaṃ “mittapaṭirūpako eso, neso me mitto”ti evaṃ paṇḍito puriso vijāneyya.

256. The meaning of those verses should be understood thus. 'One who crosses over shame' means one who transgresses shame, who is shameless (`ahirika`), without modesty (`nillajja`). 'Being disgusted' means seeing it as if it were impure. For a shameless person is disgusted by shame, seeing it as if it were impure; therefore, one does not associate with him or cling to him. For this reason, it is said, 'being disgusted.' 'Speaking thus: "I am yours"' means speaking in a way such as, 'Friend, I am your companion, your well-wisher, desiring your happiness; even my life is given up for your sake.' 'Not undertaking deeds that can be done' means that even after speaking thus, he does not undertake for his friend deeds that are possible to do, not accepting them for the purpose of performing them. Or, it means not showing even a little respect in his mind towards him, and moreover, when tasks arise, showing only calamity. 'He is not my friend; thus should one know him' means a wise person should know such a one thus: 'This is a counterfeit friend; he is not my friend.'

257. Ananvayanti yaṃ atthaṃ dassāmi, karissāmīti ca bhāsati, tena ananugataṃ. Piyaṃ vācaṃ yo mittesu pakubbatīti yo atītānāgatehi padehi paṭisantharanto niratthakena saṅgaṇhanto [P 1.0298] kevalaṃ byañjanacchāyāmatteneva piyaṃ mittesu vācaṃ pavatteti. Akarontaṃ bhāsamānaṃ, parijānanti paṇḍitāti evarūpaṃ yaṃ bhāsati, taṃ akarontaṃ, kevalaṃ vācāya bhāsamānaṃ “vacīparamo nāmesa amitto mittapaṭirūpako”ti evaṃ paricchinditvā paṇḍitā jānanti.

257. 'Not following through' means not being in accordance with what one says, such as, 'I will give,' or 'I will do.' 'One who utters pleasant speech to friends' means one who makes polite conversation with words about the past and future, wins one over with what is useless, and produces pleasant speech towards friends merely with the semblance of fine words. 'The wise understand one who speaks but does not act' means that the wise, having discerned, know such a one who speaks but does not do what he says—one who merely speaks with words—thus: 'This one is named "one for whom speech is the highest," an enemy, a counterfeit friend.'

258. Na so mitto yo sadā appamatto, bhedāsaṅkī randhamevānupassīti yo bhedameva āsaṅkamāno katamadhurena upacārena sadā appamatto viharati, yaṃkiñci assatiyā amanasikārena [V 1.0272] kataṃ, aññāṇakena vā akataṃ, “yadā maṃ garahissati, tadā naṃ etena paṭicodessāmī”ti evaṃ randhameva anupassati, na so mitto sevitabboti.

258. 'He is not a friend who is always vigilant, suspecting a breach and ever looking for a fault.' This means one who, ever suspecting a breach, dwells always vigilant with feigned sweet courtesy. Regarding anything done through forgetfulness or inattention, or not done through ignorance, he thinks, 'When he reproaches me, then I will charge him in return with this.' Thus he is ever looking for a fault. Such a one is not a friend to be associated with.

Evaṃ bhagavā “kīdiso mitto na sevitabbo”ti imaṃ ādipañhaṃ vissajjetvā dutiyaṃ vissajjetuṃ “yasmiñca setī”ti imaṃ upaḍḍhagāthamāha. Tassattho [M 1.0313] yasmiñca mitte mitto tassa hadayamanupavisitvā sayanena yathā nāma pitu urasi putto “imassa mayi urasi sayante dukkhaṃ vā anattamanatā vā bhaveyyā”tiādīhi aparisaṅkamāno nibbisaṅko hutvā seti, evamevaṃ dāradhanajīvitādīsu vissāsaṃ karonto mittabhāvena nibbisaṅko seti. Yo ca parehi kāraṇasataṃ kāraṇasahassampi vatvā abhejjo, sa ve mitto sevitabboti.

Thus the Blessed One, having answered the initial question, 'What kind of friend should not be associated with?' spoke this half-verse, 'And in whom one lies down...' to answer the second question. Its meaning is: a friend lies down in a friend, having entered his heart, just as a son lies on his father's chest without apprehension, thinking, 'There will be no suffering or displeasure for him while I lie on his chest,' and so on, thus lying down free from anxiety. In the same way, placing trust in him regarding wife, wealth, life, and so on, he lies down free from anxiety through friendship. And one who, though others speak a hundred or a thousand reasons, is indivisible—he indeed is a friend to be associated with.

259. Evaṃ bhagavā “kīdiso mitto sevitabbo”ti evaṃ dutiyapañhaṃ vissajjetvā tatiyaṃ vissajjetuṃ “pāmujjakaraṇa”nti gāthamāha. Tassattho – pāmujjaṃ karotīti pāmujjakaraṇaṃ. Ṭhānanti kāraṇaṃ. Kiṃ pana tanti? Vīriyaṃ. Tañhi dhammūpasañhitaṃ pītipāmojjasukhamuppādanato pāmujjakaraṇanti vuccati. Yathāha “svākhāte, bhikkhave, dhammavinaye yo āraddhavīriyo, so sukhaṃ viharatī”ti (a. ni. 1.319). Pasaṃsaṃ āvahatīti pasaṃsāvahanaṃ. Ādito dibbamānusakasukhānaṃ[P 1.0299], pariyosāne nibbānasukhassa āvahanato phalūpacārena sukhaṃ. Phalaṃ paṭikaṅkhamāno phalānisaṃso. Bhāvetīti vaḍḍheti. Vahanto porisaṃ dhuranti purisānucchavikaṃ bhāraṃ ādāya viharanto etaṃ sammappadhānavīriyasaṅkhātaṃ ṭhānaṃ bhāveti, īdiso payogo sevitabboti.

259. Thus the Blessed One, having answered the second question, 'What kind of friend should be associated with?' spoke the verse beginning 'pāmujjakaraṇa' to answer the third. Its meaning is: 'A cause of joy' (`pāmujjakaraṇa`) is so called because it produces joy (`pāmujja`). 'State' (`ṭhāna`) means cause. What is that? It is energy (`vīriya`). For that, being connected with the Dhamma, is called 'a cause of joy' because it gives rise to the happiness of rapture and joy. As it is said: 'Monks, in this well-taught Dhamma and Discipline, one who has aroused energy dwells happily.' 'Praise-bringing' (`pasaṃsāvahana`) is so called because it brings praise. It is called 'happiness' (`sukha`) figuratively, due to its fruit, because it brings divine and human happiness in the beginning, and the happiness of Nibbāna in the end. 'Having the fruit as its benefit' (`phalānisaṃso`) means one who expects the fruit. 'Develops' (`bhāveti`) means cultivates. 'Bearing a man's burden' means that while dwelling having taken up a burden befitting a man, one develops this state known as right exertion and energy. Such an effort should be cultivated.

260. Evaṃ bhagavā “kīdiso payogo payuñjitabbo”ti tatiyapañhaṃ vissajjetvā catutthaṃ vissajjetuṃ “pavivekarasa”nti gāthamāha. Tattha pavivekoti kilesavivekato jātattā aggaphalaṃ vuccati, tassa rasoti assādanaṭṭhena taṃsampayuttaṃ sukhaṃ. Upasamopi kilesūpasamante jātattā nibbānasaṅkhātaupasamārammaṇattā vā tadeva, dhammapītirasopi ariyadhammato anapetāya nibbānasaṅkhāte dhamme uppannāya pītiyā rasattā tadeva. Taṃ pavivekarasaṃ upasamassa ca rasaṃ pitvā tadeva dhammapītirasaṃ pivaṃ niddaro hoti nippāpo, pivitvāpi kilesapariḷāhābhāvena niddaro, pivantopi pahīnapāpattā nippāpo hoti, tasmā etaṃ rasānamagganti. Keci pana “jhānanibbānapaccavekkhaṇānaṃ kāyacittaupadhivivekānañca vasena pavivekarasādayo tayo eva ete dhammā”ti yojenti[M 1.0314], purimameva sundaraṃ. Evaṃ bhagavā catutthapañhaṃ vissajjento arahattanikūṭena [V 1.0273] desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi. Desanāpariyosāne brāhmaṇo bhagavato santike pabbajitvā katipāheneva paṭisambhidāppatto arahā ahosīti.

260. Thus the Blessed One, having answered the third question, 'What kind of effort should be applied?' spoke the verse beginning 'the taste of seclusion' to answer the fourth. Therein, 'seclusion' (`paviveka`) refers to the supreme fruit, as it is born from seclusion from the defilements. 'Its taste' (`rasa`) means the happiness associated with it, in the sense of savoring. 'Peace' (`upasama`) is also that very thing, as it is born when the defilements are pacified, or because it has the peace called Nibbāna as its object. 'The taste of Dhamma-rapture' is also that very thing, as it is the taste of the rapture that has arisen in the Dhamma called Nibbāna, which is not separate from the noble nature. Having drunk that taste of seclusion and the taste of peace, drinking that very taste of Dhamma-rapture, one becomes free from distress and free from evil. Having drunk it, one is free from distress due to the absence of the fever of defilements; while drinking it, one is free from evil because evil has been abandoned. Therefore, this is the highest of tastes. Some, however, connect it thus: 'These three things—the taste of seclusion and so on—are based on jhāna, Nibbāna, and reviewing, and on the seclusion of body, mind, and substrata.' But the former explanation is better. Thus the Blessed One, in answering the fourth question, concluded the discourse with the peak of arahantship. At the end of the discourse, the brahmin went forth in the presence of the Blessed One and in just a few days became an Arahant who had attained the analytical knowledges.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddakanikāya,

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya hirisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Here ends the explanation of the Hiri Sutta in the Commentary on the Sutta Nipāta.

Paṭhamo bhāgo niṭṭhito.

The first part is concluded.

Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Khuddakanikāye

In the Khuddaka Nikāya

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā

The Commentary on the Sutta Nipāta

(Dutiyo bhāgo)

(The Second Part)

2. Cūḷavaggo

2. The Minor Division

4. Maṅgalasuttavaṇṇanā

4. The Explanation of the Maṅgala Sutta

Evaṃ [V 2.0001][M 2.0001][P 1.0300] me sutanti maṅgalasuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Jambudīpe kira tattha tattha nagaradvārasanthāgārasabhādīsu mahājanā sannipatitvā hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ datvā nānappakāraṃ sītāharaṇādibāhirakakathaṃ kathāpenti, ekekā kathā catumāsaccayena niṭṭhāti. Tattha ekadivasaṃ maṅgalakathā samuṭṭhāsi – “kiṃ nu kho maṅgalaṃ, kiṃ diṭṭhaṃ maṅgalaṃ, sutaṃ maṅgalaṃ, mutaṃ maṅgalaṃ, ko maṅgalaṃ jānātī”ti?

Thus have I heard—the Maṅgala Sutta. What is its origin? In Jambudīpa, it is said, great crowds of people, having gathered in various places such as city gates, assembly halls, and public forums, would give silver and gold to have various kinds of external tales recited, such as that of the abduction of Sītā. Each tale would conclude after four months. There, on one day, a discussion on blessings arose: 'What, indeed, is a blessing? Is what is seen a blessing, what is heard a blessing, or what is sensed a blessing? Who knows what a blessing is?'

Atha [V 2.0002] diṭṭhamaṅgaliko nāmeko puriso āha – “ahaṃ maṅgalaṃ jānāmi, diṭṭhaṃ loke maṅgalaṃ, diṭṭhaṃ nāma abhimaṅgalasammataṃ rūpaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ – idhekacco kālasseva vuṭṭhāya cātakasakuṇaṃ vā passati, beluvalaṭṭhiṃ vā gabbhiniṃ vā kumārake vā alaṅkatapaṭiyatte puṇṇaghaṭaṃ vā allarohitamacchaṃ vā ājaññaṃ vā ājaññarathaṃ vā usabhaṃ vā gāviṃ vā kapilaṃ vā, yaṃ vā panaññampi kiñci evarūpaṃ abhimaṅgalasammataṃ rūpaṃ passati, idaṃ vuccati diṭṭhamaṅgala”nti. Tassa vacanaṃ ekacce aggahesuṃ, ekacce nāggahesuṃ. Ye nāggahesuṃ, te tena saha vivadiṃsu.

Then a man named Diṭṭhamaṅgalika said: 'I know what a blessing is. In the world, what is seen is a blessing; a visible form is what is considered a great blessing. For instance, when someone, having arisen early in the morning, sees a cuckoo, or a bamboo staff, a pregnant woman, well-adorned young boys, a full water pot, a fresh rohita fish, a thoroughbred horse, a chariot drawn by thoroughbreds, a bull, a cow, a tawny cow, or any other such form considered a great blessing—this is called a visible blessing.' Some accepted his words; others did not. Those who did not accept them disputed with him.

Atha [M 2.0002] sutamaṅgaliko nāmeko puriso āha – “cakkhu nāmetaṃ, bho, sucimpi asucimpi passati, tathā sundarampi asundarampi, manāpampi amanāpampi. Yadi tena diṭṭhaṃ maṅgalaṃ siyā, sabbampi maṅgalaṃ siyā, tasmā na diṭṭhaṃ maṅgalaṃ, apica kho pana sutaṃ maṅgalaṃ, sutaṃ nāma abhimaṅgalasammato saddo. Seyyathidaṃ – idhekacco kālasseva vuṭṭhāya vaḍḍhāti vā vaḍḍhamānāti vā puṇṇāti vā phussāti vā sumanāti vā sirīti vā sirivaḍḍhāti vā ajja sunakkhattaṃ sumuhuttaṃ sudivasaṃ sumaṅgalanti evarūpaṃ vā yaṃkiñci abhimaṅgalasammataṃ saddaṃ suṇāti, idaṃ vuccati sutamaṅgala”nti. Tassapi vacanaṃ ekacce aggahesuṃ, ekacce nāggahesuṃ. Ye nāggahesuṃ, te tena saha vivadiṃsu.

Then a man named Sutamaṅgalika said: 'Friend, this eye sees what is pure and impure, likewise what is beautiful and ugly, what is pleasant and unpleasant. If what is seen were thereby a blessing, then everything seen would be a blessing. Therefore, what is seen is not a blessing. But indeed, what is heard is a blessing; a sound is what is considered a great blessing. For instance, when someone, having arisen early, hears words such as "Prosper!", "Prospering!", "Full!", "Auspicious!", "Pleasant!", "Splendor!", "Increasing Splendor!", or "Today is a good constellation, a good moment, a good day, a good blessing!", or any other such sound considered a great blessing—this is called a heard blessing.' His words, too, some accepted, and some did not. Those who did not accept them disputed with him.

Atha mutamaṅgaliko nāmeko puriso āha – “sotampi hi nāmetaṃ bho sādhumpi asādhumpi manāpampi amanāpampi suṇāti. Yadi tena sutaṃ maṅgalaṃ siyā, sabbampi maṅgalaṃ siyā, tasmā na sutaṃ maṅgalaṃ, apica kho pana mutaṃ maṅgalaṃ, mutaṃ nāma abhimaṅgalasammataṃ gandharasaphoṭṭhabbaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ – idhekacco kālasseva vuṭṭhāya padumagandhādipupphagandhaṃ vā ghāyati, phussadantakaṭṭhaṃ vā khādati, pathaviṃ vā āmasati, haritasassaṃ vā allagomayaṃ vā kacchapaṃ vā tilavāhaṃ vā pupphaṃ vā phalaṃ vā āmasati, phussamattikāya vā sammā limpati, phussasāṭakaṃ vā nivāseti, phussaveṭhanaṃ vā dhāreti, yaṃ vā panaññampi kiñci evarūpaṃ abhimaṅgalasammataṃ gandhaṃ vā ghāyati, rasaṃ vā sāyati, phoṭṭhabbaṃ vā phusati, idaṃ vuccati mutamaṅgala”nti. Tassapi vacanaṃ ekacce aggahesuṃ, ekacce nāggahesuṃ.

Then a man named Mutamaṅgalika said: 'Friend, this ear hears what is good and bad, what is pleasant and unpleasant. If what is heard were thereby a blessing, then everything heard would be a blessing. Therefore, what is heard is not a blessing. But indeed, what is sensed is a blessing; what is considered a great blessing are odors, tastes, and tangible objects. For instance, when someone, having arisen early, smells the fragrance of a lotus or other flowers; chews a tooth-stick with a pleasant touch; touches the earth, green grain, fresh cow dung, a tortoise, a sesame plant, a flower, or a fruit; anoints themselves well with clay that is pleasant to the touch; wears a garment that is pleasant to the touch; or puts on a head-wrap that is pleasant to the touch; or when one smells any other such odor, tastes any such flavor, or feels any such tangible object considered a great blessing—this is called a sensed blessing.' His words, too, some accepted, and some did not.

Tattha na diṭṭhamaṅgaliko sutamutamaṅgalike asakkhi saññāpetuṃ. Na tesaṃ aññataro itare dve. Tesu ca manussesu ye diṭṭhamaṅgalikassa vacanaṃ gaṇhiṃsu, te “diṭṭhaṃyeva maṅgala”nti gatā. Ye sutamutamaṅgalikānaṃ vacanaṃ gaṇhiṃsu, te “sutaṃyeva mutaṃyeva maṅgala”nti gatā. Evamayaṃ maṅgalakathā sakalajambudīpe pākaṭā jātā.

Therein, the Diṭṭhamaṅgalika was not able to convince the Sutamaṅgalika and the Mutamaṅgalika, nor was any one of the three able to convince the other two. And among those people, those who accepted the words of the Diṭṭhamaṅgalika adopted the view: 'Only what is seen is a blessing.' Those who accepted the words of the Sutamaṅgalika and the Mutamaṅgalika adopted the views: 'Only what is heard is a blessing,' and 'Only what is sensed is a blessing.' In this way, this discussion about blessings became well-known throughout all of Jambudīpa.

Atha sakalajambudīpe manussā gumbagumbā hutvā “kiṃ nu kho maṅgala”nti maṅgalāni cintayiṃsu[V 2.0003]. Tesaṃ manussānaṃ ārakkhadevatā taṃ kathaṃ sutvā tatheva maṅgalāni cintayiṃsu. Tāsaṃ devatānaṃ bhummadevatā mittā honti, atha tato sutvā bhummadevatāpi tatheva maṅgalāni cintayiṃsu. Tāsampi devatānaṃ ākāsaṭṭhadevatā mittā honti, ākāsaṭṭhadevatānaṃ cātumahārājikadevatā. Eteneva upāyena yāva sudassīdevatānaṃ [M 2.0003] akaniṭṭhadevatā mittā honti, atha tato sutvā akaniṭṭhadevatāpi tatheva gumbagumbā hutvā maṅgalāni cintayiṃsu. Evaṃ dasasahassacakkavāḷesu sabbattha maṅgalacintā udapādi. Uppannā ca sā “idaṃ maṅgalaṃ idaṃ maṅgala”nti vinicchiyamānāpi appattā eva vinicchayaṃ dvādasa vassāni aṭṭhāsi. Sabbe manussā ca devā ca brahmāno ca ṭhapetvā ariyasāvake diṭṭhasutamutavasena tidhā bhinnā. Ekopi “idameva maṅgala”nti yathābhuccato niṭṭhaṅgato nāhosi, maṅgalakolāhalaṃ loke uppajji.

Then, throughout all of Jambudīpa, people formed into groups and pondered on blessings, asking, 'What, indeed, is a blessing?' Hearing this discussion, their guardian deities likewise pondered on blessings. The earth-dwelling devas are friends of those deities; hearing it from them, the earth-dwelling devas also pondered on blessings in the same way. The sky-dwelling devas are friends of those devas, and the devas of the Four Great Kings are friends of the sky-dwelling devas. By this method, the chain of friends extends up to the Akaniṭṭha devas, who are friends of the Sudassī devas. Hearing of it, the Akaniṭṭha devas also formed into groups and pondered on blessings. Thus, this pondering on blessings arose everywhere throughout the ten-thousand world-systems. And having arisen, though it was deliberated upon—'This is a blessing! That is a blessing!'—it stood for twelve years without ever reaching a conclusion. All humans, devas, and brahmās, with the exception of the noble disciples, were split into three factions according to what was seen, heard, or sensed. Not even one being came to the conclusion in accordance with reality, 'This alone is a blessing.' An uproar concerning blessings arose in the world.

Kolāhalaṃ nāma pañcavidhaṃ – kappakolāhalaṃ, cakkavattikolāhalaṃ, buddhakolāhalaṃ, maṅgalakolāhalaṃ, moneyyakolāhalanti. Tattha kāmāvacaradevā muttasirā vikiṇṇakesā rudammukhā assūni hatthehi puñchamānā rattavatthanivatthā ativiya virūpavesadhārino hutvā, “vassasatasahassassa accayena kappuṭṭhānaṃ bhavissati. Ayaṃ loko vinassissati, mahāsamuddo sussissati, ayañca mahāpathavī sineru ca pabbatarājā uḍḍhayhissati vinassissati, yāva brahmalokā lokavināso bhavissati. Mettaṃ, mārisā, bhāvetha, karuṇaṃ muditaṃ upekkhaṃ, mārisā, bhāvetha, mātaraṃ upaṭṭhahatha, pitaraṃ upaṭṭhahatha, kule jeṭṭhāpacāyino hotha, jāgaratha mā pamādatthā”ti manussapathe vicaritvā ārocenti. Idaṃ kappakolāhalaṃ nāma.

An uproar, so-called, is of five kinds: the uproar of the eon, the uproar of a wheel-turning monarch, the uproar of a Buddha, the uproar of the blessing, and the uproar of sagacity. Among these, the devas of the sense-sphere, with loosened hair and dishevelled hair, with weeping faces, wiping away tears with their hands, dressed in red garments, having assumed an extremely unsightly appearance, wander along the paths of humans and announce: 'Good sirs, after a hundred thousand years have passed, the end of the eon will occur. This world will be destroyed, the great ocean will dry up, and this great earth and Sineru, the king of mountains, will be consumed by fire and destroyed. The destruction of the world will extend as far as the Brahmā world. Good sirs, cultivate loving-kindness! Good sirs, cultivate compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity! Attend to your mother, attend to your father! Be respectful to the elders in your family! Be vigilant, do not be heedless!' This is called the uproar of the eon.

Kāmāvacaradevāyeva “vassasatassaccayena cakkavattirājā loke uppajjissatī”ti manussapathe vicaritvā ārocenti. Idaṃ cakkavattikolāhalaṃ nāma.

The devas of the sense-sphere themselves, traveling along the paths of humans, announce: 'After a hundred years, a wheel-turning monarch will arise in the world.' This is called the uproar of a wheel-turning monarch.

Suddhāvāsā pana devā brahmābharaṇena alaṅkaritvā brahmaveṭhanaṃ sīse katvā pītisomanassajātā buddhaguṇavādino “vassasahassassa accayena buddho loke uppajjissatī”ti manussapathe vicaritvā ārocenti. Idaṃ buddhakolāhalaṃ nāma.

But the Suddhāvāsa devas, having adorned themselves with the ornaments of a Brahmā and placed a Brahmā-headdress upon their heads, filled with joy and gladness, speaking in praise of the Buddha's virtues, wander along the paths of humans and announce: 'After a thousand years have passed, a Buddha will arise in the world.' This is called the uproar of the Buddha.

Suddhāvāsā eva devā manussānaṃ cittaṃ ñatvā “dvādasannaṃ vassānaṃ accayena sammāsambuddho maṅgalaṃ kathessatī”ti manussapathe vicaritvā ārocenti. Idaṃ maṅgalakolāhalaṃ nāma.

The Suddhāvāsa devas themselves, knowing the minds of humans, wander along the paths of humans and announce: 'After twelve years have passed, the Perfectly and Completely Enlightened One will teach on the blessing.' This is called the uproar of the blessing.

Suddhāvāsā [M 2.0004] eva devā “sattannaṃ vassānaṃ accayena aññataro bhikkhu bhagavatā saddhiṃ samāgamma moneyyapaṭipadaṃ pucchissatī”ti manussapathe vicaritvā ārocenti. Idaṃ moneyyakolāhalaṃ [V 2.0004] nāma. Imesu pañcasu kolāhalesu diṭṭhamaṅgalādivasena tidhā bhinnesu devamanussesu idaṃ maṅgalakolāhalaṃ loke uppajji.

The Suddhāvāsa devas themselves wander along the paths of humans and announce: 'After seven years have passed, a certain monk will approach the Blessed One and ask about the practice of sagacity.' This is called the uproar of sagacity. Among these five uproars, this uproar of the blessing arose in the world among devas and humans who were divided into three factions over what is seen as a blessing, and so forth.

Atha devesu ca manussesu ca vicinitvā vicinitvā maṅgalāni alabhamānesu dvādasannaṃ vassānaṃ accayena tāvatiṃsakāyikā devatā saṅgamma samāgamma evaṃ samacintesuṃ – “seyyathāpi nāma, mārisā, gharasāmiko antogharajanānaṃ, gāmasāmiko gāmavāsīnaṃ, rājā sabbamanussānaṃ, evamevaṃ ayaṃ sakko devānamindo amhākaṃ aggo ca seṭṭho ca yadidaṃ puññena tejena issariyena paññāya dvinnaṃ devalokānaṃ adhipati. Yaṃnūna mayaṃ sakkaṃ devānamindaṃ etamatthaṃ puccheyyāmā”ti. Tā sakkassa santikaṃ gantvā sakkaṃ devānamindaṃ taṅkhaṇānurūpanivāsanābharaṇasassirikasarīraṃ aḍḍhateyyakoṭiaccharāgaṇaparivutaṃ pāricchattakamūle paṇḍukambalavarāsane nisinnaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ ṭhatvā etadavocuṃ – “yagghe, mārisa, jāneyyāsi, etarahi maṅgalapañhā samuṭṭhitā, eke diṭṭhaṃ maṅgalanti vadanti, eke sutaṃ maṅgalanti vadanti, eke mutaṃ maṅgalanti vadanti. Tattha mayañca aññe ca aniṭṭhaṅgatā, sādhu vata no tvaṃ yāthāvato byākarohī”ti. Devarājā pakatiyāpi paññavā “ayaṃ maṅgalakathā kattha paṭhamaṃ samuṭṭhitā”ti āha. “Mayaṃ deva cātumahārājikānaṃ assumhā”ti āhaṃsu. Tato cātumahārājikā ākāsaṭṭhadevatānaṃ, ākāsaṭṭhadevatā bhummadevatānaṃ, bhummadevatā manussārakkhadevatānaṃ, manussārakkhadevatā “manussaloke samuṭṭhitā”ti āhaṃsu.

Then, as devas and humans, having sought and sought, were not discovering what a blessing is, after twelve years had passed, the deities of the Tāvatiṃsa realm gathered together and deliberated thus: 'Good sirs, just as the master of a house is foremost among the people of the household, the village headman among the villagers, and the king among all humans, so too is this Sakka, lord of the devas, our foremost and chief—by merit, power, sovereignty, and wisdom—and ruler of the two deva worlds. What if we were to ask Sakka, lord of the devas, about this matter?' They then went to Sakka's presence and found him seated at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree on the excellent Paṇḍukambala stone seat, his body glorious with attire and ornaments befitting the occasion, surrounded by a retinue of two and a half crores of celestial nymphs. Having paid homage to him, they stood to one side and said this: 'Pray, good sir, may you know that a question concerning the blessing has now arisen. Some say a blessing is what is seen, some say it is what is heard, and others say it is what is cognized. In this matter, we and others have not reached a conclusion. It would be good, sir, if you would explain it to us as it truly is.' The king of the devas, who was wise by nature, asked: 'Where did this talk of the blessing first arise?' 'We, lord, heard it from the Four Great Kings,' they replied. Then the Four Great Kings said they heard it from the sky-dwelling devas, the sky-dwelling devas from the earth-dwelling devas, the earth-dwelling devas from the devas who guard humans, and the devas who guard humans declared: 'It arose in the human world.'

Atha devānamindo “sammāsambuddho kattha vasatī”ti pucchi. “Manussaloke, devā”ti āhaṃsu. “Taṃ bhagavantaṃ koci pucchī”ti āha. “Na koci devā”ti. “Kiṃ nu kho nāma tumhe mārisā aggiṃ chaḍḍetvā khajjopanakaṃ ujjāletha, ye anavasesamaṅgaladesakaṃ taṃ bhagavantaṃ atikkamitvā maṃ pucchitabbaṃ maññatha? Āgacchatha, mārisā, taṃ bhagavantaṃ pucchāma, addhā sassirikaṃ pañhabyākaraṇaṃ labhissāmā”ti ekaṃ devaputtaṃ āṇāpesi – “tvaṃ bhagavantaṃ pucchā”ti. So devaputto taṅkhaṇānurūpena [M 2.0005] alaṅkārena attānaṃ alaṅkaritvā vijjuriva vijjotamāno devagaṇaparivuto jetavanamahāvihāraṃ āgantvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ ṭhatvā maṅgalapañhaṃ pucchanto gāthāya ajjhabhāsi. Bhagavā tassa taṃ pañhaṃ vissajjento imaṃ suttamabhāsi.

Then the lord of the devas asked, "Where does the Perfectly and Completely Enlightened One dwell?" "In the human world, O Lord," they replied. "Has anyone asked that Blessed One?" he said. "No one, O Lord." "What is this, good sirs, that you, having abandoned the fire, would light a firefly, thinking that you should ask me after passing over that Blessed One, who teaches on the blessing without remainder? Come, good sirs, let us ask that Blessed One; surely we shall obtain a glorious explanation of the question." He commanded a certain devaputta, "You ask the Blessed One." That devaputta, adorning himself with ornaments appropriate for the occasion, shining like lightning, surrounded by a host of devas, approached the Jetavana Mahāvihāra, paid homage to the Blessed One, stood to one side, and while asking the question about the blessing, addressed him in verse. The Blessed One, answering his question, spoke this discourse.

Tattha evaṃ me sutantiādīnamattho saṅkhepato kasibhāradvājasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ vutto, vitthāraṃ pana icchantehi papañcasūdaniyā majjhimaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttanayena gahetabbo. Kasibhāradvājasutte ca “magadhesu viharati dakkhiṇāgirismiṃ ekanāḷāyaṃ brāhmaṇagāme”ti vuttaṃ, idha “sāvatthiyaṃ viharati [V 2.0005] jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme”ti. Tasmā “sāvatthiya”nti imaṃ padaṃ ādiṃ katvā idha apubbapadavaṇṇanaṃ karissāma.

Therein, the meaning of 'Thus have I heard' and so on has been stated in brief in the commentary on the Kasibhāradvāja Sutta. However, those who wish for a detailed explanation should understand it according to the method described in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary to the Majjhima Nikāya. In the Kasibhāradvāja Sutta it is said, 'He was dwelling among the Magadhans at Dakkhiṇāgiri in the brahmin village of Ekanāḷā,' whereas here it is said, 'He was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park.' Therefore, taking the word 'Sāvatthī' as the starting point, we shall now provide a commentary on the words not previously explained herein.

Seyyathidaṃ, sāvatthiyanti evaṃnāmake nagare. Taṃ kira savatthassa nāma isino nivāsaṭṭhānaṃ ahosi. Tasmā yathā kusambassa nivāso kosambī, kākaṇḍassa nivāso kākaṇḍīti, evaṃ itthiliṅgavasena “sāvatthī”ti vuccati. Porāṇā pana vaṇṇayanti – yasmā tasmiṃ ṭhāne satthasamāyoge “kiṃbhaṇḍamatthī”ti pucchite “sabbamatthī”ti āhaṃsu, tasmā taṃ vacanamupādāya “sāvatthī”ti vuccati. Tassaṃ sāvatthiyaṃ. Etenassa gocaragāmo dīpito hoti. Jeto nāma rājakumāro, tena ropitasaṃvaḍḍhitattā tassa jetassa vananti jetavanaṃ, tasmiṃ jetavane. Anāthānaṃ piṇḍo etasmiṃ atthīti anāthapiṇḍiko, tassa anāthapiṇḍikassa. Anāthapiṇḍikena gahapatinā catupaṇṇāsakoṭipariccāgena niṭṭhāpitārāmeti attho. Etenassa pabbajitānurūpanivāsokāso dīpito hoti.

That is to say, in a city named Sāvatthī. It is said that this was the dwelling place of the sage named Savattha. Therefore, just as the dwelling of Kusamba is Kosambī, and the dwelling of Kākaṇḍa is Kākaṇḍī, so too, by way of the feminine gender, it is called 'Sāvatthī.' The ancients, however, explain it thus: because at that place, during a gathering of a caravan, when asked, 'What goods are there?' they replied, 'Everything is here,' therefore, based on that statement, it is called 'Sāvatthī.' In that Sāvatthī. By this, his alms-resort village is indicated. There was a prince named Jeta; because it was planted and nurtured by him, it is Jeta's grove, hence Jetavana. In that Jetavana. He in whom there is alms-food for the helpless is Anāthapiṇḍika. Of that Anāthapiṇḍika. The meaning is: in the monastery completed by the householder Anāthapiṇḍika through an expenditure of fifty-four crores. By this, a dwelling place suitable for renunciants is indicated for him.

Athāti avicchedatthe, khoti adhikārantaranidassanatthe nipāto. Tena avicchinneyeva tattha bhagavato vihāre “idamadhikārantaraṃ udapādī”ti dasseti. Kiṃ tanti? Aññatarā devatātiādi. Tattha aññatarāti aniyamitaniddeso. Sā hi nāmagottato apākaṭā, tasmā “aññatarā”ti vuttā. Devo eva devatā, itthipurisasādhāraṇametaṃ. Idha pana puriso eva so devaputto, kintu sādhāraṇanāmavasena “devatā”ti vutto.

The word 'atha' is in the sense of uninterruptedness; the particle 'kho' is in the sense of indicating a different subject matter. By this, it shows that without interruption, in the Blessed One’s dwelling, 'this different subject matter arose.' What is that? 'A certain deity,' and so forth. Therein, 'a certain' is an indefinite designation. For that deity was not well-known by name or clan; therefore, she is called 'a certain.' A deva is indeed a devatā; this term is common to both male and female. Here, however, that devaputta was in fact a male, but he is called 'devatā' by way of the common term.

Abhikkantāya [M 2.0006] rattiyāti ettha abhikkantasaddo khayasundarābhirūpaabbhanumodanādīsu dissati. Tattha “abhikkantā, bhante, ratti, nikkhanto paṭhamo yāmo, ciranisinno bhikkhusaṅgho. Uddisatu, bhagavā bhikkhūnaṃ pātimokkha”nti evamādīsu (cūḷava. 383; a. ni. 8.20; udā. 45) khaye dissati. “Ayaṃ imesaṃ catunnaṃ puggalānaṃ abhikkantataro ca paṇītataro cā”ti evamādīsu (a. ni. 4.100) sundare.

In the phrase 'abhikkantāya rattiyā,' the word 'abhikkanta' is seen in the senses of 'passed,' 'excellent,' 'beautiful form,' 'approval,' and so on. Therein, in passages such as, 'Venerable sir, the night has passed, the first watch is over, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus has been seated for a long time. Let the Blessed One recite the Pātimokkha to the bhikkhus,' it is seen in the sense of 'passed.' In passages such as, 'This one is more excellent and more sublime than these four persons,' it is in the sense of 'excellent.'

“Ko me vandati pādāni, iddhiyā yasasā jalaṃ;

Abhikkantena vaṇṇena, sabbā obhāsayaṃ disā”ti. (vi. va. 857) –

“Who is it that worships my feet, blazing with power and glory, with surpassing beauty, illuminating all directions?”

Evamādīsu abhirūpe. “Abhikkantaṃ, bho gotama, abhikkantaṃ, bho gotamā”ti evamādīsu (a. ni. 2.16; pārā. 15) abbhanumodane. Idha pana khaye. Tena abhikkantāya rattiyā, parikkhīṇāya rattiyāti vuttaṃ hoti.

In such passages as this, it is in the sense of 'beautiful form.' In passages such as, 'Excellent, good Gotama! Excellent, good Gotama!' it is in the sense of 'approval.' Here, however, it is in the sense of 'passed.' Therefore, 'abhikkantāya rattiyā' means 'when the night had passed'; thus it is said.

Abhikkantavaṇṇāti [V 2.0006] ettha abhikkantasaddo abhirūpe, vaṇṇasaddo pana chavithutikulavaggakāraṇasaṇṭhānappamāṇarūpāyatanādīsu dissati. Tattha “suvaṇṇavaṇṇosi bhagavā”ti evamādīsu (ma. ni. 2.399; su. ni. 553) chaviyaṃ. “Kadā saññūḷhā pana te, gahapati, ime samaṇassa gotamassa vaṇṇā”ti evamādīsu (ma. ni. 2.77) thutiyaṃ. “Cattārome, bho gotama, vaṇṇā”ti evamādīsu (dī. ni. 3.115) kulavagge. “Atha kena nu vaṇṇena, gandhatthenoti vuccatī”ti evamādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.234) kāraṇe. “Mahantaṃ hatthirājavaṇṇaṃ abhinimminitvā”ti evamādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.138) saṇṭhāne. “Tayo pattassa vaṇṇā”ti evamādīsu pamāṇe. “Vaṇṇo gandho raso ojā”ti evamādīsu rūpāyatane. So idha chaviyaṃ daṭṭhabbo. Tena abhikkantavaṇṇā abhirūpacchavīti vuttaṃ hoti.

In 'abhikkantavaṇṇā,' the word 'abhikkanta' is in the sense of 'beautiful form.' The word 'vaṇṇa,' however, is seen in the senses of complexion, praise, class, cause, shape, measure, the sense-base of form, and so on. Therein, in passages such as, 'The Blessed One is of golden complexion,' it is in the sense of complexion. In passages such as, 'But when, householder, did you become so well-versed in these praises of the ascetic Gotama?' it is in the sense of praise. In passages such as, 'There are, good Gotama, these four classes,' it is in the sense of class. In passages such as, 'For what reason, then, is one called a "scent-thief"?' it is in the sense of cause. In passages such as, 'Having created the great form of a king of elephants,' it is in the sense of shape. In passages such as, 'There are three sizes of the bowl,' it is in the sense of measure. In passages such as, 'Form, scent, taste, nutritive essence,' it is in the sense of the sense-base of form. Here, it should be understood in the sense of complexion. Therefore, 'abhikkantavaṇṇā' means 'of beautiful complexion'; thus it is said.

Kevalakappanti ettha kevalasaddo anavasesayebhuyyaabyāmissaanatirekadaḷhatthavisaṃyogādianekattho. Tathā hissa “kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ parisuddhaṃ brahmacariya”nti evamādīsu (dī. ni. 1.255; pārā. 1) anavasesatā attho. “Kevalakappā ca aṅgamāgadhā pahūtaṃ khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyaṃ ādāya upasaṅkamissantī”ti [M 2.0007] evamādīsu (mahāva. 43) yebhuyyatā. “Kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hotī”ti evamādīsu (vibha. 225) abyāmissatā. “Kevalaṃ saddhāmattakaṃ nūna ayamāyasmā”ti evamādīsu (mahāva. 244) anatirekatā. “Āyasmato bhante anuruddhassa bāhiko nāma saddhivihāriko kevalakappaṃ saṅghabhedāya ṭhito”ti evamādīsu (a. ni. 4.243) daḷhatthatā. “Kevalī vusitavā uttamapurisoti vuccatī”ti evamādīsu (saṃ. ni. 3.57) visaṃyogo. Idha panassa anavasesato attho adhippeto.

In 'kevalakappaṃ,' the word 'kevala' has many meanings, such as: without remainder, mostly, unmixed, not exceeding, firm, and disjoined. For instance, in passages such as 'the holy life that is wholly complete and pure,' its meaning is 'without remainder.' In passages such as, 'Almost all of Aṅga and Magadha will approach, bringing abundant food to eat and to drink,' it means 'mostly.' In passages such as, 'There is the arising of this sheer mass of suffering,' it means 'unmixed.' In passages such as, 'Surely this venerable one is one of mere faith,' it means 'not exceeding.' In passages such as, 'Venerable sir, the venerable Anuruddha's co-resident named Bāhika was firmly set on schism in the Saṅgha for a whole aeon,' it means 'firm.' In passages such as, 'One who is accomplished, who has lived the life, is called a supreme person,' it means 'disjoined.' Here, however, its meaning is intended as 'without remainder.'

Kappasaddo panāyaṃ abhisaddahanavohārakālapaññattichedanavikappalesasamantabhāvādianekattho. Tathā hissa “okappaniyametaṃ bhoto gotamassa, yatā taṃ arahato sammāsambuddhassā”ti evamādīsu (ma. ni. 1.387) abhisaddahanamattho. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, pañcahi samaṇakappehi phalaṃ paribhuñjitu”nti evamādīsu (cūḷava. 250) vohāro. “Yena sudaṃ niccakappaṃ viharāmī”ti evamādīsu (ma. ni. 1.387) kālo. “Iccāyasmā kappo”ti evamādīsu (su. ni. 1098; cūḷani. kappamāṇavapucchā 117) paññatti. “Alaṅkato kappitakesamassū”ti evamādīsu (jā. 2.22.1368) chedanaṃ. “Kappati dvaṅgulakappo”ti evamādīsu (cūḷava. 446) vikappo. “Atthi kappo nipajjitu”nti evamādīsu (a. ni. 8.80) leso. “Kevalakappaṃ veḷuvanaṃ obhāsetvā”ti evamādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.94) samantabhāvo. Idha panassa samantabhāvo atthoti adhippeto. Yato kevalakappaṃ jetavananti ettha anavasesaṃ samantato jetavananti evamattho daṭṭhabbo.

The term 'kappa' has many meanings, such as acceptance, usage, time, designation, cutting, choice, slight possibility, and entirety. For example, in passages like 'This is worthy of acceptance by the Venerable Gotama, as is fitting for the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One' (Majjhima Nikāya 1.387), it means acceptance. In 'I allow, monks, the eating of fruit within five ascetic observances' (Cūḷavagga 250), it refers to usage. In 'Where indeed I dwell continually' (Majjhima Nikāya 1.387), it denotes time. In 'Thus the Venerable Kappa' (Sutta Nipāta 1098; Cūḷaniddesa, Kappamāṇavapucchā 117), it signifies designation. In 'Adorned with hair and beard having been cut' (Jātaka 2.22.1368), it means cutting. In 'A two-finger allowance is allowable' (Cūḷavagga 446), it indicates choice. In 'Is there an opportunity to lie down?' (Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.80), it refers to a slight possibility. In 'Having illuminated the entire bamboo grove' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.94), it conveys entirety. Here, however, its intended meaning is entirety. Thus, in the phrase 'the entire Jetavana,' it should be understood to mean 'the Jetavana completely, without exception, on all sides.'

Obhāsetvāti [V 2.0007] ābhāya pharitvā, candimā viya sūriyo viya ca ekobhāsaṃ ekapajjotaṃ karitvāti attho.

`Obhāsetvā` means: having pervaded with light, like the moon and like the sun, having made a single radiance, a single effulgence. This is the meaning.

Yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamīti bhummatthe karaṇavacanaṃ, yato yattha bhagavā, tattha upasaṅkamīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Yena vā kāraṇena bhagavā devamanussehi upasaṅkamitabbo, teneva kāraṇena upasaṅkamīti evampettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Kena ca kāraṇena bhagavā upasaṅkamitabbo? Nānappakāraguṇavisesādhigamādhippāyena sāduphalūpabhogādhippāyena dijagaṇehi niccaphalitamahārukkho viya. Upasaṅkamīti ca gatāti [M 2.0008] vuttaṃ hoti. Upasaṅkamitvāti upasaṅkamanapariyosānadīpanaṃ. Atha vā evaṃ gatā tato āsannataraṃ ṭhānaṃ bhagavato samīpasaṅkhātaṃ gantvātipi vuttaṃ hoti. Bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvāti bhagavantaṃ vanditvā paṇamitvā namassitvā.

`Yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami`: herein, the instrumental case is used in the sense of the locative. Thus, the meaning should be understood as: where the Blessed One was, there he approached. Or, for whatever reason the Blessed One is to be approached by gods and humans, for that very reason he approached—thus the meaning should also be understood here. And for what reason is the Blessed One to be approached? With the intention of attaining various kinds of special qualities, just as a great, ever-fruitful tree is approached by flocks of birds with the intention of enjoying sweet fruit. `Upasaṅkami` means 'went.' `Upasaṅkamitvā` indicates the conclusion of the act of approaching. Or alternatively, it also means: having gone thus, he then went to a nearer place, designated as the vicinity of the Blessed One. `Bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā` means: having venerated, bowed down to, and saluted the Blessed One.

Ekamantanti bhāvanapuṃsakaniddeso, ekokāsaṃ ekapassanti vuttaṃ hoti. Bhummatthe vā upayogavacanaṃ. Aṭṭhāsīti nisajjādipaṭikkhepo, ṭhānaṃ kappesi, ṭhitā ahosīti attho.

`Ekamantaṃ` is an exposition in the abstract neuter; it means 'in a single space,' 'to one side.' Or, it is the accusative case used in the sense of the locative. `Aṭṭhāsi` means the rejection of sitting; she adopted the posture of standing. The meaning is 'she was standing.'

Kathaṃ ṭhitā pana sā ekamantaṃ ṭhitā ahūti?

But how was she standing, when she stood to one side?

“Na pacchato na purato, nāpi āsannadūrato;

Na kacche nopi paṭivāte, na cāpi oṇatuṇṇate;

Ime dose vivajjetvā, ekamantaṃ ṭhitā ahū”ti.

"Not behind, not in front, nor too near or too far; not at the side, nor downwind, nor in a place too low or too high; having avoided these faults, she stood to one side."

Kasmā panāyaṃ aṭṭhāsi eva, na nisīdīti? Lahuṃ nivattitukāmatāya. Devatā hi kañcideva atthavasaṃ paṭicca sucipuriso viya vaccaṭṭhānaṃ manussalokaṃ āgacchanti. Pakatiyā panetāsaṃ yojanasatato pabhuti manussaloko duggandhatāya paṭikūlo hoti, na tattha abhiramanti. Tena sā āgatakiccaṃ katvā lahuṃ nivattitukāmatāya na nisīdi. Yassa ca gamanādiiriyāpathaparissamassa vinodanatthaṃ nisīdanti, so devānaṃ parissamo natthi, tasmāpi na nisīdi. Ye ca mahāsāvakā bhagavantaṃ parivāretvā ṭhitā, te patimānesi, tasmāpi na nisīdi. Apica bhagavati gāraveneva na nisīdi. Devānañhi nisīditukāmānaṃ āsanaṃ nibbattati, taṃ anicchamānā nisajjāya cittampi akatvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi.

But why did she just stand, and not sit down? Because she wished to return quickly. For deities, on account of some purpose, come to the human world like a clean person going to a latrine. By nature, the human world is repulsive to them due to its foul smell from a hundred yojanas away, and they do not delight in it. Therefore, having completed the task for which she came, she wished to return quickly and did not sit down. Moreover, the fatigue from postures such as movement, for the removal of which one sits, does not exist for deities; therefore she did not sit. And she respected the great disciples who stood surrounding the Blessed One; therefore she did not sit. Furthermore, out of reverence for the Blessed One, she did not sit. For when deities wish to sit, a seat arises for them, but not desiring that, without even forming the intention of sitting, she stood to one side.

Ekamantaṃ ṭhitā kho sā devatāti evaṃ imehi kāraṇehi ekamantaṃ ṭhitā kho sā devatā. Bhagavantaṃ gāthāya ajjhabhāsīti bhagavantaṃ gāthāya akkharapadaniyamitaganthitena vacanena abhāsīti attho.

The phrase 'that deity, standing to one side' means that for these reasons, that deity stood to one side. 'Addressed the Blessed One in verse'—this means she spoke to the Blessed One with a verse, a composition of words with measured syllables and phrases.

261. Tattha [V 2.0008] bahūti aniyamitasaṅkhyāniddeso. Tena anekasatā anekasahassā anekasatasahassāti vuttaṃ hoti. Dibbantīti devā, pañcahi kāmaguṇehi kīḷanti, attano vā siriyā jotantīti attho. Apica tividhā devā sammutiupapattivisuddhivasena. Yathāha –

261. Herein, `bahū` is an indication of an unspecified number. Thus, it means many hundreds, many thousands, many hundred thousands. They are called `devā` because they shine (`dibbanti`); the meaning is that they revel with the five strands of sensual pleasure, or that they glow with their own splendor. Moreover, devas are of three kinds by way of convention, arising, and purity. As it is said:

“Devāti [M 2.0009] tayo devā sammutidevā, upapattidevā, visuddhidevā. Tattha sammutidevā nāma rājāno, deviyo, rājakumārā. Upapattidevā nāma cātumahārājike deve upādāya taduttaridevā. Visuddhidevā nāma arahanto vuccantī”ti (cūḷani. dhotakamāṇavapucchāniddesa 32, pārāyanānugītigāthāniddesa 119).

"Devas are of three kinds: conventional devas, devas by arising, and purified devas. Herein, conventional devas are kings, queens, and princes. Devas by arising are the devas beginning with the realm of the Four Great Kings and those above them. Purified devas are called arahants." (Cūḷaniddesa, Dhotakamāṇavapucchāniddesa 32; Pārāyanānugītigāthāniddesa 119)

Tesu idha upapattidevā adhippetā. Manuno apaccāti manussā. Porāṇā pana bhaṇanti – manassa ussannatāya manussā. Te jambudīpakā, aparagoyānakā, uttarakurukā, pubbavidehakāti catubbidhā. Idha jambudīpakā adhippetā. Maṅgalanti imehi sattāti maṅgalāni, iddhiṃ vuddhiñca pāpuṇantīti attho. Acintayunti cintesuṃ. Ākaṅkhamānāti icchamānā patthayamānā pihayamānā. Sotthānanti sotthibhāvaṃ, sabbesaṃ diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikānaṃ sobhanānaṃ sundarānaṃ kalyāṇānaṃ dhammānamatthitanti vuttaṃ hoti. Brūhīti desehi pakāsehi ācikkha vivara vibhaja uttānīkarohi. Maṅgalanti iddhikāraṇaṃ vuddhikāraṇaṃ sabbasampattikāraṇaṃ. Uttamanti visiṭṭhaṃ pavaraṃ sabbalokahitasukhāvahanti ayaṃ gāthāya anupubbapadavaṇṇanā.

Among them, devas by birth are intended here. 'Offspring of Manu' (Manuno apaccā) are humans (manussā). The ancients, however, say: on account of the excellence of mind (manassa ussannatāya), they are humans (manussā). They are of four kinds: those of Jambudīpa, Aparagoyāna, Uttarakuru, and Pubbavideha. Here, those of Jambudīpa are intended. 'Blessings' (maṅgalāni): by these, beings prosper (maṅgalanti); the meaning is that they attain accomplishment and growth. 'They pondered' (acintayun) means they thought (cintesuṃ). 'Desiring' (ākaṅkhamānā) means wishing, aspiring, and longing. 'For well-being' (sotthānaṃ) means a state of well-being; it is said to be the existence of all things that are beautiful, good, and wholesome, pertaining to the present life and the next. 'Declare' (brūhi) means teach, make known, tell, reveal, analyze, and make plain. 'Blessing' (maṅgalaṃ) means the cause of accomplishment, the cause of growth, the cause of all success. 'The highest' (uttamaṃ) means distinguished, excellent, bringing welfare and happiness to the whole world. This is the sequential explanation of the words of the verse.

Ayaṃ pana piṇḍattho – so devaputto dasasahassacakkavāḷesu devatā maṅgalapañhaṃ sotukāmatāya imasmiṃ ekacakkavāḷe sannipatitvā ekavālaggakoṭiokāsamatte dasapi vīsampi tiṃsampi cattālīsampi paññāsampi saṭṭhipi sattatipi asītipi sukhumattabhāve nimminitvā sabbadevamārabrahmāno siriyā ca tejasā ca adhigayha virocamānaṃ paññattavarabuddhāsane nisinnaṃ bhagavantaṃ parivāretvā ṭhitā disvā tasmiṃ ca samaye anāgatānampi sakalajambudīpakānaṃ manussānaṃ cetasā cetoparivitakkamaññāya sabbadevamanussānaṃ vicikicchāsallasamuddharaṇatthaṃ āha – “bahū devā manussā ca, maṅgalāni acintayuṃ, ākaṅkhamānā sotthānaṃ attano sotthibhāvaṃ icchantā, brūhi maṅgalamuttamaṃ, tesaṃ devānaṃ anumatiyā manussānañca anuggahena mayā puṭṭho samāno yaṃ sabbesameva amhākaṃ ekantahitasukhāvahanato uttamaṃ maṅgalaṃ, taṃ no anukampaṃ upādāya brūhi bhagavā”ti.

This, however, is the summary meaning. That devaputta, seeing the devas from the ten thousand world-systems who were desirous of hearing the question on blessings assembled in this one world-system—having created, in a space the size of a single hair-tip, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, sixty, seventy, and even eighty subtle forms, they stood surrounding the Blessed One, who was seated on the prepared, excellent Buddha-seat, shining and surpassing all devas, Māras, and Brahmās with glory and majesty—and at that time, having known with his mind the thoughts of all the humans of Jambudīpa who had not yet arrived, spoke for the purpose of extracting the dart of doubt for all devas and humans: '"Many devas and humans have pondered on blessings, desiring well-being"—that is, wishing for their own state of well-being—"Declare the highest blessing." Being asked by me with the consent of those devas and for the benefit of humans, that which is the highest blessing as it brings certain welfare and happiness to all of us, please declare that to us out of compassion, O Blessed One.'

262. Evametaṃ [M 2.0010] devaputtassa vacanaṃ sutvā bhagavā “asevanā ca bālāna”nti gāthamāha. Tattha asevanāti abhajanā apayirupāsanā. Bālānanti balanti assasantīti bālā, assasitapassasitamattena jīvanti, na paññājīvitenāti adhippāyo. Tesaṃ bālānaṃ paṇḍitānanti [V 2.0009] paṇḍantīti paṇḍitā, sandiṭṭhikasamparāyikesu atthesu ñāṇagatiyā gacchantīti adhippāyo. Tesaṃ paṇḍitānaṃ. Sevanāti bhajanā payirupāsanā taṃsahāyatā taṃsampavaṅkatā. Pūjāti sakkāragarukāramānanavandanā. Pūjaneyyānanti pūjārahānaṃ. Etaṃ maṅgalamuttamanti yā ca bālānaṃ asevanā, yā ca paṇḍitānaṃ sevanā, yā ca pūjaneyyānaṃ pūjā, taṃ sabbaṃ sampiṇḍetvā āha etaṃ maṅgalamuttamanti. Yaṃ tayā puṭṭhaṃ “brūhi maṅgalamuttama”nti, ettha tāva etaṃ maṅgalamuttamanti gaṇhāhīti vuttaṃ hoti. Ayametissā gāthāya padavaṇṇanā.

262. Thus, having heard this speech of the devaputta, the Blessed One spoke the verse beginning, 'Not associating with fools.' Therein, 'not associating' (asevanā) means not frequenting, not attending upon. 'Of fools' (bālānaṃ): they are called 'fools' (bālā) because they are foolish (balanti); the meaning is that they live merely by breathing in and out, not by the life of wisdom. Of those fools. 'Of the wise' (paṇḍitānaṃ): they are called 'wise' (paṇḍitā) because they are discerning (paṇḍanti); the meaning is that they proceed by way of knowledge in matters concerning the present life and the next. Of those wise ones. 'Associating' (sevanā) means frequenting, attending upon, companionship with them, and inclination towards them. 'Honor' (pūjā) means respect, reverence, esteem, and veneration. 'Of those worthy of honor' (pūjaneyyānaṃ) means of those deserving of honor. 'This is the highest blessing' (etaṃ maṅgalamuttamaṃ): having combined all of this—the non-association with fools, the association with the wise, and the honoring of those worthy of honor—He said, 'This is the highest blessing.' Regarding what was asked by you, 'Declare the highest blessing,' it is said, 'For now, understand this to be the highest blessing.' This is the explanation of the words of this verse.

Atthavaṇṇanā panassā evaṃ veditabbā – evametaṃ devaputtassa vacanaṃ sutvā bhagavā imaṃ gāthamāha. Tattha yasmā catubbidhā kathā pucchitakathā, apucchitakathā, sānusandhikathā, ananusandhikathāti. Tattha “pucchāmi taṃ, gotama, bhūripaññaṃ, kathaṃkaro sāvako sādhu hotī”ti (su. ni. 378) ca, “kathaṃ nu tvaṃ, mārisa, oghamatarī”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.1) ca evamādīsu pucchitena kathikā pucchitakathā. “Yaṃ pare sukhato āhu, tadariyā āhu dukkhato”ti evamādīsu (su. ni. 767) apucchitena attajjhāsayavaseneva kathitā apucchitakathā. Sabbāpi buddhānaṃ kathā “sanidānāhaṃ, bhikkhave, dhammaṃ desemī”ti (a. ni. 3.126; kathā. 806) vacanato sānusandhikathā. Ananusandhikathā imasmiṃ sāsane natthi. Evametāsu kathāsu ayaṃ devaputtena pucchitena bhagavatā kathitattā pucchitakathā. Pucchitakathāyañca yathā cheko puriso kusalo maggassa, kusalo amaggassa, maggaṃ puṭṭho paṭhamaṃ vijahitabbaṃ ācikkhitvā pacchā gahetabbaṃ ācikkhati – “asukasmiṃ nāma ṭhāne dvedhāpatho hoti, tattha vāmaṃ muñcitvā dakkhiṇaṃ gaṇhathā”ti, evaṃ sevitabbāsevitabbesu asevitabbaṃ ācikkhitvā sevitabbaṃ ācikkhati. Bhagavā ca maggakusalapurisasadiso. Yathāha –

The explanation of its meaning, however, should be understood thus: Having heard this speech of the devaputta, the Blessed One spoke this verse. Therein, discourse is fourfold: questioned discourse, unasked discourse, connected discourse, and unconnected discourse. Among these, in cases such as, 'I ask you, Gotama, of vast wisdom, how does a disciple become good?' and, 'How, sir, did you cross the flood?', discourse spoken because one was questioned is called questioned discourse. In cases such as, 'What others call happiness, the noble ones call suffering,' discourse spoken not because one was questioned, but by the power of one's own inclination, is called unasked discourse. All discourses of the Buddhas are connected discourse, according to the statement, 'Monks, I teach the Dhamma with its causal basis.' There is no unconnected discourse in this Dispensation. Among these types of discourse, this one is a questioned discourse, as it was spoken by the Blessed One after being questioned by the devaputta. And in a questioned discourse, it is just as when a skilled person, an expert on the path, is asked the way, he first points out what should be abandoned and afterwards points out what should be taken, saying: 'At such and such a place, the path forks; there, leaving the left, take the right.' In the same way, concerning those who should and should not be associated with, having first pointed out who should not be associated with, He then points out who should be associated with. And the Blessed One is like a person skilled in the path. As it is said:

“Puriso maggakusaloti kho, tissa, tathāgatassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ arahato sammāsambuddhassā”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.84).

'Tissa, "a person skilled in the path" is indeed a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.'

So [M 2.0011] hi kusalo imassa lokassa, kusalo parassa lokassa, kusalo maccudheyyassa, kusalo amaccudheyyassa, kusalo māradheyyassa, kusalo amāradheyyassāti. Tasmā paṭhamaṃ asevitabbaṃ ācikkhitvā sevitabbaṃ ācikkhanto āha – “asevanā ca bālānaṃ, paṇḍitānañca sevanā”ti. Vijahitabbamaggo viya hi paṭhamaṃ bālā na sevitabbā na payirupāsitabbā, tato gahetabbamaggo viya paṇḍitā sevitabbā payirupāsitabbāti.

For he is skilled regarding this world and skilled regarding the next world; skilled regarding the domain of death and skilled regarding what is beyond the domain of death; skilled regarding the domain of Māra and skilled regarding what is beyond the domain of Māra. Therefore, first pointing out who is not to be associated with, and then pointing out who is to be associated with, He said: 'Not associating with fools, and associating with the wise.' For just as a path is to be abandoned, so first fools are not to be associated with, not to be attended upon. Then, just as a path is to be taken, so the wise are to be associated with, to be attended upon.

Kasmā pana bhagavatā maṅgalaṃ kathentena paṭhamaṃ bālānaṃ asevanā paṇḍitānañca sevanā kathitāti? Vuccate – yasmā imaṃ diṭṭhādīsu maṅgaladiṭṭhiṃ bālasevanāya devamanussā gaṇhiṃsu, sā [V 2.0010] ca amaṅgalaṃ, tasmā nesaṃ taṃ idhalokatthaparalokatthabhañjakaṃ akalyāṇamittasaṃsaggaṃ garahantena ubhayalokatthasādhakañca kalyāṇamittasaṃsaggaṃ pasaṃsantena bhagavatā paṭhamaṃ bālānaṃ asevanā paṇḍitānañca sevanā kathitāti.

Why then, when the Blessed One was speaking about blessings, did he first mention not associating with fools and associating with the wise? It is said—because devas and humans have adopted this view of blessings in visible things and so on by associating with fools, and that is not a true blessing; therefore, by condemning their association with bad friends, which destroys benefit in this world and the next, and by praising association with good friends, which accomplishes benefit in both worlds, the Blessed One first spoke of not associating with fools and associating with the wise.

Tattha bālā nāma ye keci pāṇātipātādiakusalakammapathasamannāgatā sattā. Te tīhākārehi jānitabbā. Yathāha – “tīṇimāni, bhikkhave, bālassa bālalakkhaṇānī”ti (a. ni. 3.3; ma. ni. 3.246) suttaṃ. Apica pūraṇakassapādayo cha satthāro devadattakokālikakaṭamodakatissakhaṇḍadeviyāputtasamuddadattaciñcamāṇavikādayo atītakāle ca dīghavidassa bhātāti ime aññe ca evarūpā sattā bālāti veditabbā.

Therein, 'fools' are any beings who are endowed with unwholesome courses of action beginning with the destruction of life. They are to be known by three characteristics. As it is said in the sutta: 'Monks, there are these three characteristics of a fool.' Furthermore, the six teachers such as Pūraṇa Kassapa; Devadatta, Kokālika, Kaṭamodakatissa, Khaṇḍadeviyāputta, Samuddadatta, and Ciñcamāṇavikā; and in the past, the brother of Dīghavida—these and other such beings are to be understood as fools.
