Te aggipadittamiva aṅgāraṃ attanā duggahitena attānañca attano vacanakārake ca vināsenti, yathā dīghavidassa bhātā catubuddhantaraṃ saṭṭhiyojanamattena attabhāvena uttāno patito mahāniraye paccati, yathā ca tassa diṭṭhiṃ abhirucikāni pañca kulasatāni tasseva sahabyataṃ upapannāni niraye paccanti. Vuttaṃ hetaṃ –

Like a blazing coal poorly grasped, they destroy both themselves and those who follow their word. Just as the brother of Dīghavida, with a body sixty yojanas in extent, fell supine into the great hell and is tormented there for the interval of four Buddhas; and just as five hundred families who delighted in his view were reborn into his company and are tormented in hell. For it has been said:

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, naḷāgārā vā tiṇāgārā vā aggi mutto kūṭāgārānipi ḍahati ullittāvalittāni nivātāni phusitaggaḷāni pihitavātapānāni, evameva kho, bhikkhave, yāni kānici [M 2.0012] bhayāni uppajjanti, sabbāni tāni bālato uppajjanti, no paṇḍitato. Ye keci upaddavā uppajjanti…pe… ye keci upasaggā…pe… no paṇḍitato. Iti kho, bhikkhave, sappaṭibhayo bālo, appaṭibhayo paṇḍito. Saupaddavo bālo, anupaddavo paṇḍito, saupasaggo bālo, anupasaggo paṇḍito”ti (a. ni. 3.1).

“Just as, monks, a fire set loose from a reed hut or a grass hut would burn down even a gabled house—plastered inside and out, sheltered from the wind, with bolts fastened and windows closed—so too, monks, whatever fears arise, all of them arise from the fool, not from the wise. Whatever calamities arise… whatever obstacles arise… not from the wise. Thus, monks, the fool is fraught with danger, the wise is free from danger. The fool is fraught with calamities, the wise is free from calamities. The fool is fraught with obstacles, the wise is free from obstacles.”

Apica pūtimacchasadiso bālo, pūtimacchabandhapattapuṭasadiso hoti tadupasevī, chaḍḍanīyataṃ jigucchanīyatañca āpajjati viññūnaṃ. Vuttañcetaṃ –

Moreover, the fool is like a rotten fish; one who associates with him is like the leaf-wrapper for a rotten fish. He becomes worthy of rejection and disgust to the discerning. And it has been said:

“Pūtimacchaṃ kusaggena, yo naro upanayhati;

Kusāpi pūtī vāyanti, evaṃ bālūpasevanā”ti. (itivu. 76; jā. 1.15.183; 2.22.1257);

“The man who wraps a rotten fish with kusa grass—the grass itself gives off a stench; so it is with association with fools.”

Akittipaṇḍito cāpi sakkena devānamindena vare diyyamāne evamāha –

And the wise Akitti, when offered a boon by Sakka, lord of the devas, said thus:

“Bālaṃ [V 2.0011] na passe na suṇe, na ca bālena saṃvase;

Bālenallāpasallāpaṃ, na kare na ca rocaye.

“May I not see a fool, nor hear one; may I not live together with a fool. May I not hold conversation or talk with a fool, nor find pleasure in it.”

“Kinnu te akaraṃ bālo, vada kassapa kāraṇaṃ;

Kena kassapa bālassa, dassanaṃ nābhikaṅkhasi.

“What has the fool done to you? Tell me the reason, Kassapa. Why, Kassapa, do you not desire to see a fool?”

“Anayaṃ nayati dummedho, adhurāyaṃ niyuñjati;

Dunnayo seyyaso hoti, sammā vutto pakuppati;

Vinayaṃ so na jānāti, sādhu tassa adassana”nti. (jā. 1.13.90-92);

“The dull-witted one leads to ruin; he engages in what is improper. Hard to guide, he thinks it for the best; when rightly spoken to, he gets angry. He does not know discipline; it is good not to see him.”

Evaṃ bhagavā sabbākārena bālūpasevanaṃ garahanto bālānaṃ asevanaṃ “maṅgala”nti vatvā idāni paṇḍitasevanaṃ pasaṃsanto “paṇḍitānañca sevanā maṅgala”nti āha. Tattha paṇḍitā nāma ye keci pāṇātipātāveramaṇiādidasakusalakammapathasamannāgatā sattā, te tīhākārehi jānitabbā. Yathāha – “tīṇimāni, bhikkhave, paṇḍitassa paṇḍitalakkhaṇānī”ti (a. ni. 3.3; ma. ni. 3.253) vuttaṃ. Apica buddhapaccekabuddhaasītimahāsāvakā aññe ca tathāgatassa sāvakā sunettamahāgovindavidhurasarabhaṅgamahosadhasutasomanimirāja- ayogharakumāraakittipaṇḍitādayo ca paṇḍitāti veditabbā.

Thus the Blessed One, in every way condemning association with fools, said that not associating with fools is a 'blessing.' Now, praising association with the wise, he said, 'and association with the wise is a blessing.' Therein, the wise are any beings endowed with the ten wholesome courses of action, beginning with abstaining from the destruction of life. They are to be known by three characteristics. As it is said: 'Monks, there are these three characteristics of a wise person.' Furthermore, the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, the eighty great disciples, and other disciples of the Tathāgata, such as Sunetta, Mahāgovinda, Vidhura, Sarabhaṅga, Mahosadha, Sutasoma, King Nimi, Ayogharakumāra, the wise Akitti, and others, are to be understood as the wise.

Te [M 2.0013] bhaye viya rakkhā, andhakāre viya padīpo, khuppipāsādidukkhābhibhave viya annapānādipaṭilābho, attano vacanakarānaṃ sabbabhayaupaddavūpasaggaviddhaṃsanasamatthā honti. Tathā hi tathāgataṃ āgamma asaṅkhyeyyā aparimāṇā devamanussā āsavakkhayaṃ pattā, brahmaloke patiṭṭhitā, devaloke patiṭṭhitā, sugatiloke uppannā. Sāriputtatthere cittaṃ pasādetvā catūhi paccayehi theraṃ upaṭṭhahitvā asīti kulasahassāni sagge nibbattāni. Tathā mahāmoggallānamahākassapappabhutīsu sabbamahāsāvakesu, sunettassa satthuno sāvakā appekacce brahmaloke uppajjiṃsu, appekacce paranimmitavasavattīnaṃ devānaṃ sahabyataṃ…pe… appekacce gahapatimahāsālakulānaṃ sahabyataṃ upapajjiṃsu. Vuttañcetaṃ –

They are like a guard in times of fear, like a lamp in darkness, like the obtaining of food and drink when overcome by the suffering of hunger and thirst; for those who follow their word, they are capable of destroying all fears, calamities, and obstacles. Indeed, by approaching the Tathāgata, countless and immeasurable devas and humans have attained the destruction of the taints, have been established in the Brahma-world, have been established in the deva-world, and have arisen in happy realms. Having generated faith in the Elder Sāriputta and attended to him with the four requisites, eighty thousand families were reborn in heaven. Likewise for all the great disciples, such as Mahāmoggallāna and Mahākassapa. Some disciples of the teacher Sunetta were reborn in the Brahma-world, some were reborn into the company of the devas of the Paranimmitavasavattī realm... some were reborn into the company of wealthy householder families. And it has been said:

“Natthi, bhikkhave, paṇḍitato bhayaṃ, natthi paṇḍitato upaddavo, natthi paṇḍitato upasaggo”ti (a. ni. 3.1).

“Monks, from the wise there is no fear, from the wise there is no calamity, from the wise there is no obstacle.”

Apica [V 2.0012] tagaramālādigandhabhaṇḍasadiso paṇḍito, tagaramālādigandhabhaṇḍapaliveṭhanapattasadiso hoti tadupasevī, bhāvanīyataṃ manuññatañca āpajjati viññūnaṃ. Vuttañcetaṃ –

Moreover, the wise one is like fragrant goods such as tagara powder and garlands; one who associates with him is like the leaf that wraps fragrant goods such as tagara powder and garlands. He becomes worthy of cultivation and pleasing to the discerning. And it has been said:

“Tagarañca palāsena, yo naro upanayhati;

Pattāpi surabhī vāyanti, evaṃ dhīrūpasevanā”ti. (itivu. 76; jā. 1.15.184; 2.22.1258);

“The man who wraps tagara powder with a palāsa leaf—the leaves themselves give off a sweet scent; so it is with association with the wise.”

Akittipaṇḍito cāpi sakkena devānamindena vare diyyamāne evamāha –

And the wise Akitti, when offered a boon by Sakka, lord of the devas, said thus:

“Dhīraṃ passe suṇe dhīraṃ, dhīrena saha saṃvase;

Dhīrenallāpasallāpaṃ, taṃ kare tañca rocaye.

One should see the wise, hear the wise, and associate with the wise; one should engage in talk and conversation with the wise, and delight in it.

“Kinnu te akaraṃ dhīro, vada kassapa kāraṇaṃ;

Kena kassapa dhīrassa, dassanaṃ abhikaṅkhasi.

What has the wise one done to you? Tell me the reason, Kassapa. Why, Kassapa, do you long to see the wise one?

“Nayaṃ nayati medhāvī, adhurāyaṃ na yuñjati;

Sunayo seyyaso hoti, sammā vutto na kuppati;

Vinayaṃ so pajānāti, sādhu tena samāgamo”ti. (jā. 1.13.94-96);

The intelligent one leads aright; he does not engage in what is improper. He is of good conduct and is superior; when rightly spoken to, he does not get angry. He understands discipline; good is association with him (Jā. 1.13.94-96).

Evaṃ bhagavā sabbākārena paṇḍitasevanaṃ pasaṃsanto, paṇḍitānaṃ sevanaṃ “maṅgala”nti vatvā idāni tāya bālānaṃ asevanāya paṇḍitānaṃ [M 2.0014] sevanāya ca anupubbena pūjaneyyabhāvaṃ upagatānaṃ pūjaṃ pasaṃsanto “pūjā ca pūjaneyyānaṃ etaṃ maṅgalamuttama”nti āha. Tattha pūjaneyyā nāma sabbadosavirahitattā sabbaguṇasamannāgatattā ca buddhā bhagavanto, tato pacchā paccekabuddhā ariyasāvakā ca. Tesañhi pūjā appakāpi dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya hoti, sumanamālākāramallikādayo cettha nidassanaṃ.

Thus, the Blessed One, in every way praising association with the wise, having declared that association with the wise is a 'blessing,' now, praising the honoring of those worthy of veneration who, through non-association with fools and association with the wise, have successively attained the venerable state, says: 'And honoring those worthy of honor—this is the highest blessing.' Herein, those worthy of honor are the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, free from all faults and endowed with all virtues, followed by the Paccekabuddhas and noble disciples. For even a small offering made to them is for long-lasting welfare and happiness; here, Sumana the garland-maker, Mallikā, and others serve as examples.

Tatthekaṃ nidassanamattaṃ bhaṇāma. Bhagavā kira ekadivasaṃ pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya rājagahaṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Atha kho sumanamālākāro rañño māgadhassa seniyassa bimbisārassa pupphāni gahetvā gacchanto addasa bhagavantaṃ nagaradvāraṃ anuppattaṃ pāsādikaṃ pasādanīyaṃ dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇāsītānubyañjanapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ buddhasiriyā jalantaṃ. Disvānassa etadahosi – “rājā pupphāni gahetvā sataṃ vā sahassaṃ vā dadeyya, tañca idhalokamattameva sukhaṃ bhaveyya, bhagavato pana pūjā appameyyaasaṅkhyeyyaphalā dīgharattaṃ hitasukhāvahā [V 2.0013] hoti. Handāhaṃ imehi pupphehi bhagavantaṃ pūjemī”ti pasannacitto ekaṃ pupphamuṭṭhiṃ gahetvā bhagavato paṭimukhaṃ khipi, pupphāni ākāsena gantvā bhagavato upari mālāvitānaṃ hutvā aṭṭhaṃsu. Mālākāro taṃ ānubhāvaṃ disvā pasannataracitto puna ekaṃ pupphamuṭṭhiṃ khipi, tāni gantvā mālākañcuko hutvā aṭṭhaṃsu. Evaṃ aṭṭha pupphamuṭṭhiyo khipi, tāni gantvā pupphakūṭāgāraṃ hutvā aṭṭhaṃsu. Bhagavā antokūṭāgāre viya ahosi, mahājanakāyo sannipati. Bhagavā mālākāraṃ passanto sitaṃ pātvākāsi. Ānandatthero “na buddhā ahetu appaccayā sitaṃ pātukarontī”ti sitakāraṇaṃ pucchi. Bhagavā āha – “eso, ānanda, mālākāro imissā pūjāya ānubhāvena satasahassakappe devesu ca manussesu ca saṃsaritvā pariyosāne sumanissaro nāma paccekabuddho bhavissatī”ti. Vacanapariyosāne ca dhammadesanatthaṃ imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi –

Here we shall relate a single illustrative account. It is said that one morning, the Blessed One, having dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Rājagaha for alms. At that time, the garland-maker Sumana, carrying flowers for King Bimbisāra Seniya of Magadha, saw the Blessed One approaching the city gate—pleasing and inspiring confidence, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man and eighty minor characteristics, blazing with the splendor of a Buddha. Upon seeing him, Sumana thought: 'Even if the king were to give a hundred or a thousand (coins) for flowers, the happiness from that would be limited to this world alone. But an offering to the Blessed One is of immeasurable, incalculable fruit, leading to welfare and happiness for a long time. Come, let me honor the Blessed One with these flowers!' With a mind filled with faith, he took a handful of flowers and threw them in front of the Blessed One. The flowers floated through the air and formed a floral canopy above the Blessed One and remained there. Seeing that power, the garland-maker, with a mind even more filled with faith, threw another handful of flowers. These too flew up and formed a floral tunic. In this way, he threw eight handfuls of flowers, which formed a floral pavilion, and the Blessed One was as if inside a pavilion. A great multitude gathered. The Blessed One, seeing the garland-maker, revealed a smile. Venerable Ānanda, knowing that Buddhas do not reveal a smile without a cause or reason, asked the cause of the smile. The Blessed One said: 'Ānanda, this garland-maker, by the power of this offering, will wander in saṃsāra among devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons and, in the end, will become a Paccekabuddha named Sumanissara.' At the conclusion of his words, he spoke this verse for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma:

“Tañca kammaṃ kataṃ sādhu, yaṃ katvā nānutappati;

Yassa patīto sumano, vipākaṃ paṭisevatī”ti. (dha. pa. 68);

That deed is well done of which one does not repent after doing it, and the result of which one experiences with joy and satisfaction (Dhp. 68).

Gāthāpariyosāne caturāsītiyā pāṇasahassānaṃ dhammābhisamayo ahosi, evaṃ appakāpi tesaṃ pūjā dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya [M 2.0015] hotīti veditabbā. Sā ca āmisapūjāva ko pana vādo paṭipattipūjāya. Yato ye kulaputtā saraṇagamanena sikkhāpadapaṭiggahaṇena uposathaṅgasamādānena catupārisuddhisīlādīhi ca attano guṇehi bhagavantaṃ pūjenti, ko tesaṃ pūjāya phalaṃ vaṇṇayissati. Te hi tathāgataṃ paramāya pūjāya pūjentīti vuttā. Yathāha –

At the conclusion of the verse, eighty-four thousand beings attained realization of the Dhamma. Thus, it should be understood that even a small offering made to them is for long-lasting welfare and happiness. And that was only a material offering; what then is to be said of the offering of practice? For when noble sons honor the Blessed One through their own virtues—such as going for refuge, undertaking the precepts, observing the Uposatha, and maintaining the fourfold purified morality—who can describe the fruit of their offerings? Indeed, they are said to honor the Tathāgata with the supreme offering. As it is said:

“Yo kho, ānanda, bhikkhu vā bhikkhunī vā upāsako vā upāsikā vā dhammānudhammapaṭipanno viharati sāmīcippaṭipanno anudhammacārī, so tathāgataṃ sakkaroti garuṃ karoti māneti pūjeti apaciyati paramāya pūjāyā”ti.

Ananda, any monk or nun, or any male or female lay follower, who dwells practicing the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma, practicing properly, living in conformity with the Dhamma—it is he who honors, respects, reveres, venerates, and pays homage to the Tathāgata with the supreme homage.

Etenānusārena paccekabuddhaariyasāvakānampi pūjāya hitasukhāvahatā veditabbā.

By this principle, it should be understood that paying homage to Paccekabuddhas and noble disciples also leads to welfare and happiness.

Apica gahaṭṭhānaṃ kaniṭṭhassa jeṭṭho bhātāpi bhaginīpi pūjaneyyā, puttassa mātāpitaro, kulavadhūnaṃ sāmikasassusasurāti evampettha pūjaneyyā veditabbā. Etesampi hi pūjā kusaladhammasaṅkhātattā āyuādivaḍḍhihetuttā ca maṅgalameva. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Furthermore, among householders, an elder brother or sister is worthy of honor for a younger sibling; parents for a child; and for daughters-in-law, their husband, mother-in-law, and father-in-law. Thus, it should be understood that these too are worthy of honor here. For indeed, honoring these, being reckoned as wholesome qualities and a cause for the increase of life and other benefits, is itself a blessing. As it is said:

“Te matteyyā bhavissanti petteyyā sāmaññā brahmaññā kule jeṭṭhāpacāyino, idaṃ kusalaṃ [V 2.0014] dhammaṃ samādāya vattissanti. Te tesaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ samādānahetu āyunāpi vaḍḍhissanti, vaṇṇenapi vaḍḍhissantī”tiādi.

They will be dutiful to their mothers, dutiful to their fathers, respectful to recluses, respectful to brahmins, and reverers of elders in their family. Having undertaken this wholesome Dhamma, they will live accordingly. Because of undertaking these wholesome qualities, they will increase in lifespan, in beauty, and so on.

Evametissā gāthāya bālānaṃ asevanā paṇḍitānaṃ sevanā pūjaneyyānaṃ pūjāti tīṇi maṅgalāni vuttāni. Tattha bālānaṃ asevanā bālasevanapaccayabhayādiparittāṇena ubhayalokahitahetuttā paṇḍitānaṃ sevanā pūjaneyyānaṃ pūjā ca tāsaṃ phalavibhūtivaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttanayeneva nibbānasugatihetuttā “maṅgala”nti veditabbā. Ito paraṃ tu mātikaṃ adassetvā eva yaṃ yattha maṅgalaṃ, taṃ vavatthapessāma, tassa ca maṅgalattaṃ vibhāvayissāmāti.

Thus, in this verse, three blessings are stated: not associating with fools, associating with the wise, and honoring those worthy of honor. Herein, not associating with fools is a blessing because it protects one from the dangers arising from associating with fools and because it is the cause of welfare in both worlds. Associating with the wise and honoring those worthy of honor are also blessings, as explained before in the description of the abundance of their fruits, because they are a cause for Nibbāna and a good destination. Henceforth, without presenting the outline, we will determine what is a blessing in each case and clarify its nature as a blessing.

Niṭṭhitā asevanā ca bālānanti imissā gāthāya atthavaṇṇanā.

Here ends the explanation of the meaning of the verse beginning 'Not associating with fools.'

263. Evaṃ [M 2.0016] bhagavā “brūhi maṅgalamuttama”nti ekaṃ ajjhesitopi appaṃ yācito bahudāyako uḷārapuriso viya ekāya gāthāya tīṇi maṅgalāni vatvā tato uttaripi devatānaṃ sotukāmatāya maṅgalānañca atthitāya yesaṃ yesaṃ yaṃ yaṃ anukūlaṃ, te te satte tattha tattha maṅgale niyojetukāmatāya ca “patirūpadesavāso cā”tiādīhi gāthāhi punapi anekāni maṅgalāni vattumāraddho.

263. Thus, although the Blessed One was requested but once, 'Speak of the highest blessing,' like a noble person who gives much though asked for little, He spoke of three blessings in a single verse. Then, beyond that, due to the devas' desire to hear, due to the existence of blessings, and due to the desire to engage those very beings in whatever blessing is suitable for each of them, He began to speak of many more blessings with verses beginning, 'Living in a suitable place,' and so on.

Tattha paṭhamagāthāya tāva patirūpoti anucchaviko. Desoti gāmopi nigamopi nagarampi janapadopi yo koci sattānaṃ nivāsokāso. Vāsoti tattha nivāso. Pubbeti purā atītāsu jātīsu. Katapuññatāti upacitakusalatā. Attāti cittaṃ vuccati, sakalo vā attabhāvo. Sammāpaṇidhīti tassa attano sammā paṇidhānaṃ niyuñjanaṃ, ṭhapananti vuttaṃ hoti. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti ayamettha padavaṇṇanā.

Herein, in the first verse, firstly, 'patirūpa' means suitable. 'Desa' means any dwelling place for beings—a village, a market town, a city, or a country. 'Vāsa' means residing there. 'Pubbe' means formerly, in past lives. 'Katapuññatā' means the state of having accumulated wholesome deeds. 'Attā' is said to be the mind, or the entire personal existence. 'Sammāpaṇidhi' means the right directing, applying, or establishing of that self; thus it is said. The remainder is in the manner already explained. This is the explanation of the words herein.

Atthavaṇṇanā pana evaṃ veditabbā patirūpadeso nāma yattha catasso parisā viharanti, dānādīni puññakiriyāvatthūni vattanti, navaṅgaṃ satthu sāsanaṃ dippati. Tattha nivāso sattānaṃ puññakiriyāya paccayattā “maṅgala”nti vuccati. Sīhaḷadīpapaviṭṭhakevaṭṭādayo cettha nidassanaṃ.

The explanation of the meaning, however, should be understood thus: A suitable place is one where the four assemblies dwell, where the grounds for meritorious action such as giving are found, and where the Teacher’s ninefold Dispensation shines. Residing there is called a 'blessing' because it is a condition for beings' performance of meritorious deeds. The fishermen and others who entered the island of Sīhaḷa are an example in this case.

Aparo nayo – patirūpadeso nāma bhagavato bodhimaṇḍappadeso, dhammacakkappavattitappadeso, dvādasayojanāya parisāya majjhe sabbatitthiyamataṃ bhinditvā yamakapāṭihāriyadassitakaṇḍambarukkhamūlappadeso, devorohanappadeso, yo vā panaññopi sāvatthirājagahādibuddhādivāsappadeso. Tattha nivāso sattānaṃ chaanuttariyapaṭilābhapaccayato “maṅgala”nti vuccati.

Another interpretation: A suitable place is the place of the Blessed One's Bodhi-maṇḍa; the place where the Wheel of Dhamma was set in motion; the place at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree where, in the midst of an assembly spanning twelve yojanas, He shattered all the doctrines of the sectarians and displayed the Twin Miracle; the place of the descent from the deva realm; or any other place where the Buddha resided, such as Sāvatthī and Rājagaha. Residing there is called a 'blessing' because it is a condition for beings to attain the six unsurpassed qualities.

Aparo [V 2.0015] nayo – puratthimāya disāya kajaṅgalaṃ nāma nigamo, tassa aparena mahāsālā, tato paraṃ paccantimā janapadā, orato majjhe. Dakkhiṇapuratthimāya disāya sallavatī nāma nadī, tato paraṃ paccantimā janapadā, orato majjhe. Dakkhiṇāya disāya setakaṇṇikaṃ nāma nigamo, tato paraṃ paccantimā janapadā, orato majjhe. Pacchimāya disāya thūṇaṃ nāma brāhmaṇagāmo, tato paraṃ paccantimā janapadā, orato majjhe. Uttarāya disāya usiraddhajo nāma pabbato, tato paraṃ paccantimā janapadā[M 2.0017], orato majjhe (mahāva. 259). Ayaṃ majjhimappadeso āyāmena tīṇi yojanasatāni, vitthārena aḍḍhateyyāni, parikkhepena navayojanasatāni honti, eso patirūpadeso nāma.

Another interpretation: In the eastern direction, there is a market town named Kajaṅgala; beyond that, Mahāsālā; and beyond that, the border countries. On this side is the middle region. In the southeastern direction, there is a river named Sallavatī; beyond that, the border countries. On this side is the middle region. In the southern direction, there is a market town named Setakaṇṇika; beyond that, the border countries. On this side is the middle region. In the western direction, there is a brahmin village named Thūṇa; beyond that, the border countries. On this side is the middle region. In the northern direction, there is a mountain named Usiraddhaja; beyond that, the border countries. On this side is the middle region. This middle region is three hundred yojanas in length, two hundred and fifty in width, and nine hundred yojanas in circumference. This is called a suitable place.

Ettha catunnaṃ mahādīpānaṃ dvisahassānaṃ parittadīpānañca issariyādhipaccakārakā cakkavattī uppajjanti, ekaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ kappasatasahassañca pāramiyo pūretvā sāriputtamahāmoggallānādayo mahāsāvakā uppajjanti, dve asaṅkhyeyyāni kappasatasahassañca pāramiyo pūretvā paccekabuddhā, cattāri aṭṭha soḷasa vā asaṅkhyeyyāni kappasatasahassañca pāramiyo pūretvā sammāsambuddhā ca uppajjanti. Tattha sattā cakkavattirañño ovādaṃ gahetvā pañcasu sīlesu patiṭṭhāya saggaparāyaṇā honti, tathā paccekabuddhānaṃ ovāde patiṭṭhāya. Sammāsambuddhasāvakānaṃ pana ovāde patiṭṭhāya saggaparāyaṇā nibbānaparāyaṇā ca honti. Tasmā tattha vāso imāsaṃ sampattīnaṃ paccayato “maṅgala”nti vuccati.

Herein, universal monarchs arise who exercise sovereignty and dominion over the four great continents and two thousand surrounding islands. Great disciples like Sāriputta and Mahāmoggallāna arise after fulfilling the perfections for one incalculable and one hundred thousand aeons. Paccekabuddhas arise after fulfilling the perfections for two incalculable and one hundred thousand aeons. And Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddhas arise after fulfilling the perfections for four, eight, or sixteen incalculable and one hundred thousand aeons. There, beings who accept the counsel of a universal monarch establish themselves in the five precepts and are bound for heaven. Likewise for those established in the counsel of Paccekabuddhas. But those established in the counsel of the disciples of a Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddha are bound for heaven and also bound for Nibbāna. Therefore, residing there is called a 'blessing' because it is a condition for these accomplishments.

Pubbe katapuññatā nāma atītajātiyaṃ buddhapaccekabuddhakhīṇāsave ārabbha upacitakusalatā, sāpi maṅgalaṃ. Kasmā? Buddhapaccekabuddhe sammukhato dassetvā buddhānaṃ vā buddhasāvakānaṃ vā sammukhā sutāya catuppadikāyapi gāthāya pariyosāne arahattaṃ pāpetīti katvā. Yo ca manusso pubbe katādhikāro ussannakusalamūlo hoti, so teneva kusalamūlena vipassanaṃ uppādetvā āsavakkhayaṃ pāpuṇāti yathā rājā mahākappino aggamahesī ca. Tena vuttaṃ “pubbe ca katapuññatā maṅgala”nti.

Having done merit in the past means the accumulation of wholesome deeds in a past life with reference to Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and those whose taints are destroyed. This too is a blessing. Why? Because by seeing Buddhas or Paccekabuddhas face to face, or by hearing even a four-lined verse in the presence of Buddhas or their disciples, one can be led to Arahantship at its conclusion. And whatever person has made a resolve in the past and has abundant wholesome roots, by that very wholesome root, they generate insight and attain the destruction of the taints, just as King Mahākappina and his chief queen did. For this reason, it is said: 'And having done merit in the past is a blessing.'

Attasammāpaṇidhi nāma idhekacco attānaṃ dussīlaṃ sīle patiṭṭhāpeti, assaddhaṃ saddhāsampadāya patiṭṭhāpeti, macchariṃ cāgasampadāya patiṭṭhāpeti. Ayaṃ vuccati “attasammāpaṇidhī”ti. Eso ca maṅgalaṃ. Kasmā? Diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaverappahānavividhānisaṃsādhigamahetutoti.

Rightly directing the self means that herein a certain person, being immoral, establishes themselves in virtue; being faithless, establishes themselves in the accomplishment of faith; being stingy, establishes themselves in the accomplishment of generosity. This is called 'rightly directing the self.' And this is a blessing. Why? Because it is the cause for abandoning enmity pertaining to this life and the next, and for the attainment of various benefits.

Evaṃ [M 2.0018] imissāpi gāthāya patirūpadesavāso, pubbe ca katapuññatā, attasammāpaṇidhīti tīṇiyeva maṅgalāni vuttāni, maṅgalattañca nesaṃ tattha tattha vibhāvitamevāti.

Thus, in this verse, just three blessings have been spoken of: living in a suitable place, having done merit in the past, and rightly directing the self. And their nature as blessings has been made clear in their respective sections.

Niṭṭhitā [V 2.0016] patirūpadesavāso cāti imissā gāthāya atthavaṇṇanā.

The explanation of the meaning of the verse beginning 'Living in a suitable place...' is concluded.

264. Idāni bāhusaccañcāti ettha bāhusaccanti bahussutabhāvo. Sippanti yaṃkiñci hatthakosallaṃ. Vinayoti kāyavācācittavinayanaṃ. Susikkhitoti suṭṭhu sikkhito. Subhāsitāti suṭṭhu bhāsitā. Yāti aniyamaniddeso. Vācāti girā byappatho. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti. Ayamettha padavaṇṇanā.

264. Now, herein, in the phrase 'bāhusaccañca': 'bāhusaccaṃ' means the state of being very learned. 'Sippaṃ' means any kind of manual skill. 'Vinayo' means the disciplining of body, speech, and mind. 'Susikkhito' means well-trained. 'Subhāsitā' means well-spoken. The word 'yā' is an indefinite reference. The word 'vācā' means utterance, expression. The remainder is in the manner already explained. This is the explanation of the words herein.

Atthavaṇṇanā pana evaṃ veditabbā – bāhusaccaṃ nāma yaṃ taṃ “sutadharo hoti sutasannicayo”ti (ma. ni. 1.339; a. ni. 4.22) ca “idha, bhikkhave, ekaccassa puggalassa bahukaṃ sutaṃ hoti suttaṃ geyyaṃ veyyākaraṇa”nti (a. ni. 4.6) ca evamādinā nayena satthusāsanadharattaṃ vaṇṇitaṃ, taṃ akusalappahānakusalādhigamahetuto anupubbena paramatthasaccasacchikiriyahetuto ca “maṅgala”nti vuccati. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

The explanation of the meaning, however, should be understood thus: 'Extensive learning' is that which is praised in such ways as, "one is a bearer of what has been heard, an accumulator of what has been heard," and, "here, monks, a certain person has heard much—discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions," and so forth, for the purpose of upholding the Teacher's dispensation. It is called a 'blessing' because it is a cause for abandoning the unwholesome and acquiring the wholesome, and because it is a cause for the gradual realization of the ultimate truth. For this was said by the Blessed One:

“Sutavā ca kho, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako akusalaṃ pajahati, kusalaṃ bhāveti, sāvajjaṃ pajahati, anavajjaṃ bhāveti, suddhamattānaṃ pariharatī”ti (a. ni. 7.67).

'Indeed, monks, a learned noble disciple abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome; he abandons what is blameworthy and develops what is blameless; he maintains himself in purity.'

Aparampi vuttaṃ –

Furthermore, it is said:

“Dhatānaṃ dhammānaṃ atthamupaparikkhati, atthaṃ upaparikkhato dhammā nijjhānaṃ khamanti, dhammanijjhānakkhantiyā sati chando jāyati, chandajāto ussahati, ussahanto tulayati, tulayanto padahati, padahanto kāyena ceva paramatthasaccaṃ sacchikaroti, paññāya ca ativijjha passatī”ti (ma. ni. 2.432).

'He examines the meaning of the teachings he has retained. For one who examines the meaning, the teachings are amenable to reflection. When the teachings are amenable to reflection, zeal arises. When zeal has arisen, he endeavors. Endeavoring, he weighs them. Weighing them, he strives. Striving, he realizes the ultimate truth with his body and, penetrating it with wisdom, he sees.'

Apica agārikabāhusaccampi yaṃ anavajjaṃ, taṃ ubhayalokahitasukhāvahanato “maṅgala”nti veditabbaṃ.

Moreover, even the extensive learning of a householder, when it is blameless, should be understood as a 'blessing' because it brings benefit and happiness in both worlds.

Sippaṃ [M 2.0019] nāma agārikasippañca anagārikasippañca. Tattha agārikasippaṃ nāma yaṃ parūparodhavirahitaṃ akusalavivajjitaṃ maṇikārasuvaṇṇakārakammādi, taṃ idhalokatthāvahanato maṅgalaṃ. Anagārikasippaṃ nāma cīvaravicāraṇasibbanādi samaṇaparikkhārābhisaṅkharaṇaṃ, yaṃ taṃ “idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu yāni tāni sabrahmacārīnaṃ uccāvacāni kiṃkaraṇīyāni, tattha dakkho hotī”tiādinā nayena tattha tattha saṃvaṇṇitaṃ, yaṃ “nāthakaraṇo dhammo”ti (dī. ni. 3.345; a. ni. 10.17) ca [V 2.0017] vuttaṃ, taṃ attano ca paresañca ubhayalokahitasukhāvahanato “maṅgala”nti veditabbaṃ.

Skill is of two kinds: the skill of a householder and the skill of one who is homeless. Therein, the skill of a householder is that which is free from harming others and devoid of unwholesomeness, such as the work of a gem-cutter or a goldsmith; this is a blessing because it brings benefit in this world. The skill of one who is homeless is the preparation of a recluse's requisites, such as the examining and sewing of robes. This is praised in various places in such ways as, "Here, monks, a monk is skilled in the various higher and lower duties to be done for his companions in the holy life." It is also called "a teaching that creates a refuge," and it should be understood as a 'blessing' because it brings benefit and happiness to oneself and others in both worlds.

Vinayo nāma agārikavinayo ca anagārikavinayo ca. Tattha agārikavinayo nāma dasaakusalakammapathaviramaṇaṃ, so tattha asaṃkilesāpajjanena ācāraguṇavavatthānena ca susikkhito ubhayalokahitasukhāvahanato maṅgalaṃ. Anagārikavinayo nāma sattāpattikkhandhe anāpajjanaṃ, sopi vuttanayeneva susikkhito. Catupārisuddhisīlaṃ vā anagārikavinayo. So yathā tattha patiṭṭhāya arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, evaṃ sikkhanena susikkhito lokiyalokuttarasukhādhigamahetuto “maṅgala”nti veditabbo.

Discipline is of two kinds: the discipline for householders and the discipline for one who is homeless. Therein, the discipline for householders is the abstention from the ten unwholesome courses of action. When this is well-mastered through the non-occurrence of defilements and the establishment of virtuous conduct, it is a blessing because it brings benefit and happiness in both worlds. The discipline for one who is homeless is the non-commission of the seven classes of offenses; this too is to be well-mastered in the manner already stated. Alternatively, the discipline for one who is homeless is the fourfold purity of morality. When this is well-mastered through such training that one, being established therein, attains arahantship, it should be understood as a 'blessing' because it is the cause for attaining worldly and supramundane happiness.

Subhāsitā vācā nāma musāvādādidosavirahitā vācā. Yathāha – “catūhi, bhikkhave, aṅgehi samannāgatā vācā subhāsitā hotī”ti. Asamphappalāpā vācā eva vā subhāsitā. Yathāha –

Well-spoken speech is speech that is free from faults such as false speech. As it is said: 'Monks, speech endowed with four factors is well-spoken.' Alternatively, speech that is not idle chatter is itself well-spoken. As it is said:

“Subhāsitaṃ uttamamāhu santo,

Dhammaṃ bhaṇe nādhammaṃ taṃ dutiyaṃ;

Piyaṃ bhaṇe nāppiyaṃ taṃ tatiyaṃ,

Saccaṃ bhaṇe nālikaṃ taṃ catuttha”nti. (saṃ. ni. 1.213; su. ni. 452);

'The good say that well-spoken speech is supreme; speak the Dhamma, not what is not Dhamma—that is the second. Speak what is pleasant, not what is unpleasant—that is the third. Speak what is true, not what is false—that is the fourth.'

Ayampi ubhayalokahitasukhāvahanato “maṅgala”nti veditabbā. Yasmā ca ayaṃ vinayapariyāpannā eva, tasmā vinayaggahaṇena etaṃ asaṅgaṇhitvā vinayo saṅgahetabbo. Athavā kiṃ iminā parissamena paresaṃ dhammadesanāvācā idha “subhāsitā vācā”ti veditabbā. Sā [M 2.0020] hi yathā patirūpadesavāso, evaṃ sattānaṃ ubhayalokahitasukhanibbānādhigamapaccayato “maṅgala”nti vuccati. Āha ca –

This too should be understood as a 'blessing' because it brings benefit and happiness in both worlds. And since this is indeed included in the discipline, the discipline should be understood as encompassing it, rather than grasping this separately. Alternatively, what is the need for this effort? Here, the speech of teaching the Dhamma to others should be understood as 'well-spoken speech.' For just as dwelling in a suitable region is a blessing, so too is this called a 'blessing' because it is a condition for beings to attain the benefit, happiness, and Nibbāna of both worlds. And it is said:

“Yaṃ buddho bhāsati vācaṃ, khemaṃ nibbānapattiyā;

Dukkhassantakiriyāya, sā ve vācānamuttamā”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.213; su. ni. 456);

'The speech that the Buddha speaks, which is safe, for the attainment of Nibbāna, for the making of an end to suffering—that is truly the best of all speech.'

Evaṃ imissā gāthāya bāhusaccaṃ, sippaṃ, vinayo susikkhito, subhāsitā vācāti cattāri maṅgalāni vuttāni, maṅgalattañca nesaṃ tattha tattha vibhāvitamevāti.

Thus, in this verse, four blessings are spoken of: extensive learning, skill, well-mastered discipline, and well-spoken speech. And their nature as blessings has been explained in each respective place.

Niṭṭhitā [V 2.0018] bāhusaccañcāti imissā gāthāya atthavaṇṇanā.

The explanation of the meaning of the verse beginning 'Extensive learning' is concluded.

265. Idāni mātāpituupaṭṭhānanti ettha mātu ca pitu cāti mātāpitu. Upaṭṭhānanti upaṭṭhahanaṃ. Puttānañca dārānañcāti puttadārassa. Saṅgaṇhanaṃ saṅgaho. Na ākulā anākulā. Kammāni eva kammantā. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti ayaṃ padavaṇṇanā.

265. Now, in the phrase `mātāpituupaṭṭhānaṃ`: `mātāpitu` is from `mātu ca pitu ca` (mother and father). `Upaṭṭhānaṃ` means `upaṭṭhahanaṃ` (attending). `Puttadārassa` is from `puttānaṃ ca dārānaṃ ca` (of sons and of wives). `Saṅgaho` means `saṅgaṇhanaṃ` (support). `Anākulā` means `na ākulā` (unconfused). `Kammantā` means `kammāni eva` (actions). The rest is as already stated. This is the word analysis.

Atthavaṇṇanā pana evaṃ veditabbā – mātā nāma janikā vuccati, tathā pitā. Upaṭṭhānaṃ nāma pādadhovanasambāhanaucchādananhāpanehi catupaccayasampadānena ca upakārakaraṇaṃ. Tattha yasmā mātāpitaro bahūpakārā puttānaṃ atthakāmā anukampakā, yaṃ puttake bahi kīḷitvā paṃsumakkhitasarīrake āgate disvā paṃsukaṃ puñchitvā matthakaṃ upasiṅghāyantā paricumbantā ca sinehaṃ uppādenti, vassasatampi mātāpitaro sīsena pariharantā puttā tesaṃ paṭikāraṃ kātuṃ asamatthā. Yasmā ca te āpādakā posakā imassa lokassa dassetāro brahmasammatā pubbācariyasammatā, tasmā tesaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ idha pasaṃsaṃ pecca saggasukhañca āvahati, tena “maṅgala”nti vuccati. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

The explanation of the meaning, however, should be understood thus: 'Mother' is said to be she who gives birth; likewise, 'father' is he who begets. 'Attending' means rendering service by washing their feet, massaging them, anointing them, bathing them, and by providing the four requisites. In this regard, since parents are of great help to their children, desiring their welfare and being compassionate; and since, when their children come back from playing outside with their bodies smeared with dust, they wipe away the dust, sniff their heads, and kiss them, thereby generating affection; even if children were to carry their parents on their heads for a hundred years, they would be unable to repay them. And because they are nurturers, supporters, showers of this world, esteemed as Brahmās, and esteemed as first teachers, therefore attending to them brings praise in this life and the bliss of heaven after death. For that reason, it is called a 'blessing.' And this was said by the Blessed One:

“Brahmāti mātāpitaro, pubbācariyāti vuccare;

Āhuneyyā ca puttānaṃ, pajāya anukampakā.

Parents are called 'Brahmā' and 'first teachers'; they are worthy of offerings from their children and compassionate towards their offspring.

“Tasmā hi ne namasseyya, sakkareyya ca paṇḍito;

Annena atha pānena, vatthena sayanena ca.

Therefore, a wise person should pay homage to and revere them with food and drink, with clothing and bedding.

“Ucchādanena [M 2.0021] nhāpanena, pādānaṃ dhovanena ca;

Tāya naṃ pāricariyāya, mātāpitūsu paṇḍitā;

Idheva naṃ pasaṃsanti, pecca sagge pamodatī”ti. (a. ni. 3.31; itivu. 106; jā. 2.20.181-183);

Through anointing, bathing, and washing their feet—by such service to their parents, the wise praise one in this very life, and after death, one rejoices in heaven.

Aparo nayo – upaṭṭhānaṃ nāma bharaṇakiccakaraṇakulavaṃsaṭṭhapanādipañcavidhaṃ, taṃ pāpanivāraṇādipañcavidhadiṭṭhadhammikahitahetuto “maṅgala”nti veditabbaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

Another method: 'Attending' refers to the fivefold duty beginning with supporting, performing their tasks, and establishing the family lineage. It should be understood as a 'blessing' because it is a cause for welfare in this present life, which is fivefold, beginning with restraining from evil. For this was said by the Blessed One:

“Pañcahi kho, gahapatiputta, ṭhānehi puttena puratthimā disā mātāpitaro paccupaṭṭhātabbā ‘bhato ne bharissāmi, kiccaṃ nesaṃ karissāmi, kulavaṃsaṃ ṭhapessāmi, dāyajjaṃ paṭipajjissāmi, atha vā pana petānaṃ kālakatānaṃ dakkhiṇaṃ anuppadassāmī’ti[V 2.0019]. Imehi kho, gahapatiputta, pañcahi ṭhānehi puttena puratthimā disā mātāpitaro paccupaṭṭhitā pañcahi ṭhānehi puttaṃ anukampanti, pāpā nivārenti, kalyāṇe nivesenti, sippaṃ sikkhāpenti, patirūpena dārena saṃyojenti, samaye dāyajjaṃ niyyādentī”ti (dī. ni. 3.267).

‘Householder’s son, a son should attend to his parents as the eastern direction in five ways: “Having been supported by them, I will support them. I will perform their duties. I will maintain the family lineage. I will act in a way that makes me worthy of my inheritance. Furthermore, when my parents have passed away, I will make dedicatory offerings on their behalf.” Householder’s son, when parents are attended to by their son in these five ways, they show compassion to their son in five ways: they restrain him from evil, they establish him in what is good, they have him trained in a skill, they arrange a suitable wife for him, and in due time, they hand over his inheritance.’

Apica yo mātāpitaro tīsu vatthūsu pasāduppādanena sīlasamādāpanena pabbajjāya vā upaṭṭhahati, ayaṃ mātāpituupaṭṭhākānaṃ aggo, tassa taṃ mātāpituupaṭṭhānaṃ mātāpitūhi katassa upakārassa paccupakārabhūtaṃ anekesaṃ diṭṭhadhammikānaṃ samparāyikānañca atthānaṃ padaṭṭhānato “maṅgala”nti vuccati.

Furthermore, one who attends to their parents by inspiring faith in the Three Jewels, by encouraging them to undertake the moral precepts, or by assisting their ordination—this is the highest form of attending to parents. For that person, such attendance to parents is a repayment for the help rendered by the parents, and because it is the foundation for numerous benefits both in this present life and in future lives, it is called a 'blessing'.

Puttadārassāti ettha attanā janitā puttāpi dhītaropi “puttā” tveva saṅkhyaṃ gacchanti. Dārāti vīsatiyā bhariyānaṃ yā kāci bhariyā. Puttā ca dārā ca puttadāraṃ, tassa puttadārassa. Saṅgahoti sammānanādīhi upakārakaraṇaṃ. Taṃ susaṃvihitakammantatādidiṭṭhadhammikahitahetuto “maṅgala”nti veditabbaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā – “pacchimā disā puttadārā veditabbā”ti (dī. ni. 3.266) ettha uddiṭṭhaṃ puttadāraṃ bhariyāsaddena saṅgaṇhitvā –

Regarding 'the support of children and wife': Here, both sons and daughters born of oneself are counted as 'children' (puttā). 'Wife' (dārā) refers to any one of the twenty kinds of wives. 'Children and wife' (puttadāra) refers to both. 'Support' (saṅgaho) means rendering assistance through respect and other such acts. Because this is a cause for welfare in this present life, such as having well-organized work, it should be understood as a 'blessing'. For this was said by the Blessed One: 'The western direction should be understood as children and wife.' Here, having stated 'children and wife', the following is taught by grouping them under the term 'wife' (bhariyā):

“Pañcahi [M 2.0022] kho, gahapatiputta, ṭhānehi sāmikena pacchimā disā bhariyā paccupaṭṭhātabbā, sammānanāya anavamānanāya anaticariyāya issariyavossaggena alaṅkārānuppadānena. Imehi kho, gahapatiputta, pañcahi ṭhānehi sāmikena pacchimā disā bhariyā paccupaṭṭhitā pañcahi ṭhānehi sāmikaṃ anukampati, susaṃvihitakammantā ca hoti, saṅgahitaparijanā ca, anaticārinī ca, sambhatañca anurakkhati, dakkhā ca hoti analasā sabbakiccesū”ti (dī. ni. 3.269).

‘Householder’s son, a husband should attend to his wife, the western direction, in five ways: by honoring her, by not disparaging her, by not being unfaithful to her, by handing over authority to her, and by providing her with adornments. Householder’s son, when a wife is attended to by her husband in these five ways, she shows compassion to her husband in five ways: her work is well-organized, the household attendants are well-managed, she is not unfaithful, she protects what he has earned, and she is skillful and tireless in all her duties.’

Ayaṃ vā aparo nayo – saṅgahoti dhammikāhi dānapiyavācaatthacariyāhi saṅgaṇhanaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ – uposathadivasesu paribbayadānaṃ, nakkhattadivasesu nakkhattadassāpanaṃ, maṅgaladivasesu maṅgalakaraṇaṃ, diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikesu atthesu ovādānusāsananti. Taṃ vuttanayeneva diṭṭhadhammikahitahetuto samparāyikahitahetuto devatāhipi namassanīyabhāvahetuto ca “maṅgala”nti veditabbaṃ. Yathāha sakko devānamindo –

Or this is another method: 'Support' (saṅgaho) means to cherish them through righteous giving, pleasant speech, and beneficial conduct. For example: providing for their expenses on Uposatha days, arranging for them to see festivals on festival days, performing auspicious ceremonies on auspicious days, and giving advice and instruction regarding matters of welfare in this present life and in future lives. As explained before, it should be understood as a 'blessing' because it is a cause for welfare in this present life, a cause for welfare in future lives, and a cause for being worthy of veneration even by deities. As Sakka, lord of the gods, has said:

“Ye gahaṭṭhā puññakarā, sīlavanto upāsakā;

Dhammena dāraṃ posenti, te namassāmi mātalī”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.264);

‘Those householders who perform meritorious deeds, virtuous lay followers who righteously support their wife—I pay homage to them, Mātali.’

Anākulā [V 2.0020] kammantā nāma kālaññutāya patirūpakāritāya analasatāya uṭṭhānavīriyasampadāya abyasanīyatāya ca kālātikkamanaappatirūpakaraṇākaraṇasithilakaraṇādiākulabhāvavirahitā kasigorakkhavaṇijjādayo kammantā. Ete attano vā puttadārassa vā dāsakammakarānaṃ vā byattatāya evaṃ payojitā diṭṭheva dhamme dhanadhaññavuḍḍhipaṭilābhahetuto “maṅgala”nti vuttā. Vuttañcetaṃ bhagavatā –

'Unhindered occupations' are occupations such as farming, cattle-herding, and trade, which are characterized by timeliness, suitability of action, diligence, endowment with energy and effort, and freedom from adversity; and which are free from hindrances such as missing the right time, unsuitable actions, inaction, and slackness. When these are thus skillfully undertaken for the benefit of oneself, one's children and wife, or one's servants and workers, they are called a 'blessing' because they are a cause for acquiring the growth of wealth and grain in this very life. And this was said by the Blessed One:

“Patirūpakārī dhuravā, uṭṭhātā vindate dhana”nti. (su. ni. 189; saṃ. ni. 1.246) ca;

“Na divā soppasīlena, rattimuṭṭhānadessinā;

Niccaṃ mattena soṇḍena, sakkā āvasituṃ gharaṃ.

‘One who acts suitably, is steadfast, and energetic, gains wealth.’ And: ‘It is not possible to maintain a household for one who is habitually sleepy by day, who is averse to rising at night, and who is constantly intoxicated and dissolute.

“Atisītaṃ atiuṇhaṃ, atisāyamidaṃ ahu;

Iti vissaṭṭhakammante, atthā accenti māṇave.

‘“It is too cold, it is too hot, it is too late in the evening!”—for the young men who thus neglect their work, opportunities pass them by.

“Yodha [M 2.0023] sītañca uṇhañca, tiṇā bhiyyo na maññati;

Karaṃ purisakiccāni, so sukhā na vihāyatī”ti. ca (dī. ni. 3.253);

And: ‘But he who regards cold and heat as no more than a blade of grass, and performs a man’s duties, does not fall away from happiness.’

“Bhoge saṃharamānassa, bhamarasseva irīyato;

Bhogā sannicayaṃ yanti, vammikovūpacīyatī”ti. (dī. ni. 3.265) –

‘For one who gathers wealth, like a bee gathering nectar, riches accumulate like a growing anthill.’

Ca evamādi.

And other such sayings.

Evaṃ imissāpi gāthāya mātupaṭṭhānaṃ, pitupaṭṭhānaṃ, puttadārassa saṅgaho, anākulā ca kammantāti cattāri maṅgalāni vuttāni, puttadārassa saṅgahaṃ vā dvidhā katvā pañca, mātāpituupaṭṭhānaṃ vā ekameva katvā tīṇi. Maṅgalattañca nesaṃ tattha tattha vibhāvitamevāti.

Thus, in this verse, four blessings are spoken of: attending to one's mother, attending to one's father, the support of one's children and wife, and unhindered occupations. Alternatively, by taking 'the support of one's children and wife' as two, there are five. Or, by taking 'attending to one's mother and father' as one, there are three. And their nature as blessings has been clearly explained in their respective contexts.

Niṭṭhitā mātāpituupaṭṭhānanti imissā gāthāya atthavaṇṇanā.

Here ends the explanation of the meaning of the verse beginning, 'Attending to one's mother and father...'

266. Idāni dānañcāti ettha dīyate imināti dānaṃ, attano santakaṃ parassa paṭipādīyatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Dhammassa cariyā, dhammā vā anapetā cariyā dhammacariyā. Ñāyante [V 2.0021] “amhākaṃ ime”ti ñātakā. Na avajjāni anavajjāni, aninditāni agarahitānīti vuttaṃ hoti. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti ayaṃ padavaṇṇanā.

266. Now, in the phrase `dānañca`: that by which something is given is `dānaṃ` (giving); it is said to be the giving of one's own property to another. `Dhammacariyā` is conduct of the Dhamma, or conduct not separate from the Dhamma. Relatives (`ñātakā`) are so called because they are known as, 'These are ours.' Not faulty (`na avajjāni`) means faultless (`anavajjāni`); it is said to mean unblamed and unreproached. The remainder is as previously stated. This is the explanation of the words.

Atthavaṇṇanā pana evaṃ veditabbā – dānaṃ nāma paraṃ uddissa subuddhipubbikā annādidasadānavatthupariccāgacetanā taṃsampayutto vā alobho. Alobhena hi taṃ vatthuṃ parassa paṭipādeti. Tena vuttaṃ “dīyate imināti dāna”nti. Taṃ bahujanapiyamanāpatādīnaṃ diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikānaṃ phalavisesānaṃ adhigamahetuto “maṅgala”nti vuttaṃ. “Dāyako sīha dānapati bahuno janassa piyo hoti manāpo”ti evamādīni cettha suttāni (a. ni. 5.34) anussaritabbāni.

The explanation of the meaning, however, should be understood thus: `Dāna` is the volition of relinquishing the ten kinds of gift-items beginning with food, dedicated to another and preceded by a good intention, or it is the non-greed associated therewith. For it is through non-greed that one gives that object to another. Therefore it is said, ‘That by which something is given is `dāna`.’ Because it is the cause for attaining special results—both in this present life and in the future—such as being dear and agreeable to many people, it is called a ‘blessing.’ And here, suttas such as the following should be recalled: ‘A giver, Sīha, a master of giving, is dear and agreeable to many people’ (AN 5.34).

Aparo nayo – dānaṃ nāma duvidhaṃ āmisadānañca, dhammadānañca. Tattha āmisadānaṃ vuttappakārameva. Idhalokaparalokadukkhakkhayasukhāvahassa pana sammāsambuddhappaveditassa dhammassa paresaṃ hitakāmatāya desanā dhammadānaṃ. Imesañca dvinnaṃ dānānaṃ etadeva aggaṃ. Yathāha –

Another method: giving is of two kinds—material giving and the gift of the Dhamma. Herein, material giving is as previously described. The teaching of the Dhamma proclaimed by the Perfectly Enlightened One—which brings happiness through the destruction of suffering in this world and the next—out of a desire for the welfare of others, is the gift of the Dhamma. And of these two kinds of giving, this one is indeed the highest. As it is said:

“Sabbadānaṃ [M 2.0024] dhammadānaṃ jināti,

Sabbarasaṃ dhammaraso jināti;

Sabbaratiṃ dhammaratī jināti,

Taṇhakkhayo sabbadukkhaṃ jinātī”ti. (dha. pa. 354);

“The gift of Dhamma surpasses all gifts; the taste of Dhamma surpasses all tastes; the delight in Dhamma surpasses all delights; the destruction of craving conquers all suffering.” (Dhp 354)

Tattha āmisadānassa maṅgalattaṃ vuttameva. Dhammadānaṃ pana yasmā atthapaṭisaṃveditādīnaṃ guṇānaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ, tasmā “maṅgala”nti vuccati. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

Therein, that material giving is a blessing has already been stated. But since the gift of Dhamma is the proximate cause for qualities such as experiencing the meaning, it is called a ‘blessing.’ For this was said by the Blessed One:

“Yathā yathā, bhikkhave, bhikkhu yathāsutaṃ yathāpariyattaṃ dhammaṃ vitthārena paresaṃ deseti, tathā tathā so tasmiṃ dhamme atthapaṭisaṃvedī ca hoti dhammapaṭisaṃvedī cā”ti evamādi (dī. ni. 3.355; a. ni. 5.26).

“Monks, in whatever way a monk teaches the Dhamma to others in detail as he has heard it and as he has learned it, in that same way he becomes one who experiences the meaning and one who experiences the Dhamma in that teaching.” And so on. (DN 33; AN 5.26)

Dhammacariyā nāma dasakusalakammapathacariyā. Yathāha – “tividhaṃ kho, gahapatayo, kāyena dhammacariyāsamacariyā hotī”ti evamādi. Sā panesā dhammacariyā saggalokūpapattihetuto “maṅgala”nti veditabbā. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā – “dhammacariyāsamacariyāhetu kho, gahapatayo, evamidhekacce sattā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjantī”ti (ma. ni. 1.441).

The practice of Dhamma is the practice of the ten wholesome courses of action. As it is said: ‘Householders, there is a threefold practice of Dhamma, of righteous conduct, by way of the body,’ and so on. This practice of Dhamma should be understood as a ‘blessing’ because it is the cause for rebirth in a heavenly world. For this was said by the Blessed One: ‘Householders, it is because of practicing the Dhamma, of practicing righteously, that some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.’ (MN 41)

Ñātakā [V 2.0022] nāma mātito vā pitito vā yāva sattamā pitāmahayugā sambandhā. Tesaṃ bhogapārijuññena vā byādhipārijuññena vā abhihatānaṃ attano samīpaṃ āgatānaṃ yathābalaṃ ghāsacchādanadhanadhaññādīhi saṅgaho pasaṃsādīnaṃ diṭṭhadhammikānaṃ sugatigamanādīnañca samparāyikānaṃ visesādhigamānaṃ hetuto “maṅgala”nti vuccati.

Relatives are those connected through the mother's or father's side up to the seventh generation of ancestors. When they, afflicted by loss of wealth or by illness, have come to one, assisting them according to one's ability with food, clothing, wealth, grain, and so on, is called a ‘blessing’ because it is the cause for achieving special advantages—both those in this present life, such as praise, and those in the future, such as going to a good destination.

Anavajjāni kammāni nāma uposathaṅgasamādānaveyyāvaccakaraṇaārāmavanaropanasetukaraṇādīni kāyavacīmanosucaritakammāni. Tāni hi nānappakārahitasukhādhigamahetuto “maṅgala”nti vuccati. “Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, visākhe, vijjati yaṃ idhekacco itthī vā puriso vā aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgataṃ uposathaṃ upavasitvā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā cātumahārājikānaṃ devānaṃ sahabyataṃ upapajjeyyā”ti evamādīni cettha suttāni (a. ni. 8.43) anussaritabbāni.

Blameless deeds are deeds of good conduct by body, speech, and mind, such as undertaking the Uposatha precepts, performing services, planting parks and groves, building bridges, and so on. These are called ‘blessings’ because they are the cause for attaining various kinds of welfare and happiness. And here, suttas such as the following should be recalled: ‘It is possible, Visākhā, that a certain woman or man here, having observed the Uposatha endowed with eight factors, with the breakup of the body, after death, might be reborn into the company of the devas of the Four Great Kings.’ (AN 8.43)

Evaṃ [M 2.0025] imissā gāthāya dānaṃ, dhammacariyā, ñātakānaṃ saṅgaho, anavajjāni kammānīti cattāri maṅgalāni vuttāni, maṅgalattañca nesaṃ tattha tattha vibhāvitamevāti.

Thus, in this verse, four blessings are stated: giving, the practice of Dhamma, assistance to relatives, and blameless deeds. And their nature as blessings has been made clear in each respective case.

Niṭṭhitā dānañcāti imissā gāthāya atthavaṇṇanā.

The explanation of the meaning of the verse beginning `dānañca` is concluded.

267. Idāni āratī viratīti ettha āratīti āramaṇaṃ. Viratīti viramaṇaṃ, viramanti vā etāya sattāti virati. Pāpāti akusalā. Madanīyaṭṭhena majjaṃ, majjassa pānaṃ majjapānaṃ, tato majjapānā. Saṃyamanaṃ saṃyamo. Appamajjanaṃ appamādo. Dhammesūti kusalesu. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti ayaṃ padavaṇṇanā.

267. Now, in the phrase `āratī virati`: `āratī` means non-delight. `Virati` means refraining, or 'beings refrain (`viramanti`) by means of this', thus it is `virati` (abstinence). `Pāpā` means from the unwholesome. `Majjaṃ` (intoxicant) is so called because of its intoxicating nature (`madanīyaṭṭhena`); the drinking (`pānaṃ`) of an intoxicant (`majja`) is `majjapānaṃ`; `tato majjapānā` means 'from the drinking of intoxicants'. `Saṃyamanaṃ` is `saṃyamo` (restraint). `Appamajjanaṃ` is `appamādo` (heedfulness). `Dhammesu` means in wholesome states. The remainder is as previously stated. This is the explanation of the words.

Atthavaṇṇanā pana evaṃ veditabbā – ārati nāma pāpe ādīnavadassāvino manasā eva anabhirati. Virati nāma kammadvāravasena kāyavācāhi viramaṇaṃ. Sā cesā virati nāma sampattavirati samādānavirati samucchedaviratīti tividhā hoti. Tattha yā kulaputtassa attano jātiṃ vā kulaṃ vā gottaṃ vā paṭicca “na me etaṃ patirūpaṃ, yvāhaṃ imaṃ pāṇaṃ haneyyaṃ, adinnaṃ ādiyeyya”ntiādinā nayena sampattavatthuto virati, ayaṃ sampattavirati nāma. Sikkhāpadasamādānavasena pana pavattā samādānavirati nāma, yassā pavattito pabhuti kulaputto pāṇātipātādīni na samācarati. Ariyamaggasampayuttā samucchedavirati nāma, yassā pavattito pabhuti ariyasāvakassa pañca bhayāni verāni vūpasantāni honti. Pāpaṃ nāma yaṃ taṃ “pāṇātipāto kho, gahapatiputta, kammakileso adinnādānaṃ…pe… kāmesumicchācāro…pe… musāvādo”ti evaṃ vitthāretvā –

The explanation of the meaning, however, should be understood thus: `Ārati` is the mental non-delight in evil for one who sees the danger in it. `Virati` is refraining with body and speech by way of the doors of action. This `virati` is threefold: abstinence on occasion (`sampattavirati`), abstinence by undertaking (`samādānavirati`), and abstinence by eradication (`samucchedavirati`). Therein, the abstinence of a person of good family from an object that has presented itself, based on consideration of one's own birth, clan, or lineage, thinking, 'It is not suitable for me that I should kill this being or take what is not given'—this is called abstinence on occasion. Abstinence that proceeds by way of undertaking the training rules, from the arising of which a person of good family no longer commits the killing of living beings and so on, is called abstinence by undertaking. Abstinence conjoined with the noble path, from the arising of which the five fears and enmities of a noble disciple are pacified, is called abstinence by eradication. Evil is that which is elaborated thus: 'The killing of living beings, householder's son, is a defilement of action; taking what is not given… sexual misconduct… false speech…'

“Pāṇātipāto [V 2.0023] adinnādānaṃ, musāvādo ca vuccati;

Paradāragamanañceva, nappasaṃsanti paṇḍitā”ti. (dī. ni. 3.245) –

Killing living beings, taking what is not given, and what is called false speech; and also going to another's wife—the wise do not praise such a person.

Evaṃ gāthāya saṅgahitaṃ kammakilesasaṅkhātaṃ catubbidhaṃ akusalaṃ, tato pāpā. Sabbāpesā ārati ca virati ca diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikabhayaverappahānādinānappakāravisesādhigamahetuto “maṅgala”nti vuccati. “Pāṇātipātā paṭivirato kho, gahapatiputta, ariyasāvako”tiādīni cettha suttāni anussaritabbāni.

Thus, the fourfold unwholesome action, known as defilement of action, is summarized in the verse. Aversion and abstinence from that evil—all this is called a 'blessing' because it is the cause for achieving various kinds of special advantages, such as the abandonment of fear and enmity in this very life and in the life to come. Here, suttas such as, 'A noble disciple, householder's son, abstains from taking life,' and so forth, should be recollected.

Majjapānā [M 2.0026] ca saṃyamo nāma pubbe vuttasurāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānā veramaṇiyāvetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Yasmā pana majjapāyī atthaṃ na jānāti, dhammaṃ na jānāti, mātupi antarāyaṃ karoti, pitu buddhapaccekabuddhatathāgatasāvakānampi antarāyaṃ karoti, diṭṭheva dhamme garahaṃ, samparāye duggatiṃ, aparāpariyāye ummādañca pāpuṇāti. Majjapānā pana saṃyato tesaṃ dosānaṃ vūpasamaṃ tabbiparītaguṇasampadañca pāpuṇāti. Tasmā ayaṃ majjapānā saṃyamo “maṅgala”nti veditabbo.

Restraint from intoxicants is a designation for abstention from liquor, spirits, and intoxicants, which are the basis of heedlessness, as previously mentioned. For one who consumes intoxicants does not know the meaning, does not know the Dhamma, and causes harm even to one's mother, to one's father, to the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples of the Tathāgata. In this very life, one incurs blame, and in the life to come, a bad destination; in subsequent existences, one also attains madness. But one who is restrained from intoxicants attains the cessation of these faults and the accomplishment of opposite qualities. Therefore, this restraint from intoxicants should be understood as a 'blessing.'

Kusalesu dhammesu appamādo nāma “kusalānaṃ vā dhammānaṃ bhāvanāya asakkaccakiriyatā asātaccakiriyatā anaṭṭhitakiriyatā olīnavuttitā nikkhittachandatā nikkhittadhuratā anāsevanā abhāvanā abahulīkammaṃ anadhiṭṭhānaṃ ananuyogo pamādo. Yo evarūpo pamādo pamajjanā pamajjitattaṃ, ayaṃ vuccati pamādo”ti (vibha. 846) ettha vuttassa pamādassa paṭipakkhanayena atthato kusalesu dhammesu satiyā avippavāso veditabbo. So nānappakārakusalādhigamahetuto amatādhigamahetuto ca “maṅgala”nti vuccati. Tattha “appamattassa ātāpino”ti (ma. ni. 2.18-19; a. ni. 5.26) ca “appamādo amatapada”nti (dha. pa. 21) ca evamādi satthusāsanaṃ anussaritabbaṃ.

Heedfulness in wholesome states is to be understood, by way of opposition to the negligence spoken of here, as, in essence, the non-separation of mindfulness from wholesome states. Negligence is defined as: 'Lack of earnestness in developing wholesome states, lack of continuity, lack of perseverance, sluggishness, relinquishing of desire, relinquishing of the burden, non-cultivation, non-development, non-frequent practice, non-determination, non-pursuit—whatever such negligence, being negligent, the state of having been negligent, this is called negligence.' (Vibh. 846) And because it is the cause of attaining various kinds of wholesomeness and the cause of attaining the deathless, it is called a 'blessing.' In this regard, the Teacher’s instruction should be recollected, such as: 'For the heedful and ardent one' (MN 2.18–19; AN 5.26) and 'Heedfulness is the path to the deathless' (Dhp. 21).

Evaṃ imissā gāthāya pāpā virati, majjapānā saṃyamo, kusalesu dhammesu appamādoti tīṇi maṅgalāni vuttāni, maṅgalattañca nesaṃ tattha tattha vibhāvitamevāti.

Thus, in this verse, three blessings are mentioned: abstinence from evil, restraint from intoxicants, and heedfulness in wholesome states. And their nature as blessings has been elucidated in their respective contexts.

Niṭṭhitā āratī viratīti imissā gāthāya atthavaṇṇanā.

The explanation of the meaning of this verse beginning 'Aversion, abstinence from evil' is concluded.

268. Idāni gāravo cāti ettha gāravoti garubhāvo. Nivātoti nīcavuttitā. Santuṭṭhīti santoso. Katassa jānanatā kataññutā. Kālenāti khaṇena samayena. Dhammassa savanaṃ dhammassavanaṃ. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti ayaṃ padavaṇṇanā.

268. Now, in the phrase 'gāravo ca,' 'reverence' (gāravo) means the state of being respectful. 'Humility' (nivāto) means humble conduct. 'Contentment' (santuṭṭhī) means satisfaction. 'Gratitude' (kataññutā) is knowing what has been done. 'In due time' (kālena) means at the right moment, at the right time. 'Listening to the Dhamma' (dhammassavanaṃ) is the hearing of the Dhamma. The rest is as has been explained—this is the word commentary.

Atthavaṇṇanā [V 2.0024] pana evaṃ veditabbā – gāravo nāma garukārapayogārahesu buddhapaccekabuddhatathāgatasāvakaācariyupajjhāyamātāpitujeṭṭhabhātikabhaginiādīsu yathānurūpaṃ garukāro garukaraṇaṃ sagāravatā. Svāyaṃ gāravo yasmā sugatigamanādīnaṃ hetu. Yathāha –

The meaning-commentary, however, should be understood as follows: 'Reverence' (gāravo) means appropriate reverence, the act of revering, and respectfulness towards those worthy of honor, such as Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, disciples of the Tathāgata, teachers, preceptors, mother, father, elder brothers, sisters, and so on. This reverence is the cause for attaining a good destination and the like. As it is said:

“Garukātabbaṃ [M 2.0027] garuṃ karoti, mānetabbaṃ māneti, pūjetabbaṃ pūjeti. So tena kammena evaṃ samattena evaṃ samādinnena kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjati. No ce kāyassa bhedā…pe… upapajjati, sace manussattaṃ āgacchati, yattha yattha paccājāyati, uccākulīno hotī”ti (ma. ni. 3.295).

One treats with respect those who should be treated with respect, esteems those who should be esteemed, and honors those who should be honored. By that action, thus completed and undertaken, after the breakup of the body, after death, one is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. If one is not reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world, after the breakup of the body... but comes to human status, then wherever one is reborn, one is of a high family.

Yathā cāha – “sattime, bhikkhave, aparihāniyā dhammā. Katame satta? Satthugāravatā”tiādi (a. ni. 7.32-33). Tasmā “maṅgala”nti vuccati.

And as it is said: 'Monks, there are these seven conditions that prevent decline. What are the seven? Respect for the Teacher...' and so on (AN 7.32-33). Therefore, reverence is called 'a blessing.'

Nivāto nāma nīcamanatā nivātavuttitā, yāya samannāgato puggalo nihatamāno nihatadappo pādapuñchanacoḷakasamo chinnavisāṇusabhasamo uddhaṭadāṭhasappasamo ca hutvā saṇho sakhilo sukhasambhāso hoti, ayaṃ nivāto. Svāyaṃ yasādiguṇapaṭilābhahetuto “maṅgala”nti vuccati. Āha ca – “nivātavutti atthaddho, tādiso labhate yasa”nti evamādi (dī. ni. 3.273).

Humility (nivāto) means lowliness of mind and humble conduct. A person endowed with this, having subdued conceit and pride, becomes like a foot-wiping cloth, like a bull with broken horns, and like a snake with fangs removed—gentle, friendly, and pleasant in conversation. This is humility. Because it is a cause for the acquisition of qualities such as fame, it is called a 'blessing.' And it is said: 'One who behaves with humility and is not stubborn, such a person gains fame,' and so on (DN 3.273).

Santuṭṭhi nāma itarītarapaccayasantoso, so dvādasavidho hoti. Seyyathidaṃ – cīvare yathālābhasantoso, yathābalasantoso, yathāsāruppasantosoti tividho. Evaṃ piṇḍapātādīsu.

Contentment (santuṭṭhi) is satisfaction with whatever requisites one obtains, and it is of twelve kinds. Namely: in regard to robes, there are three kinds—satisfaction with whatever one obtains, satisfaction according to one's strength, and satisfaction with what is appropriate. It is similar with almsfood and the other requisites.

Tassāyaṃ pabhedavaṇṇanā – idha bhikkhu cīvaraṃ labhati sundaraṃ vā asundaraṃ vā, so teneva yāpeti, aññaṃ na pattheti, labhantopi na gaṇhāti, ayamassa cīvare yathālābhasantoso. Atha pana ābādhiko hoti, garuṃ cīvaraṃ pārupanto oṇamati vā kilamati vā. So sabhāgena bhikkhunā saddhiṃ taṃ parivattetvā lahukena yāpentopi santuṭṭhova hoti, ayamassa cīvare yathābalasantoso. Aparo bhikkhu paṇītapaccayalābhī hoti, so paṭṭacīvarādīnaṃ aññataraṃ mahagghaṃ cīvaraṃ labhitvā “idaṃ therānaṃ cirapabbajitānaṃ bahussutānañca anurūpa”nti tesaṃ datvā attanā saṅkārakūṭā vā aññato vā kutoci nantakāni uccinitvā saṅghāṭiṃ katvā dhārentopi santuṭṭhova hoti, ayamassa cīvare yathāsāruppasantoso.

This is the detailed explanation: Here, a monk obtains a robe, whether beautiful or ugly, and he makes do with just that, not longing for another. Even if offered another, he does not take it. This is his contentment with robes as they are obtained. Then again, a monk may be ill, and feels weighed down or exhausted while wearing a heavy robe. He exchanges it with a suitable monk for a lighter one and, while making do with that, remains content. This is his contentment with robes according to his strength. Another monk is a recipient of fine requisites. Having received an expensive robe, such as one of silk, he thinks, 'This is suitable for the elders, for those long ordained, and for the very learned,' and gives it to them. For himself, he gathers discarded rags from a rubbish heap or elsewhere, stitches them into a patchwork robe, and, while wearing it, remains content. This is his contentment with robes according to what is appropriate.

Idha [M 2.0028] pana bhikkhu piṇḍapātaṃ labhati lūkhaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā, so teneva yāpeti, aññaṃ na pattheti, labhantopi na gaṇhāti, ayamassa piṇḍapāte yathālābhasantoso. Atha pana ābādhiko [V 2.0025] hoti, lūkhaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ bhuñjitvā bāḷhaṃ rogātaṅkaṃ pāpuṇāti, so sabhāgassa bhikkhuno taṃ datvā tassa hatthato sappimadhukhīrādīni bhuñjitvā samaṇadhammaṃ karontopi santuṭṭhova hoti, ayamassa piṇḍapāte yathābalasantoso. Aparo bhikkhu paṇītaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ labhati, so “ayaṃ piṇḍapāto therānaṃ cirapabbajitānaṃ aññesañca paṇītapiṇḍapātaṃ vinā ayāpentānaṃ sabrahmacārīnaṃ anurūpo”ti tesaṃ datvā attanā piṇḍāya caritvā missakāhāraṃ bhuñjantopi santuṭṭhova hoti, ayamassa piṇḍapāte yathāsāruppasantoso.

Here, a monk obtains almsfood, whether coarse or fine, and subsists on just that, not longing for anything else, and even when obtaining more, he does not take it. This is his contentment with almsfood according to what is received. Or else, if he is ill and, having eaten coarse almsfood, experiences a severe attack of disease, he may give that almsfood to a monk of like disposition and, having consumed ghee, curd, honey, milk, and the like from that one's hand, even while performing the ascetic's duty, he is content. This is his contentment with almsfood according to his strength. Another monk obtains fine almsfood and thinks, 'This almsfood is suitable for the elders, for those long ordained, and for other fellow practitioners of the holy life who cannot subsist without fine almsfood.' Having given it to them, he himself goes for alms and, even while eating mixed food, he is content. This is his contentment with almsfood according to what is suitable.

Idha pana bhikkhuno senāsanaṃ pāpuṇāti, so teneva santussati, puna aññaṃ sundaratarampi pāpuṇantaṃ na gaṇhāti, ayamassa senāsane yathālābhasantoso. Atha pana ābādhiko hoti, nivātasenāsane vasanto ativiya pittarogādīhi āturīyati, so sabhāgassa bhikkhuno taṃ datvā tassa pāpuṇanake savātasītalasenāsane vasitvā samaṇadhammaṃ karontopi santuṭṭhova hoti, ayamassa senāsane yathābalasantoso. Aparo bhikkhu sundaraṃ senāsanaṃ pattampi na sampaṭicchati “sundarasenāsanaṃ pamādaṭṭhānaṃ, tatra nisinnassa thinamiddhaṃ okkamati, niddābhibhūtassa ca puna paṭibujjhato kāmavitakkā samudācarantī”ti, so taṃ paṭikkhipitvā abbhokāsarukkhamūlapaṇṇakuṭīsu yattha katthaci nivasantopi santuṭṭhova hoti, ayamassa senāsane yathāsāruppasantoso.

Here, a monk obtains a lodging, and he is content with that. When he comes across another, more beautiful one, he does not take it. This is his contentment with lodging according to what is obtained. Or else, if he is ill, dwelling in a windless lodging, he is greatly afflicted by bile diseases and the like. Giving that lodging to a monk of like disposition, he dwells in a well-ventilated, cool lodging that he obtains, and even while performing the ascetic's duty, he is content. This is his contentment with lodging according to his strength. Another monk, even when having obtained a beautiful lodging, does not accept it, thinking, 'A beautiful lodging is a basis for negligence. For one sitting there, sloth and torpor descend. And for one overcome by sleep, upon waking again, sensual thoughts arise.' Rejecting it, he dwells contentedly in the open air, at the foot of a tree, or in a leaf-hut—wherever he may stay. This is his contentment with lodging according to what is suitable.

Idha pana bhikkhu bhesajjaṃ labhati harītakaṃ vā āmalakaṃ vā, so teneva yāpeti, aññehi laddhaṃ sappimadhuphāṇitādimpi na pattheti, labhantopi na gaṇhāti, ayamassa gilānapaccaye yathālābhasantoso. Atha pana ābādhiko telena atthiko phāṇitaṃ labhati, so taṃ sabhāgassa bhikkhuno datvā tassa hatthato telena bhesajjaṃ katvā samaṇadhammaṃ karontopi santuṭṭhova hoti, ayamassa gilānapaccaye yathābalasantoso. Aparo bhikkhu ekasmiṃ bhājane pūtimuttaharītakaṃ [M 2.0029] ṭhapetvā ekasmiṃ catumadhuraṃ “gaṇhatha, bhante, yadicchasī”ti vuccamāno sacassa tesaṃ dvinnaṃ aññatarenapi byādhi vūpasammati, atha “pūtimuttaharītakaṃ nāma buddhādīhi vaṇṇitaṃ, ayañca pūtimuttabhesajjaṃ nissāya pabbajjā, tattha te yāvajīvaṃ ussāho karaṇīyo”ti (mahāva. 128) vuttanti cintento catumadhurabhesajjaṃ paṭikkhipitvā muttaharītakena bhesajjaṃ karontopi paramasantuṭṭhova hoti, ayamassa gilānapaccaye yathāsāruppasantoso.

Here, a monk obtains medicine—whether harītaka or āmalaka—and subsists on just that. He does not long for other things obtained from others, such as ghee, honey, or molasses, nor does he take them even if he receives them. This is his contentment with requisites for the sick according to what is received. Or else, a sick monk in need of oil obtains molasses. He gives it to a monk of like disposition and, from that monk's hand, having prepared medicine with oil, performs the ascetic's duty while remaining content. This is his contentment with requisites for the sick according to his strength. Another monk has harītaka steeped in putrid urine placed in one vessel and a fourfold sweet remedy in another. When told, 'Venerable sir, take whichever you wish,' even if his illness would be alleviated by either of the two, reflecting, 'The medicine of harītaka steeped in putrid urine is praised by the Buddha and others, and this ordination depends on the medicine of putrid urine. Therein, you should make an effort for as long as life lasts' (Mahāvagga 128), he rejects the fourfold sweet remedy and, while preparing medicine with the harītaka steeped in urine, remains supremely content. This is his contentment with requisites for the sick according to what is suitable.

Evaṃ pabhedo sabbopeso santoso santuṭṭhīti vuccati. Sā atricchatāpāpicchatāmahicchatādīnaṃ pāpadhammānaṃ pahānādhigamahetuto sugatihetuto ariyamaggasambhārabhāvato cātuddisādibhāvahetuto ca “maṅgala”nti veditabbā. Āha ca –

Thus, this contentment in all its divisions is called `santuṭṭhī`. It should be understood as a 'blessing' because it is a cause for abandoning evil states—such as excessive desire, evil desire, and great desire—and for attaining wholesome states; because it is a cause for a good destination; because it is a condition for the requisites of the Noble Path; and because it is a cause for being unhindered in the four directions. And it is said:

“Cātuddiso [V 2.0026] appaṭigho ca hoti,

Santussamāno itarītarenā”ti. (su. ni. 42; cūḷani. khaggavisāṇasuttaniddesa 128) evamādi;

'Being content with whatever is at hand,

One is of the four directions and unopposed.'

Kataññutā nāma appassa vā bahussa vā yena kenaci katassa upakārassa punappunaṃ anussaraṇabhāvena jānanatā. Apica nerayikādidukkhaparittāṇato puññāni eva pāṇīnaṃ bahūpakārāni, tato tesampi upakārānussaraṇatā “kataññutā”ti veditabbā. Sā sappurisehi pasaṃsanīyatādinānappakāravisesādhigamahetuto “maṅgala”nti vuttā. Āha ca – “dveme, bhikkhave, puggalā dullabhā lokasmiṃ. Katame dve? Yo ca pubbakārī, yo ca kataññū katavedī”ti (a. ni. 2.120).

Gratitude is the quality of knowing, by way of repeated remembrance, any help received from anyone, whether small or great. Moreover, since merits protect beings from suffering such as that of hell and are thus of great benefit to living beings, the remembrance of the benefit of those merits, too, should be understood as 'gratitude'. It is called a 'blessing' because it is a cause for attaining various special qualities, such as being praiseworthy to good people. As it is said: 'Monks, these two persons are rare in the world. Which two? The one who helps first, and the one who is grateful and acknowledges what has been done' (Aṅguttara Nikāya 2.120).

Kālena dhammassavanaṃ nāma yasmiṃ kāle uddhaccasahagataṃ cittaṃ hoti, kāmavitakkādīnaṃ vā aññatarena abhibhūtaṃ, tasmiṃ kāle tesaṃ vinodanatthaṃ dhammassavanaṃ. Apare āhu – pañcame pañcame divase dhammassavanaṃ kālena dhammassavanaṃ nāma. Yathāha āyasmā anuruddho “pañcāhikaṃ kho pana mayaṃ, bhante, sabbarattiṃ dhammiyā kathāya sannisīdāmā”ti (ma. ni. 1.327; mahāva. 466).

Listening to the Dhamma at the right time refers to occasions when the mind is accompanied by restlessness or is overwhelmed by sensual thoughts and the like; at such times, listening to the Dhamma is for the purpose of dispelling them. Others say that listening to the Dhamma every fifth day is called listening to the Dhamma at the right time. As the Venerable Anuruddha said: 'Venerable sir, every fifth day we gather together all night for Dhamma discussion' (Majjhima Nikāya 1.327; Mahāvagga 466).

Apica yasmiṃ kāle kalyāṇamitte upasaṅkamitvā sakkā hoti attano kaṅkhāpaṭivinodakaṃ dhammaṃ sotuṃ, tasmiṃ kālepi dhammassavanaṃ “kālena dhammassavana”nti veditabbaṃ. Yathāha – “te kālena kālaṃ upasaṅkamitvā [M 2.0030] paripucchati paripañhatī”tiādi (dī. ni. 3.358). Tadetaṃ kālena dhammassavanaṃ nīvaraṇappahānacaturānisaṃsaāsavakkhayādinānappakāravisesādhigamahetuto “maṅgala”nti veditabbaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Furthermore, whenever one can approach spiritual friends and listen to the Dhamma in order to dispel one’s doubts, that too is to be understood as 'listening to the Dhamma at the right time.' As it is said: 'They approach from time to time, inquire, and question,' etc. (Dīgha Nikāya 3.358). This timely hearing of the Dhamma is to be understood as a 'blessing' because it is a cause for the attainment of various special qualities, such as the abandonment of the hindrances, the four benefits, and the destruction of the taints. As it is stated:

“Yasmiṃ, bhikkhave, samaye ariyasāvako aṭṭhiṃ katvā manasi katvā sabbaṃ cetaso samannāharitvā ohitasoto dhammaṃ suṇāti, pañcassa nīvaraṇāni tasmiṃ samaye na hontī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.219) ca.

Monks, at a time when a noble disciple, paying proper attention, applying his mind, concentrating with his whole mind, and with an attentive ear, listens to the Dhamma, at that time the five hindrances are not present in him.

“Sotānugatānaṃ, bhikkhave, dhammānaṃ…pe… suppaṭividdhānaṃ cattāro ānisaṃsā pāṭikaṅkhā”ti (a. ni. 4.191) ca.

Monks, for those who follow the teachings with the ear... and have well penetrated their meaning, four benefits are to be expected.

“Cattārome, bhikkhave, dhammā kālena kālaṃ sammā bhāviyamānā sammā anuparivattiyamānā [V 2.0027] anupubbena āsavānaṃ khayaṃ pāpenti. Katame cattāro? Kālena dhammassavana”nti ca evamādīni (a. ni. 4.147).

Monks, these four things, when rightly developed and rightly cultivated in turn from time to time, lead gradually to the destruction of the taints. What four? Listening to the Dhamma at the proper time.

Evaṃ imissā gāthāya gāravo, nivāto, santuṭṭhi, kataññutā, kālena dhammassavananti pañca maṅgalāni vuttāni, maṅgalattañca nesaṃ tattha tattha vibhāvitamevāti.

Thus, in this verse, five blessings are mentioned: reverence, humility, contentment, gratitude, and listening to the Dhamma at the proper time. And their nature as blessings has been explained in their respective contexts.

Niṭṭhitā gāravo ca nivāto cāti imissā gāthāya atthavaṇṇanā.

Here ends the explanation of the meaning of the verse beginning 'Reverence and humility'.

269. Idāni khantī cāti ettha khamanaṃ khanti. Padakkhiṇaggāhitāya sukhaṃ vaco asminti suvaco, suvacassa kammaṃ sovacassaṃ, sovacassassa bhāvo sovacassatā. Kilesānaṃ samitattā samaṇā. Dassananti pekkhanaṃ. Dhammassa sākacchā dhammasākacchā. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti ayaṃ padavaṇṇanā.

269. Now, regarding 'and patience' (khanti ca): here, forbearance (khamanaṃ) is patience (khanti). One for whom speech is easy due to his skillful acceptance is called 'suvaco' (easy to speak to). The quality of being easy to speak to is 'sovacassaṃ,' and the state of being easy to speak to is 'sovacassatā.' Ascetics (samaṇā) are so called because their defilements are pacified (kilesānaṃ samitattā). 'Seeing' (dassana) means viewing (pekkhanaṃ). Discussion of the Dhamma (dhammasākacchā) is discussion (sākacchā) of the Dhamma (dhammassa). The rest should be understood in the manner already stated. This is the word-by-word explanation.

Atthavaṇṇanā pana evaṃ veditabbā khanti nāma adhivāsanakkhanti, yāya samannāgato bhikkhu dasahi akkosavatthūhi akkosante, vadhabandhādīhi vā vihiṃsante puggale asuṇanto viya ca apassanto viya ca nibbikāro hoti khantivādī viya. Yathāha –

The explanation of the meaning, however, should be understood as follows: Patience (khanti) is the patience of endurance (adhivāsanakkhanti). A monk endowed with it remains unperturbed—as if not hearing or seeing, like the ascetic who preached patience (Khantivādī)—when people revile him with the ten grounds for abuse or harm him with killing, binding, and the like. As it is said:

“Ahū atītamaddhānaṃ, samaṇo khantidīpano;

Taṃ khantiyāyeva ṭhitaṃ, kāsirājā achedayī”ti. (jā. 1.4.51);

“In a time long past, there was a recluse, an exponent of patience; him, though established only in patience, the king of Kāsi had cut up.”

Bhaddakato [M 2.0031] vā manasi karoti tato uttari aparādhābhāvena āyasmā puṇṇatthero viya. Yathāha –

Or, like the Venerable Puṇṇa Thera, he takes it in a good way and, beyond that, remains free from offense. As it is said:

“Sace maṃ, bhante, sunāparantakā manussā akkosissanti paribhāsissanti, tattha me evaṃ bhavissati ‘bhaddakā vatime sunāparantakā manussā, subhaddakā vatime sunāparantakā manussā, yaṃ me nayime pāṇinā pahāraṃ dentī’”tiādi (ma. ni. 3.396; saṃ. ni. 4.88).

“Venerable sir, if the people of Sunāparanta should revile and abuse me, then it will occur to me: ‘These people of Sunāparanta are good, these people of Sunāparanta are truly good, in that they do not give me a blow with their hand!’” and so on.
