Yāya ca samannāgato isīnampi pasaṃsanīyo hoti. Yathāha sarabhaṅgo isi –

And one endowed with it is praiseworthy even to sages. As the sage Sarabhaṅga said:

“Kodhaṃ vadhitvā na kadāci socati,

Makkhappahānaṃ isayo vaṇṇayanti;

Sabbesaṃ [V 2.0028] vuttaṃ pharusaṃ khametha,

Etaṃ khantiṃ uttamamāhu santo”ti. (jā. 2.17.64);

“Having slain anger, one never grieves; the abandonment of contempt the sages praise. One should endure all harsh words spoken; this patience the good call supreme.”

Devatānampi pasaṃsanīyo hoti. Yathāha sakko devānamindo –

He is praiseworthy even to deities. As Sakka, lord of the devas, said:

“Yo have balavā santo, dubbalassa titikkhati;

Tamāhu paramaṃ khantiṃ, niccaṃ khamati dubbalo”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.250-251);

“Whoever, being strong, endures the weak—that they call the supreme patience; the weak one must always endure.”

Buddhānampi pasaṃsanīyo hoti. Yathāha bhagavā –

He is praiseworthy even to the Buddhas. As the Blessed One has said:

“Akkosaṃ vadhabandhañca, aduṭṭho yo titikkhati;

Khantībalaṃ balānīkaṃ, tamahaṃ brūmi brāhmaṇa”nti. (dha. pa. 399);

“He who, free from anger, endures abuse, killing, and binding, who has the strength of patience, a mighty army—him I call a brahmin.”

Sā panesā khanti etesañca idha vaṇṇitānaṃ aññesañca guṇānaṃ adhigamahetuto “maṅgala”nti veditabbā.

This patience should be understood as a 'blessing' because it is a cause for attaining these qualities praised here and others as well.

Sovacassatā nāma sahadhammikaṃ vuccamāne vikkhepaṃ vā tuṇhībhāvaṃ vā guṇadosacintanaṃ vā anāpajjitvā ativiya ādarañca gāravañca nīcamanatañca purakkhatvā “sādhū”ti vacanakaraṇatā. Sā sabrahmacārīnaṃ santikā ovādānusāsanīpaṭilābhahetuto dosappahānaguṇādhigamahetuto ca “maṅgala”nti vuccati.

'Receptivity' (sovacassatā) is, when spoken to by a fellow practitioner of the Dhamma, to respond with 'Sādhu!' without falling into distraction, silence, or consideration of virtues and faults, but rather with great respect, reverence, and humility. It is called a 'blessing' (maṅgala) because it is a cause for obtaining advice and instruction from one's companions in the holy life, and because it leads to the abandonment of faults and the attainment of virtues.

Samaṇānaṃ [M 2.0032] dassanaṃ nāma upasamitakilesānaṃ bhāvitakāyavacīcittapaññānaṃ uttamadamathasamathasamannāgatānaṃ pabbajitānaṃ upasaṅkamanupaṭṭhānaanussaraṇasavanadassanaṃ, sabbampi omakadesanāya “dassana”nti vuttaṃ. Taṃ “maṅgala”nti veditabbaṃ. Kasmā? Bahūpakārattā. Āha ca – “dassanampahaṃ, bhikkhave, tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ bahūpakāraṃ vadāmī”tiādi (itivu. 104). Yato hitakāmena kulaputtena sīlavante bhikkhū gharadvāraṃ sampatte disvā yadi deyyadhammo atthi, yathābalaṃ deyyadhammena patimānetabbā. Yadi natthi, pañcapatiṭṭhitaṃ katvā vanditabbā. Tasmiṃ asampajjamāne añjaliṃ paggahetvā namassitabbā, tasmimpi asampajjamāne pasannacittena piyacakkhūhi sampassitabbā. Evaṃ dassanamūlakenāpi hi puññena anekāni jātisahassāni cakkhumhi rogo vā dāho vā ussadā vā piḷakā vā na honti, vippasannapañcavaṇṇasassirikāni honti cakkhūni ratanavimāne ugghāṭitamaṇikavāṭasadisāni[V 2.0029], satasahassakappamattaṃ devesu ca manussesu ca sabbasampattīnaṃ lābhī hoti. Anacchariyañcetaṃ, yaṃ manussabhūto sappaññajātiko sammā pavattitena samaṇadassanamayena puññena evarūpaṃ vipākasampattiṃ anubhaveyya, yattha tiracchānagatānampi kevalaṃ saddhāmattakajanitassa samaṇadassanassa evaṃ vipākasampattiṃ vaṇṇayanti –

The 'sight of ascetics' refers to approaching, attending upon, recollecting, hearing, and seeing those who have gone forth—those who have pacified defilements, cultivated body, speech, mind, and wisdom, and are endowed with supreme taming and calm. All these, by way of a general designation, are called 'sight.' This should be understood as a 'blessing.' Why? Because it is greatly beneficial. And it is said: 'Monks, I declare that seeing those monks is of great benefit,' and so on. Therefore, when a clansman who desires his own welfare sees virtuous monks arriving at his house door, if there is something to give, they should be honored with an offering according to his ability. If there is nothing, they should be venerated with the five-point prostration. If that is not possible, they should be revered by raising the joined palms. If that too is not possible, they should be looked upon with a serene mind and loving eyes. Indeed, even through the merit rooted in such sight, for many thousands of lifetimes, no disease, burning, swelling, or boil arises in the eyes. The eyes become very clear, radiant with five colors, like opened jeweled doors in a celestial mansion. For a hundred thousand eons, one becomes a recipient of all prosperity among gods and humans. And it is no wonder that a human being, born with wisdom, should experience such a perfection of result through the merit consisting of the proper sight of ascetics, when they praise such a perfection of result even for animals from the mere sight of ascetics generated only by faith:

“Ulūko maṇḍalakkhiko,

Vediyake ciradīghavāsiko;

Sukhito vata kosiyo ayaṃ,

Kāluṭṭhitaṃ passati buddhavaraṃ.

“The owl with round eyes, dwelling long in Vediyaka; happy indeed is this owl, he sees the excellent Buddha arisen at the proper time.”

“Mayi cittaṃ pasādetvā, bhikkhusaṅghe anuttare;

Kappānaṃ satasahassāni, duggatiṃ so na gacchati.

“Having clarified his mind towards me, and towards the unsurpassed Sangha of monks; for a hundred thousand eons, he does not go to a state of woe.”

“Devalokā cavitvāna, kusalakammena codito;

Bhavissati anantañāṇo, somanassoti vissuto”ti. (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.144; khu. pā. aṭṭha. 5.10);

Having passed away from the heavenly realm, impelled by wholesome deeds, he will become one of limitless wisdom, renowned as Somanassa.

Kālena dhammasākacchā nāma padose vā paccūse vā dve suttantikā bhikkhū aññamaññaṃ suttantaṃ sākacchanti, vinayadharā vinayaṃ, ābhidhammikā abhidhammaṃ[M 2.0033], jātakabhāṇakā jātakaṃ, aṭṭhakathikā aṭṭhakathaṃ, līnuddhatavicikicchāparetacittavisodhanatthaṃ vā tamhi tamhi kāle sākacchanti, ayaṃ kālena dhammasākacchā. Sā āgamabyattiādīnaṃ guṇānaṃ hetuto “maṅgala”nti vuccatīti.

Timely discussion of the Dhamma means that in the evening or at dawn two monks learned in the Suttas discuss the Suttas with each other; those versed in the Vinaya discuss the Vinaya; those skilled in the Abhidhamma discuss the Abhidhamma; those who recite the Jātakas discuss the Jātakas; and those learned in the commentaries discuss the commentaries. Or, they discuss at an appropriate time for the purpose of purifying a mind overcome by sloth, agitation, and doubt. This is called timely discussion of the Dhamma. Because it is a cause for qualities such as proficiency in the scriptures and eloquence, it is called 'auspicious'.

Evaṃ imissā gāthāya khanti, sovacassatā, samaṇadassanaṃ, kālena dhammasākacchāti cattāri maṅgalāni vuttāni, maṅgalattañca nesaṃ tattha tattha vibhāvitamevāti.

Thus, in this verse, four blessings are spoken of: patience, being easy to admonish, the sight of ascetics, and timely discussion of the Dhamma. And their nature as blessings has been clearly shown in each respective case.

Niṭṭhitā khantī cāti imissā gāthāya atthavaṇṇanā.

The explanation of the meaning of the verse beginning with 'Patience...' is concluded.

270. Idāni tapo cāti ettha pāpake akusale dhamme tapatīti tapo. Brahmaṃ cariyaṃ, brahmānaṃ vā cariyaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, seṭṭhacariyanti vuttaṃ hoti. Ariyasaccānaṃ dassanaṃ ariyasaccāna dassanaṃ. Ariyasaccāni dassanantipi eke, taṃ na sundaraṃ. Nikkhantaṃ vānatoti nibbānaṃ, sacchikaraṇaṃ [V 2.0030] sacchikiriyā, nibbānassa sacchikiriyā nibbānasacchikiriyā. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti ayaṃ padavaṇṇanā.

270. Now, in the verse beginning 'Austerity...', the meaning should be understood as follows. Because it burns away evil, unwholesome states, it is 'austerity' (tapo). 'The holy life' (brahmacariya) means noble conduct, or the conduct of holy ones; it is said to be the supreme conduct. 'The vision of the Noble Truths' (ariyasaccānaṃ dassanaṃ) is the seeing of the Noble Truths. Some read it as 'the Noble Truths are a vision' (ariyasaccāni dassanaṃ), but this is not elegant. Because it is a 'going forth' (nikkhantaṃ) from 'craving' (vāna), it is called 'nibbāna'. Realization (sacchikaraṇaṃ) is the act of realizing (sacchikiriyā); the act of realizing Nibbāna is 'nibbānasacchikiriyā'. The rest is just as was said previously. This is the explanation of the terms.

Atthavaṇṇanā pana evaṃ veditabbā – tapo nāma abhijjhādomanassādīnaṃ tapanato indriyasaṃvaro, kosajjassa vā tapanato vīriyaṃ. Tena hi samannāgato puggalo ātāpīti vuccati. Svāyaṃ abhijjhādippahānajhānādipaṭilābhahetuto “maṅgala”nti veditabbo.

The explanation of the meaning, however, should be understood thus: 'Austerity' (tapo) means the restraint of the senses, because it burns away covetousness, dejection, and so on; or it means energy, because it burns away sloth. A person endowed with that is called 'ardent' (ātāpī). This austerity should be understood as 'auspicious' because it is a cause for abandoning covetousness and so on, and for attaining jhāna and so on.

Brahmacariyaṃ nāma methunaviratisamaṇadhammasāsanamaggānaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tathā hi “abrahmacariyaṃ pahāya brahmacārī hotī”ti (dī. ni. 1.194; ma. ni. 1.292) evamādīsu methunavirati brahmacariyanti vuccati. “Bhagavati no, āvuso, brahmacariyaṃ vussatī”ti evamādīsu (ma. ni. 1.257) samaṇadhammo. “Na tāvāhaṃ, pāpima, parinibbāyissāmi, yāva me idaṃ brahmacariyaṃ na iddhañceva bhavissati phītañca vitthārikaṃ bāhujañña”nti evamādīsu (dī. ni. 2.168; saṃ. ni. 5.822; udā. 51) sāsanaṃ. “Ayameva kho, bhikkhu, ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo brahmacariyaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ, sammādiṭṭhī”ti evamādīsu (saṃ. ni. 5.6) maggo. Idha pana ariyasaccadassanena parato maggassa gahitattā avasesaṃ sabbampi vaṭṭati. Tañcetaṃ uparūpari nānappakāravisesādhigamahetuto “maṅgala”nti veditabbaṃ.

'The holy life' (brahmacariya) is a term for abstinence from sexual intercourse, the duties of a contemplative, the Teaching, and the Path. For instance, in passages like, "having given up unchastity, one becomes a celibate," abstinence from sexual intercourse is called the holy life. In passages like, "Friend, it is in the presence of the Blessed One that the holy life is lived by us," it refers to the duties of a contemplative. In passages like, "Pāpima, I will not attain final Nibbāna until this holy life of mine is successful, prosperous, widespread, and known to many," it refers to the Teaching. In passages like, "Monks, this Noble Eightfold Path is itself the holy life, that is: right view…," it refers to the Path. Here, however, since the Path is taken up subsequently with the seeing of the Noble Truths, all the other meanings are applicable. And this should be understood as 'auspicious' because it is the cause for attaining various superior distinctions, higher and higher.

Ariyasaccāna [M 2.0034] dassanaṃ nāma kumārapañhe vuttatthānaṃ catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ abhisamayavasena maggadassanaṃ. Taṃ saṃsāradukkhavītikkamahetuto “maṅgala”nti vuccati.

'The vision of the Noble Truths' means the seeing of the Path by way of penetrating the four Noble Truths, whose meaning was stated in the Kumārapañha. Because it is the cause for overcoming the suffering of saṃsāra, it is called 'auspicious'.

Nibbānasacchikiriyā nāma idha arahattaphalaṃ “nibbāna”nti adhippetaṃ. Tampi hi pañcagativānanena vānasaññitāya taṇhāya nikkhantattā “nibbāna”nti vuccati. Tassa patti vā paccavekkhaṇā vā “sacchikiriyā”ti vuccati. Itarassa pana nibbānassa ariyasaccānaṃ dassaneneva sacchikiriyā siddhā, tenetaṃ idha na adhippetaṃ. Evamesā nibbānasacchikiriyā diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārādihetuto “maṅgala”nti veditabbā.

The 'realization of Nibbāna': here, the fruit of arahantship is intended by the term 'Nibbāna'. For that too is called 'Nibbāna' because it is a going forth from craving—designated as 'vāna' (weaving)—which weaves one through the five destinations. The attainment of that, or the reviewing of it, is called 'the act of realizing'. As for the other Nibbāna, its realization is accomplished by the very seeing of the Noble Truths; therefore, that is not intended here. Thus, this act of realizing Nibbāna should be understood as 'auspicious' because it is a cause for dwelling happily in this very life, and so on.

Evaṃ imissāpi gāthāya tapo, brahmacariyaṃ, ariyasaccāna dassanaṃ, nibbānasacchikiriyāti cattāri maṅgalāni vuttāni, maṅgalattañca nesaṃ tattha tattha vibhāvitamevāti.

Thus, in this verse also, four blessings are spoken of: austerity, the holy life, the vision of the Noble Truths, and the realization of Nibbāna. And their nature as blessings has been clearly shown in each respective case.

Niṭṭhitā tapo cāti imissā gāthāya atthavaṇṇanā.

The explanation of the meaning of the verse beginning with 'Austerity...' is concluded.

271. Idāni [V 2.0031] phuṭṭhassa lokadhammehīti ettha phuṭṭhassāti phusitassa chupitassa sampattassa. Loke dhammā lokadhammā, yāva lokappavatti, tāva anivattakā dhammāti vuttaṃ hoti. Cittanti mano mānasaṃ. Yassāti navassa vā majjhimassa vā therassa vā. Na kampatīti na calati, na vedhati. Asokanti nissokaṃ abbūḷhasokasallaṃ. Virajanti vigatarajaṃ viddhaṃsitarajaṃ. Khemanti abhayaṃ nirupaddavaṃ. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti ayaṃ tāva padavaṇṇanā.

271. Now, regarding 'touched by worldly conditions': here 'touched' means contacted, affected, or come upon. 'Worldly conditions' are phenomena in the world; it is said that they are inevitable phenomena as long as the world persists. 'Mind' means 'mano' or 'mānasaṃ'. 'Whose' applies whether one is a junior, middle, or senior elder. 'Does not tremble' means it does not waver, does not quake. 'Sorrowless' means without sorrow, with the dart of sorrow extracted. 'Stainless' means with defilement gone, with defilement destroyed. 'Secure' means without fear, without trouble. The rest is just as was said previously. This, for now, is the explanation of the terms.

Atthavaṇṇanā pana evaṃ veditabbā – phuṭṭhassa lokadhammehi yassa cittaṃ na kampati, yassa lābhālābhādīhi aṭṭhahi lokadhammehi phuṭṭhassa ajjhotthaṭassa cittaṃ na kampati, na calati, na vedhati, tassa taṃ cittaṃ kenaci akampanīyalokuttarabhāvāvahanato “maṅgala”nti veditabbaṃ.

The explanation of the meaning, however, should be understood as follows: 'For one whose mind does not tremble when touched by worldly conditions'—that is, one whose mind, when touched and overwhelmed by the eight worldly conditions such as gain and loss, does not tremble, does not waver, does not shake—that mind of theirs should be understood as 'auspicious' because it brings about an unshakable, supramundane state.

Kassa pana etehi phuṭṭhassa cittaṃ na kampati? Arahato khīṇāsavassa, na aññassa kassaci. Vuttañhetaṃ –

But whose mind does not tremble when touched by these? An Arahant's, one whose taints are destroyed, and no one else's. For it has been said:

“Selo yathā ekagghano, vātena na samīrati;

Evaṃ rūpā rasā saddā, gandhā phassā ca kevalā.

Just as a solid rock is not stirred by the wind, so all sights, sounds, smells, tastes, and touches...

“Iṭṭhā [M 2.0035] dhammā aniṭṭhā ca, na pavedhenti tādino;

Ṭhitaṃ cittaṃ vippamuttaṃ, vayañcassānupassatī”ti. (a. ni. 6.55; mahāva. 244);

...and desirable and undesirable objects do not cause such a one to tremble. For one who constantly sees passing away, the mind is firm and liberated.

Asokaṃ nāma khīṇāsavasseva cittaṃ. Tañhi yo “soko socanā socitattaṃ antosoko antoparisoko cetaso parinijjhāyitatta”ntiādinā (vibha. 237) nayena vuccati soko, tassa abhāvato asokaṃ. Keci nibbānaṃ vadanti, taṃ purimapadena nānusandhiyati. Yathā ca asokaṃ, evaṃ virajaṃ khemantipi khīṇāsavasseva cittaṃ. Tañhi rāgadosamoharajānaṃ vigatattā virajaṃ, catūhi ca yogehi khemattā khemaṃ. Yato etaṃ tena tenākārena tamhi tamhi pavattikkhaṇe gahetvā niddiṭṭhavasena tividhampi appavattakkhandhatādilokuttamabhāvāvahanato āhuneyyādibhāvāvahanato ca “maṅgala”nti veditabbaṃ.

Sorrowless (`asokaṃ`) refers to the mind of one whose taints are destroyed. For it is called sorrowless due to the absence of sorrow (`soka`), which is described in the manner beginning, 'Sorrow is grieving, grief, the state of grieving, inner sorrow, inner deep sorrow, the burning in the mind' (Vibh 237). Some say this refers to Nibbāna, but that does not connect with the preceding phrase. And just as it is sorrowless, so too the mind of one whose taints are destroyed is stainless (`virajaṃ`) and secure (`khemaṃ`). For it is stainless due to being devoid of the dust of lust, hatred, and delusion, and secure due to its security from the four yokes. Therefore, this threefold quality, taken in this or that manner at each moment of its occurrence, as has been pointed out, is to be understood as a 'blessing' because it brings about the supramundane state, such as the non-continuation of the aggregates, and because it brings about the state of being worthy of offerings and so forth.

Evaṃ imissā gāthāya aṭṭhalokadhammehi akampitacittaṃ, asokacittaṃ, virajacittaṃ, khemacittanti cattāri maṅgalāni vuttāni, maṅgalattañca nesaṃ tattha tattha vibhāvitamevāti.

Thus, in this verse, four blessings are stated: a mind unshaken by the eight worldly conditions, a sorrowless mind, a stainless mind, and a secure mind. And their nature as blessings has been explained in each respective place.

Niṭṭhitā phuṭṭhassa lokadhammehīti imissā gāthāya atthavaṇṇanā.

The exposition of the meaning of the verse beginning 'When touched by worldly conditions' is completed.

272. Evaṃ [V 2.0032] bhagavā “asevanā ca bālāna”ntiādīhi dasahi gāthāhi aṭṭhatiṃsa maṅgalāni kathetvā idāni etāneva attanā vuttamaṅgalāni thunanto “etādisāni katvānā”ti imaṃ avasānagāthamabhāsi.

272. Thus, having taught the thirty-eight blessings through the ten verses beginning with 'Not associating with fools,' the Blessed One, now praising these very blessings he had spoken, uttered this concluding verse: 'Having done such things...'

Tassāyaṃ atthavaṇṇanā – etādisānīti etāni īdisāni mayā vuttappakārāni bālānaṃ asevanādīni. Katvānāti katvā. Katvāna katvā karitvāti hi atthato anaññaṃ. Sabbatthamaparājitāti sabbattha khandhakilesābhisaṅkhāradevaputtamārappabhedesu catūsu paccatthikesu ekenapi aparājitā hutvā, sayameva te cattāro māre parājetvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Makāro cettha padasandhikaraṇamattoti viññātabbo.

This is the exposition of its meaning: 'Such things' (`etādisāni`) refers to these things of such a kind as I have described, beginning with not associating with fools. 'Having done' (`katvāna`) means `katvā`; for `katvā` and `karitvā` are not different in meaning. 'Unconquered everywhere' (`sabbattha-m-aparājitā`) means being unconquered by even one of the four enemies in all respects: the aggregates, defilements, formations, and Māra, the son of a god. This means having oneself conquered those four Māras. The 'm' here should be understood as merely for the purpose of euphonic conjunction.

Sabbattha sotthiṃ gacchantīti etādisāni maṅgalāni katvā catūhi mārehi aparājitā hutvā sabbattha idhalokaparalokesu ṭhānacaṅkamanādīsu ca sotthiṃ gacchanti, bālasevanādīhi ye uppajjeyyuṃ āsavā vighātapariḷāhā[M 2.0036], tesaṃ abhāvā sotthiṃ gacchanti, anupaddutā anupasaṭṭhā khemino appaṭibhayā gacchantīti vuttaṃ hoti. Anunāsiko cettha gāthābandhasukhatthaṃ vuttoti veditabbo.

'They go in safety everywhere' (`sabbattha sotthiṃ gacchanti`) means that, having performed such blessings and being unconquered by the four Māras, they go in safety everywhere—in this world and the next, in standing, walking, and so on. Because the afflictions, vexations, and fevers that might arise from associating with fools and so on do not exist, they go in safety; it is said that they go unmolested, unassailed, secure, and fearless. The nasal consonant here should be understood as stated for the sake of metrical ease in the verse.

Taṃ tesaṃ maṅgalamuttamanti iminā gāthāpādena bhagavā desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi. Kathaṃ? Evaṃ devaputta ye etādisāni karonti, te yasmā sabbattha sotthiṃ gacchanti, tasmā taṃ bālānaṃ asevanādi aṭṭhatiṃsavidhampi tesaṃ etādisakārakānaṃ maṅgalaṃ uttamaṃ seṭṭhaṃ pavaranti gaṇhāhīti.

With the line of the verse, 'That is their supreme blessing' (`taṃ tesaṃ maṅgalamuttamaṃ`), the Blessed One concluded the teaching. How? 'Thus, O devaputta, because those who do such things go in safety everywhere, therefore you should understand that this thirty-eight-fold blessing, beginning with not associating with fools, is for them—for those who perform such actions—a supreme, best, and most excellent blessing.'

Evañca bhagavatā niṭṭhāpitāya desanāya pariyosāne koṭisatasahassadevatā arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu, sotāpattisakadāgāmianāgāmiphalappattānaṃ gaṇanā asaṅkhyeyyā ahosi. Atha bhagavā dutiyadivase ānandattheraṃ āmantesi – “imaṃ, ānanda, rattiṃ aññatarā devatā maṃ upasaṅkamitvā maṅgalapañhaṃ pucchi. Athassāhaṃ aṭṭhatiṃsa maṅgalāni abhāsiṃ, uggaṇha, ānanda, imaṃ maṅgalapariyāyaṃ, uggahetvā bhikkhū vācehī”ti. Thero uggahetvā bhikkhū vācesi. Tayidaṃ ācariyaparamparābhataṃ yāvajjatanā pavattati, evamidaṃ brahmacariyaṃ iddhañceva phītañca vitthārikaṃ bāhujaññaṃ puthubhūtaṃ yāva devamanussehi suppakāsitanti veditabbaṃ.

And so, at the conclusion of the teaching delivered by the Blessed One, a hundred thousand koṭis of devas attained Arahantship, and the number of those who attained the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, and non-returning was incalculable. Then, on the following day, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: 'Ānanda, last night a certain deity approached me and asked the question on blessings. I then spoke of the thirty-eight blessings. Learn this discourse on blessings, Ānanda, and having learned it, teach it to the monks.' The Elder learned it and taught it to the monks. This, handed down through the lineage of teachers, continues to this day. Thus, it should be understood that this holy life is successful, thriving, widespread, known to many, extensive, and well-proclaimed among gods and humans.

Idāni etesveva maṅgalesu ñāṇaparicayapāṭavatthaṃ ayaṃ ādito pabhuti yojanā – evamime idhalokaparalokalokuttarasukhakāmā sattā bālajanasevanaṃ pahāya, paṇḍite nissāya, pūjaneyye pūjentā, patirūpadesavāsena pubbe katapuññatāya ca kusalappavattiyaṃ codiyamānā, attānaṃ sammā paṇidhāya, bāhusaccasippavinayehi alaṅkatattabhāvā, vinayānurūpaṃ subhāsitaṃ bhāsamānā[V 2.0033], yāva gihibhāvaṃ na vijahanti, tāva mātāpituupaṭṭhānena porāṇaṃ iṇamūlaṃ visodhayamānā, puttadārasaṅgahena navaṃ iṇamūlaṃ payojayamānā, anākulakammantatāya dhanadhaññādisamiddhiṃ pāpuṇantā, dānena bhogasāraṃ dhammacariyāya jīvitasārañca gahetvā, ñātisaṅgahena sakajanahitaṃ anavajjakammantatāya parajanahitañca karontā, pāpaviratiyā parūpaghātaṃ majjapānasaṃyamena attūpaghātañca vivajjetvā, dhammesu appamādena kusalapakkhaṃ vaḍḍhetvā, vaḍḍhitakusalatāya gihibyañjanaṃ ohāya pabbajitabhāve ṭhitāpi buddhabuddhasāvakupajjhācariyādīsu gāravena nivātena ca vattasampadaṃ ārādhetvā, santuṭṭhiyā paccayagedhaṃ [M 2.0037] pahāya, kataññutāya sappurisabhūmiyaṃ ṭhatvā, dhammassavanena cittalīnataṃ pahāya, khantiyā sabbaparissaye abhibhavitvā, sovacassatāya sanāthamattānaṃ katvā, samaṇadassanena paṭipattipayogaṃ passantā, dhammasākacchāya kaṅkhāṭṭhāniyesu dhammesu kaṅkhaṃ paṭivinodetvā, indriyasaṃvaratapena sīlavisuddhiṃ samaṇadhammabrahmacariyena cittavisuddhiṃ tato parā ca catasso visuddhiyo sampādentā, imāya paṭipadāya ariyasaccadassanapariyāyaṃ ñāṇadassanavisuddhiṃ patvā arahattaphalasaṅkhātaṃ nibbānaṃ sacchikaronti. Yaṃ sacchikatvā sinerupabbato viya vātavuṭṭhīhi aṭṭhahi lokadhammehi avikampamānacittā asokā virajā khemino honti. Ye ca khemino, te sabbattha ekenāpi aparājitā honti, sabbattha ca sotthiṃ gacchanti. Tenāha bhagavā –

Now, for the sake of proficiency in knowledge and familiarity concerning these very blessings, this is the application from the beginning onwards: Here, beings desiring happiness in this world, the next world, and the supramundane bliss, having abandoned the company of fools, relying on the wise, honoring those worthy of honor, urged by residence in a suitable location and past meritorious deeds, being impelled towards wholesome activity, rightly directing themselves, adorned with extensive learning, skills, and discipline, speaking well in accordance with discipline, as long as they do not abandon the householder life, they purify the ancient debt by attending to their parents and create a new debt by providing for their wives and children. Through unconfused activities, they attain wealth, grain, and prosperity. Taking the essence of wealth through generosity and the essence of life through righteous conduct, they bring about the welfare of their own people by supporting relatives and the welfare of others by blameless deeds. Avoiding evil, refraining from harming others, and abstaining from intoxicating drinks that harm oneself, they cultivate the side of merit through diligence in the Dhamma. Having grown in virtue, even if they later abandon the signs of a householder and remain in the monastic life, they perfect their conduct through reverence and humility toward the Buddha, his disciples, preceptors, and teachers. Content, they abandon craving for requisites, stand on the ground of gratitude as good persons, dispel mental lethargy by listening to the Dhamma, overcome all adversities with patience, make themselves amenable to instruction, see the application of the practice by observing ascetics, and clear doubts about doubtful matters through Dhamma discussions. Through restraint of the senses and austerity, they accomplish purity of virtue; through the ascetic's holy life, they accomplish purity of mind. Then, they fulfill the four further purifications. By this practice, they attain the purification of knowledge and vision, which is the method of seeing the Noble Truths, and realize Nibbāna, known as the fruit of arahantship. Having realized this, their minds remain unshaken by the eight worldly conditions, just as Mount Sineru is by wind and storms; they become sorrowless, stainless, and secure. Those who are secure are invincible everywhere and go everywhere in safety. Therefore, the Blessed One has said—

“Etādisāni katvāna, sabbatthamaparājitā;

Sabbattha sotthiṃ gacchanti, taṃ tesaṃ maṅgalamuttama”nti.

'Having done such deeds, they are undefeated everywhere; Everywhere they go in safety—this is their supreme blessing.'

Iti paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

Thus, in the Paramatthajotikā, the commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya,

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya maṅgalasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Maṅgala Sutta of the Suttanipāta is completed.

5. Sūcilomasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Sūciloma Sutta

Evaṃ [V 2.0034][P 1.0301] me sutanti sūcilomasuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Atthavaṇṇanānayenevassa uppatti āvi bhavissati. Atthavaṇṇanāyañca “evaṃ me suta”ntiādi vuttatthameva. Gayāyaṃ viharati ṭaṅkitamañce sūcilomassa yakkhassa bhavaneti ettha pana kā gayā, ko ṭaṅkitamañco, kasmā ca bhagavā tassa yakkhassa bhavane viharatīti? Vuccate – gayāti gāmopi titthampi vuccati, tadubhayampi idha vaṭṭati. Gayāgāmassa hi avidūre dese viharantopi “gayāyaṃ viharatī”ti vuccati, tassa ca gāmassa samīpe avidūre dvārasantike so ṭaṅkitamañco. Gayātitthe viharantopi “gayāyaṃ viharatī”ti vuccati, gayātitthe ca so ṭaṅkitamañco. Ṭaṅkitamañcoti catunnaṃ pāsāṇānaṃ upari vitthataṃ pāsāṇaṃ āropetvā kato pāsāṇamañco[M 2.0038]. Taṃ nissāya yakkhassa bhavanaṃ āḷavakassa bhavanaṃ viya. Yasmā vā pana bhagavā taṃ divasaṃ paccūsasamaye mahākaruṇāsamāpattito vuṭṭhāya buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ volokento sūcilomassa ca kharalomassa cāti dvinnampi yakkhānaṃ sotāpattiphalūpanissayaṃ addasa, tasmā pattacīvaraṃ ādāya antoaruṇeyeva nānādisāhi sannipatitassa janassa kheḷasiṅghāṇikādinānappakārāsucinissandakilinnabhūmibhāgampi taṃ titthappadesaṃ āgantvā tasmiṃ ṭaṅkitamañce nisīdi sūcilomassa yakkhassa bhavane. Tena vuttaṃ “ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā gayāyaṃ viharati ṭaṅkitamañce sūcilomassa yakkhassa bhavane”ti.

Thus have I heard—the Sūciloma Sutta. What is its origin? Its origin will become manifest through the method of the commentary. In the commentary, the meaning of “Thus have I heard” and so on has already been stated. “At Gayā, dwelling on the stone slab in the abode of the yakkha Sūciloma”—here, what is Gayā? What is the stone slab? And why did the Blessed One dwell in that yakkha’s abode? It is said: Gayā refers to both a village and a ford, and both are applicable here. For one dwelling in a place not far from the village of Gayā is said to “dwell at Gayā,” and that stone slab was near that village, not far from the gate. And one dwelling at the Gayā ford is said to “dwell at Gayā,” and that stone slab was at the Gayā ford. A stone slab (ṭaṅkitamañca) is a stone couch made by placing a broad stone on top of four stones. Associated with it was the yakkha’s abode, like the dwelling of Āḷavaka. Or it may be that on that day, at dawn, the Blessed One arose from the attainment of great compassion and, surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, saw the supporting condition for the fruit of stream-entry in both yakkhas, Sūciloma and Kharaloma. Therefore, taking his bowl and robe, just before sunrise, he went to that ford—a place where the ground was soiled with various kinds of impurities such as spit and mucus discharged by people who had gathered from various directions—and sat down on that stone slab in the abode of the yakkha Sūciloma. Thus it is said: “At one time, the Blessed One was dwelling at Gayā, on the stone slab in the abode of the yakkha Sūciloma.”

Tena kho pana samayenāti yaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā tattha viharati, tena samayena. Kharo ca yakkho sūcilomo ca yakkho bhagavato avidūre atikkamantīti. Ke te yakkhā, kasmā ca atikkamantīti? Vuccate – tesu tāva eko atīte saṅghassa telaṃ anāpucchā gahetvā attano sarīraṃ makkhesi. So tena kammena niraye paccitvā gayāpokkharaṇitīre yakkhayoniyaṃ nibbatto. Tasseva cassa kammassa vipākāvasesena virūpāni aṅgapaccaṅgāni ahesuṃ[P 1.0302], iṭṭhakacchadanasadisañca kharasamphassaṃ cammaṃ. So kira yadā paraṃ bhiṃsāpetukāmo hoti, tadā chadaniṭṭhakasadisāni cammakapālāni ukkhipitvā bhiṃsāpeti. Evaṃ so kharasamphassattā kharo yakkhotveva nāmaṃ labhi.

“At that time”: this means at the time when the Blessed One was dwelling there. The yakkha Kharo and the yakkha Sūciloma were passing by not far from the Blessed One. Who were those yakkhas, and why were they passing by? It is said: One of them, in a past life, took oil belonging to the Sangha without asking and anointed his body. Because of that kamma, after being tormented in hell, he was reborn in the yakkha state on the bank of the Gayā pond. As a residual result of that same kamma, his limbs were deformed and his skin had a rough texture like a roof tile. It is said that whenever he wanted to frighten someone, he would raise up flaps of skin that resembled roof tiles and thus frighten them. In this way, because of his rough texture, he received the name “Kharo” (the Rough One).

Itaro [V 2.0035] kassapassa bhagavato kāle upāsako hutvā māsassa aṭṭha divase vihāraṃ gantvā dhammaṃ suṇāti. So ekadivasaṃ dhammassavane ghosite saṅghārāmadvāre attano khettaṃ kelāyanto ugghosanaṃ sutvā “sace nhāyāmi, ciraṃ bhavissatī”ti kiliṭṭhagattova uposathāgāraṃ pavisitvā mahagghe bhummattharaṇe anādarena nipajjitvā supi. Bhikkhu evāyaṃ, na upāsakoti saṃyuttabhāṇakā. So tena ca aññena kammena ca niraye paccitvā gayāpokkharaṇiyā tīre yakkhayoniyaṃ nibbatto. So tassa kammassa vipākāvasesena duddasiko ahosi, sarīre cassa sūcisadisāni lomāni ahesuṃ. So hi bhiṃsāpetabbake satte sūcīhi vijjhanto viya bhiṃsāpeti. Evaṃ so sūcisadisalomattā sūcilomo yakkhotveva nāmaṃ labhi. Te attano gocaratthāya bhavanato [M 2.0039] nikkhamitvā muhuttaṃ gantvā gatamaggeneva nivattitvā itaraṃ disābhāgaṃ gacchantā bhagavato avidūre atikkamanti.

The other, in the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, having been a lay follower, would go to the monastery on the eighth day of the month to listen to the Dhamma. One day, when the call to listen to the Dhamma was announced, he was ploughing his field at the gate of the Saṅgha's park. Hearing the announcement and thinking, “If I bathe, it will be long,” he entered the Uposatha hall with his body still soiled, lay down disrespectfully on a valuable floor covering, and fell asleep. The reciters of the Saṃyutta Nikāya say: “This one was a bhikkhu, not a lay follower.” Because of that kamma and another, after being tormented in hell, he was reborn in the yakkha state on the bank of the Gayā pond. As a residual result of that kamma, he was frightful to see, and on his body were hairs like needles. Indeed, he would frighten beings as if piercing them with needles. Thus, because he had needle-like hairs, he received the name “Sūciloma the yakkha.” Having left their abode to find food, they went for a short while, then returned by the same path and, while going in another direction, passed by not far from the Blessed One.

Atha kho kharoti kasmā te evamāhaṃsu? Kharo samaṇakappaṃ disvā āha. Sūcilomo pana “yo bhāyati na so samaṇo, samaṇapaṭirūpakattā pana samaṇako hotī”ti evaṃladdhiko. Tasmā tādisaṃ bhagavantaṃ maññamāno “neso samaṇo, samaṇako eso”ti sahasāva vatvāpi puna vīmaṃsitukāmo āha – “yāvāhaṃ jānāmī”ti. “Atha kho”ti evaṃ vatvā tato. Sūcilomo yakkhoti ito pabhuti yāva apica kho te samphasso pāpakoti, tāva uttānatthameva kevalañcettha bhagavato kāyanti attano kāyaṃ bhagavato upanāmesīti evaṃ sambandho veditabbo.

Regarding 'Then Kharo...': why did they speak thus? Kharo spoke having seen the guise of an ascetic. Sūciloma, however, was of the view: “One who is afraid is not an ascetic; but because he is a counterfeit of an ascetic, he is a mere ascetic.” Therefore, thinking of the Blessed One in this way, although he had hastily said, “This is not an ascetic, this is a mere ascetic,” wishing to investigate again, he said, “Until I know…” Having spoken thus, then from the words “the yakkha Sūciloma” up to “and also your contact is evil,” the meaning is straightforward. Here, however, regarding the phrase concerning the Blessed One's body, the connection should be understood thus: he brought his own body near to the Blessed One’s body.

Tato abhāyantaṃ bhagavantaṃ [P 1.0303] disvā “pañhaṃ taṃ samaṇā”tiādimāha. Kiṃ kāraṇā? So hi cintesi – “imināpi nāma me evaṃ kharena amanussasamphassena manusso samāno ayaṃ na bhāyati, handāhaṃ etaṃ buddhavisaye pañhaṃ pucchāmi, addhā ayaṃ tattha na sampāyissati, tato naṃ evaṃ viheṭhessāmī”ti. Bhagavā taṃ sutvā “na khvāhaṃ taṃ āvuso”tiādimāha. Taṃ sabbaṃ āḷavakasutte vuttanayeneva sabbākārehi veditabbaṃ.

Then, seeing that the Blessed One was unafraid, he said: “I will ask you a question, ascetic,” and so on. For what reason? For he thought: “This one, though a human being, is not afraid even of this harsh contact with a non-human such as me. Come now, I will ask him a question within the domain of a Buddha. Surely he will not succeed with it, and then I will vex him thus.” Having heard this, the Blessed One replied, “I do not, friend…” and so on. This entire matter should be understood in all its aspects according to the method explained in the Āḷavaka Sutta.

273. Atha kho sūcilomo yakkho bhagavantaṃ gāthāya ajjhabhāsi “rāgo ca doso cā”ti. Tattha rāgadosā vuttanayā eva. Kutonidānāti kiṃnidānā kiṃhetukā. Kutoti paccattavacanassa to-ādeso veditabbo, samāse cassa lopābhāvo. Atha vā nidānāti jātā uppannāti attho, tasmā kutonidānā, kutojātā, kutouppannāti vuttaṃ hoti. Aratī ratī lomahaṃso kutojāti yāyaṃ “pantesu vā senāsanesu aññataraññataresu vā adhikusalesu dhammesu arati [V 2.0036] aratitā anabhirati anabhiramaṇā ukkaṇṭhitā paritassitā”ti (vibha. 856) evaṃ vibhattā arati, yā ca pañcasu kāmaguṇesu rati, yo ca lomahaṃsasamuṭṭhāpanato “lomahaṃso”tveva saṅkhyaṃ gato cittutrāso. Ime tayo dhammā kutojā kutojātāti pucchati[M 2.0040]. Kuto samuṭṭhāyāti kuto uppajjitvā. Manoti kusalacittaṃ, vitakkāti uragasutte vuttā nava kāmavitakkādayo. Kumārakā dhaṅkamivossajantīti yathā gāmadārakā kīḷantā kākaṃ suttena pāde bandhitvā ossajanti khipanti, evaṃ kusalamanaṃ akusalavitakkā kuto samuṭṭhāya ossajantīti pucchati.

273. Then the yakkha Sūciloma addressed the Blessed One with a verse: “Lust and hatred…” Herein, lust and hatred are as already explained. “From what origin?” means: what is their origin, what is their cause? The word `kuto` is formed with the ablative suffix `-to`, which is not elided here in the compound. Or, “origin” (`nidāna`) has the meaning of born, arisen; therefore it is said: “from what origin, from what birth, from what arising?” “Discontent, delight, and horror—from what are they born?”: this refers to the discontent that is analyzed thus: “in regard to remote lodgings or to certain higher wholesome states, there is discontent, discontentedness, dissatisfaction, displeasure, weariness, vexation”; the delight in the five cords of sensual pleasure; and the mental terror that is counted as “horror” because it causes one’s hair to stand on end. He asks from what these three things are born. “From where do they arise?” means from where do they originate? “Mind” means the wholesome mind. “Thoughts” refers to those beginning with sensual thought mentioned in the Uraga Sutta. “As boys let loose a crow”: just as village boys at play tie a crow’s foot with a string and let it go, that is, toss it, so he asks, from where do unwholesome thoughts arise and let loose the wholesome mind?

274. Athassa bhagavā te pañhe vissajjento “rāgo cā”ti dutiyagāthamabhāsi. Tattha itoti attabhāvaṃ sandhāyāha. Attabhāvanidānā hi rāgadosā. Aratiratilomahaṃsā ca attabhāvato jātā, kāmavitakkādiakusalavitakkā ca attabhāvatoyeva [P 1.0304] samuṭṭhāya kusalamano ossajanti, tena tadaññaṃ pakatiādikāraṇaṃ paṭikkhipanto āha – “itonidānā itojā ito samuṭṭhāyā”ti. Saddasiddhi cettha purimagāthāya vuttanayeneva veditabbā.

274. Then the Blessed One, answering his questions, spoke the second verse, beginning: “Lust…” Herein, “from this” is said with reference to selfhood. For lust and hatred have selfhood as their origin. Discontent, delight, and horror are born from selfhood. And unwholesome thoughts such as sensual thought, having arisen from this very selfhood, let loose the wholesome mind. Thus, rejecting any other cause such as nature, he says: “From this as their origin, from this they are born, from this they arise.” The word formation here should be understood in the same way as explained for the previous verse.

275-6. Evaṃ te pañhe vissajjetvā idāni yvāyaṃ “itonidānā”tiādīsu “attabhāvanidānā attabhāvato jātā attabhāvato samuṭṭhāyā”ti attho vutto, taṃ sādhento āha – “snehajā attasambhūtā”ti. Ete hi sabbepi rāgādayo vitakkapariyosānā taṇhāsnehena jātā, tathā jāyantā ca pañcupādānakkhandhabhede attabhāvapariyāye attani sambhūtā. Tenāha – “snehajā attasambhūtā”ti. Idāni tadatthajotikaṃ upamaṃ karoti “nigrodhasseva khandhajā”ti. Tattha khandhesu jātā khandhajā, pārohānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yathā nigrodhassa khandhajā nāma pārohā āporasasinehe sati jāyanti, jāyantā ca tasmiṃyeva nigrodhe tesu tesu sākhappabhedesu sambhavanti, evametepi rāgādayo ajjhattataṇhāsnehe sati jāyanti, jāyantā ca tasmiṃyeva attabhāve tesu tesu cakkhādibhedesu dvārārammaṇavatthūsu sambhavanti. Tasmā veditabbametaṃ “attabhāvanidānā attabhāvajā attabhāvasamuṭṭhānā ca ete”ti.

Having thus answered his questions, now, to establish the meaning that was stated in the phrase “from this as their origin,” etc.—namely, “originating from selfhood, born from selfhood, arising from selfhood”—the Blessed One says: “Born of affection, arisen from self.” For all these states, from lust to thoughts, are born from the affection of craving. And being born thus, they arise in the self, a term for selfhood which is divided into the five aggregates subject to clinging. Hence he says: “Born of affection, arisen from self.” Now, to illuminate this meaning, he gives a simile: “Like the trunk-born shoots of a banyan.” Herein, “trunk-born” means born from the trunk; this is a term for aerial roots. What is meant? Just as the aerial roots of a banyan tree, called “trunk-born,” arise when there is the moisture of sap, and having arisen, they grow on that very banyan tree, on its various branches, so too these states from lust onwards arise when there is the affection of internal craving. And having arisen, they grow in that very selfhood, in its various divisions such as the eye, that is, in the sense doors, objects, and bases. Therefore it should be understood that these states have selfhood as their origin, are born from selfhood, and arise from selfhood.

Avasesadiyaḍḍhagāthāya pana ayaṃ sabbasaṅgāhikā atthavaṇṇanā – evaṃ attasambhūtā ca ete puthū visattā kāmesu. Rāgopi hi pañcakāmaguṇikādivasena, dosopi āghātavatthādivasena, aratiādayopi tassa tasseva bhedassa vasenāti sabbathā sabbepime kilesā puthū anekappakārā [M 2.0041] hutvā vatthudvārārammaṇādivasena tesu tesu vatthukāmesu tathā tathā visattā laggā laggitā [V 2.0037] saṃsibbitvā ṭhitā. Kimiva? Māluvāva vitatā vane, yathā vane vitatā māluvā tesu tesu rukkhassa sākhapasākhādibhedesu visattā hoti laggā laggitā saṃsibbitvā ṭhitā, evaṃ puthuppabhedesu vatthukāmesu visattaṃ kilesagaṇaṃ ye naṃ pajānanti yatonidānaṃ, te naṃ vinodenti suṇohi yakkha[P 1.0305].

In the remaining one and a half stanzas, this is the comprehensive explanation of the meaning: 'Thus, arisen from self, these diverse defilements are attached to sensual pleasures.' For lust, by way of the five cords of sensual pleasure and so on; hatred, by way of the grounds for resentment and so on; and discontent and the rest, by way of the various divisions of those very states—thus in every way, all these defilements, being diverse and manifold, cling in various ways to their respective sensual objects through bases, doors, and objects. Like what? Like a māluvā creeper spread out in the forest. Just as a māluvā creeper spread out in the forest clings to the various branches and twigs of a tree, stuck fast and entwined, so too the host of defilements is attached to the diverse sensual objects. Those who understand it, knowing its source of origin, dispel it—listen, O yakkha.

Tattha yatonidānanti bhāvanapuṃsakaniddeso, tena kiṃ dīpeti? Ye sattā naṃ kilesagaṇaṃ “yatonidānaṃ uppajjatī”ti evaṃ jānanti, te naṃ “taṇhāsnehasnehite attabhāve uppajjatī”ti ñatvā taṃ taṇhāsnehaṃ ādīnavānupassanādibhāvanāñāṇagginā visosentā vinodenti pajahanti byantīkaronti ca, etaṃ amhākaṃ subhāsitaṃ suṇohi yakkhāti. Evamettha attabhāvajānanena dukkhapariññaṃ taṇhāsneharāgādikilesagaṇavinodanena samudayappahānañca dīpeti.

Herein, 'its source of origin' is a neuter designation of an abstract noun. What does this indicate? Those beings who know that this host of defilements arises 'from such a source,' knowing that 'it arises in an individual existence drenched with the moisture of craving,' dry up that moisture of craving with the fire of knowledge developed by contemplating danger and so on; they dispel it, abandon it, and terminate it. 'This is our well-spoken word—listen, O yakkha.' Thus, herein, through knowledge of individual existence, the full understanding of suffering is shown; and through the dispelling of the host of defilements such as lust born from the moisture of craving, the abandonment of the origin is also shown.

Ye ca naṃ vinodenti, te duttaraṃ oghamimaṃ taranti atiṇṇapubbaṃ apunabbhavāya. Etena maggabhāvanaṃ nirodhasacchikiriyañca dīpeti. Ye hi naṃ kilesagaṇaṃ vinodenti, te avassaṃ maggaṃ bhāventi. Na hi maggabhāvanaṃ vinā kilesavinodanaṃ atthi. Ye ca maggaṃ bhāventi, te duttaraṃ pakatiñāṇena kāmoghādiṃ catubbidhampi oghamimaṃ taranti. Maggabhāvanā hi oghataraṇaṃ. Atiṇṇapubbanti iminā dīghena addhunā supinantenapi avītikkantapubbaṃ. Apunabbhavāyāti nibbānāya. Evamimaṃ catusaccadīpikaṃ gāthaṃ suṇantā “sutvā dhammaṃ dhārenti, dhatānaṃ dhammānaṃ atthamupaparikkhantī”tiādikaṃ kathaṃ subhāviniyā paññāya anukkamamānā te dvepi sahāyakā yakkhā gāthāpariyosāneyeva sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahiṃsu, pāsādikā ca ahesuṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇā dibbālaṅkāravibhūsitāti.

Those who dispel it cross this flood, so hard to cross, not crossed before, for no more becoming. This indicates the development of the path and the realization of cessation. For those who dispel the host of defilements assuredly develop the path, for without developing the path there is no dispelling of defilements. And those who develop the path cross this fourfold flood—beginning with the flood of sensuality—which is so hard to cross, by means of natural wisdom. Development of the path is indeed the crossing of the flood. 'Not crossed before' means never crossed before, even in a dream, throughout this long journey. 'For no more becoming' means for Nibbāna. Thus, hearing this stanza illuminating the Four Truths, and reflecting step by step on the meaning of the Dhamma they had heard and retained, with their well-developed wisdom, these two companion yakkhas became established in the fruit of stream-entry at the very end of the stanza. And they became inspiring, golden in hue, and adorned with divine ornaments.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya,

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya sūcilomasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Here ends the explanation of the Sūciloma Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary.

6. Kapilasutta-(dhammacariyasutta)-vaṇṇanā

6. Explanation of the Kapila Sutta (Dhammacariya Sutta)

Dhammacariyanti [V 2.0038][M 2.0042] kapilasuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Hemavatasutte vuttanayeneva parinibbute kassape bhagavati dve kulaputtā bhātaro nikkhamitvā sāvakānaṃ santike pabbajiṃsu. Jeṭṭho sodhano nāma, kaniṭṭho kapilo nāma. Tesaṃ mātā sādhanī nāma, kaniṭṭhabhaginī tāpanā nāma. Tāpi bhikkhunīsu [P 1.0306] pabbajiṃsu. Tato te dvepi hemavatasutte vuttanayeneva “sāsane kati dhurānī”ti pucchitvā sutvā ca jeṭṭho “vāsadhuraṃ pūressāmī”ti pañca vassāni ācariyupajjhāyānaṃ santike vasitvā pañcavasso hutvā yāva arahattaṃ, tāva kammaṭṭhānaṃ sutvā araññaṃ pavisitvā vāyamanto arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Kapilo “ahaṃ tāva taruṇo, vuḍḍhakāle vāsadhuraṃ paripūressāmī”ti ganthadhuraṃ ārabhitvā tepiṭako ahosi. Tassa pariyattiṃ nissāya parivāro, parivāraṃ nissāya lābho ca udapādi.

The Dhammacariya Sutta is the Kapila Sutta. What is its origin? As was stated in the Hemavata Sutta, after the Blessed One Kassapa had attained Parinibbāna, two brothers, sons of good family, went forth from home and were ordained in the presence of the disciples. The elder was named Sodhana, the younger was named Kapila. Their mother was named Sādhanī and their younger sister was named Tāpanā. They too were ordained among the bhikkhunīs. Then those two, in the way stated in the Hemavata Sutta, asked, 'How many yokes are there in the dispensation?' Having heard the answer, the elder thought, 'I will fulfill the yoke of residence.' After dwelling for five years in the presence of his teachers and preceptors, he became a monk of five years' standing. Having received a meditation subject leading up to arahantship, he entered the forest, strove, and attained arahantship. Kapila thought, 'I am still young; I will fulfill the yoke of residence in my old age.' He undertook the yoke of study and became a master of the Tipiṭaka. Dependent on his scriptural learning a following arose, and dependent on his following, gain arose.

So bāhusaccamadena matto paṇḍitamānī anaññātepi aññātamānī hutvā parehi vuttaṃ kappiyampi akappiyaṃ, akappiyampi kappiyaṃ, sāvajjampi anavajjaṃ, anavajjampi sāvajjanti bhaṇati. So pesalehi bhikkhūhi, “mā, āvuso kapila, evaṃ avacā”tiādinā nayena ovadiyamāno “tumhe kiṃ jānātha rittamuṭṭhisadisā”tiādīhi vacanehi khuṃsento vambhentoyeva carati. Bhikkhū tassa bhātuno sodhanattherassāpi etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. Sopi naṃ upasaṅkamitvā āha – “āvuso kapila, sāsanassa āyu nāma tumhādisānaṃ sammāpaṭipatti. Mā, āvuso kapila, kappiyampi akappiyaṃ, akappiyampi kappiyaṃ, sāvajjampi anavajjaṃ, anavajjampi sāvajjanti vadehī”ti. So tassapi vacanaṃ nādiyi. Tato naṃ sodhanatthero dvattikkhattuṃ vatvā –

Intoxicated with the pride of his great learning, conceited, and with the conceit of knowing what he did not know, he would declare what was permissible as impermissible, what was impermissible as permissible, what was faulty as faultless, and what was faultless as faulty. When admonished by virtuous monks with words like, 'Friend Kapila, do not speak thus,' he went about scolding and disparaging them, saying, 'What do you know? You are like empty fists!' The monks reported this matter to his brother, the Elder Sodhana. He too approached him and said, 'Friend Kapila, the life of the Dispensation is the right practice of those like you. Do not, friend Kapila, declare what is permissible as impermissible, what is impermissible as permissible, what is faulty as faultless, and what is faultless as faulty.' But he paid no heed to his words either. Then, after admonishing him two or three times, the Elder Sodhana said:

“Ekavācampi dvivācaṃ, bhaṇeyya anukampako;

Tatuttariṃ na bhāseyya, dāsovayyassa santike”ti. (jā. 2.19.34) –

'A compassionate person might speak once or twice; beyond that one should not speak, like a slave in the presence of his master.'

Parivajjetvā “tvameva, āvuso, sakena kammena paññāyissasī”ti pakkāmi. Tato pabhuti naṃ pesalā bhikkhū chaḍḍesuṃ.

Having avoided him, he departed, saying, 'You yourself, friend, will be known by your own kamma.' From then on, the virtuous monks shunned him.

So [V 2.0039][M 2.0043] durācāro hutvā durācāraparivuto viharanto ekadivasaṃ “uposathaṃ osāressāmī”ti sīhāsanaṃ abhiruyha citrabījaniṃ gahetvā nisinno “vattati, āvuso, ettha bhikkhūnaṃ pātimokkho”ti tikkhattuṃ āha. Atheko bhikkhupi “mayhaṃ [P 1.0307] vattatī”ti na avoca. Na ca tassa tesaṃ vā pātimokkho vattati. Tato so “pātimokkhe sutepi asutepi vinayo nāma natthī”ti āsanā vuṭṭhāsi. Evaṃ kassapassa bhagavato sāsanaṃ osakkāpesi vināsesi. Atha sodhanatthero tadaheva parinibbāyi. Sopi kapilo evaṃ taṃ sāsanaṃ osakkāpetvā kālakato avīcimahāniraye nibbatti, sāpissa mātā ca bhaginī ca tasseva diṭṭhānugatiṃ āpajjitvā pesale bhikkhū akkosamānā paribhāsamānā kālaṃ katvā niraye nibbattiṃsu.

Living as one of bad conduct and surrounded by those of bad conduct, one day, thinking, 'I will lead the Uposatha ceremony,' he ascended the lion seat, took the ceremonial fan, and sat down. He said three times: 'Friends, does the Pātimokkha proceed for the monks here?' But not a single monk said, 'It proceeds for me.' And the Pātimokkha did not proceed for him or for them. Then he rose from his seat, declaring, 'Whether the Pātimokkha is heard or not heard, there is no such thing as Vinaya!' Thus he caused the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa to decline and perish. That very day, the Elder Sodhana attained Parinibbāna. And Kapila, having thus caused the dispensation to decline, passed away and was reborn in the great Avīci hell. His mother and sister, having adopted his views, abused and reviled the virtuous monks; and when they passed away, they too were reborn in hell.

Tasmiṃyeva ca kāle pañcasatā purisā gāmaghātādīni katvā corikāya jīvantā janapadamanussehi anubaddhā palāyamānā araññaṃ pavisitvā tattha kiñci gahanaṃ vā paṭisaraṇaṃ vā apassantā avidūre pāsāṇe vasantaṃ aññataraṃ āraññikaṃ bhikkhuṃ disvā vanditvā “amhākaṃ, bhante, paṭisaraṇaṃ hothā”ti bhaṇiṃsu. Thero “tumhākaṃ sīlasadisaṃ paṭisaraṇaṃ natthi, sabbe pañca sīlāni samādiyathā”ti āha. Te “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā sīlāni samādiyiṃsu. Thero “tumhe sīlavanto, idāni attano jīvitaṃ vināsentesupi mā mano padūsayitthā”ti āha. Te “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchiṃsu. Atha te jānapadā sampattā ito cito ca maggamānā te core disvā sabbeva jīvitā voropesuṃ. Te kālaṃ katvā kāmāvacaradevaloke nibbattiṃsu. Tesu jeṭṭhakacoro jeṭṭhakadevaputto ahosi, itare tasseva parivārā.

At that very time, five hundred men were living by theft, having committed village massacres and other such crimes. Pursued by the people of the countryside, they fled and entered the forest. Seeing no thicket or refuge there, they saw a certain forest-dwelling monk dwelling on a rock not far away. They approached, paid homage, and said: 'Venerable sir, be our refuge!' The elder replied: 'There is no refuge for you like moral virtue. All of you should undertake the five precepts.' They agreed, saying, 'Very well,' and undertook the precepts. The elder then said: 'You are now virtuous. Do not corrupt your minds even toward those who are destroying your lives.' They agreed, saying, 'Very well.' Then the country-folk arrived, and searching here and there, they saw the thieves and deprived them all of life. Having passed away, they were reborn in a sense-sphere heavenly world. The chief of the thieves became the chief deva-son; the others became his retinue.

Te anulomapaṭilomaṃ saṃsarantā ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ devaloke khepetvā amhākaṃ bhagavato kāle devalokato cavitvā jeṭṭhakadevaputto sāvatthidvāre kevaṭṭagāmo atthi, tattha pañcasatakulajeṭṭhassa kevaṭṭassa pajāpatiyā kucchimhi paṭisandhiṃ aggahesi, itare avasesakevaṭṭapajāpatīnaṃ. Evaṃ tesaṃ ekadivasaṃyeva paṭisandhiggahaṇañca gabbhavuṭṭhānañca ahosi. Atha kevaṭṭajeṭṭho “atthi nu kho imasmiṃ gāme aññepi dārakā ajja jātā”ti vicinanto te dārake disvā “ime me [P 1.0308] puttassa sahāyakā bhavissantī”ti sabbesaṃ posāvanikaṃ adāsi. Te sabbe sahāyakā [M 2.0044] sahapaṃsuṃ kīḷantā anupubbena vayappattā ahesuṃ. Yasojo tesaṃ aggo ahosi.

Wandering forwards and backwards through saṃsāra, after spending one Buddha-interval in the deva world, they passed away from there in the time of our Blessed One. The chief deva-son took conception in the womb of the wife of the chief fisherman of five hundred families in a fishermen's village at a gate of Sāvatthī; the others took conception in the wombs of the wives of the remaining fishermen. Thus their conception and their birth from the womb occurred on the very same day. Then the chief fisherman, wondering, 'Are there any other boys born in this village today?' saw those boys and thought, 'These will be my son's companions.' He provided for the upbringing of all of them. Playing together in the dust, they all gradually came of age. Yasojo was their leader.

Kapilopi [V 2.0040] tadā niraye pakkāvasesena aciravatiyā suvaṇṇavaṇṇo duggandhamukho maccho hutvā nibbatti. Athekadivasaṃ sabbepi kevaṭṭadārakā jālāni gahetvā “macche bandhissāmā”ti nadiṃ gantvā jālāni pakkhipiṃsu. Tesaṃ jālaṃ so maccho pāvisi. Taṃ disvā sabbo kevaṭṭagāmo uccāsaddamahāsaddo ahosi – “amhākaṃ puttā paṭhamaṃ macche bandhantā suvaṇṇamacchaṃ bandhiṃsu, vuḍḍhi nesaṃ dārakānaṃ, idāni ca no rājā pahūtaṃ dhanaṃ dassatī”ti. Atha te pañcasatāpi dārakasahāyakā macchaṃ nāvāya pakkhipitvā nāvaṃ ukkhipitvā rañño santikaṃ agamaṃsu. Rājā disvā “kiṃ etaṃ bhaṇe”ti āha. “Maccho devā”ti. Rājā suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ macchaṃ disvā “bhagavā etassa vaṇṇakāraṇaṃ jānissatī”ti macchaṃ gāhāpetvā bhagavato santikaṃ agamāsi. Macchassa mukhavivaraṇakāle jetavanaṃ ativiya duggandhaṃ hoti.

At that time Kapila, due to the remainder of his kamma from hell, was reborn as a golden-colored fish with a foul-smelling mouth in the Aciravati River. One day, all the young fishermen took their nets and went to the river, thinking, “We will catch fish.” They cast their nets, and that fish entered their net. Seeing this, the entire fishing village erupted in loud shouts and a great clamor: “Our sons, catching fish for the first time, have caught a golden fish! Prosperity to these boys! And now the king will give us abundant wealth!” Then those five hundred companion boys put the fish in a boat, carried the boat, and went into the king’s presence. Seeing it, the king asked: “What is this, sirs?” “A fish, Your Majesty.” Seeing the golden-colored fish, the king thought, “The Blessed One will know the reason for its color.” He had the fish taken and went to the Blessed One. When the fish’s mouth was opened, the Jeta Grove became exceedingly foul-smelling.

Rājā bhagavantaṃ pucchi – “kasmā, bhante, maccho suvaṇṇavaṇṇo jāto, kasmā cassa mukhato duggandho vāyatī”ti? Ayaṃ, mahārāja, kassapassa bhagavato pāvacane kapilo nāma bhikkhu ahosi, bahussuto āgatāgamo. Attano vacanaṃ agaṇhantānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ akkosakaparibhāsako. Tassa ca bhagavato sāsanavināsako. Yaṃ so tassa bhagavato sāsanaṃ vināsesi, tena kammena avīcimahāniraye nibbatti, vipākāvasesena ca idāni maccho jāto. Yaṃ dīgharattaṃ buddhavacanaṃ vācesi, buddhassa vaṇṇaṃ kathesi, tassa nissandena īdisaṃ vaṇṇaṃ paṭilabhi. Yaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ akkosakaparibhāsako ahosi, tenassa mukhato duggandho vāyati. “Ullapāpemi naṃ mahārājā”ti? “Āma bhagavā”ti. Atha bhagavā [P 1.0309] macchaṃ ālapi – “tvaṃsi kapilo”ti? “Āma bhagavā, ahaṃ kapilo”ti. “Kuto āgatosī”ti? “Avīcimahānirayato bhagavā”ti. “Sodhano kuhiṃ gato”ti? “Parinibbuto bhagavā”ti. “Sādhanī kuhiṃ gatā”ti? “Mahāniraye nibbattā bhagavā”ti. “Tāpanā kuhiṃ gatā”ti? “Mahāniraye nibbattā bhagavā”ti. “Idāni tvaṃ kuhiṃ gamissasī”ti? “Mahānirayaṃ bhagavā”ti. Tāvadeva vippaṭisārābhibhūto nāvaṃ sīsena paharitvā kālakato mahāniraye nibbatti. Mahājano saṃviggo ahosi lomahaṭṭhajāto. Atha [M 2.0045] bhagavā tattha sampattagahaṭṭhapabbajitaparisāya taṅkhaṇānurūpaṃ dhammaṃ desento imaṃ suttamabhāsi.

The king asked the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, why was this fish born with a golden color, and why does a foul stench emanate from its mouth?” “Great King, in the dispensation of the Buddha Kassapa, there was a bhikkhu named Kapila who was very learned and had mastered the scriptures. He was an abuser and reviler of bhikkhus who did not accept his word, and he was a destroyer of that Blessed One’s Dispensation. Because of that kamma of having destroyed the Blessed One’s Dispensation, he was reborn in the Avīci great hell, and by the residue of that kamma he has now been born as a fish. Because for a long time he expounded the word of the Buddha and spoke of the Buddha’s qualities, as a consequence he has obtained such a color. But because he was an abuser and reviler of bhikkhus, a foul stench emanates from his mouth.” “Shall I make him speak, Great King?” “Yes, Blessed One.” Then the Blessed One addressed the fish: “Are you Kapila?” “Yes, Blessed One, I am Kapila.” “From where have you come?” “From the Avīci great hell, Blessed One.” “Where has Sodhana gone?” “He has attained final Nibbāna, Blessed One.” “Where has Sādhanī gone?” “She has been reborn in the great hell, Blessed One.” “Where has Tāpanā gone?” “She has been reborn in the great hell, Blessed One.” “And where will you go now?” “To the great hell, Blessed One.” At that very moment, overcome with remorse, he struck his head against the boat, passed away, and was reborn in the great hell. The great assembly was struck with a sense of urgency, and the hair on their bodies stood on end. Then the Blessed One, for the assembly of householders and monastics gathered there, taught the Dhamma appropriate to the occasion and spoke this discourse.

277-8. Tattha dhammacariyanti kāyasucaritādi dhammacariyaṃ. Brahmacariyanti maggabrahmacariyaṃ. Etadāhu vasuttamanti etaṃ ubhayampi lokiyalokuttaraṃ sucaritaṃ saggamokkhasukhasampāpakattā vasuttamanti āhu ariyā. Vasuttamaṃ nāma uttamaratanaṃ, anugāmikaṃ attādhīnaṃ rājādīnaṃ asādhāraṇanti adhippāyo.

Here, righteous conduct means righteous conduct such as good bodily conduct. The holy life means the holy life of the path. This, they say, is the supreme good: the noble ones say that both these forms of good conduct—the mundane and the supramundane—are the supreme good because they lead to the attainment of the happiness of the heavenly worlds and liberation. The meaning is that the supreme good is the supreme jewel; it is one’s constant companion, dependent on oneself, and not shared with kings and others.

Ettāvatā [V 2.0041] “gahaṭṭhassa vā pabbajitassa vā sammāpaṭipattiyeva paṭisaraṇa”nti dassetvā idāni paṭipattivirahitāya pabbajjāya asārakattadassanena kapilaṃ aññe ca tathārūpe garahanto “pabbajitopi ce hotī”ti evamādimāha.

Having thus shown that “for a householder or one gone forth, right practice is the only refuge,” now, by showing the worthlessness of the going forth that is devoid of practice, and by censuring Kapila and others of a similar kind, he spoke the words beginning: “Even though one has gone forth….”

Tatrāyaṃ atthavaṇṇanā – yo hi koci gihibyañjanāni apanetvā bhaṇḍukāsāvādigahaṇamattaṃ upasaṅkamanena pabbajitopi ce hoti pubbe vuttatthaṃ agārasmā anagāriyaṃ, so ce mukharajātiko hoti pharusavacano, nānappakārāya vihesāya abhiratattā vihesābhirato, hirottappābhāvena magasadisattā mago, jīvitaṃ tassa pāpiyo, tassa evarūpassa jīvitaṃ atipāpaṃ atihīnaṃ. Kasmā? Yasmā imāya micchāpaṭipattiyā rāgādimanekappakāraṃ rajaṃ vaḍḍheti attano.

This is the explanation of the meaning: If someone has gone forth from the home life into homelessness as explained before—having removed the marks of a householder and merely by taking up the shaven head, ochre robes, and so on, and by approaching the Sangha—and if he is of an abusive nature, harsh in speech, one who delights in vexation because he is fond of various kinds of vexation, a beast because he is like a beast in his lack of shame and moral fear, his life is a very evil one. The life of such a one is extremely evil and base. Why? Because by this wrong practice he increases for himself the many kinds of dust such as lust.

279. Na kevalañca imināva kāraṇenassa jīvitaṃ pāpiyo, apica kho pana ayaṃ evarūpo mukharajātikattā kalahābhirato bhikkhu subhāsitassa atthavijānanasammohanena [P 1.0310] mohadhammena āvuto, “mā, āvuso kapila, evaṃ avaca, imināpi pariyāyena taṃ gaṇhāhī”ti evamādinā nayena pesalehi bhikkhūhi akkhātampi na jānāti dhammaṃ buddhena desitaṃ. Yo dhammo buddhena desito, taṃ nānappakārena attano vuccamānampi na jānāti. Evampissa jīvitaṃ pāpiyo.

279. And not only for this reason is his life a very evil one. But further, a bhikkhu of this sort, being of an abusive nature and delighting in quarrels, is veiled by the state of delusion which bewilders his understanding of the meaning of what is well spoken. Even when it is explained to him by amiable bhikkhus in ways beginning, “Friend Kapila, do not speak so; grasp it in this way too,” he does not understand the Dhamma taught by the Buddha. Though the Dhamma taught by the Buddha is explained to him in various ways, he does not understand it when it is spoken. In this way, too, his life is a very evil one.

280. Tathā so evarūpo vihesābhiratattā vihesaṃ bhāvitattānaṃ bhāvitatte khīṇāsavabhikkhū sodhanattherapabhutike “na tumhe vinayaṃ jānātha, na suttaṃ na abhidhammaṃ, vuḍḍhapabbajitā”tiādinā nayena vihesanto[M 2.0046]. Upayogappavattiyañhi idaṃ sāmivacanaṃ. Atha vā yathāvutteneva nayena “vihesaṃ bhāvitattānaṃ karonto”ti pāṭhaseso veditabbo. Evaṃ nippariyāyameva sāmivacanaṃ sijjhati. Avijjāya purakkhatoti bhāvitattavihesane ādīnavadassanapaṭicchādikāya avijjāya purakkhato pesito payojito sesapabbajitānaṃ bhāvitattānaṃ vihesabhāvena pavattaṃ diṭṭheva dhamme cittavibādhanena saṅkilesaṃ, āyatiñca nirayasampāpanena maggaṃ nirayagāminaṃ na jānāti.

280. Similarly, such a one, delighting in vexation, vexes those with developed minds—the bhikkhus who are arahants, such as the Elder Sodhana and others—with such words as: “You don’t know the Vinaya, you don’t know the Sutta, you don’t know the Abhidhamma, you old monks!” Here, the genitive case (bhāvitattānaṃ) is used with the force of the objective. Alternatively, the ellipsis should be understood as “inflicting vexation upon those with developed minds” in the way just stated. In this way the genitive is established without ambiguity. Sent on by ignorance: sent on, dispatched, and spurred by the ignorance that conceals the danger in vexing those with developed minds, he does not know the defilement consisting in mental affliction in this very life, which occurs through his vexatious behavior toward the other monastics with developed minds, nor the path leading to hell, which in the future brings about rebirth there.

281. Ajānanto ca tena maggena catubbidhāpāyabhedaṃ vinipātaṃ samāpanno. Tattha ca vinipāte gabbhā gabbhaṃ tamā tamaṃ ekekanikāye satakkhattuṃ sahassakkhattumpi mātukucchito mātukucchiṃ candimasūriyehipi aviddhaṃsanīyā asurakāyatamā tamañca samāpanno. Sa ve tādisako [V 2.0042] bhikkhu pecca ito paralokaṃ gantvā ayaṃ kapilamaccho viya nānappakāraṃ dukkhaṃ nigacchati.

281. And not knowing, by that path he arrives at ruin, the fourfold plane of misery. And there in that ruin, he passes from womb to womb, from darkness to darkness. In each single realm, a hundred times, a thousand times, even a hundred thousand times, he passes from a mother’s womb to a mother’s womb, and he arrives at the darkness of darkness of the asura world, which cannot be illuminated even by the moon and sun. Indeed, such a bhikkhu, having departed from this world and gone to the next, undergoes various kinds of suffering, just like this fish Kapila.

282. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Gūthakūpo yathā assa, sampuṇṇo gaṇavassiko,yathā vaccakuṭigūthakūpo gaṇavassiko anekavassiko bahūni vassāni mukhato gūthena pūriyamāno sampuṇṇo assa, so udakakumbhasatehi [P 1.0311] udakakumbhasahassehi dhoviyamānopi duggandhadubbaṇṇiyānapagamā dubbisodho hoti, evameva yo evarūpo assa dīgharattaṃ saṃkiliṭṭhakammanto gūthakūpo viya gūthena pāpena sampuṇṇattā sampuṇṇo puggalo, so dubbisodho hi sāṅgaṇo, cirakālaṃ tassa aṅgaṇassa vipākaṃ paccanubhontopi na sujjhati. Tasmā vassagaṇanāya aparimāṇampi kālaṃ sa ve tādisako bhikkhu pecca dukkhaṃ nigacchatīti. Atha vā ayaṃ imissā gāthāya sambandho – yaṃ vuttaṃ “sa ve tādisako bhikkhu, pecca dukkhaṃ nigacchatī”ti, tatra siyā tumhākaṃ “sakkā panāyaṃ tathā kātuṃ, yathā pecca dukkhaṃ na nigaccheyyā”ti. Na sakkā. Kasmā? Yasmā gūthakūpo…pe… sāṅgaṇoti.

282. For what reason? Just as a cesspool, full for many years: Just as a latrine cesspool that has been full for a number of years, for many years, being filled with filth at its opening, would be hard to clean even if washed with hundreds or thousands of pots of water, as its foul smell and discoloration would not depart; so too, a person of such a kind, whose deeds have been defiled for a long time, is a person who is full, being filled with the filth of evil like a cesspool. For he is stained and hard to clean: even after experiencing the result of that stain for a long time, he is not purified. Therefore, for a time that is immeasurable by the count of years, such a bhikkhu, having departed, undergoes suffering. Or, this is the connection for this verse: Regarding the statement, “Such a bhikkhu, having departed, undergoes suffering,” you might think: “But is it possible for him to act in such a way that he would not undergo suffering after death?” It is not possible. Why? Because a cesspool … for he is stained.

283-4. Yato [M 2.0047] paṭikacceva yaṃ evarūpaṃ jānātha, bhikkhavo gehanissitaṃ, yaṃ evarūpaṃ pañcakāmaguṇanissitaṃ jāneyyātha abhūtaguṇapatthanākārappavattāya pāpikāya icchāya samannāgatattā pāpicchaṃ, kāmavitakkādīhi samannāgatattā pāpasaṅkappaṃ, kāyikavītikkamādinā veḷudānādibhedena ca pāpācārena samannāgatattā pāpācāraṃ, vesiyādipāpagocarato pāpagocaraṃ, sabbe samaggā hutvāna abhinibbajjiyātha naṃ. Tattha abhinibbajjiyāthāti vivajjeyyātha mā bhajeyyātha, mā cassa abhinibbajjanamatteneva appossukkataṃ āpajjeyyātha, apica kho pana kāraṇḍavaṃ niddhamatha, kasambuṃ apakassatha, taṃ kacavarabhūtaṃ puggalaṃ kacavaramiva anapekkhā niddhamatha, kasaṭabhūtañca naṃ khattiyādīnaṃ majjhe paviṭṭhaṃ pabhinnapaggharitakuṭṭhaṃ caṇḍālaṃ viya apakassatha, hatthe vā sīse vā gahetvā nikkaḍḍhatha. Seyyathāpi [P 1.0312] āyasmā mahāmoggallāno taṃ puggalaṃ pāpadhammaṃ bāhāya gahetvā bahidvārakoṭṭhakā nikkhāmetvā sūcighaṭikaṃ adāsi, evaṃ apakassathāti dasseti. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Saṅghārāmo nāma sīlavantānaṃ kato, na dussīlānaṃ.

From the very moment, monks, you recognize someone of such a kind—dependent on households, attached to the five strands of sensual pleasures—know him as one of wicked desires, possessed of a wicked wish that proceeds from aspiring after qualities he does not possess; know him as one of evil thoughts, possessed of evil thoughts such as sensual thought; know him as one of evil conduct, possessed of evil conduct through bodily transgressions such as offering bamboo staffs; and know him as one of evil resort, resorting to prostitutes and other wicked places. All united, you should expel him. Here, 'you should expel him' means you should avoid him, not associate with him. Nor should you become unconcerned merely by having expelled him. Moreover, cast out the rubbish, remove the dregs. Cast off that person who is like rubbish, disregarding him as one would rubbish. Remove him who is like dregs, just as one would remove an outcaste with oozing leprosy who has entered among the nobles. Seize him by the arm or the head and drag him out. Just as the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna seized that person of wicked nature by the arm, threw him outside the gatehouse, and applied the bolt, so should you remove him—this is what is shown. For what reason? The monastery is made for the virtuous, not for the unvirtuous.

285-6. Yato etadeva tato palāpe vāhetha, assamaṇe samaṇamānine, yathā hi palāpā anto taṇḍularahitāpi bahi thusehi vīhī viya dissanti, evaṃ pāpabhikkhū anto sīlādivirahitāpi bahi kāsāvādiparikkhārena bhikkhū viya dissanti. Tasmā “palāpā”ti vuccanti. Te palāpe vāhetha, opunātha, vidhamatha paramatthato assamaṇe vesamattena samaṇamānine[V 2.0043]. Evaṃ niddhamitvāna…pe… patissatā. Tattha kappayavhoti kappetha, karothāti vuttaṃ hoti. Patissatāti aññamaññaṃ sagāravā sappatissā. Tato samaggā nipakā, dukkhassantaṃ karissathāti athevaṃ tumhe suddhā suddhehi saṃvāsaṃ kappentā, diṭṭhisīlasāmaññatāya samaggā, anupubbena paripākagatāya paññāya nipakā, sabbassevimassa vaṭṭadukkhādino dukkhassa antaṃ karissathāti arahattanikūṭeneva desanaṃ niṭṭhapesi.

Therefore, winnow out the chaff—those who are not ascetics but presume to be ascetics. For just as chaff, though empty of rice within, appears from the outside to be paddy because of the husks, so too wicked monks, though devoid of virtue and so on within, appear from the outside to be monks because of their saffron robes and other requisites. Hence they are called 'chaff.' Winnow out that chaff, separate it, scatter it—those who are in reality not ascetics but presume to be ascetics merely by their guise. Having thus cast them out ... be respectful. Here, 'arrange your association' means you should arrange it, you should do it. 'Respectful' means mutually reverential and deferential. 'Then, united and prudent, you will make an end of suffering' means: thus you, being pure and arranging your association with the pure, united by a commonality of view and virtue, prudent with wisdom that has gradually matured, will make an end of all this suffering of the round and so on. He concluded the discourse with the pinnacle of arahantship.

Desanāpariyosāne te pañcasatā kevaṭṭaputtā saṃvegamāpajjitvā dukkhassantakiriyaṃ patthayamānā bhagavato santike pabbajitvā nacirasseva dukkhassantaṃ [M 2.0048] katvā bhagavatā saddhiṃ āneñjavihārasamāpattidhammaparibhogena ekaparibhogā ahesuṃ. Sā ca nesaṃ evaṃ bhagavatā saddhiṃ ekaparibhogatā udāne vuttayasojasuttavaseneva veditabbāti.

At the end of the discourse, those five hundred sons of fishermen, experiencing a sense of spiritual urgency and aspiring to make an end of suffering, went forth in the presence of the Blessed One. Not long afterwards, they made an end of suffering and came to share the same enjoyment with the Blessed One through the enjoyment of the Dhamma of the attainment of the imperturbable abiding. And this sharing of the same enjoyment with the Blessed One should be understood in the way stated in the Udāna in the Yasoja Sutta.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Collection

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya kapilasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Kapila Sutta in the Commentary on the Sutta-Nipāta is concluded.

7. Brāhmaṇadhammikasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Explanation of the Brāhmaṇadhammika Sutta

Evaṃ [V 2.0044] me sutanti brāhmaṇadhammikasuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Ayameva yāssa nidāne “atha kho sambahulā”tiādinā nayena vuttā. Tattha [P 1.0313] sambahulāti bahū aneke. Kosalakāti kosalaraṭṭhavāsino. Brāhmaṇamahāsālāti jātiyā brāhmaṇā mahāsāratāya mahāsālā. Yesaṃ kira nidahitvā ṭhapitaṃyeva asītikoṭisaṅkhyaṃ dhanamatthi, te “brāhmaṇamahāsālā”ti vuccanti. Ime ca tādisā, tena vuttaṃ “brāhmaṇamahāsālā”ti. Jiṇṇāti jajjarībhūtā jarāya khaṇḍiccādibhāvamāpāditā. Vuḍḍhāti aṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ vuḍḍhimariyādaṃ pattā. Mahallakāti jātimahallakatāya samannāgatā, cirakālappasutāti vuttaṃ hoti. Addhagatāti addhānaṃ gatā, dve tayo rājaparivaṭṭe atītāti adhippāyo. Vayo anuppattāti pacchimavayaṃ sampattā. Apica jiṇṇāti porāṇā, cirakālappavattakulanvayāti vuttaṃ hoti. Vuḍḍhāti sīlācārādiguṇavuḍḍhiyuttā. Mahallakāti vibhavamahantatāya samannāgatā mahaddhanā mahābhogā. Addhagatāti maggapaṭipannā brāhmaṇānaṃ vatacariyādimariyādaṃ avītikkamma caramānā. Vayo anuppattāti jātivuḍḍhabhāvampi antimavayaṃ anuppattāti evampettha yojanā veditabbā. Sesamettha pākaṭameva.

'Thus have I heard'—this is the Brāhmaṇadhammika Sutta. What is its origin? The very one stated in its introduction by the passage beginning: 'Then a number of…' Herein, 'a number of' means many, numerous. 'Kosalan' means inhabitants of the Kosala country. 'Great brahmin householders' means they were brahmins by birth and 'great householders' on account of their great wealth. It is said that those who have eighty crores of wealth stored away are called 'great brahmin householders.' Since these were such, they are called 'great brahmin householders.' 'Aged' means decrepit, having reached a state of having broken teeth, etc., through old age. 'Venerable' means they had reached the full measure of growth of their limbs. 'Senior' means they were endowed with seniority by birth; that is, they were born long ago. 'Advanced in life's span' means they had traversed the road of life; the sense is that two or three reigns of kings had passed. 'Come to the last stage of life' means they had reached the final age. Alternatively: 'aged' means ancient, that is, belonging to a long-standing family lineage. 'Venerable' means endowed with the growth of good qualities such as virtue and conduct. 'Senior' means endowed with great status, of great wealth and property. 'Advanced in life's span' means they had entered upon the path, conducting themselves without transgressing the code of the brahmins concerning vows, observances, and so on. 'Come to the last stage of life' means that their seniority by birth had also reached the final age. This is how the connection of terms should be understood here. The rest is clear.

Bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodiṃsūti khamanīyādīni pucchantā aññamaññaṃ samappavattamodā ahesuṃ. Yāya ca “kacci bhoto gotamassa khamanīyaṃ, kacci yāpanīyaṃ, appābādhaṃ, appātaṅkaṃ, balaṃ, lahuṭṭhānaṃ, phāsuvihāro”tiādikāya kathāya sammodiṃsu, taṃ pītipāmojjasaṅkhātasammodajananato sammodituṃ arahato ca sammodanīyaṃ, atthabyañjanamadhuratāya sucirampi [M 2.0049] kālaṃ sāretuṃ nirantaraṃ pavattetuṃ arahato saritabbabhāvato ca sāraṇīyaṃ. Suyyamānasukhato ca sammodanīyaṃ, anussariyamānasukhato sāraṇīyaṃ, tathā byañjanaparisuddhatāya sammodanīyaṃ, atthaparisuddhatāya sāraṇīyanti evaṃ anekehi pariyāyehi sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ [P 1.0314] vītisāretvā pariyosāpetvā niṭṭhāpetvā yenatthena āgatā, taṃ pucchitukāmā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Taṃ –

'They exchanged courteous greetings with the Blessed One' means that they asked about his health and so on, and thus their mutual gladness proceeded smoothly. The talk with which they exchanged greetings—'I hope Master Gotama is comfortable and well, with little affliction or sickness, with strength, a light body, and abiding in comfort'—is called 'gladdening' because it generates gladness consisting of joy and delight and is worthy of one who should be gladdened. It is called 'memorable' because, due to its sweetness of meaning and phrasing, it is fit to be recalled and kept going without interruption for a long time. It is gladdening because it is pleasant to hear, and memorable because it is pleasant to recollect. Likewise, it is gladdening because of its purity of phrasing, and memorable because of its purity of meaning. Having in these many ways exchanged and concluded this gladdening and memorable talk, they sat down to one side, wishing to ask about the matter for which they had come.

“Na pacchato na purato, nāpi āsannadūrato;

Na passe nāpi paṭivāte, na cāpi oṇatuṇṇate”ti. –

Not behind, not in front, not too near or too far; not to the side, not upwind, and not on ground that is too low or too high.

Ādinā [V 2.0045] nayena maṅgalasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttameva.

This has been explained in this way in the commentary on the Maṅgala Sutta.

Evaṃ ekamantaṃ nisinnā kho te brāhmaṇamahāsālā bhagavantaṃ etadavocuṃ – “kiṃ ta”nti? “Sandissanti nu kho”tiādi. Taṃ sabbaṃ uttānatthameva. Kevalañhettha brāhmaṇānaṃ brāhmaṇadhammeti desakālādidhamme chaḍḍetvā yo brāhmaṇadhammo, tasmiṃyeva. Tena hi brāhmaṇāti yasmā maṃ tumhe yācittha, tasmā brāhmaṇā suṇātha, sotaṃ odahatha, sādhukaṃ manasi karotha, yoniso manasi karotha. Tathā payogasuddhiyā suṇātha, āsayasuddhiyā sādhukaṃ manasi karotha. Avikkhepena suṇātha, paggahena sādhukaṃ manasi karothātiādinā nayena etesaṃ padānaṃ pubbe avuttopi adhippāyo veditabbo. Atha bhagavatā vuttaṃ taṃ vacanaṃ sampaṭicchantā “evaṃ bho”ti kho te brāhmaṇamahāsālā bhagavato paccassosuṃ, bhagavato vacanaṃ abhimukhā hutvā assosuṃ. Atha vā paṭissuṇiṃsu. “Suṇātha sādhukaṃ manasi karothā”ti vuttamatthaṃ kattukāmatāya paṭijāniṃsūti vuttaṃ hoti. Atha tesaṃ evaṃ paṭissutavataṃ bhagavā etadavoca – “kiṃ ta”nti? “Isayo pubbakā”tiādi.

Thus seated to one side, those great brahmin householders said this to the Blessed One. What was that? The passage beginning, 'Are they seen...?' All of that is clear in meaning. Here, however, 'the Dhamma of the brahmins' refers only to the Dhamma of the brahmins, setting aside teachings about place, time, and so on. 'Well then, brahmins': since you have asked me, therefore, 'listen, brahmins, lend your ear, apply your minds well, apply your minds systematically.' That is: listen with purity of application; apply your minds well with purity of intention. Listen without distraction; apply your minds well with exertion—in this way, the meaning of these phrases, though not previously explained, should be understood. Then, accepting the Blessed One's words, those great brahmin householders replied to the Blessed One, 'Yes, venerable sir,' and they listened to the Blessed One's words with attention. Or: they gave their assent; that is, they promised their intention to do what was said: 'Listen and apply your minds well.' Then, to them who had thus assented, the Blessed One said this. What was that? The passage beginning, 'The seers of the past...'

287. Tattha paṭhamagāthāya tāva saññatattāti sīlasaṃyamena saṃyatacittā. Tapassinoti indriyasaṃvaratapayuttā. Attadatthamacārisunti mantajjhenabrahmavihārabhāvanādiṃ attano atthaṃ akaṃsu. Sesaṃ pākaṭameva.

287. Therein, in the first verse, 'self-restrained' means with minds restrained by moral discipline. 'Ascetics' means they were engaged in the austerity of sense restraint. 'They lived for their own welfare' means they pursued their own welfare by such means as the recitation of sacred texts and the cultivation of the divine abodes. The rest is clear.

288. Dutiyagāthādīsupi ayaṃ saṅkhepavaṇṇanā – na pasū brāhmaṇānāsunti porāṇānaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ pasū na āsuṃ, na te pasupariggahamakaṃsu. Na hiraññaṃ na dhāniyanti hiraññañca [P 1.0315] brāhmaṇānaṃ antamaso jatumāsakopi nāhosi[M 2.0050], tathā vīhisāliyavagodhūmādi pubbaṇṇāparaṇṇabhedaṃ dhāniyampi tesaṃ nāhosi. Te hi nikkhittajātarūparajatā asannidhikārakāva hutvā kevalaṃ sajjhāyadhanadhaññā attano mantajjhenasaṅkhāteneva dhanena dhaññena ca samannāgatā ahesuṃ.
