Yo cāyaṃ mettādivihāro seṭṭhattā anugāmikattā ca brahmanidhīti vuccati, tañca brahmaṃ nidhimapālayuṃ sadā tassa bhāvanānuyogena.

288. In the second verse and those that follow, this is the brief explanation: 'The brahmins had no cattle'—the ancient brahmins did not have cattle; they did not acquire livestock. 'No gold or grain'—the brahmins did not possess gold, not even a lac-sealed coin, nor did they have grain such as rice, paddy, barley, and wheat, of either the early or late harvest. Having given up gold and silver and being averse to storing things up, their only wealth and grain was study; they were endowed with the wealth and grain consisting of the recitation of sacred texts. And that which is called the 'brahmic treasure'—the abodes of loving-kindness and so on, so called because of their excellence and because they are conducive to the goal—that brahmic treasure they always protected by their devotion to its cultivation.

289. Evaṃ vihārīnaṃ yaṃ nesaṃ pakataṃ āsi, yaṃ etesaṃ pakataṃ ete brāhmaṇe uddissa kataṃ ahosi. Dvārabhattaṃ upaṭṭhitanti “brāhmaṇānaṃ dassāmā”ti sajjetvā tehi tehi dāyakehi attano attano gharadvāre ṭhapitabhattaṃ. Saddhāpakatanti saddhāya pakataṃ, saddhādeyyanti vuttaṃ hoti. Esānanti esantīti esā, tesaṃ esānaṃ, esamānānaṃ pariyesamānānanti vuttaṃ hoti. Dātaveti [V 2.0046] dātabbaṃ. Tadamaññisunti taṃ amaññiṃsu, taṃ dvāre sajjetvā ṭhapitaṃ bhattaṃ saddhādeyyaṃ pariyesamānānaṃ etesaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ dātabbaṃ amaññiṃsu dāyakā janā, na tato paraṃ. Anatthikā hi te aññena ahesuṃ, kevalaṃ ghāsacchādanaparamatāya santuṭṭhāti adhippāyo.

289. For those living thus, whatever was prepared for them was done for the sake of those brahmins. 'A meal at the door is ready': this means a meal placed at their own house doors by various donors, who prepared it with the thought, 'We will give it to the brahmins.' 'Prepared with faith' means prepared through faith; that is to say, a gift of faith. 'Of those seeking': this means of those who are seeking, that is, of those searching. 'To be given' means it should be given. 'They thought thus': the donors considered that this meal, prepared and placed at the door as a gift of faith, should be given to these brahmins who were seeking, and nothing beyond that. For they had no need of anything else, being content with the bare necessities of food and clothing—this is the meaning.

290. Nānārattehīti nānāvidharāgarattehi vatthehi vicitrattharaṇatthatehi, sayanehi ekabhūmikadvibhūmikādipāsādavarehi. Āvasathehīti evarūpehi upakaraṇehi. Phītā janapadā raṭṭhā ekekappadesabhūtā janapadā ca keci keci sakalaraṭṭhā ca “namo brāhmaṇāna”nti sāyaṃ pātaṃ brāhmaṇe deve viya namassiṃsu.

290. “With various colors” means with garments dyed in various hues, on beds with diverse coverings spread out, in splendid one-story or two-story mansions and so on. “With dwellings” means with such furnishings. Prosperous districts and kingdoms, some being individual regions and others entire kingdoms, paid homage to the brahmins morning and evening as if to gods, saying, “Homage to the brahmins.”

291. Te evaṃ namassiyamānā lokena avajjhā brāhmaṇā āsuṃ, na kevalañca avajjhā, ajeyyā vihiṃsitumpi anabhibhavanīyattā ajeyyā ca ahesuṃ. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Dhammarakkhitā, yasmā dhammena rakkhitā. Te hi pañca varasīladhamme rakkhiṃsu, “dhammo have rakkhati dhammacāri”nti (jā. 1.10.102; 1.15.385) dhammarakkhitā hutvā avajjhā ajeyyā ca ahesunti [P 1.0316] adhippāyo. Na ne koci nivāresīti te brāhmaṇe kulānaṃ dvāresu sabbaso bāhiresu ca abbhantaresu ca sabbadvāresu yasmā tesu piyasammatesu varasīlasamannāgatesu [M 2.0051] mātāpitūsu viya ativissatthā manussā ahesuṃ, tasmā “idaṃ nāma ṭhānaṃ tayā na pavisitabba”nti na koci nivāresi.

291. Thus honored by the world, those brahmins were inviolable. Not only were they inviolable, but also unconquerable; because they could not be harmed or overpowered, they were unconquerable. For what reason? They were protected by the Dhamma, for they were guarded by the Dhamma. They indeed protected the five excellent virtuous principles, and as it is said, 'The Dhamma indeed protects one who lives by the Dhamma.' Being protected by the Dhamma, they were inviolable and unconquerable—this is the meaning. 'No one hindered them': because people had complete trust in those brahmins—who were beloved, esteemed, and endowed with excellent virtue—as if they were their own parents, no one hindered them at any of the doors of the families, whether outer or inner, saying, 'You must not enter this place.'

292. Evaṃ dhammarakkhitā kuladvāresu anivāritā carantā aṭṭha ca cattālīsañcāti aṭṭhacattālīsaṃ vassāni kumārabhāvato pabhuti caraṇena komāraṃ brahmacariyaṃ cariṃsu te. Yepi brāhmaṇacaṇḍālā ahesuṃ, ko pana vādo brahmasamādīsūti evamettha adhippāyo veditabbo. Evaṃ brahmacariyaṃ carantā eva hi vijjācaraṇapariyeṭṭhiṃ acaruṃ brāhmaṇā pure, na abrahmacārino hutvā. Tattha vijjāpariyeṭṭhīti mantajjhenaṃ. Vuttañcetaṃ “so aṭṭhacattālīsa vassāni komāraṃ brahmacariyaṃ carati mante adhīyamāno”ti (a. ni. 5.192). Caraṇapariyeṭṭhīti sīlarakkhaṇaṃ. “Vijjācaraṇapariyeṭṭhu”ntipi pāṭho, vijjācaraṇaṃ pariyesituṃ acarunti attho.

292. Thus, protected by the Dhamma and moving unhindered at the doors of families, they lived the youthful holy life for forty-eight years from their youth onwards. Even the brahmin-outcasts did so, so what need be said of those equal to Brahma and so on?—this is the meaning to be understood here. It was indeed while living the holy life that the brahmins of old undertook the quest for knowledge and conduct, not after becoming uncelibate. Here, 'the quest for knowledge' is the study of the sacred texts. And this is said: 'For forty-eight years he lives the youthful holy life, studying the sacred texts.' 'The quest for conduct' is the protection of virtue. There is also the reading 'vijjācaraṇapariyeṭṭhuṃ,' meaning they wandered in search of knowledge and conduct.

293. Yathāvuttañca kālaṃ brahmacariyaṃ caritvā tato paraṃ gharāvāsaṃ kappentāpi na brāhmaṇā aññamagamuṃ khattiyaṃ vā vessādīsu aññataraṃ vā, ye ahesuṃ devasamā vā mariyādā vāti adhippāyo. Tathā sataṃ vā sahassaṃ vā datvā napi bhariyaṃ kiṇiṃsu te, seyyathāpi etarahi ekacce kiṇanti. Te hi dhammena dāraṃ pariyesanti. Kathaṃ? Aṭṭhacattālīsaṃ vassāni brahmacariyaṃ [V 2.0047] caritvā brāhmaṇā kaññābhikkhaṃ āhiṇḍanti – “ahaṃ aṭṭhacattālīsa vassāni ciṇṇabrahmacariyo, yadi vayappattā dārikā atthi, detha me”ti. Tato yassa vayappattā dārikā hoti, so taṃ alaṅkaritvā nīharitvā dvāre ṭhitasseva brāhmaṇassa hatthe udakaṃ āsiñcanto “imaṃ te, brāhmaṇa, bhariyaṃ posāvanatthāya dammī”ti [P 1.0317] vatvā deti.

293. Having lived the holy life for the aforesaid time, even when arranging a household life afterwards, the brahmins did not go to another woman—that is, to a khattiya, a vessa, or another such—but only to one who was like a goddess and of good conduct; this is the meaning. Nor did they buy a wife after giving a hundred or a thousand, as some do nowadays. For they sought a wife in accordance with the Dhamma. How? Having lived the holy life for forty-eight years, a brahmin would wander begging for a maiden, saying: 'I have lived the holy life for forty-eight years. If there is a girl of suitable age, give her to me.' Then one who had a girl of suitable age would adorn her, bring her out, and while the brahmin was standing at the door, would pour water on his hands and give her to him, saying: 'Brahmin, I give you this wife for the purpose of supporting her.'

Kasmā pana te evaṃ ciraṃ brahmacariyaṃ caritvāpi dāraṃ pariyesanti, na yāvajīvaṃ brahmacārino hontīti? Micchādiṭṭhivasena. Tesañhi evaṃdiṭṭhi hoti – “yo puttaṃ na uppādeti, so kulavaṃsacchedakaro hoti, tato niraye paccatī”ti. Cattāro kira abhāyitabbaṃ bhāyanti gaṇḍuppādo kikī kuntanī brāhmaṇāti. Gaṇḍuppādā kira mahāpathaviyā khayabhayena [M 2.0052] mattabhojino honti, na bahuṃ mattikaṃ khādanti. Kikī sakuṇikā ākāsapatanabhayena aṇḍassa upari uttānā seti. Kuntanī sakuṇikā pathavikampanabhayena pādehi bhūmiṃ na suṭṭhu akkamati. Brāhmaṇā kulavaṃsūpacchedabhayena dāraṃ pariyesanti. Āha cettha –

But why, after living the holy life for so long, do they seek a wife instead of remaining celibate for life? Because of wrong view. For they hold the view: 'One who does not beget a son becomes a destroyer of the family lineage and is tormented in hell.' It is said that four beings fear what is not to be feared: the earthworm, the kiki bird, the kuntani bird, and the brahmin. The earthworm, it seems, fearing the depletion of the great earth, is a moderate eater and does not consume much soil. The kiki bird, fearing falling from the sky, lies on its back over its egg. The kuntani bird, fearing an earthquake, does not tread firmly on the ground with its feet. The brahmins, fearing the cutting off of the family lineage, seek a wife. On this it is said:

“Gaṇḍuppādo kikī ceva, kuntī brāhmaṇadhammiko;

Ete abhayaṃ bhāyanti, sammūḷhā caturo janā”ti.

“The earthworm and the kiki bird, the kunti and the pious brahmin; these four deluded beings fear what is not to be feared.”

Evaṃ dhammena dāraṃ pariyesitvāpi ca sampiyeneva saṃvāsaṃ saṅgantvā samarocayuṃ, sampiyeneva aññamaññaṃ pemeneva kāyena ca cittena ca missībhūtā saṅghaṭitā saṃsaṭṭhā hutvā saṃvāsaṃ samarocayuṃ, na appiyena na niggahena cāti vuttaṃ hoti.

And having sought a wife in accordance with the Dhamma, they came together and delighted in their cohabitation only out of mutual affection. They delighted in their cohabitation only out of mutual affection, having become blended, joined, and mixed with each other through love in body and mind, not out of dislike or coercion—this is what is meant.

294. Evaṃ sampiyeneva saṃvāsaṃ karontāpi ca aññatra tamhāti, yo so utusamayo, yamhi samaye brāhmaṇī brāhmaṇena upagantabbā, aññatra tamhā samayā ṭhapetvā taṃ samayaṃ ututo virataṃ utuveramaṇiṃ pati bhariyaṃ, yāva puna so samayo āgacchati, tāva aṭṭhatvā antarāyeva. Methunaṃ dhammanti methunāya dhammāya. Sampadānavacanapattiyā kiretaṃ upayogavacanaṃ. Nāssu gacchantīti neva gacchanti. Brāhmaṇāti ye honti devasamā ca mariyādā cāti adhippāyo.

294. And even while cohabiting only out of mutual affection, 'except for that' means: there is the fertile season, the time when the brahmin woman is to be approached by the brahmin. 'Except for that time' means setting aside that time, abstaining from intercourse with the wife outside the fertile period, not engaging in relations in the interim until that season returns. 'The act of intercourse' means 'for the purpose of intercourse.' This is a term of application in the sense of the dative. 'They did not go' means they never went. 'Brahmins' means those who are like gods and who observe limits—this is the meaning.

295. Avisesena pana sabbepi brahmacariyañca…pe… avaṇṇayuṃ. Tattha brahmacariyanti methunavirati. Sīlanti sesāni cattāri sikkhāpadāni. Ajjavanti ujubhāvo, atthato asaṭhatā [V 2.0048] amāyāvitā ca. Maddavanti [P 1.0318] mudubhāvo, atthato atthaddhatā anatimānitā ca. Tapoti indriyasaṃvaro. Soraccanti suratabhāvo sukhasīlatā appaṭikūlasamācāratā. Avihiṃsāti pāṇiādīhi avihesikajātikatā sakaruṇabhāvo. Khantīti adhivāsanakkhanti. Iccete guṇe avaṇṇayuṃ. Yepi nāsakkhiṃsu sabbaso paṭipattiyā ārādhetuṃ, tepi tattha sāradassino hutvā vācāya vaṇṇayiṃsu pasaṃsiṃsu.

295. But without distinction, they all praised celibacy ... and so on. Here, 'celibacy' is abstinence from sexual intercourse. 'Virtue' is the remaining four training rules. 'Honesty' is uprightness, that is, non-deceitfulness and non-craftiness. 'Gentleness' is softness, that is, non-stubbornness and non-conceit. 'Austerity' is restraint of the sense faculties. 'Meekness' is a gentle nature, an agreeable character, inoffensive conduct. 'Non-harming' is the nature of not vexing beings with one's hands and so on, a compassionate nature. 'Patience' is enduring patience. Thus they praised these qualities. Even those who were unable to accomplish them completely in practice, seeing their substance, praised and commended them with speech.

296. Evaṃ vaṇṇentānañca yo nesaṃ…pe… nāgamā, yo etesaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ paramo brahmā ahosi, brahmasamo nāma uttamo brāhmaṇo [M 2.0053] ahosi, daḷhena parakkamena samannāgatattā daḷhaparakkamo. Sa vāti vibhāvane vā-saddo, tena so evarūpo brāhmaṇoti tameva vibhāveti. Methunaṃ dhammanti methunasamāpattiṃ. Supinantepi nāgamāti supinepi na agamāsi.

296. And of those who praised thus, he who among them... did not go, was the highest Brahmā among these brahmins; he was the highest brahmin, named 'equal to Brahmā'. He was 'firm in exertion' because he was endowed with firm effort. The particle 'vā' in 'sa vā' is for clarification; it thereby clarifies that very brahmin as being of such a kind. 'The act of intercourse' means engagement in intercourse. 'He did not go even in a dream' means he did not go even in a dream.

297. Tato tassa vattaṃ…pe… avaṇṇayuṃ. Imāya gāthāya navamagāthāya vuttaguṇeyeva ādiantavasena niddisanto devasame brāhmaṇe pakāseti. Te hi viññujātikā paṇḍitā tassa brahmasamassa brāhmaṇassa vattaṃ anusikkhanti pabbajjāya jhānabhāvanāya ca, te ca ime brahmacariyādiguṇe paṭipattiyā eva vaṇṇayantīti. Te sabbepi brāhmaṇā pañcakanipāte doṇasutte (a. ni. 5.192) vuttanayeneva veditabbā.

297. Then his conduct... they praised. By this verse and the ninth verse, indicating the qualities already stated by way of their beginning and end, he reveals the brahmins who were like gods. For those wise and intelligent ones train in conformity with the conduct of that brahmin who is equal to Brahmā, by way of renunciation and the development of jhāna, and they praise these qualities—celibacy and so on—by means of practice itself. All these brahmins should be understood in the way stated in the Doṇa Sutta in the Book of the Fives (AN 5.192).

298. Idāni mariyāde brāhmaṇe dassento āha – “taṇḍulaṃ sayana”nti. Tassattho – tesu ye honti mariyādā, te brāhmaṇā sace yaññaṃ kappetukāmā honti, atha āmakadhaññapaṭiggahaṇā paṭiviratattā nānappakārakaṃ taṇḍulañca, mañcapīṭhādibhedaṃ sayanañca, khomādibhedaṃ vatthañca, gosappitilatelādibhedaṃ sappitelañca yāciya dhammena, “uddissa ariyā tiṭṭhanti, esā ariyāna yācanā”ti evaṃ vuttena uddissaṭhānasaṅkhātena dhammena yācitvā, atha yo yaṃ icchati dātuṃ, tena taṃ dinnataṇḍulādiṃ samodhānetvā saṃkaḍḍhitvā. “Samudānetvā”tipi pāṭho, ekoyevattho. Tato yaññamakappayunti tato gahetvā dānamakaṃsu[P 1.0319].

298. Now, showing the brahmins who observed limits, he says: 'Rice, bedding....' The meaning is this: Among them, those brahmins who observed limits, if they wished to arrange a sacrifice, then, because they abstained from accepting raw grain, having righteously requested various kinds of rice; bedding of different kinds such as couches and chairs; cloth of different kinds such as linen; and ghee and oil of different kinds such as cow's ghee and sesame oil—having requested this in accordance with the Dhamma designated as 'standing for a purpose,' as in the saying, 'The noble ones stand for a purpose; this is the asking of the noble ones'—then, whatever anyone wished to give, they combined and collected that given rice and so on. There is also the reading 'samudānetvā,' with the same meaning. 'Then they arranged a sacrifice' means that, having taken from this, they made a gift.

299. Karontā ca evametasmiṃ upaṭṭhitasmiṃ dānasaṅkhāte yaññasmiṃ nāssu gāvo haniṃsu te, na te gāviyo haniṃsu. Gāvīmukhena cettha sabbapāṇā vuttāti veditabbā. Kiṃkāraṇā na haniṃsūti? Brahmacariyādiguṇayuttattā. Apica visesato yathā mātā…pe… nāssu gāvo haniṃsu te. Tattha yāsu jāyanti osadhāti yāsu pittādīnaṃ bhesajjabhūtā pañca gorasā jāyanti.

299. And while performing it, in this sacrifice designated as giving that had been prepared, they did not kill cows, nor did they kill cattle. Here, it should be understood that all living beings are meant by the expression 'cows.' For what reason did they not kill them? Because they were endowed with such virtues as the holy life. Moreover, specifically, 'just as a mother... (etc.) ... they did not kill cows.' Therein, the words 'in whom medicines are produced' mean that in them are produced the five products of the cow, which are a medicine for such ailments as those of the bile.

300. Annadātiādīsu [V 2.0049] yasmā pañca gorase paribhuñjantānaṃ khudā vūpasammati, balaṃ vaḍḍhati, chavivaṇṇo vippasīdati, kāyikamānasikaṃ sukhaṃ uppajjati[M 2.0054], tasmā annadā baladā vaṇṇadā sukhadā cetāti veditabbā. Sesamettha uttānatthameva.

300. In regard to 'givers of food,' etc.: because for those who consume the five products of the cow, hunger is allayed, strength increases, the complexion becomes bright, and bodily and mental happiness arises, therefore they should be understood as givers of food, givers of strength, givers of beauty, and givers of happiness. The rest here has an obvious meaning.

301. Evaṃ te yaññesu gāvo ahanantā puññappabhāvānuggahitasarīrā sukhumālā…pe… sukhamedhittha yaṃ pajā. Tattha sukhumālā mudutaluṇahatthapādāditāya, mahākāyā ārohapariṇāhasampattiyā, vaṇṇavanto suvaṇṇavaṇṇatāya saṇṭhānayuttatāya ca, yasassino lābhaparivārasampadāya. Sehi dhammehīti sakehi cārittehi. Kiccākiccesu ussukāti kiccesu “idaṃ kātabbaṃ”, akiccesu “idaṃ na kātabba”nti ussukkamāpannā hutvāti attho. Evaṃ te porāṇā brāhmaṇā evarūpā hutvā dassanīyā pasādanīyā lokassa paramadakkhiṇeyyā imāya paṭipattiyā yāva loke avattiṃsu, tāva vigataītibhayupaddavā hutvā nānappakārakaṃ sukhaṃ edhittha pāpuṇi, sukhaṃ vā edhittha sukhaṃ vuḍḍhiṃ agamāsi. Ayaṃ pajāti sattalokaṃ nidasseti.

301. Thus, not killing cows in their sacrifices, their bodies supported by the power of their merit, they were delicate... (etc.) ... this generation prospered in happiness. Therein, 'delicate' is because of the softness and tenderness of their hands, feet, etc.; 'large-bodied' is because of their excellent height and girth; 'radiant' is because of their golden complexion and well-proportioned form; 'renowned' is because of their endowment with gain and retinue. 'By their own principles' means by their own conduct. 'Zealous in what should and should not be done' means they were zealous about what should be done, thinking, 'This should be done,' and about what should not be done, thinking, 'This should not be done.' Thus those ancient brahmins, being of such a kind, were lovely to see, inspiring confidence, the world's supreme field for offerings. For as long as they continued in the world in accordance with this practice, they were free from calamities, fear, and troubles, and they prospered in and attained various kinds of happiness; or, they prospered in happiness, they went to growth in happiness. 'This generation' indicates the world of beings.

302-3. Kālaccayena pana sambhinnamariyādabhāvaṃ āpajjitukāmānaṃ tesaṃ āsi vipallāso…pe… bhāgaso mite. Tattha vipallāsoti viparītasaññā. Aṇuto aṇunti lāmakaṭṭhena parittaṭṭhena appassādaṭṭhena aṇubhūtato kāmaguṇato uppannaṃ jhānasāmaññanibbānasukhāni upanidhāya saṅkhyampi anupagamanena aṇuṃ kāmasukhaṃ, lokuttarasukhaṃ vā upanidhāya aṇubhūtato attanā paṭiladdhalokiyasamāpattisukhato aṇuṃ appakatopi appakaṃ kāmasukhaṃ disvāti adhippāyo. Rājino cāti rañño ca. Viyākāranti sampattiṃ. Ājaññasaṃyutteti assājānīyasaṃyutte. Sukateti dārukammalohakammena suniṭṭhite. Cittasibbaneti sīhacammādīhi alaṅkaraṇavasena [P 1.0320] citrasibbane. Nivesaneti gharavatthūni. Niveseti tattha patiṭṭhāpitagharāni. Vibhatteti āyāmavitthāravasena vibhattāni. Bhāgaso miteti aṅgaṇadvārapāsādakūṭāgārādivasena koṭṭhāsaṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ katvā mitāni. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Tesaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ aṇuto aṇusaññitaṃ kāmasukhañca rañño byākārañca alaṅkatanāriyo ca vuttappakāre rathe ca nivesane nivese ca disvā dukkhesuyeva etesu vatthūsu “sukha”nti pavattattā pubbe pavattanekkhammasaññāvipallāsasaṅkhātā viparītasaññā āsi.

302–3. 'But with the passing of time, a distortion arose in them... (etc.) ... measured out in parts.' Therein, 'distortion' means distorted perception. 'From the subtle to the subtle': this refers to seeing a subtle sensual pleasure. It is called subtle because it is trifling, limited, and of little gratification, arising from a subtle sense object; and it is subtle because it is insignificant when compared to the bliss of jhāna, the fruits of recluseship, and Nibbāna. Or, it is subtle when compared to supramundane bliss, and even more subtle than the worldly bliss of attainment that one has oneself obtained. This is the intention. 'And of the king' means of the ruler. 'Splendor' means prosperity. 'Yoked with thoroughbreds' means yoked with thoroughbred horses. 'Well-made' means well-finished with woodwork and metalwork. 'With colorful trappings' means with colorful decorations such as lion skins. 'Mansions' means housing sites. 'Residences' means the houses established there. 'Apportioned' means divided according to length and breadth. 'Measured out in parts' means measured by creating sections for courtyards, gates, palaces, gabled chambers, etc. What is meant? Having seen that subtle sensual pleasure, the king's splendor, adorned women, the aforementioned chariots, mansions, and residences, a distorted perception arose in those brahmins. This was a distortion of their former perception of renunciation, since a perception of 'happiness' occurred in regard to these things that are in fact suffering.

304. Te [M 2.0055] evaṃ viparītasaññā hutvā gomaṇḍalaparibyūḷhaṃ…pe… brāhmaṇā. Tattha gomaṇḍalaparibyūḷhanti goyūthehi parikiṇṇaṃ. Nārīvaragaṇāyutanti varanārīgaṇasaṃyuttaṃ. Uḷāranti vipulaṃ[V 2.0050]. Mānusaṃ bhoganti manussānaṃ nivesanādibhogavatthuṃ. Abhijjhāyiṃsūti “aho vatidaṃ amhākaṃ assā”ti taṇhaṃ vaḍḍhetvā abhipatthayamānā jhāyiṃsu.

304. Thus having distorted perception, they coveted... 'surrounded by herds of cattle... (etc.) ... the brahmins.' Therein, 'surrounded by herds of cattle' means encircled by herds of cattle. 'Attended by troops of choice women' means accompanied by groups of excellent women. 'Vast' means extensive. 'Human enjoyment' means the basis for enjoyment for humans, such as mansions. 'They coveted' means they yearned for it, increasing their craving and desiring it, thinking, 'Oh, that this might be ours!'

305. Evaṃ abhijjhāyantā ca “ete manussā sunhātā suvilittā kappitakesamassū āmuttamaṇiābharaṇā pañcahi kāmaguṇehi paricārenti, mayaṃ pana evaṃ tehi namassiyamānāpi sedamalakiliṭṭhagattā parūḷhakacchanakhalomā bhogarahitā paramakāruññataṃ pattā viharāma. Ete ca hatthikkhandhaassapiṭṭhisivikāsuvaṇṇarathādīhi vicaranti, mayaṃ pādehi. Ete dvibhūmikādipāsādatalesu vasanti, mayaṃ araññarukkhamūlādīsu. Ete ca gonakādīhi attharaṇehi atthatāsu varaseyyāsu sayanti, mayaṃ taṭṭikācammakhaṇḍādīni attharitvā bhūmiyaṃ. Ete nānārasāni bhojanāni bhuñjanti, mayaṃ uñchācariyāya yāpema. Kathaṃ nu kho mayampi etehi sadisā bhaveyyāmā”ti cintetvā “dhanaṃ icchitabbaṃ, na sakkā dhanarahitehi ayaṃ sampatti pāpuṇitu”nti ca avadhāretvā vede bhinditvā dhammayutte purāṇamante nāsetvā adhammayutte kūṭamante ganthetvā dhanatthikā okkākarājānamupasaṅkamma sotthivacanādīni payuñjitvā “amhākaṃ, mahārāja, brāhmaṇavaṃse paveṇiyā āgataṃ porāṇamantapadaṃ atthi, taṃ mayaṃ ācariyamuṭṭhitāya [P 1.0321] na kassaci bhaṇimhā, taṃ mahārājā sotumarahatī”ti ca vatvā assamedhādiyaññaṃ vaṇṇayiṃsu. Vaṇṇayitvā ca rājānaṃ ussāhentā “yaja, mahārāja, evaṃ pahūtadhanadhañño tvaṃ, natthi te yaññasambhāravekallaṃ, evañhi te yajato sattakulaparivaṭṭā sagge uppajjissantī”ti avocuṃ. Tena nesaṃ taṃ pavattiṃ dassento āha bhagavā “te tattha mante…pe… bahu te dhana”nti.

305. And while coveting thus, they thought: 'These people are well-bathed, well-anointed, with trimmed hair and beards, adorned with jeweled ornaments, and they amuse themselves with the five cords of sensual pleasure. But we, though honored by them, live with sweaty, dirty bodies, with overgrown armpit-hair, nails, and body-hair, bereft of possessions, having reached a state of extreme pitiableness. These people travel on the backs of elephants and horses, in palanquins, golden chariots, and so on, while we go on foot. They dwell on the floors of two-storied palaces and the like, while we live in the forest at the foot of trees. They sleep on excellent beds spread with coverings such as long-fleeced woolen blankets, while we sleep on the ground, having spread out mats of woven grass, pieces of hide, and the like. They eat foods of various flavors, while we sustain ourselves by gleaning. How, now, can we become like them?' Reflecting thus, they concluded: 'Wealth must be sought; this prosperity cannot be attained by those without wealth.' Then, having corrupted the Vedas, having destroyed the ancient verses connected with the Dhamma, and having composed fraudulent verses unconnected with the Dhamma, desiring wealth, they approached King Okkāka. Having uttered words of blessing and so on, they said: 'Great king, in our brahmin lineage there is an ancient corpus of verses that has come down by tradition. Out of the teacher's closed fist, we have not told it to anyone. The great king deserves to hear it.' And they praised the horse sacrifice and other sacrifices. Having praised them and urging on the king, they said: 'Sacrifice, great king! You have abundant wealth and grain; for you there is no lack of sacrificial requisites. If you sacrifice thus, seven generations of your family will be reborn in heaven.' To show this course of theirs, the Blessed One said: 'They, having composed verses there... (etc.) ... you have much wealth.'

Tattha tatthāti tasmiṃ, yaṃ bhogamabhijjhāyiṃsu, tannimittanti vuttaṃ hoti. Nimittatthe hi etaṃ bhummavacanaṃ. Tadupāgamunti tadā upāgamuṃ. Pahūtadhanadhaññosīti pahūtadhanadhañño bhavissasi, abhisamparāyanti adhippāyo. Āsaṃsāyañhi anāgatepi vattamānavacanaṃ icchanti saddakovidā. Yajassūti [M 2.0056] yajāhi. Vittaṃ dhananti jātarūpādiratanameva vittikāraṇato vittaṃ, samiddhikāraṇato dhananti vuttaṃ. Atha vā vittanti vittikāraṇabhūtameva ābharaṇādi upakaraṇaṃ, yaṃ “pahūtavittūpakaraṇo”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.331) āgacchati. Dhananti hiraññasuvaṇṇādi. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Te brāhmaṇā mante ganthetvā tadā okkākaṃ upāgamuṃ. Kinti? “Mahārāja, bahū te vittañca dhanañca, yajassu, āyatimpi pahūtadhanadhañño bhavissasī”ti.

Therein, 'there' means 'in that,' that is, concerning the enjoyment they coveted; it is said to be 'on account of that.' For this locative expression is used in the sense of a reason. 'Then they approached' means they approached at that time. 'You have abundant wealth and grain' means 'you will have abundant wealth and grain in the future'; this is the intention. For in the sense of hope, those skilled in grammar allow the present tense even for the future. 'Sacrifice' means 'you should sacrifice.' 'Possessions and wealth': jewels such as gold are called 'possessions' because they are a cause of finding, and 'wealth' because they are a cause of prosperity. Alternatively, 'possessions' means equipment such as ornaments that are a cause of finding, as comes in such passages as 'with abundant possessions and equipment.' 'Wealth' means silver, gold, and so on. What is meant? Those brahmins, having composed the verses, then approached Okkāka. How? By saying: 'Great king, you have many possessions and much wealth; sacrifice, and in the future too you will have abundant wealth and grain.'

306. Evaṃ kāraṇaṃ vatvā saññāpentehi tato ca rājā…pe… adā dhanaṃ. Tattha saññattoti [V 2.0051] ñāpito. Rathesabhoti mahārathesu khattiyesu akampiyaṭṭhena usabhasadiso. “Assamedha”ntiādīsu assamettha medhantīti assamedho, dvīhi pariyaññehi yajitabbassa ekavīsatiyūpassa ṭhapetvā bhūmiñca purise ca avasesasabbavibhavadakkhiṇassa yaññassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Purisamettha medhantīti purisamedho, catūhi pariyaññehi yajitabbassa saddhiṃ bhūmiyā assamedhe vuttavibhavadakkhiṇassa yaññassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sammamettha pāsantīti sammāpāso, divase divase sammaṃ khipitvā tassa patitokāse vediṃ katvā saṃhārimehi yūpādīhi sarassatinadiyā nimuggokāsato pabhuti paṭilomaṃ gacchantena [P 1.0322] yajitabbassa satrayāgassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Vājamettha pivantīti vājapeyyo. Ekena pariyaññena sattarasahi pasūhi yajitabbassa beluvayūpassa sattarasakadakkhiṇassa yaññassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Natthi ettha aggaḷāti niraggaḷo, navahi pariyaññehi yajitabbassa saddhiṃ bhūmiyā ca purisehi ca assamedhe vuttavibhavadakkhiṇassa sabbamedhapariyāyanāmassa assamedhavikappassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sesamettha pākaṭameva.

306. When they had thus stated the reason and were persuading him, then the king... (etc.) ... gave wealth. Therein, 'persuaded' means informed. 'A bull among chariot-warriors' means like a bull among the great chariot-warrior khattiyas on account of being unshakable. In 'horse sacrifice,' etc.: 'horse sacrifice' is so called because they sacrifice a horse here; this is the designation for a sacrifice to be performed with two surrounding sacrifices and twenty-one posts, in which, excluding the land and the men, all remaining property is the sacrificial gift. 'Human sacrifice' is so called because they sacrifice a man here; this is the designation for a sacrifice to be performed with four surrounding sacrifices, in which the sacrificial gift is the property described in the horse sacrifice together with the land. 'The peg-throw' is so called because they throw a peg here; every day, having thrown the peg, on the spot where it falls they construct an altar; this is the designation for a protracted sacrifice to be performed with portable posts and so on, proceeding upstream from the place where the Sarasvatī river goes underground. 'The drink of strength' is so called because they drink a strength-giving beverage here; this is the designation for a sacrifice to be performed with one surrounding sacrifice and seventeen animals, with a seventeenfold sacrificial gift. 'The unobstructed' is so called because there is no bolt here; this is the designation for a variant of the horse sacrifice, a name that is a synonym for the 'all-sacrifice,' to be performed with nine surrounding sacrifices, in which the sacrificial gift is the property described in the horse sacrifice together with the land and the men. The rest here is evident.

307-8. Idāni yaṃ vuttaṃ “brāhmaṇānamadā dhana”nti, taṃ dassento “gāvo sayanañcā”ti gāthādvayamāha. So hi rājā “dīgharattaṃ lūkhāhārena kilantā pañca gorase paribhuñjantū”ti nesaṃ sapuṅgavāni goyūthāneva adāsi, tathā “dīgharattaṃ thaṇḍilasāyitāya thūlasāṭakanivāsanena [M 2.0057] ekaseyyāya pādacārena rukkhamūlādivāsena ca kilantā gonakādiatthatavarasayanādīsu sukhaṃ anubhontū”ti nesaṃ mahagghāni sayanādīni ca adāsi. Evametaṃ nānappakārakaṃ aññañca hiraññasuvaṇṇādidhanaṃ adāsi. Tenāha bhagavā – “gāvo sayanañca vatthañca…pe… brāhmaṇānamadā dhana”nti.

307-8. Now, to show what was said, “He gave wealth to the brahmins,” he speaks the two verses beginning: “Cows and beds….” For that king gave them herds of cattle complete with bulls, thinking: “Let them enjoy the five products of the cow, since they have long been exhausted by coarse food.” Similarly, he gave them costly beds and other items, thinking: “Since they have long been exhausted by sleeping on the bare ground, wearing coarse garments, sleeping in one place, walking on foot, and dwelling at the roots of trees, let them now enjoy comfort on excellent beds with coverings such as woolen blankets.” Thus he gave them this and other various kinds of wealth, including gold and bullion. Therefore the Blessed One said: “Cows and beds and garments… he gave wealth to the brahmins.”

309-10. Evaṃ tassa rañño santikā te ca tattha…pe… puna mupāgamuṃ. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Tassa rañño santikā te brāhmaṇā tesu yāgesu dhanaṃ labhitvā dīgharattaṃ divase divase evameva ghāsacchādanaṃ pariyesitvā nānappakārakaṃ vatthukāma sannidhiṃ samarocayuṃ. Tato tesaṃ icchāvatiṇṇānaṃ khīrādipañcagorasassādavasena rasataṇhāya otiṇṇacittānaṃ “khīrādīnipi tāva gunnaṃ sādūni, addhā imāsaṃ maṃsaṃ sādutaraṃ bhavissatī”ti evaṃ maṃsaṃ paṭicca bhiyyo taṇhā pavaḍḍhatha. Tato cintesuṃ – “sace mayaṃ māretvā khādissāma, gārayhā bhavissāma, yaṃnūna mante gantheyyāmā”ti. Atha punapi vedaṃ bhinditvā tadanurūpe te tattha mante ganthetvā te brāhmaṇā tannimittaṃ [P 1.0323] kūṭamante ganthetvā okkākarājānaṃ puna upāgamiṃsu. Imamatthaṃ bhāsamānā “yathā āpo ca…pe… bahu te dhana”nti.

309-10. Thus those brahmins approached him again from near the king. What is meant? Having received wealth from that king at those sacrifices, those brahmins for a long time sought food and clothing day after day and took delight in accumulating a store of various kinds of material treasures. Then, as they had given in to desire, their minds were overcome by craving for tastes on account of their enjoying the flavor of the five products of the cow, such as milk. Their craving grew all the more on account of meat, and they thought: “The milk and so on of cows is delicious; surely their meat must be even more delicious.” Then they considered: “If we kill and eat them, we will be censurable. Let us compose some mantras.” Then, breaking with the Veda, they composed mantras appropriate for that. Having composed deceitful mantras for that purpose, those brahmins approached King Okkāka again. Speaking on this matter, they recited the verse beginning: “Just as water… much is your wealth.”

Kiṃ [V 2.0052] vuttaṃ hoti? Amhākaṃ, mahārāja, mantesu etadāgataṃ yathā āpo hatthadhovanādisabbakiccesu pāṇīnaṃ upayogaṃ gacchati, natthi tesaṃ tatonidānaṃ pāpaṃ. Kasmā? Yasmā parikkhāro so hi pāṇinaṃ, upakaraṇatthāya uppannoti adhippāyo. Yathā cāyaṃ mahāpathavī gamanaṭṭhānādisabbakiccesu kahāpaṇasaṅkhātaṃ hiraññaṃ suvaṇṇarajatādibhedaṃ dhanaṃ, yavagodhūmādibhedaṃ dhāniyañca, saṃvohārādisabbakiccesu upayogaṃ gacchati, evaṃ gāvo manussānaṃ sabbakiccesu upayogagamanatthāya uppannā. Tasmā etā hanitvā nānappakārake yāge yajassu bahu te vittaṃ, yajassu bahu te dhananti.

What is meant? “Great king, this has come down in our mantras: just as water is of use to living beings for all purposes such as washing hands, and there is no evil for them on that account—why? because it is a requisite for living beings; the intention is that it has arisen for their use—and just as this great earth is of use for all purposes such as walking and standing, and wealth such as coins, bullion, gold, and silver, and grain such as barley and wheat, are of use for all purposes such as trade, so too cows have arisen for the purpose of being useful to humans in all their affairs. Therefore, having slain them, sacrifice in various sacrifices. You have much property; sacrifice! You have much wealth; sacrifice!”

311-12. Evaṃ purimanayeneva tato ca rājā…pe… aghātayi, yaṃ tato pubbe kañci sattaṃ na pādā…pe… ghātayi. Tadā kira brāhmaṇā yaññāvāṭaṃ gāvīnaṃ pūretvā maṅgalausabhaṃ bandhitvā rañño mūlaṃ netvā “mahārāja, gomedhayaññaṃ yajassu, evaṃ te brahmalokassa maggo visuddho bhavissatī”ti [M 2.0058] āhaṃsu. Rājā katamaṅgalakicco khaggaṃ gahetvā puṅgavena saha anekasatasahassā gāvo māresi. Brāhmaṇā yaññāvāṭe maṃsāni chinditvā khādiṃsu, pītakodātarattakambale ca pārupitvā māresuṃ. Tadupādāya kira gāvo pārute disvā ubbijjanti. Tenāha bhagavā – “na pādā…pe… ghātayī”ti.

311-12. Thus, in the same way as before: “Then the king… had them slain.” He had slain those whom previously he had not harmed, not even 'with a foot...' It is said that at that time the brahmins filled the sacrificial pit with cows, tied up a ceremonial bull, led it to the king, and said: “Great king, perform the cow-sacrifice! In this way the path to the brahmā-world will be purified for you.” The king, having performed the auspicious rites, took a sword and, along with the bull, slaughtered many hundreds of thousands of cows. The brahmins cut up the meat in the sacrificial pit and ate it; and having draped themselves in yellow, white, and red blankets, they killed. It is said that ever since then, cows are startled when they see people draped in such things. Therefore the Blessed One said: “Not with his foot… he had slain.”

313. Tato devāti evaṃ tasmiṃ rājini gāviyo ghātetumāraddhe atha tadanantarameva taṃ goghātakaṃ disvā ete cātumahārājikādayo devā ca, pitaroti brāhmaṇesu laddhavohārā brahmāno ca, sakko devānamindo ca, pabbatapādanivāsino dānavayakkhasaññitā asurarakkhasā ca “adhammo adhammo”ti evaṃ vācaṃ nicchārentā “dhi manussā, dhi manussā”ti ca vadantā pakkanduṃ. Evaṃ bhūmito pabhuti so saddo muhuttena yāva brahmalokā agamāsi, ekadhikkāraparipuṇṇo loko ahosi. Kiṃ kāraṇaṃ? Yaṃ satthaṃ nipatī gave, yasmā gāvimhi satthaṃ nipatīti vuttaṃ hoti.

313. Then the devas: When that king had begun to have the cows slain, right afterwards, seeing that cow-slaughterer, these devas headed by the Four Great Kings, and the fathers—that is, the Brahmās who are designated as such among the brahmins—and Sakka, lord of the devas, and the asuras and rakkhasas known as dānavas and yakkhas who dwell at the feet of the mountains, all cried out, uttering the words, “This is unrighteousness! This is unrighteousness!” and saying, “Fie on human beings! Fie on human beings!” Thus, starting from the earth, that sound in an instant went as far as the Brahmā-world. The world was filled with a single cry of reproach. What is the reason? Because the knife fell on the cows; that is to say, the knife fell on a cow.

314. Na kevalañca devādayo pakkanduṃ, ayamaññopi loke anattho [P 1.0324] udapādi – ye hi te tayo rogā pure āsuṃ, icchā anasanaṃ jarā, kiñci kiñcideva patthanataṇhā ca khudā ca paripākajarā cāti vuttaṃ hoti. Te pasūnañca samārambhā, aṭṭhānavutimāgamuṃ, cakkhurogādinā bhedena aṭṭhanavutibhāvaṃ pāpuṇiṃsūti attho.

314. Not only did the devas and others cry out, but this other calamity also arose in the world. For those three diseases that existed before—desire, starvation, and old age (that is to say, craving that consists in wishing for this or that, hunger, and the decay of old age)—from that onslaught on cattle, came to be ninety-eight. The meaning is that they reached the state of ninety-eight through such divisions as eye-disease.

315. Idāni bhagavā taṃ pasusamārambhaṃ nindanto āha “eso adhammo”ti. Tassattho eso [V 2.0053] pasusamārambhasaṅkhāto kāyadaṇḍādīnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ daṇḍānaṃ aññataradaṇḍabhūto dhammato apetattā adhammo okkanto ahu, pavatto āsi, so ca kho tato pabhuti pavattattā purāṇo, yassa okkamanato pabhuti kenaci pādādinā ahiṃsanato adūsikāyo gāvo haññanti. Yā ghātentā dhammā dhaṃsanti cavanti parihāyanti yājakā yaññayājino janāti.

315. Now the Blessed One, censuring that onslaught on cattle, said: “This is unrighteousness.” Its meaning is this: this, the so-called onslaught on cattle, being one of the three rods such as the bodily rod, is unrighteousness because it is contrary to Dhamma. It was inflicted, it was set in motion. And because it has been in motion ever since, it is ancient. From the time of its infliction, innocent, unblemished cows are slain, though they had not been hurt by anyone with foot or the like. The sacrificers, the people who perform sacrifices, in slaying them, fall away, shift, and decline from the Dhamma.

316. Evameso aṇudhammoti evaṃ eso lāmakadhammo hīnadhammo, adhammoti vuttaṃ hoti. Yasmā vā ettha dānadhammopi appako atthi[M 2.0059], tasmā taṃ sandhāyāha “aṇudhammo”ti. Porāṇoti tāva cirakālato pabhuti pavattattā porāṇo. Viññūhi pana garahitattā viññūgarahitoti veditabbo. Yasmā ca viññugarahito, tasmā yattha edisakaṃ passati, yājakaṃ garahatī jano. Kathaṃ? “Abbudaṃ brāhmaṇehi uppāditaṃ, gāvo vadhitvā maṃsaṃ khādantī”ti evamādīni vatvāti ayamettha anussavo.

316. Thus this is a minor practice: thus this is a base practice, an inferior practice; it is unrighteousness, is what is said. Or, because there is a small element of the practice of giving here, with reference to that he said ‘a minor practice.’ Ancient: it is ancient because it has been in motion for such a long time. But it should be understood as censured by the wise because it is censured by the wise. And since it is censured by the wise, wherever one sees such a thing, the people censure the sacrificer. How? By saying such things as: “This monstrous thing was created by the brahmins, who kill cattle and eat the meat.” This is the report here.

317. Evaṃ dhamme viyāpanneti evaṃ porāṇe brāhmaṇadhamme naṭṭhe. “Viyāvatte”tipi pāṭho, viparivattitvā aññathā bhūteti attho. Vibhinnā suddavessikāti pubbe samaggā viharantā suddā ca vessā ca te vibhinnā. Puthū vibhinnā khattiyāti khattiyāpi bahū aññamaññaṃ bhinnā. Patiṃ bhariyāvamaññathāti bhariyā ca gharāvāsatthaṃ issariyabale ṭhapitā puttabalādīhi upetā hutvā patiṃ avamaññatha, paribhavi avamaññi na sakkaccaṃ upaṭṭhāsi.

317. Thus when the practice was violated: thus when the ancient brahminical practice was lost. There is also the reading ‘viyāvatte,’ meaning having been transformed and become otherwise. Suddas and vessas were divided: the suddas and the vessas, who had formerly dwelt in harmony, were divided. Khattiyas were divided in many ways: many khattiyas were also divided from one another. A wife would despise her husband: a wife, established in the power of authority for the sake of household life and endowed with the strength of sons and so on, would despise her husband; she would scorn him, look down on him, and not attend to him respectfully.

318. Evaṃ aññamaññaṃ vibhinnā samānā khattiyā brahmabandhū ca…pe… kāmānaṃ vasamanvagunti. Khattiyā ca brāhmaṇā ca ye caññe vessasuddā yathā saṅkaraṃ nāpajjanti, evaṃ attano attano gottena rakkhitattā gottarakkhitā. Te sabbepi taṃ jātivādaṃ niraṃkatvā, “ahaṃ khattiyo, ahaṃ brāhmaṇo”ti etaṃ sabbampi nāsetvā [P 1.0325] pañcakāmaguṇasaṅkhātānaṃ kāmānaṃ vasaṃ anvaguṃ āsattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu, kāmahetu na kiñci akattabbaṃ nākaṃsūti vuttaṃ hoti.

318. Thus, being divided from one another, khattiyas and brahmin-kin… came under the sway of sensual pleasures. Khattiyas, brahmins, and the others—vessas and suddas—who were protected by their own respective clans so that they would not fall into a confusion of castes, are ‘clan-protected.’ All of them, having disregarded that doctrine of birth and having destroyed all that—“I am a khattiya,” “I am a brahmin”—came under the sway of sensual pleasures, that is, the five strands of sensual pleasure. They became attached. It is said that for the sake of sensual pleasures, there was nothing improper that they would not do.

Evamettha bhagavā “isayo pubbakā”tiādīhi navahi gāthāhi porāṇānaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ vaṇṇaṃ bhāsitvā “yo nesaṃ paramo”ti gāthāya brahmasamaṃ, “tassa vattamanusikkhantā”ti gāthāya devasamaṃ, “taṇḍulaṃ sayana”ntiādikāhi catūhi gāthāhi mariyādaṃ, “tesaṃ āsi vipallāso”tiādīhi sattarasahi gāthāhi sambhinnamariyādaṃ, tassa vippaṭipattiyā devādīnaṃ pakkandanādidīpanatthañca dassetvā desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi. Brāhmaṇacaṇḍālo pana idha avuttoyeva. Kasmā? Yasmā vipattiyā akāraṇaṃ. Brāhmaṇadhammasampattiyā hi brahmasamadevasamamariyādā kāraṇaṃ [V 2.0054][M 2.0060] honti, vipattiyā sambhinnamariyādo. Ayaṃ pana doṇasutte (a. ni. 5.192) vuttappakāro brāhmaṇacaṇḍālo brāhmaṇadhammavipattiyāpi akāraṇaṃ. Kasmā? Vipanne dhamme uppannattā. Tasmā taṃ adassetvāva desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi. Etarahi pana sopi brāhmaṇacaṇḍālo dullabho. Evamayaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ dhammo vinaṭṭho. Tenevāha doṇo brāhmaṇo – “evaṃ sante mayaṃ, bho gotama, brāhmaṇacaṇḍālampi na pūremā”ti. Sesamettha vuttanayameva.

Thus here the Blessed One, having spoken in praise of the ancient brahmins with the nine verses beginning “The ancient seers,” concluded the discourse by showing: with the verse “The one among them who was supreme,” their likeness to Brahmā; with the verse “Training in his conduct,” their likeness to the devas; with the four verses beginning “Rice, a bed,” their boundary; with the seventeen verses beginning “There was a deviation for them,” the corrupted boundary, and also illuminating the crying out of the devas and others because of that wrong practice. But the brahmin-outcaste is not mentioned here. Why? Because he is not a cause of the decline. For the accomplishment of the brahminical practice, the causes are the likeness to Brahmā, the likeness to the devas, and the boundary; for the decline, the cause is the corrupted boundary. But this brahmin-outcaste of the type mentioned in the Doṇa Sutta is not a cause of the decline of the brahminical practice. Why? Because he arose after the practice was violated. Therefore the Blessed One concluded the discourse without showing him. But nowadays even that brahmin-outcaste is rare. Thus this practice of the brahmins has been lost. That is why the brahmin Doṇa said: “This being so, Master Gotama, we do not even fulfill the role of a brahmin-outcaste.” The rest is in the way already stated.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya brāhmaṇadhammikasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Brāhmaṇadhammika Sutta in the Commentary on the Suttanipāta is finished.

8. Dhammasutta-(nāvāsutta)-vaṇṇanā

8. The Explanation of the Dhamma Sutta (Nāvā Sutta)

319. Yasmā [V 2.0055] hi dhammanti dhammasuttaṃ, “nāvāsutta”ntipi vuccati. Kā uppatti? Idaṃ suttaṃ āyasmantaṃ sāriputtattheraṃ ārabbha vuttaṃ. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana dvinnaṃ aggasāvakānaṃ uppattito pabhuti veditabbo. Seyyathidaṃ – anuppanne [P 1.0326] kira bhagavati dve aggasāvakā ekaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ kappasatasahassañca pāramiyo pūretvā devaloke nibbattā. Tesaṃ paṭhamo cavitvā rājagahassa avidūre upatissagāmo nāma brāhmaṇānaṃ bhogagāmo atthi, tattha saṭṭhiadhikapañcakoṭisatadhanavibhavassa gāmasāmino brāhmaṇassa rūpasārī nāma brāhmaṇī, tassā kucchiyaṃ paṭisandhiṃ aggahesi. Dutiyo tassevāvidūre kolitagāmo nāma brāhmaṇānaṃ bhogagāmo atthi. Tattha tathārūpavibhavasseva gāmasāmino brāhmaṇassa moggallānī nāma brāhmaṇī, tassā kucchiyaṃ taṃ divasameva paṭisandhiṃ aggahesi. Evaṃ tesaṃ ekadivasameva paṭisandhiggahaṇañca gabbhavuṭṭhānañca ahosi. Ekadivaseyeva ca nesaṃ ekassa upatissagāme jātattā upatisso, ekassa kolitagāme jātattā kolitoti nāmamakaṃsu.

319. Because it is about the Dhamma, it is the Dhammasutta; it is also called the Nāvā Sutta. What is its origin? This discourse was spoken with reference to the Venerable Sāriputta the Elder. This is the summary; the detailed account, however, should be understood from the arising of the two chief disciples onwards. It is as follows: Before the Blessed One arose, it is said, the two chief disciples, having fulfilled the perfections for one incalculable and one hundred thousand aeons, were reborn in the deva world. The first of them passed away from there and took conception in the womb of a brahmin woman named Rūpasārī, the wife of a village-head brahmin possessing wealth of five hundred and sixty crores, in a prosperous brahmin village named Upatissagāma, not far from Rājagaha. The second took conception on that very day in the womb of a brahmin woman named Moggallānī, the wife of a village-head brahmin of similar wealth, in a prosperous brahmin village named Kolitagāma, also not far from there. Thus their conception and their birth from the womb occurred on the same day. And on the same day they were named: because one was born in Upatissagāma, he was named Upatissa; because the other was born in Kolitagāma, he was named Kolita.

Te [M 2.0061] sahapaṃsuṃ kīḷantā sahāyakā anupubbena vuḍḍhiṃ pāpuṇiṃsu, ekamekassa ca pañcapañcamāṇavakasatāni parivārā ahesuṃ. Te uyyānaṃ vā nadītitthaṃ vā gacchantā saparivārāyeva gacchanti. Eko pañcahi suvaṇṇasivikāsatehi, dutiyo pañcahi ājaññarathasatehi. Tadā ca rājagahe kālānukālaṃ giraggasamajjo nāma hoti. Sāyanhasamaye nagaravemajjhe yattha sakalaaṅgamagadhavāsino abhiññātā khattiyakumārādayo sannipatitvā supaññattesu mañcapīṭhādīsu nisinnā samajjavibhūtiṃ passanti. Atha te sahāyakā tena parivārena saddhiṃ tattha gantvā paññattāsanesu nisīdiṃsu. Tato upatisso samajjavibhūtiṃ passanto mahājanakāyaṃ sannipatitaṃ disvā “ettako janakāyo vassasataṃ appatvāva marissatī”ti cintesi. Tassa maraṇaṃ āgantvā nalāṭante patiṭṭhitaṃ viya ahosi, tathā kolitassa. Tesaṃ anekappakāresu naṭesu naccantesu dassanamattepi cittaṃ na nami, aññadatthu saṃvegoyeva udapādi.

They, friends who played together in the dust, gradually grew up, and each had a retinue of five hundred young brahmins. When they went to a park or a river ford, they went with their retinues. One went with five hundred golden palanquins, the other with five hundred thoroughbred chariots. At that time in Rājagaha a festival called the Hilltop Festival was held from time to time. In the evening, in the middle of the city, well-known khattiya youths and others from all over Aṅga and Magadha would gather and, seated on well-prepared couches, chairs, and so on, watch the splendor of the festival. Then those two friends, along with their retinues, went there and sat on the prepared seats. There, Upatissa, watching the splendor of the festival and seeing the great crowd that had gathered, thought: “This whole crowd of people will die without reaching a hundred years.” It was as if death had come and stood on his forehead; the same was true for Kolita. Though actors of many kinds were dancing, their minds did not incline in the least toward watching them; on the contrary, only a sense of spiritual urgency arose in them.

Atha vuṭṭhite samajje pakkantāya parisāya sakaparivārena pakkantesu tesu sahāyesu kolito [V 2.0056] upatissaṃ pucchi – “kiṃ, samma, nāṭakādidassanena tava pamodanamattampi [P 1.0327] nāhosī”ti? So tassa taṃ pavattiṃ ārocetvā tampi tatheva paṭipucchi. Sopi tassa attano pavattiṃ ārocetvā “ehi, samma, pabbajitvā amataṃ gavesāmā”ti āha. “Sādhu sammā”ti upatisso taṃ sampaṭicchi. Tato dvepi janā taṃ sampattiṃ chaḍḍetvā punadeva rājagahamanuppattā. Tena ca samayena rājagahe sañcayo nāma paribbājako paṭivasati. Te tassa santike pañcahi māṇavakasatehi saddhiṃ pabbajitvā katipāheneva tayo vede sabbañca paribbājakasamayaṃ uggahesuṃ. Te tesaṃ satthānaṃ ādimajjhapariyosānaṃ upaparikkhantā pariyosānaṃ adisvā ācariyaṃ pucchiṃsu – “imesaṃ satthānaṃ ādimajjhaṃ dissati, pariyosānaṃ pana na dissati ‘idaṃ nāma imehi satthehi pāpuṇeyyāti, yato uttari pāpuṇitabbaṃ natthī’”ti. Sopi āha – “ahampi tesaṃ tathāvidhaṃ pariyosānaṃ na passāmī”ti. Te āhaṃsu – “tena hi mayaṃ imesaṃ pariyosānaṃ gavesāmā”ti. Te ācariyo “yathāsukhaṃ gavesathā”ti āha. Evaṃ te tena anuññātā amataṃ gavesamānā āhiṇḍantā jambudīpe pākaṭā ahesuṃ. Tehi khattiyapaṇḍitādayo pañhaṃ puṭṭhā uttaruttariṃ na sampāyanti. “Upatisso [M 2.0062] kolito”ti vutte pana “ke ete, na kho mayaṃ jānāmā”ti bhaṇantā natthi, evaṃ vissutā ahesuṃ.

Then, when the festival was over and the crowd had departed, as the two friends were leaving with their retinues, Kolita asked Upatissa: “Friend, did you get no pleasure at all from watching the plays and so on?” Upatissa told him what had happened and asked him the same in return. Kolita also recounted his own experience and said: “Come, friend, let us go forth and seek the Deathless.” Upatissa agreed, saying: “Good, friend.” Thereupon, both men abandoned their fortune and went back to Rājagaha. At that time, a wanderer named Sañjaya was residing in Rājagaha. They went forth under him along with their five hundred young men and within a few days mastered the three Vedas and the entire system of the wanderers. Examining the beginning, middle, and end of their teacher’s doctrines, they did not see a final goal. So they asked their teacher: “In these doctrines, the beginning and middle are seen, but the end is not seen—that is, a goal to be attained by these doctrines beyond which there is nothing further to be reached.” He replied: “I too do not see such a final goal in them.” They said: “In that case, we will seek their final goal ourselves.” Their teacher said: “Seek as you please.” Thus permitted by him, they wandered in search of the Deathless and became well-known throughout Jambudīpa. When questioned by them, learned khattiyas and others could not provide a conclusive answer. But when “Upatissa and Kolita” were mentioned, there was no one who would say, “Who are they? We do not know them”—so famous had they become.

Evaṃ tesu amatapariyesanaṃ caramānesu amhākaṃ bhagavā loke uppajjitvā pavattitavaradhammacakko anupubbena rājagahamanuppatto. Te ca paribbājakā sakalajambudīpaṃ caritvā tiṭṭhatu amataṃ, antamaso pariyosānapañhavissajjanamattampi alabhantā punadeva rājagahaṃ agamaṃsu. Atha kho āyasmā assaji pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvāti yāva tesaṃ pabbajjā, tāva sabbaṃ pabbajjākkhandhake (mahāva. 60) āgatanayeneva vitthārato daṭṭhabbaṃ.

While they were thus wandering in search of the Deathless, our Blessed One arose in the world and, having set rolling the excellent Wheel of the Dhamma, in due course arrived at Rājagaha. And those wanderers, having roamed all over Jambudīpa, returned once more to Rājagaha without finding the Deathless, without obtaining even so much as an answer to their question about the final goal. Then, the entire story, from “the Venerable Assaji, having dressed in the morning…” up to their going forth, should be understood in detail in the way it is given in the Pabbajjākkhandhaka (Mahāvagga 60).

Evaṃ pabbajitesu tesu dvīsu sahāyakesu āyasmā sāriputto aḍḍhamāsena [P 1.0328] sāvakapāramīñāṇaṃ sacchākāsi. So yadā assajittherena saddhiṃ ekavihāre vasati, tadā bhagavato upaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā anantaraṃ therassa upaṭṭhānaṃ gacchati “pubbācariyo me ayamāyasmā, etamahaṃ nissāya bhagavato sāsanaṃ aññāsi”nti gāravena. Yadā pana assajittherena saddhiṃ ekavihāre na vasati, tadā yassaṃ disāyaṃ thero vasati, taṃ disaṃ oloketvā pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā añjaliṃ paggayha namassati. Taṃ disvā keci bhikkhū kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “sāriputto aggasāvako hutvā disaṃ namassati, ajjāpi maññe brāhmaṇadiṭṭhi appahīnā”ti. Atha bhagavā dibbāya sotadhātuyā taṃ kathāsallāpaṃ sutvā paññattavarabuddhāsane nisinnaṃyeva attānaṃ dassento bhikkhū āmantesi – “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti[V 2.0057]? Te taṃ pavattiṃ ācikkhiṃsu. Tato bhagavā “na, bhikkhave, sāriputto disaṃ namassati, yaṃ nissāya sāsanaṃ aññāsi, taṃ attano ācariyaṃ vandati namassati sammāneti, ācariyapūjako, bhikkhave, sāriputto”ti vatvā tattha sannipatitānaṃ dhammadesanatthaṃ imaṃ suttamabhāsi.

When these two friends had thus gone forth, the Venerable Sāriputta realized the knowledge of a disciple’s perfection in half a month. When he lived in the same monastery with the Elder Assaji, he would go to attend upon the Blessed One and immediately afterwards go to attend upon the Elder, thinking with reverence: “This venerable one is my first teacher; it was through reliance on him that I came to know the Blessed One’s teaching.” But when he was not living in the same monastery with the Elder Assaji, he would look toward the direction where the Elder was staying, venerate him with the five-point prostration, and pay homage with his palms joined. Seeing this, some bhikkhus started a discussion: “Sāriputta, though he is a chief disciple, pays homage to the directions. We think he has still not abandoned his brahminical view.” Then the Blessed One, hearing their conversation with his divine ear-element, revealed himself seated on the excellent prepared Buddha-seat and addressed the bhikkhus: “For what talk, bhikkhus, are you now gathered together?” They told him the account. Thereupon the Blessed One said: “No, bhikkhus, Sāriputta does not pay homage to a direction. He venerates, pays homage to, and honors the teacher through reliance on whom he came to know the teaching. Sāriputta, bhikkhus, is one who honors his teacher.” Having said this, in order to teach the Dhamma to those assembled there, the Blessed One spoke this discourse.

Tattha yasmā hi dhammaṃ puriso vijaññāti yato puggalā piṭakattayappabhedaṃ pariyattidhammaṃ vā, pariyattiṃ sutvā adhigantabbaṃ navalokuttarappabhedaṃ paṭivedhadhammaṃ vā puriso vijaññā jāneyya vedeyya. “Yassā”tipi pāṭho, so evattho. Indaṃva naṃ devatā pūjayeyyāti yathā sakkaṃ devānamindaṃ dvīsu devalokesu devatā pūjenti, evaṃ so puggalo taṃ puggalaṃ kālasseva vuṭṭhāya upāhanaomuñcanādiṃ sabbaṃ vattapaṭivattaṃ karonto [M 2.0063] pūjeyya sakkareyya garukareyya. Kiṃ kāraṇaṃ? So pūjito…pe… pātukaroti dhammaṃ, so ācariyo evaṃ pūjito tasmiṃ antevāsimhi pasannacitto pariyattipaṭivedhavasena bahussuto desanāvaseneva pariyattidhammañca, desanaṃ sutvā yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipattiyā adhigantabbaṃ paṭivedhadhammañca [P 1.0329] pātukaroti deseti, desanāya vā pariyattidhammaṃ, upamāvasena attanā adhigatapaṭivedhadhammaṃ pātukaroti.

Therein, From whom a person might know the Dhamma: from whichever person one might know, understand, and experience either the Dhamma of learning, comprised in the three Piṭakas, or the Dhamma of penetration, comprised in the nine supramundane states, which is to be realized after hearing the teaching. The reading “yassā” is also found; it has the same meaning. He should honor him as the devas honor Indra: just as the devas in the two deva worlds honor Sakka, lord of the devas, so that person should honor, revere, and respect that person, rising early and performing all the duties and services, such as removing his sandals. For what reason? Being honored… he makes the Dhamma manifest: that teacher, being thus honored, with a mind pleased with that disciple, being learned, makes manifest both the Dhamma of learning by way of teaching, and the Dhamma of penetration, which is to be realized through practice in accordance with the instructions after hearing the teaching. Or, by his teaching he makes manifest the Dhamma of learning, and by way of analogy he makes manifest the Dhamma of penetration that he himself has realized.

320. Tadaṭṭhikatvāna nisamma dhīroti evaṃ pasannena ācariyena pātukataṃ dhammaṃ aṭṭhikatvāna suṇitvā upadhāraṇasamatthatāya dhīro puriso. Dhammānudhammaṃ paṭipajjamānoti lokuttaradhammassa anulomattā anudhammabhūtaṃ vipassanaṃ bhāvayamāno. Viññū vibhāvī nipuṇo ca hotīti viññutāsaṅkhātāya paññāya adhigamena viññū, vibhāvetvā paresampi pākaṭaṃ katvā ñāpanasamatthatāya vibhāvī, paramasukhumatthapaṭivedhatāya nipuṇo ca hoti. Yo tādisaṃ bhajati appamattoti yo tādisaṃ pubbe vuttappakāraṃ bahussutaṃ appamatto tappasādanaparo hutvā bhajati.

320. Attentively heeding, the wise one: a wise person is one who, because of his ability to reflect, listens attentively, taking to heart the Dhamma made manifest by the pleased teacher. Practicing the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma: developing insight, which is the conformable Dhamma because of its conformity to the supramundane Dhamma. Becomes discerning, perceptive, and astute: he is discerning through the attainment of the wisdom called discernment; he is perceptive because of his ability to make things known to others by clarifying them; and he is astute because of his penetration of the most subtle meaning. One who resorts to such a one, diligent: one who, being diligent and intent on pleasing him, resorts to such a learned person of the kind described before.

321. Evaṃ paṇḍitācariyasevanaṃ pasaṃsitvā idāni bālācariyasevanaṃ nindanto “khuddañca bāla”nti imaṃ gāthamāha. Tattha khuddanti khuddena kāyakammādinā samannāgataṃ, paññābhāvato bālaṃ. Anāgatatthanti anadhigatapariyattipaṭivedhatthaṃ. Usūyakanti issāmanakatāya antevāsikassa vuḍḍhiṃ asahamānaṃ. Sesamettha pākaṭameva padato. Adhippāyato pana yo bahucīvarādilābhī ācariyo antevāsikānaṃ cīvarādīni na sakkoti dātuṃ, dhammadāne pana aniccadukkhānattavacanamattampi na sakkoti. Etehi khuddatādidhammehi samannāgatattā taṃ khuddaṃ bālaṃ anāgatatthaṃ usūyakaṃ ācariyaṃ upasevamāno “pūtimacchaṃ kusaggenā”ti (itivu. 76; jā. 1.15.183) vuttanayena sayampi bālo hoti. Tasmā idha sāsane kiñci appamattakampi [V 2.0058] pariyattidhammaṃ paṭivedhadhammaṃ vā avibhāvayitvā ca avijānitvā ca yassa dhammesu kaṅkhā, taṃ ataritvā maraṇaṃ upetīti evamassa attho veditabbo.

321. Having thus praised associating with wise teachers, now, condemning association with foolish teachers, he speaks this verse: 'A petty fool.' Herein, 'petty' means endowed with petty bodily actions, etc., and 'fool' means lacking wisdom. 'One who has not attained the goal' means not having attained the goal of scriptural learning and penetration. 'Jealous' means being unable to bear the progress of the pupil due to envy. The rest here is clear from the words. But as to the meaning, a teacher who gains much in the way of robes, etc., but is unable to give robes, etc., to his pupils, nor even speak a single word on impermanence, suffering, and non-self when giving the Dhamma. Because of being endowed with such qualities as pettiness, one who associates with such a petty, foolish, jealous teacher who has not attained the goal—in the way it is said, 'like a rotten fish with a blade of kusa grass'—becomes a fool oneself. Therefore, in this Dispensation, without having discerned or understood even a little of the Dhamma of the scriptures or the Dhamma of penetration, one who has doubt about the teachings dies without having crossed over it. This is the meaning to be understood.

322-3. Idāni tassevatthassa pākaṭakaraṇatthaṃ “yathā naro”ti gāthādvayamāha. Tattha āpaganti nadiṃ. Mahodakanti bahuudakaṃ. Salilanti ito [M 2.0064] cito ca gataṃ, vitthiṇṇanti vuttaṃ [P 1.0330] hoti. “Sarita”ntipi pāṭho, so evattho. Sīghasotanti hārahārikaṃ, vegavatinti vuttaṃ hoti. Kiṃ soti ettha “so vuyhamāno”ti iminā ca sokārena tassa narassa niddiṭṭhattā nipātamatto sokāro. Kiṃ sūti vuttaṃ hoti yathā “na bhavissāmi nāma so, vinassissāmi nāma so”ti. Dhammanti pubbe vuttaṃ duvidhameva. Anisāmayatthanti anisāmetvā atthaṃ. Sesamettha pākaṭameva padato.

322–323. Now, to make that meaning clear, he speaks the two verses beginning 'As a man.' Herein, 'river' means a stream. 'Great water' means abundant water. 'Water' means gone here and there, that is to say, 'vast.' The reading 'stream' is also found, with the same meaning. 'Swift current' means carrying away, that is to say, 'impetuous.' Regarding the phrase `kiṃ so`: here, since that man is indicated by the `so` in 'he (`so`) being carried away,' the `so` is merely a particle. It is said to be used in the sense found in: 'I will not be, indeed; I will perish, indeed.' 'Dhamma' means the twofold Dhamma previously mentioned. `Anisāmayatthaṃ` means `anisāmetvā atthaṃ`: without having investigated the meaning. The rest here is clear from the words.

Adhippāyato pana yathā yo kocideva naro vuttappakāraṃ nadiṃ otaritvā tāya nadiyā vuyhamāno anusotagāmī sotameva anugacchanto pare pāratthike kiṃ sakkhati pāraṃ netuṃ. “Sakkatī”tipi pāṭho. Tatheva duvidhampi dhammaṃ attano paññāya avibhāvayitvā bahussutānañca santike atthaṃ anisāmetvā sayaṃ avibhāvitattā ajānanto anisāmitattā ca avitiṇṇakaṅkho pare kiṃ sakkhati nijjhāpetuṃ pekkhāpetunti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. “So vata, cunda, attanā palipapalipanno”tiādikañcettha (ma. ni. 1.87) suttapadaṃ anussaritabbaṃ.

But as to the intention, it is as if some person, having entered a river of the kind described and being carried along by that river, going downstream, following only the current—how could he take others who desire the far shore to the far shore? There is also the reading, 'sakkatī.' In the same way, one who has not developed the twofold Dhamma with his own wisdom and has not ascertained the meaning in the presence of the learned, being ignorant because he has not developed it himself, and, because he has not ascertained it, having not overcome doubt—how could he cause others to understand or to see clearly? Thus the meaning should be understood here. And in this connection, the sutta passage beginning, 'Indeed, Cunda, himself sunk in mire...' (MN 1.87) should be recalled.

324-5. Evaṃ bālasevanāya bālassa paraṃ nijjhāpetuṃ asamatthatāya pākaṭakaraṇatthaṃ upamaṃ vatvā idāni “yo tādisaṃ bhajati appamatto”ti ettha vuttassa paṇḍitassa pare nijjhāpetuṃ samatthatāya pākaṭakaraṇatthaṃ “yathāpi nāva”nti gāthādvayamāha. Tattha phiyenāti dabbipadarena. Rittenāti veḷudaṇḍena. Tatthāti tassaṃ nāvāyaṃ. Tatrūpayaññūti tassā nāvāya āharaṇapaṭiharaṇādiupāyajānanena maggapaṭipādanena upāyaññū. Sikkhitasikkhatāya sukusalahatthatāya ca kusalo. Uppannupaddavapaṭikārasamatthatāya mutīmā. Vedagūti vedasaṅkhātehi catūhi maggañāṇehi gato. Bhāvitattoti tāyeva maggabhāvanāya bhāvitacitto. Bahussutoti pubbe vuttanayeneva. Avedhadhammoti aṭṭhahi lokadhammehi [P 1.0331] akampaniyasabhāvo. Sotāvadhānūpanisūpapanneti sotaodahanena ca maggaphalānaṃ upanissayena ca upapanne. Sesaṃ uttānapadatthameva. Adhippāyayojanāpi sakkā purimanayeneva jānitunti na vitthāritā.

Having thus spoken a simile to make clear the inability of a fool to cause others to understand, which is due to associating with fools—now, to make clear the ability of the wise person mentioned in the phrase 'one who, being heedful, associates with such a one...' to cause others to understand, he speaks the two verses beginning 'Just as a boat...' Therein, 'with a paddle' means with a wooden spoon-like board. 'With a steering oar' means with a bamboo pole. 'Therein' means in that boat. 'One who knows the means thereto' means one who knows the means by knowing the methods for that boat, such as moving it forward and back, and by setting the course. 'Skillful' means being so due to being well-trained and having a very deft hand. 'Intelligent' means being capable of counteracting any dangers that arise. 'Vedagū' means one who has gone by means of the four path-knowledges called 'vedas'. 'One with a cultivated self' means one whose mind is cultivated through the development of that very path. 'Learned' is as explained before. 'Of an unshakeable nature' means having a nature that is not shaken by the eight worldly conditions. 'Endowed with attentiveness of ear and a basis for attainment' means endowed with attentive listening and with the supporting condition for the paths and fruits. The rest has a plain meaning. The application of the intention can also be known in the same way as before, so it is not elaborated.

326. Evaṃ [V 2.0059][M 2.0065] paṇḍitassa pare nijjhāpetuṃ samatthabhāvapākaṭakaraṇatthaṃ upamaṃ vatvā tassā paṇḍitasevanāya niyojento “tasmā have”ti imaṃ avasānagāthamāha. Tatrāyaṃ saṅkhepattho – yasmā upanissayasampannā paṇḍitasevanena visesaṃ pāpuṇanti, tasmā have sappurisaṃ bhajetha. Kīdisaṃ sappurisaṃ bhajetha? Medhāvinañceva bahussutañca, paññāsampattiyā ca medhāvinaṃ vuttappakārasutadvayena ca bahussutaṃ. Tādisañhi bhajamāno tena bhāsitassa dhammassa aññāya atthaṃ evaṃ ñatvā ca yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjamāno tāya paṭipattiyā paṭivedhavasena viññātadhammo so maggaphalanibbānappabhedaṃ lokuttarasukhaṃ labhetha adhigaccheyya pāpuṇeyyāti arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ samāpesīti.

326. Thus, having spoken a simile to make clear the ability of the wise to cause others to understand, and while enjoining association with the wise, he speaks this concluding verse: 'Therefore, indeed...' Here is the condensed meaning: Because those endowed with supporting conditions attain distinction through association with the wise, 'therefore, indeed, one should associate with a good person.' What kind of good person should one associate with? One who is wise and learned: wise through the accomplishment of wisdom, and learned through the twofold learning as described. For by associating with such a person, having understood the meaning of the Dhamma spoken by him, and having known it thus, practicing as instructed, that person, having come to know the Dhamma through penetration by means of that practice, would obtain, attain, and reach the supramundane happiness, which is distinguished as path, fruition, and Nibbāna. Thus he concluded the teaching with the peak of arahantship.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the commentary on the Khuddaka collection,

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya dhammasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

the explanation of the Nātha Sutta in the Commentary on the Suttanipāta is concluded.

9. Kiṃsīlasuttavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the What is Virtue? Sutta

327. Kiṃsīloti [V 2.0060] kiṃsīlasuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Āyasmato sāriputtassa gihisahāyako eko therasseva pituno vaṅgantabrāhmaṇassa sahāyassa brāhmaṇassa putto saṭṭhikoṭiadhikaṃ pañcasatakoṭidhanaṃ pariccajitvā āyasmato sāriputtattherassa santike pabbajitvā sabbaṃ buddhavacanaṃ pariyāpuṇi. Tassa thero bahuso ovaditvā kammaṭṭhānamadāsi, so tena visesaṃ nādhigacchati. Tato thero “buddhaveneyyo eso”ti ñatvā taṃ ādāya bhagavato santikaṃ gantvā taṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha puggalaṃ aniyametvā “kiṃsīlo”ti pucchi. Athassa bhagavā tato paraṃ abhāsi. Tattha kiṃsīloti kīdisena vārittasīlena samannāgato, kīdisapakatiko vā. Kiṃsamācāroti kīdisena cārittena yutto. Kāni kammāni [P 1.0332] brūhayanti kāni kāyakammādīni vaḍḍhento. Naro sammā niviṭṭhassāti abhirato naro sāsane sammā patiṭṭhito bhaveyya. Uttamatthañca pāpuṇeti sabbatthānaṃ uttamaṃ arahattañca pāpuṇeyyāti vuttaṃ hoti.

9. Kiṃsīlo means the Kiṃsīla Sutta. What is its origin? A lay friend of the Venerable Sāriputta—the son of a brahmin who was a friend of the elder’s own father, the brahmin Vaṅganta—renounced wealth of five hundred and sixty koṭis, went forth under the Venerable Elder Sāriputta, and mastered the entire word of the Buddha. The elder often advised him and gave him a meditation subject, but he did not attain any distinction through it. Then the elder, knowing, “This one is to be trained by a Buddha,” took him and went to the Blessed One. With reference to that monk, yet without specifying the individual, he asked, “Of what virtue?” Thereupon, the Blessed One spoke further to him. Herein, “of what virtue” means: with what kind of restraining virtue is one endowed, or of what kind of nature? “Of what conduct” means: endowed with what kind of behavior? “Cultivating what actions” means: developing what kinds of bodily actions and so on? “A person rightly dedicated” means: a person delighting in it would be rightly established in the Dispensation. “And would attain the highest goal” means: he would attain arahantship, the highest of all goals—this is what is said.

328. Tato [M 2.0066] bhagavā “sāriputto aḍḍhamāsūpasampanno sāvakapāramippatto, kasmā ādikammikaputhujjanapañhaṃ pucchatī”ti āvajjento “saddhivihārikaṃ ārabbhā”ti ñatvā pucchāya vuttaṃ cārittasīlaṃ avibhajitvāva tassa sappāyavasena dhammaṃ desento “vuḍḍhāpacāyī”tiādimāha.

327. Then the Blessed One, reflecting, “Sāriputta, ordained for but half a month, has attained the perfection of a disciple. Why does he ask a beginner's, a worldling's question?” and knowing, “He asks with reference to his co-resident,” without analyzing the virtue of conduct mentioned in the question, taught the Dhamma in a way suitable for that monk, saying, “Respectful towards elders,” and so on.

Tattha paññāvuḍḍho, guṇavuḍḍho, jātivuḍḍho, vayovuḍḍhoti cattāro vuḍḍhā. Jātiyā hi daharopi bahussuto bhikkhu appassutamahallakabhikkhūnamantare bāhusaccapaññāya vuḍḍhattā paññāvuḍḍho. Tassa hi santike mahallakabhikkhūpi buddhavacanaṃ pariyāpuṇanti, ovādavinicchayapañhavissajjanāni ca paccāsīsanti. Tathā daharopi bhikkhu adhigamasampanno guṇavuḍḍho nāma. Tassa hi ovāde patiṭṭhāya mahallakāpi vipassanāgabbhaṃ gahetvā arahattaphalaṃ pāpuṇanti. Tathā daharopi rājā khattiyo muddhāvasitto brāhmaṇo vā sesajanassa vandanārahato jātivuḍḍho nāma. Sabbo pana paṭhamajāto vayovuḍḍho nāma. Tattha yasmā paññāya sāriputtattherassa sadiso natthi ṭhapetvā bhagavantaṃ, tathā guṇenapi aḍḍhamāsena sabbasāvakapāramīñāṇassa paṭividdhattā. Jātiyāpi so brāhmaṇamahāsālakule uppanno, tasmā tassa bhikkhuno vayena samānopi so imehi [V 2.0061] tīhi kāraṇehi vuḍḍho. Imasmiṃ panatthe paññāguṇehi eva vuḍḍhabhāvaṃ sandhāya bhagavā āha – “vuḍḍhāpacāyī”ti. Tasmā tādisānaṃ vuḍḍhānaṃ apacitikaraṇena vuḍḍhāpacāyī, tesameva vuḍḍhānaṃ lābhādīsu usūyavigamena anusūyako ca siyāti ayamādipādassa attho.

Herein, there are four kinds of elders: the elder in wisdom, the elder in virtue, the elder by birth, and the elder in age. For a learned monk, though young by birth, is an elder in wisdom among unlearned senior monks on account of his great learning and wisdom. Indeed, even senior monks learn the Buddha’s word from him and hope for his instruction, decisions, and answers to questions. Similarly, a young monk who has attained an attainment is called an elder in virtue. For by establishing themselves in his instruction, even senior monks, having undertaken insight meditation, attain the fruit of arahantship. Likewise, a young anointed khattiya king or a brahmin, worthy of veneration from other people, is called an elder by birth. But anyone who is born earlier is called an elder in age. Herein, since there is none equal to the Venerable Sāriputta in wisdom except for the Blessed One, and since he had penetrated the knowledge of all the perfections of a disciple in just half a month, and since he was born into a great brahmin family, he is an elder for these three reasons, even if another monk is his equal in age. In this context, however, the Blessed One said, “Respectful towards elders,” with reference to seniority in wisdom and virtue alone. Therefore, by showing reverence to such elders one is “respectful towards elders”; and by the removal of envy towards those same elders in regard to gains and so on, one would be “unresentful.” This is the meaning of the first line.

Kālaññū cassāti ettha pana rāge uppanne tassa vinodanatthāya garūnaṃ dassanaṃ gacchantopi kālaññū, dose… mohe… kosajje uppanne tassa vinodanatthāya garūnaṃ dassanaṃ gacchantopi kālaññū, yato evaṃ kālaññū ca assa garūnaṃ [P 1.0333] dassanāya. Dhammiṃ kathanti samathavipassanāyuttaṃ. Erayitanti vuttaṃ. Khaṇaññūti tassā kathāya khaṇavedī, dullabho vā ayaṃ īdisāya kathāya savanakkhaṇoti jānanto. Suṇeyya sakkaccāti taṃ kathaṃ sakkaccaṃ suṇeyya. Na kevalañca tameva, aññānipi buddhaguṇādipaṭisaṃyuttāni subhāsitāni sakkaccameva suṇeyyāti attho.

“And he would be a knower of the right time”: Herein, when lust has arisen, he is a knower of the right time for going to see his teachers to dispel it; when hatred… delusion… laziness has arisen, he is a knower of the right time for going to see his teachers to dispel it. Thus he would be a knower of the right time for seeing his teachers. “A talk on the Dhamma” means one connected with serenity and insight. “Uttered” is what is said. “A knower of the opportunity” means one who recognizes the opportunity for that talk, knowing, “This opportunity to hear such a talk is rare.” “He should listen attentively” means he should listen to that talk attentively. The meaning is that he should listen attentively not only to that, but also to other well-spoken words connected with the qualities of the Buddha and so on.

329. “Kālaññū cassa garūnaṃ dassanāyā”ti ettha vuttanayañca attano uppannarāgādivinodanakālaṃ ñatvāpi garūnaṃ santikaṃ gacchanto kālena gacche garūnaṃ [M 2.0067] sakāsaṃ, “ahaṃ kammaṭṭhāniko dhutaṅgadharo cā”ti katvā na cetiyavandanabodhiyaṅgaṇabhikkhācāramaggaatimajjhanhikavelādīsu yattha katthaci ṭhitamācariyaṃ disvā paripucchanatthāya upasaṅkameyya, sakasenāsane pana attano āsane nisinnaṃ vūpasantadarathaṃ sallakkhetvā kammaṭṭhānādividhipucchanatthaṃ upasaṅkameyyāti attho. Evaṃ upasaṅkamantopi ca thambhaṃ niraṃkatvā nivātavutti thaddhabhāvakaraṃ mānaṃ vināsetvā nīcavutti pādapuñchanacoḷakachinnavisāṇusabhauddhatadāṭhasappasadiso hutvā upasaṅkameyya. Atha tena garunā vuttaṃ atthaṃ dhammaṃ…pe… samācare ca. Atthanti bhāsitatthaṃ. Dhammanti pāḷidhammaṃ. Saṃyamanti sīlaṃ. Brahmacariyanti avasesasāsanabrahmacariyaṃ. Anussare ceva samācare cāti atthaṃ kathitokāse anussareyya, dhammaṃ saṃyamaṃ brahmacariyaṃ kathitokāse anussareyya, anussaraṇamatteneva ca atussanto taṃ sabbampi samācare samācareyya samādāya vatteyya. Tāsaṃ kathānaṃ attani pavattane ussukkaṃ kareyyāti attho. Evaṃ karonto hi kiccakaro hoti.

329. Regarding “And he would be a knower of the right time for seeing his teachers”: The method here is that, even when one knows the time to dispel one’s own arisen lust, etc., one should go to the teachers’ presence at a proper time. One should not, thinking, “I am a meditator and an ascetic practitioner,” approach a teacher to ask questions after seeing him standing anywhere—at a shrine, in the Bodhi tree enclosure, on the alms-round path, or after midday. Rather, the meaning is that one should approach to ask about the method of the meditation subject and so on after observing that the teacher is seated on his own seat in his dwelling, with his agitation calmed. And when approaching in this way, one should do so having gotten rid of stiffness, being humble; having destroyed conceit, which causes stubbornness, being lowly; having become like a foot-wiping rag, like a bull with broken horns, or like a snake with its fangs removed. Then one should practice the meaning, the Dhamma… spoken by that teacher. “Meaning” is the meaning of what was said. “Dhamma” is the Dhamma text. “Restraint” is virtue. “Holy life” is the remaining holy life of the Dispensation. “He should recollect and practice”: one should recollect the meaning in the context in which it was spoken; one should recollect the Dhamma, restraint, and holy life in the context in which they were spoken. And not being satisfied with mere recollection, he should practice it all; he should practice it, having undertaken it he should live by it. The meaning is that one should strive to apply those teachings to oneself. For by doing so, one becomes one who does what is to be done.

330. Tato parañca dhammārāmo dhammarato dhamme ṭhito dhammavinicchayaññū bhaveyya. Sabbapadesu cettha dhammoti samathavipassanā, ārāmo ratīti ekova attho, dhamme ārāmo assāti dhammārāmo. Dhamme rato, na [P 1.0334] aññaṃ pihetīti dhammarato. Dhamme ṭhito dhammaṃ vattanato. Dhammavinicchayaṃ jānāti “idaṃ udayañāṇaṃ idaṃ vayañāṇa”nti dhammavinicchayaññū, evarūpo [V 2.0062] assa. Atha yāyaṃ rājakathāditiracchānakathā taruṇavipassakassa bahiddhārūpādīsu abhinandanuppādanena taṃ samathavipassanādhammaṃ sandūseti, tasmā “dhammasandosavādo”ti vuccati, taṃ nevācare dhammasandosavādaṃ, aññadatthu āvāsagocarādisappāyāni sevanto tacchehi nīyetha subhāsitehi. Samathavipassanāpaṭisaṃyuttānevettha tacchāni, tathārūpehi subhāsitehi nīyetha nīyeyya, kālaṃ khepeyyāti attho.

330. Furthermore, one should be one who delights in the Dhamma, is fond of the Dhamma, is established in the Dhamma, and is skilled in discerning the Dhamma. Here, in all instances, “Dhamma” means serenity and insight. “Delight” and “fondness” have the same meaning. “One who delights in the Dhamma” means one whose delight is in the Dhamma. “Fond of the Dhamma” means one is fond of the Dhamma and does not long for anything else. “Established in the Dhamma” means one is grounded in the Dhamma. “Skilled in discerning the Dhamma” means one knows, “This is the knowledge of arising, this is the knowledge of passing away.” One should be of such a nature. Now, any talk such as talk about kings and other animal-level talk—which, for a young insight meditator, corrupts that Dhamma of serenity and insight by producing delight in external forms and so on—is called “talk that corrupts the Dhamma.” One should not engage in such talk that corrupts the Dhamma. Instead, frequenting suitable things like dwelling places and alms-resorts, one should pass the time with true, well-spoken words. Here, “true” refers only to those things connected with serenity and insight. The meaning is that one should be led by such well-spoken words—that is, one should pass one's time.

331. Idāni “dhammasandosavāda”nti ettha atisaṅkhepena vuttaṃ samathavipassanāyuttassa bhikkhuno upakkilesaṃ pākaṭaṃ karonto tadaññenapi upakkilesena saddhiṃ “hassaṃ jappa”nti imaṃ gāthamāha. Hāsantipi pāṭho. Vipassakena [M 2.0068] hi bhikkhunā hasanīyasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ sitamattameva kātabbaṃ, niratthakakathājappo na bhāsitabbo, ñātibyasanādīsu paridevo na kātabbo, khāṇukaṇṭakādimhi manopadoso na uppādetabbo. Māyākatanti vuttā māyā, tividhaṃ kuhanaṃ, paccayesu giddhi, jātiādīhi māno, paccanīkasātatāsaṅkhāto sārambho, pharusavacanalakkhaṇaṃ kakkasaṃ, rāgādayo kasāvā, adhimattataṇhālakkhaṇā mucchāti ime ca dosā sukhakāmena aṅgārakāsu viya, sucikāmena gūthaṭhānaṃ viya, jīvitukāmena āsivisādayo viya ca pahātabbā.
