Hitvā ca ārogyamadādivigamā vītamadena cittavikkhepābhāvā ṭhitattena caritabbaṃ. Evaṃ paṭipanno hi sabbupakkilesaparisuddhāya bhāvanāya na cirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. Tenāha bhagavā – “hassaṃ jappaṃ…pe… ṭhitatto”ti.

331. Now, to make manifest the defilement of a monk devoted to serenity and insight, which was stated very briefly in the phrase “talk that corrupts the Dhamma,” he spoke this verse, “Laughter and chatter…,” along with other defilements. There is also the reading “laughing.” For a monk practicing insight, when a laughable matter arises, only a slight smile should be made; meaningless talk and chatter should not be spoken; lamentation over the misfortune of relatives and so on should not be done; and mental aversion should not be produced over stumps, thorns, and the like. Deceit, called “māyā”; threefold scheming; greed for requisites; conceit regarding birth and so on; contentiousness, characterized by opposition; harshness, characterized by harsh speech; the stains of lust and so on; and infatuation, characterized by excessive craving—these faults should be abandoned by one who desires happiness, like a pit of embers; by one who desires purity, like a place of filth; and by one who desires to live, like venomous snakes and poisons. And having abandoned them, one should live with a steadfast mind, free from intoxication through the removal of the intoxication of health and so on, and free from mental distraction. For one who practices thus attains arahantship in no long time through a development fully purified of all defilements. Therefore the Blessed One said: “Laughter and chatter… with a steadfast mind.”

332. Idāni yvāyaṃ “hassaṃ jappa”ntiādinā nayena upakkileso vutto, tena samannāgato bhikkhu yasmā sāhaso hoti avīmaṃsakārī, ratto rāgavasena [P 1.0335] duṭṭho dosavasena gacchati, pamatto ca hoti kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ bhāvanāya asātaccakārī, tathārūpassa ca “suṇeyya sakkacca subhāsitānī”tiādinā nayena vutto ovādo niratthako, tasmā imassa saṃkilesassa puggalādhiṭṭhānāya desanāya sutādivuddhipaṭipakkhabhāvaṃ dassento “viññātasārānī”ti imaṃ gāthamāha.

332. Now, since a monk endowed with that defilement spoken of by the method beginning “Laughter and chatter…” is rash, one who acts without investigation, goes along impassioned by lust and corrupted by hatred, and is heedless, one who does not act continuously in the development of wholesome states, for such a one the instruction spoken by the method beginning “He should listen attentively to well-spoken words” is useless. Therefore, to show that this defilement is the opposite of the growth in learning and so on, by means of a teaching based on a person, he spoke this verse: “Having understood the essentials…”

Tassattho – yāni hetāni samathavipassanāpaṭisaṃyuttāni subhāsitāni, tesaṃ vijānanaṃ sāro. Yadi viññātāni sādhu, atha saddamattameva gahitaṃ, na kiñci kataṃ hoti, yena etāni sutamayena ñāṇena viññāyanti, taṃ sutaṃ, etañca sutamayañāṇaṃ viññātasamādhisāraṃ, tesu viññātesu dhammesu yo samādhi cittassāvikkhepo tathattāya paṭipatti, ayamassa sāro. Na hi vijānanamatteneva koci attho sijjhati. Yo panāyaṃ naro rāgādivasena vattanato sāhaso[V 2.0063], kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ bhāvanāya asātaccakāritāya pamatto, so saddamattaggāhīyeva hoti. Tena tassa atthavijānanābhāvato sā subhāsitavijānanapaññā ca, tathattāya paṭipattiyā abhāvato sutañca na vaḍḍhatīti.

The meaning of this is: The essence is understanding those well-spoken words connected with serenity and insight. If they are well understood, it is good; but if only the sound is grasped, nothing is accomplished. That by which these are understood through knowledge born of learning is learning itself; and this knowledge born of learning has concentration based on understanding as its essence. When these teachings are understood, the concentration that is the mind's undistractedness and the practice for the sake of suchness—this is its essence. For by mere understanding alone no purpose is accomplished. But that person who is reckless, being driven by lust and so on, and is heedless from not constantly engaging in the development of wholesome qualities—he only grasps the sound. Therefore, for him, due to his lack of understanding the meaning, that wisdom which understands well-spoken teachings does not grow; nor does his learning increase, due to his lack of practice for the sake of suchness.

333. Evaṃ [M 2.0069] pamattānaṃ sattānaṃ paññāparihāniṃ sutaparihāniñca dassetvā idāni appamattānaṃ tadubhayasārādhigamaṃ dassento āha – “dhamme ca ye…pe… sāramajjhagū”ti. Tattha ariyappavedito dhammo nāma samathavipassanādhammo. Ekopi hi buddho samathavipassanādhammaṃ adesetvā parinibbuto nāma natthi. Tasmā etasmiṃ dhamme ca ye ariyappavedite ratā niratā appamattā sātaccānuyogino, anuttarā te vacasā manasā kammunā ca, te catubbidhena vacīsucaritena tividhena manosucaritena tividhena kāyasucaritena ca samannāgatattā vacasā manasā kammunā ca anuttarā, avasesasattehi asamā aggāvisiṭṭhā. Ettāvatā saddhiṃ pubbabhāgasīlena ariyamaggasampayuttaṃ sīlaṃ dasseti. Evaṃ parisuddhasīlā te santisoraccasamādhisaṇṭhitā, sutassa paññāya ca sāramajjhagū, ye ariyappavedite dhamme ratā, te na kevalaṃ vācādīhi anuttarā honti, apica kho pana santisoracce samādhimhi ca saṇṭhitā hutvā sutassa [P 1.0336] paññāya ca sāramajjhagū adhigatā icceva veditabbā. Āsaṃsāyaṃ bhūtavacanaṃ. Tattha santīti nibbānaṃ, soraccanti sundare ratabhāvena yathābhūtapaṭivedhikā paññā, santiyā soraccanti santisoraccaṃ, nibbānārammaṇāya maggapaññāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Samādhīti taṃsampayuttova maggasamādhi. Saṇṭhitāti tadubhaye patiṭṭhitā. Sutapaññānaṃ sāraṃ nāma arahattaphalavimutti. Vimuttisārañhi idaṃ brahmacariyaṃ.

333. Thus, having shown the decline in wisdom and learning among heedless beings, now, to demonstrate the attainment of the essence of both by the heedful, it is said: 'Those who delight in the Dhamma proclaimed by the Noble Ones... have reached the essence of learning and wisdom.' Herein, the Dhamma proclaimed by the Noble Ones is the Dhamma of serenity and insight. For not a single Buddha has attained final Nibbāna without teaching the Dhamma of serenity and insight. Therefore, those who delight in, are devoted to, and are heedful with persistent application in this Dhamma proclaimed by the Noble Ones—they are unsurpassed in speech, mind, and action. Being endowed with fourfold good verbal conduct, threefold good mental conduct, and threefold good bodily conduct, they are unsurpassed in speech, mind, and action, incomparable and distinguished among other beings. To this extent, along with the preliminary virtue, the virtue associated with the noble path is shown. Thus, those of purified virtue, established in calmness, gentleness, and concentration, have reached the essence of learning and wisdom. Those who delight in the Dhamma proclaimed by the Noble Ones are not only unsurpassed in speech and so on, but also, having become established in calmness, gentleness, and concentration, they are to be understood as having attained the essence of learning and wisdom. This is a statement of what is true. Herein, 'calmness' is Nibbāna; 'gentleness' is the wisdom that penetrates things as they truly are, from delighting in the beautiful; 'calmness and gentleness' is a designation for the path-wisdom that has Nibbāna as its object. 'Concentration' is the path-concentration associated with it. 'Established' means established in both. The essence of learning and wisdom is the liberation of arahantship. For this holy life has liberation as its essence.

Evamettha bhagavā dhammena pubbabhāgapaṭipadaṃ, “anuttarā vacasā”tiādīhi sīlakkhandhaṃ, santisoraccasamādhīhi paññākkhandhasamādhikkhandheti tīhipi imehi khandhehi aparabhāgapaṭipadañca dassetvā sutapaññāsārena akuppavimuttiṃ dassento arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ samāpesi. Desanāpariyosāne ca so bhikkhu sotāpattiphalaṃ patvā puna na cirasseva aggaphale arahatte patiṭṭhāsīti.

Thus, here the Blessed One showed the preliminary practice by means of the Dhamma; with phrases such as 'unsurpassed in speech,' he showed the aggregate of virtue; and with calmness-and-gentleness and concentration, he showed the aggregate of wisdom and the aggregate of concentration. Having thus shown the subsequent practice with these three aggregates, he concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of arahantship, demonstrating unshakable liberation, which is the essence of learning and wisdom. At the conclusion of the teaching, that bhikkhu attained the fruit of stream-entry and not long afterwards was established in the supreme fruit, arahantship.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Minor Texts,

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya kiṃsīlasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

the explanation of the Kiṃsīla Sutta in the Commentary on the Suttanipāta is concluded.

10. Uṭṭhānasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Explanation of the Uṭṭhāna Sutta

334. Uṭṭhahathāti [V 2.0064][M 2.0070] uṭṭhānasuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharanto rattiṃ jetavanavihāre vasitvā pubbaṇhasamayaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā pācīnadvārena nagarā nikkhamitvā migāramātupāsādaṃ agamāsi divāvihāratthāya. Āciṇṇaṃ kiretaṃ bhagavato rattiṃ jetavanavihāre vasitvā migāramātupāsāde divāvihārūpagamanaṃ, rattiñca migāramātupāsāde vasitvā jetavane divāvihārūpagamanaṃ. Kasmā? Dvinnaṃ kulānaṃ anuggahatthāya mahāpariccāgaguṇaparidīpanatthāya ca. Migāramātupāsādassa ca heṭṭhā pañca kūṭāgāragabbhasatāni honti, yesu pañcasatā bhikkhū vasanti. Tattha yadā bhagavā heṭṭhāpāsāde vasati, tadā bhikkhū bhagavato gāravena uparipāsādaṃ nāruhanti. Taṃ divasaṃ pana bhagavā uparipāsāde kūṭāgāragabbhaṃ pāvisi, tena heṭṭhāpāsāde pañcapi gabbhasatāni pañcasatā bhikkhū pavisiṃsu. Te ca sabbeva navā honti adhunāgatā imaṃ [P 1.0337] dhammavinayaṃ uddhatā unnaḷā pākatindriyā. Te pavisitvā divāseyyaṃ supitvā sāyaṃ uṭṭhāya mahātale sannipatitvā “ajja bhattagge tuyhaṃ kiṃ ahosi, tvaṃ kattha agamāsi, ahaṃ āvuso kosalarañño gharaṃ, ahaṃ anāthapiṇḍikassa, tattha evarūpo ca evarūpo ca bhojanavidhi ahosī”ti nānappakāraṃ āmisakathaṃ kathentā uccāsaddamahāsaddā ahesuṃ.

334. The Uṭṭhāna Sutta is the sutta beginning 'Arise!' What is its origin? At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī. Having spent the night in the Jeta's Grove monastery, in the morning, surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he entered Sāvatthī for alms. After leaving the city through the eastern gate, he went to the mansion of Migāra's mother for the day's sojourn. It was the Blessed One’s regular practice to spend the night in the Jeta's Grove monastery and go to the mansion of Migāra's mother for the day’s sojourn, or to spend the night in the mansion of Migāra's mother and go to Jeta's Grove for the day’s sojourn. Why? To favor both families and to display the quality of great generosity. Beneath the mansion of Migāra's mother, there were five hundred gabled chambers where five hundred bhikkhus resided. When the Blessed One stayed in the lower mansion, the bhikkhus, out of reverence for him, did not ascend to the upper mansion. But on that day, the Blessed One entered a gabled chamber in the upper mansion; therefore, five hundred bhikkhus entered the five hundred chambers in the lower mansion. All of them were new, recently come to this Dhamma-Vinaya, agitated, arrogant, and with unrestrained sense faculties. After entering, they slept during the day. Rising in the evening, they gathered on the great terrace and engaged in various kinds of worldly talk, saying: 'Today, what did you get at the meal hall? Where did you go?' 'Friend, I went to the house of the Kosalan king.' 'I went to Anāthapiṇḍika’s house. There was such and such a variety of food.' Thus they were making loud and great noises.

Bhagavā taṃ saddaṃ sutvā “ime mayā saddhiṃ vasantāpi evaṃ pamattā, aho ayuttakārino”ti mahāmoggallānattherassa āgamanaṃ cintesi. Tāvadeva āyasmā mahāmoggallāno bhagavato cittaṃ ñatvā iddhiyā āgamma pādamūle vandamānoyeva ahosi. Tato naṃ bhagavā āmantesi – “ete te, moggallāna, sabrahmacārino pamattā, sādhu ne saṃvejehī”ti. “Evaṃ bhante”ti kho so āyasmā mahāmoggallāno bhagavato paṭissuṇitvā tāvadeva āpokasiṇaṃ samāpajjitvā karīsabhūmiyaṃ ṭhitaṃ mahāpāsādaṃ nāvaṃ viya mahāvāto pādaṅguṭṭhakena kampesi saddhiṃ patiṭṭhitapathavippadesena. Atha te bhikkhū bhītā vissaraṃ karontā sakasakacīvarāni chaḍḍetvā catūhi dvārehi nikkhamiṃsu. Bhagavā tesaṃ attānaṃ dassento aññena dvārena gandhakuṭiṃ pavisanto viya ahosi, te bhagavantaṃ disvā vanditvā aṭṭhaṃsu[M 2.0071]. Bhagavā “kiṃ, bhikkhave, bhītatthā”ti pucchi, te “ayaṃ, bhante, migāramātupāsādo kampito”ti āhaṃsu[V 2.0065]. “Jānātha, bhikkhave, kenā”ti? “Na jānāma, bhante”ti. Atha bhagavā “tumhādisānaṃ, bhikkhave, muṭṭhassatīnaṃ asampajānānaṃ pamādavihārīnaṃ saṃvegajananatthaṃ moggallānena kampito”ti vatvā tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ dhammadesanatthaṃ imaṃ suttamabhāsi.

Hearing that sound, the Blessed One thought, 'Even while living with me, these bhikkhus are so heedless. Alas, they act improperly.' He considered the arrival of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna. At that very moment, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, knowing the Blessed One's thought, arrived by psychic power and was already paying homage at his feet. Then the Blessed One addressed him: 'Moggallāna, these fellow monks are heedless. It would be good to stir them with a sense of urgency.' 'Yes, Venerable Sir,' replied the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. Having assented to the Blessed One, he immediately entered the water-kasiṇa. He then shook the great mansion with his big toe as if a great wind were shaking a boat, along with the area of ground upon which it was established. Then those frightened bhikkhus cried out and, abandoning their robes, fled through the four doors. The Blessed One, showing himself to them, appeared as if entering the fragrant chamber by another door. Seeing the Blessed One, they paid homage and stood there. The Blessed One asked, 'Why, bhikkhus, are you frightened?' They replied, 'Venerable Sir, this mansion of Migāra's mother has been shaken.' 'Do you know by whom, bhikkhus?' 'We do not know, Venerable Sir.' Then the Blessed One said, 'Moggallāna shook it to generate a sense of urgency for bhikkhus like you, who are forgetful, not clearly comprehending, and dwelling in heedlessness.' Having said this, he spoke this discourse to teach those bhikkhus the Dhamma.

Tattha uṭṭhahathāti āsanā uṭṭhahatha ghaṭatha vāyamatha, mā kusītā hotha. Nisīdathāti pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā kammaṭṭhānānuyogatthāya nisīdatha. Ko attho supitena voti ko tumhākaṃ anupādāparinibbānatthāya pabbajitānaṃ [P 1.0338] supitena attho. Na hi sakkā supantena koci attho pāpuṇituṃ. Āturānañhi kā niddā, sallaviddhāna ruppatanti yatra ca nāma appakepi sarīrappadese uṭṭhitena cakkhurogādinā rogena āturānaṃ ekadvaṅgulamattampi paviṭṭhena ayasallaaṭṭhisalladantasallavisāṇasallakaṭṭhasallānaṃ aññatarena sallena ruppamānānaṃ manussānaṃ niddā natthi, tattha tumhākaṃ sakalacittasarīrasantānaṃ bhañjitvā uppannehi nānappakārakilesarogehi āturānañhi kā niddā rāgasallādīhi ca pañcahi sallehi antohadayaṃ pavisiya viddhattā sallaviddhānaṃ ruppataṃ.

Herein, 'arise' (uṭṭhahatha) means: rise from your seats, strive, make an effort, do not be lazy. 'Sit' (nisīdatha) means: sit down, having folded your legs crosswise, for the purpose of applying yourselves to your meditation subject. 'What use is sleep to you?' means: for you who have gone forth for the sake of final Nibbāna without clinging, what use is sleep? For no purpose can be achieved by one who is sleeping. 'For the afflicted, what sleep is there? For those pierced by a dart, who are in pain?' means: just as for those afflicted by a disease such as an eye disease that has arisen in even a small part of the body, or for people who are in pain because they have been pierced by a dart of iron, bone, tooth, horn, or wood that has penetrated even one or two finger-breadths, there is no sleep; so for you, who are afflicted by the various diseases of the defilements that have arisen and shattered the entire continuity of your mind and body, and who are in pain, having been pierced by the five darts beginning with the dart of lust that have entered and penetrated into your hearts—what sleep can there be?

335. Evaṃ vatvā puna bhagavā bhiyyosomattāya te bhikkhū ussāhento saṃvejento ca āha – “uṭṭhahatha…pe… vasānuge”ti. Tatrāyaṃ sādhippāyayojanā atthavaṇṇanā – evaṃ kilesasallaviddhānañhi vo, bhikkhave, kālo pabujjhituṃ. Kiṃ kāraṇaṃ? Maṇḍapeyyamidaṃ, bhikkhave, brahmacariyaṃ, satthā sammukhībhūto, ito pubbe pana vo dīgharattaṃ suttaṃ, girīsu suttaṃ, nadīsu suttaṃ, samesu suttaṃ, visamesu suttaṃ, rukkhaggesupi suttaṃ adassanā ariyasaccānaṃ, tasmā tassā niddāya antakiriyatthaṃ uṭṭhahatha nisīdatha daḷhaṃ sikkhatha santiyā.

335. Having said this, the Blessed One, in order to further encourage and rouse those bhikkhus, said: 'Arise... lest you fall under the sway of the King of Death.' Herein, this is the explanation of the meaning with its intended application: 'For you, bhikkhus, who have been pierced by the dart of the defilements, it is time to awaken. For what reason? I shall make this holy life known, bhikkhus; the Teacher is present before you. But before this, you have slept for a long time—slept on mountains, slept in rivers, slept on level ground, slept on uneven ground, even slept in the tops of trees—because you did not see the Noble Truths. Therefore, to make an end of that sleep, arise, sit, and train resolutely for peace.'

Tattha purimapādassattho vuttanayo eva. Dutiyapāde pana santīti tisso santiyo – accantasanti, tadaṅgasanti, sammutisantīti, nibbānavipassanādiṭṭhigatānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Idha pana accantasanti nibbānamadhippetaṃ, tasmā nibbānatthaṃ daḷhaṃ sikkhatha, asithilaparakkamā hutvā sikkhathāti vuttaṃ hoti. Kiṃ kāraṇaṃ? Mā vo pamatte viññāya, maccurājā amohayittha vasānuge[M 2.0072], mā tumhe “pamattā ete”ti evaṃ ñatvā maccurājapariyāyanāmo māro vasānuge amohayittha, yathā tassa vasaṃ gacchatha, evaṃ vasānuge karonto mā amohayitthāti vuttaṃ hoti.

Here, the meaning of the first line is as stated before. In the second line, the word 'peace' (santi) refers to three kinds of peace: absolute peace, temporary peace, and conventional peace. This is a designation for Nibbāna, insight, and right view. Here, however, absolute peace, Nibbāna, is intended. Thus, it is said: 'Train yourselves resolutely for the sake of Nibbāna; train, having become unremitting in effort.' What is the reason? 'Lest the King of Death, knowing you to be heedless, should delude you who are under his sway.' This means: Lest Māra, whose alternative name is the King of Death, knowing, 'These are heedless,' should delude you who are under his sway; lest he, making you subject to his sway, should delude you so that you fall under his power.

336. Yato tassa vasaṃ anupagacchantā yāya devā manussā ca…pe… samappitā, yāya devā ca manussā ca atthikā rūpasaddagandharasaphoṭṭhabbatthikā, taṃ rūpādiṃ sitā nissitā allīnā [V 2.0066] hutvā tiṭṭhanti, taratha samatikkamatha etaṃ nānappakāresu visayesu visaṭavitthiṇṇavisālattā [P 1.0339] visattikaṃ bhavabhogataṇhaṃ. Khaṇo vo mā upaccagā, ayaṃ tumhākaṃ samaṇadhammakaraṇakkhaṇo mā atikkami. Yesañhi ayamevarūpo khaṇo atikkamati, ye ca imaṃ khaṇaṃ atikkamanti, te khaṇātītā hi socanti nirayamhi samappitā, nirassādaṭṭhena nirayasaññite catubbidhepi apāye patiṭṭhitā “akataṃ vata no kalyāṇa”ntiādinā nayena socanti.

336. Wherefore, those who fall under his sway are those gods and humans who are attached by that craving. By that craving, gods and humans who desire forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tactile objects, remain clinging, dependent, and attached to these forms and so on. Cross over, transcend this craving for existence and sensual pleasures, which is clinging because it is pervasive, extensive, and widespread among various sense objects. Do not let the moment pass you by; this is your moment to practice the ascetic's duty—do not let it pass. For those for whom such a moment passes, and who miss this opportunity, having let the moment pass, they grieve, consigned to hell. Established in the fourfold states of woe, called 'hell' in the sense of being without delight, they lament in the manner of, 'Alas, we have done no good,' and so on.

337. Evaṃ bhagavā te bhikkhū ussāhetvā saṃvejetvā ca idāni tesaṃ taṃ pamādavihāraṃ vigarahitvā sabbeva te appamāde niyojento “pamādo rajo”ti imaṃ gāthamāha. Tattha pamādoti saṅkhepato sativippavāso, so cittamalinaṭṭhena rajo. Taṃ pamādamanupatito pamādānupatito, pamādānupatitattā aparāparuppanno pamādo eva, sopi rajo. Na hi kadāci pamādo nāma arajo atthi. Tena kiṃ dīpeti? Mā tumhe “daharā tāva mayaṃ pacchā jānissāmā”ti vissāsamāpajjittha. Daharakālepi hi pamādo rajo, majjhimakālepi therakālepi pamādānupatitattā mahārajo saṅkārakūṭo eva hoti, yathā ghare ekadvedivasiko rajo rajo eva, vaḍḍhamāno pana gaṇavassiko saṅkārakūṭo eva hoti. Evaṃ santepi pana paṭhamavaye buddhavacanaṃ pariyāpuṇitvā itaravayesu samaṇadhammaṃ karonto, paṭhamavaye vā pariyāpuṇitvā majjhimavaye suṇitvā pacchimavaye samaṇadhammaṃ karontopi bhikkhu pamādavihārī na hoti appamādānulomapaṭipadaṃ paṭipannattā. Yo pana sabbavayesu pamādavihārī divāseyyaṃ āmisakathañca anuyutto, seyyathāpi tumhe, tasseva so paṭhamavaye pamādo rajo, itaravayesu pamādānupatito mahāpamādo ca mahārajo evāti.

337. Thus, the Blessed One, having encouraged and stirred those monks to urgency, now rebuked their dwelling in heedlessness and, urging them all toward diligence, spoke this verse: 'Heedlessness is dust.' Herein, 'heedlessness' (pamāda) is, in brief, the absence of mindfulness; it is dust in the sense that it stains the mind. Following that heedlessness is 'heedlessness-following' (pamādānupatito); and because of following heedlessness, the heedlessness that arises again and again is also dust. Indeed, heedlessness is never not dust. What does this illustrate? Do not fall into complacency, thinking, 'We are still young; we will understand later.' For even in youth, heedlessness is dust; in middle age and old age, due to following heedlessness, it becomes great dust, a very rubbish heap. Just as in a house, dust of one or two days is merely dust, but as it increases over many years, it becomes a rubbish heap. Even so, a monk who learns the Buddha’s word in his early years and practices the ascetic's life in his later years, or who learns in his early years, listens in his middle years, and practices the ascetic's life in his final years, is not one who dwells heedlessly, because he has undertaken a practice that conforms with diligence. But for one who dwells heedlessly in all stages of life, devoted to sleeping by day and to talk of worldly things—just like you—for him, heedlessness in the first stage of life is dust, but in the later stages, by following heedlessness, it becomes great heedlessness and great dust indeed.

Evaṃ [M 2.0073] tesaṃ pamādavihāraṃ vigarahitvā appamāde niyojento āha – “appamādena vijjāya, abbahe sallamattano”ti, tassattho – yasmā evameso sabbadāpi pamādo rajo, tasmā satiavippavāsasaṅkhātena appamādena āsavānaṃ khayañāṇasaṅkhātāya ca vijjāya paṇḍito kulaputto uddhare attano hadayanissitaṃ rāgādipañcavidhaṃ sallanti arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ samāpesi. Desanāpariyosāne saṃvegamāpajjitvā tameva dhammadesanaṃ manasi karitvā paccavekkhamānā vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā pañcasatāpi te bhikkhū arahatte patiṭṭhahiṃsūti.

Thus, having rebuked their dwelling in heedlessness and urging them toward diligence, he said: 'With diligence and knowledge, one should pull out one's own arrow.' The meaning of this is: because this heedlessness is always dust, therefore, with diligence, described as the non-absence of mindfulness, and with knowledge, described as the wisdom of the destruction of the taints, a wise son of good family should extract the fivefold arrow of passion and so forth that is based in his own heart. Thus, he concluded the discourse with the pinnacle of Arahantship. At the conclusion of the discourse, having felt a sense of urgency, having paid attention to that very Dhamma teaching and reflected upon it, those five hundred monks began insight meditation and were established in Arahantship.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddakapāṭha,

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya uṭṭhānasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

In the Suttanipāta Commentary, the explanation of the Uṭṭhāna Sutta is concluded.

11. Rāhulasuttavaṇṇanā

11. The Explanation of the Rāhula Sutta.

338. Kacci [V 2.0067][P 1.0340] abhiṇhasaṃvāsāti rāhulasuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Bhagavā sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambujjhitvā bodhimaṇḍato anupubbena kapilavatthuṃ gantvā tattha rāhulakumārena “dāyajjaṃ me samaṇa dehī”ti dāyajjaṃ yācito sāriputtattheraṃ āṇāpesi – “rāhulakumāraṃ pabbājehī”ti. Taṃ sabbaṃ khandhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (mahāva. aṭṭha. 105) vuttanayeneva gahetabbaṃ. Evaṃ pabbajitaṃ pana rāhulakumāraṃ vuḍḍhippattaṃ sāriputtattherova upasampādesi, mahāmoggallānatthero assa kammavācācariyo ahosi. Taṃ bhagavā “ayaṃ kumāro jātiādisampanno, so jātigottakulavaṇṇapokkharatādīni nissāya mānaṃ vā madaṃ vā mā akāsī”ti daharakālato pabhuti yāva na ariyabhūmiṃ pāpuṇi, tāva ovadanto abhiṇhaṃ imaṃ suttamabhāsi. Tasmā cetaṃ suttapariyosānepi vuttaṃ “itthaṃ sudaṃ bhagavā āyasmantaṃ rāhulaṃ imāhi gāthāhi abhiṇhaṃ ovadatī”ti. Tattha paṭhamagāthāyaṃ ayaṃ saṅkhepattho “kacci tvaṃ, rāhula, abhiṇhaṃ saṃvāsahetu jātiādīnaṃ aññatarena vatthunā na paribhavasi paṇḍitaṃ, ñāṇapadīpassa dhammadesanāpadīpassa ca dhāraṇato ukkādhāro manussānaṃ [M 2.0074] kacci apacito tayā, kacci niccaṃ pūjito tayā”ti āyasmantaṃ sāriputtaṃ sandhāya bhaṇati.

338. The Rāhula Sutta begins: 'Kacci abhiṇhasaṃvāsā...' What is its origin? After attaining perfect self-awakening, the Blessed One traveled in due course from the seat of Awakening to Kapilavatthu. There, when Prince Rāhula requested his inheritance, saying, 'Ascetic, give me my inheritance,' the Blessed One instructed the Elder Sāriputta, 'Ordain Prince Rāhula.' All this should be understood in the way it is told in the Khandhaka Commentary. When Prince Rāhula, who had thus gone forth, reached the proper age, the Elder Sāriputta himself gave him the higher ordination, and the Elder Mahāmoggallāna was his preceptor for the formal act. The Blessed One, thinking, 'This prince is endowed with noble birth and other advantages; let him not, on account of his birth, clan, family, complexion, beauty, and so on, give rise to conceit or pride,' frequently admonished him with this sutta from a young age until he reached the noble stage. Therefore, it is also said at the conclusion of the sutta: 'In this way, the Blessed One frequently exhorted the Venerable Rāhula with these verses.' Therein, this is the concise meaning of the first verse: 'Rāhula, I hope that because of frequent association you do not disrespect the wise one—whether on account of birth or any other reason—who is a torch-bearer for humans because he upholds the lamp of wisdom and the lamp of the Dhamma teaching. Is he honored by you? Is he constantly revered by you?' He says this referring to the Venerable Sāriputta.

339. Evaṃ vutte āyasmā rāhulo “nāhaṃ bhagavā nīcapuriso viya saṃvāsahetu mānaṃ vā madaṃ vā karomī”ti dīpento imaṃ paṭigāthamāha “nāhaṃ abhiṇhasaṃvāsā”ti. Sā uttānatthā eva.

339. When this was said, the Venerable Rāhula, indicating, 'Blessed One, I do not act with conceit or arrogance on account of association, like a base person,' recited this responsive verse: 'Nāhaṃ abhiṇhasaṃvāsā...' Its meaning is indeed clear.

340. Tato naṃ bhagavā uttariṃ ovadanto pañca kāmaguṇetiādikā avasesagāthāyo āha. Tattha yasmā pañca kāmaguṇā sattānaṃ piyarūpā piyajātikā ativiya sattehi icchitā patthitā[P 1.0341], mano ca nesaṃ ramayanti, te cāyasmā rāhulo hitvā saddhāya gharā nikkhanto, na rājābhinīto, na corābhinīto, na iṇaṭṭo, na bhayaṭṭo, na jīvikāpakato, tasmā naṃ bhagavā “pañca kāmaguṇe hitvā, piyarūpe manorame, saddhāya gharā nikkhammā”ti samuttejetvā imassa nekkhammassa patirūpāya paṭipattiyā niyojento āha – “dukkhassantakaro bhavā”ti.

340. Then, the Blessed One, further exhorting him, spoke the remaining verses, beginning with 'the five strands of sensual pleasure.' Herein, because the five strands of sensual pleasure are of a dear form and a dear nature to beings, and are highly desired and longed for by them, and because they delight their minds, and the Venerable Rāhula, having abandoned them, went forth from home out of faith—not led out by a king, not led out by thieves, not on account of debt, and not for the sake of livelihood—therefore the Blessed One, encouraging him, said, 'Having abandoned the five strands of sensual pleasure, of a dear form and delightful to the mind, you went forth from home out of faith.' Then, directing him toward the practice suitable for this renunciation, he said, 'Be one who makes an end of suffering.'

Tattha [V 2.0068] siyā “nanu cāyasmā dāyajjaṃ patthento balakkārena pabbājito, atha kasmā bhagavā āha – ‘saddhāya gharā nikkhammā’”ti vuccate – nekkhammādhimuttattā. Ayañhi āyasmā dīgharattaṃ nekkhammādhimutto padumuttarasammāsambuddhassa puttaṃ uparevataṃ nāma sāmaṇeraṃ disvā saṅkho nāma nāgarājā hutvā satta divase dānaṃ datvā tathābhāvaṃ patthetvā tato pabhuti patthanāsampanno abhinīhārasampanno satasahassakappe pāramiyo pūretvā antimabhavaṃ upapanno. Evaṃ nekkhammādhimuttatañcassa bhagavā jānāti. Tathāgatabalaññatarañhi etaṃ ñāṇaṃ. Tasmā āha – “saddhāya gharā nikkhammā”ti. Atha vā dīgharattaṃ saddhāyeva gharā nikkhamma idāni dukkhassantakaro bhavāti ayamettha adhippāyo.

Herein, it might be asked: 'Was not the venerable one ordained by force while seeking an inheritance? Why then did the Blessed One say, "you went forth from home out of faith"?' To this it is said: Because of his inclination towards renunciation. For this venerable one, for a long time inclined towards renunciation, upon seeing the novice named Uparevata, the son of the Perfectly Enlightened One Padumuttara, became a nāga king named Saṅkha, gave alms for seven days, and aspired to such a state. From then on, endowed with aspiration and endowed with resolution, he fulfilled the perfections for one hundred thousand aeons and reached his final existence. Thus the Blessed One knows his inclination towards renunciation. For this knowledge is one of the powers of the Tathāgata. Therefore He said, 'you went forth from home out of faith.' Or alternatively, the meaning here is this: 'Having for a long time gone forth from home out of faith, now be one who makes an end of suffering.'

341. Idānissa ādito pabhuti vaṭṭadukkhassa antakiriyāya paṭipattiṃ dassetuṃ “mitte bhajassu kalyāṇe”tiādimāha. Tattha sīlādīhi adhikā kalyāṇamittā nāma, te bhajanto himavantaṃ nissāya mahāsālā mūlādīhi viya sīlādīhi vaḍḍhati. Tenāha – “mitte bhajassu kalyāṇe”ti. Pantañca sayanāsanaṃ, vivittaṃ appanigghosanti yañca sayanāsanaṃ pantaṃ dūraṃ vivittaṃ appākiṇṇaṃ appanigghosaṃ, yattha migasūkarādisaddena araññasaññā [M 2.0075] uppajjati, tathārūpaṃ sayanāsanañca bhajassu. Mattaññū hohi bhojaneti pamāṇaññū hohi, paṭiggahaṇamattaṃ paribhogamattañca jānāhīti attho. Tattha paṭiggahaṇamattaññunā deyyadhammepi appe dāyakepi appaṃ dātukāme appameva gahetabbaṃ, deyyadhamme appe dāyake pana bahuṃ dātukāmepi appameva gahetabbaṃ, deyyadhamme pana bahutare [P 1.0342] dāyakepi appaṃ dātukāme appameva gahetabbaṃ, deyyadhammepi bahutare dāyakepi bahuṃ dātukāme attano balaṃ jānitvā gahetabbaṃ. Apica mattāyeva vaṇṇitā bhagavatāti paribhogamattaññunā puttamaṃsaṃ viya akkhabbhañjanamiva ca yoniso manasi karitvā bhojanaṃ paribhuñjitabbanti.

341. Now, to show him the practice from the beginning for making an end to the suffering of the round, He said, 'Associate with good friends,' and so on. Herein, those who are superior in virtue and so on are called 'good friends.' By associating with them, one grows in virtue and so on, just as great sāl trees, relying on the Himālaya, grow by their roots and so on. Therefore He said: 'Associate with good friends.' And 'a remote lodging, secluded and with little noise' means a lodging that is remote, distant, secluded, uncrowded, and with little noise, where from the sound of deer, boars, and so on, the perception of 'forest' arises; one should frequent such a lodging. 'Be moderate in eating' means be one who knows the measure; know the measure in receiving and the measure in consuming. Herein, one who knows the measure in receiving should take only a little when the alms-material is meager and the donors wish to give little; when the alms-material is meager but the donors wish to give much, one should still take only a little; when the alms-material is plentiful but the donors wish to give little, one should take only a little; and when the alms-material is plentiful and the donors also wish to give much, one should take an amount after knowing one's own capacity. Furthermore, since moderation itself has been praised by the Blessed One, one who knows the measure in consuming should consume food after reflecting wisely upon it as being like a son's flesh or like axle-grease.

342. Evamimāya gāthāya brahmacariyassa upakārabhūtāya kalyāṇamittasevanāya niyojetvā senāsanabhojanamukhena ca paccayaparibhogapārisuddhisīle samādapetvā idāni yasmā cīvarādīsu taṇhāya micchāājīvo hoti, tasmā taṃ paṭisedhetvā ājīvapārisuddhisīle samādapento “cīvare piṇḍapāte cā”ti imaṃ gāthamāha. Tattha paccayeti gilānappaccaye. Etesūti etesu catūsu cīvarādīsu bhikkhūnaṃ taṇhuppādavatthūsu. Taṇhaṃ mākāsīti “hirikopīnapaṭicchādanādiatthameva te cattāro paccayā niccāturānaṃ purisānaṃ paṭikārabhūtā jajjaragharassevimassa atidubbalassa kāyassa upatthambhabhūtā”tiādinā nayena ādīnavaṃ passanto taṇhaṃ mā janesi, ajanento anuppādento viharāhīti vuttaṃ hoti. Kiṃ kāraṇaṃ? Mā [V 2.0069] lokaṃ punarāgami. Etesu hi taṇhaṃ karonto taṇhāya ākaḍḍhiyamāno punapi imaṃ lokaṃ āgacchati. So tvaṃ etesu taṇhaṃ mākāsi, evaṃ sante na puna imaṃ lokaṃ āgamissasīti.

342. Thus, with this verse that is beneficial to the holy life, having directed him to the cultivation of good friends, and by way of lodging and food having made him undertake the virtue of purity in the use of requisites, now, because wrong livelihood arises from craving for robes and so on, the Blessed One, in order to reject that craving and make him undertake the virtue of purity of livelihood, spoke this verse beginning, 'Regarding robes and almsfood….' Herein, 'requisites' refers to the requisites for the sick. 'Regarding these' refers to these four things beginning with robes, which are grounds for the arising of craving in bhikkhus. 'Do not have craving' means: seeing the danger in this way—'These four requisites are only for the purpose of covering the private parts, etc.; they are a remedy for a person who is constantly ill and a support for this extremely feeble body, which is like a dilapidated house'—do not generate craving. It means: dwell without generating it, without producing it. For what reason? 'Do not come to the world again.' For one who creates craving for these things, being dragged by that craving, comes to this world again. You, therefore, should not have craving for these things; this being so, you will not come to this world again.

Evaṃ vutte āyasmā rāhulo “cīvare taṇhaṃ mākāsīti maṃ bhagavā āhā”ti cīvarapaṭisaṃyuttāni dve dhutaṅgāni samādiyi paṃsukūlikaṅgañca, tecīvarikaṅgañca. “Piṇḍapāte taṇhaṃ mākāsīti maṃ bhagavā āhā”ti piṇḍapātapaṭisaṃyuttāni pañca dhutaṅgāni samādiyi – piṇḍapātikaṅgaṃ, sapadānacārikaṅgaṃ, ekāsanikaṅgaṃ, pattapiṇḍikaṅgaṃ, khalupacchābhattikaṅganti. “Senāsane taṇhaṃ mākāsīti maṃ bhagavā āhā”ti senāsanapaṭisaṃyuttāni [M 2.0076] cha dhutaṅgāni samādiyi – āraññikaṅgaṃ, abbhokāsikaṅgaṃ, rukkhamūlikaṅgaṃ, yathāsanthatikaṅgaṃ, sosānikaṅgaṃ, nesajjikaṅganti. “Gilānappaccaye taṇhaṃ mākāsīti maṃ bhagavā āhā”ti sabbappaccayesu yathālābhaṃ yathābalaṃ yathāsāruppanti tīhi [P 1.0343] santosehi santuṭṭho ahosi, yathā taṃ subbaco kulaputto padakkhiṇaggāhī anusāsaninti.

When this was said, the Venerable Rāhula reflected, 'The Blessed One told me, "Do not have craving for robes,"' and he undertook the two ascetic practices connected with robes: the refuse-rag wearer’s practice and the triple-robe wearer’s practice. He reflected, 'The Blessed One told me, "Do not have craving for almsfood,"' and he undertook the five ascetic practices connected with almsfood: the alms-gatherer’s practice, the sequential-goer’s practice, the one-session-eater’s practice, the bowl-food-eater's practice, and the practice of refusing food offered later. He reflected, 'The Blessed One told me, "Do not have craving for lodging,"' and he undertook the six ascetic practices connected with lodging: the forest-dweller’s practice, the open-air-dweller’s practice, the tree-root-dweller’s practice, the any-lodging-user’s practice, the charnel-ground-dweller’s practice, and the sitter’s practice. He reflected, 'The Blessed One told me, "Do not have craving for medicinal requisites,"' and he became content with all requisites with the three kinds of contentment—contentment with whatever is obtained, with what is according to one's strength, and with what is suitable—just as an amenable son of good family is one who accepts instruction respectfully.

343. Evaṃ bhagavā āyasmantaṃ rāhulaṃ ājīvapārisuddhisīle samādapetvā idāni avasesasīle samathavipassanāsu ca samādapetuṃ “saṃvuto pātimokkhasmi”ntiādimāha. Tattha saṃvuto pātimokkhasminti ettha bhavassūti pāṭhaseso. Bhavāti antimapadena vā sambandho veditabbo, tathā dutiyapade. Evametehi dvīhi vacanehi pātimokkhasaṃvarasīle, indriyasaṃvarasīle ca samādapesi. Pākaṭavasena cettha pañcindriyāni vuttāni. Lakkhaṇato pana chaṭṭhampi vuttaṃyeva hotīti veditabbaṃ. Sati kāyagatā tyatthūti evaṃ catupārisuddhisīle patiṭṭhitassa tuyhaṃ catudhātuvavatthānacatubbidhasampajaññānāpānassatiāhārepaṭikūlasaññābhāvanādibhedā kāyagatā sati atthu bhavatu, bhāvehi nanti attho. Nibbidābahulo bhavāti saṃsāravaṭṭe ukkaṇṭhanabahulo sabbaloke anabhiratasaññī hohīti attho.

343. Thus, having made the Venerable Rāhula undertake the virtue of purity of livelihood, the Blessed One now, in order to make him undertake the remaining virtues and serenity and insight, says, “Restrained in the Pātimokkha,” and so on. Herein, regarding “Restrained in the Pātimokkha,” the remainder of the phrase should be supplied as “may you be.” The word “be” should be understood as connected with the last word, and similarly with the second phrase. Thus, with these two statements, He made him undertake the virtue of Pātimokkha restraint and the virtue of restraint of the sense faculties. Here, the five sense faculties are mentioned explicitly, but it should be understood that by its characteristic the sixth is also stated. “May mindfulness directed to the body be yours”: thus, for you who are established in the fourfold purity of virtue, may there be mindfulness directed to the body, which is differentiated as the analysis of the four elements, the four kinds of clear comprehension, mindfulness of breathing, the development of the perception of repulsiveness in food, and so on; the meaning is, “develop it.” “Be full of disenchantment”: the meaning is, be greatly weary of the round of existence, perceiving no delight in the whole world.

344. Ettāvatā nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ upacārabhūmiṃ dassetvā idāni appanābhūmiṃ dassento “nimittaṃ parivajjehī”tiādimāha. Tattha nimittanti rāgaṭṭhāniyaṃ subhanimittaṃ. Teneva naṃ parato visesento āha – “subhaṃ rāgūpasañhita”nti. Parivajjehīti amanasikārena pariccajāhi. Asubhāya cittaṃ bhāvehīti yathā saviññāṇake aviññāṇake vā kāye asubhabhāvanā sampajjati, evaṃ cittaṃ bhāvehi. Ekaggaṃ susamāhitanti upacārasamādhinā ekaggaṃ, appanāsamādhinā susamāhitaṃ. Yathā te īdisaṃ cittaṃ hoti, tathā naṃ bhāvehīti attho.

344. Having thus shown the stage of access pertaining to penetration, He now shows the stage of absorption, saying, “Avoid the sign,” and so on. Herein, “the sign” refers to the beautiful sign that is a basis for lust. To further clarify this, He says, “the beautiful, associated with lust.” “Avoid it”—abandon it by non-attention. “Develop the mind on the unattractive”—develop the mind just as the meditation on the unattractive succeeds with regard to a sentient or non-sentient body. “Unified and well-composed”—unified by access concentration, well-composed by absorption concentration. The meaning is: develop it so that your mind becomes like this.

345. Evamassa [V 2.0070] appanābhūmiṃ dassetvā vipassanaṃ dassento “animitta”ntiādimāha. Tattha animittañca bhāvehīti evaṃ nibbedhabhāgiyena samādhinā samāhitacitto vipassanaṃ bhāvehīti vuttaṃ hoti. Vipassanā hi “aniccānupassanāñāṇaṃ niccanimittato vimuccatīti animitto vimokkho”tiādinā [M 2.0077] nayena rāganimittādīnaṃ vā aggahaṇena animittavohāraṃ labhati. Yathāha –

345. Having thus shown him the stage of absorption, He now shows him insight, saying, “Develop the signless.” Herein, “develop the signless” means that one whose mind is composed by the concentration pertaining to penetration should develop insight. For insight gains the designation “signless” by not grasping the signs of lust, etc., according to the method: “The knowledge of contemplating impermanence is liberated from the sign of permanence, thus it is the signless liberation.” As it is said:

“So khvāhaṃ, āvuso, sabbanimittānaṃ amanasikārā animittaṃ cetosamādhiṃ upasampajja [P 1.0344] viharāmi. Tassa mayhaṃ, āvuso, iminā vihārena viharato nimittānusāri viññāṇaṃ hotī”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.340).

“Indeed, friends, by not attending to any signs, I enter and dwell in the signless concentration of mind. While I dwell in this state, friends, my consciousness follows after signs.”

Mānānusayamujjahāti imāya animittabhāvanāya aniccasaññaṃ paṭilabhitvā “aniccasaññino, meghiya, anattasaññā saṇṭhāti, anattasaññī asmimānasamugghātaṃ pāpuṇātī”ti evamādinā (a. ni. 9.3; udā. 31) anukkamena mānānusayaṃ ujjaha pajaha pariccajāhīti attho. Tato mānābhisamayā, upasanto carissasīti athevaṃ ariyamaggena mānassa abhisamayā khayā vayā pahānā paṭinissaggā upasanto nibbuto sītibhūto sabbadarathapariḷāhavirahito yāva anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbāsi, tāva suññatānimittāppaṇihitānaṃ aññataraññatarena phalasamāpattivihārena carissasi viharissasīti arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi.

“Abandon the underlying tendency to conceit”: the meaning is that by means of this development of the signless, having acquired the perception of impermanence, one should sequentially abandon, give up, and relinquish the underlying tendency to conceit, in accordance with such passages as: “For one with the perception of impermanence, Meghiya, the perception of not-self is established. One with the perception of not-self attains the uprooting of the conceit ‘I am.’” “Then, from the full understanding of conceit, you will wander calmed”: then, by the noble path, through the full understanding, destruction, fading away, abandonment, and relinquishment of conceit, you will wander calmed, extinguished, become cool, devoid of all distress and burning. Until you attain final Nibbāna with the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining, you will dwell, faring by way of the fruition attainment of one or another of emptiness, signlessness, or wishlessness. Thus He concluded the discourse with the peak of arahantship.

Tato paraṃ “itthaṃ sudaṃ bhagavā”tiādi saṅgītikārakānaṃ vacanaṃ. Tattha itthaṃ sudanti itthaṃ su idaṃ, evamevāti vuttaṃ hoti. Sesamettha uttānatthameva. Evaṃ ovadiyamāno cāyasmā rāhulo paripākagatesu vimuttiparipācaniyesu dhammesu cūḷarāhulovādasuttapariyosāne anekehi devatāsahassehi saddhiṃ arahatte patiṭṭhāsīti.

Thereafter, the words beginning “Thus indeed the Blessed One…” are those of the compilers of the canon. Herein, “thus indeed” means “thus, truly,” that is, “just so.” The rest here has a plain meaning. Being thus advised, the Venerable Rāhula, when his qualities conducive to liberation had matured, was established in arahantship at the conclusion of the Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta, along with many thousands of devas.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya,

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya rāhulasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Rāhula Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary is concluded.

12. Nigrodhakappasutta-(vaṅgīsasutta)-vaṇṇanā

12. The Commentary to the Nigrodhakappa Sutta (Vaṅgīsa Sutta)

Evaṃ [V 2.0071] me sutanti nigrodhakappasuttaṃ, “vaṅgīsasutta”ntipi vuccati. Kā uppatti? Ayameva yāssa nidāne vuttā. Tattha evaṃ metiādīni vuttatthāneva, yato [M 2.0078] tāni aññāni ca tathāvidhāni chaḍḍetvā avuttanayameva vaṇṇayissāma. Aggāḷave cetiyeti āḷaviyaṃ aggacetiye. Anuppanne hi bhagavati aggāḷavagotamakādīni anekāni cetiyāni ahesuṃ yakkhanāgādīnaṃ bhavanāni. Tāni uppanne bhagavati manussā vināsetvā vihāre akaṃsu, teneva ca nāmena vohariṃsu. Tato [P 1.0345] aggāḷavacetiyasaṅkhāte vihāre viharatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Āyasmato vaṅgīsassāti ettha āyasmāti piyavacanaṃ, vaṅgīsoti tassa therassa nāmaṃ. So jātito pabhuti evaṃ veditabbo – so kira paribbājakassa putto paribbājikāya kucchimhi jāto aññataraṃ vijjaṃ jānāti, yassānubhāvena chavasīsaṃ ākoṭetvā sattānaṃ gatiṃ jānāti. Manussāpi sudaṃ attano ñātīnaṃ kālakatānaṃ susānato sīsāni ānetvā taṃ tesaṃ gatiṃ pucchanti. So “asukaniraye nibbatto, asukamanussaloke”ti vadati. Te tena vimhitā tassa bahuṃ dhanaṃ denti. Evaṃ so sakalajambudīpe pākaṭo ahosi.

“Thus have I heard”—this is the Nigrodhakappa Sutta, which is also called the “Vaṅgīsa Sutta.” What is its origin? It is the same as that stated in its introduction. Here, the meaning of “Thus have I heard” and similar phrases is as previously explained. Therefore, omitting those and other such details, we will explain only what has not been explained. “At Aggāḷava Shrine” means at the chief shrine in Āḷavī. Before the Blessed One arose, there were many shrines in Āḷavī, such as Aggāḷava and Gotamaka, which were the dwellings of yakkhas and nāgas. When the Blessed One appeared, people destroyed these and built monasteries, yet they continued to refer to them by the same names. Thus, it is said that he dwelt in the monastery known as Aggāḷava Shrine. “Of the Venerable Vaṅgīsa”: here, “venerable” is an affectionate term, and “Vaṅgīsa” is the name of that elder. From birth, he should be understood thus: it is said that he was the son of a male wanderer, born from the womb of a female wanderer, and he knew a certain science. By its power, he could tap on a skull and know a being's destination. People would even bring the skulls of their deceased relatives from the charnel ground and ask him about their destination. He would say, “This one was reborn in such-and-such a hell; this one in such-and-such a human world.” Astonished by this, they would give him much wealth. In this way, he became famous throughout all of Jambudīpa.

So satasahassakappaṃ pūritapāramī abhinīhārasampanno pañcahi purisasahassehi parivuto gāmanigamajanapadarājadhānīsu vicaranto sāvatthiṃ anuppatto. Tena ca samayena bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati, sāvatthivāsino purebhattaṃ dānaṃ datvā pacchābhattaṃ sunivatthā supārutā pupphagandhādīni gahetvā dhammassavanatthāya jetavanaṃ gacchanti. So te disvā “mahājanakāyo kuhiṃ gacchatī”ti pucchi. Athassa te ācikkhiṃsu – “buddho loke uppanno, so bahujanahitāya dhammaṃ deseti, tattha gacchāmā”ti. Sopi tehi saddhiṃ saparivāro gantvā bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammoditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Atha naṃ bhagavā āmantesi – “kiṃ, vaṅgīsa, jānāsi kira tādisaṃ vijjaṃ, yāya sattānaṃ chavasīsāni ākoṭetvā gatiṃ pavedesī”ti? “Evaṃ, bho gotama, jānāmī”ti. Bhagavā niraye nibbattassa sīsaṃ āharāpetvā dassesi, so nakhena ākoṭetvā “niraye nibbattassa sīsaṃ bho gotamā”ti āha. Evaṃ sabbagatinibbattānaṃ sīsāni dassesi, sopi tatheva ñatvā ārocesi. Athassa bhagavā khīṇāsavasīsaṃ dassesi, so punappunaṃ ākoṭetvā [V 2.0072] na aññāsi. Tato bhagavā “avisayo [M 2.0079] te ettha vaṅgīsa, mameveso [P 1.0346] visayo, khīṇāsavasīsa”nti vatvā imaṃ gāthamabhāsi –

Having perfected his perfections for a hundred thousand eons and fulfilled his aspiration, surrounded by five thousand men, wandering through villages, market towns, country districts, and royal cities, he arrived at Sāvatthī. At that time, the Blessed One was dwelling in Sāvatthī. The residents of Sāvatthī, having given alms in the morning, would in the afternoon get well-dressed and well-robed, take flowers, perfumes, and so on, and go to Jetavana to listen to the Dhamma. Seeing them, he asked, 'Where is this great crowd going?' They replied, 'A Buddha has arisen in the world, teaching the Dhamma for the welfare of many people. We are going there.' He too, along with his retinue, went there, exchanged courteous greetings with the Blessed One, and sat to one side. Then the Blessed One addressed him: 'Vaṅgīsa, is it true that you know such a science by which you tap on the skulls of beings and declare their destination?' 'Yes, Venerable Gotama, I know it,' he replied. The Blessed One had the skull of one reborn in hell brought and showed it to him. Tapping it with his fingernail, he said, 'This is the skull of one reborn in hell, Venerable Gotama.' Similarly, skulls of those reborn in all destinations were shown, and he, knowing them, declared them accordingly. Then the Blessed One showed him the skull of one whose taints are destroyed. Tapping it repeatedly, he could not recognize it. Thereupon the Blessed One said, 'This is beyond your scope, Vaṅgīsa. This is my domain—the skull of one whose taints are destroyed,' and he spoke this verse:

“Gatī migānaṃ pavanaṃ, ākāso pakkhinaṃ gati;

Vibhavo gati dhammānaṃ, nibbānaṃ arahato gatī”ti. (pari. 339);

The forest is the destination of beasts, the sky is the destination of birds; cessation is the destination of phenomena, Nibbāna is the destination of the Arahant.

Vaṅgīso gāthaṃ sutvā “imaṃ me, bho gotama, vijjaṃ dehī”ti āha. Bhagavā “nāyaṃ vijjā apabbajitānaṃ sampajjatī”ti āha. So “pabbājetvā vā maṃ, bho gotama, yaṃ vā icchasi, taṃ katvā imaṃ vijjaṃ dehī”ti āha. Tadā ca bhagavato nigrodhakappatthero samīpe hoti, taṃ bhagavā āṇāpesi – “tena hi, nigrodhakappa, imaṃ pabbājehī”ti. So taṃ pabbājetvā tacapañcakakammaṭṭhānaṃ ācikkhi. Vaṅgīso anupubbena paṭisambhidāppatto arahā ahosi. Etadagge ca bhagavatā niddiṭṭho “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ paṭibhānavantānaṃ yadidaṃ vaṅgīso”ti (a. ni. 1.212).

Hearing the verse, Vaṅgīsa said, 'Venerable Gotama, give me this science.' The Blessed One replied, 'This science is not accomplished by those who have not gone forth.' He said, 'Venerable Gotama, having ordained me, and having done whatever you wish, give me this science.' At that time, the Elder Nigrodhakappa was near the Blessed One. The Blessed One instructed him: 'Well then, Nigrodhakappa, give him the going forth.' He gave him the going forth and taught him the meditation subject of the five items ending with the skin. Vaṅgīsa gradually attained the analytical knowledges and became an arahant. And he was designated by the Blessed One as the foremost, thus: 'Monks, the foremost among my bhikkhu disciples who are quick-witted is this one, namely, Vaṅgīsa.'

Evaṃ samudāgatassa āyasmato vaṅgīsassa upajjhāyo vajjāvajjādiupanijjhāyanena evaṃ laddhavohāro nigrodhakappo nāma thero. Kappoti tassa therassa nāmaṃ, nigrodhamūle pana arahattaṃ adhigatattā “nigrodhakappo”ti bhagavatā vutto. Tato naṃ bhikkhūpi evaṃ voharanti. Sāsane thirabhāvaṃ pattoti thero. Aggāḷave cetiye aciraparinibbuto hotīti tasmiṃ cetiye aciraparinibbuto hoti. Rahogatassa paṭisallīnassāti gaṇamhā vūpakaṭṭhattā rahogatassa kāyena, paṭisallīnassa cittena tehi tehi visayehi paṭinivattitvā sallīnassa. Evaṃ cetaso parivitakko udapādīti iminā ākārena vitakko uppajji. Kasmā pana udapādīti. Asammukhattā diṭṭhāsevanattā ca. Ayañhi tassa parinibbānakāle na sammukhā ahosi, diṭṭhapubbañcānena assa hatthakukkuccādipubbāsevanaṃ, tādisañca akhīṇāsavānampi hoti khīṇāsavānampi pubbaparicayena.

The preceptor of the Venerable Vaṅgīsa, who had come to be thus, was the elder named Nigrodhakappa, who received this designation by closely watching over faults and virtues. 'Kappa' was that elder's name, but because he attained arahantship at the foot of a banyan tree, he was called 'Nigrodhakappa' by the Blessed One. Thereafter, the bhikkhus also referred to him thus. An elder (thera) is one who has attained stability in the Dispensation. 'He had recently attained final Nibbāna at the Aggāḷava Shrine' means he had passed away not long before at that shrine. 'Secluded and withdrawn': secluded in body because he was physically apart from the group; withdrawn in mind, having turned back and retreated from various sense objects. 'Thus a thought arose in his mind': in this way a thought occurred to him. But why did it arise? Because he was not in his presence and because he had observed his habits. For at the time of his final Nibbāna, Vaṅgīsa was not present, and he had previously seen his former habits, such as fidgetiness of hands. And such behavior occurs in both those whose taints are not destroyed and those whose taints are destroyed, due to past habituation.

Tathā hi piṇḍolabhāradvājo pacchābhattaṃ divāvihāratthāya udenassa uyyānameva gacchati [P 1.0347] pubbe rājā hutvā tattha paricāresīti iminā pubbaparicayena, gavampatitthero tāvatiṃsabhavane suññaṃ devavimānaṃ gacchati devaputto hutvā tattha paricāresīti iminā pubbaparicayena. Pilindavaccho bhikkhū vasalavādena samudācarati abbokiṇṇāni pañca jātisatāni [M 2.0080] brāhmaṇo hutvā tathā abhāsīti iminā pubbaparicayena. Tasmā asammukhattā diṭṭhāsevanattā cassa evaṃ cetaso [V 2.0073] parivitakko udapādi “parinibbuto nu kho me upajjhāyo, udāhu no parinibbuto”ti. Tato paraṃ uttānatthameva. Ekaṃsaṃ cīvaraṃ katvāti ettha pana puna saṇṭhāpanena evaṃ vuttaṃ. Ekaṃsanti ca vāmaṃsaṃ pārupitvā ṭhitassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Yato yathā vāmaṃsaṃ pārupitvā ṭhitaṃ hoti, tathā cīvaraṃ katvāti evamassattho veditabbo. Sesaṃ pākaṭameva.

For indeed, the Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja, after the meal, goes to Udena's park for the day's abiding because in the past, having been a king, he frequented that place—this is due to past habituation. The Elder Gavampati goes to an empty celestial mansion in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven because in the past, having been a deva, he frequented that place—this is due to past habituation. The Venerable Pilindavaccha addresses the bhikkhus with the term 'outcaste' because for five hundred unbroken births, having been a brahmin, he spoke thus—this is due to past habituation. Therefore, because he was not in his presence and because he had observed his habits, this thought arose in his mind: 'Has my preceptor attained final Nibbāna, or has he not?' From here on, the meaning is plain. 'Having arranged his robe over one shoulder': here, however, this is said by way of arranging it again. 'Over one shoulder' is a designation for one who stands having covered the left shoulder. Therefore, the meaning should be understood as: 'having arranged his robe just as one stands with the left shoulder covered.' The rest is obvious.

346. Anomapaññanti omaṃ vuccati parittaṃ lāmakaṃ, na omapaññaṃ, anomapaññaṃ, mahāpaññanti attho. Diṭṭheva dhammeti paccakkhameva, imasmiṃyeva attabhāveti vā attho. Vicikicchānanti evarūpānaṃ parivitakkānaṃ. Ñātoti pākaṭo. Yasassīti lābhaparivārasampanno abhinibbutattoti guttacitto apariḍayhamānacitto vā.

346. 'One of non-inferior wisdom': 'inferior' (oma) is said to be what is limited, base. Not inferior wisdom is non-inferior wisdom; the meaning is 'of great wisdom.' 'In this very life' means directly, or the meaning is 'in this very same existence.' 'Of doubts' refers to such thoughts. 'Known' means manifest. 'Famous' means endowed with gain and a retinue. 'Fully quenched' means with a guarded mind or a mind that is not burning.

347. Tayā katanti nigrodhamūle nisinnattā “nigrodhakappo”ti vadatā tayā katanti yathā attanā upalakkheti, tathā bhaṇati. Bhagavā pana na nisinnattā eva taṃ tathā ālapi, apica kho tattha arahattaṃ pattattā. Brāhmaṇassāti jātiṃ sandhāya bhaṇati. So kira brāhmaṇamahāsālakulā pabbajito. Namassaṃ acarīti namassamāno vihāsi. Mutyapekkhoti nibbānasaṅkhātaṃ vimuttiṃ apekkhamāno, nibbānaṃ patthentoti vuttaṃ hoti. Daḷhadhammadassīti bhagavantaṃ ālapati. Daḷhadhammo hi nibbānaṃ abhijjanaṭṭhena, tañca bhagavā dasseti. Tasmā taṃ “daḷhadhammadassī”ti āha.

347. “Made by you” means: the name “Nigrodhakappa” was made by you who said it because he was sitting at the foot of a banyan tree. He speaks as he himself conceives it. The Blessed One, however, did not address him thus merely because he sat there, but rather because he had attained arahantship there. “Of the brahmin” means he speaks with reference to his birth. It is said that he had gone forth from a great sāl-tree brahmin family. “He paid homage” means he dwelled paying homage. “Seeking liberation” means seeking the liberation called Nibbāna; that is to say, he was aspiring for Nibbāna. “Seer of the stable Dhamma”: he addresses the Blessed One. For Nibbāna is the stable Dhamma because of its indestructible nature, and the Blessed One reveals it. Therefore, he calls him “Seer of the stable Dhamma.”

348. Sakyātipi bhagavantameva kulanāmena ālapati. Mayampi sabbeti niravasesaparisaṃ saṅgaṇhitvā attānaṃ dassento bhaṇati. Samantacakkhūtipi bhagavantameva sabbaññutaññāṇena ālapati. Samavaṭṭhitāti sammā avaṭṭhitā ābhogaṃ katvā ṭhitā. Noti amhākaṃ. Savanāyāti [P 1.0348] imassa pañhassa veyyākaraṇassavanatthāya. Sotāti sotindriyāni. Tuvaṃ no satthā tvamanuttarosīti thutivacanamattamevetaṃ.

348. “O Sakyan”: he addresses the Blessed One by his clan name. “We all”: including the entire assembly without exception and presenting himself, he speaks. “O One with Vision all around”: he addresses the Blessed One by his knowledge of omniscience. “Are ready”: well prepared, standing having given attention. “Our” means “of us.” “To hear”: for the purpose of hearing the explanation of this question. “Ear” means the ear-faculties. “You are our Teacher, you are the unsurpassed”: this is merely a statement of praise.

349. Chindeva [M 2.0081] no vicikicchanti akusalavicikicchāya nibbicikiccho so, vicikicchāpatirūpakaṃ pana taṃ parivitakkaṃ sandhāyevamāha. Brūhi metanti brūhi me etaṃ, yaṃ mayā yācitosi “taṃ sāvakaṃ sakya, mayampi sabbe aññātumicchāmā”ti, brūvanto ca taṃ brāhmaṇaṃ parinibbutaṃ vedaya bhūripañña majjheva no bhāsa, parinibbutaṃ ñatvā mahāpaññaṃ bhagavā majjheva amhākaṃ sabbesaṃ bhāsa, yathā sabbeva mayaṃ jāneyyāma. Sakkova devāna sahassanettoti idaṃ pana thutivacanameva. Apicassa ayaṃ adhippāyo – yathā sakko sahassanetto devānaṃ majjhe [V 2.0074] tehi sakkaccaṃ sampaṭicchitavacano bhāsati, evaṃ amhākaṃ majjhe amhehi sampaṭicchitavacano bhāsāti.

349. “Cut off our doubt”: he is free from unwholesome doubt, without doubt; but he speaks thus referring to that discursive thought which resembles doubt. “Tell me” means: tell me this, since you have been asked by me, “that disciple, O Sakyan, we too all wish to know.” Speaking thus, he says: “Make known that brahmin who has attained final Nibbāna, O one of vast wisdom; speak in our midst.” “Having known that he has attained final Nibbāna, O greatly wise one, speak, O Blessed One, in the midst of us all, so that we may all know.” “Like Sakka, the thousand-eyed one among the gods”: this is just a statement of praise. Moreover, this is his intention: just as Sakka, the thousand-eyed one, speaks among the gods with words that are respectfully accepted by them, so may you speak among us with words that are to be respectfully accepted by us.

350. Ye kecīti imampi gāthaṃ bhagavantaṃ thunantoyeva vattukāmataṃ janetuṃ bhaṇati. Tassattho ye keci abhijjhādayo ganthā tesaṃ appahāne mohavicikicchānaṃ pahānābhāvato “mohamaggā”ti ca “aññāṇapakkhā”ti ca “vicikicchaṭṭhānā”ti ca vuccanti. Sabbe te tathāgataṃ patvā tathāgatassa desanābalena viddhaṃsitā na bhavanti nassanti. Kiṃ kāraṇaṃ? Cakkhuñhi etaṃ paramaṃ narānaṃ, yasmā tathāgato sabbaganthavidhamanapaññācakkhujananato narānaṃ paramaṃ cakkhunti vuttaṃ hoti.

350. He speaks this verse beginning “Whatever” while praising the Blessed One in order to arouse the desire to speak. Its meaning is: whatever fetters there are, such as covetousness and so on, are called “paths of delusion,” “partisans of ignorance,” and “occasions for doubt” because of the non-abandonment of delusion and doubt when those fetters are not abandoned. All of them, on reaching the Tathāgata, are demolished by the power of the Tathāgata’s teaching; they do not exist, they perish. What is the reason? “For this is the supreme eye for human beings.” This means that because the Tathāgata generates the eye of wisdom that demolishes all fetters, he is called the supreme eye for human beings.

351. No ce hi jātūti imampi gāthaṃ thunantoyeva vattukāmataṃ janentova bhaṇati. Tattha jātūti ekaṃsavacanaṃ. Purisoti bhagavantaṃ sandhāyāha. Jotimantoti paññājotisamannāgatā sāriputtādayo. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yadi bhagavā yathā puratthimādibhedo vāto abbhaghanaṃ vihanati, evaṃ desanāvegena kilese na vihaneyya[P 1.0349]. Tathā yathā abbhaghanena nivuto loko tamova hoti ekandhakāro, evaṃ aññāṇanivutopi tamovassa. Yepi ime dāni jotimanto khāyanti sāriputtādayo, tepi narā na tapeyyunti.

351. He speaks this verse beginning “If ever” while praising him and arousing the desire to speak. Here, “ever” (jātu) is a word expressing certainty. “A man” refers to the Blessed One. “Radiant ones” refers to Sāriputta and others endowed with the light of wisdom. This is what is meant: If the Blessed One did not dispel the defilements with the force of his teaching—just as a wind from the east and other directions scatters a mass of clouds—then just as the world enveloped by a mass of clouds would be sheer darkness, a single gloom, so too, one enveloped by ignorance would be darkness. And even these who now appear as radiant ones, Sāriputta and others, those men would not shine.

352. Dhīrā cāti imampi gāthaṃ purimanayeneva bhaṇati. Tassattho dhīrā ca paṇḍitā purisā pajjotakarā bhavanti, paññāpajjotaṃ uppādenti. Tasmā ahaṃ taṃ vīra padhānavīriyasamannāgato bhagavā tatheva maññe dhīroti ca [M 2.0082] pajjotakarotveva ca maññāmi. Mayañhi vipassinaṃ sabbadhamme yathābhūtaṃ passantaṃ bhagavantaṃ jānantā eva upāgamumhā, tasmā parisāsu no āvikarohi kappaṃ, nigrodhakappaṃ ācikkha pakāsehīti.

352. “And the wise”: he speaks this verse too in the same way as before. Its meaning is: wise and learned men become illuminators; they generate the light of wisdom. Therefore, “O hero”—O Blessed One endowed with striving energy—“I consider you to be just so”: I consider you to be wise and an illuminator. “For we have approached” the Blessed One knowing him as one of insight, as one who sees all things as they really are. “Therefore, make Kappa manifest to us in the assemblies; declare, explain Nigrodhakappa.”

353. Khippanti imampi gāthaṃ purimanayeneva bhaṇati. Tassattho khippaṃ giraṃ eraya lahuṃ acirāyamāno vacanaṃ bhāsa, vagguṃ manoramaṃ bhagavā. Yathā suvaṇṇahaṃso gocarapaṭikkanto jātassaravanasaṇḍaṃ disvā gīvaṃ paggayha uccāretvā rattatuṇḍena saṇikaṃ ataramāno vagguṃ giraṃ nikūjati nicchāreti, evameva tvampi saṇikaṃ nikūja, iminā mahāpurisalakkhaṇaññatarena bindussarena suvikappitena suṭṭhuvikappitena abhisaṅkhatena. Ete mayaṃ sabbeva ujugatā avikkhittamānasā hutvā tava nikūjitaṃ suṇomāti.

353. “Swiftly”: he speaks this verse too in the same way as before. Its meaning is: “Swiftly utter your voice,” speak your word quickly, without delay, a lovely and delightful word, O Blessed One. Just as a golden goose, having returned from its feeding ground, on seeing a thicket by a natural lake, raises its neck and, with its red beak, slowly, without hurrying, coos, letting out a lovely call, so you too should “coo slowly” with this well-formed, well-fashioned, well-prepared voice with its rounded tone, which is one of the marks of a great man. “We will all listen,” having become upright and with undistracted minds, to your cooing.

354. Pahīnajātimaraṇanti [V 2.0075] imampi gāthaṃ purimanayeneva bhaṇati. Tattha na sesetīti aseso, taṃ asesaṃ. Sotāpannādayo viya kiñci asesetvā pahīnajātimaraṇanti vuttaṃ hoti. Niggayhāti suṭṭhu yācitvā nibandhitvā. Dhonanti dhutasabbapāpaṃ. Vadessāmīti kathāpessāmi dhammaṃ. Na kāmakāro hi puthujjanānanti puthujjanānameva hi kāmakāro natthi, yaṃ patthenti ñātuṃ vā vattuṃ vā, taṃ na sakkonti. Saṅkheyyakāro ca tathāgatānanti tathāgatānaṃ pana vīmaṃsakāro paññāpubbaṅgamā kiriyā. Te yaṃ patthenti ñātuṃ vā vattuṃ vā, taṃ sakkontīti adhippāyo.

354. He speaks this verse beginning “Having abandoned birth and death” in the same way as before. Here, “aseso” means one who does not leave a remainder; “asesaṃ” is the accusative. It is said that he has abandoned birth and death “without remainder,” not like stream-enterers and others who abandon them while still having some remainder. “Having urged him” means having strongly requested and insisted. “The washed one” (dhonaṃ) means one who has shaken off all evil. “I will get him to speak” means I will get him to speak the Dhamma. “For worldlings have no freedom of will”: for worldlings indeed have no freedom of will; what they wish to know or to say, they cannot. “But Tathāgatas act with deliberation”: for Tathāgatas, however, action is preceded by wisdom and investigation. The intention is that whatever they wish to know or to say, they can.

355. Idāni taṃ saṅkheyyakāraṃ [P 1.0350] pakāsento “sampannaveyyākaraṇa”nti gāthamāha. Tassattho – tathā hi tava bhagavā idaṃ samujjupaññassa tattha tattha samuggahītaṃ vuttaṃ pavattitaṃ sampannaveyyākaraṇaṃ, “santatimahāmatto sattatālamattaṃ abbhuggantvā parinibbāyissati, suppabuddho sakko sattame divase pathaviṃ pavisissatī”ti evamādīsu aviparītaṃ diṭṭhaṃ. Tato pana suṭṭhutaraṃ añjaliṃ paṇāmetvā āha – ayamañjalī pacchimo suppaṇāmito, ayamaparopi añjalī suṭṭhutaraṃ paṇāmito. Mā mohayīti mā no akathanena mohayi jānaṃ jānanto kappassa gatiṃ. Anomapaññāti bhagavantaṃ ālapati.

355. Now, making clear that matter of inquiry, he speaks the verse beginning 'A perfect explanation.' Its meaning is: 'Indeed, Blessed One, this perfect explanation of yours, spoken and set forth in response to the well-put question, compiled here and there, is seen to be unerring in such cases as: “Santati the great minister will rise to the height of seven palm trees and attain final Nibbāna; Suppabuddha the Sakyan will enter the earth on the seventh day.” Then, having extended his hands in reverential salutation even more properly, he says: “This is the last salutation, well extended; this final salutation too is extended even more properly.” “Do not delude”: do not delude us by not speaking, you who know, who understand the destiny of Kappa. “O one of excellent wisdom”: he addresses the Blessed One.

356. Parovaranti [M 2.0083] imaṃ pana gāthaṃ aparenapi pariyāyena amohanameva yācanto āha. Tattha parovaranti lokiyalokuttaravasena sundarāsundaraṃ dūresantikaṃ vā. Ariyadhammanti catusaccadhammaṃ. Viditvāti paṭivijjhitvā. Jānanti sabbaṃ ñeyyadhammaṃ jānanto. Vācābhikaṅkhāmīti yathā ghammani ghammatatto puriso kilanto tasito vāriṃ, evaṃ te vācaṃ abhikaṅkhāmi. Sutaṃ pavassāti sutasaṅkhātaṃ saddāyatanaṃ pavassa pagghara muñca pavattehi. “Sutassa vassā”tipi pāṭho, vuttappakārassa saddāyatanassa vuṭṭhiṃ vassāti attho.

356. He speaks this verse beginning 'Things high and low' also in another way, requesting just this: non-delusion. Here, 'things high and low' means the worldly and the supramundane, the beautiful and the ugly, or the far and the near. 'The noble Dhamma' means the Dhamma of the Four Truths. 'Having known' means having penetrated. 'You know': knowing every knowable thing. 'I long for your speech': just as a man afflicted by the heat in the hot season, weary and thirsty, longs for water, so I long for your speech. 'Rain down what is to be heard': rain down, let flow, release, set in motion the sound-base designated as 'what is to be heard.' There is also the reading 'sutassa vassā,' which means: 'rain a shower' of the sound-base of the kind described.

357. Idāni yādisaṃ vācaṃ abhikaṅkhati, taṃ pakāsento –

357. Now, explaining what kind of speech he longs for:

“Yadatthikaṃ brahmacariyaṃ acarī,

Kappāyano kaccissa taṃ amoghaṃ;

Nibbāyi so ādu saupādiseso,

Yathā vimutto ahu taṃ suṇomā”ti. –

“For what purpose Kappāyana lived the holy life, was it not in vain for him? Did he attain Nibbāna, or with a residue remaining? How he was liberated—that we wish to hear.”

Gāthamāha[V 2.0076]. Tattha kappāyanoti kappameva pūjāvasena bhaṇati. Yathā vimuttoti “kiṃ anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā yathā asekkhā, udāhu upādisesāya yathā sekkhā”ti pucchati. Sesamettha pākaṭameva.

He speaks the verse. Here, 'Kappāyana': he speaks of Kappa by this name as a sign of respect. 'How he was liberated': he asks, 'Was it with the Nibbāna-element with no residue remaining, like one beyond training, or with the Nibbāna-element with a residue remaining, like one in training?' The rest here is plain.

358. Evaṃ dvādasahi gāthāhi yācito bhagavā taṃ viyākaronto –

Thus entreated with twelve verses, the Blessed One, explaining it, said:

“Acchecchi taṇhaṃ idha nāmarūpe, (iti bhagavā)

Kaṇhassa sotaṃ dīgharattānusayitaṃ;

Atāri jātiṃ maraṇaṃ asesaṃ,

Iccabravī bhagavā pañcaseṭṭho”ti. –

“He cut off craving here in name-and-form,” (said the Blessed One) “the stream of the Dark One that has long lain latent. He crossed over birth and death completely,” thus spoke the Blessed One, the best of the five.

Gāthamāha. Tattha purimapadassa tāva attho – yāpi imasmiṃ nāmarūpe kāmataṇhādibhedā taṇhādīgharattaṃ appahīnaṭṭhena anusayitā kaṇhanāmakassa mārassa “sota”ntipi vuccati, taṃ kaṇhassa sotabhūtaṃ dīgharattānusayitaṃ [P 1.0351] idha nāmarūpe taṇhaṃ kappāyano chindīti. Iti bhagavāti idaṃ panettha saṅgītikārānaṃ vacanaṃ. Atāri jātiṃ maraṇaṃ asesanti so [M 2.0084] taṃ taṇhaṃ chetvā asesaṃ jātimaraṇaṃ atāri, anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbāyīti dasseti. Iccabravī bhagavā pañcaseṭṭhoti vaṅgīsena puṭṭho bhagavā etadavoca pañcannaṃ paṭhamasissānaṃ pañcavaggiyānaṃ seṭṭho, pañcahi vā saddhādīhi indriyehi, sīlādīhi vā dhammakkhandhehi ativisiṭṭhehi cakkhūhi ca seṭṭhoti saṅgītikārānamevidaṃ vacanaṃ.

358. He speaks the verse. First, the meaning of the first line is this: that craving in this name-and-form—differentiated as sensual craving, etc.—which has long lain latent because it was unabandoned, is also called the 'stream' of Māra, the Dark One. Kappāyana cut off that craving in this name-and-form, which had become the stream of the Dark One and had long lain latent. '(said the Blessed One)': this here is a statement by the redactors. 'He crossed over birth and death completely': having cut off that craving, he crossed over birth and death completely. This shows that he attained final Nibbāna with the Nibbāna-element with no residue remaining. 'Thus spoke the Blessed One, the best of the five': questioned by Vaṅgīsa, the Blessed One said this. He is the best of the five first disciples, the group of five; or he is the best because of the five faculties of faith, etc., or because of the aggregates of virtue, etc., and because of his five exceedingly distinguished eyes. This too is a statement by the redactors.

359. Evaṃ vutte bhagavato bhāsitamabhinandamānaso vaṅgīso “esa sutvā”tiādigāthāyo āha. Tattha paṭhamagāthāya isisattamāti bhagavā isi ca sattamo ca uttamaṭṭhena vipassīsikhīvessabhūkakusandhakoṇāgamanakassapanāmake cha isayo attanā saha satta karonto pātubhūtotipi isisattamo, taṃ ālapanto āha. Na maṃ vañcesīti yasmā parinibbuto, tasmā tassa parinibbutabhāvaṃ icchantaṃ maṃ na vañcesi, na visaṃvādesīti attho. Sesamettha pākaṭameva.

When this was said, Vaṅgīsa, his mind delighting in the Blessed One's utterance, spoke the verses beginning, 'Hearing this…' Here, in the first verse, 'the seventh sage': the Blessed One is a sage and he is the seventh. In the sense of being the highest, he is also the seventh sage because he appeared making seven along with himself and the six sages named Vipassī, Sikhī, Vessabhū, Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and Kassapa. Addressing him as such, he speaks. 'You did not deceive me': since he has attained final Nibbāna, the meaning is, 'You did not deceive me, who wished for his state of final Nibbāna; you did not mislead me.' The rest here is plain.

360. Dutiyagāthāya yasmā mutyapekkho vihāsi, tasmā taṃ sandhāyāha “yathāvādī tathākārī, ahu buddhassa sāvako”ti. Maccuno jālaṃ tatanti tebhūmakavaṭṭe vitthataṃ mārassa taṇhājālaṃ. Māyāvinoti bahumāyassa. “Tathā māyāvino”tipi keci paṭhanti, tesaṃ yo anekāhi [V 2.0077] māyāhi anekakkhattumpi bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkami, tassa tathā māyāvinoti adhippāyo.

In the second verse, because he dwelt aspiring for liberation, it is said in reference to him: 'As he spoke, so he acted; he was a disciple of the Buddha.' 'The net of Death is spread' means Māra's net of craving spread out in the three-realmed round of existence. 'Of the deceiver' means of one with much deceit. Some also read, 'Thus, of the deceiver'; for them, the intention is this: of that one who is thus deceitful, who approached the Blessed One many times with various deceits.

361. Tatiyagāthāya ādīti kāraṇaṃ. Upādānassāti vaṭṭassa. Vaṭṭañhi upādātabbaṭṭhena idha “upādāna”nti vuttaṃ, tasseva upādānassa ādiṃ avijjātaṇhādibhedaṃ kāraṇaṃ addasa kappoti evaṃ vattuṃ vaṭṭati bhagavāti adhippāyena vadati. Accagā vatāti atikkanto vata. Maccudheyyanti maccu ettha dhiyatīti maccudheyyaṃ, tebhūmakavaṭṭassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Taṃ suduttaraṃ maccudheyyaṃ accagā vatāti vedajāto bhaṇati. Sesamettha pākaṭamevāti.

359. In the third verse, 'origin' means cause. 'Of clinging' means of the round of existence. For here the round of existence is called 'clinging' in the sense of being something to be clung to. He speaks with the intention that it is fitting for the Blessed One to say this because Kappa saw the origin of that very clinging, which is the cause differentiated as ignorance, craving, and so on. 'Indeed, he has gone beyond' means he has truly transcended. 'The realm of Death' means 'that wherein death is established'; this is a designation for the three-realmed round of existence. 'He has indeed gone beyond that realm of Death, so hard to cross'—thus speaks the one in whom joy has arisen. The rest here is clear.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

360. In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya:

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya nigrodhakappasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

361. The explanation of the Nigrodhakappa Sutta in the Commentary on the Suttanipāta is concluded.

13. Sammāparibbājanīyasutta-(mahāsamayasutta)-vaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Sammāparibbājanīya Sutta (The Mahāsamaya Sutta)

362. Pucchāmi [V 2.0078][M 2.0085][P 1.0352] muniṃ pahūtapaññanti sammāparibbājanīyasuttaṃ, “mahāsamayasutta”ntipi vuccati mahāsamayadivase kathitattā. Kā uppatti? Pucchāvasikā uppatti. Nimmitabuddhena hi puṭṭho bhagavā imaṃ suttamabhāsi, taṃ saddhiṃ pucchāya “sammāparibbājanīyasutta”nti vuccati. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthārato pana sākiyakoliyānaṃ uppattito pabhuti porāṇehi vaṇṇīyati.

362. 'I ask the sage of abundant wisdom'—this is the Sammāparibbājanīya Sutta. It is also called the 'Mahāsamaya Sutta' because it was spoken on the day of the great assembly. What is its origin? The origin is based on a question. For the Blessed One spoke this discourse when questioned by a created Buddha, and together with the question, it is called the 'Sammāparibbājanīya Sutta.' This is the summary here. In detail, however, it is explained by the ancients, starting from the origin of the Sakyans and Koliyans.

Tatrāyaṃ uddesamaggavaṇṇanā – paṭhamakappikānaṃ kira rañño mahāsammatassa rojo nāma putto ahosi. Rojassa vararojo, vararojassa kalyāṇo, kalyāṇassa varakalyāṇo, varakalyāṇassa mandhātā, mandhātussa varamandhātā, varamandhātussa uposatho, uposathassa varo, varassa upavaro, upavarassa maghadevo, maghadevassa paramparā caturāsīti khattiyasahassāni ahesuṃ. Tesaṃ parato tayo okkākavaṃsā ahesuṃ. Tesu tatiyaokkākassa pañca mahesiyo ahesuṃ – hatthā, cittā, jantu, jālinī, visākhāti. Ekekissā pañca pañca itthisatāni parivārā. Sabbajeṭṭhāya cattāro puttā – okkāmukho, karakaṇḍu, hatthiniko, sinipuroti; pañca dhītaro – piyā, suppiyā, ānandā, vijitā, vijitasenāti. Evaṃ sā nava putte labhitvā kālamakāsi.

Herein is the explanation of the introductory path. It is said that King Mahāsammata, of the first aeon, had a son named Roja. Roja's son was Vararoja, Vararoja's was Kalyāṇa, Kalyāṇa's was Varakalyāṇa, Varakalyāṇa's was Mandhātā, Mandhātā's was Varamandhātā, Varamandhātā's was Uposatha, Uposatha's was Vara, Vara's was Upavara, and Upavara's was Maghadeva. Maghadeva's lineage consisted of eighty-four thousand khattiya kings. After them, there were three Okkāka dynasties. The third Okkāka had five chief queens: Hatthā, Cittā, Jantu, Jālinī, and Visākhā. Each had a retinue of five hundred women. The eldest queen had four sons—Okkāmukha, Karakaṇḍu, Hatthinika, and Sinipura—and five daughters—Piyā, Suppiyā, Ānandā, Vijitā, and Vijitasenā. Thus, having borne nine children, she passed away.

Atha rājā aññaṃ daharaṃ abhirūpaṃ rājadhītaraṃ ānetvā aggamahesiṭṭhāne ṭhapesi. Sāpi jantuṃ nāma ekaṃ puttaṃ vijāyi. Taṃ jantukumāraṃ pañcamadivase alaṅkaritvā rañño dassesi. Rājā tuṭṭho mahesiyā varaṃ adāsi. Sā ñātakehi saddhiṃ mantetvā puttassa rajjaṃ yāci. Rājā “nassa vasali, mama puttānaṃ antarāyamicchasī”ti nādāsi. Sā punappunaṃ [P 1.0353] raho rājānaṃ paritosetvā “na, mahārāja, musāvādo vaṭṭatī”tiādīni vatvā yācati eva. Atha rājā putte āmantesi – “ahaṃ, tātā, tumhākaṃ kaniṭṭhaṃ jantukumāraṃ disvā tassa mātuyā sahasā varaṃ adāsiṃ. Sā [M 2.0086] puttassa rajjaṃ pariṇāmetuṃ icchati. Tumhe mamaccayena āgantvā rajjaṃ kāreyyāthā”ti aṭṭhahi amaccehi saddhiṃ uyyojesi. Te bhaginiyo ādāya caturaṅginiyā senāya nagarā nikkhamiṃsu. “Kumārā pituaccayena āgantvā rajjaṃ kāressanti, gacchāma ne upaṭṭhahāmā”ti cintetvā bahū manussā anubandhiṃsu. Paṭhamadivase yojanamattā [V 2.0079] senā ahosi, dutiyadivase dviyojanamattā, tatiyadivase tiyojanamattā. Kumārā cintesuṃ – “mahā ayaṃ balakāyo, sace mayaṃ kañci sāmantarājānaṃ akkamitvā janapadaṃ gaṇhissāma, sopi no na pahossati, kiṃ paresaṃ pīḷaṃ katvā laddharajjena, mahā jambudīpo, araññe nagaraṃ māpessāmā”ti himavantābhimukhā agamiṃsu.

Then the king brought another young and beautiful princess and established her in the position of chief queen. She too gave birth to a son named Jantu. On the fifth day, she adorned Prince Jantu and presented him to the king. The king, pleased, granted the queen a boon. She consulted with her kinsmen and asked for the kingdom for her son. The king refused, saying: 'Perish, you outcaste woman! You wish to bring harm to my sons!' But she, again and again, privately pleased the king and kept pleading, saying such things as, 'O great king, it is not right to speak falsely.' Then the king addressed his sons: 'My dears, when I saw your youngest brother, Prince Jantu, I hastily granted his mother a boon. She wishes to have the kingdom made over to her son. You should return after my passing and take the kingdom.' He sent them away with eight ministers. Taking their sisters, they departed from the city with a four-limbed army. Thinking, 'The princes will return after their father's passing to take the kingdom; let us go and attend on them,' many people followed. On the first day the army was a yojana in extent, on the second day two yojanas, and on the third day three yojanas. The princes thought: 'This is a great body of troops. If we were to attack some neighboring king and seize his country, even that would not be sufficient for us. What is the use of a kingdom gained by oppressing others? Jambudīpa is vast. Let us have a city built in the forest.' So they set out towards the Himalayas.
