Tattha nagaramāpanokāsaṃ pariyesamānā himavati kapilo nāma ghoratapo tāpaso paṭivasati pokkharaṇitīre mahāsākasaṇḍe, tassa vasanokāsaṃ gatā. So te disvā pucchitvā sabbaṃ pavattiṃ sutvā tesu anukampaṃ akāsi. So kira bhummajālaṃ nāma vijjaṃ jānāti, yāya uddhaṃ asītihatthe ākāse ca heṭṭhā bhūmiyañca guṇadose passati. Athekasmiṃ padese sūkaramigā sīhabyagghādayo tāsetvā paripātenti, maṇḍūkamūsikā sappe bhiṃsāpenti. So te disvā “ayaṃ bhūmippadeso pathavīagga”nti tasmiṃ padese assamaṃ māpesi. Tato so rājakumāre āha – “sace mama nāmena nagaraṃ karotha, demi vo imaṃ okāsa”nti. Te tathā paṭijāniṃsu. Tāpaso “imasmiṃ okāse ṭhatvā caṇḍālaputtopi cakkavattiṃ balena atisetī”ti vatvā “assame rañño gharaṃ māpetvā nagaraṃ māpethā”ti taṃ okāsaṃ datvā sayaṃ avidūre pabbatapāde assamaṃ katvā vasi. Tato [P 1.0354] kumārā tattha nagaraṃ māpetvā kapilassa vutthokāse katattā “kapilavatthū”ti nāmaṃ āropetvā tattha nivāsaṃ kappesuṃ.

While searching for a place to build a city, they came to the dwelling of an ascetic of fierce austerities named Kapila, who lived in the Himalayas on the shore of a lotus pond in a great grove of sāl trees. Seeing them and questioning them, and having heard their whole story, he took compassion on them. It is said that he knew a science called the Earth-Net, by which he could see the good and bad qualities of the ground for eighty cubits up into the sky and down below. Now in one place, boars and deer were frightening and routing lions, tigers, and the like, while frogs and mice were terrifying snakes. Seeing this, he thought, 'This plot of land is the best on earth,' and had his hermitage built in that place. Then he said to the princes: 'If you build a city in my name, I will give you this site.' They agreed to do so. The ascetic said: 'Standing on this site, even the son of an outcaste surpasses a wheel-turning monarch in power.' Then, giving them the site, he said: 'Have a palace for the king built at my hermitage, and then build the city.' He himself made a hermitage at the foot of a mountain not far away and dwelt there. Then the princes had a city built there, and because it was made on the site where Kapila had dwelt, they gave it the name 'Kapilavatthu' and took up residence there.

Atha amaccā “ime kumārā vayappattā, yadi nesaṃ pitā santike bhaveyya, so āvāhavivāhaṃ kāreyya. Idāni pana amhākaṃ bhāro”ti cintetvā kumārehi saddhiṃ mantesuṃ. Kumārā “amhākaṃ sadisā khattiyadhītaro na passāma, tāsampi bhaginīnaṃ sadise khattiyakumāre, jātisambhedañca [M 2.0087] na karomā”ti. Te jātisambhedabhayena jeṭṭhabhaginiṃ mātuṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā avasesāhi saṃvāsaṃ kappesuṃ. Tesaṃ pitā taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā “sakyā vata, bho kumārā, paramasakyā vata, bho kumārā”ti udānaṃ udānesi. Ayaṃ tāva sakyānaṃ uppatti. Vuttampi cetaṃ bhagavatā –

Then the ministers thought: 'These princes have come of age. If their father were present, he would arrange their marriages. But now the responsibility is ours.' They consulted with the princes. The princes said: 'We do not see khattiya maidens who are our equals, nor khattiya princes who are the equals of our sisters. We will not cause a confusion of caste.' Fearing a confusion of caste, they established their eldest sister in the position of a mother and cohabited with the remaining sisters. Their father, hearing of this affair, uttered an inspired utterance: 'Capable indeed, sirs, are the princes! Supremely capable indeed, sirs, are the princes!' This is the origin of the Sakyans. And this was also said by the Blessed One:

“Atha kho, ambaṭṭha, rājā okkāko amacce pārisajje āmantesi – ‘kahaṃ nu kho, bho, etarahi kumārā sammantī’ti. Atthi, deva, himavantapasse pokkharaṇiyā tīre mahāsākasaṇḍo, tatthetarahi kumārā sammanti. Te jātisambhedabhayā sakāhi bhaginīhi saddhiṃ saṃvāsaṃ kappentīti. Atha kho, ambaṭṭha, rājā okkāko udānaṃ udānesi – ‘sakyā vata, bho kumārā, paramasakyā vata, bho kumārā’ti, tadagge kho pana[V 2.0080], ambaṭṭha, sakyā paññāyanti, so ca sakyānaṃ pubbapuriso”ti (dī. ni. 1.267).

'Then, Ambaṭṭha, King Okkāka addressed his ministers and assembly members: "Where, sirs, are the princes living now?" "Your majesty, there is a great grove of sāl trees on a slope of the Himalayas, by the shore of a lotus pond. The princes are living there now. Fearing a confusion of caste, they are cohabiting with their own sisters." Then, Ambaṭṭha, King Okkāka uttered an inspired utterance: "Capable indeed, sirs, are the princes! Supremely capable indeed, sirs, are the princes!" From that time onwards, Ambaṭṭha, the Sakyans came to be known, and he was the primordial ancestor of the Sakyans.'

Tato nesaṃ jeṭṭhabhaginiyā kuṭṭharogo udapādi, koviḷārapupphasadisāni gattāni ahesuṃ. Rājakumārā “imāya saddhiṃ ekato nisajjaṭṭhānabhojanādīni karontānampi upari esa rogo saṅkamatī”ti cintetvā uyyānakīḷaṃ gacchantā viya taṃ yāne āropetvā araññaṃ pavisitvā pokkharaṇiṃ khaṇāpetvā [P 1.0355] taṃ tattha khādanīyabhojanīyehi saddhiṃ pakkhipitvā upari padaraṃ paṭicchādāpetvā paṃsuṃ datvā pakkamiṃsu. Tena ca samayena rāmo nāma rājā kuṭṭharogī orodhehi ca nāṭakehi ca jigucchiyamāno tena saṃvegena jeṭṭhaputtassa rajjaṃ datvā araññaṃ pavisitvā tattha paṇṇamūlaphalāni paribhuñjanto nacirasseva arogo suvaṇṇavaṇṇo hutvā, ito cito ca vicaranto mahantaṃ susirarukkhaṃ disvā tassabbhantare soḷasahatthappamāṇaṃ taṃ kolāpaṃ sodhetvā, dvārañca vātapānañca katvā nisseṇiṃ bandhitvā tattha vāsaṃ kappesi. So aṅgārakaṭāhe aggiṃ katvā rattiṃ vissarañca sussarañca suṇanto sayati. So “asukasmiṃ padese sīho saddamakāsi, asukasmiṃ byaggho”ti sallakkhetvā pabhāte tattha gantvā vighāsamaṃsaṃ ādāya pacitvā khādati.

Then their eldest sister developed leprosy, and her limbs became like koviḷāra flowers. The princes thought: “If we sit, stand, and eat together with her, this disease might spread to us.” So, pretending to go for an outing in the park, they placed her in a carriage, entered the forest, had a pit dug, and after placing her there with food, they had it covered with a roof of planks, scattered earth over it, and departed. At that time, a king named Rāma, who was afflicted with leprosy and loathed by his harem and dancers, was so overcome with distress that he handed over the kingdom to his eldest son and entered the forest. There, subsisting on leaves, roots, and fruits, he soon became free from disease and took on a golden complexion. Wandering about, he saw a large hollow tree. After cleaning out the hollow inside it—which measured sixteen cubits—he made a door and a window, fastened a ladder, and took up residence there. He would make a fire in a charcoal pan at night and lie down listening to harsh and pleasant sounds. Noting, “In such-and-such a place a lion roared, in such-and-such a place a tiger,” he would go there in the morning, collect the meat from their leftovers, cook it, and eat.

Athekadivasaṃ so paccūsasamaye aggiṃ jāletvā nisīdi. Tena ca samayena tassā rājadhītāya gandhaṃ ghāyitvā byaggho taṃ padesaṃ khaṇitvā [M 2.0088] padaratthare vivaramakāsi. Tena vivarena sā byagghaṃ disvā bhītā vissaramakāsi. So taṃ saddaṃ sutvā “itthisaddo eso”ti ca sallakkhetvā pātova tattha gantvā “ko etthā”ti āha. “Mātugāmo sāmī”ti. “Nikkhamā”ti. “Na nikkhamāmī”ti. “Kiṃ kāraṇā”ti? “Khattiyakaññā aha”nti. Evaṃ sobbhe nikhātāpi mānameva karoti. So sabbaṃ pucchitvā “ahampi khattiyo”ti jātiṃ ācikkhitvā “ehi dāni khīre pakkhittasappi viya jāta”nti āha. Sā “kuṭṭharoginīmhi sāmi, na sakkā nikkhamitu”nti āha. So “katakammo dāni ahaṃ sakkā tikicchitu”nti nisseṇiṃ datvā taṃ uddharitvā attano vasanokāsaṃ netvā sayaṃ paribhuttabhesajjāni eva datvā nacirasseva arogaṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇamakāsi. So tāya saddhiṃ saṃvāsaṃ kappesi. Sā paṭhamasaṃvāseneva gabbhaṃ gaṇhitvā dve putte vijāyi, punapi dveti evaṃ soḷasakkhattuṃ vijāyi. Evaṃ te dvattiṃsa bhātaro ahesuṃ. Te anupubbena vuḍḍhippatte pitā sabbasippāni sikkhāpesi.

One day at dawn, he lit a fire and sat down. At that time, a tiger, smelling the scent of the princess, dug at that spot and made an opening in the plank covering. Seeing the tiger through the opening, she was frightened and let out a loud cry. Hearing her cry and recognizing it as a woman’s voice, he went there early in the morning and asked: “Who is here?” “A woman, sir.” “Come out.” “I cannot come out.” “For what reason?” “I am a khattiya maiden.” Thus, though buried in a pit, she still maintained her pride. After questioning her fully, he told her his own lineage, saying: “I too am a khattiya. Come now, it has turned out like ghee added to milk.” She replied: “Sir, I am a leper; I cannot come out.” He thought: “I am now skilled and able to treat her,” so he gave her a ladder, lifted her out, took her to his dwelling, and gave her the very same medicines that he himself had used. Before long, he made her healthy and golden-skinned. He lived together with her. From their very first union, she conceived and gave birth to two sons. Again she bore two, and so on, giving birth sixteen times. Thus there came to be thirty-two brothers. As they grew up in due course, their father taught them all the arts.

Athekadivasaṃ [V 2.0081][P 1.0356] eko rāmarañño nagaravāsī pabbate ratanāni gavesanto taṃ padesaṃ āgato rājānaṃ disvā aññāsi. “Jānāmahaṃ, deva, tumhe”ti āha. “Kuto tvaṃ āgatosī”ti ca tena puṭṭho “nagarato devā”ti āha. Tato naṃ rājā sabbaṃ pavattiṃ pucchi. Evaṃ tesu samullapamānesu te dārakā āgamiṃsu. So te disvā “ime ke devā”ti pucchi. “Puttā me bhaṇe”ti. “Imehi dāni, deva, dvattiṃsakumārehi parivuto vane kiṃ karissasi, ehi rajjamanusāsā”ti? “Alaṃ, bhaṇe, idheva sukha”nti. So “laddhaṃ dāni me kathāpābhata”nti nagaraṃ gantvā rañño puttassārocesi. Rañño putto “pitaraṃ ānessāmī”ti caturaṅginiyā senāya tattha gantvā nānappakārehi pitaraṃ yāci. Sopi “alaṃ, tāta kumāra, idheva sukha”nti neva icchi. Tato rājaputto “na dāni rājā āgantuṃ icchati, handassa idheva nagaraṃ māpemī”ti cintetvā taṃ kolarukkhaṃ uddharitvā gharaṃ katvā nagaraṃ māpetvā kolarukkhaṃ apanetvā katattā “kolanagara”nti ca byagghapathe katattā “byagghapajja”nti cāti dve nāmāni āropetvā agamāsi.

One day, a city-dweller from King Rāma’s kingdom, who was searching for gems in the mountains, came to that place. Seeing the king, he recognized him and said: “I know you, Your Majesty.” When the king asked, “Where have you come from?” he replied, “From the city, Your Majesty.” Then the king asked him for all the news. While they were conversing, the boys arrived. Seeing them, the visitor asked: “Who are these, Your Majesty?” “They are my sons, my good man.” “Your Majesty, what will you do in the forest, surrounded by these thirty-two princes? Come and rule the kingdom.” “Enough, my good man. I am happy right here.” The man thought, “Now I have a story to bring back,” and he went to the city and informed the king’s son. The king’s son thought, “I will bring my father back,” and went there with a four-limbed army and pleaded with his father in many ways. But his father did not consent, saying: “Enough, my dear prince. I am happy right here.” Then the prince thought: “Since the king does not wish to return, I will have a city built for him right here.” He had that kola tree uprooted, a house built, and a city established. Because it was established by removing the kola tree, it was named ‘Kolanagara,’ and because it was established on the tiger’s path, it was also called ‘Byagghapajja.’ Having given it these two names, he departed.

Tato [M 2.0089] vayappatte kumāre mātā āṇāpesi – “tātā, tumhākaṃ kapilavatthuvāsino sakyā mātulā honti, dhītaro nesaṃ gaṇhathā”ti. Te yaṃ divasaṃ khattiyakaññāyo nadīkīḷanaṃ gacchanti, taṃ divasaṃ gantvā nadītitthaṃ uparundhitvā nāmāni sāvetvā patthitā patthitā rājadhītaro gahetvā agamaṃsu. Sakyarājāno sutvā “hotu bhaṇe, amhākaṃ ñātakā evā”ti tuṇhī ahesuṃ. Ayaṃ koliyānaṃ uppatti.

Then, when the princes came of age, their mother instructed them: “My dears, the Sakyans who dwell in Kapilavatthu are your maternal uncles. You should take their daughters as wives.” On a day when the khattiya maidens were going to play in the river, the princes went and blocked the river ford. Having announced their own names, they each took the royal daughter they desired and departed. When the Sakyan kings heard about this, they said: “So be it, my good sirs. They are our kinsmen, after all,” and they remained silent. This is the origin of the Koliyans.

Evaṃ tesaṃ sākiyakoliyānaṃ aññamaññaṃ āvāhavivāhaṃ karontānaṃ āgato vaṃso yāva sīhahanurājā, tāva vitthārato veditabbo – sīhahanurañño kira pañca puttā ahesuṃ [P 1.0357] – suddhodano, amitodano, dhotodano, sakkodano, sukkodanoti. Tesu suddhodane rajjaṃ kārayamāne tassa pajāpatiyā añjanarañño dhītāya mahāmāyādeviyā kucchimhi pūritapāramī mahāpuriso jātakanidāne vuttanayena tusitapurā cavitvā paṭisandhiṃ gahetvā anupubbena katamahābhinikkhamano sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambujjhitvā pavattitavaradhammacakko anukkamena kapilavatthuṃ gantvā suddhodanamahārājādayo ariyaphale patiṭṭhāpetvā janapadacārikaṃ pakkamitvā punapi aparena samayena paccāgantvā pannarasahi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ kapilavatthusmiṃ viharati nigrodhārāme.

Thus the lineage that came from the Sakyans and Koliyans intermarrying with one another should be understood in detail up to King Sīhahanu. King Sīhahanu, it is said, had five sons: Suddhodana, Amitodana, Dhotodana, Sakkodana, and Sukkodana. While Suddhodana was ruling, the Great Being, who had fulfilled his perfections, passed away from the Tusita realm and took conception in the womb of his consort, Queen Mahāmāyā, the daughter of King Añjana, just as described in the Jātaka Nidāna. In due course, he made the Great Renunciation, fully awakened to perfect self-enlightenment, and set in motion the excellent Wheel of the Dhamma. Then, traveling in stages, he went to Kapilavatthu, where he established King Suddhodana and others in the noble fruits. After departing on a tour of the country, he later returned and was dwelling at the Banyan Grove in Kapilavatthu with fifteen hundred bhikkhus.

Tattha viharante ca bhagavati sākiyakoliyānaṃ udakaṃ paṭicca kalaho ahosi. Kathaṃ? Nesaṃ [V 2.0082] kira ubhinnampi kapilapurakoliyapurānaṃ antare rohiṇī nāma nadī pavattati. Sā kadāci appodakā hoti, kadāci mahodakā. Appodakakāle setuṃ katvā sākiyāpi koliyāpi attano attano sassapāyanatthaṃ udakaṃ ānenti. Tesaṃ manussā ekadivasaṃ setuṃ karontā aññamaññaṃ bhaṇḍantā “are tumhākaṃ rājakulaṃ bhaginīhi saddhiṃ saṃvāsaṃ kappesi kukkuṭasoṇasiṅgālāditiracchānā viya, tumhākaṃ rājakulaṃ susirarukkhe vāsaṃ kappesi pisācillikā viyā”ti evaṃ jātivādena khuṃsetvā attano attano rājūnaṃ ārocesuṃ. Te kuddhā yuddhasajjā hutvā rohiṇīnadītīraṃ sampattā. Evaṃ sāgarasadisaṃ balaṃ aṭṭhāsi.

While the Blessed One was dwelling there, a quarrel arose between the Sakyans and Koliyans concerning water. How so? Between their two cities, Kapilapura and Koliyapura, flows the Rohiṇī river. Sometimes it has little water, sometimes much. In times of little water, both the Sakyans and the Koliyans would build a weir to divert water to irrigate their respective crops. One day, while the people were building the weir, they quarreled with one another, saying: “Hey, your royal family cohabited with their sisters like animals such as chickens, dogs, and jackals! Your royal family lived in a hollow tree like goblins!” Thus, having reviled each other with insults about their lineage, they reported the matter to their respective kings. Enraged, they prepared for battle and assembled on the bank of the Rohiṇī river. Thus an army like the ocean stood ready.

Atha [M 2.0090] bhagavā “ñātakā kalahaṃ karonti, handa, ne vāressāmī”ti ākāsenāgantvā dvinnaṃ senānaṃ majjhe aṭṭhāsi. Tampi āvajjetvā sāvatthito āgatoti eke. Evaṃ ṭhatvā ca pana [P 1.0358] attadaṇḍasuttaṃ (su. ni. 941 ādayo) abhāsi. Taṃ sutvā sabbe saṃvegappattā āvudhāni chaḍḍetvā bhagavantaṃ namassamānā aṭṭhaṃsu, mahagghañca āsanaṃ paññāpesuṃ. Bhagavā oruyha paññattāsane nisīditvā “kuṭhārīhattho puriso”tiādikaṃ phandanajātakaṃ (jā. 1.13.14), “vandāmi taṃ kuñjarā”tiādikaṃ laṭukikajātakaṃ (jā. 1.5.39).

Then the Blessed One thought: “My kinsmen are quarreling. I must go and stop them.” He traveled through the air and stood poised between the two armies. (Some say that he came from Sāvatthī after adverting to the situation.) Standing there, he recited the Attadaṇḍa Sutta. Hearing it, all were filled with a sense of spiritual urgency. They threw down their weapons and stood paying homage to the Blessed One. They prepared a magnificent seat. The Blessed One descended, sat down on the prepared seat, and related the Phandana Jātaka, which begins “A man with an axe in his hand,” and the Laṭukika Jātaka, which begins “I salute you, O elephant.”

“Sammodamānā gacchanti, jālamādāya pakkhino;

Yadā te vivadissanti, tadā ehinti me vasa”nti. (jā. 1.1.33) –

“Rejoicing together, the birds fly off, taking the net with them; but when they fall into dispute, they will come under my power.”

Imaṃ vaṭṭakajātakañca kathetvā puna tesaṃ cirakālappavattaṃ ñātibhāvaṃ dassento imaṃ mahāvaṃsaṃ kathesi. Te “pubbe kira mayaṃ ñātakā evā”ti ativiya pasīdiṃsu. Tato sakyā aḍḍhateyyakumārasate, koliyā aḍḍhateyyakumārasateti pañca kumārasate bhagavato parivāratthāya adaṃsu. Bhagavā tesaṃ pubbahetuṃ disvā “etha bhikkhavo”ti āha. Te sabbe iddhiyā nibbattaaṭṭhaparikkhārayuttā ākāse abbhuggantvā āgamma bhagavantaṃ vanditvā aṭṭhaṃsu. Bhagavā te ādāya mahāvanaṃ agamāsi. Tesaṃ pajāpatiyo dūte pāhesuṃ, te tāhi nānappakārehi palobhiyamānā ukkaṇṭhiṃsu. Bhagavā tesaṃ ukkaṇṭhitabhāvaṃ ñatvā himavantaṃ dassetvā tattha kuṇālajātakakathāya (jā. 2.21.289 kuṇālajātakaṃ) tesaṃ anabhiratiṃ vinodetukāmo āha – “diṭṭhapubbo vo, bhikkhave, himavā”ti? “Na bhagavā”ti. “Etha, bhikkhave, pekkhathā”ti attano iddhiyā te ākāsena nento “ayaṃ suvaṇṇapabbato, ayaṃ rajatapabbato, ayaṃ maṇipabbato”ti nānappakāre pabbate dassetvā kuṇāladahe manosilātale paccuṭṭhāsi. Tato “himavante sabbe catuppadabahuppadādibhedā tiracchānagatā pāṇā āgacchantu, sabbesañca pacchato [V 2.0083] kuṇālasakuṇo”ti adhiṭṭhāsi. Āgacchante ca te jātināmaniruttivasena vaṇṇento “ete, bhikkhave, haṃsā, ete koñcā[P 1.0359], ete cakkavākā, karavīkā, hatthisoṇḍakā, pokkharasātakā”ti tesaṃ dassesi.

Having related this Vaṭṭaka Jātaka, and then, to show them their long-standing kinship, he related this great lineage. They were exceedingly pleased, saying, 'Indeed, in the past we were kinsmen.' Then the Sakyans gave two hundred and fifty young men and the Koliyans gave two hundred and fifty young men, thus five hundred young men, to attend upon the Blessed One. Seeing their past cause, the Blessed One said: 'Come, bhikkhus.' All of them, furnished with the eight requisites created by psychic power, rose up into the air, approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and stood by. The Blessed One took them and went to the Great Wood. Their wives sent messengers, and being enticed by them in various ways, they became discontented. Knowing their discontent, the Blessed One, wishing to dispel their dissatisfaction by showing them the Himalayas and relating the story of the Kuṇāla Jātaka, asked: 'Bhikkhus, have you seen the Himalayas before?' 'No, Blessed One.' 'Come, bhikkhus, look.' Leading them through the air by his psychic power, he showed them various mountains, saying, 'This is the Golden Mountain, this is the Silver Mountain, this is the Jewel Mountain,' and he alighted on the Manosilā plateau by Lake Kuṇāla. Then he made a determination: 'Let all animals of the Himalayas—quadrupeds, multipeds, and other kinds of creatures—come here, and let the kuṇāla bird come behind all of them.' As they came, he described them according to their species, name, and dialect, showing them: 'Bhikkhus, these are swans, these are herons, these are ruddy sheldrakes, these are karavīkas, these are hatthisoṇḍakas, these are pokkharasātakas.'

Te [M 2.0091] vimhitahadayā passantā sabbapacchato āgacchantaṃ dvīhi dijakaññāhi mukhatuṇḍakena ḍaṃsitvā gahitakaṭṭhavemajjhe nisinnaṃ sahassadijakaññāparivāraṃ kuṇālasakuṇaṃ disvā acchariyabbhutacittajātā bhagavantaṃ āhaṃsu – “kacci, bhante, bhagavāpi idha kuṇālarājā bhūtapubbo”ti? “Āma, bhikkhave, mayāvesa kuṇālavaṃso kato. Atīte hi mayaṃ cattāro janā idha vasimhā – nārado devilo isi, ānando gijjharājā, puṇṇamukho phussakokilo, ahaṃ kuṇālo sakuṇo”ti sabbaṃ mahākuṇālajātakaṃ kathesi. Taṃ sutvā tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ purāṇadutiyikāyo ārabbha uppannā anabhirati vūpasantā. Tato tesaṃ bhagavā saccakathaṃ kathesi, kathāpariyosāne sabbapacchimako sotāpanno, sabbauparimo anāgāmī ahosi, ekopi puthujjano vā arahā vā natthi. Tato bhagavā te ādāya punadeva mahāvane oruhi. Āgacchamānā ca te bhikkhū attanova iddhiyā āgacchiṃsu.

With amazed hearts, they watched and saw the kuṇāla bird, surrounded by a thousand young female birds, coming last of all, seated in the middle of a stick held by being bitten with the beaks of two young female birds. Their minds filled with wonder and amazement, they said to the Blessed One: 'Venerable sir, could it be that the Blessed One was formerly the king of the kuṇālas here?' 'Yes, bhikkhus, this lineage of kuṇālas was indeed established by me. In the past, we four persons lived here: the rishi Nārada Devala, Ānanda the vulture king, Puṇṇamukha the spotted cuckoo, and I was Kuṇāla the bird.' Then he related the entire Mahākuṇāla Jātaka. Having heard it, the dissatisfaction that had arisen in those bhikkhus concerning their former wives subsided. Then the Blessed One gave them a discourse on the truths. At the conclusion of the discourse, the most junior among them became a stream-enterer and the most senior became a non-returner; not one was a worldling or an arahant. Then the Blessed One, taking them, descended again into the Great Wood. And those bhikkhus came by their own psychic power.

Atha nesaṃ bhagavā uparimaggatthāya puna dhammaṃ desesi. Te pañcasatāpi vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā arahatte patiṭṭhahiṃsu. Paṭhamaṃ patto paṭhamameva agamāsi “bhagavato ārocessāmī”ti. Āgantvā ca “abhiramāmahaṃ bhagavā, na ukkaṇṭhāmī”ti vatvā bhagavantaṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Evaṃ te sabbepi anukkamena āgantvā bhagavantaṃ parivāretvā nisīdiṃsu jeṭṭhamāsauposathadivase sāyanhasamaye. Tato pañcasatakhīṇāsavaparivutaṃ varabuddhāsane nisinnaṃ bhagavantaṃ ṭhapetvā asaññasatte ca arūpabrahmāno ca sakaladasasahassacakkavāḷe avasesadevatādayo maṅgalasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttanayena sukhumattabhāve nimminitvā samparivāresuṃ “vicitrapaṭibhānaṃ dhammadesanaṃ sossāmā”ti. Tattha cattāro khīṇāsavabrahmāno samāpattito [P 1.0360] vuṭṭhāya brahmagaṇaṃ apassantā “kuhiṃ gatā”ti āvajjetvā tamatthaṃ ñatvā pacchā āgantvā okāsaṃ alabhamānā cakkavāḷamuddhani ṭhatvā paccekagāthāyo abhāsiṃsu. Yathāha –

Then the Blessed One again taught them the Dhamma for the sake of the higher paths. All five hundred, having undertaken insight meditation, became established in arahantship. The one who attained it first went first, thinking, 'I will inform the Blessed One.' Having approached, he said, 'I delight, Blessed One, I am not discontented,' paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat down to one side. In this way, all of them came in succession and, having surrounded the Blessed One, sat down in the evening on the Uposatha day of the month of Jeṭṭha. Then, with the exception of the non-percipient beings and the formless brahmās, the remaining devas and others in the entire ten-thousandfold world-system, having created subtle bodies for themselves in the way described in the commentary on the Maṅgala Sutta, gathered around the Blessed One, who was seated on the excellent Buddha-seat surrounded by the five hundred arahants, thinking, 'We will listen to a Dhamma discourse of varied brilliance.' There, four brahmās who were arahants, having emerged from their attainment and not seeing the host of brahmās, considered, 'Where have they gone?' Having understood the matter, they came afterwards, but not finding a space, they stood at the summit of the world-sphere and each recited a verse. As it is said:

“Atha kho catunnaṃ suddhāvāsakāyikānaṃ devatānaṃ etadahosi – ‘ayaṃ, kho, bhagavā sakkesu viharati kapilavatthusmiṃ mahāvane mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ pañcamattehi bhikkhusatehi sabbeheva arahantehi. Dasahi ca lokadhātūhi devatā yebhuyyena sannipatitā honti bhagavantaṃ dassanāya bhikkhusaṅghañca[M 2.0092]. Yaṃnūna mayampi yena bhagavā [V 2.0084] tenupasaṅkameyyāma, upasaṅkamitvā bhagavato santike paccekaṃ gāthaṃ bhāseyyāmā’”ti (dī. ni. 2.331; saṃ. ni. 1.37).

Then it occurred to four devas of the Pure Abodes: ‘The Blessed One is dwelling among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu, in the Great Wood, together with a great Saṅgha of bhikkhus, with five hundred bhikkhus, all of them arahants. And devas from ten world-systems have for the most part assembled to see the Blessed One and the Bhikkhu Saṅgha. Let us also go to the Blessed One and, having approached, each speak a verse in his presence.’

Sabbaṃ sagāthāvagge vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ gantvā ca tattha eko brahmā puratthimacakkavāḷamuddhani okāsaṃ labhitvā tattha ṭhito imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi –

The entire matter should be understood in the way it is stated in the Sagāthāvagga. Having gone there, one brahmā found a space at the summit of the eastern world-sphere, stood there, and recited this verse:

“Mahāsamayo pavanasmiṃ…pe…

Dakkhitāye aparājitasaṅgha”nti. (dī. ni. 2.332; saṃ. ni. 1.37);

‘A great assembly in the forest grove… for seeing the unconquered Saṅgha.’

Imañcassa gāthaṃ bhāsamānassa pacchimacakkavāḷapabbate ṭhito saddaṃ assosi.

And as he was reciting this verse, one standing on the mountain of the western world-sphere heard the sound.

Dutiyo pacchimacakkavāḷamuddhani okāsaṃ labhitvā tattha ṭhito taṃ gāthaṃ sutvā imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi –

The second one, having found a space at the summit of the western world-sphere, stood there, and having heard that verse, recited this verse:

“Tatra bhikkhavo samādahaṃsu…pe…

Indriyāni rakkhanti paṇḍitā”ti. (dī. ni. 2.332; saṃ. ni. 1.37);

‘There the bhikkhus concentrated their minds… the wise ones guard their faculties.’

Tatiyo dakkhiṇacakkavāḷamuddhani okāsaṃ labhitvā tattha ṭhito taṃ gāthaṃ sutvā imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi –

The third one, having found a space at the summit of the southern world-sphere, stood there, and having heard that verse, recited this verse:

“Chetvā khīlaṃ chetvā palighaṃ…pe… susunāgā”ti. (dī. ni. 2.332; saṃ. ni. 1.37);

‘Having cut the stake, having broken the bar… the young nāgas well-tamed.’

Catuttho uttaracakkavāḷamuddhani okāsaṃ labhitvā tattha ṭhito taṃ gāthaṃ sutvā imaṃ gāthamabhāsi –

The fourth one, having found a space at the summit of the northern world-sphere, stood there, and having heard that verse, recited this verse:

“Ye keci buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gatāse…pe…

Devakāyaṃ paripūressantī”ti. (dī. ni. 2.332; saṃ. ni. 1.37);

‘Those who have gone for refuge to the Buddha… will go on to fill the host of devas.’

Tassapi [V 2.0085] taṃ saddaṃ dakkhiṇacakkavāḷamuddhani ṭhito assosi. Evaṃ tadā ime cattāro brahmāno parisaṃ thometvā ṭhitā ahesuṃ, mahābrahmāno ekacakkavāḷaṃ chādetvā aṭṭhaṃsu.

One standing on the summit of the southern world-sphere also heard his sound. Thus at that time these four brahmās stood praising the assembly, and the Great Brahmās stood covering one world-sphere.

Atha bhagavā devaparisaṃ oloketvā bhikkhūnaṃ ārocesi [P 1.0361] – “yepi te, bhikkhave, ahesuṃ atītamaddhānaṃ arahanto sammāsambuddhā, tesampi bhagavantānaṃ etapparamāyeva devatā sannipatitā ahesuṃ. Seyyathāpi mayhaṃ [M 2.0093] etarahi, yepi te, bhikkhave, bhavissanti anāgatamaddhānaṃ arahanto sammāsambuddhā, tesampi bhagavantānaṃ etapparamāyeva devatā sannipatitā bhavissanti seyyathāpi mayhaṃ etarahī”ti. Tato taṃ devaparisaṃ bhabbābhabbavasena dvidhā vibhaji “ettakā bhabbā, ettakā abhabbā”ti. Tattha “abhabbaparisā buddhasatepi dhammaṃ desente na bujjhati, bhabbaparisā sakkā bodhetu”nti ñatvā puna bhabbapuggale cariyavasena chadhā vibhaji “ettakā rāgacaritā, ettakā dosa-moha-vitakka-saddhā-buddhicaritā”ti. Evaṃ cariyavasena pariggahetvā “assā parisāya kīdisā dhammadesanā sappāyā”ti dhammakathaṃ vicinitvā puna taṃ parisaṃ manasākāsi – “attajjhāsayena nu kho jāneyya, parajjhāsayena, aṭṭhuppattivasena, pucchāvasenā”ti. Tato “pucchāvasena jāneyyā”ti ñatvā “pañhaṃ pucchituṃ samattho atthi, natthī”ti puna sakalaparisaṃ āvajjetvā “natthi kocī”ti ñatvā “sace ahameva pucchitvā ahameva vissajjeyyaṃ, evamassā parisāya sappāyaṃ na hoti. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ nimmitabuddhaṃ māpeyyanti pādakajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya manomayiddhiyā abhisaṅkharitvā nimmitabuddhaṃ māpesi. Sabbaṅgapaccaṅgī lakkhaṇasampanno pattacīvaradharo ālokitavilokitādisampanno hotū”ti adhiṭṭhānacittena saha pāturahosi. So pācīnalokadhātuto āgantvā bhagavato samasame āsane nisinno evaṃ āgantvā yāni bhagavatā imamhi samāgame cariyavasena cha suttāni (su. ni. 854 ādayo, 868 ādayo, 884 ādayo, 901 ādayo, 921 ādayo) kathitāni. Seyyathidaṃ – purābhedasuttaṃ kalahavivādasuttaṃ cūḷabyūhaṃ mahābyūhaṃ tuvaṭakaṃ idameva sammāparibbājanīyanti. Tesu rāgacaritadevatānaṃ sappāyavasena kathetabbassa imassa suttassa pavattanatthaṃ pañhaṃ pucchanto “pucchāmi muniṃ pahūtapañña”nti [P 1.0362] imaṃ gāthamāha.

Then the Blessed One, surveying the assembly of devas, addressed the bhikkhus: 'Bhikkhus, for those Blessed Ones, Arahants, Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones who were in the past, the assembly of devas was just as great as it is for me now. And, bhikkhus, for those Blessed Ones, Arahants, Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones who will be in the future, the assembly of devas will be just as great as it is for me now.' Then he divided that assembly of devas into two based on their capacity: 'This many have capacity, this many are without capacity.' Therein, knowing that 'an assembly without capacity does not awaken even if a hundred Buddhas teach the Dhamma, but an assembly with capacity can be awakened,' he further divided the capable individuals into six types based on their temperament: 'This many are of lustful temperament, this many are of hateful, deluded, speculative, faithful, and intellectual temperament.' Having thus classified them by temperament, he investigated, 'What kind of Dhamma teaching would be suitable for this assembly?' Then he directed his mind to that assembly: 'Should I know this by my own disposition, by another's disposition, by way of an incident, or by way of a question?' Realizing, 'I should know it by way of a question,' he again adverted to the entire assembly: 'Is there anyone here capable of asking a question?' Seeing there was no one, he thought: 'If I myself were to ask and I myself answer, it would not be suitable for this assembly. Suppose I were to create a mind-made Buddha.' Having entered the jhāna that is the basis for psychic power and emerged from it, with his mind-made psychic power he fashioned a mind-made Buddha. He resolved: 'Let him be complete in all major and minor limbs, endowed with the marks, wearing the robe and bowl, accomplished in looking ahead and looking around, and so on,' and with this thought of resolution, he appeared. He came from the eastern world-system and sat on a seat equal to the Blessed One's. In this assembly, the Blessed One spoke six suttas based on temperament: namely, the Purābheda Sutta, the Kalahavivāda Sutta, the Cūḷabyūha Sutta, the Mahābyūha Sutta, the Tuvaṭaka Sutta, and this very Sammāparibbājanīya Sutta. Among these, in order to set in motion this sutta which was to be taught for the benefit of the devas of lustful temperament, the mind-made Buddha, asking a question, recited this verse: 'I ask the sage of abundant wisdom...'

Tattha pahūtapaññanti mahāpaññaṃ. Tiṇṇanti caturoghatiṇṇaṃ. Pāraṅgatanti nibbānappattaṃ. Parinibbutanti saupādisesanibbānavasena parinibbutaṃ. Ṭhitattanti lokadhammehi akampanīyacittaṃ. Nikkhamma gharā panujja kāmeti vatthukāme panuditvā gharāvāsā nikkhamma. Kathaṃ bhikkhu sammā so loke paribbajeyyāti so bhikkhu kathaṃ loke sammā paribbajeyya vihareyya anupalitto lokena hutvā, lokaṃ atikkameyyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Sesamettha vuttanayameva.

Here, 'of abundant wisdom' means of great wisdom. 'Crossed over' means having crossed over the four floods. 'Gone to the far shore' means having attained Nibbāna. 'Fully extinguished' means fully extinguished by way of the Nibbāna with residue remaining. 'Of steadfast self' means with a mind unshaken by worldly conditions. 'Having gone forth from home, having banished sensual pleasures' means having banished sensual pleasures for things and having gone forth from the household life. 'How might a bhikkhu rightly wander in the world?' means: How might that bhikkhu rightly wander in the world, how might he dwell, unstained by the world, having transcended the world?—this is what is said. The rest here is in the way already stated.

363. Atha [V 2.0086][M 2.0094] bhagavā yasmā āsavakkhayaṃ appatvā loke sammā paribbajanto nāma natthi, tasmā tasmiṃ rāgacaritādivasena pariggahite sabbapuggalasamūhe taṃ taṃ tesaṃ tesaṃ samānadosānaṃ devatāgaṇānaṃ āciṇṇadosappahānatthaṃ “yassa maṅgalā”ti ārabhitvā arahattanikūṭeneva khīṇāsavapaṭipadaṃ pakāsento pannarasa gāthāyo abhāsi.

363. Then, because there is no one who rightly wanders in the world without having attained the destruction of the taints, the Blessed One—in order to dispel the habitual faults of the various groups of devas with similar defilements within that entire assembly of individuals classified by temperament such as the lustful—began with 'For whom auspicious signs...' and spoke fifteen verses, proclaiming the path of the one whose taints are destroyed, which culminates in arahantship.

Tattha paṭhamagāthāya tāva maṅgalāti maṅgalasutte vuttānaṃ diṭṭhamaṅgalādīnametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Samūhatāti suṭṭhu ūhatā paññāsatthena samucchinnā. Uppātāti “ukkāpātadisāḍāhādayo evaṃ vipākā hontī”ti evaṃ pavattā uppātābhinivesā. Supināti “pubbaṇhasamaye supinaṃ disvā idaṃ nāma hoti, majjhanhikādīsu idaṃ, vāmapassena sayatā diṭṭhe idaṃ nāma hoti, dakkhiṇapassādīhi idaṃ, supinante candaṃ disvā idaṃ nāma hoti, sūriyādayo disvā ida”nti evaṃ pavattā supinābhinivesā. Lakkhaṇāti daṇḍalakkhaṇavatthalakkhaṇādipāṭhaṃ paṭhitvā “iminā idaṃ nāma hotī”ti evaṃ pavattā lakkhaṇābhinivesā. Te sabbepi brahmajāle vuttanayeneva veditabbā. So maṅgaladosavippahīnoti aṭṭhatiṃsa mahāmaṅgalāni ṭhapetvā avasesā maṅgaladosā [P 1.0363] nāma. Yassa panete maṅgalādayo samūhatā, so maṅgaladosavippahīno hoti. Atha vā maṅgalānañca uppātādidosānañca pahīnattā maṅgaladosavippahīno hoti, na maṅgalādīhi suddhiṃ pacceti ariyamaggassa adhigatattā. Tasmā sammā so loke paribbajeyya, so khīṇāsavo sammā loke paribbajeyya anupalitto lokenāti.

Here, in the first verse, 'auspicious signs' (maṅgalā) is a term for what is mentioned in the Maṅgala Sutta, such as auspicious signs by sight. 'Well-uprooted' (samūhatā) means well-removed, cut off by the sword of wisdom. 'Portents' (uppātā) are adherences to portents that proceed thus: 'Portents such as the fall of a meteor, a blaze in a direction, etc., have such and such results.' 'Dreams' (supinā) are adherences to dreams that proceed thus: 'If one sees a dream in the morning, such a thing will happen; at midday and so on, such a thing; if seen while lying on the left side, such a thing will happen; on the right side and so on, such a thing; if at the end of a dream one sees the moon, such a thing will happen; if one sees the sun, etc., such a thing.' 'Signs' (lakkhaṇā) are adherences to signs that proceed thus: 'Having studied the lore on the signs of sticks, cloth, etc., by this such a thing will happen.' All these should be understood in the way explained in the Brahmajāla Sutta. 'He is freed from the fault of auspicious signs': setting aside the thirty-eight great auspicious signs, the rest are called the fault of auspicious signs. One for whom these auspicious signs and so on are well-uprooted is freed from the fault of auspicious signs. Or, because he has abandoned the faults of auspicious signs, portents, and so on, he is freed from the fault of auspicious signs; he does not expect purity from auspicious signs and so on, as he has attained the noble path. Therefore he would rightly wander in the world—that one whose taints are destroyed would rightly wander in the world, unstained by the world.

364. Dutiyagāthāya rāgaṃ vinayetha mānusesu, dibbesu kāmesu cāpi bhikkhūti mānusesu ca dibbesu ca kāmaguṇesu anāgāmimaggena anuppattidhammataṃ nento rāgaṃ vinayetha. Atikkamma bhavaṃ samecca dhammanti evaṃ rāgaṃ vinetvā tato paraṃ arahattamaggena sabbappakārato pariññābhisamayādayo sādhento catusaccabhedampi samecca dhammaṃ imāya paṭipadāya tividhampi atikkamma bhavaṃ. Sammā soti sopi bhikkhu sammā loke paribbajeyya.

364. In the second verse: 'A bhikkhu should dispel lust for human and also for celestial sensual pleasures' means that regarding human and celestial sense-pleasures, he should dispel lust, leading them to a state of non-arising by means of the path of the non-returner. 'Having transcended existence and penetrated the Dhamma' means: having thus dispelled lust, thereafter, by means of the path of arahantship, accomplishing in all ways full understanding, penetration, and so on, and penetrating the Dhamma with its distinction into the four truths, by this practice he transcends the threefold existence. 'Rightly so' means: that bhikkhu too would rightly wander in the world.

365. Tatiyagāthāya “anurodhavirodhavippahīno”ti sabbavatthūsu pahīnarāgadoso. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva sabbagāthāsu ca “sopi bhikkhu sammā [M 2.0095] loke paribbajeyyā”ti yojetabbaṃ. Ito parañhi yojanampi avatvā avuttanayameva vaṇṇayissāma.

365. In the third verse, 'having abandoned attraction and aversion' means having abandoned lust and hatred in regard to all things. The rest is in the way already stated, and in all the verses the phrase 'that bhikkhu too would rightly wander in the world' should be connected. From here on, without stating the connection, we will explain only what has not already been explained.

366. Catutthagāthāya sattasaṅkhāravasena duvidhaṃ piyañca appiyañca veditabbaṃ, tattha chandarāgapaṭighappahānena hitvā. Anupādāyāti catūhi upādānehi kañci dhammaṃ aggahetvā. Anissito [V 2.0087] kuhiñcīti aṭṭhasatabhedena taṇhānissayena dvāsaṭṭhibhedena diṭṭhinissayena ca kuhiñci rūpādidhamme bhave vā anissito. Saṃyojaniyehi vippamuttoti sabbepi tebhūmakadhammā dasavidhasaṃyojanassa visayattā saṃyojaniyā, tehi sabbappakārato maggabhāvanāya pariññātattā ca vippamuttoti attho. Paṭhamapādena cettha rāgadosappahānaṃ vuttaṃ, dutiyena upādānanissayābhāvo, tatiyena sesākusalehi akusalavatthūhi ca vippamokkho. Paṭhamena vā rāgadosappahānaṃ, dutiyena tadupāyo, tatiyena tesaṃ pahīnattā saṃyojaniyehi vippamokkhoti veditabbo.

366. In the fourth verse: The dear and the undear should be understood as twofold, by way of beings and formations. Therein, one abandons them by abandoning desire-and-lust and aversion. 'Not grasping' means not grasping any phenomenon by the four kinds of clinging. 'Not dependent anywhere' means not dependent on any phenomena such as form, etc., or on any existence, by dependence on craving with its one hundred and eight modes or by dependence on views with its sixty-two kinds. 'Freed from the things that fetter' means: all phenomena of the three planes are 'things that fetter' because they are the domain of the ten fetters; one is freed from them in all ways because they have been fully understood by the development of the path. Here, by the first line the abandonment of lust and hatred is stated; by the second, the absence of clinging and dependence; by the third, liberation from the remaining unwholesome states and the bases for the unwholesome. Or, by the first, the abandonment of lust and hatred; by the second, the means for this; by the third, liberation from the things that fetter because of their abandonment, is to be understood.

367. Pañcamagāthāya upadhīsūti khandhupadhīsu. Ādānanti ādātabbaṭṭhena [P 1.0364] teyeva vuccanti. Anaññaneyyoti aniccādīnaṃ sudiṭṭhattā “idaṃ seyyo”ti kenaci anetabbo. Sesaṃ uttānapadatthameva. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ādānesu catutthamaggena sabbaso chandarāgaṃ vinetvā so vinītachandarāgo, tesu upadhīsu na sārameti, sabbe upadhī asārakatteneva passati. Tato tesu duvidhenapi nissayena anissito aññena vā kenaci “idaṃ seyyo”ti anetabbo khīṇāsavo bhikkhu sammā so loke paribbajeyya.

367. In the fifth verse, 'in acquisitions' (upadhīsu) means in the aggregates as acquisitions. 'Grasping' (ādāna): those same things are so called in the sense that they are to be grasped. 'Not to be led by another' (anaññaneyyo) means: because impermanence, etc., are well seen, he is not to be led by anyone with the thought, 'This is better.' The rest has a plain meaning. This is what is said: Having entirely dispelled desire-and-lust for what is grasped by means of the fourth path, he, with desire-and-lust dispelled, does not regard them as an essence in those acquisitions; he sees all acquisitions as being without essence. Then, being undependent on them through the two kinds of dependence, and not to be led by another with the thought, 'This is better,' that bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed would rightly wander in the world.

368. Chaṭṭhagāthāya aviruddhoti etesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ duccaritānaṃ pahīnattā sucaritehi saddhiṃ aviruddho. Viditvā dhammanti maggena catusaccadhammaṃ ñatvā. Nibbānapadābhipatthayānoti anupādisesaṃ khandhaparinibbānapadaṃ patthayamāno. Sesaṃ uttānatthameva.

368. In the sixth verse, 'unopposed' (aviruddho) means: because these three kinds of misconduct have been abandoned, he is unopposed to good conduct. 'Having known the Dhamma' (viditvā dhammaṃ) means having known the Dhamma of the four truths by means of the path. 'Aspiring for the state of Nibbāna' (nibbānapadābhipatthayāno) means aspiring for the state of the final Nibbāna of the aggregates, the Nibbāna without residue remaining. The rest has a plain meaning.

369. Sattamagāthāya akkuṭṭhoti dasahi akkosavatthūhi abhisatto. Na sandhiyethāti na upanayhetha na kuppeyya. Laddhā parabhojanaṃ [M 2.0096] na majjeti parehi dinnaṃ saddhādeyyaṃ labhitvā “ahaṃ ñāto yasassī lābhī”ti na majjeyya. Sesaṃ uttānatthameva.

369. In the seventh verse, 'when reviled' (akkuṭṭho) means when cursed with the ten grounds for abuse. 'He is not hostile' (na sandhiyetha) means: he does not bear resentment, he does not become angry. 'Having received another's food, he is not intoxicated' (laddhā parabhojanaṃ na majjeti) means: having received a faithful offering given by others, he is not intoxicated, thinking, 'I am well-known, famous, and a recipient of gains.' The rest has a plain meaning.

370. Aṭṭhamagāthāya lobhanti visamalobhaṃ. Bhavanti kāmabhavādibhavaṃ. Evaṃ dvīhi padehi bhavabhogataṇhā vuttā. Purimena vā sabbāpi taṇhā, pacchimena kammabhavo. Virato chedanabandhanā cāti evametesaṃ kammakilesānaṃ pahīnattā parasattachedanabandhanā ca viratoti. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

370. In the eighth verse, 'lobhaṃ' refers to unrighteous greed. 'Bhavaṃ' refers to existence, such as sensual existence and so on. Thus, by these two phrases, craving for existence and enjoyments is stated. Or, by the first phrase, all craving is stated, while by the latter, kamma-becoming is stated. 'Virato chedanabandhanā ca' means that because these kamma and defilements have been abandoned, one abstains from cutting and binding others. The rest is as previously stated.

371. Navamagāthāya sāruppaṃ attano viditvāti attano bhikkhubhāvassa patirūpaṃ anesanādiṃ pahāya sammāesanādiājīvasuddhiṃ aññañca sammāpaṭipattiṃ tattha patiṭṭhahanena viditvā. Na hi ñātamatteneva kiñci hoti. Yathātathiyanti yathātathaṃ yathābhūtaṃ. Dhammanti khandhāyatanādibhedaṃ [P 1.0365] yathābhūtañāṇena, catusaccadhammaṃ vā maggena viditvā. Sesaṃ uttānatthameva.

371. In the ninth verse, 'sāruppaṃ attano viditvā' means: having known what is suitable for oneself—that is, for one’s state as a bhikkhu—by abandoning improper seeking and so on, and by establishing oneself in right seeking, purity of livelihood, and other right practices. For nothing comes from mere knowing. 'Yathātathiyaṃ' means in accordance with reality, as it actually is. 'Dhammaṃ' means: having known the Dhamma with its divisions into aggregates, sense bases, etc., by means of the knowledge of things as they have come to be; or having known the Dhamma of the Four Truths by means of the path. The rest has a plain meaning.

372. Dasamagāthāya [V 2.0088] so nirāso anāsisānoti yassa ariyamaggena vināsitattā anusayā ca na santi, akusalamūlā ca samūhatā, so nirāso nittaṇho hoti. Tato āsāya abhāvena kañci rūpādidhammaṃ nāsīsati. Tenāha “nirāso anāsisāno”ti. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

372. In the tenth verse, 'so nirāso anāsisāno' means: he for whom the underlying tendencies no longer exist, having been destroyed by the noble path, and for whom the unwholesome roots have been eradicated, is without hope, without craving. Therefore, due to the absence of hope, he does not long for any phenomenon such as form. Hence it is said, 'nirāso anāsisāno.' The rest is as previously stated.

373. Ekādasamagāthāya āsavakhīṇoti khīṇacaturāsavo. Pahīnamānoti pahīnanavavidhamāno. Rāgapathanti rāgavisayabhūtaṃ tebhūmakadhammajātaṃ. Upātivattoti pariññāpahānehi atikkanto. Dantoti sabbadvāravisevanaṃ hitvā ariyena damathena dantabhūmiṃ patto. Parinibbutoti kilesaggivūpasamena sītibhūto. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

373. In the eleventh verse, 'āsavakhīṇo' means one whose four taints are destroyed. 'Pahīnamāno' means one who has abandoned the nine kinds of conceit. 'Rāgapathaṃ' refers to the mass of phenomena in the three planes that has become the object of lust. 'Upātivatto' means one who has transcended by means of full understanding and abandonment. 'Danto' means one who has abandoned frequenting all sense doors and has attained the state of being tamed by the noble taming. 'Parinibbuto' means one who has become cooled by the subsiding of the fire of the defilements. The rest is as previously stated.

374. Dvādasamagāthāya saddhoti buddhādiguṇesu parappaccayavirahitattā sabbākārasampannena aveccappasādena samannāgato, na parassa saddhāya paṭipattiyaṃ gamanabhāvena. Yathāha – “na khvāhaṃ ettha bhante bhagavato saddhāya [M 2.0097] gacchāmī”ti (a. ni. 5.34). Sutavāti vositasutakiccattā paramatthikasutasamannāgato. Niyāmadassīti saṃsārakantāramūḷhe loke amatapuragāmino sammattaniyāmabhūtassa maggassa dassāvī, diṭṭhamaggoti vuttaṃ hoti. Vaggagatesu na vaggasārīti vaggagatā nāma dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhigatikā aññamaññaṃ paṭilomattā, evaṃ vaggāhi diṭṭhīhi gatesu sattesu na vaggasārī – “idaṃ ucchijjissati, idaṃ tatheva bhavissatī”ti evaṃ diṭṭhivasena agamanato. Paṭighanti paṭighātakaṃ, cittavighātakanti vuttaṃ hoti. Dosavisesanamevetaṃ. Vineyyāti vinetvā. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

374. In the twelfth verse, 'saddho' means one endowed with confirmed confidence in the qualities of the Buddha and so on, a confidence complete in all respects and free from reliance on another, not proceeding by another’s faith in a practice. As it is said: “Venerable sir, I do not proceed in this matter out of faith in the Blessed One” (AN 5.34). 'Sutavā' means one endowed with the ultimate learning, as the task of learning has been concluded. 'Niyāmadassī' means a seer of the path—which is the right fixed course leading to the deathless city for a world lost in the wilderness of saṃsāra; this means one who has seen the path. 'Vaggagatesu na vaggasārī': those who have gone to factions are the adherents of the sixty-two views, which are mutually opposed; thus, among beings who have gone by way of such factious views, he is not a faction-goer, because he does not proceed by way of views such as “this will be annihilated” or “this will remain the same.” 'Paṭighaṃ' means that which strikes back; that is, mental vexation. This is just a designation for hatred. 'Vineyya' means having trained. The rest is as previously stated.

375. Terasamagāthāya saṃsuddhajinoti saṃsuddhena arahattamaggena vijitakileso. Vivaṭṭacchadoti vivaṭarāgadosamohachadano. Dhammesu vasīti catusaccadhammesu [P 1.0366] vasippatto. Na hissa sakkā te dhammā yathā ñātā kenaci aññathā kātuṃ, tena khīṇāsavo “dhammesu vasī”ti vuccati. Pāragūti pāraṃ vuccati nibbānaṃ, taṃ gato, saupādisesavasena adhigatoti vuttaṃ hoti. Anejoti apagatataṇhācalano. Saṅkhāranirodhañāṇakusaloti saṅkhāranirodho vuccati nibbānaṃ, tamhi ñāṇaṃ ariyamaggapaññā, tattha kusalo, catukkhattuṃ bhāvitattā chekoti vuttaṃ hoti.

375. In the thirteenth verse, 'saṃsuddhajino' means one who has conquered the defilements through the thoroughly purified path of arahantship. 'Vivaṭṭacchado' means one whose covering of lust, hatred, and delusion has been removed. 'Dhammesu vasī' means one who has attained mastery over the Dhamma of the Four Truths. Because no one can make those dhammas—as they have been known by him—otherwise, the one whose taints are destroyed is called a “master in the dhammas.” 'Pāragū' means one who has gone to the far shore—Nibbāna is called the far shore; this means he has attained it by way of the Nibbāna-element with residue remaining. 'Anejo' means one from whom the agitation of craving has departed. 'Saṅkhāranirodhañāṇakusalo' means skilled in the knowledge of the cessation of formations: the cessation of formations is called Nibbāna; the knowledge in that is the wisdom of the noble path; he is skilled in that, and because it has been developed four times, he is called an expert.

376. Cuddasamagāthāya atītesūti pavattiṃ patvā atikkantesu pañcakkhandhesu. Anāgatesūti pavattiṃ appattesu pañcakkhandhesu eva. Kappātītoti “ahaṃ mama”nti kappanaṃ sabbampi vā taṇhādiṭṭhikappaṃ atīto. Aticca suddhipaññoti atīva suddhipañño, atikkamitvā [V 2.0089] vā suddhipañño. Kiṃ atikkamitvā? Addhattayaṃ. Arahā hi yvāyaṃ avijjāsaṅkhārasaṅkhāto atīto addhā, jātijarāmaraṇasaṅkhāto anāgato addhā, viññāṇādibhavapariyanto paccuppanno ca addhā, taṃ sabbampi atikkamma kaṅkhaṃ vitaritvā paramasuddhippattapañño hutvā ṭhito. Tena vuccati “aticca suddhipañño”ti. Sabbāyatanehīti dvādasahāyatanehi. Arahā hi evaṃ kappātīto. Kappātītattā aticca suddhipaññattā ca āyatiṃ na kiñci āyatanaṃ upeti. Tenāha – “sabbāyatanehi vippamutto”ti.

376. In the fourteenth verse, 'atītesu' refers to the five aggregates that have passed away after having occurred. 'Anāgatesu' refers to the five aggregates that have not yet occurred. 'Kappātīto' means one who has transcended all conceiving of “I” and “mine,” or the entire conceiving rooted in craving and views. 'Aticca suddhipañño' means one of exceedingly pure wisdom, or one of pure wisdom by having transcended. What has been transcended? The three periods of time. For the Arahant has transcended the past period of time, designated as ignorance and formations; the future period of time, designated as birth, aging, and death; and the present period of time, which ends with existence, starting from consciousness. Having transcended all this, dispelled doubt, and become one established in wisdom that has attained supreme purity, he is called 'aticca suddhipañño,' ‘one of surpassing pure wisdom.’ 'Sabbāyatanehi' means from the twelve sense bases. For an Arahant is thus beyond conceiving. Because he is beyond conceiving and is of surpassing pure wisdom, he does not approach any sense base in the future. Hence it is said, 'sabbāyatanehi vippamutto,' ‘liberated from all sense bases.’

377. Pannarasamagāthāya [M 2.0098] aññāya padanti ye te “saccānaṃ caturo padā”ti vuttā, tesu ekekapadaṃ pubbabhāgasaccavavatthāpanapaññāya ñatvā. Samecca dhammanti tato paraṃ catūhi ariyamaggehi catusaccadhammaṃ samecca. Vivaṭaṃ disvāna pahānamāsavānanti atha paccavekkhaṇañāṇena āsavakkhayasaññitaṃ nibbānaṃ vivaṭaṃ pākaṭamanāvaṭaṃ disvā. Sabbupadhīnaṃ parikkhayāti sabbesaṃ khandhakāmaguṇakilesābhisaṅkhārabhedānaṃ upadhīnaṃ parikkhīṇattā katthaci asajjamāno bhikkhu sammā so loke paribbajeyya vihareyya, anallīyanto lokaṃ gaccheyyāti desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi.

377. In the fifteenth verse, 'aññāya padaṃ' means: having known the state. This means having known each one of those states called “the four states of the truths” with the preliminary wisdom that ascertains the truths. 'Samecca dhammaṃ' means: having penetrated the Dhamma. This means thereafter having penetrated the Dhamma of the Four Truths with the four noble paths. 'Vivaṭaṃ disvāna pahānamāsavānaṃ' means: having seen the destruction of the taints as uncovered. This means then, with the knowledge of reviewing, having seen Nibbāna—which is designated as the destruction of the taints—as uncovered, manifest, and unobstructed. 'Sabbupadhīnaṃ parikkhayā' means: because of the complete destruction of all substrates—the substrates of the aggregates, the cords of sensual pleasure, the defilements, and the formations—the bhikkhu, not clinging anywhere, would wander rightly in the world. This means he would dwell, he would move through the world, without clinging. Thus he concluded the teaching.

378. Tato [P 1.0367] so nimmito dhammadesanaṃ thomento “addhā hi bhagavā”ti imaṃ gāthamāha. Tattha yo so evaṃ vihārīti yo so maṅgalādīni samūhanitvā sabbamaṅgaladosappahānavihārī, yopi so dibbamānusakesu kāmesu rāgaṃ vineyya bhavātikkamma dhammābhisamayavihārīti evaṃ tāya tāya gāthāya niddiṭṭhabhikkhuṃ dassento āha. Sesaṃ uttānameva. Ayaṃ pana yojanā – addhā hi bhagavā tatheva etaṃ yaṃ tvaṃ “yassa maṅgalā samūhatā”tiādīni vatvā tassā tassā gāthāya pariyosāne “sammā so loke paribbajeyyā”ti avaca. Kiṃ kāraṇaṃ? Yo so evaṃvihārī bhikkhu, so uttamena damathena danto, sabbāni ca dasapi saṃyojanāni caturo ca yoge vītivatto hoti. Tasmā sammā so loke paribbajeyya, natthi me ettha vicikicchāti iti desanāthomanagāthampi vatvā arahattanikūṭeneva desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi. Suttapariyosāne koṭisatasahassadevatānaṃ aggaphalappatti ahosi, sotāpattisakadāgāmianāgāmiphalappattā pana gaṇanato asaṅkhyeyyāti.

378. Then that created being, praising the Dhamma teaching, spoke this verse: “Truly, Blessed One….” Herein, 'yo so evaṃ vihārī' (that one who dwells thus) refers to the bhikkhu who dwells having abolished auspicious signs and so on, having abandoned all faults connected with auspicious signs; or it refers to the one who dwells having penetrated the Dhamma, having overcome lust for divine and human sensual pleasures and transcended becoming. Thus he spoke, pointing out the bhikkhu indicated in each respective verse. The rest is plain. This, however, is the construction: “Truly, Blessed One, it is just so, that you spoke about one ‘for whom auspicious signs are abolished,’ etc., and at the conclusion of each respective verse you said, ‘Rightly would he wander in the world.’ For what reason? Because that bhikkhu who dwells thus is tamed with the supreme taming and has passed beyond all ten fetters and the four yokes. Therefore, rightly would he wander in the world. I have no doubt about this.” Having spoken this verse praising the teaching, he concluded the discourse with the very pinnacle of arahantship. At the end of the discourse, a hundred thousand crores of devas attained the highest fruit, while those who attained the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, and non-returning were innumerable.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the commentary on a book of the Minor Collection,

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya sammāparibbājanīyasuttavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Sammāparibbājanīya Sutta in the Commentary on the Suttanipāta.

Niṭṭhitā.

It is finished.

14. Dhammikasuttavaṇṇanā

14. Commentary on the Dhammika Sutta

Evaṃ [V 2.0090][M 2.0099] me sutanti dhammikasuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Tiṭṭhamāne kira bhagavati lokanāthe dhammiko nāma upāsako ahosi nāmena ca paṭipattiyā ca. So kira saraṇasampanno sīlasampanno bahussuto piṭakattayadharo anāgāmī abhiññālābhī ākāsacārī ahosi. Tassa parivārā pañcasatā upāsakā, tepi tādisā eva ahesuṃ. Tassekadivasaṃ uposathikassa rahogatassa paṭisallīnassa majjhimayāmāvasānasamaye evaṃ parivitakko udapādi – “yaṃnūnāhaṃ agāriyaanagāriyānaṃ paṭipadaṃ puccheyya”nti. So pañcahi upāsakasatehi parivuto bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā tamatthaṃ pucchi, bhagavā cassa byākāsi. Tattha [P 1.0368] pubbe vaṇṇitasadisaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ, apubbaṃ vaṇṇayissāma.

Thus have I heard—the Dhammika Sutta. What is its origin? It is said that while the Blessed One, the Lord of the World, was still living, there was a lay follower named Dhammika, who was righteous both in name and in practice. He was accomplished in the refuges and in virtue, very learned, a bearer of the three Piṭakas, a non-returner, an obtainer of higher knowledge, and one who could travel through the sky. His retinue consisted of five hundred lay followers, and they too were of the same kind. One day, while observing the Uposatha, having gone to a secluded place for solitary retreat, at the end of the middle watch of the night this thought arose in him: “Why don’t I ask about the practice for both householders and the homeless?” Accompanied by his five hundred lay followers, he approached the Blessed One and asked him about this matter, and the Blessed One explained it to him. Therein, what is similar to what has been previously explained should be understood in the manner already stated; we shall now explain what is new.

379. Tattha paṭhamagāthāya tāva kathaṃkaroti kathaṃ karonto kathaṃ paṭipajjanto. Sādhu hotīti sundaro anavajjo atthasādhano hoti. Upāsakāseti upāsakāicceva vuttaṃ hoti. Sesamatthato pākaṭameva. Ayaṃ pana yojanā – yo vā agārā anagārameti pabbajati, ye vā agārino upāsakā, etesu duvidhesu sāvakesu kathaṃkaro sāvako sādhu hotīti.

379. Therein, regarding the first verse: 'acting in what way' means doing what, practicing how. 'Is good' means is excellent, blameless, and conducive to what is beneficial. 'Upāsakāse' simply means 'lay followers.' The rest is evident in meaning. Now this is the construction: whether one goes forth from home to homelessness, or whether they are householders who are lay followers—among these two kinds of disciples, by acting in what way is a disciple good?

380-1. Idāni evaṃ puṭṭhassa bhagavato byākaraṇasamatthataṃ dīpento “tuvañhī”ti gāthādvayamāha. Tattha gatinti ajjhāsayagatiṃ. Parāyaṇanti nipphattiṃ. Atha vā gatinti nirayādipañcappabhedaṃ. Parāyaṇanti gatito paraṃ ayanaṃ gativippamokkhaṃ parinibbānaṃ, na catthi tulyoti tayā sadiso natthi. Sabbaṃ tuvaṃ ñāṇamavecca dhammaṃ, pakāsesi satte anukampamānoti tvaṃ bhagavā yadatthi ñeyyaṃ nāma, taṃ anavasesaṃ avecca paṭivijjhitvā satte anukampamāno sabbaṃ ñāṇañca dhammañca pakāsesi. Yaṃ yaṃ yassa hitaṃ hoti, taṃ taṃ tassa āvikāsiyeva desesiyeva, na te atthi ācariyamuṭṭhīti vuttaṃ hoti. Virocasi vimaloti dhūmarajādivirahito viya cando, rāgādimalābhāvena vimalo virocasi. Sesamettha uttānatthameva.

Now, explaining the ability of the Blessed One to answer when questioned thus, he speaks two verses beginning with “For you....” Herein, “destination” (gati) means the inclination of intention. “Final goal” (parāyaṇa) means accomplishment. Alternatively, “destination” refers to the fivefold classification of destinations, such as hell. “Final goal” means the going beyond destinations, the liberation from destinations, which is final Nibbāna. “There is none equal to you” means there is none like you. “You have fully understood all knowledge and the Dhamma, and out of compassion you reveal it to beings”: this means that you, O Blessed One, having fully comprehended and penetrated without remainder whatever is to be known, out of compassion for beings, have revealed all knowledge and the Dhamma. Whatever is beneficial for each, that you have made clear and taught to them. Thus it is said, “There is no closed fist of the teacher.” “You shine immaculate”: like the moon free from smoke and dust, you shine immaculate, free from the stains of lust and so forth. The rest here is clear in meaning.

382. Idāni yesaṃ tadā bhagavā dhammaṃ desesi, te devaputte kittetvā bhagavantaṃ pasaṃsanto “āgañchī te santike”ti gāthādvayamāha. Tattha [M 2.0100] nāgarājā erāvaṇo nāmāti ayaṃ kira [V 2.0091] erāvaṇo nāma devaputto kāmarūpī dibbe vimāne vasati. So yadā sakko uyyānakīḷaṃ gacchati, tadā diyaḍḍhasatayojanaṃ kāyaṃ abhinimminitvā tettiṃsa kumbhe māpetvā erāvaṇo nāma hatthī hoti. Tassa ekekasmiṃ kumbhe dve dve dantā honti, ekekasmiṃ dante satta satta [P 1.0369] pokkharaṇiyo, ekekissā pokkharaṇiyā satta satta paduminiyo, ekekissā paduminiyā satta satta pupphāni, ekekasmiṃ pupphe satta satta pattāni, ekekasmiṃ patte satta satta accharāyo naccanti padumaccharāyotveva vissutā sakkassa nāṭakitthiyo, yā ca vimānavatthusmimpi “bhamanti kaññā padumesu sikkhitā”ti (vi. va. 1034) āgatā. Tesaṃ pana tettisaṃkumbhānaṃ majjhe sudassanakumbho nāma tiṃsayojanamatto hoti, tattha yojanappamāṇo maṇipallaṅko tiyojanubbedhe pupphamaṇḍape attharīyati. Tattha sakko devānamindo accharāsaṅghaparivuto dibbasampattiṃ paccanubhoti. Sakke pana devānaminde uyyānakīḷāto paṭinivatte puna taṃ rūpaṃ saṃharitvāna devaputtova hoti. Taṃ sandhāyāha – “āgañchi te santike nāgarājā erāvaṇo nāmā”ti. Jinoti sutvāti “vijitapāpadhammo esa bhagavā”ti evaṃ sutvā. Sopi tayā mantayitvāti tayā saddhiṃ mantayitvā, pañhaṃ pucchitvāti adhippāyo. Ajjhagamāti adhiagamā, gatoti vuttaṃ hoti. Sādhūti sutvāna patītarūpoti taṃ pañhaṃ sutvā “sādhu bhante”ti abhinanditvā tuṭṭharūpo gatoti attho.

382. Now, praising the Blessed One by mentioning the devaputtas to whom the Blessed One had taught the Dhamma on that occasion, he (Dhammika) spoke two verses beginning with: “There came into your presence….” Therein, “the Nāga king named Erāvaṇa”: it is said that this Erāvaṇa is a devaputta who can assume any form at will and who dwells in a divine mansion. When Sakka goes to the pleasure garden, this devaputta creates for himself a body one hundred and fifty yojanas in size with thirty-three heads, and thus becomes the elephant named Erāvaṇa. On each of his heads are two tusks. On each tusk are seven lotus ponds. In each pond are seven lotus plants. In each lotus plant are seven flowers. On each flower are seven petals. On each petal seven celestial nymphs dance; they are renowned as the lotus-nymphs, Sakka’s dancing girls, who are also mentioned in the Vimānavatthu: “Maidens skilled in dancing on lotuses whirl about.” Among those thirty-three heads, the central one, called Sudassana, is thirty yojanas in size. There, a jeweled couch a yojana in size is spread out in a flower pavilion three yojanas high. There Sakka, lord of the devas, surrounded by a host of celestial nymphs, enjoys divine bliss. But when Sakka, lord of the devas, returns from the pleasure garden, Erāvaṇa withdraws that form and becomes a devaputta again. It is with reference to this that he says: “The Nāga king named Erāvaṇa came into your presence.” “Having heard ‘the Victor’”: this means having heard, “This Blessed One has conquered all evil states.” “He too, having consulted with you”: this means having consulted with you with the intention of asking a question. “He approached”: this means he went. “Having heard ‘Excellent!’ and being of a pleased appearance”: the meaning is that having heard the question, he rejoiced, saying, “Excellent, venerable sir!” and came with a pleased appearance.

383. Rājāpi taṃ vessavaṇo kuveroti ettha so yakkho rañjanaṭṭhena rājā, visāṇāya rājadhāniyā rajjaṃ kāretīti vessavaṇo, purimanāmena kuveroti veditabbo. So kira kuvero nāma brāhmaṇamahāsālo hutvā dānādīni puññāni katvā visāṇāya rājadhāniyā adhipati hutvā nibbatto. Tasmā “kuvero vessavaṇo”ti vuccati. Vuttañcetaṃ āṭānāṭiyasutte –

383. “The king Vessavaṇa Kuvera also”: here, that yakkha is a king (rājā) in the sense of delighting (rañjana). And because he rules in the capital city of Visāṇā, he is called Vessavaṇa; he should be understood by his former name as Kuvera. It is said that he, by the name of Kuvera, having been a wealthy brahmin, performed meritorious deeds such as giving and was reborn as the lord of the capital city of Visāṇā. Therefore, he is called “Kuvera Vessavaṇa.” And this is stated in the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta:

“Kuverassa kho pana, mārisa, mahārājassa visāṇā nāma rājadhānī, tasmā kuvero mahārājā ‘vessavaṇo’ti pavuccatī”ti (dī. ni. 3.291) –

“Indeed, friends, the great king Kuvera has a capital named Visāṇā. Therefore, the great king Kuvera is called ‘Vessavaṇa.’”

Sesamettha pākaṭameva.

The rest here is clear.

Tattha [M 2.0101] siyā – kasmā pana dūratare tāvatiṃsabhavane vasanto erāvaṇo paṭhamaṃ āgato, vessavaṇo pacchā, ekanagareva [P 1.0370] vasanto ayaṃ upāsako sabbapacchā, kathañca so tesaṃ āgamanaṃ aññāsi, yena evamāhāti? Vuccate – vessavaṇo kira tadā anekasahassapavāḷapallaṅkaṃ dvādasayojanaṃ nārivāhanaṃ abhiruyha pavāḷakuntaṃ uccāretvā dasasahassakoṭiyakkhehi [V 2.0092] parivuto “bhagavantaṃ pañhaṃ pucchissāmī”ti ākāsaṭṭhakavimānāni pariharitvā maggena maggaṃ āgacchanto veḷukaṇḍakanagare nandamātāya upāsikāya nivesanassa uparibhāgaṃ sampatto. Upāsikāya ayamānubhāvo – parisuddhasīlā hoti, niccaṃ vikālabhojanā paṭiviratā, piṭakattayadhārinī, anāgāmiphale patiṭṭhitā. Sā tamhi samaye sīhapañjaraṃ ugghāṭetvā utuggahaṇatthāya māluteritokāse ṭhatvā aṭṭhakapārāyanavagge parimaṇḍalehi padabyañjanehi madhurena sarena bhāsati. Vessavaṇo tattheva yānāni ṭhapetvā yāva upāsikā “idamavoca bhagavā magadhesu viharanto pāsāṇake cetiye paricārakasoḷasannaṃ brāhmaṇāna”nti nigamanaṃ abhāsi, tāva sabbaṃ sutvā vaggapariyosāne suvaṇṇamurajasadisaṃ mahantaṃ gīvaṃ paggahetvā “sādhu sādhu bhaginī”ti sādhukāramadāsi. Sā “ko etthā”ti āha. “Ahaṃ bhagini vessavaṇo”ti. Upāsikā kira paṭhamaṃ sotāpannā ahosi, pacchā vessavaṇo. Taṃ so dhammato sahodarabhāvaṃ sandhāya upāsikaṃ bhaginivādena samudācarati. Upāsikāya ca “vikālo, bhātika bhadramukha, yassa dāni kālaṃ maññasī”ti vutto “ahaṃ bhagini tayi pasanno pasannākāraṃ karomī”ti āha. Tena hi bhadramukha, mama khette nipphannaṃ sāliṃ kammakarā āharituṃ na sakkonti, taṃ tava parisāya āṇāpehīti. So “sādhu bhaginī”ti yakkhe āṇāpesi. Te aḍḍhaterasa koṭṭhāgārasatāni pūresuṃ. Tato pabhuti koṭṭhāgāraṃ [P 1.0371] ūnaṃ nāma nāhosi, “nandamātu koṭṭhāgāraṃ viyā”ti loke nidassanaṃ ahosi. Vessavaṇo koṭṭhāgārāni pūretvā bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkami. Bhagavā “vikāle āgatosī”ti āha. Atha bhagavato sabbaṃ ārocesi. Iminā kāraṇena āsannatarepi cātumahārājikabhavane vasanto vessavaṇo pacchā āgato. Erāvaṇassa pana na kiñci antarā karaṇīyaṃ ahosi, tena so paṭhamataraṃ āgato.

Here one might ask: Why did Erāvaṇa, dwelling in the more distant Tāvatiṃsa realm, arrive first, while Vessavaṇa came later, and this lay follower, living in the same city, came last of all? And how did he know of their arrival, so as to speak thus? It is said: Vessavaṇa, at that time, mounted his twelve-yojana-wide palanquin carried by women, which was adorned with thousands of corals. Raising a coral lance and surrounded by ten thousand crores of yakkhas, he set out with the thought, “I will ask the Blessed One a question.” Avoiding the celestial mansions fixed in the sky, he came along the path and arrived above the residence of the lay follower Nandamātā in the city of Veḷukaṇḍaka. This was the spiritual power of that lay follower: she was of purified morality, always refrained from eating at the wrong time, was a bearer of the three Piṭakas, and was established in the fruit of non-returning. At that time, she had opened her lion-window and was standing in a place stirred by a gentle breeze to take the air, reciting with a melodious voice the Aṭṭhakavagga and the Pārāyanavagga with well-rounded words and syllables. Vessavaṇa stopped his vehicles right there and listened until the lay follower recited the conclusion: “Thus spoke the Blessed One while dwelling at the Pāsāṇaka Cetiya in Magadha, to the sixteen attendant brahmins.” Having heard the entire recitation, at the end of the sections, he stretched out his great neck, which was like a golden drum, and gave his approval, saying, “Excellent, excellent, sister!” She asked, “Who is there?” He replied, “I am Vessavaṇa, sister.” It is said that the lay follower had become a stream-enterer first, and Vessavaṇa later. Referring to their kinship in the Dhamma, he addressed the lay follower with the term “sister.” When she said, “It is the wrong time, brother, good sir. You may now do that for which you deem it the time,” he replied, “Sister, I am pleased with you and wish to show a sign of my pleasure.” “Then, good sir, the workers cannot harvest the rice that has ripened in my field. Please command your retinue to do it.” He said, “Very well, sister,” and commanded the yakkhas. They filled twelve hundred and fifty storehouses. From then on, her storehouses were never empty, and it became a saying in the world: “Like Nandamātā’s storehouse!” After filling the storehouses, Vessavaṇa approached the Blessed One. The Blessed One said, “You have come at the wrong time.” Then he related the entire matter to the Blessed One. For this reason, though dwelling in the nearer Cātumahārājika realm, Vessavaṇa arrived later. As for Erāvaṇa, he had no business to attend to on the way, so he arrived earlier.

Ayaṃ [M 2.0102] pana upāsako kiñcāpi anāgāmī pakatiyāva ekabhattiko, tathāpi tadā uposathadivasoti katvā uposathaṅgāni adhiṭṭhāya sāyanhasamayaṃ sunivattho supāruto pañcasataupāsakaparivuto jetavanaṃ gantvā dhammadesanaṃ sutvā attano gharaṃ āgamma tesaṃ upāsakānaṃ saraṇasīlauposathānisaṃsādibhedaṃ upāsakadhammaṃ kathetvā te upāsake uyyojesi. Tesañca tasseva ghare muṭṭhihatthappamāṇapādakāni pañca kappiyamañcasatāni pāṭekkovarakesu paññattāni honti. Te attano attano ovarakaṃ pavisitvā samāpattiṃ appetvā nisīdiṃsu, upāsakopi tathevākāsi. Tena ca samayena sāvatthinagare sattapaññāsa kulasatasahassāni vasanti, manussagaṇanāya aṭṭhārasakoṭimanussā. Tena paṭhamayāme hatthiassamanussabherisaddādīhi sāvatthinagaraṃ mahāsamuddo viya ekasaddaṃ hoti. Majjhimayāmasamanantare so saddo paṭippassambhati[V 2.0093]. Tamhi kāle upāsako samāpattito vuṭṭhāya attano guṇe āvajjetvā “yenāhaṃ maggasukhena phalasukhena sukhito viharāmi, idaṃ sukhaṃ kaṃ nissāya laddha”nti cintetvā “bhagavantaṃ nissāyā”ti bhagavati cittaṃ pasādetvā “bhagavā etarahi katamena vihārena viharatī”ti āvajjento dibbena cakkhunā erāvaṇavessavaṇe disvā dibbāya sotadhātuyā dhammadesanaṃ sutvā cetopariyañāṇena tesaṃ pasannacittataṃ [P 1.0372] ñatvā “yaṃnūnāhampi bhagavantaṃ ubhayahitaṃ paṭipadaṃ puccheyya”nti cintesi. Tasmā so ekanagare vasantopi sabbapacchā āgato, evañca nesaṃ āgamanaṃ aññāsi. Tenāha – “āgañchi te santike nāgarājā…pe… so cāpi sutvāna patītarūpo”ti.

Now this lay follower, though a non-returner and by nature one who eats only a single meal a day, nevertheless, because it was the Uposatha day, undertook the Uposatha precepts. In the evening, well-dressed and properly attired, accompanied by five hundred lay followers, he went to Jetavana, listened to the Dhamma teaching, and upon returning to his home, explained to those lay followers the Dhamma for lay followers, with its various aspects such as the benefits of the refuges, the precepts, and the Uposatha. Then he dismissed those lay followers. And for them, in his house, five hundred suitable couches, each with legs the size of a fist, were arranged in separate private rooms. They entered their respective rooms, attained meditative absorption, and sat down. The lay follower also did the same. At that time, fifty-seven hundred-thousand families dwelt in the city of Sāvatthī, with a population of eighteen crore people. During the first watch of the night, with the sounds of elephants, horses, people, and drums, the city of Sāvatthī was as noisy as the great ocean. Shortly after the middle watch began, that sound subsided. At that time, the lay follower emerged from his meditative attainment, reflected on his own virtues, and thought: “By relying on whom have I obtained this happiness of the path and fruit with which I now dwell?” Having considered, “It is by relying on the Blessed One,” he aroused confidence in the Blessed One and reflected: “In which state is the Blessed One now dwelling?” While reflecting, with his divine eye he saw Erāvaṇa and Vessavaṇa; with his divine ear element, he heard the Dhamma teaching; and with his knowledge encompassing the minds of others, he knew their minds were confident. He then thought: “Why should I not also ask the Blessed One about the practice that is beneficial for both?” Therefore, although he lived in the same city, he arrived last, and thus he knew of their arrival. Hence he said: “The Nāga king came to your presence… and he too, having heard, was delighted.”

384. Idāni ito bahiddhā lokasammatehi samaṇabrāhmaṇehi ukkaṭṭhabhāvena bhagavantaṃ pasaṃsanto “ye kecime”ti gāthādvayamāha. Tattha titthiyāti nandavacchasaṃkiccehi ādipuggalehi tīhi titthakarehi kate diṭṭhititthe jātā, tesaṃ sāsane pabbajitā pūraṇādayo cha satthāro. Tattha nāṭaputto nigaṇṭho, avasesā ājīvakāti te sabbe dassento āha “ye kecime titthiyā vādasīlā”ti, “mayaṃ sammā paṭipannā, aññe micchā paṭipannā”ti evaṃ vādakaraṇasīlā lokaṃ mukhasattīhi vitudantā vicaranti. Ājīvakā vāti te ekajjhamuddiṭṭhe bhinditvā dasseti. Nātitarantīti nātikkamanti. Sabbeti aññepi ye [M 2.0103] keci titthiyasāvakādayo, tepi pariggaṇhanto āha. “Ṭhito vajantaṃ viyā”ti yathā koci ṭhito gativikalo sīghagāminaṃ purisaṃ gacchantaṃ nātitareyya, evaṃ te paññāgatiyā abhāvena te te atthappabhede bujjhituṃ asakkontā ṭhitā, atijavanapaññaṃ bhagavantaṃ nātitarantīti attho.

384. Now, praising the Blessed One for his supreme excellence in comparison with ascetics and brahmins outside of this teaching who are esteemed by the world, he speaks two verses beginning with “Ye kecime.” Here, “titthiyā” (sectarians) refers to those who arose in the heretical views established by the three original founders—Nanda, Vaccha, and Saṅkicca—in whose teaching the six teachers, Pūraṇa and others, have gone forth. Among them, Nāṭaputta is the Nigaṇṭha, and the rest are Ājīvikas. Pointing to all of them, he says, “Whatever sectarians there are, fond of debate”—that is, those who are disposed to argue, claiming, “We are practicing rightly, others are practicing wrongly,” and wander the world piercing it with their mouth-spears. The phrase “or the Ājīvikas” shows them distinctly after they were indicated collectively. “Nātitaranti” means they do not surpass. “Sabbe” (all) includes any other disciples of the sectarians and so on, encompassing them all. “Ṭhito vajantaṃ viyā” (like one standing still a man who is walking) means that just as someone standing still, impaired in movement, cannot surpass a swift-walking man, so too, lacking the movement of wisdom, they remain stationary, unable to comprehend the various distinctions of meaning, and thus cannot surpass the Blessed One, whose wisdom is exceedingly swift.

385. Brāhmaṇā vādasīlā vuddhā cāti ettāvatā caṅkītārukkhapokkharasātijāṇussoṇiādayo dasseti, api brāhmaṇā santi kecīti iminā majjhimāpi daharāpi kevalaṃ brāhmaṇā santi atthi upalabbhanti kecīti evaṃ assalāyanavāseṭṭhaambaṭṭhauttaramāṇavakādayo dasseti. Atthabaddhāti “api nu kho imaṃ pañhaṃ byākareyya, imaṃ kaṅkhaṃ chindeyyā”ti evaṃ atthabaddhā bhavanti. Ye cāpi aññeti aññepi ye “mayaṃ vādino”ti evaṃ maññamānā [P 1.0373] vicaranti khattiyapaṇḍitabrāhmaṇabrahmadevayakkhādayo aparimāṇā. Tepi sabbe tayi atthabaddhā bhavantīti dasseti.

385. “And aged brahmins fond of debate” indicates elders such as Caṅkī, Tārukkha, Pokkharasāti, and Jāṇussoṇi. “There are also some brahmins” indicates middle-aged and young brahmins, that is, some mere brahmins exist, are found, such as Assalāyana, Vāseṭṭha, Ambaṭṭha, the young brahmin Uttara, and others. “Atthabaddhā” (bound to the meaning) means they become bound to the meaning, thinking, “Might he answer this question? Might he cut off this doubt?” “And whatever others” refers to countless others—wise khattiyas, brahmins, Brahmā deities, yakkhas, and more—who wander about considering themselves to be debaters. He shows that all of them become bound to the meaning in regard to you.

386-7. Evaṃ nānappakārehi bhagavantaṃ pasaṃsitvā idāni dhammeneva taṃ pasaṃsitvā dhammakathaṃ yācanto “ayañhi dhammo”ti gāthādvayamāha. Tattha ayañhi dhammoti sattatiṃsa bodhipakkhiyadhamme [V 2.0094] sandhāyāha. Nipuṇoti saṇho duppaṭivijjho. Sukhoti paṭividdho samāno lokuttarasukhamāvahati, tasmā sukhāvahattā “sukho”ti vuccati. Suppavuttoti sudesito. Sussūsamānāti sotukāmamhāti attho. Taṃ no vadāti taṃ dhammaṃ amhākaṃ vada. “Tvaṃ no”tipi pāṭho, tvaṃ amhākaṃ vadāti attho. Sabbepime bhikkhavoti taṅkhaṇaṃ nisinnāni kira pañca bhikkhusatāni honti, tāni dassento yācati. Upāsakā cāpīti attano parivāre aññe ca dasseti. Sesamettha pākaṭameva.

Having thus praised the Blessed One in various ways, now praising him by means of the Dhamma itself and requesting a Dhamma talk, he speaks two verses beginning, “For this is the Dhamma.” Herein, “For this is the Dhamma” refers to the thirty-seven requisites of enlightenment. “Subtle” means refined and difficult to penetrate. “Blissful” means that when penetrated, it brings the bliss of the supramundane; thus, because it brings bliss, it is called “blissful.” “Well-expounded” means well-taught. “Wishing to hear” means “we desire to hear.” “Teach us that” means “speak that Dhamma to us.” There is also the variant reading, “You teach us,” meaning “you speak to us.” “All these monks” refers to the five hundred monks said to have been seated at that moment; pointing to them, he makes the request. “And lay followers also” indicates his own retinue and others. The rest here is clear.

388. Atha bhagavā anagāriyapaṭipadaṃ tāva dassetuṃ bhikkhū āmantetvā “suṇātha me bhikkhavo”tiādimāha. Tattha dhammaṃ dhutaṃ tañca carātha sabbeti kilese dhunātīti dhuto, evarūpaṃ kilesadhunanakaṃ paṭipadādhammaṃ sāvayāmi vo, tañca mayā sāvitaṃ sabbe caratha paṭipajjatha, mā pamāditthāti vuttaṃ hoti. Iriyāpathanti gamanādicatubbidhaṃ. Pabbajitānulomikanti samaṇasāruppaṃ satisampajaññayuttaṃ. Araññe kammaṭṭhānānuyogavasena pavattamevāti apare. Sevetha nanti taṃ iriyāpathaṃ bhajeyya[M 2.0104]. Atthadasoti hitānupassī. Mutīmāti buddhimā. Sesamettha gāthāya pākaṭameva.

388. Then the Blessed One, in order to first show the practice of the homeless life, addressed the monks, saying, “Listen to me, monks,” and so on. Herein, regarding `dhammaṃ dhutaṃ tañca carātha sabbe`: a Dhamma is called `dhuta` because it shakes off (`dhunāti`) defilements. The meaning is this: 'I will proclaim to you a Dhamma of practice of this kind, one that shakes off defilements. And when I have proclaimed it, all of you should practice it, undertake it; do not be negligent.' “Posture” refers to the four kinds: walking, etc. “Suitable for one gone forth” means what is befitting an ascetic, endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension. Others say it is what is pursued by way of devotion to a meditation subject in the forest. “One should resort to it” means one should cultivate that posture. “Seeing the goal” means seeing what is beneficial. “Wise” means intelligent. The rest of the verse here is clear.

389. No ve vikāleti evaṃ pabbajitānulomikaṃ iriyāpathaṃ sevamāno ca divāmajjhanhikavītikkamaṃ upādāya vikāle na careyya bhikkhu, yuttakāle eva pana gāmaṃ piṇḍāya careyya. Kiṃ kāraṇaṃ? Akālacāriñhi sajanti saṅgā, akālacāriṃ puggalaṃ rāgasaṅgādayo aneke saṅgā sajanti parissajanti upaguhanti allīyanti. Tasmā vikāle na [P 1.0374] caranti buddhā, tasmā ye catusaccabuddhā ariyapuggalā, na te vikāle piṇḍāya carantīti. Tena kira samayena vikālabhojanasikkhāpadaṃ appaññattaṃ hoti, tasmā dhammadesanāvasenevettha puthujjanānaṃ ādīnavaṃ dassento imaṃ gāthamāha. Ariyā pana saha maggapaṭilābhā eva tato paṭiviratā honti, esā dhammatā.

389. “Not at the wrong time”: A bhikkhu who is cultivating a posture suitable for one gone forth should not wander at the wrong time, that is, after midday has passed; rather, he should wander for alms in the village only at the proper time. For what reason? Because attachments cling to one who wanders at the wrong time. Numerous attachments such as the attachment of lust cling to, embrace, envelop, and adhere to a person who wanders at the wrong time.
