Therefore the Buddhas do not wander at the wrong time; that is, those noble persons who have awakened to the Four Truths do not wander for alms at the wrong time. It is said that at that time the training rule concerning eating at the wrong time had not yet been laid down. Therefore he spoke this verse in the course of his Dhamma discourse to show the danger for worldlings. But the noble ones refrain from this as soon as they attain the path; this is the nature of the matter.

390. Evaṃ vikālacariyaṃ paṭisedhetvā “kāle carantenapi evaṃ caritabba”nti dassento āha “rūpā ca saddā cā”ti. Tassattho – ye te rūpādayo nānappakārakaṃ madaṃ janentā satte sammadayanti, tesu piṇḍapātapārisuddhisuttādīsu (ma. ni. 3.438 ādayo) vuttanayena chandaṃ vinodetvā yuttakāleneva pātarāsaṃ paviseyyāti. Ettha ca pāto asitabboti pātarāso, piṇḍapātassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Yo yattha labbhati, so padesopi taṃ yogena “pātarāso”ti idha vutto. Yato piṇḍapātaṃ labhati, taṃ okāsaṃ gaccheyyāti evamettha attho veditabbo.

390. Having thus forbidden wandering at the wrong time, to show how one should conduct oneself even when wandering at the proper time, he said, “Forms and sounds, etc.” The meaning is this: Regarding those forms and other sense objects that generate various kinds of intoxication and delude beings, one should dispel desire for them in the manner taught in the Piṇḍapātapārisuddhisutta and other suttas, and go for the morning meal only at the appropriate time. Here, `pātarāsa` (morning meal) means what is to be eaten in the morning; this is a name for almsfood. The place where it is obtained is also called `pātarāsa` by association with it. The meaning to be understood here is that one should go to the place where one obtains almsfood.

391. Evaṃ [V 2.0095] paviṭṭho –

391. Having entered thus:

“Piṇḍañca bhikkhu samayena laddhā,

Eko paṭikkamma raho nisīde;

Ajjhattacintī na mano bahiddhā,

Nicchāraye saṅgahitattabhāvo”.

“A bhikkhu, having obtained alms at the proper time, should withdraw alone and sit in seclusion. Reflecting inwardly, with a restrained self, he should not send his mind outwards.”

Tattha piṇḍanti missakabhikkhaṃ, sā hi tato tato samodhānetvā sampiṇḍitaṭṭhena “piṇḍo”ti vuccati. Samayenāti antomajjhanhikakāle. Eko paṭikkammāti kāyavivekaṃ sampādento adutiyo nivattitvā. Ajjhattacintīti tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā khandhasantānaṃ cintento. Na mano bahiddhā [M 2.0105] nicchārayeti bahiddhā rūpādīsu rāgavasena cittaṃ na nīhare. Saṅgahitattabhāvoti suṭṭhu gahitacitto.

Herein, piṇḍa (almsfood) means mixed alms; it is called piṇḍa because it is gathered from here and there and lumped together. At the proper time means during the time before noon. Withdrawing alone means, having achieved bodily seclusion, turning back without a companion. Reflecting inwardly means contemplating the continuity of the aggregates by imposing the three characteristics on it. He should not send his mind outward means he should not lead his mind out through lust toward external objects such as forms. With a restrained self means with a well-grasped mind.

392. Evaṃ viharanto ca –

392. And dwelling thus:

“Sacepi so sallape sāvakena,

Aññena vā kenaci bhikkhunā vā;

Dhammaṃ paṇītaṃ tamudāhareyya,

Na pesuṇaṃ nopi parūpavādaṃ”.

“If he should converse with a disciple or with any other bhikkhu, he should speak on the sublime Dhamma, not on slander or the blame of others.”

Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? So yogāvacaro kiñcideva sotukāmatāya upagatena sāvakena vā kenaci aññatitthiyagahaṭṭhādinā vā idheva pabbajitena bhikkhunā vā saddhiṃ sacepi sallape, atha yvāyaṃ maggaphalādipaṭisaṃyutto [P 1.0375] dasakathāvatthubhedo vā atappakaṭṭhena paṇīto dhammo. Taṃ dhammaṃ paṇītaṃ udāhareyya, aññaṃ pana pisuṇavacanaṃ vā parūpavādaṃ vā appamattakampi na udāhareyyāti.

What is meant? If that meditator converses with a disciple who has approached out of a desire to listen, or with any other person such as an adherent of another teaching or a householder, or with a bhikkhu who has gone forth in this very dispensation, he should speak that sublime Dhamma connected with the path, fruit, and so on, or the ten topics of discussion. But he should not utter even the slightest slander or criticism of others.

393. Idāni tasmiṃ parūpavāde dosaṃ dassento āha “vādañhi eke”ti. Tassattho – idhekacce moghapurisā parūpavādasañhitaṃ nānappakāraṃ viggāhikakathābhedaṃ vādaṃ paṭiseniyanti virujjhanti, yujjhitukāmā hutvā senāya paṭimukhaṃ gacchantā viya honti, te mayaṃ lāmakapaññe na pasaṃsāma. Kiṃ kāraṇaṃ? Tato tato ne pasajanti saṅgā, yasmā te tādisake puggale [V 2.0096] tato tato vacanapathato samuṭṭhāya vivādasaṅgā sajanti allīyanti. Kiṃ kāraṇā sajantīti? Cittañhi te tattha gamenti dūre, yasmā te paṭiseniyantā cittaṃ tattha gamenti, yattha gataṃ samathavipassanānaṃ dūre hotīti.

393. Now, pointing out the fault in such criticism of others, he says: ‘For some engage in disputes.’ The meaning is this: Here, certain foolish persons engage in or oppose various kinds of contentious and divisive talk connected with criticizing others; eager to quarrel, they are like those advancing to face an enemy army. We do not praise such persons of meager wisdom. For what reason? Because from this and that, attachments are generated for them. For in such people, attachments to disputes arise from this and that topic of speech and cling to them. For what reason do they cling? Because they send their minds far away to that. For in opposing, they send their minds to that place, and when it has gone there, it is far from serenity and insight.

394-5. Evaṃ parittapaññānaṃ pavattiṃ dassetvā idāni mahāpaññānaṃ pavattiṃ dassento āha “piṇḍaṃ vihāraṃ…pe… sāvako”ti. Tattha vihārena patissayo, sayanāsanena mañcapīṭhanti tīhipi padehi senāsanameva vuttaṃ. Āpanti udakaṃ. Saṅghāṭirajūpavāhananti paṃsumalādino saṅghāṭirajassa dhovanaṃ. Sutvāna dhammaṃ sugatena desitanti sabbāsavasaṃvarādīsu “paṭisaṅkhā yoniso cīvaraṃ paṭisevati sītassa paṭighātāyā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.23; a. ni. 6.58) nayena bhagavatā desitaṃ dhammaṃ sutvā. Saṅkhāya seve [M 2.0106] varapaññasāvakoti etaṃ idha piṇḍanti vuttaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ, vihārādīhi vuttaṃ senāsanaṃ, āpamukhena dassitaṃ gilānapaccayaṃ, saṅghāṭiyā cīvaranti catubbidhampi paccayaṃ saṅkhāya “yāvadeva imassa kāyassa ṭhitiyā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.23; a. ni. 6.58) nayena paccavekkhitvā seve varapaññasāvako, sevituṃ sakkuṇeyya varapaññassa tathāgatassa sāvako sekkho vā puthujjano vā, nippariyāyena ca arahā. So hi caturāpasseno “saṅkhāyekaṃ paṭisevati, saṅkhāyekaṃ [P 1.0376] adhivāseti, saṅkhāyekaṃ parivajjeti, saṅkhāyekaṃ vinodetī”ti (dī. ni. 3.308; ma. ni. 2.168; a. ni. 10.20) vutto. Yassā ca saṅkhāya seve varapaññasāvako, tasmā hi piṇḍe…pe… yathā pokkhare vāribindu, tathā hotīti veditabbo.

Having thus shown the conduct of those with meager wisdom, now, to show the conduct of those with great wisdom, he says: 'Almsfood, dwelling... the disciple.' Herein, by 'dwelling' (vihāra) a residence is meant; by 'bed' (sayana) and 'seat' (āsana), a couch and a chair are meant—thus with these three terms, lodging (senāsana) is indicated. 'Water' (āpa) means water. Saṅghāṭirajūpavāhanaṃ means the washing of dust, dirt, and the like from the outer robe. 'Having heard the Dhamma taught by the Sugata' means having listened to the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One concerning the restraint of all taints and so on, by the method beginning: 'Reflecting wisely, he uses the robe only for protection from cold...' 'A disciple of excellent wisdom uses it after reflection' means this: here, 'alms' refers to almsfood; 'dwelling,' etc., refers to lodging; by 'water,' the requisite of medicine for the sick is indicated; and by 'outer robe' (saṅghāṭi), the robe requisite is indicated. A disciple of excellent wisdom should use the fourfold requisite after reflecting by the method beginning: 'Only for the support of this body...' A disciple of the Tathāgata of excellent wisdom—whether a trainee, an ordinary person, or, unequivocally, an arahant—is able to use them thus. For he is said to be one who relies on the four requisites with reflection: 'Reflecting, he uses one; reflecting, he endures one; reflecting, he avoids one; reflecting, he dispels one.' And because a disciple of excellent wisdom uses them after reflection, therefore, regarding almsfood... he is like a drop of water on a lotus leaf—so it should be understood.

396. Evaṃ khīṇāsavapaṭipattiṃ dassento arahattanikūṭena anagāriyapaṭipadaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā idāni agāriyapaṭipadaṃ dassetuṃ “gahaṭṭhavattaṃ pana vo”tiādimāha. Tattha paṭhamagāthāya tāva sāvakoti agāriyasāvako. Sesaṃ uttānatthameva. Ayaṃ pana yojanā – yo mayā ito pubbe kevalo abyāmisso sakalo paripuṇṇo bhikkhudhammo kathito. Esa khettavatthuādipariggahehi sapariggahena na labbhā phassetuṃ na sakkā adhigantunti.

396. Thus, having shown the practice of one whose taints are destroyed, culminating in arahantship, and having concluded the path of homelessness, now, to show the path of the householder, he begins with: 'But as for the duties of a householder…' Herein, in the first verse, the term 'disciple' refers to a householder disciple. The rest is clear in meaning. This is the explanation: That monastic Dhamma taught by me before—pure, unmixed, whole, and complete—cannot be contacted or attained by one who has possessions, such as fields and property.

397. Evaṃ tassa bhikkhudhammaṃ paṭisedhetvā gahaṭṭhadhammameva dassento āha “pāṇaṃ na hane”ti. Tattha purimaḍḍhena tikoṭiparisuddhā pāṇātipātāveramaṇi vuttā, pacchimaḍḍhena sattesu hitapaṭipatti. Tatiyapādo cettha khaggavisāṇasutte (su. ni. 35 ādayo) catutthapāde thāvaratasabhedo mettasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ (su. ni. 143 ādayo) sabbappakārato vaṇṇito. Sesaṃ uttānatthameva. Uppaṭipāṭiyā pana yojanā kātabbā – tasathāvaresu sabbesu bhūtesu nidhāya daṇḍaṃ [V 2.0097] na hane na ghātayeyya nānujaññāti. “Nidhāya daṇḍa”nti ito vā paraṃ “vatteyyā”ti pāṭhaseso āharitabbo. Itarathā hi na pubbenāparaṃ sandhiyati.

397. Having thus rejected the monastic practice for him and showing only the householder's practice, he says: 'One should not kill a living being.' Herein, by the first half-verse, abstinence from taking life, purified in three aspects, is stated; by the latter half-verse, conduct beneficial to beings. The third line here is explained in the commentary on the Khaggavisāṇa Sutta (Snp 35ff), and the fourth line, concerning the distinction between stationary and moving beings, is explained in all its aspects in the commentary on the Mettā Sutta (Snp 143ff). The rest is clear in meaning. The explanation, however, should be construed in reverse order: 'Having laid down the rod toward all beings, whether moving or stationary, one should neither kill, nor cause to be killed, nor approve of killing.' After 'Having laid down the rod,' the elliptical phrase 'one should conduct oneself' must be supplied. Otherwise, the preceding part does not connect with what follows.

398. Evaṃ paṭhamasikkhāpadaṃ dassetvā idāni dutiyasikkhāpadaṃ dassento āha “tato adinna”nti. Tattha kiñcīti appaṃ vā bahuṃ vā. Kvacīti [M 2.0107] gāme vā araññe vā. Sāvakoti agāriyasāvako. Bujjhamānoti “parasantakamida”nti jānamāno. Sabbaṃ adinnaṃ parivajjayeyyāti evañhi paṭipajjamāno sabbaṃ adinnaṃ parivajjeyya, no aññathāti dīpeti. Sesamettha vuttanayañca pākaṭañcāti.

398. Having thus shown the first training rule, now showing the second training rule, he says: 'Then, what is not given…' Herein, 'anything' means little or much. 'Anywhere' means in the village or the forest. 'Disciple' refers to a householder disciple. 'Knowing' means knowing, 'This belongs to another.' He explains that the line 'should avoid all that is not given' means that by practicing in this way one would avoid all that is not given, and not otherwise. The rest here follows the method already stated and is clear.

399. Evaṃ dutiyasikkhāpadampi tikoṭiparisuddhaṃ dassetvā ukkaṭṭhaparicchedato pabhuti tatiyaṃ dassento āha “abrahmacariya”nti. Tattha asambhuṇantoti asakkonto.

399. Having thus shown the second training rule also as purified in three aspects, now, beginning from the highest division, while showing the third, he says: 'Unchastity…' Therein, 'not being able' (asambhuṇanto) means being incapable (asakkonto).

400. Idāni catutthasikkhāpadaṃ dassento [P 1.0377] āha “sabhaggato vā”ti. Tattha sabhaggatoti santhāgārādigato. Parisaggatoti pūgamajjagato. Sesamettha vuttanayañca pākaṭañcāti.

400. Now, while showing the fourth training rule, he says: 'Or in an assembly…' Therein, 'in an assembly' means having gone to a meeting hall or the like. 'In a gathering' means having gone into the midst of a company. The rest here follows the method already stated and is clear.

401. Evaṃ catutthasikkhāpadampi tikoṭiparisuddhaṃ dassetvā pañcamaṃ dassento āha “majjañca pāna”nti. Tattha majjañca pānanti gāthābandhasukhatthaṃ evaṃ vuttaṃ. Ayaṃ panattho “majjapānañca na samācareyyā”ti. Dhammaṃ imanti imaṃ majjapānaveramaṇīdhammaṃ. Ummādanantanti ummādanapariyosānaṃ. Yo hi sabbalahuko majjapānassa vipāko, so manussabhūtassa ummattakasaṃvattaniko hoti. Iti naṃ viditvāti iti naṃ majjapānaṃ ñatvā. Sesamettha vuttanayañca pākaṭañcāti.

401. Having thus shown the fourth training rule also as purified in three aspects, while showing the fifth, he says: 'And the drinking of intoxicants…' Therein, 'And the drinking of intoxicants' is stated thus for metrical ease in the verse. The meaning, however, is: 'And one should not engage in the drinking of intoxicants.' 'This Dhamma' means this Dhamma of abstaining from the drinking of intoxicants. 'Ending in madness' means having madness as its culmination. For the very lightest result of drinking intoxicants is that it leads to madness for one who is a human being. 'Knowing it thus' means thus knowing this drinking of intoxicants. The rest here follows the method already stated and is clear.

402. Evaṃ pañcamasikkhāpadampi tikoṭiparisuddhaṃ dassetvā idāni purimasikkhāpadānampi majjapānameva saṃkilesakarañca bhedakarañca dassetvā daḷhataraṃ tato veramaṇiyaṃ niyojento āha “madā hi pāpāni karontī”ti. Tattha madāti madahetu. Hikāro padapūraṇamatte nipāto. Pāpāni karontīti pāṇātipātādīni sabbākusalāni karonti. Ummādanaṃ mohananti paraloke ummādanaṃ ihaloke mohanaṃ. Sesaṃ uttānatthameva.

402. Having thus shown the fifth training rule also as purified in three aspects, now, showing that the drinking of intoxicants itself is a cause of defilement and a cause of division for the previous training rules as well, and enjoining a stronger abstinence from it, he says: 'For from intoxication they do evil deeds…' Therein, 'from intoxication' (madā) means because of intoxication. The particle hi is merely a metrical expletive. 'Do evil deeds' means they do all unwholesome deeds, such as taking life. 'Maddening and deluding' means maddening in the next world and deluding in this world. The rest has a plain meaning.

403-4. Ettāvatā agāriyasāvakassa niccasīlaṃ dassetvā idāni uposathaṅgāni dassento [V 2.0098] “pāṇaṃ na hane”ti gāthādvayamāha. Tattha abrahmacariyāti aseṭṭhacariyabhūtā. Methunāti methunadhammasamāpattito. Rattiṃ na bhuñjeyya vikālabhojananti rattimpi na bhuñjeyya, divāpi kālātikkantabhojanaṃ [M 2.0108] na bhuñjeyya. Na ca gandhanti ettha gandhaggahaṇena vilepanacuṇṇādīnipi gahitānevāti veditabbāni. Mañceti kappiyamañce. Santhateti taṭṭikādīhi kappiyattharaṇehi atthate. Chamāyaṃ pana gonakādisanthatāyapi vaṭṭati. Aṭṭhaṅgikanti pañcaṅgikaṃ viya tūriyaṃ, na aṅgavinimuttaṃ. Dukkhantagunāti vaṭṭadukkhassa antagatena. Sesamettha pākaṭameva. Pacchimaḍḍhuṃ pana saṅgītikārakehi vuttantipi āhu.

Having thus far shown the constant virtue of a householder disciple, now, to show the Uposatha factors, he states the two verses beginning: 'One should not kill a living being…' Therein, 'unchastity' (abrahmacariyā) means being ignoble conduct. 'From sexual intercourse' (methunā) means from engaging in the act of sexual intercourse. 'One should not eat at night, which is eating at the wrong time' means one should not eat at night, nor should one eat food that is past the proper time during the day. 'Nor perfumes': here, by the term 'perfumes,' it should be understood that ointments, powders, and so on are also included. 'On a bed' means on an allowable bed. 'On a spread' means on an allowable covering, such as a mat, that is spread out. On the ground, however, even a spread such as a long-haired goat's-wool coverlet is allowable. 'Eight-factored' means like a five-limbed musical instrument, not lacking any part. 'One who has gone to the end of suffering' means by one who has gone to the end of the suffering of the round. The rest here is clear. Some say, however, that the last half-verse was spoken by the compilers of the canon.

405. Evaṃ uposathaṅgāni dassetvā idāni uposathakālaṃ dassento āha “tato ca pakkhassā”ti. Tattha tatoti [P 1.0378] padapūraṇamatte nipāto. Pakkhassupavassuposathanti evaṃ parapadena yojetabbaṃ “pakkhassa cātuddasiṃ pañcadasiṃ aṭṭhaminti ete tayo divase upavassa uposathaṃ, etaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikauposathaṃ upagamma vasitvā”ti. Pāṭihāriyapakkhañcāti ettha pana vassūpanāyikāya purimabhāge āsāḷhamāso, antovassaṃ tayo māsā, kattikamāsoti ime pañca māsā “pāṭihāriyapakkho”ti vuccanti. Āsāḷhakattikaphagguṇamāsā tayo evāti apare. Pakkhuposathadivasānaṃ purimapacchimadivasavasena pakkhe pakkhe terasīpāṭipadasattamīnavamīsaṅkhātā cattāro cattāro divasāti apare. Yaṃ ruccati, taṃ gahetabbaṃ. Sabbaṃ vā pana puññakāmīnaṃ bhāsitabbaṃ. Evametaṃ pāṭihāriyapakkhañca pasannamānaso susamattarūpaṃ suparipuṇṇarūpaṃ ekampi divasaṃ apariccajanto aṭṭhaṅgupetaṃ uposathaṃ upavassāti sambandhitabbaṃ.

405. Having thus shown the factors of the Uposatha, now, indicating the time for the Uposatha, he says: ‘Then, of the fortnight.’ Therein, ‘then’ is a particle merely for filling out the phrase. The phrase ‘observe the Uposatha of the fortnight’ should be connected with the following words thus: ‘On the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth days of the fortnight, one should observe the Uposatha; having undertaken this eight-factored Uposatha, one should dwell thus.’ As to ‘and the Pāṭihāriya-pakkha’: here, the month of Āsāḷha before the rains retreat, the three months within the rains, and the month of Kattika—these five months are called the ‘Pāṭihāriya-pakkha.’ Others say it is just the three months: Āsāḷha, Kattika, and Phagguṇa. Still others say that with respect to the Uposatha days of the fortnight, based on the preceding and succeeding days, in each fortnight there are four days, namely, the thirteenth, the first, the seventh, and the ninth. Whichever is preferred should be adopted. Or else, all should be mentioned for those who desire merit. Thus, this should be connected as follows: ‘And during the Pāṭihāriya-pakkha, with a confident mind, having undertaken it well and in a fully complete way, not omitting even a single day, one should observe the Uposatha endowed with eight factors.’

406. Evaṃ uposathakālaṃ dassetvā idāni tesu kālesu etaṃ uposathaṃ upavassa yaṃ kātabbaṃ, taṃ dassento āha “tato ca pāto”ti. Etthāpi tatoti padapūraṇamatte nipāto, anantaratthe vā, athāti vuttaṃ hoti. Pātoti aparajjudivasapubbabhāge. Upavutthuposathoti upavasitauposatho. Annenāti yāgubhattādinā. Pānenāti aṭṭhavidhapānena. Anumodamānoti anupamodamāno, nirantaraṃ modamānoti attho. Yathārahanti attano anurūpena, yathāsatti yathābalanti vuttaṃ hoti. Saṃvibhajethāti bhājeyya patimāneyya. Sesaṃ pākaṭameva.

406. Having thus shown the time for the Uposatha, now, indicating what should be done at those times after observing this Uposatha, he says: ‘And then in the morning.’ Here too, ‘then’ is a particle merely for filling out the phrase, or it is in the sense of ‘immediately after’; that is to say, it means ‘then.’ ‘In the morning’ means in the early part of the next day. ‘Having observed the Uposatha’ means one who has dwelt observing the Uposatha. ‘With food’ means with rice gruel, boiled rice, and so on. ‘With drink’ means with the eight kinds of drinks. ‘Rejoicing’ means rejoicing again and again; the meaning is continuously delighting. ‘As is fit’ means in a way suitable to oneself; that is to say, according to one’s ability, according to one’s strength. ‘One should share’ means one should divide, one should apportion. The rest is self-evident.

407. Evaṃ [M 2.0109] upavutthuposathassa kiccaṃ vatvā idāni yāvajīvikaṃ garuvattaṃ ājīvapārisuddhiñca kathetvā tāya paṭipadāya adhigantabbaṭṭhānaṃ dassento āha “dhammena mātāpitaro”ti. Tattha dhammenāti dhammaladdhena bhogena[P 1.0379]. Bhareyyāti poseyya. Dhammikaṃ so vaṇijjanti sattavaṇijjā, satthavaṇijjā, visavaṇijjā, maṃsavaṇijjā, surāvaṇijjāti imā pañca [V 2.0099] adhammavaṇijjā vajjetvā avasesā dhammikavaṇijjā. Vaṇijjāmukhena cettha kasigorakkhādi aparopi dhammiko vohāro saṅgahito. Sesamuttānatthameva. Ayaṃ pana yojanā – so niccasīlauposathasīladānadhammasamannāgato ariyasāvako payojaye dhammikaṃ vaṇijjaṃ, tato laddhena ca dhammato anapetattā dhammena bhogena mātāpitaro bhareyya. Atha so gihī evaṃ appamatto ādito pabhuti vuttaṃ imaṃ vattaṃ vattayanto kāyassa bhedā ye te attano ābhāya andhakāraṃ vidhametvā ālokakaraṇena sayampabhāti laddhanāmā cha kāmāvacaradevā, te sayampabhe nāma deve upeti bhajati allīyati, tesaṃ nibbattaṭṭhāne nibbattatīti.

407. Having thus stated the duty of one who has observed the Uposatha, now, after speaking of lifelong reverence and purity of livelihood, indicating the destination to be attained by that practice, he says: ‘Righteously one’s parents.’ Herein, ‘righteously’ means with wealth acquired righteously. ‘Should support’ means should nourish. As to ‘righteous commerce’: having avoided the five kinds of unrighteous commerce—that is, trade in living beings, trade in weapons, trade in poison, trade in meat, and trade in intoxicants—the remainder is righteous commerce. And here, by way of commerce, other righteous occupations such as agriculture and cattle-rearing are included. The rest has an obvious meaning. This, however, is the construction: that noble disciple, endowed with constant virtue, the Uposatha virtue, and the practice of giving, should engage in righteous commerce. Then, with the wealth obtained from that, which is righteous because it is not disconnected from the Dhamma, he should support his parents. Then that householder, being thus diligent, pursuing this practice that has been spoken of from the outset, on the breakup of the body, approaches, resorts to, and cleaves to the gods named the Self-Luminous—the six classes of sense-sphere devas who have obtained the name ‘Self-Luminous’ because they dispel darkness with their own radiance by making light—that is, he is reborn in the place where they have been reborn.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddakapāṭha

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya dhammikasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Here ends the explanation of the Dhammika Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary.

Niṭṭhito ca dutiyo vaggo atthavaṇṇanānayato, nāmena

And the second chapter is finished, according to the method of explaining the meaning, named:

Cūḷavaggoti.

The Minor Chapter.

3. Mahāvaggo

3. The Great Chapter

1. Pabbajjāsuttavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Discourse on the Going Forth

408. Pabbajjaṃ [V 2.0100][M 2.0110][P 2.0381] kittayissāmīti pabbajjāsuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Bhagavati kira sāvatthiyaṃ viharante āyasmato ānandassa parivitakko udapādi – “sāriputtādīnaṃ mahāsāvakānaṃ pabbajjā kittitā, taṃ bhikkhū ca upāsakā ca jānanti. Bhagavato pana akittitā, yaṃnūnāhaṃ kitteyya”nti. So jetavanavihāre āsane nisīditvā cittabījaniṃ gahetvā bhikkhūnaṃ bhagavato pabbajjaṃ kittento imaṃ suttamabhāsi.

408. The Pabbajjā Sutta is so called because it begins, ‘I will extol the going forth.’ What is its origin? It is said that while the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī, a reflection arose in the Venerable Ānanda: ‘The going forth of the great disciples such as Sāriputta has been extolled, and the bhikkhus and lay followers know it. But the Blessed One’s has not been extolled. Let me now extol it!’ Then, having sat down on his seat in the Jetavana monastery and taken a painted fan, while extolling the Blessed One’s going forth to the bhikkhus, he spoke this sutta.

Tattha yasmā pabbajjaṃ kittentena yathā pabbaji, taṃ kittetabbaṃ. Yathā ca pabbaji, taṃ kittentena yathā vīmaṃsamāno pabbajjaṃ rocesi, taṃ kittetabbaṃ. Tasmā “pabbajjaṃ kittayissāmī”ti vatvā “yathā pabbajī”tiādimāha. Cakkhumāti pañcahi cakkhūhi cakkhumā cakkhusampannoti attho. Sesamādigāthāya uttānameva.

Herein, since one who extols the going forth must extol how he went forth, and since one who extols how he went forth must extol how he, upon reflection, came to approve of the going forth, therefore, having said, ‘I will extol the going forth,’ he then says, ‘As he went forth,’ and so on. ‘One with vision’ means one who has vision, one endowed with the five kinds of eyes; this is the meaning. The rest is obvious from the opening verse.

409. Idāni “yathā vīmaṃsamāno”ti tamatthaṃ pakāsento āha “sambādhoya”nti. Tattha sambādhoti puttadārādisampīḷanena kilesasampīḷanena ca kusalakiriyāya okāsarahito. Rajassāyatananti kambojādayo viya assādīnaṃ, rāgādirajassa uppattideso. Abbhokāsoti vuttasambādhapaṭipakkhabhāvena ākāso viya vivaṭā. Iti disvāna pabbajīti iti gharāvāsapabbajjāsu byādhijarāmaraṇehi suṭṭhutaraṃ codiyamānahadayo ādīnavamānisaṃsañca vīmaṃsitvā, mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhamitvā[P 2.0382], anomānadītīre khaggena kese chinditvā, tāvadeva ca dvaṅgulamattasaṇṭhitasamaṇasāruppakesamassu hutvā ghaṭikārena brahmunā upanīte aṭṭha parikkhāre gahetvā “evaṃ nivāsetabbaṃ pārupitabba”nti kenaci ananusiṭṭho anekajātisahassapavattitena attano pabbajjāciṇṇeneva sikkhāpiyamāno pabbaji. Ekaṃ kāsāvaṃ nivāsetvā ekaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ karitvā ekaṃ cīvaraṃ khandhe karitvā mattikāpattaṃ aṃse ālaggetvā pabbajitavesaṃ adhiṭṭhāsīti vuttaṃ hoti. Sesamettha uttānameva.

409. Now, explaining the meaning of ‘how he reflected,’ he says, ‘This is a confined space.’ Herein, ‘a confined space’ means being without opportunity for wholesome deeds due to the oppression of wife, children, and so on, and the oppression of the defilements. ‘A basis for dust’ means a place where the dust of passion and so on arises. ‘The open air’ is open like the sky, being the opposite of what was described as a confined space. ‘Having seen this, he went forth’ means this: his heart being deeply stirred by sickness, aging, and death in both the household life and the going forth, and having reflected upon the danger and the advantage, he undertook the great renunciation. On the bank of the river Anomā, he cut off his hair with a sword, and at that very moment his hair and beard became suitable for an ascetic, remaining at a length of two finger-breadths. Then, having received the eight requisites brought by Ghaṭikāra Brahmā, he went forth, being instructed by his own practice of renunciation cultivated over many thousands of lives, without being instructed by anyone on how one should wear the lower robe and the upper robe. That is to say, having put on one ochre robe, made another his upper robe, placed a patchwork cloak on his shoulder, and slung an earthenware bowl from his shoulder, he adopted the guise of one gone forth. The rest here is obvious.

410. Evaṃ [V 2.0101] bhagavato pabbajjaṃ kittetvā tato paraṃ pabbajitapaṭipattiṃ anomānadītīraṃ hitvā padhānāya gamanañca pakāsetuṃ “pabbajitvāna kāyenā”tiādiṃ [M 2.0111] sabbamabhāsi. Tattha kāyena pāpakammaṃ vivajjayīti tividhaṃ kāyaduccaritaṃ vajjesi. Vacīduccaritanti catubbidhaṃ vacīduccaritaṃ. Ājīvaṃ parisodhayīti micchājīvaṃ hitvā sammājīvameva pavattayi.

410. Having thus extolled the Blessed One's going forth, in order to show his practice after going forth and his journey for striving after leaving the bank of the river Anomā, he spoke the entire passage beginning with: ‘Having gone forth, with the body.’ Here, ‘he avoided evil action with the body’ means he avoided the threefold bodily misconduct. ‘Verbal misconduct’ means the fourfold verbal misconduct. ‘He purified his livelihood’ means that, having abandoned wrong livelihood, he pursued only right livelihood.

411. Evaṃ ājīvaṭṭhamakasīlaṃ sodhetvā anomānadītīrato tiṃsayojanappamāṇaṃ sattāhena agamā rājagahaṃ buddho. Tattha kiñcāpi yadā rājagahaṃ agamāsi, tadā buddho na hoti, tathāpi buddhassa pubbacariyāti katvā evaṃ vattuṃ labbhati – “idha rājā jāto, idha rajjaṃ aggahesī”tiādi lokiyavohāravacanaṃ viya. Magadhānanti magadhānaṃ janapadassa nagaranti vuttaṃ hoti. Giribbajanti idampi tassa nāmaṃ. Tañhi paṇḍavagijjhakūṭavebhāraisigilivepullanāmakānaṃ pañcannaṃ girīnaṃ majjhe vajo viya ṭhitaṃ, tasmā “giribbaja”nti vuccati. Piṇḍāya abhihāresīti bhikkhatthāya tasmiṃ nagare cari. So kira nagaradvāre ṭhatvā cintesi – “sacāhaṃ rañño bimbisārassa attano āgamanaṃ nivedeyyaṃ, ‘suddhodanassa putto siddhattho nāma kumāro āgato’ti bahumpi me paccayaṃ abhihareyya. Na kho pana me taṃ patirūpaṃ pabbajitassa ārocetvā paccayagahaṇaṃ, handāhaṃ piṇḍāya carāmī”ti devadattiyaṃ paṃsukūlacīvaraṃ pārupitvā mattikāpattaṃ gahetvā pācīnadvārena [P 2.0383] nagaraṃ pavisitvā anugharaṃ piṇḍāya acari. Tenāha āyasmā ānando – “piṇḍāya abhihāresī”ti. Ākiṇṇavaralakkhaṇoti sarīre ākiritvā viya ṭhapitavaralakkhaṇo vipulavaralakkhaṇo vā. Vipulampi hi “ākiṇṇa”nti vuccati. Yathāha – “ākiṇṇaluddo puriso, dhāticelaṃva makkhito”ti (jā. 1.6.118; 1.9.106). Vipulaluddoti attho.

411. Having thus purified the virtue with livelihood as the eighth factor, the Buddha went to Rājagaha, a journey of thirty yojanas from the bank of the river Anomā, in seven days. Although he was not yet a Buddha when he went to Rājagaha, it is permissible to speak thus on the grounds that it was the Buddha's former practice, just like the worldly expression: ‘Here the king was born, here he took the throne,’ and so on. ‘Of the Magadhans’ means the city of the country of the Magadhans. ‘Giribbaja’ is also its name. For it stands like a cattle-pen in the midst of the five mountains named Paṇḍava, Gijjhakūṭa, Vebhāra, Isigili, and Vepulla; therefore it is called ‘Giribbaja.’ ‘He went about for almsfood’ means he wandered for alms in that city. It is said that, standing at the city gate, he thought: ‘If I were to inform King Bimbisāra of my arrival, he would bring me many requisites, thinking, “Prince Siddhattha, the son of Suddhodana, has come.” But it is not proper for me, one who has gone forth, to receive requisites after having announced myself. Come now, I will wander for alms.’ Having donned the robe of rags given by a deva and taken an earthenware bowl, he entered the city by the eastern gate and went for alms from house to house in succession. Therefore the Venerable Ānanda said: ‘He went about for almsfood.’ ‘Replete with the excellent marks’ means having the excellent marks as if strewn over his body, or having abundant excellent marks. For ‘replete’ (ākiṇṇa) can also mean ‘abundant.’ As it is said: ‘A man replete with greed, smeared like a dyer’s cloth.’ The meaning is ‘abundant greed.’

412. Tamaddasāti tato kira purimāni satta divasāni nagare nakkhattaṃ ghositaṃ ahosi. Taṃ divasaṃ pana “nakkhattaṃ vītivattaṃ, kammantā payojetabbā”ti bheri cari. Atha mahājano rājaṅgaṇe sannipati. Rājāpi “kammantaṃ saṃvidahissāmī”ti sīhapañjaraṃ vivaritvā balakāyaṃ passanto taṃ piṇḍāya abhihārentaṃ mahāsattaṃ addasa. Tenāha āyasmā ānando – “tamaddasā bimbisāro, pāsādasmiṃ patiṭṭhito”ti. Imamatthaṃ abhāsathāti imaṃ atthaṃ amaccānaṃ abhāsi.

412. He saw him: it is said that for the previous seven days a festival had been proclaimed in the city. On that day, however, the drum was beaten, announcing: 'The festival has passed; work should be undertaken.' Then a great crowd gathered in the royal courtyard. The king, too, thinking, 'I will arrange the work,' opened the lion-window and, while observing his troops, saw the Great Being going about for alms. Therefore the Venerable Ānanda said: 'Bimbisāra saw him, standing in the palace.' He spoke this matter means he spoke this matter to his ministers.

413. Idāni [M 2.0112] taṃ tesaṃ amaccānaṃ bhāsitamatthaṃ dassento āha – “imaṃ bhonto”ti. Tattha imanti so rājā bodhisattaṃ dasseti, bhontoti amacce ālapati. Nisāmethāti passatha. Abhirūpoti dassanīyaṅgapaccaṅgo. Brahmāti ārohapariṇāhasampanno. Sucīti parisuddhachavivaṇṇo. Caraṇenāti gamanena.

413. Now, to show the meaning of what was said to those ministers, the text says: 'Behold this one, sirs.' Here, ‘this one’ (imaṃ): the king points out the Bodhisatta. ‘Sirs’ (bhonto): he addresses the ministers. ‘Behold’ (nisāmetha) means 'look.' ‘Handsome’ (abhirūpo) means possessing beautiful limbs and features. ‘Stately’ (brahmā) means endowed with height and girth. ‘Pure’ (sucī) means having a pure skin-complexion. ‘By his deportment’ (caraṇena) means by his manner of walking.

414-5. Nīcakulāmivāti [V 2.0102] nīcakulā iva pabbajito na hotīti attho. Makāro padasandhikaro. Kuhiṃ bhikkhu gamissatīti ayaṃ bhikkhu kuhiṃ gamissati, ajja kattha vasissatīti jānituṃ rājadūtā sīghaṃ gacchantu. Dassanakāmā hi mayaṃ assāti iminā adhippāyena āha. Guttadvāro okkhittacakkhutāya, susaṃvuto satiyā. Guttadvāro vā satiyā, susaṃvuto pāsādikena saṅghāṭicīvaradhāraṇena.

414–415. Like one from a low family: the meaning is that he is not one who has gone forth like someone from a low family. The 'm' is for euphonic conjunction. Where will the bhikkhu go?: to find out where this bhikkhu will go and where he will dwell today, the king's messengers should go quickly. He spoke with this intention: 'For we desire to see him.' With guarded doors: due to his downcast eyes. Well-restrained: by mindfulness. Alternatively, with guarded doors: by mindfulness; well-restrained: by the graceful way he wears his outer robe.

416. Khippaṃ pattaṃ apūresīti sampajānattā patissatattā ca adhikaṃ agaṇhanto “alaṃ ettāvatā”ti ajjhāsayapūraṇena khippaṃ pattaṃ apūresi. Munīti monatthāya paṭipannattā appattamunibhāvopi muniicceva vutto, lokavohārena vā. Lokiyā hi amonasampattampi pabbajitaṃ “munī”ti bhaṇanti. Paṇḍavaṃ abhihāresīti taṃ pabbataṃ abhiruhi. So kira manusse pucchi “imasmiṃ nagare pabbajitā kattha vasantī”ti. Athassa [P 2.0384] te “paṇḍavassa upari puratthābhimukhapabbhāre”ti ārocesuṃ. Tasmā tameva paṇḍavaṃ abhihāresi “ettha vāso bhavissatī”ti evaṃ cintetvā.

416. He quickly filled his bowl: because he was clearly comprehending and mindful, he did not take an excessive amount, and by fulfilling his intention of 'this much is enough,' he quickly filled his bowl. The sage: because he had undertaken the practice for the sake of sagehood, though he had not yet attained the state of a sage, he is still called a 'sage'; or else this is by worldly convention. For worldly people call even a renunciant who has not attained the accomplishment of sagehood a 'sage.' He approached Mount Paṇḍava: he ascended that mountain. It is said he asked the people: 'Where in this city do the renunciants dwell?' Then they informed him: 'On a ledge facing east on Mount Paṇḍava.' Therefore he approached that very Mount Paṇḍava, thinking, 'My dwelling will be here.'

419-23. Byagghusabhova sīhova girigabbhareti giriguhāyaṃ byaggho viya usabho viya sīho viya ca nisinnoti attho. Ete hi tayo seṭṭhā vigatabhayabheravā girigabbhare nisīdanti, tasmā evaṃ upamaṃ akāsi. Bhaddayānenāti hatthiassarathasivikādinā uttamayānena. Sayānabhūmiṃ yāyitvāti yāvatikā bhūmi hatthiassādinā yānena sakkā gantuṃ, taṃ gantvā. Āsajjāti patvā, samīpamassa gantvāti attho. Upāvisīti nisīdi. Yuvāti yobbanasampanno. Daharoti jātiyā taruṇo. Paṭhamuppattiko susūti tadubhayavisesanameva. Yuvā susūti atiyobbano. Paṭhamuppattikoti paṭhameneva yobbanavesena uṭṭhito. Daharo cāsīti sati ca daharatte susu bālako viya khāyasīti.

419–423. Like a tiger, a bull, or a lion in a mountain lair: the meaning is that he sat like a tiger, a bull, and a lion in a mountain cave. For these three are supreme, devoid of fear and dread, and they sit in a mountain lair; therefore this comparison was made. With a fine vehicle: with a superior vehicle, such as an elephant, horse, chariot, or palanquin. Having gone as far as a vehicle could go: having gone as far as it is possible to go by a vehicle such as an elephant or horse. Approached: having reached; the meaning is, having gone near him. He sat down: he took a seat. Young: endowed with youth. Tender: young by birth. In the first flush of youth, very young: this is a qualification of both the preceding. Young, very young: extremely youthful. In the first flush of youth: arisen in the first stage of youth. And he was tender: while being of tender age, he appeared like a very young boy.

424-5. Anīkagganti [M 2.0113] balakāyaṃ senāmukhaṃ. Dadāmi bhoge bhuñjassūti ettha “ahaṃ te aṅgamagadhesu yāvicchasi, tāva dadāmi bhoge. Taṃ tvaṃ sobhayanto anīkaggaṃ nāgasaṅghapurakkhato bhuñjassū”ti evaṃ sambandho veditabbo. Ujuṃ janapado rājāti “dadāmi bhoge bhuñjassu, jātiṃ akkhāhi pucchito”ti evaṃ kira vutto mahāpuriso cintesi – “sace ahaṃ rajjena atthiko assaṃ, cātumahārājikādayopi maṃ attano attano rajjena nimanteyyuṃ, gehe ṭhito eva vā cakkavattirajjaṃ kāreyyaṃ. Ayaṃ pana rājā ajānanto evamāha – ‘handāhaṃ, taṃ jānāpemī’”ti bāhaṃ uccāretvā attano āgatadisābhāgaṃ niddisanto “ujuṃ janapado rājā”tiādimāha. Tattha himavantassa [V 2.0103] passatoti bhaṇanto sassasampattivekallābhāvaṃ dasseti. Himavantañhi nissāya pāsāṇavivarasambhavā mahāsālāpi pañcahi vuddhīhi vaḍḍhanti, kimaṅgaṃ [P 2.0385] pana khette vuttāni sassāni. Dhanavīriyena sampannoti bhaṇanto sattahi ratanehi avekallattaṃ, pararājūhi atakkanīyaṃ vīrapurisādhiṭṭhitabhāvañcassa dasseti. Kosalesu niketinoti bhaṇanto navakarājabhāvaṃ paṭikkhipati. Navakarājā hi niketīti na vuccati. Yassa pana ādikālato pabhuti anvayavasena so eva janapado nivāso, so niketīti vuccati. Tathārūpo ca rājā suddhodano, yaṃ sandhāyāha “kosalesu niketino”ti. Tena anvayāgatampi bhogasampattiṃ dīpeti.

424–425. The head of the army: the body of troops, the front of the army. In the phrase 'I give you possessions; enjoy them,' the connection should be understood thus: 'I will give you as many possessions in Anga and Magadha as you wish. Enjoy them, gracing the head of the army, preceded by a host of elephants.' Straight on, O king, is a country: It is said that when he was told, 'I give you possessions; enjoy them. Being asked, declare your birth,' the Great Being thought: 'If I were in need of a kingdom, even the Cātumahārājika devas and others would invite me to their respective kingdoms, or while remaining at home I could exercise the rule of a wheel-turning monarch. But this king, not knowing this, speaks thus. Well now, I will let him know.' Raising his arm and pointing to the region from which he had come, he said, 'Straight on, O king, is a country,' and so on. Therein, by saying 'at the foot of the Himalayas,' he shows there is no lack of abundant crops. For, being near the Himalayas, even great sāl trees that spring up in the crevices of rocks grow with the five kinds of growth; how much more so the crops sown in the fields. By saying 'endowed with wealth and energy,' he shows that it is not lacking in the seven treasures and that it is established with heroic men who are unassailable by other kings. By saying 'inhabitants of Kosala,' he rejects the status of being a new king. For a new king is not called an 'inhabitant' (niketī). But one for whom that very country has been a dwelling place from the beginning of time by way of lineage is called an 'inhabitant.' Such was King Suddhodana, in reference to whom it is said, 'inhabitants of Kosala.' By this he also indicates the abundance of wealth that has come down through his lineage.

426. Ettāvatā attano bhogasampattiṃ dīpetvā “ādiccā nāma gottena, sākiyā nāma jātiyā”ti iminā jātisampattiñca ācikkhitvā yaṃ vuttaṃ raññā “dadāmi bhoge bhuñjassū”ti, taṃ paṭikkhipanto āha – “tamhā kulā pabbajitomhi, na kāme abhipatthaya”nti. Yadi hi ahaṃ kāme abhipatthayeyyaṃ, na īdisaṃ dhanavīriyasampannaṃ dvāsītisahassavīrapurisasamākulaṃ kulaṃ chaḍḍetvā pabbajeyyanti ayaṃ kirettha adhippāyo.

426. Having thus indicated his abundance of possessions, and having also declared his noble birth with the words, 'Ādiccas by clan, Sākyans by birth,' he rejected what the king had said—'I give you possessions; enjoy them'—by saying: 'From that family I have gone forth; I do not long for sensual pleasures.' The intention here, it is said, is this: 'For if I longed for sensual pleasures, I would not have gone forth after abandoning such a family, endowed with wealth and energy and filled with eighty-two thousand heroic men.'

427. Evaṃ rañño vacanaṃ paṭikkhipitvā tato paraṃ attano pabbajjāhetuṃ dassento āha – “kāmesvādīnavaṃ disvā, nekkhammaṃ daṭṭhu khemato”ti. Etaṃ “pabbajitomhī”ti iminā sambandhitabbaṃ. Tattha daṭṭhūti disvā[M 2.0114]. Sesamettha ito purimagāthāsu ca yaṃ yaṃ na vicāritaṃ, taṃ taṃ sabbaṃ uttānatthattā eva na vicāritanti veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ attano pabbajjāhetuṃ vatvā padhānatthāya gantukāmo rājānaṃ āmantento āha – “padhānāya gamissāmi, ettha me rañjatī mano”ti. Tassattho – yasmāhaṃ, mahārāja, nekkhammaṃ daṭṭhu khemato pabbajito, tasmā taṃ paramatthanekkhammaṃ nibbānāmataṃ sabbadhammānaṃ aggaṭṭhena padhānaṃ patthento padhānatthāya gamissāmi, ettha me padhāne rañjati mano, na kāmesūti. Evaṃ vutte kira rājā bodhisattaṃ āha – “pubbeva metaṃ, bhante, sutaṃ ‘suddhodanarañño kira putto siddhatthakumāro [P 2.0386] cattāri pubbanimittāni disvā pabbajitvā buddho bhavissatī’ti, sohaṃ, bhante, tumhākaṃ adhimuttiṃ disvā evaṃpasanno ‘addhā buddhattaṃ pāpuṇissathā’ti. Sādhu, bhante, buddhattaṃ patvā paṭhamaṃ mama vijitaṃ okkameyyāthā”ti.

427. Having thus rejected the king's words, he then, showing the reason for his own going forth, said: 'Having seen the danger in sensual pleasures, and seeing renunciation as security.' This should be connected with the phrase 'I have gone forth.' Here, daṭṭhu means 'having seen.' Whatever else here and in the preceding verses has not been explained should be understood as not having been explained because its meaning is plain. Having thus stated the reason for his going forth, as he wished to go to strive, he addressed the king, saying: 'I will go to strive; in this my mind delights.' The meaning is: 'Great king, since I have gone forth having seen renunciation as security, therefore, aspiring for that supreme renunciation—the deathless Nibbāna, which is the foremost because it is the highest of all things—I will go to strive. My mind delights in this striving, not in sensual pleasures.' When this was said, it is said the king replied to the Bodhisatta: 'Venerable sir, I have heard this before: "It is said that the son of King Suddhodana, Prince Siddhattha, having seen the four portents, will go forth and become a Buddha." Seeing your resolve, venerable sir, I am so confident: "Surely you will attain Buddhahood." It is good, venerable sir. Having attained Buddhahood, may you first set foot in my kingdom.'

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya pabbajjāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Here ends the explanation of the Pabbajjā Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary.

2. Padhānasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Padhāna Sutta

428. Taṃ [V 2.0104] maṃ padhānapahitattanti padhānasuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? “Padhānāya gamissāmi, ettha me rañjatī mano”ti āyasmā ānando pabbajjāsuttaṃ niṭṭhāpesi. Bhagavā gandhakuṭiyaṃ nisinno cintesi – “mayā chabbassāni padhānaṃ patthayamānena dukkarakārikā katā, taṃ ajja bhikkhūnaṃ kathessāmī”ti. Atha gandhakuṭito nikkhamitvā buddhāsane nisinno “taṃ maṃ padhānapahitatta”nti ārabhitvā imaṃ suttamabhāsi.

428. The Padhāna Sutta is so called because it begins with 'Taṃ maṃ padhānapahitattaṃ' (Me, resolved on striving). What is its origin? With the words, 'I will go to strive; in this my mind delights,' the Venerable Ānanda concluded the Pabbajjā Sutta. The Blessed One, seated in the Fragrant Cottage, reflected: 'For six years, while desiring striving, I performed difficult practices. Today, I shall relate this to the bhikkhus.' Then, emerging from the Fragrant Cottage and seated on the Buddha’s seat, he began this sutta with 'Taṃ maṃ padhānapahitattaṃ' and delivered it.

Tattha taṃ manti dvīhipi vacanehi attānameva niddisati. Padhānapahitattanti nibbānatthāya pesitacittaṃ pariccattaattabhāvaṃ vā. Nadiṃ nerañjaraṃ patīti lakkhaṇaṃ niddisati. Lakkhaṇañhi padhānapahitattāya nerañjarā nadī. Teneva cettha upayogavacanaṃ. Ayaṃ panattho “nadiyā nerañjarāyā”ti, nerañjarāya tīreti vuttaṃ hoti. Viparakkammāti atīva parakkamitvā. Jhāyantanti appāṇakajjhānamanuyuñjantaṃ[M 2.0115]. Yogakkhemassa pattiyāti catūhi yogehi khemassa nibbānassa adhigamatthaṃ.

Here, by the two words 'taṃ maṃ,' he indicates himself. 'Padhānapahitattaṃ' means a mind directed towards Nibbāna, or one who has relinquished his selfhood. 'Nadiṃ nerañjaraṃ pati' indicates the characteristic. For the characteristic for one resolved on striving is indeed the Nerañjarā River. Therefore, a case indicating relation is used here. The meaning here is 'nadiyā nerañjarāya,' which means 'on the bank of the Nerañjarā.' 'Viparakkamma' means having striven exceedingly. 'Jhāyantaṃ' refers to one engaged in the meditation of non-breathing. 'Yogakkhemassa pattiyā' means for the attainment of Nibbāna, which is security from the four bonds.

429. Namucīti māro. So hi attano visayā nikkhamitukāme devamanusse na muñcati, antarāyaṃ nesaṃ karoti, tasmā “namucī”ti vuccati. Karuṇaṃ vācanti anuddayāyuttaṃ vācaṃ. Bhāsamāno upāgamīti idaṃ uttānameva. Kasmā pana upāgato? Mahāpuriso kira ekadivasaṃ cintesi – “sabbadā āhāraṃ pariyesamāno jīvite sāpekkho hoti, na ca sakkā jīvite sāpekkhena amataṃ adhigantu”nti[P 2.0387]. Tato āhārupacchedāya paṭipajji, tena kiso dubbaṇṇo ca ahosi. Atha māro “ayaṃ sambodhāya maggo hoti, na hotīti ajānanto atighoraṃ tapaṃ karoti, kadāci mama visayaṃ atikkameyyā”ti bhīto “idañcidañca vatvā vāressāmī”ti āgato. Tenevāha – “kiso tvamasi dubbaṇṇo, santike maraṇaṃ tavā”ti.

429. 'Namucī' refers to Māra. For he does not release gods and humans who wish to escape his domain, but obstructs them; hence he is called 'Namucī.' 'Karuṇaṃ vācaṃ' means a speech endowed with compassion. 'Bhāsamāno upāgamīti' is straightforward. But why did he approach? The Great Being, it is said, once reflected: 'Always seeking food, one remains attached to life, and it is impossible to attain the Deathless while attached to life.' Thus, he undertook the cessation of food, becoming emaciated and discolored. Then Māra, fearing, 'This may or may not be the path to enlightenment, but he performs severe austerities; perhaps he will escape my domain,' thought, 'I will dissuade him by saying such and such,' and came. Therefore, he said: 'You are emaciated and discolored; death is near you.'

430. Evañca pana vatvā athassa maraṇasantikabhāvaṃ sāvento āha – “sahassabhāgo maraṇassa, ekaṃso tava jīvita”nti. Tassattho – sahassaṃ bhāgānaṃ assāti sahassabhāgo. Ko so[V 2.0105]? Maraṇassa paccayoti pāṭhaseso. Eko aṃsoti ekaṃso. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ayaṃ appāṇakajjhānādisahassabhāgo tava maraṇassa paccayo, tato pana te eko eva bhāgo jīvitaṃ, evaṃ santike maraṇaṃ tavāti. Evaṃ maraṇassa santikabhāvaṃ sāvetvā atha naṃ jīvite samussāhento āha “jīva bho jīvitaṃ seyyo”ti. Kathaṃ seyyoti ce. Jīvaṃ puññāni kāhasīti.

430. Having said this, he then announced the imminence of death, saying: 'A thousand shares are of death, one share is of your life.' Its meaning is: 'Having a thousand shares' means 'sahassabhāgo.' What is that? The implied remainder of the text is 'the cause of death.' 'One share' means 'ekaṃso.' This is what is meant: 'This thousandfold meditation without breathing and the like is a cause of your death; from that, only one share is your life. Thus, death is near you.' Having thus announced the imminence of death, he then encouraged him to persist in life, saying: 'Live, sir, life is better.' If it is asked, 'How is it better?' He replies: 'Living, you can perform meritorious deeds.'

431. Atha attanā sammatāni puññāni dassento āha – “carato ca te brahmacariya”nti. Tattha brahmacariyanti kālena kālaṃ methunaviratiṃ sandhāyāha, yaṃ tāpasā karonti. Jūhatoti juhantassa. Sesamettha pākaṭameva.

431. Then, pointing out the meritorious deeds he himself approved of, he said: 'And for one who fares on the holy life...' Here, 'brahmacariya' refers to periodic abstinence from sexual intercourse, as practiced by ascetics. 'Jūhato' means 'to one who sacrifices.' The rest here is evident.

432. Duggo maggoti imaṃ pana aḍḍhagāthaṃ padhānavicchandaṃ janento āha. Tattha appāṇakajjhānādigahanattā dukkhena gantabboti duggo, dukkhitakāyacittena [M 2.0116] kattabbattā dukkaro, santikamaraṇena tādisenāpi pāpuṇituṃ asakkuṇeyyato durabhisambhavoti evamattho veditabbo. Ito paraṃ imā gāthā bhaṇaṃ māro, aṭṭhā buddhassa santiketi ayamupaḍḍhagāthā saṅgītikārehi vuttā. Sakalagāthāpīti eke. Bhagavatā eva pana paraṃ viya attānaṃ niddisantena sabbamettha evaṃjātikaṃ vuttanti ayamamhākaṃ khanti. Tattha aṭṭhāti aṭṭhāsi. Sesaṃ uttānameva.

432. He spoke this half-verse, 'The difficult path,' to cause him to abandon the striving. Therein, it is called 'duggo' (difficult to traverse) because it is hard to traverse due to the impenetrability of the meditation of non-breathing and so forth; 'dukkaro' (hard to do) because it requires painful physical and mental effort; and 'durabhisambhavo' (hard to master) because even one near death may not be able to attain it. This is the meaning to be understood. From here on, 'Māra, speaking these verses, stood near the Buddha'—this half-verse was spoken by the compilers. Some hold that the entire verse was. However, our acceptance is that the Blessed One himself spoke all such things here, referring to himself as if he were another. Therein, 'aṭṭhā' means 'he stood' (aṭṭhāsi). The rest is clear.

433. Chaṭṭhagāthāya yenatthenāti ettha paresaṃ antarāyakaraṇena attano atthena tvaṃ, pāpima, āgatosīti ayamadhippāyo[P 2.0388]. Sesaṃ uttānameva.

433. In the sixth verse, regarding 'yenatthena' (for what purpose), the meaning is this: 'You have come, O Wicked One, for your own sake by causing obstruction to others.' The rest is self-explanatory.

434. “Jīvaṃ puññāni kāhasī”ti idaṃ pana vacanaṃ paṭikkhipanto “aṇumattopī”ti imaṃ gāthamāha. Tattha puññenāti vaṭṭagāmiṃ mārena vuttaṃ puññaṃ sandhāya bhaṇati. Sesaṃ uttānameva.

434. Rejecting this statement, 'Jīvaṃ puññāni kāhasi' (Living, you will perform meritorious deeds), he speaks this verse: 'Aṇumattopi' (even a little). Here, 'puññena' refers to the merit pertaining to the round of existence, as spoken by Māra. The rest is self-explanatory.

435. Idāni “ekaṃso tava jīvita”nti idaṃ vacanaṃ ārabbha māraṃ santajjento “atthi saddhā”ti imaṃ gāthamāha. Tatrāyamadhippāyo – are, māra, yo anuttare santivarapade assaddho bhaveyya, saddhopi vā kusīto, saddho āraddhavīriyo samānopi vā duppañño, taṃ tvaṃ jīvitamanupucchamāno sobheyyāsi, mayhaṃ pana anuttare santivarapade okappanasaddhā atthi, tathā kāyikacetasikamasithilaparakkamatāsaṅkhātaṃ vīriyaṃ, vajirūpamā paññā ca mama vijjati, so tvaṃ evaṃ maṃ pahitattaṃ uttamajjhāsayaṃ kiṃ jīvamanupucchasi, kasmā jīvitaṃ pucchasi. Paññā [V 2.0106] ca mamāti ettha ca saddena sati samādhi ca. Evaṃ sante yehi pañcahi indriyehi samannāgatā nibbānaṃ pāpuṇanti, tesu ekenāpi avirahitaṃ evaṃ maṃ pahitattaṃ kiṃ jīvamanupucchasi? Nanu – ekāhaṃ jīvitaṃ seyyo, vīriyamārabhato daḷhaṃ (dha. pa. 112). Paññavantassa jhāyino, passato udayabbayanti (dha. pa. 111, 113).

435. Now, taking up Māra’s statement, 'Ekaṃso tava jīvitaṃ' (one share is of your life), he admonishes him with this verse: 'Atthi saddhā' (there is faith). Herein, the meaning is this: 'O Māra, if someone were faithless in the supreme, peaceful state, or even if faithful but lazy, or faithful and energetic but unwise, then you might rightly question their life. But in me, there is unwavering faith in the supreme, peaceful state, as well as bodily and mental exertion free from slackness—known as energy—and wisdom like a diamond. Why then do you, with such a resolute mind and lofty aspiration, question my life? Why ask about my life? And here, by the word 'ca' in 'Paññā ca mama,' mindfulness and concentration are also included. Thus, being endowed with the five faculties by which beings attain Nibbāna, not lacking even one, why do you question my life, who am so resolute? Indeed: 'Better a single day of life for one who rouses his energy firmly' (Dhp. 112), and for 'the wise meditator, seeing rise and fall' (Dhp. 111, 113).

436-8. Evaṃ māraṃ santajjetvā attano dehacittappavattiṃ dassento “nadīnamapī”pi gāthāttayamāha. Tamatthato pākaṭameva. Ayaṃ pana adhippāyavaṇṇanā [M 2.0117] – yvāyaṃ mama sarīre appāṇakajjhānavīriyavegasamuṭṭhito vāto vattati, loke gaṅgāyamunādīnaṃ nadīnampi sotāni ayaṃ visosaye, kiñca me evaṃ pahitattassa catunāḷimattaṃ lohitaṃ na upasoseyya. Na kevalañca me lohitameva sussati, apica kho pana tamhi lohite sussamānamhi baddhābaddhabhedaṃ sarīrānugataṃ [P 2.0389] pittaṃ, asitapītādipaṭicchādakaṃ catunāḷimattameva semhañca, kiñcāparaṃ tattakameva muttañca ojañca sussati, tesu ca sussamānesu maṃsānipi khīyanti, tassa me evaṃ anupubbena maṃsesu khīyamānesu bhiyyo cittaṃ pasīdati, na tveva tappaccayā saṃsīdati. So tvaṃ īdisaṃ cittamajānanto sarīramattameva disvā bhaṇasi “kiso tvamasi dubbaṇṇo, santike maraṇaṃ tavā”ti. Na kevalañca me cittameva pasīdati, apica kho pana bhiyyo sati ca paññā ca samādhi mama tiṭṭhati, aṇumattopi pamādo vā sammoho vā cittavikkhepo vā natthi, tassa mayhaṃ evaṃ viharato ye keci samaṇabrāhmaṇā atītaṃ vā addhānaṃ anāgataṃ vā etarahi vā opakkamikā vedanā vedayanti, tāsaṃ nidassanabhūtaṃ pattassa uttamavedanaṃ. Yathā aññesaṃ dukkhena phuṭṭhānaṃ sukhaṃ, sītena uṇhaṃ, uṇhena sītaṃ, khudāya bhojanaṃ, pipāsāya phuṭṭhānaṃ udakaṃ apekkhate cittaṃ, evaṃ pañcasu kāmaguṇesu ekakāmampi nāpekkhake cittaṃ. “Aho vatāhaṃ subhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā sukhaseyyaṃ sayeyya”nti īdisenākārena mama cittaṃ na uppannaṃ, passa, tvaṃ māra, sattassa suddhatanti.

436–438. Having thus rebuked Māra, he showed the functioning of his own body and mind, and spoke three verses beginning with 'Nadīnamapi' (Even the rivers). Their meaning is clear enough. But here is the explanation of the intention: 'Whatever wind arises in my body from the force of the energy of breathless absorption, it could dry up the streams of rivers like the Ganges and Yamunā in the world—how much more this mere four nāḷis of blood in one like me, so resolute? Not only does my blood dry up, but also the bile in my body, whether bound or unbound, which envelops what is eaten and drunk—just four nāḷis in measure—and likewise the phlegm, and moreover, the same amount of urine and nutrient essence dries up. As these dry up, the flesh also wastes away. As my flesh wastes away thus gradually, my mind becomes even more serene; it does not become sluggish on account of that. You, not knowing such a mind and seeing only the body, say, 'You are emaciated and discolored; death is near you.' Not only does my mind become serene, but moreover, my mindfulness, wisdom, and concentration are firmly established. There is not the slightest heedlessness, delusion, or distraction of mind. For me dwelling thus, the highest feeling has been attained, which is an example for whatever ascetics or brahmins in the past, future, or present endure painful feelings due to affliction. Just as the minds of others, when afflicted by suffering, long for happiness; when afflicted by cold, for warmth; when afflicted by heat, for coolness; when afflicted by hunger, for food; when afflicted by thirst, for water—so my mind does not long for even a single sensual pleasure among the five strands of sensual desire. 'Oh, that I might eat fine food and lie on a comfortable bed'—such a thought has not arisen in my mind. See, Māra, the purity of this being.

439-41. Evaṃ attano suddhataṃ dassetvā “nivāressāmi ta”nti āgatassa mārassa manorathabhañjanatthaṃ mārasenaṃ kittetvā tāya aparājitabhāvaṃ dassento “kāmā te paṭhamā senā”tiādikā cha gāthāyo āha.

439–441. Having thus shown his own purity, in order to shatter the wish of Māra who had come thinking, 'I will prevent him,' he enumerated the army of Māra and, demonstrating that he was unconquered by it, spoke six verses beginning with 'Sensual desire is your first army.'

Tattha yasmā āditova agāriyabhūte satte vatthukāmesu kilesakāmā mohayanti, te abhibhuyya anagāriyabhāvaṃ upagatānaṃ pantesu vā senāsanesu aññataraññataresu vā adhikusalesu dhammesu arati uppajjati. Vuttañcetaṃ “pabbajitena kho, āvuso, abhirati dukkarā”ti [V 2.0107] (saṃ. ni. 4.331). Tato te parapaṭibaddhajīvikattā khuppipāsā bādheti, tāya bādhitānaṃ [M 2.0118] pariyesanataṇhā cittaṃ kilamayati, atha nesaṃ [P 2.0390] kilantacittānaṃ thinamiddhaṃ okkamati. Tato visesamanadhigacchantānaṃ durabhisambhavesu araññavanapatthesu senāsanesu viharataṃ utrāsasaññitā bhīru jāyati, tesaṃ ussaṅkitaparisaṅkitānaṃ dīgharattaṃ vivekarasamanassādayamānānaṃ viharataṃ “na siyā nu kho esa maggo”ti paṭipattiyaṃ vicikicchā uppajjati, taṃ vinodetvā viharataṃ appamattakena visesādhigamena mānamakkhathambhā jāyanti, tepi vinodetvā viharataṃ tato adhikataraṃ visesādhigamaṃ nissāya lābhasakkārasilokā uppajjanti, lābhādimucchitā dhammapatirūpakāni pakāsentā micchāyasaṃ adhigantvā tattha ṭhitā jātiādīhi attānaṃ ukkaṃsenti, paraṃ vambhenti, tasmā kāmādīnaṃ paṭhamasenādibhāvo veditabbo.

Here, because from the very beginning sensual pleasures as objects and sensual pleasures as defilements delude beings in the household life, for those who have overcome them and gone forth into homelessness, discontent arises in regard to remote lodgings or to higher wholesome states. And this was said: 'Friend, delight is difficult for one who has gone forth.' Then, because their livelihood is dependent on others, hunger and thirst afflict them. For those afflicted by these, the craving for what is sought fatigues their minds. Then, for those with fatigued minds, sloth and torpor descend upon them. For those not attaining any distinction, dwelling in forest-and-woodland tracts that are hard to endure, fear and timidity arise. As they dwell for a long time, suspicious and anxious, not savoring the taste of seclusion, doubt about the practice arises in them: 'Could it be that this is not the path?' As they dwell having dispelled that, with the attainment of some slight distinction, conceit, denigration, and obstinacy arise. As they dwell having dispelled these too, relying on the attainment of a greater distinction, gain, honor, and renown arise. Intoxicated by gain and the rest, proclaiming counterfeit Dhamma, they acquire a wrong reputation and, established in that, they exalt themselves on the basis of birth, etc., and disparage others. Therefore, it should be understood that sensual pleasures and so on constitute the first army and so on.

442-3. Evametaṃ dasavidhaṃ senaṃ uddisitvā yasmā sā kaṇhadhammasamannāgatattā kaṇhassa namucino upakārāya saṃvattati, tasmā naṃ tava senāti niddisanto āha – “esā namuci te senā, kaṇhassābhippahārinī”ti. Tattha abhippahārinīti samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ ghātanī nippothanī, antarāyakarīti attho. Na naṃ asūro jināti, jetvā ca labhate sukhanti evaṃ tava senaṃ asūro kāye ca jīvite ca sāpekkho puriso na jināti, sūro pana jināti, jetvā ca maggasukhaṃ phalasukhañca adhigacchati. Yasmā ca labhate sukhaṃ, tasmā sukhaṃ patthayamāno ahampi esa muñjaṃ parihareti. Saṅgāmāvacarā anivattino purisā attano anivattanakabhāvaviññāpanatthaṃ sīse vā dhaje vā āvudhe vā muñjatiṇaṃ bandhanti, taṃ ayampi pariharaticceva maṃ dhārehi. Tava senāya parājitassa dhiratthu mama jīvitaṃ, tasmā evaṃ dhārehi – saṅgāme me mataṃ seyyo, yañce jīve parājito, yena jīvitena parājito jīve, tasmā jīvitā tayā sammāpaṭipannānaṃ antarāyakarena saddhiṃ saṅgāme mataṃ mama seyyoti attho.

Having thus pointed out the tenfold army, because it is endowed with dark qualities and conduces to the benefit of the Dark One, Namuci, he points to it as 'your army,' saying: 'This, Namuci, is your army, the assaulting force of the Dark One.' Here, 'assaulting' means slaughtering and crushing ascetics and brahmins, causing obstruction. 'No coward conquers it, but having conquered it one finds happiness': thus your army is not conquered by a coward, a person concerned for his body and life, but a hero conquers it, and having conquered it he attains the happiness of the path and the happiness of the fruit. And because one finds happiness, therefore, wishing for happiness, 'I too wear this muñja grass.' Warriors who do not retreat in battle tie muñja grass on their heads, banners, or weapons to make known their state of not turning back. 'This one also wears it; thus understand me. Shame on the life of one defeated by your army! Therefore, understand this: "Better for me is death in battle than that I should live defeated."' The meaning is: 'Than that life by which one would live defeated, better for me is death in battle with you who are an obstructor of those practicing rightly.'

444. Kasmā mataṃ seyyoti ce? Yasmā pagāḷhettha…pe… subbatā, ettha kāmādikāya attukkaṃsanaparavambhanapariyosānāya tava senāya pagāḷhā nimuggā anupaviṭṭhā eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā na [P 2.0391] dissanti, sīlādīhi guṇehi nappakāsanti, andhakāraṃ paviṭṭhā viya honti. Ete evaṃ pagāḷhā samānā [M 2.0119] sacepi kadāci ummujjitvā nimujjanapuriso viya “sāhu saddhā”tiādinā nayena ummujjanti, tathāpi tāya senāya ajjhotthaṭattā tañca maggaṃ na jānanti khemaṃ nibbānagāmīnaṃ, sabbepi buddhapaccekabuddhādayo yena gacchanti subbatāti. Imaṃ pana gāthaṃ sutvā māro puna kiñci avatvā eva pakkāmi.

444. And why is death better? Because 'Immersed in it... the virtuous.' Here, some ascetics and brahmins, plunged, sunken, and entered into your army—which begins with sensual pleasures and ends with self-exaltation and disparagement of others—are not seen; they do not shine with qualities such as virtue, as if they have entered into darkness. Even if these, being so plunged, should sometimes emerge—like a man who dives and emerges, saying 'Good is faith!' and so on—still, because they are overwhelmed by that army, 'they do not know that path,' the safe way to Nibbāna, 'by which all the virtuous ones'—the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and others—'go.' Having heard this verse, Māra departed without saying anything more.

445-6. Pakkante [V 2.0108] pana tasmiṃ mahāsatto tāya dukkarakārikāya kiñcipi visesaṃ anadhigacchanto anukkamena “siyā nu kho añño maggo bodhāyā”tiādīni cintetvā oḷārikāhāraṃ āhāretvā, balaṃ gahetvā, visākhapuṇṇamadivase pageva sujātāya pāyāsaṃ paribhuñjitvā, bhadravanasaṇḍe divāvihāraṃ nisīditvā, tattha aṭṭha samāpattiyo nibbattento divasaṃ vītināmetvā sāyanhasamaye mahābodhimaṇḍābhimukho gantvā sotthiyena dinnā aṭṭha tiṇamuṭṭhiyo bodhimūle vikiritvā dasasahassalokadhātudevatāhi katasakkārabahumāno –

445-6. But after he had departed, the Great Being, not attaining any distinction by that practice of austerities, gradually thought, 'Could there be another way to enlightenment?' and so on. Having consumed coarse food and regained his strength, on the full-moon day of Visākha he ate the milk-rice offered by Sujātā early in the morning. He sat down for the day's abiding in the Bhadravana grove, and he spent the day there producing the eight attainments. In the evening, he went towards the terrace of great enlightenment, scattered at the foot of the Bodhi tree the eight handfuls of grass given by Sotthiya, and, having received honor and esteem from the devas of the ten-thousand-world-system—

“Kāmaṃ taco ca nhāru ca, aṭṭhi ca avasissatu;

Upasussatu nissesaṃ, sarīre maṃsalohita”nti. –

"Willingly, let skin, sinews, and bone remain; let the flesh and blood in my body dry up completely."

Caturaṅgavīriyaṃ adhiṭṭhahitvā “na dāni buddhattaṃ apāpuṇitvā pallaṅkaṃ bhindissāmī”ti paṭiññaṃ katvā aparājitapallaṅke nisīdi. Taṃ ñatvā māro pāpimā “ajja siddhattho paṭiññaṃ katvā nisinno, ajjeva dānissa sā paṭiññā paṭibāhitabbā”ti bodhimaṇḍato yāva cakkavāḷamāyataṃ dvādasayojanavitthāraṃ uddhaṃ navayojanamuggataṃ mārasenaṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā diyaḍḍhayojanasatappamāṇaṃ girimekhalaṃ hatthirājānaṃ āruyha bāhusahassaṃ māpetvā nānāvudhāni gahetvā “gaṇhatha, hanatha, paharathā”ti bhaṇanto āḷavakasutte vuttappakārā vuṭṭhiyo māpesi, tā mahāpurisaṃ patvā tattha vuttappakārā eva sampajjiṃsu. Tato vajiraṅkusena hatthiṃ kumbhe paharitvā mahāpurisassa samīpaṃ netvā “uṭṭhehi, bho siddhattha, pallaṅkā”ti āha. Mahāpuriso “na uṭṭhahāmi mārā”ti [P 2.0392] vatvā taṃ dhajiniṃ samantā vilokento imā gāthāyo abhāsi “samantā dhajini”nti.

Having resolved upon the fourfold striving and made the vow, 'I will not break up this cross-legged posture until I have attained Buddhahood,' he sat down on the unconquered seat. Knowing this, Māra the Evil One thought, 'Today Siddhattha has sat down after making a vow. Today that vow of his must be thwarted.' He raised Māra's army—twelve yojanas wide and nine yojanas high, extending from the Bodhi terrace to the Cakkavāḷa range—and mounting the elephant king Girimekhala, who was one hundred and fifty yojanas in size, he created a thousand arms, took up various weapons, and shouting, 'Seize! Slay! Strike!' he created rains of the kind described in the Āḷavaka Sutta. Reaching the Great Being, they turned out just as described there. Then, striking the elephant on its frontal globes with a diamond goad, he brought it near the Great Being and said, 'Rise, Siddhattha, from this seat!' The Great Being said, 'I will not rise, Māra!' and looking all around at that army, he uttered these verses: 'Seeing the army all around...'

Tattha [M 2.0120] dhajininti senaṃ. Yuttanti uyyuttaṃ. Savāhananti girimekhalanāgarājasahitaṃ. Paccuggacchāmīti abhimukho upari gamissāmi, so ca kho tejeneva, na kāyena. Kasmā? Mā maṃ ṭhānā acāvayi, maṃ etasmā ṭhānā aparājitapallaṅkā māro mā cālesīti vuttaṃ hoti. Nappasahatīti sahituṃ na sakkoti, nābhibhavati vā. Āmaṃ pattanti kācajātaṃ mattikābhājanaṃ. Asmanāti pāsāṇena. Sesamettha pākaṭameva.

Herein, `dhajiniṃ` means army. `Yuttaṃ` means arrayed. `Savāhanaṃ` means together with the elephant king Girimekhala. `Paccuggacchāmi` means: I will go up to meet it face to face, and that with my spiritual power, not with my body. Why? 'May he not make me move from my place.' This means: 'May Māra not dislodge me from this place, the unconquered seat.' `Nappasahati` means: he is not able to endure, or he does not overwhelm. `Āmaṃ pattaṃ` means an unbaked clay pot. `Asmanā` means with a stone. The rest here is evident.

447-8. Idāni “etaṃ te mārasenaṃ bhinditvā tato paraṃ vijitasaṅgāmo sampattadhammarājābhiseko idaṃ karissāmī”ti dassento āha “vasīkaritvā”ti. Tattha vasīkaritvā saṅkappanti maggabhāvanāya sabbaṃ micchāsaṅkappaṃ pahāya sammāsaṅkappasseva pavattanena vasīkaritvā [V 2.0109] saṅkappaṃ. Satiñca sūpatiṭṭhitanti kāyādīsu catūsu ṭhānesu attano satiñca suṭṭhu upaṭṭhitaṃ karitvā evaṃ vasīkatasaṅkappo suppatiṭṭhitassati raṭṭhā raṭṭhaṃ vicarissāmi devamanussabhede puthū sāvake vinayanto. Atha mayā vinīyamānā te appamattā…pe… na socare, taṃ nibbānāmatamevāti adhippāyo.

447-8. Now, to show, 'Having shattered this army of Māra, and thereafter, as a victor in battle who has attained the consecration of a Dhamma King, I will do this,' he says, 'Having brought under control.' Herein, 'having brought thought under control' means: having brought thought under control by abandoning all wrong thought through the development of the path and by making only right thought proceed. 'And mindfulness well established' means: having made one's own mindfulness well established in the four stations, on the body, etc. Thus, with thought brought under control and mindfulness well established, 'I will wander from country to country, training many disciples' among devas and humans. Then, those being trained by me, 'being diligent... will not grieve'—the intention here is the deathless Nibbāna itself.

449-51. Atha māro imā gāthāyo sutvā āha – “evarūpaṃ pakkhaṃ disvā na bhāyasi bhikkhū”ti? “Āma, māra, na bhāyāmī”ti. “Kasmā na bhāyasī”ti? “Dānādīnaṃ pāramipuññānaṃ katattā”ti. “Ko etaṃ jānāti dānādīni tvamakāsī”ti? “Kiṃ ettha pāpima sakkhikiccena, apica ekasmiṃyeva bhave vessantaro hutvā yaṃ dānamadāsiṃ, tassānubhāvena sattakkhattuṃ chahi pakārehi sañjātakampā ayaṃ mahāpathavīyeva sakkhī”ti. Evaṃ vutte udakapariyantaṃ katvā mahāpathavī kampi bheravasaddaṃ muñcamānā, yaṃ sutvā māro asanihato viya bhīto dhajaṃ paṇāmetvā palāyi saddhiṃ parisāya. Atha mahāpuriso tīhi yāmehi tisso vijjā sacchikatvā aruṇuggamane “anekajātisaṃsāraṃ…pe… taṇhānaṃ khayamajjhagā”ti [P 2.0393] imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi. Māro udānasaddena āgantvā “ayaṃ‘buddho aha’nti paṭijānāti, handa naṃ anubandhāmi ābhisamācārikaṃ passituṃ. Sacassa kiñci kāyena vā vācāya vā khalitaṃ bhavissati, viheṭhessāmi na”nti pubbe bodhisattabhūmiyaṃ [M 2.0121] chabbassāni anubandhitvā buddhattaṃ pattaṃ ekaṃ vassaṃ anubandhi. Tato bhagavato kiñci khalitaṃ apassanto “satta vassānī”ti imā nibbejanīyagāthāyo abhāsi.

449-51. Then, having heard these verses, Māra said: 'Seeing such a faction, are you not afraid, bhikkhu?' 'No, Māra, I am not afraid.' 'Why are you not afraid?' 'Because of having made the merit of the perfections such as giving.' 'Who knows that you have performed acts of giving and so on?' 'What need is there for a witness here, Evil One? Moreover, in the single existence when I was Vessantara, because of the gift I gave, this great earth itself, which quaked seven times in six ways, is my witness.' When this was said, the great earth quaked down to its water boundary, emitting a terrifying sound. Hearing this, Māra, terrified as if struck by a thunderbolt, lowered his banner and fled with his retinue. Then the Great Being, having realized the three true knowledges in the three watches of the night, at the break of dawn uttered this solemn utterance: 'Through the round of many births... I have reached the destruction of craving.' Hearing the sound of the solemn utterance, Māra came and thought: 'This one is claiming, "I am the Buddha." Come now, I will follow him to observe his higher conduct. If he has any fault in body or speech, I will harass him.' Having followed him for six years previously when he was a bodhisatta, he followed him for one year after he attained Buddhahood. Then, not seeing any fault in the Blessed One, he uttered these verses of discouragement: 'For seven years...'

Tattha otāranti randhaṃ vivaraṃ. Nādhigacchissanti nādhigamiṃ. Medavaṇṇanti medapiṇḍasadisaṃ. Anupariyagāti parito parito agamāsi. Mudunti mudukaṃ. Vindemāti adhigaccheyyāma. Assādanāti sādubhāvo. Vāyasettoti vāyaso etto. Sesamettha pākaṭameva.

Herein, 'an opportunity' means a flaw, an opening. 'They will not find'; 'I did not find.' 'Resembling fat' means resembling a lump of fat. 'He went all around' means he went around and around. 'Soft' means soft. 'We might find' means we might attain. 'Gratification' means savoriness. 'The crow here' means the crow from here. The rest here is clear.

Ayaṃ pana yojanā – satta vassāni bhagavantaṃ otārāpekkho anubandhiṃ katthaci avijahanto padāpadaṃ, evaṃ anubandhitvāpi ca otāraṃ nādhigamiṃ. Sohaṃ yathā nāma medavaṇṇaṃ pāsāṇaṃ medasaññī vāyaso ekasmiṃ passe mukhatuṇḍakena vijjhitvā assādaṃ avindamāno “appeva nāma ettha mudu vindema, api ito assādanā siyā”ti samantā tatheva vijjhanto anupariyāyitvā katthaci assādaṃ aladdhā “pāsāṇovāya”nti nibbijja pakkameyya, evamevāhaṃ bhagavantaṃ kāyakammādīsu attano parittapaññāmukhatuṇḍakena vijjhanto samantā anupariyagā “appeva nāma katthaci aparisuddhakāyasamācārādimudubhāvaṃ vindema, kutoci assādanā [V 2.0110] siyā”ti, te dāni mayaṃ assādaṃ alabhamānā kākova selamāsajja nibbijjāpema gotamaṃ āsajja tato gotamā nibbijja apemāti. Evaṃ vadato kira mārassa satta vassāni nipphalaparissamaṃ nissāya balavasoko udapādi. Tenassa visīdamānaṅgapaccaṅgassa beluvapaṇḍu nāma vīṇā kacchato patitā. Yā [P 2.0394] sakiṃ kusalehi vāditā cattāro māse madhurassaraṃ muñcati, yaṃ gahetvā sakko pañcasikhassa adāsi. Taṃ so patamānampi na bujjhi. Tenāha bhagavā –

Now this is the application: For seven years, I followed the Blessed One step by step, seeking an opportunity, never leaving him. Yet, even after following him thus, I did not find an opportunity. Just as a crow, perceiving a stone the color of fat to be fat, might peck at it with its beak, and finding no savor, might think, 'Perhaps we will find something soft here, perhaps there might be some gratification here!' and then, after pecking all around and finding no gratification, it would become disgusted and depart, thinking, 'This is just a stone'—in the same way, I kept probing the Blessed One with the beak of my limited wisdom, examining his bodily actions and so on, thinking, 'Perhaps somewhere I will find the softness of impure bodily conduct; perhaps there might be some gratification from some quarter.' But now we, finding no gratification, are leaving Gotama, disappointed, just like the crow that approached the rock. It is said that as Māra spoke thus, a strong sorrow arose in him on account of his seven years of fruitless effort. As he was despairing and his limbs were sinking, his lute named Beluvapaṇḍu fell from his armpit. That lute, when played once by a skilled person, would produce sweet sounds for four months; Sakka had taken it and given it to Pañcasikha. But Māra did not notice it even as it was falling. Therefore the Blessed One said:

452.

452.

“Tassa sokaparetassa, vīṇā kacchā abhassatha;

Tato so dummano yakkho, tatthevantaradhāyathā”ti.

For him, overcome by sorrow, the lute slipped from his armpit; then that dejected yakkha vanished right there.

Saṅgītikārakā āhaṃsūti eke, amhākaṃ panetaṃ nakkhamatīti.

Some say that the compilers of the canon spoke thus, but this is not acceptable to us.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Collection.

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya padhānasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Padhāna Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary is concluded.

3. Subhāsitasuttavaṇṇanā

3. The Explanation of the Subhāsita Sutta

Evaṃ [V 2.0111][M 2.0122] me sutanti subhāsitasuttaṃ. Attajjhāsayato cassa uppatti. Bhagavā hi subhāsitappiyo, so attano subhāsitasamudācārappakāsanena sattānaṃ dubbhāsitasamudācāraṃ paṭisedhento imaṃ suttamabhāsi. Tattha evaṃ me sutantiādi saṅgītikāravacanaṃ. Tattha tatra kho bhagavā…pe… bhadanteti te bhikkhūti etaṃ apubbaṃ, sesaṃ vuttanayameva. Tasmā apubbapadavaṇṇanatthamidaṃ vuccati – tatrāti desakālaparidīpanaṃ. Tañhi yaṃ samayaṃ viharati, tatra samaye, yasmiñca ārāme viharati, tatra ārāmeti dīpeti. Bhāsitabbayutte vā desakāle dīpeti. Na hi bhagavā ayutte dese kāle vā dhammaṃ bhāsati. “Akālo kho, tāva, bāhiyā”tiādi (udā. 10) cettha sādhakaṃ. Khoti padapūraṇamatte avadhāraṇādikālatthe vā nipāto. Bhagavāti lokagaruparidīpanaṃ. Bhikkhūti kathāsavanayuttapuggalaparidīpanaṃ. Āmantesīti ālapi abhāsi sambodhesi.

'Thus have I heard'—this is the Subhāsita Sutta. Its origin was from his own disposition. For the Blessed One is fond of what is well spoken, and by demonstrating his own practice of well-spoken speech, he spoke this sutta to restrain beings from ill-spoken speech. Herein, 'Thus have I heard,' and so forth, is the utterance of the compilers of the canon. Herein, 'There the Blessed One…' up to '"Venerable sir," said those bhikkhus'—this is new; the rest is in the manner already stated. Therefore, this is said to explain the new words: 'There' indicates the place and time. For it clarifies the time when he was dwelling, and the monastery where he was dwelling. Or it clarifies the suitable place and time for speaking. For the Blessed One does not teach the Dhamma in unsuitable places or at unsuitable times. 'It is not the time now, Bāhiya,' etc., is the proof here. 'Kho' is a particle that is merely a verse-filler or has the meaning of emphasis, time, etc. 'The Blessed One' indicates the Teacher of the world. 'Bhikkhus' indicates the persons fit to hear the discourse. 'Addressed' means he called to, spoke to, addressed.

Bhikkhavoti āmantanākāraparidīpanaṃ. Tañca bhikkhanasīlatādiguṇayogasiddhattā vuttaṃ. Tena nesaṃ hīnādhikajanasevitaṃ [P 2.0395] vuttiṃ pakāsento uddhatadīnabhāvaniggahaṃ karoti. “Bhikkhavo”ti iminā ca karuṇāvipphārasommahadayanayananipātapubbaṅgamena vacanena te attano mukhābhimukhe karitvā teneva kathetukamyatādīpakena vacanena tesaṃ sotukamyataṃ janeti, teneva ca sambodhanatthena vacanena sādhukasavanamanasikārepi te niyojeti. Sādhukasavanamanasikārāyattā hi sāsanasampatti. Aparesupi devamanussesu vijjamānesu kasmā bhikkhū eva āmantesīti ce? Jeṭṭhaseṭṭhāsannasadāsannihitabhāvato. Sabbaparisasādhāraṇā hi ayaṃ dhammadesanā, na pāṭipuggalikā. Parisāya ca jeṭṭhā bhikkhū paṭhamuppannattā, seṭṭhā anagāriyabhāvaṃ ādiṃ katvā satthu cariyānuvidhāyakattā sakalasāsanapaṭiggāhakattā ca. Āsannā tattha nisinnesu satthu santikattā, sadā sannihitā satthu santikāvacarattā. Tena bhagavā sabbaparisasādhāraṇaṃ dhammaṃ desento bhikkhū eva āmantesi. Apica bhājanaṃ te imāya kathāya yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipattisabbhāvatotipi te eva [M 2.0123] āmantesi. Bhadanteti gāravādhivacanametaṃ. Te bhikkhūti ye bhagavā āmantesi, te evaṃ bhagavantaṃ ālapantā bhagavato paccassosunti.

'Bhikkhus'—this indicates the mode of address. And it is said because of their attainment of qualities such as the habit of alms-seeking. By this, revealing their livelihood, which is frequented by both the lowly and the eminent, he suppresses arrogance and dejection. And by this word 'Bhikkhus,' preceded by the casting of a glance from eyes filled with compassion and a gentle heart, having turned them towards his face, by that word indicating his desire to speak to them, he generates in them a desire to listen, and by that same address, he also engages them in careful listening and attention. For the accomplishment of the teaching depends on careful listening and attention. If it is asked why he addressed only the bhikkhus though other devas and humans were present, it is because they are the eldest, the best, the nearest, and always present. For this Dhamma teaching is common to the entire assembly, not for a specific individual. And in the assembly, the bhikkhus are the eldest, being the first to arise; the best, because, having undertaken the homeless life, they follow the Teacher's conduct and are the receptacles of the entire teaching. They are near, being seated in the Teacher's presence, and always present, attending on him. Thus, the Blessed One, teaching the Dhamma common to the whole assembly, addressed the bhikkhus. Moreover, he addressed them because they are vessels for this discourse, being capable of practice in accordance with the instruction. 'Venerable Sir'—this is a term of reverence. 'Those bhikkhus'—this means that those whom the Blessed One addressed, thus replied to the Blessed One.

Catūhi [V 2.0112] aṅgehīti catūhi kāraṇehi avayavehi vā. Musāvādāveramaṇiādīni hi cattāri subhāsitavācāya kāraṇāni. Saccavacanādayo cattāro avayavā, kāraṇatthe ca aṅgasaddo. Catūhīti nissakkavacanaṃ hoti, avayavatthe karaṇavacanaṃ. Samannāgatāti samanuāgatā pavattā yuttā ca. Vācāti samullapanavācā. Yā sā “vācā girā byappatho”ti (dha. sa. 636) ca, “nelā kaṇṇasukhā”ti (dī. ni. 1.9; ma. ni. 3.14) ca evamādīsu āgacchati. Yā pana “vācāya ce kataṃ kamma”nti (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1 kāyakammadvāra) evaṃ viññatti ca, “yā catūhi vacīduccaritehi ārati virati…pe… ayaṃ vuccati sammāvācā”ti [P 2.0396] (dha. sa. 299; vibha. 206) evaṃ virati ca, “pharusavācā, bhikkhave, āsevitā bhāvitā bahulīkatā nirayasaṃvattanikā hotī”ti (a. ni. 8.40) evaṃ cetanā ca vācāti āgacchati, sā idha na adhippetā. Kasmā? Abhāsitabbato. Subhāsitā hotīti suṭṭhu bhāsitā hoti. Tenassā atthāvahanataṃ dīpeti. Na dubbhāsitāti na duṭṭhu bhāsitā. Tenassā anatthānāvahanataṃ dīpeti. Anavajjāti vajjasaṅkhātarāgādidosavirahitā. Tenassā kāraṇasuddhiṃ vuttadosābhāvañca dīpeti. Ananuvajjā cāti anuvādavimuttā. Tenassā sabbākārasampattiṃ dīpeti. Viññūnanti paṇḍitānaṃ.
