Tena nindāpasaṃsāsu bālā appamāṇāti dīpeti.

'With four factors' means with four causes or components. For abstinence from false speech and so forth are the four causes for well-spoken speech. Truthful speech and the other three are the four components, and the word 'factor' here has the sense of cause. The word 'with four' is a statement of separation; in the sense of components, it is a statement of instrument. 'Endowed' means accompanied by, proceeding with, and connected. 'Speech' refers to speech that articulates. It is the same as what is mentioned in phrases like 'speech, utterance, expression' and 'gentle, pleasing to the ear' and similar contexts. However, the 'speech' that is mentioned in phrases like 'action done by speech,' which refers to intimation; or 'abstaining, refraining from the four kinds of verbal misconduct... this is called right speech,' which refers to abstinence; or 'harsh speech, bhikkhus, when cultivated, developed, and frequently practiced, leads to hell,' which refers to volition—such 'speech' is not intended here. Why? Because these are not what is spoken. 'It is well-spoken' means it is excellently spoken. This highlights its ability to convey benefit. 'Not ill-spoken' means it is not badly spoken. This highlights its not conveying what is harmful. 'Blameless' means free from the faults called 'blame,' such as lust and other defilements. This highlights the purity of its cause and the absence of the stated faults. 'And irreproachable' means free from censure. This highlights its perfection in all aspects. 'By the wise' means by the learned. This shows that in blame and praise, fools are no measure.

Katamehi catūhīti kathetukamyatāpucchā. Idhāti imasmiṃ sāsane. Bhikkhaveti yesaṃ kathetukāmo, tadālapanaṃ. Bhikkhūti vuttappakāravācābhāsanakapuggalanidassanaṃ. Subhāsitaṃyeva bhāsatīti puggalādhiṭṭhānāya desanāya catūsu vācaṅgesu aññataraṅganiddesavacanaṃ. No dubbhāsitanti tasseva vācaṅgassa paṭipakkhabhāsananivāraṇaṃ. Tena “musāvādādayopi kadāci vattabbā”ti diṭṭhiṃ nisedheti. “No dubbhāsita”nti iminā vā micchāvācappahānaṃ dīpeti, “subhāsita”nti iminā pahīnamicchāvācena satā bhāsitabbavacanalakkhaṇaṃ. Tathā pāpassa akaraṇaṃ, kusalassa upasampadaṃ[M 2.0124]. Aṅgaparidīpanatthaṃ pana abhāsitabbaṃ pubbe avatvā bhāsitabbamevāha. Esa nayo dhammaṃyevātiādīsupi.

'By which four?' is a question expressing the desire to explain. 'Here' means in this Dispensation. 'Bhikkhus' is an address to those to whom he wishes to speak. 'A bhikkhu' indicates the person who speaks in the manner described. 'One speaks only what is well-spoken'—this is a statement specifying one of the four factors of speech in a teaching that is based on a person. 'Not what is ill-spoken'—this prevents speaking the opposite of that same factor of speech. Thereby, it rejects the view that 'false speech and the like should also sometimes be spoken.' By 'not what is ill-spoken' it indicates the abandoning of wrong speech; by 'what is well-spoken' it signifies the characteristic of the speech that should be spoken by one who has abandoned wrong speech. This is like the non-doing of evil and the undertaking of the wholesome. However, for the purpose of explaining the factors, he states what should be spoken without first stating what should not be spoken. This is the method also in such phrases as 'one speaks only the Dhamma,' and so forth.

Ettha ca “subhāsitaṃyeva bhāsati no dubbhāsita”nti iminā pisuṇadosarahitaṃ samaggakaraṇavacanaṃ vuttaṃ, “dhammaṃyeva bhāsati no adhamma”nti iminā samphadosarahitaṃ dhammato anapetaṃ mantāvacanaṃ vuttaṃ, itarehi dvīhi pharusālikarahitāni piyasaccavacanāni vuttāni. Imehi khotiādinā pana tāni aṅgāni paccakkhato dassento taṃ vācaṃ nigameti. Visesato cettha “imehi kho, bhikkhave[P 2.0397], catūhi aṅgehi samannāgatā vācā subhāsitā hotī”ti bhaṇanto [V 2.0113] yadaññe paṭiññādīhi avayavehi nāmādīhi padehi liṅgavacanavibhattikālakārakādīhi sampattīhi ca samannāgataṃ vācaṃ “subhāsita”nti maññanti, taṃ dhammato paṭisedheti. Avayavādisampannāpi hi pesuññādisamannāgatā vācā dubbhāsitāva hoti attano paresañca anatthāvahattā. Imehi pana catūhi aṅgehi samannāgatā sacepi milakkhubhāsāpariyāpannā ghaṭaceṭikāgītikapariyāpannā vā hoti, tathāpi subhāsitā eva lokiyalokuttarahitasukhāvahattā. Sīhaḷadīpe maggapasse sassaṃ rakkhantiyā sīhaḷaceṭikāya sīhaḷakeneva jātijarāmaraṇapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ gītaṃ gāyantiyā sutvā maggaṃ gacchantā saṭṭhimattā vipassakabhikkhū cettha arahattaṃ pattā nidassanaṃ. Tathā tisso nāma āraddhavipassako bhikkhu padumasarasamīpena gacchanto padumasare padumāni bhañjitvā bhañjitvā –

Here, by 'he speaks only what is well-spoken, not what is ill-spoken,' is meant speech that creates harmony, being free from the fault of slander. By 'he speaks only the Dhamma, not what is not the Dhamma,' is meant thoughtful speech, free from the fault of frivolous chatter and not deviating from the Dhamma. By the other two are meant pleasant and truthful words, which are devoid of harshness and falsehood. Then, by the passage beginning 'imehi kho,' he concludes by pointing out these factors directly. In particular, when he says, 'Monks, speech endowed with these four factors is well-spoken,' he thereby refutes the opinion of others who think that speech is 'well-spoken' when it is endowed with components such as propositions, with words such as nouns, and with accomplishments such as correctness of gender, number, case, tense, and agent. For even if speech is accomplished in its components, if it is accompanied by slander and so on, it is still ill-spoken because it brings harm to oneself and others. But speech endowed with these four factors, even if it is in a barbarian's tongue or is included in the songs of water-pot slave girls, is still well-spoken because it brings worldly and supramundane welfare and happiness. An example of this is on the island of Sri Lanka, where about sixty monks practicing insight meditation attained arahantship upon hearing a song connected with birth, aging, and death being sung in the Sinhalese language by a Sinhalese slave girl who was guarding the crops by the side of the road. Similarly, a monk named Tissa, who had undertaken insight meditation, was walking near a lotus pond, and breaking off lotuses one after another—

“Pāto phullaṃ kokanadaṃ, sūriyālokena bhajjiyate;

Evaṃ manussattagatā sattā, jarābhivegena maddīyantī”ti. –

"At dawn, a fully blossomed red lotus is shattered by the sunlight; so too, beings who have attained human existence are crushed by the onrush of old age."

Imaṃ gītaṃ gāyantiyā ceṭikāya sutvā arahattaṃ patto, buddhantare ca aññataro puriso sattahi puttehi saddhiṃ vanā āgamma aññatarāya itthiyā musalena taṇḍule koṭṭentiyā –

Having heard this song sung by the slave girl, he attained arahantship. And in the time of another Buddha, a certain man, coming from the forest with his seven sons, heard a certain woman pounding rice with a pestle and singing—

“Jarāya [M 2.0125] parimadditaṃ etaṃ, milātachavicammanissitaṃ;

Maraṇena bhijjati etaṃ, maccussa ghasamāmisaṃ.

"Crushed by old age is this, founded on withered skin and hide; Shattered by death is this, a morsel of flesh for Death.

“Kimīnaṃ ālayaṃ etaṃ, nānākuṇapena pūritaṃ;

Asucissa bhājanaṃ etaṃ, kadalikkhandhasamaṃ ida”nti. –

"This is an abode of worms, filled with various kinds of carrion; This is a vessel of impurity, like the trunk of a plantain tree."

Imaṃ [P 2.0398] gītikaṃ sutvā saha puttehi paccekabodhiṃ patto, aññe ca īdisehi upāyehi ariyabhūmiṃ pattā nidassanaṃ. Anacchariyaṃ panetaṃ, yaṃ bhagavatā āsayānusayakusalena “sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā”tiādinā nayena vuttā gāthāyo sutvā pañcasatā bhikkhū arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu, aññe ca khandhāyatanādipaṭisaṃyuttā kathā sutvā aneke devamanussāti. Evaṃ imehi catūhi aṅgehi samannāgatā vācā sacepi milakkhubhāsāpariyāpannā, ghaṭaceṭikāgītikapariyāpannā vā hoti, tathāpi “subhāsitā”ti veditabbā. Subhāsitattā eva ca anavajjā ca ananuvajjā ca viññūnaṃ atthatthikānaṃ kulaputtānaṃ atthapaṭisaraṇānaṃ, no byañjanapaṭisaraṇānanti.

Having heard this little song, he attained the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha together with his sons. And this is an example of how others have attained the noble stage by similar means. It is no wonder that when they heard the verses spoken by the Blessed One—who is skilled in dispositions and underlying tendencies—by the method beginning 'All conditioned things are impermanent,' five hundred monks attained arahantship, and many devas and humans did so upon hearing discourses connected with the aggregates, sense bases, and so on. Thus, speech endowed with these four factors, even if it is in a barbarian's tongue or is included in the songs of water-pot slave girls, is still to be understood as 'well-spoken.' And precisely because it is well-spoken, it is blameless and irreproachable for the wise, for clansmen who seek the meaning, who have the meaning as their resort, not the letter.

Idamavoca [V 2.0114] bhagavāti idaṃ subhāsitalakkhaṇaṃ bhagavā avoca. Idaṃ vatvāna sugato, athāparaṃ etadavoca satthāti idañca lakkhaṇaṃ vatvā atha aññampi etaṃ avoca satthā. Idāni vattabbagāthaṃ dassetvā sabbametaṃ saṅgītikārakā āhaṃsu. Tattha aparanti gāthābandhavacanaṃ sandhāya vuccati. Taṃ duvidhaṃ hoti – pacchā āgataparisaṃ assavanasussavanaādhāraṇadaḷhīkaraṇādīni vā sandhāya tadatthadīpakameva ca. Pubbe kenaci kāraṇena parihāpitassa atthassa dīpanena atthavisesadīpakañca “purisassa hi jātassa, kuṭhārī jāyate mukhe”tiādīsu (su. ni. 662) viya. Idha pana tadatthadīpakameva.

'The Blessed One spoke this' means: the Blessed One spoke this characteristic of well-spoken speech. 'Having said this, the Sugata, then the Teacher said this further' means: having spoken this characteristic, the Teacher then also spoke this other thing. Having now shown the verse to be spoken, the redactors of the council said all this. Herein, 'further' is said with reference to the speech bound in verse. This is of two kinds: it can be simply an illuminator of that same meaning, with reference to a later-arriving assembly for the sake of their hearing, listening well, retaining, strengthening, etc.; or it can be an illuminator of a special meaning by explaining a meaning that was previously omitted for some reason, as in passages such as 'For when a person is born, an axe is born in his mouth' (Snp 662). Here, however, it is simply an illuminator of that same meaning.

453. Tattha santoti buddhādayo. Te hi subhāsitaṃ “uttamaṃ seṭṭha”nti vaṇṇayanti. Dutiyaṃ tatiyaṃ catutthanti idaṃ pana pubbe niddiṭṭhakkamaṃ upādāya vuttaṃ. Gāthāpariyosāne pana vaṅgīsatthero bhagavato subhāsite pasīdi.

453. Herein, 'the peaceful' means the Buddhas and others. For they praise well-spoken speech as 'supreme, best.' 'The second, the third, and the fourth' is said with reference to the order indicated previously. At the conclusion of the verses, the Elder Vaṅgīsa gained confidence in the Blessed One’s well-spoken words.

So yaṃ pasannākāraṃ akāsi, yañca vacanaṃ bhagavā abhāsi, taṃ dassentā saṅgītikārakā “atha kho āyasmā”tiādimāhaṃsu. Tattha [M 2.0126] paṭibhāti manti mama bhāgo pakāsati[P 2.0399]. Paṭibhātu tanti tava bhāgo pakāsatu. Sāruppāhīti anucchavikāhi. Abhitthavīti pasaṃsi.

In order to show the expression of confidence he made and the words the Blessed One spoke, the redactors of the council said the passage beginning, 'Then the Venerable…' Herein, 'it occurs to me' means 'my part becomes manifest.' 'May it occur to you' means 'may your part become manifest.' 'With suitable (verses)' means 'with fitting (verses).' 'He extolled' means 'he praised.'

454. Na tāpayeti vippaṭisārena na tāpeyya. Na vihiṃseyyāti aññamaññaṃ bhindanto na bādheyya. Sā ve vācāti sā vācā ekaṃseneva subhāsitā. Ettāvatā apisuṇavācāya bhagavantaṃ thometi.

454. 'One should not torment oneself' means: one should not torment oneself with remorse. 'Nor does one harm another' means: one should not harm another by causing division among others. 'That indeed is speech' means: that speech is definitely well-spoken. With this, he praises the Blessed One for his non-slanderous speech.

455. Paṭinanditāti haṭṭhena hadayena paṭimukhaṃ gantvā nanditā sampiyāyitā. Yaṃ anādāya pāpāni, paresaṃ bhāsate piyanti yaṃ vācaṃ bhāsanto paresaṃ pāpāni appiyāni paṭikkūlāni pharusavacanāni anādāya atthabyañjanamadhuraṃ piyameva vacanaṃ bhāsati, taṃ piyavācameva bhāseyyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Imāya gāthāya piyavacanena bhagavantaṃ abhitthavi.

455. 'Welcomed' means welcomed face-to-face with a joyful heart, delighted, cherished. 'What one speaks that is pleasing to others, without having taken up what is evil' means: when one speaks, one does not take up the evil, unpleasing, repulsive, and harsh words of others, but speaks only pleasing words that are sweet in meaning and expression. Thus it is said that one should speak only pleasant speech. With this verse, he extolled the Blessed One for his pleasant speech.

456. Amatāti amatasadisā sādubhāvena. Vuttampi cetaṃ “saccaṃ have sādutaraṃ rasāna”nti (saṃ. ni. 1.73; su. ni. 184). Nibbānāmatapaccayattā vā amatā. Esa dhammo sanantanoti yāyaṃ saccavācā nāma, esa porāṇo dhammo cariyā paveṇī, idameva hi porāṇānaṃ āciṇṇaṃ, na te alikaṃ bhāsiṃsu. Tenevāha – “sacce atthe ca dhamme ca, ahu [V 2.0115] santo patiṭṭhitā”ti. Tattha sacce patiṭṭhitattā eva attano ca paresañca atthe patiṭṭhitā. Atthe patiṭṭhitattā eva ca dhamme patiṭṭhitā hontīti veditabbā. Paraṃ vā dvayaṃ saccavisesanamicceva veditabbaṃ. Sacce patiṭṭhitā. Kīdise? Atthe ca dhamme ca, yaṃ paresaṃ atthato anapetattā atthaṃ anuparodhaṃ karotīti vuttaṃ hoti. Satipi ca anuparodhakaratte dhammato anapetattā dhammaṃ, yaṃ dhammikameva atthaṃ sādhetīti vuttaṃ hoti. Imāya gāthāya saccavacanena bhagavantaṃ abhitthavi.

456. 'Deathless' means like the deathless because of its sweetness. And this is said: 'Truth, indeed, is the sweetest of tastes.' Or it is deathless because it is a condition for the deathless, Nibbāna. 'This is the eternal Dhamma' means: this which is called truthful speech is the ancient Dhamma, the conduct, the tradition. For this is what the ancients were accustomed to; they did not speak falsely. Therefore it is said: 'In truth, in welfare, and in the Dhamma, the peaceful were established.' Herein, it is because they are established in truth that they are established in their own welfare and that of others. And it should be understood that it is because they are established in welfare that they are established in the Dhamma. Or, the latter two should be understood simply as qualifiers of 'truth.' Established in truth. Of what kind? In welfare and in the Dhamma. This means that because it does not deviate from the welfare of others, it does not obstruct their welfare. And although it does not cause obstruction, because it does not deviate from the Dhamma, it accomplishes only a righteous welfare. With this verse, he extolled the Blessed One for his truthful speech.

457. Khemanti abhayaṃ nirupaddavaṃ. Kena kāraṇenāti ce? Nibbānappattiyā dukkhassantakiriyāya, yasmā kilesanibbānaṃ pāpeti, vaṭṭadukkhassa ca antakiriyāya saṃvattatīti attho. Atha vā yaṃ buddho nibbānappattiyā dukkhassantakiriyāyāti dvinnaṃ nibbānadhātūnamatthāya khemamaggappakāsanato khemaṃ vācaṃ bhāsati, sā ve vācānamuttamāti sā vācā sabbavācānaṃ [P 2.0400] seṭṭhāti [M 2.0127] evamettha attho veditabbo. Imāya gāthāya mantāvacanena bhagavantaṃ abhitthavanto arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesīti ayamettha apubbapadavaṇṇanā. Sesaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbanti.

457. 'Secure' means safe, free from affliction. If it is asked, 'For what reason?' For the attainment of Nibbāna, for making an end of suffering. The meaning is that since it makes one attain the nibbāna of the defilements, it conduces to the ending of the suffering of the round. Or, because the Buddha speaks the secure word for the sake of attaining Nibbāna, for making an end of suffering—that is, for the sake of the two Nibbāna-elements by revealing the secure path—'that is indeed the ultimate among speeches' means that speech is the best of all speeches. Thus the meaning should be understood here. Extolling the Blessed One with this verse of thoughtful speech, he concluded the discourse with the peak of arahantship. This here is the explanation of the unprecedented words. The rest should be understood in the way already stated.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya subhāsitasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Subhāsita Sutta in the Commentary on the Suttanipāta is finished.

4. Pūraḷāsasutta-(sundarikabhāradvājasutta)-vaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Pūraḷāsa Sutta (Sundarikabhāradvāja Sutta)

Evaṃ [V 2.0116] me sutanti pūraḷāsasuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Bhagavā pacchābhattakiccāvasāne buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ volokento sundarikabhāradvājabrāhmaṇaṃ arahattassa upanissayasampannaṃ disvā “tattha mayi gate kathā pavattissati, tato kathāvasāne dhammadesanaṃ sutvā esa brāhmaṇo pabbajitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇissatī”ti ca ñatvā tattha gantvā kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā imaṃ suttamabhāsi.

Thus have I heard—this is the Pūraḷāsa Sutta. What is its origin? The Blessed One, at the conclusion of his duties after the meal, was surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, and he saw the brahmin Sundarikabhāradvāja who was endowed with the supporting conditions for arahantship. Having known: 'When I go there, a conversation will arise. Then, at the conclusion of the conversation, after hearing the Dhamma teaching, this brahmin will go forth and attain arahantship,' he went there, initiated a conversation, and spoke this sutta.

Tattha evaṃ me sutantiādi saṅgītikārakānaṃ vacanaṃ. Kiṃjacco bhavantiādi tassa brāhmaṇassa, na brāhmaṇo nomhītiādi bhagavato. Taṃ sabbampi samodhānetvā “pūraḷāsasutta”nti vuccati. Tattha vuttasadisaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ, avuttaṃ vaṇṇayissāma, tañca kho uttānatthāni padāni anāmasantā. Kosalesūti kosalā nāma jānapadino rājakumārā. Tesaṃ nivāso ekopi janapado ruḷhisaddena “kosalā”ti vuccati. Tasmiṃ kosalesu janapade. Keci pana “yasmā pubbe mahāpanādaṃ rājakumāraṃ nānānāṭakādīni disvā sitamattampi akarontaṃ sutvā rājā āṇāpesi ‘yo mama puttaṃ hasāpeti, sabbābharaṇehi naṃ alaṅkaromī’ti. Tato naṅgalāni chaḍḍetvā mahājanakāyo sannipati. Te ca manussā atirekasattavassāni nānākīḷikādayo dassentāpi taṃ nāsakkhiṃsu hasāpetuṃ. Tato sakko devanaṭaṃ pesesi, so dibbanāṭakaṃ [P 2.0401] dassetvā hasāpesi. Atha te manussā attano attano vasanokāsābhimukhā pakkamiṃsu. Te paṭipathe mittasuhajjādayo disvā paṭisanthāramakaṃsu ‘kacci bho kusalaṃ, kacci bho kusala’nti[M 2.0128]. Tasmā taṃ ‘kusala’nti saddaṃ upādāya so padeso ‘kosalo’ti vuccatī”ti vaṇṇayanti. Sundarikāya nadiyā tīreti sundarikāti evaṃnāmikāya nadiyā tīre.

Herein, 'Thus have I heard,' and so on, is the utterance of the reciters at the council. 'Of what birth are you?' and so on, is the brahmin's. 'I am not a brahmin,' and so on, is the Blessed One's. Combining all this, it is called the 'Pūraḷāsa Sutta.' Herein, what has been said should be understood in the manner it has been said; we will explain what has not been said, without touching upon the words with obvious meanings. Kosalesu: the Kosalans are the royal princes who are inhabitants of the country. Their residence, though a single country, is called 'Kosala' by convention. In that Kosalan country. Some, however, explain it thus: 'Formerly, having heard that Prince Mahāpanāda did not even smile upon seeing various dramas and the like, the king issued an order: "Whoever makes my son laugh, I will adorn him with every ornament." Then a great crowd assembled, leaving their plows. But though those people showed him various kinds of entertainment for more than seven years, they could not make him laugh. Then Sakka sent a divine actor, who made him laugh by showing him a celestial drama. Then those people departed towards their own dwelling places. On the way, seeing friends and companions, they exchanged greetings, saying: "Are you well, sir? Are you well?" (kacci bho kusalaṃ). Therefore, based on that word kusala, that region came to be called 'Kosala'.' Sundarikāya nadiyā tīre (on the bank of the river Sundarikā) means: on the bank of the river named Sundarikā.

Tena kho panāti yena samayena bhagavā taṃ brāhmaṇaṃ vinetukāmo gantvā tassā nadiyā tīre sasīsaṃ pārupitvā rukkhamūle nisajjāsaṅkhātena iriyāpathavihārena viharati. Sundarikabhāradvājoti so brāhmaṇo tassā nadiyā tīre vasati aggiñca juhati, bhāradvājoti cassa gottaṃ, tasmā evaṃ vuccati. Aggiṃ juhatīti āhutipakkhipanena jāleti. Aggihuttaṃ paricaratīti [V 2.0117] agyāyatanaṃ sammajjanūpalepanabalikammādinā payirupāsati. Ko nu kho imaṃ habyasesaṃ bhuñjeyyāti so kira brāhmaṇo aggimhi juhitvā avasesaṃ pāyāsaṃ disvā cintesi – “aggimhi tāva pakkhittapāyāso mahābrahmunā bhutto, ayaṃ pana avaseso atthi. Taṃ yadi brahmuno mukhato jātassa brāhmaṇasseva dadeyyaṃ, evaṃ me pitarā saha puttopi santappito bhaveyya, suvisodhito ca brahmalokagāmimaggo assa, handāhaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ gavesāmī”ti. Tato brāhmaṇadassanatthaṃ uṭṭhāyāsanā catuddisā anuvilokesi – “ko nu kho imaṃ habyasesaṃ bhuñjeyyā”ti.

Tena kho pana (At that time): at the time when the Blessed One, wishing to train that brahmin, went to the bank of that river, covered himself including his head, and was dwelling at the foot of a tree in the posture of sitting. Sundarikabhāradvāja: that brahmin dwells on the bank of that river and tends the fire; Bhāradvāja is his clan name, thus he is so called. Aggiṃ juhati (He tends the fire) means: he kindles it by casting in oblations. Aggihuttaṃ paricarati (He attends to the fire-oblation) means: he serves the fire-place by sweeping, smearing, making offerings, and so on. Ko nu kho imaṃ habyasesaṃ bhuñjeyyā (Now who might eat this remainder of the oblation?): it is said that the brahmin, having made his offering in the fire and seeing the remaining rice-porridge, thought: 'The rice-porridge cast into the fire has been eaten by Mahābrahmā, but this remainder exists. If I were to give it to a brahmin born from Brahmā’s mouth, then my son and I would be gratified along with my father, and the path leading to the Brahmā-world would be well-cleared. Well now, I will look for a brahmin.' Then, rising from his seat to see a brahmin, he looked around in the four directions, thinking: 'Now who might eat this remainder of the oblation?'

Aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūleti tasmiṃ vanasaṇḍe seṭṭharukkhamūle. Sasīsaṃ pārutanti saha sīsena pārutakāyaṃ. Kasmā pana bhagavā evamakāsi, kiṃ nārāyanasaṅkhātabalopi hutvā nāsakkhi himapātaṃ sītavātañca paṭibāhitunti? Atthetaṃ kāraṇaṃ. Na hi buddhā sabbaso kāyapaṭijagganaṃ karonti eva, apica bhagavā “āgate brāhmaṇe sīsaṃ vivarissāmi, maṃ disvā brāhmaṇo kathaṃ pavattessati, athassa kathānusārena dhammaṃ desessāmī”ti kathāpavattanatthaṃ evamakāsi. Disvāna vāmena…pe… tenupasaṅkamīti [P 2.0402] so kira bhagavantaṃ disvā brāhmaṇo “ayaṃ sasīsaṃ pārupitvā sabbarattiṃ padhānamanuyutto, imassa dakkhiṇodakaṃ datvā imaṃ habyasesaṃ dassāmī”ti brāhmaṇasaññī hutvā eva upasaṅkami. Muṇḍo ayaṃ bhavaṃ, muṇḍako ayaṃ bhavanti sīse vivaritamatteva kesantaṃ disvā “muṇḍo”ti āha. Tato suṭṭhutaraṃ olokento parittampi sikhaṃ adisvā [M 2.0129] hīḷento “muṇḍako”ti āha. Evarūpā hi nesaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ diṭṭhi. Tato vāti yattha ṭhito addasa, tamhā padesā muṇḍāpīti kenaci kāraṇena muṇḍitasīsāpi honti.

Aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle (at the foot of a certain tree) means: at the foot of the best tree in that forest grove. Sasīsaṃ pārutaṃ (covered including his head) means: with his body covered along with his head. But why did the Blessed One do this? Was he, though possessing the strength of Nārāyaṇa, unable to ward off the falling snow and the cold wind? There is a reason. Buddhas do not always attend to the care of the body. Moreover, the Blessed One did so to initiate a conversation, thinking: 'When the brahmin comes, I will uncover my head. Seeing me, the brahmin will start a conversation, and then I will teach him the Dhamma according to the course of the conversation.' Disvāna vāmena…pe… tenupasaṅkami (Having seen with his left... he approached): it is said that when the brahmin saw the Blessed One, he thought, 'This person has been striving all night, covered including his head. I will give him this remainder of the oblation after giving the dedicatory water,' and so he approached, perceiving him to be a brahmin. Muṇḍo ayaṃ bhavaṃ, muṇḍako ayaṃ bhavaṃ (This venerable one is a shaveling, this venerable one is a mere shaveling): as soon as the Blessed One uncovered his head, seeing his hair, he said, 'A shaveling!' Then, looking more closely and not seeing even a small topknot, he said scornfully, 'A mere shaveling!' For such is the view of those brahmins. Tato vā (Thence): from the place where he stood and saw him. Muṇḍāpi (shavelings too): for some reason their heads are shaven.

458. Na brāhmaṇo nomhīti ettha nakāro paṭisedhe, nokāro avadhāraṇe “na no sama”ntiādīsu (khu. pā. 6.3; su. ni. 226) viya. Tena nevamhi brāhmaṇoti dasseti. Na rājaputtoti khattiyo namhi. Na vessāyanoti vessopi namhi. Udakoci nomhīti aññopi suddo vā caṇḍālo vā koci na homīti evaṃ ekaṃseneva jātivādasamudācāraṃ paṭikkhipati. Kasmā? Mahāsamuddaṃ pattā viya hi nadiyo pabbajjūpagatā kulaputtā jahanti purimāni nāmagottāni. Pahārādasuttañcettha (a. ni. 8.19) sādhakaṃ. Evaṃ jātivādaṃ paṭikkhipitvā yathābhūtamattānaṃ āvikaronto āha – “gottaṃ pariññāya puthujjanānaṃ, akiñcano manta carāmi loke”ti. Kathaṃ gottaṃ pariññāsīti ce? Bhagavā hi tīhi pariññāhi pañcakkhandhe pariññāsi, tesu ca pariññātesu gottaṃ pariññātameva hoti. Rāgādikiñcanānaṃ pana abhāvena so akiñcano mantā jānitvā ñāṇānuparivattīhi kāyakammādīhi [V 2.0118] carati. Tenāha – “gottaṃ…pe… loke”ti. Mantā vuccati paññā, tāya cesa carati. Tenevāha – “mantaṃ carāmi loke”ti chandavasena rassaṃ katvā.

458. In the phrase Na brāhmaṇo nomhi (I am not a brahmin), the particle na is for negation, and the particle no is for emphasis, as in na no sama (not equal to us). Thus he shows: 'I am certainly not a brahmin.' Na rājaputto (Not a prince) means: I am not a khattiya. Na vessāyano (Not a vessa-son) means: I am not a vessa. Udakoci nomhi (Nor am I anyone else) means: I am not a sudda or a caṇḍāla or anyone else. In this way he categorically rejects the conventions of birth-distinction. Why? Because just as rivers that have reached the great ocean give up their former names and families, so clansmen who have gone forth give up their former names and clans. The Pahārāda Sutta (AN 8.19) is evidence here. Having thus rejected birth-distinction, revealing his true nature, he said: 'Having fully understood the clan of ordinary people, possessionless, a knower, I wander in the world.' How did he fully understand clan? The Blessed One fully understood the five aggregates by means of the three kinds of full understanding; and when these were fully understood, clan was also fully understood. Because of the absence of impediments such as lust, he is possessionless. As a knower (mantā), having known, he fares on with bodily actions, etc., that revolve in accordance with knowledge. Thus he said: 'Having fully understood the clan... I wander in the world.' Mantā is called wisdom; he fares on with that. Therefore he said mantaṃ carāmi loke, shortening the vowel for the sake of the meter.

459-60. Evaṃ attānaṃ āvikatvā idāni “evaṃ oḷārikaṃ liṅgampi disvā pucchitabbāpucchitabbaṃ na jānāsī”ti brāhmaṇassa upārambhaṃ āropento āha – “saṅghāṭivāsī…pe… gottapañha”nti. Ettha ca chinnasaṅghaṭitaṭṭhena tīṇipi cīvarāni “saṅghāṭī”ti adhippetāni, tāni nivāseti paridahatīti [P 2.0403] saṅghāṭivāsī. Agahoti ageho, nittaṇhoti adhippāyo. Nivāsāgāraṃ pana bhagavato jetavane mahāgandhakuṭikarerimaṇḍalamāḷakosambakuṭicandanamālādianekappakāraṃ, taṃ sandhāya na yujjati. Nivuttakesoti apanītakeso, ohāritakesamassūti vuttaṃ hoti. Abhinibbutattoti atīva vūpasantapariḷāhacitto, guttacitto vā. Alippamāno idha māṇavehīti upakaraṇasinehassa pahīnattā manussehi alitto asaṃsaṭṭho ekantavivitto. Akallaṃ maṃ brāhmaṇāti yvāhaṃ [M 2.0130] evaṃ saṅghāṭivāsī…pe… alippamāno idha māṇavehi, taṃ maṃ tvaṃ, brāhmaṇa, pākatikāni nāmagottāni atītaṃ pabbajitaṃ samānaṃ appatirūpaṃ gottapañhaṃ pucchasīti.

459-60. Having thus revealed himself, he now reproaches the brahmin, saying: 'Seeing such a gross sign, you do not know what is fit and unfit to be asked.' He said: 'Wearing the patchwork robe... a question about clan.' Here, because they are cut and sewn together, all three robes are intended by the word saṅghāṭī. Saṅghāṭivāsī (wearing the patchwork robe) means one who wears them, who puts them on. Agaho (houseless) means without a house; the meaning is 'without craving.' This is not said in reference to the Blessed One's dwelling place, which was of many kinds, such as the Great Fragrant Chamber, the Kareri-tree Pavilion, the Kosamba Hut, and the Sandalwood Pavilion in the Jeta Grove. Nivuttakeso (with hair cut off) means with hair removed; that is, with hair and beard shaved. Abhinibbutatto (with self extinguished) means with a mind whose feverish distress is extremely well-calmed, or with a guarded mind. Alippamāno idha māṇavehi (unsmeared here by men) means, because affection for requisites has been abandoned, he is unsullied by people, unassociated, completely secluded. Akallaṃ maṃ brāhmaṇa (It is not proper, brahmin, for you to ask me) means: 'Brahmin, you ask me—who am thus one who wears the patchwork robe... unsmeared here by men, who have gone forth and am beyond ordinary name and clan—an improper question about clan.'

Evaṃ vutte upārambhaṃ mocento brāhmaṇo āha – pucchanti ve, bho brāhmaṇā, brāhmaṇebhi saha “brāhmaṇo no bhava”nti. Tattha brāhmaṇo noti brāhmaṇo nūti attho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – nāhaṃ bho akallaṃ pucchāmi. Amhākañhi brāhmaṇasamaye brāhmaṇā brāhmaṇehi saha samāgantvā “brāhmaṇo nu bhavaṃ, bhāradvājo nu bhava”nti evaṃ jātimpi gottampi pucchanti evāti.

When this was said, the brahmin, deflecting the reproach, said: 'Sirs, brahmins indeed ask other brahmins: "Are you a brahmin, sir?"' Here, brāhmaṇo no means brāhmaṇo nu (are you a brahmin?). This is what is said: 'Sir, I am not asking improperly. For it is our brahmin custom that when brahmins meet with other brahmins, they ask about both birth and clan, saying: "Are you a brahmin, sir? Are you a Bhāradvāja, sir?"'

461-2. Evaṃ vutte bhagavā brāhmaṇassa cittamudubhāvakaraṇatthaṃ mantesu attano pakataññutaṃ pakāsento āha – “brāhmaṇo hi ce tvaṃ brūsi…pe… catuvīsatakkhara”nti. Tassattho – sace tvaṃ “brāhmaṇo ahaṃ”ti brūsi, mañca abrāhmaṇaṃ brūsi, tasmā bhavantaṃ sāvittiṃ pucchāmi tipadaṃ catuvīsatakkharaṃ, taṃ me brūhīti. Ettha ca bhagavā paramatthavedānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ piṭakānaṃ ādibhūtaṃ paramatthabrāhmaṇehi sabbabuddhehi pakāsitaṃ atthasampannaṃ byañjanasampannañca “buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, dhammaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, saṅghaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmī”ti imaṃ ariyasāvittiṃ sandhāya pucchati. Yadipi hi brāhmaṇo aññaṃ vadeyya, addhā naṃ bhagavā “nāyaṃ, brāhmaṇa, ariyassa vinaye sāvittīti vuccatī”ti tassa asārakattaṃ dassetvā idheva patiṭṭhāpeyya. Brāhmaṇo pana “sāvittiṃ pucchāmi tipadaṃ [P 2.0404] catuvīsatakkhara”nti idaṃ attano samayasiddhaṃ sāvittilakkhaṇabyañjanakaṃ brahmassarena nicchāritavacanaṃ sutvāva “addhāyaṃ samaṇo brāhmaṇasamaye [V 2.0119] niṭṭhaṃ gato, ahaṃ pana aññāṇena ‘abrāhmaṇo aya’nti paribhaviṃ, sādhurūpo mantapāragū brāhmaṇova eso”ti niṭṭhaṃ gantvā “handa naṃ yaññavidhiṃ dakkhiṇeyyavidhiñca pucchāmī”ti tamatthaṃ pucchanto “kiṃnissitā…pe… loke”ti imaṃ visamagāthāpadattayamāha. Tassattho – kiṃnissitā kimadhippāyā kiṃ patthentā isayo ca khattiyā ca brāhmaṇā ca aññe ca manujā devatānaṃ atthāya yaññaṃ akappayiṃsu. Yaññamakappayiṃsūti makāro padasandhikaro. Akappayiṃsūti saṃvidahiṃsu akaṃsu. Puthūti bahū annapānadānādinā bhedena anekappakāre puthū vā isayo manujā khattiyā brāhmaṇā ca kiṃnissitā [M 2.0131] yaññamakappayiṃsu. Kathaṃ nesaṃ taṃ kammaṃ samijjhatīti iminādhippāyena pucchati.

461-2. When this was said, the Blessed One, in order to soften the brahmin’s mind and to reveal his own profound knowledge of the sacred verses, said: 'If you say you are a brahmin…pe… the twenty-four syllable verse.' The meaning is: If you say, 'I am a brahmin,' and call me a non-brahmin, then I ask you about the Sāvittī, the three-footed, twenty-four-syllable verse—tell it to me. Here, the Blessed One asks this with reference to the noble Sāvittī—'I go for refuge to the Buddha, I go for refuge to the Dhamma, I go for refuge to the Saṅgha'—which is the foundation of the three Piṭakas, the ultimate Vedas, is rich in meaning and phrasing, and was proclaimed by all the Buddhas, the supreme brahmins who have realized the ultimate truth. For if the brahmin were to recite something else, the Blessed One would surely show its lack of substance by saying, 'This, brahmin, is not called the Sāvittī in the discipline of the noble ones,' and would establish him right there. But when he heard the Buddha's words, which described the Sāvittī established in his own tradition and were uttered with a Brahmā-like voice, he concluded: 'Surely this ascetic is well-versed in brahminical lore, whereas I, out of ignorance, disparaged him as a non-brahmin. He is truly a brahmin of good character, a master of the sacred verses.' Having concluded this, he thought, 'Come, I will ask him about the sacrificial procedure and the proper recipients of offerings.' Asking about this matter, he spoke these three irregular verse-lines: 'Relying on what…pe… in the world.' The meaning is: Relying on what, with what intention, desiring what, did the seers, khattiyas, brahmins, and other humans perform sacrifices for the sake of the deities? In yaññamakappayiṃsu, the 'm' is a euphonic consonant. Akappayiṃsu means they arranged, they performed. Puthū means many; that is, relying on what did the many seers, humans, khattiyas, and brahmins, of various kinds distinguished by giving food and drink, perform sacrifices? He asks with the intention: 'How does that action of theirs succeed?'

463. Athassa bhagavā tamatthaṃ byākaronto “yadantagū vedagū yaññakāle. Yassāhutiṃ labhe tassijjheti brūmī”ti idaṃ sesapadadvayamāha. Tattha yadantagūti yo antagū, okārassa akāro, dakāro ca padasandhikaro “asādhāraṇamaññesa”ntiādīsu (khu. pā. 8.9) makāro viya. Ayaṃ pana attho – yo vaṭṭadukkhassa tīhi pariññāhi antagatattā antagū, catūhi ca maggañāṇavedehi kilese vijjhitvā gatattā vedagū, so yassa isimanujakhattiyabrāhmaṇānaṃ aññatarassa yaññakāle yasmiṃ kismiñci āhāre paccupaṭṭhite antamaso vanapaṇṇamūlaphalādimhipi āhutiṃ labhe, tato kiñci deyyadhammaṃ labheyya, tassa taṃ yaññakammaṃ ijjhe samijjheyya, mahapphalaṃ bhaveyyāti brūmīti.

463. Then the Blessed One, explaining that meaning, spoke these remaining two lines: 'One who has reached the end, a knower of the Vedas, at the time of sacrifice—if he should receive an offering, that sacrifice succeeds, I say.' Herein, yadantagū means yo antagū (one who has reached the end); the 'o' sound changes to 'a', and the 'd' is a euphonic consonant, like the 'm' in 'asādhāraṇamaññesaṃ' (Khp 8.9). The meaning is this: One who, having reached the end of the suffering of the round of existence through the threefold full understanding, is an 'end-reacher' (antagū), and who, having pierced the defilements with the fourfold path-knowledge, is a 'Veda-knower' (vedagū)—at the time of sacrifice, when any offering, be it food or even forest leaves, roots, or fruits, is presented to one among seers, humans, khattiyas, or brahmins, if he receives any gift-worthy thing, I declare that his sacrificial act will succeed, be accomplished, and be of great fruit.

464. Atha brāhmaṇo taṃ bhagavato paramatthayogagambhīraṃ atimadhuragiranibbikārasarasampannaṃ desanaṃ sutvā [P 2.0405] sarīrasampattisūcitañcassa sabbaguṇasampattiṃ sambhāvayamāno pītisomanassajāto “addhā hi tassā”ti gāthamāha. Tattha iti brāhmaṇoti saṅgītikārānaṃ vacanaṃ, sesaṃ brāhmaṇassa. Tassattho – addhā hi tassa mayhaṃ hutamijjhe, ayaṃ ajja deyyadhammo ijjhissati samijjhissati mahapphalo bhavissati yaṃ tādisaṃ vedagumaddasāma, yasmā tādisaṃ bhavantarūpaṃ vedaguṃ addasāma. Tvaññeva hi so vedagū, na añño. Ito pubbe pana tumhādisānaṃ vedagūnaṃ antagūnañca adassanena amhādisānaṃ yaññe paṭiyattaṃ añño jano bhuñjati pūraḷāsaṃ carukañca pūvañcāti.

464. Then the brahmin, having heard the Blessed One’s teaching—profound in its connection to the ultimate meaning, supremely sweet in speech, flawless and rich in tone—and appreciating the perfection of all virtues indicated by his physical perfection, became filled with joy and gladness and spoke this verse: 'Surely, for him…' Herein, 'Thus the brahmin…' is the compilers’ statement; the rest belongs to the brahmin. The meaning is: Surely my sacrifice offered to him will succeed; this gift today will succeed, will be accomplished, and will be of great fruit, for we have seen such a Veda-knower; because we have seen such a one who has reached the end of existence, a Veda-knower. Indeed, you are that Veda-knower, no other. But before this, not having seen such Veda-knowers and end-reachers as you, other people would consume the sacrificial cake, the gruel, and the sweet cakes prepared for our sacrifices.

465. Tato bhagavā attani pasannaṃ vacanapaṭiggahaṇasajjaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ viditvā yathāssa suṭṭhu pākaṭā honti, evaṃ nānappakārehi dakkhiṇeyye pakāsetukāmo “tasmātiha tva”nti gāthamāha. Tassattho – yasmā mayi pasannosi, tasmā pana iha tvaṃ, brāhmaṇa, upasaṅkamma pucchāti attānaṃ [V 2.0120] dassento āha. Idāni ito pubbaṃ atthenaatthikapadaṃ parapadena sambandhitabbaṃ – atthena atthiko tassa atthatthikabhāvassa anurūpaṃ kilesaggivūpasamena santaṃ, kodhadhūmavigamena vidhūmaṃ, dukkhābhāvena [M 2.0132] anīghaṃ, anekavidhaāsābhāvena nirāsaṃ appevidha ekaṃsena idha ṭhitova idha vā sāsane abhivinde lacchasi adhigacchissasi sumedhaṃ varapaññaṃ khīṇāsavadakkhiṇeyyanti. Atha vā yasmā mayi pasannosi, tasmātiha, tvaṃ brāhmaṇa, atthena atthiko samāno upasaṅkamma puccha santaṃ vidhūmaṃ anīghaṃ nirāsanti attānaṃ dassento āha. Evaṃ pucchanto appevidha abhivinde sumedhaṃ khīṇāsavadakkhiṇeyyanti evampettha yojanā veditabbā.

465. Then the Blessed One, knowing the brahmin was pleased with him and ready to receive his words, and wishing to explain in various ways those worthy of offerings so they would become very clear to him, spoke this verse: 'Therefore, you here…' The meaning is this. First, one way to construe the verse: 'Because you are pleased with me, therefore, brahmin, approach and ask.' The Buddha says this pointing to himself. 'You who have need of the goal'—in a way suitable to that state—'might find here'—that is, established in this very life or in this Dispensation, you will certainly find, get, attain—one who is 'peaceful' through the calming of the fire of defilements, 'smokeless' through the departure of the smoke of anger, 'untroubled' through the absence of suffering, 'free from craving' through the absence of many kinds of hope; you might find, O wise one, one of excellent wisdom, a worthy recipient whose taints are destroyed. Or else, the construction is: 'Because you are pleased with me, therefore, brahmin, being one who has need of the goal, approach and ask me'—he said this, pointing to himself as one who is 'peaceful, smokeless, untroubled, and free from craving.' 'Asking thus, you might find here, O wise one, a worthy recipient whose taints are destroyed.' Thus the construction should be understood here.

466. Atha brāhmaṇo yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjamāno bhagavantaṃ āha – “yaññe ratohaṃ…pe… brūhi meta”nti. Tattha yañño yāgo dānanti atthato ekaṃ. Tasmā [P 2.0406] dānarato ahaṃ, tāya eva dānārāmatāya dānaṃ dātukāmo, na pana jānāmi, evaṃ ajānantaṃ anusāsatu maṃ bhavaṃ. Anusāsanto ca uttāneneva nayena yattha hutaṃ ijjhate brūhi metanti evamettha atthayojanā veditabbā. “Yathāhuta”ntipi pāṭho.

466. Then the brahmin, following the instruction, said to the Blessed One: 'I delight in sacrifice…pe… tell me this.' Herein, sacrifice (yañña), offering (yāga), and gift (dāna) are the same in meaning. Therefore, the meaning is: 'I delight in giving, and because of that very delight in giving, I desire to give, but I do not know. Instruct me, venerable sir, who am thus unknowing. And in instructing me, explain in a straightforward manner where an offering succeeds.' Thus the connection of meaning should be understood here. There is also the reading 'as offered' (yathāhutaṃ).

467. Athassa bhagavā vattukāmo āha – “tena hi…pe… desessāmī”ti. Ohitasotassa cassa anusāsanatthaṃ tāva “mā jātiṃ pucchī”ti gāthamāha. Tattha mā jātiṃ pucchīti yadi hutasamiddhiṃ dānamahapphalataṃ paccāsīsasi, jātiṃ mā puccha. Akāraṇañhi dakkhiṇeyyavicāraṇāya jāti. Caraṇañca pucchāti apica kho sīlādiguṇabhedaṃ caraṇaṃ puccha. Etañhi dakkhiṇeyyavicāraṇāya kāraṇaṃ.

467. Then the Blessed One, wishing to speak, said: 'Then listen…pe… I will teach.' And for the purpose of instructing him, as he was listening attentively, he first spoke the verse: 'Do not ask about birth…' Herein, 'Do not ask about birth' means: if you hope for the success of the offering and the great fruit of the gift, do not ask about birth. For birth is not a reason for investigating the worthiness of a recipient. 'But ask about conduct' means: you should ask about conduct, which is distinguished by qualities such as virtue. For this is a reason for investigating the worthiness of a recipient.

Idānissa tamatthaṃ vibhāvento nidassanamāha – “kaṭṭhā have jāyati jātavedo”tiādi. Tatrāyamadhippāyo – idha kaṭṭhā aggi jāyati, na ca so sālādikaṭṭhā jāto eva aggikiccaṃ karoti, sāpānadoṇiādikaṭṭhā jāto na karoti, apica kho attano acciādiguṇasampannattā eva karoti. Evaṃ na brāhmaṇakulādīsu jāto eva dakkhiṇeyyo hoti, caṇḍālakulādīsu jāto na hoti, apica kho nīcākulīnopi uccākulīnopi khīṇāsavamuni dhitimā hirīnisedho ājāniyo hoti, imāya dhitihiripamukhāya guṇasampattiyā jātimā uttamadakkhiṇeyyo hoti. So hi dhitiyā guṇe dhārayati, hiriyā dose nisedheti. Vuttañcetaṃ “hiriyā hi santo na karonti pāpa”nti. Tena te brūmi –

Now, explaining this meaning, he gives an illustration, beginning: 'From wood, indeed, is born fire…' Herein, this is the intention: In this world, fire is born from wood, but that fire does not perform the function of fire simply because it is born from wood such as sāl wood; nor does it fail to perform its function because it is born from wood such as a trough or a boat; rather, it performs it precisely because it possesses qualities such as flame. Similarly, one is not worthy of offerings simply because one is born in a brahmin family, nor is one unworthy because born in a low family such as that of an outcaste. Rather, whether of low birth or high birth, a sage whose taints are destroyed, who is resolute and restrained by a sense of shame, becomes a noble thoroughbred. By this possession of qualities, with resolution and shame foremost, one becomes truly high-born, the highest worthy of offerings. For by resolution one upholds virtues, and by a sense of shame one prevents faults. And it was said: 'For out of a sense of shame the good do not do evil.' Therefore, I say to you:

“Mā [V 2.0121][M 2.0133] jātiṃ pucchī caraṇañca puccha,

Kaṭṭhā have jāyati jātavedo;

Nīcākulīnopi munī dhitīmā,

Ājāniyo hoti hirīnisedho”ti. –

'Do not ask about birth, but ask about conduct;

From wood, indeed, is fire born.

A sage, though from a lowly family, if resolute,

Becomes a noble thoroughbred, restrained by a sense of shame.'

Esa saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana assalāyanasuttānusārena (ma. ni. 2.401 ādayo) veditabbo.

This is the summary. The detailed explanation, however, should be understood in accordance with the Assalāyana Sutta (MN 93).

468. Evametaṃ [P 2.0407] bhagavā cātuvaṇṇisuddhiyā anusāsitvā idāni yattha hutaṃ ijjhate, yathā ca hutaṃ ijjhate, tamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “saccena danto”tiādigāthamāha. Tattha saccenāti paramatthasaccena. Tañhi patto danto hoti. Tenāha – “saccena danto”ti. Damasā upetoti indriyadamena samannāgato. Vedantagūti vedehi vā kilesānaṃ antaṃ gato, vedānaṃ vā antaṃ catutthamaggañāṇaṃ gato. Vūsitabrahmacariyoti puna vasitabbābhāvato vutthamaggabrahmacariyo. Kālena tamhi habyaṃ paveccheti attano deyyadhammaṭṭhitakālaṃ tassa sammukhībhāvakālañca upalakkhetvā tena kālena tādise dakkhiṇeyye deyyadhammaṃ paveccheyya, paveseyya paṭipādeyya.

468. Having thus instructed on the purification of the four castes, the Blessed One now speaks the verse beginning with 'Tamed by truth' to show where an offering succeeds and how an offering succeeds. Herein, 'by truth' means by ultimate truth. For one who has attained it is tamed. Hence it is said: 'Tamed by truth.' 'Endowed with restraint' means possessing control over the senses. 'One who has gone to the end of the Vedas' means one who has gone to the end of defilements by means of the Vedas (knowledges), or one who has gone to the end of the Vedas, which is the fourth path-knowledge. 'One who has lived the holy life' means one who has completed the holy life of the path, since there is no further need to live it. 'At the right time, one should present an offering to him' means, having noted the time when one's gift-worthy things are available and the time when such a worthy recipient is present, at that time one should present, give, or provide the gift-worthy thing to such a worthy recipient.

469-71. Kāmeti vatthukāme ca kilesakāme ca. Susamāhitindriyāti suṭṭhu samāhitaindriyā, avikkhittaindriyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Candova rāhuggahaṇā pamuttāti yathā cando rāhuggahaṇā, evaṃ kilesaggahaṇā pamuttā ye atīva bhāsanti ceva tapanti ca. Satāti satisampannā. Mamāyitānīti taṇhādiṭṭhimamāyitāni.

469-71. 'Desires' refers to both sensual objects and defilement-desires. 'With well-composed faculties' means with faculties well-composed, that is, with faculties undistracted. 'Like the moon freed from Rāhu's grasp' means: just as the moon is freed from Rāhu's grasp, so those who are freed from the grasp of the defilements shine and blaze exceedingly. 'Mindful' means endowed with mindfulness. 'Things made 'mine'' refers to things appropriated as 'mine' through craving and views.

472. Yo kāme hitvāti ito pabhuti attānaṃ sandhāya vadati. Tattha kāme hitvāti kilesakāme pahāya. Abhibhuyyacārīti tesaṃ pahīnattā vatthukāme abhibhuyyacārī. Jātimaraṇassa antaṃ nāma nibbānaṃ vuccati, tañca yo vedi attano paññābalena aññāsi. Udakarahado vāti ye ime anotattadaho kaṇṇamuṇḍadaho rathakāradaho chaddantadaho kuṇāladaho mandākinidaho sīhappapātadahoti himavati satta mahārahadā aggisūriyasantāpehi asamphuṭṭhattā [M 2.0134] niccaṃ sītalā, tesaṃ aññataro udakarahadova sīto parinibbutakilesapariḷāhattā.

472. From the words 'He who, having abandoned desires,' he speaks referring to himself. Therein, 'having abandoned desires' means having abandoned the defilement-desires. 'One who fares having overcome' means that because those have been abandoned, he fares having overcome sensual objects. The end of birth and death is called Nibbāna, and 'he who knew it' means he understood it by the power of his own wisdom. 'Like a lake of water' means: just as these seven great lakes in the Himalayas—Anotatta, Kaṇṇamuṇḍa, Rathakāra, Chaddanta, Kuṇāla, Mandākinī, and Sīhappapāta—are perpetually cool because they are untouched by the heat of fire and the sun, so he is cool like one of those lakes of water, because the fever of the defilements has been extinguished.

473. Samoti tulyo. Samehīti vipassiādīhi buddhehi. Te hi paṭivedhasamattā “samā”ti vuccanti. Natthi tesaṃ paṭivedhenādhigantabbesu guṇesu, pahātabbesu vā dosesu vemattatā[V 2.0122], addhānaāyukulappamāṇābhinikkhamanapadhānabodhirasmīhi pana nesaṃ vemattatā hoti. Tathā hi te heṭṭhimaparicchedena [P 2.0408] catūhi asaṅkhyeyyehi kappasatasahassena ca pāramiyo pūrenti, uparimaparicchedena soḷasahi asaṅkhyeyyehi kappasatasahassena ca. Ayaṃ nesaṃ addhānavemattatā. Heṭṭhimaparicchedena ca vassasatāyukakāle uppajjanti, uparimaparicchedena vassasatasahassāyukakāle. Ayaṃ nesaṃ āyuvemattatā. Khattiyakule vā brāhmaṇakule vā uppajjanti. Ayaṃ kulavemattatā. Uccā vā honti aṭṭhāsītihatthappamāṇā, nīcā vā pannarasaaṭṭhārasahatthappamāṇā. Ayaṃ pamāṇavemattatā. Hatthiassarathasivikādīhi nikkhamanti vehāsena vā. Tathā hi vipassikakusandhā assarathena nikkhamiṃsu, sikhīkoṇāgamanā hatthikkhandhena, vessabhū sivikāya, kassapo vehāsena, sakyamuni assapiṭṭhiyā. Ayaṃ nekkhammavemattatā. Sattāhaṃ vā padhānamanuyuñjanti, aḍḍhamāsaṃ, māsaṃ, dvemāsaṃ, temāsaṃ, catumāsaṃ, pañcamāsaṃ, chamāsaṃ, ekavassaṃ dviticatupañcachavassāni vā. Ayaṃ padhānavemattatā. Assattho vā bodhirukkho hoti nigrodhādīnaṃ vā aññataro. Ayaṃ bodhivemattatā. Byāmāsītianantapabhāyuttā honti. Tattha byāmappabhā vā asītippabhā vā sabbesaṃ samānā, anantappabhā pana dūrampi gacchati āsannampi, ekagāvutaṃ dvigāvutaṃ yojanaṃ anekayojanaṃ cakkavāḷapariyantampi, maṅgalassa buddhassa sarīrappabhā dasasahassacakkavāḷaṃ agamāsi. Evaṃ santepi manasā cintāyattāva sabbabuddhānaṃ, yo yattakamicchati, tassa tattakaṃ gacchati. Ayaṃ rasmivemattatā. Imā aṭṭha vemattatā ṭhapetvā avasesesu paṭivedhenādhigantabbesu guṇesu, pahātabbesu vā dosesu natthi nesaṃ viseso, tasmā “samā”ti vuccanti. Evametehi samo samehi.

473. 'Equal' (samo) means alike (tulyo). 'With the equal' (samehi) means with the Buddhas such as Vipassī. For they are called 'equal' because of the sameness of their penetration. There is no difference among them in the qualities to be attained through penetration or in the faults to be abandoned. However, there is a difference among them in regard to duration, lifespan, family, stature, renunciation, striving, Bodhi tree, and radiance. For they fulfill the perfections for four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons as the lower limit, and for sixteen incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons as the upper limit. This is the difference among them in duration. They arise when the lifespan is a hundred years as the lower limit, and when the lifespan is a hundred thousand years as the upper limit. This is the difference among them in lifespan. They are born in a khattiya family or a brahmin family. This is the difference among them in family. They are tall, eighty-eight cubits in stature, or short, fifteen or eighteen cubits in stature. This is the difference among them in stature. They go forth by elephant, horse, chariot, palanquin, or through the air. For Vipassī and Kakusandha went forth by horse and chariot; Sikhī and Koṇāgamana on an elephant's back; Vessabhū in a palanquin; Kassapa through the air; and Sakyamuni on a horse's back. This is the difference among them in renunciation. They engage in striving for seven days, or half a month, a month, two, three, four, five, or six months, or two, three, four, five, or six years. This is the difference among them in striving. The Bodhi tree is an Assattha, or one of the others such as a Nigrodha. This is the difference among them in the Bodhi tree. They are endowed with a fathom-wide radiance, an eighty-cubit radiance, and an infinite radiance. Therein, the fathom-wide radiance and the eighty-cubit radiance are the same for all, but the infinite radiance goes far or near: one league, two leagues, a yojana, many yojanas, even to the edge of the world-sphere. The bodily radiance of the Buddha Maṅgala extended for ten thousand world-spheres. Even so, for all Buddhas it is dependent on their mental resolve: it extends as far as each one wishes. This is the difference among them in radiance. Setting aside these eight differences, in the remaining qualities to be attained through penetration or in the faults to be abandoned, there is no distinction among them. Therefore they are called 'equal.' Thus he is equal with these who are equal.

Visamehi [M 2.0135] dūreti na samā visamā, paccekabuddhādayo avasesasabbasattā. Tehi visamehi asadisatāya dūre. Sakalajambudīpaṃ pūretvā pallaṅkena pallaṅkaṃ saṅghaṭṭetvā nisinnā paccekabuddhāpi hi guṇehi ekassa sammāsambuddhassa kalaṃ nāgghanti soḷasiṃ[P 2.0409], ko pana vādo sāvakādīsu. Tenāha – “visamehi dūre”ti. Tathāgato hotīti ubhayapadehi dūreti yojetabbaṃ. Anantapaññoti aparimitapañño. Lokiyamanussānañhi paññaṃ upanidhāya aṭṭhamakassa paññā adhikā, tassa paññaṃ upanidhāya sotāpannassa. Evaṃ yāva arahato paññaṃ upanidhāya paccekabuddhassa paññā adhikā, paccekabuddhassa paññaṃ pana upanidhāya tathāgatassa paññā adhikāti na vattabbā, anantā icceva pana vattabbā. Tenāha – “anantapañño”ti. Anūpalittoti taṇhādiṭṭhilepehi alitto. Idha vā huraṃ vāti idhaloke vā paraloke vā. Yojanā panettha – samo samehi visamehi dūre tathāgato hoti. Kasmā? Yasmā anantapañño anupalitto idha vā huraṃ vā, tena tathāgato arahati pūraḷāsanti.

'Far from the unequal': The unequal are those who are not equal, that is, the Paccekabuddhas and all remaining beings. He is far from those unequal ones because of his incomparability. For even if Paccekabuddhas were to fill the whole of Jambudīpa, sitting with their cross-legged seats touching, in terms of qualities they would not be worth a sixteenth part of a single Perfectly Self-Enlightened One—what then to say of disciples and others? Therefore it is said: 'far from the unequal.' The words 'the Tathāgata is' should be construed with both phrases. 'Of infinite wisdom' means of immeasurable wisdom. For compared to the wisdom of worldly people, the wisdom of the eighth person is superior; compared to his wisdom, that of a stream-enterer is superior. In this way, up to the wisdom of an Arahant, the wisdom of a Paccekabuddha is superior. But compared to the wisdom of a Paccekabuddha, the wisdom of the Tathāgata should not be said to be superior; rather, it should just be said to be infinite. Therefore it is said: 'of infinite wisdom.' 'Unstained' means unsmeared by the smearing of craving and views. 'Here or beyond' means in this world or in the next world. The construction here is: 'The Tathāgata is equal with the equal and far from the unequal.' Why? Because he is of infinite wisdom and unstained here or beyond. Therefore the Tathāgata is worthy of the sacrificial cake.

474. Yamhi [V 2.0123] na māyāti ayaṃ pana gāthā aññā ca īdisā māyādidosayuttesu brāhmaṇesu dakkhiṇeyyasaññāpahānatthaṃ vuttāti veditabbā. Tattha amamoti sattasaṅkhāresu “idaṃ mamā”ti pahīnamamāyitabhāvo.

474. This verse, 'In whom there is no deceit,' and other verses like it, should be understood as spoken to abandon the perception that brahmins endowed with deceit and other faults are worthy of offerings. Herein, 'without 'mine'' means the state of having abandoned making anything 'mine' in regard to beings and formations with the thought, 'This is mine.'

475. Nivesananti taṇhādiṭṭhinivesanaṃ. Tena hi mano tīsu bhavesu nivisati, tena taṃ “nivesanaṃ manaso”ti vuccati. Tattheva vā nivisati taṃ hitvā gantuṃ asamatthatāya. Tenapi “nivesana”nti vuccati. Pariggahāti taṇhādiṭṭhiyo eva, tāhi pariggahitadhammā vā. Kecīti appamattakāpi. Anupādiyānoti tesaṃ nivesanapariggahānaṃ abhāvā kañci dhammaṃ anupādiyamāno.

475. 'Settlements' are the settling down of craving and views. For by that the mind settles down in the three kinds of existence; therefore it is called 'a settlement of the mind.' Or else, it settles down right there, being unable to abandon it and go. For that reason too it is called a 'settlement.' 'Possessions' are craving and views themselves, or the things possessed by them. 'Any' means even a few. 'Not clinging' means not clinging to any phenomenon because of the absence of those settlements and possessions.

476. Samāhito maggasamādhinā. Udatārīti uttiṇṇo. Dhammaṃ caññāsīti sabbañca ñeyyadhammaṃ aññāsi. Paramāya diṭṭhiyāti sabbaññutaññāṇena.

476. 'Concentrated' means by the concentration of the path. 'He has crossed up' means he has crossed over. 'And he has understood the Dhamma' means he has understood all knowable phenomena. 'With the supreme vision' means with the knowledge of omniscience.

477. Bhavāsavāti [M 2.0136] bhavataṇhājhānanikantisassatadiṭṭhisahagatā rāgā. Vacīti vācā. Kharāti kakkhaḷā pharusā. Vidhūpitāti daḍḍhā. Atthagatāti atthaṅgatā. Na santīti vidhūpitattā atthaṅgatattā ca. Ubhayehi pana ubhayaṃ yojetabbaṃ sabbadhīti sabbesu khandhāyatanādīsu.

477. 'The taint of existence' means lust accompanied by craving for existence, delight in the jhānas, and the eternalist view. 'Speech' means speech. 'Harsh' means rough, abusive. 'Dispelled' means burnt up. 'Gone to rest' means set, disappeared. 'They are no more' because they have been dispelled and have gone to rest. Further, both terms should be applied to both items. 'In every way' means in all the aggregates, sense bases, and so on.

478. Mānasattesūti mānena laggesu. Dukkhaṃ pariññāyāti vaṭṭadukkhaṃ tīhi pariññāhi parijānitvā. Sakhettavatthunti sahetupaccayaṃ, saddhiṃ kammakilesehīti vuttaṃ hoti.

478. 'Among those attached by conceit' means among those stuck by conceit. 'Having fully understood suffering' means having fully understood the suffering of the round by means of the three kinds of full understanding. 'With its field and ground' means with its cause and condition; that is to say, together with kamma and defilements.

479. Āsaṃ anissāyāti taṇhaṃ anallīyitvā. Vivekadassīti [P 2.0410] nibbānadassī. Paravediyanti parehi ñāpetabbaṃ. Diṭṭhimupātivattoti dvāsaṭṭhibhedampi micchādiṭṭhiṃ atikkanto. Ārammaṇāti paccayā, punabbhavakāraṇānīti vuttaṃ hoti.

479. 'Not relying on hope' means not cleaving to craving. 'A seer of seclusion' means a seer of Nibbāna. 'To be known by others' means to be made known by others. 'He has passed beyond views' means he has overcome wrong view in all its sixty-two forms. 'Supports' means conditions; that is to say, the causes for renewed existence.

480. Paroparāti varāvarā sundarāsundarā. Parā vā bāhirā, aparā ajjhattikā. Sameccāti ñāṇena paṭivijjhitvā. Dhammāti khandhāyatanādayo dhammā. Upādānakhaye vimuttoti nibbāne nibbānārammaṇato vimutto, nibbānārammaṇavimuttilābhīti attho.

480. 'Higher and lower' means superior and inferior, beautiful and unbeautiful. Or, 'higher' are external, 'lower' are internal. 'Having fully understood' means having penetrated with knowledge. 'Phenomena' means phenomena such as the aggregates and sense bases. 'Liberated in the destruction of clinging' means liberated in Nibbāna by taking Nibbāna as object; the meaning is that he is one who has obtained liberation with Nibbāna as its object.

481. Saṃyojanaṃjātikhayantadassīti saṃyojanakkhayantadassī jātikkhayantadassī ca. Saṃyojanakkhayantena cettha saupādisesā nibbānadhātu, jātikkhayantena anupādisesā vuttā. Khayantoti hi accantakhayassa samucchedappahānassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Anunāsikalopo cettha “vivekajaṃ [V 2.0124] pītisukha”ntiādīsu viya na kato. Yopānudīti yo apanudi. Rāgapathanti rāgārammaṇaṃ, rāgameva vā. Rāgopi hi duggatīnaṃ pathattā “rāgapatho”ti vuccati kammapatho viya. Suddho nidoso vimalo akācoti parisuddhakāyasamācārāditāya suddho. Yehi “rāgadosā ayaṃ pajā, dosadosā, mohadosā”ti vuccati. Tesaṃ abhāvā nidoso. Aṭṭhapurisamalavigamā vimalo, upakkilesābhāvato akāco. Upakkiliṭṭho hi upakkilesena “sakāco”ti vuccati. Suddho vā yasmā niddoso, niddosatāya vimalo, bāhiramalābhāvena vimalattā akāco. Samalo hi [M 2.0137] “sakāco”ti vuccati. Vimalattā vā āguṃ na karoti, tena akāco. Āgukiriyā hi upaghātakaraṇato “kāco”ti vuccati.

481. 'A seer of the final destruction of fetters and birth' means a seer of the destruction of the fetters and a seer of the destruction of birth. Here, by 'destruction of the fetters' the Nibbāna-element with residue remaining is stated; by 'destruction of birth,' the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining. For 'final destruction' is a designation for utter destruction, for eradication by cutting off. Here the elision of the nasal has not been done, as in cases like 'vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ'. 'Who has dispelled' means 'who has driven away.' 'The path of lust' means the object of lust, or lust itself. For lust is also called 'the path of lust' because it is a path to the bad destinations, like 'the path of kamma.' 'Pure, faultless, stainless, and unblemished': he is pure because of purity of bodily conduct, and so on. He is faultless because of the absence of those faults by which it is said: 'This generation is at fault through lust, at fault through hatred, at fault through delusion.' He is stainless because the eight stains of a person have departed; he is unblemished because of the absence of imperfections. For one who is defiled by an imperfection is called 'blemished.' Or: he is pure because he is faultless; because he is faultless, he is stainless; because he is stainless through the absence of external stains, he is unblemished. For one with a stain is called 'blemished.' Or, because he is stainless, he does no wrong; therefore he is unblemished. For the doing of wrong is called a 'blemish' because it causes injury.

482. Attano attānaṃ nānupassatīti ñāṇasampayuttena cittena vipassanto attano khandhesu aññaṃ attānaṃ nāma na passati, khandhamattameva passati. Yā cāyaṃ “attanāva attānaṃ sañjānāmī”ti tassa saccato thetato diṭṭhi uppajjati, tassā abhāvā attano attānaṃ nānupassati, aññadatthu paññāya [P 2.0411] khandhe passati. Maggasamādhinā samāhito, kāyavaṅkādīnaṃ abhāvā ujjugato, lokadhammehi akampanīyato ṭhitatto, taṇhāsaṅkhātāya ejāya pañcannaṃ cetokhilānañca aṭṭhaṭṭhānāya kaṅkhāya ca abhāvā anejo akhilo akaṅkho.

482. 'One does not observe a self in oneself' means that when contemplating with a mind associated with knowledge, one does not see in one's own aggregates any other thing called a 'self'; one sees only the aggregates. And since that view, 'I perceive the self by means of the self,' which might arise as true and firm, is absent, one does not observe a self in oneself; rather, one sees the aggregates with wisdom. Composed by the concentration of the path, straightened by the absence of bodily crookedness and the like, steadfast because unshakeable by worldly conditions, and because of the absence of the agitation identified as craving, of the five kinds of mental barrenness, and of doubt on eight grounds—one is unagitated, without barrenness, and free from doubt.

483. Mohantarāti mohakāraṇā mohapaccayā, sabbakilesānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sabbesu dhammesu ca ñāṇadassīti sacchikatasabbaññutaññāṇo. Tañhi sabbesu dhammesu ñāṇaṃ, tañca bhagavā passi, “adhigataṃ me”ti sacchikatvā vihāsi. Tena vuccati “sabbesu dhammesu ca ñāṇadassī”ti. Sambodhinti arahattaṃ. Anuttaranti paccekabuddhasāvakehi asādhāraṇaṃ. Sivanti khemaṃ nirupaddavaṃ sassirikaṃ vā. Yakkhassāti purisassa. Suddhīti vodānatā. Ettha hi mohantarābhāvena sabbadosābhāvo, tena saṃsārakāraṇasamucchedo antimasarīradhāritā, ñāṇadassitāya sabbaguṇasambhavo. Tena anuttarā sambodhipatti, ito parañca pahātabbamadhigantabbaṃ vā natthi. Tenāha – “ettāvatā yakkhassa suddhī”ti.

483. 'Obstructed by delusion' means caused by delusion, conditioned by delusion; this is a designation for all defilements. 'And a seer of knowledge in all things' means one who has realized the knowledge of omniscience. For that is the knowledge in all things, and the Blessed One saw it; having realized it as 'attained by me,' he dwelled. Therefore it is said, 'and a seer of knowledge in all things.' 'Enlightenment' means arahantship. 'Unsurpassed' means not shared with paccekabuddhas and disciples. 'Auspicious' means secure, untroubled, or glorious. 'Of the yakkha' means of the person. 'Purification' means purity. Here, through the absence of the obstruction of delusion there is the absence of all faults; thereby the cause of saṃsāra is cut off and one bears one's final body, and through possession of knowledge and vision all good qualities arise. Thus there is the attainment of unsurpassed enlightenment, and beyond this there is nothing further to be abandoned or to be realized. Therefore he said: 'To this extent is the purification of the yakkha.'

484. Evaṃ vutte brāhmaṇo bhiyyosomattāya bhagavati pasanno pasannākāraṃ karonto āha “hutañca mayha”nti. Tassattho – yamahaṃ ito pubbe brahmānaṃ ārabbha aggimhi ajuhaṃ, taṃ me hutaṃ saccaṃ vā hoti, alikaṃ vāti na jānāmi. Ajja pana idaṃ hutañca mayhaṃ hutamatthu saccaṃ, saccahutameva atthūti yācanto bhaṇati. Yaṃ tādisaṃ vedagunaṃ alatthaṃ, yasmā idheva ṭhito bhavantarūpaṃ [V 2.0125] vedaguṃ alatthaṃ. Brahmā hi sakkhi, paccakkhameva hi tvaṃ brahmā, yato paṭiggaṇhātu me bhagavā, paṭiggahetvā [M 2.0138] ca bhuñjatu me bhagavā pūraḷāsanti taṃ habyasesaṃ upanāmento āha.

484. When this was said, the brahmin, with even greater satisfaction and with faith in the Blessed One, showing his pleasure, said: 'And my offering!' The meaning is: 'Whatever I previously offered in the fire with respect to Brahma, I do not know if that offering of mine was true or false. But today, may this offering of mine be a true offering, may it be a truly well-made offering.' Speaking thus, he makes a request. 'Since I have found such a master of the sacred lore; for standing right here I have found a master of the lore who has gone beyond becoming. For Brahma is directly perceived; you are indeed Brahma manifest. Therefore, let the Blessed One accept from me, and having accepted, let the Blessed One eat my sacrificial cake.' Presenting the remainder of the oblation, he said this.

487. Atha bhagavā kasibhāradvājasutte vuttanayena gāthādvayamabhāsi. Tato brāhmaṇo “ayaṃ attanā na icchati, kampi caññaṃ sandhāya ‘kevalinaṃ mahesiṃ khīṇāsavaṃ kukkuccavūpasantaṃ annena pānena upaṭṭhahassū’ti bhaṇatī”ti evaṃ gāthāya atthaṃ asallakkhetvā taṃ ñātukāmo [P 2.0412] āha “sādhāhaṃ bhagavā”ti. Tattha sādhūti āyācanatthe nipāto. Tathāti yena tvamāha, tena pakārena. Vijaññanti jāneyyaṃ. Yanti yaṃ dakkhiṇeyyaṃ yaññakāle pariyesamāno upaṭṭhaheyyanti pāṭhaseso. Pappuyyāti patvā. Tava sāsananti tava ovādaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti. Sādhāhaṃ bhagavā tava ovādaṃ āgamma tathā vijaññaṃ ārocehi me taṃ kevalinanti adhippāyo. Yo dakkhiṇaṃ bhuñjeyya mādisassa, yaṃ cāhaṃ yaññakāle pariyesamāno upaṭṭhaheyyaṃ, tathārūpaṃ me dakkhiṇeyyaṃ dassehi, sace tvaṃ na bhuñjasīti.

487. Then the Blessed One spoke two verses in the manner stated in the Kasibhāradvāja Sutta. Then the brahmin, not understanding the meaning of the verse, thought: 'He himself does not wish for it, but with reference to someone else he says: "You should serve with food and drink the consummate one, the great seer, whose taints are destroyed, whose remorse is stilled."' Wishing to know this, he said: 'Good, Blessed One.' Here, 'good' is a particle in the sense of a request. 'Thus' means in the way that you have spoken. 'May I know' means 'I would know.' 'Whom'—the rest of the passage is: 'whom, as a worthy recipient, I might serve, seeking at the time of sacrifice.' 'May I attain' means 'having reached.' 'Your teaching' means 'your instruction.' This is what is said. The intention is: 'Good, Blessed One, having come to your instruction, may I know thus; declare that consummate one to me.' The meaning is: 'Show me such a one worthy of offerings who would eat the offering of one like me, whom I might serve, seeking at the time of sacrifice, if you yourself do not eat.'

488-90. Athassa bhagavā pākaṭena nayena tathārūpaṃ dakkhiṇeyyaṃ dassento “sārambhā yassā”ti gāthāttayamāha. Tattha sīmantānaṃ vinetāranti sīmāti mariyādā sādhujanavutti, tassā antā pariyosānā aparabhāgāti katvā sīmantā vuccanti kilesā, tesaṃ vinetāranti attho. Sīmantāti buddhaveneyyā sekkhā ca puthujjanā ca, tesaṃ vinetārantipi eke. Jātimaraṇakovidanti “evaṃ jāti evaṃ maraṇa”nti ettha kusalaṃ. Moneyyasampannanti paññāsampannaṃ, kāyamoneyyādisampannaṃ vā. Bhakuṭiṃ vinayitvānāti yaṃ ekacce dubbuddhino yācakaṃ disvā bhakuṭiṃ karonti, taṃ vinayitvā, pasannamukhā hutvāti attho. Pañjalikāti paggahitaañjalino hutvā.

Then the Blessed One, showing in a clear way such a one worthy of offerings, spoke three verses beginning: 'For whom there are no contentions…' Here, 'a subduer of the limits': 'sīmā' is a boundary, the conduct of good people. Its 'antā' (ends), its conclusions, its final parts, are called 'sīmantā,' which are the defilements. The meaning is 'a subduer of them.' Some say 'sīmantā' are those to be trained by the Buddha—learners and worldlings—and 'vinetāra' is a trainer of them. 'Expert in birth and death' means skilled in this: 'thus is birth, thus is death.' 'Endowed with sagehood' means endowed with wisdom, or endowed with sagehood of body, speech, and mind. 'Having dispelled a frown': some foolish people, on seeing a beggar, make a frown; having dispelled that, the meaning is 'having become bright-faced.' 'With hands joined in reverence' means having raised the hands in the añjali gesture.

491. Atha brāhmaṇo bhagavantaṃ thomayamāno “buddho bhava”nti gāthamāha. Tattha āyāgoti āyajitabbo, tato tato āgamma vā yajitabbametthātipi āyāgo, deyyadhammānaṃ adhiṭṭhānabhūtoti vuttaṃ hoti[M 2.0139]. Sesamettha ito purimagāthāsu ca yaṃ na vaṇṇitaṃ, taṃ sakkā avaṇṇitampi jānitunti uttānatthattāyeva na vaṇṇitaṃ. Ito paraṃ pana kasibhāradvājasutte vuttanayamevāti.

491. Then the brahmin, praising the Blessed One, spoke the verse: 'You are the Buddha.' Here, 'āyāga' means worthy of sacrifice, or 'āyāga' is a place where one should make offerings, having come from here and there; it is said to be the basis for things to be given. The rest here and in the preceding verses that has not been commented upon can be known even without commentary because its meaning is plain, and for that very reason it has not been commented upon. From here on, however, it is just according to the method stated in the Kasibhāradvāja Sutta.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka.

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya pūraḷāsasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Pūraḷāsa Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary is finished.

5. Māghasuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Explanation of the Māgha Sutta

Evaṃ [V 2.0126][P 2.0413] me sutanti māghasuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Ayameva yāssa nidāne vuttā. Ayañhi māgho māṇavo dāyako ahosi dānapati. Tassetadahosi – “sampattakapaṇaddhikādīnaṃ dānaṃ dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ hoti, udāhu noti samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ etamatthaṃ pucchissāmi, samaṇo kira gotamo atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ jānātī”ti. So bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā pucchi. Bhagavā cassa pucchānurūpaṃ byākāsi. Tayidaṃ saṅgītikārānaṃ brāhmaṇassa bhagavatoti tiṇṇampi vacanaṃ samodhānetvā “māghasutta”nti vuccati.

Thus have I heard—the Māgha Sutta. What is its origin? It is the same as what was stated in its introduction. For this Māgha, the young brahmin, was a donor and a patron of gifts. It occurred to him: 'Is a gift given to those who have arrived, the poor, travellers, and so on, of great fruit, or not? I will ask the ascetic Gotama about this matter, for it is said that the ascetic Gotama knows the past, the future, and the present.' So he approached the Blessed One and asked. And the Blessed One answered him in accordance with his question. The Reciters, combining the speech of the three—the brahmin, the Blessed One, and so on—called it the 'Māgha Sutta'.

Tattha rājagaheti evaṃnāmake nagare. Tañhi mandhātumahāgovindādīhi pariggahitattā “rājagaha”nti vuccati. Aññepettha pakāre vaṇṇayanti. Kiṃ tehi, nāmametaṃ tassa nagarassa? Taṃ panetaṃ buddhakāle ca cakkavattikāle ca nagaraṃ hoti, sesakāle suññaṃ hoti yakkhapariggahitaṃ, tesaṃ vasantavanaṃ hutvā tiṭṭhati. Evaṃ gocaragāmaṃ dassetvā nivāsaṭṭhānamāha – “gijjhakūṭe pabbate”ti. So ca gijjhā tassa kūṭesu vasiṃsu, gijjhasadisāni vāssa kūṭāni, tasmā “gijjhakūṭo”ti vuccatīti veditabbo.

Herein, 'at Rājagaha' means in the city of that name. Because it was occupied by kings such as Mandhātā and Mahāgovinda, it is called 'Rājagaha.' Others describe it here in other ways. But what of them? This is just the name of that city. Now, during the time of a Buddha and the time of a wheel-turning monarch it is a city; at other times it is deserted, possessed by yakkhas, and stands as their dwelling grove. Having thus shown the alms-resort village, he states the dwelling place: 'on the Vulture Peak mountain.' And it should be understood that it is called 'Vulture Peak' either because vultures dwelt on its peaks or because its peaks resembled vultures.

Atha kho…pe… avocāti ettha māghoti tassa brāhmaṇassa nāmaṃ. Māṇavoti antevāsivāsaṃ anatītabhāvena vuccati, jātiyā pana mahallako. “Pubbāciṇṇavasenā”ti eke piṅgiyo māṇavo viya. So hi vīsavassasatikopi pubbāciṇṇavasena “piṅgiyo māṇavo” tveva saṅkhaṃ agamāsi. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

In the phrase 'Then…pe… he said,' 'Māgha' is the name of that brahmin. He is called 'young brahmin' because he had not gone beyond the student’s life, though by birth he was an old man. Some say it is by force of long-standing habit, like the young brahmin Piṅgiya. For though he was one hundred and twenty years old, by force of long-standing habit he was still reckoned as 'the young brahmin Piṅgiya.' The rest is in the way already stated.

Ahañhi[M 2.0140], bho gotama…pe… pasavāmīti ettha dāyako dānapatīti dāyako ceva dānapati ca. Yo hi aññassa santakaṃ tenāṇatto deti, sopi dāyako hoti, tasmiṃ pana dāne issariyābhāvato na dānapati. Ayaṃ pana attano santakaṃyeva deti. Tenāha – “ahañhi, bho gotama[P 2.0414], dāyako dānapatī”ti. Ayameva hi ettha attho, aññatra pana antarantarā maccherena abhibhuyyamāno dāyako anabhibhūto dānapatītiādināpi nayena vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Vadaññūti yācakānaṃ vacanaṃ jānāmi vuttamatteyeva “ayamidamarahati ayamida”nti purisavisesāvadhāraṇena [V 2.0127] bahūpakārabhāvagahaṇena vā. Yācayogoti yācituṃ yutto. Yo hi yācake disvāva bhakuṭiṃ katvā pharusavacanādīni bhaṇati, so na yācayogo hoti. Ahaṃ pana na tādisoti dīpeti. Dhammenāti adinnādānanikativañcanādīni vajjetvā bhikkhācariyāya, yācanāyāti attho. Yācanā hi brāhmaṇānaṃ bhogapariyesane dhammo, yācamānānañca nesaṃ parehi anuggahakāmehi dinnā bhogā dhammaladdhā nāma dhammādhigatā ca honti, so ca tathā pariyesitvā labhi. Tenāha – “dhammena bhoge pariyesāmi…pe… dhammādhigatehī”ti. Bhiyyopi dadāmīti tato uttaripi dadāmi, pamāṇaṃ natthi, ettha laddhabhogappamāṇena dadāmīti dasseti.

In the passage beginning, 'For I, good Gotama… I generate,' 'a donor, a lord of gifts' means he is both a donor and a lord of gifts. For one who gives what belongs to another, being authorized by that person, is a donor, but since he lacks mastery over that gift, he is not a lord of gifts. This one, however, gives what is his own. Hence he said: 'For I, good Gotama, am a donor, a lord of gifts.' This is the meaning here. Elsewhere, however, it is permissible to explain it by the method whereby a donor who is from time to time overcome by stinginess is a (mere) donor, while one who is not overcome is a lord of gifts, and so on. 'Generous' means: 'I know the speech of supplicants'; as soon as they have spoken, I know, 'This one deserves this, that one deserves that,' by determining the distinction between persons or by grasping their great need. 'Approachable for requests' means fit to be asked. For one who, on seeing supplicants, frowns and utters harsh words and the like, is not approachable for requests. He indicates: 'But I am not like that.' 'Righteously' means: avoiding the taking of what is not given, fraud, deception, and the like, by the practice of asking; this is the meaning. For asking is the righteous way for brahmins to seek wealth, and the wealth given to them by others who wish to support them when they ask is called 'righteously obtained' and 'righteously acquired.' And he seeks and obtains it in that way. Hence he said: 'I seek wealth righteously… from what is righteously acquired.' 'I give still more' means: 'I give even beyond that, there is no limit.' Here it shows: 'I give in proportion to the wealth I have obtained.'

Tagghāti ekaṃsavacane nipāto. Ekaṃseneva hi sabbabuddhapaccekabuddhasāvakehi pasatthaṃ dānaṃ antamaso tiracchānagatānampi dīyamānaṃ. Vuttañcetaṃ “sabbattha vaṇṇitaṃ dānaṃ, na dānaṃ garahitaṃ kvacī”ti. Tasmā bhagavāpi ekaṃseneva taṃ pasaṃsanto āha – “taggha tvaṃ māṇava…pe… pasavasī”ti. Sesaṃ uttānatthameva. Evaṃ bhagavatā “bahuṃ so puññaṃ pasavatī”ti vuttepi dakkhiṇeyyato dakkhiṇāvisuddhiṃ sotukāmo brāhmaṇo uttari bhagavantaṃ pucchi. Tenāhu saṅgītikārā – “atha kho māgho māṇavo bhagavantaṃ gāthāya ajjhabhāsī”ti. Taṃ atthato vuttanayameva.

'Taggha' is a particle in the sense of definite affirmation. For giving is definitely praised by all Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples, even when given to animals. And this has been said: 'Everywhere giving is extolled; nowhere is giving censured.' Therefore the Blessed One, praising it definitely, said: 'Indeed, young man… you generate (much merit).' The rest has a plain meaning. Thus, even though the Blessed One had said, 'He generates much merit,' the brahmin, wishing to hear about the purity of the offering with respect to the worthy recipients, questioned the Blessed One further. Hence the Reciters said: 'Then the young man Māgha addressed the Blessed One in verse.' The meaning of this is in the way already stated.

492. Pucchāmahantiādigāthāsu [P 2.0415] pana vadaññunti vacanaviduṃ, sabbākārena sattānaṃ vuttavacanādhippāyaññunti vuttaṃ hoti. Sujjheti dakkhiṇeyyavasena suddhaṃ mahapphalaṃ bhaveyya. Yojanā panettha – yo yācayogo dānapati [M 2.0141] gahaṭṭho puññatthiko hutvā paresaṃ annapānaṃ dadaṃ yajati, na aggimhi āhutimattaṃ pakkhipanto, tañca kho puññapekkhova na paccupakārakalyāṇakittisaddādiapekkho, tassa evarūpassa yajamānassa hutaṃ kathaṃ sujjheyyāti?

492. But in the verses beginning, 'I ask,' 'generous' means knowing speech; that is, in all ways knowing the intention of the words spoken by beings. 'Would be purified' means it would become pure, of great fruit, on account of the worthy recipients. The construction here is: When a householder who is a donor approachable for requests, being a seeker of merit, sacrifices by giving food and drink to others—not just by casting an oblation into the fire—and does so only in expectation of merit, not in expectation of a return favor, a good reputation, fame, and so on, how would the sacrifice of such a sacrificer be purified?

493. Ārādhaye dakkhiṇeyyebhi tādīti tādiso yācayogo dakkhiṇeyyehi ārādhaye sampādaye sodhaye, mahapphalaṃ taṃ hutaṃ kareyya, na aññathāti attho. Imināssa “kathaṃ hutaṃ yajamānassa sujjhe” iccetaṃ byākataṃ hoti.

493. 'One such should propitiate with worthy recipients' means: such a one, who is approachable for requests, should propitiate, accomplish, purify by means of worthy recipients; he would make that sacrifice be of great fruit, not otherwise; this is the meaning. By this, his question, 'How would the sacrifice of the sacrificer be purified?' is answered.

494. Akkhāhi me bhagavā dakkhiṇeyyeti ettha yo yācayogo dadaṃ paresaṃ yajati, tassa me bhagavā dakkhiṇeyye akkhāhīti evaṃ yojanā veditabbā.

494. Herein, in the phrase 'Declare to me, Blessed One, the worthy recipients,' the construction should be understood thus: 'For me—one who is approachable for requests and who sacrifices by giving to others—declare, O Blessed One, the worthy recipients.'

495. Athassa [V 2.0128] bhagavā nānappakārehi nayehi dakkhiṇeyye pakāsento “ye ve asattā”tiādikā gāthāyo abhāsi. Tattha asattāti rāgādisaṅgavasena alaggā. Kevalinoti pariniṭṭhitakiccā. Yatattāti guttacittā.

495. Then the Blessed One, making known the worthy recipients by various methods, spoke the verses beginning: 'Those who are indeed unattached.' Therein, 'unattached' means not clinging by way of the attachment of lust and so on. 'Perfected' means those whose task is finished. 'Self-controlled' means those with a guarded mind.

496-7. Dantā anuttarena damathena, vimuttā paññācetovimuttīhi, anīghā āyatiṃ vaṭṭadukkhābhāvena, nirāsā sampati kilesābhāvena. Imissā pana gāthāya dutiyagāthā bhāvanānubhāvappakāsananayena vuttāti veditabbā. “Bhāvanānuyogamanuyuttassa, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno viharato kiñcāpi na evaṃ icchā uppajjeyya ‘aho vata me anupādāya āsavehi cittaṃ vimucceyyā’ti (a. ni. 7.71), atha khvāssa anupādāya āsavehi cittaṃ vimuccatī”ti idaṃ cettha suttaṃ sādhakaṃ.

496–497. 'Tamed' by the unsurpassed taming. 'Liberated' by the liberation by wisdom and the liberation of mind.
