'Untroubled' because of the absence of the suffering of the round of rebirths in the future. 'Without longing' at present because of the absence of defilements. But the second verse of this pair should be understood as spoken by way of revealing the power of meditative development. And this sutta is the proof here: 'Monks, for a bhikkhu who dwells devoted to the practice of meditation, even if the wish does not arise in him, “Oh, that my mind might be liberated from the taints without clinging!” (AN 7.71), still his mind is liberated from the taints without clinging.'

498-502. Rāgañca…pe… yesu na māyā…pe… na taṇhāsu upātipannāti kāmataṇhādīsu nādhimuttā. Vitareyyāti vitaritvā. Taṇhāti rūpataṇhādichabbidhā[P 2.0416]. Bhavābhavāyāti sassatāya vā ucchedāya vā. Atha vā bhavassa abhavāya bhavābhavāya, punabbhavābhinibbattiyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Idha vā huraṃ vāti idaṃ pana “kuhiñci loke”ti imassa vitthāravacanaṃ.

498–502. 'Lust'…pe… 'in whom there is no deceit'…pe… 'not fallen into cravings' means not intent on the cravings for sensual pleasures and so on. 'Vitareyya' (one should cross over) means having crossed over. 'Craving' is the sixfold kind, such as craving for forms. 'For existence and non-existence' means for eternalism or for annihilationism. Or, 'for existence and non-existence' means for the generation of renewed existence. 'Here or hereafter' is an extensive explanation of the phrase 'anywhere in the world.'

504. Ye [M 2.0142] vītarāgā…pe… samitāvinoti samitavanto, kilesavūpasamakārinoti attho. Samitāvitattā ca vītarāgā akopā. Idha vippahāyāti idhaloke vattamāne khandhe vihāya, tato paraṃ yesaṃ gamanaṃ natthīti vuttaṃ hoti. Ito paraṃ “ye kāme hitvā agahā caranti, susaññatattā tasaraṃva ujju”nti imampi gāthaṃ keci paṭhanti.

504. 'Those who are free from lust'…pe… 'calmed' means possessing calm; the meaning is those who cause the stilling of the defilements. And because they are calmed, they are free from lust and imperturbable. 'Having abandoned here' means having abandoned the aggregates that exist in this world; it is said that beyond that there is no further going for them. After this some also recite this verse: 'Those who, having abandoned sensual pleasures, wander homeless, well-restrained, straight like a shuttle.'

506-8. Jahitvāti hitvā. “Jahitvānā”tipi pāṭho, ayamevattho. Attadīpāti attano guṇe eva attano dīpaṃ katvā vicarantā khīṇāsavā vuccanti. Ye hetthāti hakāro nipāto padapūraṇamatte. Ayaṃ panattho – ye ettha khandhāyatanādisantāne yathā idaṃ khandhāyatanādi tathā jānanti, yaṃsabhāvaṃ taṃsabhāvaṃyeva sañjānanti aniccādivasena jānantā. Ayamantimā natthi punabbhavoti ayaṃ no antimā jāti, idāni natthi punabbhavoti evañca ye jānantīti.

506–8. Having abandoned means having left behind. Jahitvānā is also a reading with the same meaning. With themselves as an island means those who wander having made their own virtues their island; they are called the destroyers of the taints. In ye hettha, the particle ha is merely a line-filler. But this is the meaning: those who know the aggregates, sense bases, etc., in this continuum of aggregates, sense bases, etc., just as they are; knowing them by way of impermanence, etc., they perceive their nature just as it is. And those who know thus: 'This is our last birth, now there is no more renewed existence.'

509. Yo vedagūti idāni attānaṃ sandhāya bhagavā imaṃ gāthamāha. Tattha satimāti chasatatavihārasatiyā [V 2.0129] samannāgato. Sambodhipattoti sabbaññutaṃ patto. Saraṇaṃ bahūnanti bahūnaṃ devamanussānaṃ bhayavihiṃsanena saraṇabhūto.

509. Now the Blessed One, referring to himself, speaks this verse beginning 'He who is a knower of the Veda.' Therein, mindful means endowed with the mindfulness of the six constant abidings. Attained to full enlightenment means having attained omniscience. A refuge for many means having become a refuge for many devas and humans by dispelling their fear and harm.

510. Evaṃ dakkhiṇeyye sutvā attamano brāhmaṇo āha – “addhā amoghā”ti. Tattha tvañhettha jānāsi yathā tathā idanti tvañhi ettha loke idaṃ sabbampi ñeyyaṃ yathā tathā jānāsi yāthāvato jānāsi, yādisaṃ taṃ tādisameva jānāsīti [P 2.0417] vuttaṃ hoti. Tathā hi te vidito esa dhammoti tathā hi te esā dhammadhātu suppaṭividdhā, yassā suppaṭividdhatā yaṃ yaṃ icchasi, taṃ taṃ jānāsīti adhippāyo.

510. Having thus heard about the worthy recipients, the brahmin, with gladdened mind, said: 'Surely, not in vain.' Therein, 'for you know this as it really is' means: for you know all that is knowable in this world just as it is, you know it in its true nature, you know it just as it is. 'For this Dhamma is known to you' means: for this Dhamma-element has been well penetrated by you, and because it has been well penetrated, whatever you wish to know, that you know; this is the intention.

511. Evaṃ so brāhmaṇo bhagavantaṃ pasaṃsitvā dakkhiṇeyyasampadāya yaññasampadaṃ ñatvā dāyakasampadāyapi taṃ chaḷaṅgaparipūraṃ yaññasampadaṃ sotukāmo “yo yācayogo”ti uttaripañhaṃ pucchi. Tatrāyaṃ yojanā – yo yācayogo dadaṃ paresaṃ yajati, tassa akkhāhi me bhagavā yaññasampadanti.

511. Thus that brahmin, having praised the Blessed One, and having understood the perfection of the sacrifice through the perfection of the recipients, also desired to hear about that perfection of the sacrifice complete with six factors through the perfection of the donor. He therefore asked a further question, beginning 'He who is a petitioner...' Herein, this is the construction: 'He who, being a petitioner, gives, sacrificing for others—explain to me, O Blessed One, the perfection of that sacrifice.'

512. Athassa [M 2.0143] bhagavā dvīhi gāthāhi akkhāsi. Tatthāyaṃ atthayojanā – yajassu māgha, yajamāno ca sabbattha vippasādehi cittaṃ, tīsupi kālesu cittaṃ pasādehi. Evaṃ te yāyaṃ –

512. Then the Blessed One explained it to him in two stanzas. Herein, this is the explanation of the meaning: Sacrifice, Māgha, and while sacrificing, make your mind thoroughly serene in every way; make your mind serene in all three periods of time. Thus your sacrifice…

“Pubbeva dānā sumano, dadaṃ cittaṃ pasādaye;

Datvā attamano hoti, esā yaññassa sampadā”ti. (a. ni. 6.37; pe. va. 305) –

“Before giving, one is glad-minded; while giving, one clarifies the mind; having given, one is gratified—this is the perfection of the sacrifice.”

Yaññasampadā vuttā, tāya sampanno yañño bhavissati. Tattha siyā “kathaṃ cittaṃ pasādetabba”nti? Dosappahānena. Kathaṃ dosappahānaṃ hoti? Yaññārammaṇatāya. Ayañhi ārammaṇaṃ yajamānassa yañño ettha patiṭṭhāya jahāti dosaṃ, ayañhi sattesu mettāpubbaṅgamena sammādiṭṭhipadīpavihatamohandhakārena cittena yajamānassa deyyadhammasaṅkhāto yañño ārammaṇaṃ hoti, so ettha yaññe ārammaṇavasena pavattiyā patiṭṭhāya deyyadhammapaccayaṃ lobhaṃ, paṭiggāhakapaccayaṃ kodhaṃ, tadubhayanidānaṃ mohanti evaṃ tividhampi jahāti dosaṃ. So evaṃ bhogesu vītarāgo, sattesu ca pavineyya dosaṃ tappahāneneva pahīnapañcanīvaraṇo anukkamena upacārappanābhedaṃ aparimāṇasattapharaṇena ekasatte vā anavasesapharaṇena appamāṇaṃ mettaṃ cittaṃ bhāvento [V 2.0130] puna bhāvanāvepullatthaṃ, rattindivaṃ satataṃ sabbairiyāpathesu appamatto hutvā tameva mettajjhānasaṅkhātaṃ sabbā disā pharate appamaññanti.

The perfection of the sacrifice has been stated; endowed with that, the sacrifice will be accomplished. Therein, one might ask: 'How should the mind be made serene?' By abandoning defilement. How is defilement abandoned? Through the sacrifice as object. For this sacrifice is the object for the sacrificer; established in this, he abandons defilement. Indeed, for the sacrificer whose mind is preceded by loving-kindness towards beings and has the darkness of delusion dispelled by the lamp of right view, this sacrifice, designated as the gift-object, is the object. Established in the process by way of the sacrifice as object, he abandons the threefold defilement: greed conditioned by the gift-object, anger conditioned by the recipient, and delusion based on both. Thus, being without lust for possessions and having removed aversion towards beings, by that very abandoning he has abandoned the five hindrances. Gradually developing the immeasurable mind of loving-kindness—distinguished as access and absorption concentration—by pervading limitless beings or by pervading a single being without remainder, and then for the sake of the full development of the cultivation, being diligent day and night, constantly, in all postures, he 'pervades all directions with the immeasurable,' that is, with what is designated as the jhāna of loving-kindness.

514. Atha brāhmaṇo taṃ mettaṃ “brahmalokamaggo aya”nti ajānanto kevalaṃ attano visayātītaṃ mettābhāvanaṃ sutvā [P 2.0418] suṭṭhutaraṃ sañjātasabbaññusambhāvano bhagavati attanā brahmalokādhimuttattā brahmalokūpapattimeva ca suddhiṃ muttiñca maññamāno brahmalokamaggaṃ pucchanto “ko sujjhatī”ti gāthamāha. Tatra ca brahmalokagāmiṃ puññaṃ karontaṃ sandhāyāha – “ko sujjhati muccatī”ti, akarontaṃ sandhāya “bajjhatī cā”ti. Kenattanāti kena kāraṇena. Sakkhi brahmajjadiṭṭhoti brahmā ajja sakkhi diṭṭho. Saccanti bhagavato brahmasamattaṃ ārabbha accādarena sapathaṃ karoti. Kathaṃ upapajjatīti accādareneva punapi pucchati. Jutimāti bhagavantaṃ ālapati.

514. Then the brahmin, not knowing that this loving-kindness is 'the path to the Brahmā-world,' and having merely heard about the development of loving-kindness that transcended his own sphere, conceived a very high estimation of the Blessed One as the Omniscient One. Being himself intent on the Brahmā-world, and thinking that purity and liberation are simply rebirth in the Brahmā-world, he asked about the path to the Brahmā-world by reciting the stanza beginning: 'Who is purified?' Therein, referring to one who performs merit leading to the Brahmā-world, he said: 'Who is purified and liberated?' And referring to one who does not, he said: 'And who is bound?' 'By what cause?' means by what reason. 'Brahmā is seen today as a witness' means Brahmā is directly witnessed today. 'Truly'—he makes an oath with great reverence with reference to the Blessed One's equality with Brahmā. 'How does one arise there?'—he asks again with great reverence. 'O Radiant One'—he addresses the Blessed One.

Tattha [M 2.0144] yasmā yo bhikkhu mettāya tikacatukkajjhānaṃ uppādetvā tameva pādakaṃ katvā vipassanto arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, so sujjhati muccati ca, tathārūpo ca brahmalokaṃ na gacchati. Yo pana mettāya tikacatukkajjhānaṃ uppādetvā “santā esā samāpattī”tiādinā nayena taṃ assādeti, so bajjhati. Aparihīnajjhāno ca teneva jhānena brahmalokaṃ gacchati, tasmā bhagavā yo sujjhati muccati ca, tassa brahmalokagamanaṃ ananujānanto anāmasitvāva taṃ puggalaṃ yo bajjhati. Tassa tena jhānena brahmalokagamanaṃ dassento brāhmaṇassa sappāyena nayena “yo yajatī”ti imaṃ gāthamāha.

Herein, a bhikkhu who generates the third and fourth jhānas through loving-kindness and, using that as a basis for insight, attains arahantship—he is purified and liberated. Such a one does not go to the Brahmā-world. But one who generates the third and fourth jhānas through loving-kindness and delights in it, thinking, 'This attainment is peaceful,' and so on—he becomes bound. And not having lost the jhāna, he goes to the Brahmā-world through that very jhāna. Therefore the Blessed One, not sanctioning going to the Brahmā-world for the one who is purified and liberated, and without even touching upon that person, spoke this stanza 'He who sacrifices…' in a manner suitable for the brahmin in order to show the going to the Brahmā-world of the one who is bound by that jhāna.

515. Tattha tividhanti tikālappasādaṃ sandhāyāha. Tena dāyakato aṅgattayaṃ dasseti. Ārādhaye dakkhiṇeyyebhi tādīti tañca so tādiso tividhasampattisādhako puggalo tividhaṃ yaññasampadaṃ dakkhiṇeyyehi khīṇāsavehi sādheyya sampādeyya. Iminā paṭiggāhakato aṅgattayaṃ dasseti. Evaṃ yajitvā sammā yācayogoti evaṃ mettajjhānapadaṭṭhānabhāvena chaḷaṅgasamannāgataṃ yaññaṃ sammā yajitvā so yācayogo tena chaḷaṅgayaññūpanissayena mettajjhānena upapajjati brahmalokanti [P 2.0419] brūmīti brāhmaṇaṃ samussāhento desanaṃ samāpesi. Sesaṃ sabbagāthāsu uttānatthameva. Ito parañca pubbe vuttanayamevāti.

515. Herein, 'threefold' refers to the serenity of mind at the three times. By this, he shows the three factors on the part of the donor. 'He should gratify the ones worthy of offerings, those such-like ones': that is, such a person, an accomplisher of the threefold perfection, should achieve and accomplish the threefold perfection of the sacrifice with those worthy of offerings, the arahants. By this, he shows the three factors on the part of the recipient. 'Having thus rightly sacrificed, the petitioner…': that is, having rightly performed a sacrifice endowed with six factors because it has the jhāna of loving-kindness as its basis, that petitioner, by means of that jhāna of loving-kindness which is supported by the six-factored sacrifice, 'is reborn in the Brahmā-world, so I say.' Thus, encouraging the brahmin, he concluded the discourse. The meaning of the rest in all the stanzas is plain. And from here on, the method is just as stated before.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

The Paramatthajotikā, Commentary on the Minor Collection

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya māghasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Here ends the explanation of the Māgha Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary.

6. Sabhiyasuttavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Sabhiya Sutta

Evaṃ [V 2.0131] me sutanti sabhiyasuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Ayameva yāssa nidāne vuttā. Atthavaṇṇanākkamepi cassa pubbasadisaṃ pubbe vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Yaṃ pana apubbaṃ, taṃ uttānatthāni padāni pariharantā vaṇṇayissāma. Veḷuvane kalandakanivāpeti veḷuvananti tassa uyyānassa nāmaṃ. Taṃ kira veḷūhi ca parikkhittaṃ ahosi aṭṭhārasahatthena ca pākārena, gopuradvāraṭṭālakayuttaṃ [M 2.0145] nīlobhāsaṃ manoramaṃ, tena “veḷuvana”nti vuccati. Kalandakānañcettha nivāpaṃ adaṃsu, tena “kalandakanivāpo”ti vuccati. Kalandakā nāma kāḷakā vuccanti. Pubbe kira aññataro rājā tattha uyyānakīḷanatthaṃ āgato surāmadena matto divāseyyaṃ supi. Parijanopissa “sutto rājā”ti pupphaphalādīhi palobhiyamāno ito cito ca pakkāmi. Atha surāgandhena aññatarasmā susirarukkhā kaṇhasappo nikkhamitvā rañño abhimukho āgacchati. Taṃ disvā rukkhadevatā “rañño jīvitaṃ dassāmī”ti kāḷakavesena āgantvā kaṇṇamūle saddamakāsi. Rājā paṭibujjhi, kaṇhasappo nivatto. So taṃ disvā “imāya mama kāḷakāya jīvitaṃ dinna”nti kāḷakānaṃ tattha nivāpaṃ paṭṭhapesi, abhayaghosanañca [P 2.0420] ghosāpesi. Tasmā taṃ tato pabhuti “kalandakanivāpo”ti saṅkhaṃ gataṃ.

The Sabhiya Sutta begins: 'Thus have I heard.' What is its origin? The very one that was stated in its introduction. In the course of explaining the meaning, what is similar to the previous should be understood in the way stated before. But what is new, we will explain by setting forth the words with their plain meaning. ‘In the Bamboo Grove, at the Kalandakas’ Feeding Ground’: ‘Bamboo Grove’ is the name of that park. It is said that it was surrounded by bamboos and by a wall eighteen cubits high, complete with gate-towers and watchtowers, gleaming blue and delightful; hence it is called ‘Veḷuvana.’ And there they gave a feeding portion to the kalandakas, so it is called ‘Kalandakanivāpa.’ Kalandakas are said to be squirrels. It is said that in the past, a certain king came there to enjoy the park and, intoxicated with liquor, fell asleep during the day. His retinue, thinking, ‘The king is asleep,’ were enticed by flowers and fruits and wandered off. Then, by the scent of the liquor, a black snake came out of a hollow tree and approached the king. Seeing it, a tree-deity thought, ‘I will give the king his life,’ and coming in the guise of a squirrel, it made a sound near his ear. The king awoke; the black snake turned back. Seeing this, he thought, ‘My life was given by this squirrel,’ and he established a feeding ground for squirrels there and had a proclamation of safety announced. Therefore, from that time on, it came to be known as ‘Kalandakanivāpa.’

Sabhiyassa paribbājakassāti sabhiyoti tassa nāmaṃ, paribbājakoti bāhira pabbajjaṃ upādāya vuccati. Purāṇasālohitāya devatāyāti na mātā na pitā, apica kho panassa mātā viya pitā viya ca hitajjhāsayattā so devaputto “purāṇasālohitā devatā”ti vutto. Parinibbute kira kassape bhagavati patiṭṭhite suvaṇṇacetiye tayo kulaputtā sammukhasāvakānaṃ santike pabbajitvā cariyānurūpāni kammaṭṭhānāni gahetvā paccantajanapadaṃ gantvā araññāyatane samaṇadhammaṃ karonti, antarantarā ca cetiyavandanatthāya dhammassavanatthāya ca nagaraṃ gacchanti. Aparena ca samayena tāvatakampi araññe vippavāsaṃ arocayamānā tattheva appamattā vihariṃsu, evaṃ viharantāpi na ca kiñci visesaṃ adhigamiṃsu. Tato nesaṃ ahosi – “mayaṃ piṇḍāya gacchantā jīvite sāpekkhā homa, jīvite sāpekkhena ca na sakkā lokuttaradhammo adhigantuṃ, puthujjanakālakiriyāpi dukkhā, handa mayaṃ nisseṇiṃ bandhitvā pabbataṃ [V 2.0132] abhiruyha kāye ca jīvite ca anapekkhā samaṇadhammaṃ karomā”ti. Te tathā akaṃsu.

‘Of the wandering ascetic Sabhiya’: ‘Sabhiya’ was his name, and ‘wandering ascetic’ refers to his adoption of the external ascetic life. ‘By a deity who was an old blood-relative’: he was neither his mother nor his father, but because that deity had a loving and beneficial attitude towards him like a mother or a father, that deity was called ‘a deity who was an old blood-relative.’ It is said that after the Blessed One Kassapa had attained final Nibbāna and a golden stupa had been established, three young men of good family went forth in the presence of the direct disciples. Having taken up meditation subjects suitable to their temperaments, they went to a remote region and practiced the ascetic life in a forest dwelling, from time to time going to the city to pay homage at the stupa and to listen to the Dhamma. After some time, no longer approving of even that much time away from the forest, they dwelt right there heedfully. Yet even while dwelling thus, they did not achieve any special attainment. Then it occurred to them: ‘When we go for alms, we are concerned with survival. With such concern for survival, it is impossible to attain the supramundane Dhamma. Even the death of an ordinary person is suffering. Come, let us fasten a ladder, climb the mountain, and practice the ascetic life free from concern for body and life.’ And so they did.

Atha nesaṃ mahāthero upanissayasampannattā tadaheva chaḷabhiññāparivāraṃ arahattaṃ sacchākāsi. So iddhiyā himavantaṃ gantvā anotatte mukhaṃ dhovitvā uttarakurūsu piṇḍāya caritvā katabhattakicco puna aññampi padesaṃ gantvā pattaṃ pūretvā anotattaudakañca nāgalatādantapoṇañca gahetvā [M 2.0146] tesaṃ santikaṃ āgantvā āha – “passathāvuso mamānubhāvaṃ, ayaṃ uttarakuruto piṇḍapāto, idaṃ himavantato udakadantapoṇaṃ ābhataṃ, imaṃ bhuñjitvā samaṇadhammaṃ karotha, evāhaṃ tumhe sadā upaṭṭhahissāmī”ti. Te taṃ sutvā āhaṃsu – “tumhe, bhante, katakiccā, tumhehi saha sallāpamattampi amhākaṃ papañco, mā dāni tumhe puna amhākaṃ [P 2.0421] santikaṃ āgamitthā”ti. So kenaci pariyāyena te sampaṭicchāpetuṃ asakkonto pakkāmi.

Then, the great elder among them, due to his being endowed with supporting conditions, attained Arahantship that very day, complete with the sixfold higher knowledge. By his psychic power, he went to the Himalayas, washed his face in Lake Anotatta, wandered for alms in Uttarakuru, and having completed his meal, he went to another region, filled his bowl, and took water from Anotatta and a toothpick made of naga creeper. Returning to their presence, he said: ‘See, friends, my power—this almsfood is from Uttarakuru; this water and toothpick have been brought from the Himalayas. Eat this and practice the ascetic duties. Thus I will always attend to you.’ Hearing this, they replied: ‘Venerable sir, you have done what had to be done. Even mere conversation with you is a proliferation for us. Do not come near us again.’ Unable to persuade them by any means, he departed.

Tato tesaṃ eko dvīhatīhaccayena pañcābhiñño anāgāmī ahosi. Sopi tatheva akāsi, itarena ca paṭikkhitto tatheva agamāsi. So taṃ paṭikkhipitvā vāyamanto pabbataṃ āruhanadivasato sattame divase kiñci visesaṃ anadhigantvāva kālakato devaloke nibbatti. Khīṇāsavattheropi taṃ divasameva parinibbāyi, anāgāmī suddhāvāsesu uppajji. Devaputto chasu kāmāvacaradevalokesu anulomapaṭilomena dibbasampattiṃ anubhavitvā amhākaṃ bhagavato kāle devalokā cavitvā aññatarissā paribbājikāya kucchimhi paṭisandhiṃ aggahesi. Sā kira aññatarassa khattiyassa dhītā, taṃ mātāpitaro “amhākaṃ dhītā samayantaraṃ jānātū”ti ekassa paribbājakassa niyyātesuṃ. Tasseko antevāsiko paribbājako tāya saddhiṃ vippaṭipajji. Sā tena gabbhaṃ gaṇhi. Taṃ gabbhiniṃ disvā paribbājikā nikkaḍḍhiṃsu. Sā aññattha gacchantī antarāmagge sabhāyaṃ vijāyi, tenassa “sabhiyo”tveva nāmaṃ akāsi. Sopi sabhiyo vaḍḍhitvā paribbājakapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā nānāsatthāni uggahetvā mahāvādī hutvā vādakkhittatāya sakalajambudīpe vicaranto attano sadisaṃ vādiṃ adisvā nagaradvāre assamaṃ kārāpetvā khattiyakumārādayo sippaṃ sikkhāpento tattha vasati.

Then, among them, one, after two or three days, became a non-returner possessing the five higher knowledges. He too acted in the same way and was likewise rejected by the other, departing in the same manner. Having rejected him, that monk strove on, but without attaining any special distinction, on the seventh day from climbing the mountain he passed away and was reborn in a deva world. The elder whose taints were destroyed attained final Nibbāna on that very day, while the non-returner was reborn in the Pure Abodes. The deity, having experienced divine bliss in forward and reverse order throughout the six sense-sphere deva worlds, passed away from the deva world in the time of our Blessed One and took rebirth in the womb of a certain female wanderer. She, it seems, was the daughter of a certain khattiya, and her parents entrusted her to a wanderer, saying, ‘Let our daughter learn another doctrine.’ One of that wanderer's disciples, a wanderer himself, misbehaved with her, and she became pregnant by him. Seeing her pregnant, the female wanderers expelled her. While going elsewhere, she gave birth on the road in a public hall, and so they named him ‘Sabhiya.’ That Sabhiya grew up, took the going-forth of a wanderer, studied various treatises, and became a great debater. Due to being undefeated in debate, he traveled all over Jambudīpa but, not finding anyone equal to him in debate, he had a hermitage built at the city gate. There he stayed, teaching arts and sciences to khattiya youths and others.

Atha bhagavā pavattitavaradhammacakko anupubbena rājagahaṃ āgantvā veḷuvane viharati kalandakanivāpe. Sabhiyo pana buddhuppādaṃ na jānāti. Atha so suddhāvāsabrahmā samāpattito vuṭṭhāya “imāhaṃ visesaṃ kassānubhāvena patto”ti āvajjento kassapassa bhagavato sāsane samaṇadhammakiriyaṃ te ca sahāye anussaritvā “tesu eko [M 2.0147] parinibbuto, eko idāni katthā”ti [V 2.0133] āvajjento “devalokā cavitvā jambudīpe uppanno buddhuppādampi na jānātī”ti ñatvā “handa naṃ buddhupasevanāya niyojemī”ti vīsati pañhe abhisaṅkharitvā rattibhāge tassa assamamāgamma [P 2.0422] ākāse ṭhatvā “sabhiya, sabhiyā”ti pakkosi. So niddāyamāno tikkhattuṃ taṃ saddaṃ sutvā nikkhamma obhāsaṃ disvā pañjaliko aṭṭhāsi. Tato taṃ brahmā āha – “ahaṃ sabhiya tavatthāya vīsati pañhe āhariṃ, te tvaṃ uggaṇha. Yo ca te samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā ime pañhe puṭṭho byākaroti, tassa santike brahmacariyaṃ careyyāsī”ti. Imaṃ devaputtaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ “purāṇasālohitāya devatāya pañhā uddiṭṭhā hontī”ti. Uddiṭṭhāti uddesamatteneva vuttā, na vibhaṅgena.

Then the Blessed One, having set in motion the excellent Wheel of the Dhamma, in due course arrived at Rājagaha and was dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, at the Kalandakas’ Feeding Ground. Sabhiya, however, did not know of the Buddha’s arising. Then that Brahmā from the Pure Abodes, having emerged from his attainment, reflected: ‘By whose power have I attained this distinction?’ Remembering the practice of the ascetic life in the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa and those companions, he reflected further: ‘Among them, one has attained final Nibbāna; where is the other one now?’ Knowing that, ‘Having passed away from the deva world, he has been reborn in Jambudīpa, yet he does not know of the Buddha’s arising,’ he thought: ‘Come now, I shall direct him to attend upon the Buddha.’ Having formulated twenty questions, he approached Sabhiya's hermitage during the night, stood in the sky, and called out: ‘Sabhiya, Sabhiya!’ Hearing that call three times while drowsy, Sabhiya came out, saw the radiance, and stood with hands clasped in reverence. Then that Brahmā said to him: ‘Sabhiya, I have brought twenty questions for you. Learn them. You should lead the holy life under whichever ascetic or brahmin can answer these questions when asked.’ It was with reference to this deity that it was said: ‘The questions were set forth by a deity who was an old blood-relative.’ ‘Set forth’ means they were stated merely in summary, not in detail.

Evaṃ vutte ca ne sabhiyo ekavacaneneva padapaṭipāṭiyā uggahesi. Atha so brahmā jānantopi tassa buddhuppādaṃ nācikkhi. “Atthaṃ gavesamāno paribbājako sayameva satthāraṃ ñassati. Ito bahiddhā ca samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ tucchabhāva”nti iminā panādhippāyena evamāha – “yo te sabhiya…pe… careyyāsī”ti. Theragāthāsu pana catukkanipāte sabhiyattherāpadānaṃ vaṇṇentā bhaṇanti “sā cassa mātā attano vippaṭipattiṃ cintetvā taṃ jigucchamānā jhānaṃ uppādetvā brahmaloke uppannā, tāya brahmadevatāya te pañhā uddiṭṭhā”ti.

When this was said, Sabhiya learned them in a single hearing, in the exact sequence of the words. Then that Brahmā, though he knew of the Buddha’s arising, did not tell him. With the intention, ‘Seeking the meaning, the wanderer will discover the Teacher for himself. And outside of this, the ascetics and brahmins are void,’ he said: ‘Whichever ascetic or brahmin, Sabhiya … you should lead the holy life under him.’ However, in the Theragāthā, in the Chapter of Fours, when commenting on the Apadāna of the Elder Sabhiya, they say: ‘His mother, reflecting on her own misconduct and feeling revulsion for it, developed jhāna and was reborn in the Brahmā world; it was by that Brahmā deity that these questions were set forth.’

Ye teti idāni vattabbānaṃ uddesapaccuddeso. Samaṇabrāhmaṇāti pabbajjūpagamanena lokasammutiyā ca samaṇā ceva brāhmaṇā ca. Saṅghinoti gaṇavanto. Gaṇinoti satthāro, “sabbaññuno maya”nti evaṃ paṭiññātāro. Gaṇācariyāti uddesaparipucchādivasena pabbajitagahaṭṭhagaṇassa ācariyā. Ñātāti abhiññātā, vissutā pākaṭāti vuttaṃ hoti. Yasassinoti lābhaparivārasampannā. Titthakarāti tesaṃ diṭṭhānugatiṃ āpajjantehi otaritabbānaṃ ogāhitabbānaṃ diṭṭhititthānaṃ kattāro. Sādhusammatā bahujanassāti “sādhavo ete santo sappurisā”ti evaṃ bahujanassa sammatā.

‘Those who’: this is a statement and explanation of the terms to be mentioned now. ‘Ascetics and brahmins’: by undertaking the going-forth and by worldly convention, they are ascetics and brahmins. ‘With a following’: possessing a group. ‘Leaders of a group’: teachers who claim, ‘We are all-knowing.’ ‘Teachers of a group’: teachers of a group of renunciants and householders by way of recitation, questioning, and so on. ‘Known’: this means well-known, famous, and renowned. ‘Illustrious’: endowed with gain and a following. ‘Founders of sects’: creators of fords of views, which are to be entered and plunged into by those who adopt the course of their views. ‘Regarded as good by many people’: regarded by the multitude as, ‘These are good, serene, and true men.’

Seyyathidanti [M 2.0148] katame teti ce-iccetasmiṃ atthe nipāto. Pūraṇoti nāmaṃ, kassapoti gottaṃ. So kira jātiyā dāso, dāsasataṃ [P 2.0423] pūrento jāto. Tenassa “pūraṇo”ti nāmamakaṃsu. Palāyitvā pana naggesu pabbajitvā “kassapo aha”nti gottaṃ uddisi, sabbaññutañca paccaññāsi. Makkhalīti nāmaṃ, gosālāya jātattā gosālotipi vuccati. Sopi kira jātiyā dāso eva, palāyitvā pabbaji, sabbaññutañca paccaññāsi. Ajitoti nāmaṃ, appicchatāya kesakambalaṃ dhāreti, tena kesakambalotipi vuccati, sopi sabbaññutaṃ paccaññāsi[V 2.0134]. Pakudhoti nāmaṃ, kaccāyanoti gottaṃ. Appicchavasena udake jīvasaññāya ca nhānamukhadhovanādi paṭikkhitto, sopi sabbaññutaṃ paccaññāsi. Sañcayoti nāmaṃ, belaṭṭho panassa pitā, tasmā belaṭṭhaputtoti vuccati, sopi sabbaññutaṃ paccaññāsi. Nigaṇṭhoti pabbajjānāmena, nāṭaputtoti pitunāmena vuccati. Nāṭoti kira nāmassa pitā, tassa puttoti nāṭaputto, sopi sabbaññutaṃ paccaññāsi. Sabbepi pañcasatapañcasatasissaparivārā ahesuṃ. Teti te cha satthāro. Te pañheti te vīsati pañhe. Teti te cha satthāro. Na sampāyantīti na sampādenti. Kopanti cittacetasikānaṃ āvilabhāvaṃ. Dosanti paduṭṭhacittataṃ, tadubhayampetaṃ mandatikkhabhedassa kodhassevādhivacanaṃ. Appaccayanti appatītatā, domanassanti vuttaṃ hoti. Pātukarontīti kāyavacīvikārena pakāsenti, pākaṭaṃ karonti.

As to `Seyyathidaṃ`: it is a particle in the sense of, 'If one asks, who are they?'. 'Pūraṇa' is his name, 'Kassapa' is his clan. It is said that he was born a slave, completing a hundred slaves, hence they named him 'Pūraṇa.' Having fled, he went forth among the naked ascetics, declared his clan as 'Kassapa,' and also claimed omniscience. 'Makkhalī' is his name; because he was born in a cow-pen, he is also called 'Gosāla.' He too, it is said, was born a slave; he fled, went forth, and claimed omniscience. 'Ajita' is his name; because he had few wishes, he wore a hair blanket, hence he is called 'Kesakambala'—he too claimed omniscience. 'Pakudha' is his name, 'Kaccāyana' is his clan. On account of his few wishes and his perception of life in water, he rejected bathing, washing the face, and so on—he too claimed omniscience. 'Sañcaya' is his name; Belaṭṭha was his father, therefore he is called 'Belaṭṭhaputta'—he too claimed omniscience. 'Nigaṇṭha' is his ordination name, 'Nāṭaputta' is his patronymic. It is said that Nāṭa was his father, so he is 'Nāṭaputta' (son of Nāṭa)—he too claimed omniscience. All of them had retinues of five hundred disciples each. By 'they' is meant these six teachers. By 'these questions' is meant the twenty questions. By 'they' is meant these six teachers. 'They do not succeed' means they do not accomplish it. By 'anger' is meant the turbid state of mind and mental factors. By 'hostility' is meant a corrupted state of mind; both these are synonyms for anger, distinguished as mild and intense. By 'resentment' is meant lack of conviction; it is said to be 'displeasure.' By 'they display' is meant they reveal it by way of bodily and verbal action; they make it manifest.

Hīnāyāti gahaṭṭhabhāvāya. Gahaṭṭhabhāvo hi pabbajjaṃ upanidhāya sīlādiguṇahīnato hīnakāmasukhapaṭisevanato vā “hīno”ti vuccati. Uccā pabbajjā. Āvattitvāti osakkitvā. Kāme paribhuñjeyyanti kāme paṭiseveyyaṃ. Iti kirassa sabbaññupaṭiññānampi pabbajitānaṃ tucchakattaṃ disvā ahosi. Uppannaparivitakkavaseneva ca āgantvā punappunaṃ vīmaṃsamānassa atha kho sabhiyassa paribbājakassa etadahosi – “ayampi kho samaṇo”ti ca “yepi kho te bhonto”ti ca “samaṇo kho daharoti na uññātabbo”ti cāti evamādi. Tattha jiṇṇātiādīni padāni vuttanayāneva. Therāti attano samaṇadhamme thirabhāvappattā. Rattaññūti [P 2.0424] ratanaññū, “nibbānaratanaṃ jānāma maya”nti evaṃ sakāya paṭiññāya lokenāpi sammatā, bahurattividū vā. Ciraṃ pabbajitānaṃ etesanti cirapabbajitā. Na uññātabboti na avajānitabbo, na nīcaṃ katvā jānitabboti vuttaṃ [M 2.0149] hoti. Na paribhotabboti na paribhavitabbo, “kimesa ñassatī”ti evaṃ na gahetabboti vuttaṃ hoti.

By 'to the low' is meant to the household life. For the household life is called 'low' in comparison with the going forth because it is deficient in virtues such as moral conduct, or because one pursues base sensual pleasures. The going forth is 'high.' By 'having reverted' is meant having drawn back. By 'I would enjoy sensual pleasures' is meant I would indulge in sensual pleasures. It seems this thought of his arose from seeing the futility of those renunciants who had even claimed omniscience. And as this thought arose, and as he came and investigated again and again, it occurred to Sabhiya the wanderer: 'This one, too, is a recluse,' and 'Those venerable ones,' and 'A young recluse should not be disdained,' and so on. Here, the words 'aged' and so on are as already explained. By 'elders' is meant those who have attained a state of firmness in their own ascetic duties. By 'of long standing' is meant knowers of the jewel; they are esteemed by the world for their own declaration, 'We know the jewel of Nibbāna,' or they are knowers of many nights. By 'of those long gone forth' is meant those who have been ordained for a long time. By 'should not be disdained' is meant he should not be despised; that is, it is said, he should not be regarded as inferior. By 'should not be scorned' is meant he should not be treated with contempt; that is, it is said, he should not be regarded thus: 'What can this one know?'

516. Kaṅkhī vecikicchīti sabhiyo bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodamāno evaṃ bhagavato rūpasampattidamūpasamasūcitaṃ sabbaññutaṃ sambhāvayamāno vigatuddhacco hutvā āha – “kaṅkhī vecikicchī”ti. Tattha “labheyyaṃ nu kho imesaṃ byākaraṇa”nti evaṃ pañhānaṃ byākaraṇakaṅkhāya kaṅkhī. “Ko nu kho imassimassa ca pañhassa attho”ti evaṃ vicikicchāya vecikicchī. Dubbalavicikicchāya vā tesaṃ pañhānaṃ atthe kaṅkhanato kaṅkhī, balavatiyā vicinanto kicchatiyeva, na sakkoti sanniṭṭhātunti vecikicchī. Abhikaṅkhamānoti ativiya patthayamāno. Tesantakaroti tesaṃ pañhānaṃ antakaro. Bhavantova evaṃ bhavāhīti dassento āha “pañhe me puṭṭho…pe… byākarohi me”ti. Tattha pañhe meti pañhe mayā. Puṭṭhoti pucchito. Anupubbanti [V 2.0135] pañhapaṭipāṭiyā anudhammanti atthānurūpaṃ pāḷiṃ āropento. Byākarohi meti mayhaṃ byākarohi.

516. As to 'doubting, perplexed': while exchanging courtesies with the Blessed One, Sabhiya, honoring the omniscience indicated by the Blessed One's accomplishment in form, his self-control, and his peacefulness, became free from restlessness and said: 'Doubting, perplexed.' Here, he is 'doubting' because of his doubt about the explanation of the questions, thus: 'Might I obtain an explanation for these?' He is 'perplexed' because of his perplexity thus: 'What indeed is the meaning of this and that question?' Alternatively, he is 'doubting' because he doubts the meaning of the questions with a weak perplexity; he is 'perplexed' because, though investigating with strong perplexity, he is troubled and unable to come to a conclusion. By 'eagerly desiring' is meant exceedingly longing. By 'the one who makes an end to them' is meant the one who makes an end to those questions. Showing, 'You should be such a one,' he said: 'When asked questions by me ... explain them to me.' Here, `pañhe me` means 'questions by me' (`pañhe mayā`). By 'asked' is meant questioned. By 'in due order' is meant in the sequence of the questions. By 'in accordance with the Dhamma' is meant applying the text in conformity with the meaning. By 'explain to me' is meant 'explain for my sake.'

517. Dūratoti so kira ito cito cāhiṇḍanto sattayojanasatamaggato āgato. Tenāha – bhagavā “dūrato āgatosī”ti, kassapassa bhagavato vā sāsanato āgatattā “dūrato āgatosī”ti naṃ āha.

517. By 'from afar': it is said that he, wandering here and there, has come from a distance of seven hundred yojanas. Therefore the Blessed One said, 'You have come from afar.' Or, because he had come from the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, he said to him, 'You have come from afar.'

518. Puccha manti imāya panassa gāthāya sabbaññupavāraṇaṃ pavāreti. Tattha manasicchasīti manasā icchasi.

518. By 'Ask me': with this verse he makes the invitation concerning omniscience. Here, by 'you wish in mind' is meant 'you wish with your mind.'

Yaṃ vatāhanti yaṃ vata ahaṃ. Attamanoti pītipāmojjasomanassehi phuṭacitto. Udaggoti kāyena cittena ca abbhunnato[P 2.0425]. Idaṃ pana padaṃ na sabbapāṭhesu atthi. Idāni yehi dhammehi attamano, te dassento āha – “pamudito pītisomanassajāto”ti.

By 'Yaṃ vatāhaṃ' is meant 'yaṃ vata ahaṃ' (what I indeed). By 'delighted' is meant with a mind pervaded by rapture, gladness, and mental joy. By 'elated' is meant uplifted in body and mind. This word, however, is not in all textual recensions. Now, showing the states by which he was delighted, he said: 'joyful, born of rapture and mental joy.'

519. Kiṃ pattinanti kiṃ pattaṃ kimadhigataṃ. Soratanti suvūpasantaṃ. “Surata”ntipi pāṭho, suṭṭhu uparatanti attho. Dantanti damitaṃ. Buddhoti vibuddho, buddhaboddhabbo vā. Evaṃ sabhiyo ekekāya gāthāya cattāro cattāro katvā pañcahi gāthāhi vīsati pañhe pucchi. Bhagavā panassa ekamekaṃ [M 2.0150] pañhaṃ ekamekāya gāthāya katvā arahattanikūṭeneva vīsatiyā gāthāhi byākāsi.

519. By 'one who has attained what?' is meant what has he reached, what has he acquired? By 'gentle' is meant well pacified. There is also the reading 'surata,' meaning 'well restrained.' By 'tamed' is meant controlled. By 'awakened' is meant enlightened, or one who has understood what is to be understood. Thus Sabhiya, by formulating four questions in each verse, asked twenty questions in five verses. The Blessed One, however, answered each single question with a single verse, explaining them in twenty verses that culminate in arahantship.

520. Tattha yasmā bhinnakileso paramatthabhikkhu, so ca nibbānappatto hoti, tasmā assa “kiṃ pattinamāhu bhikkhuna”nti imaṃ pañhaṃ byākaronto “pajjenā”tiādimāha. Tassattho – yo attanā bhāvitena maggena parinibbānagato kilesaparinibbānaṃ patto, parinibbānagatattā eva ca vitiṇṇakaṅkho vipattisampattihānibuddhiucchedasassataapuññapuññabhedaṃ vibhavañca bhavañca vippahāya, maggavāsaṃ vusitavā khīṇapunabbhavoti ca etesaṃ thutivacanānaṃ araho, so bhikkhūti.

520. Here, since a bhikkhu in the ultimate sense is one who has shattered the defilements and has attained Nibbāna, in answering the question, 'What do they call the attainment of a bhikkhu?,' he spoke the verse beginning 'By the path...' Its meaning is this: One who, by the path developed by himself, has gone to final Nibbāna, having attained the final Nibbāna of the defilements; and just because he has gone to final Nibbāna, he has crossed over doubt; having abandoned the distinctions of failure and success, decline and growth, annihilationism and eternalism, demerit and merit, and having left behind both non-becoming and becoming; and who is worthy of these words of praise: 'he has lived the life of the path' and 'his renewed existence is destroyed'—he is a bhikkhu.

521. Yasmā pana vippaṭipattito suṭṭhu uparatabhāvena nānappakārakilesavūpasamena ca sorato hoti, tasmā tamatthaṃ dassento “sabbattha upekkhako”tiādinā nayena dutiyapañhabyākaraṇamāha. Tassattho – yo sabbattha rūpādīsu ārammaṇesu “cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā neva sumano [V 2.0136] hoti, na dummano”ti evaṃ pavattāya chaḷaṅgupekkhāya upekkhako, vepullappattāya satiyā satimā, na so hiṃsati neva hiṃsati kañci tasathāvarādibhedaṃ sattaṃ sabbaloke sabbasmimpi loke, tiṇṇoghattā tiṇṇo, samitapāpattā samaṇo, āvilasaṅkappappahānā anāvilo. Yassa cime rāgadosamohamānadiṭṭhikilesaduccaritasaṅkhātā sattussadā keci oḷārikā vā sukhumā vā na santi, so imāya upekkhāvihāritāya sativepullatāya ahiṃsakatāya ca vippaṭipattito suṭṭhu uparatabhāvena iminā oghādinānappakārakilesavūpasamena [P 2.0426] ca soratoti.

521. And since one is 'gentle' (sorata) through being well restrained from wrong practice and through the calming of the various kinds of defilements, showing this meaning, he gave the explanation to the second question by the method beginning 'equanimous everywhere.' Its meaning is this: One who is equanimous towards all objects such as forms by means of the six-factored equanimity that proceeds thus: 'Having seen a form with the eye, he is neither glad nor sad'; who is mindful with a mindfulness that has reached fullness; he does not harm, he never harms any being at all, whether moving or stationary, in the whole world. He is 'one who has crossed' (tiṇṇo) because he has crossed the flood; he is a 'recluse' (samaṇo) because his evils are pacified; he is 'untroubled' (anāvilo) because he has abandoned turbid thoughts. One in whom these seven 'uproars'—namely, lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, views, defilements, and misconduct—do not exist at all, whether coarse or subtle, is 'gentle' because of this dwelling in equanimity, this fullness of mindfulness, and this harmlessness, and because of being well restrained from wrong practice, and because of this calming of the various kinds of defilements such as the floods.

522. Yasmā ca bhāvitindriyo nibbhayo nibbikāro danto hoti, tasmā tamatthaṃ dassento “yassindriyānī”ti gāthāya tatiyapañhaṃ byākāsi. Tassattho – yassa cakkhādīni chaḷindriyāni gocarabhāvanāya aniccāditilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā vāsanābhāvanāya satisampajaññagandhaṃ gāhāpetvā ca bhāvitāni, tāni ca kho yathā ajjhattaṃ gocarabhāvanāya, evaṃ pana bahiddhā ca sabbaloketi yattha yattha indriyānaṃ vekallatā vekallatāya vā sambhavo, tattha tattha nābhijjhādivasena bhāvitānīti [M 2.0151] evaṃ nibbijjha ñatvā paṭivijjhitvā imaṃ parañca lokaṃ sakasantatikkhandhalokaṃ parasantatikkhandhalokañca adandhamaraṇaṃ maritukāmo kālaṃ kaṅkhati, jīvitakkhayakālaṃ āgameti patimāneti, na bhāyati maraṇassa. Yathāha thero –

522. And since one with developed faculties is fearless, unperturbed, and tamed, showing this meaning, he explained the third question with the verse beginning 'Whose faculties...' Its meaning is this: One whose six faculties, beginning with the eye, have been developed by applying the three characteristics of impermanence, etc., through development regarding their objects, and by making them acquire the 'scent' of mindfulness and clear comprehension through development of the latent tendencies. And these faculties are developed not only internally through development regarding their objects, but also externally, in the entire world. That is, wherever there is a defect in the faculties or a possibility of a defect, they are developed by way of not having longing, etc. Having thus known and penetrated this world and the next—the world of one's own stream of aggregates and the world of others' streams of aggregates—and desiring to die a blameless death, he awaits his time, he looks for the time of the exhaustion of his life-span; he does not fear death. As the elder said:

“Maraṇe me bhayaṃ natthi, nikanti natthi jīvite”; (Theragā. 20);

“Nābhikaṅkhāmi maraṇaṃ, nābhikaṅkhāmi jīvitaṃ;

Kālañca paṭikaṅkhāmi, nibbisaṃ bhatako yathā”ti. (theragā. 606);

"I have no fear of death, no craving for life." (Theragā. 20) "I do not long for death, I do not long for life; I await my time, like a hireling for his wages." (Theragā. 606)

Bhāvito sa dantoti evaṃ bhāvitindriyo so dantoti.

By 'developed, he is tamed' is meant: thus, with faculties developed, he is tamed.

523. Yasmā pana buddho nāma buddhisampanno kilesaniddā vibuddho ca, tasmā tamatthaṃ dassento “kappānī”ti gāthāya catutthapañhaṃ byākāsi. Tattha kappānīti taṇhādiṭṭhiyo. Tā hi tathā tathā vikappanato “kappānī”ti vuccanti. Viceyyāti aniccādibhāvena sammasitvā. Kevalānīti sakalāni. Saṃsāranti yo cāyaṃ –

523. Because a Buddha is one endowed with wisdom, awakened from the slumber of defilements, therefore, to explain that meaning, he answered the fourth question with the verse beginning 'Kappāni'. Here, 'kappāni' refers to craving and views. For they are called 'kappāni' because they discriminate in various ways. 'Viceyya' means having scrutinized through the nature of impermanence and so forth. 'Kevalāni' means all. 'Saṃsāra' refers to that which is—

“Khandhānañca paṭipāṭi, dhātuāyatanāna ca;

Abbocchinnaṃ vattamānā, saṃsāroti pavuccatī”ti. –

"The uninterrupted continuity of aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, ongoing, is called saṃsāra."

Evaṃ [V 2.0137] khandhādipaṭipāṭisaṅkhāto saṃsāro, taṃ saṃsārañca kevalaṃ viceyya. Ettāvatā khandhānaṃ mūlabhūtesu kammakilesesu khandhesu cāti evaṃ tīsupi vaṭṭesu vipassanaṃ āha. Dubhayaṃ cutūpapātanti sattānaṃ cutiṃ upapātanti imañca [P 2.0427] ubhayaṃ viceyya ñatvāti attho. Etena cutūpapātañāṇaṃ āha. Vigatarajamanaṅgaṇaṃ visuddhanti rāgādirajānaṃ vigamā aṅgaṇānaṃ abhāvā malānañca vigamā vigatarajamanaṅgaṇaṃ visuddhaṃ. Pattaṃ jātikhayanti nibbānaṃ pattaṃ. Tamāhu buddhanti taṃ imāya lokuttaravipassanāya cutūpapātañāṇabhedāya buddhiyā sampannattā imāya ca vigatarajāditāya kilesaniddā vibuddhattā tāya paṭipadāya jātikkhayaṃ pattaṃ buddhamāhu.

Thus, saṃsāra is designated as the sequence of aggregates and so on. And by the words 'having investigated that entire saṃsāra,' insight is described regarding the three rounds: into kamma and defilements, which are the root of the aggregates, and into the aggregates themselves. ‘Both passing away and rebirth’ means to investigate and know both the passing away and rebirth of beings. By this, the knowledge of passing away and rebirth is indicated. ‘Free from dust, without blemish, purified’ means free from the dust of lust and other defilements, devoid of blemishes, and free from stains, thus ‘free from dust, without blemish, purified’. ‘Having attained the destruction of birth’ means having attained Nibbāna. They call him a Buddha because he is endowed with the wisdom of supramundane insight, distinguished by the knowledge of passing away and rebirth, and because he is awakened from the slumber of defilements through this freedom from dust, etc., and because he has attained the destruction of birth through that practice.

Atha vā kappāni viceyya kevalānīti “anekepi saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭakappe amutrāsi”ntiādinā (itivu. 99; pārā. 12) nayena vicinitvāti attho. Etena paṭhamavijjamāha. Saṃsāraṃ dubhayaṃ cutūpapātanti sattānaṃ cutiṃ upapātanti imañca ubhayaṃ saṃsāraṃ [M 2.0152] “ime vata bhonto sattā”tiādinā nayena vicinitvāti attho. Etena dutiyavijjamāha. Avasesena tatiyavijjamāha. Āsavakkhayañāṇena hi vigatarajāditā ca nibbānappatti ca hotīti. Tamāhu buddhanti evaṃ vijjattayabhedabuddhisampannaṃ taṃ buddhamāhūti.

Alternatively, ‘having examined the aeons completely’ means having investigated in the manner of ‘in many aeons of contraction and expansion, I was there,’ and so on (Itivuttaka 99; Pārā. 12). By this, the first knowledge is stated. ‘The twofold saṃsāra, passing away and rebirth’ means having investigated both the passing away and rebirth of beings, and this entire saṃsāra, in the manner of ‘Indeed, these beings,’ and so on. By this, the second knowledge is stated. By the remainder, the third knowledge is stated. For through the knowledge of the destruction of the taints, one becomes free from dust, etc., and attains Nibbāna. They call him a Buddha—thus, they call him a Buddha who is endowed with wisdom distinguished by the three knowledges.

525. Evaṃ paṭhamagāthāya vuttapañhe vissajjetvā dutiyagāthāya vuttapañhesupi yasmā brahmabhāvaṃ seṭṭhabhāvaṃ patto paramatthabrāhmaṇo bāhitasabbapāpo hoti, tasmā tamatthaṃ dassento “bāhitvā”ti gāthāya paṭhamaṃ pañhaṃ byākāsi. Tassattho – yo catutthamaggena bāhitvā sabbapāpakāni ṭhitatto, ṭhito icceva vuttaṃ hoti. Bāhitapāpattā eva ca vimalo, vimalabhāvaṃ brahmabhāvaṃ seṭṭhabhāvaṃ patto, paṭippassaddhasamādhivikkhepakarakilesamalena aggaphalasamādhinā sādhusamāhito, saṃsārahetusamatikkamena saṃsāramaticca pariniṭṭhitakiccatāya kevalī, so taṇhādiṭṭhīhi anissitattā asito, lokadhammehi nibbikārattā “tādī”ti ca pavuccati. Evaṃ thutiraho sa brahmā so brāhmaṇoti.

525. Having thus answered the questions stated in the first verse, then regarding the questions in the second verse, because the ultimate brahmin who has attained the state of Brahmā, the highest state, is one who has warded off all evil, he, showing that meaning, explained the first question with the verse beginning ‘having warded off.’ Its meaning is this: one who, through the fourth path, having warded off all evil, is steadfast; indeed, it is said ‘steadfast.’ And because of having warded off evil, he is stainless. Having attained the stainless state, the state of Brahmā, the highest state, he is well-composed with the concentration of the highest fruition, the defilements that disturb concentration being utterly calmed. Having transcended the cause of saṃsāra, he has completed his task by going beyond saṃsāra, thus he is ‘the perfect one.’ Because he is not dependent on craving and views, he is ‘unattached.’ Unaffected by worldly conditions, he is called ‘such a one.’ Thus, he is worthy of praise—that Brahmā, that brahmin.

526. Yasmā pana samitapāpatāya samaṇo, nhātapāpatāya [P 2.0428] nhātako, āgūnaṃ akaraṇena ca nāgoti pavuccati, tasmā tamatthaṃ dassento tato aparāhi tīhi gāthāhi tayo pañhe byākāsi. Tattha samitāvīti ariyamaggena kilese sametvā ṭhito. Samaṇo pavuccate tathattāti tathārūpo samaṇo pavuccatīti. Ettāvatā pañho byākato hoti, sesaṃ tasmiṃ samaṇe sabhiyassa bahumānajananatthaṃ thutivacanaṃ. Yo hi samitāvī, so puññapāpānaṃ apaṭisandhikaraṇena [V 2.0138] pahāya puññapāpaṃ rajānaṃ vigamena virajo, aniccādivasena ñatvā imaṃ parañca lokaṃ jātimaraṇaṃ upātivatto tādi ca hoti.

526. However, since one who has pacified evil is called a recluse (samaṇa), one who has bathed away evil is called a bathed one (nhātaka), and one who does no offense is called a nāga, therefore, explaining that meaning, he answered the three questions with the next three verses. Here, ‘one who has pacified’ means one who has subdued the defilements through the noble path and stands firm. ‘He is called a recluse because of that state’ means one of such a nature is called a recluse. To this extent, the question is answered. The rest is words of praise to inspire reverence for that recluse in Sabhiya. For one who has pacified, having abandoned merit and demerit by preventing a new linking for rebirth, is free from dust by the disappearance of defilements, and knowing this world and the next through impermanence, etc., has transcended birth and death—such a one is also ‘such a one’.

527. Ninhāya…pe… nhātakoti ettha pana yo ajjhattabahiddhāsaṅkhāte sabbasmimpi āyatanaloke ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇavasena uppattirahāni sabbapāpakāni maggañāṇena ninhāya dhovitvā tāya ninhātapāpakatāya taṇhādiṭṭhikappehi kappiyesu devamanussesu kappaṃ na eti, taṃ nhātakamāhūti evamattho daṭṭhabbo.

527. However, regarding ‘having bathed…pe… one who is bathed’: Here, the meaning to be understood is that one who, by means of the knowledge of the path, has bathed and washed away all evil that is liable to arise based on internal and external objects in the entire world of sense bases, designated as internal and external, and because of that bathing away of evil, does not come into a cycle among gods and humans who are subject to cycles formed by craving and views—him they call ‘one who is bathed’.

528. Catutthagāthāyapi āguṃ na karoti kiñci loketi yo loke appamattakampi pāpasaṅkhātaṃ āguṃ na karoti, nāgo pavuccate tathattāti[M 2.0153]. Ettāvatā pañho byākato hoti, sesaṃ pubbanayeneva thutivacanaṃ. Yo hi maggena pahīnaāguttā āguṃ na karoti, so kāmayogādike sabbayoge dasasaññojanabhedāni ca sabbabandhanāni visajja jahitvā sabbattha khandhādīsu kenaci saṅgena na sajjati, dvīhi ca vimuttīhi vimutto, tādi ca hotīti.

528. In the fourth verse, ‘He does no offense whatsoever in the world’ refers to one who commits no offense, however slight, deemed as evil in the world. ‘He is called a nāga because of that state’. Thus far, the question is answered; the rest is a eulogy in the previous manner. For one who, his offenses having been abandoned by the path, commits no offense, has cast off and relinquished all yokes, beginning with the yoke of sensual desire, and all bondages, which are the ten fetters. He is not attached anywhere to the aggregates and so on by any attachment, is liberated by the two liberations, and becomes a stable one.

530. Evaṃ dutiyagāthāya vuttapañhe vissajjetvā tatiyagāthāya vuttapañhesupi yasmā “khettānī”ti āyatanāni vuccanti. Yathāha – “cakkhupetaṃ cakkhāyatanaṃpetaṃ…pe… khettampetaṃ vatthupeta”nti (dha. sa. 596-598). Tāni vijeyya vijetvā abhibhavitvā, viceyya vā aniccādibhāvena vicinitvā upaparikkhitvā kevalāni anavasesāni, visesato pana saṅgahetubhūtaṃ dibbaṃ mānusakañca brahmakhettaṃ, yaṃ dibbaṃ [P 2.0429] dvādasāyatanabhedaṃ tathā mānusakañca, yañca brahmakhettaṃ chaḷāyatane cakkhāyatanādidvādasāyatanabhedaṃ, taṃ sabbampi vijeyya viceyya vā. Yato yadetaṃ sabbesaṃ khettānaṃ mūlabandhanaṃ avijjābhavataṇhādi, tasmā sabbakhettamūlabandhanā pamutto. Evametesaṃ khettānaṃ vijitattā vicinitattā vā khettajino nāma hoti, tasmā “khettānī”ti imāya gāthāya paṭhamapañhaṃ byākāsi. Tattha keci “kammaṃ khettaṃ, viññāṇaṃ bījaṃ, taṇhā sneho”ti (a. ni. 3.77) vacanato kammāni khettānīti vadanti. Dibbaṃ mānusakañca brahmakhettanti ettha ca devūpagaṃ kammaṃ dibbaṃ, manussūpagaṃ kammaṃ mānusakaṃ, brahmūpagaṃ kammaṃ brahmakhettanti vaṇṇayanti. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

530. Having thus answered the questions posed in the second verse, regarding the questions in the third verse, since ‘fields’ are said to refer to the sense bases—as it is said: ‘This is the eye, this is the eye-base…pe… this is the field, this is the object’ (Dhs. 596-598)—he conquers them, overcomes them, or discerns them thoroughly, examining their nature as impermanent, etc., leaving nothing unexamined. Specifically, he conquers or discerns the divine and human fields, as well as the Brahmā-field, which are the basis for grasping. The divine field consists of the twelve sense bases, and likewise the human field. The Brahmā-field consists of the twelve sense bases beginning with the eye-base within the six sense bases. He conquers or discerns all of this. Since the root bondage of all these fields is ignorance, craving for existence, etc., he is therefore freed from the root bondage of all fields. Thus, because he has conquered or discerned these fields, he is called a conqueror of fields. Hence, the first question is explained in this verse using ‘fields’. Here, some say, ‘Action is the field, consciousness the seed, craving the moisture’ (AN 3.77), and thus interpret actions as fields. Regarding the divine and human fields, as well as the Brahmā-field, here they explain that action leading to the deva realm is divine, action leading to the human realm is human, and action leading to the Brahmā realm is the Brahmā-field. The rest is as previously explained.

531. Yasmā pana sakaṭṭhena kosasadisattā “kosānī”ti kammāni vuccanti, tesañca lunanā samucchedanā kusalo hoti, tasmā tamatthaṃ dassento “kosānī”ti gāthāya dutiyapañhaṃ byākāsi. Tassattho – lokiyalokuttaravipassanāya visayato kiccato ca aniccādibhāvena kusalākusalakammasaṅkhātāni [V 2.0139] kosāni viceyya kevalāni, visesato pana saṅgahetubhūtaṃ aṭṭhakāmāvacarakusalacetanābhedaṃ dibbaṃ mānusakañca navamahaggatakusalacetanābhedañca brahmakosaṃ viceyya. Tato imāya maggabhāvanāya avijjābhavataṇhādibhedā sabbakosānaṃ mūlabandhanā pamutto, evametesaṃ kosānaṃ lunanā “kusalo”ti pavuccati, tathattā tādī ca hotīti. Atha vā sattānaṃ [M 2.0154] dhammānañca nivāsaṭṭhena asikosasadisattā “kosānī”ti tayo bhavā dvādasāyatanāni ca veditabbāni. Evamettha yojanā kātabbā.

531. However, since by their own meaning, being like a sheath, actions are called ‘sheaths’ (kosāni), and he is skilled in cutting and eradicating them, therefore, explaining that meaning, he answered the second question in the verse with ‘sheaths’. Its meaning is this: having thoroughly examined the sheaths, which are the wholesome and unwholesome kammas, by way of their impermanence, etc., through worldly and supramundane insight with respect to object and function, completely; specifically, having examined the divine and human sheaths, which consist of the eight types of sense-sphere wholesome volitions, and the Brahmā sheath, which consists of the nine types of sublime wholesome volitions, which are the basis for grasping. Then, through this path-development, one is freed from the root bonds of all sheaths, such as ignorance, craving for existence, etc. Thus, he is called ‘skilled’ in cutting these sheaths, and because of that state, he is also ‘such a one’. Alternatively, the three realms of existence and the twelve sense bases should be understood as ‘sheaths’ because they are the dwelling places of beings and phenomena, resembling a sword-sheath. The explanation should be applied in this way.

532. Yasmā ca na kevalaṃ paṇḍatīti imināva “paṇḍito”ti vuccati, apica kho pana paṇḍarāni ito upagato pavicayapaññāya allīnotipi “paṇḍito”ti vuccati, tasmā tamatthaṃ dassento “dubhayānī”ti gāthāya tatiyapañhaṃ byākāsi[P 2.0430]. Tassattho – ajjhattaṃ bahiddhā cāti evaṃ ubhayāni aniccādibhāvena viceyya. Paṇḍarānīti āyatanāni. Tāni hi pakatiparisuddhattā ruḷhiyā ca evaṃ vuccanti, tāni viceyya imāya paṭipattiyā niddhantamalattā suddhipañño paṇḍitoti pavuccati tathattā, yasmā tāni paṇḍarāni paññāya ito hoti, sesamassa thutivacanaṃ. So hi pāpapuññasaṅkhātaṃ kaṇhasukkaṃ upātivatto tādī ca hoti, tasmā evaṃ thuto.

532. And since one is called ‘wise’ not merely because one is discerning, but also because one has approached bright things with the wisdom of discrimination, being intent on them, one is therefore called ‘wise.’ Explaining that meaning, he answered the third question in the verse with ‘both.’ Its meaning is this: one should examine both internal and external phenomena as impermanent, etc. ‘Bright things’ refers to the sense bases. For they are naturally pure and are thus conventionally called so. Having examined them through this practice, one whose wisdom is cleansed of defilements is called ‘wise’ because of that state, since one has gone to these bright things with wisdom. The rest is a word of praise for him. For he has transcended the black and white, reckoned as unwholesome and wholesome, and is also a stable one; therefore, he is thus praised.

533. Yasmā pana “monaṃ vuccati ñāṇaṃ, yā paññā pajānanā…pe… sammādiṭṭhi, tena ñāṇena samannāgato munī”ti vuttaṃ, tasmā tamatthaṃ dassento “asatañcā”ti gāthāya catutthapañhaṃ byākāsi. Tassattho – yvāyaṃ akusalakusalappabhedo asatañca satañca dhammo, taṃ ajjhattaṃ bahiddhāti imasmiṃ sabbaloke pavicayañāṇena asatañca satañca ñatvā dhammaṃ tassa ñātattā eva rāgādibhedato sattavidhaṃ saṅgaṃ taṇhādiṭṭhibhedato duvidhaṃ jālañca aticca atikkamitvā ṭhito. So tena monasaṅkhātena pavicayañāṇena samannāgatattā muni. Devamanussehi pūjanīyoti idaṃ panassa thutivacanaṃ. So hi khīṇāsavamunittā devamanussānaṃ pūjāraho hoti, tasmā evaṃ thuto.

533. Because it is said, 'Sagehood is called knowledge, which is wisdom, understanding... right view. One endowed with that knowledge is a sage,' therefore, to explain this meaning, he answered the fourth question with the verse 'and of the unreal.' Its meaning is this: Having known with the knowledge of investigation the unreal and the real Dhamma—that which is divided into unwholesome and wholesome—internally and externally in this whole world, and simply because of having known it, he stands, having overcome and transcended the sevenfold bond in terms of lust and so forth, and the twofold net in terms of craving and views. Because he is endowed with that knowledge of investigation, called sagehood, he is a sage. 'Worthy of worship by devas and humans' is a word of praise for him. For, due to his sagehood as one with destroyed outflows, he is worthy of worship by devas and humans, and thus is praised.

535. Evaṃ tatiyagāthāya vuttapañhe vissajjetvā catutthagāthāya vuttapañhesupi yasmā yo catūhi maggañāṇavedehi kilesakkhayaṃ karonto gato, so paramatthato vedagū nāma hoti. Yo ca sabbasamaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ satthasaññitāni vedāni, tāyeva maggabhāvanāya kiccato aniccādivasena viceyya. Tattha chandarāgappahānena tameva [M 2.0155] sabbaṃ vedamaticca yā vedapaccayā vā aññathā vā uppajjanti vedanā[P 2.0431], tāsu sabbavedanāsu vītarāgo hoti, tasmā tamatthaṃ dassento “idaṃ [V 2.0140] pattina”nti avatvā “vedānī”ti gāthāya paṭhamapañhaṃ byākāsi. Yasmā vā yo pavicayapaññāya vedāni viceyya, tattha chandarāgappahānena sabbaṃ vedamaticca vattati, so satthasaññitāni vedāni gato ñāto atikkanto ca hoti. Yo vedanāsu vītarāgo, sopi vedanāsaññitāni vedāni gato atikkanto ca hoti. Vedāni gatotipi vedagū, tasmā tampi atthaṃ dassento “idaṃ pattina”nti avatvā imāya gāthāya paṭhamapañhaṃ byākāsi.

535. Having thus answered the question stated in the third verse, regarding the questions stated in the fourth verse: Because one who, by means of the four path-knowledges, brings about the destruction of defilements and has thus gone beyond, he is in the ultimate sense called a ‘master of knowledge’ (vedagū). And one who, through the development of the path, examines the knowledges (vedāni) regarded as scripture by all ascetics and brahmins, discerning them in terms of impermanence and so on; and there, by abandoning desire and lust, having transcended all that knowledge, is free from lust regarding all feelings that arise either conditioned by knowledge or otherwise—therefore, to show that meaning, instead of saying 'this is attained,' he answered the first question with the verse beginning 'vedāni.' Or, because one who examines the knowledges with the wisdom of discrimination, and by abandoning desire and lust for them, abides having transcended all knowledge, he has gone to, known, and transcended the knowledges regarded as scripture. One who is free from lust regarding feelings has also gone to and transcended the knowledges designated as feelings. By having gone to the knowledges, one is a ‘master of knowledge’; therefore, to show that meaning as well, instead of saying 'this is attained,' he answered the first question with this verse.

536. Yasmā pana dutiyapañhe “anuvidito”ti anubuddho vuccati, so ca anuvicca papañcanāmarūpaṃ ajjhattaṃ attano santāne taṇhāmānadiṭṭhibhedaṃ papañcaṃ tappaccayā nāmarūpañca aniccānupassanādīhi anuvicca anuviditvā, na kevalañca ajjhattaṃ, bahiddhā ca rogamūlaṃ, parasantāne ca imassa nāmarūparogassa mūlaṃ avijjābhavataṇhādiṃ, tameva vā papañcaṃ anuvicca tāya bhāvanāya sabbesaṃ rogānaṃ mūlabandhanā, sabbasmā vā rogānaṃ mūlabandhanā, avijjābhavataṇhādibhedā, tasmā eva vā papañcā pamutto hoti, tasmā taṃ dassento “anuviccā”ti gāthāya dutiyapañhaṃ byākāsi.

536. Regarding the second question, ‘anuvidito’ means one who has thoroughly understood. Such a one, having investigated and thoroughly understood—internally, within their own continuity, the proliferation divided into craving, conceit, and views, and the name-and-form conditioned by it, through contemplation of impermanence and so on; and not only internally, but also externally, the root of disease, and in the continuities of others, the root of this disease of name-and-form, namely ignorance, craving for existence, and so on. Or, having investigated that very proliferation, through that development one is liberated from the root-bondage of all diseases—or from all the root-bondages of diseases, which are divided into ignorance, craving for existence, and so forth—and thus from that proliferation itself. Therefore, to show that, he answered the second question with the verse beginning ‘anuviccā.’

537. “Kathañca vīriyavā”ti ettha pana yasmā yo ariyamaggena sabbapāpakehi virato, tathā viratattā ca āyatiṃ apaṭisandhitāya nirayadukkhaṃ aticca ṭhito vīriyavāso vīriyaniketo, so khīṇāsavo “vīriyavā”ti vattabbataṃ arahati, tasmā tamatthaṃ dassento “virato”ti gāthāya tatiyapañhaṃ byākāsi. Padhānavā dhīro tādīti imāni panassa thutivacanāni. So hi padhānavā maggajhānapadhānena, dhīro kilesārividdhaṃsanasamatthatāya, tādī nibbikāratāya, tasmā evaṃ thuto. Sesaṃ yojetvā vattabbaṃ.

537. As for 'And how is one energetic?': here, because one who, by the Noble Path, is abstinent from all evil, and due to being thus abstinent, stands having transcended the suffering of hell through non-relinking in the future—being a dwelling of energy, a home of energy—that one whose outflows are destroyed deserves to be called ‘energetic.’ Therefore, to show that meaning, he answered the third question with the verse beginning ‘virato.’ ‘Striving, wise, such a one’—these are words of praise for him. For he is ‘striving’ through the exertion of the path-jhanas, ‘wise’ due to his ability to destroy the enemy of the defilements, and ‘such a one’ due to being unperturbed. Thus, he is praised. The rest should be connected and stated.

538. “Ājāniyo kinti nāma hotī”ti ettha pana yasmā [P 2.0432] pahīnasabbavaṅkadoso kāraṇākāraṇaññū asso vā hatthī vā “ājāniyo hotī”ti [M 2.0156] loke vuccati, na ca tassa sabbaso te dosā pahīnā eva, khīṇāsavassa pana te pahīnā, tasmā so “ājāniyo”ti paramatthato vattabbataṃ arahatīti dassento “yassā”ti gāthāya catutthapañhaṃ byākāsi. Tassattho – ajjhattaṃ bahiddhā cāti evaṃ ajjhattabahiddhāsaññojanasaṅkhātāni yassa assu lunāni bandhanāni paññāsatthena chinnāni padālitāni. Saṅgamūlanti yāni tesu tesu vatthūsu saṅgassa sajjanāya anatikkamanāya mūlaṃ honti, atha vā yassa assu lunāni rāgādīni bandhanāni yāni ajjhattaṃ bahiddhā ca saṅgamūlāni honti, so sabbasmā saṅgānaṃ mūlabhūtā sabbasaṅgānaṃ vā mūlabhūtā bandhanā pamutto “ājāniyo”ti vuccati, tathattā tādi ca hotīti.

538. As for 'Why is one called a thoroughbred?': Here, because a horse or an elephant that has abandoned all crooked faults and knows cause and non-cause is called a 'thoroughbred' in the world—although for them those faults are not entirely abandoned, whereas for one whose outflows are destroyed, they are abandoned. Therefore, to show that such a one deserves to be called a 'thoroughbred' in the ultimate sense, he answered the fourth question with the verse beginning 'yassa.' Its meaning is this: one for whom the bonds known as internal and external fetters are cut, severed by the sword of wisdom, and destroyed. 'Root of attachment' means that which, in regard to various objects, is the root for attachment, for clinging, and for not overcoming. Or, one for whom the bonds of lust and so on, which are the roots of attachment both internally and externally, are cut; he, being liberated from all bonds that are the root of attachments, or that are the root of all attachments, is called a 'thoroughbred,' and because of that state, is also a 'stable one.'

540. Evaṃ [V 2.0141] catutthagāthāya vuttapañhe vissajjetvā pañcamagāthāya vuttapañhesupi yasmā yaṃ chandajjhenamattena akkharacintakā sottiyaṃ vaṇṇayanti, vohāramattasottiyo so. Ariyo pana bāhusaccena nissutapāpatāya ca paramatthasottiyo hoti, tasmā tamatthaṃ dassento “idaṃ pattina”nti avatvā “sutvā”ti gāthāya paṭhamapañhaṃ byākāsi. Tassattho – yo imasmiṃ loke sutamayapaññākiccavasena sutvā kātabbakiccavasena vā sutvā vipassanūpagaṃ sabbadhammaṃ aniccādivasena abhiññāya sāvajjānavajjaṃ yadatthi kiñci, imāya paṭipadāya kilese kilesaṭṭhāniye ca dhamme abhibhavitvā abhibhūti saṅkhaṃ gato, taṃ sutvā sabbadhammaṃ abhiññāya loke sāvajjānavajjaṃ yadatthi kiñci, abhibhuṃ sutavattā sottiyoti āhu. Yasmā ca yo akathaṃkathī kilesabandhanehi vimutto, rāgādīhi īghehi anīgho ca hoti sabbadhi sabbesu dhammesu khandhāyatanādīsu, tasmā taṃ akathaṃkathiṃ vimuttaṃ anīghaṃ sabbadhi nissutapāpakattāpi “sottiyo”ti āhūti.

540. Having thus answered the question stated in the fourth verse, regarding the questions stated in the fifth verse also: Because those who ponder letters merely out of delight and inclination are praised as 'learned,' such a one is learned only in a conventional sense. A noble one, however, through extensive learning and having cast out evil, is learned in the ultimate sense. Therefore, to show that meaning, without saying 'this is by attainment,' he explained the first question with the verse beginning 'sutvā.' Its meaning is this: one who in this world, having heard for the purpose of wisdom based on learning or for the purpose of doing what ought to be done, directly knows all phenomena conducive to insight by way of impermanence and so forth, and whatever exists that is blameworthy and blameless; and by this practice, having overcome defilements and the states that are the basis for defilements, has reached the state of an overcomer—such a one, having heard and directly known all phenomena, whatever is blameworthy or blameless in the world, they call an overcomer, a 'sottiya' (learned one), on account of his learning. And because one who is free from doubt, liberated from the bonds of defilements, is untroubled by troubles such as lust, and is untroubled in every way regarding all phenomena such as the aggregates and sense bases, therefore, that one who is free from doubt, liberated, and untroubled in every way, they also call a 'sottiya' because he has cast out evil.

541. Yasmā pana hitakāmena janena [P 2.0433] araṇīyato ariyo hoti, abhigamanīyatoti attho. Tasmā yehi guṇehi so araṇīyo hoti, te dassentā “chetvā”ti gāthāya dutiyapañhaṃ byākāsi. Tassattho – cattāri āsavāni dve ca ālayāni paññāsatthena chetvā vidvā viññū vibhāvī catumaggañāṇī so punabbhavavasena na upeti [M 2.0157] gabbhaseyyaṃ, kañci yoniṃ na upagacchati, kāmādibhedañca saññaṃ tividhaṃ. Kāmaguṇasaṅkhātañca paṅkaṃ panujja panuditvā taṇhādiṭṭhikappānaṃ aññatarampi kappaṃ na eti, evaṃ āsavacchedādiguṇasamannāgataṃ tamāhu ariyoti. Yasmā vā pāpakehi ārakattā ariyo hoti anaye ca anirīyanā, tasmā tampi atthaṃ dassento imāya gāthāya dutiyapañhaṃ byākāsi. Āsavādayo hi pāpakā dhammā anayasammatā, te cānena chinnā panunnā, na ca tehi kampati, iccassa te ārakā honti, na ca tesu irīyati tasmā ārakāssa honti pāpakā dhammāti imināpatthena. Anaye na irīyatīti imināpatthena tamāhu ariyoti ca evampettha yojanā veditabbā. “Vidvā so na upeti gabbhaseyya”nti idaṃ pana imasmiṃ atthavikappe thutivacanameva hoti.

541. Furthermore, because he is to be approached by people who wish for their welfare, he is an 'ariya' (noble one); 'worthy of being approached' is the meaning. Therefore, showing the qualities by which he is to be approached, he explained the second question with the verse beginning 'chetvā.' Its meaning is this: having cut off the four taints and the two attachments with the sword of wisdom, the wise, discerning, insightful one, possessing the knowledge of the four paths, does not enter a womb again by way of renewed existence, does not go to any particular womb, nor does he entertain the threefold perception, such as that of sensual pleasures. Having driven out and dispelled the mire known as sensual qualities, he does not come to any speculation of craving or views. Thus, they call one endowed with qualities such as the cutting off of the taints an 'ariya.' Alternatively, he is an 'ariya' because he is far from evil things and does not proceed into a wrong course. Therefore, to show this meaning as well, he explained the second question with this verse. For the taints and so forth are evil states, considered a wrong course; they have been cut off and driven out by him, and he is not shaken by them. Thus, they are far from him, and he does not proceed into them. Therefore, the construction should be understood here in this way: they call him an 'ariya' with the meaning that evil states are far from him, and with the meaning that he does not proceed into a wrong course. The phrase 'the wise one does not enter a womb again' is, in this explanation of the meaning, merely a statement of praise.

542. “Kathaṃ caraṇavā”ti ettha pana yasmā caraṇehi pattabbaṃ patto “caraṇavā”ti vattabbataṃ arahati, tasmā taṃ dassento “yo idhā”ti gāthāya tatiyapañhaṃ byākāsi. Tattha yo idhāti yo imasmiṃ sāsane. Caraṇesūti sīlādīsu hemavatasutte (su. ni. 153 ādayo) vuttapannarasadhammesu. Nimittatthe bhummavacanaṃ. Pattipattoti pattabbaṃ patto. Yo caraṇanimittaṃ caraṇahetu caraṇapaccayā pattabbaṃ arahattaṃ pattoti vuttaṃ hoti. Caraṇavā soti so [V 2.0142] imāya caraṇehi pattabbapattiyā caraṇavā hotīti. Ettāvatā pañho byākato hoti, sesamassa thutivacanaṃ. Yo hi caraṇehi pattipatto, so kusalo ca hoti cheko, sabbadā ca ājānāti nibbānadhammaṃ[P 2.0434], niccaṃ nibbānaninnacittatāya sabbattha ca khandhādīsu na sajjati. Dvīhi ca vimuttīhi vimuttacitto hoti, paṭighā yassa na santīti.

542. Regarding 'How is one endowed with conduct?': because one who has attained what is to be attained through conduct deserves to be called 'endowed with conduct,' to show this he explained the third question with the verse beginning 'yo idhā.' Therein, 'yo idhā' means 'who in this teaching.' 'Caraṇesu' (in conduct) refers to the fifteen qualities beginning with virtue, mentioned in the Hemavata Sutta. The locative case is used in the sense of cause. 'Pattipatto' means 'one who has attained what is to be attained.' It is said that one who, on account of conduct, as a cause of conduct, as a condition for conduct, has attained what is to be attained—arahantship. 'Caraṇavā so' means that he is endowed with conduct because of this attainment of what is to be attained through conduct. Thus far, the question has been answered; the rest is a statement of praise. For one who has attained what is to be attained through conduct is skilled and expert; he always understands the state of Nibbāna; with a mind constantly inclined toward Nibbāna, he does not cling anywhere to the aggregates and so forth. His mind is liberated through the two kinds of liberation, and for him, there are no forms of aversion.

543. Yasmā pana kammādīnaṃ paribbājanena paribbājako nāma hoti, tasmā tamatthaṃ dassento “dukkhavepakka”nti gāthāya catutthapañhaṃ byākāsi. Tattha vipāko eva vepakkaṃ, dukkhaṃ vepakkamassāti dukkhavepakkaṃ. Pavattidukkhajananato sabbampi tedhātukakammaṃ vuccati. Uddhanti atītaṃ. Adhoti anāgataṃ. Tiriyaṃ vāpi majjheti paccuppannaṃ. Tañhi na uddhaṃ na adho, tiriyaṃ ubhinnañca antarā, tena “majjhe”ti vuttaṃ. Paribbājayitvāti nikkhāmetvā niddhametvā[M 2.0158]. Pariññacārīti paññāya paricchinditvā caranto. Ayaṃ tāva apubbapadavaṇṇanā. Ayaṃ pana adhippāyayojanā – yo tiyaddhapariyāpannampi dukkhajanakaṃ yadatthi kiñci kammaṃ, taṃ sabbampi ariyamaggena taṇhāvijjāsinehe sosento apaṭisandhijanakabhāvakaraṇena paribbājayitvā tathā paribbājitattā eva ca taṃ kammaṃ pariññāya caraṇato pariññacārī. Na kevalañca kammameva, māyaṃ mānamathopi lobhakodhaṃ imepi dhamme pahānapariññāya pariññacārī, pariyantamakāsi nāmarūpaṃ, nāmarūpassa ca pariyantamakāsi paribbājesi iccevattho. Imesaṃ kammādīnaṃ paribbājanena taṃ paribbājakamāhu. Pattipattanti idaṃ panassa thutivacanaṃ.

543. Furthermore, since one is called a 'paribbājaka' (wanderer) because of wandering away from actions and so forth, to show that meaning, he explained the fourth question with the verse beginning 'dukkhavepakka.' Here, 'vepakka' is simply 'vipāka' (result); it is called 'dukkhavepakka' because its result is suffering. All action within the three realms is so called because it generates the suffering of ongoing existence. 'Uddhaṃ' (upwards) means the past. 'Adho' (downwards) means the future. 'Tiriyaṃ vāpi majjhe' (across or in the middle) means the present. For it is neither upwards nor downwards, but across and between the two; hence, it is called 'majjhe.' 'Paribbājayitvā' means having expelled, having driven away. 'Pariññacārī' means one who fares having comprehended with wisdom. This, for a start, is the explanation of the unfamiliar terms. Now, this is the application of the intended meaning: one who, regarding whatever action there is that generates suffering and is included in the three periods of time, dries up the moisture of craving and ignorance by means of the noble path, and by making it incapable of producing a new life, causes it to be abandoned; and because he has thus caused it to be abandoned and because he fares having fully understood that action, he is a 'pariññacārī.' And not only action, but he is also a 'pariññacārī' with respect to these states—deceit, conceit, as well as greed and anger—through the full understanding that is abandonment. He made an end of name-and-form; 'he made an end of name-and-form' means he caused it to be abandoned. Because of this wandering away from these things, action and so forth, they call him a 'paribbājaka.' The word 'pattipattanti' is a statement of praise for him.

544. Evaṃ pañhabyākaraṇena tuṭṭhassa pana sabhiyassa “yāni ca tīṇī”tiādīsu abhitthavanagāthāsu osaraṇānīti ogahaṇāni titthāni, diṭṭhiyoti attho. Tāni yasmā sakkāyadiṭṭhiyā saha brahmajāle vuttadvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhigatāni gahetvā tesaṭṭhi honti, yasmā ca tāni aññatitthiyasamaṇānaṃ pavādabhūtāni satthāni sitāni upadisitabbavasena, na uppattivasena. Uppattivasena pana yadetaṃ “itthī puriso”ti saññakkharaṃ [P 2.0435] vohāranāmaṃ, yā cāyaṃ micchāparivitakkānussavādivasena “evarūpena attanā bhavitabba”nti bālānaṃ viparītasaññā uppajjati, tadubhayanissitāni tesaṃ vasena uppajjanti, na attapaccakkhāni. Tāni ca bhagavā vineyya vinayitvā oghatamagā oghatamaṃ oghandhakāraṃ agā atikkanto. “Oghantamagā”tipi pāṭho, oghānaṃ antaṃ agā, tasmā āha “yāni ca tīṇi…pe… tamagā”ti.

544. Thus, for Sabhiya, who was pleased by the answering of the questions, in the verses of praise beginning 'yāni ca tīṇi,' 'osaraṇāni' means immersions, landing places; the meaning is 'views.' Because these, when taken together with the sixty-two views mentioned in the Brahmajāla Sutta along with identity view, become sixty-three; and because they are the doctrines of other sectarian ascetics, adhered to in the sense of being taught, not in the sense of arising. As for their arising, they arise dependent on both this conventional name, the signifier 'woman, man,' and the perverted perception that arises in fools through wrong reflection, tradition, and so on, thinking, 'I must be of such a nature'; they arise through the influence of these, not being self-realized. And the Blessed One, having disciplined and removed them, went beyond the flood's darkness; he went beyond, he surpassed the flood's gloom. There is also the reading 'oghantamagā,' meaning he went to the end of the floods. Therefore, he said, 'yāni ca tīṇi…pe… tamagā.'

545. Tato paraṃ vaṭṭadukkhassa antaṃ pārañca nibbānaṃ tappattiyā dukkhābhāvato tappaṭipakkhato [V 2.0143] ca taṃ sandhāyāha, “antagūsi pāragū dukkhassā”ti. Atha vā pāragū bhagavā nibbānaṃ gatattā, taṃ ālapanto āha, “pāragū antagūsi dukkhassā”ti ayamettha sambandho. Sammā ca buddho sāmañca buddhoti sammāsambuddho. Taṃ maññeti tameva maññāmi, na aññanti accādarena bhaṇati. Jutimāti paresampi andhakāravidhamanena jutisampanno. Mutimāti aparappaccayañeyyañāṇasamatthāya mutiyā paññāya [M 2.0159] sampanno. Pahūtapaññoti anantapañño. Idha sabbaññutaññāṇamadhippetaṃ. Dukkhassantakarāti āmantento āha. Atāresi manti kaṅkhāto maṃ tāresi.

545. Furthermore, referring to Nibbāna, which is the end and the far shore of the suffering of the round—because of the absence of suffering upon its attainment and because it is its opposite—he says, 'You have gone to the end, you have gone beyond suffering.' Alternatively, because the Blessed One has gone to the far shore, having gone to Nibbāna, addressing him, he says, 'You have gone beyond, you have gone to the end of suffering.' This is the connection here. 'Rightly awakened and awakened by himself,' thus he is the Perfectly Self-Awakened One. 'I consider him' means 'I consider him alone, not another'; he speaks with extreme reverence. 'Radiant' means endowed with radiance by dispelling the darkness of others as well. 'Wise' means endowed with wisdom, with insight capable of knowledge not dependent on another. 'Of abundant wisdom' means of infinite wisdom. Here, the knowledge of omniscience is intended. 'O maker of the end of suffering,' he says, addressing him. 'You have helped me across' means 'you have helped me across from doubt.'

546-9. Yaṃ metiādigāthāya namakkārakaraṇaṃ bhaṇati. Tattha kaṅkhittanti vīsatipañhanissitaṃ atthaṃ sandhāyāha. So hi tena kaṅkhito ahosi. Monapathesūti ñāṇapathesu. Vinaḷīkatāti vigatanaḷā katā, ucchinnāti vuttaṃ hoti. Nāga nāgassāti ekaṃ āmantanavacanaṃ, ekassa “bhāsato anumodantī”ti iminā sambandho. “Dhammadesana”nti pāṭhaseso. Sabbe devāti ākāsaṭṭhā ca bhūmaṭṭhā ca. Nāradapabbatāti tepi kira dve devagaṇā paññavanto, tepi anumodantīti sabbaṃ pasādena ca namakkārakaraṇaṃ bhaṇati[P 2.0436].
