546-9. With the verse beginning 'Yaṃ me,' he speaks of making obeisance. Therein, 'my doubt' refers to the matter based on the twenty questions, for he had been in doubt because of that. 'In the paths of sagehood' means in the paths of knowledge. 'Made reedless' means made with reeds gone; that is to say, cut off. 'Nāga, of the Nāga': one is a term of address; one is connected with 'they rejoice in him speaking.' 'The teaching of the Dhamma' is the rest of the text. 'All the devas' means those dwelling in the sky and those dwelling on the earth. 'Nārada and Pabbata': it is said that those two groups of devas are wise, and they too rejoice. He says all this with faith and while making obeisance.

550-53. Anumodanārahaṃ byākaraṇasampadaṃ sutvā “namo te”ti añjaliṃ paggahetvā āha. Purisājaññāti purisesu jātisampannaṃ. Paṭipuggaloti paṭibhāgo puggalo tuvaṃ buddho catusaccapaṭivedhena, satthā anusāsaniyā satthavāhatāya ca, mārābhibhū catumārābhibhavena, muni buddhamuni. Upadhīti khandhakilesakāmaguṇābhisaṅkhārabhedā cattāro. Vaggūti abhirūpaṃ. Puññe cāti lokiye na limpasi tesaṃ akaraṇena, pubbe katānampi vā āyatiṃ phalūpabhogābhāvena. Taṃnimittena vā taṇhādiṭṭhilepena. Vandati satthunoti evaṃ bhaṇanto gopphakesu pariggahetvā pañcapatiṭṭhitaṃ vandi.

550-53. Having heard the accomplishment of the explanation, which was worthy of rejoicing, he raised his hands in reverence and said, 'Homage to you.' 'Thoroughbred of men' means one of noble birth among men. 'Peerless individual' means you are an individual without counterpart: the Buddha through the penetration of the four truths; the Teacher through instruction and leading the caravan; the Conqueror of Māra through conquering the four Māras; the Sage, the Buddha-Sage. 'Substrates' means the four kinds: the aggregates, defilements, sensual pleasures, and formations. 'Lovely' means beautiful. 'And in merits' means you are not smeared by worldly merits, either by not performing them, or because of the non-enjoyment in the future of the fruit of those done previously; or by the stain of craving and views on account of that. 'He worships the Teacher' means, saying thus, he grasped his ankles and worshipped with the five-point prostration.

Aññatitthiyapubboti aññatitthiyo eva. Ākaṅkhatīti icchati. Āraddhacittāti abhirādhitacittā. Apica mettha puggalavemattatā viditāti apica mayā ettha aññatitthiyānaṃ parivāse puggalanānattaṃ viditaṃ, na sabbeneva parivasitabbanti. Kena pana na parivasitabbaṃ? Aggiyehi jaṭilehi, sākiyena jātiyā, liṅgaṃ vijahitvā āgatena. Avijahitvā āgatopi ca yo maggaphalapaṭilābhāya hetusampanno hoti, tādisova sabhiyo paribbājako. Tasmā bhagavā “tava pana, sabhiya, titthiyavattapūraṇatthāya parivāsakāraṇaṃ natthi, atthatthiko tvaṃ ‘maggaphalapaṭilābhāya hetusampanno’ti viditametaṃ mayā”ti tassa pabbajjaṃ anujānanto [M 2.0160] āha – “apica [V 2.0144] mettha puggalavemattatā viditā”ti. Sabhiyo pana attano ādaraṃ dassento āha “sace bhante”ti. Taṃ sabbaṃ aññañca tathārūpaṃ uttānatthattā pubbe vuttanayattā ca idha na vaṇṇitaṃ, yato pubbe vaṇṇitānusārena veditabbanti.

'Formerly of another sect' means simply one of another sect. 'Desires' means wishes. 'With an ardent mind' means with a mind that is pleased. 'Moreover, the difference among individuals is known to me here' means: moreover, the diversity among individuals regarding probation for those from other sects is known to me here, and that not all must undergo probation. But by whom must probation not be undergone? By fire-worshippers, by matted-hair ascetics, by one of the Sakyan clan by birth, and by one who has come having abandoned their outward signs. And even one who has come without abandoning them, if he is endowed with the cause for attaining the path and its fruit—Sabhiya the wanderer was such a one. Therefore the Blessed One, granting him ordination, said: 'But for you, Sabhiya, there is no reason for probation to fulfill the practices of other sects; it is known to me that you are one who seeks the goal, endowed with the cause for attaining the path and its fruit.' And further, 'the difference among individuals is known to me here.' But Sabhiya, showing his own respect, said, 'If, venerable sir...' All this and other such matters, being of plain meaning and following the previously stated method, are not explained here, since they are to be understood according to what was explained before.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya sabhiyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Here ends the explanation of the Sabhiya Sutta in the Commentary on the Suttanipāta.

7. Selasuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Explanation of the Sela Sutta

Evaṃ [V 2.0145][P 2.0437] me sutanti selasuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Ayameva yāssa nidāne vuttā. Atthavaṇṇanākkamepi cassa pubbasadisaṃ pubbe vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Yaṃ pana apubbaṃ, taṃ uttānatthāni padāni pariharantā vaṇṇayissāma. Aṅguttarāpesūti aṅgā eva so janapado, gaṅgāya pana yā uttarena āpo, tāsaṃ avidūrattā “uttarāpo”tipi vuccati. Kataragaṅgāya uttarena yā āpoti? Mahāmahīgaṅgāya.

'Thus have I heard' begins the Sela Sutta. What is its origin? It is the same as what was stated in its introduction. In the sequence of the explanation of the meaning, too, it should be understood as similar to the preceding, in the way previously stated. As for what is new, we will explain it, leaving aside the words of plain meaning. 'In Aṅguttarāpa' means that country is Aṅga itself. But because of the proximity of the waters that are north of the Ganges, it is also called 'Uttarāpa.' North of which Ganges are these waters? Of the great Mahī-Ganges.

Tatrāyaṃ tassā nadiyā āvibhāvatthaṃ ādito pabhuti vaṇṇanā – ayaṃ kira jambudīpo dasasahassayojanaparimāṇo. Tattha catusahassayojanaparimāṇo padeso udakena ajjhotthaṭo “samuddo”ti saṅkhaṃ gato. Tisahassayojanapamāṇe manussā vasanti. Tisahassayojanapamāṇe himavā patiṭṭhito ubbedhena pañcayojanasatiko caturāsītisahassakūṭehi paṭimaṇḍito samantato sandamānapañcasatanadīvicitto. Yattha āyāmavitthārena gambhīratāya ca paññāsapaññāsayojanā diyaḍḍhayojanasataparimaṇḍalā pūraḷāsasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttā anotattādayo satta mahāsarā patiṭṭhitā.

Here is the description of that river from the beginning, regarding its appearance: This Jambudīpa is said to be ten thousand yojanas in extent. Therein, a region four thousand yojanas in extent is submerged by water and is called “the ocean.” Humans dwell in an area three thousand yojanas in extent. The Himavā mountain, adorned with eighty-four thousand peaks and variegated with five hundred rivers flowing all around, is established in an area three thousand yojanas in extent, with a height of five hundred yojanas. There, the seven great lakes, beginning with Anotatta, are established, each fifty yojanas in length, width, and depth, and one hundred and fifty yojanas in circumference, as described in the commentary on the Pūraḷāsa Sutta.

Tesu anotatto sudassanakūṭaṃ, citrakūṭaṃ, kāḷakūṭaṃ, gandhamādanakūṭaṃ, kelāsakūṭanti imehi pañcahi pabbatehi parikkhitto. Tattha sudassanakūṭaṃ suvaṇṇamayaṃ dviyojanasatubbedhaṃ antovaṅkaṃ kākamukhasaṇṭhānaṃ tameva [M 2.0161] saraṃ paṭicchādetvā ṭhitaṃ, citrakūṭaṃ sabbaratanamayaṃ, kāḷakūṭaṃ añjanamayaṃ, gandhamādanakūṭaṃ sānumayaṃ abbhantare muggavaṇṇaṃ [P 2.0438] nānappakāraosadhasañchannaṃ kāḷapakkhuposathadivase ādittamiva aṅgāraṃ jalantaṃ tiṭṭhati, kelāsakūṭaṃ rajatamayaṃ. Sabbāni sudassanena samānubbedhasaṇṭhānāni tameva saraṃ paṭicchādetvā ṭhitāni. Sabbāni devānubhāvena nāgānubhāvena ca vassanti, nadiyo ca tesu sandanti. Taṃ sabbampi udakaṃ anotattameva pavisati. Candimasūriyā dakkhiṇena vā uttarena vā gacchantā pabbatantarena taṃ obhāsenti, ujuṃ gacchantā na obhāsenti. Tenevassa “anotatta”nti saṅkhā udapādi.

Among them, Anotatta is surrounded by five peaks: Sudassanakūṭa, Citrakūṭa, Kāḷakūṭa, Gandhamādanakūṭa, and Kelāsakūṭa. There, Sudassanakūṭa is made of gold, two hundred yojanas high, curved inward, shaped like a crow’s beak, and stands covering that very lake. Citrakūṭa is made of all kinds of jewels, Kāḷakūṭa is made of antimony, Gandhamādanakūṭa is a plateau-mountain, its interior the color of mung beans, covered with various kinds of medicinal herbs, and on the Uposatha day of the dark fortnight, it stands blazing like a glowing ember. Kelāsakūṭa is made of silver. All are of the same height and shape as Sudassanakūṭa and stand covering that very lake. On all of them it rains by the power of the devas and the nāgas, and rivers flow on them. All that water enters only Anotatta. The sun and moon, whether going south or north, illuminate it by passing between the mountains, but when going straight over, they do not illuminate it. For that reason, the name “Anotatta” arose.

Tattha manoharasilātalāni nimmacchakacchapāni phalikasadisanimmalūdakāni nahānatitthāni suppaṭiyattāni [V 2.0146] honti, yesu buddhapaccekabuddhakhīṇāsavā isigaṇā ca nhāyanti, devayakkhādayo ca uyyānakīḷikaṃ kīḷanti.

There, well-prepared bathing places are found, with delightful rocky surfaces, free from fish and turtles, and with water as clear as crystal. In these, Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, Arahants, and groups of sages bathe, while devas, yakkhas, and others enjoy garden sports.

Catūsu cassa passesu sīhamukhaṃ, hatthimukhaṃ, assamukhaṃ, usabhamukhanti cattāri mukhāni honti, yehi catasso nadiyo sandanti. Sīhamukhena nikkhantanadītīre sīhā bahutarā honti, hatthimukhādīhi hatthiassausabhā. Puratthimadisato nikkhantanadī anotattaṃ tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā itarā tisso nadiyo anupagamma pācīnahimavanteneva amanussapathaṃ gantvā mahāsamuddaṃ pavisati. Pacchimadisato ca uttaradisato ca nikkhantanadiyopi tatheva padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pacchimahimavanteneva uttarahimavanteneva ca amanussapathaṃ gantvā mahāsamuddaṃ pavisanti. Dakkhiṇadisato nikkhantanadī pana taṃ tikkhattuṃ [P 2.0439] padakkhiṇaṃ katvā dakkhiṇena ujukaṃ pāsāṇapiṭṭheneva saṭṭhiyojanāni gantvā pabbataṃ paharitvā vuṭṭhāya pariṇāhena tigāvutapamāṇā udakadhārā hutvā ākāsena saṭṭhi yojanāni gantvā tiyaggaḷe nāma pāsāṇe patitā, pāsāṇo udakadhārāvegena bhinno. Tatra paññāsayojanapamāṇā tiyaggaḷā nāma pokkharaṇī jātā. Pokkharaṇiyā kūlaṃ bhinditvā pāsāṇaṃ pavisiya saṭṭhi yojanāni gatā. Tato ghanapathaviṃ bhinditvā umaṅgena saṭṭhi yojanāni gantvā viñjhaṃ nāma tiracchānapabbataṃ paharitvā hatthatale pañcaṅgulisadisā pañcadhārā hutvā pavattati. Sā tikkhattuṃ anotattaṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā gataṭṭhāne “āvaṭṭagaṅgā”ti vuccati[M 2.0162]. Ujukaṃ pāsāṇapiṭṭhena saṭṭhi yojanāni gataṭṭhāne “kaṇhagaṅgā”ti vuccati. Ākāsena saṭṭhi yojanāni gataṭṭhāne “ākāsagaṅgā”ti vuccati. Tiyaggaḷapāsāṇe paññāsayojanokāse “tiyaggaḷapokkharaṇī”ti vuccati. Kūlaṃ bhinditvā pāsāṇaṃ pavisiya saṭṭhi yojanāni gataṭṭhāne “bahalagaṅgā”ti vuccati. Pathaviṃ bhinditvā umaṅgena saṭṭhi yojanāni gataṭṭhāne “umaṅgagaṅgā”ti vuccati. Viñjhaṃ nāma tiracchānapabbataṃ paharitvā pañcadhārā hutvā pavattaṭṭhāne “gaṅgā, yamunā, aciravatī, sarabhū, mahī”ti pañcadhā vuccati. Evametā pañca mahāgaṅgā himavatā sambhavanti. Tāsu yā ayaṃ pañcamī mahī nāma, sā idha “mahāmahīgaṅgā”ti adhippetā. Tassā gaṅgāya uttarena yā āpo, tāsaṃ avidūrattā so janapado “aṅguttarāpo”ti veditabbo. Tasmiṃ janapade aṅguttarāpesu.

On its four sides are four mouths: a lion’s mouth, an elephant’s mouth, a horse’s mouth, and an ox’s mouth, from which four rivers flow. On the banks of the river emerging from the lion’s mouth, lions are most numerous; from the mouths of the elephant, horse, and ox, elephants, horses, and oxen are most numerous. The river emerging from the eastern direction circles Lake Anotatta three times clockwise and, without joining the other three rivers, travels along the eastern Himavanta through a path inaccessible to humans and enters the great ocean. The rivers emerging from the western and northern directions similarly circle it clockwise and, traveling along the western and northern Himavanta through a path inaccessible to humans, enter the great ocean. The river emerging from the southern direction, however, circles it three times clockwise and then flows straight south along a rocky plateau for sixty yojanas. Striking a mountain, it rises up and, becoming a stream of water three gāvutas in circumference, travels sixty yojanas through the sky and falls on a rock called Tiyaggaḷa. The rock is shattered by the force of the water stream, and there a pond fifty yojanas in extent, called Tiyaggaḷa Pokkharaṇī, is formed. Breaking the bank of the pond, the water enters the rock and travels sixty yojanas. Then, piercing the solid earth, it flows through a tunnel for sixty yojanas and strikes a transverse mountain called Viñjha. There, it divides into five streams resembling the five fingers on the palm of a hand. The place where it flows after circling Lake Anotatta three times is called “Āvaṭṭa Gaṅgā.” The stretch where it flows straight along the rocky plateau for sixty yojanas is called “Kaṇha Gaṅgā.” The stretch where it travels sixty yojanas through the sky is called “Ākāsa Gaṅgā.” The fifty-yojana space at the Tiyaggaḷa rock is called “Tiyaggaḷa Pokkharaṇī.” The stretch where it travels sixty yojanas after breaking the bank and entering the rock is called “Bahala Gaṅgā.” The stretch where it flows sixty yojanas through a tunnel after piercing the earth is called “Umaṅga Gaṅgā.” The place where it flows as five streams after striking the transverse mountain Viñjha is called by five names: Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Aciravatī, Sarabhū, and Mahī. Thus, these five great rivers originate from the Himavanta. Among them, the fifth one, called Mahī, is here intended as “Mahāmahī Gaṅgā.” The waters to the north of this Gaṅgā, on account of their proximity, cause that region to be known as “Aṅguttarāpa.” In that region, in Aṅguttarāpa.

Cārikaṃ caramānoti addhānagamanaṃ kurumāno[P 2.0440]. Tattha bhagavato duvidhā cārikā turitacārikā, aturitacārikā ca. Tattha dūrepi bhabbapuggale disvā sahasā gamanaṃ turitacārikā. Sā mahākassapapaccuggamanādīsu daṭṭhabbā. Taṃ paccuggacchanto hi bhagavā muhutteneva tigāvutaṃ agamāsi, āḷavakadamanatthaṃ tiṃsayojanaṃ, tathā aṅgulimālassatthāya. Pukkusātissa [V 2.0147] pana pañcattālīsayojanaṃ, mahākappinassa vīsayojanasataṃ, dhaniyassatthāya sattayojanasataṃ addhānaṃ agamāsi. Ayaṃ turitacārikā nāma. Gāmanigamanagarapaṭipāṭiyā pana piṇḍapātacariyādīhi lokaṃ anuggaṇhantassa gamanaṃ aturitacārikā nāma. Ayaṃ idha adhippetā. Evaṃ cārikaṃ caramāno. Mahatāti saṅkhyāmahatā guṇamahatā ca. Bhikkhusaṅghenāti samaṇagaṇena. Aḍḍhateḷasehīti aḍḍhena teḷasahi, dvādasahi satehi paññāsāya ca bhikkhūhi saddhinti vuttaṃ hoti. Yena…pe… tadavasarīti āpaṇabahulatāya so nigamo “āpaṇo” tveva nāmaṃ labhi. Tasmiṃ kira vīsatiāpaṇamukhasahassāni vibhattāni ahesuṃ. Yena disābhāgena maggena vā so aṅguttarāpānaṃ raṭṭhassa nigamo osaritabbo, tena avasari tadavasari agamāsi, taṃ nigamaṃ anupāpuṇīti vuttaṃ hoti.

“While traveling on a journey” means making a journey. Here, the Blessed One had two kinds of journeys: swift journeys and leisurely journeys. Among these, seeing a capable person even from afar and suddenly going to them is called a swift journey. This can be seen in instances like going forth to meet Mahākassapa and others. For example, when going forth to meet him, the Blessed One covered three gāvutas in a moment; to subdue Āḷavaka, thirty yojanas; and likewise for Aṅgulimāla. For Pukkusāti, however, he traveled forty-five yojanas; for Mahākappina, one hundred and twenty yojanas; and for Dhaniya, seven hundred yojanas. This is called a swift journey. On the other hand, traveling through villages, towns, and cities in sequence, while benefiting the world through alms rounds and other activities, is called a leisurely journey. This is what is intended here. “While traveling on a journey.” “With a great…” means great in number and great in virtue. “With a company of bhikkhus…” means with a community of ascetics. “With twelve and a half hundred…” means with twelve hundred and fifty bhikkhus, it is said. Regarding “To where… he approached that place”: Due to its abundance of shops, that town came to be named simply “Āpaṇa” (Market). It is said that twenty thousand shop-fronts were arranged there. The meaning is: by whichever direction or path that town of the Aṅguttarāpans was to be approached, by that way he approached it, went to it, and arrived at that town.

Keṇiyo jaṭiloti keṇiyoti nāmena, jaṭiloti tāpaso. So kira brāhmaṇamahāsālo, dhanarakkhaṇatthāya pana tāpasapabbajjaṃ samādāya rañño paṇṇākāraṃ datvā bhūmibhāgaṃ gahetvā tattha assamaṃ kāretvā vasati kulasahassassa nissayo hutvā. Assamepi cassa eko [M 2.0163] tālarukkho divase divase ekaṃ suvaṇṇaphalaṃ muñcatīti vadanti. So divā kāsāyāni dhāreti jaṭā ca bandhati, rattiṃ yathāsukhaṃ pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappito samaṅgībhūto paricāreti. Sakyaputtoti uccākulaparidīpanaṃ. Sakyakulā pabbajitoti saddhāya pabbajitabhāvaparidīpanaṃ, kenaci pārijuññena anabhibhūto aparikkhīṇaṃyeva taṃ [P 2.0441] kulaṃ pahāya saddhāya pabbajitoti vuttaṃ hoti. Taṃ kho panāti itthambhūtākhyānatthe upayogavacanaṃ, tassa kho pana bhoto gotamassāti attho. Kalyāṇoti kalyāṇaguṇasamannāgato, seṭṭhoti vuttaṃ hoti. Kittisaddoti kittiyeva thutighoso vā.

“Keṇiya the matted-haired ascetic”: Keṇiya is his name, and ‘matted-haired ascetic’ means a hermit. It is said that he was a wealthy brahmin, but for the sake of protecting his wealth, he took up the ascetic life and, having given the king a tribute, obtained a piece of land. There he had a hermitage built and lived, becoming the support for a thousand families. And in his hermitage, it is said, there was a palm tree that daily dropped one golden fruit. By day, he wore ochre robes and bound his hair in matted locks, but at night, as he pleased, he enjoyed himself, complete and furnished with the five strands of sensual pleasure. “Sakyaputta” highlights his noble lineage. “Having gone forth from the Sakyan clan” signifies that he went forth out of faith. It means that, uninfluenced by any deficiency, he left his clan out of faith while its wealth was still unexhausted, and went forth. “Now then”—this phrase is used to describe something as it is. The meaning is: “of that venerable Gotama.” “Kalyāṇa” means endowed with excellent qualities—it signifies the best. “Kittisadda” refers to fame, the sound of praise, or the voice of renown.

Itipi so bhagavāti ādimhi pana ayaṃ tāva yojanā – so bhagavā itipi arahaṃ, itipi sammāsambuddho…pe… itipi bhagavāti, iminā ca iminā ca kāraṇenāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha ārakattā, arīnaṃ arānañca hatattā paccayādīnaṃ arahattā, pāpakaraṇe rahābhāvāti imehi tāva kāraṇehi so bhagavā arahanti veditabbo. Ārakā hi so sabbakilesehi maggena savāsanānaṃ kilesānaṃ viddhaṃsitattāti ārakattā arahaṃ. Te cānena kilesārayo maggena hatāti arīnaṃ hatattāpi arahaṃ. Yañcetaṃ avijjābhavataṇhāmayanābhi, puññādiabhisaṅkhārānaṃ jarāmaraṇanemi, āsavasamudayamayena akkhena vijjhitvā tibhavarathe samāyojitaṃ anādikālapavattaṃ saṃsāracakkaṃ. Tassānena bodhimaṇḍe vīriyapādehi sīlapathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhāya saddhāhatthena kammakkhayakarañāṇapharasuṃ gahetvā sabbe arā hatāti arānaṃ hatattātipi arahaṃ[V 2.0148]. Aggadakkhiṇeyyattā ca cīvarādipaccaye sakkāragarukārādīni ca arahatīti paccayādīnaṃ arahattāpi arahaṃ. Yathā ca loke keci paṇḍitamānino bālā asilokabhayena raho pāpaṃ karonti, evaṃ nāyaṃ kadāci karotīti pāpakaraṇe rahābhāvatopi arahaṃ. Hoti cettha –

“Indeed, that Blessed One…” Now, at the beginning, this is the explanation: “Indeed, that Blessed One is thus an Arahant, thus a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One… thus the Blessed One,” and it is said because of this and that reason. Here, that Blessed One is to be understood as an Arahant because of these reasons: because of being distant from defilements, because of destroying enemies and spokes, because of being worthy of requisites, and because of the absence of doing evil in secret. For he is an Arahant because he is distant from all defilements, as the path has destroyed the defilements along with their latent tendencies. And he is an Arahant because he has destroyed those defilements, the enemies, with the path. And that wheel of saṃsāra, which has been revolving since beginningless time, joined to the chariot of the three existences, pierced by the axle of the origin of the taints, with the felloe of aging and death, with the nave of ignorance and craving for existence, and with volitional formations beginning with merit. He, standing on the ground of virtue at the seat of enlightenment with the feet of effort, having grasped the axe of knowledge that destroys kamma with the hand of faith, has destroyed all the spokes—thus, he is an Arahant because of destroying the spokes. And he is an Arahant because he is worthy of requisites, being the foremost recipient of offerings and worthy of honor and respect regarding requisites such as robes. And just as in the world some foolish people who think themselves wise do evil in secret out of fear of blame, this one never does so—thus, he is an Arahant because of the absence of doing evil in secret. And here it is said:

“Ārakattā hatattā ca, kilesārīna so muni;

Hatasaṃsāracakkāro, paccayādīna cāraho;

Na raho karoti pāpāni, arahaṃ tena pavuccatī”ti.

“Because that sage is distant from and has destroyed the defilement-enemies, has destroyed the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra, and is worthy of requisites and the like; and because he does no evil in secret, he is therefore called an ‘Arahant’.”

Sammā sāmañca saccānaṃ buddhattā sammāsambuddho. Atisayavisuddhāhi vijjāhi abbhuttamena caraṇena ca samannāgatattā [P 2.0442] vijjācaraṇasampanno. Sobhanagamanattā [M 2.0164] sundaraṃ ṭhānaṃ gatattā suṭṭhu gatattā sammā gadattā ca sugato. Sabbathāpi viditalokattā lokavidū. So hi bhagavā sabhāvato samudayato nirodhato nirodhūpāyatoti sabbathā khandhāyatanādibhedaṃ saṅkhāralokaṃ avedi, “eko loko sabbe sattā āhāraṭṭhitikā. Dve lokā nāmañca rūpañca. Tayo lokā tisso vedanā. Cattāro lokā cattāro āhārā. Pañca lokā pañcupādānakkhandhā. Cha lokā cha ajjhattikāni āyatanāni. Satta lokā satta viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo. Aṭṭha lokā aṭṭha lokadhammā. Nava lokā nava sattāvāsā. Dasa lokā dasāyatanāni. Dvādasa lokā dvādasāyatanāni. Aṭṭhārasa lokā aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.112) evaṃ sabbathā saṅkhāralokaṃ avedi. Sattānaṃ āsayaṃ jānāti, anusayaṃ jānāti, caritaṃ jānāti, adhimuttiṃ jānāti, apparajakkhe mahārajakkhe tikkhindriye mudindriye svākāre dvākāre suviññāpaye duviññāpaye bhabbe abhabbe satte jānātīti sabbathā sattalokaṃ avedi. Tathā ekaṃ cakkavāḷaṃ āyāmato vitthārato ca yojanānaṃ dvādasa satasahassāni tīṇi sahassāni aḍḍhapañcamāni ca satāni, parikkhepato chattiṃsa satasahassāni dasa sahassāni aḍḍhuḍḍhāni ca satāni.

He is a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One (sammāsambuddho) because he has awakened (buddhattā) to the truths (saccānaṃ) rightly (sammā) and by himself (sāmaṃ). He is accomplished in knowledge and conduct (vijjācaraṇasampanno) because he is endowed with exceedingly pure knowledges (atisayavisuddhāhi vijjāhi) and unexcelled conduct (abbhuttamena caraṇena). He is the Well-Gone One (sugato) because he has gone beautifully (sobhanagamanattā), has gone to a beautiful place (sundaraṃ ṭhānaṃ gatattā), has gone well (suṭṭhu gatattā), and has spoken rightly (sammā gadattā). He is the Knower of the World (lokavidū) because he has known the world in every way (sabbathāpi viditalokattā). Indeed, that Blessed One knew the conditioned world (saṅkhāraloka)—with its distinctions of aggregates, sense bases, and so on—in every way: as to its nature, its origin, its cessation, and the way leading to its cessation: “One world: all beings are sustained by nutriment. Two worlds: name and form. Three worlds: three kinds of feeling. Four worlds: four kinds of nutriment. Five worlds: five aggregates subject to clinging. Six worlds: six internal sense bases. Seven worlds: seven stations of consciousness. Eight worlds: eight worldly conditions. Nine worlds: nine abodes of beings. Ten worlds: ten sense bases. Twelve worlds: twelve sense bases. Eighteen worlds: eighteen elements” (Ps. 1.112). Thus, in every way, he knew the conditioned world. He knows the dispositions of beings, their underlying tendencies, their behavior, their inclinations. He knows beings with little dust, much dust, keen faculties, dull faculties, good demeanor, bad demeanor, easy to instruct, difficult to instruct, capable, incapable. Thus, in every way, he knew the world of beings. Further, he knew one world-system (cakkavāḷa) to be one million, two hundred and three thousand, four hundred and fifty yojanas in length and breadth, and three million, six hundred and ten thousand, three hundred and fifty yojanas in circumference.

Tattha –

Herein it is said:

Duve satasahassāni, cattāri nahutāni ca;

Ettakaṃ bahalattena, saṅkhātāyaṃ vasundharā.

Two hundred thousand and forty thousand yojanas;

So vast in thickness, this earth has been reckoned.

Cattāri [V 2.0149] satasahassāni, aṭṭheva nahutāni ca;

Ettakaṃ bahalattena, jalaṃ vāte patiṭṭhitaṃ.

Four hundred thousand and eighty thousand yojanas;

So much water, resting upon the wind, is established.

Nava satasahassāni, māluto nabhamuggato;

Saṭṭhi ceva sahassāni, esā lokassa saṇṭhiti”.

Nine hundred thousand and sixty thousand yojanas, the wind rises to the sky;

This is the world's foundation.

Evaṃ saṇṭhite cettha yojanānaṃ –

When this is thus established, the measurement in yojanas is as follows:

Caturāsīti sahassāni, ajjhogāḷho mahaṇṇave;

Accuggato [P 2.0443] tāvadeva, sineru pabbatuttamo.

The supreme Mount Sineru is eighty-four thousand yojanas submerged in the great ocean, and rises up just as high.

Tato [M 2.0165] upaḍḍhupaḍḍhena, pamāṇena yathākkamaṃ;

Ajjhogāḷhuggatā dibbā, nānāratanacittitā.

Then, in due order, the divine mountains, adorned with various jewels, are submerged and rise up by half of the preceding one's measure.

Yugandharo īsadharo, karavīko sudassano;

Nemindharo vinatako, assakaṇṇo giri brahā.

Yugandhara, Īsadhara, Karavīka, Sudassana, Nemindhara, Vinataka, and the great mountain Assakaṇṇa.

Ete satta mahāselā, sinerussa samantato;

Mahārājānamāvāsā, devayakkhanisevitā.

These seven great mountains surround Sineru; they are the abodes of the Great Kings, frequented by devas and yakkhas.

Yojanānaṃ satānucco, himavā pañca pabbato;

Yojanānaṃ sahassāni, tīṇi āyatavitthato.

The Himavā mountain, with its five peaks, is five hundred yojanas high; it is three thousand yojanas in length and breadth.

Caturāsītisahassehi, kūṭehi paṭimaṇḍito;

Tipañcayojanakkhandha-parikkhepā nagavhayā.

It is adorned with eighty-four thousand peaks. The Nāga tree has a trunk with a circumference of fifteen yojanas.

Paññāsayojanakkhandha-sākhāyāmā samantato;

Sattayojanavitthiṇṇā, tāvadeva ca uggatā.

The trunk is fifty yojanas high and the branches are of equal length, extending all around; they are seven yojanas wide and rise up just as high.

Jambū [V 2.0150] yassānubhāvena, jambudīpo pakāsito;

Dve asītisahassāni, ajjhogāḷho mahaṇṇave.

By the power of this Jambu tree, Jambudīpa is so-named. It is eighty-two thousand yojanas submerged in the great ocean.

Accuggato tāvadeva, cakkavāḷasiluccayo;

Parikkhipitvā taṃ sabbaṃ, cakkavāḷamayaṃ ṭhito”.

The Cakkavāḷa mountain range rises up just as high; having encircled all that, it stands, forming the world-sphere.

Tattha candamaṇḍalaṃ ekūnapaññāsayojanaṃ, sūriyamaṇḍalaṃ paññāsayojanaṃ, tāvatiṃsabhavanaṃ dasasahassayojanaṃ, tathā asurabhavanaṃ avīcimahānirayo jambudīpo ca. Aparagoyānaṃ sattasahassayojanaṃ, tathā pubbavideho, uttarakuru aṭṭhasahassayojano. Ekameko cettha mahādīpo pañcasatapañcasataparittadīpaparivāro. Taṃ sabbampi ekaṃ cakkavāḷaṃ ekā lokadhātu. Cakkavāḷantaresu lokantarikanirayā. Evaṃ anantāni cakkavāḷāni anantā lokadhātuyo, anantena buddhañāṇena aññāsīti sabbathā okāsalokaṃ avedi. Evaṃ so bhagavā sabbathā. Viditalokattā lokavidūti veditabbo.

Therein, the moon's disc is forty-nine yojanas, the sun's disc is fifty yojanas, the Tāvatiṃsa heaven is ten thousand yojanas, and likewise the Asura realm, the Avīci great hell, and Jambudīpa. Aparagoyāna is seven thousand yojanas, likewise Pubbavideha, and Uttarakuru is eight thousand yojanas. Each of these great continents is surrounded by five hundred small islands. All that together forms one world-sphere, one world-system. In the space between world-spheres are the Lokantarika hells. Thus, with his boundless Buddha-knowledge, he knew that there are endless world-spheres and endless world-systems, and so in every way he knew the world of space (okāsaloka). Thus, that Blessed One, having known the world in all aspects, is to be understood as the Knower of the World.

Attano pana guṇehi visiṭṭhatarassa kassaci abhāvā anuttaro. Vicittehi vinayanūpāyehi purisadamme sāretīti purisadammasārathi. Diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaparamatthehi [M 2.0166][P 2.0444] yathārahaṃ anusāsati nitthāreti cāti satthā. Devamanussaggahaṇaṃ ukkaṭṭhaparicchedavasena bhabbapuggalapariggahavasena ca kataṃ, nāgādikepi pana esa lokiyatthena anusāsati. Yadatthi neyyaṃ nāma, sabbassa buddhattā vimokkhantikañāṇavasena buddho. Yato pana so –

Since there is no one more distinguished than himself on account of his own qualities, he is the Unsurpassed One (anuttaro). He is the Charioteer of Persons to be Tamed (purisadammasārathi) because he guides those capable of being tamed with diverse and skillful methods of training. He is the Teacher (satthā) because he instructs and brings to completion appropriately with regard to benefits in this life, benefits in the next life, and the ultimate benefit. The inclusion of 'gods and humans' is made on account of the distinction of excellence and on account of the inclusion of capable individuals; but he also instructs beings such as nāgas with worldly matters. Because he has understood all that is knowable by means of knowledge that culminates in liberation, he is the Buddha. And since he—

“Bhagyavā bhaggavā yutto, bhagehi ca vibhattavā;

Bhattavā vantagamano, bhavesu bhagavā tato”ti.

“He is fortunate, he has broken (the defilements), he is endowed (with qualities), and he has analyzed the parts (of the teaching);

He has partaken (of the Dhamma), he has abandoned travel in states of becoming; therefore, he is the Blessed One.”

Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthārato panetāni padāni visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.124-125) vuttāni.

This is a summary here; however, these terms are explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga (Vism. 1.124–125).

So imaṃ lokanti so bhagavā imaṃ lokaṃ. Idāni vattabbaṃ nidasseti. Sadevakantiādīni kasibhāradvājaāḷavakasuttesu vuttanayāneva. Sayanti sāmaṃ aparaneyyo hutvā. Abhiññāti abhiññāya. Sacchikatvāti paccakkhaṃ katvā. Pavedetīti bodheti ñāpeti pakāseti. So dhammaṃ deseti…pe… pariyosānakalyāṇanti so bhagavā sattesu kāruññataṃ paṭicca [V 2.0151] anuttaraṃ vivekasukhaṃ hitvāpi dhammaṃ deseti. Tañca kho appaṃ vā bahuṃ vā desento ādikalyāṇādippakārameva deseti. Kathaṃ? Ekagāthāpi hi samantabhaddakattā dhammassa paṭhamapādena ādikalyāṇā, dutiyatatiyapādehi majjhekalyāṇā, pacchimapādena pariyosānakalyāṇā. Ekānusandhikaṃ suttaṃ nidānena ādikalyāṇaṃ, nigamanena pariyosānakalyāṇaṃ, sesena majjhekalyāṇaṃ. Nānānusandhikaṃ paṭhamānusandhinā ādikalyāṇaṃ, pacchimena pariyosānakalyāṇaṃ, sesehi majjhekalyāṇaṃ. Sakalopi sāsanadhammo attano atthabhūtena sīlena ādikalyāṇo, samathavipassanāmaggaphalehi majjhekalyāṇo, nibbānena pariyosānakalyāṇo. Sīlasamādhīhi vā ādikalyāṇo, vipassanāmaggehi majjhekalyāṇo, phalanibbānehi pariyosānakalyāṇo. Buddhasubodhitāya vā ādikalyāṇo, dhammasudhammatāya majjhekalyāṇo, saṅghasuppaṭipattiyā pariyosānakalyāṇo[P 2.0445]. Taṃ sutvā tathattāya paṭipannena adhigantabbāya abhisambodhiyā vā ādikalyāṇo, paccekabodhiyā majjhekalyāṇo, sāvakabodhiyā pariyosānakalyāṇo[M 2.0167]. Suyyamāno cesa nīvaraṇādivikkhambhanato savanenapi kalyāṇameva āvahatīti ādikalyāṇo, paṭipajjamāno samathavipassanāsukhāvahanato paṭipattiyāpi kalyāṇameva āvahatīti majjhekalyāṇo, tathā paṭipanno ca paṭipattiphale niṭṭhite tādibhāvāvahanato paṭipattiphalenapi kalyāṇameva āvahatīti pariyosānakalyāṇo. Nāthappabhavattā ca pabhavasuddhiyā ādikalyāṇo, atthasuddhiyā majjhekalyāṇo, kiccasuddhiyā pariyosānakalyāṇo. Yato appaṃ vā bahuṃ vā desento ādikalyāṇādippakārameva desetīti veditabbo.

“This world”—that is, the Blessed One refers to this world. Now he shows what is to be stated. The phrases beginning with “with its gods” are to be understood in the same way as explained in the Kasibhāradvāja Sutta and the Āḷavaka Sutta. “He himself knows” (sayaṃ) means that he is independent, not led by others. “Directly knowing” (abhiññā) means by direct knowledge. “Having realized” (sacchikatvā) means having directly experienced. “He proclaims” (pavedeti) means he makes known, informs, and reveals. “He teaches the Dhamma… up to ‘good in the end’”—that is, the Blessed One, out of compassion for beings, teaches the Dhamma even having abandoned the unsurpassed bliss of seclusion. And whether teaching a little or much, he teaches in a way that is entirely “good in the beginning” and so forth. How so? Even a single verse, because of the Dhamma’s all-around auspiciousness, is good in the beginning with its first line, good in the middle with its second and third lines, and good in the end with its final line. A discourse with a single sequence is good in the beginning with its introduction, good in the middle with the rest, and good in the end with its conclusion. A discourse with multiple sequences is good in the beginning with its first sequence, good in the middle with the intermediate ones, and good in the end with the last. The entire dispensation of the Dhamma is good in the beginning with virtue, which is its own benefit; good in the middle with serenity, insight, the path, and the fruits; and good in the end with Nibbāna. Or it is good in the beginning with virtue and concentration, good in the middle with insight and the paths, and good in the end with the fruits and Nibbāna. Or it is good in the beginning due to the Buddha’s perfect awakening, good in the middle due to the Dhamma’s well-taught nature, and good in the end due to the Saṅgha’s good practice. Having heard it, for one practicing accordingly, it is good in the beginning for the complete awakening to be attained, good in the middle for individual awakening, and good in the end for the awakening of disciples. Even while being heard, it brings benefit by suppressing hindrances and so forth, thus being good in the beginning by hearing; while being practiced, it brings the joy of serenity and insight, thus being good in the middle by practice; and when one has practiced accordingly and the fruit of practice is complete, it brings the attainment of such a state, thus being good in the end by the fruit of practice. Because it originates from the Protector, it is good in the beginning due to purity of origin, good in the middle due to purity of meaning, and good in the end due to purity of action. Thus, whether teaching a little or much, it should be understood that he teaches in a way that is entirely “good in the beginning” and so forth.

Sātthaṃ sabyañjananti evamādīsu pana yasmā imaṃ dhammaṃ desento sāsanabrahmacariyaṃ maggabrahmacariyañca pakāseti, nānānayehi dīpeti, tañca yathāsambhavaṃ atthasampattiyā sātthaṃ, byañjanasampattiyā sabyañjanaṃ. Saṅkāsanapakāsanavivaraṇavibhajanauttānīkaraṇapaññattiatthapadasamāyogato sātthaṃ, akkharapadabyañjanākāraniruttiniddesasampattiyā sabyañjanaṃ. Atthagambhīratāpaṭivedhagambhīratāhi sātthaṃ, dhammagambhīratādesanāgambhīratāhi sabyañjanaṃ. Atthapaṭibhānapaṭisambhidāvisayato sātthaṃ, dhammaniruttipaṭisambhidāvisayato sabyañjanaṃ. Paṇḍitavedanīyato sarikkhakajanappasādakanti sātthaṃ, saddheyyato lokiyajanappasādakanti sabyañjanaṃ. Gambhīrādhippāyato sātthaṃ, uttānapadato sabyañjanaṃ. Upanetabbassābhāvato sakalaparipuṇṇabhāvena kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ, apanetabbassa abhāvato niddosabhāvena parisuddhaṃ. Sikkhattayapariggahitattā brahmabhūtehi seṭṭhehi caritabbato tesañca cariyabhāvato brahmacariyaṃ. Tasmā “sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ…pe… brahmacariyaṃ pakāsetī”ti vuccati.

“Meaningful and well-expressed”—in these and similar cases, because when expounding this Dhamma, he reveals the holy life of the Dispensation and the holy life of the path, illuminating it through various methods. And it is meaningful (sātthaṃ) in terms of the attainment of meaning as is possible, and well-expressed (sabyañjanaṃ) in terms of the attainment of expression. It is meaningful due to the combination of indicating, expounding, explaining, analyzing, making clear, formulating, and combining meaningful phrases. It is well-expressed due to the excellence in syllables, words, expressions, form, etymology, and definition. It is meaningful because of the profundity of meaning and the profundity of penetration. It is well-expressed because of the profundity of the Dhamma and the profundity of the exposition. It is meaningful in terms of the scope of the analytical insights into meaning and inspired speech. It is well-expressed in terms of the scope of the analytical insights into Dhamma and language. It is meaningful because it is to be understood by the wise and delights those of similar disposition. It is well-expressed because it is trustworthy and delights worldly people. It is meaningful due to its profound intention. It is well-expressed due to its plain wording. Because there is nothing to be added, it is entirely complete in every way, perfectly complete. Because there is nothing to be removed, it is utterly pure and flawless. Since it is embraced by the threefold training and is to be lived by the supreme ones who have become Brahma, and because it is their way of life, it is called the holy life. Therefore, it is said: “meaningful and well-expressed… it reveals the holy life.”

Apica [V 2.0152] yasmā sanidānaṃ sauppattikañca desento ādikalyāṇaṃ deseti, vineyyānaṃ anurūpato atthassa aviparītatāya hetudāharaṇayogato ca majjhekalyāṇaṃ[P 2.0446], sotūnaṃ saddhāpaṭilābhena nigamanena ca pariyosānakalyāṇaṃ. Evaṃ desento ca brahmacariyaṃ pakāseti. Tañca paṭipattiyā adhigamabyattito sātthaṃ, pariyattiyā āgamabyattito sabyañjanaṃ, sīlādipañcadhammakkhandhayuttato kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ, nirupakkilesato nittharaṇatthāya pavattito lokāmisanirapekkhato ca [M 2.0168] parisuddhaṃ, seṭṭhaṭṭhena brahmabhūtānaṃ buddhapaccekabuddhasāvakānaṃ cariyato brahmacariyanti vuccati, tasmāpi “so dhammaṃ deseti…pe… brahmacariyaṃ pakāsetī”ti vuccati.

Moreover, because he teaches the Dhamma with its causes and its arising, he teaches what is good in the beginning. By presenting the middle in a way suitable to those to be trained, ensuring the meaning is not distorted, and through the application of reasons and examples, he teaches what is good in the middle. Through the listeners’ acquisition of faith and the conclusion, he teaches what is good in the end. Thus, teaching in this way, he reveals the holy life. And that holy life is meaningful (sātthaṃ) because of its clarity of realization through practice; it is well-expressed (sabyañjanaṃ) because of its clarity of tradition through study; it is perfectly complete (kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ) because it is endowed with the five aggregates of Dhamma beginning with virtue; it is utterly pure (parisuddhaṃ) because it is free from defilements, it proceeds for the sake of deliverance, and it is independent of worldly allurements. It is called the holy life (brahmacariyaṃ) because it is the conduct of those who have become Brahma—the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples—in the sense of being supreme. For this reason too, it is said: “He teaches the Dhamma… he reveals the holy life.”

Sādhu kho panāti sundaraṃ kho pana, atthāvahaṃ sukhāvahanti vuttaṃ hoti. Dhammiyā kathāyāti pānakānisaṃsapaṭisaṃyuttāya. Ayañhi keṇiyo sāyanhasamaye bhagavato āgamanaṃ assosi. “Tucchahattho bhagavantaṃ dassanāya gantuṃ lajjamāno vikālabhojanā viratānampi pānakaṃ kappatī”ti cintetvā pañcahi kājasatehi susaṅkhataṃ badarapānaṃ gāhāpetvā agamāsi. Yathāha bhesajjakkhandhake “atha kho keṇiyassa jaṭilassa etadahosi, kiṃ nu kho ahaṃ samaṇassa gotamassa harāpeyya”nti (mahāva. 300) sabbaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tato naṃ bhagavā yathā sekkhasutte (ma. ni. 2.22 ādayo) sākiye āvasathānisaṃsapaṭisaṃyuttāya kathāya, gosiṅgasālavane (ma. ni. 1.325 ādayo) tayo kulaputte sāmaggirasānisaṃsapaṭisaṃyuttāya, rathavinīte (ma. ni. 1.252 ādayo) jātibhūmake bhikkhū dasakathāvatthupaṭisaṃyuttāya, evaṃ taṅkhaṇānurūpāya pānakānisaṃsapaṭisaṃyuttāya kathāya pānakadānānisaṃsaṃ sandassesi, tathārūpānaṃ puññānaṃ punapi kattabbatāya niyojento samādapesi, abbhussāhaṃ janento samuttejesi, sandiṭṭhikasamparāyikena phalavisesena pahaṃsento sampahaṃsesi. Tenāha “dhammiyā kathāya…pe… sampahaṃsesī”ti. So bhiyyosomattāya bhagavati pasanno bhagavantaṃ nimantesi, bhagavā cassa tikkhattuṃ paṭikkhipitvā adhivāsesi. Tenāha “atha kho keṇiyo jaṭilo…pe… adhivāsesi [P 2.0447] bhagavā tuṇhībhāvenā”ti.

“Excellent indeed” (sādhu kho pana)—that is, it is beautiful, beneficial, and brings happiness. “With a Dhamma talk” (dhammiyā kathāya)—that is, one connected with the benefits of drinks. For this Keṇiya heard of the Blessed One’s arrival in the evening. Thinking, “Empty-handed, I am ashamed to go see the Blessed One. Even for those who abstain from eating at the wrong time, a drink is permissible,” he had well-prepared jujube drink carried on five hundred poles and went. As stated in the Bhesajjakkhandhaka: “Then the ascetic Keṇiya thought, ‘What could I offer to the ascetic Gotama?’” (Mahāvagga 300)—all should be understood accordingly. Then the Blessed One, just as in the Sekkha Sutta (Majjhima Nikāya 2.22 ff.) he spoke to the Sakyans with a discourse connected with the benefits of lodging; in the Gosingasala Grove (Majjhima Nikāya 1.325 ff.) to the three clansmen with a discourse connected with the benefits of concord; and in the Rathavinita Sutta (Majjhima Nikāya 1.252 ff.) to the monks of Jātibhūmi with a discourse connected with the ten topics of discourse—similarly, at that moment, with a discourse connected with the benefits of drinks, he demonstrated the benefits of giving drinks, encouraged them to perform such merits again, roused their enthusiasm, and gladdened and delighted them with the special fruits visible in this life and in the future. Therefore, it is said: “with a Dhamma talk… he delighted them.” Being even more pleased with the Blessed One, he invited him. The Blessed One declined three times but then consented. Therefore, it is said: “Then the ascetic Keṇiya… the Blessed One consented by silence.”

Kimatthaṃ pana paṭikkhipi bhagavāti? Punappunaṃ yācanāya cassa puññavuḍḍhi bhavissati, bahutarañca paṭiyādessati, tato aḍḍhatelasānaṃ bhikkhusatānaṃ paṭiyattaṃ aḍḍhasoḷasannaṃ pāpuṇissatīti. Kuto aparāni tīṇi satānīti ce? Appaṭiyatteyeva hi bhatte selo brāhmaṇo tīhi māṇavakasatehi saddhiṃ pabbajissati, taṃ disvā bhagavā evamāhāti. Mittāmacceti mitte ca kammakare ca. Ñātisālohiteti samānalohite ekayonisambandhe puttadhītādayo [V 2.0153] avasesabandhave ca. Yenāti [M 2.0169] yasmā. Meti mayhaṃ. Kāyaveyyāvaṭikanti kāyena veyyāvaccaṃ. Maṇḍalamāḷaṃ paṭiyādetīti setavitānamaṇḍapaṃ karoti.

Why then did the Blessed One decline? So that by repeated requests his merit would increase, and he would prepare much more. Thus, what was prepared for twelve hundred and fifty monks would suffice for fifteen hundred and fifty. If it is asked, “From where would the other three hundred come?”—it is because while the meal was still unprepared, the brahmin Sela would go forth with three hundred young men. Seeing this, the Blessed One spoke thus. “Friends and companions” (mittāmaccā) refers to friends and workers. “Relatives and kin” (ñātisālohitā) means those of the same bloodline, connected by one womb, such as sons, daughters, and other remaining relatives. “Because of whom” (yena)—that is, because. “My” (me)—that is, for me. “Bodily service” (kāyaveyyāvaṭikaṃ)—that is, service performed with the body. “Prepares a pavilion” (maṇḍalamāḷaṃ paṭiyādeti) means he makes a white canopy and pavilion.

Tiṇṇaṃ vedānanti irubbedayajubbedasāmavedānaṃ. Saha nighaṇḍunā ca keṭubhena ca sanighaṇḍukeṭubhānaṃ. Nighaṇḍūti nāmanighaṇḍurukkhādīnaṃ vevacanappakāsakaṃ satthaṃ. Keṭubhanti kiriyākappavikappo kavīnaṃ upakārāya satthaṃ. Saha akkharappabhedena sākkharappabhedānaṃ. Akkharappabhedoti sikkhā ca nirutti ca. Itihāsapañcamānanti athabbanavedaṃ catutthaṃ katvā “itiha āsa itiha āsā”ti īdisavacanapaṭisaṃyutto purāṇakathāsaṅkhāto itihāso pañcamo etesanti itihāsapañcamā. Tesaṃ itihāsapañcamānaṃ. Padaṃ tadavasesañca byākaraṇaṃ ajjheti vedeti cāti padako veyyākaraṇo. Lokāyate vitaṇḍavādasatthe mahāpurisalakkhaṇādhikāre ca dvādasasahasse mahāpurisalakkhaṇasatthe anūno paripūrakārīti lokāyatamahāpurisalakkhaṇesu anavayo, avayo na hotīti vuttaṃ hoti. Avayo nāma yo tāni atthato ca ganthato ca sandhāretuṃ na sakkoti.

“The three Vedas” (tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ) means the Rigveda, Yajurveda, and Samaveda. `Sanighaṇḍukeṭubhānaṃ` means: along with the Nighaṇḍu and the Keṭubha. The Nighaṇḍu is a text that explains the synonyms of names, trees, and so on. The Keṭubha is a text on the arrangement and modification of poetic composition, useful for poets. `Sākkharappabhedānaṃ` means: along with the analysis of syllables. The analysis of syllables (`akkharappabheda`) means phonetics (`sikkhā`) and etymology (`nirutti`). “The Itihāsa as the fifth” (`itihāsapañcamānaṃ`): having made the Atharvaveda the fourth, the Itihāsa—which consists of ancient tales connected with such phrases as “thus it was, thus it was”—is the fifth of these; hence they are called `itihāsapañcamā`. One who studies and knows the Pada text and the rest, which is grammar, is a `padako` (an expert in the Pada text) and a `veyyākaraṇo` (a grammarian). Regarding `lokāyatamahāpurisalakkhaṇesu anavayo` (“faultless in the Lokāyata and the marks of a great man”): in the Lokāyata, the science of sophistry, and in the science of the great man’s marks, which has a section on the marks of a great man in twelve thousand verses, he is not deficient (`anūno`), a fulfiller (`paripūrakārī`). Thus, he is `anavayo`, which is to say he is not `avayo` (deficient). One who is deficient (`avayo`) is one who is unable to retain them in meaning and in text.

Jaṅghāya hitaṃ vihāraṃ [P 2.0448] jaṅghāvihāraṃ, cirāsanādijanitaṃ parissamaṃ vinodetuṃ jaṅghāpasāraṇatthaṃ adīghacārikanti vuttaṃ hoti. Anucaṅkamamānoti caṅkamamāno eva. Anuvicaramānoti ito cito ca caramāno. Keṇiyassa jaṭilassa assamoti keṇiyassa assamaṃ nivesanaṃ. Āvāhoti kaññāgahaṇaṃ. Vivāhoti kaññādānaṃ. Mahāyaññoti mahāyajanaṃ. Māgadhoti magadhānaṃ issaro. Mahatiyā senāya samannāgatattā seniyo. Bimbīti suvaṇṇaṃ, tasmā sārasuvaṇṇasadisavaṇṇatāya bimbisāro. So me nimantitoti so mayā nimantito.

A walk beneficial for the legs is a `jaṅghāvihāra`. It is said to be a short walk for stretching the legs to relieve the fatigue caused by prolonged sitting. `Anucaṅkamamāno` means simply walking back and forth. `Anuvicaramāno` means walking here and there. `Keṇiyassa jaṭilassa assamo` means the hermitage, the abode of Keṇiya. `Āvāha` means the taking of a bride. `Vivāha` means the giving away of a bride. `Mahāyañña` means a great sacrifice. `Māgadha` means the ruler of the Magadhas. `Seniyo` means one possessing an army, because he is endowed with a great army. `Bimbī` means gold; therefore, he is Bimbisāra because his complexion resembles refined gold. `So me nimantito` means 'he has been invited by me'.

Atha brāhmaṇo pubbe katādhikārattā buddhasaddaṃ sutvāva amatenevābhisitto vimhayarūpattā āha – “buddhoti, bho keṇiya, vadesī”ti. Itaro yathābhūtaṃ ācikkhanto āha – “buddhoti, bho sela, vadāmī”ti. Tato naṃ punapi daḷhīkaraṇatthaṃ pucchi, itaropi tatheva ārocesi. Atha kappasatasahassehipi buddhasaddassa dullabhabhāvaṃ dassento [M 2.0170] āha – “ghosopi kho eso dullabho lokasmiṃ yadidaṃ buddho”ti. Tattha yadidanti nipāto, yo esoti vuttaṃ hoti.

Then the brahmin, because of his previously performed meritorious deeds, upon hearing the word 'Buddha,' was as if sprinkled with nectar and, being filled with wonder, said: 'Keṇiya, friend, do you say 'Buddha'?' The other, explaining it as it truly was, replied: 'Sela, friend, I say 'Buddha'.' Then he asked him again to confirm it, and the other likewise informed him. Then, showing the rarity of the word 'Buddha' even in hundreds of thousands of aeons, he said: 'Indeed, this sound is rare in the world, namely, 'Buddha'.' Here, `yadidaṃ` is a particle, meaning 'which this is'.

Atha brāhmaṇo buddhasaddaṃ sutvā “kiṃ nu kho so saccameva buddho, udāhu nāmamattamevassa buddho”ti vīmaṃsitukāmo cintesi, abhāsi eva vā “āgatāni kho pana…pe… vivaṭṭacchado”ti. Tattha “mantesū”ti vedesu. “Tathāgato kira uppajjissatī”ti paṭikacceva [V 2.0154] suddhāvāsadevā brāhmaṇavesena lakkhaṇāni pakkhipitvā vede vācenti “tadanusārena mahesakkhā sattā tathāgataṃ jānissantī”ti. Tena pubbe vedesu mahāpurisalakkhaṇāni āgacchanti. Parinibbute pana tathāgate kamena antaradhāyanti, tena etarahi natthi. Mahāpurisassāti paṇidhisamādānañāṇasamādānakaruṇādiguṇamahato purisassa[P 2.0449]. Dveva gatiyoti dve eva niṭṭhā. Kāmañcāyaṃ gatisaddo “pañca kho imā, sāriputta, gatiyo”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.153) bhavabhede, “gatī migānaṃ pavana”ntiādīsu (pari. 339) nivāsaṭṭhāne, “evaṃ adhimattagatimanto”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.161) paññāyaṃ, “gatigata”ntiādīsu (cūḷava. 204) visaṭabhāve vattati, idha pana niṭṭhāyaṃ veditabbo. Tattha kiñcāpi yehi lakkhaṇehi samannāgato rājā hoti cakkavatti, na tehi eva buddho. Jātisāmaññato pana tāniyeva tānīti vuccanti. Tasmā vuttaṃ “yehi samannāgatassā”ti.

Then the brahmin, hearing the word 'Buddha,' wishing to investigate whether 'is he truly a Buddha, or is his name merely 'Buddha' (nāmamattamevassa buddho)?' reflected, or rather, spoke thus: 'Indeed, it has been said... with the covering removed (vivaṭṭacchado).' Therein, 'in the mantras' (mantesu) means in the Vedas (vedesu). 'The Tathāgata will arise' (Tathāgato kira uppajjissatīti) — even beforehand (paṭikacceva), the Suddhāvāsa deities, in the guise of brahmins (brāhmaṇavesena), inserted the characteristics (lakkhaṇāni pakkhipitvā) into the Vedas and had them recited, thinking: 'So that beings of great power (mahesakkhā sattā) may recognize the Tathāgata accordingly (tadanusārena).' Therefore, previously the marks of a great man (mahāpurisalakkhaṇāni) appeared in the Vedas. But after the Tathāgata's Parinibbāna, they gradually disappeared (kamena antaradhāyanti); hence they are not found now (etarahi natthi). 'Of a great man' (Mahāpurisassa) means of a man great with qualities such as the undertaking of an aspiration (paṇidhisamādāna), the undertaking of knowledge (ñāṇasamādāna), and compassion (karuṇā). 'Only two destinies' (Dveva gatiyo) means only two conclusions (dve eva niṭṭhā). Moreover, this word 'gati' (gatisaddo) is used in various senses: in 'There are, Sāriputta, these five destinies' (Majjhima Nikāya 1.153), it refers to types of existence (bhavabhede); in 'the destiny of deer in the forest' (Parivāra 339), it means a dwelling place (nivāsaṭṭhāne); in 'thus, those of excessive destiny' (Majjhima Nikāya 1.161), it refers to wisdom (paññāyaṃ); in 'gone to destiny' (Cūḷavagga 204), it denotes pervasiveness (visaṭabhāve). Here, however, it should be understood as referring to the conclusion (niṭṭhāyaṃ). Therein, although one endowed with those marks (yehi lakkhaṇehi samannāgato) becomes a wheel-turning monarch (rājā hoti cakkavatti), he is not a Buddha by those same marks. But in terms of commonality of type (jātisāmaññato), those very marks are called the same (tāniyeva tānīti). Therefore, it is said, 'one endowed with them' (yehi samannāgatassā).

Sace agāraṃ ajjhāvasatīti yadi agāre vasati. Rājā hoti cakkavattīti catūhi acchariyadhammehi saṅgahavatthūhi ca lokaṃ rañjanato rājā. Cakkaratanaṃ vatteti, catūhi sampatticakkehi, vattati, tehi ca paraṃ vatteti, parahitāya ca iriyāpathacakkānaṃ vatto etasmiṃ atthīti cakkavatti. Ettha ca rājāti sāmaññaṃ, cakkavattīti visesanaṃ. Dhammena caratīti dhammiko, ñāyena samena vattatīti attho. Dhammena rajjaṃ labhitvā rājā jātoti dhammarājā. Parahitadhammakaraṇena vā dhammiko, attahitadhammakaraṇena dhammarājā. Caturantāya issaroti cāturanto, catusamuddantāya cattubbidhadīpavibhūsitāya ca pathaviyā issaroti attho. Ajjhattaṃ kodhādipaccatthike bahiddhā ca sabbarājāno vijesīti vijitāvī. Janapadatthāvariyappattoti janapade dhuvabhāvaṃ thāvarabhāvaṃ patto, na sakkā kenaci [M 2.0171] cāletuṃ, janapado vā tamhi thāvariyappatto anussukko sakammanirato acalo asampavedhītipi janapadatthāvariyappatto.

'If he lives in a house' (Sace agāraṃ ajjhāvasati) means if he dwells in a house (yadi agāre vasati). 'He becomes a wheel-turning monarch' (Rājā hoti cakkavatti) means a king (rājā) because he delights the world (lokaṃ rañjanato) with the four marvelous qualities (catūhi acchariyadhammehi) and the bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthūhi). He is a wheel-turner (cakkavatti) because he sets the wheel-treasure (cakkaratanaṃ) in motion (vatteti); he proceeds (vattati) with the four wheels of accomplishment (catūhi sampatticakkehi), and by them he causes others to proceed (paraṃ vatteti); and because the turning (vatto) of the wheels of deportment (iriyāpathacakkānaṃ) for the welfare of others (parahitāya) exists in him. Here, 'king' (rājā) is the general term (sāmaññaṃ), and 'wheel-turner' (cakkavatti) is the specific attribute (visesanaṃ). 'He rules righteously' (Dhammena carati) means he is righteous (dhammiko), meaning he acts with justice and impartiality (ñāyena samena vattati). Having obtained kingship by righteousness, he is a righteous king (dhammarājā). Or, he is righteous (dhammiko) by performing righteous deeds for others' welfare (parahitadhammakaraṇena), and a righteous king (dhammarājā) by performing righteous deeds for his own welfare (attahitadhammakaraṇena). 'Sovereign of the four quarters' (Caturantāya issaro) means he is a ruler of the four quarters (cāturanto), meaning he is the lord (issaro) of the earth (pathaviyā) bounded by the four oceans (catusamuddantāya) and adorned with the four kinds of continents (cattubbidhadīpavibhūsitāya). `Vijitāvī` (victorious) means one who has conquered his internal enemies, such as anger, and externally, all kings. 'Established in the stability of the country' (Janapadatthāvariyappattoti) means he has attained permanence (dhuvabhāvaṃ) and stability (thāvarabhāvaṃ) in the country (janapade), so he cannot be shaken by anyone (na sakkā kenaci cāletuṃ). Or, it means the country (janapado) has attained stability (thāvariyappatto) in him, being untroubled (anussukko), devoted to its own duties (sakammanirato), unshaken (acalo), and undisturbed (asampavedhī)—thus, he is 'established in the stability of the country'.

Seyyathidanti nipāto, tassa [P 2.0450] etāni katamānīti attho. Cakkaratanaṃ…pe… pariṇāyakaratanameva sattamanti tāni sabbappakārato ratanasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttāni. Tesu ayaṃ cakkavattirājā cakkaratanena ajitaṃ jināti, hatthiassaratanehi vijite yathāsukhamanuvicarati, pariṇāyakaratanena vijitamanurakkhati, sesehi upabhogasukhamanubhavati. Paṭhamena cassa ussāhasattiyogo, hatthiassagahapatiratanehi pabhusattiyogo, pariṇāyakaratanena mantasattiyogo suparipuṇṇo hoti, itthimaṇiratanehi ca tividhasattiyogaphalaṃ. So itthimaṇiratanehi bhogasukhamanubhoti, sesehi issariyasukhaṃ. Visesato cassa purimāni tīṇi adosakusalamūlajanitakammānubhāvena [V 2.0155] sampajjanti, majjhimāni alobhakusalamūlajanitakammānubhāvena, pacchimamekaṃ amohakusalamūlajanitakammānubhāvenāti veditabbaṃ.

'Seyyathidaṃ' is a particle, meaning 'what are these?' (tassa etāni katamānīti attho). The Wheel-Treasure... up to... the Counselor-Treasure as the seventh (pariṇāyakaratanameva sattamaṃ) — these are all described in every way (sabbappakārato) in the commentary on the Ratana Sutta (ratanasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ). Among these, this Wheel-Turning Monarch (cakkavattirājā) conquers the unconquered (ajitaṃ jināti) with the Wheel-Treasure (cakkaratanena); he roams freely (yathāsukhaṃ anuvicarati) in the conquered territories (vijite) with the Elephant- and Horse-Treasures (hatthiassaratanehi); he protects his conquests (vijitaṃ anurakkhati) with the Counselor-Treasure (pariṇāyakaratanena); and he experiences the pleasure of enjoyment (upabhogasukhaṃ anubhavati) with the remaining treasures (sesehi). With the first treasure, he has the power of effort (ussāhasattiyogo); with the Elephant-, Horse-, and Householder-Treasures, the power of dominion (pabhusattiyogo); with the Counselor-Treasure, his power of counsel (mantasattiyogo) is perfectly complete (suparipuṇṇo hoti); and with the woman- and gem-treasures (itthimaṇiratanehi), there is the fruit of the threefold power (tividhasattiyogaphalaṃ). He experiences the pleasure of enjoyment (bhogasukhaṃ anubhoti) with the woman- and gem-treasures (itthimaṇiratanehi), and the pleasure of sovereignty (issariyasukhaṃ) with the others (sesehi). Specifically, it should be understood that his first three (purimāni tīṇi) treasures arise from the karmic result (kammānubhāvena) produced by the wholesome root of non-hatred (adosakusalamūlajanita); the middle ones (majjhimāni) from the karmic result produced by the wholesome root of non-greed (alobhakusalamūlajanita); and the last one (pacchimamekaṃ) from the karmic result produced by the wholesome root of non-delusion (amohakusalamūlajanita).

Parosahassanti atirekasahassaṃ. Sūrāti abhīrukajātikā. Vīraṅgarūpāti devaputtasadisakāyā, evaṃ tāveke. Ayaṃ panettha sabhāvo vīrāti uttamasūrā vuccanti, vīrānaṃ aṅgaṃ vīraṅgaṃ, vīrakāraṇaṃ vīriyanti vuttaṃ hoti. Vīraṅgaṃ rūpaṃ etesanti vīraṅgarūpā, vīriyamayasarīrā viyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Parasenappamaddanāti sace paṭimukhaṃ tiṭṭheyya parasenā, taṃ pamaddituṃ samatthāti adhippāyo. Dhammenāti “pāṇo na hantabbo”tiādinā (dī. ni. 2.244; ma. ni. 3.257) pañcasīladhammena. Arahaṃ hoti sammāsambuddho loke vivaṭṭacchadoti ettha rāgadosamohamānadiṭṭhiavijjāduccaritachadanehi sattahi paṭicchanne kilesandhakāre loke taṃ chadanaṃ vivaṭṭetvā samantato sañjātāloko hutvā ṭhitoti vivaṭṭacchado. Tattha paṭhamena padena pūjārahatā, dutiyena tassā hetu yasmā sammāsambuddhoti. Tatiyena buddhattahetu vivaṭṭacchadatā vuttāti [P 2.0451] veditabbā. Atha vā vivaṭṭo ca vicchado cāti vivaṭṭacchado, vaṭṭarahito chadanarahito cāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tena arahaṃ vaṭṭābhāvena sammāsambuddho chadanābhāvenāti evaṃ purimapadadvayasseva hetudvayaṃ vuttaṃ hoti. Dutiyena vesārajjena cettha purimasiddhi, paṭhamena dutiyasiddhi, tatiyacatutthehi [M 2.0172] tatiyasiddhi hoti. Purimañca dhammacakkhuṃ, dutiyaṃ buddhacakkhuṃ, tatiyaṃ samantacakkhuṃ sādhetīti veditabbaṃ.

'Parosahassaṃ' means more than a thousand (atirekasahassaṃ). 'Sūrā' means those of fearless nature (abhīrukajātikā). 'Vīraṅgarūpā' means having bodies resembling divine beings (devaputtasadisakāyā); so say some (evaṃ tāveke). Here, however, the true meaning (sabhāvo) is this: `vīrā` are called the most excellent of the brave (uttamasūrā); `vīraṅga` is the 'limb' of heroes (`vīrānaṃ aṅgaṃ`); it is said that the cause of heroism (`vīrakāraṇaṃ`) is energy (`vīriya`). 'Vīraṅgarūpā' means 'having heroic form,' that is, they are as if bodies made of energy (vīriyamayasarīrā viya) — this is what is said. 'Crushing enemy armies' (Parasenappamaddanā) means that if an enemy army (parasenā) should stand in opposition (paṭimukhaṃ tiṭṭheyya), he is able to crush it (taṃ pamaddituṃ samattha) — this is the intention (adhippāyo). 'By righteousness' (Dhammena) refers to the five precepts (pañcasīladhammena), such as 'living beings should not be killed' (pāṇo na hantabbo) (Dī. Ni. 2.244; Ma. Ni. 3.257). 'The Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, with the covering removed in the world' (Arahaṃ hoti sammāsambuddho loke vivaṭṭacchado) — here, in the world (loke) covered by the darkness of defilements (kilesandhakāre), concealed by the seven coverings (sattahi paṭicchanne) of lust, hatred, delusion, pride, wrong view, ignorance, and misconduct (rāgadosamohamānadiṭṭhiavijjāduccarita), having removed that covering (taṃ chadanaṃ vivaṭṭetvā) and having become one whose light has arisen everywhere (samantato sañjātāloko hutvā), he stands as one with the covering removed (vivaṭṭacchado). Here, by the first term (paṭhamena padena) is stated deservingness of homage (pūjārahatā); by the second (dutiyena), the reason for that, namely, because he is the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One (yasmā sammāsambuddhoti). By the third (tatiyena), the state of having the covering removed (vivaṭṭacchadatā) is stated as the cause of Buddhahood (buddhattahetu) — this should be understood. Or alternatively, 'vivaṭṭacchado' means both 'uncovered' (vivaṭṭa) and 'without a covering' (vicchada); that is, without the cycle (vaṭṭarahito) and without covering (chadanarahito) — this is what is said. Thus, two reasons are stated for the two previous terms themselves (purimapadadvayasseva): 'Arahant' due to the absence of the cycle (vaṭṭābhāvena), and 'Perfectly Self-Enlightened One' due to the absence of covering (chadanābhāvena). Here, by the second confidence (dutiyena vesārajjena), there is the accomplishment of the first; by the first, the accomplishment of the second; and by the third and fourth, the accomplishment of the third occurs. And it should be understood that the first (purimaṃ) establishes the eye of Dhamma (dhammacakkhu), the second (dutiyaṃ) the eye of a Buddha (buddhacakkhu), and the third (tatiyaṃ) the all-seeing eye (samantacakkhu).

Idāni bhagavato santikaṃ gantukāmo āha – “kahaṃ pana bho…pe… sammāsambuddho”ti. Evaṃ vuttetiādīsu yenesāti yena disābhāgena esā. Nīlavanarājīti nīlavaṇṇarukkhapanti. Vanaṃ kira meghapantisadisaṃ. Yattha bhagavā tadā vihāsi, taṃ niddisanto āha – “yenesā bho, sela, nīlavanarājī”ti. Tattha “so viharatī”ti ayaṃ panettha pāṭhaseso, bhummatthe vā karaṇavacanaṃ. Pade padanti padasamīpe padaṃ. Tena turitagamanaṃ paṭisedheti. Durāsadā hīti kāraṇaṃ āha, yasmā te durāsadā, tasmā evaṃ bhonto āgacchantūti. Kiṃ pana kāraṇā durāsadāti ce? Sīhāva ekacarā. Yathā hi sīhā sahāyakiccābhāvato ekacarā, evaṃ tepi vivekakāmatāya. “Yadā cāha”ntiādinā pana te māṇavake upacāraṃ sikkhāpeti. Tattha mā opātethāti mā pavesetha, mā kathethāti vuttaṃ hoti. Āgamentūti paṭimānentu, yāva kathā pariyosānaṃ gacchati, tāva tuṇhī bhavantūti attho.

Now, wishing to go to the Blessed One, he said: 'But where, sir... is the Perfectly Enlightened One?' In phrases like 'When this was said' (Evaṃ vutte), 'yenesā' means 'by which direction this is.' 'The blue forest grove' (nīlavanarājī) refers to a row of trees with a blue color. The forest, it is said, resembled a line of clouds. Pointing out where the Blessed One was dwelling at that time, he said: 'By which direction, sir Sela, is that blue forest grove?' Here, 'he dwells there' is the remainder of the text, or it may be an instrumental case in the sense of location. 'Step by step' (pade padaṃ) means placing one foot near the other. This discourages hurried movement. 'For they are hard to approach' (durāsadā hi) states the reason: 'Because they are hard to approach, therefore, sirs, come in this manner.' But why are they hard to approach? 'Like lions, they wander alone.' Just as lions wander alone due to the absence of the need for companions, so too do they, out of love for seclusion. Then, with the phrase 'and when I,' he instructs those young men in proper conduct. Here, 'mā opātetha' means 'do not enter,' that is, 'do not speak' is what is said. 'Let them wait' (āgamentu) means 'let them await'; the meaning is that they should remain silent until the conversation reaches its conclusion.

Samannesīti gavesi. Yebhuyyenāti bahukāni addasa, appakāni nāddasa. Tato yāni na addasa[V 2.0156], tāni dīpento āha “ṭhapetvā dve”ti. Kaṅkhatīti kaṅkhaṃ uppādeti patthanaṃ “aho vata passeyya”nti. Vicikicchatīti tato tato tāni vicinanto kicchati na sakkoti daṭṭhuṃ. Nādhimuccatīti tāya vicikicchāya sanniṭṭhānaṃ na gacchati. Na sampasīdatīti tato “paripuṇṇalakkhaṇo aya”nti bhagavati pasādaṃ [P 2.0452] nāpajjati. Kaṅkhāya vā sudubbalavimati vuttā, vicikicchāya majjhimā, anadhimuccanatāya balavatī, asampasādena tehi tīhi dhammehi cittassa kālussiyabhāvo.

‘He sought out’ means he searched. ‘For the most part’ means he saw many, but few he did not see. Then, pointing out those he did not see, he said, ‘except for two.’ ‘He is doubtful’ means he gives rise to doubt, wishing, ‘Oh, if only I could see!’ ‘He is uncertain’ means, while investigating them here and there, he is troubled and cannot see. ‘He does not become decided’ means he does not reach a conclusion due to that uncertainty. ‘He does not become confident’ means he does not attain faith in the Blessed One, thinking, ‘This one is endowed with the complete marks.’ By doubt, very weak perplexity is meant; by uncertainty, a middling one; by indecision, a strong one; and by lack of confidence, the mind's state of impurity due to these three states.

Kosohiteti vatthikosena paṭicchanne. Vatthaguyheti aṅgajāte. Bhagavato hi varavāraṇasseva kosohitaṃ vatthaguyhaṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ padumagabbhasamānaṃ. Taṃ so vatthapaṭicchannattā apassanto antomukhagatāya ca jivhāya pahūtabhāvaṃ asallakkhento tesu dvīsu lakkhaṇesu kaṅkhī ahosi [M 2.0173] vicikicchī. Tathārūpanti kathaṃ rūpaṃ? Kimettha amhehi vattabbaṃ, vuttametaṃ nāgasenatthereneva milindaraññā puṭṭhena (mi. pa. 4.3.3) –

‘Kosohita’ means covered by a sheath. ‘Vatthaguyha’ means the private parts. Indeed, the Blessed One’s private parts are hidden in a sheath like those of a great elephant, golden-hued, resembling the calyx of a lotus. Not seeing it because it was covered by his robe, and not discerning the largeness of his tongue, which was withdrawn into his mouth, he was doubtful and uncertain about those two characteristics. Regarding ‘such a form,’ what kind of form is it? What should we say about this? This has already been stated by the Elder Nāgasena when questioned by King Milinda (Miln. 4.3.3).

“Dukkaraṃ, bhante nāgasena, bhagavatā katanti. Kiṃ, mahārājāti? Mahājanena hirikaraṇokāsaṃ brahmāyubrāhmaṇassa ca antevāsiuttarassa ca bāvarissa antevāsīnaṃ soḷasannaṃ brāhmaṇānañca selassa brāhmaṇassa antevāsīnaṃ tisatamāṇavānañca dassesi, bhanteti. Na, mahārāja, bhagavā guyhaṃ dasseti, chāyaṃ bhagavā dasseti, iddhiyā abhisaṅkharitvā nivāsananivatthaṃ kāyabandhanabaddhaṃ cīvarapārutaṃ chāyārūpakamattaṃ dasseti, mahārājāti. Chāyārūpe diṭṭhe sati diṭṭho eva nanu, bhanteti. Tiṭṭhatetaṃ, mahārāja, hadayarūpaṃ disvā bujjhanakasatto bhaveyya, hadayamaṃsaṃ nīharitvā dasseyya sammāsambuddhoti. Kallosi, bhante, nāgasenā”ti (mi. pa. 4.3.3).

‘Venerable Nāgasena, what the Blessed One did was difficult.’ ‘What is it, great king?’ ‘He showed an occasion for shame to the great multitude, to the brahmin Brahmāyu and his disciple Uttara, to the sixteen brahmin disciples of Bāvarī, and to the three hundred pupils of the brahmin Sela, venerable sir.’ ‘No, great king, the Blessed One does not show what is hidden. The Blessed One shows a shadow. Having created it by psychic power, he shows a mere shadow-like form, wearing the under-robe and girdle, and covered with the outer robe, great king.’ ‘When a shadow-like form is seen, is it not truly seen, venerable sir?’ ‘Let that be, great king. If a being could be awakened by seeing the heart’s form, the Perfectly Enlightened One could show it by drawing out the heart’s flesh.’ ‘You are skilled, venerable Nāgasena.’ (Miln. 4.3.3).

Ninnāmetvāti nīharitvā. Kaṇṇasotānumasanena cettha dīghabhāvo, nāsikāsotānumasanena tanubhāvo, nalāṭacchādanena puthulabhāvo pakāsitoti veditabbo. Ācariyapācariyānanti ācariyānañceva ācariyācariyānañca. Sake vaṇṇeti attano guṇe.

‘Ninnāmetvā’ means having drawn out. Here, the length is to be understood as indicated by the touching of the ear-opening, the slenderness by the touching of the nose-opening, and the breadth by the covering of the forehead. ‘Ācariyapācariyānaṃ’ means of both teachers and the teachers of teachers. ‘Sake vaṇṇe’ means one’s own qualities.

554. Paripuṇṇakāyoti lakkhaṇehi paripuṇṇatāya ahīnaṅgapaccaṅgatāya ca paripuṇṇasarīro[P 2.0453]. Surucīti sundarasarīrappabho. Sujātoti ārohapariṇāhasampattiyā saṇṭhānasampattiyā ca sunibbatto. Cārudassanoti sucirampi passantānaṃ atittijanakaṃ appaṭikūlaṃ ramaṇīyaṃ cāru eva dassanaṃ assāti cārudassano. Keci pana bhaṇanti “cārudassanoti [V 2.0157] sundaranetto”ti. Suvaṇṇavaṇṇoti suvaṇṇasadisavaṇṇo. Asīti bhavasi. Etaṃ sabbapadehi yojetabbaṃ. Susukkadāṭhoti suṭṭhu sukkadāṭho. Bhagavato hi dāṭhāhi candakiraṇā viya ativiya paṇḍararaṃsiyo niccharanti. Tenāha – “susukkadāṭhosī”ti.

554. ‘Paripuṇṇakāya’ means complete in body due to the perfection of the characteristics and not lacking any major or minor limbs. ‘Surucī’ means having a beautiful bodily radiance. ‘Sujāta’ means well-formed due to the accomplishment of height and girth, and the accomplishment of shape. ‘Cārudassana’ means having a pleasing appearance, not repulsive, delightful, and charming to behold, even for those who look for a long time, causing no satiety. Some, however, say, ‘Cārudassana’ means having beautiful eyes. ‘Suvaṇṇavaṇṇa’ means having a color like gold. ‘Asi’ means ‘you are.’ This should be connected with all the terms. ‘Susukkadāṭha’ means having very white teeth. Indeed, from the Blessed One’s teeth, exceedingly bright and white rays emanate, like moonbeams. Therefore it is said, ‘You have very white teeth.’

555. Mahāpurisalakkhaṇāti pubbe vuttabyañjanāneva vacanantarena nigamento āha.

555. ‘Mahāpurisalakkhaṇāni’ refers to the previously mentioned minor marks, which he now summarizes with a different expression.

556. Idāni [M 2.0174] tesu lakkhaṇesu attano abhirucitehi lakkhaṇehi bhagavantaṃ thunanto āha – “pasannanetto”tiādi. Bhagavā hi pañcavaṇṇapasādasampattiyā pasannanetto, paripuṇṇacandamaṇḍalasadisamukhattā sumukho, ārohapariṇāhasampattiyā brahā, bahmujugattatāya uju, jutimantatāya patāpavā. Yampi cettha pubbe vuttaṃ, taṃ “majjhe samaṇasaṅghassā”ti iminā pariyāyena thunatā puna vuttaṃ. Īdiso hi evaṃ virocati. Esa nayo uttaragāthāyapi.

556. Now, praising the Blessed One with the marks that appeal to him, he says: ‘with serene eyes,’ and so on. Indeed, the Blessed One has serene eyes due to the perfection of the five-hued clarity, a beautiful face like a full moon, is majestic due to the accomplishment of height and girth, upright due to a very straight body, and radiant due to brilliance. What was previously stated here is now praised again with the phrase: ‘in the midst of the Sangha of ascetics.’ Indeed, such a one shines forth in this way. This same method applies to the following verse as well.

557-8. Uttamavaṇṇinoti uttamavaṇṇasampannassa. Jambusaṇḍassāti jambudīpassa. Pākaṭena issariyaṃ vaṇṇayanto āha, apica cakkavatti catunnampi dīpānaṃ issaro hoti.

557-8. ‘Uttamavaṇṇin’ means one endowed with supreme complexion. ‘Jambusaṇḍassa’ refers to Jambudīpa. Describing manifest sovereignty, he says, ‘Moreover, a wheel-turning monarch is the ruler of all four continents.’

559. Khattiyāti jātikhattiyā. Bhojāti bhogiyā. Rājānoti ye keci rajjaṃ kārentā. Anuyantāti anugāmino sevakā. Rājābhirājāti rājūnaṃ pūjaniyo rājā hutvā, cakkavattīti adhippāyo. Manujindoti manussādhipati paramissaro hutvā.

559. ‘Khattiyā’ means those of the warrior caste by birth. ‘Bhojā’ means those who possess wealth. ‘Rājāno’ refers to any who exercise kingship. ‘Anuyantā’ means followers and servants. ‘Rājābhirājā’ means a king worthy of homage among kings, implying a wheel-turning monarch. ‘Manujinda’ means the overlord and supreme ruler of men.

560. Evaṃ vutte bhagavā “ye te bhavanti arahanto sammāsambuddhā, te sake vaṇṇe bhaññamāne attānaṃ pātukarontī”ti imaṃ selassa manorathaṃ pūrento āha “rājāhamasmī”ti. Tatrāyamadhippāyo – yaṃ kho maṃ tvaṃ sela yācasi “rājā arahasi bhavituṃ cakkavattī”ti, ettha appossukko hoti, rājāhamasmi, sati ca rājatte yathā añño rājā samānopi yojanasataṃ vā anusāsati, dve tīṇi vā cattāri vā pañca vā yojanasatāni yojanasahassaṃ vā cakkavatti hutvāpi [P 2.0454] catudīpapariyantamattaṃ vā, nāhamevaṃ paricchinnavisayo. Ahañhi dhammarājā anuttaro bhavaggato avīcipariyantaṃ katvā tiriyaṃ appameyyā lokadhātuyo anusāsāmi. Yāvatā hi apadadvipadādibhedā sattā, ahaṃ tesaṃ aggo. Na hi me koci sīlena vā…pe… vimuttiñāṇadassanena vā paṭibhāgo atthi. Svāhaṃ evaṃ dhammarājā anuttaro anuttareneva catusatipaṭṭhānādibhedabodhipakkhiyasaṅkhātena dhammena cakkaṃ vattemi “idaṃ pajahatha, idaṃ upasampajja viharathā”tiādinā āṇācakkaṃ, “idaṃ kho pana, bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ ariyasacca”ntiādinā [V 2.0158] (saṃ. ni. 5.1081; mahāva. 14) pariyattidhammena dhammacakkameva vā. Cakkaṃ appaṭivattiyanti [M 2.0175] yaṃ cakkaṃ appaṭivattiyaṃ hoti samaṇena vā…pe… kenaci lokasminti.

560. When this was said, the Blessed One, fulfilling Sela’s wish by declaring, ‘Those who are Arahants, Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones, reveal themselves when their own virtues are praised,’ said, ‘I am a king.’ Here is the meaning: ‘Sela, as for when you request, “You deserve to be a wheel-turning king,” in this matter, be without concern—I am a king. Whereas another king, even if equal, might rule over a hundred leagues, or two, three, four, or five hundred leagues, or even a thousand leagues, and a wheel-turning monarch, even having become one, might rule only to the extent of the four continents, my domain is not so limited. For I am the Dhamma King, unsurpassed, having made the space from the highest realm of existence down to Avīci the limit, I teach throughout immeasurable world-systems in all directions. Indeed, as far as beings extend, with their divisions into footless, two-footed, and so on, I am their foremost. Indeed, no one is my equal in virtue… or in the knowledge and vision of liberation. Thus, I, the supreme Dhamma King, turn the wheel with the unsurpassed Dhamma consisting of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, beginning with the four foundations of mindfulness, commanding, “Abandon this, attain this, and dwell thus,” which is the wheel of command, and also the wheel of the teaching with the textual Dhamma, “This, monks, is the noble truth of suffering,” and so on. ‘The wheel that cannot be turned back’ means the wheel that cannot be turned back by any ascetic… or anyone in the world.

561-2. Evaṃ attānaṃ āvikarontaṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā pītisomanassajāto selo daḷhikaraṇatthaṃ “sambuddho paṭijānāsī”ti gāthādvayamāha. Tattha ko nu senāpatīti dhammarañño bhoto, dhammena pavattitassa dhammacakkassa anuppavattako senāpati koti pucchi.

561-2. Seeing the Blessed One thus revealing himself, Sela, filled with joy and gladness, spoke two verses to strengthen his conviction, beginning, ‘Do you claim to be the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One?’ Here, ‘Who then is your commander?’ asks who the commander of the Dhamma King might be—the one who continues the turning of the wheel of Dhamma, which is set in motion by Dhamma.

563. Tena ca samayena bhagavato dakkhiṇapasse āyasmā sāriputto nisinno hoti suvaṇṇapuñjo viya siriyā sobhamāno, taṃ dassento bhagavā “mayā pavattita”nti gāthamāha. Tattha anujāto tathāgatanti tathāgatahetu anujāto, tathāgatena hetunā jātoti attho.

563. At that time, the Venerable Sāriputta was seated on the Blessed One’s right side, gleaming with glory like a heap of gold. Pointing to him, the Blessed One spoke the verse beginning, 'Set in motion by me.' Here, 'born after the Tathāgata' means born because of the Tathāgata; that is, born by the cause of the Tathāgata.

564. Evaṃ “ko nu senāpatī”ti pañhaṃ byākaritvā yaṃ selo āha – “sambuddho paṭijānāsī”ti, tatra naṃ nikkaṅkhaṃ kātukāmo “nāhaṃ paṭiññāmatteneva paṭijānāmi, apicāhaṃ iminā kāraṇena buddho”ti ñāpetuṃ “abhiññeyya”nti gāthamāha. Tattha abhiññeyyanti vijjā ca vimutti ca. Maggasaccasamudayasaccāni pana bhāvetabbapahātabbāni, hetuvacanena pana phalasiddhito tesaṃ phalāni nirodhasaccadukkhasaccānipi vuttāneva bhavanti. Yato sacchikātabbaṃ sacchikataṃ, pariññeyyaṃ pariññātanti evampettha vuttameva hoti. Evaṃ [P 2.0455] catusaccabhāvanāphalañca vijjāvimuttiṃ dassento “bujjhitabbaṃ bujjhitvā buddho jātosmī”ti yuttena hetunā buddhattaṃ sādheti.

564. Having thus answered the question, ‘Who then is your commander?’, when Sela said, ‘Do you claim to be the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One?’, the Blessed One, wishing to remove his doubt, declared, ‘I do not claim merely by assertion, but because of this reason I am a Buddha,’ and spoke the verse beginning with ‘What should be directly known.’ Here, ‘what should be directly known’ refers to knowledge and liberation. The truths of the path and the origin, however, are to be developed and abandoned. By the statement of the cause, their fruits—the truths of cessation and suffering—are also said to be established. Since what should be realized has been realized, and what should be fully understood has been fully understood, it is stated thus. In this way, showing both the fruit of the development of the four truths and knowledge-liberation, he establishes his Buddhahood with the fitting reason: ‘Having awakened to what should be awakened, I have become the Buddha.’

565-7. Evaṃ nippariyāyena attānaṃ pātukatvā attani kaṅkhāvitaraṇatthaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ abhittharayamāno “vinayassū”ti gāthāttayamāha. Tattha sallakattoti rāgasallādisattasallakattano. Brahmabhūtoti seṭṭhabhūto. Atituloti tulaṃ atīto upamaṃ atīto, nirūpamoti attho. Mārasenappamaddanoti “kāmā te paṭhamā senā”tiādikāya “pare ca avajānātī”ti (su. ni. 440; mahāni. 28; cūḷani. nandamāṇavapucchāniddesa 47) evaṃ vuttāya māraparisasaṅkhātāya mārasenāya [M 2.0176] pamaddano. Sabbāmitteti khandhakilesābhisaṅkhāramaccudevaputtamārādike sabbapaccatthike. Vasīkatvāti attano vase vattetvā. Akutobhayoti kutoci abhayo.

565-7. Having thus revealed himself directly, to dispel doubt about himself and to urge the brahmin, he spoke three verses beginning, 'Dispel your doubt...'. Here, 'the dart-puller' is the remover of the seven darts, such as the dart of lust. 'Brahmā-become' means become the best. 'Beyond compare' means beyond measure, beyond comparison—that is, incomparable. 'The crusher of Māra’s army' refers to the crushing of Māra’s host, described as 'sensual pleasures are your first army' and so forth, up to 'and despises others.' 'All enemies' refers to all adversaries, such as the aggregates, defilements, volitional formations, the god of death, and Māra, the son of a god. 'Having mastered' means having brought under his control. 'Fearless from any quarter' means fearless from anywhere.

568-70. Evaṃ vutte selo brāhmaṇo tāvadeva bhagavati sañjātappasādo pabbajjāpekkho [V 2.0159] hutvā “imaṃ bhavanto”ti gāthāttayamāha yathā taṃ paripākagatāya upanissayasampattiyā sammā codiyamāno. Tattha kaṇhābhijātikoti caṇḍālādinīcakule jāto.

568-70. When this was said, the brahmin Sela immediately gained confidence in the Blessed One and, aspiring to go forth, spoke three verses beginning with 'Let the venerable ones hear this,' as one rightly admonished, his supporting conditions having reached maturity. Here, 'born of the dark lineage' means born in a low family, such as that of outcastes and the like.

571. Tato tepi māṇavakā tatheva pabbajjāpekkhā hutvā “etañce ruccati bhoto”ti gāthamāhaṃsu yathā taṃ tena saddhiṃ katādhikārā kulaputtā.

571. Then those young men also, aspiring to ordination in the same way, spoke the verse beginning, 'If this is pleasing to you, sir,' like the noble youths who had made an aspiration with him.

572. Atha selo tesu māṇavakesu tuṭṭhacitto te dassento pabbajjaṃ yācamāno “brāhmaṇā”ti gāthamāha.

572. Then Sela, pleased with those young men, pointed them out and, requesting ordination, spoke the verse beginning 'Brahmins...'

573.
