Tato bhagavā yasmā selo atīte padumuttarassa bhagavato sāsane tesaṃyeva tiṇṇaṃ purisasatānaṃ gaṇaseṭṭho hutvā tehi saddhiṃ pariveṇaṃ kārāpetvā dānādīni puññāni ca katvā kamena devamanussasampattiṃ anubhavamāno pacchime bhave tesaṃyeva ācariyo hutvā nibbatto, tañca nesaṃ kammaṃ vimuttiparipākāya paripakkaṃ ehibhikkhubhāvassa [P 2.0456] ca upanissayabhūtaṃ, tasmā te sabbeva ehibhikkhupabbajjāya pabbājento “svākkhāta”nti gāthamāha. Tattha sandiṭṭhikanti paccakkhaṃ. Akālikanti maggānantaraphaluppattito na kālantare pattabbaphalaṃ. Yatthāti yannimittā. Maggabrahmacariyanimittā hi pabbajjā appamattassa sativippavāsavirahitassa tīsu sikkhāsu sikkhato amoghā hoti. Tenāha – “svākkhātaṃ…pe… sikkhato”ti.

573. Then, because in a past life, during the dispensation of the Blessed One Padumuttara, Sela had been the chief of a group of those same three hundred men, and together with them had a monastery built and performed meritorious deeds such as giving, in due course experiencing the prosperity of devas and humans, and in his last existence was reborn as their teacher; and because that deed of theirs had ripened towards liberation and had become a supporting condition for the 'Come, bhikkhu' status, therefore, while ordaining them all with the 'Come, bhikkhu' ordination, the Blessed One spoke the verse beginning with 'Well-proclaimed.' Herein, 'directly visible' means immediately evident. 'Timeless' means that since the fruit arises immediately after the path, it is not a fruit to be obtained after some time. 'Wherein' means for what reason. For the going forth, which is for the sake of the holy life of the path, is not in vain for one who is diligent, free from any lapse in mindfulness, and trains in the three trainings. Therefore, it is said: 'Well-proclaimed... for one who trains.'

Evañca vatvā “etha bhikkhavo”ti bhagavā avoca. Te sabbe pattacīvaradharā hutvā ākāsenāgamma bhagavantaṃ abhivādesuṃ. Evamimaṃ tesaṃ ehibhikkhubhāvaṃ sandhāya saṅgītikārā “alattha kho selo…pe… upasampada”nti āhaṃsu.

And having spoken thus, the Blessed One said, 'Come, bhikkhus.' They all, bearing bowl and robe, came through the air and paid homage to the Blessed One. With reference to this 'Come, bhikkhu' state of theirs, the compilers of the canon said: 'Sela indeed attained... the higher ordination.'

Bhuttāvinti [M 2.0177] bhuttavantaṃ. Onītapattapāṇinti pattato onītapāṇiṃ, apanītahatthanti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha “upagantvā”ti pāṭhaseso daṭṭhabbo. Itarathā hi bhagavantaṃ ekamantaṃ nisīdīti na yujjati.

'Having eaten' means one who has finished eating. 'With hand withdrawn from the bowl' means the hand is withdrawn from the bowl; that is to say, the hand is removed. Herein, 'having approached' should be understood as completing the text. Otherwise, 'he sat down to one side of the Blessed One' would not be grammatically sound.

574. Aggihuttamukhāti bhagavā keṇiyassa cittānukūlavasena anumodanto evamāha. Tattha aggiparicariyaṃ vinā brāhmaṇānaṃ yaññābhāvato “aggihuttamukhā yaññā”ti vuttaṃ. Aggihuttaseṭṭhā [V 2.0160] aggihuttapadhānāti attho. Vede sajjhāyantehi paṭhamaṃ sajjhāyitabbato sāvittī “chandaso mukha”nti vuttā. Manussānaṃ seṭṭhato rājā “mukha”nti vutto. Nadīnaṃ ādhārato paṭisaraṇato ca sāgaro “mukha”nti vutto. Candayogavasena “ajja kattikā ajja rohinī”ti sañjānanato ālokakaraṇato sommabhāvato ca “nakkhattānaṃ mukhaṃ cando”ti vutto. Tapantānaṃ aggattā ādicco “tapataṃ mukha”nti vutto. Dakkhiṇeyyānaṃ pana aggattā visesena tasmiṃ samaye buddhappamukhaṃ saṅghaṃ sandhāya “puññaṃ ākaṅkhamānānaṃ, saṅgho ve yajataṃ mukha”nti vutto. Tena saṅgho puññassa āyamukhanti dasseti.

574. 'The fire oblation is the chief of sacrifices'—the Blessed One, expressing appreciation in accordance with Keṇiya's mind, spoke thus. Herein, because brahmins have no sacrifice without fire worship, it is said, 'the fire oblation is the chief of sacrifices.' The meaning is: the fire oblation is the best, the fire oblation is the principal. Because the Sāvitrī is to be recited first by those who recite the Vedas, it is called 'the mouth of the Vedic hymns.' Among humans, the king is called 'the chief' because he is the best. Of rivers, the ocean is called 'the mouth' because it is their repository and refuge. Because by conjunction with the moon one recognizes, 'Today is Kattikā, today is Rohiṇī,' and because it gives light and is gentle, it is said, 'the moon is the mouth of the constellations.' Because the sun is the chief of those that give heat, it is said, 'the sun is the mouth of things that give heat.' But among those worthy of offerings, because the Sangha headed by the Buddha is especially pre-eminent at that time, it is said, 'for those who desire merit, the Sangha is indeed the mouth for those making offerings.' Thus, it shows that the Sangha is the source of the arising of merit.

576. Yaṃ taṃ saraṇanti aññabyākaraṇagāthamāha. Tassattho [P 2.0457] – pañcahi cakkhūhi cakkhumā bhagavā, yasmā mayaṃ ito aṭṭhame divase taṃ saraṇaṃ agamamha, tasmā sattarattena tava sāsane anuttarena damathena dantamha. Aho te saraṇassa ānubhāvoti.

576. He spoke the verse declaring the attainment of final knowledge, beginning 'That refuge.' Its meaning is: O Blessed One, possessor of the five eyes, you are the one with the Eye. Since we went for refuge to you a week ago, we have, in seven nights, been tamed by the unsurpassed taming in your dispensation. Ah, the power of your refuge!

577-8. Tato paraṃ bhagavantaṃ dvīhi gāthāhi thunitvā tatiyāya vandanaṃ yācati –

Then, after praising the Blessed One with two verses, with a third he requests to pay homage:

579.

579.

“Bhikkhavo tisatā ime, tiṭṭhanti pañjalīkatā;

Pāde vīra pasārehi, nāgā vandantu satthuno”ti.

'These three hundred bhikkhus stand with hands held in reverence. O Hero, extend your feet; let these noble ones pay homage to the Teacher.'

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

From the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya.

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya selasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Here ends the explanation of the Sela Sutta in the Commentary on the Suttanipāta.

8. Sallasuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Explanation of the Salla Sutta

580. Animittanti [V 2.0161][M 2.0178] sallasuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Bhagavato kira upaṭṭhāko eko upāsako, tassa putto kālamakāsi. So puttasokābhibhūto sattāhaṃ nirāhāro ahosi. Taṃ anukampanto bhagavā tassa gharaṃ gantvā sokavinodanatthaṃ imaṃ suttamabhāsi.

580. The Salla Sutta begins with the word 'Animittaṃ' (Without a sign). What is its origin? It is said that a certain lay follower, an attendant of the Blessed One, had a son who passed away. Overcome by grief for his son, he went without food for seven days. Out of compassion for him, the Blessed One went to his house and spoke this sutta to dispel his sorrow.

Tattha animattanti kiriyākāranimittavirahitaṃ. Yathā hi “yadāhaṃ akkhiṃ vā nikhaṇissāmi, bhamukaṃ vā ukkhipissāmi, tena nimittena taṃ bhaṇḍaṃ avaharā”tiādīsu kiriyākāranimittamatthi, na evaṃ jīvite. Na hi sakkā laddhuṃ “yāvāhaṃ idaṃ vā idaṃ vā karomi, tāva tvaṃ jīva, mā mīyā”ti. Anaññātanti ato eva na sakkā ekaṃsena aññātuṃ “ettakaṃ vā ettakaṃ vā kālaṃ iminā jīvitabba”nti gatiyā āyupariyantavasena vā. Yathā hi cātumahārājikādīnaṃ parimitaṃ āyu, na tathā maccānaṃ, evampi ekaṃsena anaññātaṃ.

Herein, 'without a sign' means devoid of any sign of its process or cause. For example, in cases like, 'When I wink my eye or raise my eyebrow, by that sign you should steal the goods,' there is a sign that is a cause for action, but it is not so with life. For it is not possible to arrange, 'As long as I do this or that, you must live and not die.' 'Unknown' means that for this very reason it is not possible to know for certain, 'One must live for such and such a length of time,' either in terms of one's future destination or the limit of one's lifespan. For just as the lifespan of the devas of the Four Great Kings and so on is fixed, it is not so for mortals; in this way too it is entirely unknown.

Kasiranti anekapaccayapaṭibaddhavuttibhāvato kicchaṃ na sukhayāpanīyaṃ. Tathā hi taṃ assāsapaṭibaddhañca, passāsapaṭibaddhañca, mahābhūtapaṭibaddhañca, kabaḷīkārāhārapaṭibaddhañca, usmāpaṭibaddhañca, viññāṇapaṭibaddhañca. Anassasantopi hi na jīvati apassasantopi. Catūsu ca dhātūsu kaṭṭhamukhādiāsīvisadaṭṭho [P 2.0458] viya kāyo pathavīdhātuppakopena tāva thaddho hoti kaliṅgarasadiso. Yathāha –

'Precarious' means difficult and not easily maintained, because its subsistence is dependent on many conditions. For it is dependent on the in-breath, the out-breath, the great elements, physical food, heat, and consciousness. For one who does not breathe in does not live, nor one who does not breathe out. And among the four elements, when the earth element is disturbed, the body, like one bitten by a Kaṭṭhamukha or other venomous snake, becomes stiff, like a log. As it is said:

“Patthaddho bhavatī kāyo, daṭṭho kaṭṭhamukhena vā;

Pathavīdhātuppakopena, hoti kaṭṭhamukheva so”ti. (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 584);

"The body becomes rigid, as if bitten by a Kaṭṭhamukha snake; due to the disturbance of the earth element, it becomes just like wood."

Āpodhātuppakopena pūtibhāvaṃ āpajjitvā paggharitapubbamaṃsalohito aṭṭhicammāvaseso hoti. Yathāha –

Due to a disturbance of the water element, the body becomes putrid, with pus, flesh, and blood flowing out, until only bones and skin remain. As it is said:

“Pūtiko [V 2.0162] bhavatī kāyo, daṭṭho pūtimukhena vā;

Āpodhātuppakopena, hoti pūtimukheva so”ti. (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 584);

"The body becomes putrid, as if bitten by a Pūtimukha snake; due to the disturbance of the water element, it itself becomes putrid."

Tejodhātuppakopena aṅgārakāsuyaṃ pakkhitto viya samantā pariḍayhati. Yathāha –

Due to a disturbance of the fire element, it burns all around as if thrown into a pit of embers. As it is said:

“Santatto [M 2.0179] bhavatī kāyo, daṭṭho aggimukhena vā;

Tejodhātuppakopena, hoti aggimukheva so”ti. (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 584);

The body is fevered, as if bitten by a fiery mouth; through the disturbance of the fire element, it is just like a fiery mouth.

Vāyodhātuppakopena sañchijjamānasandhibandhano pāsāṇehi koṭṭetvā sañcuṇṇiyamānaṭṭhiko viya ca hoti. Yathāha –

When the wind element is disturbed, the ligaments of the joints are severed, and the bones are crushed as if pounded by stones. As it is said:

“Sañchinno bhavatī kāyo, daṭṭho satthamukhena vā;

Vāyodhātuppakopena, hoti satthamukheva so”ti. (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 584);

The body is cut apart, or struck by the edge of a sword; through the disturbance of the wind element, it is just like the edge of a sword.

Dhātuppakopabyāpannakāyopi ca na jīvati. Yadā pana tā dhātuyo aññamaññaṃ patiṭṭhānādikiccaṃ sādhentāpi samaṃ vahanti, tadā jīvitaṃ pavattati. Evaṃ mahābhūtapaṭibaddhañca jīvitaṃ. Dubbhikkhādīsu pana āhārupacchedena sattānaṃ jīvitakkhayo pākaṭo eva. Evaṃ kabaḷīkārāhārapaṭibaddhañca jīvitaṃ. Tathā asitapītādiparipāke kammajateje khīṇe sattā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇantāpi pākaṭā eva. Evaṃ usmāpaṭibaddhañca jīvitaṃ. Viññāṇe pana niruddhe niruddhato pabhuti sattānaṃ na hoti jīvitanti evampi loke pākaṭameva. Evaṃ viññāṇapaṭibaddhañca jīvitaṃ. Evaṃ anekapaccayapaṭibaddhavuttibhāvato kasiraṃ veditabbaṃ.

A body afflicted by the disturbance of the elements does not live. But when those elements, while performing their respective functions such as providing support, flow evenly, then life continues. Thus, life is dependent on the great elements. Moreover, in times of famine and the like, the end of life in beings due to the deprivation of food is clearly evident. Thus, life is dependent on edible food. Similarly, when the kamma-produced heat involved in the digestion of what is eaten and drunk is exhausted, beings clearly experience the end of life. Thus, life is dependent on heat. Furthermore, when consciousness ceases, from the moment of cessation onwards, beings no longer have life—this too is plainly evident in the world. Thus, life is dependent on consciousness. In this way, because its subsistence is dependent on many conditions, it should be understood as precarious.

Parittañcāti appakaṃ, devānaṃ jīvitaṃ upanidhāya tiṇagge ussāvabindusadisaṃ, cittakkhaṇato uddhaṃ abhāvena vā parittaṃ. Atidīghāyukopi hi satto atītena cittena jīvittha na jīvati na jīvissati, anāgatena [P 2.0459] jīvissati na jīvati na jīvittha, paccuppannena jīvati na jīvittha na jīvissati. Vuttañcetaṃ –

‘Brief’ means little; compared to the life of the gods, it is like a drop of dew on a blade of grass, or it is brief because of its non-existence after a mind-moment. For even a being with a very long lifespan has lived with the past mind, does not live with it now, and will not live with it in the future; will live with the future mind, does not live with it now, and has not lived with it in the past; lives with the present mind, has not lived with it in the past, and will not live with it in the future. And it was said:

“Jīvitaṃ attabhāvo ca, sukhadukkhā ca kevalā;

Ekacittasamāyuttā, lahuso vattate khaṇo.

Life and individuality, and all pleasure and pain, are bound to a single mind-moment; the moment passes swiftly.

“Cullāsītisahassāni[V 2.0163], kappā tiṭṭhanti ye marū;

Natveva tepi jīvanti, dvīhi cittehi saṃyutā”ti. (mahāni. 10);

For eighty-four thousand aeons do the Maras remain; yet even they do not live connected with two successive mind-moments.

Tañca dukkhena saṃyutanti tañca jīvitaṃ evaṃ animittamanaññātaṃ kasiraṃ parittañca samānampi sītuṇhaḍaṃsamakasādisamphassakhuppipāsāsaṅkhāradukkhavipariṇāmadukkhadukkhadukkhehi saṃyutaṃ. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yasmā īdisaṃ maccānaṃ jīvitaṃ, tasmā [M 2.0180] tvaṃ yāva taṃ parikkhayaṃ na gacchati, tāva dhammacariyameva brūhaya, mā puttamanusocāti.

And that life is bound up with suffering—thus, even though it is signless, unknown, precarious, and brief, it is still connected with the suffering of cold and heat, the touch of gadflies and mosquitoes, hunger and thirst, the suffering of formations, the suffering of change, and suffering-as-suffering. What is being said? Because such is the life of mortals, therefore, until it comes to its destruction, cultivate only the practice of the Dhamma. Do not grieve for your son.

581. Athāpi maññeyyāsi “sabbūpakaraṇehi puttaṃ anurakkhantassāpi me so mato, tena socāmī”ti, evampi mā soci. Na hi so upakkamo atthi, yena jātā na miyyare, na hi sakkā kenaci upakkamena jātā sattā mā marantūti rakkhitunti vuttaṃ hoti. Tato yasmā so “jaraṃ patvā nāma, bhante, maraṇaṃ anurūpaṃ, atidaharo me putto mato”ti cintesi, tasmā āha “jarampi patvā maraṇaṃ, evaṃdhammā hi pāṇino”ti, jaraṃ patvāpi appatvāpi maraṇaṃ, natthi ettha niyamoti vuttaṃ hoti.

581. And if you should think, ‘Even though I protected my son with all means, he still died, therefore I grieve,’ do not grieve even so. For there is no undertaking by which those who are born may not die. It is said that by no undertaking can born beings be protected so that they will not die. Therefore, since he thought, ‘Venerable sir, death is appropriate for one who has reached old age, but my son died very young,’ the Blessed One said: ‘Even having reached old age, there is death, for such is the nature of living beings.’ This means that whether having reached old age or not, death occurs; there is no fixed rule in this matter.

582. Idāni tamatthaṃ nidassanena sādhento “phalānamiva pakkāna”ntiādimāha. Tassattho – yathā phalānaṃ pakkānaṃ yasmā sūriyuggamanato pabhuti sūriyātapena santappamāne rukkhe pathaviraso ca āporaso ca pattato sākhaṃ sākhato khandhaṃ khandhato mūlanti evaṃ anukkamena mūlato pathavimeva pavisati, ogamanato pabhuti pana pathavito mūlaṃ mūlato khandhanti evaṃ anukkamena sākhāpattapallavādīni puna ārohati, evaṃ ārohanto ca paripākagate phale vaṇṭamūlaṃ na pavisati. Atha sūriyātapena tappamāne vaṇṭamūle pariḷāho uppajjati. Tena tāni phalāni pāto pāto niccakālaṃ patanti, nesaṃ pāto patanato bhayaṃ hoti, patanā bhayaṃ hotīti attho. Evaṃ jātānaṃ maccānaṃ niccaṃ maraṇato bhayaṃ[P 2.0460]. Pakkaphalasadisā hi sattāti.

582. Now, establishing that meaning with an example, he says, ‘Like ripe fruits...’ and so on. The meaning is this: Just as for ripe fruits, from the rising of the sun, when the tree is scorched by the sun's heat, the earth's essence and the water's essence, in sequence, pass from leaf to branch, from branch to trunk, from trunk to root, and thus from the root enter the very earth. But from sunset onward, they rise again from the earth to the root, from the root to the trunk, and so on in that order, ascending again to the branches, leaves, and shoots. Thus, when ascending, they do not enter the base of the stalk of a fruit that has reached full ripeness. Then, when the base of the stalk is scorched by the sun's heat, a burning arises. Because of this, those fruits fall constantly, every morning. For them there is fear from falling in the morning; the meaning is, there is fear of falling. Similarly, for beings who are born, there is constant fear from death. For beings are indeed like ripe fruits.

583-6. Kiñca bhiyyo “yathāpi kumbhakārassa…pe… jīvita”nti. Tasmā “daharā ca…pe… parāyaṇā”ti evaṃ gaṇha, evañca gahetvā “tesaṃ maccu…pe… ñātī vā pana ñātake”ti evampi gaṇha. Yasmā ca na pitā tāyate puttaṃ, ñātī vā pana ñātake, tasmā pekkhataṃyeva…pe… nīyati.

583-6. Furthermore, ‘Just as a potter’s... life...’ and so on. Therefore, grasp it thus: ‘Both young... bound for death.’ And having grasped it thus, also grasp: ‘Of them, death... nor relatives their kinsmen.’ And because a father does not protect a son, nor relatives their kinsmen, therefore even while relatives are watching... one is led away.

Tattha [V 2.0164] ayaṃ yojanā – passamānānaṃyeva ñātīnaṃ “amma, tātā”tiādinā nayena puthu anekappakārakaṃ lālapataṃyeva maccānaṃ ekameko [M 2.0181] macco yathā go vajjho evaṃ nīyati, evaṃ passa, upāsaka, yāva atāṇo lokoti.

Here is the explanation: Even while the relatives are looking on and lamenting profusely in many ways—‘Mother! Father!’ and so on—one by one, mortals are led away like a cow to the slaughter. See this, lay follower, how the world is without refuge.

587. Tattha ye buddhapaccekabuddhādayo dhitisampannā, te “evamabbhāhato loko maccunā ca jarāya ca, so na sakkā kenaci parittāṇaṃ kātu”nti yasmā jānanti, tasmā dhīrā na socanti viditvā lokapariyāyaṃ. Imaṃ lokasabhāvaṃ ñatvā na socantīti vuttaṃ hoti.

587. In this regard, those endowed with steadfastness—Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and others—know that ‘The world is thus afflicted by death and old age; it is not possible for anyone to provide protection.’ Therefore, the steadfast do not grieve, having understood the way of the world. This means that knowing this nature of the world, they do not grieve.

588. Tvaṃ pana yassa maggaṃ…pe… paridevasi. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yassa mātukucchiṃ āgatassa āgatamaggaṃ vā ito cavitvā aññattha gatassa gatamaggaṃ vā na jānāsi, tassa ime ubho ante asampassaṃ niratthaṃ paridevasi. Dhīrā pana te passantā viditvā lokapariyāyaṃ na socantīti.

588. But you lament for him whose path... and so on. What is being said? You do not know the path of his coming, when he came into his mother’s womb, nor the path of his going, when, having departed from here, he went elsewhere. Not seeing these two extremes, you lament uselessly. But the wise, seeing them and knowing the ways of the world, do not grieve.

589. Idāni “niratthaṃ paridevasī”ti ettha vuttaparidevanāya niratthakabhāvaṃ sādhento “paridevayamāno ce”tiādimāha. Tattha udabbaheti ubbaheyya dhāreyya, attani sañjaneyyāti attho. Sammūḷho hiṃsamattānanti sammūḷho hutvā attānaṃ bādhento. Kayirā ce naṃ vicakkhaṇoti yadi tādiso kañci atthaṃ udabbahe, vicakkhaṇopi naṃ paridevaṃ kareyya.

589. Now, to establish the futility of the lamentation mentioned as 'uselessly grieves,' he says, 'Even if one were to lament...' and so on. Here, 'udabbaheti' means to uphold, to bear, to produce within oneself. The meaning of 'sammūḷho hiṃsamattānaṃ' is 'being deluded and harming oneself.' 'Kayirā ce naṃ vicakkhaṇo' means if such a person were to attain any benefit, even a discerning one would lament over it.

590. Na hi ruṇṇenāti etthāyaṃ yojanā – na pana koci ruṇṇena vā sokena vā cetaso santiṃ pappoti, apica kho pana rodato socato ca bhiyyo assa uppajjate dukkhaṃ, sarīrañca dubbaṇṇiyādīhi upahaññatīti.

590. 'Not by weeping...' Here is the explanation: No one attains peace of mind by weeping or sorrowing. Moreover, for one who weeps and sorrows, suffering only increases, and the body is afflicted by ugliness and the like.

591. Na tena petāti tena paridevanena kālakatā na pālenti na yāpenti, na taṃ tesaṃ upakārāya hoti. Tasmā niratthā paridevanāti.

591. By that lamentation, the departed are neither protected nor maintained; it is of no benefit to them. Therefore, lamentation is futile.

592. Na kevalañca niratthā, anatthampi āvahati. Kasmā? Yasmā sokamappajahaṃ [P 2.0461] …pe… vasamanvagū. Tattha anutthunantoti anusocanto. Vasamanvagūti vasaṃ gato.

592. Not only is it futile, but it also brings harm. Why? Because, not abandoning sorrow… he is subservient to it. Here, anutthunanto means 'lamenting'. Vasamanvagūti means 'gone under its control'.

593. Evampi [M 2.0182] niratthakattaṃ anatthāvahattañca sokassa dassetvā idāni sokavinayatthaṃ ovadanto [V 2.0165] “aññepi passā”tiādimāha. Tattha gamineti gamike, paralokagamanasajje ṭhiteti vuttaṃ hoti. Phandantevidha pāṇinoti maraṇabhayena phandamāneyeva idha satte.

593. Having thus shown the futility and harmfulness of sorrow, now advising for the sake of sorrow's overcoming, he says, “See others too…”. Here, gamineti means 'going', meaning 'established in readiness to depart for the other world'. Phandantevidha pāṇinoti means 'beings here trembling with the fear of death'.

594. Yena yenāti yenākārena maññanti “dīghāyuko bhavissati, arogo bhavissatī”ti. Tato taṃ aññathāyeva hoti, so evaṃ maññito maratipi, rogīpi hoti. Etādiso ayaṃ vinābhāvo maññitappaccanīkena hoti, passa, upāsaka, lokasabhāvanti evamettha adhippāyayojanā veditabbā.

594. “In whatever way…” means in whatever manner they think, “He will live long, he will be free from disease,” it turns out quite otherwise. The one so thought of may die or become sick. Such is this state of separation, contrary to expectation. “See, lay follower, the nature of the world”—this is how the connection of meaning should be understood here.

596. Arahato sutvāti imaṃ evarūpaṃ arahato dhammadesanaṃ sutvā. Neso labbhā mayā itīti so peto “idāni mayā puna jīvatū”ti na labbhā iti parijānanto, vineyya paridevitanti vuttaṃ hoti.

596. “Having heard from the Arahant…” means having heard such a teaching of the Dhamma from an Arahant. Understanding, 'It is not possible for me to make that departed one live again,' one should remove lamentation; this is what is meant.

597. Kiñca bhiyyo – “yathā saraṇamādittaṃ…pe… dhaṃsaye”ti. Tattha dhīro dhitisampadāya, sapañño sābhāvikapaññāya, paṇḍito bāhusaccapaññāya, kusalo cintakajātikatāya veditabbo. Cintāmayasutamayabhāvanāmayapaññāhi vā yojetabbaṃ.

597. What more? “Just as a burning shelter… destroys.” Here, the wise one (dhīro) should be understood as possessing resolution; the sagacious one (sapañño), with innate wisdom; the learned one (paṇḍito), with wisdom from vast learning; the skillful one (kusalo), as being of a reflective nature. Or, it should be connected with wisdom born of thinking, wisdom born of learning, and wisdom born of development.

598-9. Na kevalañca sokameva, paridevaṃ…pe… sallamattano. Tattha pajappanti taṇhaṃ. Domanassanti cetasikadukkhaṃ. Abbaheti uddhare. Sallanti etameva tippakāraṃ dunnīharaṇaṭṭhena antovijjhanaṭṭhena ca sallaṃ. Pubbe vuttaṃ sattavidhaṃ rāgādisallaṃ vā. Etasmiñhi abbūḷhe salle abbūḷhasallo…pe… nibbutoti arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi. Tattha asitoti taṇhādiṭṭhīhi anissito. Pappuyyāti pāpuṇitvā. Sesaṃ idha ito pubbe vuttattā uttānatthameva, tasmā na vaṇṇitaṃ.

Not only sorrow, but lamentation… the dart of oneself. There, pajappanti means 'craving'. Domanassa means 'mental suffering'. Abbaheti means 'he would pull out'. Salla means this very dart, hard to extract because it pierces within. Or the previously mentioned seven kinds of darts, such as lust. For when this dart is removed, one is without the dart… extinguished—thus, the teaching was concluded with the pinnacle of arahantship. Here, asito means 'unattached to craving and views'. Pappuyya means 'having attained'. The rest here, having been stated before, is of plain meaning; therefore, it is not elaborated upon.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

From the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya sallasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Salla Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary is concluded.

9. Vāseṭṭhasuttavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Vāseṭṭha Sutta

Evaṃ [V 2.0166][M 2.0183][P 2.0462] me sutanti vāseṭṭhasuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Ayameva yāssa nidāne vuttā atthavaṇṇanaṃ panassa vuttanayāni uttānatthāni ca padāni pariharantā karissāma. Icchānaṅgaloti gāmassa nāmaṃ. Brāhmaṇamahāsālānaṃ caṅkī tārukkho todeyyoti vohāranāmametaṃ. Pokkharasāti jāṇussoṇīti nemittikaṃ. Tesu kira eko himavantapasse pokkharaṇiyā padume nibbatto, aññataro tāpaso taṃ padumaṃ gahetvā tattha sayitaṃ dārakaṃ disvā saṃvaḍḍhetvā rañño dassesi. Pokkhare sayitattā “pokkharasātī”ti cassa nāmamakāsi. Ekassa ṭhānantare nemittikaṃ. Tena kira jāṇussoṇināmakaṃ purohitaṭṭhānaṃ laddhaṃ, so teneva paññāyi.

“Thus have I heard”—this is the Vāseṭṭha Sutta. What is its origin? It is this very one, whose occasion has been stated. We shall now provide the explanation of its meaning, preserving the stated methods and the words of plain meaning. Icchānaṅgala was the name of a village. Caṅkī, Tārukkha, and Todeyya were the designation names of great brahmin householders. Pokkharasāti and Jāṇussoṇī were names based on a characteristic sign. Among them, it is said, one was born from a lotus in a pond on the slopes of the Himalayas. A certain ascetic, after plucking the lotus, saw the child lying there, raised him, and presented him to the king. Because he was found lying on a lotus (pokkhara), he gave him the name “Pokkharasāti.” For another, the name was based on a characteristic sign in a different instance. It is said that he obtained the position of royal chaplain under the name Jāṇussoṇī, and thus he became known.

Te sabbepi aññe ca abhiññātā abhiññātā brāhmaṇamahāsālā kasmā icchānaṅgale paṭivasantīti? Vedasajjhāyanaparivīmaṃsanatthaṃ. Tena kira samayena kosalajanapade vedakā brāhmaṇā vedānaṃ sajjhāyakaraṇatthañca atthūpaparikkhaṇatthañca tasmiṃyeva gāme sannipatanti. Tena tepi antarantarā attano bhogagāmato āgamma tattha paṭivasanti.

Why do all those and other well-known and distinguished great brahmin householders dwell at Icchānaṅgala? For the purpose of reciting and examining the Vedas. At that time, it is said, in the Kosala country, brahmins who knew the Vedas would gather in that very village for the purpose of reciting the Vedas and investigating their meaning. Therefore, they too, from time to time, would come from their own wealthy villages and dwell there.

Vāseṭṭhabhāradvājānanti vāseṭṭhassa ca bhāradvājassa ca. Ayamantarākathāti yaṃ attano sahāyakabhāvānurūpaṃ kathaṃ kathentā anuvicariṃsu, tassā kathāya antarā vemajjheyeva ayaṃ aññā kathā udapādīti vuttaṃ hoti. Saṃsuddhagahaṇikoti saṃsuddhakucchiko, saṃsuddhāya brāhmaṇiyā eva kucchismiṃ nibbattoti adhippāyo. “Samavepākiniyā gahaṇiyā”tiādīsu hi udaraggi “gahaṇī”ti vuccati. Idha pana mātukucchi. Yāva sattamāti mātu mātā, pitu pitāti evaṃ paṭilomena yāva satta jātiyo. Ettha ca pitāmaho ca pitāmahī ca pitāmahā, tathā mātāmaho ca mātāmahī ca mātāmahā, pitāmahā ca mātāmahā [P 2.0463] ca pitāmahāyeva. Pitāmahānaṃ yugaṃ pitāmahayugaṃ. Yuganti āyuppamāṇaṃ. Abhilāpamattameva cetaṃ, atthato pana pitāmahāyeva pitāmahayugaṃ. Akkhittoti jātiṃ ārabbha “kiṃ so”ti kenaci anavaññāto[M 2.0184]. Anupakkuṭṭhoti jātisandosavādena anupakkuṭṭhapubbo. Vatasampannoti ācārasampanno. Saññāpetunti ñāpetuṃ bodhetuṃ, nirantaraṃ kātunti vuttaṃ hoti. Āyāmāti gacchāma.

Vāseṭṭhabhāradvājānaṃ means of Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja. “This intermediate discussion” means it is said that while they were conversing in a manner befitting their friendly association, this other discussion arose in the middle of their conversation. Saṃsuddhagahaṇiko means 'born from a pure womb', meaning 'born in the womb of a pure brahmin woman'. For in phrases like “from a woman with equal digestion,” the term gahaṇī refers to the digestive fire. Here, however, it means the mother’s womb. “Up to the seventh” means the mother’s mother, the father’s father, and so on, backwards up to seven generations. Here, the paternal grandfather and grandmother are referred to as grandfathers; similarly, the maternal grandfather and grandmother are referred to as grandfathers. The paternal grandfathers and maternal grandfathers are simply grandfathers. The generation of grandfathers is the grandfather-generation. Yuga here means a lifespan. But this is merely a figure of speech; in reality, the grandfather-generation is simply the grandfathers. Akkhitto means 'unblemished', meaning 'not disparaged by anyone regarding birth, as in “What is he?”'. Anupakkuṭṭho means 'unreproached', meaning 'never before reproached with criticism of lineage'. Vatasampanno means 'endowed with observances', meaning 'one accomplished in conduct'. Saññāpetuṃ means 'to convince', meaning 'to make known, to enlighten; it means to do so uninterruptedly'. Āyāma means 'let us go'.

600. Anuññātapaṭiññātāti [V 2.0167] “tevijjā tumhe”ti evaṃ mayaṃ ācariyehi ca anuññātā attanā ca paṭijānimhāti attho. Asmāti bhavāma. Ubhoti dvepi janā. Ahaṃ pokkharasātissa, tārukkhassāyaṃ māṇavoti ahaṃ pokkharasātissa jeṭṭhantevāsī aggasisso, ayaṃ tārukkhassāti adhippāyena bhaṇati ācariyasampattiṃ attano sampattiñca dīpento.

600. Anuññātapaṭiññātā means “We have been acknowledged and have assented,” meaning “we are the threefold knowers” according to our teachers and ourselves. Asma means “we are.” Ubho refers to both people. “I am Pokkharasāti’s, and this young man is Tārukkha’s” means “I am Pokkharasāti’s foremost senior disciple, and this is Tārukkha’s,” thus speaking, he reveals the teacher’s accomplishment and his own accomplishment.

601. Tevijjānanti tivedānaṃ. Kevalinoti niṭṭhaṅgatā. Asmaseti amha bhavāma. Idāni taṃ kevalibhāvaṃ vitthārento āha – “padakasmā…pe… sādisā”ti. Tattha jappeti vede. Kammunāti dasavidhena kusalakammapathakammunā. Ayañhi pubbe sattavidhaṃ kāyavacīkammaṃ sandhāya “yato kho bho sīlavā hotī”ti āha. Tividhaṃ manokammaṃ sandhāya “vatasampanno”ti āha. Tena samannāgato hi ācārasampanno hoti.

601. Tevijjānaṃ means 'of the three Vedas'. Kevalino means 'one who has reached completion'. Asmase means “we are.” Now, elaborating on that state of being a kevalin, he says: “padakasmā… sādisā.” There, jappeti means 'he recites the Vedas'. Kammunā means 'by means of the tenfold wholesome course of action'. For earlier, referring to the sevenfold bodily and verbal action, he said, “yato kho bho sīlavā hotī.” And referring to the threefold mental action, he said, “vatasampanno.” For one endowed with that is accomplished in conduct.

602-5. Idāni taṃ vacanantarena dassento āha – “ahañca kammunā brūmī”ti. Khayātītanti ūnabhāvaṃ atītaṃ, paripuṇṇanti attho. Peccāti upagantvā. Namassantīti namo karonti. Cakkhuṃ loke samuppannanti avijjandhakāre loke, taṃ andhakāraṃ vidhamitvā lokassa diṭṭhadhammikādiatthasandassanena cakkhu hutvā samuppannaṃ.

Now, to show that meaning through another statement, he says: “And I declare by action.” Khayātītaṃ means 'having passed beyond deficiency', meaning 'complete'. Pecca means 'having approached'. Namassanti means 'they pay homage'. Cakkhuṃ loke samuppannaṃ means, in the world shrouded by the darkness of ignorance, having dispelled that darkness and having become an eye arisen in the world by revealing benefits both in this life and beyond.

606. Evaṃ abhitthavitvā vāseṭṭhena yācito bhagavā dvepi [P 2.0464] jane saṅgaṇhanto āha – “tesaṃ vo ahaṃ byakkhissa”ntiādi. Tattha byakkhissanti byākarissāmi. Anupubbanti tiṭṭhatu tāva brāhmaṇacintā, kīṭapaṭaṅgatiṇarukkhato pabhuti vo anupubbaṃ byakkhissanti evamettha adhippāyo veditabbo, evaṃ vitthārakathāya vinetabbā hi te māṇavakā. Jātivibhaṅganti jātivitthāraṃ. Aññamaññā hi jātiyoti tesaṃ tesañhi pāṇānaṃ jātiyo aññā aññā nānappakārāti attho.

606. Thus, having been praised and then entreated by Vāseṭṭha, the Blessed One, embracing both people, said, “I will explain to you,” and so on. Here, byakkhissaṃ means 'I will expound'. Anupubbaṃ means: “Let the brahmin’s thought stand for now; I will explain to you gradually, starting from insects, moths, grass, and trees”—this is the intended meaning here. For these young men should be guided by a detailed explanation. Jātivibhaṅga means 'the detailed exposition of birth'. “For the births are diverse” means the births of those beings are indeed diverse, of various kinds—this is the meaning.

607. Tato [M 2.0185] pāṇānaṃ jātivibhaṅge kathetabbe “tiṇarukkhepi jānāthā”ti anupādinnakānaṃ tāva kathetuṃ āraddho. Taṃ kimatthamiti ce? Upādinnesu sukhañāpanatthaṃ. Anupādinnesu hi jātibhede gahite upādinnesu so pākaṭataro hoti. Tattha tiṇāni nāma antopheggūni bahisārāni. Tasmā tālanāḷikerādayopi tiṇasaṅgahaṃ gacchanti. Rukkhā nāma bahipheggū antosārā. Tiṇāni ca rukkhā ca tiṇarukkhā. Te upayogabahuvacanena dassento āha – “tiṇarukkhepi jānāthā”ti. Na cāpi paṭijānareti “mayaṃ tiṇā, mayaṃ rukkhā”ti evampi na paṭijānanti. Liṅgaṃ jātimayanti apaṭijānantānampi ca tesaṃ jātimayameva saṇṭhānaṃ [V 2.0168] attano mūlabhūtatiṇādisadisameva hoti. Kiṃ kāraṇaṃ? Aññamaññā hi jātiyo, yasmā aññā tiṇajāti, aññā rukkhajāti; tiṇesupi aññā tālajāti, aññā nāḷikerajātīti evaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ.

607. Then, when the classification of births among beings was to be explained, he began by speaking of those not appropriated: “You know even grass and trees.” What is the purpose of this? To make the matter easily understood in the case of those that are appropriated. For when distinctions of birth among the unappropriated are grasped, those among the appropriated become clearer. Here, tiṇāni (grasses) refers to those with pith inside and sapwood outside. Thus, even palms and coconut trees fall under the category of grass. Rukkhā (trees) are those with sapwood outside and pith inside. Tiṇāni ca rukkhā ca (grasses and trees) are referred to collectively in the plural for usage, hence he says, “You know even grass and trees.” And they do not claim, “We are grass, we are trees”—they do not claim thus. “Their characteristics are born of their kind”—even though they do not claim anything, their forms are indeed born of their kind, resembling their root origins like grass and so on. Why is this? Because their kinds are diverse—one kind is grass, another kind is trees; among grasses, one kind is palms, another kind is coconut trees—this should be elaborated in detail.

Tena kiṃ dīpeti? Yaṃ jātivasena nānā hoti, taṃ attano paṭiññaṃ paresaṃ vā upadesaṃ vināpi aññajātito visesena gayhati. Yadi ca jātiyā brāhmaṇo bhaveyya, sopi attano paṭiññaṃ paresaṃ vā upadesaṃ vinā khattiyato vessasuddato vā visesena gayheyya, na ca gayhati, tasmā na jātiyā brāhmaṇoti. Parato pana “yathā etāsu jātīsū”ti imāya gāthāya etamatthaṃ vacībhedeneva āvikarissati.

What does this indicate? Whatever is diverse by birth is grasped as distinct from other kinds without any self-declaration or instruction by others. And if a brahmin were such by birth, he too would be grasped as distinct from a khattiya, a vessa, or a sudda without any self-declaration or instruction by others—but he is not so grasped. Therefore, a brahmin is not a brahmin by birth. Furthermore, with the verse “just as among these kinds,” he will reveal this meaning through a variety of expressions.

608. Evaṃ anupādinnesu jātibhedaṃ dassetvā upādinnesu taṃ dassento “tato kīṭe”ti evamādimāha. Tattha kīṭāti kimayo. Paṭaṅgāti [P 2.0465] paṭaṅgāyeva. Yāva kunthakipilliketi kunthakipillikaṃ pariyantaṃ katvāti attho.

608. Having thus shown the distinctions of birth among the unappropriated, he then shows them among the appropriated, saying, “Then the insects,” and so on. Here, kīṭā means worms. Paṭaṅgā are indeed moths. Yāva kunthakipilliketi means taking ants and termites as the limit—this is the meaning.

609. Khuddaketi kāḷakakaṇḍakādayo. Mahallaketi sasabiḷārādayo. Sabbe hi te anekavaṇṇā.

609. Khuddakā refers to black ants and the like. Mahallakā refers to rabbits, cats, and the like. All of them are of various colors.

610. Pādūdareti udarapāde, udaraṃyeva yesaṃ pādāti vuttaṃ hoti. Dīghapiṭṭhiketi sappānañhi sīsato yāva naṅguṭṭhā piṭṭhi eva hoti, tena te “dīghapiṭṭhikā”ti vuccanti. Tepi anekappakārā āsīvisādibhedena.

610. Pādūdarā means 'belly-footed'; that is to say, those for whom the belly itself is their feet. Dīghapiṭṭhikā refers to snakes, for their back extends from the head all the way to the tail; hence they are called 'long-backed'. These too are of many kinds, distinguished as venomous snakes and so on.

611. Odaketi [M 2.0186] udakamhi jāte. Macchāpi anekappakārā rohitamacchādibhedena.

611. “Odaka” refers to those born in water. Fish are also of many kinds, distinguished as the rohita fish and so on.

612. Pakkhīti sakuṇe. Te hi pakkhānaṃ atthitāya “pakkhī”ti vuccanti. Pattehi yantīti pattayānā. Vehāse gacchantīti vihaṅgamā. Tepi anekappakārā kākādibhedena.

612. “Pakkhī” means birds. They are called “pakkhī” because they possess wings. “Pattayānā” means those who travel by means of wings. “Vihaṅgamā” means those who go through the sky. They too are of many kinds, distinguished as crows and so forth.

613. Evaṃ thalajalākāsagocarānaṃ pāṇānaṃ jātibhedaṃ dassetvā idāni yenādhippāyena taṃ dassesi, taṃ āvikaronto “yathā etāsū”ti gāthamāha. Tassattho saṅkhepato pubbe vuttādhippāyavaṇṇanāvaseneva veditabbo.

613. Having thus shown the diversity of species among beings that dwell on land, in water, and in the sky, now, revealing the intention for which that was shown, he speaks the verse “yathā etāsū.” Its meaning should be understood briefly in accordance with the previously stated explanation of the intention.

614-6. Vitthārato [V 2.0169] panettha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ sayameva dassento “na kesehī”tiādimāha. Tatrāyaṃ yojanā – yaṃ vuttaṃ “natthi manussesu liṅgaṃ jātimayaṃ puthū”ti, taṃ evaṃ natthīti veditabbaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ, na kesehīti. Na hi “brāhmaṇānaṃ īdisā kesā honti, khattiyānaṃ īdisā”ti niyamo atthi yathā hatthiassamigādīnanti iminā nayena sabbaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Liṅgaṃ jātimayaṃ neva, yathā aññāsu jātisūti idaṃ pana vuttassevatthassa nigamananti veditabbaṃ. Tassa yojanā – tadeva yasmā imehi kesādīhi natthi manussesu liṅgaṃ jātimayaṃ puthu, tasmā veditabbametaṃ “brāhmaṇādibhedesu manussesu liṅgaṃ jātimayaṃ neva yathā aññāsu jātīsū”ti.

614-6. Here, elaborating further on what should be said, he states “na kesehī” and so on. The explanation is as follows: What was said—“among humans there are no various birth-based characteristics”—should be understood as being thus: For example, “not by hair.” For there is no rule that “Brahmins have such hair, Kshatriyas have such hair,” as is the case with elephants, horses, deer, and so on. In this way, everything should be connected. “A birth-based characteristic does not exist, as in other species”—this, however, should be understood as a conclusion to what was stated. Its reasoning is: Since, by these things such as hair, various birth-based characteristics do not exist among humans, therefore it should be understood thus: “Among humans with distinctions such as Brahmins, a birth-based characteristic does not exist, as in other species.”

617. Idāni evaṃ jātibhede asantepi brāhmaṇo khattiyoti idaṃ nānattaṃ yathā jātaṃ, taṃ dassetuṃ “paccatta”nti gāthamāha. Tassattho – etaṃ tiracchānānaṃ viya yonisiddhameva kesādisaṇṭhānānattaṃ manussesu [P 2.0466] brāhmaṇādīnaṃ attano attano sarīresu na vijjati. Avijjamānepi pana etasmiṃ yadetaṃ brāhmaṇo khattiyoti nānattavidhānapariyāyaṃ vokāraṃ, taṃ vokārañca manussesu samaññāya pavuccati, vohāramattena vuccatīti.

617. Now, even though such birth-based distinctions do not exist, to show how the difference of “Brahmin,” “Kshatriya,” and so on, has arisen, the verse “paccatta” is spoken. Its meaning is: This kind of difference in bodily form, such as hair, established by birth as it is in animals, does not exist in the individual bodies of humans such as Brahmins. But even though this does not exist, that diverse mode of designation which is “Brahmin,” “Kshatriya,” and so on—that designation is spoken of among humans by convention; it is spoken merely by usage.

619-625. Ettāvatā [M 2.0187] bhagavā bhāradvājassa vādaṃ niggahetvā idāni yadi jātiyā brāhmaṇo bhaveyya, ājīvasīlācāravipannopi brāhmaṇo bhaveyya. Yasmā pana porāṇā brāhmaṇā tassa brāhmaṇabhāvaṃ na icchanti loke ca aññepi paṇḍitamanussā, tasmā vāseṭṭhassa vādapaggahaṇatthaṃ taṃ dassento “yo hi koci manussesū”tiādikā aṭṭha gāthāyo āha. Tattha gorakkhanti khettarakkhaṃ, kasikammanti vuttaṃ hoti. Pathavī hi “go”ti vuccati, tappabhedo ca khettaṃ. Puthusippenāti tantavāyakammādinānāsippena. Vohāranti vaṇijjaṃ. Parapessenāti paresaṃ veyyāvaccena. Issatthanti āvudhajīvikaṃ, usuñca sattiñcāti vuttaṃ hoti. Porohiccenāti purohitakammena.

619-625. Having thus refuted Bhāradvāja’s argument, the Blessed One now shows that if one were a brahmin by birth, then even one deficient in livelihood, virtue, and conduct would be a brahmin. But since the ancient brahmins did not accept such a person’s brahminhood, nor did other wise people in the world, therefore, to support Vāseṭṭha’s argument, he spoke the eight verses beginning with “Whoever among men.” There, “gorakkha” means the protection of fields, which is to say, agriculture. For the earth is called “go,” and a division of that is a field. “Puthusippena” refers to various crafts such as weaving. “Vohāra” means trade. “Parapessena” means service to others. “Issattha” refers to a livelihood by weapons, which is to say, by arrow and spear. “Porohiccena” means the work of a royal chaplain.

626. Evaṃ brāhmaṇasamayena ca lokavohārena ca ājīvasīlācāravipannassa abrāhmaṇabhāvaṃ sādhetvā evaṃ sante na jātiyā brāhmaṇo, guṇehi pana brāhmaṇo hoti. Tasmā yattha yattha kule jāto yo guṇavā, so brāhmaṇo, ayamettha ñāyoti evametaṃ ñāyaṃ atthato āpādetvā puna tadeva ñāyaṃ vacībhedena pakāsento āha “na cāhaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ brūmī”ti.

626. Having thus established, through brahminical convention and worldly usage, the non-brahmin status of one deficient in livelihood, virtue, and conduct, it follows that one is not a brahmin by birth, but one becomes a brahmin by qualities. Therefore, in whatever family one is born, whoever is virtuous is a brahmin; this is the principle here. Having thus demonstrated this principle in terms of its meaning, he reveals that very principle again with a difference in wording, saying, “And I do not call one a brahmin.”

Tassattho – ahaṃ pana yvāyaṃ catūsu yonīsu yattha katthaci jāto, tatrāpi vā visesena yo [V 2.0170] brāhmaṇasamaññitāya mātari sambhūto, taṃ yonijaṃ mattisambhavaṃ yā cāyaṃ “ubhato sujāto”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.303; ma. ni. 2.424) nayena brāhmaṇehi brāhmaṇassa parisuddhauppattimaggasaṅkhātā yoni kathīyati, “saṃsuddhagahaṇiko”ti iminā ca mātusampatti, tatopi jātasambhūtattā “yonijo mattisambhavo”ti ca vuccati, tampi yonijaṃ mattisambhavaṃ iminā ca yonijamattisambhavamattena brāhmaṇaṃ na brūmi[P 2.0467]. Kasmā? Yasmā “bho bho”ti vacanamattena aññehi sakiñcanehi visiṭṭhattā bhovādī nāma so hoti, sace hoti sakiñcano. Yo panāyaṃ yattha katthaci kule jātopi rāgādikiñcanābhāvena akiñcano, sabbagahaṇapaṭinissaggena ca anādāno, akiñcanaṃ anādānaṃ tamahaṃ brūmi brāhmaṇaṃ. Kasmā? Yasmā bāhitapāpoti.

The meaning is this: I do not call someone a brahmin merely because they are born in any of the four kinds of birth, or even if they are born specifically from a mother designated as a brahmin—one born from a womb, from a mother. And that womb is described by brahmins according to the method beginning with “well-born on both sides” (D. I, 303; M. II, 424), which is called the way of pure birth for a brahmin; and by this, “of pure lineage,” is meant maternal excellence. Because of being born and arisen from that, he is called “born from a womb, from a mother.” Even such a one, born from a womb, from a mother, I do not call a brahmin merely on account of this. Why? Because merely by the utterance “bho, bho,” being distinguished from others who have attachments, he is called a “bhovādī,” if he has attachments. But whoever, though born in any family, is without attachments due to the absence of defilements like greed, and due to the relinquishment of all grasping, is one who does not grasp—such a one, without attachments and not grasping, I call a brahmin. Why? Because they have cast out evil.

627. Kiñca [M 2.0188] bhiyyo – “sabbasaṃyojanaṃ chetvā”tiādikā sattavīsati gāthā. Tattha sabbasaṃyojananti dasavidhaṃ saṃyojanaṃ. Na paritassatīti taṇhāya na tassati. Tamahanti taṃ ahaṃ rāgādīnaṃ saṅgānaṃ atikkantattā saṅgātigaṃ, catunnampi yogānaṃ abhāvena visaṃyuttaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ vadāmīti attho.

627. What more? The twenty-seven verses beginning, “Having cut off all fetters.” Here, “all fetters” means the ten fetters. “He does not tremble” means he is not tormented by craving. The meaning is: I call that person a brahmin who is 'gone beyond attachment' (saṅgātigaṃ), because he has transcended the bonds of lust and so on, and 'unyoked' (visaṃyuttaṃ), because of the absence of the four yokes.

628. Naddhinti nayhanabhāvena pavattaṃ kodhaṃ. Varattanti bandhanabhāvena pavattaṃ taṇhaṃ. Sandānaṃ sahanukkamanti anusayānukkamasahitaṃ dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhisandānaṃ, idaṃ sabbampi chinditvā ṭhitaṃ avijjāpalighassa ukkhittattā ukkhittapalighaṃ catunnaṃ saccānnaṃ buddhattā buddhaṃ ahaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ vadāmīti attho.

628. “The thong” (naddhi) means anger, which proceeds with the nature of tying. “The strap” (varatta) means craving, which proceeds with the nature of binding. “The tether with its sequence” (sandānaṃ sahanukkamaṃ) means the tether of the sixty-two views together with the sequence of underlying tendencies. The meaning is: I call that person a brahmin who, having cut all this, is “one with the bar lifted” (ukkhittapalighaṃ) because the bar of ignorance has been lifted, and is “awakened” (buddhaṃ) because he has awakened to the four truths.

629. Aduṭṭhoti evaṃ dasahi akkosavatthūhi akkosañca pāṇiādīhi pothanañca andubandhanādīhi bandhanañca yo akuddhamānaso hutvā adhivāsesi, khantibalena samannāgatattā khantībalaṃ, punappunaṃ uppattiyā anīkabhūtena teneva khantībalānīkena samannāgatattā balānīkaṃ taṃ evarūpaṃ ahaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ vadāmīti attho.

629. ‘Unangered’—one who, though subjected to the ten grounds for abuse, beating with hands and so on, and imprisonment with chains and so on, endures with an unangered mind. Because he is endowed with the power of patience, he has ‘the power of patience.’ Because he is endowed with that very army of the power of patience, which has become a formidable force through repeated arising, he is one with ‘an army of strength.’ Such a one I call a brahmin—this is the meaning.

630. Vatantanti dhutavatena samannāgataṃ, catupārisuddhisīlena sīlavantaṃ, taṇhāussadābhāvena anussadaṃ, chaḷindriyadamanena dantaṃ, koṭiyaṃ ṭhitena attabhāvena antimasārīraṃ tamahaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ vadāmīti attho.

630. ‘Practicing austerity’—endowed with ascetic practices. ‘Virtuous’—possessing the fourfold purified virtue. ‘Without swelling’—free from the swelling of craving. ‘Tamed’—restrained in the six senses. ‘With his final body’—with his being established on the limit, he is one with his final body. Him I call a brahmin—this is the meaning.

631. Yo [V 2.0171] na limpatīti evameva yo abbhantare duvidhepi kāme na limpati, tasmiṃ kāme na saṇṭhāti, tamahaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ vadāmīti attho.

631. ‘He does not cling’—just so, one who does not cling internally to the two kinds of sensual pleasures, does not linger in them—such a one I call a brahmin—this is the meaning.

632. Dukkhassāti khandhadukkhassa. Pannabhāranti ohitakkhandhabhāraṃ catūhi yogehi sabbakilesehi vā visaṃyuttaṃ tamahaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ vadāmīti [P 2.0468] attho.

632. ‘Of suffering’ means the suffering of the aggregates. ‘Having laid down the burden’ means having laid down the burden of the aggregates, being detached from the four yokes or from all defilements. I call him a brahmin—this is the meaning.

633. Gambhīrapaññanti gambhīresu khandhādīsu pavattāya paññāya samannāgataṃ, dhammojapaññāya medhāviṃ, “ayaṃ duggatiyā, ayaṃ sugatiyā, ayaṃ nibbānassa maggo, ayaṃ amaggo”ti evaṃ magge amagge ca chekatāya maggāmaggassa [M 2.0189] kovidaṃ, arahattasaṅkhātaṃ uttamatthamanuppattaṃ tamahaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ vadāmīti attho.

633. ‘Deep in wisdom’—endowed with wisdom that operates in the profound aggregates and so on. ‘Wise’—endowed with Dhamma-penetrating wisdom, intelligent. ‘Skilled in the path and the not-path’—because he is expert in distinguishing the path and the not-path, knowing, “This leads to a bad destination, this to a good destination, this is the path to Nibbāna, this is not the path.” ‘Attained to the highest goal’—having reached the supreme goal, that is, arahantship. Such a one I call a brahmin—this is the meaning.

634. Asaṃsaṭṭhanti dassanasavanasamullāpaparibhogakāyasaṃsaggānaṃ abhāvena asaṃsaṭṭhaṃ. Ubhayanti gihīhi ca anagārehi cāti ubhayehipi asaṃsaṭṭhaṃ. Anokasārinti anālayacāriṃ, taṃ evarūpaṃ ahaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ vadāmīti attho.

634. ‘Unmingled’—unmingled due to the absence of association by way of seeing, hearing, conversing, using, and bodily contact. ‘With both’—unmingled with both householders and the homeless. ‘Wandering without a home’—living without attachment. Such a one I call a brahmin—this is the meaning.

635. Nidhāyāti nikkhipitvā oropetvā. Tasesu thāvaresu cāti taṇhātāsena tasesu taṇhābhāvena thiratāya thāvaresu. Yo na hantīti yo evaṃ sabbasattesu vigatapaṭighatāya nikkhittadaṇḍo neva kañci sayaṃ hanati, na aññena ghāteti, tamahaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ vadāmīti attho.

635. ‘Having laid down’ means having put aside, having relinquished. ‘Among the trembling and the firm’ refers to those agitated by craving and those steadfast due to the absence of craving. ‘Who does not strike’ means one who, having laid down the rod towards all beings due to the absence of ill will, neither strikes any being himself nor causes another to strike. Such a one I call a brahmin—this is the meaning.

636. Aviruddhanti āghātavasena viruddhesupi lokiyamahājanesu āghātābhāvena aviruddhaṃ, hatthagate daṇḍe vā satthe vā avijjamānepi paresaṃ pahāradānato aviratattā attadaṇḍesu janesu nibbutaṃ nikkhittadaṇḍaṃ, pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ “ahaṃ mama”nti gahitattā sādānesu, tassa gahaṇassa abhāvena anādānaṃ taṃ evarūpaṃ ahaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ vadāmīti attho.

636. ‘Unconflicted’ means unconflicted due to the absence of resentment, even among worldly people who are in conflict. Among people who have taken up the rod, who do not refrain from striking others, he is extinguished, having laid down the rod. Among those who are grasping, who grasp the five aggregates as ‘I’ or ‘mine,’ he is non-grasping due to the absence of that grasping. Such a one I call a brahmin—this is the meaning.

637. Āraggāti yassete rāgādayo ayañca paraguṇamakkhaṇalakkhaṇo makkho āraggā sāsapo viya papatito, yathā sāsapo āragge na santiṭṭhati, evaṃ citte na tiṭṭhati, tamahaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ vadāmīti attho.

637. ‘From the point of an awl’ means that for him, lust and other defilements, and this envy characterized by disparaging others’ good qualities, fall away like a mustard seed from the point of an awl; just as a mustard seed does not stay on the point of an awl, so these do not remain in his mind. Such a one I call a brahmin—this is the meaning.

638. Akakkasanti apharusaṃ. Viññāpaninti atthaviññāpaniṃ. Saccanti bhūtaṃ. Nābhisajeti [V 2.0172] yāya girāya aññaṃ kujjhāpanavasena na laggāpeyya. Khīṇāsavo nāma evarūpameva giraṃ bhāseyya. Tasmā tamahaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ vadāmīti attho.

638. ‘Not harsh’ means not rough. ‘That makes known’ means speech that makes known the meaning. ‘True’ means what is actual. ‘By which he would offend no one’ means that by his speech he does not cause another to become angry. One whose cankers are destroyed speaks just such words. Therefore, I call him a brahmin—this is the meaning.

639. Sāṭakābharaṇādīsu dīghaṃ vā rassaṃ vā, maṇimuttādīsu aṇuṃ vā thūlaṃ vā mahagghaappagghavasena subhaṃ vā asubhaṃ vā yo puggalo imasmiṃ [M 2.0190] loke parapariggahitaṃ nādiyati, tamahaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ [P 2.0469] vadāmīti attho.

639. Whether long or short, regarding garments, ornaments, and so on; or small or large, regarding gems, pearls, and so on; or fine or foul, in the sense of valuable or of little value—one who in this world does not take what is possessed by another, him I call a brahmin—this is the meaning.

640. Nirāsāsanti nittaṇhaṃ. Visaṃyuttanti sabbakilesehi viyuttaṃ tamahaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ vadāmīti attho.

640. ‘Without hopes’ means without craving. ‘Detached’ means detached from all defilements; such a one I call a brahmin—this is the meaning.

641. Ālayāti taṇhā. Aññāya akathaṃkathīti aṭṭha vatthūni yathābhūtaṃ jānitvā aṭṭhavatthukāya vicikicchāya nibbicikiccho. Amatogadhamanuppattanti amataṃ nibbānaṃ ogahetvā anuppattaṃ tamahaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ vadāmīti attho.

641. ‘Attachments’ means craving. ‘Having understood, is without doubt’ means that having truly understood the eight grounds, he is free from doubt concerning the eight objects of doubt. ‘Who has plunged into the deathless’ means he has plunged into and reached the deathless, Nibbāna. Such a one I call a brahmin—this is the meaning.

642. Ubhoti dvepi puññāni pāpāni ca chaḍḍetvāti attho. Saṅganti rāgādibhedaṃ saṅgaṃ. Upaccagāti atikkanto. Tamahaṃ vaṭṭamūlasokena asokaṃ, abbhantare rāgarajādīnaṃ abhāvena virajaṃ, nirupakkilesatāya suddhaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ vadāmīti attho.

642. ‘Both bonds’ means having abandoned both merit and demerit. ‘Bondage’ refers to attachments such as lust. ‘Has transcended’ means has gone beyond. Him I call a brahmin who is sorrowless, stainless, and pure: sorrowless, being free from the sorrow that is the root of the cycle; stainless, due to the absence of the dust of passion and so on within; and pure, due to being undefiled—this is the meaning.

643. Vimalanti abbhādimalavirahitaṃ. Suddhanti nirupakkilesaṃ. Vippasannanti pasannacittaṃ. Anāvilanti kilesāvilattavirahitaṃ. Nandībhavaparikkhīṇanti tīsu bhavesu parikkhīṇataṇhaṃ tamahaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ vadāmīti attho.

643. ‘Stainless’ means free from stains such as clouds. ‘Pure’ means free from defilements. ‘Serene’ means serene-minded. ‘Untroubled’ means free from the turbidity of defilements. ‘Whose delight in existence is exhausted’ means one whose craving for existence in the three realms is exhausted. Such a one I call a brahmin—this is the meaning.

644. Yo bhikkhu imaṃ rāgapalipathañceva kilesaduggañca saṃsāravaṭṭañca catunnaṃ saccānaṃ appaṭivijjhanakamohañca atīto, cattāro oghe tiṇṇo hutvā pāraṃ anuppatto, duvidhena jhānena jhāyī, taṇhāya abhāvena anejo, kathaṃkathāya abhāvena akathaṃkathī, upādānānaṃ abhāvena anupādiyitvā kilesanibbānena nibbuto, tamahaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ vadāmīti attho.

644. That monk who has transcended this treacherous path of lust, this fortress of defilements, this cycle of existence, and the delusion of not penetrating the Four Noble Truths; who has crossed the four floods and reached the far shore; who is meditative with twofold meditation, unshaken due to the absence of craving, without doubt due to the absence of questioning, and who, not clinging due to the absence of attachments, is extinguished through the extinction of defilements—him I call a brahmin—this is the meaning.

645. Yo puggalo, idha loke, ubhopi kāme hitvā anāgāro hutvā paribbajati, taṃ parikkhīṇakāmañceva parikkhīṇabhavañca ahaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ vadāmīti attho.

645. That person who, in this world, has abandoned both kinds of sensual pleasure and, having become homeless, wanders forth—him, with sensual pleasure and existence exhausted, I call a brahmin—this is the meaning.

646. Yo [V 2.0173][M 2.0191] idha loke chadvārikaṃ taṇhaṃ jahitvā gharāvāsena anatthiko anāgāro hutvā paribbajati, taṇhāya ceva bhavassa ca parikkhīṇattā taṇhābhavaparikkhīṇaṃ tamahaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ vadāmīti attho.

646. Whoever in this world has abandoned craving at the six sense doors and, having no need for the household life, becomes a homeless one and wanders forth—him, with craving and existence exhausted, I call a brahmin—this is the meaning.

647. Mānusakaṃ yoganti mānusakaṃ āyuñceva pañcavidhakāmaguṇe ca. Dibbayogepi eseva nayo. Upaccagāti yo mānusakaṃ yogaṃ hitvā dibbaṃ atikkanto, taṃ sabbehi catūhi yogehi visaṃyuttaṃ ahaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ vadāmīti attho.

647. “Human bond” (mānusakaṃ yogaṃ) refers to human lifespan and the five kinds of sensual pleasures. The same principle applies to divine bonds. “Upaccagā” means one who, having abandoned the human bond, has transcended the divine. Him, disjoined from all four bonds, I call a brahmin.

648. Ratinti pañcakāmaguṇaratiṃ. Aratinti araññavāse ukkaṇṭhitattaṃ. Sītibhūtanti [P 2.0470] nibbutaṃ, nirupadhinti nirupakkilesaṃ, vīranti taṃ evarūpaṃ sabbaṃ khandhalokaṃ abhibhavitvā ṭhitaṃ vīriyavantaṃ ahaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ vadāmīti attho.

648. “Rati” means delight in the five strands of sensual pleasure. “Arati” means discontent with forest dwelling. “Sītibhūta” means extinguished. “Nirupadhi” means without defilements. “Vīra” refers to the heroic one who, having overcome that entire aggregate-world, stands firm with vigor—him I call a brahmin.

649. Yo vedīti yo sattānaṃ sabbākārena cutiñca paṭisandhiñca pākaṭaṃ katvā jānāti, tamahaṃ alaggatāya asattaṃ, paṭipattiyā suṭṭhu gatattā sugataṃ, catunnaṃ saccānaṃ buddhatāya buddhaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ vadāmīti attho.

649. “One who knows” (yo vedī) is one who, in every way, knows distinctly the passing away and rebirth of beings. Him, unattached because of non-clinging, well-gone in practice, awakened to the Four Noble Truths, I call a brahmin.

650. Yassāti yassete devādayo gatiṃ na jānanti, tamahaṃ āsavānaṃ khīṇatāya khīṇāsavaṃ, kilesehi ārakattā arahantaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ vadāmīti attho.

650. Whose destiny the gods and others do not know—him, a khīṇāsava due to the destruction of the influxes, an arahant because of being far from defilements, I call a brahmin.

651. Pureti atītakkhandhesu. Pacchāti anāgatesu. Majjheti paccuppannesu. Kiñcananti yassetesu ṭhānesu taṇhāgāhasaṅkhātaṃ kiñcanaṃ natthi. Tamahaṃ rāgakiñcanādīhi akiñcanaṃ. Kassaci gahaṇassa abhāvena anādānaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ vadāmīti attho.

651. “Before” (pure) refers to past aggregates. “After” (paccha) refers to future aggregates. “In the middle” (majjhe) refers to present aggregates. “Anything” (kiñcanaṃ) means that for whom there is no impediment, in the form of craving and grasping, in these states. Him, having nothing on account of the absence of the impediment of lust and so on, not grasping because of the absence of any grasping, I call a brahmin.

652. Acchambhitattena usabhasadisatāya usabhaṃ, uttamaṭṭhena pavaraṃ, vīriyasampattiyā vīraṃ, mahantānaṃ sīlakkhandhādīnaṃ esitattā mahesiṃ, tiṇṇaṃ mārānaṃ vijitattā vijitāvinaṃ, ninhātakilesatāya nhātakaṃ, catusaccabuddhatāya buddhaṃ taṃ evarūpaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ vadāmīti attho.

652. A bull for being fearless and bull-like, supreme in the highest sense, a hero for his attainment of energy, a great seer for seeking the great aggregates of virtue and so on, a conqueror for having conquered the three Māras, one who has bathed for having washed off defilements, awakened for having awakened to the four truths—such a one I call a brahmin.

653. Yo pubbenivāsaṃ pākaṭaṃ katvā jānāti, chabbīsatidevalokabhedaṃ saggaṃ, catubbidhaṃ apāyañca dibbacakkhunā passati, atho jātikkhayasaṅkhātaṃ arahattaṃ patto, tamahaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ vadāmīti attho.

653. One who makes past lives manifest and knows them, who with the divine eye perceives heaven, with its twenty-six deva realms, and the fourfold state of misery, and who has attained arahantship, known as the destruction of birth—him I call a brahmin.

654. Evaṃ [V 2.0174][M 2.0192] bhagavā guṇato brāhmaṇaṃ vatvā “ye ‘jātito brāhmaṇo’ti abhinivesaṃ karonti, te idaṃ vohāramattaṃ ajānantā, sā ca nesaṃ diṭṭhi duddiṭṭhī”ti dassento “samaññā hesā”ti gāthādvayamāha. Tassattho – “yadidaṃ brāhmaṇo khattiyo bhāradvājo vāseṭṭho”ti nāmagottaṃ pakappitaṃ, samaññā hesā lokasmiṃ, paññattivohāramattanti veditabbaṃ. Kasmā? Yasmā sammuccā samudāgataṃ samanuññāya [P 2.0471] āgataṃ. Tañhi tattha tattha jātakāleyevassa ñātisālohitehi pakappitaṃ kataṃ. No cetaṃ evaṃ pakappeyyuṃ, na koci kañci disvā “ayaṃ brāhmaṇo”ti vā “bhāradvājo”ti vā jāneyya.

654. Having thus spoken of the brahmin in terms of qualities, the Blessed One, showing that those who insist, “a brahmin is so by birth,” do not understand this mere convention, and that their view is a wrong view, declared two verses beginning with “It is a designation.” The meaning is this: Whatever name or clan is assigned—whether brahmin, khattiya, Bhāradvāja, or Vāseṭṭha—it is a designation in the world, to be understood as a mere concept and convention. Why? Because it has arisen from convention, come about by agreement. For it was assigned and created by relatives and kinsmen at the time of birth in various places. If they had not assigned it thus, no one, upon seeing another, would know, ‘This is a brahmin’ or ‘This is a Bhāradvāja.’”

655. Evaṃ pakappitañcetaṃ dīgharattamanusayitaṃ diṭṭhigatamajānataṃ, “pakappitaṃ nāmagottaṃ, nāmagottamattametaṃ saṃvohāratthaṃ pakappita”nti ajānantānaṃ sattānaṃ hadaye dīgharattaṃ diṭṭhigatamanusayitaṃ, tassa anusayitattā taṃ nāmagottaṃ ajānantā te pabruvanti “jātiyā hoti brāhmaṇo”ti, ajānantāyeva evaṃ vadantīti vuttaṃ hoti.

655. Thus this designation is a view that has long been latent for those who do not know. For beings who do not know that “A name and clan are designated; this is merely a name and clan designated for the sake of convention,” this view has long been latent in their hearts. Because it has been latent, they, not understanding this matter of name and clan, declare, “One is a brahmin by birth.” It is said that they speak thus only out of ignorance.

656-7. Evaṃ “ye ‘jātito brāhmaṇo’ti abhinivesaṃ karonti, te idaṃ vohāramattamajānantā, sā ca nesaṃ diṭṭhi duddiṭṭhī”ti dassetvā idāni nippariyāyameva jātivādaṃ paṭikkhipanto kammavādañca niropento “na jaccā”tiādimāha. Tattha “kammunā brāhmaṇo hoti, kammunā hoti abrāhmaṇo”ti imissā upaḍḍhagāthāya atthavitthāraṇatthaṃ “kassako kammunā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha kammunāti paccuppannena kasikammādinibbattakacetanākammunā.

656-7. Having shown that “those who insist ‘a brahmin is such by birth’ do not understand this mere convention, and that view of theirs is a wrong view,” now, rejecting the doctrine of birth without qualification and establishing the doctrine of action, he says, “Not by birth,” etc. Here, to expand on the meaning of the half-verse “By action one is a brahmin, by action one is a non-brahmin,” it is said “A farmer by action,” etc. Herein, “by action” means by the present volitional action that produces farming and so on.

659. Paṭiccasamuppādadassāti “iminā paccayena evaṃ hotī”ti evaṃ paṭiccasamuppādadassāvino. Kammavipākakovidāti sammānāvamānārahe kule kammavasena uppatti hoti, aññāpi hīnapaṇītatā hīnapaṇīte kamme vipaccamāne hotīti evaṃ kammavipākakusalā.

659. “Seers of dependent origination” (paṭiccasamuppādadassā) are those who see thus: “With this as a condition, this comes to be.” “Skilled in the results of actions” (kammavipākakovidā) means they are skilled in the results of actions thus: birth in families worthy of respect or disrespect occurs by the power of action, and other inferior or superior states arise when inferior or superior actions ripen.

660. “Kammunāvattatī”ti gāthāya pana “loko”ti vā “pajā”ti vā “sattā”ti vā ekoyeva attho, vacanamattameva nānaṃ. Purimapadena cettha [M 2.0193] “atthi brahmā mahābrahmā…pe… seṭṭho sajitā vasī pitā bhūtabhabyāna”nti (dī. ni. 1.42) imissā diṭṭhiyā [P 2.0472] nisedho veditabbo. Kammunā hi vattati tāsu tāsu gatīsu uppajjati loko, tassa ko sajitāti? Dutiyena “evaṃ kammunā uppannopi ca pavattiyampi atītapaccuppannabhedena kammunā eva [V 2.0175] pavattati, sukhadukkhāni paccanubhonto hīnapaṇītādibhāvaṃ āpajjanto pavattatī”ti dasseti. Tatiyena tamevatthaṃ nigameti “evaṃ sabbathāpi kammanibandhanā sattā kammeneva baddhā hutvā pavattanti, na aññathā”ti. Catutthena tamatthaṃ upamāya vibhāveti rathassāṇīva yāyatoti. Yathā rathassa yāyato āṇi nibandhanaṃ hoti, na tāya anibaddho yāti, evaṃ lokassa uppajjato ca pavattato ca kammaṃ nibandhanaṃ, na tena anibaddho uppajjati nappavattati.

660. In the verse “The world revolves by kamma,” the terms “world,” “creatures,” or “beings” all convey the same meaning; only the wording differs. Here, by the first line, the refutation of the view that “there is a Brahmā, a Great Brahmā… the best, the creator, the controller, the father of all that have been and will be” (DN 1.18) should be understood. For it is by kamma that the world revolves, arising in various destinies—so who is its creator? The second line shows that “even having arisen by kamma, it also revolves by kamma alone in its continuation, divided into past and present; experiencing pleasure and pain, it revolves, attaining inferior and superior states.” The third line concludes that same meaning: “Thus, in every way, beings are bound by kamma. Bound by kamma, they revolve, not otherwise.” The fourth line illustrates this meaning with the simile: “like the axle-pin of a moving chariot.” Just as the axle-pin is the binding for a moving chariot, and it does not move unbound by it, so too, kamma is the binding for the world's arising and revolving; unbound by it, it neither arises nor revolves.

661. Idāni yasmā evaṃ kammanibandhano loko, tasmā seṭṭhena kammunā seṭṭhabhāvaṃ dassento “tapenā”ti gāthādvayamāha. Tattha tapenāti indriyasaṃvarena. Brahmacariyenāti sikkhānissitena vuttāvasesaseṭṭhacariyena. Saṃyamenāti sīlena. Damenāti paññāya. Etena seṭṭhaṭṭhena brahmabhūtena kammunā brāhmaṇo hoti. Kasmā? Yasmā etaṃ brāhmaṇamuttamaṃ, yasmā etaṃ kammaṃ uttamo brāhmaṇabhāvoti vuttaṃ hoti. “Brahmāna”ntipi pāṭho, tassattho – brahmaṃ ānetīti brahmānaṃ, brahmabhāvaṃ āneti āvahati detīti vuttaṃ hoti.

661. Now, because the world is thus bound by kamma, to show that the state of excellence is attained by excellent kamma, he speaks the pair of verses beginning with “By austerity.” Herein, “by austerity” means by restraint of the senses. “By the holy life” means by the remaining excellent conduct based on the training. “By self-control” means by morality. “By taming” means by wisdom. By this kamma, which is excellent and has become sublime, one becomes a brahmin. Why? Because this is the highest for a brahmin, and because this kamma is the highest state of a brahmin, so it is said. There is also a reading “Brahmāna,” the meaning of which is: it brings Brahma, thus it is called Brahmāna; meaning it brings, conveys, and gives the state of Brahma, so it is said.

662. Dutiyagāthāya santoti santakileso. Brahmā sakkoti brahmā ca sakko ca. Yo evarūpo, so na kevalaṃ brāhmaṇo, apica kho brahmā ca sakko ca so vijānataṃ paṇḍitānaṃ, evaṃ vāseṭṭha jānāhīti vuttaṃ hoti. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti.

662. In the second verse, “peaceful” means one whose defilements are stilled. “Brahma and Sakka” refers to Brahma and Sakka. Whoever is such, that one is not only a brahmin, but indeed Brahma and Sakka among the wise who understand. Vāseṭṭha, know it thus—this is what is said. The rest is according to the manner already stated.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

The Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddakapāṭha.

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya vāseṭṭhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Vāseṭṭha Sutta in the Commentary on the Suttanipāta is completed.

10. Kokālikasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Explanation of the Kokālika Sutta

Evaṃ [V 2.0176][M 2.0194][P 2.0473] me sutanti kokālikasuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Imassa suttassa uppatti atthavaṇṇanāyameva āvi bhavissati. Atthavaṇṇanāya cassa evaṃ me sutantiādi vuttanayameva. Atha kho kokālikoti ettha pana ko ayaṃ kokāliko, kasmā ca upasaṅkamīti? Vuccate – ayaṃ kira kokālikaraṭṭhe kokālikanagare kokālikaseṭṭhissa putto pabbajitvā pitarā kārāpite vihāreyeva paṭivasati “cūḷakokāliko”ti nāmena, na devadattassa sisso. So hi brāhmaṇaputto “mahākokāliko”ti paññāyi.

Thus have I heard—the Kokālika Sutta. What is its origin? The origin of this sutta will become clear in the explanation of its meaning. And the explanation of its meaning is in the same manner as has been stated for “Thus have I heard,” and so on. Now, regarding “Kokālika”—who is this Kokālika, and why did he approach? It is said: This one, it seems, was the son of the Kokālika merchant in the city of Kokālika in the country of Kokālika. Having gone forth, he resided in the very monastery built by his father and was known by the name “Cūḷakokālika.” He was not a disciple of Devadatta, for it was a brahmin’s son who was known as “Mahākokālika.”

Bhagavati kira sāvatthiyaṃ viharante dve aggasāvakā pañcamattehi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ janapadacārikaṃ caramānā upakaṭṭhāya vassūpanāyikāya vivekavāsaṃ vasitukāmā te bhikkhū uyyojetvā attano pattacīvaramādāya tasmiṃ janapade taṃ nagaraṃ patvā taṃ vihāraṃ agamaṃsu. Tattha te kokālikena saddhiṃ sammoditvā taṃ āhaṃsu – “āvuso, mayaṃ idha temāsaṃ vasissāma, mā kassaci āroceyyāsī”ti. So “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇitvā temāse atīte itaradivasaṃ pageva nagaraṃ pavisitvā ārocesi – “tumhe aggasāvake idhāgantvā vasamāne na jānittha, na te koci paccayenāpi nimantetī”ti. Nagaravāsino “kasmā no, bhante, nārocayitthā”ti. Kiṃ ārocitena, kiṃ nāddasatha dve bhikkhū vasante, nanu ete aggasāvakāti. Te khippaṃ sannipatitvā sappiguḷavatthādīni ānetvā kokālikassa purato nikkhipiṃsu. So cintesi – “paramappicchā aggasāvakā ‘payuttavācāya uppanno lābho’ti ñatvā na sādiyissanti, asādiyantā addhā ‘āvāsikassa dethā’ti bhaṇissanti, handāhaṃ imaṃ lābhaṃ gāhāpetvā gacchāmī”ti[P 2.0474]. So tathā akāsi, therā disvāva payuttavācāya uppannabhāvaṃ ñatvā “ime paccayā neva amhākaṃ na kokālikassa vaṭṭantī”ti cintetvā “āvāsikassa dethā”ti avatvā paṭikkhipitvā pakkamiṃsu. Tena kokāliko “kathañhi nāma attanā aggaṇhantā mayhampi na dāpesu”nti domanassaṃ uppādesi.

When the Blessed One was residing at Sāvatthī, it is said, his two chief disciples, along with about five hundred monks, were traveling through the countryside. As the rains-residence was approaching, wishing to dwell in seclusion, they sent the monks away and, taking their own bowls and robes, reached a city in that region and went to a monastery there. There, they exchanged greetings with Kokālika and said to him, “Friend, we will stay here for three months—do not inform anyone.” He agreed, saying, “Very well.” When the three months had passed, on the very next day, he entered the city early and announced, “You did not know that the chief disciples had come here and were staying—no one invited them even for requisites!” The townspeople said, “Why, venerable sir, did you not inform us?” He replied, “What was the use of informing you? Did you not see two monks staying here? Surely, these are the chief disciples!” Quickly gathering, they brought ghee, molasses, cloth, and other things and placed them before Kokālika. He thought, “The chief disciples are of extremely few wishes. Knowing that these gains arose from calculated speech, they will not accept them. Surely, if they do not accept them, they will say, ‘Give them to the resident monk.’ Come now, I will have these gains taken and then depart.” The elders, as soon as they saw them, knew that the gains had arisen from calculated speech and reflected, “These requisites are suitable neither for us nor for Kokālika.” Without saying, “Give them to the resident monk,” they rejected them and departed. At this, Kokālika became distressed, thinking, “How could they, not taking it themselves, not have it given to me either?”

Te [M 2.0195] bhagavato santikaṃ agamaṃsu. Bhagavā ca pavāretvā sace attanā janapadacārikaṃ na gacchati, aggasāvake peseti – “caratha, bhikkhave, cārikaṃ bahujanahitāyā”tiādīni (mahāva. 32) vatvā[V 2.0177]. Idamāciṇṇaṃ tathāgatānaṃ. Tena kho pana samayena attanā agantukāmo hoti. Atha kho ime punadeva uyyojesi – “gacchatha, bhikkhave, caratha cārika”nti. Te pañcamattehi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ cārikaṃ caramānā anupubbena tasmiṃ raṭṭhe tameva nagaraṃ agamaṃsu. Nāgarā there sañjānitvā saha parikkhārehi dānaṃ sajjetvā nagaramajjhe maṇḍapaṃ katvā dānaṃ adaṃsu, therānañca parikkhāre upanāmesuṃ. Therā gahetvā bhikkhusaṅghassa adaṃsu. Taṃ disvā kokāliko cintesi – “ime pubbe appicchā ahesuṃ, idāni lobhābhibhūtā pāpicchā jātā, pubbepi appicchasantuṭṭhapavivittasadisā maññe, ime pāpicchā asantaguṇaparidīpakā pāpabhikkhū”ti. So there upasaṅkamitvā “āvuso, tumhe pubbe appicchā santuṭṭhā pavivittā viya ahuvattha, idāni panattha pāpabhikkhū jātā”ti vatvā pattacīvaramādāya tāvadeva taramānarūpo nikkhamitvā gantvā “bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocessāmī”ti sāvatthābhimukho gantvā anupubbena bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkami. Ayamettha kokāliko, iminā kāraṇena upasaṅkami. Tena vuttaṃ “atha kho kokāliko bhikkhu yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamī”tiādi.

They went to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, after the Pavāraṇā ceremony, if he himself did not go on a journey through the countryside, would send his chief disciples, saying, “Go, monks, wander for the welfare of many,” and so on (Mahāvagga 32). This is the custom of the Tathāgatas. At that time, however, he himself did not wish to go. So he sent them out again, saying, “Go, monks, wander on your journey.” Traveling with about five hundred monks, they gradually reached that very city in that country. The citizens, recognizing the elders, prepared offerings along with requisites, set up a pavilion in the middle of the city, and gave alms, presenting the requisites to the elders. The elders accepted them and gave them to the community of monks. Seeing this, Kokālika thought, “Before, they were of few wishes, but now, overcome by greed, they have become of evil wishes. I thought they used to seem like those of few wishes, content, and secluded. These are monks of evil wishes, evil monks who display qualities they do not possess.” Approaching the elders, he said, “Friends, before you seemed to be of few wishes, content, and secluded, but now you have become evil monks.” Then, taking his bowl and robe, he immediately left in haste, thinking, “I will report this matter to the Blessed One.” He set out toward Sāvatthī and gradually approached the Blessed One. This here is Kokālika, and for this reason he approached. Therefore, it is said, “Then the monk Kokālika approached the Blessed One,” and so on.

Bhagavā taṃ turitaturitaṃ āgacchantaṃ disvāva āvajjetvā aññāsi – “aggasāvake akkositukāmo āgato”ti. “Sakkā nu kho paṭisedhetu”nti ca āvajjento “na sakkā, theresu aparajjhitvā [P 2.0475] āgato, ekaṃsena padumaniraye uppajjissatī”ti addasa. Evaṃ disvāpi pana “sāriputtamoggallānepi nāma garahantaṃ sutvā na nisedhetī”ti parūpavādamocanatthaṃ ariyūpavādassa mahāsāvajjabhāvadassanatthañca “mā heva”ntiādinā nayena tikkhattuṃ paṭisedhesi. Tattha mā hevanti mā evamāha, mā evaṃ abhaṇīti attho. Pesalāti piyasīlā. Saddhāyikoti saddhāgamakaro, pasādāvahoti vuttaṃ hoti. Paccayikoti paccayakaro, “evameta”nti sanniṭṭhāvahoti vuttaṃ hoti.

Seeing him coming in great haste, the Blessed One, having turned his mind, understood: 'He has come intending to insult the chief disciples.' And reflecting, 'Is it possible to restrain him?' he saw: 'It is not possible. He has come having offended the elders; he will certainly be reborn in the Paduma hell.' Even having seen this, in order to avert reproach from others, and to show the great fault of reviling the noble ones, he restrained him three times with the phrase 'Do not say so,' etc., in this manner. Here, 'Do not say so' means 'Do not say thus,' 'Do not speak in this way'—this is the meaning. 'Gentle' means of amiable conduct. 'Faith-inspiring' means one who causes the arising of faith, bringing confidence—this is said. 'Trustworthy' means one who inspires trust, bringing certainty—'Thus it is'—this is said.

Acirapakkantassāti pakkantassa sato na cireneva sabbo kāyo phuṭo ahosīti kesaggamattampi okāsaṃ avajjetvā sakalasarīraṃ aṭṭhīni [M 2.0196] bhinditvā uggatāhi pīḷakāhi ajjhotthaṭaṃ ahosi. Tattha yasmā buddhānubhāvena tathārūpaṃ kammaṃ buddhānaṃ sammukhībhāve vipākaṃ na deti, dassanūpacāre pana vijahitamatte deti, tasmā tassa acirapakkantassa pīḷakā uṭṭhahiṃsu. Teneva vuttaṃ “acirapakkantassa ca kokālikassā”ti. Atha kasmā tattheva na aṭṭhāsīti ce? Kammānubhāvena. Okāsakatañhi kammaṃ avassaṃ vipaccati, taṃ tassa tattha ṭhātuṃ na deti. So kammānubhāvena codiyamāno uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkāmi. Kaḷāyamattiyoti caṇakamattiyo[V 2.0178]. Beluvasalāṭukamattiyoti taruṇabeluvamattiyo. Pabhijjiṃsūti bhijjiṃsu. Tāsu bhinnāsu sakalasarīraṃ panasapakkaṃ viya ahosi. So pakkena gattena anayabyasanaṃ patvā dukkhābhibhūto jetavanadvārakoṭṭhake sayi. Atha dhammassavanatthaṃ āgatāgatā manussā taṃ disvā “dhi kokālika, dhi kokālika, ayuttamakāsi, attanoyeva mukhaṃ nissāya anayabyasanaṃ pattosī”ti āhaṃsu. Tesaṃ sutvā ārakkhadevatā [P 2.0476] dhikkāraṃ akaṃsu, ārakkhadevatānaṃ ākāsaṭṭhadevatāti iminā upāyena yāva akaniṭṭhabhavanā ekadhikkāro udapādi.

‘Not long after he had departed’ means that soon after he had departed, his entire body was covered, without even a hair’s breadth of space being left untouched; he was overwhelmed by boils that had erupted, shattering his bones. There, because the power of the Buddhas prevents such kamma from ripening in their presence, it ripens only when they are no longer in sight. Therefore, soon after Kokālika had departed, the boils arose. Hence it is said, ‘not long after Kokālika had departed.’ But why did he not stay there? Due to the power of kamma. For kamma, when it has found its opportunity, inevitably ripens; it did not allow him to remain there. Driven by the force of his kamma, he rose from his seat and departed. ‘Like a chickpea’ means the size of a chickpea. ‘Like a young beluva fruit’ means the size of a young beluva fruit. ‘They burst’ means they split open. When they burst, his entire body became like a ripe jackfruit. Overcome by suffering, he reached ruin with his festering body and lay down at the gatehouse of Jetavana. Then, people who came to hear the Dhamma saw him and said, ‘Shame on you, Kokālika! Shame on you, Kokālika! You acted wrongly and have brought ruin upon yourself by your own words.’ Hearing this, the guardian deities uttered their reproach, and through this means, from the deities of the sky up to the Akaniṭṭha heavens, a single cry of condemnation arose.

Tadā ca turū nāma bhikkhu kokālikassa upajjhāyo anāgāmiphalaṃ patvā suddhāvāsesu nibbatto hoti. Sopi samāpattiyā vuṭṭhito taṃ dhikkāraṃ sutvā āgamma kokālikaṃ ovadi sāriputtamoggallānesu cittappasādajananatthaṃ. So tassāpi vacanaṃ aggahetvā aññadatthu tameva aparādhetvā kālaṃ katvā padumaniraye uppajji. Tenāha – “atha kho kokāliko bhikkhu tenevābādhena…pe… āghātetvā”ti.

At that time, a monk named Tudu, Kokālika’s preceptor, having attained the fruit of non-returning, had been reborn in the Pure Abodes. Having emerged from meditative attainment, he heard that reproach and came to admonish Kokālika, in order to generate confidence of mind in Sāriputta and Moggallāna. But Kokālika did not accept his words and, on the contrary, offended him as well, and so he died and was reborn in the Paduma Hell. Therefore, it is said: ‘Then the monk Kokālika, by that very illness… having harbored resentment…’

Atha kho brahmā sahampatīti ko ayaṃ brahmā, kasmā ca bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā etadavocāti?
