Ayaṃ kassapassa bhagavato sāsane sahako nāma bhikkhu anāgāmī hutvā suddhāvāsesu uppanno, tattha naṃ “sahampati brahmā”ti sañjānanti. So pana “ahaṃ bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā padumanirayaṃ kittessāmi, tato bhagavā bhikkhūnaṃ ārocessati. Kathānusandhikusalā bhikkhū tatthāyuppamāṇaṃ pucchissanti, bhagavā ācikkhanto ariyūpavāde ādīnavaṃ pakāsessatī”ti iminā kāraṇena bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā [M 2.0197] etadavoca. Bhagavā tatheva akāsi, aññataropi bhikkhu pucchi. Tena ca puṭṭho “seyyathāpi bhikkhū”tiādimāha.

‘Then Brahmā Sahampati’ – who was this Brahmā, and why did he approach the Blessed One and speak thus? This was a monk named Sahaka in the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, who became a non-returner and was reborn in the Pure Abodes. There, they recognize him as ‘Brahmā Sahampati.’ He thought, ‘I will approach the Blessed One and proclaim the Paduma Hell, so that the Blessed One may inform the monks. The monks, skilled in following up the conversation, will ask about the lifespan there, and the Blessed One, while explaining, will reveal the danger in reviling the Noble Ones.’ For this reason, he approached the Blessed One and spoke thus. The Blessed One acted accordingly, and a certain monk asked. Being questioned thus, he spoke beginning with, ‘Suppose, monks…’

Tattha vīsatikhārikoti māgadhakena patthena cattāro patthā kosalaraṭṭhe eko pattho hoti, tena patthena cattāro patthā āḷhakaṃ, cattāri āḷhakāni doṇaṃ, catudoṇā mānikā, catumānikā khārī, tāya khāriyā vīsatikhāriko. Tilavāhoti tilasakaṭaṃ. Abbudo nirayoti abbudo nāma koci paccekanirayo natthi, avīcimhiyeva abbudagaṇanāya paccanokāso pana “abbudo nirayo”ti vutto. Esa nayo nirabbudādīsu.

Here, ‘twenty khārī’ means: Four patthas by the Magadhan measure make one pattha in the Kosalan country. Four of that Kosalan pattha make one āḷhaka. Four āḷhakas make one doṇa. Four doṇas make one mānikā. Four mānikās make one khārī. Twenty of that khārī is meant. ‘Tilavāha’ means a cartload of sesame seeds. ‘Abbuda hell’ does not refer to any individual hell named Abbuda. Rather, it is a term for a place of rebirth within the Avīci hell, where the duration is reckoned in abbudas. The same principle applies to Nirabbuda and the others.

Tattha vassagaṇanāpi evaṃ veditabbā [P 2.0477] – yatheva hi sataṃ satasahassāni koṭi hoti, evaṃ sataṃ satasahassakoṭiyo pakoṭi nāma hoti, sataṃ satasahassapakoṭiyo koṭippakoṭi nāma, sataṃ satasahassakoṭippakoṭiyo nahutaṃ, sataṃ satasahassanahutāni ninnahutaṃ, sataṃ satasahassaninnahutāni [V 2.0179] ekaṃ abbudaṃ, tato vīsatiguṇaṃ nirabbudaṃ. Esa nayo sabbattha. Keci pana “tattha tattha paridevanānattenapi kammakaraṇanānattenapi imāni nāmāni laddhānī”ti vadanti, apare “sītanarakā eva ete”ti.

Here, the calculation of years should be understood thus: Just as one hundred times one hundred thousand is a koṭi, so one hundred times one hundred thousand koṭis is a pakoṭi. One hundred times one hundred thousand pakoṭis is a koṭippakoṭi. One hundred times one hundred thousand koṭippakoṭis is a nahuta. One hundred times one hundred thousand nahutas is a ninnahuta. One hundred times one hundred thousand ninnahutas is one abbuda. Twenty times this is a nirabbuda. This is the method everywhere. Some say, ‘These names were obtained based on the varying degrees of lamentation and the varying types of actions performed there.’ Others say, ‘These are simply cold hells.’

Athāparanti tadatthavisesatthadīpakaṃ gāthābandhaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Pāṭhavasena vuttavīsatigāthāsu hi ettha “sataṃ sahassāna”nti ayamekā eva gāthā vuttatthadīpikā, sesā visesatthadīpikā eva, avasāne gāthādvayameva pana mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vinicchitapāṭhe natthi. Tenāvocumha “vīsatigāthāsū”ti.

‘And further’ is said with reference to the composition of verses that illuminates the meaning and its particular details. Among the twenty verses stated according to the textual reading, only the verse beginning with ‘a hundred thousand’ illuminates the meaning that was stated, while the rest illuminate the particular details. However, the final two verses are not found in the Mahāaṭṭhakathā’s established reading. Therefore, we said, ‘in the twenty verses.’

663. Tattha kuṭhārīti attacchedakaṭṭhena kuṭhārisadisā pharusavācā. Chindatīti kusalamūlasaṅkhātaṃ attano mūlaṃyeva nikantati.

663. Here, ‘axe’ refers to harsh speech, which is like an axe in that it cuts its own self. ‘Cuts’ means it severs one’s own root, namely, the root consisting of wholesome qualities.

664. Nindiyanti ninditabbaṃ. Taṃ vā nindati yo pasaṃsiyoti yo uttamaṭṭhena pasaṃsāraho puggalo, taṃ vā so pāpicchatādīni āropetvā garahati. Vicinātīti upacināti. Kalinti aparādhaṃ.

664. ‘One blames what is blameworthy.’ Or, he blames one who is praiseworthy—that person who is worthy of praise in the highest sense—or he reviles him by falsely attributing evil desires and other faults to him. ‘He accumulates’ means he gathers. ‘Kali’ means offense.

665. Ayaṃ kalīti ayaṃ aparādho. Akkhesūti jūtakīḷanaakkhesu. Sabbassāpi sahāpi attanāti sabbena attano dhanenapi attanāpi saddhiṃ. Sugatesūpi [M 2.0198] suṭṭhu gatattā, sundarañca ṭhānaṃ gatattā sugatanāmakesu buddhapaccekabuddhasāvakesu. Manaṃ padosayeti yo manaṃ padūseyya. Tassāyaṃ manopadoso eva mahattaro kalīti vuttaṃ hoti.

665. ‘This is Kali’ means this is a fault. ‘In dice’ refers to dice used for gambling. ‘Even with all his own wealth and himself’ means with all his wealth and even with himself. ‘Even toward the Sugatas’—those who have gone well, the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples, so named because they have gone to an excellent state and have gone to a beautiful destination. ‘Corrupts the mind’—whoever would corrupt the mind. For him, this corruption of mind is indeed the greatest fault, it is said.

666. Kasmā? Yasmā sataṃ sahassānaṃ…pe… pāpakaṃ, yasmā vassagaṇanāya ettako so kālo, yaṃ kālaṃ ariyagarahī [P 2.0478] vācaṃ manañca paṇidhāya pāpakaṃ nirayaṃ upeti, tattha paccatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Idañhi saṅkhepena padumaniraye āyuppamāṇaṃ.

666. Why? Because for a hundred thousand… evil… because in the counting of years such is the period, the period during which one who disparages the noble ones, having directed speech and mind toward evil, goes to the evil hell, there he is tormented—so it is said. For this is, in brief, the life-span in the Paduma hell.

667. Idāni aparenapi nayena “ayameva mahattaro kali, yo sugatesu manaṃ padūsaye”ti imamatthaṃ vibhāvento “abhūtavādī”ti ādimāha. Tattha abhūtavādīti ariyūpavādavasena alikavādī. Nirayanti padumādiṃ. Pecca samā bhavantīti ito paṭigantvā nirayūpapattiyā samā bhavanti. Paratthāti paraloke.

667. Now, by another method, explaining the meaning of ‘this indeed is the greatest Kali, he who corrupts his mind toward the Sugatas,’ he begins with ‘a speaker of untruth.’ Here, ‘a speaker of untruth’ means one who speaks falsely by way of disparaging the noble ones. ‘Hell’ refers to Paduma and others. ‘After death, they become equal’ means having departed from here, they become equal in their rebirth in hell. ‘In the next world’ means in the other world.

668. Kiñca [V 2.0180] bhiyyo – yo appaduṭṭhassāti. Tattha manopadosābhāvena appaduṭṭho, avijjāmalābhāvena suddho, pāpicchābhāvena anaṅgaṇoti veditabbo. Appaduṭṭhattā vā suddhassa, suddhattā anaṅgaṇassāti evampettha yojetabbaṃ.

668. And what is more – ‘one who is uncorrupted.’ Here, ‘uncorrupted’ means free from mental corruption; ‘pure’ means free from the stain of ignorance; and ‘flawless’ means free from evil desires—this should be understood. Or, because he is uncorrupted, he is pure; because he is pure, he is flawless—thus it should be connected here.

669. Evaṃ sugatesu manopadosassa mahattarakalibhāvaṃ sādhetvā idāni vāritavatthugāthā nāma cuddasa gāthā āha. Imā kira kokālikaṃ mīyamānameva ovadantenāyasmatā mahāmoggallānena vuttā, “mahābrahmunā”ti eke. Tāsaṃ iminā suttena saddhiṃ ekasaṅgahatthaṃ ayamuddeso “yo lobhaguṇe anuyutto”tiādi. Tattha paṭhamagāthāya tāva “guṇo”ti niddiṭṭhattā anekakkhattuṃ pavattattā vā lobhoyeva lobhaguṇo, taṇhāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Avadaññūti avacanaññū buddhānampi ovādaṃ aggahaṇena. Maccharīti pañcavidhamacchariyena. Pesuṇiyaṃ anuyuttoti aggasāvakānaṃ bhedakāmatāya. Sesaṃ pākaṭameva. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yo, āvuso kokālika, tumhādiso anuyuttalobhataṇhāya lobhaguṇe anuyutto assaddho kadariyo avadaññū maccharī pesuṇiyaṃ anuyutto, so vacasā paribhāsati aññaṃ abhāsaneyyampi puggalaṃ. Tena taṃ vadāmi [P 2.0479] “mukhaduggā”ti gāthāttayaṃ.

669. Having thus established that mental corruption toward the Sugatas is the greatest demerit, he now speaks fourteen verses called the ‘Verses on Restrained Conduct.’ These were reportedly spoken by the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna to admonish Kokālika as he was dying—some say by Mahābrahmā. For the purpose of combining them with this discourse, their summary is as follows: ‘One who is devoted to the quality of greed,’ etc. Here, in the first verse, since it is specified as a ‘quality’ and because it occurs repeatedly, greed itself is the ‘quality of greed,’ which is a term for craving. ‘Unreceptive to advice’ means not understanding what is said, by not accepting the counsel even of the Buddhas. ‘Miserly’ refers to the five kinds of miserliness. ‘Devoted to slander’ means desiring to create a schism among the chief disciples. The rest is clear. This is what is said: ‘Friend Kokālika, one like you, devoted to greed and craving, attached to the quality of greed, faithless, stingy, unreceptive to advice, miserly, and devoted to slander, verbally abuses another, even a person who should not be spoken to in such a way. Therefore, I say to you the three verses beginning with “Foul-mouthed.”’

670. Tassāyaṃ [M 2.0199] anuttānapadattho – mukhadugga mukhavisama, vibhūta vigatabhūta, alikavādi, anariya asappurisa, bhūnahu bhūtihanaka, vuḍḍhināsaka, purisanta antimapurisa, kali alakkhipurisa, avajāta buddhassa avajātaputta.

670. The meaning of these difficult words is as follows: ‘Foul-mouthed’ means one with a wicked mouth; ‘vibhūta’ means one whose goodness has departed; a liar; ‘un-noble’ means not a good person; ‘destroyer of beings’ means a killer of beings; a destroyer of growth; ‘last of men’ means the lowest of men; ‘Kali’ means a man of misfortune; ‘degenerate’ means a degenerate son of the Buddha.

671. Rajamākirasīti kilesarajaṃ attani pakkhipasi. Papatanti sobbhaṃ. “Papāta”ntipi pāṭho, so evattho. “Papada”ntipi pāṭho, mahānirayanti attho.

671. ‘You scatter dust upon yourself’ means you cast the dust of defilements upon yourself. ‘You fall into a pit.’ There is also the reading ‘papāta,’ which has the same meaning. There is also the reading ‘papada,’ which means the great hell.

672. Eti hatanti ettha ha-iti nipāto, tanti taṃ kusalākusalakammaṃ. Atha vā hatanti gataṃ paṭipannaṃ, upacitanti attho. Suvāmīti sāmi tassa kammassa katattā. So hi taṃ kammaṃ labhateva, nāssa taṃ nassatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Yasmā ca labhati, tasmā dukkhaṃ mando…pe… kibbisakārī.

672. Regarding ‘eti hatanti’: here, ‘ha’ is a particle, and ‘taṃ’ refers to that wholesome or unwholesome kamma. Alternatively, ‘hataṃ’ means gone to, undertaken, or accumulated. Regarding ‘suvāmī’: ‘master’ means the owner of that kamma, because of having done it. For he surely receives that kamma; it does not perish for him, so it is said. And because he receives it, therefore ‘the fool suffers… the evil-doer.’

673. Idāni yaṃ dukkhaṃ mando passati, taṃ pakāsento “ayosaṅkusamāhataṭṭhāna”ntiādimāha. Tattha purimaupaḍḍhagāthāya tāva attho – yaṃ taṃ ayosaṅkusamāhataṭṭhānaṃ sandhāya bhagavatā “tamenaṃ, bhikkhave, nirayapālā pañcavidhabandhanaṃ nāma kāraṇaṃ [V 2.0181] karontī”ti (ma. ni. 3.250; a. ni. 3.36) vuttaṃ, taṃ upeti, evaṃ upento ca tattheva ādittāya lohapathaviyā nipajjāpetvā nirayapālehi pañcasu ṭhānesu ākoṭiyamānaṃ tattaṃ khilasaṅkhātaṃ tiṇhadhāramayasūlamupeti, yaṃ sandhāya bhagavatā vuttaṃ “tattaṃ ayokhilaṃ hatthe gamentī”tiādi. Tato parā upaḍḍhagāthā anekāni vassasahassāni tattha paccitvā pakkāvasesānubhavanatthaṃ anupubbena khārodakanadītīraṃ gatassa yaṃ taṃ “tattaṃ ayoguḷaṃ mukhe pakkhipanti, tattaṃ tambalohaṃ mukhe āsiñcantī”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tattha ayoti lohaṃ. Guḷasannibhanti beluvasaṇṭhānaṃ. Ayogahaṇena cettha tambalohaṃ, itarena ayoguḷaṃ [P 2.0480] veditabbaṃ. Patirūpanti katakammānurūpaṃ.

673. Now, to clarify the suffering that the fool experiences, it is said: “the place struck by an iron spike,” and so on. Here, first, is the meaning of the initial half-verse: he goes to that place struck by an iron spike, which the Blessed One referred to when he said, “Then, monks, the hell-guardians inflict what is called the fivefold torture.” And going thus, having been laid down on the blazing iron ground there, while being struck by the hell-guardians in five places, he approaches a red-hot, sharp-edged iron stake called a khila, which the Blessed One referred to when he said: “They drive a red-hot iron stake into his hand,” and so on. The subsequent half-verse was spoken in reference to one who, after being tormented there for many thousands of years, gradually reaches the shore of the river of caustic water in order to experience the remaining results. It refers to what was said: “They force a red-hot iron ball into his mouth; they pour molten bronze into his mouth.” Here, ‘ayo’ means iron. ‘Guḷasannibha’ means having the shape of a beluva fruit. By the word ‘ayo’ here, molten bronze is to be understood, and by the other word, an iron ball. ‘Patirūpaṃ’ means corresponding to the deeds done.

674. Tato parāsu gāthāsu na hi vaggūti “gaṇhatha, paharathā”tiādīni vadantā nirayapālā madhuravācaṃ na vadanti. Nābhijavantīti na [M 2.0200] sumukhabhāvena abhimukhā javanti, na sumukhā upasaṅkamanti, anayabyasanamāvahantā eva upasaṅkamantīti vuttaṃ hoti. Na tāṇamupentīti tāṇaṃ leṇaṃ paṭisaraṇaṃ hutvā na upagacchanti, gaṇhantā hanantā eva upentīti vuttaṃ hoti. Aṅgāre santhate sayantīti aṅgārapabbataṃ āropitā samānā anekāni vassasahassāni santhate aṅgāre senti. Ginisampajjalitanti samantato jalitaṃ sabbadisāsu ca sampajjalitaṃ aggiṃ. Pavisantīti mahāniraye pakkhittā samānā ogāhanti. Mahānirayo nāma yo so “catukkaṇṇo”ti (a. ni. 3.36) vutto, naṃ yojanasate ṭhatvā passataṃ akkhīni bhijjanti.

674. In the following verses, "they do not speak sweetly" means the hell-wardens do not utter such words as, "Seize him, strike him," in a pleasant voice. "They do not approach kindly" means they do not rush forward with friendly faces; it means they approach bringing only misfortune and disaster. "They do not offer protection" means they do not come as a refuge or shelter; it means they come only to seize and strike. "They lie on a bed of coals" means, having been made to ascend the mountain of coals, they lie on the spread-out coals for many thousands of years. "Blazing with fire" means the fire is blazing all around, completely blazing in every direction. "They enter" means, having been thrown into the Great Hell, they plunge in. The Great Hell is the one described as "four-cornered," where the eyes of one who sees it from a hundred yojanas away burst.

675. Jālena ca onahiyānāti ayojālena paliveṭhetvā migaluddakā migaṃ viya hananti. Idaṃ devadūte avuttakammakāraṇaṃ. Andhaṃva timisamāyantīti andhakaraṇena andhameva bahalandhakārattā “timisa”nti saññitaṃ dhūmaroruvaṃ nāma narakaṃ gacchanti. Tatra kira nesaṃ kharadhūmaṃ ghāyitvā akkhīni bhijjanti, tena “andhaṃvā”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ vitatañhi yathā mahikāyoti tañca andhatimisaṃ mahikāyo viya vitataṃ hotīti attho. “Vitthata”ntipi pāṭho. Idampi devadūte avuttakammakāraṇameva.

675. "And covered with a net" means they are killed by being enveloped in an iron net, just as hunters kill a deer. This refers to an action not mentioned in the Devadūta Sutta. "Blind, they enter the gloom" means they go to a hell named Dhūmaroruva, which is called "gloom" on account of its dense darkness, and they are blind because of its blinding effect. There, it is said, their eyes burst after inhaling the acrid smoke; hence it is said, "blind, as it were." "For that is spread out like a mass of mist" means that this blinding gloom is spread out like a mass of mist. "Vitthata" is also a reading. This too refers to an action not mentioned in the Devadūta Sutta.

676. Atha lohamayanti ayaṃ pana lohakumbhī pathavipariyantikā catunahutādhikāni dveyojanasatasahassāni gambhīrā samatittikā tatralohapūrā hoti. Paccanti hi tāsu cirarattanti tāsu kumbhīsu dīgharattaṃ paccanti. Agginisamāsūti aggisamāsu[P 2.0481]. Samuppilavāteti samuppilavantā[V 2.0182], sakimpi uddhaṃ sakimpi adho gacchamānā pheṇuddehakaṃ paccantīti vuttaṃ hoti. Devadūte vuttanayeneva taṃ veditabbaṃ.

676. "Then, this iron cauldron," refers to an iron cauldron extending to the periphery of the earth, two hundred and forty thousand yojanas deep, filled to the brim with molten metal. "There, they are roasted for a long time," means they are roasted for a long time in those cauldrons. "Like fire" means like fire. "Bobbing up and down" means, while bobbing up, sometimes going up and sometimes going down, they are roasted like a mass of foam. This should be understood in the same way as described in the Devadūta Sutta.

677. Pubbalohitamisseti pubbalohitamissāya lohakumbhiyā. Tattha kinti tattha. Yaṃ yaṃ disakanti disaṃ vidisaṃ. Adhisetīti gacchati. “Abhisetī”tipi pāṭho, tattha yaṃ yaṃ disaṃ allīyati apassayatīti attho. Kilissatīti bādhīyati. “Kilijjatī”tipi pāṭho, pūti hotīti attho. Samphusamānoti tena pubbalohitena phuṭṭho samāno. Idampi devadūte avuttakammakāraṇaṃ.

677. "Mixed with pus and blood" refers to an iron cauldron mixed with pus and blood. "There, in whatever direction" means in any direction or intermediate direction. "He lies upon" means he goes. "Abhiseti" is also a reading, meaning he clings to or leans upon any direction. "He is afflicted" means he is tormented. "Kilijjati" is also a reading, meaning he becomes putrid. "Being in contact" means being touched by that pus and blood. This too refers to an action not mentioned in the Devadūta Sutta.

678. Puḷavāvasatheti [M 2.0201] puḷavānaṃ āvāse. Ayampi lohakumbhīyeva devadūte “gūthanirayo”ti vuttā, tattha patitassa sūcimukhapāṇā chaviādīni chinditvā aṭṭhimiñjaṃ khādanti. Gantuṃ na hi tīramapatthīti apagantuṃ na hi tīraṃ atthi. “Tīravamatthī”tipi pāṭho, soyevattho. Tīrameva ettha “tīrava”nti vuttaṃ. Sabbasamā hi samantakapallāti yasmā tassā kumbhiyā uparibhāgepi nikujjitattā sabbattha samā samantato kaṭāhā, tasmā apagantuṃ tīraṃ natthīti vuttaṃ hoti.

678. "In the dwelling of worms" means in the abode of worms. This too is an iron cauldron, called the "Excrement Hell" in the Devadūta Sutta. There, for one who has fallen in, needle-mouthed creatures cut through the skin and so on and devour the bone marrow. "For there is no shore to go to" means there is no shore to escape to. "Tīravamatthi" is also a reading; the meaning is the same. Here, "tīrava" is used for "shore." "For all around are level basins" means that because the upper part of that cauldron is curved inwards, the basins are level everywhere all around; therefore, it is said there is no shore to escape to.

679. Asipattavanaṃ devadūte vuttanayameva. Tañhi dūrato ramaṇīyaṃ ambavanaṃ viya dissati, athettha lobhena nerayikā pavisanti, tato nesaṃ vāteritāni pattāni patitvā aṅgapaccaṅgāni chindanti. Tenāha – “taṃ pavisanti samucchidagattā”ti. Taṃ pavisanti tato suṭṭhu chinnagattā hontīti. Jivhaṃ baḷisena gahetvā ārajayārajayā vihanantīti tattha asipattavane vegena dhāvitvā patitānaṃ musāvādīnaṃ nerayikānaṃ nirayapālā jivhaṃ baḷisena nikkaḍḍhitvā yathā manussā allacammaṃ bhūmiyaṃ pattharitvā khilehi ākoṭenti, evaṃ ākoṭetvā pharasūhi phāletvā phāletvā ekamekaṃ [P 2.0482] koṭiṃ chindetvā vihananti, chinnachinnā koṭi punappunaṃ samuṭṭhāti. “Āracayāracayā”tipi pāṭho, āviñchitvā āviñchitvāti attho. Etampi devadūte avuttakammakāraṇaṃ.

679. The Sword-leaf Forest is as described in the Devadūta Sutta. From a distance, it appears delightful like a mango grove, and hell-beings enter it out of greed. Then leaves stirred by the wind fall and sever their major and minor limbs. Therefore it is said: "They enter it with their bodies thoroughly cut up." This means that when they enter it, their bodies become thoroughly cut up. "Having seized their tongue with a hook, they stretch it out again and again and torment them" means that in that Sword-leaf Forest, when hell-beings who were liars fall after running with speed, the hell-wardens pull out their tongues with a hook. Just as people spread a wet hide on the ground and pin it down with stakes, so too they pin it down, and splitting it again and again with axes, they torment them by cutting off each single tip. The severed tip grows back again and again. "Āracayāracayā" is also a reading, meaning "stretching and stretching." This too refers to an action not mentioned in the Devadūta Sutta.

680. Vetaraṇinti devadūte “mahatī khārodakā nadī”ti (ma. ni. 3.269) vuttanadiṃ. Sā kira gaṅgā viya udakabharitā dissati. Athettha nhāyissāma pivissāmāti nerayikā patanti. Tiṇhadhārakhuradhāranti tiṇhadhāraṃ khuradhāraṃ, tikkhadhārakhuradhāravatinti vuttaṃ hoti. Tassā kira nadiyā uddhamadho ubhayatīresu ca tiṇhadhārā khurā paṭipāṭiyā ṭhapitā viya [V 2.0183] tiṭṭhanti, tena sā “tiṇhadhārā khuradhārā”ti vuccati. Taṃ tiṇhadhārakhuradhāraṃ udakāsāya upenti allīyantīti attho. Evaṃ upentā ca pāpakammena coditā tattha mandā papatanti bālāti attho.

680. Vetaraṇī is the river mentioned in the Devadūta Sutta as "a great river of caustic water." It is said to appear full of water like the Ganges. Thinking, "Here we will bathe and drink," the hell-beings fall in. "With sharp edges, with razor blades" means sharp-edged and razor-edged; that is to say, possessing blades sharp as razors. It is said that along both banks of this river, above and below, sharp-edged razors stand as if arranged in rows. Thus, it is called "with sharp edges, with razor blades." Hoping for water, they approach and cling to that place of sharp razor-blades. And approaching thus, driven by their evil kamma, the foolish ones, the simpletons, fall in there.

681. Sāmā sabalāti etaṃ parato “soṇā”ti iminā yojetabbaṃ. Sāmavaṇṇā kammāsavaṇṇā ca soṇā khādantīti vuttaṃ hoti[M 2.0202]. Kākolagaṇāti kaṇhakākagaṇā. Paṭigiddhāti suṭṭhu sañjātagedhā hutvā, “mahāgijjhā”ti eke. Kulalāti kulalapakkhino, “senānametaṃ nāma”nti eke. Vāyasāti akaṇhakākā. Idampi devadūte avuttakammakāraṇaṃ. Tattha vuttānipi pana kānici idha na vuttāni, tāni etesaṃ purimapacchimabhāgattā vuttāneva hontīti veditabbāni.

681. "Sāmā sabalā" should be connected with the following "soṇā." The meaning is that dogs, being dark and variegated in color, devour. "Kākolagaṇā" means a flock of black crows. "Paṭigiddhā" means having become exceedingly greedy; some say "great vultures." "Kulalā" refers to kulala birds; some say this is a name for hawks. "Vāyasā" means non-black crows. This too is a cause of kamma not mentioned in the Devadūta Sutta. However, some things mentioned there are not mentioned here; they should be understood as having been stated, by virtue of being part of the preceding and succeeding sections.

682. Idāni sabbamevetaṃ narakavuttiṃ dassetvā ovadanto “kicchā vatāya”nti gāthamāha. Tassattho – kicchā vata ayaṃ idha narake nānappakārakammakaraṇabhedā vutti, yaṃ jano phusati kibbisakārī. Tasmā idha jīvitasese jīvitasantatiyā vijjamānāya idha loke ṭhitoyeva samāno saraṇagamanādikusaladhammānuṭṭhānena kiccakaro naro siyā bhaveyya. Kiccakaro bhavantopi ca sātaccakāritāvaseneva bhaveyya, na pamajje muhuttampi na pamādamāpajjeyyāti ayamettha [P 2.0483] samuccayavaṇṇanā. Yasmā pana vuttāvasesāni padāni pubbe vuttanayattā uttānatthattā ca suviññeyyāneva, tasmā anupadavaṇṇanā na katāti.

682. Now, having shown all this conduct of hell, he advises, speaking the verse, "Difficult indeed is this." The meaning is: difficult indeed is this conduct here in hell, with its various kinds of tortures and their distinctions, which a person who commits evil deeds experiences. Therefore, here, while a remainder of life or the continuity of life still exists, while still standing in this world, a person should be one who does what should be done by practicing wholesome qualities such as going for refuge. Even when one has become one who does what should be done, one should be persistent in doing so, and not be heedless even for a moment, not falling into negligence. This is the combined explanation here. However, because the remaining words are easily understood due to their clear meaning and the method previously stated, a word-by-word explanation is not given.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

The Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddakapāṭha.

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya kokālikasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Kokālika Sutta in the Commentary on the Suttanipāta is complete.

11. Nālakasuttavaṇṇanā

11. The Explanation of the Nālaka Sutta

685. Ānandajāteti [V 2.0184] nālakasuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Padumuttarassa kira bhagavato sāvakaṃ moneyyapaṭipadaṃ paṭipannaṃ disvā tathattaṃ abhikaṅkhamāno tato pabhuti kappasatasahassaṃ pāramiyo pūretvā asitassa isino bhāgineyyo nālako nāma tāpaso bhagavantaṃ dhammacakkappavattitadivasato sattame divase “aññātameta”ntiādīhi dvīhi gāthāhi moneyyapaṭipadaṃ pucchi. Tassa bhagavā “moneyyaṃ te upaññissa”ntiādinā nayena taṃ byākāsi. Parinibbute pana bhagavati saṅgītiṃ karontenāyasmatā mahākassapena āyasmā ānando tameva moneyyapaṭipadaṃ puṭṭho yena yadā ca samādapito nālako bhagavantaṃ pucchi[M 2.0203]. Taṃ sabbaṃ pākaṭaṃ katvā dassetukāmo “ānandajāte”tiādikā vīsati vatthugāthāyo vatvā abhāsi. Taṃ sabbampi “nālakasutta”nti vuccati.

685. The Nālaka Sutta is also known as the Ānandajāta. What is its origin? It is said that, desiring to attain such a state after seeing a disciple of the Blessed One Padumuttara practicing the path of sagely conduct, from that time onward he fulfilled the perfections for a hundred thousand eons. Then, Nālaka, the ascetic, nephew of the seer Asita, on the seventh day after the Blessed One had set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma, asked about the path of sagely conduct with the two verses beginning, "This is known." The Blessed One explained it to him with the method beginning, "I will teach you sagely conduct." However, after the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, when the Venerable Mahākassapa was holding the council, the Venerable Ānanda was questioned about that very path of sagely conduct—by whom and when Nālaka had been inspired to ask the Blessed One. Wishing to make all of this clear, he spoke twenty introductory verses beginning, "Joy having arisen." All of this is called the "Nālaka Sutta."

Tattha ānandajāteti samiddhijāte vuddhippatte. Patīteti tuṭṭhe. Atha vā ānandajāteti pamudite. Patīteti somanassajāte. Sucivasaneti akiliṭṭhavasane. Devānañhi kapparukkhanibbattāni vasanāni rajaṃ vā malaṃ vā na gaṇhanti. Dussaṃ gahetvāti idha dussasadisattā “dussa”nti laddhavohāraṃ dibbavatthaṃ ukkhipitvā. Asito isīti kaṇhasarīravaṇṇattā evaṃladdhanāmo isi. Divāvihāreti divāvihāraṭṭhāne. Sesaṃ padato uttānameva.

Therein, "ānandajāte" means: when prosperity had arisen, when growth had been attained. "Patīte" means: pleased. Alternatively, "ānandajāte" means: delighted; "patīte" means: when gladness had arisen. "Sucivasane" means: wearing unsoiled garments. For the garments produced from the divine wishing-trees do not gather dust or dirt. "Dussaṃ gahetvā" means: having lifted up the divine garment, which has gained the designation "cloth" because of its resemblance to cloth. "Asito isīti": the seer was so named because of his dark body color. "Divāvihāre" means: in the place for daytime abiding. The rest is clear from the words themselves.

Sambandhato pana – ayaṃ kira suddhodanassa pitu sīhahanurañño purohito suddhodanassapi anabhisittakāle sippācariyo hutvā abhisittakāle purohitoyeva ahosi. Tassa sāyaṃ pātaṃ rājupaṭṭhānaṃ āgatassa rājā daharakāle viya nipaccakāraṃ akatvā añjalikammamattameva karoti. Dhammatā kiresā [P 2.0484] pattābhisekānaṃ sakyarājūnaṃ. Purohito tena nibbijjitvā “pabbajjāmahaṃ mahārājā”ti āha. Rājā tassa nicchayaṃ ñatvā “tena hi, ācariya, mameva uyyāne vasitabbaṃ, yathā te ahaṃ abhiṇhaṃ passeyya”nti yāci. So “evaṃ hotū”ti paṭissuṇitvā tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā raññā upaṭṭhahiyamāno uyyāneyeva vasanto kasiṇaparikammaṃ katvā aṭṭha samāpattiyo pañcābhiññāyo ca nibbattesi. So tato pabhuti rājakule [V 2.0185] bhattakiccaṃ katvā himavantacātumahārājikabhavanādīnaṃ aññataraṃ gantvā divāvihāraṃ karoti. Athekadivasaṃ tāvatiṃsabhavanaṃ gantvā ratanavimānaṃ pavisitvā dibbaratanapallaṅke nisinno samādhisukhaṃ anubhavitvā sāyanhasamayaṃ vuṭṭhāya vimānadvāre ṭhatvā ito cito ca vilokento saṭṭhiyojanāya mahāvīthiyā celukkhepaṃ katvā bodhisattaguṇapasaṃsitāni thutivacanāni vatvā kīḷante sakkappamukhe deve addasa. Tenāha āyasmā ānando – “ānandajāte…pe… divāvihāre”ti.

Regarding the connection—it is said that this one was the family priest of King Sīhahanu, the father of Suddhodana. He also became the teacher of Suddhodana before his coronation and remained his priest after the coronation. Morning and evening, when he came to attend upon the king, the king no longer offered the same respectful welcome as when he was a youth, but merely performed the añjali gesture. This, it is said, was the custom for the Sakyan kings after their coronation. Disenchanted by this, the priest said, "Great king, I will go forth." Knowing his resolve, the king entreated him, "Then, teacher, you must dwell in my park so that I may see you often." He agreed, saying, "So be it," and after going forth as an ascetic, he lived in the park, supported by the king. There, he practiced the preliminary meditation on the kasiṇas and attained the eight meditative absorptions and the five higher knowledges. From then on, after taking his meal at the royal household, he would go to one of the divine abodes—such as the Himavanta or the realm of the Four Great Kings—to spend the day. One day, having gone to the Tāvatiṃsa realm, he entered a jeweled mansion and sat upon a celestial jeweled couch, enjoying the bliss of concentration. In the evening, he rose and stood at the mansion’s doorway, gazing around. He saw Sakka and the other prominent gods sporting about on the great thoroughfare sixty yojanas wide, tossing cloths and speaking words of praise extolling the virtues of the Bodhisatta. Thus, the Venerable Ānanda said: "Ānandajāte…pe… divāvihāre."

686. Tato so evaṃ disvāna deve…pe… kiṃ paṭicca. Tattha udaggeti abbhunnatakāye. Cittiṃ karitvānāti ādaraṃ katvā. Kalyarūpoti tuṭṭharūpo. Sesaṃ uttānatthameva.

686. Then, having seen the devas thus…pe… depending on what? Therein, "udagga" means with uplifted bodies. "Cittiṃ karitvāna" means having shown respect. "Kalyarūpo" means of pleased appearance. The rest is clear in meaning.

687. Idāni [M 2.0204] “yadāpi āsī”tiādigāthā uttānasambandhā eva. Padattho pana paṭhamagāthāya tāva saṅgamoti saṅgāmo. Jayo surānanti devānaṃ jayo.

687. Now, the verse beginning with "yadāpi āsī" is indeed straightforward in its connection. As for the meaning of the words, first, in that verse, "saṅgamo" means battle. "Jayo surānaṃ" means victory for the gods.

Tassāvibhāvatthaṃ ayamanupubbikathā veditabbā – sakko kira magadharaṭṭhe macalagāmavāsī tettiṃsamanussaseṭṭho magho nāma māṇavo hutvā satta vattapadāni pūretvā tāvatiṃsabhavane nibbatti saddhiṃ parisāya. Tato pubbadevā “āgantukadevaputtā āgatā, sakkāraṃ nesaṃ karissāmā”ti vatvā dibbapadumāni [P 2.0485] upanāmesuṃ, upaḍḍharajjena ca nimantesuṃ. Sakko upaḍḍharajjena asantuṭṭho sakaparisaṃ saññāpetvā ekadivasaṃ surāmadamatte te pāde gahetvā sinerupabbatapāde khipi. Tesaṃ sinerussa heṭṭhimatale dasasahassayojanaṃ asurabhavanaṃ nibbatti pāricchattakapaṭicchannabhūtāya citrapāṭaliyā upasobhitaṃ. Tato te satiṃ paṭilabhitvā tāvatiṃsabhavanaṃ apassantā “aho re naṭṭhā mayaṃ pānamadadosena, na dāni mayaṃ suraṃ pivimhā, asuraṃ pivimhā, na dānimhā surā, asurā dāni jātamhā”ti. Tato pabhuti “asurā”icceva uppannasamaññā hutvā “handa dāni devehi saddhiṃ saṅgāmemā”ti sineruṃ parito ārohiṃsu. Tato sakko asure yuddhena abbhuggantvā punapi samudde pakkhipitvā catūsu dvāresu attanā sadisaṃ indapaṭimaṃ māpetvā ṭhapesi. Tato asurā “appamatto vatāyaṃ sakko niccaṃ rakkhanto tiṭṭhatī”ti cintetvā punadeva nagaraṃ agamiṃsu. Tato devā attano jayaṃ ghosentā mahāvīthiyaṃ celukkhepaṃ karontā nakkhattaṃ kīḷiṃsu. Atha asito atītānāgate cattālīsakappe anussarituṃ samatthatāya “kiṃ nu kho imehi pubbepi evaṃ kīḷitapubba”nti āvajjento taṃ devāsurasaṅgāme devavijayaṃ disvā āha –

To clarify this matter, the following sequential account should be understood: It is said that Sakka, in the country of Magadha, residing in the village of Macala, was once a young man named Magha, the foremost of thirty-three men. Having fulfilled the seven vows, he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven together with his company. Then, the previous gods, saying, "Guest deities have arrived; let us honor them," offered divine lotuses and invited them to share half the kingdom. Unsatisfied with half the kingdom, Sakka instructed his company and, one day, while they were intoxicated with liquor, seized them by the feet and hurled them to the foot of Mount Sineru. There, at the lower level of Sineru, for ten thousand yojanas, the Asura realm arose, adorned by the Citrapāṭalī tree and overshadowed by the Pāricchattaka tree. Then, regaining their senses and not seeing the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, they cried, "Alas! We are ruined by the fault of intoxicating drink! Now we have drunk not sura, but asura! Now we are no longer suras, but have become asuras!" From then on, the designation "Asuras" arose, and they thought, "Come now, let us do battle with the gods!" So they ascended Sineru on all sides. Then Sakka, having gone up against the asuras in battle, threw them back into the ocean and had an image of Indra, identical to himself, created and placed at the four gates. Then the asuras, thinking, "Indeed, this Sakka is vigilant and stands constantly on guard," went back to their city. Then the gods, proclaiming their victory, tossed cloths and played festive games in the great street. Then Asita, being able to remember forty aeons into the past and future, considering, "Have they ever played like this before?", and seeing the gods' victory in the battle between the gods and asuras, said—

“Yadāpi [V 2.0186] āsī asurehi saṅgamo,

Jayo surānaṃ asurā parājitā;

Tadāpi netādiso lomahaṃsano”ti.

"Even when there was a battle with the asuras, and the victory was to the suras, the asuras defeated; even then, there was no such hair-raising thrill."

Tasmimpi kāle etādiso lomahaṃsano pamodo na āsi. Kimabbhutaṃ daṭṭhu marū pamoditāti ajja pana kiṃ abbhutaṃ disvā evaṃ devā pamuditāti.

Even at that time, such a hair-raising joy did not arise. What marvel did the gods see to be so delighted? But today, what marvel have the gods seen that they are so delighted?

688. Dutiyagāthāya [M 2.0205] seḷentīti mukhena usseḷanasaddaṃ muñcanti. Gāyanti nānāvidhāni gītāni, vādayanti aṭṭhasaṭṭhi tūriyasahassāni, phoṭentīti apphoṭenti. Pucchāmi vohanti attanā āvajjetvā ñātuṃ samatthopi tesaṃ vacanaṃ sotukāmatāya pucchati. Merumuddhavāsineti sinerumuddhani vasante. Sinerussa hi heṭṭhimatale dasayojanasahassaṃ [P 2.0486] asurabhavanaṃ, majjhimatale dvisahassaparittadīpaparivārā cattāro mahādīpā, uparimatale dasayojanasahassaṃ tāvatiṃsabhavanaṃ. Tasmā devā “merumuddhavāsino”ti vuccanti. Mārisāti deve āmanteti, nidukkhā nirābādhāti vuttaṃ hoti.

688. In the second verse, 'seḷenti' means they emit a sound of exultation with their mouths. 'Gāyanti' means they sing various kinds of songs; 'vādayanti' means they play sixty-eight thousand musical instruments; 'phoṭenti' means they clap their hands. 'Pucchāmi vo' means, though capable of understanding by reflecting on it himself, he asks out of a desire to hear their words. 'Merumuddhavāsino' refers to those dwelling on the summit of Mount Meru. For at the lower level of Mount Meru lies the ten-thousand-yojana realm of the asuras; in the middle level are the four great continents surrounded by two thousand minor islands; and at the upper level is the ten-thousand-yojana realm of the Tāvatiṃsa gods. Therefore, the gods are called 'dwellers on Meru’s summit.' 'Mārisā' is how he addresses the gods, meaning 'you who are free from suffering and affliction.'

689. Athassa tamatthaṃ ārocentehi devehi vuttāya tatiyagāthāya bodhisattoti bujjhanakasatto, sammāsambodhiṃ gantuṃ araho satto ratanavaroti vararatanabhūto. Tenamha tuṭṭhāti tena kāraṇena mayaṃ tuṭṭhā. So hi buddhattaṃ patvā tathā dhammaṃ desessati, yathā mayañca aññe ca devagaṇā sekkhāsekkhabhūmiṃ pāpuṇissāma. Manussāpissa dhammaṃ sutvā ye na sakkhissanti parinibbātuṃ, te dānādīni katvā devaloke paripūressantīti ayaṃ kira nesaṃ adhippāyo. Tattha “tuṭṭhā kalyarūpā”ti kiñcāpi idaṃ padadvayaṃ atthato abhinnaṃ, tathāpi “kimabbhutaṃ daṭṭhu marū pamoditā, kiṃ devasaṅgho atiriva kalyarūpo”ti imassa pañhadvayassa vissajjanatthaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

689. Then, in the third verse, spoken by the gods explaining this matter: 'bodhisatto' means a being who is to awaken. 'ratanavaro' means a supreme jewel-like being, a being worthy of attaining perfect enlightenment. 'Tenamha tuṭṭhā' means 'for that reason we are pleased.' For when he attains Buddhahood, he will teach the Dhamma in such a way that we and other hosts of gods will reach the stages of learners and non-learners. Even humans who hear his Dhamma but are not able to attain final Nibbāna will, by performing acts of generosity and so forth, fill up the heavenly world—this, it seems, is their intention. Here, although the two phrases 'tuṭṭhā kalyarūpā' are not different in meaning, it should be understood that they are spoken to answer the two questions: 'What wonder have the Maruts seen that they are so delighted?' and 'Why is the assembly of gods so exceedingly splendid?'

690. Idāni yena adhippāyena bodhisatte jāte tuṭṭhā ahesuṃ, taṃ āvikarontehi vuttāya catutthagāthāya sattaggahaṇena devamanussaggahaṇaṃ, pajāgahaṇena sesagatiggahaṇaṃ. Evaṃ dvīhi padehi pañcasupi gatīsu seṭṭhabhāvaṃ dasseti. Tiracchānāpi hi sīhādayo asantāsādiguṇayuttā, tepi ayameva atiseti. Tasmā “pajānamuttamo”ti vutto. Devamanussesu pana ye attahitāya paṭipannādayo cattāro puggalā, tesu ubhayahitapaṭipanno aggapuggalo [V 2.0187] ayaṃ, naresu ca usabhasadisattā narāsabho. Tenassa thutiṃ bhaṇantā idampi padadvayamāhaṃsu.

690. Now, in the fourth verse, spoken by those revealing the intention with which they rejoiced at the Bodhisatta's birth: by the term 'satta' (beings), gods and humans are included; by the term 'pajā' (creatures), the remaining destinations are included. Thus, with these two terms, his supremacy among the five destinations is shown. For even among animals, lions and others possess qualities such as fearlessness, yet this one surpasses them. Therefore, he is called 'the highest among creatures.' Among gods and humans, there are four types of individuals, such as those who have embarked on the path for their own benefit; among them, this one, who has embarked on the path for the benefit of both, is the foremost individual. And among men, because he is like a bull, he is a 'narāsabho,' a bull among men. Therefore, uttering his praise, they spoke these two terms as well.

691. Pañcamagāthāya [M 2.0206] taṃ saddanti taṃ devehi vuttavacanasaddaṃ. Avasarīti otari. Tada bhavananti tadā bhavanaṃ.

691. In the fifth verse, 'taṃ saddaṃ' means that sound, the sound of the words spoken by the gods. 'Avasarī' means he descended. 'Tadā bhavanaṃ' means 'then the mansion.'

692. Chaṭṭhagāthāya tatoti asitassa vacanato anantaraṃ. Ukkāmukhevāti ukkāmukhe eva, mūsāmukheti vuttaṃ hoti. Sukusalasampahaṭṭhanti sukusalena suvaṇṇakārena [P 2.0487] saṅghaṭṭitaṃ, saṅghaṭṭentena tāpitanti adhippāyo. Daddallamānanti vijjotamānaṃ. Asitavhayassāti asitanāmassa dutiyena nāmena kaṇhadevilassa isino.

692. In the sixth verse, 'tato' means immediately after Asita’s words. 'Ukkāmukhe' means 'in the mouth of a furnace'; it is said to mean 'in the mouth of a crucible.' 'Sukusalasampahaṭṭhaṃ' means 'fashioned by a very skilled goldsmith'; the meaning is that it was heated while being fashioned. 'Daddallamānaṃ' means 'shining brightly.' 'Asitavhayassa' means of the sage named Asita, whose second name is Kaṇhadevila.

693. Sattamagāthāya tārāsabhaṃ vāti tārānaṃ usabhasadisaṃ, candanti adhippāyo. Visuddhanti abbhādiupakkilesarahitaṃ. Saradarivāti sarade iva. Ānandajātoti savanamatteneva uppannāya pītiyā pītijāto. Alattha pītinti disvā punapi pītiṃ labhi.

693. In the seventh verse, 'tārāsabhaṃ vā' means 'like the bull among the stars'; the meaning is the moon. 'Visuddhaṃ' means 'pure,' free from defilements such as clouds. 'Saradariva' means 'as in autumn.' 'Ānandajāto' means 'joy arose,' that is, joy arose in him from the joy that had arisen merely upon hearing. 'Alattha pītiṃ' means 'he obtained joy,' that is, upon seeing, he obtained joy again.

694. Tato paraṃ bodhisattassa devehi sadā payujjamānasakkāradīpanatthaṃ vuttaaṭṭhamagāthāya anekasākhanti anekasalākaṃ. Sahassamaṇḍalanti rattasuvaṇṇamayasahassamaṇḍalayuttaṃ. Chattanti dibbasetacchattaṃ. Vītipatantīti sarīraṃ bījamānā patanuppatanaṃ karonti.

694. Thereafter, to illustrate the honors constantly bestowed upon the Bodhisatta by the devas, regarding the eighth verse that was spoken: 'Anekasākhanti' means 'many-branched,' that is, with many standards. 'Sahassamaṇḍalanti' means 'with a thousand circles,' that is, adorned with a thousand discs made of red gold. 'Chattanti' means 'a parasol,' that is, a divine white parasol. 'Vītipatantīti' means 'they fall around,' that is, fanning the body, they rise and fall.

695. Navamagāthāya jaṭīti jaṭilo. Kaṇhasirivhayoti kaṇhasaddena ca sirisaddena ca avhayamāno. Taṃ kira “sirikaṇho”tipi avhayanti āmantenti, ālapantīti vuttaṃ hoti. Paṇḍukambaleti rattakambale. Adhikārato cettha “kumāra”nti vattabbaṃ, pāṭhaseso vā kātabbo. Purimagāthāya ca ahatthapāsagataṃ sandhāya “disvā”ti vuttaṃ. Idha pana hatthapāsagataṃ paṭiggahaṇatthaṃ upanītaṃ, tasmā puna vacanaṃ “disvā”ti. Purimaṃ vā dassanapītilābhāpekkhaṃ gāthāvasāne “vipulamalattha pīti”nti vacanato, idaṃ paṭiggahāpekkhaṃ avasāne “sumano paṭiggahe”ti vacanato. Purimañca kumārasambandhameva, idaṃ setacchattasambandhampi. Disvāti satasahassagghanake gandhārarattakambale suvaṇṇanikkhaṃ viya kumāraṃ “chattaṃ marū”ti ettha vuttappakāraṃ setacchattaṃ dhāriyantaṃ muddhani disvā. Keci pana “idaṃ mānusakaṃ chattaṃ sandhāya vutta”nti bhaṇanti. Yatheva hi devā, evaṃ manussāpi chattacāmaramorahatthatālavaṇṭavāḷabījanihatthā mahāpurisaṃ upagacchantīti. Evaṃ santepi [M 2.0207] na tassa [P 2.0488] vacanena kocipi atisayo atthi, tasmā yathāvuttameva [V 2.0188] sundaraṃ. Paṭiggaheti ubhohi hatthehi paṭiggahesi. Isiṃ kira vandāpetuṃ kumāraṃ upanesuṃ. Athassa pādā parivattitvā isissa matthake patiṭṭhahiṃsu. So tampi acchariyaṃ disvā udaggacitto sumano paṭiggahesi.

695. In the ninth verse, 'jaṭī' means 'one with matted hair,' that is, an ascetic with matted hair. 'Kaṇhasirivhayoti' means 'being called by Kaṇha and Siri,' that is, being called by the name Kaṇha and the name Siri. It is said that they also called him 'Sirikaṇha,' meaning they addressed or spoke to him. 'Paṇḍukambale' means 'on a yellow blanket,' that is, on a red blanket. Here, due to context, 'kumāra' (prince) should be understood, or the remainder of the passage should be supplied. In the previous verse, 'disvā' (having seen) was said with reference to seeing him when he was not within arm's reach. Here, however, he was brought within arm's reach for the purpose of receiving; hence, the repetition of the word 'disvā.' Or, the former use of 'disvā' refers to the expectation of gaining joy from seeing, as indicated by the phrase 'he obtained abundant joy' at the end of the verse; this latter use refers to the expectation of acceptance, as indicated by the phrase 'he gladly accepted' at the end. The former seeing relates only to the prince, while this seeing also connects to the white parasol. 'Disvāti' means 'having seen,' that is, seeing the white parasol of the kind mentioned in 'chattaṃ marū' being held over the head of the prince, who was like a golden nikkha on a red Gandhāra blanket worth a hundred thousand. Some, however, say that this refers to a human parasol, for just as devas do, humans also approach great beings with parasols, yak-tail whisks, peacock-feather fans, palm-leaf fans, and fly-whisks in hand. Even so, there is no special significance in his words, so the aforementioned explanation is preferable. 'Paṭiggaheti' means 'he accepted,' that is, he accepted with both hands. They say they brought the prince to make him pay homage to the sage. Then his feet turned and rested on the sage’s head. Seeing this marvel too, he, with elated mind, gladly accepted him.

696. Dasamagāthāyaṃ jigīsakoti jigīsanto magganto pariyesanto, upaparikkhantoti vuttaṃ hoti. Lakkhaṇamantapāragūti lakkhaṇānaṃ vedānañca pāraṃ gato. Anuttarāyanti anuttaro ayaṃ. So kira attano abhimukhāgatesu mahāsattassa pādatalesu cakkāni disvā tadanusārena sesalakkhaṇāni jigīsanto sabbaṃ lakkhaṇasampattiṃ disvā “addhāyaṃ buddho bhavissatī”ti ñatvā evamāha.

696. In the tenth verse, 'jigīsako' means 'one who desires to conquer,' that is, one who seeks, searches, or investigates. 'Lakkhaṇamantapāragū' means 'one who has gone to the far shore of marks and mantras,' that is, one who has gone to the far shore of marks and the Vedas. 'Anuttarāyaṃ' means 'this is unsurpassed,' that is, this one is unsurpassed. It is said that he saw the wheels on the soles of the Great Being who had approached him and, in accordance with that, seeking the remaining marks, seeing all the perfection of marks, he knew, 'Assuredly, this one will become a Buddha,' and thus spoke.

697. Ekādasāyaṃ athattano gamananti paṭisandhivasena arūpagamanaṃ. Akalyarūpo gaḷayati assukānīti taṃ attano arūpūpapattiṃ anussaritvā “na dānāhaṃ assa dhammadesanaṃ sotuṃ lacchāmī”ti atuṭṭharūpo balavasokābhibhavena domanassajāto hutvā assūni pāteti gaḷayati. “Garayatī”tipi pāṭho. Yadi panesa rūpabhave cittaṃ nameyya, kiṃ tattha na uppajjeyya, yenevaṃ rodatīti? Na na uppajjeyya, akusalatāya panetaṃ vidhiṃ na jānāti. Evaṃ santepi domanassuppattiyevassa ayuttā samāpattilābhena vikkhambhitattāti ce? Na, vikkhambhitattā eva. Maggabhāvanāya samucchinnā hi kilesā na uppajjanti, samāpattilābhīnaṃ pana balavapaccayena uppajjanti. Uppanne kilese parihīnajjhānattā kutassa arūpagamananti ce? Appakasirena punādhigamato. Samāpattilābhino hi uppanne kilese balavavītikkamaṃ anāpajjantā vūpasantamatteyeva kilesavege puna taṃ visesaṃ appakasirenevādhigacchanti, “parihīnavisesā ime”tipi duviññeyyā honti, tādiso ca eso. No ce kumāre bhavissati antarāyoti na bhavissati nu kho imasmiṃ kumāre [P 2.0489] antarāyo.

697. In the eleventh verse, 'athattano gamana' (then his going) refers to his going to the formless realm through rebirth-linking. 'Akalyarūpo gaḷayati assukāni' (the unhappy one sheds tears) means that, reflecting on his own rebirth in the formless realm, he becomes discontent, thinking, 'Now I will not get to hear his Dhamma teaching,' and overwhelmed by strong sorrow, he becomes distressed and sheds tears. There is also a variant reading, 'garayati' (he grieves). But if his mind were inclined toward the realm of form, why would he not be reborn there, that he weeps thus? It is not that he would not be reborn there, but due to unskillfulness he does not know this method. Even so, is not the arising of distress inappropriate for him, since his defilements are suppressed by the attainment? No, it is because they are merely suppressed. Defilements eradicated by path development do not arise, but for those who have attained meditative absorption, they can arise due to strong conditions. If defilements arise, how can he go to the formless realm, having fallen from jhāna? Because he can regain it again with little difficulty. Those who attain absorption, when defilements arise, do not commit grave transgressions; as soon as the force of the defilements subsides, they easily regain that special attainment. They are hard to recognize as 'those who have fallen from their special state,' and such a one is he. 'No ce kumāre bhavissati antarāyo' (if there is no obstacle for the boy) means 'will there indeed be no obstacle for this boy?'

698. Dvādasāyaṃ na orakāyanti ayaṃ orako paritto na hoti. Uttaragāthāya vattabbaṃ buddhabhāvaṃ sandhāyāha.

698. In the twelfth verse, 'na orakāyaṃ' (not of an inferior kind) means 'this one is not inferior or limited.' He spoke with reference to the state of Buddhahood, which is to be stated in the following verse.

699. Terasāyaṃ [M 2.0208] sambodhiyagganti sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ. Tañhi aviparītabhāvena sammā bujjhanato sambodhi, katthaci āvaraṇābhāvena sabbañāṇuttamato “agga”nti vuccati. Phusissatīti pāpuṇissati. Paramavisuddhadassīti nibbānadassī. Tañhi ekantavisuddhattā paramavisuddhaṃ. Vitthārikassāti vitthārikaṃ assa. Brahmacariyanti sāsanaṃ.

699. In the thirteenth verse, 'sambodhiyagga' (the pinnacle of enlightenment) refers to omniscient knowledge. For because one awakens perfectly without deviation, it is called enlightenment (sambodhi), and because it is the highest of all knowledge due to the absence of any obstruction, it is called the 'pinnacle' (agga). 'Phusissati' (will touch) means 'will attain.' 'Paramavisuddhadassī' (the seer of supreme purity) means 'the seer of Nibbāna.' For because it is utterly pure, Nibbāna is supremely pure. 'Vitthārikassā' means 'it will be widespread for him.' 'Brahmacariya' (the holy life) refers to the Dispensation.

700. Cuddasāyaṃ [V 2.0189] athantarāti antarāyeva assa, sambodhippattito orato evāti vuttaṃ hoti. Na sossanti na suṇissaṃ. Asamadhurassāti asamavīriyassa. Aṭṭoti āturo. Byasanaṃ gatoti sukhavināsaṃ patto. Aghāvīti dukkhito, sabbaṃ domanassuppādameva sandhāyāha. Domanassena hi so āturo. Tañcassa sukhabyasanato byasanaṃ, sukhavināsanatoti vuttaṃ hoti. Tena ca so cetasikaaghabhūtena aghāvī.

700. In the fourteenth verse, 'athantarā' (then an obstacle) means 'there would indeed be an obstacle for him,' that is, only before attaining enlightenment. 'Na sossāmi' (I will not hear) means 'I will not get to hear.' 'Asamadhurassā' (of the one with an unequalled burden) means 'of the one with unequalled energy.' 'Aṭṭo' (afflicted) means 'diseased.' 'Byasanaṃ gato' (gone to ruin) means 'having attained the destruction of happiness.' 'Aghāvī' (the suffering one) means 'the sorrowful one'—all this refers to the arising of displeasure. For he is afflicted by displeasure. And that ruin for him is the destruction of happiness, meaning the loss of happiness. Thus, he is a suffering one due to that mental affliction.

701. Pannarasāyaṃ vipulaṃ janetvānāti vipulaṃ janetvā. Ayameva vā pāṭho. Niggamāti niggato. Evaṃ niggato ca so bhāgineyyaṃ sayanti sakaṃ bhāgineyyaṃ, attano bhaginiyā puttanti vuttaṃ hoti. Samādapesīti attano appāyukabhāvaṃ ñatvā kaniṭṭhabhaginiyā ca puttassa nālakassa māṇavakassa upacitapuññataṃ attano balena ñatvā “vuḍḍhippatto pamādampi āpajjeyyā”ti naṃ anukampamāno bhaginiyā gharaṃ gantvā “kahaṃ nālako”ti. “Bahi, bhante, kīḷatī”ti. “Ānetha na”nti āṇāpetvā taṅkhaṇaṃyeva tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbājetvā samādapesi ovadi anusāsi. Kathaṃ? “Buddhoti ghosaṃ…pe… brahmacariya”nti soḷasamagāthamāha.

701. In the fifteenth verse, 'vipulaṃ janetvāna' (having produced abundantly) means 'having produced abundantly.' Or this is the correct reading. 'Niggama' (gone out) means 'he went forth.' Thus, having gone forth, he initiated his nephew—meaning his own nephew, the son of his sister; it is said. 'Samādapesi' (he encouraged him) means that, knowing his own short lifespan and recognizing through his own power the accumulated merit of the young Nālaka, the son of his youngest sister, and out of compassion, thinking, 'Having reached maturity, he might still fall into negligence,' he went to his sister’s house and asked, 'Where is Nālaka?' She replied, 'Outside, venerable sir, playing.' He commanded, 'Bring him here,' and at that very moment, he ordained him into the ascetic life and encouraged, advised, and instructed him. How? He spoke sixteen verses, from 'The word "Buddha"' up to 'the holy life'.

702. Tattha yada paratoti yadā parato. Dhammamagganti paramadhammassa nibbānassa maggaṃ, dhammaṃ vā aggaṃ saha paṭipadāya nibbānaṃ. Tasminti tassa santike. Brahmacariyanti samaṇadhammaṃ.

702. Therein, 'yada parato' (when from another) means 'when from another.' 'Dhammamaggaṃ' (the path of Dhamma) means 'the path to the supreme Dhamma, Nibbāna,' or 'the supreme Dhamma, Nibbāna, together with the practice.' 'Tasmiṃ' (in that) means 'in his presence.' 'Brahmacariyaṃ' (the holy life) refers to the ascetic's practice.

703. Sattarasāyaṃ tādināti tassaṇṭhitena, tasmiṃ samaye kilesavikkhambhane [P 2.0490] samādhilābhe ca sati vikkhambhitakilesena samāhitacittena cāti adhippāyo. Anāgate paramavisuddhadassināti “ayaṃ nālako anāgate kāle bhagavato santike paramavisuddhaṃ nibbānaṃ passissatī”ti [M 2.0209] evaṃ diṭṭhattā so isi iminā pariyāyena “anāgate paramavisuddhadassī”ti vutto. Tena anāgate paramavisuddhadassinā. Upacitapuññasañcayoti padumuttarato pabhuti katapuññasañcayo. Patikkhanti āgamayamāno. Parivasīti pabbajitvā tāpasavesena vasi. Rakkhitindriyoti rakkhitasotindriyo hutvā. So kira tato pabhuti udake na nimujji “udakaṃ pavisitvā sotindriyaṃ vināseyya, tato dhammassavanabāhiro bhaveyya”nti cintetvā.

703. In the seventeenth verse, 'tādinā' (by such a one) means 'by one established in that state'; the meaning is that at that time, with defilements suppressed and concentration attained, one has a mind with defilements suppressed and composed. 'Anāgate paramavisuddhadassī' (in the future, one who sees supreme purity) means that the sage, having seen that 'this Nālaka in a future time will see the supremely pure Nibbāna in the presence of the Blessed One,' is thus called 'one who sees supreme purity in the future' by this means. Therefore, by him who sees supreme purity in the future. 'Upacitapuññasañcayo' (with an accumulated store of merit) means 'the accumulation of merit made since the time of the Buddha Padumuttara.' 'Patikkhaṃ' (awaiting) means 'expecting, anticipating.' 'Parivasī' (he lived) means 'having gone forth, he lived in ascetic garb.' 'Rakkhitindriyo' (with guarded faculties) means 'having guarded his ear faculty.' It is said that from then on, he did not submerge himself in water, thinking, 'If I enter the water, I might impair my ear faculty, and then I would be unable to hear the Dhamma.'

704. Aṭṭhārasāyaṃ sutvāna ghosanti so nālako evaṃ parivasanto anupubbena bhagavatā sambodhiṃ patvā bārāṇasiyaṃ dhammacakke pavattite taṃ “bhagavatā dhammacakkaṃ pavattitaṃ, sammāsambuddho [V 2.0190] vata so bhagavā uppanno”tiādinā nayena jinavaracakkavattane pavattaghosaṃ attano atthakāmāhi devatāhi āgantvā ārocitaṃ sutvā. Gantvāna disvā isinisabhanti sattāhaṃ devatāhi moneyyakolāhale kayiramāne sattame divase isipatanaṃ gantvā “nālako āgamissati, tassa dhammaṃ desessāmī”ti iminā ca abhisandhinā varabuddhāsane nisinnaṃ disvā nisabhasadisaṃ isinisabhaṃ bhagavantaṃ. Pasannoti saha dassaneneva pasannacitto hutvā. Moneyyaseṭṭhanti ñāṇuttamaṃ, maggañāṇanti vuttaṃ hoti. Samāgate asitāvhayassa sāsaneti asitassa isino ovādakāle anuppatte. Tena hi – “yadā vivarati dhammamaggaṃ, tadā gantvā samayaṃ paripucchamāno carassu tasmiṃ bhagavati brahmacariya”nti anusiṭṭho, ayañca so kālo. Tena vuttaṃ – “samāgate asitāvhayassa sāsane”ti. Sesamettha pākaṭameva.

704. In the eighteenth verse, 'sutvāna ghosaṃ' (having heard the sound) means: that Nālaka, while living thus, when the Blessed One had gradually attained enlightenment and set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion at Bārāṇasī, heard that proclamation concerning the turning of the wheel by the supreme Victor, which was announced by deities who came desiring his welfare, saying: 'The Blessed One has set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion; indeed the Blessed One, the Fully Enlightened One, has arisen,' and so forth. 'Gantvāna disvā isinisabhaṃ' (having gone and seen the bull among sages) means: while the deities were making a joyous uproar about the sage's path for seven days, on the seventh day, having gone to Isipatana, he saw the Blessed One, the bull among sages, who is like a bull, seated on the excellent Buddha-throne with this intention: 'Nālaka will come; I shall teach him the Dhamma.' 'Pasanno' (delighted) means: having become delighted in mind at the very sight of him. 'Moneyyaseṭṭhaṃ' (the foremost sagehood) means the highest knowledge; that is to say, the knowledge of the path. 'Samāgate asitāvhayassa sāsane' (when the instruction of the one named Asita had arrived) means: when the time for the advice of the sage Asita had come. For he had been instructed: 'When he reveals the path of Dhamma, then go and, inquiring at the proper time, live the holy life under that Blessed One.' And this was that time. Hence it is said: 'When the instruction of the one named Asita had arrived.' The rest here is quite clear.

Ayaṃ tāva vatthugāthāvaṇṇanā.

Thus far is the commentary on the introductory verses.

705. Pucchāgāthādvaye aññātametanti viditaṃ mayā etaṃ. Yathātathanti aviparītaṃ. Ko adhippāyo? Yaṃ asito “sambodhiyaggaṃ phusissatāyaṃ kumāro”ti ñatvā “buddhoti [P 2.0491] ghosaṃ yada parato suṇosi, sambodhippatto vivarati dhammamagga”nti maṃ avaca, tadetaṃ mayā asitassa vacanaṃ ajja bhagavantaṃ sakkhiṃ disvā “yathātathamevā”ti aññātanti. Taṃ tanti tasmā taṃ. Sabbadhammāna pāragunti hemavatasutte vuttanayena chahi ākārehi. Sabbadhammānaṃ pāragataṃ.

705. In the two verses of questioning, 'aññātametaṃ' (this is known) means 'this is known by me.' 'Yathātathaṃ' (as it truly is) means 'without distortion.' What is the meaning? 'That word of Asita—who, knowing "this prince will touch the summit of enlightenment," told me, "When you hear from another the sound ‘Buddha!’, one who has attained enlightenment is revealing the path of Dhamma"—is known by me today as being just as it truly is, having seen the Blessed One with my own eyes.' 'Taṃ' means 'therefore, that one.' 'Sabbadhammāna pāraguṃ' (one who has gone to the far shore of all things) means one who has gone to the far shore of all things in six ways, according to the method stated in the Hemavata Sutta.

706. Anagāriyupetassāti [M 2.0210] anagāriyaṃ upetassa, pabbajitassāti attho. Bhikkhācariyaṃ jigīsatoti ariyehi āciṇṇaṃ anupakkiliṭṭhaṃ bhikkhācariyaṃ pariyesamānassa. Moneyyanti munīnaṃ santakaṃ. Uttamaṃ padanti uttamapaṭipadaṃ. Sesamettha pākaṭameva.

706. 'Anagāriyupetassa' means 'of one who has entered the homeless life'; that is, of one who has gone forth. 'Bhikkhācariyaṃ jigīsato' means 'of one seeking the alms-round,' that is, of one searching for the untainted alms-round practiced by the noble ones. 'Moneyyaṃ' means 'that which belongs to the sages.' 'Uttamaṃ padaṃ' (the highest state) means 'the supreme practice.' The rest here is quite clear.

707. Athassa evaṃ puṭṭho bhagavā “moneyyaṃ te upaññissa”ntiādinā nayena moneyyapaṭipadaṃ byākāsi. Tattha upaññissanti upaññāpeyyaṃ, vivareyyaṃ paññāpeyyanti attho. Dukkaraṃ durabhisambhavanti kātuñca dukkhaṃ kayiramānañca sambhavituṃ sahituṃ dukkhanti vuttaṃ hoti. Ayaṃ panettha adhippāyo – ahaṃ te moneyyaṃ paññāpeyyaṃ, yadi naṃ kātuṃ vā abhisambhotuṃ vā sukhaṃ bhaveyya, evaṃ pana dukkaraṃ durabhisambhavaṃ puthujjanakālato pabhuti kiliṭṭhacittaṃ anuppādetvā paṭipajjitabbato. Tathā hi naṃ ekassa buddhassa ekova sāvako karoti ca sambhoti cāti.

707. Then, having been asked thus, the Blessed One explained the practice of sagehood in the manner beginning, 'I will explain sagehood to you.' Therein, 'I will explain' means 'I would make it known, I would reveal it, I would declare it.' 'Hard to do, hard to accomplish' means it is difficult to do and, while being done, difficult to accomplish or endure; so it is said. This is the meaning here: 'I would explain sagehood to you, if it were easy to do or to accomplish. But it is hard to do and hard to accomplish, because it must be practiced from the time one is an ordinary person without giving rise to a defiled mind.' For indeed, of one Buddha, only one disciple performs and accomplishes it.

Evaṃ [V 2.0191] bhagavā moneyyassa dukkarabhāvaṃ durabhisambhavatañca dassento nālakassa ussāhaṃ janetvā tamassa vattukāmo āha “handa te naṃ pavakkhāmi, santhambhassu daḷho bhavā”ti. Tattha handāti byavasāyatthe nipāto. Te naṃ pavakkhāmīti tuyhaṃ taṃ moneyyaṃ pavakkhāmi. Santhambhassūti dukkarakaraṇasamatthena vīriyūpatthambhena attānaṃ upatthambhaya. Daḷho bhavāti durabhisambhavasahanasamatthāya asithilaparakkamatāya thiro hoti. Kiṃ vuttaṃ [P 2.0492] hoti? Yasmā tvaṃ upacitapuññasambhāro, tasmāhaṃ ekantabyavasitova hutvā evaṃ dukkaraṃ durabhisambhavampi samānaṃ tuyhaṃ taṃ moneyyaṃ pavakkhāmi, santhambhassu daḷho bhavāti.

Thus, the Blessed One, showing the difficulty and arduous nature of sagehood, inspired Nālaka’s enthusiasm and, wishing to speak to him about it, said, "Come, I will explain it to you. Be steadfast and firm." Here, 'come' is a particle indicating resolution. 'I will explain it to you' means 'I will explain that sagehood to you.' 'Be steadfast' means support yourself with the support of energy capable of doing what is difficult. 'Be firm' means be steady with unrelaxed exertion, capable of enduring what is hard to accomplish. What is being said? "Because you have accumulated a mass of merit, therefore I, being utterly resolute, will explain that sagehood to you, though it is difficult and hard to accomplish. Be steadfast and firm."

708. Evaṃ paramasallekhaṃ moneyyavattaṃ vattukāmo nālakaṃ santhambhane daḷhībhāve ca niyojetvā paṭhamaṃ tāva gāmūpanibaddhakilesappahānaṃ dassento “samānabhāga”nti upaḍḍhagāthamāha. Tattha samānabhāganti samabhāgaṃ ekasadisaṃ ninnānākaraṇaṃ. Akkuṭṭhavanditanti akkosañca vandanañca.

708. Thus, wishing to speak of the supreme effacement, the conduct of a sage, and having enjoined Nālaka to be steadfast and firm, the Blessed One, first showing the abandoning of defilements connected with the village, spoke the half-verse beginning, 'with equal mind.' Here, 'with equal mind' means with an equal share, alike, without making distinctions. 'Reviled and praised' means insult and praise.

Idāni yathā taṃ samānabhāgaṃ kayirati, taṃ upāyaṃ dassento “manopadosa”nti upaḍḍhagāthamāha. Tassattho – akkuṭṭho manopadosaṃ rakkheyya, vandito santo anuṇṇato care, raññāpi vandito samāno “maṃ vandatī”ti uddhaccaṃ nāpajjeyya.

Now, to show the method by which such equal-mindedness is to be practiced, he spoke the half-verse beginning, 'corruption of mind.' The meaning is this: When reviled, one should guard against corruption of mind; when venerated, one should fare forth calmly and without haughtiness; even when venerated by a king, one should not become excited, thinking, 'He venerates me.'

709. Idāni [M 2.0211] araññūpanibaddhakilesappahānaṃ dassento “uccāvacā”ti gāthamāha. Tassattho – araññasaññite dāyepi iṭṭhāniṭṭhavasena uccāvacā nānappakārā ārammaṇā niccharanti, cakkhādīnaṃ āpāthamāgacchanti, te ca kho aggisikhūpamā pariḷāhajanakaṭṭhena. Yathā vā ḍayhamāne vane aggisikhā nānappakāratāya uccāvacā niccharanti, sadhūmāpi, vidhūmāpi, nīlāpi, pītāpi, rattāpi, khuddakāpi, mahantāpi, evaṃ sīhabyagghamanussāmanussavividhavihaṅgavirutapupphaphalapallavādibhedavasena nānappakāratāya dāye uccāvacā ārammaṇā niccharanti bhiṃsanakāpi, rajanīyāpi, dosanīyāpi, mohanīyāpi. Tenāha – “uccāvacā niccharanti, dāye aggisikhūpamā”ti. Evaṃ niccharantesu ca uccāvacesu ārammaṇesu yā kāci uyyānavanacārikaṃ gatā samānā pakatiyā vā vanacāriniyo kaṭṭhahārikādayo rahogataṃ disvā hasitalapitaruditadunnivatthādīhi nāriyo muniṃ palobhenti, tā su taṃ mā palobhayuṃ, tā nāriyo taṃ mā palobhayuṃ. Yathā na palobhenti, tathā karohīti vuttaṃ hoti.

709. Now, to show the abandoning of defilements connected with the forest, he speaks the verse beginning 'various.' Its meaning is this: In a forest so designated, various kinds of objects, pleasant and unpleasant, arise in diverse ways, coming into the range of the eye and other senses; and they are like flames of fire, due to their nature of causing torment. Just as in a burning forest, flames of fire arise in various forms—some smoky, some smokeless, some blue, some yellow, some red, some small, some large—so too in the forest, objects arise in diverse forms through the distinctions of lions, tigers, humans, non-humans, the cries of various birds, flowers, fruits, shoots, and so on. Some are frightening, some alluring, some provoking aversion, some deluding. Therefore, it is said: 'Various things arise, like flames of fire in the forest.' And when such diverse objects arise, whatever women—whether those who have gone to the forest for a stroll, or forest-dwellers by nature such as wood-gatherers—seeing the sage in solitude, might try to entice him with laughter, chatter, crying, or improper dress, let them not entice him. Those women should not entice him. What is meant is: 'You should act in such a way that they do not entice you.'

710-11. Evamassa [P 2.0493] bhagavā gāme ca araññe ca paṭipattividhiṃ dassetvā idāni sīlasaṃvaraṃ [V 2.0192] dassento “virato methunā dhammā”ti gāthādvayamāha. Tattha hitvā kāme paropareti methunadhammato avasesepi sundare ca asundare ca pañca kāmaguṇe hitvā. Tappahānena hi methunavirati susampannā hoti. Tenāha – “hitvā kāme paropare”ti. Ayamettha adhippāyo. “Aviruddho”tiādīni pana padāni “na haneyya, na ghātaye”ti ettha vuttāya pāṇātipātāveramaṇiyā sampattidassanatthaṃ vuttāni. Tatrāyaṃ saṅkhepavaṇṇanā – parapakkhiyesu pāṇesu aviruddho, attapakkhiyesu asāratto, sabbepi sataṇhanittaṇhatāya tasathāvare pāṇe jīvitukāmatāya amaritukāmatāya sukhakāmatāya dukkhapaṭikūlatāya ca “yathā ahaṃ tathā ete”ti attasamānatāya tesu virodhaṃ vinento teneva pakārena “yathā ete tathā aha”nti paresaṃ samānatāya ca attani anurodhaṃ vinento evaṃ ubhayathāpi anurodhavirodhavippahīno hutvā maraṇapaṭikūlatāya attānaṃ upamaṃ katvā pāṇesu ye keci tase vā thāvare vā pāṇe na haneyya sāhatthikādīhi payogehi, na ghātaye āṇattikādīhīti.

710-11. Having thus shown the way of practice in both village and forest, the Blessed One now teaches restraint in morality by stating the two verses beginning with 'abstaining from sexual activity.' Herein, 'having abandoned sensual pleasures both high and low' means abandoning all five strands of sensual desire, whether beautiful or ugly, including those apart from sexual activity. For by their abandoning, abstinence from sexual activity is well accomplished. Hence it is said: 'having abandoned sensual pleasures both high and low.' This is the meaning here. The phrases 'not hostile' and so forth, however, are stated to show the attainment in relation to the abstention from killing living beings, as explained in 'one should not kill or cause to kill.' Herein, this is the brief explanation: not hostile toward living beings of opposing factions, not attached to those of one's own faction; and toward all beings, moving or stationary, whether with craving or without, seeing them as equal to oneself in their desire for life, aversion to death, longing for happiness, and dislike of suffering, thinking, 'Just as I am, so are they,' thus removing hostility toward them. Similarly, by considering, 'Just as they are, so am I,' one removes partiality toward oneself. In this way, having abandoned both partiality and hostility, and having made oneself the standard due to an aversion to death, one should not kill any living being—whether moving or stationary—by one's own hand or other means, nor cause others to kill, by command or otherwise.

712. Evamassa [M 2.0212] methunaviratipāṇātipātaviratimukhena saṅkhepato pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlaṃ vatvā “hitvā kāme”tiādīhi indriyasaṃvarañca dassetvā idāni ājīvapārisuddhiṃ dassento “hitvā icchañcā”tiādimāha. Tassattho – yāyaṃ taṇhā ekaṃ laddhā dutiyaṃ icchati, dve laddhā tatiyaṃ, satasahassaṃ laddhā taduttarimpi icchatīti evaṃ appaṭiladdhavisayaṃ icchanato “icchā”ti vuccati, yo cāyaṃ paṭiladdhavisayalubbhano lobho. Taṃ hitvā icchañca lobhañca yattha satto puthujjano, yasmiṃ cīvarādipaccaye tehi icchālobhehi puthujjano satto laggo paṭibaddho tiṭṭhati, tattha taṃ ubhayampi hitvā paccayatthaṃ [P 2.0494] ājīvapārisuddhiṃ avirodhento ñāṇacakkhunā cakkhumā hutvā imaṃ moneyyapaṭipadaṃ paṭipajjeyya. Evañhi paṭipanno tareyya narakaṃ imaṃ, duppūraṇaṭṭhena narakasaññitaṃ micchājīvahetubhūtaṃ imaṃ paccayataṇhaṃ tareyya, imāya vā paṭipadāya tareyyāti vuttaṃ hoti.

712. Having thus briefly explained the morality of the Pātimokkha restraint by way of abstaining from sexual activity and from killing living beings, and having shown the restraint of the senses with phrases like 'having abandoned sensual pleasures,' now, to illustrate purity of livelihood, he says, 'having abandoned craving and greed.' The meaning is this: That which, having obtained one thing, desires a second; having obtained two, desires a third; having obtained a hundred thousand, still desires even more—this desiring of an unobtained object is called 'craving' (icchā); and there is that greed which is covetousness for an object that has been obtained. Having abandoned both that craving and greed to which an ordinary person is attached—that is, the robes and other requisites to which an ordinary person is attached, bound, and tied by that craving and greed—one should, without obstructing purity of livelihood for the sake of requisites, become one with vision through the eye of wisdom and undertake this path of sagehood. For one who practices thus would cross over this hell; one would cross over this craving for requisites, which is the cause of wrong livelihood and is designated as 'hell' because it is difficult to fill. Or, it is said, one would cross over by means of this path.

713. Evaṃ paccayataṇhāpahānamukhena ājīvapārisuddhiṃ dassetvā idāni bhojane mattaññutāmukhena paccayaparibhogasīlaṃ tadanusārena ca yāva arahattappatti, tāva paṭipadaṃ dassento “ūnūdaro”ti gāthamāha. Tassattho – dhammena samena laddhesu itarītaracīvarādīsu paccayesu āhāraṃ tāva āhārento –

713. Having thus illustrated purity of livelihood through abandoning craving for requisites, now, to show the virtue of using requisites through moderation in eating, and accordingly the practice leading up to the attainment of arahantship, he speaks the verse beginning, 'with a stomach not too full.' The meaning is this: when consuming food among the various requisites such as robes etc. obtained righteously and justly—

“Cattāro pañca ālope, abhutvā udakaṃ pive;

Alaṃ phāsuvihārāya, pahitattassa bhikkhuno”ti. (theragā. 983) –

“Leaving four or five morsels uneaten, one should drink water; this is sufficient for the easeful abiding of a monk with a resolute mind.”

Vuttanayena [V 2.0193] ūnaudaro assa, na vātabharitabhastā viya uddhumātudaro, bhattasammadapaccayā thinamiddhaṃ parihareyyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Ūnūdaro hontopi ca mitāhāro assa bhojane mattaññū, “neva davāyā”tiādinā paccavekkhaṇena guṇato dosato ca paricchinnāhāro. Evaṃ mitāhāro samānopi paccayadhutaṅgapariyattiadhigamavasena catubbidhāya appicchatāya appiccho assa. Ekaṃsena hi moneyyapaṭipadaṃ paṭipannena bhikkhunā evaṃ appicchena bhavitabbaṃ. Tattha ekekasmiṃ paccaye tīhi santosehi santussanā paccayappicchatā. Dhutaṅgadharasseva sato “dhutavāti maṃ pare jānantū”ti anicchanatā dhutaṅgappicchatā. Bahussutasseva sato “bahussutoti [M 2.0213] maṃ pare jānantū”ti anicchanatā pariyattiappicchatā majjhantikattherassa viya. Adhigamasampannasseva sato “adhigato ayaṃ kusalaṃ dhammanti maṃ pare jānantū”ti anicchanatā adhigamappicchatā. Sā ca arahattādhigamato oraṃ veditabbā. Arahattādhigamatthañhi ayaṃ paṭipadāti. Evaṃ appicchopi ca arahattamaggena [P 2.0495] taṇhāloluppaṃ hitvā alolupo assa. Evaṃ alolupo hi sadā icchāya nicchāto aniccho hoti nibbuto, yāya icchāya chātā honti sattā khuppipāsāturā viya atittā, tāya icchāya aniccho hoti anicchattā ca nicchāto hoti anāturo paramatittippatto. Evaṃ nicchātattā nibbuto hoti vūpasantasabbakilesapariḷāhoti evamettha uppaṭipāṭiyā yojanā veditabbā.

According to the method stated, his belly should be less than full, not bloated like a wind-filled bellows. It is said that he should avoid sluggishness and drowsiness caused by the stupor of food. Even while his belly is less than full, he should be moderate in eating, knowing the right measure in food, discerning the qualities and faults of food through reflection as stated in 'not for amusement,' etc. Thus, though moderate in eating, he should be of few wishes in four ways, namely, regarding requisites, ascetic practices, learning, and attainment. For a monk who has fully undertaken the path of sagehood must be thus of few wishes. Herein, fewness of wishes regarding each requisite is achieved through three kinds of satisfaction. For one who observes ascetic practices, it is the absence of desire for others to know him as 'an ascetic'—this is fewness of wishes regarding ascetic practices. For one who is learned, it is the absence of desire for others to know him as 'learned'—this is fewness of wishes regarding learning, like the elder Majjhantika. For one accomplished in attainment, it is the absence of desire for others to know him as 'having attained this wholesome state'—this is fewness of wishes regarding attainment. This should be understood as before the attainment of arahantship, for this path is for the attainment of arahantship. Thus, though of few wishes, he should abandon craving’s greed through the path to arahantship and be free from greed. Being thus free from greed, he is always without craving for desire, without desire, quenched. By that desire by which beings are afflicted—unsatisfied like those tormented by hunger and thirst—he is without that desire. Being without desire, he is without craving, unafflicted, having reached supreme satisfaction. Thus, being without craving, he is quenched, with the torment of all defilements completely stilled. In this way, the connection here should be understood in reverse order.

714. Evaṃ yāva arahattappatti, tāvapaṭipadaṃ kathetvā idāni taṃ paṭipadaṃ paṭipannassa bhikkhuno arahattappattiniṭṭhaṃ dhutaṅgasamādānaṃ senāsanavattañca kathento “sa piṇḍacāra”nti gāthādvayamāha. Tattha sa piṇḍacāraṃ caritvāti so bhikkhu bhikkhaṃ caritvā bhattakiccaṃ vā katvā. Vanantamabhihārayeti apapañcito gihipapañcena vanaṃ eva gaccheyya. Upaṭṭhito rukkhamūlasminti rukkhamūle ṭhito vā hutvā. Āsanūpagatoti āsanaṃ upagato vā hutvā, nisinnoti vuttaṃ hoti. Munīti moneyyapaṭipadaṃ paṭipanno. Ettha ca “piṇḍacāraṃ caritvā”ti iminā piṇḍapātikaṅgaṃ vuttaṃ. Yasmā pana ukkaṭṭhapiṇḍapātiko sapadānacārī ekāsaniko pattapiṇḍiko khalupacchābhattiko ca hotiyeva, tecīvarikapaṃsukūlampi ca samādiyateva, tasmā imānipi cha vuttāneva honti. “Vanantamabhihāraye”ti iminā pana āraññikaṅgaṃ vuttaṃ, “upaṭṭhito rukkhamūlasmi”nti iminā rukkhamūlikaṅgaṃ, “āsanūpagato”ti iminā nesajjikaṅgaṃ. Yathākkamaṃ pana etesaṃ anulomattā abbhokāsikayathāsanthatikasosānikaṅgāni vuttāniyeva hontīti evametāya gāthāya terasa dhutaṅgāni nālakattherassa kathesi.

714. Thus, having explained the practice leading up to the attainment of arahantship, now, explaining the undertaking of ascetic practices and the duties concerning dwellings that bring the monk practicing that path to the culmination of arahantship, he states two verses beginning with 'sa piṇḍacāra.' Herein, 'having gone for alms' means that the monk, having gone for alms or having completed his meal duties. 'He should go to the forest edge' means he should go to the forest itself, avoiding the proliferation of household life. 'Standing at the foot of a tree' means standing or having stood at the foot of a tree. 'Having approached a seat' means having approached a seat, or in other words, having sat down. 'The sage' refers to one practicing the path of sagehood. Here, 'having gone for alms' indicates the alms-food-eater's practice. Since the strict alms-food-eater, the one who walks systematically for alms, the one who eats in one sitting, the bowl-food-eater, and the one who refuses later food also undertake the three-robe and rag-robe practices, these six are also implied. 'He should go to the forest edge' indicates the forest-dweller's practice; 'standing at the foot of a tree' indicates the tree-root-dweller's practice; 'having approached a seat' indicates the sitter's practice. Accordingly, in sequence, because they are suitable to these, the open-air-dweller's, the any-bed-user's, and the charnel-ground-dweller's practices are also implied. Thus, through this verse, he taught the venerable Nālaka the thirteen ascetic practices.

715. Sa jhānapasuto dhīroti so anuppannassa jhānassa uppādanena uppannassa āvajjanasamāpajjanādhiṭṭhānavuṭṭhānapaccavekkhaṇehi [V 2.0194] ca jhānesu pasuto anuyutto. Dhīroti dhitisampanno. Vanante ramito siyāti vane [M 2.0214] abhirato siyā, gāmantasenāsane nābhirameyyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Jhāyetha [P 2.0496] rukkhamūlasmiṃ, attānamabhitosayanti na kevalaṃ lokiyajjhānapasutoyeva siyā, apica kho tasmiṃyeva rukkhamūle sotāpattimaggādisampayuttena lokuttarajjhānenāpi attānaṃ atīva tosento jhāyetha. Paramassāsappattiyā hi lokuttarajjhāneneva cittaṃ atīva tussati, na aññena. Tenāha – “attānamabhitosaya”nti. Evamimāya gāthāya jhānapasutatāya vanantasenāsanābhiratiṃ arahattañca kathesi.

715. “He, intent on jhāna, the wise” refers to one who is devoted to and engaged in jhāna, both by generating the unarisen jhāna and by adverting to, attaining, determining, emerging from, and reviewing the arisen jhāna. “The wise” means endowed with steadfastness. “He should delight in the forest edge” means he should find joy in the forest; he should not delight in a dwelling at the village outskirts—thus it is said. “He should meditate at the foot of a tree, thoroughly satisfying himself” means he should not only be intent on mundane jhāna but also, right there at the foot of a tree, meditate with supramundane jhāna associated with the path of stream-entry and so on, greatly delighting himself. For the mind is greatly satisfied only by supramundane jhāna, which is the attainment of supreme relief, not by anything else. Hence it is said, 'thoroughly satisfying himself.' Thus, through this verse, he spoke of devotion to jhāna, delight in a forest dwelling, and arahantship.

716. Idāni yasmā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ sutvā nālakatthero vanantamabhihāretvā nirāhāropi paṭipadāpūraṇe atīva ussukko ahosi, nirāhārena ca samaṇadhammaṃ kātuṃ na sakkā. Tathā karontassa hi jīvitaṃ nappavattati, kilese pana anuppādentena āhāro pariyesitabbo, ayamettha ñāyo. Tasmā tassa bhagavā aparāparesupi divasesu piṇḍāya caritabbaṃ, kilesā pana na uppādetabbāti dassanatthaṃ arahattappattiniṭṭhaṃyeva bhikkhācāravattaṃ kathento “tato ratyā vivasāne”tiādikā cha gāthāyo abhāsi. Tattha tatoti “sa piṇḍacāraṃ caritvā, vanantamabhihāraye”ti ettha vuttapiṇḍacāravanantābhihārato uttaripi. Ratyā vivasāneti rattisamatikkame, dutiyadivaseti vuttaṃ hoti. Gāmantamabhihārayeti ābhisamācārikavattaṃ katvā yāva bhikkhācāravelā, tāva vivekamanubrūhetvā gatapaccāgatavatte vuttanayena kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasi karonto gāmaṃ gaccheyya. Avhānaṃ nābhinandeyyāti “bhante, amhākaṃ ghare bhuñjitabba”nti nimantanaṃ, “deti nu kho na deti nu kho sundaraṃ nu kho deti asundaraṃ nu kho detī”ti evarūpaṃ vitakkaṃ bhojanañca paṭipadāpūrako bhikkhu nābhinandeyya, nappaṭiggaṇheyyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Yadi pana balakkārena pattaṃ gahetvā pūretvā denti, paribhuñjitvā samaṇadhammo kātabbo, dhutaṅgaṃ na kuppati, tadupādāya pana taṃ gāmaṃ na pavisitabbaṃ. Abhihārañca gāmatoti sace gāmaṃ paviṭṭhassa pātisatehipi bhattaṃ abhiharanti[P 2.0497], tampi nābhinandeyya, tato ekasitthampi nappaṭiggaṇheyya, aññadatthu gharapaṭipāṭiyā piṇḍapātameva careyyāti.
