716. Now, because having heard this Dhamma teaching, the elder Nālaka, having resorted to the forest, was exceedingly diligent in fulfilling his practice even without food. Yet, it is not possible to practice the ascetic life without food. For one who does so, life does not continue; but food should be sought by one who does not give rise to defilements—this is the principle here. Therefore, to show him that one should go for alms on subsequent days, but that defilements should not be produced, the Blessed One, speaking on the practice of alms-gathering which culminates in the attainment of Arahantship, uttered the six verses beginning, 'Then, at the break of day.' Therein, 'then' means subsequent to the alms-round and resorting to the forest mentioned in the phrase, 'having gone for alms, he should resort to the forest.' 'At the break of day' means at the passing of the night; that is to say, on the second day. 'He should resort to the village' means that having performed the duties of proper conduct until the time for the alms-round, and having cultivated seclusion until then, he should go to the village while keeping the meditation subject in mind according to the method described in the section on the duty of going and returning. 'He should not delight in an invitation' means a monk who is fulfilling his practice should not delight in an invitation such as, 'Venerable sir, you should eat in our house,' nor in the food, entertaining such thoughts as, 'Will they give or not? Will they give something fine or not? Will they give something plain or not?' It means he should not accept. If, however, they forcefully take his bowl, fill it, and give it to him, he should eat it and then practice the ascetic life; his ascetic observance is not violated. But on account of that, he should not enter that village again. 'And an offering from the village' means that if, after he has entered the village, they bring him food, even hundreds of portions, he should not delight in it. He should not accept even a single grain of rice from it; instead, he should go for alms from house to house in regular order.

717. Na [M 2.0215] munī gāmamāgamma, kulesu sahasā careti so ca monatthāya paṭipannako muni gāmaṃ gato samāno kulesu sahasā na care, sahasokitādiananulomikaṃ gihisaṃsaggaṃ na āpajjeyyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Ghāsesanaṃ chinnakatho, na vācaṃ payutaṃ bhaṇeti chinnakatho viya hutvā obhāsaparikathānimittaviññattipayuttaṃ ghāsesanavācaṃ na bhaṇeyya. Sace ākaṅkheyya, gilāno samāno [V 2.0195] gelaññapaṭibāhanatthāya bhaṇeyya. Senāsanatthāya vā viññattiṃ ṭhapetvā obhāsaparikathānimittapayuttaṃ, avasesapaccayatthāya pana agilāno neva kiñci bhaṇeyyāti.

717. 'A sage, having come to a village, should not act hastily among families' means that a sage who is practicing for sagehood, having gone to a village, should not act hastily among families; that is to say, he should not engage in impetuous and other unsuitable association with householders. 'Seeking sustenance, with talk cut off, he should not utter speech employed for it' means that, being as if his talk were cut off, he should not utter speech for the sake of seeking sustenance that is connected with making an opening, talking around the subject, making signs, or making a request. If he wishes, being ill, he may speak for the purpose of warding off his illness. Or, setting aside a request for lodging, if he is not ill, he should not speak at all regarding other requisites in a way connected with making an opening, talking around the subject, making signs, or making a request.

718-9. Alatthaṃ yadidanti imissā pana gāthāya ayamattho – gāmaṃ piṇḍāya paviṭṭho appamattakepi kismiñci laddhe “alatthaṃ yaṃ idaṃ sādhū”ti cintetvā aladdhe “nālatthaṃ kusala”nti tampi “sundara”nti cintetvā ubhayeneva lābhālābhena so tādī nibbikāro hutvā rukkhaṃvupanivattati, yathāpi puriso phalagavesī rukkhaṃ upagamma phalaṃ laddhāpi aladdhāpi ananunīto appaṭihato majjhattoyeva hutvā gacchati, evaṃ kulaṃ upagamma lābhaṃ laddhāpi aladdhāpi majjhattova hutvā gacchatīti. Sa pattapāṇī ti gāthā uttānatthāva.

718-719. Now, the meaning of this verse beginning 'What I have obtained' is as follows: Having entered a village for alms, if even a little of something is obtained, he reflects, 'What I have obtained is good.' If nothing is obtained, he reflects, 'Not obtaining is skillful,' thinking of this too as 'good.' Thus, such a one, being unperturbed by both gain and loss, returns to the foot of a tree. Just as a man seeking fruit, having approached a tree, goes away remaining neutral, neither attracted nor repelled, whether he obtains fruit or not; even so, having approached a family, he goes away remaining neutral whether he obtains alms or not. The verse beginning 'He, with bowl in hand' has a plain meaning.

720. Uccāvacāti imissā gāthāya sambandho – evaṃ bhikkhācāravattasampanno hutvāpi tāvatakeneva tuṭṭhiṃ anāpajjitvā paṭipadaṃ ārodheyya. Paṭipattisārañhi sāsanaṃ. Sā cāyaṃ uccāvacā…pe… mutanti. Tassattho – sā cāyaṃ maggapaṭipadā uttamanihīnabhedato uccāvacā buddhasamaṇena pakāsitā. Sukhāpaṭipadā hi khippābhiññā uccā, dukkhāpaṭipadā dandhābhiññā avacā. Itarā dve ekenaṅgena uccā, ekena avacā. Paṭhamā eva vā uccā, itarā tissopi avacā. Tāya cetāya uccāya avacāya vā paṭipadāya na pāraṃ diguṇaṃ yanti. “Duguṇa”nti vā pāṭho, ekamaggena [P 2.0498] dvikkhattuṃ nibbānaṃ na yantīti attho. Kasmā? Yena maggena ye kilesā pahīnā, tesaṃ puna appahātabbato. Etena parihānadhammābhāvaṃ dīpeti. Nayidaṃ ekaguṇaṃ mutanti tañca idaṃ pāraṃ ekakkhattuṃyeva phusanārahampi na hoti. Kasmā? Ekena maggena sabbakilesappahānābhāvato. Etena ekamaggeneva arahattābhāvaṃ dīpeti.

720. The connection to this verse beginning 'High and low' is as follows: even when endowed with such conduct in alms-seeking, one should not become content with merely that, but should ascend the Path. For the essence of the Teaching is the practice. And this path is 'high and low... liberated.' Its meaning is: this path of practice is declared by the great sage to be high and low according to the distinction between superior and inferior. The pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge is high; the painful practice with slow direct knowledge is low. The other two are high in one aspect and low in another. Or, the first alone is high, and the other three are low. By that high or low practice, 'they do not go to the beyond twice.' Or, the reading is 'twofold' (duguṇaṃ), meaning they do not go to Nibbāna twice by one and the same path. Why? Because the defilements that have been abandoned by a certain path do not have to be abandoned again. By this, he shows that there is no falling away. 'Nor is this considered a single-fold thing' means that this 'beyond' is not something that can be attained by a single contact. Why? Because all defilements are not abandoned by a single path. By this, he shows that Arahantship is not attained by one path alone.

721. Idāni [M 2.0216] paṭipadānisaṃsaṃ dassento “yassa ca visatā”ti gāthamāha. Tassattho – yassa ca evaṃ paṭipannassa bhikkhuno tāya paṭipadāya pahīnattā aṭṭhasatataṇhāvicaritabhāvena visatattā visatā taṇhā natthi, tassa kilesasotacchedena chinnasotassa kusalākusalappahānena kiccākiccappahīnassa rāgajo vā dosajo vā appamattakopi pariḷāho na vijjatīti.

721. Now, to show the benefit of the practice, he spoke the verse beginning, 'For whom craving is scattered.' Its meaning is this: For the monk who practices thus, for whom, because it has been abandoned through that practice, there is no craving, which is called 'scattered' (visatā) because it is scattered by way of the one hundred and eight operations of craving. For him, whose stream is cut off because the stream of defilements has been severed, for whom what should and should not be done is abandoned because the wholesome and unwholesome have been abandoned, there exists no fever born of lust or born of hatred, not even the slightest.

722. Idāni yasmā imā gāthāyo sutvā nālakattherassa cittaṃ udapādi – “yadi ettakaṃ moneyyaṃ sukaraṃ na dukkaraṃ, sakkā appakasirena pūretu”nti, tasmāssa bhagavā “dukkarameva moneyya”nti dassento puna “moneyyaṃ te upaññissa”ntiādimāha. Tattha upaññissanti upaññāpeyyaṃ, kathayissanti vuttaṃ hoti. Khuradhārā upamā assāti khuradhārūpamo[V 2.0196]. Bhaveti bhaveyya. Ko adhippāyo? Moneyyaṃ paṭipanno bhikkhu khuradhāraṃ upamaṃ katvā paccayesu vatteyya. Yathā madhudiddhaṃ khuradhāraṃ lihanto, chedato, jivhaṃ rakkhati, evaṃ dhammena laddhe paccaye paribhuñjanto cittaṃ kilesuppattito rakkheyyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Paccayā hi parisuddhena ñāyena laddhuñca anavajjaparibhogena paribhuñjituñca na sukhena sakkāti bhagavā paccayanissitameva bahuso bhaṇati. Jivhāya tālumāhacca, udare saññato siyāti jivhāya tāluṃ uppīḷetvāpi rasataṇhaṃ vinodento kiliṭṭhena maggena uppannapaccaye asevanto udare saṃyato siyā.

722. Now, since upon hearing these verses, the mind of the Elder Nālaka arose—'If this much of the sage's practice is easy, not difficult, it can be fulfilled with little difficulty'—therefore, the Blessed One, showing that 'the sage's practice is indeed difficult,' spoke again beginning with 'I will explain to you the sage's practice.' Herein, 'I will explain' means I will make known, it is said. 'Like a razor's edge' means having the simile of a razor's edge. 'He should be' means he should be or become. What is the meaning? A monk practicing the sage's practice should conduct himself with regard to requisites, making the razor's edge his simile. Just as one licking a razor's edge smeared with honey guards the tongue from being cut, so too, enjoying requisites righteously obtained, he should guard the mind from the arising of defilements—this is what is meant. For it is not easy to obtain requisites by a pure method and to enjoy them with blameless enjoyment; thus the Blessed One often speaks concerning requisites. 'With the tongue pressing the palate, restrained in the belly' means pressing the tongue against the palate, dispelling craving for tastes, not indulging in requisites arisen through a defiled path, and being restrained in the belly.

723. Alīnacitto ca siyāti [P 2.0499] niccaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ bhāvanāya aṭṭhitakāritāya akusītacitto ca bhaveyya. Na cāpi bahu cintayeti ñātijanapadāmaravitakkavasena ca bahuṃ na cinteyya. Nirāmagandho asito, brahmacariyaparāyaṇoti nikkileso ca hutvā taṇhādiṭṭhīhi kismiñci bhave anissito sikkhāttayasakalasāsanabrahmacariyaparāyaṇo eva bhaveyya.

723. He should be one with an unslothful mind, constantly devoted to the cultivation of wholesome qualities, with steadfast application, and not lazy-minded. And he should not think too much—he should not engage in excessive thought in terms of relatives, country, or immortality. 'Free from the stench of defilements, unattached, wholly devoted to the holy life' means that being without defilements, not dependent on any existence through craving and views, he should be wholly devoted to the holy life, which is the threefold training and the entire teaching.

724-5. Ekāsanassāti vivittāsanassa. Āsanamukhena cettha sabbairiyāpathā vuttā. Yato sabbairiyāpathesu ekībhāvassa sikkheyyāti vuttaṃ hotīti veditabbaṃ. Ekāsanassāti ca sampadānavacanametaṃ. Samaṇūpāsanassa [M 2.0217] cāti samaṇehi upāsitabbassa aṭṭhatiṃsārammaṇabhāvanānuyogassa, samaṇānaṃ vā upāsanabhūtassa aṭṭhatiṃsārammaṇabhedasseva. Idampi sampadānavacanameva, upāsanatthanti vuttaṃ hoti. Ettha ca ekāsanena kāyaviveko, samaṇūpāsanena cittaviveko vutto hotīti veditabbo. Ekattaṃ monamakkhātanti evamidaṃ kāyacittavivekavasena “ekattaṃ mona”nti akkhātaṃ. Eko ce abhiramissasīti idaṃ pana uttaragāthāpekkhaṃ padaṃ, “atha bhāhisi dasadisā”ti iminā assa sambandho.

724-725. 'Of a single seat' means of a secluded seat. Here, by 'seat' all postures are meant. Therefore, it should be understood that one should train in being unified in all postures. 'Of a single seat' is a dative term. And 'of the practice of ascetics' refers either to the application to the cultivation of the thirty-eight meditation objects, as practiced by ascetics, or to the thirty-eightfold division of objects that is the practice for ascetics. This too is a dative term, meaning 'for the purpose of practice.' And here, it should be understood that physical seclusion is indicated by 'of a single seat,' and mental seclusion by 'of the practice of ascetics.' 'Singleness is called sagehood' means that in terms of physical and mental seclusion, 'singleness is called sagehood' is declared. 'If you delight in being alone' is a phrase anticipating the next verse, and is connected with 'then you will blaze in the ten directions.'

Bhāhisīti bhāsissasi pakāsessasi. Imaṃ paṭipadaṃ bhāvento sabbadisāsu kittiyā pākaṭo bhavissasīti vuttaṃ hoti. Sutvā dhīrānantiādīnaṃ pana catunnaṃ padānaṃ ayamattho – yena ca kittighosena bhāhisi dasadisā taṃ dhīrānaṃ jhāyīnaṃ kāmacāginaṃ nighosaṃ sutvā atha tvaṃ tena uddhaccaṃ anāpajjitvā bhiyyo hiriñca saddhañca kareyyāsi, tena ghosena harāyamāno “niyyānikapaṭipadā aya”nti saddhaṃ uppādetvā uttari paṭipattimeva brūheyyāsi. Māmakoti evañhi sante mama sāvako hotīti.

'You will blaze' means you will shine forth, you will make known. Practicing this path, you will become renowned through your fame in all directions—so it has been said. Regarding the four lines beginning with 'Having heard the wise,' this is their meaning: having heard that sound of fame by which you blaze in the ten directions—the acclaim of the wise, the meditators, those who have abandoned sensual desires—then, without giving way to restlessness because of it, you should further cultivate moral shame and faith. Being humbled by that acclaim, producing faith thinking, 'This is the path leading to liberation,' you should further develop the higher practice. 'Māmaka' means, if it is so, then he is my disciple.

726. Taṃ nadīhīti yaṃ taṃ mayā “hiriñca saddhañca bhiyyo kubbethā”ti vadatā “uddhaccaṃ [V 2.0197] na kātabba”nti vuttaṃ, taṃ iminā nadīnidassanenāpi jānātha, tabbipariyāyañca sobbhesu ca padaresuca jānātha. Sobbhesūti mātikāsu[P 2.0500]. Padaresūti darīsu. Kathaṃ? Saṇantā yanti kusobbhā, tuṇhī yanti mahodadhīti. Kusobbhā hi sobbhapadarādibhedā sabbāpi kunnadiyo saṇantā saddaṃ karontā uddhatā hutvā yanti, gaṅgādibhedā pana mahānadiyo tuṇhī yanti, evaṃ “moneyyaṃ pūremī”ti uddhato hoti amāmako, māmako pana hiriñca saddhañca uppādetvā nīcacittova hoti.

726. 'That by rivers' means that what I said, 'You should further cultivate moral shame and faith,' and 'Restlessness should not be done,' understand that also through this river simile. And understand its opposite in the terms 'sobbha' and 'padara.' 'Sobbha' means channels. 'Padara' means clefts. How? 'Small streams flow noisily, while great oceans flow silently.' Indeed, all small rivers, whether channels, clefts, or of other kinds, flow noisily, making sound, being agitated. But great rivers like the Ganges flow silently. Similarly, one who is agitated, thinking, 'I am fulfilling the sage's practice,' is not my disciple, while my disciple, having produced moral shame and faith, remains with a humble mind.

727-9. Kiñca bhiyyo – yadūnakaṃ…pe… paṇḍitoti. Tattha siyā – sace aḍḍhakumbhūpamo bālo saṇantatāya, rahado pūrova paṇḍito santatāya, atha kasmā buddhasamaṇo evaṃ dhammadesanābyāvaṭo hutvā bahuṃ bhāsatīti iminā sambandhena “yaṃ samaṇo”ti gāthamāha. Tassattho – yaṃ buddhasamaṇo bahuṃ bhāsati upetaṃ atthasañhitaṃ, atthupetaṃ [M 2.0218] dhammupetañca hitena ca saṃhitaṃ, taṃ na uddhaccena, apica kho jānaṃ so dhammaṃ deseti divasampi desento nippapañcova hutvā. Tassa hi sabbaṃ vacīkammaṃ ñāṇānuparivatti. Evaṃ desento ca “idamassa hitaṃ idamassa hita”nti nānappakārato jānaṃ so bahu bhāsati, na kevalaṃ bahubhāṇitāya. Avasānagāthāya sambandho – evaṃ tāva sabbaññutaññāṇena samannāgato buddhasamaṇo jānaṃ so dhammaṃ deseti, jānaṃ so bahu bhāsati. Tena desitaṃ pana dhammaṃ nibbedhabhāgiyeneva ñāṇena yo ca jānaṃ saṃyatatto, jānaṃ na bahu bhāsati, sa muni monamarahati, sa muni monamajjhagāti. Tassattho – taṃ dhammaṃ jānanto saṃyatatto guttacitto hutvā yaṃ bhāsitaṃ sattānaṃ hitasukhāvahaṃ na hoti, taṃ jānaṃ na bahu bhāsati. So evaṃvidho monatthaṃ paṭipannako muni moneyyapaṭipadāsaṅkhātaṃ monaṃ arahati. Na kevalañca arahatiyeva, apica kho pana sa muni arahattamaggañāṇasaṅkhātaṃ monaṃ ajjhagā icceva veditabboti arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi.

727-9. What more? ‘That which is deficient… a wise one.’ Here it might be said: if a fool is like a half-full pot because of its noise, and a wise one is like a full pond because of its stillness, then why is the ascetic Buddha so engaged in teaching the Dhamma and speaking much? In this connection, he spoke the verse beginning with “Whatever an ascetic.” Its meaning is: Whatever the ascetic Buddha speaks much is endowed with meaning, conducive to the goal, conducive to the Dhamma, and connected with welfare; it is not due to restlessness. Rather, knowing, he teaches the Dhamma, expounding it even for a whole day while remaining free from conceptual proliferation. For him, all verbal action revolves in accordance with knowledge. Teaching thus, knowing in various ways, “This is for their welfare, this is for their welfare,” he speaks much—not merely for the sake of much speaking. The connection with the concluding verse is this: Thus, endowed with the knowledge of omniscience, the ascetic Buddha teaches the Dhamma knowingly and speaks much knowingly. But regarding the Dhamma taught by him, one who, knowing it through the knowledge that partakes of penetration, is self-restrained, and, knowing, does not speak much—that sage is worthy of sagehood, that sage has attained sagehood. Its meaning is: Knowing that Dhamma, being self-restrained and guarded in mind, and knowing that what is spoken does not bring welfare and happiness to beings, one does not speak much. Such a one, a sage who has entered upon the path for the sake of sagehood, is worthy of the sagehood called the practice of a sage. Not only is he worthy, but it should be understood that that sage has also attained the sagehood known as the knowledge of the path to arahantship. Thus, he concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of arahantship.

Taṃ sutvā nālakatthero tīsu ṭhānesu appiccho ahosi dassane savane pucchāyāti. So hi desanāpariyosāne pasannacitto [P 2.0501] bhagavantaṃ vanditvā vanaṃ paviṭṭho, puna “aho vatāhaṃ bhagavantaṃ passeyya”nti lolabhāvaṃ na janesi. Ayamassa dassane appicchatā. Tathā “aho vatāhaṃ puna dhammadesanaṃ suṇeyya”nti lolabhāvaṃ na janesi. Ayamassa savane appicchatā. Tathā “aho vatāhaṃ puna moneyyapaṭipadaṃ puccheyya”nti lolabhāvaṃ na janesi. Ayamassa pucchāya appicchatā.

Having heard that, the elder Nālaka became of few wishes in three respects: seeing, hearing, and questioning. Indeed, at the conclusion of the teaching, with a clear and confident mind, he paid homage to the Blessed One and entered the forest. He did not generate longing, thinking, “Oh, that I might see the Blessed One again!” This was his being of few wishes in regard to seeing. Similarly, he did not generate longing, thinking, “Oh, that I might hear the Dhamma teaching again!” This was his being of few wishes in regard to hearing. Likewise, he did not generate longing, thinking, “Oh, that I might ask about the practice of a sage again!” This was his being of few wishes in regard to questioning.

So evaṃ appiccho samāno pabbatapādaṃ pavisitvā ekavanasaṇḍe dve divasāni na vasi[V 2.0198], ekarukkhamūle dve divasāni na nisīdi, ekagāme dve divasāni piṇḍāya na pāvisi. Iti vanato vanaṃ, rukkhato rukkhaṃ, gāmato gāmaṃ āhiṇḍanto anurūpapaṭipadaṃ paṭipajjitvā aggaphale patiṭṭhāsi. Atha yasmā moneyyapaṭipadaṃ ukkaṭṭhaṃ katvā pūrento bhikkhu satteva māsāni jīvati, majjhimaṃ katvā pūrento satta vassāni, mandaṃ katvā pūrento soḷasa vassāni. Ayañca ukkaṭṭhaṃ katvā pūresi, tasmā satta māse ṭhatvā attano āyusaṅkhāraparikkhayaṃ ñatvā nhāyitvā nivāsetvā kāyabandhanaṃ bandhitvā diguṇaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ pārupitvā dasabalābhimukho pañcapatiṭṭhitaṃ vanditvā añjaliṃ [M 2.0219] paggahetvā hiṅgulakapabbataṃ nissāya ṭhitakova anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbāyi. Tassa parinibbutabhāvaṃ ñatvā bhagavā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ tattha gantvā sarīrakiccaṃ katvā dhātuyo gāhāpetvā cetiyaṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā agamāsīti.

Thus, being of few wishes, he entered the foot of a mountain. He did not stay two days in a single grove, nor sit two days at the foot of a single tree, nor enter a single village for alms for two days. Wandering from forest to forest, from tree to tree, from village to village, he undertook a fitting practice and was established in the highest fruit. Then, because a monk perfecting the practice of a sage intensely lives only seven months, perfecting it moderately seven years, and perfecting it weakly sixteen years—and because he perfected it intensely—therefore, after seven months, knowing the exhaustion of his life-formation, having bathed, put on his lower robe, fastened his belt, draped his double outer robe, facing the Ten-Powered One, paid homage with the five-point prostration, raised his joined hands, and, leaning against the Hiṅgulaka Mountain, while still standing he attained final Nibbāna through the Nibbāna-element without remainder. Knowing he had attained final Nibbāna, the Blessed One went there with the community of monks, performed the rites for the body, had the relics collected, established a stupa, and then departed.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the commentary on a text of the Khuddaka collection.

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya nālakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

In the Suttanipāta Commentary, the explanation of the Nālaka Sutta is finished.

12. Dvayatānupassanāsuttavaṇṇanā

12. The Explanation of the Discourse on the Contemplation of Dyads

Evaṃ [V 2.0199] me sutanti dvayatānupassanāsuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Imassa suttassa attajjhāsayato uppatti. Attajjhāsayena hi bhagavā imaṃ suttaṃ desesi. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro panassa atthavaṇṇanāyameva āvi bhavissati. Tattha [P 2.0502] evaṃ me sutantiādīni vuttanayāneva. Pubbārāmeti sāvatthinagarassa puratthimadisāyaṃ ārāme. Migāramātu pāsādeti ettha visākhā upāsikā attano sasurena migārena seṭṭhinā mātuṭṭhāne ṭhapitattā “migāramātā”ti vuccati. Tāya migāramātuyā navakoṭiagghanakaṃ mahālatāpiḷandhanaṃ vissajjetvā kārāpito pāsādo heṭṭhā ca upari ca pañca pañca gabbhasatāni katvā sahassakūṭāgāragabbho, so “migāramātupāsādo”ti vuccati. Tasmiṃ migāramātu pāsāde.

“Thus have I heard”—this is the Discourse on the Contemplation of Dyads. What is its origin? The origin of this discourse is from the Master’s own intention. Indeed, the Blessed One taught this discourse out of his own intention. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation will become clear in the exposition of the meaning itself. In this context, “Thus have I heard” and so forth are as previously explained. “In the Eastern Park” means in the monastery to the east of the city of Sāvatthī. “In the Mansion of Migāra’s Mother”—here, the lay follower Visākhā, having been placed in the position of a mother by her father-in-law, the merchant Migāra, is called “Migāramātā” (Migāra’s Mother). The mansion called “Migāramātā’s Mansion” is the one she had built by giving up the great creeper ornament worth nine crores; it was constructed with five hundred chambers below and five hundred above, a hall with a thousand gabled chambers. In that Mansion of Migāra’s Mother.

Tena kho pana samayena bhagavāti yaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiṃ nissāya pubbārāme migāramātu pāsāde viharati, tena samayena. Tadahuposatheti tasmiṃ ahu uposathe, uposathadivaseti vuttaṃ hoti. Pannaraseti idaṃ uposathaggahaṇena sampattāvasesuposathapaṭikkhepavacanaṃ. Puṇṇāya puṇṇamāya rattiyāti pannarasadivasattā divasagaṇanāya abbhādiupakkilesavirahattā rattiguṇasampattiyā ca puṇṇattā puṇṇāya, paripuṇṇacandattā puṇṇamāya ca rattiyā. Bhikkhusaṅghaparivutoti bhikkhusaṅghena parivuto. Abbhokāse nisinno hotīti migāramātu ratanapāsādapariveṇe abbhokāse upari appaṭicchanne okāse paññattavarabuddhāsane nisinno hoti. Tuṇhībhūtaṃ tuṇhībhūtanti atīva tuṇhībhūtaṃ, yato yato vā anuviloketi[M 2.0220], tato tato tuṇhībhūtaṃ, tuṇhībhūtaṃ vācāya, puna tuṇhībhūtaṃ kāyena. Bhikkhusaṅghaṃ anuviloketvāti taṃ parivāretvā nisinnaṃ anekasahassabhikkhuparimāṇaṃ tuṇhībhūtaṃ tuṇhībhūtaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ “ettakā ettha sotāpannā, ettakā sakadāgāmino, ettakā anāgāmino ettakā āraddhavipassakā kalyāṇaputhujjanā, imassa bhikkhusaṅghassa kīdisī dhammadesanā sappāyā”ti sappāyadhammadesanāparicchedanatthaṃ ito cito ca viloketvā.

At that time, the Blessed One: at the time when the Blessed One was dwelling near Sāvatthī, in the Eastern Park, at the mansion of Migāra’s mother. On that day it was the uposatha: on that day was the uposatha; it was the uposatha day, is what is said. The fifteenth: this is a statement that, by specifying this uposatha, rejects the other remaining uposathas. On the full, full-moon night: because it was the fifteenth day by the counting of days, because it was free from the defilements of clouds and so forth, and because the qualities of the night were complete, it was ‘full’; and because the moon was perfectly full, it was a ‘full-moon’ night. Surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus: he was surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Seated in the open: he was seated in the open, in an uncovered space above, within the precincts of Migāra’s mother’s jeweled mansion, on the prepared, excellent Buddha-seat. Utterly silent: exceedingly silent; wherever he looked, there was silence—silent in speech, and again, silent in body. Having surveyed the Saṅgha of bhikkhus: having looked here and there at the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, numbering many thousands, who were seated surrounding him in utter silence, in order to determine a suitable Dhamma teaching, thinking: ‘Here there are this many stream-enterers, this many once-returners, this many non-returners, this many virtuous worldlings who have undertaken insight meditation. What kind of Dhamma teaching would be suitable for this Saṅgha of bhikkhus?’

Ye [P 2.0503] te, bhikkhave, kusalā dhammāti ye te ārogyaṭṭhena anavajjaṭṭhena iṭṭhaphalaṭṭhena kosallasambhūtaṭṭhena ca kusalā sattatiṃsabodhipakkhiyadhammā, tajjotakā vā pariyattidhammā. Ariyā [V 2.0200] niyyānikā sambodhagāminoti upagantabbaṭṭhena ariyā, lokato niyyānaṭṭhena niyyānikā, sambodhasaṅkhātaṃ arahattaṃ gamanaṭṭhena sambodhagāmino. Tesaṃ vo bhikkhave…pe… savanāya, tesaṃ bhikkhave kusalānaṃ…pe… sambodhagāmīnaṃ kā upanisā, kiṃ kāraṇaṃ, kiṃ payojanaṃ tumhākaṃ savanāya, kimatthaṃ tumhe te dhamme suṇāthāti vuttaṃ hoti. Yāvadeva dvayatānaṃ dhammānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ ñāṇāyāti ettha yāvadevāti paricchedāvadhāraṇavacanaṃ. Dve avayavā etesanti dvayā, dvayā eva dvayatā, tesaṃ dvayatānaṃ. “Dvayāna”ntipi pāṭho. Yathābhūtaṃ ñāṇāyāti aviparītañāṇāya. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yadetaṃ lokiyalokuttarādibhedena dvidhā vavatthitānaṃ dhammānaṃ vipassanāsaṅkhātaṃ yathābhūtañāṇaṃ, etadatthāya na ito bhiyyoti, savanena hi ettakaṃ hoti, taduttari visesādhigamo bhāvanāyāti. Kiñca dvayataṃ vadethāti ettha pana sace, vo bhikkhave, siyā, kiñca tumhe, bhante, dvayataṃ vadethāti ayamadhippāyo. Padattho pana “kiñca dvayatābhāvaṃ vadethā”ti.

Those, bhikkhus, are wholesome dhammas: this refers to the thirty-seven factors of awakening, which are wholesome in the sense of being healthy, blameless, yielding desirable results, and born of skill; or they are the scriptural teachings that illuminate them. Noble, leading out, and conducive to awakening: they are ‘noble’ because they are to be approached; ‘leading out’ because they lead out from the world; and ‘conducive to awakening’ because they lead to the attainment of arahantship, which is called awakening. For you, bhikkhus... for the sake of hearing: what is the proximate cause, what is the reason, what is the purpose for your hearing of these wholesome... conducive to awakening dhammas? This means: 'For what purpose do you listen to these dhammas?' Just for the sake of the true knowledge of dualities: here, ‘just for’ is a term indicating limitation and determination. Those that have two parts are dual; duality is just the dual things; of those dualities. There is also the reading ‘of the two.’ For the sake of true knowledge: for the sake of non-perverted knowledge. What is being said? That is, for the sake of true knowledge, which is called insight, regarding phenomena divided into two categories such as worldly and supramundane—this much is the purpose, nothing beyond this. For through hearing, this much is achieved; the attainment of distinction beyond that comes through cultivation. And what is this duality you speak of?: here, if it were to be asked, “Bhikkhus, what duality would you speak of, venerable sir?”—this is the intended meaning. But in terms of the word’s meaning, it is, “And what would you speak of regarding the state of duality?”

(1) Tato bhagavā dvayataṃ dassento “idaṃ dukkha”nti evamādimāha. Tattha dvayatānaṃ catusaccadhammānaṃ “idaṃ dukkhaṃ, ayaṃ dukkhasamudayo”ti evaṃ lokiyassa ekassa avayavassa sahetukassa vā dukkhassa dassanena ayaṃ ekānupassanā, itarā lokuttarassa dutiyassa avayavassa saupāyassa vā nirodhassa dassanena dutiyānupassanā. Paṭhamā cettha tatiyacatutthavisuddhīhi hoti, dutiyā pañcamavisuddhiyā. Evaṃ sammā dvayatānupassinoti iminā vuttanayena sammā dvayadhamme anupassantassa satiyā [M 2.0221] avippavāsena appamattassa, kāyikacetasikavīriyātāpena ātāpino kāye ca jīvite ca nirapekkhattā[P 2.0504], pahitattassa. Pāṭikaṅkhanti icchitabbaṃ. Diṭṭheva dhamme aññāti asmiṃyeva attabhāve arahattaṃ. Sati vā upādisese anāgāmitāti “upādisesa”nti punabbhavavasena upādātabbakkhandhasesaṃ vuccati, tasmiṃ vā sati anāgāmibhāvo paṭikaṅkhoti dasseti. Tattha kiñcāpi heṭṭhimaphalānipi evaṃ dvayatānupassinova honti, uparimaphalesu pana ussāhaṃ janento evamāha.

Then the Blessed One, showing the twofold, spoke thus, beginning with “This is suffering.” Herein, the twofold refers to the four noble truths. “This is suffering; this is the origin of suffering”—thus, by seeing one mundane aspect of suffering, together with its cause, this is one contemplation. The other, by seeing the second supramundane aspect of cessation, together with its means, is the second contemplation. Here, the first is associated with the third and fourth purifications, while the second is associated with the fifth purification. Thus, “rightly contemplating the twofold” means that one who rightly contemplates the twofold Dhamma with unwavering mindfulness, being ardent with bodily and mental exertion, unconcerned with body and life, and with a resolute self, can expect. “Direct knowledge in this very life” means arahantship in this very existence. Or, if there is a remainder of clinging, non-returning: “remainder of clinging” means the remaining aggregates liable to be grasped as a basis for renewed existence; when there is such a remainder, the state of non-returning is to be expected. Although even the lower fruits come about through contemplating this twofold, he speaks thus inspiring effort towards the higher fruits.

Idamavocātiādi saṅgītikārānaṃ vacanaṃ. Tattha idanti “ye te, bhikkhave”tiādivuttanidassanaṃ. Etanti idāni “ye dukkha”nti evamādivattabbagāthābandhanidassanaṃ. Imā ca gāthā catusaccadīpakattā vuttatthadīpikā eva, evaṃ santepi gāthārucikānaṃ pacchā āgatānaṃ pubbe vuttaṃ asamatthatāya anuggahetvā “idāni yadi vadeyya sundara”nti ākaṅkhantānaṃ vikkhittacittānañca atthāya vuttā. Visesatthadīpikā vāti avipassake [V 2.0201] vipassake ca dassetvā tesaṃ vaṭṭavivaṭṭadassanato, tasmā visesatthadassanatthameva vuttā. Esa nayo ito parampi gāthāvacanesu.

“This was said,” and so forth, is the statement of the compilers. Here, “this” refers to the illustration stated beginning with, “Those, bhikkhus…” “This” now refers to the verse composition to be stated beginning with, “Those who are suffering…” These verses, being illuminators of the four noble truths, are indeed clarifiers of the meaning already stated. Even so, for those who like verses and have come later, unable to grasp what was previously said due to their own inability, and longing and thinking, “Now, if one would speak beautifully…” and also for those of distracted minds, these verses were spoken. Or, being indicators of a special meaning, they were spoken to show the distinction between those without insight and those with insight, showing them the round and the escape from the round. Therefore, they were spoken precisely for the sake of showing a special meaning. This method applies to the subsequent utterances of verses as well.

730. Tattha yattha cāti nibbānaṃ dasseti. Nibbāne hi dukkhaṃ sabbaso uparujjhati, sabbappakāraṃ uparujjhati, sahetukaṃ uparujjhati, asesañca uparujjhati. Tañca magganti tañca aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ.

730. Here, “where” points to Nibbāna. For in Nibbāna, suffering ceases completely, ceases in every manner, ceases with its cause, and ceases without remainder. “And that” refers to the Noble Eightfold Path.

731-3. Cetovimuttihīnā te, atho paññāvimuttiyāti ettha arahattaphalasamādhi rāgavirāgā cetovimutti, arahattaphalapaññā avijjāvirāgā paññāvimuttīti veditabbā. Taṇhācaritena vā appanājhānabalena kilese vikkhambhetvā adhigataṃ arahattaphalaṃ rāgavirāgā cetovimutti, diṭṭhicaritena upacārajjhānamattaṃ nibbattetvā vipassitvā adhigataṃ arahattaphalaṃ avijjāvirāgā paññāvimutti. Anāgāmiphalaṃ vā kāmarāgaṃ sandhāya rāgavirāgā cetovimutti, arahattaphalaṃ sabbappakārato avijjāvirāgā paññāvimuttīti. Antakiriyāyāti vaṭṭadukkhassa antakaraṇatthāya[P 2.0505]. Jātijarūpagāti jātijaraṃ upagatā, jātijarāya vā upagatā, na parimuccanti jātijarāyāti evaṃ veditabbā. Sesamettha ādito pabhuti pākaṭameva. Gāthāpariyosāne ca saṭṭhimattā bhikkhū taṃ [M 2.0222] desanaṃ uggahetvā vipassitvā tasmiṃyeva āsane arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Yathā cettha, evaṃ sabbavāresu.

731-3. Those deficient in liberation of mind, and also in liberation by wisdom—here, it should be understood that the concentration of the fruit of arahantship, through dispassion for lust, is liberation of mind; the wisdom of the fruit of arahantship, through dispassion for ignorance, is liberation by wisdom. Or, for one with a craving temperament, having suppressed the defilements through the power of absorption jhāna, the attainment of the fruit of arahantship is liberation of mind through dispassion for lust. For one with a speculative temperament, having generated only access concentration and developed insight, the attainment of the fruit of arahantship is liberation by wisdom through dispassion for ignorance. Or, the fruit of non-returning, with reference to sensual lust, is liberation of mind through dispassion for lust; the fruit of arahantship, in every way, is liberation by wisdom through dispassion for ignorance. To make an end means for the purpose of making an end to the suffering of the round. Subject to birth and aging means they have come to birth and aging, or are overcome by birth and aging; they are not freed from birth and aging—thus it should be understood. The rest here is clear from the beginning. At the conclusion of the verses, about sixty bhikkhus, having grasped that teaching and developed insight, attained arahantship right there in their seats. As it is here, so it is in all cases.

(2) Ato eva bhagavā “siyā aññenapi pariyāyenā”tiādinā nayena nānappakārato dvayatānupassanaṃ āha. Tattha dutiyavāre upadhipaccayāti sāsavakammapaccayā. Sāsavakammañhi idha “upadhī”ti adhippetaṃ. Asesavirāganirodhāti asesaṃ virāgena nirodhā, asesavirāgasaṅkhātā vā nirodhā.

(2) Therefore, the Blessed One, in the way beginning with “There might be another method,” explained the contemplation of the twofold in various ways. Here, in the second instance, conditioned by substrate means conditioned by kamma with taints. For here, kamma with taints is intended by the term “substrate.” Complete cessation through dispassion means cessation through complete dispassion, or cessation defined as complete dispassion.

734. Upadhinidānāti kammapaccayā. Dukkhassa jātippabhavānupassīti vaṭṭadukkhassa jātikāraṇaṃ “upadhī”ti anupassanto. Sesamettha pākaṭameva. Evaṃ ayampi vāro cattāri saccāni dīpetvā arahattanikūṭeneva vutto. Yathā cāyaṃ, evaṃ sabbavārā.

734. With substrate as source means conditioned by kamma. One who contemplates the origin of birth of suffering means one who contemplates that 'substrate' is the cause of birth for the suffering of the round. The rest here is clear. Thus, this section too, having illuminated the four truths, is spoken with arahantship as its pinnacle. As this section is, so are all the sections.

(3) Tattha tatiyavāre avijjāpaccayāti bhavagāmikammasambhāraavijjāpaccayā. Dukkhaṃ pana sabbattha vaṭṭadukkhameva.

(3) Here, in the third instance, with ignorance as condition means conditioned by the ignorance that is the accumulation of kamma leading to becoming. And suffering, in all cases, is simply the suffering of the round.

735. Jātimaraṇasaṃsāranti [V 2.0202] khandhanibbattiṃ jātiṃ khandhabhedaṃ maraṇaṃ khandhapaṭipāṭiṃ saṃsārañca. Vajantīti gacchanti upenti. Itthabhāvaññathābhāvanti imaṃ manussabhāvaṃ ito avasesaaññanikāyabhāvañca. Gatīti paccayabhāvo.

735. The cycle of birth and death means birth as the production of aggregates, death as the breaking up of aggregates, and the round of existence as the continuity of aggregates. They proceed means they go, they approach. This state and another state means this human state, and the state in other remaining realms besides this. Gati means the state of being a condition.

736. Avijjā hāyanti avijjā hi ayaṃ. Vijjāgatā ca ye sattāti ye ca arahattamaggavijjāya kilese vijjhitvā gatā khīṇāsavasattā. Sesamuttānatthameva.

736. This is ignorance means 'for this is ignorance.' And those beings who have attained knowledge means those beings whose taints are destroyed, who have gone beyond after piercing the defilements with the knowledge of the path to arahantship. The rest has an obvious meaning.

(4) Catutthavāre saṅkhārapaccayāti puññāpuññāneñjābhisaṅkhārapaccayā.

(4) In the fourth instance, conditioned by volitional formations means conditioned by meritorious, demeritorious, and imperturbable volitional formations.

738-9. Etamādīnavaṃ ñatvāti yadidaṃ dukkhaṃ saṅkhārapaccayā, etaṃ ādīnavanti ñatvā. Sabbasaṅkhārasamathāti sabbesaṃ vuttappakārānaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ maggañāṇena samathā, upahatatāya phalasamatthatāyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Saññānanti kāmasaññādīnaṃ maggeneva uparodhanā. Etaṃ ñatvā yathātathanti etaṃ [P 2.0506] dukkhakkhayaṃ aviparītaṃ ñatvā. Sammaddasāti sammādassanā. Sammadaññāyāti saṅkhataṃ aniccādito, asaṅkhatañca niccādito ñatvā. Mārasaṃyoganti tebhūmakavaṭṭaṃ. Sesamuttānatthameva.

738-9. Knowing this drawback means knowing this as a drawback, namely, that this suffering is conditioned by volitional formations. The calming of all volitional formations means from the calming of all volitional formations of the kind described by means of the knowledge of the path; this is said to be due to their destruction and the competence of the fruit. Of perceptions means from the cessation of perceptions of sensual pleasure and so on by the path itself. Knowing this as it truly is means knowing this cessation of suffering without distortion. Seeing rightly means right seeing. Through right knowing means having known the conditioned as impermanent, etc., and the unconditioned as permanent, etc. The bondage of Māra means the round of the three realms. The rest has an obvious meaning.

(5) Pañcamavāre [M 2.0223] viññāṇapaccayāti kammasahajātaabhisaṅkhāraviññāṇapaccayā.

(5) In the fifth instance, with consciousness as condition means conditioned by consciousness that is a volitional formation co-nascent with kamma.

741. Nicchātoti nittaṇho. Parinibbutoti kilesaparinibbānena parinibbuto hoti. Sesaṃ pākaṭameva.

741. Free from hunger means without craving. Fully extinguished means one is extinguished through the full extinguishment of defilements. The rest is clear.

(6) Chaṭṭhavāre phassapaccayāti abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇasampayuttaphassapaccayāti attho. Evaṃ ettha padapaṭipāṭiyā vattabbāni nāmarūpasaḷāyatanāni avatvā phasso vutto. Tāni hi rūpamissakattā kammasampayuttāneva na honti, idañca vaṭṭadukkhaṃ kammato vā sambhaveyya kammasampayuttadhammato vāti.

(6) In the sixth instance, the meaning of with contact as condition is: conditioned by contact associated with consciousness that is a volitional formation. Thus here, without stating name-and-form and the six sense bases, which ought to be stated in the sequence of links, contact is stated. For these, being mixed with form, are not necessarily associated with kamma. And this suffering of the round may arise either from kamma or from phenomena associated with kamma.

742-3. Bhavasotānusārinanti taṇhānusārinaṃ. Pariññāyāti tīhi pariññāhi parijānitvā. Aññāyāti arahattamaggapaññāya ñatvā. Upasame ratāti phalasamāpattivasena nibbāne ratā. Phassābhisamayāti phassanirodhā. Sesaṃ pākaṭameva.

742-3. Following the stream of becoming means following craving. Having fully understood means having fully understood through the three kinds of full understanding. Having known means having known with the wisdom of the path of arahantship. Delighting in peace means delighting in Nibbāna by way of the attainment of fruition. The comprehension of contact means the cessation of contact. The rest is clear.

(7) Sattamavāre [V 2.0203] vedanāpaccayāti kammasampayuttavedanāpaccayā.

(7) In the seventh instance, with feeling as condition means conditioned by feeling associated with kamma.

744-5. Adukkhamasukhaṃ sahāti adukkhamasukhena saha. Etaṃ dukkhanti ñatvānāti etaṃ sabbaṃ vedayitaṃ “dukkhakāraṇa”nti ñatvā, vipariṇāmaṭṭhitiaññāṇadukkhatāhi vā dukkhaṃ ñatvā. Mosadhammanti nassanadhammaṃ. Palokinanti jarāmaraṇehi palujjanadhammaṃ. Phussa phussāti udayabbayañāṇena phusitvā phusitvā. Vayaṃ passanti ante bhaṅgameva passanto. Evaṃ tattha vijānatīti evaṃ tā vedanā vijānāti, tattha vā dukkhabhāvaṃ vijānāti. Vedanānaṃ khayāti tato paraṃ maggañāṇena kammasampayuttānaṃ vedanānaṃ khayā. Sesamuttānameva.

744-5. Together with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling means together with feeling that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant. Having known this as suffering means having known all that is felt as 'the cause of suffering,' or having known it as suffering due to the suffering of change, instability, and ignorance. Of a deceptive nature means of a nature to be destroyed. Perishable means of a nature to be broken up by aging and death. Having touched and touched means having touched again and again with the knowledge of arising and passing away. Seeing its passing away means seeing only its dissolution at the end. Thus one understands there means one thus understands those feelings, or one understands the state of suffering there. From the destruction of feelings means: thereafter, from the destruction of feelings associated with kamma by means of the knowledge of the path. The rest has an obvious meaning.

(8) Aṭṭhamavāre taṇhāpaccayāti kammasambhārataṇhāpaccayā[P 2.0507].

(8) In the eighth instance, with craving as condition means conditioned by the craving that is the accumulation of kamma.

747. Etamādīnavaṃ ñatvā, taṇhaṃ dukkhassa sambhavanti etaṃ dukkhassa sambhavaṃ taṇhāya ādīnavaṃ ñatvā. Sesamuttānameva.

747. Having known this drawback, craving, the origin of suffering means having known this drawback of craving, which is the origin of suffering. The rest has an obvious meaning.

(9) Navamavāre upādānapaccayāti kammasambhāraupādānapaccayā.

(9) In the ninth instance, with clinging as condition means conditioned by the clinging that is the accumulation of kamma.

748-9. Bhavoti [M 2.0224] vipākabhavo khandhapātubhāvo. Bhūto dukkhanti bhūto sambhūto vaṭṭadukkhaṃ nigacchati. Jātassa maraṇanti yatrāpi “bhūto sukhaṃ nigacchatī”ti bālā maññanti, tatrāpi dukkhameva dassento āha – “jātassa maraṇaṃ hotī”ti. Dutiyagāthāya yojanā – aniccādīhi sammadaññāya paṇḍitā upādānakkhayā jātikkhayaṃ nibbānaṃ abhiññāya na gacchanti punabbhavanti.

748-9. “Becoming” refers to resultant becoming and the manifestation of the aggregates. “What has come to be is suffering” means that what has arisen, what has come into being, undergoes the suffering of the round. “For one who is born, there is death”—even where fools imagine, “What has come to be attains happiness,” there too, showing only suffering, he says: “For one who is born, there is death.” The explanation of the second verse: The wise, having rightly understood impermanence and so forth, and having directly known Nibbāna, the destruction of clinging and the destruction of birth, do not go to renewed existence.

(10) Dasamavāre ārambhapaccayāti kammasampayuttavīriyapaccayā.

(10) In the tenth instance, “with exertion as condition” means with energy associated with kamma as condition.

751. Anārambhe vimuttinoti anārambhe nibbāne vimuttassa. Sesamuttānameva.

751. “Liberation in non-exertion” means of one who is liberated in Nibbāna, which is non-exertion. The rest is self-explanatory.

(11) Ekādasamavāre āhārapaccayāti kammasampayuttāhārapaccayā. Aparo nayo – catubbidhā sattā rūpūpagā, vedanūpagā, saññūpagā, saṅkhārūpagāti. Tattha ekādasavidhāya kāmadhātuyā sattā rūpūpagā kabaḷīkārāhārasevanato. Rūpadhātuyā sattā aññatra asaññehi vedanūpagā phassāhārasevanato. Heṭṭhā tividhāya arūpadhātuyā sattā saññūpagā saññābhinibbattamanosañcetanāhārasevanato[V 2.0204]. Bhavagge sattā saṅkhārūpagā saṅkhārābhinibbattaviññāṇāhārasevanatoti. Evampi yaṃ kiñci dukkhaṃ sambhoti, sabbaṃ āhārapaccayāti veditabbaṃ.

(11) In the eleventh section, “with nutriment as condition” means with nutriment associated with kamma as condition. Another method: There are four kinds of beings—those sustained by form, feeling, perception, and volitional formations. Here, beings of the elevenfold sensuous realm are sustained by form due to partaking of edible food. Beings of the form realm, except for the non-percipient beings, are sustained by feeling due to partaking of contact as food. Beings of the threefold formless realm below are sustained by perception due to partaking of mental volition born of perception as food. Beings at the peak of existence are sustained by volitional formations due to partaking of consciousness born of volitional formations as food. Thus, whatever suffering arises, all should be understood as having nutriment as its condition.

755. Ārogyanti nibbānaṃ. Saṅkhāya sevīti cattāro paccaye paccavekkhitvā sevamāno, “pañcakkhandhā dvādasāyatanāni aṭṭhārasadhātuyo”ti evaṃ vā lokaṃ saṅkhāya “aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattā”ti ñāṇena sevamāno. Dhammaṭṭhoti catusaccadhamme ṭhito. Saṅkhyaṃ nopetīti “devo”ti vā “manusso”ti vā ādikaṃ saṅkhyaṃ na gacchati. Sesamuttānameva.

755. “Health” is Nibbāna. “One who uses with reflection” means one who uses the four requisites after reflecting on them, or one who uses after reckoning the world thus: “The five aggregates, the twelve sense bases, the eighteen elements,” or who uses with the knowledge of “impermanent, suffering, not-self.” “Established in Dhamma” means established in the four noble truths. “He does not resort to reckoning” means he does not go to a reckoning such as “deva” or “human.” The rest is self-explanatory.

(12) Dvādasamavāre [P 2.0508] iñjitapaccayāti taṇhāmānadiṭṭhikammakilesaiñjitesu yato kutoci kammasambhāriñjitapaccayā.

(12) In the twelfth section, “with agitation as condition” means with agitation from the accumulation of kamma as condition, which arises from any of the agitations of craving, conceit, views, kamma, and defilements.

757. Ejaṃ vossajjāti taṇhaṃ cajitvā. Saṅkhāre uparundhiyāti kammaṃ kammasampayutte ca saṅkhāre nirodhetvā. Sesamuttānameva.

757. “Having abandoned agitation” means having given up craving. “Having restrained formations” means having ceased kamma and the formations associated with kamma. The rest is self-explanatory.

(13) Terasamavāre [M 2.0225] nissitassa calitanti taṇhāya taṇhādiṭṭhimānehi vā khandhe nissitassa sīhasutte (saṃ. ni. 3.78) devānaṃ viya bhayacalanaṃ hoti. Sesamuttānameva.

(13) In the thirteenth instance, “trembling of one who is dependent” means that for one dependent on the aggregates through craving, or through craving, views, and conceit, there is trembling from fear, like that of the devas in the Sīhasutta (Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.78). The rest is self-explanatory.

(14) Cuddasamavāre rūpehīti rūpabhavehi rūpasamāpattīhi vā. Arūpāti arūpabhavā arūpasamāpattiyo vā. Nirodhoti nibbānaṃ.

(14) In the fourteenth section, “from forms” means from the form realms or the form attainments. “Formless” means the formless realms or the formless attainments. “Cessation” means Nibbāna.

761. Maccuhāyinoti maraṇamaccu kilesamaccu devaputtamaccuhāyino, tividhampi taṃ maccuṃ hitvā gāminoti vuttaṃ hoti. Sesamuttānameva.

761. “One who has overcome death” means one who has overcome the death of mortality, the death of defilements, and the death of Devaputta Māra; it is said that such a one is a “goer,” having abandoned that threefold death. The rest is self-explanatory.

(15) Pannarasamavāre yanti nāmarūpaṃ sandhāyāha. Tañhi lokena dhuvasubhasukhattavasena “idaṃ sacca”nti upanijjhāyitaṃ diṭṭhamālokitaṃ. Tadamariyānanti idaṃ ariyānaṃ, anunāsikaikāralopaṃ katvā vuttaṃ. Etaṃ musāti etaṃ dhuvādivasena gahitampi musā, na tādisaṃ hotīti. Puna yanti nibbānaṃ sandhāyāha. Tañhi lokena rūpavedanādīnamabhāvato “idaṃ musā natthi kiñcī”ti upanijjhāyitaṃ. Tadamariyānaṃ etaṃ saccanti taṃ idaṃ ariyānaṃ etaṃ nikkilesasaṅkhātā subhabhāvā, pavattidukkhapaṭipakkhasaṅkhātā sukhabhāvā, accantasantisaṅkhātā [V 2.0205] niccabhāvā ca anapagamanena paramatthato “sacca”nti yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya sudiṭṭhaṃ.

(15) In the fifteenth section, “that which” refers to name-and-form. For this is meditated upon, seen, and regarded by the world as “this is true” in the sense of being permanent, beautiful, pleasant, and self. The phrase `Tad amariyānaṃ` (That which is for the non-noble) is explained as `idaṃ ariyānaṃ` (this is for the noble ones), stated with the elision of the nasal and the vowel ‘i’. “This is false” means that even though grasped as permanent and so on, it is false, not being such. Again, “that which” refers to Nibbāna. For this is meditated upon by the world as “this is false, there is nothing here,” due to the absence of form, feeling, etc. The phrase `Tad amariyānaṃ etaṃ saccaṃ` (That which is for the non-noble is this truth) means that for the noble ones, this is rightly seen with perfect wisdom as it really is as “the truth” in the ultimate sense by its unchanging nature, because of its beautiful nature known as stainlessness, its blissful nature known as the opposite of the suffering of existence, and its permanent nature known as utter peace.

762-3. Anattani attamāninti anattani nāmarūpe attamāniṃ. Idaṃ saccanti maññatīti idaṃ nāmarūpaṃ dhuvādivasena “sacca”nti maññati. Yena yena hīti yena yena rūpe vā vedanāya vā “mama rūpaṃ, mama vedanā”tiādinā nayena maññanti. Tato tanti tato maññitākārā taṃ nāmarūpaṃ hoti aññathā. Kiṃ kāraṇaṃ? Tañhi tassa musā hoti, yasmā taṃ yathāmaññitākārā [P 2.0509] musā hoti, tasmā aññathā hotīti attho. Kasmā pana musā hotīti? Mosadhammañhi ittaraṃ, yasmā yaṃ ittaraṃ parittapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, taṃ mosadhammaṃ nassanadhammaṃ hoti, tathārūpañca nāmarūpanti. Saccābhisamayāti saccāvabodhā. Sesamuttānameva.

762-3. “Conceiving self in what is not-self” means conceiving of name-and-form, which is not-self, as self. “Imagines, ‘This is true’” means one imagines this name-and-form as “true” in terms of permanence and so on. “In whatever way” means in whatever form or feeling they imagine in the manner of “my form, my feeling,” etc. “From that” means that from that way of imagining, that name-and-form becomes otherwise. Why? Because that imagining is false for one. The meaning is: since that name-and-form is false in the way it is imagined, therefore it becomes otherwise. But why is it false? Because what is transient is of a deceptive nature. Since whatever is transient, of limited appearance, is of a deceptive nature, subject to destruction—and such is name-and-form. “Realization of the truth” means understanding the truth. The rest is self-explanatory.

(16) Soḷasamavāre yanti chabbidhamiṭṭhārammaṇaṃ sandhāyāha. Tañhi lokena salabhamacchamakkaṭādīhi padīpabaḷisalepādayo viya “idaṃ sukha”nti [M 2.0226] upanijjhāyitaṃ. Tadamariyānaṃ etaṃ dukkhanti taṃ idaṃ ariyānaṃ “kāmā hi citrā madhurā manoramā, virūparūpena mathenti citta”ntiādinā (su. ni. 50; cūḷani. khaggavisāṇasuttaniddesa 136) nayena “etaṃ dukkha”nti yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya sudiṭṭhaṃ. Puna yanti nibbānameva sandhāyāha. Tañhi lokena kāmaguṇābhāvā “dukkha”nti upanijjhāyitaṃ. Tadamariyānanti taṃ idaṃ ariyānaṃ paramatthasukhato “etaṃ sukha”nti yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya sudiṭṭhaṃ.

(16) In the sixteenth section, “that which” is said referring to the six kinds of desirable objects. For the world meditates upon them as “this is pleasure,” like moths, fish, and monkeys towards lamps, bait, and birdlime. The phrase `Tad amariyānaṃ etaṃ dukkhaṃ` (That which is for the non-noble is this suffering) means that for the noble ones, as stated: “For sensual pleasures are diverse, sweet, delightful, but with various forms they torment the mind,” etc. (Snp 50; Cnd 136), this is rightly seen with perfect wisdom as it really is as “this is suffering.” Again, “that which” refers to Nibbāna itself. For the world, due to the absence of sensual qualities, meditates upon it as “suffering.” The phrase `Tad amariyānaṃ` (That which is for the non-noble) means that for the noble ones, because it is ultimate bliss, this is rightly seen with perfect wisdom as it really is as “this is pleasure.”

765-6. Kevalāti anavasesā. Iṭṭhāti icchitā patthitā. Kantāti piyā. Manāpāti manavuḍḍhikarā. Yāvatatthīti vuccatīti yāvatā ete cha ārammaṇā atthīti vuccanti. Vacanabyattayo veditabbo. Ete voti ettha voti nipātamattaṃ.

765-6. “Kevalā” means without remainder. “Iṭṭhā” means desired, wished for. “Kantā” means dear. “Manāpā” means delighting the mind. “As long as they exist, it is said” means “as long as these six objects exist,” they are called. A change of grammatical number should be understood. Here, in “ete vo,” “vo” is merely a particle.

767-8. Sukhanti diṭṭhamariyehi, sakkāyassuparodhananti “sukha”miti ariyehi pañcakkhandhanirodho diṭṭho, nibbānanti vuttaṃ hoti. Paccanīkamidaṃ hotīti paṭilomamidaṃ dassanaṃ hoti. Passatanti passantānaṃ, paṇḍitānanti vuttaṃ hoti. Yaṃ pareti ettha yanti vatthukāme sandhāyāha. Puna yaṃ pareti ettha nibbānaṃ.

767-8. Regarding 'Happiness is seen by the noble ones in the cessation of personal identity': the cessation of the five aggregates is seen by the noble ones as 'happiness', which is to say, Nibbāna. 'This is contrary' means this is a contrary view. 'For those who see' refers to those who see, meaning the wise. Here, 'what others...' refers to material sensual pleasures. Again, 'what others...' here refers to Nibbāna.

769-71. Passāti sotāraṃ ālapati. Dhammanti nibbānadhammaṃ. Sampamūḷhetthaviddasūti sampamūḷhā ettha aviddasū bālā. Kiṃkāraṇaṃ sampamūḷhā? Nivutānaṃ tamo hoti [P 2.0510], andhakāro apassataṃ[V 2.0206], bālānaṃ avijjāya nivutānaṃ otthaṭānaṃ andhabhāvakaraṇo tamo hoti, yena nibbānadhammaṃ daṭṭhuṃ na sakkonti. Satañca vivaṭaṃ hoti, āloko passatāmivāti satañca sappurisānaṃ paññādassanena passataṃ ālokova vivaṭaṃ hoti nibbānaṃ. Santike na vijānanti, magā dhammassakovidāti yaṃ attano sarīre tacapañcakamattaṃ paricchinditvā anantarameva adhigantabbato, attano khandhānaṃ vā nirodhamattato santike nibbānaṃ, taṃ evaṃ santike santampi na vijānanti magabhūtā janā maggāmaggadhammassa saccadhammassa vā akovidā, sabbathā bhavarāga…pe… susambudho. Tattha māradheyyānupannehīti tebhūmakavaṭṭaṃ anupannehi.

769-71. 'See!' addresses the listener. 'The Dhamma' refers to the Dhamma of Nibbāna. 'Herein the ignorant are deluded' means the deluded and ignorant fools are here. Why are they deluded? For the veiled, there is darkness; for those who do not see, there is blindness. The fools, veiled by ignorance, enveloped and obscured, have a darkness that causes blindness, preventing them from seeing the Dhamma of Nibbāna. But for the virtuous, it is open, like light for those who see—Nibbāna is open like light for those who see with the vision of wisdom. 'Though near, they do not know it'—though Nibbāna is near, because it can be attained immediately after discerning the mere five constituents of the body beginning with the skin in one's own body, or because it is near as the mere cessation of one's own aggregates, these people, like deer, do not understand it, being unskilled in the path and not-path or in the true Dhamma. In every way, by craving for existence... etc. ...it is not fully understood. Therein, 'by those not subject to Māra's domain' means by those not fallen into the round of the three planes of existence.

772. Pacchimagāthāya [M 2.0227] sambandho “evaṃ asusambudhaṃ ko nu aññatra mariyehī”ti. Tassattho – ṭhapetvā ariye ko nu añño nibbānapadaṃ jānituṃ arahati, yaṃ padaṃ catutthena ariyamaggena sammadaññāya anantarameva anāsavā hutvā kilesaparinibbānena parinibbanti, sammadaññāya vā anāsavā hutvā ante anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbantīti arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi.

772. The connection with the last verse is: 'Thus, who else but the noble ones can understand this not well-understood state?' Its meaning is: except for the noble ones, who else is worthy of knowing the state of Nibbāna? Having fully understood that state with the fourth noble path, they immediately become without taints and attain final Nibbāna through the extinguishing of the defilements; or, having fully understood and become without taints, at the end they attain final Nibbāna in the Nibbāna-element without remainder. Thus, he concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of arahantship.

Attamanāti tuṭṭhamanā. Abhinandunti abhinandiṃsu. Imasmiñca pana veyyākaraṇasminti imasmiṃ soḷasame veyyākaraṇe. Bhaññamāneti bhaṇiyamāne. Sesaṃ pākaṭameva.

'Glad' means pleased in mind. 'They rejoiced' means they rejoiced. 'And in this exposition' refers to this sixteenth exposition. 'While it was being spoken' means while it was being recited. The rest is clear.

Evaṃ sabbesupi soḷasasu veyyākaraṇesu saṭṭhimatte saṭṭhimatte katvā saṭṭhiadhikānaṃ navannaṃ bhikkhusatānaṃ anupādāya āsavehi cittāni vimucciṃsu, soḷasakkhattuṃ cattāri cattāri katvā catusaṭṭhi saccānettha veneyyavasena nānappakārato desitānīti.

Thus, in all sixteen expositions, with about sixty monks each time, the minds of nine hundred and sixty monks were liberated from the taints without clinging. Sixteen times, four each were made, totaling sixty-four truths taught here in various ways according to the capacity of those to be guided.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

Of the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya dvayatānupassanāsuttavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Dvayatānupassanā Sutta in the Commentary on the Suttanipāta

Niṭṭhittā.

It is finished.

Niṭṭhito ca tatiyo vaggo atthavaṇṇanānayato, nāmena

And so the third chapter is completed, according to the method of explaining the meaning, named:

Mahāvaggoti.

The Great Chapter.

4. Aṭṭhakavaggo

4. The Chapter of the Octads

1. Kāmasuttavaṇṇanā

1. The Explanation of the Kāmasutta

773. Kāmaṃ [V 2.0207][M 2.0228][P 2.0511] kāmayamānassāti kāmasuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Bhagavati kira sāvatthiyaṃ viharante aññataro brāhmaṇo sāvatthiyā jetavanassa ca antare aciravatīnadītīre “yavaṃ vapissāmī”ti khettaṃ kasati. Bhagavā bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto piṇḍāya pavisanto taṃ disvā āvajjento addasa – “assa brāhmaṇassa yavā vinassissantī”ti, puna upanissayasampattiṃ āvajjento cassa sotāpattiphalassa upanissayaṃ addasa. “Kadā pāpuṇeyyā”ti āvajjento “sasse vinaṭṭhe sokābhibhūto dhammadesanaṃ sutvā”ti addasa. Tato cintesi – “sacāhaṃ tadā eva brāhmaṇaṃ upasaṅkamissāmi, na me ovādaṃ sotabbaṃ maññissati. Nānārucikā hi brāhmaṇā, handa, naṃ ito pabhutiyeva saṅgaṇhāmi, evaṃ mayi muducitto hutvā tadā ovādaṃ sossatī”ti brāhmaṇaṃ upasaṅkamitvā āha – “kiṃ, brāhmaṇa, karosī”ti. Brāhmaṇo “evaṃ uccākulīno samaṇo gotamo mayā saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ karotī”ti tāvatakeneva bhagavati pasannacitto hutvā “khettaṃ, bho gotama, kasāmi yavaṃ vapissāmī”ti āha. Atha sāriputtatthero cintesi – “bhagavā brāhmaṇena saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ akāsi, na ca ahetu appaccayā tathāgatā evaṃ karonti, handāhampi tena saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ karomī”ti brāhmaṇaṃ upasaṅkamitvā tatheva paṭisanthāramakāsi. Evaṃ mahāmoggallānatthero sesā ca asīti mahāsāvakā. Brāhmaṇo atīva attamano ahosi.

773. The Kāmasutta begins with 'For one desiring sensual pleasures'. What is its origin? It is said that while the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī, a certain brahmin was plowing a field between Sāvatthī and Jetavana, on the bank of the Aciravatī River, intending to sow barley. The Blessed One, entering for alms surrounded by the Sangha of monks, saw him and, while reflecting, perceived, "This brahmin's barley will be destroyed." Then, reflecting on his potential for attainment, he perceived that he had the potential for the fruit of stream-entry. Wondering when he might attain it, he perceived that it would be when, overcome by sorrow after the crops were ruined, he would hear the Dhamma teaching. Then he thought, "If I approach the brahmin right now, he will not think my advice is to be listened to. For brahmins have diverse inclinations. Well now, let me win him over from this moment on, so that when his mind has softened toward me, he will then listen to my advice." Approaching the brahmin, he said, "What are you doing, brahmin?" The brahmin, thinking, "The ascetic Gotama, so highly born, is engaging in friendly conversation with me," became pleased with the Blessed One just for that and said, "I am plowing the field, good Gotama, to sow barley." Then the Venerable Sāriputta thought, "The Blessed One has engaged in friendly conversation with the brahmin, and the Tathāgatas do not act so without cause or reason. Well now, let me also engage in friendly conversation with him." Approaching the brahmin, he did the same. Likewise, the Venerable Mahā Moggallāna and the other eighty great disciples did the same. The brahmin was exceedingly delighted.

Atha bhagavā sampajjamānepi sasse ekadivasaṃ katabhattakicco sāvatthito jetavanaṃ gacchanto maggā okkamma brāhmaṇassa santikaṃ gantvā āha – “sundaraṃ te, brāhmaṇa, yavakkhetta”nti. “Evaṃ, bho gotama, sundaraṃ, sace sampajjissati, tumhākampi saṃvibhāgaṃ [P 2.0512] karissāmī”ti. Athassa catumāsaccayena yavā nipphajjiṃsu. Tassa “ajja vā sve vā lāyissāmī”ti ussukkaṃ kurumānasseva mahāmegho uṭṭhahitvā sabbarattiṃ vassi. Aciravatī nadī pūrā āgantvā sabbaṃ yavaṃ vahi. Brāhmaṇo sabbarattiṃ anattamano hutvā pabhāte nadītīraṃ gato sabbaṃ sassavipattiṃ disvā “vinaṭṭhomhi, kathaṃ dāni jīvissāmī”ti balavasokaṃ uppādesi[V 2.0208]. Bhagavāpi tameva [M 2.0229] rattiṃ paccūsasamaye buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ volokento “ajja brāhmaṇassa dhammadesanākālo”ti ñatvā bhikkhācāravattena sāvatthiṃ pavisitvā brāhmaṇassa gharadvāre aṭṭhāsi. Brāhmaṇo bhagavantaṃ disvā “sokābhibhūtaṃ maṃ assāsetukāmo samaṇo gotamo āgato”ti cintetvā āsanaṃ paññāpetvā pattaṃ gahetvā bhagavantaṃ nisīdāpesi. Bhagavā jānantova brāhmaṇaṃ pucchi – “kiṃ brāhmaṇa paduṭṭhacitto vihāsī”ti? Āma, bho gotama, sabbaṃ me yavakkhettaṃ udakena vūḷhanti. Atha bhagavā “na, brāhmaṇa, vipanne domanassaṃ, sampanne ca somanassaṃ kātabbaṃ. Kāmā hi nāma sampajjantipi vipajjantipī”ti vatvā tassa brāhmaṇassa sappāyaṃ ñatvā dhammadesanāvasena imaṃ suttamabhāsi. Tattha saṅkhepato padatthasambandhamattameva vaṇṇayissāma, vitthāro pana niddese (mahāni. 1) vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Yathā ca imasmiṃ sutte, evaṃ ito paraṃ sabbasuttesu.

Then the Blessed One, while the crops were growing, having finished his meal duties for the day, was going from Sāvatthī to Jetavana when, turning off the road, he approached a brahmin and said, “Your barley field is beautiful, brahmin.” “Yes, Venerable Gotama, it is beautiful. If it prospers, I will also share it with you.” Then, after four months, the barley ripened. As he was eagerly preparing, thinking, “Today or tomorrow I will reap,” a great cloud arose and rained all night. The Aciravatī River, being full, came and swept away all the barley. The brahmin, distressed all night, went to the riverbank at dawn and, seeing the complete destruction of his crop, gave rise to a strong sorrow, thinking, “I am ruined! How will I live now?” That same night, at dawn, the Blessed One surveyed the world with the Buddha’s eye and knew, “Today is the time to teach the brahmin.” Having entered Sāvatthī for his alms-round, he stood at the brahmin’s door. Seeing the Blessed One, the brahmin thought, “The ascetic Gotama has come wishing to console me, who am overwhelmed by sorrow.” He then prepared a seat, took the Blessed One's bowl, and had him sit down. The Blessed One, though knowing, asked the brahmin, “Brahmin, why are you dwelling with a troubled mind?” “Yes, Venerable Gotama, my entire barley field has been swept away by water.” Then the Blessed One said, “Brahmin, one should not feel sorrow over loss, nor joy over gain. For sensual pleasures indeed succeed and also fail.” Having said this, and understanding what was suitable for that brahmin, he spoke this discourse by way of a Dhamma teaching. Here, we will explain only the connection of words and their meaning in brief; the detailed explanation, however, should be understood as stated in the Niddesa (Mahāni. 1). And as in this discourse, so too in all subsequent discourses.

Tattha kāmanti manāpiyarūpāditebhūmakadhammasaṅkhātaṃ vatthukāmaṃ, kāmayamānassāti icchamānassa. Tassa ce taṃ samijjhatīti tassa kāmayamānassa sattassa taṃ kāmasaṅkhātaṃ vatthu samijjhati ce, sace so taṃ labhatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Addhā pītimano hotīti ekaṃsaṃ tuṭṭhacitto hoti. Laddhāti labhitvā. Maccoti satto. Yadicchatīti yaṃ icchati.

Herein, 'kāma' refers to objective sensual pleasure (vatthukāma), which is designated as a phenomenon pertaining to the three planes of existence, such as pleasing forms and other sense objects. 'Kāmayamānassāti' means 'of one who desires,' that is, 'of one who wishes.' 'Tassa ce taṃ samijjhati' means if that object, designated as a sensual pleasure, succeeds for that desiring being—that is to say, if he obtains it. 'Addhā pītimano hoti' means he is certainly of joyful mind, that is, he becomes decidedly delighted in mind. 'Laddhā' means having obtained. 'Macco' means a mortal, a being. 'Yadicchati' means whatever he desires.

774. Tassa ce kāmayānassāti tassa puggalassa kāme icchamānassa, kāmena vā yāyamānassa. Chandajātassāti [P 2.0513] jātataṇhassa. Jantunoti sattassa. Te kāmā parihāyantīti te kāmā parihāyanti ce. Sallaviddhova ruppatīti atha ayomayādinā sallena viddho viya pīḷīyati.

774. 'Tassa ce kāmayānassa' means of that person who desires sensual pleasures, or who strives for sensual pleasures. 'Chandajātassa' means of one in whom craving is born. 'Jantuno' means of a being. 'Te kāmā parihāyanti' means if those sensual pleasures decline. 'Sallaviddhova ruppati' means then he is afflicted as if pierced by a dart made of iron or the like.

775. Tatiyagāthāya saṅkhepattho – yo pana ime kāme tattha chandarāgavikkhambhanena vā samucchedena vā attano pādena sappassa siraṃ iva parivajjeti. So bhikkhu sabbaṃ lokaṃ visaritvā ṭhitattā loke visattikāsaṅkhātaṃ taṇhaṃ sato hutvā samativattatīti.

775. The condensed meaning of the third verse is this: whoever avoids these sensual pleasures—as one would a snake’s head with one’s foot—through the suppression or the eradication of desire and lust for them; that monk, being mindful, overcomes the craving known as attachment in the world, because he stands steadfast, having dismissed the entire world.

776-8. Tato [M 2.0230] parāsaṃ tissannaṃ gāthānaṃ ayaṃ saṅkhepattho – yo etaṃ sālikkhettādiṃ khettaṃ vā gharavatthādiṃ vatthuṃ vā kahāpaṇasaṅkhātaṃ hiraññaṃ vā goassabhedaṃ gavāssaṃ vā itthisaññikā thiyo vā ñātibandhavādī bandhū vā aññe vā manāpiyarūpādī puthu kāme anugijjhati, taṃ puggalaṃ abalasaṅkhātā kilesā balīyanti sahanti maddanti, saddhābalādivirahena vā abalaṃ taṃ puggalaṃ abalā kilesā balīyanti, abalattā balīyantīti attho. Atha taṃ kāmagiddhaṃ kāme rakkhantaṃ [V 2.0209] pariyesantañca sīhādayo ca pākaṭaparissayā kāyaduccaritādayo ca apākaṭaparissayā maddanti, tato apākaṭaparissayehi abhibhūtaṃ taṃ puggalaṃ jātiādidukkhaṃ bhinnaṃ nāvaṃ udakaṃ viya anveti. Tasmā kāyagatāsatiādibhāvanāya jantu sadā sato hutvā vikkhambhanasamucchedavasena rūpādīsu vatthukāmesu sabbappakārampi kilesakāmaṃ parivajjento kāmāni parivajjaye. Evaṃ te kāme pahāya tappahānakaramaggeneva catubbidhampi tare oghaṃ tareyya tarituṃ sakkuṇeyya. Tato yathā puriso udakagarukaṃ nāvaṃ siñcitvā lahukāya nāvāya appakasireneva pāragū bhaveyya, pāraṃ gaccheyya, evameva attabhāvanāvaṃ kilesūdakagarukaṃ siñcitvā lahukena attabhāvena pāragū bhaveyya, sabbadhammapāraṃ nibbānaṃ gato bhaveyya, arahattappattiyā gaccheyya ca, anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbātīti arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi. Desanāpariyosāne [P 2.0514] brāhmaṇo ca brāhmaṇī ca sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahiṃsūti.

776-8. The condensed meaning of the following three verses is this: whoever is greedy for various sensual pleasures—such as fields of rice and other crops, property like houses and land, gold in the form of coins, cattle and horses, women, or relatives and friends, or other various pleasing forms—that person, being weak, is overpowered, overwhelmed, and crushed by the defilements. Or, because that person is weak due to a lack of the power of faith and so on, the defilements overpower him; the meaning is that they overpower him because of his weakness. Then, that person who is greedy for sensual pleasures, while guarding and seeking them, is crushed by obvious dangers such as lions and by hidden dangers such as bodily misconduct. Thereafter, being overcome by hidden dangers, the suffering of birth and so on follows that person, just as water follows a broken boat. Therefore, a being, being always mindful by developing mindfulness of the body and so on, should avoid sensual pleasures, avoiding every kind of defilement-desire regarding objective sensual pleasures such as forms, by way of suppression and eradication. Having thus abandoned those sensual pleasures, by that very path that causes their abandonment, one could cross the fourfold flood. Then, just as a person, having bailed out a boat heavy with water, would, with a light boat, reach the far shore with little effort, so too, having bailed out the boat of one's being, heavy with the water of defilements, one would, with a lightened being, reach the far shore. One would go to Nibbāna, the far shore of all phenomena, would attain Arahantship, and would attain final Nibbāna with the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining. He concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of Arahantship. At the end of the teaching, the brahmin and his wife were established in the fruit of stream-entry.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya.

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya kāmasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Here ends the explanation of the Kāma Sutta in the Commentary on the Suttanipāta.

2. Guhaṭṭhakasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Guhaṭṭhaka Sutta.

779. Satto [V 2.0210][M 2.0231] guhāyanti guhaṭṭhakasuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Bhagavati kira sāvatthiyaṃ viharante āyasmā piṇḍolabhāradvājo kosambiyaṃ gaṃṅgātīre āvaṭṭakaṃ nāma utenassa uyyānaṃ, tattha agamāsi sītale padese divāvihāraṃ nisīditukāmo. Aññadāpi cāyaṃ gacchateva tattha pubbāsevanena yathā gavampatitthero tāvatiṃsabhavananti vuttanayametaṃ vaṅgīsasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ. So tattha gaṅgātīre sītale rukkhamūle samāpattiṃ appetvā divāvihāraṃ nisīdi. Rājāpi kho uteno taṃ divasaṃyeva uyyānakīḷikaṃ gantvā bahudeva divasabhāgaṃ naccagītādīhi uyyāne kīḷitvā pānamadamatto ekissā itthiyā aṅke sīsaṃ katvā sayi. Sesitthiyo “sutto rājā”ti uṭṭhahitvā uyyāne pupphaphalādīni gaṇhantiyo theraṃ disvā hirottappaṃ upaṭṭhāpetvā “mā saddaṃ akatthā”ti aññamaññaṃ nivāretvā appasaddā upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā theraṃ samparivāretvā nisīdiṃsu. Thero samāpattito vuṭṭhāya tāsaṃ dhammaṃ desesi, tā tuṭṭhā “sādhu sādhū”ti vatvā suṇanti.

779. The Guhaṭṭhaka Sutta: “The Cave-Dweller.” What is its origin? When the Blessed One was residing at Sāvatthī, the Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja, wanting to spend the midday rest in a cool place, went to a park named Āvaṭṭaka belonging to King Udena, on the banks of the Ganges near Kosambī. He often went there due to his previous association with the place, just as the elder Gavampati frequented the Tāvatiṃsa heaven—as mentioned in the commentary to the Vaṅgīsa Sutta. There, by the Ganges, under a cool tree, having attained meditative absorption, he sat for his midday rest. On that same day, King Udena also had gone to the park for recreation. After enjoying much of the day with dancing, singing, and other amusements, intoxicated with drink, he lay down with his head on the lap of one of his women. The other women, thinking, “The king is asleep,” rose and wandered through the park gathering flowers and fruits. Seeing the elder, they aroused shame and fear of wrongdoing. Silencing each other with, “Do not make a noise,” they approached quietly, paid homage, and sat surrounding him. Emerging from his meditative state, the elder taught them the Dhamma. Delighted, they listened, exclaiming, “Excellent, excellent!”

Rañño sīsaṃ aṅkenādāya nisinnitthī “imā maṃ ohāya kīḷantī”ti tāsu issāpakatā ūruṃ cāletvā rājānaṃ pabodhesi. Rājā paṭibujjhitvā itthāgāraṃ apassanto “kuhiṃ imā vasaliyo”ti āha. Sā āha – “tumhesu abahukatā ‘samaṇaṃ ramayissāmā’ti gatā”ti. So kuddho therābhimukho agamāsi. Tā itthiyo rājānaṃ disvā ekaccā uṭṭhahiṃsu, ekaccā “mahārāja, pabbajitassa santike dhammaṃ suṇāmā”ti na uṭṭhahiṃsu. So tena bhiyyosomattāya [P 2.0515] kuddho theraṃ avanditvāva “kimatthaṃ āgatosī”ti āha. “Vivekatthaṃ mahārājā”ti. So “vivekatthāya āgatā evaṃ itthāgāraparivutā nisīdantī”ti vatvā “tava vivekaṃ kathehī”ti āha. Thero visāradopi vivekakathāya “nāyaṃ aññātukāmo pucchatī”ti tuṇhī ahosi. Rājā “sace na kathesi, tambakipillikehi taṃ khādāpessāmī”ti aññatarasmiṃ asokarukkhe tambakipillikapuṭaṃ gaṇhanto attanova upari vikiri. So sarīraṃ puñchitvā aññaṃ puṭaṃ gahetvā therābhimukho agamāsi. Thero “sacāyaṃ rājā mayi aparajjheyya[M 2.0232], apāyābhimukho bhaveyyā”ti taṃ anukampamāno iddhiyā ākāsaṃ abbhuggantvā gato.

The woman who was sitting with the king’s head on her lap, thinking, “These women are playing, having left me,” stirred with jealousy, moved her thigh, and woke the king. The king, waking up and not seeing the women of the inner chamber, asked, “Where are these wretches?” She replied, “Disregarding you, they have gone, saying, ‘We will amuse ourselves with the ascetic.’” Angered, he went toward the elder. Seeing the king, some of the women stood up, while others, saying, “Great king, we are listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the ascetic,” did not rise. He, even more furious because of that, without even saluting the elder, asked, “Why have you come here?” “For solitude, great king,” he replied. The king, saying, “Having come for solitude, you sit surrounded by the women of the inner chamber? Speak of your solitude!” Though confident in speaking of solitude, the elder remained silent, thinking, “He is not asking with the desire to understand.” The king, threatening, “If you do not speak, I will have you eaten by red ants!” took hold of a nest of red ants on a certain asoka tree and scattered it over himself. Brushing off his body, he took another nest and advanced toward the elder. The elder, thinking, “If this king should do wrong against me, he would be facing ruin,” pitying him, rose into the sky by his psychic power and departed.

Tato [V 2.0211] itthiyo āhaṃsu – “mahārāja, aññe rājāno īdisaṃ pabbajitaṃ disvā pupphagandhādīhi pūjenti, tvaṃ tambakipillikapuṭena āsādetuṃ āraddho ahosi, kulavaṃsaṃ nāsetuṃ uṭṭhito”ti. So attano dosaṃ ñatvā tuṇhī hutvā uyyānapālaṃ pucchi – “aññampi divasaṃ thero idhāgacchatī”ti? “Āma, mahārājā”ti. Tena hi yadā āgacchati, tadā me āroceyyāsīti. So ekadivasaṃ there āgate ārocesi. Rājāpi theraṃ upasaṅkamitvā pañhaṃ pucchitvā pāṇehi saraṇaṃ gato ahosi. Tambakipillikapuṭena āsāditadivase pana thero ākāsenāgantvā puna pathaviyaṃ nimujjitvā bhagavato gandhakuṭiyaṃ ummujji. Bhagavāpi kho dakkhiṇena passena sato sampajāno sīhaseyyaṃ kappayamāno theraṃ disvā “kiṃ, bhāradvāja, akāle āgatosī”ti āha. Thero “āma bhagavā”ti vatvā sabbaṃ taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesi. Taṃ sutvā bhagavā “kiṃ karissati tassa vivekakathā kāmaguṇagiddhassā”ti vatvā dakkhiṇena passena nipanno eva therassa dhammadesanatthaṃ imaṃ suttamabhāsi.

Then the women said, “Great king, other kings, upon seeing such a recluse, honor him with flowers, perfumes, and the like. But you were intent on harassing him with a nest of red ants, having arisen to destroy your family line.” Realizing his fault, the king fell silent and asked the park keeper, “Does the elder come here on other days as well?” “Yes, great king,” he replied. “Then, when he comes again, inform me,” the king instructed. One day, when the elder arrived, the park keeper informed the king. The king approached the elder, asked him a question, and went for refuge to him with his life. On the day he was harassed with the nest of red ants, the elder had come through the sky, then submerged into the earth, and emerged in the Blessed One’s fragrant dwelling. The Blessed One, reclining on his right side, mindful and fully aware, in the lion's posture, saw the elder and said, “Why, Bhāradvāja, have you come at an unseasonable time?” The elder replied, “Yes, Blessed One,” and recounted the entire incident. Hearing this, the Blessed One said, “What will talk of seclusion do for one greedy for sensual pleasures?” Then, while still lying on his right side, he spoke this sutta for the elder’s instruction.

Tattha sattoti laggo. Guhāyanti kāye. Kāyo hi rāgādīnaṃ vāḷānaṃ vasanokāsato “guhā”ti vuccati. Bahunābhichannoti bahunā rāgādikilesajālena abhicchanno. Etena ajjhattabandhanaṃ vuttaṃ. Tiṭṭhanti rāgādivasena tiṭṭhanto. Naroti satto. Mohanasmiṃ pagāḷhoti mohanaṃ vuccati kāmaguṇā. Ettha hi devamanussā muyhanti, tesu ajjhogāḷho hutvā[P 2.0516]. Etena bahiddhābandhanaṃ vuttaṃ. Dūre vivekā hi tathāvidho soti so tathārūpo naro tividhāpi kāyavivekādikā vivekā dūre anāsanne. Kiṃkāraṇā? Kāmā hi loke na hi suppahāyā, yasmā loke kāmā suppahāyā na hontīti vuttaṃ hoti.

There, 'a being' means an attached one. 'In a cave' refers to the body. For the body is called a 'cave' because it is the dwelling place for the wild beasts of lust and other defilements. 'Covered with much' means covered by the net of defilements such as lust. By this, internal bondage is stated. 'Dwelling' means dwelling by way of lust and other defilements. 'A man' means a being. 'Plunged into delusion'—delusion refers to the objects of sensual pleasure. For here, gods and humans are deluded, being deeply immersed in them. By this, external bondage is stated. 'Far from seclusion'—such a person, such a being, is far from the three kinds of seclusion, such as bodily seclusion. Why? Because sensual pleasures in the world are indeed not easy to abandon. Thus, it is said that sensual pleasures in the world are not easily abandoned.

780. Evaṃ paṭhamagāthāya “dūre vivekā tathāvidho”ti sādhetvā puna tathāvidhānaṃ sattānaṃ dhammataṃ āvikaronto “icchānidānā”ti gāthamāha. Tattha icchānidānāti taṇhāhetukā. Bhavasātabaddhāti sukhavedanādimhi bhavasāte baddhā. Te duppamuñcāti te bhavasātavatthubhūtā [M 2.0233] dhammā, te vā tattha baddhā icchānidānā sattā duppamocayā. Na hi aññamokkhāti aññena ca mocetuṃ na sakkonti. Kāraṇavacanaṃ vā etaṃ, te sattā duppamuñcā. Kasmā? Yasmā aññena mocetabbā na honti. Yadi pana muñceyyuṃ, sakena thāmena muñceyyunti ayamassa attho.
