Pacchā pure vāpi apekkhamānāti anāgate atīte vā kāme apekkhamānā. Imeva kāme purimeva jappanti ime vā paccuppanne kāme purime vā duvidhepi atītānāgate balavataṇhāya patthayamānā. Imesañca dvinnaṃ padānaṃ “te duppamuñcā na hi aññamokkhā”ti iminā saha sambandho [V 2.0212] veditabbo, itarathā “apekkhamānā jappaṃ kiṃ karonti kiṃ vā katā”ti na paññāyeyyuṃ.

780. Thus, having established in the first verse that “such a one is far from seclusion,” he now reveals the nature of such beings by stating the verse beginning with “icchānidānā.” Herein, “icchānidānā” means caused by craving. “Bhavasātabaddhā” means bound to the pleasure of existence, such as pleasant feeling. “Te duppamuñcā” means those phenomena that are the basis for the pleasure of existence, or those beings bound there, originating from craving, are hard to release. “Na hi aññamokkhā” means they cannot be freed by another. Or this is a statement of reason: those beings are hard to release. Why? Because they are not to be freed by another. If, however, they were to be freed, they would be freed by their own strength—this is the meaning. “Pacchā pure vāpi apekkhamānā” means longing for sensual pleasures in the future or the past. “Imeva kāme purimeva jappanti” means they desire these present sensual pleasures, or both the former kinds—past and future—due to powerful craving. And the connection of these two phrases should be understood with “they are hard to release, for they are not freed by another.” Otherwise, it would not be clear what those who are “longing” and “craving” do or have done.

781-2. Evaṃ paṭhamagāthāya “dūre vivekā tathāvidho”ti sādhetvā dutiyagāthāya ca tathāvidhānaṃ sattānaṃ dhammataṃ āvikatvā idāni nesaṃ pāpakammakaraṇaṃ āvikaronto “kāmesu giddhā”ti gāthamāha. Tassattho – te sattā kāmesu paribhogataṇhāya giddhā pariyesanādimanuyuttattā pasutā sammohamāpannattā pamūḷhā avagamanatāya maccharitāya buddhādīnaṃ vacanaṃ anādiyanatāya ca avadāniyā. Kāyavisamādimhi visame niviṭṭhā antakāle maraṇadukkhūpanītā “kiṃsū bhavissāma ito cutāse”ti paridevayantīti. Yasmā etadeva, tasmā hi sikkhetha…pe… māhu dhīrāti. Tattha sikkhethāti tisso sikkhā āpajjeyya. Idhevāti [P 2.0517] imasmiṃyeva sāsane. Sesamuttānameva.

781-2. Thus, having established in the first verse that “such a one is far from seclusion,” and having revealed the nature of such beings in the second verse, he now reveals their performance of evil deeds by stating the verse beginning with “kāmesu giddhā.” Its meaning is this: those beings are greedy for sensual pleasures due to craving for enjoyment; they are engrossed, being devoted to seeking and the like; they are bewildered, having fallen into delusion; and they are incorrigible due to their lack of understanding, their miserliness, and their failure to heed the words of the Buddha and others. They are entrenched in wrong conduct, such as bodily misconduct, and at the time of death, afflicted by the suffering of death, they lament, “What shall we become after passing from here?” Because it is just so, therefore: “One should train… say the wise.” Herein, “sikkhetha” means one should undertake the threefold training. “Idheva” means right here in this very Dispensation. The rest is self-evident.

783. Idāni ye tathā na karonti, tesaṃ byasanappattiṃ dassento “passāmī”ti gāthamāha. Tattha passāmīti maṃsacakkhuādīhi pekkhāmi. Loketi apāyādimhi. Pariphandamānanti ito cito ca phandamānaṃ. Pajaṃ imanti imaṃ sattakāyaṃ. Taṇhagatanti taṇhāya gataṃ abhibhūtaṃ, nipātitanti adhippāyo. Bhavesūti kāmabhavādīsu. Hīnā narāti hīnakammantā narā. Maccumukhe lapantīti antakāle sampatte maraṇamukhe paridevanti. Avītataṇhāseti avigatataṇhā. Bhavābhavesūti kāmabhavādīsu. Atha vā bhavābhavesūti bhavabhavesu, punappunabhavesūti vuttaṃ hoti.

783. Now, to show the misfortune of those who do not act accordingly, he speaks the verse beginning with “Passāmi.” Here, “Passāmi” means I see with the physical eye and so forth. “Loke” refers to the woeful states and the like. “Pariphandamānaṃ” means trembling here and there. “Pajaṃ imaṃ” refers to this host of beings. “Taṇhagataṃ” means gone to craving, overcome by it; the meaning intended is ‘felled.’ “Bhavesu” refers to the realms of sensual existence and so forth. “Hīnā narā” means men of base actions. “Maccumukhe lapanti” means they lament at the mouth of death when their end has come. “Avītataṇhāse” means with craving un-departed. “Bhavābhavesu” refers to the realms of sensual existence and so forth. Alternatively, “bhavābhavesu” means in this or that state of existence, that is to say, in repeated existences.

784. Idāni yasmā avītataṇhā evaṃ phandanti ca lapanti ca, tasmā taṇhāvinaye samādapento “mamāyite”ti gāthamāha. Tattha mamāyiteti taṇhādiṭṭhimamattehi “mama”nti pariggahite vatthusmiṃ. Passathāti sotāre [M 2.0234] ālapanto āha. Etampīti etampi ādīnavaṃ. Sesaṃ pākaṭameva.

784. Now, because those with craving un-departed thus tremble and lament, he speaks the verse beginning with “Mamāyite” in order to encourage the removal of craving. Here, “mamāyite” refers to a thing claimed as “mine” through the “mineness” of craving and views. “Passatha,” he says, addressing the listeners. “Etampi” means this danger also. The rest is manifest.

785. Evamettha paṭhamagāthāya assādaṃ, tato parāhi catūhi ādīnavañca dassetvā idāni saupāyaṃ nissaraṇaṃ nissaraṇānisaṃsañca dassetuṃ sabbāhi vā etāhi kāmānaṃ ādīnavaṃ okāraṃ saṃkilesañca dassetvā idāni nekkhamme ānisaṃsaṃ dassetuṃ “ubhosu antesū”ti gāthādvayamāha. Tattha ubhosu antesūti phassaphassasamudayādīsu dvīsu paricchedesu. Vineyya chandanti chandarāgaṃ vinetvā. Phassaṃ pariññāyāti cakkhusamphassādiphassaṃ, phassānusārena vā [V 2.0213] taṃsampayutte sabbepi arūpadhamme, tesaṃ vatthudvārārammaṇavasena rūpadhamme cāti sakalampi nāmarūpaṃ tīhi pariññāhi parijānitvā. Anānugiddhoti rūpādīsu sabbadhammesu agiddho. Yadattagarahī tadakubbamānoti yaṃ attanā garahati, taṃ akurumāno. Nalippatī diṭṭhasutesu dhīroti so evarūpo dhitisampanno dhīro diṭṭhesu ca sutesu ca dhammesu dvinnaṃ lepānaṃ ekenapi lepena na lippati. Ākāsamiva nirupalitto accantavodānappatto hoti.

785. Thus, having shown the gratification in the first verse, and the danger in the subsequent four, he now speaks the two verses beginning with ‘Ubhosu antesu’ to show the escape with its means and the benefit of escape. Or, having shown the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures by all these verses, he now speaks them to show the benefit in renunciation. Herein, ‘ubhosu antesu’ (at both ends) refers to the two divisions, such as contact and the origin of contact. ‘Vineyya chandaṃ’ (having subdued desire) means having subdued desire and lust. ‘Phassaṃ pariññāya’ (having fully understood contact) means having fully understood contact, such as eye-contact, through the three kinds of full understanding; or, in accordance with contact, all associated immaterial phenomena, and also the material phenomena by way of their bases, doors, and objects—thus, the whole of name-and-form. ‘Anānugiddho’ (not greedy) means not greedy for any phenomena, such as forms. ‘Yadattagarahī tadakubbamāno’ (not doing what he himself would censure) means not doing that which he censures in himself. ‘Nalippatī diṭṭhasutesu dhīro’ (the wise one is not stained by what is seen and heard) means such a wise one, endowed with fortitude, is not stained by phenomena seen or heard with even one of the two kinds of stain. He is like space, unstained, having attained ultimate purity.

786. Saññaṃ pariññāti gāthāya pana ayaṃ saṅkhepattho – na kevalañca [P 2.0518] phassameva, apica kho pana kāmasaññādibhedaṃ saññampi, saññānusārena vā pubbe vuttanayeneva nāmarūpaṃ tīhi pariññāhi parijānitvā imāya paṭipadāya catubbidhampi vitareyya oghaṃ, tato so tiṇṇogho taṇhādiṭṭhipariggahesu taṇhādiṭṭhilepappahānena nopalitto khīṇāsavamuni rāgādisallānaṃ abbūḷhattā abbūḷhasallo sativepullappattiyā appamatto caraṃ, pubbabhāge vā appamatto caraṃ tena appamādacārena abbūḷhasallo hutvā sakaparattabhāvādibhedaṃ nāsīsatī lokamimaṃ parañca, aññadatthu carimacittanirodhā nirupādāno jātavedova parinibbātīti arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi dhammanettiṭṭhapanameva karonto, na uttariṃ imāya desanāya maggaṃ vā phalaṃ vā uppādesi khīṇāsavassa desitattāti.

786. Now, the brief meaning of the verse beginning ‘Saññaṃ pariññāya’ is this: having fully understood not only contact, but also perception in its divisions of sensual perception and so forth—or, in accordance with perception, name-and-form in the manner previously stated—through the three kinds of full understanding, by this practice one may cross the fourfold flood. Then, having crossed the flood, unstained by the graspings of craving and views through the abandoning of the stains of craving and views, the sage whose taints are destroyed, having drawn out the darts of lust and so forth, fares heedfully, having attained an abundance of mindfulness. Or, faring heedfully in the preliminary stage, and by that heedful conduct having become one with dart drawn out, he does not long for this world or the next, distinguished as his own existence or another’s. Rather, with the cessation of the final consciousness, being without clinging, he is fully extinguished like a fire. Thus he concludes the discourse with the pinnacle of Arahantship, merely establishing the standard of the Dhamma, not generating any further path or fruit by this teaching, since it was taught for one whose taints are destroyed.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya guhaṭṭhakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Here ends the explanation of the Guhaṭṭhaka Sutta in the Commentary on the Suttanipāta.

3. Duṭṭhaṭṭhakasuttavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Duṭṭhaṭṭhaka Sutta.

787. Vadanti [V 2.0214][M 2.0235] ve duṭṭhamanāpīti duṭṭhaṭṭhakasuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Ādigāthāya tāva uppatti – munisuttanayena bhagavato bhikkhusaṅghassa ca uppannalābhasakkāraṃ asahamānā titthiyā sundariṃ paribbājikaṃ uyyojesuṃ. Sā kira janapadakalyāṇī setavatthaparibbājikāva ahosi. Sā sunhātā sunivatthā mālāgandhavilepanavibhūsitā bhagavato dhammaṃ sutvā sāvatthivāsīnaṃ jetavanato nikkhamanavelāya sāvatthito nikkhamitvā jetavanābhimukhī gacchati. Manussehi ca “kuhiṃ gacchasī”ti pucchitā “samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ sāvake cassa ramayituṃ gacchāmī”ti vatvā jetavanadvārakoṭṭhake vicaritvā jetavanadvārakoṭṭhake pidahite nagaraṃ pavisitvā pabhāte puna jetavanaṃ gantvā gandhakuṭisamīpe pupphāni vicinantī viya carati[P 2.0519]. Buddhupaṭṭhānaṃ āgatehi ca manussehi “kimatthaṃ āgatāsī”ti pucchitā yaṃkiñcideva bhaṇati. Evaṃ aḍḍhamāsamatte vītikkante titthiyā taṃ jīvitā voropetvā parikhātaṭe nikkhipitvā pabhāte “sundariṃ na passāmā”ti kolāhalaṃ katvā rañño ca ārocetvā tena anuññātā jetavanaṃ pavisitvā vicinantā viya taṃ nikkhittaṭṭhānā uddharitvā mañcakaṃ āropetvā nagaraṃ abhiharitvā upakkosaṃ akaṃsu. Sabbaṃ pāḷiyaṃ (udā. 38) āgatanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

787. The Duṭṭhaṭṭhaka Sutta begins with 'Vadanti ve duṭṭhamanāpi'. What is its origin? First, the origin of the opening verse: following the manner of the Muni Sutta, the sectarians, unable to bear the gain and honor that arose for the Blessed One and the community of bhikkhus, instigated the female wandering ascetic Sundarī. She was, it is said, a country beauty, a wandering ascetic clad in white. Well-bathed, well-dressed, and adorned with garlands, perfumes, and cosmetics, she would leave Sāvatthī and go towards Jetavana at the time when the residents of Sāvatthī were departing from Jetavana after having heard the Dhamma. When people asked her, 'Where are you going?' she replied, 'I am going to delight the ascetic Gotama and his disciples.' She wandered near the gatehouse of Jetavana, and when the gatehouse was closed, she entered the city. In the morning, she returned to Jetavana and walked around near the Fragrant Hut as if picking flowers. When people who had come to attend upon the Buddha asked her, 'Why have you come?' she would say whatever came to mind. After about half a month had passed in this way, the sectarians deprived her of life, threw her into a trench, and in the morning raised an uproar, saying, 'We do not see Sundarī!' They reported it to the king and, with his permission, entered Jetavana. Pretending to search, they recovered her from the place where she was thrown, placed her on a stretcher, carried her into the city, and began to slander. All this should be understood in accordance with the way it is found in the Pāli text (Udāna 38).

Bhagavā taṃ divasaṃ paccūsasamaye buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ volokento “titthiyā ajja ayasaṃ uppādessantī”ti ñatvā “tesaṃ saddahitvā mādise cittaṃ pakopetvā mahājano apāyābhimukho mā ahosī”ti gandhakuṭidvāraṃ pidahitvā antogandhakuṭiyaṃyeva acchi, na nagaraṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Bhikkhū pana dvāraṃ pidahitaṃ disvā pubbasadisameva pavisiṃsu. Manussā bhikkhū disvā nānappakārehi akkosiṃsu. Atha āyasmā ānando bhagavato taṃ pavattiṃ ārocetvā “titthiyehi, bhante, mahāayaso uppādito, na sakkā idha vasituṃ, vipulo jambudīpo, aññattha gacchāmā”ti āha. Tatthapi ayase uṭṭhite kuhiṃ gamissasi ānandāti? “Aññaṃ nagaraṃ bhagavā”ti. Atha bhagavā “āgamehi, ānanda, sattāhamevāyaṃ saddo bhavissati, sattāhaccayena yehi ayaso [M 2.0236] kato, tesaṃyeva upari patissatī”ti vatvā ānandattherassa dhammadesanatthaṃ “vadanti ve”ti imaṃ gāthamabhāsi.

The Blessed One, at dawn that day, surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, knew: 'Today, the sectarians will create disgrace.' Thinking: 'Lest the great populace, having believed them and provoked their minds against one such as I, should be headed for the planes of misery,' He closed the door of the Fragrant Hut and remained inside the Fragrant Hut itself, not entering the city for alms. The bhikkhus, however, seeing the door closed, entered just as before. People, seeing the bhikkhus, reviled them in various ways. Then the Venerable Ānanda informed the Blessed One of that event and said: 'Venerable sir, the sectarians have created great disgrace; it is not possible to stay here. Jambudīpa is vast; let us go elsewhere.' 'Where will you go, Ānanda, if disgrace arises there too?' 'To another city, Blessed One.' Then the Blessed One said: 'Wait, Ānanda. This uproar will last for only seven days. After seven days, it will fall back upon those who created the disgrace.' Having spoken thus, for the sake of teaching the Dhamma to the Elder Ānanda, He recited this verse: 'Vadanti ve...'

Tattha [V 2.0215] vadantīti bhagavantaṃ bhikkhusaṅghañca upavadanti. Duṭṭhamanāpi eke athopi ve saccamanāti ekacce duṭṭhacittā, ekacce tathasaññinopi hutvā, titthiyā duṭṭhacittā, ye tesaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā saddahiṃsu, te saccamanāti adhippāyo. Vādañca jātanti etaṃ akkosavādaṃ [P 2.0520] uppannaṃ. Muni no upetīti akārakatāya ca akuppanatāya ca buddhamuni na upeti. Tasmā munī natthi khilo kuhiñcīti tena kāraṇena ayaṃ muni rāgādikhilehi natthi khilo kuhiñcīti veditabbo.

Herein, 'vadanti' means they blame the Blessed One and the community of bhikkhus. 'Some with malevolent minds, and some with minds on truth': some have malevolent minds, while some perceive it as true. The sectarians are those with malevolent minds. Those who, having heard their words, believed them, are intended by 'with minds on truth'. 'And a dispute having arisen' means this abusive speech arose. 'The sage does not engage' means the Buddha-sage does not engage, due to not being the perpetrator and due to being imperturbable. Therefore, 'the sage has no mental barrenness anywhere' means for that reason this sage should be understood as having no mental barrenness anywhere from lust and so forth.

788. Imañca gāthaṃ vatvā bhagavā ānandattheraṃ pucchi, “evaṃ khuṃsetvā vambhetvā vuccamānā bhikkhū, ānanda, kiṃ vadantī”ti. Na kiñci bhagavāti. “Na, ānanda, ‘ahaṃ sīlavā’ti sabbattha tuṇhī bhavitabbaṃ, loke hi nābhāsamānaṃ jānanti missaṃ bālehi paṇḍita”nti vatvā, “bhikkhū, ānanda, te manusse evaṃ paṭicodentū”ti dhammadesanatthāya “abhūtavādī nirayaṃ upetī”ti imaṃ gāthamabhāsi. Thero taṃ uggahetvā bhikkhū āha – “manussā tumhehi imāya gāthāya paṭicodetabbā”ti. Bhikkhū tathā akaṃsu. Paṇḍitamanussā tuṇhī ahesuṃ. Rājāpi rājapurise sabbato pesetvā yesaṃ dhuttānaṃ lañjaṃ datvā titthiyā taṃ mārāpesuṃ, te gahetvā niggayha taṃ pavattiṃ ñatvā titthiye paribhāsi. Manussāpi titthiye disvā leḍḍunā paharanti, paṃsunā okiranti “bhagavato ayasaṃ uppādesu”nti. Ānandatthero taṃ disvā bhagavato ārocesi, bhagavā therassa imaṃ gāthamabhāsi “sakañhi diṭṭhiṃ…pe… vadeyyā”ti.

788. Having spoken this verse, the Blessed One asked the Elder Ānanda: 'Ānanda, when the bhikkhus are thus abused and scorned, what do they say?' 'Nothing, Blessed One.' 'Ānanda, one should not remain silent everywhere, thinking, "I am virtuous," for in the world, a wise person is not recognized when mingled with fools and not speaking.' Having said this, for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma, he instructed: 'Ānanda, let the bhikkhus reprove those people thus,' and he spoke this verse: 'One who speaks what is not true goes to hell.' The Elder, having learned it, told the bhikkhus: 'You should reprove those people with this verse.' The bhikkhus did so. The wise among the people became silent. The king, too, having sent his royal officers everywhere, seized those rogues to whom the sectarians had given a bribe to have her killed. Having punished them and learned of the event, he rebuked the sectarians. The people, too, seeing the sectarians, struck them with clods and showered them with dust, saying: 'They have created disgrace for the Blessed One!' The Elder Ānanda, seeing this, reported it to the Blessed One, who then spoke this verse to the Elder: 'For one's own view... one would say.'

Tassattho – yāyaṃ diṭṭhi titthiyajanassa “sundariṃ māretvā samaṇānaṃ sakyaputtiyānaṃ avaṇṇaṃ pakāsetvā etenupāyena laddhaṃ sakkāraṃ sādiyissāmā”ti, so taṃ diṭṭhiṃ kathaṃ atikkameyya, atha kho so ayaso tameva titthiyajanaṃ paccāgato taṃ diṭṭhiṃ accetuṃ asakkontaṃ. Yo vā sassatādivādī, sopi sakaṃ diṭṭhiṃ kathaṃ accayeyya tena diṭṭhicchandena anunīto tāya ca diṭṭhiruciyā niviṭṭho, apica kho pana sayaṃ samattāni [M 2.0237] pakubbamāno attanāva paripuṇṇāni tāni diṭṭhigatāni karonto yathā jāneyya, tatheva vadeyyāti.

Its meaning is this: How could that sectarian person overcome this view: 'Having killed Sundarī, we will proclaim the dispraise of the ascetics, the sons of the Sakyan, and by this means enjoy the honor we have gained'? Indeed, that disgrace returned to that very sectarian person, unable to overcome that view. Or how could one who holds doctrines of eternalism and so forth abandon his own view, being led on by desire for that view and settled in his preference for that view? Moreover, personally adopting them and making those views complete by himself, he would speak just as he knows.

789. Atha rājā sattāhaccayena taṃ kuṇapaṃ chaḍḍāpetvā sāyanhasamayaṃ [P 2.0521] vihāraṃ gantvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā āha – “nanu, bhante, īdise ayase uppanne mayhampi ārocetabbaṃ siyā”ti. Evaṃ vutte bhagavā, “na, mahārāja, ‘ahaṃ sīlavā guṇasampanno’ti paresaṃ ārocetuṃ [V 2.0216] ariyānaṃ patirūpa”nti vatvā tassā aṭṭhuppattiyaṃ “yo attano sīlavatānī”ti avasesagāthāyo abhāsi.

789. Then, after seven days, the king had that corpse disposed of. In the evening, he went to the monastery, paid homage to the Blessed One, and said: 'Venerable sir, when such a misfortune arose, should I not have been informed?' When this was said, the Blessed One replied: 'Great king, it is not proper for noble ones to announce to others, “I am virtuous, I am endowed with good qualities.”' Having said this, in response to that occurrence, he spoke the remaining verses beginning with: 'One who his own virtuous practices...'

Tattha sīlavatānīti pātimokkhādīni sīlāni āraññikādīni dhutaṅgavatāni ca. Anānupuṭṭhoti apucchito. Pāvāti vadati. Anariyadhammaṃ kusalā tamāhu, yo ātumānaṃ sayameva pāvāti yo evaṃ attānaṃ sayameva vadati, tassa taṃ vādaṃ “anariyadhammo eso”ti kusalā evaṃ kathenti.

Here, 'virtuous practices' refers to the precepts such as the Pātimokkha, and the ascetic practices such as forest-dwelling. 'Unasked' means not questioned. 'Declares' means speaks. 'The wise call that an ignoble quality, for one who praises himself': this means the wise say of one who thus praises himself, of that speech, 'This is an ignoble quality.'

790. Santoti rāgādikilesavūpasamena santo, tathā abhinibbutatto. Itihanti sīlesu akatthamānoti “ahamasmi sīlasampanno”tiādinā nayena iti sīlesu akatthamāno, sīlanimittaṃ attūpanāyikaṃ vācaṃ abhāsamānoti vuttaṃ hoti. Tamariyadhammaṃ kusalā vadantīti tassa taṃ akatthanaṃ “ariyadhammo eso”ti buddhādayo khandhādikusalā vadanti. Yassussadā natthi kuhiñci loketi yassa khīṇāsavassa rāgādayo satta ussadā kuhiñci loke natthi, tassa taṃ akatthanaṃ “ariyadhammo eso”ti evaṃ kusalā vadantīti sambandho.

790. 'Peaceful' means peaceful through the calming of defilements such as lust, and thus completely stilled. 'Thus not boasting about virtues' means not saying, 'I am accomplished in virtue,' and so forth, thereby not boasting about virtues; that is to say, not speaking words that bring the self forward on account of virtue. 'The wise call this the noble quality': Buddhas and others skilled in the aggregates and so forth say of such non-boasting, 'This is a noble quality.' 'For whom there are no conceits anywhere in the world': For the one whose taints are destroyed, the seven kinds of conceits, such as lust, do not exist anywhere in the world. The connection is that the wise say of such non-boasting, 'This is a noble quality.'

791. Evaṃ khīṇāsavapaṭipattiṃ dassetvā idāni diṭṭhigatikānaṃ titthiyānaṃ paṭipattiṃ rañño dassento āha – “pakappitā saṅkhatā”ti. Tattha pakappitāti parikappitā. Saṅkhatāti paccayābhisaṅkhatā. Yassāti yassa kassaci diṭṭhigatikassa. Dhammāti diṭṭhiyo. Purakkhatāti purato katā. Santīti saṃvijjanti. Avīvadātāti avodātā. Yadattani passati ānisaṃsaṃ, taṃ nissito kuppapaṭiccasantinti yassete diṭṭhidhammā purakkhatā avodātā santi, so evaṃvidho yasmā attani tassā diṭṭhiyā diṭṭhidhammikañca [M 2.0238][P 2.0522] sakkārādiṃ, samparāyikañca gativisesādiṃ ānisaṃsaṃ passati, tasmā tañca ānisaṃsaṃ, tañca kuppatāya ca paṭiccasamuppannatāya ca sammutisantitāya ca kuppapaṭiccasantisaṅkhātaṃ diṭṭhiṃ nissitova hoti, so tannissitattā attānaṃ vā ukkaṃseyya pare vā vambheyya abhūtehipi guṇadosehi.

791. Having thus shown the practice of one whose taints are destroyed, now revealing to the king the practice of sectarians holding wrong views, he said: 'Fabricated, conditioned...' Here, 'fabricated' means mentally constructed. 'Conditioned' means conditioned by causes. 'Of whom' refers to any holder of wrong views. 'Doctrines' means the views. 'Held foremost' means placed ahead. 'Exist' means are present. 'Impure' means not stainless. 'Whatever benefit one sees for oneself, relying on that, one relies on what is unstable and conditionally arisen': For one whose views are held foremost and are impure, because he sees for himself the worldly benefits of such views—such as honor—and the afterlife benefits—such as special rebirths—therefore, relying on that benefit and on the view termed 'unstable, conditionally arisen, and conventional' (because of its instability, its dependent origination, and its conventional nature), he might exalt himself or disparage others based on unreal virtues and faults.

792. Evaṃ nissitena ca diṭṭhīnivesā…pe… ādiyatī ca dhammanti. Tattha diṭṭhīnivesāti idaṃsaccābhinivesasaṅkhātāni diṭṭhinivesanāni. Na hi svātivattāti sukhena ativattitabbā na honti. Dhammesu niccheyya samuggahītanti dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhidhammesu taṃ taṃ samuggahitaṃ abhiniviṭṭhaṃ dhammaṃ nicchinitvā pavattattā diṭṭhinivesā na hi svātivattāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tasmā naro tesu nivesanesu, nirassatī ādiyatī ca dhammanti yasmā na hi svātivattā[V 2.0217], tasmā naro tesuyeva diṭṭhinivesanesu ajasīlagosīlakukkurasīlapañcātapamaruppapātaukkuṭikappadhānakaṇṭakāpassayādibhedaṃ satthāradhammakkhānagaṇādibhedañca taṃ taṃ dhammaṃ nirassati ca ādiyati ca jahati ca gaṇhāti ca vanamakkaṭo viya taṃ taṃ sākhanti vuttaṃ hoti. Evaṃ nirassanto ca ādiyanto ca anavaṭṭhitacittattā asantehipi guṇadosehi attano vā parassa vā yasāyasaṃ uppādeyya.

792. Thus, for one who is dependent, entrenchments in views... and he adopts a doctrine. Herein, 'entrenchments in views' refers to the entrenchments in views known as the insistence 'this alone is true.' 'Are not easily overcome' means they are not to be easily overcome. 'Having decisively grasped among doctrines' means that because he proceeds having decided upon that particular firmly grasped and adhered to doctrine among the sixty-two speculative views, it is said that entrenchments in views are not easily overcome. 'Therefore, a person, regarding those entrenchments, rejects and adopts a doctrine': because they are not easily overcome, a person, regarding those very entrenchments in views, rejects and adopts, abandons and grasps, this or that doctrine—with its distinctions such as goat-practice, cow-practice, dog-practice, the five austerities, throwing oneself from a cliff, the squatting posture, lying on thorns, and so on, and with its distinctions of teachers, doctrines, explanations, groups, and so on—like a monkey in the forest grasping this or that branch, it is said. Thus, by rejecting and adopting, due to an unsteady mind, with non-existent virtues and faults, he might produce fame or disgrace for himself or for others.

793. Yo panāyaṃ sabbadiṭṭhigatādidosadhunanāya paññāya samannāgatattā dhono, tassa dhonassa hi…pe… anūpayo so. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Dhonadhammasamannāgamā dhonassa dhutasabbapāpassa arahato katthaci loke tesu tesu bhavesu pakappitā diṭṭhi natthi, so tassā diṭṭhiyā abhāvena, yāya ca attanā kataṃ pāpakammaṃ paṭicchādentā titthiyā māyāya mānena vā etaṃ agatiṃ gacchanti, tampi māyañca mānañca pahāya dhono rāgādīnaṃ dosānaṃ kena gaccheyya, diṭṭhadhamme samparāye vā nirayādīsu gativisesesu kena saṅkhaṃ gaccheyya, anūpayo so, so hi taṇhādiṭṭhiupayānaṃ dvinnaṃ abhāvena anūpayoti.

793. But one who is endowed with wisdom for the shaking off of all faults such as wrong views is 'purified' (dhona). For such a purified one... he is without attachments. What is meant? For the purified one, the Arahant who has shaken off all evil, endowed with the qualities of the purified, there is no fabricated view anywhere in the world, in these various states of existence. Because of the absence of that view—and having abandoned that deceit and pride by which sectarians, concealing the evil deeds done by themselves, go to a wrong course—the purified one, by what defilements such as lust could he be defined? In this present life or the next, among various destinies such as hell, by what could he be reckoned? He is without attachments, for he is without the two attachments of craving and views, hence he is 'without attachments.'

794. Yo pana tesaṃ [P 2.0523] dvinnaṃ bhāvena upayo hoti, so upayo hi…pe… diṭṭhimidheva sabbanti. Tattha upayoti taṇhādiṭṭhinissito. Dhammesu upeti vādanti “ratto”ti vā “duṭṭho”ti vā evaṃ tesu [M 2.0239] tesu dhammesu upeti vādaṃ. Anūpayaṃ kena kathaṃ vadeyyāti taṇhādiṭṭhipahānena anūpayaṃ khīṇāsavaṃ kena rāgena vā dosena vā kathaṃ “ratto”ti vā “duṭṭho”ti vā vadeyya, evaṃ anupavajjo ca so kiṃ titthiyā viya katapaṭicchādako bhavissatīti adhippāyo. Attā nirattā na hi tassa atthīti tassa hi attadiṭṭhi vā ucchedadiṭṭhi vā natthi, gahaṇaṃ muñcanaṃ vāpi attanirattasaññitaṃ natthi. Kiṃkāraṇā natthīti ce? Adhosi so diṭṭhimidheva sabbaṃ, yasmā so idheva attabhāve ñāṇavātena sabbaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ adhosi, pajahi, vinodesīti arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi. Taṃ sutvā rājā attamano bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā pakkāmīti.

794. Now, whoever is attached by reason of the existence of those two, that attachment is indeed… ‘the view itself is all.’ Herein, ‘attachment’ means being rooted in craving and view. ‘He approaches things with a view’ means he approaches those various things with a statement, saying ‘lustful’ or ‘hateful.’ ‘How could one who is free from attachment speak of anything in any way?’: Through the abandonment of craving and view, one is free from attachment—how could one whose taints are destroyed be called ‘lustful’ or ‘hateful’ by any greed or hatred? Thus, being without fault, why would such a one be a concealer of what has been done, like the sectarians? This is the meaning. ‘For him, there is no self or non-self’: Indeed, for him, there is no self-view or annihilation-view, nor any grasping or releasing conceived as self or non-self. If it is asked, ‘Why is this so?’: ‘Because he has shaken off all views right here’—since, with the wind of wisdom, he has shaken off, abandoned, and dispelled all that pertains to views in this very existence. Thus, he concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of arahantship. Having heard this, the king, delighted, paid homage to the Blessed One and departed.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

From the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya.

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya duṭṭhaṭṭhakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Duṭṭhaṭṭhaka Sutta in the Sutta Nipāta Commentary is concluded.

4. Suddhaṭṭhakasuttavaṇṇanā

4. The Explanation of the Suddhaṭṭhaka Sutta

795. Passāmi [V 2.0218] suddhanti suddhaṭṭhakasuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Atīte kira kassapassa bhagavato kāle bārāṇasivāsī aññataro kuṭumbiko pañcahi sakaṭasatehi paccantajanapadaṃ agamāsi bhaṇḍaggahaṇatthaṃ. Tattha vanacarakena saddhiṃ mittaṃ katvā tassa paṇṇākāraṃ datvā pucchi – “kacci, te samma, candanasāraṃ diṭṭhapubba”nti? “Āma sāmī”ti ca vutte teneva saddhiṃ candanavanaṃ pavisitvā sabbasakaṭāni candanasārassa pūretvā tampi vanacarakaṃ “yadā, samma, bārāṇasiṃ āgacchasi, tadā candanasāraṃ gahetvā āgaccheyyāsī”ti vatvā bārāṇasiṃyeva agamāsi. Athāparena samayena sopi vanacarako candanasāraṃ gahetvā tassa gharaṃ agamāsi. So taṃ disvā sabbaṃ paṭisanthāraṃ katvā sāyanhasamaye candanasāraṃ pisāpetvā samuggaṃ pūretvā “gaccha, samma, nhāyitvā āgacchā”ti attano purisena saddhiṃ nhānatitthaṃ [P 2.0524] pesesi. Tena ca samayena bārāṇasiyaṃ ussavo hoti. Atha bārāṇasivāsino pātova dānaṃ [M 2.0240] datvā sāyaṃ suddhavatthanivatthā mālāgandhādīni gahetvā kassapassa bhagavato mahācetiyaṃ vandituṃ gacchanti. So vanacarako te disvā “mahājano kuhiṃ gacchatī”ti pucchi. “Vihāraṃ cetiyavandanatthāyā”ti ca sutvā sayampi agamāsi. Tattha manusse haritālamanosilādīhi nānappakārehi cetiye pūjaṃ karonte disvā kiñci citraṃ kātuṃ ajānanto taṃ candanaṃ gahetvā mahācetiye suvaṇṇiṭṭhakānaṃ. Upari kaṃsapātimattaṃ maṇḍalaṃ akāsi. Atha tattha sūriyuggamanavelāyaṃ sūriyarasmiyo uṭṭhahiṃsu. So taṃ disvā pasīdi, patthanañca akāsi “yattha yattha nibbattāmi, īdisā me rasmiyo ure uṭṭhahantū”ti. So kālaṃ katvā tāvatiṃsesu nibbatti. Tassa ure rasmiyo uṭṭhahiṃsu, candamaṇḍalaṃ viyassa uramaṇḍalaṃ virocati, “candābho devaputto”tveva ca naṃ sañjāniṃsu.

795. The Suddhaṭṭhaka Sutta begins with the words 'Passāmi suddhaṃ' (I see the pure). What is its origin? Indeed, in the past, during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, a certain householder from Varanasi went to a frontier region with five hundred carts to acquire merchandise. There, he befriended a forest dweller, gave him a present, and asked, "Friend, have you ever seen sandalwood?" When the man replied, "Yes, master," they entered the sandalwood forest together, filled all the carts with sandalwood, and the householder told the forest dweller, "Friend, when you come to Varanasi, bring sandalwood with you." Then he returned to Varanasi. Some time later, the forest dweller took sandalwood and went to the householder’s home. Seeing him, the householder welcomed him warmly, had the sandalwood ground in the evening, filled a casket with it, and said, "Go, friend, bathe and return," sending him to the bathing place with one of his servants. At that time, there was a festival in Varanasi. The residents of Varanasi, having given alms in the morning, dressed in clean robes in the evening, took flowers and perfumes, and went to pay homage to the great stupa of the Blessed One Kassapa. The forest dweller saw them and asked, "Where is the crowd going?" Hearing they were going to the monastery to venerate the stupa, he went as well. There, he saw people making offerings to the stupa with various items like yellow orpiment and red arsenic. Not knowing how to make any special offering, he took the sandalwood and made a circular mark the size of a bronze bowl on the golden bricks of the great stupa. Then, at sunrise, rays of light arose there. Seeing this, he was delighted and made an aspiration: "Wherever I am reborn, may such rays of light rise from my chest." After his death, he was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa devas. Rays of light arose from his chest, and his chest shone like a moon disc. They recognized him as "the moon-like deva prince."

So tāya sampattiyā chasu devalokesu anulomapaṭilomato ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ khepetvā amhākaṃ bhagavati uppanne sāvatthiyaṃ brāhmaṇamahāsālakule nibbatti, tathevassa ure candamaṇḍalasadisaṃ rasmimaṇḍalaṃ ahosi. Nāmakaraṇadivase cassa maṅgalaṃ katvā brāhmaṇā taṃ maṇḍalaṃ disvā “dhaññapuññalakkhaṇo ayaṃ kumāro”ti vimhitā “candābho” tveva nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Taṃ vayappattaṃ brāhmaṇā gahetvā alaṅkaritvā rattakañcukaṃ pārupāpetvā rathe āropetvā “mahābrahmā [V 2.0219] aya”nti pūjetvā “yo candābhaṃ passati, so yasadhanādīni labhati, samparāyañca saggaṃ gacchatī”ti ugghosentā gāmanigamarājadhānīsu āhiṇḍanti. Gatagataṭṭhāne manussā “esa kira bho [P 2.0525] candābho nāma, yo etaṃ passati, so yasadhanasaggādīni labhatī”ti uparūpari āgacchanti, sakalajambudīpo cali. Brāhmaṇā tucchahatthakānaṃ āgatānaṃ na dassenti, sataṃ vā sahassaṃ vā gahetvā āgatānameva dassenti. Evaṃ candābhaṃ gahetvā anuvicarantā brāhmaṇā kamena sāvatthiṃ anuppattā.

With that prosperity, having spent one Buddha-interval in the six heavenly realms, moving back and forth, he was reborn in a great Brahmin family in Sāvatthī when our Blessed One arose. Similarly, on his chest was a radiant circle like the moon's orb. On his naming day, the Brahmins performed an auspicious ceremony and, seeing that circle, were astonished and declared, "This boy has the marks of prosperity and merit!" They named him "Candābha." When he came of age, the Brahmins took him, adorned him, dressed him in a red tunic, placed him on a chariot, and honored him, proclaiming, "This is the Great Brahmā! Whoever sees Candābha gains fame, wealth, and other things, and in the next life, goes to heaven!" They traveled through villages, towns, and royal cities, proclaiming this. Wherever they went, people would say, "This, they say, is Candābha! Whoever sees him gains fame, wealth, heaven, and other things!" People flocked to see him, and all of Jambudīpa was stirred. The Brahmins did not show him to those who came empty-handed but only to those who brought a hundred or a thousand. Thus, taking Candābha and wandering about, the Brahmins gradually arrived in Sāvatthī.

Tena ca samayena bhagavā pavattitavaradhammacakko anupubbena sāvatthiṃ āgantvā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane bahujanahitāya dhammaṃ desento. Atha candābho sāvatthiṃ patvā samuddapakkhantakunnadī viya apākaṭo ahosi, candābhoti bhaṇantopi natthi. So sāyanhasamaye mahājanakāyaṃ [M 2.0241] mālāgandhādīni ādāya jetavanābhimukhaṃ gacchantaṃ disvā “kuhiṃ gacchathā”ti pucchi. “Buddho loke uppanno, so bahujanahitāya dhammaṃ deseti, taṃ sotuṃ jetavanaṃ gacchāmā”ti ca tesaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā sopi brāhmaṇagaṇaparivuto tattheva agamāsi. Bhagavā ca tasmiṃ samaye dhammasabhāyaṃ varabuddhāsane nisinnova hoti. Candābho bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamma madhurapaṭisanthāraṃ katvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi, tāvadeva cassa so āloko antarahito. Buddhālokassa hi samīpe asītihatthabbhantare añño āloko nābhibhoti. So “āloko me naṭṭho”ti nisīditvāva uṭṭhāsi, uṭṭhahitvā ca gantumāraddho. Atha naṃ aññataro puriso āha – “kiṃ bho candābha, samaṇassa gotamassa bhīto gacchasī”ti. Nāhaṃ bhīto gacchāmi, apica me imassa tejena āloko na sampajjatīti punadeva bhagavato purato nisīditvā pādatalā paṭṭhāya yāva kesaggā rūparaṃsilakkhaṇādisampattiṃ disvā “mahesakkho samaṇo gotamo, mama ure appamattako āloko uṭṭhito, tāvatakenapi maṃ gahetvā brāhmaṇā sakalajambudīpaṃ vicaranti. Evaṃ varalakkhaṇasampattisamannāgatassa samaṇassa gotamassa neva māno uppanno, addhā ayaṃ anomaguṇasamannāgato bhavissati satthā devamanussāna”nti ativiya pasannacitto bhagavantaṃ vanditvā [P 2.0526] pabbajjaṃ yāci. Bhagavā aññataraṃ theraṃ āṇāpesi – “pabbājehi na”nti. So taṃ pabbājetvā tacapañcakakammaṭṭhānaṃ ācikkhi. So vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā na cireneva arahattaṃ patvā “candābhatthero”ti vissuto ahosi. Taṃ ārabbha bhikkhū kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “kiṃ nu kho, āvuso, ye candābhaṃ addasaṃsu. Te yasaṃ vā dhanaṃ vā labhiṃsu, saggaṃ vā gacchiṃsu, visuddhiṃ vā pāpuṇiṃsu tena cakkhudvārikarūpadassanenā”ti. Bhagavā tassaṃ aṭṭhuppattiyaṃ imaṃ suttamabhāsi.

At that time, the Blessed One, having set in motion the excellent Wheel of the Dhamma, gradually arrived at Sāvatthī and was dwelling in Jeta’s Grove, teaching the Dhamma for the welfare of many people. Then Candābha, having reached Sāvatthī, became as inconspicuous as a small river flowing into the ocean—no one even spoke of him as 'Candābha.' One evening, seeing a large crowd carrying flowers and perfumes heading toward Jeta’s Grove, he asked, 'Where are you going?' They replied, 'A Buddha has arisen in the world. He teaches the Dhamma for the welfare of many people. We are going to Jeta’s Grove to listen to him.' Hearing their words, he too, surrounded by a group of brahmins, went there. At that time, the Blessed One was seated on the excellent Buddha-seat in the Dhamma hall. Candābha approached the Blessed One, exchanged pleasant greetings, and sat to one side. Immediately, his own radiance vanished. For within eighty cubits of the Buddha’s light, no other light can prevail. Thinking, 'My light has disappeared,' he stood up right after sitting down. As he began to leave, a certain man said to him, 'Why, Candābha, are you leaving? Are you afraid of the ascetic Gotama?' 'I am not leaving out of fear. Rather, my light cannot manifest in his presence.' He then sat again before the Blessed One and, starting from the soles of his feet up to the tips of his hair, observed the perfection of his form, rays, and marks. Seeing these, he thought, 'The ascetic Gotama is mighty. The small light that arose in my chest—even with that light alone, brahmins take me with them and travel throughout all of Jambudīpa. Yet this ascetic Gotama, endowed with such excellent marks, has no trace of pride. Surely, he must be a teacher endowed with peerless virtues for gods and humans.' With a heart exceedingly pleased, he paid homage to the Blessed One and requested to go forth. The Blessed One instructed a certain elder, 'Have him go forth.' After ordaining him, the elder taught him the meditation subject of the fivefold repulsiveness of the body. He began insight meditation and, before long, attained arahantship, becoming renowned as 'The Elder Candābha.' In connection with him, the monks raised a discussion: 'Friends, those who saw Candābha—did they gain fame, wealth, heaven, or purity through that sight of form at the eye-door?' On that occasion when the matter arose, the Blessed One spoke this discourse.

Tattha [V 2.0220] paṭhamagāthāya tāvattho – na, bhikkhave, evarūpena dassanena suddhi hoti. Apica kho kilesamalinattā asuddhaṃ, kilesarogānaṃ avigamā sarogameva candābhaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ aññaṃ vā evarūpaṃ disvā diṭṭhigatiko bālo abhijānāti “passāmi suddhaṃ paramaṃ arogaṃ, tena ca diṭṭhisaṅkhātena dassanena saṃsuddhi narassa hotī”ti, so evaṃ abhijānanto taṃ dassanaṃ “parama”nti ñatvā tasmiṃ dassane suddhānupassī samāno [M 2.0242] taṃ dassanaṃ “maggañāṇa”nti pacceti. Taṃ pana maggañāṇaṃ na hoti. Tenāha – “diṭṭhena ce suddhī”ti dutiyagāthaṃ.

First, the meaning of the first verse is this: 'Monks, purity does not come from such seeing.' And indeed, seeing the brahmin Candābha or another of such kind—who is impure due to the stain of defilements and still diseased because the diseases of defilements have not departed—the foolish one, holding wrong views, recognizes: 'I see the pure, supreme, and disease-free. Through this so-called vision, a person becomes purified.' Thus recognizing, regarding that vision as 'supreme,' and contemplating purity in that vision, he accepts that vision as 'knowledge of the path.' But that is not knowledge of the path. Therefore, He said the second verse: 'If purity comes through vision...'

796. Tassattho – tena rūpadassanasaṅkhātena diṭṭhena yadi kilesasuddhi narassa hoti. Tena vā ñāṇena so yadi jātiādidukkhaṃ pajahāti. Evaṃ sante ariyamaggato aññena asuddhimaggeneva so sujjhati, rāgādīhi upadhīhi saupadhiko eva samāno sujjhatīti āpannaṃ hoti, na ca evaṃvidho sujjhati. Tasmā diṭṭhī hi naṃ pāva tathā vadānaṃ, sā naṃ diṭṭhiyeva “micchādiṭṭhiko aya”nti katheti diṭṭhianurūpaṃ “sassato loko”tiādinā nayena tathā tathā vadanti.

796. The meaning of that is: If purity from defilements comes to a person through what is called vision of form, or if through that knowledge one abandons the suffering of birth and so forth—if this were so, then one would be purified by an impure path other than the noble path. It would follow that one is purified while still being burdened with attachments like lust, etc.—but one of such kind is not purified. Therefore, their view is truly corrupt, and that view itself declares of those who speak thus: 'This one holds wrong view.' They speak in accordance with their view, saying, 'The world is eternal,' and so on.

797. Na brāhmaṇoti tatiyagāthā. Tassattho – yo pana bāhitapāpattā brāhmaṇo hoti, so maggena adhigatāsavakkhayo khīṇāsavabrāhmaṇo ariyamaggañāṇato aññena abhimaṅgalasammatarūpasaṅkhāte [P 2.0527] diṭṭhe tathāvidhasaddasaṅkhāte sute avītikkamasaṅkhāte sīle hatthivatādibhede vate pathaviādibhede mute ca uppannena micchāñāṇena suddhiṃ na āha. Sesamassa brāhmaṇassa vaṇṇabhaṇanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. So hi tedhātukapuññe sabbasmiñca pāpe anūpalitto, tassa pahīnattā attadiṭṭhiyā yassa kassaci vā gahaṇassa pahīnattā attañjaho, puññābhisaṅkhārādīnaṃ akaraṇato nayidha pakubbamānoti vuccati. Tasmā naṃ evaṃ pasaṃsanto āha. Sabbasseva cassa purimapādena sambandho veditabbo – puññe ca pāpe ca anūpalitto, attañjaho nayidha pakubbamāno, na brāhmaṇo aññato suddhimāhāti.

797. 'Not a brahmin' introduces the third verse. Its meaning is: One who is a brahmin by having warded off evil, who has attained the destruction of taints through the path, a brahmin whose taints are destroyed—such a one does not declare purity by means of any wrong knowledge arisen in regard to what is seen (such as forms considered auspicious), what is heard (such as similar sounds), precepts (considered inviolable), vows (such as the elephant-vow), or what is sensed (such as the earth element). The rest is spoken in praise of that brahmin. For he is unstained by merit pertaining to the three realms and by all evil; having abandoned self-view and any kind of grasping, he has relinquished the self; because of not making formations of merit and so forth, he is called 'not creating here.' Therefore, praising him thus, it is said. The connection of all this with the preceding line should be understood: 'Unstained by merit or evil, having relinquished the self, not creating here, a brahmin does not declare purity from another source.'

798. Evaṃ na brāhmaṇo aññato suddhimāhāti vatvā idāni ye diṭṭhigatikā aññato suddhiṃ bruvanti, tesaṃ tassā diṭṭhiyā anibbāhakabhāvaṃ dassento “purimaṃ pahāyā”ti gāthamāha. Tassattho – te hi aññato suddhivādā samānāpi yassā diṭṭhiyā appahīnattā gahaṇamuñcanaṃ hoti. Tāya purimaṃ satthārādiṃ pahāya aparaṃ nissitā ejāsaṅkhātāya taṇhāya anugatā abhibhūtā rāgādibhedaṃ na taranti saṅgaṃ, tañca atarantā taṃ taṃ dhammaṃ uggaṇhanti ca nirassajanti ca makkaṭova sākhanti.

798. Thus, having said, 'a brahmin does not declare purity from another,' now, showing the unliberating nature of that view for those who are attached to views and declare purity from another, he speaks the verse: “Having abandoned the former.” Its meaning is this: for though they are proponents of purity from another, because of the non-abandonment of that view, there is grasping and releasing. By that, having abandoned the former, such as a teacher, and relying on another, they are followed by craving, which is agitation, and being overcome, they do not cross over the attachment of lust and the like. And not crossing it, they grasp and reject various teachings, like a monkey on a branch.

799. Pañcamagāthāya [V 2.0221][M 2.0243] sambandho – yo ca so “diṭṭhī hi naṃ pāva tathā vadāna”nti vutto, so sayaṃ samādāyāti. Tattha sayanti sāmaṃ. Samādāyāti gahetvā. Vatānīti hatthivatādīni. Uccāvacanti aparāparaṃ hīnapaṇītaṃ vā satthārato satthārādiṃ. Saññasattoti kāmasaññādīsu laggo. Vidvā ca vedehi samecca dhammanti paramatthavidvā ca arahā catūhi maggañāṇavedehi catusaccadhammaṃ abhisameccāti. Sesaṃ pākaṭameva.

799. The connection with the fifth verse is this: the one described as “for views indeed affect him who speaks thus,” he himself takes up. Herein, 'sayaṃ' means 'personally.' 'Samādāya' means 'having taken up.' 'Vatāni' refers to vows like the elephant-vow and so forth. 'Uccāvacaṃ' means 'high and low,' that is, one after another, inferior or superior, from one teacher to another and so forth. 'Saññasatto' means 'attached to sensual perceptions and the like.' And 'the wise one, having comprehended the Dhamma with knowledge' means the Arahant, wise in the ultimate truth, having fully understood the Dhamma of the Four Truths with the four knowledges of the path. The rest is clear.

800. Sa sabbadhammesu visenibhūto, yaṃ [P 2.0528] kiñci diṭṭhaṃva sutaṃ mutaṃ vāti sobhūripañño khīṇāsavo yaṃ kiñci diṭṭhaṃ vā sutaṃ vā mutaṃ vā tesu sabbadhammesu mārasenaṃ vināsetvā ṭhitabhāvena visenibhūto. Tamevadassinti taṃ evaṃ visuddhadassiṃ. Vivaṭaṃ carantanti taṇhacchadanādivigamena vivaṭaṃ hutvā carantaṃ. Kenīdha lokasmiṃ vikappayeyyāti kena idha loke taṇhākappena vā diṭṭhikappena vā koci vikappeyya, tesaṃ vā pahīnattā rāgādinā pubbe vuttenāti.

800. “He is unopposed among all phenomena, whatever is seen, heard, or sensed”—this refers to the one of vast wisdom, whose taints are destroyed, who is unopposed among all those phenomena, whether seen, heard, or sensed, by having destroyed Māra’s army and being firmly established. “That very seer” means him who has such purified vision. “Walking openly” means walking, having become open through the removal of the covering of craving and the like. “By what in this world could one define him?” means by what in this world could anyone define him through the conceptualization of craving or the conceptualization of views, since these have been abandoned by him, along with lust and the like as previously stated.

801. Na kappayantīti gāthāya sambandho attho ca – kiñca bhiyyo? Te hi tādisā santo dvinnaṃ kappānaṃ purekkhārānañca kenaci na kappayanti na purekkharonti, paramatthaaccantasuddhiadhigatattā anaccantasuddhiṃyeva akiriyasassatadiṭṭhiṃ accanta suddhīti na te vadanti. Ādānaganthaṃ gathitaṃ visajjāti catubbidhampi rūpādīnaṃ ādāyakattā ādānaganthaṃ attano cittasantāne gathitaṃ baddhaṃ ariyamaggasatthena visajja chinditvā. Sesaṃ pākaṭameva.

801. “They do not form conceptions”—the connection and meaning of the verse is this: what more is there to say? For such beings, being thus, do not form conceptions or give preference based on any of the two conceptions or preferences. Having attained ultimate, utter purity, they do not declare non-ultimate purity—the doctrine of inaction or eternalism—to be ultimate purity. “Having relinquished the knot of grasping” means having, with the sword of the noble path, cut off and relinquished the fourfold knot of grasping for forms and the like, which is tied and bound in one's own mental continuum, because it is the cause of grasping for forms and so forth. The rest is clear.

802. Sīmātigoti gāthā ekapuggalādhiṭṭhānāya desanāya vuttā. Pubbasadiso eva panassā sambandho, so evaṃ atthavaṇṇanāya saddhiṃ veditabbo – kiñca bhiyyo so īdiso bhūripañño catunnaṃ kilesasīmānaṃ atītattā sīmātigo bāhitapāpattā ca brāhmaṇo, itthambhūtassa ca tassa natthi paracittapubbenivāsañāṇehi ñatvā vā maṃsacakkhudibbacakkhūhi disvā vā kiñci samuggahītaṃ, abhiniviṭṭhanti vuttaṃ hoti. So ca kāmarāgābhāvato na rāgarāgī, rūpārūparāgābhāvato na virāgaratto[M 2.0244]. Yato evaṃvidhassa “idaṃ para”nti kiñci idha uggahitaṃ natthīti arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi.

802. The verse 'Sīmātigo' was spoken as an instruction based on a single individual. Its connection is similar to the previous one, and it should be understood along with the explanation of its meaning in this way: what more is there to say? Such a one, of vast wisdom, having transcended the four boundaries of defilements, is 'Sīmātigo' (one who has gone beyond boundaries), and being one who has cast out evil, he is a brahmin. And for such a one, there is nothing grasped, whether known through the knowledge of others' minds and past lives, or seen with the fleshly eye and the divine eye, that is clung to. And being free from sensual lust, he is not one who lusts with passion; being free from lust for form and formless realms, he is not one who delights in dispassion. Since for one of such a nature there is nothing grasped here as 'this is supreme,' the teaching is concluded with the pinnacle of Arahantship.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya.

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya suddhaṭṭhakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Suddhaṭṭhaka Sutta in the Commentary on the Suttanipāta is concluded.

5. Paramaṭṭhakasuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Explanation of the Paramaṭṭhaka Sutta

803. Paramanti [V 2.0222][P 2.0529] diṭṭhīsūti paramaṭṭhakasuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Bhagavati kira sāvatthiyaṃ viharante nānātitthiyā sannipatitvā attano attano diṭṭhiṃ dīpentā “idaṃ paramaṃ, idaṃ parama”nti kalahaṃ katvā rañño ārocesuṃ. Rājā sambahule jaccandhe sannipātāpetvā “imesaṃ hatthiṃ dassethā”ti āṇāpesi. Rājapurisā andhe sannipātāpetvā hatthiṃ purato sayāpetvā “passathā”ti āhaṃsu. Te hatthissa ekamekaṃ aṅgaṃ parāmasiṃsu. Tato raññā “kīdiso, bhaṇe, hatthī”ti puṭṭho yo soṇḍaṃ parāmasi, so “seyyathāpi, mahārāja, naṅgalīsā”ti bhaṇi. Ye dantādīni parāmasiṃsu, te itaraṃ “mā bho rañño purato musā bhaṇī”ti paribhāsitvā “seyyathāpi, mahārāja, bhittikhilo”tiādīni āhaṃsu. Rājā taṃ sabbaṃ sutvā “īdiso tumhākaṃ samayo”ti titthiye uyyojesi. Aññataro piṇḍacāriko taṃ pavattiṃ ñatvā bhagavato ārocesi. Bhagavā tassaṃ aṭṭhuppattiyaṃ bhikkhū āmantetvā “yathā, bhikkhave, jaccandhā hatthiṃ ajānantā taṃ taṃ aṅgaṃ parāmasitvā vivadiṃsu, evaṃ titthiyā vimokkhantikadhammaṃ ajānantā taṃ taṃ diṭṭhiṃ parāmasitvā vivadantī”ti vatvā dhammadesanatthaṃ imaṃ suttamabhāsi.

803. The Paramaṭṭhaka Sutta is the one that begins, 'Supreme, among views...' What is its origin? It is said that when the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī, various sectarians gathered and, proclaiming their own respective views, quarreled, saying, “This is supreme, this is supreme,” and reported the matter to the king. The king had many men born blind assembled and ordered, “Show them an elephant.” The king's men gathered the blind men, had an elephant lie before them, and said, “Behold.” They each touched a single part of the elephant. Then, when asked by the king, “What, sirs, is an elephant like?” the one who touched the trunk said, “Great king, it is like a plow-pole.” Those who touched the tusks and other parts scolded the other, saying, “Do not, sir, speak falsely before the king,” and said, “Great king, it is like a wall-post,” and so on. Hearing all this, the king dismissed the sectarians, saying, “Such is your doctrine.” A certain alms-gathering monk, learning of this event, reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, on that occasion, addressed the monks: “Monks, just as those men born blind, not knowing the elephant, touched this or that part and argued, so too do the sectarians, not knowing the Dhamma that leads to liberation, grasp at this or that view and quarrel.” Having said this, he spoke this sutta to teach the Dhamma.

Tattha paramanti diṭṭhīsu paribbasānoti “idaṃ parama”nti gahetvā sakāya sakāya diṭṭhiyā vasamāno. Yaduttari kuruteti yaṃ attano satthārādiṃ seṭṭhaṃ karoti. Hīnāti aññe tato sabbamāhāti taṃ attano satthārādiṃ ṭhapetvā tato aññe sabbe “hīnā ime”ti āha. Tasmā vivādāni avītivattoti tena kāraṇena so diṭṭhikalahe avītivattova hoti.

Therein, 'paramanti diṭṭhīsu paribbasāno' (dwelling on 'supreme' among views) means dwelling under the sway of one's own particular view, having grasped it as 'this is supreme.' 'Yaduttari kurute' (what one makes supreme) means that one makes one's own teacher and so forth the best. 'Hīnāti aññe tato sabbamāhā' (he calls all others inferior to that) means that, having established his own teacher and so forth, he says of all others, “These are inferior.” 'Tasmā vivādāni avītivatto' (therefore he does not overcome disputes) means that for that reason, he is one who has not overcome quarrels about views.

804. Dutiyagāthāya [M 2.0245] attho – evaṃ avītivatto ca yaṃ diṭṭhe sute sīlavate muteti etesu vatthūsu uppannadiṭṭhisaṅkhāte attani pubbe vuttappakāraṃ ānisaṃsaṃ passati. Tadeva so tattha sakāya diṭṭhiyā ānisaṃsaṃ “idaṃ seṭṭha”nti [P 2.0530] abhinivisitvā aññaṃ sabbaṃ parasatthārādikaṃ nihīnato passati.

804. The meaning of the second verse is this: being thus not overcome, one perceives in what is seen, heard, in precepts and vows, or cognized—in these objects, which are reckoned as views that have arisen in oneself—the benefits of the kind previously stated. Thus, having adhered to the benefits of his own view there, thinking, "This is supreme," he regards all others, such as other teachers and so on, as inferior.

805. Tatiyagāthāya attho – evaṃ passato cassa yaṃ attano satthārādiṃ nissito aññaṃ parasatthārādiṃ hīnaṃ passati taṃ pana dassanaṃ ganthameva kusalā vadanti, bandhananti vuttaṃ hoti[V 2.0223]. Yasmā etadeva, tasmā hi diṭṭhaṃva sutaṃ mutaṃ vā sīlabbataṃ bhikkhu na nissayeyya, nābhiniveseyyāti vuttaṃ hoti.

805. The meaning of the third verse is this: For one who sees in this way, relying on his own teacher and so on, and regarding other teachers and so on as inferior—that very seeing is called a fetter by the skilled; it is said to be bondage. Because it is just that, therefore a bhikkhu should not rely on what is seen, heard, or cognized, or on precepts and vows, nor should he adhere to them.

806. Catutthagāthāya attho – na kevalaṃ diṭṭhasutādiṃ na nissayeyya, apica kho pana asañjātaṃ uparūpari diṭṭhimpi lokasmiṃ na kappayeyya, na janeyyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Kīdisaṃ? Ñāṇena vā sīlavatena vāpi, samāpattiñāṇādinā ñāṇena vā sīlavatena vā yā kappiyati, etaṃ diṭṭhiṃ na kappeyya. Na kevalañca diṭṭhiṃ na kappayeyya, apica kho pana mānenapi jātiādīhi vatthūhi samoti attānamanūpaneyya, hīno na maññetha visesi vāpīti.

806. The meaning of the fourth verse is this: not only should one not rely on what is seen, heard, and so on, but it is also said that one should not construct or generate any view not yet arisen, again and again, in the world. What kind? One should not construct a view which is constructed by knowledge or by precepts and vows, that is, by knowledge such as that of meditative attainments or by precepts and vows. And not only should one not construct views, but one should also not, through conceit regarding birth and other things, bring oneself to be equal, nor should one conceive oneself as inferior or superior.

807. Pañcamagāthāya attho – evañhi diṭṭhiṃ akappento amaññamāno ca attaṃ pahāya anupādiyāno idha vā yaṃ pubbe gahitaṃ, taṃ pahāya aparaṃ aggaṇhanto tasmimpi vuttappakāre ñāṇe duvidhaṃ nissayaṃ no karoti. Akaronto ca sa ve viyattesu nānādiṭṭhivasena bhinnesu sattesu na vaggasārī chandādivasena agacchanadhammo hutvā dvāsaṭṭhiyā diṭṭhīsu kiñcipi diṭṭhiṃ na pacceti, na paccāgacchatīti vuttaṃ hoti.

807. The meaning of the fifth verse is this: Thus, not constructing views and not conceiving, having abandoned the self and not clinging, and not grasping another after abandoning what was previously grasped here—such a one does not make twofold reliance on knowledge of the kind stated. Not doing so, he does not become a partisan among beings distinguished and divided by way of various views, having become one whose nature is not to proceed by way of desire and so on, and he does not return to any of the sixty-two views; that is to say, he does not come back to them.

808-10. Idāni yo so imāya gāthāya vutto khīṇāsavo, tassa vaṇṇabhaṇanatthaṃ “yassūbhayante”tiādikā tisso gāthāyo āha. Tattha ubhayanteti pubbe vuttaphassādibhede. Paṇidhīti taṇhā. Bhavābhavāyāti punappunabhavāya. Idha vā huraṃ vāti sakattabhāvādibhede idha vā parattabhāvādibhede parattha vā. Diṭṭhe vāti diṭṭhasuddhiyā vā. Esa nayo [M 2.0246] sutādīsu. Saññāti saññāsamuṭṭhāpikā diṭṭhi. Dhammāpi [P 2.0531] tesaṃ na paṭicchitāseti dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhigatadhammāpi tesaṃ “idameva saccaṃ moghamañña”nti evaṃ na paṭicchitā. Pāraṅgato na pacceti tādīti nibbānapāraṃ gato tena tena maggena pahīne kilese puna nāgacchati, pañcahi ca ākārehi tādī hotīti. Sesaṃ pākaṭamevāti.

Now, to speak in praise of that one whose taints are destroyed, who was spoken of in this verse, he spoke three verses beginning with "yassūbhayante." Here, "ubhayante" refers to the previously mentioned distinctions such as contact. "Paṇidhī" means craving. "Bhavābhavāya" means for repeated becoming. "Idha vā huraṃ vā" refers to distinctions such as one's own state of being here, or another's state of being elsewhere. "Diṭṭhe vā" means by purity of view. This same method applies to what is heard and so on. "Saññā" means a view that gives rise to perception. "Dhammāpi tesaṃ na paṭicchitāse" means that even the doctrines included in the sixty-two views are not accepted by them thus: "This alone is true, all else is false." "Pāraṅgato na pacceti tādī" means that one who has gone to the far shore of Nibbāna does not return to the defilements abandoned by that particular path, and is 'such a one' (tādī), that is, stable, in five ways. The rest is self-evident.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

From the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya.

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya paramaṭṭhakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Discourse on the Supreme Eight in the Commentary on the Suttanipāta is concluded.

6. Jarāsuttavaṇṇanā

6. The Explanation of the Jarā Sutta

811. Appaṃ [V 2.0224] vata jīvitanti jarāsuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ vassaṃ vasitvā yāni tāni buddhānaṃ sarīrārogyasampādanaṃ anuppannasikkhāpadapaññāpanaṃ veneyyadamanaṃ tathārūpāya aṭṭhuppattiyā jātakādikathanantiādīni janapadacārikānimittāni, tāni samavekkhitvā janapadacārikaṃ pakkāmi. Anupubbena cārikaṃ caramāno sāyaṃ sāketaṃ anuppatto añjanavanaṃ pāvisi. Sāketavāsino sutvā “akālo idāni bhagavantaṃ dassanāyā”ti vibhātāya rattiyā mālāgandhādīni gahetvā bhagavato santikaṃ gantvā pūjanavandanasammodanādīni katvā parivāretvā aṭṭhaṃsu yāva bhagavato gāmappavesanavelā, atha bhagavā bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto piṇḍāya pāvisi. Taṃ aññataro sāketako brāhmaṇamahāsālo nagarā nikkhanto nagaradvāre addasa. Disvā puttasinehaṃ uppādetvā “ciradiṭṭhosi, putta, mayā”ti paridevayamāno abhimukho agamāsi. Bhagavā bhikkhū saññāpesi – “ayaṃ, bhikkhave, brāhmaṇo yaṃ icchati, taṃ karotu, na vāretabbo”ti.

811. The Jarā Sutta begins: "How short, indeed, is this life." What is its origin? On one occasion, the Blessed One, having spent the rains residence in Sāvatthī, considered the reasons for wandering through the country—such as promoting the health of the Buddhas' bodies, the laying down of training rules not yet arisen, the taming of those who can be tamed, and telling the Jātakas and so on when a suitable occasion arises—and set out on a journey through the country. Wandering in due course, he arrived at Sāketa in the evening and entered the Añjana Grove. The residents of Sāketa heard of his arrival and thought, "It is now an unsuitable time to see the Blessed One." When the night grew bright, they took garlands, perfumes, and so on, went to the Blessed One, made offerings, paid homage, exchanged friendly greetings, and then surrounded him and waited until it was time for the Blessed One to enter the village. Then the Blessed One, surrounded by the community of bhikkhus, entered for alms. A certain wealthy brahmin of Sāketa, who was leaving the city, saw him at the city gate. Seeing him, he felt a father's love arise and, lamenting, "It has been long, my son, since I have seen you," he went towards him. The Blessed One informed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus, let this brahmin do as he wishes; he is not to be stopped."

Brāhmaṇopi vacchagiddhinīva gāvī āgantvā bhagavato [P 2.0532] kāyaṃ purato ca pacchato ca dakkhiṇato ca vāmato cāti samantā āliṅgi “ciradiṭṭhosi, putta, ciraṃ vinā ahosī”ti bhaṇanto. Yadi pana so tathā kātuṃ na labheyya, hadayaṃ phāletvā mareyya. So bhagavantaṃ avoca – “bhagavā tumhehi saddhiṃ āgatabhikkhūnaṃ ahameva bhikkhaṃ dātuṃ samattho, mameva [M 2.0247] anuggahaṃ karothā”ti. Adhivāsesi bhagavā tuṇhībhāvena. Brāhmaṇo bhagavato pattaṃ gahetvā purato gacchanto brāhmaṇiyā pesesi – “putto me āgato, āsanaṃ paññāpetabba”nti. Sā tathā katvā āgamanaṃ passantī ṭhitā bhagavantaṃ antaravīthiyaṃyeva disvā puttasinehaṃ uppādetvā “ciradiṭṭhosi, putta, mayā”ti pādesu gahetvā roditvā gharaṃ atinetvā sakkaccaṃ bhojesi. Bhuttāvino brāhmaṇo pattaṃ apanāmesi. Bhagavā tesaṃ sappāyaṃ viditvā dhammaṃ desesi, desanāpariyosāne ubhopi sotāpannā ahesuṃ. Atha bhagavantaṃ yāciṃsu – “yāva, bhante, bhagavā imaṃ nagaraṃ upanissāya viharati, amhākaṃyeva ghare bhikkhā gahetabbā”ti. Bhagavā “na buddhā evaṃ ekaṃ nibaddhaṭṭhānaṃyeva gacchantī”ti paṭikkhipi. Te āhaṃsu – “tena hi, bhante, bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ piṇḍāya caritvāpi tumhe idheva bhattakiccaṃ katvā dhammaṃ desetvā vihāraṃ gacchathā”ti. Bhagavā tesaṃ anuggahatthāya [V 2.0225] tathā akāsi. Manussā brāhmaṇañca brāhmaṇiñca “buddhapitā buddhamātā” tveva vohariṃsu. Tampi kulaṃ “buddhakula”nti nāmaṃ labhi.

The brahmin, like a cow yearning for her calf, approached the Blessed One, embracing his body from the front, the back, the right, and the left, all around, saying, "It has been long since I saw you, my child. It has been long since we were apart." If he had not been able to do so, his heart would have burst, and he would have died. He said to the Blessed One, "Venerable sir, I alone am capable of providing alms to the monks who have come with you. Please show me this favor." The Blessed One consented by remaining silent. The brahmin took the Blessed One’s bowl and went ahead, sending a message to his wife: "My son has arrived. Prepare a seat." She did so and stood waiting for his arrival. Seeing the Blessed One in the street itself, her motherly love arose, and she cried, "It has been long since I saw you, my child," clasping his feet. She led him into the house and respectfully served him a meal. When the Blessed One had finished his meal, the brahmin took away the bowl. Knowing what was beneficial for them, the Blessed One taught the Dhamma. At the end of the teaching, both husband and wife became stream-enterers. Then they requested, "Venerable sir, as long as the Blessed One remains near this city, let the monks receive alms only in our house." The Blessed One declined, saying, "Buddhas do not go to only one fixed place." They then said, "Then, venerable sir, after walking for alms with the Sangha, please take your meal here, teach the Dhamma, and then return to the monastery." For their benefit, the Blessed One agreed to do so. People called the brahmin and his wife "the Buddha’s father" and "the Buddha’s mother." That family also came to be known as "the Buddha’s family."

Ānandatthero bhagavantaṃ pucchi – “ahaṃ bhagavato mātāpitaro jānāmi, ime pana kasmā vadanti ‘ahaṃ buddhamātā ahaṃ buddhapitā’”ti. Bhagavā āha – “nirantaraṃ me, ānanda, brāhmaṇī ca brāhmaṇo ca pañca jātisatāni mātāpitaro ahesuṃ, pañca jātisatāni mātāpitūnaṃ jeṭṭhakā, pañca jātisatāni kaniṭṭhakā. Te pubbasineheneva kathentī”ti imañca gāthamabhāsi –

Venerable Ānanda asked the Blessed One: "I know the Blessed One's parents, so why do these people say, 'I am the Buddha's mother, I am the Buddha's father'?" The Blessed One replied: "Ānanda, without interruption, this brahmin and brahmini were my parents for five hundred lifetimes; for five hundred lifetimes they were elder siblings to my parents, and for five hundred lifetimes they were younger siblings to my parents. They speak thus out of past affection." And he spoke this verse:

“Pubbeva [P 2.0533] sannivāsena, paccuppannahitena vā;

Evaṃ taṃ jāyate pemaṃ, uppalaṃva yathodake”ti. (jā. 1.2.174);

"Through former association, or present benefit,

Thus affection springs up, like a lotus in water."

Tato bhagavā sākete yathābhirantaṃ viharitvā puna cārikaṃ caramāno sāvatthimeva agamāsi. Sopi brāhmaṇo ca brāhmaṇī ca bhikkhū upasaṅkamitvā patirūpaṃ dhammadesanaṃ sutvā sesamagge pāpuṇitvā anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbāyiṃsu. Nagare brāhmaṇā sannipatiṃsu “amhākaṃ [M 2.0248] ñātake sakkarissāmā”ti. Sotāpannasakadāgāmianāgāmino upāsakāpi sannipatiṃsu upāsikāyo ca “amhākaṃ sahadhammike sakkarissāmā”ti. Te sabbepi kambalakūṭāgāraṃ āropetvā mālāgandhādīhi pūjentā nagarā nikkhāmesuṃ.

Then the Blessed One, having stayed in Sāketa as long as he pleased, set out wandering again and came to Sāvatthī. That brahmin and his wife, having approached the monks and heard a suitable Dhamma teaching, attained the remaining paths and passed away into the Nibbāna element without residue. The brahmins of the city gathered, saying, "We will honor our relatives." The lay followers who were stream-enterers, once-returners, and non-returners also gathered, along with the laywomen, saying, "We will honor our fellow Dhamma practitioners." They all placed them in a blanket-covered pavilion, honored them with garlands, perfumes, and so on, and carried them out of the city.

Bhagavāpi taṃ divasaṃ paccūsasamaye buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ volokento tesaṃ parinibbānabhāvaṃ ñatvā “tattha mayi gate dhammadesanaṃ sutvā bahujanassa dhammābhisamayo bhavissatī”ti ñatvā pattacīvaramādāya sāvatthito āgantvā āḷāhanameva pāvisi. Manussā disvā “mātāpitūnaṃ sarīrakiccaṃ kātukāmo bhagavā āgato”ti vanditvā aṭṭhaṃsu. Nāgarāpi kūṭāgāraṃ pūjentā āḷāhanaṃ ānetvā bhagavantaṃ pucchiṃsu – “gahaṭṭhaariyasāvakā kathaṃ pūjetabbā”ti. Bhagavā “yathā asekkhā pūjiyanti, tathā pūjetabbā ime”ti adhippāyena tesaṃ asekkhamunibhāvaṃ dīpento imaṃ gāthamāha –

The Blessed One, that very day at dawn, surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, knew of their passing into Nibbāna. Knowing that, "When I go there and teach the Dhamma, many people will gain insight into the Dhamma," he took his bowl and robe, left Sāvatthī, and entered the cremation ground itself. Seeing him, the people paid homage and stood aside, thinking, "The Blessed One has come to perform the funeral rites for his parents." The townspeople, honoring the pavilion, brought it to the cremation ground and asked the Blessed One, "How should noble lay disciples be honored?" The Blessed One, with the intention of revealing their status as non-learners, said, "They should be honored just as those who are beyond training are honored," and spoke this verse:

“Ahiṃsakā ye munayo, niccaṃ kāyena saṃvutā;

Te yanti accutaṃ ṭhānaṃ, yattha gantvā na socare”ti. (dha. pa. 225);

"Those sages who are harmless, ever restrained in body, go to the unshakeable state, where, having gone, they grieve no more."

Tañca parisaṃ oloketvā taṅkhaṇānurūpaṃ dhammaṃ desento imaṃ suttamabhāsi.

Then, surveying the assembly and teaching the Dhamma appropriate to the occasion, he spoke this discourse.

Tattha [V 2.0226] appaṃ vata jīvitaṃ idanti “idaṃ vata manussānaṃ jīvitaṃ appaṃ parittaṃ ṭhitiparittatāya sarasaparittatāyā”ti sallasuttepi vuttanayametaṃ. Oraṃ vassasatāpi miyyatīti vassasatā oraṃ kalalādikālepi miyyati. Aticcāti vassasataṃ atikkamitvā. Jarasāpi miyyatīti jarāyapi miyyati.

Here, "life is short indeed" means, "This life of humans is indeed short, limited, and fleeting." This is the meaning stated in the Sallasutta. "Even before a hundred years, one dies" means one dies even before reaching a hundred years, even in the embryonic stage. "Exceeding that" means exceeding a hundred years. "One dies of old age" means one dies also of old age.

812-6. Mamāyiteti mamāyitavatthukāraṇā. Vinābhāvasantamevidanti [P 2.0534] santavinābhāvaṃ vijjamānavinābhāvameva idaṃ, na sakkā avinābhāvena bhavitunti vuttaṃ hoti. Māmakoti mama upāsako bhikkhu vāti saṅkhaṃ gato, buddhādīni vā vatthūni mamāyamāno. Saṅgatanti samāgataṃ diṭṭhapubbaṃ vā. Piyāyitanti piyaṃ kataṃ. Nāmaṃyevāvasissati akkheyyanti sabbaṃ rūpādidhammajātaṃ pahīyati, nāmamattameva tu avasissati “buddharakkhito, dhammarakkhito”ti evaṃ saṅkhātuṃ kathetuṃ. Munayoti khīṇāsavamunayo. Khemadassinoti nibbānadassino.

812-6. "Mamāyita" means having the basis for attachment as its cause. "Vinābhāvasantam eva idaṃ" means this is merely a state of separation—only separation exists; it is said that it is impossible for it to be without separation. "Māmaka" refers to one who is counted as "mine", whether a lay devotee or a monk, or one who claims "mine" over objects such as the Buddha, etc. "Saṅgata" means that which has been encountered or seen before. "Piyāyita" means made dear. "Only the name will remain, to be designated"—all phenomena such as form, etc., are abandoned, and only the mere name remains, to be designated or spoken of, for example, as "Buddharakkhito, Dhammarakkhito." "Munayo" refers to the arahants whose defilements are destroyed. "Khemadassino" means those who see Nibbāna.

817. Sattamagāthā [M 2.0249] evaṃ maraṇabbhāhate loke anurūpapaṭipattidassanatthaṃ vuttā. Tattha patilīnacarassāti tato tato patilīnaṃ cittaṃ katvā carantassa. Bhikkhunoti kalyāṇaputhujjanassa sekkhassa vā. Sāmaggiyamāhu tassa taṃ, yo attānaṃ bhavane na dassayeti tassetaṃ patirūpamāhu, yo evaṃpaṭipanno nirayādibhede bhavane attānaṃ na dasseyya. Evañhi so imamhā maraṇā mucceyyāti adhippāyo.

817. The seventh verse is spoken to show the appropriate practice in a world afflicted by death. Here, 'one who dwells withdrawn' means one who wanders with a mind withdrawn from this and that. 'A monk' means a virtuous worldling or a trainee. Regarding the line, 'They say that this is fitting for him, who does not show himself in existence,' this means it is said to be suitable for one who, practicing thus, would not show himself in the divisions of existence such as hell. The intention is: 'Thus, he would be freed from this death.'

818-20. Idāni yo “attānaṃ bhavane na dassaye”ti evaṃ khīṇāsavo vibhāvito, tassa vaṇṇabhaṇanatthaṃ ito parā tisso gāthāyo āha. Tattha sabbatthāti dvādasasu āyatanesu. Yadidaṃ diṭṭhasutaṃ mutesu vāti ettha pana yadidaṃ diṭṭhasutaṃ, ettha vā mutesu vā dhammesu evaṃ muni na upalimpatīti evaṃ sambandho veditabbo. Dhono na hi tena maññati, yadidaṃ diṭṭhasutaṃ mutesu vāti atrāpi yadidaṃ diṭṭhasuttaṃ, tena vatthunā na maññati, mutesu vā dhammesu na maññatīti evameva sambandho veditabbo. Na hi so rajjati no virajjatīti. Bālaputhujjanā viya na rajjati, kalyāṇaputhujjanasekkhā viya na virajjati, rāgassa pana khīṇattā “virāgo”tveva saṅkhaṃ gacchati. Sesaṃ sabbattha pākaṭamevāti. Desanāpariyosāne caturāsītiyā pāṇasahassānaṃ dhammābhisamayo ahosīti.

818-20. Now, to praise the Arahant, who is thus described as 'one who does not show himself in existence,' three verses are spoken from this point onward. Here, 'in all respects' refers to the twelve sense bases. Regarding 'And whatever is seen, heard, or sensed'—here, in regard to 'whatever is seen or heard,' or in the case of sensed phenomena, the sage does not cling. This is how the connection should be understood. Regarding 'The purified one does not conceive by means of that which is seen, heard, or sensed'—here too, in regard to 'whatever is seen or heard,' one does not conceive by means of that object, nor does one conceive in relation to sensed phenomena. This is how the connection should be understood. Regarding 'For he is neither attached nor detached'—unlike foolish ordinary people, he is not attached, and unlike virtuous ordinary people or trainees, he is not detached; rather, because lust is destroyed, he is simply reckoned as 'dispassionate.' The rest is clear throughout. At the conclusion of the teaching, eighty-four thousand beings attained realization of the Dhamma.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

From the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Minor Collection.

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya jarāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Jarā Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary is concluded.

7. Tissametteyyasuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Explanation of the Tissametteyya Sutta

821. Methunamanuyuttassāti [V 2.0227][P 2.0535] tissametteyyasuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Bhagavati kira sāvatthiyaṃ viharante tissametteyyā nāma dve sahāyā sāvatthiṃ agamaṃsu. Te sāyanhasamayaṃ mahājanaṃ jetavanābhimukhaṃ gacchantaṃ disvā “kuhiṃ gacchathā”ti pucchiṃsu. Tato tehi “buddho loke uppanno, bahujanahitāya dhammaṃ deseti, taṃ sotuṃ jetavanaṃ gacchāmā”ti vutte [M 2.0250] “mayampi sossāmā”ti agamaṃsu. Te avañjhadhammadesakassa bhagavato dhammadesanaṃ sutvā parisantare nisinnāva cintesuṃ – “na sakkā agāramajjhe ṭhitenāyaṃ dhammo paripūretu”nti. Atha pakkante mahājane bhagavantaṃ pabbajjaṃ yāciṃsu. Bhagavā “ime pabbājehī”ti aññataraṃ bhikkhuṃ āṇāpesi. So te pabbājetvā tacapañcakakammaṭṭhānaṃ datvā araññavāsaṃ gantumāraddho. Metteyyo tissaṃ āha – “āvuso, upajjhāyo araññaṃ gacchati, mayampi gacchāmā”ti. Tisso “alaṃ āvuso, bhagavato dassanaṃ dhammassavanañca ahaṃ pihemi, gaccha tva”nti vatvā na agamāsi. Metteyyo upajjhāyena saha gantvā araññe samaṇadhammaṃ karonto na cirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi saddhiṃ ācariyupajjhāyehi. Tissassāpi jeṭṭhabhātā byādhinā kālamakāsi. So taṃ sutvā attano gāmaṃ agamāsi, tatra naṃ ñātakā palobhetvā uppabbājesuṃ. Metteyyopi ācariyupajjhāyehi saddhiṃ sāvatthiṃ āgato. Atha bhagavā vutthavasso janapadacārikaṃ caramāno anupubbena taṃ gāmaṃ pāpuṇi. Tattha metteyyo bhagavantaṃ vanditvā “imasmiṃ, bhante, gāme mama gihisahāyo atthi, muhuttaṃ tāva āgametha anukampaṃ upādāyā”ti vatvā gāmaṃ pavisitvā taṃ bhagavato santikaṃ ānetvā ekamantaṃ ṭhito tassatthāya ādigāthāya bhagavantaṃ pañhaṃ [P 2.0536] pucchi. Tassa bhagavā byākaronto avasesagāthāyo abhāsi. Ayamassa suttassa uppatti.

821. "Methunamanuyuttassā" is the Tissametteyya Sutta. What is its origin? It is said that while the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī, two friends named Tissa and Metteyya came to Sāvatthī. In the evening, seeing a large crowd heading towards Jetavana, they asked, "Where are you going?" Thereupon they were told, "A Buddha has arisen in the world, teaching the Dhamma for the welfare of many. We are going to Jetavana to listen." When this was said, they replied, "We too will listen," and went along. After hearing the Dhamma teaching of the Blessed One, who taught the infallible Dhamma, they sat aside in the assembly and reflected: "This Dhamma cannot be fully realized while living at home." When the crowd departed, they requested the going forth from the Blessed One. The Blessed One instructed a certain bhikkhu, saying, "Give them the going forth." That bhikkhu ordained them, gave them the meditation subject on the five parts ending with the skin, and then set out to go to the forest. Metteyya said to Tissa, "Friend, the preceptor is going to the forest. Let us go too." Tissa replied, "Enough, friend. I long to see the Blessed One and hear the Dhamma. You go." So he did not go. Metteyya went with the preceptor to the forest, practiced the duties of a recluse, and before long attained arahantship together with his teachers and preceptors. Meanwhile, Tissa’s elder brother died of an illness. Hearing this, Tissa returned to his village. There, his relatives enticed him and made him disrobe. Metteyya, together with his teachers and preceptors, returned to Sāvatthī. Later, the Blessed One, having completed the rains retreat, set out on a tour of the countryside and eventually arrived at that village. There, Metteyya paid homage to the Blessed One and said, "Venerable sir, a former householder friend of mine lives in this village. Please wait for a moment out of compassion." Then he entered the village, brought Tissa to the Blessed One, stood to one side, and for his sake asked the Blessed One a question with the first verse. The Blessed One answered him and spoke the remaining verses. This is the origin of this sutta.

Tattha methunamanuyuttassāti methunadhammasamāyuttassa. Itīti evamāha. Āyasmāti piyavacanametaṃ, tissoti nāmaṃ tassa therassa. So hi tissoti nāmena. Metteyyoti gottaṃ, gottavaseneva cesa pākaṭo ahosi. Tasmā aṭṭhuppattiyaṃ vuttaṃ “tissametteyyā nāma dve sahāyā”ti. Vighātanti upaghātaṃ. Brūhīti ācikkha. Mārisāti piyavacanametaṃ, nidukkhāti vuttaṃ hoti. Sutvāna tava sāsananti tava vacanaṃ sutvā. Viveke sikkhissāmaseti sahāyaṃ ārabbha dhammadesanaṃ yācanto bhaṇati. So pana sikkhitasikkhoyeva.

Here, 'methunamanuyuttassa' means one who is engaged in sexual intercourse. 'Iti' means he spoke thus. 'Āyasmā' (Venerable) is a term of endearment; 'Tissa' is the name of that elder. Indeed, he was known by the name Tissa. 'Metteyya' is the clan name, and he was well-known by this clan name. Therefore, in the account of the origin, it is said: "Two friends named Tissa and Metteyya." 'Vighāta' (distress) means harm. 'Brūhi' (speak) means tell. 'Mārisa' (Sir) is a term of endearment; it means 'one free from suffering'. 'Sutvāna tava sāsanaṃ' (having heard your teaching) means having heard your word. 'Viveke sikkhissāmase' (we will train in seclusion)—he speaks, requesting a Dhamma teaching concerning his friend. But he himself had already completed the training.

822. Mussate [V 2.0228] vāpi sāsananti pariyattipaṭipattito duvidhampi sāsanaṃ nassati. Vāpīti padapūraṇamattaṃ. Etaṃ tasmiṃ anāriyanti tasmiṃ puggale etaṃ anariyaṃ, yadidaṃ micchāpaṭipadā.

822. 'Mussate vāpi sāsanaṃ' (even the Teaching is forgotten) means the Dispensation in both its aspects—learning and practice—is lost. 'Vāpi' is merely a verse-filler. 'Etaṃ tasmiṃ anāriyaṃ' (this is ignoble in him) means in that person this is ignoble, that is to say, wrong practice.

823. Eko [M 2.0251] pubbe caritvānāti pabbajjāsaṅkhātena vā gaṇavossaggaṭṭhena vā pubbe eko viharitvā. Yānaṃ bhantaṃva taṃ loke, hīnamāhu puthujjananti taṃ vibbhantakaṃ puggalaṃ yathā hatthiyānādiyānaṃ adantaṃ visamaṃ ārohati, ārohakampi bhañjati, papātepi papatati. Evaṃ kāyaduccaritādivisamārohanena narakādīsu, atthabhañjanena jātipapātādīsu papatanena ca yānaṃ bhantaṃva āhu hīnaṃ puthujjanañca āhūti.

823. 'Eko pubbe caritvāna' (having first lived alone) means having previously lived alone either in the sense of the going forth (pabbajjā) or in the sense of abandoning a group. Regarding the line, 'Yānaṃ bhantaṃva taṃ loke, hīnamāhu puthujjanaṃ' (like a runaway vehicle in the world, they call him low, an ordinary person): this means that person who has gone astray is like an untamed, unsteady vehicle, such as an elephant-vehicle. When one mounts it, it breaks the rider and falls into a precipice. Similarly, because of unsteadily mounting bodily misconduct and so on, one falls into hell and the like; and because of breaking one’s purpose and falling into the precipices of birth and so on, they call him low and an ordinary person, like a runaway vehicle.

824-5. Yaso kitti cāti lābhasakkāro pasaṃsā ca. Pubbeti pabbajitabhāve. Hāyate vāpi tassa sāti tassa vibbhantakassa sato so ca yaso sā ca kitti hāyati. Etampi disvāti etampi pubbe yasakittīnaṃ bhāvaṃ pacchā ca hāniṃ disvā. Sikkhetha methunaṃ vippahātaveti tisso sikkhā sikkhetha. Kiṃ kāraṇaṃ? Methunaṃ vippahātave, methunappahānatthāyāti vuttaṃ hoti.
