Yo hi methunaṃ na vippajahati, saṅkappehi…pe… tathāvidho[P 2.0537]. Tattha paretoti samannāgato. Paresaṃ nigghosanti upajjhāyādīnaṃ nindāvacanaṃ. Maṅku hotīti dummano hoti.

824-5. 'Yaso kitti ca' (fame and renown) means gain, honor, and praise. 'Pubbe' (previously) means in the state of having gone forth. 'Hāyate vāpi tassa sā' (even his fame declines) means for that person who has gone astray, both that fame and that renown decline. 'Seeing this too' means having seen this state of fame and renown before, and its decline afterward. 'Sikkhetha methunaṃ vippahātave' (train to abandon sexual intercourse) means one should train in the threefold training. For what reason? 'To abandon sexual intercourse' means for the sake of giving up sexual intercourse, it is said. For one who does not give up sexual intercourse is affected by thoughts… and so on… such a one. There, 'pareto' (affected) means endowed. 'The reproach of others' means the condemning words of preceptors and so on. 'Maṅku hoti' (he becomes dejected) means he becomes downcast.

826. Ito parā gāthā pākaṭasambandhā eva. Tāsu satthānīti kāyaduccaritādīni. Tāni hi attano paresañca chedanaṭṭhena “satthānī”ti vuccanti. Tesu cāyaṃ visesato codito musāvacanasatthāneva karoti – “iminā kāraṇenāhaṃ vibbhanto”ti bhaṇanto. Tenevāha – “esa khvassa mahāgedho, mosavajjaṃ pagāhatī”ti. Tattha esa khvassāti esa kho assa. Mahāgedhoti mahābandhanaṃ. Katamoti ce? Yadidaṃ mosavajjaṃ pagāhati, svāssa musāvādajjhogāho mahāgedhoti veditabbo.

826. The verses beyond this are clearly connected in meaning. In them, 'satthāni' (weapons) refer to bodily misconduct and so on. These are called 'weapons' because they cut down oneself and others. Among these, this person is specifically accused of wielding the weapon of false speech—saying, "Because of this reason, I have gone astray." Therefore, it is said: "Indeed, this is his great fetter—he plunges into false speech." Here, 'esa khvassa' means 'esa kho assa'. 'Mahāgedha' (great fetter) means a great bondage. What is it? It is this plunging into false speech. Thus, his immersion in false speech should be understood as a great fetter.

827. Mandova parikissatīti pāṇavadhādīni karonto tatonidānañca dukkhamanubhonto bhogapariyesanarakkhanāni ca karonto momūho viya parikilissati.

827. 'Mandova parikissati' (he is afflicted as if deluded) means that one who engages in killing living beings and the like, experiences suffering as a result of that, and seeks and protects wealth, is afflicted like one who is utterly deluded.

828-9. “Etamādīnavaṃ ñatvā, muni pubbāpare idhā”ti etaṃ “yaso kitti ca yā pubbe, hāyatevāpi tassa sā”ti ito pabhuti vutte pubbāpare idha imasmiṃ sāsane pubbato apare samaṇabhāvato vibbhantakabhāve [M 2.0252] ādīnavaṃ muni ñatvā. Etadariyānamuttamanti yadidaṃ vivekacariyā[V 2.0229], etaṃ buddhādīnaṃ ariyānaṃ uttamaṃ, tasmā vivekaññeva sikkhethāti adhippāyo. Na tena seṭṭho maññethāti tena ca vivekena na attānaṃ “seṭṭho aha”nti maññeyya, tena thaddho na bhaveyyāti vuttaṃ hoti.

828-9. 'Etamādīnavaṃ ñatvā, muni pubbāpare idha' (Knowing this danger, the sage here in what came before and after) means: the sage, having known this danger here in this Dispensation—as stated from 'The fame and renown one had before declines...' onward—in what came before and after, that is, in the state of having gone astray from the former state of being a recluse. 'Etadariyānamuttamaṃ' (This is the supreme way of the noble ones) means that this practice of seclusion is the highest for the noble ones, such as the Buddha. Therefore, the meaning is that one should train only in seclusion. 'Na tena seṭṭho maññetha' (One should not think oneself superior because of it) means one should not think, "I am superior," because of that seclusion. It is said that one should not become arrogant because of it.

830. Rittassāti vivittassa kāyaduccaritādīhi virahitassa. Oghatiṇṇassa pihayanti, kāmesu gadhitā pajāti vatthukāmesu laggā sattā tassa caturoghatiṇṇassa pihayanti iṇāyikā viya āṇaṇyassāti arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi. Desanāpariyosāne tisso sotāpattiphalaṃ patvā pacchā pabbajitvā arahattaṃ sacchākāsīti.

830. 'Rittassā' (of one who is empty) means of one who is secluded, devoid of bodily misconduct and so on. 'Oghatiṇṇassa pihayanti, kāmesu gadhitā pajā' (beings attached to sensual pleasures envy the one who has crossed the flood) means that beings who are attached to sensual pleasures, clinging to sense-objects, envy the one who has crossed the four floods, just as debtors envy one who is free from debt. Thus, he concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of arahantship. At the end of the teaching, Tissa attained the fruit of stream-entry, and later, having gone forth, realized arahantship.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

From the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya tissametteyyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Tissametteyya Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary is completed.

8. Pasūrasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Exposition of the Pasūra Sutta

831. Idheva [V 2.0230][P 2.0538] suddhīti pasūrasuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Bhagavati kira sāvatthiyaṃ viharante pasūro nāma paribbājako mahāvādī, so “ahamasmi sakalajambudīpe vādena aggo, tasmā yathā jambudīpassa jambupaññāṇaṃ, evaṃ mamāpi bhavituṃ arahatī”ti jambusākhaṃ dhajaṃ katvā sakalajambudīpe paṭivādaṃ anāsādento anupubbena sāvatthiṃ āgantvā nagaradvāre vālikatthalaṃ katvā tattha sākhaṃ ussāpetvā “yo mayā saddhiṃ vādaṃ kātuṃ samattho, so imaṃ sākhaṃ bhañjatū”ti vatvā nagaraṃ pāvisi. Taṃ ṭhānaṃ mahājano parivāretvā aṭṭhāsi. Tena ca samayena āyasmā sāriputto bhattakiccaṃ katvā sāvatthito nikkhamati. So taṃ disvā sambahule gāmadārake pucchi – “kiṃ etaṃ dārakā”ti, te sabbaṃ ācikkhiṃsu. “Tena hi naṃ tumhe uddharitvā pādehi bhañjatha, ‘vādatthiko vihāraṃ āgacchatū’ti ca bhaṇathā”ti vatvā pakkāmi.

831. The Pasūra Sutta is so called because it deals with the statement 'Purity is here alone.' What is its origin? It is said that when the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī, there was a wanderer named Pasūra who was a great debater. He thought, "I am the foremost in debate in all of Jambudīpa. Just as the Jambu tree is the symbol of Jambudīpa, so too should I be." He made a banner with a Jambu branch and traveled throughout Jambudīpa seeking a counter-debater, but found none. Gradually, he arrived at Sāvatthī. At the city gate, he prepared a sandy area, planted the branch there, and declared, "Whoever is capable of debating with me, let him break this branch." Then he entered the city. A large crowd gathered around that spot and stood there. At that time, Venerable Sāriputta, having completed his meal duties, was leaving Sāvatthī. Seeing this, he asked many village children, "What is this, children?" They explained everything to him. He said, "Then you all pull it up and break it with your feet, and say, 'If anyone wishes to debate, let him come to the monastery.'" Having said this, he left.

Paribbājako [M 2.0253] piṇḍāya caritvā katabhattakicco āgantvā uddharitvā bhaggaṃ sākhaṃ disvā “kenidaṃ kārita”nti pucchi. “Buddhasāvakena sāriputtenā”ti ca vutte pamudito hutvā “ajja mama jayaṃ samaṇassa ca parājayaṃ paṇḍitā passantū”ti pañhavīmaṃsake kāraṇike ānetuṃ sāvatthiṃ pavisitvā vīthisiṅghāṭakacaccaresu vicaranto “samaṇassa gotamassa aggasāvakena saha vāde paññāpaṭibhānaṃ sotukāmā bhonto nikkhamantū”ti ugghosesi. “Paṇḍitānaṃ vacanaṃ sossāmā”ti sāsane pasannāpi appasannāpi bahū manussā nikkhamiṃsu. Tato pasūro mahājanaparivuto “evaṃ vutte evaṃ bhaṇissāmī”tiādīni vitakkento vihāraṃ agamāsi. Thero “vihāre uccāsaddamahāsaddo janabyākulañca mā ahosī”ti jetavanadvārakoṭṭhake āsanaṃ paññāpetvā nisīdi.

The wanderer, having gone for alms and completed his meal, returned and upon seeing the branch pulled up and broken, asked, "Who had this done?" When told, "By the Buddha's disciple Sāriputta," he was delighted and said, "Today, let the wise witness my victory and the ascetic's defeat!" He then entered Sāvatthī to summon questioners and arbiters, wandering through the streets, crossroads, and public squares, proclaiming, "Let those who wish to hear the wisdom and ready wit in a debate with the ascetic Gotama's chief disciple come forth!" Many people, both those confident in the teaching and those not confident, came out, saying, "We will listen to the words of the wise." Then Pasūra, surrounded by a great crowd, went to the monastery, pondering, "If he says this, I will say that," and so on. The elder, thinking, "Let there not be loud noise and great commotion in the monastery, nor a disturbance from the crowd," had a seat prepared at the gatehouse of Jetavana and sat down.

Paribbājako theraṃ upasaṅkamitvā “tvaṃ, bho, pabbajita, mayhaṃ jambudhajaṃ bhañjāpesī”ti āha. “Āma paribbājakā”ti ca vutte “hotu no, bho, kāci kathāpavattī”ti āha. “Hotu paribbājakā”ti ca therena sampaṭicchite “tvaṃ, samaṇa, puccha, ahaṃ vissajjessāmī”ti [P 2.0539] āha. Tato naṃ thero avaca “kiṃ, paribbājaka, dukkaraṃ pucchā, udāhu [V 2.0231] vissajjana”nti. Vissajjanaṃ bho, pabbajita, pucchāya kiṃ dukkaraṃ. Taṃ yo hi koci yaṃkiñci pucchatīti. “Tena hi, paribbājaka, tvaṃ puccha, ahaṃ vissajjessāmī”ti evaṃ vutte paribbājako “sādhurūpo bhikkhu ṭhāne sākhaṃ bhañjāpesī”ti vimhitacitto hutvā theraṃ pucchi – “ko purisassa kāmo”ti. “Saṅkapparāgo purisassa kāmo”ti (a. ni. 6.63) thero āha. So taṃ sutvā there viruddhasaññī hutvā parājayaṃ āropetukāmo āha – “citravicitrārammaṇaṃ pana bho, pabbajita, purisassa kāmaṃ na vadesī”ti? “Āma, paribbājaka, na vademī”ti. Tato naṃ paribbājako yāva tikkhattuṃ paṭiññaṃ kārāpetvā “suṇantu bhonto samaṇassa vāde dosa”nti pañhavīmaṃsake ālapitvā āha – “bho, pabbajita, tumhākaṃ sabrahmacārino araññe viharantī”ti? “Āma, paribbājaka, viharantī”ti. “Te tattha viharantā kāmavitakkādayo vitakke vitakkentī”ti? “Āma, paribbājaka, puthujjanā sahasā vitakkentī”ti. “Yadi evaṃ tesaṃ samaṇabhāvo kuto? Nanu te agārikā kāmabhogino hontī”ti evañca pana vatvā athāparaṃ etadavoca –

The wanderer approached the elder and said, "You, sir, a renunciant, had my Jambu banner broken." When it was said, "Yes, wanderer," he replied, "Let there be some discussion between us, sir." When the elder agreed, saying, "Very well, wanderer," the wanderer said, "You, ascetic, ask, and I will answer." Then the elder said to him, "What, wanderer, is more difficult—asking or answering?" "Answering is difficult, sir renunciant. What is difficult about asking? For anyone can ask anything." "Then, wanderer, you ask, and I will answer," said the elder. When this was said, the wanderer, astonished, thought, "This well-composed bhikkhu rightly had the branch broken," and asked the elder, "What is a man’s sensual desire?" The elder replied, "Lustful intention is a man’s sensual desire" (AN 6.63). Hearing this, the wanderer, perceiving a contradiction in the elder's statement, and seeking to impute defeat, said, "But, sir renunciant, do you not say that a man’s sensual desire is varied and diverse objects?" "No, wanderer, I do not say that," replied the elder. Then the wanderer made him admit this up to three times and, calling out to those skilled in questioning, said, "Listen, sirs, to the fault in the ascetic’s statement!" Then he asked, "Sir renunciant, do your fellow spiritual practitioners dwell in the forest?" "Yes, wanderer, they dwell there." "While dwelling there, do they think thoughts of sensual desire and the like?" "Yes, wanderer, ordinary people impulsively think such thoughts." "If so, from where is their status as ascetics? Are they not householders enjoying sensual pleasures?" Having said this, he then added—

“Na [M 2.0254] te ve kāmā yāni citrāni loke,

Saṅkapparāgañca vadesi kāmaṃ;

Saṅkappayaṃ akusale vitakke,

Bhikkhupi te hessati kāmabhogī”ti. (saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.34);

"Those varied things in the world are not sensual pleasures; you speak of lustful intention as sensual pleasure. By thinking unwholesome thoughts, even your monk will be an enjoyer of sensual pleasures."

Atha thero paribbājakassa vāde dosaṃ dassento āha – “kiṃ, paribbājaka, saṅkapparāgaṃ purisassa kāmaṃ na vadesi, citravicitrārammaṇaṃ vadesī”ti? “Āma, bho, pabbajitā”ti. Tato naṃ thero yāva tikkhattuṃ paṭiññaṃ kārāpetvā “suṇātha, āvuso, paribbājakassa vāde dosa”nti pañhavīmaṃsake ālapitvā āha – “āvuso pasūra, tava satthā atthī”ti? “Āma, pabbajita, atthī”ti. “So cakkhuviññeyyaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ passati saddārammaṇādīni [P 2.0540] vā sevatī”ti? “Āma, pabbajita, sevatī”ti. “Yadi evaṃ tassa satthubhāvo kuto, nanu so agāriko kāmabhogī hotī”ti evañca pana vatvā athāparaṃ etadavoca –

Then the elder, pointing out the fault in the wanderer's statement, said: "Wanderer, do you maintain that a man's sensual desire is not lustful intention, but rather varied and diverse objects?" "Yes, sir renunciant," he replied. Then the elder, having made him affirm this up to three times, addressed those skilled in questioning, saying: "Listen, friends, to the fault in the wanderer's statement." And he asked: "Friend Pasūra, do you have a teacher?" "Yes, renunciant, I do." "Does he see forms cognizable by the eye, or does he engage with sense objects such as sounds?" "Yes, renunciant, he engages with them." "If so, from where is his status as a teacher? Is he not a householder enjoying sensual pleasures?" Having said this, he then spoke further:

“Te ve kāmā yāni citrāni loke,

Saṅkapparāgaṃ na vadesi kāmaṃ;

Passanto [V 2.0232] rūpāni manoramāni,

Suṇanto saddāni manoramāni.

"Those varied things in the world are indeed sensual pleasures; you do not call lustful intention 'sensual pleasure.' Seeing lovely forms, hearing delightful sounds,

“Ghāyanto gandhāni manoramāni,

Sāyanto rasāni manoramāni;

Phusanto phassāni manoramāni,

Satthāpi te hessati kāmabhogī”ti.

"Smelling delightful fragrances, tasting delightful flavors, touching delightful tangibles, even your teacher will be an enjoyer of sensual pleasures."

Evaṃ vutte nippaṭibhāno paribbājako “ayaṃ pabbajito mahāvādī, imassa santike pabbajitvā vādasatthaṃ sikkhissāmī”ti sāvatthiṃ pavisitvā pattacīvaraṃ pariyesitvā jetavanaṃ paviṭṭho tattha lāludāyiṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ kāyūpapannaṃ sarīrākārākappesu samantapāsādikaṃ disvā “ayaṃ bhikkhu mahāpañño mahāvādī”ti mantvā tassa santike pabbajitvā taṃ vādena niggahetvā saliṅgena taṃyeva titthāyatanaṃ pakkamitvā puna “samaṇena gotamena saddhiṃ vādaṃ karissāmī”ti sāvatthiyaṃ purimanayeneva ugghosetvā mahājanaparivuto “evaṃ samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ niggahessāmī”tiādīni vadanto [M 2.0255] jetavanaṃ agamāsi. Jetavanadvārakoṭṭhake adhivatthā devatā “ayaṃ abhājanabhūto”ti mukhabandhamassa akāsi. So bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā mūgo viya nisīdi. Manussā “idāni pucchissati, idāni pucchissatī”ti tassa mukhaṃ ulloketvā “vadehi, bho pasūra, vadehi, bho pasūrā”ti uccāsaddamahāsaddā ahesuṃ. Atha bhagavā “kiṃ pasūro vadissatī”ti vatvā tattha sampattaparisāya dhammadesanatthaṃ imaṃ suttaṃ abhāsi.

When this was said, the wanderer was left speechless. Thinking, "This renunciant is a great debater. I will go forth under him and learn the science of debate," he entered Sāvatthī, sought a bowl and robes, and then entered Jetavana. There, he saw Lāludāyī, golden-skinned, well-proportioned, and pleasing in every way with respect to his bodily form and features. Considering, "This monk is very wise and a great debater," he went forth under him. But after defeating him in debate, he left that very sectarian residence in his own guise and thought, "I will debate with the ascetic Gotama." As before, he proclaimed in Sāvatthī, surrounded by a great crowd, saying, "I will refute the ascetic Gotama!" and so on, and went to Jetavana. At the gatehouse of Jetavana, a deity who dwelt there thought, "This one is an unworthy vessel," and sealed his mouth. He approached the Blessed One and sat down like a mute. The people, watching his face, said, "Now he will ask, now he will ask!" and there were loud shouts and great noises, "Speak, Pasūra! Speak, Pasūra!" Then the Blessed One, saying, "What will Pasūra say?" spoke this discourse for the sake of teaching the Dhamma to the assembly gathered there.

Tattha paṭhamagāthāya tāva ayaṃ saṅkhepo – ime diṭṭhigatikā attano diṭṭhiṃ sandhāya idheva suddhī iti vādayanti nāññesu dhammesu visuddhimāhu. Evaṃ sante attano satthārādīni [P 2.0541] nissitā tattheva “esa vādo subho”ti evaṃ subhaṃ vadānā hutvā puthū samaṇabrāhmaṇā “sassato loko”tiādīsu paccekasaccesu niviṭṭhā.

Here is the summary of the first verse: these adherents of views, with reference to their own view, declare, 'Purity is here alone,' and do not speak of purification in other teachings. This being so, relying on their own teachers and so on, and proclaiming right there, 'This doctrine is excellent,' many ascetics and brahmins become entrenched in their individual truths, such as 'the world is eternal,' and so on.

832. Evaṃ niviṭṭhā ca – te vādakāmāti gāthā. Tattha bālaṃ dahantī mithu aññamaññanti “ayaṃ bālo ayaṃ bālo”ti evaṃ dvepi janā aññamaññaṃ bālaṃ dahanti, bālato passanti. Vadanti te aññasitā kathojjanti te aññamaññaṃ satthārādiṃ nissitā kalahaṃ vadanti. Pasaṃsakāmā kusalā vadānāti pasaṃsatthikā ubhopi “mayaṃ kusalavādā paṇḍitavādā”ti evaṃsaññino hutvā.

832. And being thus entrenched—the verse says, 'they are eager for debate.' Here, 'they scorch the fool, one against the other' means, saying, 'This is a fool, this is a fool,' both people scorch each other as a fool, see each other as a fool. 'They speak, relying on another, causing quarrels' means they, relying on each other's teachers and so on, speak in quarrels. 'Desiring praise, proclaiming themselves skilled' means both, being desirous of praise, hold the perception, 'We are skilled speakers, wise speakers.'

833. Evaṃ [V 2.0233] vadānesu ca tesu eko niyamato eva – yutto kathāyanti gāthā. Tattha yutto kathāyanti vivādakathāya ussukko. Pasaṃsamicchaṃ vinighāti hotīti attano pasaṃsaṃ icchanto “kathaṃ nu kho niggahessāmī”tiādinā nayena pubbeva sallāpā kathaṃkathī vinighātī hoti. Apāhatasminti pañhavīmaṃsakehi “atthāpagataṃ te bhaṇitaṃ, byañjanāpagataṃ te bhaṇita”ntiādinā nayena apahārite vāde. Nindāya so kuppatīti evaṃ apāhatasmiñca vāde uppannāya nindāya so kuppati. Randhamesīti parassa randhameva gavesanto.

833. And among such speakers, one is certainly 'engaged in debate,' as the verse says. Here, 'engaged in debate' means eager for argument. 'Desiring praise, he becomes a destroyer' refers to one who, seeking self-praise, becomes hesitant and destructive before the discussion, thinking, 'How shall I refute him?' 'When he is struck down' means when his argument is struck down by questioners who say, 'Your statement lacks meaning, your statement lacks expression,' and so on. 'He flares up at criticism' means he becomes angry at the criticism that arises when his argument is thus struck down. 'He seeks flaws' means constantly searching for the flaws of others.

834. Na [M 2.0256] kevalañca kuppati, apica kho pana yamassa vādanti gāthā. Tattha parihīnamāhu apāhatanti atthabyañjanādito apāhataṃ parihīnaṃ vadanti. Paridevatīti tato nimittaṃ so “aññaṃ mayā āvajjita”ntiādīhi vippalapati. Socatīti “tassa jayo”tiādīni ārabbha socati. Upaccagā manti anutthunātīti “so maṃ vādena vādaṃ atikkanto”tiādinā nayena suṭṭhutaraṃ vippalapati.

834. Not only does he flare up, but also, as the verse states. Here, 'they call it deficient, rejected' means they say it is rejected and deficient in terms of meaning and expression. 'He laments'—from that cause, he babbles, saying, 'I must have been inattentive,' and so on. 'He grieves'—he grieves focusing on things like 'He has won,' and so forth. 'He wails'—he babbles profusely, saying, 'He has surpassed me in debate,' and so on.

835. Ete vivādā samaṇesūti ettha pana samaṇā vuccanti bāhiraparibbājakā. Etesu ugghāti nighāti hotīti etesu vādesu jayaparājayādivasena cittassa ugghātaṃ nighātañca pāpuṇanto ugghātī nighātī ca hoti. Virame kathojjanti pajaheyya kalahaṃ. Na haññadatthatthi pasaṃsalābhāti na hi ettha pasaṃsalābhato añño attho atthi.

835. 'These disputes among ascetics'—here, 'ascetics' refers to outside wanderers. 'In these, there is elation and dejection'—in these disputes, due to victory or defeat, one experiences mental elation and dejection, and thus becomes elated and dejected. 'Refrain from quarreling'—one should abandon strife. 'There is no other benefit beyond praise and gain'—indeed, in this, there is no other meaning than praise and gain.

836-7. Chaṭṭhagāthāya attho – yasmā ca na haññadatthatthi pasaṃsalābhā, tasmā paramaṃ lābhaṃ labhantopi “sundaro aya”nti tattha diṭṭhiyā pasaṃsito vā [P 2.0542] pana hoti taṃ vādaṃ parisāya majjhe dīpetvā, tato so tena jayatthena tuṭṭhiṃ vā dantavidaṃsakaṃ vā āpajjanto hasati, mānena ca uṇṇamati. Kiṃ kāraṇaṃ? Yasmā taṃ jayatthaṃ pappuyya yathāmāno jāto, evaṃ uṇṇamato ca yā uṇṇatīti gāthā. Tattha mānātimānaṃ vadate panesoti eso pana taṃ uṇṇatiṃ “vighātabhūmī”ti abujjhamāno mānañca atimānañca vadatiyeva.

836-7. The meaning of the sixth verse is: Because there is no other meaning than praise and gain, therefore, even attaining the highest gain, and being praised for their view as 'beautiful,' they proclaim that doctrine in the midst of an assembly. Then, delighted by that victory, they either laugh, displaying their teeth, or swell with pride. What is the reason? Because, having attained that victory, pride arises, and thus, they swell with that swelling—so says the verse. Here, 'it speaks of pride and excessive pride.' But not understanding that this swelling is 'a ground for ruin,' he indeed speaks of pride and excessive pride.

838. Evaṃ vāde dosaṃ dassetvā idāni tassa vādaṃ asampaṭicchanto “sūro”ti gāthamāha. Tattha rājakhādāyāti rājakhādanīyena, bhattavetanenāti vuttaṃ hoti. Abhigajjameti paṭisūramicchanti yathā so paṭisūraṃ icchanto abhigajjanto eti, evaṃ diṭṭhigatiko diṭṭhigatikanti dasseti. Yeneva so, tena palehīti yena so tuyhaṃ paṭisūro, tena gaccha. Pubbeva [V 2.0234] natthi yadidaṃ yudhāyāti yaṃ pana idaṃ kilesajātaṃ yuddhāya siyā, taṃ etaṃ pubbeva natthi, bodhimūleyeva pahīnanti dasseti. Sesagāthā pākaṭasambandhāyeva.

838. Having thus shown the fault in debate, now, not accepting that view, he speaks the verse beginning 'a hero.' Here, 'for royal food' means 'by royal food,' which is to say, by food and wages. 'Comes roaring' means desiring a counter-champion. Just as one desiring a counter-champion comes roaring, so it is shown that one who adheres to a view seeks another who adheres to a view. 'Go to him by that very way' means 'Go to where that counter-champion of yours is.' 'There was nothing before for battle' means that whatever group of defilements there might be for battle, this was not there from before, having been abandoned at the very root of enlightenment. The remaining verses are clear in their connection.

839-40. Tattha vivādayantīti vivadanti. Paṭisenikattāti paṭilomakārako. Visenikatvāti kilesasenaṃ vināsetvā. Kiṃ labhethoti [M 2.0257] paṭimallaṃ kiṃ labhissasi. Pasūrāti taṃ paribbājakaṃ ālapati. Yesīdha natthīti yesaṃ idha natthi.

839-40. Here, 'disputing' means they dispute. 'Being an opponent' means acting contrarily. 'Being without an army' means having destroyed the army of defilements. 'What would you gain?' means 'What rival would you gain?' 'Pasūra' addresses that wanderer. 'For whom there is not here' means 'for whom there is nothing here'.

841. Pavitakkanti “jayo nu kho me bhavissatī”ti ādīni vitakkento. Dhonena yugaṃ samāgamāti dhutakilesena buddhena saddhiṃ yugaggāhaṃ samāpanno. Na hi tvaṃ sakkhasi sampayātaveti kotthukādayo viya sīhādīhi, dhonena saha yugaṃ gahetvā ekapadampi sampayātuṃ yugaggāhameva vā sampādetuṃ na sakkhissasīti. Sesaṃ sabbattha pākaṭamevāti.

841. 'Pondering' means thinking 'Will victory be mine?' and so on. 'You have met the yoke with the Pure One' means you have entered into a yoke-contest with the Buddha, who has shaken off defilements. 'You cannot advance' means just as jackals and others cannot advance with lions and others, you will not be able to advance even a single step yoked with the Pure One, nor even to complete the yoke-contest. The rest is clear throughout.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya pasūrasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Pasūra Sutta in the Suttanipāta commentary is finished.

9. Māgaṇḍiyasuttavaṇṇanā

9. The Explanation of the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta

842. Disvāna [V 2.0235] taṇhanti māgaṇḍiyasuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharanto paccūsasamaye [P 2.0543] buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ volokento kurūsu kammāsadhammanigamavāsino māgaṇḍiyassa nāma brāhmaṇassa sapajāpatikassa arahattūpanissayaṃ disvā tāvadeva sāvatthito tattha gantvā kammāsadhammassa avidūre aññatarasmiṃ vanasaṇḍe nisīdi suvaṇṇobhāsaṃ muñcamāno. Māgaṇḍiyopi taṅkhaṇaṃ tattha mukhadhovanatthaṃ gato suvaṇṇobhāsaṃ disvā “kiṃ ida”nti ito cito ca pekkhamāno bhagavantaṃ disvā attamano ahosi. Tassa kira dhītā suvaṇṇavaṇṇā, taṃ bahū khattiyakumārādayo vārayantā na labhanti. Brāhmaṇo evaṃladdhiko hoti “samaṇasseva naṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇassa dassāmī”ti. So bhagavantaṃ disvā “ayaṃ me dhītāya samānavaṇṇo, imassa naṃ dassāmī”ti cittaṃ uppādesi. Tasmā disvāva attamano ahosi. So vegena gharaṃ gantvā brāhmaṇiṃ āha – “bhoti bhoti mayā dhītāya samānavaṇṇo puriso diṭṭho, alaṅkarohi dārikaṃ, tassa naṃ dassāmā”ti. Brāhmaṇiyā [M 2.0258] dārikaṃ gandhodakena nhāpetvā vatthapupphālaṅkārādīhi alaṅkarontiyā eva bhagavato bhikkhācāravelā sampattā. Atha bhagavā kammāsadhammaṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi.

842. “Having seen Taṇhā…”: this is the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta. What is its origin? At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī. In the early morning, surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, he saw in the Kuru country, among the people of the market town of Kammāsadhamma, a brahmin named Māgaṇḍiya and his wife, who had the supporting condition for attaining arahantship. Immediately, he left Sāvatthī and went there, sitting in a grove not far from Kammāsadhamma, radiating a golden glow. At that very moment, Māgaṇḍiya had gone there to wash his face. Seeing the golden radiance, he wondered, 'What is this?' Looking around here and there, he saw the Blessed One and was delighted. It is said that his daughter had a golden complexion, and many khattiya princes and others sought her but did not obtain her. The brahmin held the view, 'I will give her only to an ascetic of golden complexion.' Seeing the Blessed One, the thought arose in him, 'This man matches my daughter’s complexion; I will give her to him.' That is why he was so pleased upon seeing him. He hurried home and said to his wife, the brahmin woman, 'Madam, madam! I have seen a man who matches our daughter’s complexion. Adorn the girl—we will give her to him.' While the brahmin woman was bathing the girl in fragrant water and adorning her with clothes, flowers, ornaments, and so on, the time for the Blessed One’s almsround arrived. Then the Blessed One entered Kammāsadhamma for alms.

Tepi kho dhītaraṃ gahetvā bhagavato nisinnokāsaṃ agamaṃsu. Tattha bhagavantaṃ adisvā brāhmaṇī ito cito ca vilokentī bhagavato nisajjaṭṭhānaṃ tiṇasanthārakaṃ addasa. Buddhānañca adhiṭṭhānabalena nisinnokāso padanikkhepo ca abyākulā honti. Sā brāhmaṇaṃ āha – “esa, brāhmaṇa, tassa tiṇasanthāro”ti? “Āma, bhotī”ti. “Tena hi, brāhmaṇa, amhākaṃ āgamanakammaṃ na sampajjissatī”ti. “Kasmā bhotī”ti? “Passa, brāhmaṇa, abyākulo tiṇasanthāro, neso kāmabhogino paribhutto”ti. Brāhmaṇo “mā, bhoti maṅgale pariyesiyamāne avamaṅgalaṃ abhaṇī”ti āha. Punapi brāhmaṇī ito cito ca vicarantī bhagavato padanikkhepaṃ disvā brāhmaṇaṃ āha “ayaṃ tassa padanikkhepo”ti? “Āma, bhotī”ti. “Passa, brāhmaṇa, padanikkhepaṃ, nāyaṃ satto kāmesu gadhito”ti. “Kathaṃ tvaṃ bhoti jānāsī”ti ca vuttā attano ñāṇabalaṃ dassentī āha –

Then, taking their daughter, they went to the place where the Blessed One was seated. Not seeing the Blessed One there, the brahmin woman looked around and saw the Blessed One’s sitting place, a spread of grass. By the power of the Buddhas’ resolve, their sitting places and footprints remain undisturbed. She said to the brahmin, 'Brahmin, is this his grass mat?' 'Yes, madam.' 'Then, brahmin, our mission will not be accomplished.' 'Why, madam?' 'Look, brahmin, the grass mat is undisturbed. It has not been used by one who indulges in sensual pleasures.' The brahmin said, 'Madam, do not utter an inauspicious word while seeking a blessing.' Again, the brahmin woman wandered about and, seeing the Blessed One’s footprint, said to the brahmin, 'Is this his footprint?' 'Yes, madam.' 'Look, brahmin, at the footprint. This being is not attached to sensual pleasures.' When asked, 'How do you know, madam?' she, demonstrating the power of her knowledge, said:

“Rattassa [V 2.0236][P 2.0544] hi ukkuṭikaṃ padaṃ bhave,

Duṭṭhassa hoti anukaḍḍhitaṃ padaṃ;

Mūḷhassa hoti sahasānupīḷitaṃ,

Vivaṭṭacchadassa idamīdisaṃ pada”nti. (a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.260-261; dha. pa. aṭṭha. 1.2 sāmāvatīvatthu; visuddhi. 1.45);

For one with lust, the footprint is on tiptoe; for one with hatred, the footprint is dragged; for one with delusion, the footprint is forcefully pressed down; for one whose covering is removed, the footprint is like this.

Ayañcarahi tesaṃ kathā vippakatā, atha bhagavā katabhattakicco tameva vanasaṇḍaṃ āgato. Brāhmaṇī bhagavato varalakkhaṇakhacitaṃ byāmappabhāparikkhittaṃ rūpaṃ disvā brāhmaṇaṃ āha – “esa tayā, brāhmaṇa, diṭṭho”ti? “Āma bhotī”ti. “Āgatakammaṃ na sampajjissateva, evarūpo nāma kāme paribhuñjissatīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī”ti. Tesaṃ evaṃ vadantānaññeva bhagavā tiṇasanthārake nisīdi. Atha brāhmaṇo dhītaraṃ vāmena hatthena gahetvā kamaṇḍaluṃ dakkhiṇena hatthena gahetvā bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “bho, pabbajita, tvañca suvaṇṇavaṇṇo ayañca dārikā, anucchavikā esā tava, imāhaṃ bhoto bhariyaṃ posāvanatthāya dammī”ti [M 2.0259] vatvā bhagavato santikaṃ gantvā dātukāmo aṭṭhāsi. Bhagavā brāhmaṇaṃ anālapitvā aññena saddhiṃ sallapamāno viya “disvāna taṇha”nti imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi.

Now, while their conversation was still unfinished, the Blessed One, having finished his meal, came to that same grove. The brahmin woman, seeing the Blessed One’s form adorned with excellent marks and surrounded by a fathom-wide aura, said to the brahmin: 'Is this the one you saw, brahmin?' 'Yes, madam.' 'The purpose of our coming will surely not succeed. It is impossible that one of such an appearance would indulge in sensual pleasures.' While they were speaking thus, the Blessed One sat down on the spread of grass. Then the brahmin, taking his daughter by the left hand and a water pot by the right hand, approached the Blessed One and said: 'O recluse, you are of golden complexion, and this girl is suitable for you. I give her to you to be your wife, to attend on you.' Having spoken thus, intending to give her, he stood near the Blessed One. Without addressing the brahmin, the Blessed One, as if conversing with another, spoke this verse: 'Having seen Taṇhā...'

Tassattho – ajapālanigrodhamūle nānārūpāni nimminitvā abhikāmamāgataṃ māradhītaraṃ disvāna taṇhaṃ aratiṃ ragañca chandamattampi me methunasmiṃ nāhosi, kimevidaṃ imissā dārikāya muttakarīsapuṇṇaṃ rūpaṃ disvā bhavissati sabbathā pādāpi naṃ samphusituṃ na icche, kutonena saṃvasitunti.

The meaning is this: At the root of the Goatherd's Banyan Tree, when Māra's daughters—Taṇhā, Arati, and Ragā—approached, having created various forms, upon seeing them not even the slightest desire for sexual union arose in me. What then of seeing this girl’s form, which is full of urine and excrement? I would not wish to touch her even with my foot, let alone cohabit with her.

843. Tato māgaṇḍiyo “pabbajitā nāma mānusake kāme pahāya dibbakāmatthāya pabbajanti, ayañca dibbepi kāme na icchati, idampi itthiratanaṃ, kā nu assa diṭṭhī”ti pucchituṃ dutiyaṃ gāthamāha. Tattha etādisaṃ ce ratananti dibbitthiratanaṃ sandhāya bhaṇati, nārinti attano dhītaraṃ sandhāya. Diṭṭhigataṃ sīlavataṃ nu jīvitanti diṭṭhiñca sīlañca [P 2.0545] vatañca jīvitañca. Bhavūpapattiñca vadesi kīdisanti attano bhavūpapattiñca kīdisaṃ vadasīti.

843. Then Māgaṇḍiya, thinking, 'Renunciants, it is said, abandon human sensual pleasures and go forth for the sake of divine sensual pleasures. But this one does not desire even divine sensual pleasures. What, then, can his view be?' spoke a second verse to ask. Therein, the words 'such a jewel' are said with reference to a divine woman-jewel, and 'woman' with reference to his own daughter. The words 'view, virtue, observance, and life' refer to view, virtue, observance, and life. 'And what kind of future existence do you declare?' means 'What kind of future existence do you declare for yourself?'

844. Ito parā dve gāthā visajjanapucchānayena pavattattā pākaṭasambandhāyeva. Tāsu paṭhamagāthāya saṅkhepattho – tassa mayhaṃ, māgaṇḍiya, dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhigatadhammesu nicchinitvā “idameva saccaṃ, moghamañña”nti evaṃ idaṃ vadāmīti samuggahitaṃ na hoti natthi na vijjati. Kiṃkāraṇā[V 2.0237]? Ahañhi passanto diṭṭhīsu ādīnavaṃ kañci diṭṭhiṃ aggahetvā saccāni pavicinanto ajjhattaṃ rāgādīnaṃ santibhāvena ajjhattasantisaṅkhātaṃ nibbānameva addasanti.

844. The two verses that follow this are clearly connected, proceeding by way of question and answer. Of these, the summary meaning of the first verse is: 'Māgaṇḍiya, for me, among the doctrines of the sixty-two views, there is not one that I have determined and taken up, thinking, “This alone is true, all else is false.” For what reason? Because, seeing the danger in views, not grasping any view, and investigating the truths, I saw for myself Nibbāna, known as inner peace, through the calming of lust and so forth within.'

845. Dutiyagāthāya saṅkhepattho – yānimāni diṭṭhigatāni tehi tehi sattehi vinicchinitvā gahitattā vinicchayāti ca attano paccayehi abhisaṅkhatabhāvādinā nayena pakappitāni cāti vuccanti. Te tvaṃ muni diṭṭhigatadhamme aggahetvā ajjhattasantīti yametamatthaṃ brūsi, ācikkha me, kathaṃ nu dhīrehi paveditaṃ kathaṃ pakāsitaṃ dhīrehi taṃ padanti.

845. The summary meaning of the second verse is: 'These doctrines of views are called “determinations” because they are adopted by various beings after deliberation, and they are called “concoctions” because they are devised by way of being conditioned by their own causes. You, O sage, not grasping these doctrines of views, speak of this matter of “inner peace.” Explain to me how that state has been made known, how it has been declared by the wise.'

846. Athassa [M 2.0260] bhagavā yathā yena upāyena taṃ padaṃ dhīrehi pakāsitaṃ, taṃ upāyaṃ sapaṭipakkhaṃ dassento “na diṭṭhiyā”ti gāthamāha. Tattha “na diṭṭhiyā”tiādīhi diṭṭhisutiaṭṭhasamāpattiñāṇabāhirasīlabbatāni paṭikkhipati. “Suddhimāhā”ti ettha vuttaṃ āha-saddaṃ sabbattha nakārena saddhiṃ yojetvā purisabyattayaṃ katvā “diṭṭhiyā suddhiṃ nāhaṃ kathemī”ti evamattho veditabbo. Yathā cettha, evaṃ uttarapadesupi. Tattha ca adiṭṭhiyā nāhāti dasavatthukaṃ sammādiṭṭhiṃ vinā na kathemi. Tathā assutiyāti navaṅgaṃ savanaṃ vinā. Añāṇāti kammassa katasaccānulomikañāṇaṃ vinā. Asīlatāti pātimokkhasaṃvaraṃ vinā. Abbatāti dhutaṅgavataṃ vinā. Nopi tenāti tesu ekamekena diṭṭhiādimattenāpi no kathemīti evamattho veditabbo. Ete ca nissajja anuggahāyāti ete ca purime diṭṭhiādibhede kaṇhapakkhiye dhamme samugghātakaraṇena nissajja, pacchime adiṭṭhiādibhede sukkapakkhiye atammayatāpajjanena anuggahāya. Santo anissāya bhavaṃ na [P 2.0546] jappeti imāya paṭipattiyā rāgādivūpasamena santo cakkhādīsu kañci dhammaṃ anissāya ekampi bhavaṃ apihetuṃ apatthetuṃ samattho siyā, ayamassa ajjhattasantīti adhippāyo.

846. Then the Blessed One, showing the method and its opposite by which the wise illuminate that state, spoke the verse beginning with “Not by view.” Here, “Not by view” and so forth reject views, hearsay, the eight attainments, knowledge, and external virtues and ascetic practices. In “speaks of purity,” the word “speaks” should be connected with the negative particle everywhere, interpreting the subject as the first person: “I do not declare purity by view.” This meaning should be understood here, as well as in the following passages. And “not without view” means: I do not speak of it without the tenfold right view. Likewise, “not without hearing” means: without the nine-limbed teaching. “Not without knowledge” means: without knowledge that accords with the truth of kamma. “Not without virtue” means: without the restraint of the Pātimokkha. “Not without ascetic practice” means: without the practice of the ascetic vows. “Nor even by that” means: I do not speak of it even by any single one of these, by mere view and so on. This is the meaning to be understood. “Having abandoned these, for support” means: having abandoned these former divisions, such as views, which belong to the dark side, by way of extirpation; and for the sake of upholding the latter divisions, such as non-views, which belong to the bright side, by way of attaining non-identification with them. “Peaceful, not depending, he does not long for existence” means: by this practice, with the calming of lust and so forth, being peaceful, he does not depend on any phenomenon such as the senses, and is capable of not desiring or seeking even a single existence. This is the meaning of his “internal peace.”

847. Evaṃ vutte vacanatthaṃ asallakkhento māgaṇḍiyo “no ce kirā”ti gāthamāha. Tattha diṭṭhādīni vuttanayāneva. Kaṇhapakkhiyāniyeva pana sandhāya ubhayatrāpi āha. Āha-saddaṃ pana nocekira-saddena yojetvā “no ce kirāha no ce kira kathesī”ti evaṃ attho daṭṭhabbo. Momuhanti atimūḷhaṃ, mohanaṃ vā. Paccentīti jānanti.

847. When this was said, Māgaṇḍiya, not considering the meaning of the words, uttered the verse beginning, “Is it not so?” Here, 'views' and so on are to be understood in the same way as before. However, he spoke in both instances with reference to the dark side. The word 'āha' should be combined with the word 'no ce kira', and the meaning should be understood as 'Is it not so, I say?' or 'Is it not so, you speak?'. 'Momuhanti' means extremely deluded or bewildering. 'Paccentīti' means they understand.

848. Athassa bhagavā taṃ diṭṭhiṃ nissāya pucchaṃ paṭikkhipanto “diṭṭhiñca nissāyā”ti gāthamāha. Tassattho – tvaṃ, māgaṇḍiya, diṭṭhiṃ nissāya punappunaṃ pucchamāno yāni te diṭṭhigatāni samuggahitāni, tesveva samuggahītesu evaṃ pamohaṃ āgato, ito ca mayā vuttaajjhattasantito [V 2.0238] paṭipattito dhammadesanato vā aṇumpi yuttasaññaṃ na passasi, tena kāraṇena tvaṃ imaṃ dhammaṃ momuhato passasīti.

848. Then the Blessed One, rejecting his question, which was based on that view, spoke the verse, “Depending on views.” The meaning is: You, Māgaṇḍiya, repeatedly asking based on your views, have become utterly bewildered by clinging to those very views you hold. Moreover, you do not see even the slightest suitable perception in what I have said—from the inner peace spoken of by me, or from the practice, or from the teaching of the Dhamma. For this reason, you perceive this Dhamma as bewildering.

849. Evaṃ samuggahitesu pamohena māgaṇḍiyassa vivādāpattiṃ dassetvā idāni tesu aññesu ca dhammesu vigatappamohassa attano nibbivādataṃ dassento “samo visesī”ti gāthamāha. Tassattho [M 2.0261] – yo evaṃ tividhamānena vā diṭṭhiyā vā maññati, so tena mānena tāya diṭṭhiyā tena vā puggalena vivadeyya. Yo pana amhādiso imāsu tīsu vidhāsu avikampamāno, samo visesīti na tassa hoti, na ca hīnoti pāṭhaseso.

849. Having thus shown Māgaṇḍiya’s falling into contention due to his bewilderment regarding what he had grasped, now, demonstrating his own absence of contention, being free from bewilderment regarding those and other phenomena, he said the verse, “Equal or superior.” The meaning of this is: One who conceives in terms of the threefold conceit or by views would contend with others because of that conceit, those views, or that person. But for one like us, unshaken in these three aspects, there is no “equal or superior,” nor is there “inferior”—this is the remaining portion of the text.

850. Kiñca bhiyyo – saccanti soti gāthā. Tassattho – so evarūpo pahīnamānadiṭṭhiko mādiso bāhitapāpattādinā nayena brāhmaṇo “idameva sacca”nti kiṃ vadeyya kiṃ vatthuṃ bhaṇeyya, kena vā kāraṇena bhaṇeyya, “mayhaṃ saccaṃ, tuyhaṃ musā”ti vā kena mānena diṭṭhiyā puggalena vā vivadeyya? Yasmiṃ mādise khīṇāsave “sadisohamasmī”ti pavattiyā samaṃ vā, itaradvayabhāvena pavattiyā visamaṃ vā maññitaṃ natthi, so samānādīsu kena vādaṃ paṭisaṃyujeyya paṭipphareyyāti. Nanu ekaṃseneva evarūpo puggalo – okaṃ pahāyāti gāthā?

850. Furthermore, the verse beginning “What truth…” The meaning is: Such a one, like me, who has abandoned conceit and views, a brahmin in the sense of having expelled evil, etc.—what truth would he speak, what thing would he say, or for what reason would he say, “My truth, your falsehood,” or with what conceit, view, or person would he dispute? In one like me, a taintless one, there is no conceiving of ‘equal’ through the occurrence of “I am similar,” nor of ‘unequal’ through the occurrence of the other two states. With whom, among equals and the like, would he engage in or exchange a dispute? Indeed, is not such a person one for whom the verse “Having abandoned home…” applies?

851. Tattha [P 2.0547] okaṃ pahāyāti rūpavatthādiviññāṇassa okāsaṃ tatra chandarāgappahānena chaḍḍetvā. Aniketasārīti rūpanimittaniketādīni taṇhāvasena asaranto. Gāme akubbaṃ muni santhavānīti gāme gihisanthavāni akaronto. Kāmehi rittoti kāmesu chandarāgābhāvena sabbakāmehi puthubhūto. Apurekkharānoti āyatiṃ attabhāvaṃ anabhinibbattento. Kathaṃ na viggayha janena kayirāti janena saddhiṃ viggāhikakathaṃ na katheyya. So evarūpo – yehi vivittoti gāthā.

851. Therein, “having abandoned home” means having abandoned the opportunity for consciousness based on form-objects and so on, by abandoning desire and lust therein. “Wandering without a home” means not delighting in the abodes of form-signs and so on through craving. “The sage, making no intimacies in the village,” means not forming familiar relationships with householders in the village. “Empty of sensual pleasures” means being separate from all sensual pleasures due to the absence of desire and lust for them. “Not putting anything forward” means not generating a future state of existence. “How would he engage in disputes with people?” means how would he engage in contentious talk with people? Such a one is as in the verse: “Secluded from which…”

852. Tattha yehīti yehi diṭṭhigatehi. Vivitto vicareyyāti ritto careyya. Na tāni uggayha vadeyya nāgoti “āguṃ na karotī”tiādinā (cūḷani. bhadrāvudhamāṇavapucchāniddesa 70; pārāyanānugītigāthāniddesa 102) nayena nāgo tāni diṭṭhigatāni uggahetvā na vadeyya. Jalambujanti jalasaññite ambumhi jātaṃ kaṇṭakanāḷaṃ vārijaṃ, padumanti vuttaṃ hoti. Yathā jalena paṅkena ca nūpalittanti taṃ padumaṃ yathā jalena ca paṅkena ca anupalittaṃ hoti, evaṃ muni santivādo agiddhoti evaṃ ajjhattasantivādo muni gedhābhāvena agiddho. Kāme [V 2.0239] ca loke ca [M 2.0262] anūpalittoti duvidhepi kāme apāyādike ca loke dvīhipi lepehi anupalitto hoti.

852. Herein, “by which” refers to by which views. “He would wander secluded” means he would wander detached. “The nāga would not grasp those and speak” means, in the sense that a nāga is one who “does no wrong,” etc. (as explained in the Cūḷaniddesa and Pārāyanānugītigāthāniddesa), the noble one does not take up those views and speak. “Water-born lotus” refers to the thorny-stemmed water-born plant, born in the water; it is called a “paduma” or lotus. “Just as it is unstained by water and mud” means just as that lotus is unstained by water and mud, “so the sage, a speaker of peace, is not greedy” means so the sage, a speaker of internal peace, is not greedy due to the absence of greed. “Unstained by sensual pleasures and the world” means he is unstained by the two defilements in both kinds of sensual pleasures and in the world, including the woeful states.

853. Kiñca bhiyyo – na vedagūti gāthā. Tattha na vedagū diṭṭhiyāyakoti catumaggavedagū mādiso diṭṭhiyāyako na hoti, diṭṭhiyā gacchanto vā, taṃ sārato paccento vā na hoti. Tattha vacanattho – yāyatīti yāyako, karaṇavacanena diṭṭhiyā yātīti diṭṭhiyāyako. Upayogatthe sāmivacanena diṭṭhiyā yātītipi diṭṭhiyāyako. Na mutiyā sa mānametīti mutarūpādibhedāya mutiyāpi so mānaṃ na eti. Na hi tammayo soti taṇhādiṭṭhivasena tammayo hoti tapparāyaṇo, ayaṃ pana na tādiso. Na kammunā nopi sutena neyyoti puññābhisaṅkhārādinā kammunā vā sutasuddhiādinā sutena vā so netabbo na hoti. Anūpanīto sa nivesanesūti so dvinnampi upayānaṃ pahīnattā sabbesu taṇhādiṭṭhinivesanesu anūpanīto. Tassa ca evaṃvidhassa – saññāvirattassāti gāthā.

853. "What more?"—the verse, "not a knower of the Vedas." Herein, "not a knower of the Vedas" means one like me, a knower of the four paths, is not a proponent of views; he does not go by views or rely on them as essence. The meaning here is: "one who goes" is a goer; by the instrumental case, "goes by views" means a proponent of views. In the sense of usage in the possessive case, "goes by views" also means a proponent of views. "He does not come to pride through what is sensed" means he does not develop pride even through what is sensed, which is differentiated as form and so on. "For he is not of that sort" means he is not defined by craving or views, nor inclined toward them; but this one is not like that. "Not to be led by deeds or by learning" means he cannot be led by meritorious formations or by purity based on learning. "Unattached in all dwellings" means, having abandoned both kinds of 'approach' (upayana), he is unattached to all dwellings of craving and views. And for one of this kind—the verse, "dispassionate toward perceptions."

854. Tattha saññāvirattassāti nekkhammasaññāpubbaṅgamāya bhāvanāya pahīnakāmādisaññassa. Iminā padena ubhatobhāgavimutto samathayāniko adhippeto. Paññāvimuttassāti vipassanāpubbaṅgamāya bhāvanāya sabbakilesehi [P 2.0548] vimuttassa. Iminā sukkhavipassako adhippeto. Saññañca diṭṭhiñca ye aggahesuṃ, te ghaṭṭayantā vicaranti loketi ye kāmasaññādikaṃ saññaṃ aggahesuṃ, te visesato gahaṭṭhā kāmādhikaraṇaṃ, ye ca diṭṭhiṃ aggahesuṃ, te visesato pabbajitā dhammādhikaraṇaṃ aññamaññaṃ ghaṭṭentā vicarantīti. Sesamettha yaṃ avuttaṃ, taṃ vuttānusāreneva veditabbaṃ. Desanāpariyosāne brāhmaṇo ca brāhmaṇī ca pabbajitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsūti.

854. Here, 'one detached from perception' refers to one who has abandoned perceptions of sensuality, etc., through meditation preceded by the perception of renunciation. This phrase indicates one liberated in both ways, who has serenity as their vehicle. 'One liberated by wisdom' refers to one liberated from all defilements through meditation preceded by insight. This phrase indicates a dry-insight meditator. 'Those who clung to perception and view'—those who clung to perceptions like sensuality were especially householders concerned with sensual matters, while those who clung to views were especially ascetics concerned with doctrinal matters, clashing with one another as they wandered the world. The rest here, whatever is unsaid, should be understood in accordance with what has already been said. At the conclusion of the teaching, both the brahmin and the brahmin’s wife went forth and attained arahantship.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

From the Paramatthajotikā, the commentary on the Minor Collection.

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya māgaṇḍiyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta in the Suttanipāta commentary is finished.

10. Purābhedasuttavaṇṇanā

10. The Explanation of the Purābheda Sutta

855. Kathaṃdassīti [V 2.0240][M 2.0263] purābhedasuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Imassa suttassa ito paresañca pañcannaṃ kalahavivādacūḷabyūhamahābyūhatuvaṭakaattadaṇḍasuttānaṃ sammāparibbājanīyassa uppattiyaṃ vuttanayeneva sāmaññato uppatti vuttā. Visesato pana yatheva tasmiṃ mahāsamaye rāgacaritadevatānaṃ sappāyavasena dhammaṃ desetuṃ nimmitabuddhena attānaṃ pucchāpetvā sammāparibbājanīyasuttamabhāsi, evaṃ tasmiṃyeva mahāsamaye “kiṃ nu kho purā sarīrabhedā kattabba”nti uppannacittānaṃ devatānaṃ cittaṃ ñatvā tāsaṃ anuggahatthaṃ aḍḍhateḷasabhikkhusataparivāraṃ nimmitabuddhaṃ ākāsena ānetvā tena attānaṃ pucchāpetvā imaṃ suttamabhāsi.

855. "How does one see?" This is the Purābheda Sutta. What is its origin? The origin of this sutta, along with the five that follow—the Kalahavivāda, Cūḷabyūha, Mahābyūha, Tuvaṭaka, and Attadaṇḍa Suttas—has been generally explained in the manner stated regarding the origin of the Sammāparibbājanīya Sutta. Specifically, just as during that great assembly, a created Buddha had himself questioned in order to teach the Dhamma in a way suitable for deities of lustful temperament, and the Sammāparibbājanīya Sutta was spoken, so too during that same great assembly, knowing the thoughts of deities who had the thought, "What should be done before the breaking up of the body?" for their benefit, a created Buddha, surrounded by twelve hundred and fifty monks, was brought through the sky, and after making him question himself, he spoke this sutta.

Tattha pucchāya tāva so nimmito kathaṃdassīti adhipaññaṃ kathaṃsīloti adhisīlaṃ, upasantoti adhicittaṃ pucchati. Sesaṃ pākaṭameva.

There, first, regarding the question, the created one asks: "How does one see?" (concerning higher wisdom); "How is one's virtue?" (concerning higher virtue); and "Is one at peace?" (concerning higher mind). The rest is clear.

856. Vissajjane pana bhagavā sarūpena adhipaññādīni avissajjetvāva adhipaññādippabhāvena yesaṃ kilesānaṃ upasamā “upasanto”ti vuccati, nānādevatānaṃ āsayānulomena tesaṃ upasamameva dīpento “vītataṇho”tiādikā gāthāyo abhāsi. Tattha ādito aṭṭhannaṃ gāthānaṃ “taṃ brūmi upasanto”ti imāya gāthāya sambandho veditabbo. Tato parāsaṃ “sa ve santoti vuccatī”ti iminā sabbapacchimena padena.

856. In his answer, the Blessed One, without directly explaining higher wisdom and so forth in their own terms, instead spoke the verses beginning "free from craving," illuminating the very pacification of those defilements by which one is called 'calmed' through the power of higher wisdom and so forth, in accordance with the inclinations of the various deities. Here, the first eight verses should be understood as connected with the verse, "Him I call 'calmed.'" The subsequent verses are linked by the very last phrase, "Truly, he is called 'peaceful.'"

Anupadavaṇṇanānayena [P 2.0549] ca – vītataṇho purā bhedāti yo sarīrabhedā pubbameva pahīnataṇho. Pubbamantamanissitoti atītaddhādibhedaṃ pubbantamanissito. Vemajjhenupasaṅkheyyoti paccuppannepi addhani “ratto”tiādinā nayena na upasaṅkhātabbo. Tassa natthi purakkhatanti tassa arahato dvinnaṃ purekkhārānaṃ abhāvā anāgate addhani purakkhatampi natthi, taṃ brūmi upasantoti evamettha yojanā veditabbā. Esa nayo sabbattha. Ito paraṃ pana yojanaṃ adassetvā anuttānapadavaṇṇanaṃyeva karissāma.

And by the method of word-by-word explanation: 'free from craving before the breakup' means one who has abandoned craving even before the breakup of the body. 'Not dependent on the past' means not dependent on the past, such as past periods. 'Not to be reckoned in the middle' means even in the present moment, one should not be reckoned by way of 'attached,' or the like. 'For him, there is no anticipation' means for that arahant, there is no anticipation even in the future, due to the absence of the two kinds of anticipations. Thus, the connection here should be understood as 'Him I call peaceful.' This is the method in all cases. From here onward, without showing the full application, we will only provide the explanation of obscure words.

857. Asantāsīti tena tena alābhakena asantasanto. Avikatthīti sīlādīhi avikatthanasīlo[V 2.0241]. Akukkucoti hatthakukkucādivirahito[M 2.0264]. Mantabhāṇīti mantāya pariggahetvā vācaṃ bhāsitā. Anuddhatoti uddhaccavirahito. Sa ve vācāyatoti so vācāya yato saṃyato catudosavirahitaṃ vācaṃ bhāsitā hoti.

857. 'Asantāsī' means not trembling due to various losses. 'Avikatthī' is one whose nature is not to boast about virtues like morality. 'Akukkuco' is devoid of misdeeds of hand and the like. 'Mantabhāṇī' speaks words after carefully considering them. 'Anuddhato' is free from agitation. 'Sa ve vācāyato' means he is controlled in speech, speaking words free from the four faults.

858. Nirāsattīti nittaṇho. Vivekadassī phassesūti paccuppannesu cakkhusamphassādīsu attādibhāvavivekaṃ passati. Diṭṭhīsu ca na nīyatīti dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhīsu kāyaci diṭṭhiyā na nīyati.

858. 'Nirāsatti' means without craving. 'Seer of detachment in contacts' means they see detachment from the state of selfhood in present contacts like eye-contact and so on. 'Not led by views' means they are not led by any of the sixty-two views.

859. Patilīnoti rāgādīnaṃ pahīnattā tato apagato. Akuhakoti avimhāpako tīhi kuhanavatthūhi. Apihālūti apihanasīlo, patthanātaṇhāya rahitoti vuttaṃ hoti. Amaccharīti pañcamaccheravirahito. Appagabbhoti kāyapāgabbhiyādivirahito. Ajegucchoti sampannasīlāditāya ajegucchanīyo asecanako manāpo. Pesuṇeyye ca no yutoti dvīhi ākārehi upasaṃharitabbe pisuṇakamme ayutto.

859. 'Patilīno' means withdrawn, having turned away from greed and other defilements because they have been abandoned. 'Akuhako' means not deceptive, free from the three grounds of deceit. 'Apihālu' means not inclined to envy, that is to say, devoid of the craving of longing. 'Amaccharī' means free from the five kinds of stinginess. 'Appagabbho' means free from bodily insolence and the like. 'Ajeguccho' means not repulsive, because of possessing virtue and other qualities, inherently pleasing and delightful. 'Pesuṇeyye ca no yuto' means not engaged in the act of slander, which can be performed in two ways.

860. Sātiyesu anassāvīti sātavatthūsu kāmaguṇesu taṇhāsanthavavirahito. Saṇhoti saṇhehi kāyakammādīhi samannāgato. Paṭibhānavāti pariyattiparipucchādhigamapaṭibhānehi samannāgato. Na saddhoti sāmaṃ adhigatadhammaṃ na kassaci saddahati. Na virajjatīti khayā rāgassa virattattā idāni na virajjati.

860. 'Not indulging in pleasures' means being free from craving and attachment to sensual objects that bring pleasure. 'Gentle' means endowed with gentle bodily actions and so forth. 'Eloquent' means endowed with the ready wit of learning, questioning, and realization. 'Not believing' means he does not believe anyone regarding the Dhamma he has himself realized. 'He does not become dispassionate' means that having already become dispassionate through the destruction of lust, he does not now become dispassionate.

861. Lābhakamyā na sikkhatīti na lābhapatthanāya suttantādīni sikkhati. Aviruddho ca taṇhāya, rasesu nānugijjhatīti virodhābhāvena ca aviruddho hutvā taṇhāya mūlarasādīsu gedhaṃ [P 2.0550] nāpajjati.

861. ‘One does not train out of a desire for gain’ means one does not study the discourses and so on with a desire for gain. ‘And unconflicted by craving, one does not greedily cling to flavors’ means that, being unconflicted due to the absence of opposition, one does not through craving fall into greed for root-flavors and the like.

862. Upekkhakoti chaḷaṅgupekkhāya samannāgato. Satoti kāyānupassanādisatiyutto.

862. 'Equanimous' means endowed with six-factored equanimity. 'Mindful' means endowed with mindfulness such as the contemplation of the body.

863. Nissayanāti taṇhādiṭṭhinissayā. Ñatvā dhammanti aniccādīhi ākārehi dhammaṃ jānitvā. Anissitoti evaṃ tehi nissayehi anissito. Tena aññatra dhammañāṇā natthi nissayānaṃ abhāvoti dīpeti bhavāya vibhavāya vāti sassatāya ucchedāya vā.

863. 'Supports' means the supports of craving and view. 'Having known the Dhamma' means having known the Dhamma through its characteristics, such as impermanence and so on. 'Without support' means unsupported by those supports. By this, it is shown that apart from knowledge of the Dhamma, there is no absence of supports for views of existence or non-existence, that is, for eternalism or annihilation.

864. Taṃ [V 2.0242][M 2.0265] brūmi upasantoti taṃ evarūpaṃ ekekagāthāya vuttaṃ upasantoti kathemi. Atarī so visattikanti so imaṃ visatādibhāvena visattikāsaṅkhātaṃ mahātaṇhaṃ atari.

864. 'That one I call peaceful' means: I declare as peaceful such a one spoken of in each verse. 'He has crossed over clinging' means: he has crossed over this great craving, known as clinging because of its spreading nature.

865. Idāni tameva upasantaṃ pasaṃsanto āha “na tassa puttā”ti evamādi. Tattha puttā atrajādayo cattāro. Ettha ca puttapariggahādayo puttādināmena vuttāti veditabbā. Te hissa na vijjanti, tesaṃ vā abhāvena puttādayo na vijjantīti.

865. Now, praising that same peaceful one, he says, 'He has no sons,' and so on. Here, 'sons' refers to the four kinds, beginning with those born of oneself. And here, it should be understood that possessions such as sons and so on are referred to by the term 'sons' and so on. For him, these do not exist; or, because of the absence of these, sons and the like do not exist.

866. Yena naṃ vajjuṃ puthujjanā, atho samaṇabrāhmaṇāti yena taṃ rāgādinā vajjena puthujjanā sabbepi devamanussā ito bahiddhā samaṇabrāhmaṇā ca ratto vā duṭṭho vāti, vadeyyuṃ. Taṃ tassa apurakkhatanti taṃ rāgādivajjaṃ tassa arahato apurakkhataṃ tasmā vādesu nejatīti taṃ kāraṇā nindāvacanesu na kampati.

866. 'By which ordinary people, and also ascetics and brahmins, might speak of him' means: by which fault of lust and so on, all ordinary people—gods and humans—and ascetics and brahmins outside this teaching, might speak of him, saying, 'He is lustful' or 'He is hateful.' 'That is not put before him' means that fault of lust and so on is not present for that Arahant. 'Therefore he is not stirred by doctrines' means for that reason he does not tremble at words of blame.

867. Na ussesu vadateti visiṭṭhesu attānaṃ antokatvā “ahaṃ visiṭṭho”ti atimānavasena na vadati. Esa nayo itaresu dvīsu. Kappaṃ neti akappiyoti so evarūpo duvidhampi kappaṃ na eti. Kasmā? Yasmā akappiyo, pahīnakappoti vuttaṃ hoti.

867. 'He does not speak among the high' means that, including himself among the superior, he does not speak out of excessive conceit, saying, 'I am superior.' This is the method for the other two cases as well. 'He does not go to speculation, being one for whom it is unfitting' means such a one does not go to either of the two kinds of speculation. Why? Because he is one for whom it is unfitting (akappiyo); that is to say, he has abandoned speculation.

868. Sakanti mayhanti pariggahitaṃ. Asatā ca na socatīti avijjamānādinā asatā ca na socati. Dhammesu ca na gacchatīti sabbesu dhammesu chandādivasena na gacchati. Sa ve santoti vuccatīti so evarūpo naruttamo “santo”ti vuccatīti arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi. Desanāpariyosāne koṭisatasahassadevatānaṃ arahattappatti ahosi, sotāpannādīnaṃ gaṇanā natthīti.

868. 'One's own' means 'mine,' 'possessed by me.' 'And he does not grieve for what is not' means he does not sorrow over what is not, such as what is non-existent and so on. 'And he does not go among phenomena' means he does not go to any phenomena by way of desire and so on. 'He is truly called "peaceful"' means such a supreme person is called 'peaceful,' thus concluding the teaching with the pinnacle of Arahantship. At the end of the teaching, a trillion devas attained Arahantship, and there was no counting of those who became stream-enterers and so forth.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya purābhedasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Purābheda Sutta in the Commentary on the Suttanipāta is concluded.

11. Kalahavivādasuttavaṇṇanā

11. The Explanation of the Kalahavivāda Sutta

869. Kuto [V 2.0243][M 2.0266][P 2.0551] pahūtā kalahā vivādāti kalahavivādasuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Idampi tasmiṃyeva mahāsamaye “kuto nu, kho, kalahādayo aṭṭha dhammā pavattantī”ti uppannacittānaṃ ekaccānaṃ devatānaṃ te dhamme āvikātuṃ purimanayeneva nimmitabuddhena attānaṃ pucchāpetvā vuttaṃ tattha pucchāvissajjanakkamena ṭhitattā sabbagāthā pākaṭasambandhāyeva.

869. The Kalahavivāda Sutta is the one that begins, 'From where have quarrels and disputes arisen?' What is its origin? This too was spoken on that very great occasion. For certain deities, the thought arose, 'From where, indeed, do these eight things—quarrels and so forth—arise?' In order to reveal those things to them, the Buddha, in the same way as before, caused himself to be questioned by a created Buddha. There, because all the verses stand in the sequence of question and answer, their connection is clear.

Anuttānapadavaṇṇanā panetāsaṃ evaṃ veditabbā – kutopahūtā kalahā vivādāti kalaho ca tassa pubbabhāgo vivādo cāti ime kuto jātā. Paridevasokā sahamaccharā cāti paridevasokā ca maccharā ca kutopahūtā. Mānātimānā sahapesuṇā cāti mānā ca atimānā ca pesuṇā ca kutopahūtā. Teti te sabbepi aṭṭha kilesadhammā. Tadiṅgha brūhīti taṃ mayā pucchitamatthaṃ brūhi yācāmi taṃ ahanti. Yācanattho hi iṅghāti nipāto.

The explanation of the difficult words in these verses should be understood thus: 'From where have quarrels and disputes arisen?' means from where are these born: quarrel, and dispute which is its preliminary part? 'Lamentation and sorrow, together with stinginess' means from where have lamentation, sorrow, and stinginess arisen? 'Conceit and arrogance, together with slander' means from where have conceit, arrogance, and slander arisen? 'These' means all those eight defiled states. 'Pray, tell me this' means 'Tell me that meaning which I have asked; I entreat you.' For the particle 'iṅgha' has the meaning of entreaty.

870. Piyappahūtāti piyavatthuto jātā. Yutti panettha niddese (mahāni. 98) vuttā eva. Maccherayuttā kalahā vivādāti iminā kalahavivādādīnaṃ na kevalaṃ piyavatthumeva, macchariyampi paccayaṃ dasseti. Kalahavivādasīsena cettha sabbepi te dhammā vuttāti veditabbā. Yathā ca etesaṃ macchariyaṃ, tathā pesuṇānañca vivādaṃ. Tenāha – “vivādajātesu ca pesuṇānī”ti.

870. 'Arisen from what is dear' means born from a dear object. The reasoning here is as stated in the Niddesa (Mahāni. 98). 'Quarrels and disputes are connected with stinginess'—by this, it is shown that not only dear objects but also stinginess is a condition for quarrels, disputes, and so forth. It should be understood that all those states are mentioned here under the heading of quarrels and disputes. And just as stinginess is a condition for these, so too is dispute for slander. Therefore, he said: 'And slander among those born from disputes.'

871. Piyāsu lokasmiṃ kutonidānā ye cāpi lobhā vicaranti loketi “piyā pahūtā kalahā”ti ye ettha vuttā. Te piyā lokasmiṃ kutonidānā, na kevalañca piyā, ye cāpi khattiyādayo lobhā vicaranti lobhahetukā lobhenābhibhūtā vicaranti, tesaṃ so lobho ca kutonidānoti dve atthe ekāya pucchāya pucchati. Āsā ca niṭṭhā cāti āsā ca tassā āsāya samiddhi ca. Ye samparāyāya narassa hontīti ye narassa samparāyāya honti, parāyanā hontīti vuttaṃ hoti. Ekā evāyampi pucchā.

871. Regarding the verse 'From what source in the world are dear things, and also the greeds that wander in the world?': The 'dear things' are those mentioned here in the phrase 'quarrels arise from dear things.' The question is: from what source in the world do those dear things arise? And not only the dear things, but also, for those such as nobles and others who wander due to greed, motivated by greed, and overcome by greed—from what source is that greed of theirs? Thus, two meanings are asked with a single question. 'Hope and fulfillment' means hope and the success of that hope. 'Which are for a person's future' means that which is for a person's future course; that is to say, their ultimate destiny. This too is a single question.

872. Chandānidānānīti [M 2.0267] kāmacchandādichandanidānāni. Ye cāpi lobhā vicarantīti ye cāpi [V 2.0244] khattiyādayo lobhā vicaranti tesaṃ lobhopi chandanidānoti dvepi atthe ekato vissajjeti. Itonidānāti chandanidānā evāti vuttaṃ hoti. “Kutonidānā kutonidānā”ti (su. ni. 273) etesu ca saddasiddhi sūcilomasutte vuttanayeneva [P 2.0552] veditabbā.

872. 'Rooted in desire' means rooted in sensual desire and other desires. 'Those who wander driven by greed'—those such as nobles and others who wander under the influence of greed—their greed too is rooted in desire. Thus, both meanings are answered together. 'From this source' means 'they are rooted in desire'—this is what is said. And the grammatical formation of 'kutonidānā kutonidānā' (from what source, from what source) in these verses should be understood in the same way as stated in the Sūciloma Sutta (Sn 273).

873. Vinicchayāti taṇhādiṭṭhivinicchayā. Ye vāpi dhammā samaṇena vuttāti ye ca aññepi kodhādīhi sampayuttā, tathārūpā vā akusalā dhammā buddhasamaṇena vuttā, te kutopahūtāti.

873. 'Discriminations' means the discriminations of craving and views. 'And those things declared by the ascetic' means: from where do those other unwholesome states associated with anger and so forth, or such unwholesome states declared by the Buddha-ascetic, originate?

874. Tamūpanissāya pahoti chandoti taṃ sukhadukkhavedanaṃ. Tadubhayavatthusaṅkhātaṃ sātāsātaṃ upanissāya saṃyogaviyogapatthanāvasena chando pahoti. Ettāvatā “chando nu lokasmiṃ kutonidāno”ti ayaṃ pañho vissajjito hoti. Rūpesu disvā vibhavaṃ bhavañcāti rūpesu vayañca uppādañca disvā. Vinicchayaṃ kubbati jantu loketi apāyādike loke ayaṃ jantu bhogādhigamanatthaṃ taṇhāvinicchayaṃ “attā me uppanno”tiādinā nayena diṭṭhivinicchayañca kurute. Yutti panettha niddese (mahāni. 102) vuttā eva. Ettāvatā “vinicchayā cāpi kutopahūtā”ti ayaṃ pañho vissajjito hoti.

874. 'Desire arises dependent on that' refers to that pleasant and painful feeling. Dependent on the agreeable and disagreeable, which are designated as the basis for both, desire arises by way of longing for union and for separation. To this extent, the question, 'What is the source of desire in the world?' is answered. 'Having seen decline and growth in forms' means having seen cessation and arising in forms. 'A being makes distinctions in the world' means in the world of the lower realms and so forth, this being makes distinctions based on craving for attaining enjoyments, and also makes distinctions based on views in the manner beginning with 'A self has arisen for me.' The connection here is as stated in the Niddesa (Mahāni. 102). To this extent, the question, 'And from what do distinctions arise?' is answered.

875. Etepi dhammā dvayameva santeti etepi kodhādayo dhammā sātāsātadvaye sante eva pahonti uppajjanti. Uppatti ca nesaṃ niddese (mahāni. 103) vuttāyeva. Ettāvatā tatiyapañhopi vissajjito hoti. Idāni yo evaṃ vissajjitesu etesu pañhesu kathaṃkathī bhaveyya, tassa kathaṃkathāpahānūpāyaṃ dassento āha – “kathaṃkathī ñāṇapathāya sikkhe”ti, ñāṇadassanañāṇādhigamanatthaṃ tisso sikkhā sikkheyyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Kiṃ kāraṇaṃ? Ñatvā pavuttā samaṇena dhammā. Buddhasamaṇena hi ñatvāva dhammā vuttā, natthi tassa dhammesu aññāṇaṃ. Attano pana ñāṇābhāvena te ajānanto na jāneyya, na desanā dosena, tasmā kathaṃkathī ñāṇapathāya sikkhe, ñatvā pavuttā samaṇena dhammāti.

875. 'These phenomena, too, exist only in duality' means these phenomena such as anger and so forth, arise only when the duality of the agreeable and disagreeable exists. Their arising has also been stated in the Niddesa (Mahāni. 103). To this extent, the third question is also answered. Now, showing the means for abandoning doubt for anyone who might be doubtful regarding these questions thus answered, he said: 'One who doubts should train in the path of knowledge.' It is said that one should train in the threefold training for the attainment of knowledge and insight. What is the reason? 'For the ascetic proclaimed the teachings after knowing them.' For the Buddha-ascetic proclaimed the teachings only after knowing them; there is no ignorance in him regarding the teachings. But one, not knowing them due to lacking knowledge oneself, would not understand, not due to a fault in the teaching. Therefore, one who doubts should train in the path of knowledge, for 'the ascetic proclaimed the teachings after knowing them.'

876-7. Sātaṃ [M 2.0268] asātañca kutonidānāti ettha sātaṃ asātanti sukhadukkhavedanā eva adhippetā. Na bhavanti heteti na bhavanti ete. Vibhavaṃ bhavañcāpi yametamatthaṃ etaṃ me pabrūhi yatonidānanti sātāsātānaṃ vibhavaṃ bhavañca etampi yaṃ atthaṃ. Liṅgabyattayo ettha kato. Idaṃ pana vuttaṃ hoti – sātāsātānaṃ vibhavo bhavo cāti yo esa attho, evaṃ me pabrūhi yatonidānanti. [V 2.0245] Ettha ca sātāsātānaṃ vibhavabhavavatthukā vibhavabhavadiṭṭhiyo eva vibhavabhavāti [P 2.0553] atthato veditabbā. Tathā hi imassa pañhassa vissajjanapakkhe “bhavadiṭṭhipi phassanidānā, vibhavadiṭṭhipi phassanidānā”ti niddese (mahāni. 105) vuttaṃ. Itonidānanti phassanidānaṃ.

876-7. In 'What is the source of the agreeable and disagreeable?', the agreeable and disagreeable are indeed intended as pleasant and painful feelings. In the phrase 'these do not exist' (na bhavanti hete), the word 'hete' means 'these' (ete). 'Decline and growth, too—this meaning, explain to me its source' refers to this meaning, which is also the decline and growth of the agreeable and disagreeable. Here, a change of gender has been made. But this is what is said: 'This meaning, which is the decline and growth of the agreeable and disagreeable—explain to me its source.' And here, 'decline and growth' should be understood in meaning as the views of decline and growth, which are based on the agreeable and disagreeable. For in the answer to this question, it is stated in the Niddesa (Mahāni. 105): 'The view of existence has contact as its source, and the view of non-existence also has contact as its source.' 'From this source' means it has contact as its source.

878. Kismiṃ vibhūte na phusanti phassāti kismiṃ vītivatte cakkhusamphassādayo pañca phassā na phusanti.

878. 'When what is dissolved do contacts not make contact?' means 'When what has been transcended do the five contacts—eye-contact and so on—not make contact?'

879. Nāmañca rūpañca paṭiccāti sampayuttakanāmaṃ vatthārammaṇarūpañca paṭicca. Rūpe vibhūte na phusanti phassāti rūpe vītivatte pañca phassā na phusanti.

879. 'Depending on name and form' means depending on associated mental factors (nāma) and the physical base or object (rūpa). 'When form is dissolved, contacts do not make contact' means when form has been transcended, the five contacts do not make contact.

880. Kathaṃ sametassāti kathaṃ paṭipannassa. Vibhoti rūpanti rūpa vibhavati, na bhaveyya vā. Sukhaṃ dukhañcāti iṭṭhāniṭṭhaṃ rūpameva pucchati.

880. 'How for one who is composed?' means 'how for one who has practiced?' 'Form vanishes' means form vanishes, or it might not exist. 'Pleasure and pain' refers to desirable and undesirable forms being inquired about.

881. Na saññasaññīti yathā sametassa vibhoti rūpaṃ, so pakatisaññāya saññīpi na hoti. Na visaññasaññīti visaññāyapi virūpāya saññāya saññī na hoti ummattako vā khittacitto vā. Nopi asaññīti saññāvirahitopi na hoti nirodhasamāpanno vā asaññasatto vā. Na vibhūtasaññīti “sabbaso rūpasaññāna”ntiādinā (dha sa. 265; vibha. 602) nayena samatikkantasaññīpi na hoti arūpajjhānalābhī. Evaṃ sametassa vibhoti rūpanti etasmiṃ saññasaññitādibhāve aṭṭhatvā yadetaṃ vuttaṃ “so evaṃ samāhite citte…pe… ākāsānañcāyatanasamāpattipaṭilābhatthāya cittaṃ abhinīharatī”ti. Evaṃ sametassa arūpamaggasamaṅgino vibhoti rūpaṃ. Saññānidānā hi papañcasaṅkhāti evaṃ paṭipannassāpi yā saññā, tannidānā taṇhādiṭṭhipapañcā appahīnā eva hontīti dasseti.

881. 'Not perceiving in perception' means that for one who is composed, form vanishes, and he is not perceiving through normal perception. 'Nor perceiving in distorted perception' means he does not perceive with a distorted or abnormal perception, like someone deranged or of unsound mind. 'Nor without perception' means he is not without perception, like someone in cessation attainment or a non-percipient being. 'Nor perceiving the vanished' means he is not perceiving through perception that has been transcended in the way beginning with 'Through the complete surmounting of all perceptions of form' (Dhs 265; Vibh 602), like one who has gained the formless jhānas. Thus, 'for one who is composed, form vanishes'—this does not refer to being in the state of perceiving in perception, etc., but refers to what was said: 'So, when his mind is thus concentrated...he directs his mind to attaining the attainment of the dimension of infinite space.' Thus, for one who is composed and endowed with the path of the formless, form vanishes. 'Because proliferation is rooted in perception'—he shows that even for such a practitioner, whatever perception there is, the proliferations of craving and views rooted in that are not abandoned.

882-3. Ettāvataggaṃ [M 2.0269] nu vadanti, heke yakkhassa suddhiṃ idha paṇḍitāse. Udāhu aññampi vadanti ettoti ettāvatā nu idha paṇḍitā samaṇabrāhmaṇā aggaṃ suddhiṃ sattassa vadanti, udāhu aññampi etto arūpasamāpattito adhikaṃ vadantīti pucchati. Ettāvataggampi vadanti heketi eke sassatavādā samaṇabrāhmaṇā paṇḍitamānino ettāvatāpi aggaṃ suddhiṃ vadanti. Tesaṃ paneke samayaṃ vadantīti tesaṃyeva eke ucchedavādā samayaṃ ucchedaṃ vadanti. Anupādisese kusalā vadānāti anupādisese kusalavādā samānā.

882-3. 'Do some, who consider themselves experts here, declare this to be the ultimate purity for the spirit? Or do they declare something beyond this?' The question asks whether learned ascetics and brahmins here declare this much as the highest purity for a being, or do they proclaim something superior beyond this formless attainment? 'Some indeed declare this to be the limit' refers to some eternalist ascetics and brahmins who think themselves learned and declare only this much as the ultimate purity. 'But some of those speak of annihilation' refers to some of those very same teachers, particularly annihilationists, who proclaim annihilation. 'Those skilled in teaching without remainder' means they are skilled in teaching about the state without remainder.

884. Ete [V 2.0246] ca ñatvā upanissitāti ete ca diṭṭhigatike [P 2.0554] sassatucchedadiṭṭhiyo nissitāti ñatvā. Ñatvā munī nissaye so vimaṃsīti nissaye ca ñatvā so vīmaṃsī paṇḍito buddhamuni. Ñatvā vimuttoti dukkhāniccādito dhamme ñatvā vimutto. Bhavābhavāya na sametīti punappunaṃ upapattiyā na samāgacchatīti arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi. Desanāpariyosāne purābhedasutte vuttasadisoyevābhisamayo ahosīti.

884. 'Knowing these are dependent' means knowing that these adherents of views are dependent on eternalist and annihilationist views. 'Knowing the dependencies, the sage investigates' means that the wise sage, the Buddha, investigates after knowing the dependencies. 'Knowing, he is liberated' means he is liberated after knowing phenomena such as suffering, impermanence, and so forth. 'He does not come to existence or non-existence' means he does not come to repeated rebirth—thus he concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of Arahantship. At the end of the discourse, the realization was just as was stated in the Purābheda Sutta.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya kalahavivādasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Kalahavivāda Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary is concluded.

12. Cūḷabyūhasuttavaṇṇanā

12. The Commentary on the Cūḷabyūha Sutta

885-6. Sakaṃsakaṃdiṭṭhiparibbasānāti [V 2.0247] cūḷabyūhasuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Idampi tasmiṃyeva mahāsamaye “sabbepi ime diṭṭhigatikā ‘sādhurūpamhā’ti bhaṇanti, kiṃ nu kho sādhurūpāva ime attanoyeva diṭṭhiyā patiṭṭhahanti, udāhu aññampi diṭṭhiṃ gaṇhantī”ti uppannacittānaṃ ekaccānaṃ devatānaṃ tamatthaṃ pakāsetuṃ purimanayeneva nimmitabuddhena attānaṃ pucchāpetvā vuttaṃ.

885-6. 'Abiding in their respective views'—this is the Cūḷabyūha Sutta. What is its origin? This too arose during that great assembly when some deities, their minds stirred, thought: 'All these adherents of views claim, “We are of a good nature.” But do they stand firm in their own views alone, or do they also adopt other views?' To clarify this matter, as before, it was spoken by a manifested Buddha who had caused himself to be questioned.

Tattha ādito dvepi gāthā pucchāgāthāyeva. Tāsu sakaṃsakaṃdiṭṭhiparibbasānāti attano attano diṭṭhiyā vasamānā. Viggayha nānā kusalā vadantīti diṭṭhibalaggāhaṃ gahetvā, tattha “kusalāmhā”ti paṭijānamānā [M 2.0270] puthu puthu vadanti ekaṃ na vadanti. Yo evaṃ jānāti sa vedi dhammaṃ idaṃ paṭikosamakevalī soti tañca diṭṭhiṃ sandhāya yo evaṃ jānāti, so dhammaṃ vedi. Idaṃ pana paṭikkosanto hīno hotīti vadanti. Bāloti hīno. Akkusaloti avidvā.

Here, the first two verses are indeed question verses. In them, 'abiding in their respective views' means abiding by their own respective views. 'Disputing, various experts speak' means, having taken a tenacious hold of their views and claiming, 'We are skilled,' they speak variously, not in unison. With reference to that view, they say: 'One who knows thus, knows the Dhamma. But one who rejects this is inferior.' 'Bālo' means inferior. 'Akkusalo' means ignorant.

887-8. Idāni tisso vissajjanagāthā honti. Tā purimaḍḍhena vuttamatthaṃ pacchimaḍḍhena paṭibyūhitvā ṭhitā. Tena byūhena uttarasuttato ca appakattā idaṃ suttaṃ “cūḷabyūha”nti nāmaṃ labhati. Tattha parassa ce dhammanti parassa diṭṭhiṃ. Sabbeva bālāti evaṃ sante sabbeva ime bālā hontīti adhippāyo. Kiṃ kāraṇaṃ? Sabbevime diṭṭhiparibbasānāti sandiṭṭhiyā ceva na vīvadātā. Saṃsuddhapaññā kusalā mutīmāti sakāya diṭṭhiyā na vivadātā na vodātā saṃkiliṭṭhāva samānā [P 2.0555] saṃsuddhapaññā ca kusalā ca mutimanto ca te honti ce. Atha vā “sandiṭṭhiyā ce pana vīvadātā” tipi pāṭho. Tassattho – sakāya pana diṭṭhiyā vodātā saṃsuddhapaññā kusalā mutimanto honti ce. Na tesaṃ kocīti evaṃ sante tesaṃ ekopi hīnapañño na hoti. Kiṃkāraṇā? Diṭṭhī hi tesampi tathā samattā, yathā itaresanti.

887-8. Now there are three reply verses. These stand having countered, with the latter half, the meaning stated in the former half. Because of that 'countering' (byūha) and its being shorter than the following sutta, this sutta obtains the name 'Cūḷabyūha' (The Lesser Array). There, 'another's teaching' means another's view. 'All are fools' means: if that is so, then all these are indeed fools. Why? Because 'all of them abide in their views'—they are not purified by their own view. 'Of purified wisdom, skilled, and wise' means: if, while being defiled, not disputing, and not purified by their own view, they are indeed of purified wisdom, skilled, and wise. Alternatively, there is also the reading 'sandiṭṭhiyā ce pana vīvadātā.' Its meaning is: if they are purified by their own view, they are of purified wisdom, skilled, and wise. 'Not one of them' means: in that case, not even one of them is of inferior wisdom. Why? Because their view is also accomplished in the same way as that of the others.

889. Na vāhametanti gāthāya saṅkhepattho – yaṃ te mithu dve dve janā aññamaññaṃ “bālo”ti āhu, ahaṃ etaṃ tathiyaṃ tacchanti neva brūmi. Kiṃkāraṇā? Yasmā sabbe te sakaṃ sakaṃ diṭṭhiṃ “idameva saccaṃ moghamañña”nti akaṃsu. Tena ca kāraṇena paraṃ “bālo”ti dahanti. Ettha ca “tathiya”nti “kathiva”nti dvepi pāṭhā.

889. The gist of the verse beginning 'I do not say this' is: When two people mutually call each other 'a fool,' I do not say this is true or real. Why? Because all of them have each declared their own view as 'only this is true, the other is false.' And for that reason, they regard another as 'a fool.' Here, both 'tathiya' and 'kathiva' are variant readings.

890. Yamāhūti [V 2.0248] pucchāgāthāya yaṃ diṭṭhisaccaṃ tathiyanti eke āhu.

890. In the question verse beginning 'What they call': that truth of a view which some declare to be real.

891. Ekañhi saccanti vissajjanagāthāya ekaṃ saccaṃ nirodho maggo vā. Yasmiṃ pajā no vivade pajānanti yamhi sacce pajānanto pajā no vivadeyya. Sayaṃ thunantīti attanā vadanti.
