891. In the reply verse, 'one truth' means the one truth, which is cessation or the path. 'About which a knowing person would not dispute' means: knowing which truth, a person would not dispute. 'They praise their own' means they speak for themselves.

892. Kasmā nūti pucchāgāthāya pavādiyāseti vādino. Udāhu te takkamanussarantīti te vādino udāhu attano takkamattaṃ anugacchanti.

892. In the question verse beginning 'Why indeed': 'disputants' means debaters. 'Or do they follow their reasoning?' means: or do those debaters merely follow their own reasoning?

893. Na [M 2.0271] hevāti vissajjanagāthāya aññatra saññāya niccānīti ṭhapetvā saññāmattena niccanti gahitaggahaṇāni. Takkañca diṭṭhīsu pakappayitvāti attano micchāsaṅkappamattaṃ diṭṭhīsu janetvā. Yasmā pana diṭṭhīsu vitakkaṃ janentā diṭṭhiyopi janenti, tasmā niddese vuttaṃ “diṭṭhigatāni janenti sañjanentī”tiādi (mahāni. 121).

893. In the reply verse beginning 'Not so indeed': 'permanent apart from perception' refers to holdings grasped as permanent merely through perception, setting other things aside. 'And having fashioned reasoning in their views' means having generated merely their own wrong conception in their views. And since, in generating thought within views, they also generate views, it is therefore said in the Niddesa: 'They generate and produce entrenched views,' and so on (Mahāni. 121).

894-5. Idāni evaṃ nānāsaccesu asantesu takkamattamanussarantānaṃ diṭṭhigatikānaṃ vippaṭipattiṃ dassetuṃ “diṭṭhe sute”tiādikā gāthāyo abhāsi. Tattha diṭṭheti diṭṭhaṃ, diṭṭhasuddhinti adhippāyo. Esa nayo sutādīsu. Ete ca nissāya vimānadassīti ete diṭṭhidhamme nissayitvā suddhibhāvasaṅkhātaṃ vimānaṃ asammānaṃ passantopi. Vinicchaye ṭhatvā pahassamāno, bālo paro akkusaloti cāhāti evaṃ vimānadassīpi tasmiṃ diṭṭhivinicchaye ṭhatvā tuṭṭhijāto hāsajāto hutvā “paro hīno ca avidvā cā”ti evaṃ vadatiyeva. Evaṃ [P 2.0556] sante yenevāti gāthā. Tattha sayamattanāti sayameva attānaṃ. Vimānetīti garahati. Tadeva pāvāti tadeva vacanaṃ diṭṭhiṃ vadati, taṃ vā puggalaṃ.

894-5. Now, to show the wrong practice of those adherents of views who, when diverse truths are non-existent, merely follow their own reasoning, the verses beginning 'In the seen, the heard,' etc., were spoken. There, 'in the seen' means the seen; the intended meaning is 'purity through the seen.' This method applies to 'the heard,' etc. And 'seeing a high station' means: relying on these views, one sees a 'high station' (vimāna) accounted as a state of purity, while disrespecting others. 'Standing in judgment and exulting, he says, “The other is a fool, unskilled”' means: thus, one who sees a high station, standing in that judgment of views, becoming pleased and joyful, indeed says, 'The other is inferior and ignorant.' This being so, there is the verse beginning 'By that very thing...' There, 'by oneself' means oneself. 'He disrespects' means he disparages. 'He speaks that very thing' means he speaks that very saying, that view, or about that person.

896. Atisāradiṭṭhiyāti gāthāyattho – so evaṃ tāya lakkhaṇātisāriniyā atisāradiṭṭhiyā samatto puṇṇo uddhumāto, tena ca diṭṭhimānena matto “paripuṇṇo ahaṃ kevalī”ti evaṃ paripuṇṇamānī sayameva attānaṃ manasā “ahaṃ paṇḍito”ti abhisiñcati. Kiṃkāraṇā? Diṭṭhī hi sā tassa tathā samattāti.

896. The meaning of the verse on 'the over-reaching view' is: Thus, being complete, full, and swollen with that overbearing, over-reaching view, and intoxicated with the conceit of that view, he has the conceit of being complete, thinking, 'I am complete, whole.' He anoints himself in his own mind, thinking, 'I am wise.' Why? Because that view of his is thus complete.

897. Parassa ceti gāthāya sambandho attho ca – kiñca bhiyyo? Yo so vinicchaye ṭhatvā pahassamāno “bālo paro akkusalo”ti cāha. Tassa parassa ce hi vacasā so tena vuccamāno [V 2.0249] nihīno hoti. Tumo sahā hoti nihīnapañño, sopi teneva saha nihīnapañño hoti. Sopi hi naṃ “bālo”ti vadati. Athassa vacanaṃ appamāṇaṃ, so pana sayameva vedagū ca dhīro ca hoti. Evaṃ sante na koci bālo samaṇesu atthi. Sabbepi hi te attano icchāya paṇḍitā.

897. The connection and meaning of the verse beginning 'Parassa ce' is as follows—what more? He who, standing in judgment, laughing, says, 'The other is a fool, unskillful.' If by another's words the one so spoken of becomes base, then the speaker too becomes of diminished wisdom along with him, for he too calls him a 'fool.' Then the accuser's word is no measure, while the other is himself a sage and a wise one. This being so, no fool exists among ascetics, for they are all wise according to their own desire.

898. Aññaṃ [M 2.0272] itoti gāthāya sambandho attho ca – “atha ce sayaṃ vedagū hoti dhīro, na koci bālo samaṇesu atthī”ti evañhi vuttepi siyā kassaci “kasmā”ti. Tattha vuccate – yasmā aññaṃ ito yābhivadanti dhammaṃ aparaddhā suddhimakevalī te, evampi titthiyā puthuso vadanti, ye ito aññaṃ diṭṭhiṃ abhivadanti, ye aparaddhā viraddhā suddhimaggaṃ, akevalino ca teti evaṃ puthutitthiyā yasmā vadantīti vuttaṃ hoti. Kasmā panevaṃ vadantīti ce? Sandiṭṭhirāgena hi te bhirattā, yasmā sakena diṭṭhirāgena abhirattāti vuttaṃ hoti.

898. The connection and meaning of the verse beginning 'Aññaṃ ito' is as follows: When it is said, 'But if one is oneself a sage and a wise one, no fool exists among ascetics,' someone might ask, 'Why?' To this it is said: Because 'those who proclaim a doctrine other than this have erred from purity and are not complete'—thus do the various sectarians speak severally. This means that the many sectarians speak thus of those who proclaim a view other than this: that they have erred, have missed the path of purity, and are incomplete. And why do they speak thus? 'Because they are deeply affected by passion for their own view'; this means that they are deeply affected by passion for their own view.

899-900. Evaṃ abhirattā ca – idheva suddhinti gāthā. Tattha sakāyaneti sakamagge daḷhaṃ vadānāti daḷhavādā. Evañca daḷhavādesu tesu yo koci titthiyo sakāyane vāpi daḷhaṃ vadāno kamettha bāloti paraṃ daheyya, saṅkhepato tattha sassatucchedasaṅkhāte vitthārato vā natthikaissarakāraṇaniyatādibhede sake āyatane “idameva sacca”nti daḷhaṃ vadāno kaṃ paraṃ ettha diṭṭhigate “bālo”ti saha dhammena [P 2.0557] passeyya, nanu sabbopi tassa matena paṇḍito eva suppaṭipanno eva ca. Evaṃ sante ca sayameva so medhagamāvaheyya paraṃ vadaṃ bālamasuddhidhammaṃ, sopi paraṃ “bālo ca asuddhidhammo ca aya”nti vadanto attanāva kalahaṃ āvaheyya. Kasmā? Yasmā sabbopi tassa matena paṇḍito eva suppaṭipanno eva ca.

899-900. And thus being deeply affected—the verse is 'Here alone is purity.' Therein, 'in their own sphere' means in their own path; 'firmly asserting' means they are of firm assertion. And among those of firm assertion, whatever sectarian, firmly asserting in his own sphere, whom could he here regard as a fool? In his own sphere—whether in brief, designated as eternalism and annihilationism, or in detail, divided into nihilism, a first cause, determinism, and so on—firmly declaring 'This alone is true,' whom else in this matter of views could he rightly see as a 'fool' along with his doctrine? Surely, according to his opinion, everyone is wise and well-practiced. This being so, he himself would bring on a quarrel by calling another a fool and of impure doctrine. By calling another 'this one is a fool and of impure doctrine,' he would bring conflict upon himself. Why? Because according to his opinion, everyone is indeed wise and well-practiced.

901. Evaṃ sabbathāpi vinicchaye ṭhatvā sayaṃ pamāya uddhaṃsa lokasmiṃ vivādameti, diṭṭhiyaṃ ṭhatvā sayañca satthārādīni minitvā so bhiyyo vivādametīti. Evaṃ pana vinicchayesu ādīnavaṃ ñatvā ariyamaggena hitvāna sabbāni vinicchayāni na medhagaṃ kubbati jantu loketi arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi. Desanāpariyosāne purābhedasutte vuttasadiso evābhisamayo ahosīti.

901. Thus, in every way, standing in judgment and measuring oneself with conceit, one enters into disputes in the world. Standing by one's own views and measuring oneself against teachers and others, one engages in disputes all the more. But having known the danger in such judgments, and having abandoned all judgments by the noble path, a being does not create quarrels in the world. Thus he concluded the teaching with the summit of Arahantship. At the end of the discourse, a realization occurred just as was described in the Purābheda Sutta.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

From the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya.

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya cūḷabyūhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Here ends the explanation of the Cūḷabyūha Sutta in the Commentary on the Suttanipāta.

13. Mahābyūhasuttavaṇṇanā

13. Commentary on the Mahābyūha Sutta

902. Ye [V 2.0250][M 2.0273] kecimeti mahābyūhasuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Idampi tasmiṃyeva mahāsamaye “kiṃ nu kho ime diṭṭhiparibbasānā viññūnaṃ santikā nindameva labhanti, udāhu pasaṃsampī”ti uppannacittānaṃ ekaccānaṃ devatānaṃ tamatthaṃ āvikātuṃ purimanayena nimmitabuddhena attānaṃ pucchāpetvā vuttaṃ. Tattha anvānayantīti anu ānayanti, punappunaṃ āharanti.

902. The Mahābyūha Sutta begins with 'Ye kecime'. What is its origin? This too was spoken during that great assembly to clarify the matter for certain deities in whose minds the thought arose: 'Do these who are obsessed with views receive only blame from the wise, or do they also receive praise?' Following the previous method, the Buddha had a created Buddha ask him the question, and then he spoke. Therein, 'anvānayanti' means 'anu ānayanti', they bring forth repeatedly, they bring it again and again.

903. Idāni yasmā te “idameva sacca”nti vadantā diṭṭhigatikā vādino kadāci katthaci pasaṃsampi labhanti, yaṃ etaṃ pasaṃsāsaṅkhātaṃ vādaphalaṃ, taṃ appaṃ rāgādīnaṃ samāya samatthaṃ na hoti, ko pana vādo dutiye nindāphale, tasmā etamatthaṃ dassento imaṃ tāva vissajjanagāthamāha. “Appañhi etaṃ na alaṃ samāya, duve vivādassa phalāni brūmī”tiādi. Tattha duve vivādassa phalānīti nindā pasaṃsā ca, jayaparājayādīni vā taṃsabhāgāni. Etampi disvāti “nindā aniṭṭhā eva, pasaṃsā nālaṃ samāyā”ti etampi vivādaphale ādīnavaṃ disvā. Khemābhipassaṃ avivādabhūminti avivādabhūmiṃ [P 2.0558] nibbānaṃ “khema”nti passamāno.

903. Now, since those debaters adhering to views, who declare, 'This alone is the truth,' sometimes and in some places receive praise—that result of debate called praise is small and not sufficient for the calming of lust and so on, so what to say of the second result, blame? Therefore, to show this meaning, he first speaks this reply verse: 'For this is little, not enough for calm; I declare the two fruits of dispute,' and so on. Herein, 'the two fruits of dispute' are blame and praise, or victory and defeat and the like, which share the same nature. The phrase 'Seeing this too' means seeing this drawback in the fruits of dispute: 'Blame is undesirable, and praise is insufficient for calm.' The phrase 'Seeing the ground of non-dispute as safety' means seeing Nibbāna, the ground of non-dispute, as 'safety.'

904. Evañhi avivadamāno – yā kācimāti gāthā. Tattha sammutiyoti diṭṭhiyo. Puthujjāti puthujjanasambhavā. So upayaṃ kimeyyāti so upagantabbaṭṭhena upayaṃ rūpādīsu ekampi dhammaṃ kiṃ upeyya, kena vā kāraṇena upeyya. Diṭṭhe sute khantimakubbamānoti diṭṭhasutasuddhīsu pemaṃ akaronto.

904. Thus, not engaging in disputes—the verse is 'Yā kācimā'. Herein, 'conventions' means views. 'Common' means arising from ordinary people. 'Why should he resort to a basis?' means: why, or for what reason, should he approach even one thing among form and so on, in the sense that it is to be resorted to? 'Not forming a preference for what is seen or heard' means not cherishing purifications based on what is seen or heard.

905. Ito bāhirā pana – sīluttamāti gāthā. Tassattho – sīlaṃyeva “uttama”nti maññamānā sīluttamā eke bhonto saṃyamamattena suddhiṃ vadanti, hatthivatādiñca vataṃ samādāya upaṭṭhitā, idheva diṭṭhiyaṃ assa satthuno suddhinti bhavūpanītā bhavajjhositā samānā vadanti, apica te kusalā vadānā “kusalā maya”nti evaṃ vādā.

905. But those outside of this—the verse is 'Sīluttamā'. Its meaning is: Some honorable ones, considering virtue itself to be supreme, are 'supreme in virtue'; they declare purity by mere restraint. Having undertaken and being established in vows such as the elephant-vow, and being led to existence and attached to existence, they say, 'Here alone, in the view of this teacher, is purity.' Moreover, they, claiming to be skilled, hold the view, 'We are skilled.'

906. Evaṃ [M 2.0274] sīluttamesu ca tesu tathā paṭipanno yo koci – sace cutoti gāthā. Tassattho – sace tato sīlavatato paravicchandanena vā anabhisambhuṇanto vā cuto hoti, so taṃ [V 2.0251] sīlabbatādikammaṃ puññābhisaṅkhārādikammaṃ vā virādhayitvā pavedhatī. Na kevalañca vedhati, apica kho taṃ sīlabbatasuddhiṃ pajappatī ca vippalapati patthayatī ca. Kimiva? Satthāva hīno pavasaṃ gharamhā. Gharamhā pavasanto satthato hīno yathā taṃ gharaṃ vā satthaṃ vā pattheyyāti.

906. Thus, among those who hold virtue as supreme, whoever practices accordingly—as the verse says, 'If one deviates.' Its meaning is: If one who is virtuous deviates, whether by disparaging another or by failing to succeed, one trembles, having failed in that action of virtue and vows or that action of meritorious formation. And not only does one tremble, but one also yearns for, laments, and longs for that purity of virtue and vows. Like what? Like a merchant separated from his caravan while away from home. Just as one living away from home, separated from his caravan, would long for that home or that caravan.

907. Evaṃ pana sīluttamānaṃ vedhakāraṇaṃ ariyasāvako – sīlabbataṃ vāpi pahāya sabbanti gāthā. Tattha sāvajjanavajjanti sabbākusalaṃ lokiyakusalañca. Etaṃ suddhiṃ asuddhinti apatthayānoti pañcakāmaguṇādibhedaṃ etaṃ suddhiṃ, akusalādibhedaṃ asuddhiñca apatthayamāno. Virato careti suddhiyā asuddhiyā ca virato careyya. Santimanuggahāyāti diṭṭhiṃ agahetvā.

907. But a noble disciple understands thus the cause of agitation for those who regard virtue as supreme—as the verse says, 'Having abandoned all rites and vows.' Herein, 'the blameworthy and the blameless' refers to all unwholesome and worldly wholesome actions. 'Not desiring this purity or impurity' means not desiring this purity—differentiated as the five strands of sensual pleasure, and so on—or this impurity—differentiated as unwholesome states, and so on. 'Let him wander detached' means he should wander detached from both purity and impurity. 'For the attainment of peace' means without grasping any view.

908. Evaṃ ito bāhirake sīluttame saṃyamena visuddhivāde tesaṃ vighātaṃ sīlabbatappahāyino arahato ca paṭipattiṃ dassetvā idāni aññathāpi suddhivāde bāhirake dassento “tamūpanissāyā”ti gāthamāha. Tassattho – santaññepi samaṇabrāhmaṇā, te jigucchitaṃ amarantapaṃ vā diṭṭhasuddhiādīsu vā aññataraññataraṃ upanissāya akiriyadiṭṭhiyā vā uddhaṃsarā hutvā bhavābhavesu avītataṇhāse [P 2.0559] suddhimanutthunanti vadanti kathentīti.

908. Thus, having shown the frustration for those outsiders who advocate purity through supreme virtue and restraint, and having shown the practice of the Arahant who has abandoned rites and vows, now, in order to show other outsiders who advocate purity in another way, the verse 'Relying on that' is spoken. Its meaning is: There are some ascetics and brahmins who, though they may be peaceful, rely on some repulsive practice, or deathless austerity, or purity by view, and so on. Or, having become arrogant with the view of non-action, and with craving for existence and non-existence not yet gone, they extol, declare, and proclaim purity.

909. Evaṃ tesaṃ avītataṇhānaṃ suddhiṃ anutthunantānaṃ yopi suddhippattameva attānaṃ maññeyya, tassapi avītataṇhattā bhavābhavesu taṃ taṃ vatthuṃ patthayamānassa hi jappitāni punappunaṃ hontiyevāti adhippāyo. Taṇhā hi āsevitā taṇhaṃ vaḍḍhayateva. Na kevalañca jappitāni, pavedhitaṃ vāpi pakappitesu, taṇhādiṭṭhīhi cassa pakappitesu vatthūsu pavedhitampi hotīti vuttaṃ hoti. Bhavābhavesu pana vītataṇhattā āyatiṃ cutūpapāto idha yassa natthi, sakena vedheyya kuhiṃva jappeti ayametissā gāthāya sambandho. Sesaṃ niddese vuttanayameva.

909. Thus, among those who extol purity while their craving is not gone, even if one were to consider oneself as having attained purity, because craving is not eradicated, one would still yearn for various objects in different realms of existence. Indeed, mutterings would arise repeatedly. For craving, when indulged, only increases craving. And not only mutterings, but agitation concerning mentally constructed things also arises. It is said that, due to craving and views, agitation also arises for him concerning those mentally constructed objects. However, for one free from craving for future existences, for whom there is no future death and rebirth here, by what should he tremble, or where would he mutter? This is the connection of this verse. The rest follows the method explained in the exposition.

910-11. Yamāhūti [M 2.0275] pucchāgāthā. Idāni yasmā ekopi ettha vādo sacco natthi, kevalaṃ diṭṭhimattakena hi te vadanti, tasmā tamatthaṃ dassento “sakañhī”ti imaṃ tāva vissajjanagāthamāha. Tattha sammutinti diṭṭhiṃ.

910-11. The question verse is 'What they say.' Now, since not even one of these doctrines is true—for they speak merely based on their own views—therefore, to explain that meaning, the reply verse 'For one's own' is first given. Herein, 'convention' means view.

912. Evametesu sakaṃ dhammaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ bruvantesu aññassa pana dhammaṃ “hīna”nti vadantesu yassa kassaci – parassa ce vambhayitena hīnoti gāthā. Tassattho – yadi parassa ninditakāraṇā hīno bhaveyya, na koci dhammesu visesi aggo bhaveyya. Kiṃ kāraṇaṃ? Puthū hi [V 2.0252] aññassa vadanti dhammaṃ, nihīnato sabbeva te samhi daḷhaṃ vadānā sakadhamme daḷhavādā eva.

912. Thus, while they declare their own doctrine to be complete and disparage the doctrine of another as 'inferior'—as the verse says, 'If by another's disparagement one becomes inferior.' Its meaning is: If one's doctrine were to become inferior because of another's censure, then no doctrine would be supreme or excellent. Why? Because many speak of the doctrine of another as inferior, yet all are firm in asserting their own, being staunch advocates of their own doctrine.

913. Kiñca bhiyyo – saddhammapūjāti gāthā. Tassattho – te ca titthiyā yathā pasaṃsanti sakāyanāni, saddhammapūjāpi nesaṃ tatheva vattati. Te hi ativiya satthārādīni sakkaronti. Tattha yadi te pamāṇā siyuṃ, evaṃ sante sabbeva vādā tathiyā bhaveyyuṃ. Kiṃ kāraṇaṃ? Suddhī hi nesaṃ paccattameva, na sā aññatra sijjhati, nāpi paramatthato. Attani diṭṭhigāhamattameva hi taṃ tesaṃ parapaccayaneyyabuddhīnaṃ.

913. Furthermore—the verse 'The honoring of one's own doctrine.' Its meaning is: Just as those sectarians praise their own systems, so too does their honoring of their own doctrine proceed. For they excessively honor their own teachers and so forth. If they were the standard, then all doctrines would be true. Why? For them, purification is purely personal; it is not accomplished otherwise, nor is it ultimately real. For those whose understanding is to be led by others, it is merely the grasping of a view within themselves.

914. Yo vā pana viparīto bāhitapāpattā brāhmaṇo, tassa – na brāhmaṇassa paraneyyamatthīti gāthā. Tassattho – brāhmaṇassa [P 2.0560] hi “sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā”tiādinā (dha. pa. 277; netti. 5) nayena sudiṭṭhattā parena netabbaṃ ñāṇaṃ natthi, diṭṭhidhammesu “idameva sacca”nti nicchinitvā samuggahītampi natthi. Taṃkāraṇā so diṭṭhikalahāni atīto, na ca so seṭṭhato passati dhammamaññaṃ aññatra satipaṭṭhānādīhi.

914. But for one who is the opposite—a brahmin because evil has been expelled—for him, the verse states: 'For a brahmin, there is nothing to be led by another.' Its meaning is: For a brahmin, because he has clearly seen according to the principle 'all conditioned phenomena are impermanent,' and so on, there is no knowledge to be led by another; nor, among doctrines, is there anything grasped after having decided, 'This alone is true.' For that reason, he has transcended disputes about views, and he does not see any other teaching as superior, apart from the foundations of mindfulness and so on.

915. Jānāmīti gāthāya sambandho attho ca – evaṃ tāva paramatthabrāhmaṇo na hi seṭṭhato passati dhammamaññaṃ, aññe pana titthiyā paracittañāṇādīhi jānantā passantāpi “jānāmi passāmi tatheva eta”nti evaṃ vadantāpi ca diṭṭhiyā suddhiṃ paccenti. Kasmā? Yasmā tesu ekopi addakkhi ce addasa cepi tena paracittañāṇādinā yathābhūtaṃ atthaṃ, kiñhi tumassa tena tassa tena dassanena kiṃ kataṃ, kiṃ dukkhapariññā sādhitā, udāhu samudayapahānādīnaṃ [M 2.0276] aññataraṃ, yato sabbathāpi atikkamitvā ariyamaggaṃ te titthiyā aññeneva vadanti suddhiṃ, atikkamitvā vā te titthiye buddhādayo aññeneva vadanti suddhinti.

915. The connection and meaning of the verse 'I know' is as follows: Thus, the brahmin in the ultimate sense does not regard any other teaching as superior. But other sectarians, though knowing and seeing by means of knowledge of others' minds and so on, and claiming, 'I know, I see, it is just so,' still presume purification by their views. Why? Because even if one among them has seen or were to see the true nature of things through that knowledge of others' minds, what then has been accomplished for him by that seeing? Has the full understanding of suffering been achieved, or the abandonment of its origin, or any other such thing? Since, having entirely bypassed the Noble Path, those sectarians declare purification in another way; or, having surpassed those sectarians, the Buddhas and others declare purification in another way.

916. Passaṃ naroti gāthāya sambandho attho ca. Kiñca bhiyyo? Yvāyaṃ paracittañāṇādīhi addakkhi, so passaṃ naro dakkhati nāmarūpaṃ, na tato paraṃ disvāna vā ñassati tānimeva nāmarūpāni niccato sukhato vā na aññathā. So evaṃ passanto kāmaṃ bahuṃ passatu appakaṃ vā nāmarūpaṃ niccato sukhato ca, athassa evarūpena dassanena na hi tena suddhiṃ kusalā vadantīti.

916. The connection and meaning of the verse 'Passaṃ naro' is as follows. What more? Whoever sees by means of knowledge of others' minds and so forth, that seeing person sees name-and-form. Having seen that, he will not know anything beyond it, and he will know those very name-and-form as permanent or pleasant, and not otherwise. Though seeing thus, whether he sees much or little of name-and-form as permanent and pleasant, the wise do not declare purification by such seeing.

917. Nivissavādīti gāthāya sambandho attho ca – tena ca dassanena suddhiyā asatiyāpi [V 2.0253] yo “jānāmi passāmi tatheva eta”nti evaṃ nivissavādī, etaṃ vā dassanaṃ paṭicca diṭṭhiyā suddhiṃ paccento “idameva sacca”nti evaṃ nivissavādī, so subbinayo na hoti taṃ tathā pakappitaṃ abhisaṅkhataṃ diṭṭhiṃ purekkharāno. So hi yaṃ satthārādiṃ nissito, tattheva subhaṃ vadāno suddhiṃ vado, “parisuddhavādo [P 2.0561] parisuddhadassano vā aha”nti attānaṃ maññamāno tattha tathaddasā so, tattha sakāya diṭṭhiyā aviparītameva so addasa. Yathā sā diṭṭhi pavattati, tatheva naṃ addasa, na aññathā passituṃ icchatīti adhippāyo.

917. The connection and meaning of the verse 'Nivissavādī' is as follows: Even though there is no purity through such a view, one who dogmatically asserts, 'I know, I see, it is just so,' or who, relying on that view and expecting purity by means of that view, declares, 'This alone is true'—such a one is not well-disciplined, holding that fabricated and constructed view foremost. For, relying on a teacher or the like, speaking of the good and declaring purity there, and thinking, 'I am one of pure speech, of pure vision,' he sees it as such therein. There, according to his own view, he sees it indeed without distortion. As that view proceeds, so he sees it, not wishing to see it otherwise—this is the meaning.

918. Evaṃ pakappitaṃ diṭṭhiṃ purekkharānesu titthiyesu – na brāhmaṇo kappamupeti saṅkhāti gāthā. Tattha saṅkhāti saṅkhāya, jānitvāti attho. Napi ñāṇabandhūti samāpattiñāṇādinā akatataṇhādiṭṭhibandhu. Tattha viggaho – nāpi assa ñāṇena kato bandhu atthīti napi ñāṇabandhu. Sammutiyoti diṭṭhisammutiyo. Puthujjāti puthujjanasambhavā. Uggahaṇanti maññeti uggahaṇanti aññe, aññe tā sammutiyo uggaṇhantīti vuttaṃ hoti.

918. Thus, regarding the sectarians who hold their fabricated views foremost—the verse 'The Brahmin does not enter into reckoning' is stated. Here, 'saṅkhāti' means 'by reckoning, having known.' 'Napi ñāṇabandhu' means he is not one for whom a bond is made by knowledge, that is, one for whom the bond of craving and views is not made by means of knowledge of meditative attainments and so forth. The analysis here is: 'Nor is there for him a bond made by knowledge,' thus 'napi ñāṇabandhu.' 'Sammutiyo' refers to the conventions of views. 'Puthujjāti' means arising from ordinary people. Regarding 'Uggahaṇanti': some say it means 'conceiving'; it means that others grasp those conventions.

919. Kiñca bhiyyo – vissajja ganthānīti gāthā. Tattha anuggahoti uggahaṇavirahito, sopi nāssa uggahoti anuggaho, na vā uggaṇhātīti anuggaho.

919. What more? – The verse is 'Vissajja ganthāni.' Here, 'anuggaho' means one who is devoid of grasping; he is 'anuggaho' because there is no grasping for him, or because he does not grasp.

920. Kiñca [M 2.0277] bhiyyo – so evarūpo – pubbāsaveti gāthā. Tattha pubbāsaveti atītarūpādīni ārabbha uppajjamānadhamme kilese. Naveti paccuppannarūpādīni ārabbha uppajjamānadhamme. Na chandagūti chandādivasena na gacchati. Anattagarahīti katākatavasena attānaṃ agarahanto.

920. What more? – Such a one – the verse is 'Pubbāsave.' Here, 'pubbāsave' refers to the defilements that are arising in relation to past forms, etc. 'Nave' refers to those arising in relation to present forms, etc. 'Na chandagū' means one does not proceed by way of desire, etc. 'Anattagarahī' means not blaming oneself in terms of what has been done and not done.

921. Evaṃ anattagarahī ca – sa sabbadhammesūti gāthā. Tattha sabbadhammesūti dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhidhammesu “yaṃ kiñci diṭṭhaṃ vā”ti evaṃpabhedesu. Pannabhāroti patitabhāro. Na kappetīti na kappiyo, duvidhampi kappaṃ na karotīti attho. Nūparatoti puthujjanakalyāṇakasekkhā viya uparatisamaṅgīpi na hoti. Na patthiyoti nittaṇho. Taṇhā hi patthiyatīti patthiyā, nāssa patthiyāti na patthiyoti. Sesaṃ tattha tattha pākaṭamevāti na vuttaṃ. Evaṃ arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi, desanāpariyosāne purābhedasutte vuttasadiso evābhisamayo ahosīti.

921. Thus, one who is not self-blaming – the verse is 'Sa sabbadhammesu.' Here, 'sabbadhammesu' refers to the sixty-two kinds of views, such as 'whatever is seen,' and so on. 'Pannabhāro' means one whose burden has been laid down. 'Na kappeti' means he is not one who conceptualizes; the meaning is that he does not engage in either of the two kinds of conceptualization. 'Nūparato' means he is not possessed of cessation like an ordinary person, a virtuous worldling, or a trainee. 'Na patthiyo' means without craving. For craving is called 'patthiyā' because it is longed for; he has no longing, thus he is 'na patthiyo.' The rest is obvious in each case, so it is not stated. Thus, he concluded the teaching with arahantship as its pinnacle. At the end of the teaching, a realization arose just like the one described in the Purābheda Sutta.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya mahābyūhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Mahābyūha Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary is concluded.

14. Tuvaṭakasuttavaṇṇanā

14. The Explanation of the Tuvaṭaka Sutta

922. Pucchāmi [V 2.0254][P 2.0562] tanti tuvaṭakasuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Idampi tasmiṃyeva mahāsamaye “kā nu kho arahattappattiyā paṭipattī”ti uppannacittānaṃ ekaccānaṃ devatānaṃ tamatthaṃ pakāsetuṃ purimanayeneva nimmitabuddhena attānaṃ pucchāpetvā vuttaṃ.

922. The Tuvaṭaka Sutta begins, 'Pucchāmi taṃ.' What is its origin? This too was spoken on that same great occasion to clarify the matter for certain deities in whose minds the thought had arisen, 'What indeed is the practice for the attainment of arahantship?' As before, a mind-created Buddha had himself questioned and then spoke.

Tattha ādigāthāya tāva pucchāmīti ettha adiṭṭhajotanādivasena pucchā vibhajitā. Ādiccabandhunti ādiccassa gottabandhuṃ. Vivekaṃ santipadañcāti vivekañca santipadañca. Kathaṃ disvāti kena kāraṇena disvā, kathaṃ pavattadassano hutvāti vuttaṃ hoti.

Therein, in the first verse, the question 'Pucchāmi' is analyzed by way of illuminating what is unseen, and so on. 'Ādiccabandhu' means a kinsman of the sun by clan. 'Vivekaṃ santipadañca' means seclusion and the state of peace. 'Kathaṃ disvā' means 'having seen for what reason'; that is to say, 'having become one who sees in what way it occurs.'

923. Atha bhagavā yasmā yathā passanto kilese uparundhati, tathā pavattadassano hutvā parinibbāti, tasmā tamatthaṃ āvikaronto nānappakārena [M 2.0278] taṃ devaparisaṃ kilesappahāne niyojento “mūlaṃ papañcasaṅkhāyā”ti ārabhitvā pañca gāthā abhāsi.

923. Then the Blessed One, because one attains final Nibbāna by seeing in what way one obstructs the defilements and by becoming one who sees how it occurs, therefore, making that meaning clear and exhorting that assembly of deities in various ways to abandon the defilements, began with 'Mūlaṃ papañcasaṅkhāya' and spoke five verses.

Tattha ādigāthāya tāva saṅkhepattho – papañcāti saṅkhātattā papañcā eva papañcasaṅkhā. Tassā avijjādayo kilesā mūlaṃ, taṃ papañcasaṅkhāya mūlaṃ asmīti pavattamānañca sabbaṃ mantāya uparundhe. Yā kāci ajjhattaṃ taṇhā upajjeyyuṃ, tāsaṃ vinayā sadā sato sikkhe upaṭṭhitassati hutvā sikkheyyāti.

Here, the summary meaning of the first verse is as follows: Because they are reckoned as 'papañca' (proliferation), they are 'papañcasaṅkhā.' The root of this is the defilements, beginning with ignorance. One should, by means of wisdom, obstruct that root of conceptual proliferation and all that proceeds as 'I am.' Whatever internal cravings might arise, for their removal one should always train mindfully, one should train having established mindfulness.

924. Evaṃ tāva paṭhamagāthāya eva tisikkhāyuttaṃ desanaṃ arahattanikūṭena desetvā puna mānappahānavasena desetuṃ “yaṃ kiñcī”ti gāthamāha. Tattha yaṃ kiñci dhammamabhijaññā ajjhattanti yaṃ kiñci uccākulīnatādikaṃ attano guṇaṃ jāneyya atha vāpi bahiddhāti atha vā bahiddhāpi ācariyupajjhāyānaṃ vā guṇaṃ jāneyya. Na tena thāmaṃ kubbethāti tena guṇena thāmaṃ na kareyya.

924. Thus, having first taught through the initial verse the teaching connected to the three trainings with arahantship as its pinnacle, he spoke the verse beginning 'Yaṃ kiñci' in order to teach further by way of the abandonment of conceit. Therein, 'whatever state one might know internally' means whatever quality of one's own one might know, such as high birth, and 'or externally' means or if one might know an external quality, such as that of one's teachers and preceptors. 'One should not become steadfast on account of that' means one should not become proud on account of that quality.

925. Idānissa akaraṇavidhiṃ dassento “seyyo na tenā”ti gāthamāha. Tassattho – tena ca mānena “seyyoha”nti [P 2.0563] vā “nīcoha”nti vā “sarikkhoha”nti vāpi na maññeyya, tehi [V 2.0255] ca uccākulīnatādīhi guṇehi phuṭṭho anekarūpehi “ahaṃ uccākulā pabbajito”tiādinā nayena attānaṃ vikappento na tiṭṭheyya.

925. Now, to explain the method of non-doing, the verse 'Seyyo na tena' is stated. Its meaning is: one should not conceive oneself as 'I am better,' or 'I am inferior,' or even 'I am equal' because of that conceit. Nor should one remain conceptualizing oneself in various ways—such as 'I am of high birth who has gone forth'—being affected by those qualities like high birth and so on.

926. Evaṃ mānappahānavasenapi desetvā idāni sabbakilesūpasamavasenapi desetuṃ “ajjhattamevā”ti gāthamāha. Tattha ajjhattamevupasameti attani eva rāgādisabbakilese upasameyya. Na aññato bhikkhu santimeseyyāti ṭhapetvā ca satipaṭṭhānādīni aññena upāyena santiṃ na pariyeseyya. Kuto nirattā vāti nirattā kuto eva.

926. Having thus taught regarding the abandonment of conceit, now, in order to teach also regarding the subsiding of all defilements, he speaks the verse, 'Ajjhattameva.' Therein, 'Ajjhattameva upasame' means one should pacify all defilements such as lust within oneself. A bhikkhu should not seek serenity from another source, nor should he seek peace by any other means apart from the foundations of mindfulness and so on. As for 'kuto nirattā vā,' it means: from where indeed could there be a non-self?

927. Idāni ajjhattaṃ upasantassa khīṇāsavassa tādibhāvaṃ dassento “majjhe yathā”ti gāthamāha. Tassattho – yathā mahāsamuddassa uparimaheṭṭhimabhāgānaṃ vemajjhasaṅkhāte catuyojanasahassappamāṇe majjhe pabbatantare ṭhitassa vā majjhe samuddassa ūmi na jāyati, ṭhitova so hoti [M 2.0279] avikampamāno, evaṃ anejo khīṇāsavo lābhādīsu ṭhito assa avikampamāno, so tādiso rāgādiussadaṃ bhikkhu na kareyya kuhiñcīti.

927. Now, to describe the state of one who has pacified internally, whose taints are destroyed, showing his suchness, the verse 'Majjhe yathā' is spoken. Its meaning is: just as in the middle of the great ocean, in the intermediate space called the middle, measuring four thousand leagues between the upper and lower regions, or in the middle of the ocean standing between mountains, no wave arises, but it remains still, unwavering; even so, the passionless one, whose taints are destroyed, should remain steadfast and unwavering amid gains and the like. Such a monk would not create any rising up of lust and the like anywhere.

928. Idāni etaṃ arahattanikūṭena desitaṃ dhammadesanaṃ abbhanumodanto tassa ca arahattassa ādipaṭipadaṃ pucchanto nimmitabuddho “akittayī”ti gāthamāha. Tattha akittayīti ācikkhi. Vivaṭacakkhūti vivaṭehi anāvaraṇehi pañcahi cakkhūhi samannāgato. Sakkhidhammanti sayaṃ abhiññātaṃ attapaccakkhaṃ dhammaṃ. Parissayavinayanti parissayavinayanaṃ. Paṭipadaṃ vadehīti idāni paṭipattiṃ vadehi. Bhaddanteti “bhaddaṃ tava atthū”ti bhagavantaṃ ālapanto āha. Atha vā bhaddaṃ sundaraṃ tava paṭipadaṃ vadehīti vuttaṃ hoti. Pātimokkhaṃ atha vāpi samādhinti tameva paṭipadaṃ bhinditvā pucchati. Paṭipadanti etena vā maggaṃ pucchati. Itarehi sīlaṃ samādhiñca pucchati.

928. Now, the created Buddha, rejoicing in this Dhamma teaching delivered with arahantship as its pinnacle and inquiring about the initial practice leading to that arahantship, spoke the verse 'Akittayī.' Herein, 'Akittayī' means he declared. 'Vivaṭacakkhū' means endowed with the five unobstructed eyes. 'Sakkhidhamma' refers to the Dhamma known by oneself, directly experienced by oneself. 'Parissayavinayana' means the removal of obstacles. 'Paṭipadaṃ vadehi' means 'now speak of the practice.' 'Bhaddante' means addressing the Blessed One with 'May it be well with you,' he said. Alternatively, it is said, 'Speak of your beautiful practice.' 'Pātimokkhaṃ atha vāpi samādhiṃ' means he asks, breaking down that very practice. With 'Paṭipadaṃ' he asks about the path. With the others, he asks about virtue and concentration.

929-30. Athassa bhagavā yasmā indriyasaṃvaro sīlassa rakkhā[P 2.0564], yasmā vā iminā anukkamena desiyamānā ayaṃ desanā tāsaṃ devatānaṃ sappāyā, tasmā indriyasaṃvarato pabhuti paṭipadaṃ dassento “cakkhūhī”tiādimāraddho. Tattha cakkhūhi neva lolassāti adiṭṭhadakkhitabbādivasena cakkhūhi lolo nevassa. Gāmakathāya āvaraye sotanti tiracchānakathāto sotaṃ āvareyya. Phassenāti rogaphassena. Bhavañca nābhijappeyyāti tassa phassassa vinodanatthāya kāmabhavādibhavañca na pattheyya. Bheravesu ca na sampavedheyyāti tassa phassassa paccayabhūtesu sīhabyagghādīsu bheravesu ca na sampavedheyya, avasesesu vā ghānindriyamanindriyavisayesu [V 2.0256] nappavedheyya. Evaṃ paripūro indriyasaṃvaro vutto hoti. Purimehi vā indriyasaṃvaraṃ dassetvā iminā “araññe vasatā bheravaṃ disvā vā sutvā vā na vedhitabba”nti dasseti.

929-30. Then the Blessed One, because restraint of the senses is the protection of virtue, and because this teaching, being delivered step by step, is beneficial to those deities, therefore, beginning with 'Cakkhūhi,' he explains the practice starting from restraint of the senses. Herein, 'Cakkhūhi neva lolassa' means he should not be greedy with the eyes in terms of what is not seen, what should be seen, etc. 'Gāmakathāya āvaraye sota' means one should restrain the ear from low talk. 'Phassena' refers to the contact of disease. 'Bhavañca nābhijappeyya' means one should not long for existence, such as sensual existence, etc., in order to eliminate that contact. 'Bheravesu ca na sampavedheyya' means one should not be agitated by terrifying things, such as lions and tigers, which are conditions for that contact, nor be agitated regarding the remaining objects of the nose, tongue, body, and mind faculties. Thus, complete restraint of the senses is described. Alternatively, having shown restraint of the senses with the earlier terms, here it is shown that 'one dwelling in the forest should not be frightened upon seeing or hearing terrifying things.'

931. Laddhā na sannidhiṃ kayirāti etesaṃ annādīnaṃ yaṃkiñci dhammena labhitvā “araññe ca senāsane vasatā sadā dullabha”nti cintetvā sannidhiṃ na kareyya.

931. 'Laddhā na sannidhiṃ kayirā' means that having rightfully obtained any food and so on, one should not hoard it, thinking, 'For one dwelling in the forest and in lodgings, it is always difficult to obtain.'

932. Jhāyī [M 2.0280] na pādalolassāti jhānābhirato ca na pādalolo assa. Virame kukkuccā nappamajjeyyāti hatthakukkuccādikukkuccaṃ vinodeyya. Sakkaccakāritāya cettha nappamajjeyya.

932. "Jhāyī na pādalolassa" means one devoted to jhāna should not be restless with his feet. "Virame kukkuccā nappamajjeyya" means one should dispel misbehavior, such as misbehavior with the hands, and should not be negligent in acting carefully in this regard.

933. Tandiṃ māyaṃ hassaṃ khiḍḍanti ālasiyañca māyañca hassañca kāyikacetasikakhiḍḍañca. Savibhūsanti saddhiṃ vibhūsāya.

933. "Tandiṃ māyaṃ hassaṃ khiḍḍaṃ" means sloth, deception, laughter, and physical and mental play. "Savibhūsanti" means together with adornment.

934-7. Āthabbaṇanti āthabbaṇikamantappayogaṃ. Supinanti supinasatthaṃ. Lakkhaṇanti maṇilakkhaṇādiṃ. No vidaheti nappayojeyya. Virutanti migādīnaṃ vassitaṃ. Pesuṇiyanti pesuññaṃ. Kayavikkayeti pañcahi sahadhammikehi saddhiṃ vañcanāvasena vā udayapatthanāvasena vā na tiṭṭheyya. Upavādaṃ bhikkhu na kareyyāti upavādakare kilese anibbattento attani parehi samaṇabrāhmaṇehi upavādaṃ na janeyya. Gāme ca nābhisajjeyyāti gāme ca gihisaṃsaggādīhi nābhisajjeyya. Lābhakamyā janaṃ na lapayeyyāti lābhakāmatāya janaṃ nālapayeyya. Payuttanti cīvarādīhi sampayuttaṃ[P 2.0565], tadatthaṃ vā payojitaṃ.

934-7. "Āthabbaṇa" refers to the application of Atharva Veda spells. "Supina" means dream lore. "Lakkhaṇa" refers to the characteristics of jewels, etc. "No vidaheti" means one should not apply it. "Viruta" refers to the cries of animals such as deer. "Pesuṇiya" means tale-bearing. "Kayavikkaya" means one should not engage in buying and selling with the five lawful co-religionists, either deceitfully or out of desire for profit. "A bhikkhu should not make accusations" means that by not producing the defilements that cause accusation, he should not give rise to accusation against himself from other ascetics and brahmins. "And he should not be attached to the village" means he should not be attached to the village through association with householders, etc. "Desiring gain, he should not cajole people" means he should not cajole people out of desire for gain. "Payutta" refers to what is connected with robes, etc., or applied for that purpose.

938-9. Mosavajje na nīyethāti musāvāde na nīyetha. Jīvitenāti jīvikāya. Sutvā rusito bahuṃ vācaṃ, samaṇānaṃ vā puthujanānanti rusito ghaṭṭito parehi tesa samaṇānaṃ vā khattiyādibhedānaṃ vā aññesaṃ puthujanānaṃ bahumpi aniṭṭhavācaṃ sutvā. Na paṭivajjāti na paṭivadeyya. Kiṃ kāraṇaṃ? Na hi santo paṭisenikaronti.

938-9. "Mosavajje na nīyetha" means one should not be drawn into lying. "Jīvitena" means by livelihood. "Sutvā rusito bahuṃ vācaṃ, samaṇānaṃ vā puthujanānaṃ" means being provoked or offended by others, having heard much unpleasant speech from ascetics, nobles, or other ordinary people. "Na paṭivajjā" means one should not retaliate. Why is that? Because the peaceful do not engage in counterattacks.

940. Etañca dhammamaññāyāti sabbametaṃ yathāvuttaṃ dhammaṃ ñatvā. Vicinanti vicinanto. Santīti nibbutiṃ ñatvāti nibbutiṃ rāgādīnaṃ santīti ñatvā.

940. "Etañca dhammaṃ aññāya" means knowing all this Dhamma as explained. "Vicinaṃ" means reflecting. "Santīti nibbutiṃ ñatvā" means knowing Nibbāna as the peace from lust and so on.

941. Kiṃkāraṇā [V 2.0257] nappamajjeiti ce – abhibhū hi soti gāthā. Tattha abhibhūti rūpādīnaṃ abhibhavitā. Anabhibhūtoti tehi anabhibhūto. Sakkhidhammamanītihamadassīti paccakkhameva anītihaṃ dhammamaddakkhi. Sadā namassamanusikkheti sadā namassanto tisso sikkhāyo sikkheyya. Sesaṃ sabbattha pākaṭameva.

941. If it is asked, "For what reason should one not be heedless?"—the verse states: "For he is a conqueror." Here, "abhibhū" means one who has overcome forms and so on. "Anabhibhūto" means not being overcome by them. "Sakkhidhammaṃ anītihaṃ adassī" means he directly saw the Dhamma, not based on tradition. "Sadā namassaṃ anusikkhe" means, always paying respect, one should train in the three trainings. The rest is clear in all respects.

Kevalaṃ [M 2.0281] pana ettha “cakkhūhi neva lolo”tiādīhi indriyasaṃvaro, “annānamatho pānāna”ntiādīhi sannidhipaṭikkhepamukhena paccayapaṭisevanasīlaṃ, methunamosavajjapesuṇiyādīhi pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlaṃ, “āthabbaṇaṃ supinaṃ lakkhaṇa”ntiādīhi ājīvapārisuddhisīlaṃ, “jhāyī assā”ti iminā samādhi, “vicinaṃ bhikkhū”ti iminā paññā, “sadā sato sikkhe”ti iminā puna saṅkhepato tissopi sikkhā, “atha āsanesu sayanesu, appasaddesu bhikkhu vihareyya, niddaṃ na bahulīkareyyā”tiādīhi sīlasamādhipaññānaṃ upakārāpakārasaṅgaṇhanavinodanāni vuttānīti. Evaṃ bhagavā nimmitassa paripuṇṇapaṭipadaṃ vatvā arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi, desanāpariyosāne purābhedasutte vuttasadisoyevābhisamayo ahosīti.

Here, indeed, restraint of the senses is indicated by such phrases as "not greedy with the eyes"; the virtue of proper use of requisites, by way of rejecting accumulation, as in "food and drink"; the virtue of Pātimokkha restraint by avoiding sexual misconduct, false speech, malicious speech, and so on; the purity of livelihood by abstaining from fortune-telling, interpreting dreams, and reading omens; concentration by "one should be a meditator"; wisdom by "a discerning monk"; and briefly, the threefold training again by "always mindful, one should train." Furthermore, regarding seats and beds, a monk should dwell in quiet places and not indulge in sleep—thus are stated the taking up of what is helpful and the dispelling of what is harmful for virtue, concentration, and wisdom. Having thus explained the complete practice for the created one, the Blessed One concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of arahantship. At the end of the discourse, the realization was just as described in the Purābheda Sutta.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya.

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya tuvaṭakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Tuvaṭaka Sutta in the Commentary on the Suttanipāta is concluded.

15. Attadaṇḍasuttavaṇṇanā

15. The Explanation of the Attadaṇḍa Sutta

942. Attadaṇḍā [V 2.0258][P 2.0566] bhayaṃ jātanti attadaṇḍasuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Yo so sammāparibbājanīyasuttassa uppattiyaṃ vuccamānāya sākiyakoliyānaṃ udakaṃ paṭicca kalaho vaṇṇito, taṃ ñatvā bhagavā “ñātakā kalahaṃ karonti, handa ne vāressāmī”ti dvinnaṃ senānaṃ majjhe ṭhatvā imaṃ suttamabhāsi.

942. "Attadaṇḍā bhayaṃ jātaṃ" (Fear is born from taking up the rod) is the Attadaṇḍa Sutta. What is its origin? In the telling of the origin of the Sammāparibbājanīya Sutta, a quarrel between the Sākyas and the Koliyas over water was described. Knowing this, the Blessed One thought, "My relatives are quarreling; come, let me restrain them." Standing between the two armies, he spoke this sutta.

Tattha paṭhamagāthāyattho – yaṃ lokassa diṭṭhadhammikaṃ vā samparāyikaṃ vā bhayaṃ jātaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ attadaṇḍā bhayaṃ jātaṃ attano duccaritakāraṇā jātaṃ, evaṃ santepi janaṃ passatha medhagaṃ, imaṃ sākiyādijanaṃ passatha aññamaññaṃ medhagaṃ hiṃsakaṃ bādhakanti. Evaṃ taṃ paṭiviruddhaṃ vippaṭipannaṃ janaṃ paribhāsitvā attano sammāpaṭipattidassanena tassa saṃvegaṃ janetuṃ āha [M 2.0282] “saṃvegaṃ kittayissāmi, yathā saṃvijitaṃ mayā”ti, pubbe bodhisatteneva satāti adhippāyo.

Here is the meaning of the first verse: whatever fear has arisen for the world, whether in this life or in a future one, all that fear is born from taking up the rod, born from one's own misconduct. Even so, behold the people engaged in quarrels—behold these Sākyas and others, harming and oppressing one another. Having thus rebuked those people who are in conflict and have gone astray, he spoke in order to stir a sense of spiritual urgency in them by showing his own right practice: "I will proclaim the spiritual urgency, as it was experienced by me"—the meaning is, as it was when he was formerly the Bodhisatta.

943. Idāni yathānena saṃvijitaṃ, taṃ pakāraṃ dassento “phandamāna”ntiādimāha. Tattha phandamānanti taṇhādīhi kampamānaṃ. Appodaketi appaudake. Aññamaññehi byāruddhe disvāti nānāsatte ca aññamaññehi saddhiṃ viruddhe disvā. Maṃ bhayamāvisīti maṃ bhayaṃ paviṭṭhaṃ.

943. Now, showing the manner in which this was experienced, he says "phandamānaṃ" (trembling) and so on. Here, "phandamānaṃ" means trembling due to craving and the like. "Appodake" means in little water. "Aññamaññehi byāruddhe disvā" means seeing various beings in conflict with one another. "Maṃ bhayaṃ āvisī" means fear entered me.

944. Samantamasāro lokoti nirayaṃ ādiṃ katvā samantato loko asāro niccasārādirahito. Disā sabbā sameritāti sabbā disā aniccatāya kampitā. Icchaṃ bhavanamattanoti attano tāṇaṃ icchanto. Nāddasāsiṃ anositanti kiñci ṭhānaṃ jarādīhi anajjhāvutthaṃ nāddakkhiṃ.

944. "Samantaṃ asāro loko" means: beginning with hell, the world on all sides is without substance, lacking any permanent substance and so on. "Disā sabbā sameritā" means all directions are shaken by impermanence. "Icchaṃ bhavanamattano" means desiring my own protection. "Nāddasāsiṃ anositaṃ" means I did not see any place not overcome by aging and so on.

945. Osānetveva byāruddhe, disvā me aratī ahūti yobbaññādīnaṃ osāne eva antagamake eva vināsake eva jarādīhi byāruddhe āhatacitte satte disvā arati me ahosi. Athettha sallanti atha [P 2.0567] etesu sattesu rāgādisallaṃ. Hadayanissitanti cittanissitaṃ.

945. "Osānetveva byāruddhe, disvā me aratī ahū" means: seeing beings with smitten minds, afflicted by aging and so on—which is the very end, the end-maker, and the destroyer of youth and so on—discontent arose in me. "Athettha sallaṃ" means: then, in these beings, there is the dart of lust and so on. "Hadayanissitaṃ" means resting on the mind.

946. “Kathaṃānubhāvaṃ [V 2.0259] salla”nti ce – yena sallena otiṇṇoti gāthā. Tattha disā sabbā vidhāvatīti sabbā duccaritadisāpi puratthimādidisāvidisāpi dhāvati. Tameva sallamabbuyha, na dhāvati na sīdatīti tameva sallaṃ uddharitvā tā ca disā na dhāvati, caturoghe ca na sīdatīti.

946. If it is asked, "Of what power is the dart?"—the verse is: "Pierced by which dart..." There, "disā sabbā vidhāvati" means one runs to all directions of misconduct, and also to the eastern direction, the other cardinal directions, and the intermediate directions. "Tameva sallaṃ abbuyha, na dhāvati na sīdati" means: having drawn out that very dart, one neither runs to those directions, nor sinks in the four floods.

947. Evaṃmahānubhāvena sallena otiṇṇesvapi ca sattesu – tattha sikkhānugīyanti, yāni loke gadhitānīti gāthā. Tassattho – ye loke pañca kāmaguṇā paṭilābhāya gijjhantīti katvā “gadhitānī”ti vuccanti, cirakālāsevitattā vā “gadhitānī”ti vuccanti, tattha taṃ nimittaṃ hatthisikkhādikā anekā sikkhā kathīyanti uggayhanti vā. Passatha yāva pamatto vāyaṃ loko, yato paṇḍito kulaputto tesu vā gadhitesu tāsu vā sikkhāsu adhimutto na siyā, aññadatthu aniccādidassanena nibbijjha sabbaso kāme attano nibbānameva sikkheti.

947. And even among beings pierced by a dart of such great power, the verse is: "There trainings are recited for those things craved in the world." Its meaning is: because they are greedily desired for the sake of obtaining the five strands of sensual pleasure in the world, they are called "gadhitāni" (craved); or because they have been indulged in for a long time, they are called "gadhitāni." In that context, for that purpose, many trainings such as elephant training are taught or learned. See how heedless this world is, for a wise person of good family would not be attached to those craved things or to those trainings; but instead, having become disillusioned with all sensual pleasures by seeing impermanence and so on, he trains solely for his own Nibbāna.

948. Idāni [M 2.0283] yathā nibbānāya sikkhitabbaṃ, taṃ dassento “sacco siyā”tiādimāha. Tattha saccoti vācāsaccena ñāṇasaccena maggasaccena ca samannāgato. Rittapesuṇoti pahīnapesuṇo. Vevicchanti macchariyaṃ.

948. Now, to show how one should train for Nibbāna, he says, "sacco siyā" (one should be truthful), and so on. There, "sacco" means endowed with truth of speech, truth of knowledge, and truth of the path. "Rittapesuṇo" means one who has abandoned slander. "Vevicchaṃ" means stinginess.

949. Niddaṃ tandiṃ sahe thīnanti pacalāyikañca kāyālasiyañca cittālasiyañcāti ime tayo dhamme abhibhaveyya. Nibbānamanasoti nibbānaninnacitto.

949. "Niddaṃ tandiṃ thīnaṃ sahe" means one should overcome these three things: drowsiness, bodily laziness, and mental laziness. "Nibbānamanaso" means with a mind inclined toward Nibbāna.

950-51. Sāhasāti rattassa rāgacariyādibhedā sāhasakaraṇā. Purāṇaṃ nābhinandeyyāti atītarūpādiṃ nābhinandeyya. Naveti paccuppanne. Hiyyamāneti vinassamāne. Ākāsaṃ na sito siyāti taṇhānissito na bhaveyya. Taṇhā hi rūpādīnaṃ ākāsanato “ākāso”ti vuccati.

950-51. "Sāhasā" means the rash actions which are the various kinds of conduct motivated by lust for one who is impassioned. "Purāṇaṃ nābhinandeyya" means one should not delight in past forms and so on. "Nave" means in the present. "Hiyyamāne" means in what is perishing. "Ākāsaṃ na sito siyā" means one should not be dependent on craving. For craving, on account of its making-space for forms and so on, is called "space."

952. “Kiṃkāraṇā ākāsaṃ na sito siyā”ti ce – “gedhaṃ brūmī”ti gāthā. Tassattho – ahañhi imaṃ ākāsasaṅkhātaṃ taṇhaṃ rūpādīsu gijjhanato gedhaṃ brūmi “gedho”ti vadāmi. Kiñca bhiyyo – avahananaṭṭhena “ogho”ti ca ājavanaṭṭhena “ājava”nti ca “idaṃ mayhaṃ, idaṃ mayha”nti jappakāraṇato “jappana”nti ca dummuñcanaṭṭhena “ārammaṇa”nti [P 2.0568] ca kampakaraṇena “pakampana”nti ca brūmi, esā ca lokassa palibodhaṭṭhena duratikkamanīyaṭṭhena ca [V 2.0260] kāmapaṅko duraccayoti. “Ākāsaṃ na sito siyā”ti evaṃ vutte vā “kimetaṃ ākāsa”nti ce? Gedhaṃ brūmīti. Evampi tassā gāthāya sambandho veditabbo. Tattha padayojanā – ākāsanti gedhaṃ brūmīti. Tathā yvāyaṃ mahoghoti vuccati. Taṃ brūmi, ājavaṃ brūmi, jappanaṃ brūmi, pakampanaṃ brūmi, yvāyaṃ sadevake loke kāmapaṅko duraccayo, taṃ brūmīti.

952. If asked, "For what reason would one not be dependent on the sky?"—the verse says, "I call it craving." Its meaning is this: I call this craving, which is reckoned as "sky," "craving" (gedha) because of its greed for forms and so on. And furthermore, due to its characteristic of dragging down, I call it "flood"; due to its driving nature, "torrent"; because it is the cause of muttering "this is mine, this is mine," I call it "muttering"; due to its characteristic of being difficult to release, "object"; and because it causes trembling, "shaking." And this, being an obstruction to the world and difficult to overcome, is the mire of sensual desires, hard to cross. If it is said, "One should not be dependent on the sky," or if it is asked, "What is this sky?"—I call it craving. Thus, the connection of this verse should be understood. Here, the word arrangement is: "sky"—I call it craving. Similarly, that which is called the great flood, that I call; the torrent, I call; the muttering, I call; the shaking, I call; that which in the world with its gods is the mire of sensual desires, hard to cross—that I call.

953. Evametaṃ gedhādipariyāyaṃ ākāsaṃ anissito – saccā avokkammāti gāthā. Tassattho – pubbe vuttā tividhāpi saccā avokkamma moneyyappattiyā munīti saṅkhyaṃ gato nibbānatthale tiṭṭhati brāhmaṇo, sa ve evarūpo sabbāni āyatanāni nissajjitvā “santo”ti vuccatīti.

953. Thus, not relying on this 'sky,' which has synonyms such as craving—the verse says, "not deviating from the truths." Its meaning is: not deviating from the previously mentioned threefold truths, having attained sagehood through sagacity, he is reckoned a sage; the brahmin stands on the ground of Nibbāna. Indeed, such a one, having relinquished all sense-bases, is called "peaceful."

954. Kiñca [M 2.0284] bhiyyo – sa ve vidvāti gāthā. Tattha ñatvā dhammanti aniccādinayena saṅkhatadhammaṃ ñatvā. Sammā so loke iriyānoti asammāiriyanakarānaṃ kilesānaṃ pahānā sammā so loke iriyamāno.

954. And further: the verse says, "He is truly wise." Here, "having known the Dhamma" means knowing conditioned phenomena by way of impermanence, etc. "He rightly fares in the world" means that, having abandoned the defilements that cause wrong conduct, he fares rightly in the world.

955. Evaṃ apihento ca – yodha kāmeti gāthā. Tattha saṅganti sattavidhaṃ saṅgañca yo accatari nājjhetīti nābhijjhāyati.

955. And thus, not longing—the verse says, "who here in regard to sensual pleasures..." Therein, "attachment" means the seven kinds of attachment. "Who has crossed beyond does not cling" means does not covet.

956. Tasmā tumhesupi yo evarūpo hotumicchati, taṃ vadāmi – yaṃ pubbeti gāthā. Tattha yaṃ pubbeti atīte saṅkhāre ārabbha uppajjanadhammaṃ kilesajātaṃ atītakammañca. Pacchā te māhu kiñcananti anāgatepi saṅkhāre ārabbha uppajjanadhammaṃ rāgādikiñcanaṃ māhu. Majjhe ce no gahessasīti paccuppanne rūpādidhammepi na gahessasi ce.

956. Therefore, whoever among you wishes to be like that, to him I speak—the verse says, "what is past..." Here, "what is past" refers to the host of defilements subject to arising and past kamma, with respect to past formations. "Let there be no impediment for you in the future" means: with respect to future formations also, let there be no impediment of greed and so on, which is subject to the nature of arising. "And if in the middle you will not grasp" means: if you will not grasp present phenomena such as form.

957. Evaṃ “upasanto carissasī”ti arahattappattiṃ dassetvā idāni arahato thutivasena ito parā gāthāyo abhāsi. Tattha sabbasoti gāthāya mamāyitanti mamattakaraṇaṃ, “mama ida”nti gahitaṃ vā vatthu. Asatā ca na socatīti avijjamānakāraṇā asantakāraṇā na socati. Na jīyatīti jānimpi na gacchati.

957. Thus, having shown the attainment of arahantship with "peaceful, you will wander," he now spoke the following verses by way of praising the arahant. Here, in the verse beginning "sabbaso," "what is possessed" means the act of making something one's own, or a thing grasped as "this is mine." "And he does not grieve over what is not" means he does not grieve for a non-existent reason, for a baseless reason. "He is not diminished" means he does not come to ruin.

958-9. Kiñca bhiyyo – yassa natthīti gāthā. Tattha [P 2.0569] kiñcananti kiñci rūpādidhammajātaṃ. Kiñca bhiyyo – aniṭṭhurīti gāthā. Tattha aniṭṭhurīti anissukī. “Aniddhurī”tipi keci paṭhanti. Sabbadhī samoti sabbattha samo, upekkhakoti adhippāyo. Kiṃ [V 2.0261] vuttaṃ hoti? Yo so “natthi me”ti na socati, tamahaṃ avikampinaṃ puggalaṃ puṭṭho samāno aniṭṭhurī ananugiddho anejo sabbadhi samoti imaṃ tasmiṃ puggale catubbidhamānisaṃsaṃ brūmīti.

Furthermore, the verse beginning "For whom there is no..." Here, "impediment" means any kind of phenomena such as form, etc. Furthermore, the verse beginning "Not harsh." Here, "not harsh" means not envious. Some also read it as "aniddhurī" (not burdened). "Everywhere the same" means equal in all respects; the meaning is "equanimous." What is being said? That person who does not grieve thinking "There is nothing for me"—when asked about that unshaken person, I declare this fourfold benefit in that person: "not harsh, not greedy, free from craving, everywhere the same."

960. Kiñca bhiyyo – anejassāti gāthā. Tattha nisaṅkhatīti puññābhisaṅkhārādīsu yo koci saṅkhāro. So hi yasmā nisaṅkhariyati nisaṅkharoti vā, tasmā “nisaṅkhatī”ti vuccati. Viyārambhāti vividhā puññābhisaṅkhārādikā [M 2.0285] ārambhā. Khemaṃ passati sabbadhīti sabbattha abhayameva passati.

960. Furthermore, the verse on "the one free from craving." Herein, "nisaṅkhati" refers to any formation whatsoever among meritorious formations and so on. For since it is formed or it forms, it is therefore called "nisaṅkhati." "Viyārambhā" means various undertakings, such as meritorious formations and the like. "He sees safety everywhere" means he sees only security everywhere.

961. Evaṃ passanto na samesūti gāthā. Tattha na vadateti “sadisohamasmī”tiādinā mānavasena samesupi attānaṃ na vadati omesupi ussesupi. Nādeti na nirassatīti rūpādīsu kañci dhammaṃ na gaṇhāti; na nissajjati. Sesaṃ sabbattha pākaṭameva. Evaṃ arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi, desanāpariyosāne pañcasatā sākiyakumārā ca koliyakumārā ca ehibhikkhupabbajjāya pabbajitā, te gahetvā bhagavā mahāvanaṃ pāvisīti.

961. Thus seeing, the verse says, "Not among equals..." Here, "he does not speak" means that through conceit, he does not speak of himself among equals, nor among inferiors, nor among superiors, with such thoughts as "I am equal." "He neither grasps nor rejects" means he does not take up nor does he relinquish any phenomenon among forms and so on. The rest is clear everywhere. Thus, he concluded the discourse with the pinnacle of arahantship. At the conclusion of the discourse, five hundred Sakyan and Koliyan youths went forth by the 'come, bhikkhu' ordination. Taking them with him, the Blessed One entered the Great Wood.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya attadaṇḍasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Here ends the explanation of the Attadaṇḍa Sutta in the Commentary on the Suttanipāta.

16. Sāriputtasuttavaṇṇanā

16. Explanation of the Sāriputta Sutta

962. Na [V 2.0262] me diṭṭhoti sāriputtasuttaṃ, “therapañhasutta”ntipi vuccati. Kā uppatti? Imassa suttassa uppatti – rājagahakassa [P 2.0570] seṭṭhissa candanaghaṭikāya paṭilābhaṃ ādiṃ katvā tāya candanaghaṭikāya katassa pattassa ākāse ussāpanaṃ āyasmato piṇḍolabhāradvājassa iddhiyā pattaggahaṇaṃ, tasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ sāvakānaṃ iddhipaṭikkhepo, titthiyānaṃ bhagavatā saddhiṃ pāṭihāriyaṃ kattukāmatā, pāṭihāriyakaraṇaṃ, bhagavato sāvatthigamanaṃ, titthiyānubandhanaṃ, sāvatthiyaṃ pasenadino buddhūpagamanaṃ kaṇḍambapātubhāvo, catunnaṃ parisānaṃ titthiyajayatthaṃ pāṭihāriyakaraṇussukkanivāraṇaṃ, yamakapāṭihāriyakaraṇaṃ, katapāṭihāriyassa bhagavato tāvatiṃsabhavanagamanaṃ, tattha temāsaṃ dhammadesanā, āyasmatā mahāmoggallānattherena yācitassa devalokato saṅkassanagare orohaṇanti imāni vatthūni antarantare ca jātakāni vitthāretvā yāva dasasahassacakkavāḷadevatāhi pūjiyamāno bhagavā majjhe maṇimayena sopānena saṅkassanagare oruyha sopānakaḷevare aṭṭhāsi –

962. The Sāriputta Sutta, which begins with 'Na me diṭṭho,' is also called the 'Therapañhasutta.' What is its origin? The origin of this sutta is as follows: beginning with the merchant of Rājagaha obtaining a block of sandalwood, the raising into the sky of a bowl made from that sandalwood, the Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja taking the bowl by means of his psychic power; on that occasion, the prohibition of psychic powers for the disciples; the heretics' desire to perform a miracle in competition with the Blessed One; the performance of the miracle; the Blessed One's journey to Sāvatthī; the heretics following him; King Pasenadi's visit to the Buddha in Sāvatthī; the appearance of the Kaṇḍamba mango tree; the prevention of the eagerness of the four assemblies to perform a miracle to defeat the heretics; the performance of the Twin Miracle; the Blessed One's ascent to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven after performing the miracle; his teaching of the Dhamma there for three months; his descent to the city of Saṅkassa from the deva-world at the request of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna—these events, with Jātaka stories elaborated in between, up to the point where the Blessed One, worshipped by the deities of the ten-thousandfold world-system, descended to the city of Saṅkassa by a jeweled staircase in the middle and stood on the base of the staircase.

“Ye [M 2.0286] jhānappasutā dhīrā, nekkhammūpasame ratā;

Devāpi tesaṃ pihayanti, sambuddhānaṃ satīmata”nti. (dha. pa. 181) –

“Those wise ones devoted to meditation, delighting in the peace of renunciation; even the gods envy them, the mindful, fully awakened ones.” (Dhp. 181)

Imissā dhammapadagāthāya vuccamānāya vuttā. Sopānakaḷevare ṭhitaṃ pana bhagavantaṃ sabbapaṭhamaṃ āyasmā sāriputto vandi, tato uppalavaṇṇā bhikkhunī, athāparo janakāyo. Tatra bhagavā cintesi – “imissaṃ parisati moggallāno iddhiyā aggoti pākaṭo, anuruddho dibbacakkhunā, puṇṇo dhammakathikattena, sāriputtaṃ panāyaṃ parisā na kenaci guṇena evaṃ aggoti jānāti, yaṃnūnāhaṃ sāriputtaṃ paññāguṇena pakāseyya”nti. Atha theraṃ pañhaṃ pucchi. Thero bhagavatā pucchitaṃ pucchitaṃ puthujjanapañhaṃ, sekkhapañhaṃ, asekkhapañhañca, sabbaṃ vissajjesi. Tadā naṃ jano “paññāya aggo”ti aññāsi[P 2.0571]. Atha bhagavā “sāriputto na idāneva paññāya aggo, atītepi paññāya aggo”ti jātakaṃ ānesi.

This was said when this Dhammapada verse was recited. First, the Venerable Sāriputta paid homage to the Blessed One, who was standing on the base of the staircase, then the bhikkhunī Uppalavaṇṇā, and afterward the rest of the crowd. There, the Blessed One thought: “In this assembly, Moggallāna is known as foremost in psychic powers, Anuruddha in the divine eye, and Puṇṇa in expounding the Dhamma. But this assembly does not know Sāriputta as foremost in any such quality. What if I were to reveal Sāriputta’s excellence in wisdom?” Then he asked the Elder a question. The Elder answered every question put to him by the Blessed One—questions for ordinary people, for trainees, and for the perfected ones. At that moment, the people recognized him as “foremost in wisdom.” Then the Blessed One declared, “Sāriputta is not only now foremost in wisdom—he was also foremost in wisdom in the past,” and he related a Jātaka.

Atīte parosahassā isayo vanamūlaphalāhārā pabbatapāde vasanti. Tesaṃ ācariyassa ābādho [V 2.0263] uppajji, upaṭṭhānāni vattanti. Jeṭṭhantevāsī “sappāyabhesajjaṃ āharissāmi, ācariyaṃ appamattā upaṭṭhahathā”ti vatvā manussapathaṃ agamāsi. Tasmiṃ anāgateyeva ācariyo kālamakāsi. Taṃ “idāni kālaṃ karissatī”ti antevāsikā samāpattimārabbha pucchiṃsu. So ākiñcaññāyatanasamāpattiṃ sandhāyāha – “natthi kiñcī”ti, antevāsino “natthi ācariyassa adhigamo”ti aggahesuṃ. Atha jeṭṭhantevāsī bhesajjaṃ ādāya āgantvā taṃ kālakataṃ disvā ācariyaṃ “kiñci pucchitthā”ti āha. Āma pucchimhā, “natthi kiñcī”ti āha, na kiñci ācariyena adhigatanti. Natthi kiñcīti vadanto ācariyo ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ pavedesi, sakkātabbo ācariyoti.

In the past, over a thousand ascetics lived at the foot of a mountain, sustaining themselves on the roots and fruits of the forest. Their teacher fell ill, and they attended to him. The senior pupil said, “I will fetch suitable medicine; attend to the teacher diligently,” and then he went to a place inhabited by humans. Before he returned, the teacher passed away. Thinking, “He is about to pass away,” the pupils asked him about his meditative attainment. He, referring to the attainment of the base of nothingness, said, “There is nothing.” The pupils took this to mean, “The teacher has no attainment.” Then the senior pupil arrived with the medicine and, seeing that the teacher had passed away, asked, “Did you ask the teacher anything?” They said, “Yes, we asked, and he said, ‘There is nothing,’ meaning the teacher had attained nothing.” The senior pupil said, “In saying ‘There is nothing,’ the teacher was indicating the base of nothingness. The teacher should be venerated.”

“Parosahassampi samāgatānaṃ,

Kandeyyuṃ te vassasataṃ apaññā;

Ekopi seyyo puriso sapañño,

Yo bhāsitassa vijānāti attha”nti. (jā. 1.1.99);

“Even if over a thousand fools were to gather, they might weep for a hundred years; but one wise person is better, who understands the meaning of what is spoken.” (Jā. 1.1.99)

Kathite [M 2.0287] ca pana bhagavatā jātake āyasmā sāriputto attano saddhivihārikānaṃ pañcannaṃ bhikkhusatānamatthāya sappāyasenāsanagocarasīlavatādīni pucchituṃ “na me diṭṭho ito pubbe”ti imaṃ thutigāthaṃ ādiṃ katvā aṭṭha gāthāyo abhāsi. Tamatthaṃ vissajjento bhagavā tato parā sesagāthāti.

When the Blessed One had related this Jātaka, the Venerable Sāriputta, for the benefit of his five hundred resident monks, wishing to inquire about suitable lodgings, alms-resorts, virtuous conduct, and so forth, recited eight verses beginning with the verse of praise, “I have not seen before this.” The Blessed One, explaining the meaning of this, then recited the remaining verses.

Tattha ito pubbeti ito saṅkassanagare otaraṇato pubbe. Vagguvadoti sundaravado. Tusitā gaṇimāgatoti tusitakāyā cavitvā mātukucchiṃ āgatattā tusitā āgato, gaṇācariyattā gaṇī. Santuṭṭhaṭṭhena vā tusitasaṅkhātā devalokā gaṇiṃ āgato tusitānaṃ vā arahantānaṃ gaṇiṃ āgatoti.

Here, 'before this' (ito pubbe) means before this descent in the city of Saṅkassa. 'Pleasant in speech' (vagguvado) means one with beautiful speech. 'Come from Tusita, the leader' (tusitā gaṇimāgato) means: having passed away from the Tusita realm and entered a mother's womb, he is 'come from Tusita'; and being a teacher of a group, he is a 'leader' (gaṇī). Or, on account of the meaning of 'contentment,' he has come to the group from the deva-world named Tusita; or he has come to the group of the 'contented ones' (tusitānaṃ), that is, the arahants.

963. Dutiyagāthāya sadevakassa lokassa yathā dissatīti sadevakassa lokassa viya manussānampi dissati. Yathā vā dissatīti [P 2.0572] tacchato aviparītato dissati cakkhumāti uttamacakkhu. Ekoti pabbajjāsaṅkhātādīhi eko. Ratinti nekkhammaratiādiṃ.

963. In the second verse, 'as is seen by the world with its devas' (sadevakassa lokassa yathā dissati) means it is seen by humans just as by the world with its devas. Or, 'as is seen' (yathā dissati) means seen truly, without distortion. 'One with the eye' (cakkhumā) means one with the supreme eye. 'Alone' (eko) means one in terms of qualities such as his going forth. 'Delight' (rati) means delight in renunciation and so forth.

964. Tatiyagāthāya bahūnamidha baddhānanti idha bahūnaṃ khattiyādīnaṃ sissānaṃ. Sissā hi [V 2.0264] ācariye paṭibaddhavuttittā “baddhā”ti vuccanti atthi pañhena āgamanti atthiko pañhena āgatomhi, atthikānaṃ vā pañhena āgamanaṃ, pañhena atthi āgamanaṃ vāti.

964. In the third verse, 'of many bound here' (bahūnamidha baddhānaṃ) refers here to many disciples, such as khattiyas and others. Disciples are called 'bound' (baddhā) because their conduct is bound to their teacher. 'Coming with a question for a purpose' (atthi pañhena āgamanaṃ) means either 'I, having a purpose, have come with a question,' or 'the coming with a question of those with a purpose,' or 'there is a coming with a question.'

965. Catutthagāthāya vijigucchatoti jātiādīhi aṭṭīyato rittamāsananti vivittaṃ mañcapīṭhaṃ. Pabbatānaṃ guhāsu vāti pabbataguhāsu vā rittamāsanaṃ bhajatoti sambandhitabbaṃ.

965. In the fourth verse, 'for one who is disgusted' (vijigucchato) means for one who is distressed by birth and so on. 'A secluded seat' (rittamāsanaṃ) refers to a secluded couch or seat. 'Or in the caves of mountains' (pabbatānaṃ guhāsu vā) means 'or in mountain caves,' and this should be connected with the phrase 'resorts to a secluded seat' (rittamāsanaṃ bhajato).

966. Pañcamagāthāya uccāvacesūti hīnapaṇītesu. Sayanesūti vihārādīsu senāsanesu. Kīvanto tattha bheravāti kittakā tattha bhayakāraṇā. “Kuvanto”tipi pāṭho, kūjantoti cassa attho. Na pana pubbenāparaṃ sandhiyati.

966. In the fifth verse, 'in high and low' (uccāvacesu) refers to the inferior and the sublime. 'In resting places' (sayanesu) means in lodgings such as monasteries. 'How many terrors are there?' (kīvanto tattha bheravā) asks how many causes for fear there are there. There is also the reading 'kuvanto,' and its meaning is 'warbling,' but the preceding does not connect with the following.

967. Chaṭṭhagāthāya katī parissayāti kittakā upaddavā. Agataṃ disanti nibbānaṃ. Tañhi agatapubbattā agataṃ tathā niddisitabbato disā cāti[M 2.0288]. Tena vuttaṃ “agataṃ disa”nti. Abhisambhaveti abhibhaveyya. Pantamhīti pariyante.

967. In the sixth verse, 'katī parissayā' asks how many dangers there are, and 'kittakā upaddavā' how many troubles. 'Agataṃ disā' refers to Nibbāna. Because it has never been reached before, it is called 'agataṃ,' and because it should be indicated as such, it is also called 'disā' (direction). Hence, it is said 'agataṃ disā.' 'Abhisambhaveti' means to overcome. 'Pantamhi' means in a remote place.

968-9. Sattamagāthāya kyāssa byappathayo assūti kīdisāni tassa vacanāni assu. Aṭṭhamagāthāya ekodi nipakoti ekaggacitto paṇḍito.

968-9. In the seventh verse, 'kyāssa byappathayo assu' asks what kind of expressions they would be. In the eighth verse, 'ekodi nipako' means one with a concentrated mind, a wise person.

970. Evaṃ āyasmatā sāriputtena tīhi gāthāhi bhagavantaṃ thometvā pañcahi gāthāhi – pañcasatānaṃ sissānamatthāya senāsanagocarasīlavatādīni pucchito bhagavā tamatthaṃ pakāsetuṃ “vijigucchamānassā”tiādinā nayena vissajjanamāraddho. Tattha paṭhamagāthāya tāvattho – jātiādīhi vijigucchamānassa rittāsanaṃ sayanaṃ sevato ce sambodhikāmassa sāriputta, bhikkhuno yadidaṃ phāsu yo phāsuvihāro yathānudhammaṃ yo ca anudhammo, taṃ te pavakkhāmi yathā pajānaṃ yathā pajānanto vadeyya, evaṃ vadāmīti.

970. Thus, after the Venerable Sāriputta praised the Blessed One with three verses and, for the sake of five hundred disciples, asked with five verses about matters such as lodgings, alms-resort, virtue, and observances, the Blessed One began to explain that matter in the manner beginning with 'vijigucchamānassa.' Here, the meaning of the first verse is this: O Sāriputta, for a monk disgusted by birth and so forth, who resorts to a secluded seat and bed while seeking awakening, I will declare to you what is suitable, what is a comfortable abiding, what is in accordance with the Dhamma, and what is the corresponding practice. I will explain this as I know it; I speak as one who knows.

971. Dutiyagāthāya pariyantacārīti sīlādīsu catūsu pariyantesu caramāno. Ḍaṃsādhipātānanti piṅgalamakkhikānañca sesamakkhikānañca. Sesamakkhikā hi tato tato adhipatitvā khādanti, tasmā “adhipātā”ti vuccanti. Manussaphassānanti [P 2.0573] corādiphassānaṃ.

971. In the second verse, 'pariyantacārī' means one who fares within the four limits, namely virtue and so forth. 'Ḍaṃsādhipātānaṃ' refers to gadflies and other flies. Other flies alight and bite from various places, hence they are called 'adhipātā.' 'Manussaphassānaṃ' means contact with thieves and the like.

972. Tatiyagāthāya paradhammikā nāma satta sahadhammikavajjā sabbepi bāhirakā. Kusalānuesīti kusaladhamme anvesamāno.

972. In the third verse, 'paradhammikā' refers to followers of other doctrines; excluding those who share the same Dhamma, they are all outsiders. 'Kusalānuesī' means one who seeks wholesome qualities.

973. Catutthagāthāya [V 2.0265] ātaṅkaphassenāti rogaphassena. Sītaṃ atuṇhanti sītañca uṇhañca. So tehi phuṭṭho bahudhāti so tehi ātaṅkādīhi anekehi ākārehi phuṭṭho samānopi. Anokoti abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇādīnaṃ anokāsabhūto.

973. In the fourth verse, 'ātaṅkaphassena' means contact with disease. 'Sītaṃ atuṇhaṃ' means cold and heat. 'So tehi phuṭṭho bahudhā' means though afflicted by these—disease and so on—in many ways. 'Anoka' means not a location for formations, consciousness, and so forth.

974. Evaṃ “bhikkhuno vijigucchato”tiādīhi tīhi gāthāhi puṭṭhamatthaṃ vissajjetvā idāni “kyāssa byappathayo”tiādinā nayena puṭṭhaṃ vissajjento “theyyaṃ na kāre”tiādimāha. Tattha phasseti phareyya[M 2.0289]. Yadāvilattaṃ manaso vijaññāti yaṃ cittassa āvilattaṃ vijāneyya, taṃ sabbaṃ “kaṇhassa pakkho”ti vinodayeyya.

974. Thus, having explained the meaning inquired about in the three verses beginning with 'bhikkhuno vijigucchato,' now explaining the question posed in the manner beginning with 'kyāssa byappathayo,' he says 'theyyaṃ na kāre' and so on. Here, 'phasseti' means 'one should touch.' 'Yadāvilattaṃ manaso vijaññā' means when one understands the turbidity of the mind; all that should be dispelled as 'belonging to the dark side.'

975. Mūlampi tesaṃ palikhañña tiṭṭheti tesaṃ kodhātimānānaṃ yaṃ avijjādikaṃ mūlaṃ, tampi palikhaṇitvā tiṭṭheyya. Addhā bhavanto abhisambhaveyyāti evaṃ piyappiyaṃ abhibhavanto ekaṃseneva abhibhaveyya, na tatra sithilaṃ parakkameyyāti adhippāyo.

975. 'Mūlampi tesaṃ palikhañña tiṭṭhe' means that having dug up even the root of their anger and conceit, which is ignorance and so on, one should stand firm. 'Addhā bhavanto abhisambhaveyyā' means that by overcoming likes and dislikes, one should certainly prevail; there should be no slackening of effort—this is the intention.

976. Paññaṃ purakkhatvāti paññaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ katvā. Kalyāṇapītīti kalyāṇāya pītiyā samannāgato. Caturo sahetha paridevadhammeti anantaragāthāya vuccamāne paridevanīyadhamme saheyya.

976. 'Paññaṃ purakkhatvāti' means having made wisdom the forerunner. 'Kalyāṇapītīti' means possessed of wholesome joy. 'Caturo sahetha paridevadhammeti' means one should endure the four lamentable conditions mentioned in the following verse.

977. Kiṃsū asissāmīti kiṃ bhuñjissāmi. Kuvaṃ vā asissanti kuhiṃ vā asissāmi. Dukkhaṃ vata settha kvajja sessanti imaṃ rattiṃ dukkhaṃ sayiṃ, ajja āgamanarattiṃ kattha sayissaṃ. Ete vitakketi ete piṇḍapātanissite dve, senāsananissite dveti cattāro vitakke. Aniketacārīti apalibodhacārī nittaṇhacārī.

977. 'Kiṃsū asissāmīti' means 'What shall I eat?'. 'Kuvaṃ vā asissanti' means 'Where shall I eat?'. 'Dukkhaṃ vata settha kvajja sessan'ti' means 'I slept poorly this night; where shall I sleep on the coming night?'. 'Ete vitakketi' refers to these four thoughts: two concerning almsfood and two concerning lodging. 'Aniketacārīti' means one who wanders without a fixed abode, free from craving.

978. Kāleti piṇḍapātakāle piṇḍapātasaṅkhātaṃ annaṃ vā cīvarakāle cīvarasaṅkhātaṃ vasanaṃ vā laddhā dhammena samenāti adhippāyo. Mattaṃ so jaññāti paṭiggahaṇe ca paribhoge ca so pamāṇaṃ jāneyya. Idhāti sāsane, nipātamattameva vā etaṃ. Tosanatthanti santosatthaṃ, etadatthaṃ mattaṃ jāneyyāti vuttaṃ hoti. So tesu guttoti so bhikkhu tesu paccayesu gutto. Yatacārīti saṃyatavihāro[P 2.0574], rakkhitiriyāpatho rakkhitakāyavacīmanodvāro cāti vuttaṃ hoti. “Yaticārī”tipi pāṭho, soyevattho. Rusitoti rosito, ghaṭṭitoti vuttaṃ hoti.

978. The phrase beginning 'Kālena' is explained thus: having obtained food, known as almsfood, at the time for almsfood, or a garment, known as a robe, at the time for robes, righteously and peacefully—this is the intention. 'Mattaṃ so jaññāti' means that he should know moderation in receiving and using. 'Idhāti' refers to this Dispensation, or it is merely a particle. 'Tosanatthanti' means for the sake of contentment; for this purpose, it is said, he should know moderation. 'So tesu guttoti' means that monk is guarded in regard to these requisites. 'Yatacārīti' means one who abides restrainedly; that is, with guarded deportment and with the doors of body, speech, and mind guarded. 'Yaticārī' is also a reading; the meaning is the same. 'Rusitoti' means angered; that is to say, agitated.

979. Jhānānuyuttoti anupannuppādanena uppannāsevanena ca jhāne anuyutto. Upekkhamārabbha samāhitattoti catutthajjhānupekkhaṃ uppādetvā samāhitacitto. Takkāsayaṃ kukkucciyūpachindeti [V 2.0266] kāmavitakkādiṃ takkañca[M 2.0290], kāmasaññādiṃ tassa takkassa āsayañca, hatthakukkuccādiṃ kukkucciyañca upacchindeyya.

979. 'Jhānānuyuttoti' means devoted to jhāna by generating the unarisen and cultivating the arisen. 'Upekkhamārabbha samāhitattoti' means having generated the equanimity of the fourth jhāna, with a composed mind. 'Takkāsayaṃ kukkucciyūpachindeti' means he should cut off thinking, such as sensual thought; the basis of that thinking, such as sensual perception; and worry, such as regret concerning actions of the hand.

980. Cudito vacībhi satimābhinandeti upajjhāyādīhi vācāhi codito samāno satimā hutvā taṃ codanaṃ abhinandeyya. Vācaṃ pamuñce kusalanti ñāṇasamuṭṭhitaṃ vācaṃ pamuñceyya. Nātivelanti ativelaṃ pana vācaṃ kālavelañca sīlavelañca atikkantaṃ nappamuñceyya. Janavādadhammāyāti janavādakathāya. Na cetayeyyāti cetanaṃ na uppādeyya.

980. 'Cudito vacībhi satimābhinandeti' means that when reproved by the words of one’s preceptor or others, one should be mindful and welcome that reproof. 'Vācaṃ pamuñce kusalanti' means one should utter skillful speech, that is, speech arisen from knowledge. 'Nātivelanti' means one should not speak excessively, transgressing the proper time and the bounds of morality. 'Janavādadhammāyāti' means for the sake of popular talk. 'Na cetayeyyāti' means one should not form the intention.

981. Athāparanti atha idāni ito parampi. Pañca rajānīti rūparāgādīni pañca rajāni. Yesaṃ satīmā vinayāya sikkheti yesaṃ upaṭṭhitassati hutvā vinayanatthaṃ tisso sikkhā sikkheyya. Evaṃ sikkhanto hi rūpesu…pe… phassesu sahetha rāgaṃ, na aññeti.

981. 'Athāparanti' means and furthermore, now, and beyond this. 'Pañca rajānīti' refers to the five defilements, such as lust for forms. 'Yesaṃ satīmā vinayāya sikkheti' means for the removal of which a mindful one trains: being of established mindfulness, one should train in the three trainings for the purpose of their removal. 'Evaṃ sikkhanto hi rūpesu…pe… phassesu sahetha rāgaṃ, na aññeti' means for one training thus would overcome lust in regard to forms… and so on… contacts, and not otherwise.

982. Tato so tesaṃ vinayāya sikkhanto anukkamena – etesu dhammesūti gāthā. Tattha etesūti rūpādīsu. Kālena so sammā dhammaṃ parivīmaṃsamānoti so bhikkhu yvāyaṃ “uddhate citte samādhissa kālo”tiādinā nayena kālo vutto, tena kālena sabbaṃ saṅkhatadhammaṃ aniccādinayena parivīmaṃsamāno. Ekodibhūto vihane tamaṃ soti so ekaggacitto sabbaṃ mohāditamaṃ vihaneyya. Natthi ettha saṃsayo. Sesaṃ sabbattha pākaṭameva.

982. Then, training for their discipline, gradually—this is the verse: "in these phenomena." Herein, "in these" refers to forms and so on. "At the proper time, rightly investigating the teaching": this means that a monk, at the time spoken of by the method beginning, "when the mind is agitated, it is the time for concentration," rightly investigates all conditioned phenomena by the method of impermanence, and so on. "Becoming unified, he would dispel the darkness": this means that, with a one-pointed mind, he would dispel all the darkness of delusion and so on. There is no doubt in this. The rest is clear in every way.

Evaṃ bhagavā arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi. Desanāpariyosāne pañcasatā bhikkhū arahattaṃ pattā, tiṃsakoṭisaṅkhyānañca devamanussānaṃ dhammābhisamayo ahosīti.
