Thus the Blessed One concluded the teaching with the attainment of Arahantship. At the end of the discourse, five hundred monks attained Arahantship, and thirty crores of devas and humans realized the Dhamma.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya,

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya sāriputtasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the Sāriputta Sutta in the Commentary to the Suttanipāta is completed.

Niṭṭhito ca catuttho vaggo atthavaṇṇanānayato, nāmena

And the fourth chapter is completed, by way of the exposition of meaning, by name:

Aṭṭhakavaggoti.

The Chapter of Eights.

5. Pārāyanavaggo

5. The Chapter on the Way to the Further Shore

Vatthugāthāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Introductory Verses

983. Kosalānaṃ [V 2.0267][M 2.0291][P 2.0575] purā rammāti pārāyanavaggassa vatthugāthā. Tāsaṃ uppatti – atīte kira bārāṇasivāsī eko rukkhavaḍḍhakī sake ācariyake adutiyo, tassa soḷasa sissā, ekamekassa sahassaṃ antevāsikā. Evaṃ te sattarasādhikasoḷasasahassā ācariyantevāsino sabbepi bārāṇasiṃ upanissāya jīvikaṃ kappentā pabbatasamīpaṃ gantvā rukkhe gahetvā tattheva nānāpāsādavikatiyo niṭṭhāpetvā kullaṃ bandhitvā gaṅgāya bārāṇasiṃ ānetvā sace rājā atthiko hoti, rañño, ekabhūmikaṃ vā…pe… sattabhūmikaṃ vā pāsādaṃ yojetvā denti. No ce, aññesampi vikiṇitvā puttadāraṃ posenti. Atha nesaṃ ekadivasaṃ ācariyo “na sakkā vaḍḍhakikammena niccaṃ jīvikaṃ kappetuṃ, dukkarañhi jarākāle etaṃ kamma”nti cintetvā antevāsike āmantesi – “tātā, udumbarādayo, appasārarukkhe ānethā”ti. Te “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇitvā ānayiṃsu. So tehi kaṭṭhasakuṇaṃ katvā tassa abbhantaraṃ pavisitvā yantaṃ pūresi. Kaṭṭhasakuṇo supaṇṇarājā viya ākāsaṃ laṅghitvā vanassa upari caritvā antevāsīnaṃ purato oruhi. Atha ācariyo sisse āha – “tātā, īdisāni kaṭṭhavāhanāni katvā sakkā sakalajambudīpe rajjaṃ gahetuṃ, tumhepi, tātā, etāni karotha, rajjaṃ gahetvā jīvissāma, dukkhaṃ vaḍḍhakisippena jīvitu”nti. Te tathā katvā ācariyassa paṭivedesuṃ. Tato ne ācariyo āha – “katamaṃ, tātā, rajjaṃ gaṇhāmā”ti? “Bārāṇasirajjaṃ ācariyā”ti. “Alaṃ, tātā, mā etaṃ rucci, mayañhi taṃ gahetvāpi ‘vaḍḍhakirājā vaḍḍhakiyuvarājā’ti vaḍḍhakivādā na muccissāma, mahanto jambudīpo, aññattha gacchāmā”ti.

983. “In the lovely city of the Kosalans…” is the introductory verse of the Pārāyanavagga. Its origin is as follows: In the past, it is said, there was a carpenter from Bārāṇasī, second to none in his craft. He had sixteen disciples, and each of them had a thousand apprentices. Thus, these sixteen thousand and seventeen teachers and apprentices all made their living depending on Bārāṇasī. They would go near a mountain, get trees, and right there, after completing various palace structures, they would bind them into a raft and bring it down the Gaṅgā to Bārāṇasī. If the king was in need, they would construct and present to the king a palace of one story… up to… seven stories. If not, they would sell to others and support their children and wives. Then one day their teacher thought, “It is not possible to make a living by the craft of carpentry forever, for this work is difficult in old age.” He addressed his apprentices: “My dears, bring trees with little heartwood, such as the udumbara.” “Very well,” they replied, and brought them. From these, he made a wooden bird, entered inside it, and set the mechanism. The wooden bird, like the king of the supaṇṇas, soared into the sky, flew over the forest, and descended in front of the apprentices. Then the teacher said to his disciples, “My dears, by making such wooden vehicles, it is possible to take the kingdom of all of Jambudīpa. You too, my dears, make these. We will take a kingdom and live. It is suffering to live by the carpenter’s craft.” They did so and reported back to their teacher. Then the teacher asked them, “Which kingdom shall we take, my dears?” “The kingdom of Bārāṇasī, teacher.” “Enough, my dears, do not wish for that. For even if we took it, we would not be free from being called ‘the carpenter king’ and ‘the carpenter crown prince.’ Jambudīpa is vast; let us go elsewhere.”

Tato saputtadārā kaṭṭhavāhanāni[P 2.0576], abhiruhitvā sajjāvudhā hutvā himavantābhimukhā gantvā himavati aññataraṃ nagaraṃ pavisitvā rañño nivesaneyeva paccuṭṭhahaṃsu. Te tattha rajjaṃ gahetvā ācariyaṃ rajje abhisiñciṃsu. So “kaṭṭhavāhano rājā”ti pākaṭo ahosi. Tampi nagaraṃ [V 2.0268] tena gahitattā “kaṭṭhavāhananagara”ntveva nāmaṃ labhi, tathā sakalaraṭṭhampi[M 2.0292]. Kaṭṭhavāhano rājā dhammiko ahosi, tathā yuvarājā amaccaṭṭhānesu ca ṭhapitā soḷasa sissā. Taṃ raṭṭhaṃ raññā catūhi saṅgahavatthūhi saṅgayhamānaṃ ativiya iddhaṃ phītaṃ nirupaddavañca ahosi. Nāgarā jānapadā rājānañca rājaparisañca ativiya mamāyiṃsu “bhaddako no rājā laddho, bhaddikā rājaparisā”ti.

Then, with their children and wives, they mounted the wooden vehicles, and having armed themselves, they went towards the Himavanta. Entering a certain city in the Himavanta, they rose up right at the king’s residence. There, having seized the kingdom, they consecrated their teacher as king. He became known as “King Kaṭṭhavāhana.” That city, because it was taken by him, received the name “Kaṭṭhavāhananagara,” as did the entire country. King Kaṭṭhavāhana was righteous, as were the sixteen disciples appointed as crown prince and ministers. That country, being managed by the king with the four means of unification, became exceedingly prosperous, affluent, and free from calamity. The townspeople and country folk greatly cherished the king and his retinue, saying, “We have gained a good king and a good royal retinue.”

Athekadivasaṃ majjhimadesato vāṇijā bhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā kaṭṭhavāhananagaraṃ āgamaṃsu paṇṇākārañca gahetvā rājānaṃ passiṃsu. Rājā “kuto āgatatthā”ti sabbaṃ pucchi. “Bārāṇasito devā”ti. So tattha sabbaṃ pavattiṃ pucchitvā – “tumhākaṃ raññā saddhiṃ mama mittabhāvaṃ karothā”ti āha. Te “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchiṃsu. So tesaṃ paribbayaṃ datvā gamanakāle sampatte puna ādarena vatvā vissajjesi. Te bārāṇasiṃ gantvā tassa rañño ārocesuṃ. Rājā “kaṭṭhavāhanaraṭṭhā āgatānaṃ vāṇijakānaṃ ajjatagge suṅkaṃ muñcāmī”ti bheriṃ carāpetvā “atthu me kaṭṭhavāhano mitto”ti dvepi adiṭṭhamittā ahesuṃ. Kaṭṭhavāhanopi ca sakanagare bheriṃ carāpesi – “ajjatagge bārāṇasito āgatānaṃ vāṇijakānaṃ suṅkaṃ muñcāmi, paribbayo ca nesaṃ dātabbo”ti. Tato bārāṇasirājā kaṭṭhavāhanassa lekhaṃ pesesi “sace tasmiṃ janapade daṭṭhuṃ vā sotuṃ vā araharūpaṃ kiñci acchariyaṃ uppajjati, amhepi dakkhāpetu ca sāvetu cā”ti. Sopissa tatheva paṭilekhaṃ pesesi. Evaṃ [P 2.0577] tesaṃ katikaṃ katvā vasantānaṃ kadāci kaṭṭhavāhanassa atimahagghā accantasukhumā kambalā uppajjiṃsu bālasūriyarasmisadisā vaṇṇena. Te disvā rājā “mama sahāyassa pesemī”ti dantakārehi aṭṭha dantakaraṇḍake likhāpetvā tesu karaṇḍakesu te kambale pakkhipitvā lākhācariyehi bahi lākhāgoḷakasadise kārāpetvā aṭṭhapi lākhāgoḷake samugge pakkhipitvā vatthena veṭhetvā rājamuddikāya lañchetvā “bārāṇasirañño dethā”ti amacce pesesi. Lekhañca adāsi “ayaṃ paṇṇākāro nagaramajjhe amaccaparivutena pekkhitabbo”ti.

One day, merchants from the Middle Country, bringing goods and gifts, came to the city of Kaṭṭhavāhana and went to see the king. The king asked, "Whence have you come?" They replied, "From Bārāṇasī, Your Majesty." He inquired about all the news there and then said, "Establish a friendship between me and your king." They agreed, saying, "So be it." He provided them with their expenses and, when the time came for their departure, dismissed them with great respect. Upon returning to Bārāṇasī, they informed their king. The king had a drum beaten to announce: "From today, I exempt merchants coming from the country of Kaṭṭhavāhana from customs duties." He declared, "Let Kaṭṭhavāhana be my friend." Thus, the two became friends though they had not seen each other. Similarly, Kaṭṭhavāhana had a drum beaten in his own city to announce: "From today, I exempt merchants coming from Bārāṇasī from customs duties, and their expenses shall be provided." After this, the king of Bārāṇasī sent a letter to Kaṭṭhavāhana: "If anything marvelous, worthy of being seen or heard, arises in your country, let us also be shown and informed of it." He also sent a reply in the same manner. While they thus lived in agreement, one day, extremely valuable and exceedingly fine blankets appeared in Kaṭṭhavāhana’s kingdom—their color resembling the rays of the morning sun. Seeing them, the king thought, "I shall send them to my friend." He had eight ivory caskets carved by ivory carvers, placed the blankets inside them, and had them covered with lac by lac-workers so that they resembled lac-balls from the outside. He then placed these eight lac-balls in a casket, wrapped it in cloth, sealed it with his royal seal, and sent ministers with the instruction, "Deliver these to the king of Bārāṇasī." He also gave a letter stating: "This gift should be viewed in the middle of the city, surrounded by ministers."

Te gantvā bārāṇasirañño adaṃsu. So lekhaṃ vācetvā amacce sannipātetvā nagaramajjhe rājaṅgaṇe lañchanaṃ bhinditvā paliveṭhanaṃ apanetvā samuggaṃ vivaritvā aṭṭha lākhāgoḷake disvā “mama sahāyo lākhāgoḷakehi kīḷanakabālakānaṃ viya mayhaṃ lākhāgoḷake pesesī”ti maṅku [M 2.0293] hutvā ekaṃ lākhāgoḷakaṃ attano nisinnāsane pahari. Tāvadeva lākhā paripati, dantakaraṇḍako vivaraṃ datvā dvebhāgo ahosi. So abbhantare kambalaṃ disvā itarepi vivari sabbattha tatheva ahosi. Ekameko kambalo dīghato soḷasahattho vitthārato aṭṭhahattho. Pasārite kambale [V 2.0269] rājaṅgaṇaṃ sūriyappabhāya obhāsitamiva ahosi. Taṃ disvā mahājano aṅguliyo vidhuni, celukkhepañca akāsi, “amhākaṃ rañño adiṭṭhasahāyo kaṭṭhavāhanarājā evarūpaṃ paṇṇākāraṃ pesesi, yuttaṃ evarūpaṃ mittaṃ kātu”nti attamano ahosi. Rājā vohārike pakkosāpetvā ekamekaṃ kambalaṃ agghāpesi, sabbepi anagghā ahesuṃ. Tato cintesi – “pacchā pesentena paṭhamaṃ pesitapaṇṇākārato atirekaṃ pesetuṃ vaṭṭati, sahāyena ca me anaggho paṇṇākāro pesito, kiṃ nu, kho, ahaṃ sahāyassa peseyya”nti? Tena ca [P 2.0578] samayena kassapo bhagavā uppajjitvā bārāṇasiyaṃ viharati. Atha rañño etadahosi – “vatthuttayaratanato aññaṃ uttamaratanaṃ natthi, handāhaṃ vatthuttayaratanassa uppannabhāvaṃ sahāyassa pesemī”ti. So –

They went and gave it to the king of Bārāṇasī. He had the letter read, assembled his ministers, and in the royal courtyard in the middle of the city, he broke the seal, removed the wrapping, opened the casket, and saw the eight lac-balls. "My friend has sent me lac-balls as if for children to play with," he thought, feeling displeased, and struck one lac-ball against his seat. Immediately, the lac fell away, and the ivory casket split into two parts. Seeing a blanket inside, he opened the others as well, and it was the same in all of them. Each blanket was sixteen hands long and eight hands wide. When the blankets were spread out, the royal courtyard was illuminated as if by the light of the sun. Seeing this, the great crowd snapped their fingers, tossed their outer garments in the air, and were delighted, saying, "Our king’s unseen friend, King Kaṭṭhavāhana, has sent such a gift; it is fitting to make such a friend." The king summoned the valuers and had each blanket appraised, but they were all priceless. Then he thought, "When sending a gift in return, it is proper to send something superior to the gift first sent. My friend has sent me a priceless gift; what, indeed, should I send to my friend?" At that time, the Blessed One Kassapa had arisen and was dwelling in Bārāṇasī. Then this thought occurred to the king: "There is no supreme jewel other than the Triple Gem. I shall send news of the arising of the Triple Gem to my friend." So he:

“Buddho loke samuppanno, hitāya sabbapāṇinaṃ;

Dhammo loke samuppanno, sukhāya sabbapāṇinaṃ;

Saṅgho loke samuppanno, puññakkhettaṃ anuttara”nti. –

"The Buddha has arisen in the world, for the welfare of all beings; the Dhamma has arisen in the world, for the happiness of all beings; the Saṅgha has arisen in the world, an unsurpassed field of merit."

Imaṃ gāthaṃ, yāva arahattaṃ, tāva ekabhikkhussa paṭipattiñca suvaṇṇapaṭṭe jātihiṅgulakena likhāpetvā sattaratanamaye samugge pakkhipitvā taṃ samuggaṃ maṇimaye samugge, maṇimayaṃ masāragallamaye, masāragallamayaṃ lohitaṅgamaye, lohitaṅgamayaṃ, suvaṇṇamaye, suvaṇṇamayaṃ rajatamaye, rajatamayaṃ dantamaye, dantamayaṃ sāramaye, sāramayaṃ samuggaṃ peḷāya pakkhipitvā peḷaṃ dussena veṭhetvā lañchetvā mattavaravāraṇaṃ sovaṇṇaddhajaṃ sovaṇṇālaṅkāra hemajālasañchannaṃ kāretvā tassupari pallaṅkaṃ paññāpetvā pallaṅke peḷaṃ āropetvā setacchattena dhāriyamānena sabbagandhapupphādīhi pūjāya kariyamānāya sabbatāḷāvacarehi thutisatāni gāyamānehi yāva attano rajjasīmā, tāva maggaṃ alaṅkārāpetvā sayameva nesi. Tatra ca ṭhatvā sāmantarājūnaṃ paṇṇākāraṃ pesesi – “evaṃ sakkarontehi ayaṃ paṇṇākāro pesetabbo”ti[M 2.0294]. Taṃ sutvā te te rājāno paṭimaggaṃ āgantvā yāva kaṭṭhavāhanassa rajjasīmā, tāva nayiṃsu.

This verse, and the practice of a single monk up to Arahantship, he had inscribed on a golden plate with native cinnabar. He had it placed in a casket made of the seven jewels, that casket in one made of jewels, the jewel casket in one of coral, the coral one in one of ruby, the ruby one in one of gold, the gold one in one of silver, the silver one in one of ivory, and the ivory one in one of heartwood. That heartwood casket he placed in a large box. The box was wrapped in cloth and sealed, and he had a majestic, excellent elephant prepared, adorned with a golden banner, golden ornaments, and covered with a net of gold. He had a palanquin placed on its back, and the box was set upon the palanquin. While a white parasol was held over it, offerings of all kinds of perfumes and flowers were made, and hundreds of hymns of praise were sung by all the musicians, he had the road decorated as far as the borders of his own kingdom, and he himself led the procession. Standing there, he sent a message to the neighboring kings: "This gift should be sent onward while honoring it in this manner." Hearing this, those kings came along the path and escorted it as far as the border of Kaṭṭhavāhana's kingdom.

Kaṭṭhavāhanopi sutvā paṭimaggaṃ āgantvā tatheva pūjento nagaraṃ pavesetvā amacce ca nāgare ca sannipātāpetvā rājaṅgaṇe paliveṭhanadussaṃ apanetvā peḷaṃ vivaritvā peḷāya samuggaṃ passitvā anupubbena sabbasamugge vivaritvā suvaṇṇapaṭṭe lekhaṃ passitvā “kappasatasahassehi atidullabhaṃ mama sahāyo paṇṇākāraratanaṃ pesesī”ti attamano hutvā “asutapubbaṃ vata suṇimhā ‘buddho loke uppanno’ti, yaṃnūnāhaṃ gantvā buddhañca passeyyaṃ dhammañca suṇeyya”nti cintetvā amacce āmantesi – “buddhadhammasaṅgharatanāni kira loke [P 2.0579] uppannāni, kiṃ kātabbaṃ maññathā”ti[V 2.0270]. Te āhaṃsu – “idheva tumhe, mahārāja, hotha, mayaṃ gantvā pavattiṃ jānissāmā”ti.

Kaṭṭhavāhana, having heard, came along the path to meet it and, likewise making offerings, entered the city. He assembled the ministers and citizens in the royal courtyard, removed the wrapping cloth, opened the box, and saw the large casket inside. Gradually, he opened all the caskets, saw the inscription on the golden plate, and, delighted, thought, "My friend has sent me a gift-jewel, extremely rare even in hundreds of thousands of eons. Truly, we have heard something unprecedented: 'A Buddha has arisen in the world!' Why do I not go and see the Buddha and hear the Dhamma?" Then he addressed the ministers: "It seems the Triple Gem—the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha—has appeared in the world. What do you think should be done?" They replied, "Stay here, great king. We will go and ascertain the facts."

Tato soḷasasahassaparivārā soḷasa amaccā rājānaṃ abhivādetvā “yadi buddho loke uppanno puna dassanaṃ natthi, yadi na uppanno, āgamissāmā”ti niggatā. Rañño pana bhāgineyyo pacchā rājānaṃ vanditvā “ahampi gacchāmī”ti āha. Tāta, tvaṃ tattha buddhuppādaṃ ñatvā puna āgantvā mama ārocehīti. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā agamāsi. Te sabbepi sabbattha ekarattivāsena gantvā bārāṇasiṃ pattā. Asampattesveva ca tesu bhagavā parinibbāyi. Te “ko buddho, kuhiṃ buddho”ti sakalavihāraṃ āhiṇḍantā sammukhasāvake disvā pucchiṃsu. Te nesaṃ “buddho parinibbuto”ti ācikkhiṃsu. Te “aho dūraddhānaṃ āgantvā dassanamattampi na labhimhā”ti paridevamānā “kiṃ, bhante, koci bhagavatā dinnaovādo atthī”ti pucchiṃsu. Āma, upāsakā atthi, saraṇattaye patiṭṭhātabbaṃ, pañcasīlāni samādātabbāni, aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgato uposatho upavasitabbo, dānaṃ dātabbaṃ, pabbajitabbanti. Te sutvā taṃ bhāgineyyaṃ amaccaṃ ṭhapetvā sabbe pabbajiṃsu. Bhāgineyyo paribhogadhātuṃ gahetvā kaṭṭhavāhanaraṭṭhābhimukho pakkāmi. Paribhogadhātu nāma bodhirukkhapattacīvarādīni. Ayaṃ pana bhagavato dhammakaraṇaṃ dhammadharaṃ vinayadharamekaṃ therañca gahetvā pakkāmi, anupubbena ca nagaraṃ gantvā “buddho loke uppanno ca parinibbutto cā”ti rañño ārocetvā bhagavatā dinnovādaṃ ācikkhi. Rājā theraṃ upasaṅkamitvā dhammaṃ sutvā vihāraṃ kārāpetvā cetiyaṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā [M 2.0295] bodhirukkhaṃ ropetvā saraṇattaye pañcasu ca niccasīlesu patiṭṭhāya aṭṭhaṅgupetaṃ uposathaṃ upavasanto dānādīni dento yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā kāmāvacaradevaloke nibbatti. Tepi soḷasasahassā pabbajitvā puthujjanakālakiriyaṃ katvā tasseva rañño parivārā sampajjiṃsu.

Then, sixteen ministers, accompanied by sixteen thousand attendants, paid homage to the king and said, “If a Buddha has arisen in the world, we will not return; if he has not arisen, we will return.” Having said this, they departed. Later, the king’s nephew paid homage to the king and said, “I too shall go.” The king replied, “My dear, when you learn there of the Buddha's arising, return and inform me.” He agreed, saying, “Very well,” and set off. All of them traveled, staying one night in each place, and reached Bārāṇasī. But even before they arrived, the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna. Wandering through the entire monastery, they asked, “Who is the Buddha? Where is the Buddha?” When they met the direct disciples, they inquired. They informed them, “The Buddha has attained final Nibbāna.” They lamented, “Alas! Having come from afar, we could not even obtain a mere glimpse!” Then they asked, “Venerable sirs, is there any instruction given by the Blessed One?” The disciples replied, “Yes, lay followers, there is: one should take refuge in the Triple Gem, observe the five precepts, keep the Uposatha with its eight factors, give alms, and go forth into homelessness.” Hearing this, all of them—except the nephew, the minister—went forth. The nephew took the relics of personal use and set out toward the kingdom of Kaṭṭhavāhana. Relics of personal use are the leaves of the Bodhi tree, robes, and so on. He also took with him the Blessed One's water-strainer and an elder who was a master of the Dhamma and Vinaya, and set off. Gradually, he reached the city and informed the king, “A Buddha has arisen in the world and has attained final Nibbāna.” He then conveyed the instruction given by the Blessed One. The king approached the elder, listened to the Dhamma, had a monastery built, established a stūpa, planted a Bodhi tree, took refuge in the Triple Gem, and established himself in the five permanent precepts. He also observed the Uposatha with its eight factors, gave alms, and so on. He lived out his lifespan and was reborn in the sensual heavenly realms. Those sixteen thousand who had gone forth, having died as worldlings, were reborn as that king’s retinue.

Te ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ devaloke khepetvā amhākaṃ bhagavati [P 2.0580] anuppanneyeva devalokato cavitvā ācariyo pasenadirañño pitu purohitassa putto jāto nāmena “bāvarī”ti, tīhi mahāpurisalakkhaṇehi samannāgato tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ pāragū, pituno ca accayena purohitaṭṭhāne aṭṭhāsi. Avasesāpi soḷasādhikasoḷasasahassā tattheva sāvatthiyā brāhmaṇakule nibbattā. Tesu soḷasa jeṭṭhantevāsino bāvarissa santike sippaṃ uggahesuṃ, itare soḷasasahassā tesaṃyeva santiketi evaṃ te punapi sabbe samāgacchiṃsu. Mahākosalarājāpi kālamakāsi, tato pasenadiṃ rajje abhisiñciṃsu. Bāvarī tassāpi purohito ahosi. Rājā pitarā dinnañca aññañca [V 2.0271] bhogaṃ bāvarissa adāsi. So hi daharakāle tasseva santike sippaṃ uggahesi. Tato bāvarī rañño ārocesi – “pabbajissāmahaṃ, mahārājā”ti. “Ācariya, tumhesu ṭhitesu mama pitā ṭhito viya hoti, mā pabbajitthā”ti. “Alaṃ, mahārāja, pabbajissāmī”ti. Rājā vāretuṃ asakkonto “sāyaṃ pātaṃ mama dassanaṭṭhāne rājuyyāne pabbajathā”ti yāci. Ācariyo soḷasasahassaparivārehi soḷasahi sissehi saddhiṃ tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā rājuyyāne vasi, rājā catūhi paccayehi upaṭṭhahati. Sāyaṃ pātañcassa upaṭṭhānaṃ gacchati.

They spent one Buddha-period in the heavenly realm. Before our Blessed One had arisen, they passed away from the heavenly realm. The teacher was born as the son of the chaplain to King Pasenadi’s father, named Bāvarī. He was endowed with the three marks of a great man and was a master of the three Vedas. After his father’s passing, he assumed the position of chaplain. The remaining sixteen thousand and sixteen were also reborn in brahmin families in Sāvatthī. Among them, sixteen chief disciples studied the crafts under Bāvarī, while the other sixteen thousand studied under them. Thus, they all came together again. The Great King of Kosala also passed away, and then they anointed Pasenadi as king. Bāvarī became his chaplain as well. The king gave Bāvarī the wealth that had been given by his father and even more, for he had studied the crafts under him from a young age. Then Bāvarī informed the king, “Great king, I wish to go forth.” The king replied, “Teacher, as long as you remain, it is as if my father were still here. Do not go forth.” But Bāvarī insisted, “Enough, great king, I will go forth.” Unable to dissuade him, the king requested, “Go forth in the royal park where I can see you morning and evening.” The teacher, along with his retinue of sixteen thousand and his sixteen disciples, took up the ascetic life and dwelt in the royal park. The king provided him with the four requisites and visited him morning and evening.

Athekadivasaṃ antevāsino ācariyaṃ āhaṃsu – “nagarasamīpe vāso nāma mahāpalibodho, vijanasampātaṃ ācariya okāsaṃ gacchāma, pantasenāsanavāso nāma bahūpakāro pabbajitāna”nti. Ācariyo “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā rañño ārocesi. Rājā tikkhattuṃ vāretvā vāretuṃ asakkonto dvesatasahassāni kahāpaṇāni datvā dve amacce āṇāpesi “yattha isigaṇo vāsaṃ icchati, tattha assamaṃ katvā dethā”ti. Tato ācariyo soḷasādhikasoḷasasahassajaṭilaparivuto amaccehi anuggahamāno uttarajanapadā dakkhiṇajanapadābhimukho [M 2.0296] agamāsi. Tamatthaṃ gahetvā āyasmā ānando saṅgītikāle pārāyanavaggassa nidānaṃ āropento imā gāthāyo abhāsi.

One day, the disciples said to the teacher, “Living near the city is a great distraction. Teacher, let us go to a secluded place, for dwelling in a remote hermitage is very beneficial for those who have gone forth.” The teacher, approvingly accepting, informed the king. Though the king tried to dissuade them three times, being unable to stop them, he gave two hundred thousand coins and ordered two ministers, “Wherever the group of ascetics wishes to dwell, build a hermitage there and give it to them.” Then the teacher, accompanied by sixteen thousand and sixteen matted-hair ascetics, and supported by the ministers, set out from the northern country towards the southern country. Taking up that subject, the Venerable Ānanda, while establishing the origin of the Pārāyana Vagga during the recitation, spoke these verses.

Tattha kosalānaṃ purāti kosalaraṭṭhassa nagarā, sāvatthitoti vuttaṃ hoti. Ākiñcaññanti akiñcanabhāvaṃ, pariggahūpakaraṇavivekanti vuttaṃ hoti.

There, 'the city of the Kosalans' means the city of the Kosala kingdom, that is, Sāvatthī. 'Ākiñcañña' means the state of having nothing, that is, seclusion from possessions and requisites.

984. So assakassa visaye[P 2.0581], aḷakassa samāsaneti so brāhmaṇo assakassa ca aḷakassa cāti dvinnampi rājūnaṃ samāsanne visaye āsanne raṭṭhe, dvinnampi raṭṭhānaṃ majjheti adhippāyo. Godhāvarī kūleti godhāvariyā nadiyā kūle. Yattha godhāvarī dvidhā bhijjitvā tiyojanappamāṇaṃ antaradīpamakāsi sabbaṃ kapiṭṭhavanasañchannaṃ, yattha pubbesarabhaṅgādayo vasiṃsu, tasmiṃ deseti adhippāyo. So kira taṃ padesaṃ disvā “ayaṃ pubbasamaṇālayo pabbajitasāruppa”nti amaccānaṃ nivedesi. Amaccā bhūmiggahaṇatthaṃ assakarañño satasahassaṃ, aḷakarañño satasahassaṃ adaṃsu. Te tañca padesaṃ aññañca dviyojanamattanti sabbampi pañcayojanamattaṃ padesaṃ adaṃsu. Tesaṃ kira rajjasīmantare so padeso hoti. Amaccā tattha assamaṃ kāretvā sāvatthito ca aññampi dhanaṃ āharāpetvā gocaragāmaṃ nivesetvā agamaṃsu. Uñche [V 2.0272] na ca phalena cāti uñchācariyāya ca vanamūlaphalena ca. Tasmā vuttaṃ “tasseva upanissāya, gāmo ca vipulo ahū”ti.

984. In the domain of Assaka and near Aḷaka—that brahmin lived in the vicinity of both King Assaka and King Aḷaka, meaning he resided in the border region between the two kingdoms, in the middle of both territories. On the banks of the Godhāvarī—this refers to the bank of the Godhāvarī River. Where the Godhāvarī split into two, creating an island three leagues wide, entirely covered with kapiṭṭha trees, where the ancient seers like Sarabhaṅga once dwelled—in that region is the meaning. Seeing this area, the brahmin reportedly told his ministers, “This is an ancient hermitage, suitable for ascetics.” The ministers, to secure the land, gave a hundred thousand to King Assaka and a hundred thousand to King Aḷaka. They granted him that area and an additional two leagues, making a total of five leagues. This land reportedly lay on the border between their kingdoms. The ministers built a hermitage there, brought more wealth from Sāvatthī and elsewhere, established a village for sustenance, and departed. 'By gleaning and by fruit' means by the practice of gleaning and by the roots and fruits of the forest. Hence, it was said, “Relying on him, the village became prosperous.”

985. Tattha tassāti tassa godhāvarīkūlassa, tassa vā brāhmaṇassa upayogatthe cetaṃ sāmivacanaṃ, taṃ upanissāyāti attho. Tato jātena āyena, mahāyaññamakappayīti tasmiṃ gāme kasikammādinā satasahassaṃ āyo uppajji, taṃ gahetvā kuṭumbikā rañño assakassa santikaṃ agamaṃsu “sādiyatu devo āya”nti. So “nāhaṃ sādiyāmi, ācariyasseva upanethā”ti āha. Ācariyopi taṃ attano aggahetvā dānayaññaṃ akappayi. Evaṃ so saṃvacchare saṃvacchare dānamadāsi.

985. Therein, 'tassa' (his) refers to the bank of the Godhāvarī or to that brahmin; this is a genitive of use, meaning it was dependent on him. From the income generated there, he performed a great sacrifice—meaning that in that village, an income of a hundred thousand arose from farming and other work. Taking this, the householders went to King Assaka and said, “May the king accept the revenue.” But the king replied, “I will not accept it; let it be offered to the teacher.” The teacher, not keeping it for himself, used it to perform a sacrificial offering. Thus, year after year, he gave alms.

986. Mahāyaññanti [M 2.0297] gāthāyattho – so evaṃ saṃvacchare saṃvacchare dānayaññaṃ yajanto ekasmiṃ saṃvacchare taṃ mahāyaññaṃ yajitvā tato gāmā nikkhamma puna pāvisi assamaṃ. Paviṭṭho [P 2.0582] ca paṇṇasālaṃ pavisitvā “suṭṭhu dinna”nti dānaṃ anumajjanto nisīdi. Evaṃ tasmiṃ paṭipaviṭṭhamhi taruṇāya brāhmaṇiyā ghare kammaṃ akātukāmāya “eso, brāhmaṇa, bāvarī godhāvarītīre anusaṃvaccharaṃ satasahassaṃ vissajjeti, gaccha tato pañcasatāni yācitvā dāsiṃ me ānehī”ti pesito añño āgañchi brāhmaṇoti.

986. 'The great sacrifice'—the meaning of the verse is this: He, while performing such annual sacrificial gifts, in one particular year, after performing that great sacrifice, having left the village, again entered his hermitage. And having entered, he went into the leaf-hut and, reflecting, 'The gift was well given,' he sat down. Meanwhile, as he had re-entered, another brahmin arrived, sent by a young brahmin woman who was unwilling to do the work in her house, saying, 'This Bāvarī, on the banks of the Godhāvarī, dispenses a hundred thousand every year. Go there, ask for five hundred, and bring me a female servant.'

987-8. Ugghaṭṭapādoti maggagamanena ghaṭṭapādatalo, paṇhikāya vā paṇhikaṃ, gopphakena vā gopphakaṃ, jaṇṇukena vā jaṇṇukaṃ āhacca ghaṭṭapādo. Sukhañca kusalaṃ pucchīti sukhañca kusalañca pucchi “kacci te, brāhmaṇa, sukhaṃ, kacci kusala”nti.

987-8. 'Ugghaṭṭapādo' means one whose soles are chafed from walking the path, or whose heel strikes heel, or ankle strikes ankle, or knee strikes knee. 'Sukhañca kusalaṃ pucchīti' means he asked about happiness and well-being: 'Are you at ease, brahmin? Are you well?'

989-91. Anujānāhīti anumaññāhi saddahāhi. Sattadhāti sattavidhena. Abhisaṅkharitvāti gomayavanapupphakusatiṇādīni ādāya sīghaṃ sīghaṃ bāvarissa assamadvāraṃ gantvā gomayena bhūmiṃ upalimpitvā pupphāni vikiritvā tiṇāni santharitvā vāmapādaṃ kamaṇḍalūdakena dhovitvā sattapādamattaṃ gantvā attano pādatale parāmasanto evarūpaṃ kuhanaṃ katvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Bheravaṃ so akittayīti bhayajanakaṃ vacanaṃ akittayi, “sace me yācamānassā”ti imaṃ gāthamabhāsīti adhippāyo. Dukkhitoti domanassajāto.

989-91. 'Anujānāhīti' means permit, approve, believe. 'Sattadhāti' means sevenfold. 'Abhisaṅkharitvāti' means: having taken cow dung, forest flowers, kusa grass, and so on, having gone quickly to Bāvarī’s hermitage door, having smeared the ground with cow dung, having scattered flowers, having spread grass, having washed his left foot with water from a water pot, having walked about seven paces, and touching his own sole while performing such deceit—this is what is meant. 'Bheravaṃ so akittayīti' means he uttered fearful words, meaning he spoke the verse, 'If to me, who am begging...'. 'Dukkhitoti' means arisen from sorrow.

992-4. Ussussatīti tassa taṃ vacanaṃ kadāci saccaṃ bhaveyyāti maññamāno sussati[V 2.0273]. Devatāti assame adhivatthā devatā eva. Muddhani muddhapāte vāti muddhe vā muddhapāte vā.

992-4. 'Ussussatīti' means he becomes anxious, thinking that his statement might sometimes be true. 'Devatāti' refers to the deity dwelling in the hermitage. 'Muddhani muddhapāte vāti' means on the head or at the splitting of the head.

995-6. Bhotī carahi jānātīti bhotī ce jānāti. Muddhādhipātañcāti muddhapātañca. Ñāṇametthāti ñāṇaṃ me ettha.

995-6. 'Bhotī carahi jānātīti' means if, lady, you know. 'Muddhādhipātañcāti' means and the splitting of the head. 'Ñāṇametthāti' means my knowledge is here.

998. Purāti ekūnatiṃsavassavayakāle. Bāvaribrāhmaṇe pana godhāvarītīre vasamāne aṭṭhannaṃ vassānaṃ accayena buddho loke udapādi. Apaccoti anuvaṃso.

998. 'Purāti' refers to the time when he was twenty-nine years old. While the brahmin Bāvarī was dwelling on the banks of the Godhāvarī, after eight years had passed the Buddha appeared in the world. 'Apaccoti' means descendant or posterity.

999. Sabbābhiññābalappattoti [M 2.0298] sabbābhiññāya balappatto, sabbā vā abhiññāyo ca balāni ca patto. Vimuttoti ārammaṇaṃ [P 2.0583] katvā pavattiyā vimuttacitto.

999. 'Sabbābhiññābalappattoti' means one who has attained power through all the higher knowledges, or one who has attained all the higher knowledges and powers. 'Vimuttoti' means his mind was liberated from the process of existence by making it an object of insight.

1001-3. Sokassāti soko assa. Pahūtapaññoti mahāpañño. Varabhūrimedhasoti uttamavipulapañño bhūte abhiratavarapañño vā. Vidhuroti vigatadhuro, appaṭimoti vuttaṃ hoti.

1001-3. 'Sokassāti' means sorrow is his. 'Pahūtapaññoti' means one of great wisdom. 'Varabhūrimedhasoti' means one of supreme and abundant wisdom, or one with excellent wisdom delighting in realities. 'Vidhuroti' means free from a yoke; 'matchless,' it is said.

1004-9. Mantapārageti vedapārage. Passavhoti passatha ajānatanti ajānantānaṃ. Lakkhaṇāti lakkhaṇāni. Byākkhātāti kathitāni, vitthāritānīti vuttaṃ hoti. Samattāti samattāni, paripuṇṇānīti vuttaṃ hoti. Dhammena manusāsatīti dhammena anusāsati.

1004-9. 'Mantapārageti' means one who has mastered the Vedas. 'Passavhoti' means 'see,' addressed to those who do not know. 'Lakkhaṇāti' means the characteristics. 'Byākkhātāti' means explained; elaborated, it is said. 'Samattāti' means complete; fulfilled, it is said. 'Dhammena manusāsatīti' means he instructs with the Dhamma.

1011. Jātiṃ gottañca lakkhaṇanti “kīva ciraṃ jāto”ti mama jātiñca gottañca lakkhaṇañca. Mante sisseti mayā paricitavede ca mama sisse ca. Manasāyeva pucchathāti ime satta pañhe citteneva pucchatha.

1011. 'Jātiṃ gottañca lakkhaṇaṃ' means my birth (for example, 'How long has he been born?'), my clan, and my marks. 'Mante sisseti' means the Vedas with which I am familiar and my pupils. 'Manasāyeva pucchathāti' means ask these seven questions with the mind alone.

1013-8. Tissametteyyoti ekoyeva esa nāmagottavasena vutto. Dubhayoti ubho. Paccekagaṇinoti visuṃ visuṃ gaṇavanto. Pubbavāsanavāsitāti pubbe kassapassa bhagavato sāsane pabbajitvā. Gatapaccāgatavattapuññavāsanāya vāsitacittā. Puramāhissatinti māhissatināmikaṃ puraṃ, nagaranti vuttaṃ hoti. Tañca nagaraṃ paviṭṭhāti adhippāyo, evaṃ sabbattha. Gonaddhanti godhapurassa nāmaṃ. Vanasavhayanti pavananagaraṃ vuccati, “vanasāvatthi”nti eke. Evaṃ vanasāvatthito kosambiṃ, kosambito ca sāketaṃ anuppattānaṃ kira tesaṃ soḷasannaṃ jaṭilānaṃ chayojanamattā parisā ahosi.

1013-8. Tissametteyya is mentioned as a single individual by name and clan. “Both” refers to the two. “Individual leaders of groups” means they each had their own following. “Shaped by past tendencies” means their minds were imbued with the wholesome tendencies of their practice of going forth and returning, having previously gone forth in the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa. “The city of Māhissatī” refers to a city named Māhissatī, that is, a town. The meaning is that they entered that city, and similarly everywhere. “Gonaddha” is the name of Godhapura. “Vanasavhaya” is said to be Pavanana town; some call it “Vanasāvatthī.” Thus, it is said that when those sixteen matted-hair ascetics arrived from Vanasāvatthī to Kosambī, and from Kosambī to Sāketa, their following was about six yojanas in extent.

1019. Atha [V 2.0274] bhagavā “bāvarissa jaṭilā mahājanaṃ saṃvaḍḍhentā āgacchanti, na ca tāva nesaṃ indriyāni paripākaṃ gacchanti, nāpi ayaṃ deso sappāyo, magadhakhette pana tesaṃ pāsāṇakacetiyaṃ sappāyaṃ. Tatra [M 2.0299] hi mayi dhammaṃ desente mahājanassa dhammābhisamayo bhavissati, sabbanagarāni ca pavisitvā āgacchantā bahutarena janena āgamissantī”ti bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto sāvatthito rājagahābhimukho [P 2.0584] agamāsi. Tepi jaṭilā sāvatthiṃ āgantvā vihāraṃ pavisitvā “ko buddho, kuhiṃ buddho”ti vicinantā gandhakuṭimūlaṃ gantvā bhagavato padanikkhepaṃ disvā “rattassa hi ukkuṭikaṃ padaṃ bhave…pe… vivaṭṭacchadassa idamīdisaṃ pada”nti (a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.260-261; dha. pa. aṭṭha. 1.20 sāmāvatīvatthu; visuddhi. 1.45) “sabbaññu buddho”ti niṭṭhaṃ gatā. Bhagavāpi anupubbena setabyakapilavatthuādīni nagarāni pavisitvā mahājanaṃ saṃvaḍḍhento pāsāṇakacetiyaṃ gato. Jaṭilāpi tāvadeva sāvatthito nikkhamitvā sabbāni tāni nagarāni pavisitvā pāsāṇakacetiyameva agamaṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ “kosambiñcāpi sāketaṃ, sāvatthiñca puruttamaṃ. Setabyaṃ kapilavatthu”ntiādi.

1019. Then the Blessed One thought: “Bāvarī’s matted-hair ascetics are coming, increasing their following, but their faculties are not yet ripe, nor is this region suitable. However, the Pāsāṇaka Cetiya in the Magadha region is suitable for them. There, when I teach the Dhamma, the great multitude will attain the realization of the Dhamma, and as they enter all the cities, they will come with many more people.” Surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he set out from Sāvatthī towards Rājagaha. Those matted-hair ascetics, having arrived in Sāvatthī and entered the monastery, searched around asking, “Who is the Buddha? Where is the Buddha?” Going to the foot of the perfumed chamber, they saw the footprints of the Blessed One and concluded: “For one who is passionate, the footprint would be on tiptoe… for one whose covering is removed, the footprint is like this.” They became convinced: “This is the All-Knowing Buddha.” The Blessed One, too, gradually entered cities such as Setabyā and Kapilavatthu, increasing his following, and went to Pāsāṇaka Cetiya. The matted-hair ascetics, too, left Sāvatthī at that very time, entered all those cities, and arrived at Pāsāṇaka Cetiya. Hence it is said: “Kosambī and Sāketa, Sāvatthī, the best of cities, Setabyā and Kapilavatthu,” and so on.

1020. Tattha māgadhaṃ puranti magadhapuraṃ rājagahanti adhippāyo. Pāsāṇakaṃ cetiyanti mahato pāsāṇassa upari pubbe devaṭṭhānaṃ ahosi. Uppanne pana bhagavati vihāro jāto. So teneva purimavohārena “pāsāṇakaṃ cetiya”nti vuccati.

1020. There, “the Magadha city” means the city of Magadha, that is, Rājagaha. Pāsāṇaka Cetiya was formerly a shrine of deities on top of a large rock. But when the Blessed One appeared, a monastery came into being. It is called “Pāsāṇaka Cetiya” by that same former designation.

1021. Tasitovudakanti te hi jaṭilā vegasā bhagavantaṃ anubandhamānā sāyaṃ gatamaggaṃ pāto, pāto gatamaggañca sāyaṃ gacchantā “ettha bhagavā”ti sutvā ativiya pītipāmojjajātā taṃ cetiyaṃ abhiruhiṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ “turitā pabbatamāruhu”nti.

1021. “Like those thirsty for water”: For those matted-hair ascetics, eagerly following the Blessed One, traveled the path they had taken in the evening by morning, and the path they had taken in the morning by evening. Hearing, “The Blessed One is here,” they were filled with intense joy and delight, and climbed up to that shrine. Hence it is said: “They hurriedly ascended the mountain.”

1024. Ekamantaṃ ṭhito haṭṭhoti tasmiṃ pāsāṇake cetiye sakkena māpitamahāmaṇḍape nisinnaṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā “kacci isayo khamanīya”ntiādinā nayena bhagavatā paṭisammodanīye kate “khamanīyaṃ bho gotamā”tiādīhi sayampi paṭisanthāraṃ katvā ajito jeṭṭhantevāsī ekamantaṃ ṭhito haṭṭhacitto hutvā manopañhe pucchi.

1024. “Standing to one side, delighted”: Seeing the Blessed One seated in the great pavilion created by Sakka at that Pāsāṇaka Cetiya, and after the Blessed One had exchanged greetings with him in words such as, “I hope the seers are well,” he too returned the greeting, saying, “We are well, Gotama,” and so on. Ajita, the senior disciple, standing to one side with a joyful mind, asked his mental questions.

1025. Tattha ādissāti “kativasso”ti evaṃ uddissa. Jammananti “amhākaṃ ācariyassa jātiṃ brūhī”ti pucchati. Pāraminti niṭṭhāgamanaṃ.

1025. There, “declaring” means specifying, as in “How many years old?” “Birth” means he asks, “Tell us the birth of our teacher.” “Perfection” means the attainment.

1026-7. Vīsaṃ [V 2.0275] vassasatanti vīsativassādhikaṃ vassasataṃ. Lakkhaṇeti mahāpurisalakkhaṇe. Etasmiṃ ito paresu ca itihāsādīsu anavayoti [M 2.0300] adhippāyo parapadaṃ vā [P 2.0585] ānetvā tesu pāramiṃ gatoti yojetabbaṃ. Pañcasatāni vācetīti pakatialasadummedhamāṇavakānaṃ pañcasatāni sayaṃ mante vāceti. Sadhammeti eke brāhmaṇadhamme, tevijjake pāvacaneti vuttaṃ hoti.

1026-7. “A hundred and twenty years” means one hundred years plus twenty years. “Marks” refers to the marks of a great man. In this and in other matters such as history, the meaning is that he is not deficient; or, by supplying another word, it should be construed as “he has gone to perfection in them.” “He teaches five hundred” means he himself teaches the mantras to five hundred brahmin youths who are by nature lazy and unwise. “True Dhamma”—some say it refers to brahminical practices, that is, what is called the teaching of the three Vedas.

1028. Lakkhaṇānaṃ pavicayanti lakkhaṇānaṃ vitthāraṃ, “katamāni tānissa gatte tīṇi lakkhaṇānī”ti pucchati.

1028. “An analysis of the marks” means a detailed explanation of the marks; he asks, “What are those three marks on his body?”

1030-31. Pucchañhīti pucchamānaṃ kametaṃ paṭibhāsatīti devādīsu kaṃ puggalaṃ etaṃ pañhavacanaṃ paṭibhāsatīti.

1030-31. “Ask, indeed” means: “To whom does this occur when asked?” That is, “To which person among the gods and so on does this question occur?”

1032-33. Evaṃ brāhmaṇo pañcannaṃ pañhānaṃ veyyākaraṇaṃ sutvā avasese dve pucchanto “muddhaṃ muddhādhipātañcā”ti āha. Athassa bhagavā te byākaronto “avijjā muddhā”ti gāthamāha. Tattha yasmā catūsu saccesu aññāṇabhūtā avijjā saṃsārassa sīsaṃ, tasmā “avijjā muddhā”ti āha. Yasmā ca arahattamaggavijjā attanā sahajātehi saddhāsatisamādhikattukamyatāchandavīriyehi samannāgatā indriyānaṃ ekarasaṭṭhabhāvamupagatattā taṃ muddhaṃ adhipāteti, tasmā “dhijjā muddhādhipātinī”tiādimāha.

1032-33. Thus, the brahmin, having heard the explanation of the five questions, asked the remaining two, saying, “The head and the smiter of the head.” Then the Blessed One, explaining them to him, spoke the verse: “Ignorance is the head.” Here, because ignorance, being the state of unknowing regarding the four truths, is the head of saṃsāra, therefore he said, “Ignorance is the head.” And because the knowledge of the path to arahantship, together with faith, mindfulness, concentration, the will to act, desire, and energy, which arise simultaneously with itself, having attained a state of single essence of the faculties, strikes down that head, therefore he said, “Knowledge is the smiter of the head,” and so on.

1034-8. Tato vedena mahatāti atha imaṃ pañhaveyyākaraṇaṃ sutvā uppannāya mahāpītiyā santhambhitvā alīnabhāvaṃ, kāyacittānaṃ udaggaṃ patvāti attho. Patitvā ca “bāvarī”ti imaṃ gāthamāha. Atha naṃ anukampamāno bhagavā “sukhito”ti gāthamāha. Vatvā ca “bāvarissa cā”ti sabbaññupavāraṇaṃ pavāresi. Tattha sabbesanti anavasesānaṃ soḷasasahassānaṃ. Tattha pucchi tathāgatanti tattha pāsāṇake cetiye, tattha vā parisāya, tesu vā pavāritesu ajito paṭhamaṃ pañhaṃ pucchīti. Sesaṃ sabbagāthāsu pākaṭamevāti.

1034-8. “Then, with great joy”: Upon hearing this explanation of the questions, he was steadied by the great joy that had arisen, and being free from sluggishness, his body and mind reached elation—this is the meaning. Having attained this, he spoke this verse, “Bāvarī.” Then, out of compassion for him, the Blessed One spoke the verse, “Happy one.” Having spoken, he then proclaimed the all-knowing one's invitation, “And for Bāvarī’s…” Here, “all” refers to the entire sixteen thousand without exception. Here, “the Tathāgata was asked” means that at the Pāsāṇaka Cetiya, or in that assembly, or among those invited, Ajita asked the first question. The rest is evident in all the verses.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

The Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Minor Collection.

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya vatthugāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the introductory verses in the Suttanipāta Commentary is completed.

1. Ajitasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Exposition of the Ajita Sutta

1039. Tasmiṃ [V 2.0276][M 2.0301][P 2.0586] pana pañhe nivutoti paṭicchādito. Kissābhilepanaṃ brūsīti kiṃ assa lokassa abhilepanaṃ vadesi.

1039. Now, in that question, ‘nivuto’ means concealed. ‘Kissābhilepanaṃ brūsi’ means ‘What do you say is the smearing of this world?’

1040. Vevicchā pamādā nappakāsatīti macchariyahetu ca pamādahetu ca nappakāsati. Macchariyaṃ hissa dānādiguṇehi pakāsituṃ na deti, pamādo sīlādīhi. Jappābhilepananti taṇhā assa lokassa makkaṭalepo viya makkaṭassa abhilepanaṃ. Dukkhanti jātiādikaṃ dukkhaṃ.

1040. ‘It does not shine forth due to doubt and heedlessness’ means that due to the cause of stinginess and the cause of heedlessness, it does not shine forth. Indeed, stinginess does not allow one to shine forth with qualities like generosity, and heedlessness with morality and so on. ‘Craving is the smearing’ means craving is a smearing for this world, like the smearing on a monkey. ‘Suffering’ means suffering, such as birth and so on.

1041. Savanti sabbadhi sotāti sabbesu rūpādiāyatanesu taṇhādikā sotā sandanti. Kiṃ nivāraṇanti tesaṃ kiṃ āvaraṇaṃ kā rakkhāti? Saṃvaraṃ brūhīti taṃ tesaṃ nivāraṇasaṅkhātaṃ saṃvaraṃ brūhi. Etena sāvasesappahānaṃ pucchati. Kena sotā pidhiyyareti kena dhammena ete sotā pidhiyyanti pacchijjanti. Etena anavasesappahānaṃ pucchati.

1041. ‘Streams flow everywhere’ means streams of craving and so on flow in all sense bases such as forms and so on. ‘What is their prevention?’ means ‘What is their obstruction? What is their protection?’ ‘Tell me the restraint’ means ‘Tell me that restraint which is called their prevention.’ By this, he asks about abandoning with remainder. ‘By what are the streams blocked?’ means ‘By what Dhamma are these streams blocked and cut off?’ By this, he asks about abandoning without remainder.

1042. Sati tesaṃ nivāraṇanti vipassanāyuttā. Kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ gatiyo samannesamānā sati tesaṃ sotānaṃ nivāraṇaṃ. Sotānaṃ saṃvaraṃ brūmīti tamevāhaṃ satiṃ sotānaṃ saṃvaraṃ brūmīti adhippāyo. Paññāyete pidhiyyareti rūpādīsu pana aniccatādipaṭivedhasādhikāya maggapaññāya ete sotā sabbaso pidhiyyantīti.

1042. ‘Mindfulness is their prevention’ refers to mindfulness associated with insight. Mindfulness, examining the courses of wholesome states, is the prevention of those streams. ‘I declare the restraint of the streams’—the intention is: ‘I declare that very mindfulness to be the restraint of the streams.’ ‘They are blocked by wisdom’ means that these streams are completely blocked by the wisdom of the path, which is effective in penetrating impermanence and so forth in forms and so on.

1043. Paññā cevāti pañhagāthāya, yā cāyaṃ tayā vuttā paññā yā ca sati, yañca tadavasesaṃ nāmarūpaṃ, etaṃ sabbampi kattha nirujjhati, etaṃ me pañhaṃ puṭṭho brūhīti evaṃ saṅkhepattho veditabbo.

1043. ‘And wisdom too’ is from the question verse. The wisdom you have spoken of, and that mindfulness, and whatever remains of name-and-form—where does all this cease? Being asked this question, explain it to me—this is the concise meaning to be understood.

1044. Vissajjanagāthāya panassa yasmā paññāsatiyo nāmeneva saṅgahaṃ gacchanti, tasmā tā visuṃ na vuttā. Ayamettha saṅkhepattho – yaṃ maṃ tvaṃ, ajita, etaṃ pañhaṃ apucchi “katthetaṃ uparujjhatī”ti, taṃ te yattha nāmañca rūpañca asesaṃ uparujjhati, taṃ [P 2.0587] vadanto vadāmi[V 2.0277], tassa, tassa hi viññāṇassa nirodhena saheva apubbaṃ acarimaṃ etthetaṃ uparujjhati. Ettheva viññāṇanirodhe nirujjhati etaṃ, viññāṇanirodhā tassa nirodho hoti. Taṃ nātivattatīti vuttaṃ hoti.

1044. Now, in the answer verse, since wisdom and mindfulness are included under the term ‘name,’ they are not mentioned separately. Here is the concise meaning: ‘Ajita, regarding the question you asked me, “Where does this cease?”, I speak, telling you where name and form cease without remainder. Indeed, with the cessation of that consciousness, this ceases right here, simultaneously, without preceding or succeeding. It ceases right here with the cessation of consciousness; its cessation occurs from the cessation of consciousness. It does not go beyond that’—so it is said.

1045. Ettāvatā [M 2.0302] ca “dukkhamassa mahabbhaya”nti iminā pakāsitaṃ dukkhasaccaṃ, “yāni sotānī”ti iminā samudayasaccaṃ paññāyete pidhiyyareti iminā maggasaccaṃ, “asesaṃ uparujjhatī”ti iminā nirodhasaccanti evaṃ cattāri saccāni sutvāpi ariyabhūmiṃ anadhigato puna sekhāsekhapaṭipadaṃ pucchanto “ye ca saṅkhātadhammāse”ti gāthamāha. Tattha saṅkhātadhammāti aniccādivasena parivīmaṃsitadhammā, arahataṃ etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sekhāti sīlādīni sikkhamānā avasesā ariyapuggalā. Puthūti bahū sattajanā. Tesaṃ me nipako iriyaṃ puṭṭho pabrūhīti tesaṃ me sekhāsekhānaṃ nipako paṇḍito tvaṃ puṭṭho paṭipattiṃ brūhīti.

1045. Thus, by ‘suffering is its great fear,’ the truth of suffering is revealed; by ‘whatever streams there are,’ the truth of origin; by ‘they are blocked by wisdom,’ the truth of the path; and by ‘ceases without remainder,’ the truth of cessation. Having heard these four truths, yet not having attained the noble stage, he, asking again about the practice of trainees and those beyond training, says the verse ‘And those who have discerned the Dhamma...’ Here, ‘those who have discerned the Dhamma’ refers to those who have investigated phenomena in terms of impermanence and so on—this is a designation for arahants. ‘Trainees’ are the remaining noble individuals who are training in virtue and so on. ‘Many’ refers to numerous beings. ‘Being asked by me, O expert one, explain their conduct’—this means, ‘You, being an expert and wise, explain to me, when asked, the practice of those trainees and those beyond training.’

1046. Athassa bhagavā yasmā sekhena kāmacchandanīvaraṇaṃ ādiṃ katvā sabbakilesā pahātabbā eva, tasmā “kāmesū”ti upaḍḍhagāthāya sekhapaṭipadaṃ dasseti. Tassattho – vatthu “kāmesu” kilesakāmena nābhigijjheyya kāyaduccaritādayo ca manaso āvilabhāvakare dhamme pajahanto manasā nāvilo siyāti. Yasmā pana asekho aniccādivasena sabbasaṅkhārādīnaṃ paritulitattā kusalo sabbadhammesu kāyānupassanāsatiādīhi ca sato sakkāyadiṭṭhiādīnaṃ bhinnattā bhikkhubhāvaṃ patto ca hutvā sabbiriyāpathesu paribbajati, tasmā “kusalo”ti upaḍḍhagāthāya asekhapaṭipadaṃ dasseti. Sesaṃ sabbattha pākaṭameva.

1046. Then, because for a trainee all defilements, beginning with the hindrance of sensual desire, must be abandoned, the Blessed One teaches the trainee’s practice in the half-verse beginning with ‘in sensual pleasures.’ Its meaning is: In regard to sensual pleasures, one should not be greedy with the greed of defilement; and abandoning bodily misconduct and other states that create mental turbidity, one's mind should not be turbid. However, because one beyond training, having weighed all conditioned things in terms of impermanence and so on, is skilled in all phenomena, and because, being mindful through contemplation of the body and so on, he has shattered identity view and so on, and having attained the state of a bhikkhu, he wanders in all postures, the Blessed One teaches the practice of one beyond training in the half-verse beginning with ‘skilled.’ The rest is quite clear everywhere.

Evaṃ bhagavā arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi, desanāpariyosāne ajito arahatte patiṭṭhāsi saddhiṃ antevāsisahassena, aññesañca anekasahassānaṃ dhammacakkhuṃ udapādi. Saha arahattappattiyā ca āyasmato ajitassa [P 2.0588] antevāsisahassassa ca ajinajaṭāvākacīrādīni antaradhāyiṃsu. Sabbeva iddhimayapattacīvaradharā, dvaṅgulakesā ehibhikkhū hutvā bhagavantaṃ namassamānā pañjalikā nisīdiṃsūti.

Thus the Blessed One concluded his teaching with the pinnacle of arahantship. At the end of the discourse, Ajita became established in arahantship together with his thousand disciples, and the eye of the Dhamma arose in many thousands of others. And upon the attainment of arahantship by Venerable Ajita and his thousand disciples, their antelope-skins, matted hair, bark garments, and so on, disappeared. All of them, wearing bowls and robes created by psychic power, with hair two fingers in length, having become ‘Come, bhikkhus!’, sat paying homage to the Blessed One with hands clasped in reverence.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

The Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Minor Collection.

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya ajitasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Ajita Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary is completed.

2. Tissametteyyasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Exposition of the Tissametteyya Sutta

1047. Kodha [V 2.0278][M 2.0303] santussitoti tissametteyyasuttaṃ. Kā uppatti? Sabbasuttānaṃ pucchāvasikā eva uppatti. Te hi brāhmaṇā “katāvakāsā pucchavho”ti bhagavatā pavāritattā attano attano saṃsayaṃ pucchiṃsu. Puṭṭho puṭṭho ca tesaṃ bhagavā byākāsi. Evaṃ pucchāvasikānevetāni suttānīti veditabbāni.

1047. The Tissametteyya Sutta, 'Who is content here?' What is its origin? The origin of all suttas is indeed due to questioning. For those brahmins, having been invited by the Blessed One with the words, 'You have been given the opportunity; ask!', each asked about their own doubts. And the Blessed One answered them as each was asked. Thus, it should be understood that these suttas are indeed based on questioning.

Niṭṭhite pana ajitapañhe “kathaṃ lokaṃ avekkhantaṃ, maccurājā na passatī”ti (su. ni. 1124; cūḷani. piṅgiyamāṇavapucchā 144) evaṃ mogharājā pucchituṃ ārabhi. Taṃ “na tāvassa indriyāni paripākaṃ gatānī”ti ñatvā bhagavā “tiṭṭha tvaṃ, mogharāja, añño pucchatū”ti paṭikkhipi. Tato tissametteyyo attano saṃsayaṃ pucchanto “kodhā”ti gāthamāha. Tattha kodha santussitoti ko idha tuṭṭho. Iñjitāti taṇhādiṭṭhivipphanditāni. Ubhantamabhiññāyāti ubho ante abhijānitvā. Mantā na lippatīti paññāya na lippati.

When Ajita's question was concluded, Mogharāja began to ask thus: 'How should one look upon the world so that the King of Death does not see one?' (Sn 1124; Cūḷaniddesa, Piṅgiyamāṇavapucchā 144). Knowing that 'his faculties had not yet matured,' the Blessed One rejected him, saying, 'Wait, Mogharāja, let another ask.' Then Tissametteyya, asking his own doubt, spoke the verse beginning with 'Kodha.' Therein, 'kodha santussito' means 'who here is content?' 'Iñjitā' means the agitations of craving, views, and so on. 'Ubhantamabhiññāya' means having fully understood both extremes. 'Mantā na lippati' (the wise one is not stained) means that by means of wisdom, he is not stained.

1048-9. Tassetamatthaṃ byākaronto bhagavā “kāmesū”ti gāthādvayamāha. Tattha kāmesu brahmacariyavāti kāmanimittaṃ brahmacariyavā, kāmesu ādīnavaṃ disvā maggabrahmacariyena samannāgatoti vuttaṃ hoti. Ettāvatā santusitaṃ dasseti, “vītataṇho”tiādīhi aniñjitaṃ[P 2.0589]. Tattha saṅkhāya nibbutoti aniccādivasena dhamme vīmaṃsitvā rāgādinibbānena nibbuto. Sesaṃ tattha tattha vuttanayattā pākaṭameva.

1048-9. Explaining this meaning, the Blessed One spoke the two verses beginning with 'Kāmesu.' Therein, 'kāmesu brahmacariyavā' (one who lives the holy life in regard to sensual pleasures) means one who lives the holy life with respect to the object of sensual pleasures; that is to say, having seen the danger in sensual pleasures, he is endowed with the holy life of the path. By this much, he shows contentment; by 'vītataṇho' (free from craving) and so on, he shows the unshaken state. Therein, 'saṅkhāya nibbuto' (having discerned, extinguished) means having investigated phenomena in terms of impermanence and so on, he is extinguished by the extinction of passion and so forth. The rest is quite clear, as it has been explained in various places.

Evaṃ bhagavā imampi suttaṃ arahattanikūṭeneva desesi. Desanāpariyosāne ayampi brāhmaṇo arahatte patiṭṭhāsi saddhiṃ antevāsisahassena, aññesañca anekasahassānaṃ dhammacakkhuṃ udapādi. Sesaṃ pubbasadisamevāti.

Thus, the Blessed One also taught this discourse with the culmination in arahantship. At the end of the teaching, this brahmin was also established in arahantship together with his thousand students, and the Dhamma-eye arose in many thousands of others. The rest is just as before.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

From the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Minor Collection.

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya tissametteyyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Tissametteyya Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary is concluded.

3. Puṇṇakasuttavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Puṇṇaka Sutta

1050. Anejanti [V 2.0279][M 2.0304] puṇṇakasuttaṃ. Imampi purimanayeneva mogharājānaṃ paṭikkhipitvā vuttaṃ. Tattha mūladassāvinti akusalamūlādidassāviṃ. Isayoti isināmakā jaṭilā. Yaññanti deyyadhammaṃ. Akappayiṃsūti pariyesanti.

1050. The Puṇṇaka Sutta, beginning with 'Aneja.' This too was spoken after rejecting Mogharāja in the same manner as before. Therein, 'mūladassāvi' means one who sees the unwholesome roots and so on. 'Isayo' (sages) refers to matted-hair ascetics called sages. 'Yaññaṃ' (sacrifice) means an offering. 'Akappayiṃsu' means 'they sought'.

1051. Āsīsamānāti rūpādīni patthayamānā. Itthattanti itthabhāvañca patthayamānā, manussādibhāvaṃ icchantāti vuttaṃ hoti. Jaraṃ sitāti jaraṃ nissitā. Jarāmukhena cettha sabbavaṭṭadukkhaṃ vuttaṃ. Tena vaṭṭadukkhanissitā tato aparimuccamānā eva kappayiṃsūti dīpeti.

1051. 'Āsīsamānā' (desiring) means desiring forms and so on. 'Itthattaṃ' (this state) means desiring this state; that is to say, desiring human existence and so on. 'Jaraṃ sitā' (relying on old age) means relying on old age. Here, by means of old age, all the suffering of the round of existence is spoken of. Thus, it is explained that being reliant on the suffering of the round of existence, and not freed from it, they indeed performed sacrifices.

1052. Kaccissu te bhagavā yaññapathe appamattā, atāruṃ jātiñca jarañca mārisāti ettha yaññoyeva yaññapatho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – kacci te yaññe appamattā hutvā yaññaṃ kappayantā vaṭṭadukkhamatariṃsūti.

1052. 'Kaccissu te, Bhagavā, yaññapathe appamattā, atāruṃ jātiñca jarañca, Mārisa?' (Were they, Blessed One, heedful on the path of sacrifice? Did they cross over birth and aging, O Mārisa?) Here, 'yaññapatho' (path of sacrifice) means sacrifice itself. This is what is said: 'Were they, being heedful in the sacrifice and performing the sacrifice, able to cross over the suffering of the round of existence?'

1053. Āsīsantīti rūpapaṭilābhādayo patthenti. Thomayantīti “suyiṭṭhaṃ suci dinna”ntiādinā nayena yaññādīni pasaṃsanti. Abhijappantīti rūpādipaṭilābhāya vācaṃ bhindanti. Juhantīti denti. Kāmābhijappanti paṭicca lābhanti rūpādipaṭilābhaṃ paṭicca punappunaṃ kāme eva abhijappanti, “aho vata amhākaṃ siyu”nti vadanti, taṇhañca tattha vaḍḍhentīti vuttaṃ [P 2.0590] hoti. Yājayogāti yāgādhimuttā. Bhavarāgarattāti evamimehi āsīsanādīhi bhavarāgeneva rattā, bhavarāgarattā vā hutvā etāni āsīsanādīni karontā nātariṃsu jātiādivaṭṭadukkhaṃ na uttariṃsūti.

1053. 'Āsīsanti' (they desire) means they desire the attainment of forms and so on. 'Thomayanti' (they praise) means they praise sacrifices and the like, in the manner of saying, 'Well-sacrificed, well-given,' and so forth. 'Abhijappanti' (they yearn) means they utter words for the attainment of forms and so on. 'Juhanti' (they offer) means they give. 'Kāmābhijappanti paṭicca lābhaṃ' (they yearn for sensual pleasures on account of gain) means that on account of gain, that is, the attainment of forms and so on, they repeatedly yearn for sensual pleasures, saying, 'Oh, that they might be ours!' Thus it is said, they increase craving in that regard. 'Yājayogā' (devoted to sacrifice) means they are devoted to sacrifice. 'Bhavarāgarattā' (impassioned by craving for existence) means that through these actions of desiring and so on, they are indeed impassioned by craving for existence; or, being impassioned by craving for existence, they perform these actions of desiring and so on, and thus they did not cross over, did not transcend, the suffering of the round of existence, which is birth and so on.

1054-5. Athakocarahīti atha idāni ko añño atārīti. Saṅkhāyāti ñāṇena vīmaṃsitvā. Paroparānīti parāni ca orāni ca, parattabhāvasakattabhāvādīni parāni ca orāni cāti vuttaṃ hoti. Vidhūmoti kāyaduccaritādidhūmavirahito. Anīghoti rāgādiīghavirahito[V 2.0280]. Atāri soti so evarūpo arahā jātijaraṃ atāri. Sesamettha pākaṭameva.

1054-5. 'Athakocarahi' means 'now then, who else has crossed over?' 'Saṅkhāya' (having discerned) means having investigated with wisdom. 'Paroparāni' (higher and lower) means both higher and lower; that is to say, states of being in others and in oneself, and so on, are both higher and lower. 'Vidhūmo' (free from smoke) means devoid of the smoke of bodily misconduct and the like. 'Anīgho' (free from distress) means devoid of the distress of lust and so on. 'Atāri so' (he has crossed over) means such an arahant has indeed crossed over birth and aging. The rest here is quite clear.

Evaṃ [M 2.0305] bhagavā imampi suttaṃ arahattanikūṭeneva desesi. Desanāpariyosāne ayampi brāhmaṇo arahatte patiṭṭhāsi saddhiṃ antevāsisahassena, aññesañca anekasatānaṃ dhammacakkhuṃ udapādi. Sesaṃ vuttasadisamevāti.

Thus, the Blessed One also taught this discourse with the culmination in arahantship. At the end of the teaching, this brahmin was also established in arahantship together with his thousand pupils, and the Dhamma-eye arose in many hundreds of others. The rest is as has been said.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

From the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Minor Collection.

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya puṇṇakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Puṇṇaka Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary is concluded.

4. Mettagūsuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Mettagū Sutta

1056. Pucchāmi [V 2.0281] tanti mettagusuttaṃ. Tattha maññāmi taṃ vedaguṃ bhāvitattanti “ayaṃ vedagū”ti ca “bhāvitatto”ti ca evaṃ taṃ maññāmi.

1056. The Mettagū Sutta begins with 'Pucchāmi taṃ' (I ask you). Therein, 'maññāmi taṃ vedaguṃ bhāvitattaṃ' (I consider you one who has attained wisdom and is well-developed) means: 'I consider you thus: "This one has attained wisdom (vedagū)" and "This one is well-developed (bhāvitatta)."'

1057. Apucchasīti ettha a-iti padapūraṇamatte nipāto, pucchasicceva attho. Pavakkhāmi yathā pajānanti yathā pajānanto ācikkhati, evaṃ ācikkhissāmi. Upadhinidānā pabhavanti dukkhāti taṇhādiupadhinidānā jātiādidukkhavisesā pabhavanti.

1057. Regarding 'Apucchasi' (you asked), here the 'a-' is merely a particle to fill out the meter; the meaning is simply 'you ask.' Regarding 'Pavakkhāmi yathā pajānaṃ' (I will explain as I know it), it means: 'As one who knows explains, so will I explain.' Regarding 'Upadhinidānā pabhavanti dukkhā' (Sufferings arise from the source of attachments), it means: the various specific sufferings such as birth arise from the source of attachments, which is craving and so on.

1058. Evaṃ upadhinidānato pabhavantesu dukkhesu – yo ve avidvāti gāthā. Tattha pajānanti saṅkhāre aniccādivasena jānanto. Dukkhassa jātippabhavānupassīti vaṭṭadukkhassa jātikāraṇaṃ “upadhī”ti anupassanto.

1058. Thus, concerning sufferings arising from the source of attachments, the verse is 'Yo ve avidvā' (Whoever, being ignorant...). Therein, 'pajānaṃ' (knowing) means knowing formations in terms of impermanence and so on. Regarding 'Dukkhassa jātippabhavānupassī' (one who sees the birth and origin of suffering), it means one who contemplates that 'attachment' (upadhi) is the cause of the birth of the suffering of the round of existence.

1059. Sokapariddavañcāti sokañca paridevañca. Tathā hi te vidito esa dhammoti yathā yathā sattā jānanti, tathā tathā paññāpanavasena vidito esa dhammoti.

1059. Regarding 'Sokapariddavañca', it means sorrow and lamentation. Regarding 'Tathā hi te vidito esa dhammo', it means: just as beings know, so this Dhamma is known by way of explanation.

1060-61. Kittayissāmi te dhammanti [P 2.0591] nibbānadhammaṃ nibbānagāminipaṭipadādhammañca te desayissāmi. Diṭṭhe dhammeti diṭṭhe dukkhādidhamme, imasmiṃyeva vā attabhāve. Anītihanti attapaccakkhaṃ. Yaṃ viditvāti yaṃ dhammaṃ “sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā”tiādinā nayena sammasanto viditvā. Tañcāhaṃ abhinandāmīti taṃ vuttapakāradhammajotakaṃ tava vacanaṃ ahaṃ patthayāmi. Dhammamuttamanti tañca dhammamuttamaṃ abhinandāmīti.

1060-61. Regarding 'Kittayissāmi te dhammaṃ' (I will proclaim the Dhamma to you), it means: I will teach you the Dhamma of Nibbāna and the Dhamma of the practice leading to Nibbāna. Regarding 'Diṭṭhe dhamme' (in this visible life), it means: in the seen phenomena of suffering, etc., or in this very existence. Regarding 'Anītihā' (without hearsay), it means: directly experienced. Regarding 'Yaṃ viditvā' (having known which), it means: having known that Dhamma by comprehending it according to the method 'all conditioned phenomena are impermanent,' etc. Regarding 'Tañcāhaṃ abhinandāmi' (And that I applaud), it means: I desire your words that illuminate the Dhamma in the manner described. Regarding 'Dhammaṃ uttamaṃ' (the supreme Dhamma), it means: and I applaud that supreme Dhamma.

1062. Uddhaṃ [M 2.0306] adho tiriyañcāpi majjheti ettha uddhanti anāgataddhā vuccati, adhoti atītaddhā, tiriyañcāpi majjheti paccuppannaddhā. Etesu nandiñca nivesanañca, panujja viññāṇanti etesu uddhādīsu taṇhañca diṭṭhinivesanañca abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇañca panudehi, panuditvā ca bhave na tiṭṭhe, evaṃ sante duvidhepi bhave na tiṭṭheyya. Evaṃ tāva panujjasaddassa panudehīti imasmiṃ atthavikappe sambandho, panuditvāti etasmiṃ pana atthavikappe bhave na tiṭṭheti [V 2.0282] ayameva sambandho. Etāni nandinivesanaviññāṇāni panuditvā duvidhepi bhave na tiṭṭheyyāti vuttaṃ hoti.

1062. Regarding 'Uddhaṃ adho tiriyañcāpi majjhe' (Above, below, and across in the middle), here 'above' refers to the future time, 'below' to the past time, and 'across in the middle' to the present time. Regarding 'Panujja nandiñca nivesanañca, viññāṇaṃ' (Having dispelled delight, dwelling, and consciousness), it means: in these—above, etc.—dispel craving, attachment to views, and volitional consciousness. Having dispelled them, one should not remain in existence; thus, one would not remain in either kind of existence. Thus, in one interpretation, the word 'panujja' (having dispelled) is connected with 'panudehi' (dispel); but in the interpretation as 'panuditvā' (having dispelled), the connection is with 'bhave na tiṭṭhe' (one should not remain in existence). It is said that having dispelled these delights, dwellings, and consciousnesses, one would not remain in either kind of existence.

1063-4. Etāni vinodetvā bhave atiṭṭhanto eso – evaṃvihārīti gāthā. Tattha idhevāti imasmiṃyeva sāsane, imasmiṃyeva vā attabhāve. Sukittitaṃ gotamanūpadhīkanti ettha anupadhikanti nibbānaṃ. Taṃ sandhāya bhagavantaṃ ālapanto āha – “sukittitaṃ gotamanūpadhīka”nti.

1063-64. The verse is about one who, 'Having removed these, not remaining in existence, dwells thus.' Here, 'idheva' (right here) means in this very Dispensation, or in this very existence. Regarding 'Sukittitaṃ gotamanūpadhīkaṃ' (Well-proclaimed by Gotama, without substratum), here 'anupadhīkaṃ' (without substratum) refers to Nibbāna. With reference to that, addressing the Blessed One, he says, 'Well-proclaimed by Gotama, without substratum.'

1065. Na kevalaṃ dukkhameva pahāsi – te cāpīti gāthā. Tattha aṭṭhitanti sakkaccaṃ, sadā vā. Taṃ taṃ namassāmīti tasmā taṃ namassāmi. Sameccāti upagantvā. Nāgāti bhagavantaṃ ālapanto āha.

1065. Not only did he abandon suffering—the verse is 'Te cāpi'. Therein, 'aṭṭhitaṃ' means diligently, or always. Regarding 'Taṃ taṃ namassāmi' (I salute him), it means: therefore I salute him. Regarding 'Samecca' (having approached), it means: having approached. Regarding 'Nāga', he says this addressing the Blessed One.

1066. Idāni taṃ bhagavā “addhā hi bhagavā pahāsi [P 2.0592] dukkha”nti evaṃ tena brāhmaṇena viditopi attānaṃ anupanetvāva pahīnadukkhena puggalena ovadanto “yaṃ brāhmaṇa”nti gāthamāha. Tassattho – yaṃ tvaṃ abhijānanto “ayaṃ bāhitapāpattā brāhmaṇo, vedehi gatattā vedagū, kiñcanābhāvena akiñcano, kāmesu ca bhavesu ca asattattā kāmabhave asatto”ti jaññā jāneyyāsi. Addhā hi so imaṃ oghaṃ atāri, tiṇṇo ca pāraṃ akhilo akaṅkho.

1066. Now, although it was known by that brahmin that 'Surely the Blessed One has abandoned suffering,' the Blessed One, without referring to himself, but instructing by way of a person who has abandoned suffering, spoke the verse beginning 'Yaṃ brāhmaṇa'. Its meaning is: You should know that one whom you recognize as a brahmin for having banished evil, a vedagū for having gone to the end of the Vedas, one with nothing for having no possessions, and unattached in the sensual existence for being unattached to sensual pleasures and existences—surely he has crossed this flood, has gone to the far shore, is whole, and without doubt.

1067. Kiñca bhiyyo – vidvā ca yoti gāthā. Tattha idhāti imasmiṃ sāsane, attabhāve vā. Visajjāti vossajjitvā. Sesaṃ sabbattha pākaṭameva.

1067. And what more? The verse is 'Vidvā ca yo'. Therein, 'idha' (here) means in this Dispensation or in this existence. Regarding 'Visajja' (having relinquished), it means: having relinquished. The rest is clear everywhere.

Evaṃ [M 2.0307] bhagavā imampi suttaṃ arahattanikūṭeneva desesi. Desanāpariyosāne ca vuttasadiso eva dhammābhisamayo ahosīti.

Thus the Blessed One taught this discourse with the very culmination of Arahantship. And at the conclusion of the teaching, there was a penetration of the Dhamma just as was described.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the commentary on the Khuddaka collection.

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya mettagūsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Mettagū Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary is concluded.

5. Dhotakasuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Explanation of the Dhotaka Sutta

1068-9. Pucchāmi [V 2.0283] tanti dhotakasuttaṃ. Tattha vācābhikaṅkhāmīti vācaṃ abhikaṅkhāmi. Sikkhe nibbānamattanoti attano rāgādīnaṃ nibbānatthāya adhisīlādīni sikkheyya. Itoti mama mukhato.

1068-69. 'Pucchāmi taṃ' is the Dhotaka Sutta. Therein, 'vācābhikaṅkhāmi' (I desire your utterance) means: I desire your utterance. Regarding 'Sikkhe nibbānamattano' (May I train for my own Nibbāna), it means: for the purpose of the extinguishing of one's own passion, etc., one should train in higher virtue, etc. Regarding 'Ito' (from here), it means: from my mouth.

1070. Evaṃ vutte attamano dhotako bhagavantaṃ abhitthavamāno kathaṃkathāpamokkhaṃ yācanto “passāmaha”nti gāthamāha. Tattha passāmahaṃ devamanussaloketi passāmi ahaṃ devamanussaloke. Taṃ taṃ namassāmīti taṃ evarūpaṃ namassāmi. Pamuñcāti pamocehi.

1070. When this was said, the delighted Dhotaka, praising the Blessed One and requesting release from doubt, spoke the verse beginning 'Passāmahaṃ'. Therein, 'passāmahaṃ devamanussaloke' (I see in the world of gods and humans) means: I see in the world of gods and humans. Regarding 'Taṃ taṃ namassāmi' (I pay homage to him), it means: I pay homage to such a one. Regarding 'Pamuñca' (Release), it means: release.

1071. Athassa bhagavā attādhīnameva kathaṃkathāpamokkhaṃ oghataraṇamukhena dassento “nāha”nti gāthamāha. Tattha nāhaṃ sahissāmīti ahaṃ na sahissāmi na sakkhissāmi, na vāyamissāmīti vuttaṃ hoti. Pamocanāyāti pamācetuṃ. Kathaṃkathinti sakaṅkhaṃ. Taresīti tareyyāsi.

1071. Then the Blessed One, showing that release from doubt is dependent on oneself, through the method of crossing the flood, spoke the verse beginning 'Nāhaṃ'. Therein, 'nāhaṃ sahissāmi' (I am not able) means: I am not able, I will not be capable, I will not strive—this is what is said. Regarding 'Pamocanāya' (for release), it means: to release. Regarding 'Kathaṃkathiṃ' (one who is doubting), it means: one with doubt. Regarding 'Taresi' (you will cross), it means: you would cross.

1072-5. Evaṃ vutte attamanataro dhotako bhagavantaṃ abhitthavamāno anusāsaniṃ yācanto “anusāsa brahme”ti gāthamāha. Tattha brahmāti seṭṭhavacanametaṃ. Tena bhagavantaṃ āmantayamāno āha – “anusāsa brahme”ti[P 2.0593]. Vivekadhammanti sabbasaṅkhāravivekanibbānadhammaṃ. Abyāpajjamānoti nānappakārataṃ anāpajjamāno. Idheva santoti idheva samāno. Asitoti anissito. Ito parā dve gāthā mettagusutte vuttanayā eva. Kevalañhi tattha dhammaṃ, idha santinti ayaṃ viseso. Tatiyagāthāyapi [M 2.0308] pubbaḍḍhaṃ tattha vutanayameva aparaḍḍhe saṅgoti sajjanaṭṭhānaṃ, laggananti vuttaṃ hoti. Sesaṃ sabbattha pākaṭameva.

1072-75. When this was said, the greatly delighted Dhotaka, praising the Blessed One and requesting instruction, spoke the verse beginning 'Anusāsa brahme'. Therein, 'brahmā' is a word for the best. Addressing the Blessed One with this, he said: 'Anusāsa brahme' (Instruct, O Brahmā). Regarding 'Vivekadhammaṃ' (the Dhamma of seclusion), it means the Dhamma of Nibbāna, which is seclusion from all conditioned phenomena. Regarding 'Abyāpajjamāno' (not being afflicted), it means: not falling into manifoldness. Regarding 'Idheva santo' (being at peace right here), it means: being at peace right here. Regarding 'Asito' (unattached), it means: unreliant. The next two verses follow the same method as explained in the Mettagū Sutta. The only difference is that there it is 'dhammaṃ', whereas here it is 'santiṃ' (peace). In the third verse also, the first half follows the method explained there. In the second half, 'saṅgo' (attachment) is a state of attachment; it is said to be 'clinging' (lagganaṃ). The rest is clear everywhere.

Evaṃ bhagavā imampi suttaṃ arahattanikūṭeneva desesi. Desanāpariyosāne ca vuttasadiso eva dhammābhisamayo ahosīti.

Thus the Blessed One taught this discourse with the very culmination of Arahantship. And at the conclusion of the teaching, there was a penetration of the Dhamma just as was described.

Paramatthajotikāya khuddaka-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Paramatthajotikā, the commentary on the Khuddaka collection.

Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathāya dhotakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Dhotaka Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary is concluded.

6. Upasīvasuttavaṇṇanā

6. The Explanation of the Upasīva Sutta.

1076. Eko [V 2.0284] ahanti upasīvasuttaṃ. Tattha mahantamoghanti mahantaṃ oghaṃ. Anissitoti puggalaṃ vā dhammaṃ vā anissito. No visahāmīti na sakkomi. Ārammaṇanti nissayaṃ. Yaṃ nissitoti yaṃ puggalaṃ vā dhammaṃ vā nissito.

1076. ‘I am alone,’ thus the Upasīva Sutta. Therein, ‘great flood’ means a great flood. ‘Without support’ means not relying on a person or a phenomenon. ‘I cannot’ means I am not able. ‘Basis’ means a support. ‘That on which one relies’ means that person or phenomenon on which one relies.

1077. Idāni yasmā so brāhmaṇo ākiñcaññāyatanalābhī tañca santampi nissayaṃ na jānāti, tenassa bhagavā tañca nissayaṃ uttari ca niyyānapathaṃ dassento “ākiñcañña”nti gāthamāha. Tattha pekkhamānoti taṃ ākiñcaññāyatanasamāpattiṃ sato samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhahitvā ca aniccādivasena passamāno. Natthīti nissāyāti taṃ “natthi kiñcī”ti pavattasamāpattiṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā. Tarassu oghanti tato pabhuti pavattāya vipassanāya yathānurūpaṃ catubbidhampi oghaṃ tarassu. Kathāhīti kathaṃkathāhi. Taṇhakkhayaṃ nattamahābhipassāti rattindivaṃ nibbānaṃ vibhūtaṃ katvā passa. Etenassa diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāraṃ katheti.

1077. Now, because that brahmin had attained the base of nothingness but did not recognize even that peaceful support, the Blessed One, showing him that support and the further path to liberation, spoke the verse beginning with ‘nothingness.’ Therein, ‘observing’ means observing that attainment of the base of nothingness, having mindfully entered and emerged from it, seeing it as impermanent and so forth. ‘By relying on “there is nothing”’ means taking as an object that attainment which occurs with ‘there is nothing whatsoever.’ ‘Cross the flood’ means from then onward, with the insight that arises, cross the four kinds of flood accordingly. ‘With uncertainties’ means with doubts. ‘Clearly see the destruction of craving day and night’ means making Nibbāna clearly visible day and night, and seeing it. Through this, he describes to him the pleasant abiding in this very life.

1078-9. Idāni “kāme pahāyā”ti sutvā vikkhambhanavasena attanā pahīne kāme sampassamāno “sabbesū”ti gāthamāha. Tattha hitvā maññanti aññaṃ tato heṭṭhā chabbidhampi samāpattiṃ [P 2.0594] hitvā. Saññāvimokkhe parameti sattasu saññāvimokkhesu uttame ākiñcaññāyatane. Tiṭṭhe nu [M 2.0309] so tattha anānuyāyīti so puggalo tattha ākiñcaññāyatanabrahmaloke avigacchamāno tiṭṭheyya nūti pucchati. Athassa bhagavā saṭṭhikappasahassamattaṃyeva ṭhānaṃ anujānanto tatiyagāthamāha.

1078-9. Now, having heard ‘having abandoned sensual pleasures,’ and seeing the sensual pleasures abandoned within himself through suppression, he speaks the verse beginning with ‘in all.’ Therein, ‘having abandoned conceit’ means having abandoned the other six kinds of attainments below that. ‘In the liberation of perception, supreme’ refers to the highest among the seven liberations of perception, the base of nothingness. ‘Would he remain there without following?’ asks whether that person would remain there in the Brahma world of the base of nothingness, without departing. Then the Blessed One, approving a duration of only sixty thousand eons, speaks the third verse.

1080. Evaṃ tassa tattha ṭhānaṃ sutvā idānissa sassatucchedabhāvaṃ pucchanto “tiṭṭhe ce”ti gāthamāha. Tattha pūgampi vassānanti anekasaṅkhyampi vassānaṃ, gaṇarāsinti attho. “Pūgampi vassānī”tipi pāṭho, tattha vibhattibyattayena sāmivacanassa paccattavacanaṃ kattabbaṃ, pūganti vā etassa bahūnīti attho vattabbo. “Pūgānī”ti vāpi paṭhanti, purimapāṭhoyeva sabbasundaro. Tattheva so sīti siyā vimuttoti so puggalo tatthevākiñcaññāyatane nānādukkhehi [V 2.0285] vimutto sītibhāvappatto bhaveyya, nibbānappatto sassato hutvā tiṭṭheyyāti adhippāyo. Cavetha viññāṇaṃ tathāvidhassāti udāhu tathāvidhassa viññāṇaṃ anupādāya parinibbāyeyyāti ucchedaṃ pucchati, paṭisandhiggahaṇatthaṃ vāpi bhaveyyāti paṭisandhimpi tassa pucchati.

1080. Having thus heard of his state there, now questioning its nature as eternalism or annihilationism, he speaks the verse beginning with ‘if he remains.’ Therein, ‘for a multitude of years’ means for an innumerable number of years, a heap of years; that is the meaning. The reading ‘pūgampi vassānī’ is also found; there, by the change of inflection, the genitive case should be made into the accusative case, or it should be understood to mean ‘many.’ Alternatively, ‘pūgāni’ is also read; the former reading is the most elegant. ‘There, liberated, he would be cooled’ means that person, right there in the base of nothingness, would be liberated from various sufferings, attain a state of coolness, reach Nibbāna, and remain eternally—that is the intention. ‘Or would the consciousness of such a one pass away?’ asks about annihilationism, whether the consciousness of such a one would attain final Nibbāna without clinging, or he also asks about his rebirth, whether it would be for the purpose of taking a new existence.

1081. Athassa bhagavā ucchedasassataṃ anupagamma tattha uppannassa ariyasāvakassa anupādāya parinibbānaṃ dassento “accī yathā”ti gāthamāha. Tattha atthaṃ paletīti atthaṃ gacchati. Na upeti saṅkhanti “asukaṃ nāma disaṃ gato”ti vohāraṃ na gacchati. Evaṃ munī nāmakāyā vimuttoti evaṃ tattha uppanno sekkhamuni pakatiyā pubbeva rūpakāyā vimutto tattha catutthamaggaṃ nibbattetvā dhammakāyassa pariññātattā puna nāmakāyāpi vimutto ubhatobhāgavimutto khīṇāsavo hutvā anupādāparinibbānasaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ paleti, na upeti saṅkhaṃ “khattiyo vā brāhmaṇo vā”ti evamādikaṃ.

1081. Then the Blessed One, without adopting either annihilationism or eternalism, showing the final Nibbāna without clinging for the noble disciple arisen there, spoke the verse beginning with ‘like a flame.’ Therein, ‘goes to rest’ means it ceases. ‘It does not come into reckoning’ means it does not enter into conventional expression such as ‘it has gone to such and such a direction.’ ‘Thus the sage, freed from the name-body’ means that the trainee-sage arisen there, being naturally freed from the form-body even before, having produced the fourth path there, and because the Dhamma-body is fully comprehended, is also freed from the name-body. Having become one liberated in both ways, one whose taints are destroyed, he goes to rest in what is designated as final Nibbāna without clinging, and does not come into reckoning as ‘a khattiya or a brahmin,’ and so on.

1082. Idāni [P 2.0595] “atthaṃ paletī”ti sutvā tassa yoniso atthaṃ asallakkhento “atthaṅgato so”ti gāthamāha. Tassattho – so atthaṅgato udāhu natthi, udāhu ve sassatiyā sassatabhāvena arogo avipariṇāmadhammo soti evaṃ taṃ me munī sādhu viyākarohi. Kiṃ kāraṇaṃ? Tathā hi te vidito esa dhammoti.

1082. Now, having heard ‘goes to rest,’ and not properly considering its meaning, he speaks the verse beginning with ‘has he gone to rest?’ Its meaning is: ‘Has he gone to rest, or does he not exist, or is he eternally healthy and not subject to change?’ O sage, please explain this well to me. What is the reason? For this Dhamma is indeed known to you.

1083. Athassa [M 2.0310] bhagavā tathā avattabbataṃ dassento “atthaṅgatassā”ti gāthamāha. Tattha atthaṅgatassāti anupādāparinibbutassa. Na pamāṇamatthīti rūpādippamāṇaṃ natthi. Yena naṃ vajjunti yena rāgādinā naṃ vadeyyuṃ. Sabbesu dhammesūti sabbesu khandhādidhammesu. Sesaṃ sabbattha pākaṭameva.

1083.
